*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library ... of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III ... FIRST SERIES*

## PATROLOGY, VOLUME XX

Saint Phoebadius; Saint Anastasius I, Pope; Faustus the Manichaean; Sulpicius Severus; Secundinus the Manichaean; Saint Chromatius; Saint Victricius of Rouen; Pammachius; Oceanus; Saint Innocent I, Pope; Saint Zosimus, Pope; Paulinus of Milan; Paulinus the Deacon; Severus of Majorca; Saint Boniface I, Pope; Saint Gaudentius of Brescia; Saint Aurelius of Carthage; the monk Bachiarius; Zacchaeus the Christian; the monk Evagrius.

### Single volume

## Volume front matter

## Series title page

### Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that appeared during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes for each volume and for each author of any importance following it; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily superior to all others if the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient form of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—are taken into account: a collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered together for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### First series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Ecclesiastical writers of the fifth century

## In the year of the Lord 400

# Saint Phoebadius, Bishop of Agen

*(From Gallandius, Library of the Ancient Fathers, vol. V.)*

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomena

Phoebadius was a Gaul by nationality and, if we follow Sulpicius—who was himself an Aquitanian and calls him “our man”—indeed belonged to the province of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0009C] Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 44.]. He governed the church of Agen, as Saint Jerome writes [Note: [Col. 0009C] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 108.]; and he may perhaps also have been born in that city, which is the capital of the Nitiobriges. The year in which he was raised to episcopal rank, however, has not been established. It certainly happened after the year 347, for he is not listed among the Gallic bishops who attended the Council of Sardica, held in that very year, as Tillemont and others observe [Note: [Col. 0009C] Tillemont, *Memoirs of Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, p. 427; Sammarthanus, *Gallicia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 895; *Literary History of France*, vol. I, part II, p. 266.].

He was certainly already distinguished by episcopal honor in the year 357, when, together with the other bishops of Gaul, he rejected and condemned the second formula of faith from Sirmium, sent into Gaul by Constantius—the formula which is seventh among the Arian professions of faith according to Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0009C] Athanasius, *On the Councils*, § 28, works, vol. I, part II, p. 744.], and which Hilary calls the blasphemy of Potamius and Hosius [Col. 0009B] [Note: [Col. 0009C] Hilary, *On the Councils*, § 10.]—and he also vigorously refuted it in a book he composed, as we learn clearly enough from his own work [Note: [Col. 0009C] Phoebadius, *Book against the Arians*, §§ 5 and 23. See below.].

After these vigorous actions, he later took part in the Council of Rimini, summoned by the same Constantius in the year 359. In that council Phoebadius played a major role in what was first undertaken for the Catholic faith against Arian faithlessness, before the bishops had been taken captive. Indeed, after almost all the others had yielded, he himself nevertheless continued with the greatest steadfastness, together with Servatio, bishop of Tongeren, to contend on behalf of the Nicene truth, as Sulpicius testifies [Note: [Col. 0010C] Sulpicius, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 44.]. Resisting with unconquered spirit every assault of the Ariomaniacs, he declared that he would rather undergo exile and every kind of punishment than accept the formula of faith devised by the Arians.

[Col. 0010A] Later, however, deceived by Valens’s trickery, he accepted and confirmed by his signature a formula altered by him as he pleased and containing, as it seemed to him, nothing except what was Catholic. That Arian bishop of Mursa had added this sort of statement to a confession of faith asserting that Christ was not a creature: “as are the other creatures”—a phrase which plainly contained the poison of the Arian heresy. For, to speak with Sulpicius [Note: [Col. 0010C] Sulpicius, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 44.], by these words the Son was denied to be like the other creatures, yet was declared to be a creature, merely superior to the others. On this matter, I ask you to consult what Saint Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0010C] Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book III, chapter 16, §§ 129–130, works, vol. II, p. 519.].

From this, therefore, you may conclude that the matter was not carried so far that Phoebadius came to profess the Arian heresy. Rather, as soon as the deception was exposed, he himself [Col. 0010B] and the other Gallic bishops, as Sulpicius says [Note: [Col. 0010C] Sulpicius, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 45.], condemned what had been done at Rimini and restored the faith of the churches to its former state. Jerome agrees [Note: [Col. 0010C] Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, § 19, works, vol. II, p. 191, Verona edition.]. This is established most fully by the proceedings reported by Hilary [Note: [Col. 0010C] Hilary, *Historical Fragment from a Letter*, fragment 11, no. 1.] and Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0010C] Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 22.]. Thus, as soon as the holy bishop detected the error, he attacked it and openly demonstrated the integrity of his faith; consequently nothing was taken away from his reputation by this event, nor was his authority in any way diminished. For it is certain that he later presided over the councils held at Valence in 374 and at Zaragoza around the year 380.

He was still alive in the year 392, when Jerome composed his book *On Illustrious Men*. Jerome writes the following about Phoebadius [Note: [Col. 0010C] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 108.]: “He lives to this day in extreme old age”; [Col. 0010C] so that he must therefore have governed the church of Agen for nearly forty years. “He was a man most distinguished for piety and learning,” [Col. 0011A] and a most vigorous opponent of Arian faithlessness. For this reason he was especially dear to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, as we understand from the letter addressed jointly to Phoebadius and Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0011D] Ambrose, letter 87, works, vol. II, p. 1106.]. His memory, moreover, is commemorated in the calendars of the church of Agen on April 25. On this subject see Dionysius Sammarthanus [Note: [Col. 0011D] Sammarthanus, *Gallicia Christiana*, vol. II, p. 896.] and the Bollandists [Note: [Col. 0011D] Bollandists, *Acts of the Saints*, April, vol. III, p. 366.] for fuller discussion.

Among the literary monuments that Phoebadius commended to posterity in defense of the faith, the greatest Doctor mentions one; as for the other works said to have been written by the same author, he professes that he had not read them [Note: [Col. 0011D] Jerome, cited above.]: “He published,” he says, “a book against the Arians. Other minor works are also said to be his, which I have not yet read.” There does indeed exist a book against the Arians [Col. 0011B], which the blessed bishop wrote to overthrow completely the second Sirmian formula, sent by the Arians into Gaul and written in Latin, as Athanasius reports [Note: [Col. 0011D] Athanasius, *On the Councils*, § 28, works, vol. I, part II, p. 744.] and Hilary records [Note: [Col. 0011D] Hilary, *On the Councils*, § 10.].

The learned Theodore Beza first published this work, together with several other writings of the ancients, at Geneva in 1570; from there it passed into the libraries of the Fathers. It was subsequently incorporated into the works of certain ancient Gallic theologians and published at Paris in 1586 through the efforts of Pierre Pithou. Caspar Barthius also published it separately, with notes, at Frankfurt in 1623. Finally, Delalande had it printed again at Paris in 1666 [Note: [Col. 0011D] Delalande, *Supplement to the Gallican Councils*, pp. 3–91.]. The work is rightly thought to have been written around the year 358, while Hosius of Cordova was still alive and had signed the aforementioned Sirmian formula, as we learn from the author himself [Col. 0011C] [Note: [Col. 0011D] Phoebadius, *Book against the Arians*, § 23, below.].

Our bishop of Agen is not said to have been the author only of this book. We have just heard Jerome relate that other minor works by the same writer existed in his time, though he himself had by no means read them. One other distinguished work still survives: *On Orthodox Faith against the Arians*. We recognize it without hesitation as a genuine work of Phoebadius, whether guided by Jerome or moved by the considerable force of the arguments advanced by the most learned men [Note: [Col. 0011D] *Literary History of France*, vol. I, part II, pp. 273 ff.] in support of the same conclusion.

This book was published among the works of Gregory Nazianzen [Note: [Col. 0011D] Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 49, works, vol. I, pp. 717 ff.] and Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0011D] Ambrose, appendix, vol. II, p. 346, Paris edition, Benedictine Fathers.]; yet learned men have clearly demonstrated that it must be denied to both of them [Col. 0012D] [Note: [Col. 0012D] Nourry on Ambrose’s Appendix, cited above; Tillemont, *Memoirs of Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IX, p. 727, note 64, on Saint Gregory of Nazianzus; *Literary History of France*, cited above.]. Nor are the opinions of those learned men more convincing who judged the work attributable either to Vigilius of Thapsus or to Gregory, bishop of the see of Eliberitana in the province of Baetica.

And with the very best reason: the context and style of the entire work plainly proclaim Phoebadius alone. First, at the beginning, the author says [Note: [Col. 0012D] Phoebadius, *On Orthodox Faith*, chapter 2, below.]: “I had already published a booklet against the Arians.” Who does not see that these words indicate a preceding work, unquestionably by Phoebadius, and entitled precisely as Jerome also called it?

Furthermore, we find the same modes of expression in both works. In both, the Book of Wisdom is cited under the name of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0012D] The same author, *Book against the Arians*, §§ 7 and 11, pp. 251–252; *On Orthodox Faith*, chapter 5, p. 261.]; and in both the Nicene Creed is called the “Nicene treatise” [Note: [Col. 0012D] The same author, *Book against the Arians*, § 27, p. 256; *On Orthodox Faith*, chapter 8, p. 264.]. [Col. 0012B] In both, the Sabellian heresy is joined with the Arian [Note: [Col. 0012D] The same author, cited above, § 13, p. 253; *On Faith*, chapter 8, p. 264.]. There is also the same teaching in both works concerning the manner in which God made himself visible to the ancient fathers [Note: [Col. 0012D] The same author, cited above, § 17, p. 254; *On Orthodox Faith*, chapter 8, p. 264.]. Finally, in both there is the same interpretation of the same scriptural passages wherever the distinction of the Persons is discussed. You may find these and many other matters treated more extensively in the writers of the literary history of Gaul, whom we have just cited once and again.

It will also be useful to note what no one has hitherto observed: namely, that Phoebadius was accustomed to release his writings to the public without the author’s name, as he himself testifies when he says [Note: [Col. 0012D] The same author, *On Orthodox Faith*, § 2, p. 257.] that “he had given a booklet against the Arians to a friend to read, and had earnestly asked him in the meantime to show it, with the author concealed, to learned and prudent men, so that, if anything seemed to anyone to have been stated too much or too little, it could be corrected on the advice of many.” This is his statement.

The holy Father must likewise have proceeded in this way when publishing the work of which we are speaking. From this, as may reasonably be conjectured, arose the occasion for attributing such a work to Gregory Nazianzen and Ambrose, such eminent Fathers of the Greek and Latin Church. Moreover, as learned men have observed, a fragment torn from the same work of Phoebadius was incorporated into the book *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*, which circulates among the works of Hilary of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0012D] Hilary, works, vol. II, p. 719, Verona edition.], and also into a sermon which for a very long time was attributed to Augustine [Note: [Col. 0012D] Augustine, works, vol. V, Appendix, sermon 113, p. 206, Paris edition of the Benedictine Fathers.]. All these considerations taken together demonstrate both the antiquity and the elegance of the work, and at the same time establish that its author was a man outstanding in learning and doctrine.

[Col. 0013A] We have printed the text of the booklet as it was reviewed against ancient manuscript codices and editions by the most learned Benedictine monk Nourry in his excellent edition of the works of Ambrose, in the appendix to volume II, pages 345–358.

A few words remain to be said about the *Booklet of Faith*, which occupies third place among the works of Phoebadius in our edition. It is, in fact, something like a compendium of the preceding treatise *On Orthodox Faith*, and it should be joined to that work not only because of the affinity of their subject matter but also because of the author’s own intention. This booklet exists among the orations of Gregory Nazianzen and is numbered 50.

Now, among scholars it is agreed [Note: [Col. 0013A] Quesnel, dissertation 14 on the works of Saint Leo, § 7, vol. II, p. 380, Lyons edition; Ballerini, works of Saint Leo, [Col. 0013B] vol. III, p. 945, 1700 edition.] that this Oration 50, which is thought to be Nazianzen’s, agrees so closely with Oration 49, which is likewise considered his, that they must have one and the same author. Since it is sufficiently clear from what was said above that the author of Oration 49 is Phoebadius, Oration 50 must therefore also rightly be assigned to him.

I do not intend to construct a longer discussion on this subject. Whoever desires fuller treatment should consult the learned men whom we have followed [Note: [Col. 0014A] *Literary History of France*, vol. I, part II, p. 279, no. 3.]. We have based our edition of this booklet on the latest edition of the Ballerini.

# The minor works of Saint Phoebadius, Bishop of Agen, against the Arians

[Col. 0013B]

## I. Book against the Arians (C, G)

### Chapter I. The occasion and subject of the discussion

[Col. 0013C]

Unless I saw that fraud of diabolical subtlety which, after occupying almost everyone’s understanding, persuades them to accept heresy as right faith and condemns right faith as heresy, I would have no discussion at all, dearest brothers, concerning the matters recently written to us. It would have been enough for conscience to hold what it believes, judging it more right to defend one’s own beliefs than to investigate foreign and alien ones.

But since, as we have said, either heresy must be accepted if we are to be called Catholics, or we shall not truly be Catholics if we do not reject heresy, necessity has brought us to this condition of discussion. It is fitting that we bring into the open the diabolical poison concealed under the appearance of religious reverence, so that both the evil hidden beneath the guise of simple words may be detected and, once the lie has been exposed, the obstructed truth may breathe again.

For what belongs to others must be destroyed in order that our own teaching may be believed. As for our own teaching, unless those other things have been destroyed so that it alone should be believed, I see no alternative but that it must be believed. Therefore, although I can bring before the public conscience the heresy blinded by diabolical fraud [Note: Before “heresy.” It seems that *however* or something similar should be supplied.], nevertheless, while I am speaking about that very matter, by giving the pledge of my faith I shall prove myself Catholic; proved so, as I hope, first before God, then before my own conscience, and also before those whom neither fear nor worldly ambition has overcome.

### Chapter II. The Arians’ deceptions

Beginning, then, with the very head of their faithlessness—not of their faith—and proceeding thereafter through the whole body, we shall prove that many things have been introduced by fraud under the common profession of faith, things which we cannot accept, while other matters have been piled together with no semblance of shame.

For “one God” is proposed not without fraud, while “two gods” are simply denied. The name “substance” is utterly rejected for this reason: so that the Son may be separated from the Father. Finally, his birth is declared unknown, although, if it is believed to be from the Father just as it is, it is sufficiently known by its very confession.

The Father is said to be greater than the Son—not, however, by the difference whereby the Father is greater than the Son, but greater in all the goods of divine glory. If the Son is inferior in these things, he will not be granted even to exist in the Father, because his eternal blessedness will receive nothing into itself except what is proper to it. But nothing is proper to God unless it is complete and perfect; nor, again, will the Father deign to be in one in whom he cannot be wholly present.

The Father is denied to have a beginning, so that the Son may be believed to have a beginning not from an author but in time. I think that whoever is said to have a beginning in this way will not be denied to be subject to an end.

The Son is then said to be subject to the Father—not, however, as a Son to a Father, but as a servant to a Lord, although we read that a servant cannot be an heir. Finally, when he is described as subject to God together with every creature, the invisible and immortal Father is proclaimed, plainly so that the Son may lie in opposition to these attributes. [Note: *Si*. We restore the text in this way. Others read *sic*.]

If, therefore, we refute these individual statements—not by human presumption but by divine authority—it will follow that Catholic faith stands in that part which accepts God as he ought to be who is God.

### Chapter III. Poison smeared with honey

“One God,” he says, “is established.”

Those who bring forward slanderous conjectures and twist the holiness of simple faith through malicious interpretation may perhaps appear unable to be refuted. But we must look to Ursacius, Valens, and Potamius, because they have very often confessed one God in the same words through insidious fraud.

I have accepted nothing simple in this profession of faith, which at first glance, by heretical subtlety, flatters the ignorant, the credulous, and the unwary in order to deceive them—just as honey commends a cup of poison.

“One God,” he says, “the almighty Father, is established.” None of us denies this, because none of us is ignorant of it. But, as can be demonstrated from their treatises, we say that here they profess not so much one God as one almighty Father. For with the same determination with which they refuse the Son, they nevertheless confess the Son as God.

I suppose they will not deny that they have accepted the other assertion; and therefore, in this faithlessness of theirs, not faith, it remains open to them to say “one God the Father” rather than “one God.” Yet throughout the whole body of their profession they refrain from denying our Lord outright, only to destroy him as God; that is, they call him “Lord” merely by name, a name by which we too are accustomed to be called.

“I said,” he says, “You are gods” (Psalm 81:6). Moses too was previously honored with this title: “I have made you,” he says, “a god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1). Let no one, therefore, think that these words complete a Catholic profession merely because we confess one God the Father and do not deny the Son to be God. For the Father can be called one God in such a way that he is one Father, not one God. And the Son can be called God in such a way that he is not God.

### Chapter IV. One God—or none. Blind heretics

“We know,” he says, “that two gods neither can nor ought to be proclaimed.”

We never utter “two gods” from our mouths either. For if God is not one and true, he is not God. But attention must be paid to the definition by which this is stated, and to the faithlessness for which the whole matter is being prepared, so that common words may rush with us into sacrilege.

They immediately explain why they have denied two gods: “Because God himself says: ‘I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’” (John 20:17). By this definition of a false interpretation, the Son is separated from the Father and placed beneath the almighty God to such an extent that both the condition of his birth and the weakness of his humanity are made to belong to us.

Finally they add: “The God of all is one.” By this statement the Lord is not absolutely denied to be God; rather, he is subjected to God the Father—not under the name of the Son, but under the condition of a creature.

And I suppose that apostolic authority will be claimed here, so that Christ may be said to be God rather than truly be God, because Scripture says: “And God gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Likewise, they appeal to the Lord himself, who denies that he is the true God when he says: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God” (John 17:3); and: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God” (Luke 18:19).

[Col. 0016B] You will hear further: “Why do you not seek honor from the one and only God? But concerning the day and the hour no one knows except the Father alone” (Matthew 24:36).

O blind guides! O men deceived by worldly ambition! You do not distinguish the twofold condition of the Lord’s power, each aspect differing according to its own proper character. Whatever is said about his humanity, you apply to God, so that God himself is associated with human weakness.

### Chapter V. The Arians’ blasphemies. The letter of Potamius

For this reason you wish this twofold condition to appear not united but confused, so that even one of your number—namely the letter of Potamius, which was sent from East and West—asserts that Christ’s flesh and spirit were coagulated through Mary’s blood and reduced to one body, and that God was thereby made passible.

This was so that no one, from the fact that he is clearly known to be impassible, should believe him to be God. You have therefore made something—I do not know what third thing—from the Spirit of God and human flesh. For he is not truly God if he ceases to be the Word—for he became flesh—nor truly man, because he was not properly flesh, but was the Word. Thus, if he is now neither of the two, I mean that very one who, against this poison, distinguished his two substances by the proper character of each.

For the Spirit in him governs his own affairs—that is, powers, works, and signs—and the flesh underwent its own sufferings. He desired food when he was tempted by the devil; he thirsted at the well of Samaria, although the prophet’s voice says: “The eternal God neither thirsts nor hungers.”

Why say more about the human emotion with which he wept for Lazarus and Jerusalem? Finally, he was distressed in the face of death. But when he expressed these things through emotion, did he not also attest them in words? For he said to Nicodemus: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John 3:6); and: “The flesh,” he says, “is weak, but the spirit is ready” (Matthew 26:41).

Spirit therefore does not become flesh, nor flesh spirit—as these excellent teachers wish—so that our Lord and God might have been made passible through this mixture of substances. They wish him to be called passible precisely so that he may not also be believed impassible.

### Chapter VI. The Council of Nicaea. The incorruptible truth

[Col. 0017A]

But why is it necessary to search out deeper matters and expose and submit to public judgment the internal poison emerging through argument, when the serpent that flees the light, winding through its coils and proceeding crookedly, has at last revealed what and how great it is and, after its victories, has poured out all its poison at once with its customary freedom of spraying it?

An edict proceeds from the bishops: “Let no one say one substance.” That is: “Let no one proclaim in the Church that the Father and the Son have one power.”

What have you done, men of blessed memory, who assembled at Nicaea from every part of the world, examined the sacred volumes, and with carefully considered language established the perfect rule of Catholic faith, giving the right hand of the common faith to those who believed correctly, and a form of belief to those who were in error?

Behold where your labor, behold where your anxious care, has ended: the seeds of the rising evil that you then killed, as far as lay within you, by a Catholic profession! What you established is forbidden to be proclaimed in the Church—the very thing which you decreed ought to be proclaimed in the Church for the exposure of heresies. What you approved is removed, and what you condemned is introduced, because a lie could not be built up unless the truth had first been destroyed.

That truth is not subject to destruction, and, as it has always been incorruptible, so it will endure forever. Yet it has punished the sacrilegious hands that attacked it as though it had been violated.

### Chapter VII. The term “substance” explained

[Col. 0017C]

“Let no one say one substance.”

What sacrilege, what crime is there in this word? In what respect does it attack the Catholic faith? Is the problem in the sound of the word, or in the interpretation of the thing itself?

I am not mistaken: the interpretation is free of blame. For “substance” means that which always exists from itself; that is, that which subsists by its own proper power within itself. This power belongs to one God alone.

I do not think that even those who deny the term are unaware that this word is customary and familiar in the divine books. David, speaking in the person of Christ, says: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance” (Psalm 69:2). Again: “My substance is in the lower parts of the earth” (Psalm 139:15). And: “My substance is always before you” (Psalm 39:8). And: “My substance is as nothing before you” (ibid., 6). “Let the creditor search out his substance” (Psalm 109:11).

Solomon also says: “Your substance and your sweetness” (Wisdom 16:20). Jeremiah says: “If they had stood in my substance” (Jeremiah 23:22, according to the Septuagint). And in Proverbs: “The substance of the rich is a fortified city” (Proverbs 10:15). Again, in the same book: “Fathers divide house and substance among their sons” (Proverbs 13:22).

Tobias also says: “If your substance should be abundant” (Tobit 4:9). And again: “My son, give alms from your substance” (ibid., 7). John likewise says: “Whoever has the substance of this world” (1 John 3:17). And in the Gospel: “Behold, I give half of my substance” (Luke 19:8).

We have gathered these examples together so that that statement might not mislead the unlearned—the statement that “substance” is not to be proclaimed because it is nowhere found in the divine Scriptures.

Therefore, if neither the word “substance” itself is new to the sacred writings nor its interpretation involves any offense, it remains for us to examine why this term is rejected. On examination, we find that they reject not the word but the power of the word.

If this becomes clear, the status of the word will be evident to us, and the understanding of those who, while seeking novel paths of profane interpretation, have departed from the straight path of the Gospels will also be shown to be faulty.

### Chapter VIII. The objections of the heretics are answered

[Col. 0018B]

Before I establish what I promised, however, we must meet the arguments proposed against us. They say that the term “substance” is indeed found in the divine books, but that it does not immediately belong to the same category of thing that we introduce. There, they say, the word “substance” signifies either power or divinity.

When we therefore defend one substance of the Father and the Son, what else do we proclaim than equal riches in both, namely, of one divinity? Concerning these riches the Apostle says: “God has made known the riches of his glory” (Colossians 1:27)—which is Christ.

We also say that the power of both is one. Concerning this the same Apostle says: “Christ is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Since this power needs no external assistance, it is called “substance,” as we said above: whatever exists as owing its existence to itself.

Therefore we declare nothing new in this term, nothing foreign, nothing incongruous with divinity, even if its meaning is extended in any direction. But, as I began to say, this whole dispute is really about something else: it is not the word but the force of the word that displeases them.

With what ears, then, could they tolerate the proclamation that the substance of the Father and the Son is one—that honor, dignity, glory, power, and majesty are truly and equally common to both—when they separate the Son from the Father and, dividing their substances, present each as existing in his own distinct character, rejecting their communion in divinity?

Here, then, is the blasphemous offense; here is the sacrilegious grievance: that one God is acknowledged in the Father and the Son.

Although the authors of this poison have died, their crimes and teaching have not died. Those authors, I say, separated the Son from the Father to such an extent that they declared with sacrilegious mouth that the Son of God was indeed created and founded before the ages, but had received from the Father the ability to live and exist; that he existed before he was born; and that he was indeed God, but was not the true God.

It is therefore fitting that the successors of this faithlessness, not faith, through whom the inheritance of evils creeps onward, should dislike the one substance, which they demand be removed as though it were a stumbling block and a divorce from unity. They do not understand that only those should be called Catholics who agree in communion with this profession.

### Chapter IX. The unknown birth of Christ. Christ from God, in God, with God.

It is something that no one could endure with equanimity: that those who assert as certain that he has a beginning should regard his birth as uncertain. Either both matters must be held concealed, since they are contemporaneous, or both ought to be known. For one cannot be known or unknown without the other. “The Son,” he says, “has a beginning, but his birth is hidden.” Is it not unjust? Who disclosed anything concerning his birth? Why did he keep silent? Indeed, how can the very birth that is asserted to be unknown be known? But here people wholly devoid of every good hope appeal against us to the authority of the prophet who says:

> “Who has recounted his birth?” (Isaiah 58:8)

They do not understand that already then, by the prophetic Spirit, those were foreseen who would give a beginning to the Word of God—that is, to the Son of God. “Who,” he says, “has recounted his birth?” This means: No human being will be able to do so. No one could, except the one who, declaring the bosom of the Father, first revealed to us the secrets of his own birth.

For we also read that the following was spoken in the same sense: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:34; 1 Corinthians 1:16). But we are taught again: “Except the Spirit who is in him.” “Who has recounted his birth?” (1 Corinthians 1:11). This means: Let no one dare to recount what he cannot recount. But why will no one be able to do so? Because the one who is without birth exists not only from him and with him, but also in him. For, begotten from the Unbegotten, the Son God was born into those divine goods that belonged to the Unbegotten; and did the Father cease to possess in the same Unbegotten what he had begotten, while possessing in himself the same one whom he had begotten?

His birth, therefore, is proclaimed unutterable because through it he is beyond conception; yet, perfect from God the Father, the Son is God. For, according to the Scriptures, we have said of the Son that he is “from him, and with him, and in him” (Romans 11:36).

## CHAPTER X. This doctrine is explained. Heretics agree with us in words, not in meaning.

So that no one may be troubled by the variety of meanings, an account must be given of the statements; and, so that what has been set forth may not be confused, it must be given briefly. “From him” refers to the author; “with him” to the Only-Begotten; “in him” to the birth of the substance. This is heard throughout. Hold fast to the mysteries of the divine dispensation. You know enough.

“Who,” he says, “has recounted his birth?” For who could recount according to nature a birth that is contrary to nature? He alone is born who is conscious of his own birth. He, understanding by nature the origin of the one for whom these goods were being prepared, was in the Father in the very condition in which he was born.

“Who,” he says, “has recounted his birth?” And they add that this was disclosed to no one, because it is known, of course, only to the Son and the Father. This is to say, without the deceit of subtle words: The Father indeed begot the Son, but no one knows from where.

The Jews likewise said: “We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John 9:29). Although at times they agree with us in the communion of words, and certain statements may seem, taken simply, to cast the disgrace of heretical perversity upon them, nevertheless, because almost all their statements [Note: [Col. 0019D] “Almost all of theirs.” It seems that words such as *verba* (“statements”) or *dicta* (“sayings”), or something similar, should be inserted, as a little earlier.] proceed against the true faith, the fewer must be understood in light of the greater—especially since, if anything contrary to the faith is accepted, the whole faith suffers loss.

“No one,” he says, “knows how the Son was begotten except the Father alone” (John 1:18). What, then, does that statement mean, by which the Lord did not wish us to remain ignorant of this? “I,” he says, “came forth from the Father, and from the bosom of the Father” (John 16:27–28).

Alas! Why did he not wish us, who pursue the darkness of ignorance, to remain ignorant? Surely he did not wish it, so that, once we knew the author, the question of his status might be removed. For there would be no need to ask who, how, or what he was, once we knew from whom he was.

But if at this point the Lord’s own statement is brought forward as confirmation, namely: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father” (Matthew 11:27), they will hear from us that they must not defraud the divine definition. For it continues: “And the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” That which cannot be revealed is not wholly hidden. It is revealed if someone proves worthy of revelation.

## CHAPTER XI. Through the Spirit of God we know hidden things.

This knowledge of the secret, then, is not concealed from us for no reason; it is revealed according to the purpose for which it is revealed. It follows that we are unworthy of knowledge, and that God must not be regarded as unjust because he punishes ignorance; he would not punish it if he had not granted knowledge.

He granted it through the Holy Spirit. Finally, “the Spirit,” he says, “of truth will declare to you all truth” (John 16:13). When he says “all truth,” he certainly excludes nothing. This is the Spirit of knowledge and truth, through whom Solomon says concerning the Lord’s birth: “I will report what wisdom is and how it came to be, and from the beginning I will investigate its birth” (Wisdom 6:24).

Therefore, through the same Spirit we can discover what we seek. The Apostle also says: “God has revealed it to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). “No one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God.” Since the same Apostle proves that this Spirit dwells in us, we can therefore, through that same Spirit, gain entry into the secrets of God.

And indeed: “Seek,” he says, “and you will find; ask, and it will be given to you; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7; Luke 11:24). And again: “Father, you have revealed to little ones what you concealed from the wise” (Matthew 11:25)—to us, surely, to whom the Lord says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of God” (Matthew 13:11); that mystery, namely, of which the Apostle says: “What was not previously known to the sons of men has now been revealed to his saints” (Ephesians 3:5).

It has indeed been revealed. For he has displayed the surpassing riches of his glory, in his goodness toward us in Christ [Note: [Col. 0021D] I would read “in Christ” with the Apostle, Ephesians 3:6.]—who himself is [Note: [Col. 0022D] “Glory.” Another reading: “in glory.”] the glory of God the Father. He himself is the true offspring of the Unbegotten.

This is the meaning of: “No one knows how the Son was begotten.” No one, certainly; but this is said of those in whom, as the Lord says, his word does not find room (John 8:37), as also of the Jews, to whom the same Lord says: “You do not know where I come from or where I am going, because you judge according to the flesh” (ibid., 14–15).

For how can no one know, if the Father says: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44:2)? How can no one know, if the Son says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclesiasticus 24:5)? Do not inquire further, and you will have nothing left to seek; for you know the whole, because what is said is the whole.

“I came forth,” he says, “from the mouth of the Most High.” This is the perfect birth of the Word; this is a beginning without beginning. This is a rising that has a beginning in birth but has none in status. For God the Begotten came forth from the God who cannot be born: one from one, true from true, full from full. Thus, in being born into those things that always existed, what was born did not begin to be from things not conceived, nor does it have a time that is naturally co-born with the timeless Father.

For it is written: “God is spirit” (John 4:24), and the eternal one was born from God. Therefore he is of that nature in which eternity consists. The Son, therefore, is not imperfect, although born, because he was born from the Perfect; nor is the one who begot diminished, because he begot from himself. For the Whole gave the whole, so that, according to the power of the Spirit, the whole might be in the whole.

## CHAPTER XII. What the evil teachers think and how they contend.

But now the evil teachers no longer restrain themselves within the secrets of their craft. They stand against the truth and against truth itself, having horns like lambs but speaking like dragons.

Wishing, therefore, to sever the Son from the Father and place him beneath God, they appeal from the Gospel: “The Father,” he says, “is greater than I” (John 14:28). And how is he greater? Immediately, with heretical presumption, they define it: In honor, glory, dignity, and majesty.

But if this is so, why is it commanded that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father? If this is so, then we blaspheme every day in our thanksgivings and sacrificial offerings, confessing these things to be common to the Father and the Son; for the Son cannot fail to possess everything that belongs to the Father, since he himself is wholly in the Father.

Finally, John says: “No one has ever seen God, except the Only-Begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18). Therefore he says: “All that is yours is mine, and what is mine is yours” (John 17:10); and: “The Son can do nothing from himself” (John 5:19); and: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

This is not a confession of weakness but an assertion of unity. For he had also said, both against weakness and in favor of unity: “The one who sent me is with me” (John 6:29); and: “The Father, remaining in me, does his works” (John 14:10); and: “The words that I speak are not mine but the Father’s” (ibid.; 7:6).

Whatever, therefore, is taken away from the Son will also be derogated from the Father. For neither does one do anything without the other, because one cannot exist without the other. The Son is not Son unless he has the Father; nor is the Father Father unless he has the Son.

“The Father,” he says, “is greater than I.” But the fullness of that same divinity is in the Son. Finally, the Apostle says: “However many the promises of God are, in him they are” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Do the Son’s acts of obedience, then, dissolve the status of his divinity? For everything that God is is dissolved in Christ if he is understood to possess a different majesty; and it will be different if the Father is greater in majesty. But since that majesty is one—belonging, obviously, to the one God—it cannot fail to be perfect. What is imperfect is unequal; and it is unequal if it is less than another.

## CHAPTER XIII. Christ, the mirror of God’s majesty, reflects the complete image of the Father. The heresy of Sabellius.

But at this point what Matthew reports will favor you: read in that same Matthew (25:31) that the Son of Man, supposedly as a private and lesser figure, will come in the majesty of the Father. Concerning this coming Luke also says: “When the Son of Man comes in his glory and the Father’s” (Luke 21:27).

The Son, therefore, is not so much declared by you to be lesser in majesty when this is said as God is denied. He—he, I say—of whom Solomon says: “He is the radiance of eternal light and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty” (Wisdom 7:26).

A spotless mirror indeed. For he preserves the face of God; and, faithfully expressing its form, he presents the complete image of the Father. What more need be said about his status, in which the Lord Christ recognized himself? “The Father,” he says, “is greater than I.”

Rightly greater, because he alone is the author without an author. Finally, the Apostle says of the Son: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9). Therefore, just as the Son is perfect in the Father, so the Father is perfect in the Son.

Finally, when our Lord said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, he added: “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14). Likewise, when John had said: “We announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father” (1 John 1:2), he added: “This life is in his Son” (ibid., 11). Thus, although both are perfect and each is perfect, there is nevertheless one perfect God in the two.

“The Father,” he says, “is greater than I” (John 14:28). Rightly greater, because he himself did not descend into the Virgin. Sabellius denied this: for him the Father and the Son are not two, that is, one person with two names. Yet he had heard the Father’s voice through Isaiah: “Behold my Son, whom I have chosen; I will place my Spirit upon him” (Isaiah 42:1). And thereafter, through the same prophet, he should recognize the Son speaking: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isaiah 61:1).

Foreseeing this heresy, the Lord said: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me?” (John 14:10–11). He certainly did not say: “I am the Father, and I am in myself,” but: “I am in the Father and the Father in me.” By this statement he struck down two heresies: the Sabellian, which says that the Father and the Son are one person, and the Arian, which says that they are two substances. Rather, as the Catholic faith confesses, he taught that there is one substance and two persons.

## CHAPTER XIV. Catholic doctrine confirmed from the sacred writings.

But what need is there of arguments, when the Lord himself has pronounced the definitive judgment? “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5:19). How can this be so if he cannot aspire to the fullness of that paternal glory?

Indeed, because he can, John rightly says: “Without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). The Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). One, certainly, by nature: for what was in the Son of Man remained in the Father’s bosom.

Finally: “You know me,” he says, “and you know where I am from; and I have not come from myself, but the one who sent me is true, whom you do not know. I know him, because I am with him, and he sent me” (John 7:28–29); and: “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (John 8:16); and: “Just as the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John 10:15).

But I do not know whether the Son could have known the Father if the Son received a beginning. The begotten could not have known the Unbegotten before he was begotten. He therefore does not know the Father in the same way that he is known by the Father. A lie must consequently be attributed to him—something that ought not to fall upon the Lord—and rightly attributed, if his assertion does not stand by reason.

But it will not stand unless he is the one who not only came forth from the Father but also is and has always been in the Father. “The Father,” he says, “has handed everything over into his hand” (John 3:35). How “everything,” unless also every time? And how every time, if he is not without a beginning?

However much you may say that he was born before all time, nevertheless, because you wish the one who was born to have begun at some point, and not to have existed as what was made, I do not know how you can maintain that he received from the Father everything, including every time.

## CHAPTER XV. Heretics speak ambiguously. One God. In God the Father, God the Son.

“The Son,” he says, “is subject to the Father, together with all those things that the Father himself subjected to him.”

You conceal this poisoned venom beneath the veil of carefully chosen words. We steadfastly proclaim what we have heard from our fathers; you, therefore, should not abandon the doctrine of your fathers. They, I say, openly declared that the God of heavenly glory was not the true God but a perfect creature of God. You, while holding the same opinion, avoid blunt blasphemy and resort to ambiguities in order to deceive the simple and unwary.

For you confess that the Son is subject to the Father, not in the name of the Father or the Son, as the holy and Catholic Church says, but—as we said above—in the condition of a creature. When you say that the Son is subject to the Father “together with all those things that the Father subjected to him,” do you not number him among creatures that were established in time?

According to you, God and our Lord has nothing greater than every creature except that he is first in number, except that those creatures also serve him, together with which he serves. He too is a servant if he serves; and although he is Lord of some, he is Lord by will, since, if he became Lord by the Lord’s will, he is serving precisely by being commanded to rule.

This is what you secretly say, and what your fathers said openly: that the Son of God was brought forth by the Father without time and established not before he was born.

What, I ask, is this dullness of heart? What forgetfulness of hope? Indeed, what so mad and blasphemous a confession as to call God the one whom you compare with all those things made from nothing?

This is also to mock the Son with the false name of divinity, if he is said to be by word what is denied in the heart; and to mark God the Father as a liar, when he says: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14); and: “I alone am the Lord” (Isaiah 63:11); and: “I will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8; 48:11); and: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God”; and: “Do not seek my name; God is my name” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

If, then, there is one God, this name belongs to one. But he will no longer be one unless, in God the Father, the Son is God.

Rightly, therefore, the Lord, in accordance with the prophet who had said, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 117:26), says: “I have come in the name of my Father” (John 5:43). What is the Father’s name except the name of God and Lord? John, recognizing it in the Son, says: “He who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” (Revelation 1:8).

## CHAPTER XVI. The Son, image of the unbegotten God, cannot have begun after God. The Father is not without the Son.

“The Father,” he says, “has no beginning.” This is to say that he has a Son. For what necessity is there to assert of the Father what is known, unless this is prejudicial to the opinion that has accepted an equivalent claim concerning the Son?

“The Father,” he says, “has no beginning.” Who denies it? But, I think, the image of the invisible and unbegotten God cannot have begun after God.

Finally, when Moses asked who he was, he replied: “I am who I am always” (Exodus 3:14). For he always was who is and always will be.

John says of him: “What was from the beginning, we have seen with our eyes” (1 John 1:1). And again: “We announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father” (ibid., 2)—and, certainly, in the Father; for what was from him could not be outside him.

Indeed, when it is said, “There was time in him,” it is not announced that he himself existed in time. For the power of the eternal substance was not made by God but came forth from God. Therefore he says: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28); and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9); and: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid., 10); and: “The one who sent me is with me” (John 8:29).

Therefore David also says: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power” (Psalm 109:3). The Word of God, that is, the Son of God, is before every beginning with the one who is from him and in him, for whom there can be no beginning.

We do indeed find Solomon speaking in the person of Wisdom—which we maintain is Christ: “The Lord created me, and before the age he founded me, and before the abyss I was begotten” (Proverbs 8:22–24). But it must not for that reason be believed that God was made. For if he was made, he was not; if he was not, he will not be. And how is he God, when both conditions are imposed to prevent him from being God?

Wisdom, therefore, is announced as born and created so that nothing might be believed to exist in nature besides God the Father himself, who is also the source of his own powers. For from this it would rightly be said: Wisdom was created from him and in him, from whom the Only-Begotten and blessed birth shone forth.

Whoever, therefore, proves that the Father was at some time without the Word, without wisdom, without reason, without power, and without the Spirit has proved that, with the Father and in the Father, the Son did not exist before every beginning.

Yet I do not know whether a Father lacking these powers could be called God. For not only will God, who is perfect in his eternity, fail to exist as such, but no creature either will be complete according to its kind unless it is perfected. For what does not exist cannot be something; and it will not exist if it lacks what it ought to be.

Everything, therefore, was lacking to the Father if anything was lacking from the whole. Something was lacking if his Son—that is, the fullness of his powers—was not without a beginning. This opinion must necessarily pass over into one or the other part of blasphemy through profane and sacrilegious definition.

Either the Father must be believed to have received a beginning together with his Son, because he could not exist without the Son—that is, without his powers—and some third god will then be the author of their beginning; or, if he alone is said to be without beginning until the generation of the Son, he must be said to have been imperfect.

For he is imperfect if he began to have what previously he had chosen not to have. But he ought always to have everything who ought always to have been perfect, because whatever has occupied the whole admits no increase.

## CHAPTER XVII. Heretics confess concerning the Son whatever they deny concerning the Father. How the Son God is visible.

“The Father,” they say, “has no beginning, is invisible, immortal, and impassible.”

They set these things forth in order to ascribe their opposites to the Son. For whatever they deny concerning the Father they confess concerning the Son; and if he is proved to have a beginning, he is rightly mortal and rightly passible.

Once the first proposition—the one that assigned a beginning to the Word of God—has been destroyed, it should already have been prejudged that the other kinds of suffering cannot apply to the Son. Nevertheless, lest we recoil in distrust before the other claims that have been profanely advanced: just as the remaining attributes included under this definition cannot be ascribed to one who has no beginning, so, if he is found akin to one of them, it is right that those attributes which had been defended should likewise be overturned.

“The Father,” he says, “is invisible.” As though we should ever find the Son visible without transformation, before he, obedient to the Father, became corporeal from eternity.

Although he appeared to Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Isaiah, and Ezekiel, the nature of that vision is nevertheless explained. He is reported to have appeared in sleep, in a mirror, and in an enigma.

Finally, when Moses requested that he be allowed to see him clearly, he said: “No one can see my face, because no one who sees it will live” (Exodus 33:20). Therefore, in this passage, let them either contend that the Father spoke—the one who says that he is invisible—or, if they do not deny that it was the Son, let them know that the speaker was invisible in his own name, as Word and as Spirit.

Finally, how the invisible God was seen is testified by the same Scripture. For it reports that God spoke with him face to face, as with a friend. Thereafter it adds that Moses asked to see his face; yet if he had seen it, he would not immediately have asked to see it. [Note: [Col. 0025D] “Had asked.” Another reading: “to have asked.”]

Jacob indeed says: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Genesis 32:30). But how was he saved by seeing that face which, if seen, kills? How had the Lord shown his face, which he later said could not be seen, except under the condition we mentioned above—in a mirror and in an enigma, in a dream and in a vision?

Thus he assumed visible material form when he willed, yet immediately remained invisible; for, if he is declared visible, he must necessarily not be from the one whom we confess to be invisible.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Son of God, preserving the bond of unity with the Father, bore a man on earth and was not absent from heaven.

But to resolve this assertion by questions from the Old Testament, they take confirmation from the New Testament. For the Lord and God, speaking of the Father, says that no one has seen the image of the Father (John 1:18). If the Son himself is the image of the Father, as the Apostle proves (Hebrews 1:3), then he denies that the Son was visible by saying that no one had seen the image of the Father.

Therefore he says: “You know neither me nor my Father” (John 8:19). Here he certainly confirms that the two are unknown, but also that the two are inseparable. For if they knew him, they would know the Father as well, because, through their indivisibility, neither could the one be known without the other nor the one be ignored without the other.

A similar argument, therefore, follows concerning mortality and passibility. If the Son has no beginning, since he always was and is in the one to whom no beginning is assigned, and if he is not visible, since he remains in the bosom of the invisible one, then he must neither be regarded as mortal nor as passible—at least in that part of the substance in which he is God.

For we know that nothing suffered in the Spirit of God, at least in his own name, because God is impassible and God is spirit (John 4:24). We know that all that suffering properly belonged to flesh and soul, that is, to the human being. In that human being, while he was suffering, the Son of God was also joined to him by nature—from the Father whom he had come from—and, preserving the bond of unity, he bore a man on earth and was not absent from heaven.

Thus he was called the mediator, thus the intermediary of both substances. The Spirit of God, therefore, was not passible, although he suffered in his own man. He did not abandon him even in his suffering, in order thereby to grant him the capacity to suffer. Unless this is accepted, the basis of our faith will not stand: namely, that he gave him the weakness of a man whom they do not deny to be God.

For if he is said to have a beginning, taught to be visible, and introduced as mortal, I do not see how he differs from the human being in whom such sufferings rule.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Ariomanites think one thing with their mouth and another in their heart.

“We confess,” they say, “the Son of God, God from God, light from light.”

It may seem sacrilegious to harass by malicious argument a profession that appears to be a perfect statement of the Catholic faith. But it must not be allowed that they take away from us what they do not hold with us by means of what they do hold with us.

We acknowledge and reverently accept the words of the common faith. But what are we to do? Such is the mad doctrine of the Ariomanites. For when it says “God from God, light from light,” it makes one God from God and another God, one light from light and another light, so that the Son is from the Father but not in the Father—that is, so that, made God by God, he is not the Only-Begotten in God.

But what more is needed here, when the writings of some of those who recently sent us this distinguished faith are preserved? Although they say “God from God, light from light,” they nevertheless teach, in heretical argument, that he is separated from the Father and completely cut off from him.

“They say that the Son of God took from Mary a man with whom he suffered.” Thus, bringing everything to a fitting conclusion, they confessed in writing what they had conceived in their minds. Their writing responds to their meaning and lays bare their hidden poisons: namely, when they say that the Son of God took from Mary a man with whom he suffered.

First, I do not see why they preferred to call him “one who suffered with” rather than openly confess him to be passible. As though “to suffer with” were something other than “to suffer.” Moreover, if God is impassible, then he is also incapable of suffering with another. He therefore did not suffer with another any more than he suffered, in the condition in which he is God.

Finally, the Apostle says: “He suffered” (2 Corinthians 13:4), namely, through the weakness of the flesh—for “the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41), while “the spirit is willing”—“but he lives through the power of God,” namely, through himself. For he himself is the power of God, possessing life in himself.

We believe that our Lord consisted of two substances, human and divine; and thus he was immortal by virtue of the divine substance and mortal by virtue of the human one: born from one and proved by the other; immortal from one and mortal from the other.

Finally, the same Apostle says: “Christ,” he says, “died” (1 Corinthians 15:3)—that is, the anointed one, for this name is derived from anointing. If, then, it was nothing other than the flesh that was anointed, the flesh alone is therefore said to have died whenever Christ’s death is announced.

## CHAPTER XX. The Son is other than the Father through distinction, not division, of persons. The Word of God is not a sound of the voice but a substantial reality.

But if someone wishes to force one of two alternatives upon us—either to define one God in isolation if we confess one, or openly to assert two if we say that both the Father is God and the Son is God—let this be understood above all: we say neither one with prejudice nor two; for, following the Lord himself, we say that there is one in two: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), so that two might be believed to exist in one power.

For he did not speak as though the Father and the Son were one person, as though the Son were confirming himself to be the Father—“I am my Son,” “Today I have begotten myself,” “Before the morning star I begot myself,” “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways,” “Before the ages he founded me,” “I and the Father are one.”

Rather, he disclosed the mystery through a distinction, not a division, of persons: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; “I and the Father are one”; and “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

The Son of the Father is seen as the true image and expressed figure of his substance; this is the Word of God—not a sound of the voice but a substantial reality, one that is corporeal through substance. For what he made from so great a substance did not exist without substance.

Nothing, therefore, is empty from the full, nothing void from the solid, because the Word of God—the Spirit of God, Christ—is equipped; and, to put it more clearly, he is the body of the Word. For the spirit too has a body, a body of its own kind. For the spirit is both invisible and incomprehensible.

Yet is God an empty and void reality? For God is spirit. Finally: “No one knows,” he says, “what is in God except the Spirit who is in him” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

We do indeed read: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34). No one, certainly—but no one outside his Spirit. The prophet calls this Spirit wise, the architect, and the wonderful counselor; and rightly so.

For this same Spirit is the Word and Wisdom of God. In his person Solomon says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present with him” (Proverbs 8:27); and: “I was with him, and he rejoiced with me” (ibid., 30).

He is not, therefore, no counselor, since through him all things that were made came to be. Finally, although this same Wisdom is the Word of God and the Spirit of God, the functions of the individual names are nevertheless proclaimed.

Wisdom was present with the Father as he created all things: “By his Word the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6). It is therefore clear that one and the same being has now come under the name of Spirit and now under the designation of Wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXI. The passage of Romans 11:36 explained.

Therefore this Word, being in the form of God (Philippians 2:6–8), endowed with wisdom and reason, with the reason and power of the Spirit—that is, possessing the whole power of God— he did not make himself equal to God the Father. Rather, taking the form of a servant, he humbled himself even to death.

For he had put on what could serve and what could die—namely, the human being whom, raised up, he displayed to heaven. As the second Adam, through obedience, he restored what the first had lost through transgression.

If anyone still asks of the Apostle about the Lord’s status—that is, about the quality of the single substance that is naturally joined to its author—let him hear briefly what the same Apostle thought when speaking of the unsearchable ways of God the Father and his formerly hidden mysteries.

“From him,” he says, “and through him, and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36).

When “through him” is said, I recognize that the Son is signified; for I read: “Through him all things were made” (John 1:3). When “in him” is proclaimed, there is nothing new; for in him the beginnings of all seeds have been established.

But when “from him” is stated, it certainly refers to the Father as the author of all things. And if this is so—as it is—how will the reasoning of those who join distinct things stand, that is, those who refer everything to one, when one is the one from whom all things are and another the one through whom all things are? One is unbegotten and the other Only-Begotten.

Unless it is in another sense that it is rightly said that all things are also from the Son, since, by nature, he is in whose heart is the one from whom all things are; and that all things are through the Father, since he is always in the one through whom all things are.

For the Father acts through understanding; the Son, who is the Father’s understanding, brings things to completion by seeing. We must not, therefore, believe that the Apostle pronounced this rashly. But we must not believe that he thought this: that the Son of God, according to the flesh, became what he was not, while according to the spirit he is what he was; for what always was cannot not have been.

## CHAPTER XXII. Who are the Patripassians? Who are the Arians? What is the rule of faith?

We must therefore hold to the principle that creeps along a difficult and narrow path, with precipices on either side. Blinded by diabolical deceit, these precipices offer broad and easy paths in order to plunge those who go beyond the limits into destruction.

For if we name one God in isolation, excluding the name of a second person, we approve the madness of that heresy which asserts that the Father himself suffered. If we admit number together with division, we join the Arians, who assert that a God was made by God and that a new substance came into existence from nothing.

We must therefore hold, as we said, to the rule that confesses the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son (John 14:20); that, preserving one substance in two persons, acknowledges the dispensation of divinity.

The Father, therefore, is God, and the Son is God, because in God the Father the Son is God. If this causes scandal to anyone, let him hear from us that the Spirit is from God, because the one who has the second person in the Son also has the third in the Holy Spirit.

Finally, the Lord says: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Advocate” (ibid., 16). The Spirit is other than the Son just as the Son is other than the Father. The Spirit is the third person just as the Son is the second person; yet all three are one God, and the three are one.

This we believe; this we hold, because this we received from the prophets; the Gospels spoke this to us; the apostles handed it down; the martyrs confessed it in their suffering. In this, too, we cling firmly in our minds to the faith. Against it, even if an angel from heaven should proclaim otherwise, let him be anathema (Galatians 1:8).

## CHAPTER XXIII. The author’s judgment concerning Hosius, bishop of Corduba.

But I am not unaware that, once all these matters have been examined and set before the public light of understanding, the name of Hosius, that most ancient priest and ever-ready defender of the faith, will be wielded against us like a battering ram, by which the rashness of contradiction may be driven back. To those who raise this engine against us I reply in a very brief statement. His authority cannot prescribe the matter, because either he is now in error or he has always been in error. For the world knows what he has maintained throughout this period, with what steadfastness he assented at Sardica and in the Council of Nicaea, and condemned the Arians. But what if he now thinks differently, and whatever he formerly condemned is now defended, while what he defended is condemned? I say again: his authority does not prescribe the matter for me. For if he believed wrongly for nearly ninety years, I shall not believe that he came to right belief after ninety years. Or if he is right now, what are we to think of those who, marked with the same faith in which he himself stood, have passed from this world? And what verdict would have been pronounced concerning him if he had fallen asleep before this synod? Therefore, as we said above, the authority of a prejudged opinion will avail nothing, because it stands in contradiction to itself. And indeed we read: “The righteousness of the righteous shall not save him on whatever day he goes astray” (Ezek. 33:12). Amen.

[Col. 0031]

## II. ON THE ORTHODOX FAITH, AGAINST THE ARIANS; OTHERWISE, A TREATISE ON THE DIVINITY AND CONSUBSTANTIALITY OF THE SON. (C, G, S)*

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0031A]

#### Confession of Faith

We believe in God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born uniquely from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον); through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. Who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, and was incarnate, and became man; who suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten, he was not,” and who say that the Son of God is mutable or changeable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them. Amen.

#### Preface

Led by love for the catholic Faith, I had some time ago published a little book against the Arians. When I had given it to a friend to read, because he approved of it, he thought it should be transcribed. I earnestly asked him, however, to conceal the author for the time being and have it read by learned and prudent men, so that, if he knew of anything that seemed to have been stated there either excessively or insufficiently, it might be corrected by the advice of many. For no one is so arrogantly confident as to claim for himself the whole of heavenly doctrine, thinking that he clearly possesses all its mysteries, when the Apostle Paul says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2); and: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). But if everything written there seemed to all to stand in accordance with the true faith, then he himself would not refuse it to those who requested it. It is clear that he did so. And because the work was judged worthy both of so catholic a confession and of a response to heresy, many wished either to read it or to copy it.

But there was someone who, whether out of zeal for learning or as a duty of charity, subjected what I had said to a more scrupulous review; and he declared certain things either superfluous or ambiguous, which some might understand otherwise than I had intended. Therefore I have once again arranged those same matters in this little book in clearer language, both to show the simplicity of my meaning and to remove any scruple from the readers.

For this is what they say can be criticized: that, when we presented the Word of God as referring to the person of the Son, we supposedly understood this Word to be such as grammarians describe it—air struck by the breath of the mouth and made perceptible to hearing. But we know not the wisdom of this world, which is being destroyed, but that wisdom which is from God, which indicates that the Word of God is God when it says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). Hence I confess that I am astonished that this could have been understood as though we denied the distinct person of the Word, who is the Son. No one merely gives a verbal name to one whom he repeatedly professes truly to exist in his own person. For how have we confessed either a true Son or a true Father, if we have not preserved the true distinctness of the persons both of the Father and of the Son?

But because we used the term “one God,” we are thought to have denied the persons. From this, what we stated has seemed plausible. We name the Father and the Son in such a way as to designate one God in these persons and names. Moreover, although the Father and the Son are called by two names, they are nevertheless one in reason and substance; and when I establish the Father and the Son, I designate the unity of their kind.

All these statements were judged capable of being understood as though the names had been placed between the Father and the Son as a first name and a surname belonging to one person, although the suspicion could have been excluded by what was said above or below. For when I had said that the Son of God was born from no other source than properly from the Father—whole from whole, complete from complete, perfect from perfect, and consummate in power—how could I have posited the Father himself as his own Son and in this way called one person by two names? Especially since, in the same book, I condemned this sect, namely the Sabellian sect, and wrote about the distinction of persons according to their names. For no one can say of one person, “they are one,” or speak of a unity of kind, unless persons are being designated.

What catholic does not know that the Father is truly Father, the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit truly the Holy Spirit, just as the Lord himself says to his apostles: “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19)? This is the perfect Trinity consisting in unity, which we profess to be of one substance. We do not create a division in God according to the condition of bodies; rather, according to the power of the divine nature, which is not material, we believe that the persons designated by the names truly exist, and we testify that the divinity is one.

Nor do we call the Son of God an extension of some part of the Father—as certain people have thought—nor [do we call him] a word without reality, as though we understood him to be the sound of a voice. Rather, we believe that the three names and three persons belong to one essence, one majesty, and one power. And for this reason we confess one God, because the unity of majesty prevents a plurality [of persons] from being called “gods.”

Finally, we name the Father and the Son in catholic fashion; but we can neither say nor ought to say “two gods”—not because the Son of God is not God, indeed because he is true God from true God, but because we know the Son of God to be from no other source than that one Father himself, and therefore we call them one God. For this the prophets handed down, this the apostles transmitted, and this the Lord himself taught when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). “One” refers, as I said, to the unity of divinity; “are” designates the persons. The Apostle also says: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. But not everyone possesses knowledge” (1 Cor. 8:6).

Since I have explained these words, which caused scruple not for me, who know what I said, but for others, I think the opportunity for a bad interpretation has been removed. For the confession of faith is clear, the person exists together with the names, and one divinity has been designated.

Or, if there is still something in the words that seems ambiguous to readers, the words should be brought into relation with their meaning; for it is not the simplicity of the words but the obstinacy of a bad understanding that gives off the odor of guilt. But when our meaning agrees with the truth, the words too must agree with the most sincere reasoning. Therefore let the academic disputant withdraw from Christian simplicity.

### CHAPTER I  
### Nothing is more dangerous than those heretics who agree with us in many respects. Although they seem to proceed soundly through everything, they corrupt the simple faith by a single word. Once the name “substance,” which they wish to remove from the evangelical and apostolic faith and from the tradition of the fathers, has been taken away, the Arian heresy is subtly introduced. By what reasoning they have tried to remove this name.

[Col. 0034A]

We know that many serious heresies have boiled over from many sources and, like poison, poured the virus of their cancer into the innermost heart. But those whose first proposition exposes the whole purpose of their mind can either be easily defeated or easily avoided. Those, however, who agree with us in many respects can easily strike minds that are innocent and devoted to God through a deceptive alliance, while defending the poison of their evils by means of our goods. For nothing can be more dangerous than these heretics, who, although they proceed soundly through everything, nevertheless corrupt the pure and simple faith of the Lord and, consequently, of the apostolic tradition by a single word, as by a drop of poison.

Therefore we must take the greatest care that something of this kind does not secretly insinuate itself into our minds or ears, because nothing drives a person so powerfully toward death as violating the faith under the pretext of faith.
