Just as gypsum mixed with water imitates milk in color, so here an enemy tradition is introduced under the appearance of a plausible confession. For this reason it is not the similarity of the confession but the meaning of the mind by which the confession itself is established that must be weighed.

Finally, if you attend more diligently and carefully, you will undoubtedly recognize that the Arian heresy has been abbreviated by a subtle shortcut and introduced by removing the name “substance,” since they wished that name to be taken away from the evangelical and apostolic faith and from the tradition of the fathers. I do not assert this on the basis of suspicion or conjecture, nor do I act, as they suppose, like an academic disputant who twists simple meanings through verbal subtlety; rather, I bring into the light of knowledge arguments that have been twisted and composed through a slender device, so that iniquity, once known and exposed, may more easily be avoided by human beings.

For what cause, or what reason, existed for striving—by no small effort—to remove what had been handed down to all the churches as something to be taught and believed, and what our fathers, apostolic men, purified by the Holy Spirit, established by catholic reasoning against all heresies, and especially against the Arian heresy, as a kind of barrier of truth by which they might block every entrance of pestilent doctrine? Surely the only reason is that those branded with the mark of Arian pollution might pretend that the Son of God is mutable and changeable, since he supposedly did not proceed from the Father’s own substance; and thus might now freely, securely, and without hesitation hand on and insinuate into the churches what they have always taught: that he had a beginning in time, an origin from nothing, and a name derived from another source, for which they have often been condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] The Laet. and Tell. manuscripts read: “I undertake this, neither by opinion,” etc.; all the better editions have the text as above.]

[Note: [Col. 0033D] The Tell. manuscript and Amerb. edition read: “what true reason exists.”]

[Note: [Col. 0034D] The Vigiliana edition reads: “purified and flooded by the Holy Spirit.”]

[Note: [Col. 0034D] *Elogium* sometimes has the same meaning as a formula of condemnation.]

### CHAPTER II  
### The refutation of the Arian heresy by the strongest arguments and the clear testimonies of sacred Scripture. They posit the Son as God from God in such a way that he was made from God, not begotten from God. They remove the term *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον) and substitute *homoiousion* (ὁμοιούσιον) for it. They understand that Wisdom who is the Son of God is a creature.

[Col. 0035A]

You see, therefore, that throughout their treatise they have set forth everything not according to evangelical faith but by deceitful malice, in order to seduce the simple. It should no longer be merely suspected but manifest to everyone that they posited God from God in the manner Arius used to teach: that he was made from God, not born from God. If he was born, he is of one substance; if he was made, he is not the true Son; and if he is not the true Son, he is not true God. Or, if he is true God but is not from the Father, then there are two beings, each possessing its own will and differing authority. Or, if they are one only through agreement and fellowship, he is nevertheless not true God in substance, as I have already said.

Thus he will be God in the sense in which Moses was God to Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1): by power, not by nature. The Son, too, will have to be believed in the sense of the words spoken through Isaiah to the people: “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Isa. 1:2); and elsewhere: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). He will also be regarded as firstborn in the same way that Israel was called God’s firstborn son (Exod. 4:22). Likewise, “firstborn of all creation” will be understood as though he were firstborn in the order of created things, so that from him they may assign a certain sequence to the creation of the world’s beings.

Finally, after removing *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, the term “of one substance,” they put in its place *homoiousion* (ὁμοιούσιον), that is, “like his maker,” although likeness is one thing and truth another. For human beings too were made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26), yet they are not God; nor should what is God be believed to have come into existence as a human being. In the same way they want the Son of God to be like God, but they say that he is like him from another source, not from that one holy and blessed substance of the Father. If he is not from the Father’s substance, he is *ex ouk ontōn* (ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων), that is, “from things that do not exist,” as Arius likewise taught. For once the Father is removed, wherever the Son may have come from, he must have both a beginning from nothing and an origin in time; nothing exists without a beginning except God alone.

Hence the Son also says, as the Lord himself stated: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He said this in order to show that the names of two persons belong to the majesty of one divinity, just as the prophet says in the voice of God: “My heart has poured forth a good Word; I speak my works to the king” (Ps. 45:2). You see, therefore, that this good Word is the Son of God, whom we believe to have been born from no other source than the Father’s breast, or, so to speak, from the womb of God’s heart. And for this reason he calls him king, because he is the King of kings, the Lord God before whom all divine works bow, who said: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

Of him the Evangelist also says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). Therefore what was in the beginning must be believed always to have existed; but it must not be from any other source than him who has no beginning—that is, from the heart of the Father—for “my heart has poured forth a good Word” (Ps. 45:2). He did not say, “In the beginning the Word was made,” but said, “In the beginning the Word was.” Whatever beginning you wish to assign to the Word, you will already be refuted, because he says, “In the beginning the Word was.”

We do not say that there are two beginnings because of the diversity of things, but because the Word, the Son, is always with the Father and was born from the Father. Therefore, since his origin has no beginning, he must be believed to be eternal with the Father, because the Father can never be named without the Son, nor the Son called without the Father. Thus the Son is always, because the Father is always.

“And the Word was God,” he says. What is God always is; for if he has not always existed, he cannot be true God. The same is true in the name “Wisdom,” because, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 1:24), he himself is the Wisdom of the Father. “I came forth,” he says, “from the mouth of the Most High” (Sir. 24:5). Therefore he is from no other source than the Father, because he is always with the Father. And for this reason he is called the Wisdom of God, so that it may never be believed that the Father existed without Wisdom, that is, without his Son.

This is that ineffable Wisdom which, according to Solomon (Prov. 8:22), is described as either founded, begotten, or created as the beginning of God’s ways.

[Note: [Col. 0036D] The manuscripts Tell. and Laet., as well as the old edition, read “which at the beginning”; and below, “but with a beginning.” Rom. and Vigil. read “but with the beginning.”]

Yet he says that it was founded in such a way as to show that it had always been with God. For what beginning will you give to God, so that you can assign a beginning to Wisdom itself? God did not establish his Wisdom as though he had once existed without Wisdom. Rather, when he says “the beginning of his ways,” he indicates the beginning of the movement of some work, so that Wisdom has this beginning: that it proceeded from God to create all things heavenly and earthly—not that it began to exist in God. Wisdom was therefore created, or rather begotten, not for itself, since it always existed, but for those things that had to be made by it. Since it could not be known how great and what sort it was, its power and strength were to be recognized from the effect of its works, so that we might fear the Creator all the more when we marvel at the things that have been made.

[Note: [Col. 0036D] The Vigil. edition reads: “so that, while we fear the Creator from the created things …”]

But if you call Wisdom created in order to understand the Son of God as a creature, the Apostle confronts you, condemning those who worship the creature, saying: “For this reason God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:24–25).

This, I say, is that Wisdom of God which says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Sir. 24:25), the founder and maker of the universe—that is, the Son of God, through whom and in whom all things exist. For, as the Apostle said: “In him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Principalities, or Powers; all things were created through him and in him. And he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1:16–17). Hence Solomon also says: “Although she is one, she can do all things; and remaining in herself, she makes all things new, and through the nations she passes into holy souls” (Wis. 7:27). Confirming this, the Apostle says that Christ dwells in the inner person (Eph. 3:16), so that through the one by whom all things were made in the beginning, all things might also be saved at the end.

### CHAPTER III  
### The arguments by which the Arians establish their heresy are answered; they especially claim that *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον) ought not to be admitted because it is not contained in the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0037B]

But you tell me that, for this reason, they worship *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, “of one substance,” rather than the Creator, while certainly maintaining the same things that the Apostle said: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess” (Phil. 2:10). And Moses says: “Let all the angels of God adore him” (Deut. 32:43, according to the Septuagint). And David says: “All kings shall adore him” (Ps. 72:11). This indeed would not be said in the Scriptures unless he himself is the Word, the Son, the maker of all things.

[Col. 0037C]

But you say that *homoousion* ought not to be named because it is not contained in the divine Scriptures. And I ask you, human being who forbids this: if it ought not to be named because it is not written, is that because it may not be believed in this way?

If it ought to be believed in this way, why should it not be confessed in this way? For the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Or if it ought not to be named because it ought not to be believed in this way, then the assertion of Arian pollution has prevailed. It denied that the Father and the Son are of one substance because it introduces the Son of God as made—sometimes from nothing, sometimes from the Father but from another substance—whenever, however, and from wherever it wished, provided that it pretended that he came into existence from elsewhere and not from that which the Father is. Although it says that he was born, it does so only in words, because it again understands everything that is born to have been made, on the grounds that we too are called begotten by God, although it is clear that we are a created work.

Or, if you are not an Arian and acknowledge that the true Son was born from the true Father, not made, why do you not say that he is of one substance with the Father? You fear in vain, human being, to confess what you believe; and you believe in vain if you do not believe in this way—and rightly you are branded a heretic.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] The Tell. manuscript and Vigil. edition read: “although you have not changed the statement.” This does not make good sense.]

And although you have changed the statement—which you think forbade the Son of God to be called a created work—when he adds, “just as one of these things that has been made,” you plainly show that he did not wish him not to be called a created work for the reason that he should not be understood to have been made. Rather, you do not want him to have been made in the same way as one of those things that have been made, but nevertheless made.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] The Gill. and Rom. editions read: “he wished him to be called a created work.” Incorrectly.]

For you speak of “made” in another sense, as though he were a perfect creature through whom all things were made, provided that you still understand him to have been made, although not in the same way as the rest.

But to return to the point: you say that the term *homoousion*, that is, “of one substance,” is not found in the divine Scriptures. Suppose for the moment that this is so, on the assumption that wherever “substance” is read, the reality of God rather than God himself is understood. Yet you also confess something else that is not written, namely, “God from God, light from light.” What do you say to this? Either hold everything with me or abandon everything. For if you fear to say “of one substance” because it is not written, you must likewise fear to confess “God from God” and “light from light.”

But I prove that “God from God,” “light from light,” and the term “of one substance” are contained in the divine Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] The Teller manuscript reads: “in the Lord’s Scriptures.”]

For when the Son of God himself, who is God, says in his Gospel, “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:27), we rightly and properly confess God from God, because we understand the Son of God, true God from true God, to have been born from God the Father. But not in the manner in which we have been called gods (Ps. 82:6), or in which Moses was called the god of Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1); rather, because he is the true Son, he was born from the true Father.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] The Vigil. edition reads: “born from the true Father, not made.”]

He must therefore truly and confidently be called God from God, and likewise light from light.

You say with me that this is not written, but you do not at all understand it with me.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] All manuscripts and editions bearing the name of Ambrose read: “You do not understand [this] with me, because it is written of the Father: ‘God is light, which illuminates every human being …’—that is, Christ in heaven—and darkness … These human beings, of course, did not recognize [him], but he himself …” We have restored the passage according to the Vigil. edition.]

For it is written of the Father: “God is light” (1 John 1:5); and of the Son: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9); and: “The light shines in the darkness” (ibid., 5)—that is, Christ in the world—and the darkness did not overcome it. Those human beings whose hearts had been blinded by the darkness of ignorance did not recognize Christ as true God and the true Son of God. But the Lord himself says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). Therefore, since the Father is light and the Son is light, rightly we say “light from light.”

But you assert “light from light” as though another light had been made from the Father, who is the true light, and as though it were not from the Father’s own substance; as though it were some other light, even if made by God, nevertheless entirely different from him who made it. For this reason you say “light from light,” not “light from the light.”

Although I have stated these things beforehand, you may not understand them with me; nevertheless, however you pronounce the words, you yourself utter them even though they are not written.

[Col. 0039A]

Do you not likewise confess with me the term “of one substance,” which you do not think is contained in the Scriptures? Or is it because there you have found a way to cover your wicked meanings in both cases by hidden deceit, so that you express the very same thing with me in the sound of your voice while separating the meaning of the statement far from mine?

The same is true of those heretics who deny the resurrection of the flesh and, in order to deceive simple minds, pronounce woe upon those who do not rise in the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] The Vigil. edition also restored this passage. In the Ambrosian manuscripts and editions it read: “They say woe to simple souls on these grounds, because they do not rise in the flesh … They will say to you: ‘Certainly he will be …’” This made no sense.]

But if you examine why they said this, although you know that they altogether deny the resurrection of the flesh, they will tell you: “Woe indeed will befall the one who has not been baptized in the flesh, so that, while the soul is in the body, it may rise through baptism from the death of its sins, as from the grave of its crimes, in that same flesh.” For they defend the resurrection in the flesh of the soul alone, through the grace of the life-giving washing, while excluding salvation for the flesh itself. By a plausible confession these people too deceive innocent minds through hidden fraud. And just as a deadly drink, tempered with the sweetness of honey, kills through its deceptive pleasantness, so this evil, through the charm of the ears, contaminates the minds of its hearers with a certain corruption and infects them with the contagion of an adhering vice.

### CHAPTER IV  
### By what argument the Arians try to prove that God is not a substance. The same argument is refuted.

Finally, even now they could name *homoousion*, as they do other terms, merely in words, if they had a way to twist it toward another meaning through a crooked interpretation. But when they saw that they were enclosed by this word, they wanted no mention of it at all, lest, by confessing it, they should appear to believe it, or, while believing it, appear to confess it. With subtle ingenuity they excused themselves by saying either that it was not written or that God ought not to be called a substance, lest he be thought corporeal.

“For God,” they say, “causes substance to exist, but God himself is not thereby reckoned as a substance; for,” they say, “every substance admits opposites. But God, who can admit nothing diverse, ought not to be called a substance.”

I would forgive you if you said this simply, if you approached this question as an ignorant person, if you were not the very one who had always asserted that the Son of God was from another substance or from things that do not exist. But since you are the very one who has often been convicted and often confessed this, then often denied it and more often condemned by changing it in another way; since even now you are disturbing everything by force, ambition, and power—

[Note: [Col. 0039D] The Ambrosian edition with the Tell. manuscript reads: “now stirring everything up in ambition.” The Vigil. edition with the Laet. manuscript reads: “with force and ambition”; the Vigil. edition alone adds: “and power.”]

[Col. 0040D]

—how do you think I can forgive you when you repeatedly reconsider the same things? But lest this perversity seem to be condemned as a matter of prejudice rather than examination, I shall answer you briefly concerning this objection.

[Col. 0040A]

You therefore forbid the term “substance” to be used of God, as though everything called substance were regarded as a thing of one and the same kind. Do you not know that heavenly things exist in one way and earthly things in another, and that even among heavenly and worldly things there is great difference? Angels have received their substances of constitution in one way, and the individual Virtues in another, just as the Apostle says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars” (1 Cor. 15:41). So also in this world there are different bodies of living creatures according to the different kinds of things; and each kind has its own substance, as the Apostle says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh” (ibid., 39).

If, then, the things made by God have different qualities of substance, do you think that God possesses a substance such as anything made has, so that it can receive opposites? Far be it from us. For what is the substance of God? It is itself what God is: simple, unique, pure, unmixed with any combination, clear, good, perfect, blessed, whole, entirely holy.

Do you think that what is God is something empty and void? For it is blasphemy to think empty the one through whom all things have been established, who brought forth all things by the Word, ordered them by reason, perfected them by power, and by whose will and command the universe is governed and all things serve.

And rightly you read that this has been written of God: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14); and: “He who is has sent me” (ibid.). The Lord and Savior himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

[Col. 0040C]

Therefore God is, in substance, by his own essence; his knowledge is eternal life, and he is as great as cannot be expressed.

[Note: [Col. 0040D] All editions and the Laet. manuscript read this way; but the Vigil. edition omitted “in his substance,” for which the Tell. manuscript substituted “in his own judgment.” The received reading should not be changed; it means the same as if one wrote “in the order of substance through his essence.”]

He is rightly esteemed when he is called inestimable—whether you wish it or not.

Therefore what a thing is, this is the substance of the thing whose existence is defended. Yet it has already been stated that neither the extent nor the quality of what God is can be conceived by the mind, estimated by the senses, or defined by the spirit. It is enough that what is believed to be is established as existing, so that from that very reality which God is comes the Son, so that he is the true Son, and the true Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father.

This is *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος), that is, “of one substance with the Father,” as the Lord himself says: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10); and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28); and: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9).

Not without reason: for the Son of God was born from God the Father, and therefore, by the unity of substance and the majesty of divinity, they are one, just as Jeremiah prophesied: “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen the Word of the Lord?” (Jer. 23:18, according to the Septuagint). And again: “If they had stood in my substance and had heard my words, I would have turned them away from their evil pursuits” (ibid., 22). And in Solomon: “My substance is sweetness” (Wis. 16:21).

### CHAPTER V  
### Since the unity of substance in the Father and the Son is confirmed not only by prophetic but also by evangelical authority, it cannot be said that *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον) is not found in the sacred writings. What is the meaning of the term. Moreover, if the Arian wishes to establish some comparison in God by means of likeness, he cannot define a more exact comparison than when he says, “light from light.”

Since, then, you recognize this unity of substance in the Father and the Son not only by prophetic but also by evangelical authority, how can you say that *homoousion* is not found in the divine Scriptures, as though *homoousion* were something other than what is said by the words: “I came forth from God the Father” (John 16:28), and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), or something other than what the prophets openly indicated concerning the substance of God?

The meaning of the term is this: you are to believe in the unity of substance in the Father and the Son, although you cannot define the reality itself, which is ineffable. Thus, whether you say “light from light,” “word from word,” “spirit from spirit,” or “Lord from Lord,” whatever you say of him, you must nevertheless believe that the Father and the Son are of one essence, and understand the Son to be from that very reality which the Father is.

For if you make some comparison in him with things that are seen, then, through the very dissimilarity of the things, you will not explain the matter but will introduce contentious disputation. Thus it is written by the voice of the one who said: “To whom will you compare me?” (Isa. 46:5).

[Note: [Col. 0041D] The Vigil. edition alone adds: “And because it is written by the voice of God …”]

Therefore, since nothing can be likened to God, it is enough to believe him as he himself is understood and as he himself willed to be believed, rather than to define him.

Finally, if, concerning this very matter that you confess with me, you wish to introduce some comparison in God, I do not know whether you could define what you compare more precisely. For example, when you say “light from light,” if you were compelled to explain it through a painstaking account, I ask how you believe light to be from light. Is it like a lamp from a lamp, or like a sun from a sun, so that under this example you introduce either two lamps or two suns, as though there were two gods? Or do you designate the brightness of the same lamp from that lamp, or the radiance of the sun shining from the same sun, as “light from light,” so that you liken the Son to the matrix and form of the Father’s light, while presenting him as the splendor of glory?

The prophet said of him: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 36:10); Solomon said: “She is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. 7:26); and the Apostle declared that our Savior is “the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15), because the image of the sun is its own light, which proceeds from the same sun.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] The word “sun” is absent from the edition; we have restored it from the Tell. manuscript, since it is necessary for the completeness of the sense.]

But how much can be said in response to these matters that generate disputes, which the Apostle forbids us to pursue (II Tim. II, 24), would take too long to explain—especially since it is established that that light which is God cannot be evaluated, grasped, or defined, and that nothing in this world can truly be compared with divine majesty. For nothing among all the things that are seen or spoken of can be evaluated by a likeness proportionate to what God is, since he surpasses the very faculties of understanding and perception.

Therefore he warned you to believe that divinity is a substance and to recognize the true Son from the true Father; but you ought not to inquire into the quality of the thing, since you cannot know what its nature or magnitude is. This is what the prophets and the apostles proclaimed.

## CHAPTER VI. What God is; whether anything can be compared with him; a certain Reason, called Λόγος (*Logos*) among the Greeks, which distinguishes the persons or names between the Father and the Son; that Reason is called by many names; why each of these names is applied to the Son.

[Col. 0042B]

Finally, according to our capacity, strength, and faith, let us contemplate what God is and see whether anything can be compared with him. Certainly this is the one of whom, even when he is spoken of, nothing adequate can be said; when he is evaluated, he cannot be evaluated; when he is compared, he cannot be compared; when he is defined, he grows beyond the definition itself. With his hand he opens heaven; in his fist he encloses the whole circuit of the world. All things do not know him in his entirety, yet they know him with fear. This world serves his name and power, and even the momentary succession and change of the elements bears witness to him. See, then, whether there can be anything to which the Father and the Son can be compared, because the Son is such as the Father is. For he would not say that he and the Father are one unless he knew himself to be such as the Father is.

There is a certain Reason, called Λόγος (*Logos*) among the Greeks, which distinguishes the persons or names between the Father and the Son, since the Son himself is also called Reason. This Reason, however, is called by many names: at one time Word, at another Power, at another Wisdom, at another Right Hand, at another Arm, at another Pearl, at another Treasure, at another Nets, at another Plow, at another Fountain, at another Rock, at another Cornerstone, at another Lamb, at another Man, at another Calf, at another Eagle, at another Lion, at another Way. Thus, although he is God, all things in all things, these names make known the mysteries of the divine dispensations; they do not properly define or display the majesty of the Son of God.

For what is the Son in relation to what the Father is? Another, yet the same.

[Note: At [Col. 0042D], the Ambrosian edition reads, “For this Word also”; Vigilantius and the Tellus manuscript read more aptly, “For this reason,” that is, on account of this matter, etc.]

For this reason he is called the Word, because he proceeded from the Father’s own divine mouth, and the Father neither commanded nor did anything without him. He is called Power because he truly comes from God and is always with God, and all the Father’s power consists in him. He is called Wisdom because, coming from the Father’s heart, he opened the heavenly secrets to believers. He is called the Right Hand because through him all divine works have been perfected. He is called the Arm because all things are held together by him. He is called the Pearl so that nothing may be regarded as more precious than it. He is called the Treasure so that all the resources and riches of the heavenly kingdoms may be recognized as stored up in him. He is called Nets because through him and in him the diverse multitude of the nations is gathered from the sea of the world into the Church, like fish through the water of baptism, where the distinction between the good and the wicked is recognized. He is called the Plow because hard hearts are brought under the sign of his cross, so that they may be prepared for the necessary seed.

[Note: The Ambrosian edition reads “so that the more necessary things may be in it”; the Tellus manuscript reads “so that the necessary things may be in it”; Vigilantius’ reading is best, as in the text.]

He is called the Fountain of living water because thirsty hearts are watered from him by the grace of heavenly water. He is called the Rock because he gives strength to believers and hardness to unbelievers. He is called the Cornerstone because, as the one Mediator, he joined together within himself both walls—the New and the Old Testament. He is called the Lamb so that Christ’s innocence and passion may be shown. He is called Man because for us human beings he deigned to be born according to the flesh.

[Col. 0043B]

He is called the Calf because he endured suffering for our salvation. He is called the Eagle because, after the venerable resurrection, he flies as king of the birds to the Father’s seat.

[Note: This is the reading of the Tellus manuscript and Vigilantius’ edition. Ambrose instead reads, “as king, he flies high to the Father,” and so forth.]

He is called the Lion because he is the King of kings, who crushed death and the devil by the power of his might. He is the Way because through him there is ascent. He is the Truth because he knows no falsehood. He is the Life because he gives life to all things.

You see, therefore, that through these names the meanings of the divine dispensations and works have been foreshadowed; yet God himself has not thereby been properly defined. The Father, then, is God immeasurable, eternal, incomprehensible, beyond evaluation. His Son also is God and our Lord, as great as the Father—but from no other source than the Father, for he says, “I came forth from the Father,” that is, light from light.

## CHAPTER VII. The removal of the occasion of error that a heretical person might derive from the establishment of two names or two persons—that is, of the Father and the Son—as though two gods were being proclaimed.

But lest a heretic derive any occasion for error from my establishing two names or two persons, namely, the Father and the Son, as though I were proclaiming two gods, as they invent two gods on the basis of difference, we name the Father and the Son in such a way that we affirm one God in these persons and names. Let philosophers look to it; let their heretical disciples look to it—those who vary according to differences of powers. For us, however, there is one God, the Father, as the Apostle said (I Cor. VIII, 6), from whom all things come, and we from him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, through whom all things come, and we through him.

For what else is meant by “two” than a substance divided into parts, with a nature separated by the very names, and with both the will to act and command and the commands themselves divided?

[Note: The Ambrosian edition, together with the Tellus manuscript and Laetus, reads “and separated from him in every respect.” Vigilantius’ more coherent reading is that given in the text.]

Moreover, although the Father and the Son are believed to be two persons, they are nevertheless one in reason and substance. For the association of unequal things is an offense against the superior, and another who is not the true God is compared to the dishonor of him who is the true God. But when I establish the Father and the Son, I assign unity of kind; and although I divide that unity among the persons, the distinctions of the persons are again marked by the same names as one, through the natural covenant of the law.

Thus the Son is as great as the Father will be seen to be: wholly from the Whole, complete from the Complete, perfect from perfect and consummate power, as the Apostle says: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Coloss. II, 9). [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “For Baruch also.” It should be observed that Ambrose too more than once cites this passage under Jeremiah’s name.]

Jeremiah too, the most widely accepted of the prophets, knowing this unity of divinity in the Father and the Son, says:

“This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him. He discovered the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36–38).

Isaiah likewise proclaims the same thing, saying:

“Thus says the Lord God: Egypt is weary, and the commerce of the Ethiopians; and the Sabaeans, men of stature, shall pass over to you. They shall be your servants, and they shall walk behind you, bound in fetters; and they shall entreat you, because God is in you, and there is no other God besides you. For you are God” (Isa. XIV, 14).

Do not suppose that I have said this with the same arrogance attributed to Sabellius, who professes that the Father himself is the Son himself. We do not force everything into a single meaning in such a way as to be caught by the deception of other heretics. Rather, because authority is recognized without distinction in the very name of the persons, and because the Son is named from the Father not by kind but personally, we consequently ascribe to the Father everything that the Son is, and to the Son everything that the Father is. Nothing will be regarded as belonging to the Father that is judged not to belong to the Son, nor to the Son what is defended as belonging to the Father, because the unity of majesty does not permit them to be called gods in the plural. For it is established that the Father and the Son are of one substance; hence each is called one God.

Above all, we fear that, unless the Father and the Son are one, the fabricated birth of the author may fall into disrepute.

[Note: The old edition reads “because where the Father”; Vigilantius reads “lest, if the Father”; the manuscripts read “because unless the Father.” In the following clause the old edition and the manuscripts have “envy may return,” but Vigilantius’ “may return into reproach” is much better.]

For this was pleasing to the heretics: that the almighty, invisible, immeasurable God should degenerate in the Son, with not merely his power but his condition changed, as though the Father could not have from himself one who was such as he himself is. We therefore defend the true Son from the true Father, who always was and is of one substance with the Father. This is what the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), that is, “another, the very same with the one”: 

[Note: The old edition reads “so that the person might be heard by name.” Vigilantius and the manuscripts read “so that the person might be heard in the names” (the manuscripts: “by name”). As for the author’s explanation of the term ὁμοούσιον as “one and the same with the one,” Ambrose gives a somewhat fuller treatment in *On the Faith*, book III, chapter 15, §126; we have noted that passage as apparently derived from Basil.]

so that the persons might be distinguished by name when heard, and not so that the names might separate the substance.

## CHAPTER VIII. The mystery of the Arian heresy is exposed. Why they refuse to believe that the Son is from the substance of the Father. The Arian arguments are answered. There is a great difference between the things that were made and the one who made all things. How God displayed himself to the patriarchs in many and varied forms, although he could not be seen according to his divinity. Conclusion of the discussion.

[Col. 0045A]

But in order to expose the entire mystery of the Arian heresy, I shall briefly explain why they refuse to believe that the Son is from the Father’s substance. They say: Since God the Father is almighty, invisible, unchangeable, immutable, perfect, always the same, and eternal, whereas the Son is visible, because he was often seen by the patriarchs, and changeable and mutable, because he displayed himself in various forms—if he were from the Father’s substance, they say, it could never have happened that he was seen as either visible or mutable before the assumption of flesh. Rather, he would have remained in the equality in which the Father exists, since he was from the Father’s substance. For what is from the Father, they believe, must be regarded as incapable of being seen, changed, or transformed.

They add to their argument that when he entered into Mary and filled the Virgin’s womb, something other than that which had come into her was certainly born from her. Hence, they say, the substance at once changed its state, lost its order, and, through immediate change, was fashioned from God into a human being, from spirit into flesh.

[Note: The Ambrosian edition and the Laetus manuscript immediately reverse the order: “it immediately changes its state and at once loses its immutability, by forming itself.” The Tellus manuscript reads “the change itself in forming”; in a second hand, “the change in forming itself.” Vigilantius’ edition, as in the text, is more appropriate.]

Every transformation, moreover, is the destruction of what previously existed. Therefore, they say: If the Son were from the Father’s substance, then the Father would now appear inferior to his own substance, either through its transmission or through its end. For this reason they preferred to believe that the Son was from another substance, so that he could be changed, transformed, and seen, since this could not be believed of the Father’s substance.

This is the cause of their error, this the origin of the Arian heresy: they do not understand the power of God and do not recognize the ordering of so great a mystery, comparing God with human conditions.

[Note: The Tellus manuscript and Vigilantius’ edition have “to whom the Son must first be answered in this place,” as in the context.]

They must first be answered by saying that the Son of God was not seen as he was as God, but as human beings were capable of receiving something from God. Secondly, in the various forms he did not himself become mutable or changeable; rather, this belongs to God’s power: when he deigns to reveal himself to individuals as he wills, he changes his appearance, not his substance. He does not lose the proper character of his nature, but adapts the manifestation of his majesty according to the capacity of the one who sees him. He himself nevertheless remains always the same in the character of his substance, as it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 28).

For although there are many things visible in this world that are transformed from one thing into another, so that they cease to be what they were and become what previously they were not—for example, when mud is shaped into a human being, it ceases to be mud; or when fish or birds emerge from water, they are no longer water, because they are something else; or when potter’s clay hardens into a vessel; or when a stone, after being fired, is dissolved into lime; or when sand is changed into glass, along with the other examples too numerous to list—there is a great difference, foolish heretic, between things that were made and the one who made everything as he willed.

Things that were made serve the condition assigned to them; but the one who made them belongs to his own will and proper jurisdiction. He cannot be changed into something other than what he is by any compulsion; rather, he shows himself as he wills and to whom he wills. For if angels have often been seen in the form of human beings, yet are nothing other than what they know themselves to be, and do not change their substance when they assume the form of a human body, how much more is this true of our Lord himself, who made all things and who by his own institution granted even to the angels the ability to do this?

Further, we approve the Son of God as having been seen by the patriarchs, as has already been said, not in such a way that everything which God is was visible in him, but so that, through an image, they might see in him the arrangements of future events that were to be fulfilled in their respective times. For who could have seen the Son of God before he assumed visible matter as he willed, or before he deigned to put on humanity itself?

Although he was seen by Abraham (Gen. XVIII, 1), he was seen in the form of a human body, so that it might be shown that in the last times he would come as a human being.

[Col. 0046C]

Jacob likewise is seen in one passage as an angel and elsewhere equally as a human being (Gen. XXVIII, 13). He therefore showed himself as an angel in order to indicate that he was the messenger of the great counsel; but as a human being, when he is also described as having wrestled with him, so that he might especially indicate the image of the future wrestling that he would have with Israel when he came as a human being. But so that Israel might believe him to be the Lord with whom he wrestled in such a great struggle under the appearance of a human being, he received the name Israel (Gen. XXXII, 24), that is, “a man seeing God.” “I saw God,” he says, “face to face, and my soul was preserved” (ibid., 30). Certainly he had seen the form of a human being that the Son of God had assumed.

He appeared to Moses in the bush in a flame of fire (Exod. III, 2), in order to show light to believers and judgment to unbelievers, because Christ is salvation to believers and punishment to unbelievers, as the Apostle says: “To some an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 16).

He went before the people of Israel by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire, as a guide on their journey (Exod. XIII, 21), in order to show the grace of baptism through the cloud and the gift of the Holy Spirit through fire. For the Apostle Paul writes that the patriarchs were baptized in the cloud (I Cor. X, 2), and the Acts of the Apostles declare that the Spirit is like fire (Acts I, 3).

You see, therefore, heretic, that throughout the divine Scriptures the figures of things were foreshown to the patriarchs in honor of God, but not God himself as he is, properly revealed. Finally, when Moses prayed that he might see God’s face clearly, what did God immediately say to him? “You cannot see my face,” he said, “for no human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20). By the very denial of the sight, the splendor is indicated—namely, a splendor as great as it must be believed to be, and which is declared invisible.

Although Moses had set out, indicated, and described the structure of heaven, the orders of the world, the changes of the elements, and finally the ornaments of the whole world—and although the Lord himself bore witness to him, saying, “There shall be no prophet like Moses my servant, to whom I spoke face to face, mouth to mouth” (Num. XII, 7–8)—he nevertheless could not see God clearly. He was rightly worthy of every prophetic gift, but not to such a degree that, being merely human, he could gaze upon God.

We defend all these words as the words of the Son, whom we know to have spoken with Moses on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXXI, 18), having come from the Father to conduct and explain these events, since from the beginning all things were to be ordered, explained, and preserved through him, so that this might establish the principal reason for the Son’s existence. Yet he is understood to have been seen in such a way that some visible matter, as I have said, had been assumed and arranged for the purpose, while his invisibility remained intact, that invisibility which the majesty diffused around him had withdrawn from the sight of all.

[Col. 0047C]

For he was not revealed to human eyes in such a way that the whole divinity appeared in him; rather, serving as a kind of mirror, when he enclosed faces conceived within his own light as though in the complete likeness of a human being,

[Note: The old edition and the Tellus manuscript read: “thus his majesty . . . might be seen within that [vision].” More concisely, Vigilantius’ edition with the Laetus manuscripts reads: “thus, of his majesty . . . . . it is seen within that [vision],” that is, the vision is granted under these conditions.]

the radiance of his majesty going before it, he appeared within that vision which displayed the image of the truth, not God himself in his proper nature.

Thus, when he deigned to put on humanity, he did not inflict any stain upon eternity by changing spirit into flesh; rather, having assumed humanity, he bestowed upon it the immortality and eternity of heavenly life. For although the Apostle says that he “emptied himself” (Philipp. II, 7) by taking the form of a servant, we do not understand him to have been emptied in such a way that the same Spirit became something other than what he had been.

[Note: Gill’s and the Roman editions read “that the same Christ should become”; other editions and manuscripts read “that the same Spirit should become.” The latter is entirely suitable, since above we read “so that he might change spirit into flesh.”]

Rather, setting aside temporarily the honor of his majesty, he put on a human body; and by assuming it he became the salvation of the nations. For when the sun is covered by a cloud, its brightness is restrained, not extinguished; and that light which, spread throughout the whole world in brilliant radiance, suffuses everything is enclosed by the very small obstruction of a cloud, not taken away. So too the man whom the Lord Jesus, our Savior—that is, God and the Son of God—put on did not obstruct God within him, but concealed him.

[Col. 0048A]

Finally, when on the mountain he raised himself somewhat beyond the human being himself (Matt. XVII, 6), the apostles, almost blinded by the brilliance of his light, fell to the ground as human beings, having endangered their lives, unless the Lord in his mercy had come to their aid by again restraining the honor of his majesty, in accordance with the saying: “No one has seen God and lived” (Exod. XXXIII, 20).

Thus, just as the sun’s brilliance remains unharmed when it does not shine all the way into our sight—for what is not seen results from the weakness of us whose eyes are covered by the darkness of clouds—

[Note: Ambrose’s edition and the manuscripts read “when it does not shine all the way to our eyes.” Vigilantius’ edition adds the negation, which the sense there necessarily requires.]

so that divine majesty, which, as I have said, had put on a body, proves that it was concealed not through any diminution of its own radiance, but through the benefit of the flesh, for whose sake the Son of God endured being the Son of Man.

Indeed, the Virgin conceived from the Spirit of God, and what she conceived she bore: namely, God joined to his human being, as I have already said. He himself said: “What is born from the flesh is flesh, and what is born from the spirit is spirit” (John III, 6), because God is spirit, and he was born from God. So too the angel said to the Virgin Mary: “The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

You see, therefore, that the Spirit himself—that is, the Son of God—came to the virgin, and that from her the Son of God and Man proceeded. Yet the Son of God was not changed by that garment of flesh; rather, he remained the same in humanity as he had been before the world, with the Father—through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made—as the Evangelist says: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I, 10).

Otherwise, it would be madness to believe that we could be liberated by the one who, in order to liberate, was lost; who, in order to be born, was overcome; who, in order to receive immortality, passed over into death. But far be it, heretic, that the meaning of your wickedness should be admitted by Catholics. For we believe the Word and Spirit—that is, the Son of God—to be immutable and unchangeable. When he put on humanity, he did not change his state, lose his order, or alter his substance; rather, he illumined the defilements of that same body with the eternal light of his splendor, so that through the passage of his body the light of the Holy Spirit and the grace of eternal life might overflow to us.

Although we believe him to have suffered and been buried, it was that man who suffered—the man whom the Son of God assumed, put on, and carried. But because everything that that man suffered was referred to its author, the Lord’s death and passion are proclaimed. For it is established that what belongs to God is immortal, while what belongs to the human being is subject to decay.

On the third day he also rose again—not God into a human being, but rather the human being into God.

He ascended into heaven, offered that most pleasing human being to his Father as a gift, and sat at the Father’s right hand, according to what is written: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1).

He sent us the Holy Spirit from what is his own and from that one substance of his, as our protector, sanctifier, and guide into eternal life, as it is written in the word of God: “I will pour out from my Spirit upon my servants and my maidservants” (Joel II, 29). And again: “The Spirit will go forth from me” (Isa. LVII, 6). Our Lord and Savior himself says: “He will receive from what is mine” (John XVI, 15)—namely, from what belongs to the Son, because the Son is from what the Father is.

Afterward, at the appointed time, he will come to judge the living and the dead, in order to give rewards to believers and punishments to unbelievers.

His kingdom is eternal and immortal; it has neither beginning nor end. To him be honor and glory for ever and ever.

You who read this, I beg you by God: do not twist the simplicity of its meaning into ambiguity or draw from it anything other than what has been said. For we confess the Father to be truly the Father, the Son of God to be truly the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit to be truly the Holy Spirit, confessing three persons of one substance and one divinity. We condemn the sect of Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius, as well as any others that oppose the rule of truth. We embrace and preserve with every effort of our soul, in the fullness of faith, the decree of the Council of Nicaea, for we know that this decree has been set against all heresies with unconquerable truth.

[Col. 0049A]

## III. BOOKLET OF FAITH. (C, S)*

[Col. 0049B]

We believe in one God, the almighty Father; and in one only-begotten Son of his, God and Lord, our Savior; and in the Holy Spirit, God. We confess not three gods—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one God.

[Note: “One.” The Vatican and Vallicellian manuscripts read “in one.” Shortly afterward, they read “in one only-begotten Son of him, Jesus Christ, God.”]

Not “one God” in the sense of a solitary being, nor the same person who is himself Father to himself and himself Son.

[Note: “He himself to himself.” The Lucensian manuscripts read “that he himself is Father and himself is Son.”]

Rather, we confess the true Father, who begot the true Son, as God from God,

[Note: As in D. Crabbe: “that is, God from God.”]

light from light, life from life, perfect from perfect, whole from whole, full from full—not created but begotten, not from nothing but from the Father, of one substance with the Father.

[Note: “Of one substance.” Quesnel reads “and of one substance.” Our manuscripts and Crabbe omit the conjunction.]

We confess the Holy Spirit, God, not unbegotten and not begotten, not created and not made, but coeternal with the Father and the Son, always in the Father and the Son.

[Note: “Coeternal.” Crabbe, together with most of our manuscripts, has different punctuation: “we venerate the coeternal one, yet one God.”]

Nevertheless, we venerate one God, because from the one Father the Son, God, was born as the whole of what belongs to the Father; and in the Father he begot the Son as the whole of what exists in him.

[Note: “Because.” Crabbe reads “who.” Shortly afterward the Lucensian, Vallicellian, and both Vatican manuscripts read “God was born, the Son.”]

The Father, in generating the Son, neither diminished nor lost the divinity of his fullness. We hold with complete certainty that everything which the Father God is, the Son born from him also is.

[Note: “What God the Father is.” Thus the Vindobonensian and Thuanean manuscripts agree, as do all the others in the remaining collections. Quesnel reads: “what the Father God is, the Son also is, and we most certainly hold that he is the same.”]

Together with the Holy Spirit we devoutly confess one God, Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of God, through whom all things were made, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible. For our salvation he descended from heaven; yet he never ceased to be in heaven. He was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

The Word became flesh and did not lose what he had been, but began to be what he had not been.

[Note: “Not changed.” All our manuscripts and the Thuanean manuscript read thus. Quesnel has “not changed, but remaining.”]

We believe that he was born as a human being without being changed, while remaining what he was—not apparently but truly; not airy but corporeal; not phantom-like but fleshly; possessing bones, blood, perception, and a soul.

[Note: “Thus truly.” The Lucensian manuscript has the better reading: “Thus we understand a true human being and a true God, so that we do not in any way hesitate to confess that he was truly God and truly human.”]

We understand him to be truly God and truly human; and we in no way hesitate to confess that he was truly human and truly God.

We must confess that this same Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified according to the Scriptures,

[Note: Quesnel reads “was crucified and died.”]

died and was buried according to the Scriptures, rose from the dead on the third day, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there we await his coming to judge the living and the dead.

We have been cleansed in his death and blood and have obtained forgiveness of sins.

[Note: Quesnel inserts “we confess forgiveness.”]

We await resurrection from him in these bodies and in the same flesh in which we now exist, just as he rose in the same flesh in which he was born, suffered, and died. And we shall receive from him, together with this flesh,

[Note: “Or our bodies.” Quesnel deleted these words, although he admits that they occur in two Thuanean manuscripts, as they are read in all five of our manuscripts from different collections. Only the Lucensian manuscript adds, after “or our bodies,” “we have received.” The Vallicellian and Vatican manuscripts more appropriately read “we shall receive,” deleting the final word *recepturos* (“shall receive”); Quesnel instead has *recepturas* (“shall receive,” feminine).]

either eternal life as the reward of good merit or the sentence of eternal punishment for sins.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 401

## SAINT ANASTASIUS I, POPE

[Col. 0051]

# PROLEGOMENA

## LIFE OF SAINT ANASTASIUS I, POPE

[Col. 0051A]

### I

*(From the* Liber Pontificalis*.)*

Anastasius, a Roman by nation, the son of Maximus, occupied the see for three years and ten days. He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were read, the priests should not sit but stand bowed. He issued a decree concerning the Church. He built the basilica called Crescentiana, in the second region, on the Mamertine Way in the city of Rome. He also decreed that no man from overseas should be admitted to clerical rank unless he produced written attestations from five bishops,

[Col. 0052A]

because at that same time Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: eight priests, five deacons, and ten bishops for various places. He was also buried in his own cemetery at the Bear with the Cap, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate then remained vacant for twenty-one days.

### II

*(From Coustant, on the Roman Pontiffs’ Letters.)*

Jerome, in Letter 16, to Principia, where he had mentioned letters sent by Siricius to the supporters of Origen, adds: “Not much time intervened. The distinguished man Anastasius succeeded to the pontificate.” By these words he indicates that those letters did not greatly benefit the persons to whom they had been sent, because Anastasius succeeded Siricius shortly afterward and took care to suppress the evil that the recently translated Latin version of Origen’s *On First Principles* had brought upon Rome.

Antonius Pagius supposes that this distinguished man was ordained on December 5 of the year 398, a Sunday. Baronius and other learned men, relying both on the chronicles of Prosper and Marcellinus Comes, in which Innocent is said to have succeeded him in the year 402, and on several ancient martyrologies, in which Anastasius’ feast day is assigned to April 27, defer his death to April 27 of the year 402.

But this is contradicted not only by Socrates,

[Col. 0053B]

who writes in book VII, chapter 9, that he occupied the Roman see for three years, but also by the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs. None of these extends his pontificate beyond three years and twenty-one or twenty-two days; most contain only three years and ten days.

Here I should incidentally point out that the learned scholar’s annotation is not accurate when he observes that a Corbie manuscript, written in the middle of the sixth century, presents the reading “Anastasius, two years … twenty-five days,” and supposes that something has been erased there. What is actually read is: “Anastasius held the see three years and twenty-one days”; nothing at all has been obliterated.

Furthermore, amid this variety in the catalogues, Pagius, adhering to those in which Anastasius is recorded as having held the see for three years and ten days, believes that he departed to heaven on December 4 of the year 401, the day on which his feast is commemorated in Jerome’s *Martyrology*.

“Rome did not deserve,” Jerome says (Letter 16, to Principia), “to keep this man long, lest the head of the world be cut off under such a bishop.” Rather, he was snatched away and transferred so that he might not attempt by his prayers to bend a sentence once pronounced.

### III

*(From Galland, Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum, vol. VIII.)*

#### 1

When Saint Siricius, Roman pontiff, was called to heaven at the end of the year 398, Saint Anastasius assumed the pontificate a few days later, that is, at the beginning of December. Saint Jerome is an authoritative witness to the short interval between pontificates:

[Note: Jerome, Letter 127, §10, works, vol. I, p. 95, new edition of Verona.]

“Not much time intervened,” he says; “the distinguished man Anastasius succeeded to the pontificate.” Elsewhere the same great Doctor calls him

[Note: The same author, Letter 130, works, vol. I, p. 986.]

“a man of the richest poverty and apostolic solicitude.”

Indeed, as we learn from his successor Innocent,

[Note: Innocent I, Letter 1.]

his merits were so great and of such a kind that they already surpassed the fellowship of human life … on account of the purity of his life and the abundance of his teaching, by which he governed the people of God with the full rigor—or perhaps vigor—of ecclesiastical authority.

This most watchful shepherd devoted all his energy chiefly to ensuring

[Note: Anastasius, Letter 1, §5, below.]

that nothing should stain the Church of Christ God and that no profane novelty should dare corrupt the intact faith of the flock entrusted to his care. His distinguished deeds must be gathered from the records of the Church.

Yet this blessed pontiff, Jerome says,

[Note: Jerome, Letter 127, cited above.]

Rome did not deserve to keep him long, lest the head of the world be cut off under such a bishop. Rather, he was snatched away and transferred so that he might not attempt by his prayers to bend a sentence once pronounced.

After completing three years and approximately five months in the pontificate, the supreme bishop died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May in the year 402. This is the opinion of Baronius,

[Note: Baronius, under the year 402, §42.]

against Papebrochius, Pagius, Coustant, and others, and defended by the learned men Tillemont,

[Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XII, p. 650, note 69, on Saint Jerome.]

Fontanini,

[Note: Fontanini, *Literary History of Aquileia*, book V, chapter 6, §6, p. 279 ff.]

Bernard de Rubeis,

[Note: Bernard de Rubeis, dissertation on Rufinus, chapter 17, p. 118.]

the Ballerini brothers,

[Note: The Ballerini, notes on the works of Noris, vol. IV, *Observations*, chapter 3, §3, p. 845.]

and Vallarsi.

[Note: Vallarsi, at the beginning of volume XI of Jerome’s works, in his life of Jerome, chapter 32, §6, p. 199.]

## 2.

Only two letters of so great a pontiff survive; one of them was published long ago, the other only recently. The former is addressed to John, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning Rufinus. In this letter Origen is said to have been condemned; but whether Rufinus too was condemned along with Origen is disputed by men of outstanding learning. Baronius [Note: Baron. ad ann. 401, § 4.], Norisius [Note: Noris. *Hist. Pelag.* lib. I, c. 2, *opp.* tom. I, p. 25.], Pagius [Note: Pagi ad ann. 401, §§ 9, 15, 16.] and Tillemontius [Note: Tillem. *Mém. eccl.* tom. XII, art. 100, p. 242.] affirm this; Huetius also seems formerly to have held the same view [Note: Huet. *Origen.* lib. II, c. 4, sect. 1, § 20, p. 206.]. But others are known, with better reason, to have championed the opposing side. Among them are Coustantius [Note: Coustant. *Epistt. Rom. Pont.* p. 723, § 7.], the Ballerini [Note: Baller. *l. c.* cap. 2, § 1, p. 827.], Bern. de Rubeis [Note: Bern. de Rub. *l. c.* cap. 17, p. 109 ff.] and, above all, Fontaninus [Note: Fontan. *l. c.* cap. 19, § 2, p. 240 ff.].

We know that this latter opinion is clearly confirmed when the text of Anastasius’s letter itself is properly considered. In that letter the holy pontiff plainly distinguishes Rufinus’s case from Origen’s. Concerning Origen he says [Note: Anast. epist. 1, § 3, below.]:

> “I have therefore conceived this in my mind: that the faith established by the tradition of the apostles and of our forefathers . . . he wished to dissolve.”

But concerning Rufinus he says [Note: The same, ibid. § 4.]:

> “I approve it if he accuses the author and exposes his detestable deed to the peoples, so that he may at last be held by just hatred—the man whom reputation had long since bound. But if the interpreter lends his consent to such great evils . . . he has constructed by his labor nothing else than this: that, as though by the judgment of his own mind, he might overthrow, under the title of an unexpected assertion, those things which alone, which first, and which among catholic Christians are held by the true faith . . .”

A little earlier he further declares [Note: The same, ibid. § 2.] “that Rufinus has the divine majesty as the judge of his conscience.” These and other statements in the same sense, which may be seen discussed at greater length by the authors cited above, most clearly prove that Rufinus was not condemned by Anastasius. Moreover, what we have noted from Vallarsius to elucidate § 5 of this letter had already been perceived by our own Hieronymus de Prato, whom it will therefore be useful to consult [Note: H. de Prato, *Dissert.* 6, ad tom. I *opp. Sulp. Sev.*, no. 36, p. 311.].

## 3.

The second letter of Anastasius, addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, was published not long ago among the writings of Jerome, together with other splendid and ancient literary documents, from a manuscript of the most ancient Ambrosian Library by the learned Vallarsius [Note: Hieron. *opp.* tom. I, epist. 95, p. 552.]. In it the holy pontiff praises the zeal and vigilance of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and declares that he himself had proscribed the errors of Origen together with their author.

This letter seems to have been written at the beginning of the year 400. During that year Simplicianus died, and Venerius succeeded him. On this matter, after the distinguished editor [Note: Vallars. edit. Hieron. tom. I, p. 552; and ibid., in the review of the letters, nos. 93, 94, 95; likewise in *Vit. Hieron.* tom. XI, p. 176.], several valuable observations may be read in Ballerini [Note: Baller. *l. c.* cap. 3, § 1, p. 842.] and especially in the aforementioned Hieronymus de Prato [Note: H. de Prato *l. c.* nos. 18, 21, p. 295 ff.]. The latter, presenting the Anastasian letter itself to the eyes of readers, also attempted to exhibit it in several places in a more correct form on the basis of conjecture. It will therefore be worthwhile to set it forth here as the learned man gives it, freed from corruption. It runs as follows:

## 4.

> **To his lord and brother Simplicianus, Anastasius.**
>
> “A shepherd is shown to exercise great solicitude and watchfulness over his flock; likewise, from a lofty tower, a careful watchman observes the condition of the city by day and night. A prudent master of a ship, in a time of storm and danger, suffers great agitation of mind, lest the ship be dashed upon the rocks by squalls and the harshest waves.
>
> With equal spirit the holy and honorable man Theophilus, our brother and fellow bishop, does not cease to watch over the interests of salvation, lest the people of God, by reading Origen in the various churches, fall into great blasphemies.
>
> Having received the letter of which you have been informed, I appeal to your holiness, so that, just as we, established in the city of Rome—which the glorious Peter, chief of the apostles, founded and confirmed by his faith—have condemned the reading, contrary to the command, of the things we have mentioned, and have earnestly requested that no departure whatever be made from the ordinances of the Gospels which the judgment of God and Christ taught from his mouth [Note: Some words seem to be missing here.], so also that what the venerable apostle Paul foretold and admonished may be recalled:
>
> ‘If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what was preached to you, let him be accursed.’”
>
> The rest is as in the published copy.

[Note: *Magister*; the manuscript has thus far *navis*. Perhaps: “the master of a ship.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads: *hora tempestatis ecoris et periculo*. Perhaps: *hora tempestatis, aequoris et periculo*—“in a time of storm, sea, and danger.”]

[Note: *Ut sicuti*. Perhaps: *ut scias uti*—“so that you may know how.”]

## 5.

After these two letters of Anastasius we have placed the *Apology* which Rufinus of Aquileia sent to the same pontiff on his own behalf. Following Coustantius, whose copy we have therefore reproduced here in the customary manner, we have nevertheless compared it with the edition of Rufinus’s works carefully prepared by Vallarsius. He based the same *Apology* on the Guarnerian manuscript and successfully restored several passages [Note: Vallars. praef. ad *opp. Rufin.* p. 16.], as is shown by the notes appended below.

Rufinus directed this *Apology* concerning his faith to the holy pontiff in order to safeguard his reputation and at the same time to repel the hostility which had been stirred up against him at the apostolic see on account of his translation of Origen’s *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*). We learn from Rufinus himself as well as from Jerome when the work was written.

When Rufinus was summoned to Rome so that he might clear away suspicions concerning his faith there in person, he offered the following excuse [Note: Rufin. *Apolog.* § 1, below, p. 249d.]:

> “Since,” he says, “I myself have been restored to my parents after nearly THIRTY YEARS, it would have been harsh and quite inhuman to abandon so quickly those whom I had visited again only after so long a time; and also because the hardship of so long a journey has made me less capable of undertaking further labors.”

Jerome, criticizing the grounds of this excuse, says the following [Note: Hieron. lib. II *adv. Rufin.* § 2.]:

> “He pleads the weariness of a long journey, as though he had been running continuously for THIRTY YEARS, or, sitting at Aquileia for TWO YEARS, had been exhausted by the labor of the preceding journey.”

From these passages the learned Bern. de Rubeis argues [Note: Bern. de Rub. *Dissert. de Rufin.* cap. 16, § 1, p. 110.] that this *Apology* was sent by Rufinus in the year 400. Rufinus, he says, had departed from Aquileia for the East in 372 and returned there in 393. Since the round number of thirty years is diminished by the particle “nearly,” the two-year period during which Rufinus was staying at Aquileia was therefore running in the year 400, which had already begun. The distinguished Coustantius holds nearly the same opinion [Note: Coustant. *Epistt. Rom. Pontiff.* p. 713, § 4.].

This *Apology* of the presbyter of Aquileia seems, in a certain sense, to comprise seven chapters, of which the first five concern doctrines: the first concerning the Trinity, the second concerning the incarnation of the Word, the third concerning the resurrection, the fourth concerning the final judgment and the eternal condemnation of the devil, and the fifth concerning the origin of souls. In the remaining two chapters Rufinus professes himself an interpreter, not a defender, of Origen. Fontaninus explains all these matters individually [Note: Fontan. *Hist. litter. Aquil.* lib. V, cap. 4.]; a reader who consults him while he discusses these matters will not waste either effort or labor.

# IV

*(From Schoenemann, Bibliotheca, vol. I.)*

## 1. Writings

Only two letters survive, one of which—that to John of Jerusalem—was published long ago, while the other—to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan—has only recently seen the light. The former seems to have been written in 401, the latter in 400, during which year Simplicianus died and Venerius was appointed in his place.

Two letters to Paulinus have perished; one to Anysius, in which Anastasius is said to have recently entrusted to him everything being conducted in the regions of Illyricum; one to Venerius, to which he refers in the letter to John of Jerusalem; one to the Africans; and finally another concerning Rufinus, sent to the East by Rufinus’s advocate.

Baluzius has shown that three fragments of letters to Ursinus belong to Anastasius II [Note: In *Coll. nova concil.* t. I, p. 1457.]. Coustantius discusses other spurious writings and a falsely attributed decree of Anastasius on the basis of Blondellus.

## 2. Editions

Because Jerome frequently refers to the letter to John of Jerusalem, it was preserved in the older collections among Jerome’s own letters; in the Benedictine edition it occupies p. 260 of volume V, which contains works by other authors. From the published editions of Jerome, this letter first entered the Roman edition of the papal letters, then was included by Baronius under the year 402, § 26, and afterward passed into the collections of councils.

Later it was published from Vatican and Beauvais manuscripts by Jean Garnier among the works of Marius Mercator, Paris, 1673, part I, appendix 1. From the same manuscripts there was added the profession of faith of the pseudonymous Rufinus, consisting of twelve anathemas.

Whereas in the earlier editions, as also in those that followed, the letter had been divided into six sections or paragraphs, Garnier divided it into twelve parts. Suspecting the eighth to be mutilated and corrupt, he freely interpolated it with a formula condemning Origen and Rufinus. He did not do this, however, with the intention of deceiving readers; rather, so that the words inserted by him might more quickly catch the eye, he took care to print them in a different type [Note: Nevertheless, as Coustantius observed, there were people who were offended by this. Because they had not examined Garnier’s notes, they thought that the change of type was intended to distinguish more easily the sentence pronounced against Origen and Rufinus, and consequently accepted Garnier’s added words as genuine words of Anastasius. This happened to Antonio Pagius in his *Critica* under the year 401, no. 9.]. In his notes on p. 112 he acknowledged them as his own and attempted to establish their authenticity in three ways. In Coustantius’s judgment, none of these arguments necessarily proves what Garnier wished, and especially the last two rest upon words of Anastasius that are either corrupt or wrongly understood.

Rejecting this interpolation, Petrus Coustantius once again presented the complete letter, carefully collated with the variations of Garnier’s and the earlier editions, and illustrated with his own notes and a preliminary discussion, in 1721, in *Epistolae Pontificum Romanorum*, vol. I, pp. 719–730. On pp. 729–738 he added an account of lost and falsely attributed writings [Note: We append Coustantius’s account to this work of Schoenemann’s. (Editor.)]. Vallarsius later produced a more polished edition in his edition of the works of Rufinus, vol. I, p. 411.

Vallarsius finally published the letter to Simplicianus—unknown to Jerome and previously known to no one—from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, together with several other letters by other authors, among the Jerome letters in volume I of his works, letter 95. It appears entirely genuine. From this source Joannes Dominicus Mansi took it and inserted it into volume I of his collection of councils. Hieronymus de Prato proposed the same letter, emended conjecturally in several places, in his edition of the works of Sulpicius Severus, vol. [1] (Verona, 1741), dissertation 6, no. 36, p. 311.

Finally, Andreas Gallandius, having added Rufinus’s *Apology to Anastasius*, inserted both letters, elucidated by the labors of Garnier, Coustantius, and Vallarsius, in *Bibliotheca Patrum et veterum Ecclesiae Scriptorum*, vol. VIII, pp. 246–251; at the same time he prefixed a dissertation on Anastasius, chapter 9 of the *Prolegomena*, p. XXI ff.

# INFORMATION CONCERNING NONEXTANT LETTERS RELATING TO POPE ANASTASIUS

## I

*(From Coustantius, Epistolae Romanae Pontificum.)*

### 1. Letters of Anastasius to Paulinus and of Paulinus to Anastasius

Paulinus, still a presbyter and later bishop of Nola, indicates several letters relating to our Anastasius at once in letter 20, addressed to Delphinus, no. 2, in the following words:

> “Let your Reverence know that your holy brother, Pope Anastasius of the City, is exceedingly fond of our humility. For as soon as he began to have the opportunity to offer us his affection, he hastened not merely to accept it from us but to press it upon us with the most devout tenderness.
>
> Not long after his ordination he sent to the bishops of Campania letters full of piety and peace in our name, both to declare his affection and to provide others with an example of his kindness. Later, after some time had passed, he also deigned to invite us to his Nativity, as he is accustomed to show this honor only to his fellow priests. Nor was he offended by our excuse; rather, accepting the service of our message, which we had offered in place of our presence, he received us in his fatherly heart even though we were absent.”

In these words four or five letters are indicated: the first, a letter from Paulinus to Anastasius immediately after the latter’s ordination, which Anastasius received kindly; the second, a letter from Anastasius in which he hastened to offer and in turn signify his goodwill to Paulinus; the third, from the same pope to the bishops of Campania, sent on Paulinus’s behalf; the fourth, by which Anastasius invited Paulinus to his Nativity, that is, to the anniversary of his ordination—contrary to the custom by which only fellow priests, namely bishops, and not ordinary presbyters, were usually invited; and the last, from Paulinus to Anastasius, excusing him for not having come when invited to the celebration of Anastasius’s Nativity.

Of all these letters, the first three are said to have been written shortly after Anastasius’s ordination and therefore belong to the year 399. Two others should likewise be assigned to the end of that year, since they were written on the occasion of the anniversary solemnity at which Anastasius celebrated the return of the day of his ordination.

## II

### 2. He Entrusts His Deputation in Illyricum to Anysius
