Anastasius also wrote to Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica, entrusting to him the administration of everything being done in the regions of Illyricum. Innocentius bears witness to this. When he delegated the same office to Anysius in letter 1, he said that he was conferring upon him what “such great and such distinguished predecessors of mine, namely Damasus of holy memory, Siricius, and the aforementioned man [Anastasius], had conferred.”

These words of Innocentius deserve notice. From them it is established that once the office of vicar of the apostolic see in Illyricum had been conferred upon a bishop of Thessalonica, it had to be renewed whenever a new bishop of the Roman see was appointed. This letter of Anastasius seems to have been sent not long after the beginning of his pontificate.

## III

### 3. Letter of John of Jerusalem to Anastasius Concerning Rufinus

During the pontificate of Anastasius, Rufinus translated Origen’s *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) into Latin. Consequently, several people who were disturbed against the translator thought that he ought to be restrained by Anastasius’s authority.

At that time John, bishop of Jerusalem, whether compelled by various rumors spread about Rufinus or by Rufinus’s own requests, consulted the blessed pope about what he thought concerning this presbyter. In this letter John extolled Anastasius with the highest praises, as may be gathered from the second preceding letter, which Anastasius sent in reply to the same bishop.

## IV

### 4. Letter of Anastasius to Venerius of Milan

In replying to John of Jerusalem, Anastasius also notes that he was sending him a letter which he had written to Venerius, bishop of Milan. In it he explained with careful attention how harmful he considered Origen’s books, recently translated into Latin by Rufinus (Letter 2, no. 5). It may therefore be suspected that Venerius too had consulted Anastasius concerning these books.

Perhaps at about the same time Anastasius was consulted by both John and Venerius on the same matter and gave replies to both at once, taking care to append to the letter written to one whatever he had replied to the other.

## V

### 5. Letter of Theophilus of Alexandria to Anastasius

In letter 71, addressed to Theophilus, Jerome says that he believes by God’s providence it came about that, at the very time when he had sent letters against Origen to the West, Theophilus also wrote against the same man to Pope Anastasius and, without knowing Jerome’s own opinion, confirmed it.

Since Jerome did not yet know what effect this letter of Theophilus had had upon Anastasius, he referred to it in letter 78, addressed to Pammachius and Marcella, writing:

> “Pray therefore to the Lord that . . . the preaching of the see of Mark the Evangelist may also be confirmed by the preaching of the see of the apostle Peter.”

That is, he prayed that Anastasius might agree with Theophilus in condemning Origen.

He nevertheless adds:

> “Although it has been spread abroad in famous discourse that the blessed Pope Anastasius also, with the same fervor—for he has the same spirit—persecuted the heretics lurking in their hiding places, and that his letters show that what was condemned in the East was condemned in the West.”

By these words Jerome plainly indicates that Anastasius’s letters against Origen, whether to Venerius of Milan or to John of Jerusalem, had already been written, but that knowledge of them had not yet reached Jerome except through rumor. Hence it is clear that Theophilus’s letter was not later than the aforesaid letters to Venerius or John.

## VI

### 6. Letter and Delegation of the Africans to Anastasius

On June 18 of the year 401, the Africans assembled at Carthage and decided to choose one from among the bishops

> “who might make known both to the venerable holy brother Anastasius, bishop of the apostolic see, and to the holy brother Venerius, priest of the Church of Milan, the need and shortage of clergy under which the African churches were suffering, and might request permission for them to promote into the clergy those children who had been baptized among the heretics.”

They thought they ought to ask this of them

> “because,” they said, “it had been prohibited by these sees”—namely, by Siricius and Ambrose.

## VII

### 7. Letter of Anastasius to the Africans

Not long afterward the Africans received a letter from Anastasius in which he displayed his goodwill toward them and his paternal concern for their church. Therefore, on September 13 of the same year 401, assembling again at Carthage, they arranged for the letter to be read to them and for the manner in which they had received it to be entered in the synodal acts as follows:

> “After the letters of our most blessed brother and fellow priest Anastasius, bishop of the Roman Church, had been read—letters in which, with the solicitude and sincerity of paternal and fraternal charity, he exhorted us not in any way to overlook the plots and wickedness of the heretical and schismatic Donatists, by which they grievously harass the Catholic African Church—we give thanks to the Lord, because he has deigned to inspire that good and holy bishop of his with such pious concern for the members of Christ, though they are separated by the diversity of lands but joined in one structure of the body.”

While recalling this with expressions of gratitude, they remain silent as to whether Anastasius had granted what they had resolved to ask from him concerning the children baptized on the Donatist side. But it may be inferred from the letter now under discussion that what they requested was granted to them by the pious pope.

## VIII

### 8. Another Letter of the Africans to Anastasius

Unless the Africans had obtained what they had requested on behalf of the children mentioned above, there would seem to have been no occasion for new letters from them to the same pope and for the following other decree, which they enacted in the same council:

> “It was resolved that letters be sent to our brothers and fellow bishops, and especially to the apostolic see, over which our aforementioned venerable brother and colleague Anastasius presides, so that he may know that Africa has great need, for the peace and benefit of the Church, that even those Donatists who, having corrected their judgment, wish to pass over to Catholic unity may, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in that place, be received in their offices, if this seems beneficial to Christian peace—
>
> “as is clearly shown to have been done in the earlier period of the same division, as the examples of many, indeed almost all, African churches in which such an error arose testify.
>
> “This is not intended to dissolve the council held overseas on this matter; rather, that decree should remain in force concerning those who wish to pass over to the Catholic Church in such a way that no compensation for unity is secured through them.
>
> “But where Catholic unity seems likely, through them, either to be fully achieved or to be assisted by the manifest gain of brotherly souls in the places where they live, the fact that the overseas council decreed something against the honor of their offices should not harm them, although salvation has been denied to no one. That is: according to the overseas council, those ordained on the Donatist side, if they wish, after correcting their position, to pass over to the Catholic Church, are not to be received in their offices, except for those through whom provision is made for Catholic unity” [*Code of the Canons of the African Church*, c. 6].

For if Anastasius had been unwilling to relax anything of the strictness of the law concerning children, how much less could they have hoped that he would relax it concerning the preservation of clerical offices?

We have thought it necessary to transcribe the whole canon because, since it clearly prescribes what ought to be written to Anastasius, we are pleased to possess in it a summary and supplement of the letter written to this pope, which has perished.

The council whose decree concerning Donatist clergy the Africans so revere, yet nevertheless think should be moderated for the sake of the unity of the Church, seems to be none other than the Council of Capua. They likewise praise another decree of that council [ibid., c. 48] concerning

> “reordinations, rebaptisms, or transfers of bishops.”

Whether Anastasius replied to these letters of the Africans is unknown. But what they did not dare to undertake without the consent of the apostolic see is known to have been accepted in Africa somewhat later.

For in the year 417 Augustine, when the Donatists objected as though it were an established practice, “How is it that after this repentance we remain among you as clergy or even as bishops?” replied:

> “This would not happen—for in truth, what must be admitted, it ought not to happen—unless it were healed by a compensation for peace itself.”

Nor is it surprising that something was then granted by the apostolic see which had been observed in Africa from the beginning of the schism, even according to the judgment of Miltiades.

That most prudent pope, as we saw above, p. 328, no. 5, had decreed, for the purpose of uprooting the schism from its roots, that in places where there were two bishops—one schismatic and the other Catholic—the one who had been ordained first should be confirmed, while another people should be provided for the other to govern.

But where there was no compensation for unity, the earlier law concerning the non-retention of offices remained wholly intact and unimpaired, as we shall see under Innocentius and other pontiffs.

## IX

### 10. Letters of Anastasius Against Rufinus Sent to the East

In the very year in which Jerome was preparing book III of his *Apology*, he mentions more than once that new letters from Anastasius against Rufinus had been sent to the East.

At one point, against Rufinus, who was trying to suggest that the letter written to John of Jerusalem in the preceding year was a forgery, Jerome says that the truth of that letter

> “is proved also by the letter of this year against you.”

And somewhat earlier:

> “Granted that I forged the letter of the preceding year. Who sent the recent writings to the East? In them Pope Anastasius adorns you with such flowers that, when you read them, you begin to wish more to defend yourself than to accuse me.”

Then, plucking some of those flowers and placing them before Rufinus’s eyes, he addresses him as follows:

> “Appeal to him in person—Anastasius—and ask why he insulted you, though absent and innocent, by sending letters against you to the East and, while you were unaware, branding you with the mark of heresy; why he said that you had translated Origen’s *On First Principles* so that, through you, they might lose the truth of the faith which they had learned from the Apostle; and why, to make you still more hated, he dared to allege that these very books had been authenticated by the testimony of your preface. It is no light charge that the bishop of so great a city brings against you, or rashly accepts when brought by another.”

If, however, we consider the manner in which Jerome, in the same work, when reporting what Anastasius had written to John about Rufinus, puts forward not so much what that pope says as what he thinks follows from his words, it may reasonably be supposed that he acted in the same way here. It is therefore highly probable that the statements Jerome records were expressed by Anastasius in less severe terms.

Perhaps these writings of Anastasius were sent to the East after that pontiff, together with the entire synod of the Westerners, had

> “received and approved the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious man [Origen],”

as Theophilus says in the sermon praised by the emperor Justinian.

## X

### 11. A Judgment Obtained by Deception from the Apostolic See

A judgment was issued by one of Innocentius’s predecessors against Photinus, a bishop of Illyricum, by which, according to Innocentius’s testimony (Letter 15, c. 14), “something more severe was decreed.”

Afterward the Macedonian bishops, taking up the case of their colleague, demonstrated that this judgment had been

> “obtained from the apostolic see through a false rumor and elicited by treachery.”

When Innocentius heard this, he first admitted that it was anxious and extremely difficult for him to “review” and reconsider “the judgments of his predecessors.” At the same time, however, he thought it harsh to deny consent to so many and such good bishops.

Therefore, having changed for the better the earlier judgment by which Photinus had been condemned, he permitted them to reinstate that bishop. The earlier judgment, however, seems to belong to no other pontiff than Anastasius, and indeed toward the end of his pontificate, so that his intervening death denied the Macedonians the opportunity and the time to demonstrate that the judgment had been obtained by deception.

When Innocentius corrected the matter, he plainly showed that he held that no one is so holy—even if he occupies the first see—that it is impossible to impose upon him in judicial matters.

## XI

### 12. Three Fragments to Be Restored to Anastasius II

Baronius, under the year 402, cites three fragments as though they belonged to a letter of our Anastasius to Ursinus. But Stephanus Baluzius, volume I of the *New Collection of Councils*, p. 1457, restored them to Anastasius II. We shall demonstrate in its proper place that they belong to him.

## XII

### 13. Two Letters Falsely Attributed to Anastasius I by Mercator

Isidorus Mercator did not spare even this pope’s name. He falsely attributed two letters to him: one addressed to all the bishops of Germany and Burgundy, the other addressed to Nerianus. The falsity of both was detected by Baronius and confirmed by conclusive arguments.

We shall establish this in its proper place, when we publish those letters together with the rest of this impostor’s collection.

## XIII

### 14.

In the published *Book of the Pontiffs* we read concerning Anastasius I:

> “He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but stand bent forward. He also decreed that no man from overseas should be admitted to the honor of the clergy for any reason unless he produced written attestations from five bishops, because at that same time Manichaeans were also discovered in the city of Rome.”

Following the wording of this book, Isidorus Mercator represents Anastasius, in letter I, chapters 1, 2, and 3, as issuing the following command:

> “While the holy Gospels are being recited in the church, let the priests and all the others present, not sitting but reverently standing bent forward in the sight of the holy Gospel, listen attentively to the Lord’s words and worship them faithfully.
>
> “Likewise, do not receive men from overseas, concerning whom you have consulted us, into the honor of the clergy unless they have been designated by the written attestations of five or more bishops . . . As for the Manichaeans whom we found in the city of Rome, etc.”

## 15.

In the copy of the *Book of the Pontiffs* once belonging to the Queen of the Swedes, which the continuators of Bollandus consider to have been written in the time of the emperor Justinian, and which they published in volume I of the *April Propylea*, p. 40, as well as in the copy of Saint Peter of Fossatensis, now in the Colbert Library, no. 1868, which ends with Pelagius II, Anastasius is said to have decreed only this:

> “He decreed that whenever the Gospels are recited, the priests should not sit.”

Nothing is said there concerning foreign clergy or Manichaeans discovered in Rome.

There is therefore no lack of grounds for suspecting that Isidorus Mercator, who prefixed the *Book of the Pontiffs* with the additions or interpolations mentioned above to his collection, was the author of these additions.

Once they have been removed, however, it is less implausible that Anastasius decreed that priests should not sit while the Gospels were being recited. For it would rightly seem contrary to the prudence of our pontiff for him to have commanded priests—most of whom were worn out by old age—not merely to stand throughout the entire time in which the Gospels were read, but even to stand bent forward. Whether this really accords with him must be considered.

## 16.

Baronius seems to have derived the occasion for this decree from a dispute that arose in Rome around that time between presbyters and deacons, when some attempted to place deacons on an equal footing with presbyters or even to put them ahead of presbyters.

As witnesses to this dispute he cites the author of the *Questions* published in the appendix to volume III of Augustine’s works, who is also thought to be earlier than Augustine, as well as Jerome, formerly letter 85, addressed to Evagrius, or rather Evangelus.

Then, says the learned Cardinal:

> “The presbyters rose up against these deacons and, according to the custom prescribed by the Roman Church, insisted that while the presbyters were sitting, the deacons ought to stand. But the dispute advanced with such persistence that even when the deacons, standing before the people, were reading the Gospel, the presbyters nevertheless did not rise from their seats. Anastasius, judging this to be an outrageous act, thought it should be corrected by such a decree.”

Here he seems to place the chief point of the dispute in the fact that, while the presbyters were sitting in church, the deacons likewise wished to sit.

But that the deacons of the Roman Church never arrogated this to themselves is expressly attested by the author published among Augustine’s works whom Baronius cites. He says in these words (*Questions*, 101, p. 92f):

> “Although the deacons of the Roman Church may seem somewhat more immodest, they nevertheless do not presume upon the dignity of sitting in the church.”

Baronius also detracts from the reputation of the many presbyters who governed the Roman churches by supposing that they committed such an act at that time. A constant law prevailed everywhere: out of reverence for the Gospel, it was to be heard only while its reading was being attended by people standing.

In book II, chapter 57, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, the following is decreed:

> “When the Gospel is read, let the presbyters and deacons and the whole people stand in complete silence.”

And Nicephorus Callistus, while recalling that the following had once prevailed in the Alexandrian church (book II, chapter 34),

> “that the bishop did not rise when the sacred Gospels were being read,”

at the same time observes that this was

> “new and unusual in all other places.”

Philostorgius, an ancient writer, also praises Theophilus the Indian because, traveling through regions by day,

> “he corrected many things that were not properly done there,”

and immediately adds:

> “For they also listened to the readings of the Gospel while sitting, and performed certain other acts against which the divine law protested.”

This sufficiently indicates that it was universally customary for the Gospel to be heard while the people stood.

Who, then, could believe that in a flourishing Church, and one most faithful to ecclesiastical customs, the spirit of contention could have prevailed among the foremost order of the clergy to such an extent that not merely one or two but the presbyters generally would, contrary to established custom, refuse the observance owed to the sacred Gospels?

# THE LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE ANASTASIUS I (C, S)

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER.

## I. This Letter Is Mentioned by Jerome and Inserted in Book II of *Against Rufinus*

Frequent mention of this letter is made in Jerome’s writings. He refers to it in Letter 8, to Demetrias, where he writes:

> “While you were still a little girl, and Anastasius, bishop of holy and blessed memory, was governing the Roman Church, a savage storm of heretics from the regions of the East attempted to defile and weaken the simplicity of the faith, which had been praised by the voice of the Apostle. But that man of richest poverty and apostolic solicitude immediately struck the noxious head and silenced the hissing mouths of the hydra.”

In Letter 78, to Pammachius and Marcella, after praising Theophilus of Alexandria because he had declared Origen a heretic, he speaks of this letter as follows:

> “Although it has been widely reported in celebrated speech that blessed Pope Anastasius also, because he is of the same spirit, pursued heretics hiding in their own caves with the same fervor, and that his letters show that what was condemned in the East was condemned in the West as well. May we number many years for him, so that, through his zeal, the revived shoots of heresy may wither and die after a long time.”

In Book III of his *Apology* he speaks of it several times, nor is he silent about it in the second book. Indeed, he testifies that a copy of it was appended by him to that book, and, addressing Rufinus, he explains why it was appended in these words:

> “If you are translating [Origen’s books] in order to accuse him as a heretic, alter nothing from the Greek, and attest this very thing in your preface: something which Pope Anastasius, with the greatest prudence, expressed in his own language in the letter which he writes against you to Bishop John—acquitting me, who did this, and accusing you, who were unwilling to do it. And lest perhaps you deny this also, I have appended a copy of his letter, so that, if you do not wish to hear a brother admonishing you, you may hear a bishop condemning you.”

## II. How It Came to Be Inserted in the Collection of Jerome’s Letters

From this too one may conjecture on what occasion it happened that this letter of Anastasius was placed among Jerome’s letters, even in the older collections of them. Those who compiled these collections, whenever they found among Jerome’s works anything that had the form of a letter, detached it from his other writings of the same kind in order to include it in a single body of letters. Thus, when they found this letter of Anastasius, as well as Rufinus’s preceding letter, appended to Jerome’s Book II of the *Apology*, they judged that both should be transferred to the class of letters.

Now both have been relegated to the volume containing works that are not Jerome’s. Whether it would be preferable to display such writings in the place that Jerome assigned to them is not for me to decide.

## III. It Is Found Prefixed to the Manuscript Works of Marius Mercator

Among the published works of Jerome, this letter of Anastasius was first transcribed in the Roman edition of the papal letters, then in Baronius, and afterward in the editions of the councils. In the Vatican and Bellovacian manuscripts it is prefixed, together with another short work entitled *The Faith of the Same Rufinus*, to the works of Marius Mercator.

Although John Garnerius acknowledges that neither work belongs in any way to Marius Mercator, he nevertheless thought that both should be published with that author’s works—not at their beginning, but at the end—and illustrated with notes. His edition presents one on page 109 and the other on page 114. He also correctly observed that the exposition of the faith which he found attributed to Rufinus was not by the presbyter of Aquileia.

## IV. Rufinus Suspects That This Letter Was Fabricated by Jerome

Rufinus indicated, not without the appearance of a troubled and uncertain mind, that he suspected this letter of Anastasius to have been fabricated by Jerome. Accordingly, Jerome addresses him as follows:

> “In the letter of holy Pope Anastasius you showed yourself slippery; and, disturbed, you could not find where to plant your foot. For now you say that it was composed by me; now that it ought to have been sent to you by him—namely, John—to whom it was sent. Again you accuse the writer of injustice.”

A little later, being himself certain of the letter’s authenticity, Jerome mocks Rufinus because he said that he expected a copy of it from the East, in these words:

> “Go rather to Rome, and, being present with him—Anastasius—demand an explanation of why he has insulted you, absent and innocent: first, because he did not receive your exposition of the faith, contained in your preceding letter … and then because he sent letters against you to the East.”

Even now, however, Peter Halloix, in *The Life of Origen*, page 333, considers the same letter suspect of being a forgery. Jerome nevertheless confirms its authenticity by other letters sent by the same pope to the East in the following year, concerning which he adds shortly afterward:

> “Let it be that I fabricated the letter of the previous year: who sent the recent writings to the East, in which Pope Anastasius adorns you with such abundant flowers that, when you read them, you will begin to want to defend yourself more than to accuse us?”

And near the end of his *Apology*:

> “But if it is his—for the letter of this year against you proves that it is—then you strive in vain and falsely to accuse a false letter.”

## V. In What Year It Was Written

The opinion of those who think that the letter under discussion was written in the year 402 cannot stand together with these two passages. For no one extends the life of Anastasius beyond 27 April of the year 402. Yet Jerome testifies that this letter was written not in the year in which that pope died, but in the year preceding it.

It follows that it must be assigned either to the year 401, if Anastasius really died in April 402, or, if his death is correctly recorded as having occurred on 4 December 401, to the year 400; and in that case Jerome composed the final part of his *Apology against Rufinus* not in 402 but in 401.

## VI. Origen Condemned by Anastasius

That Origen was condemned in this letter is clear both from several passages of Jerome and from the words of the letter itself. As I have already observed, Jerome, in Letter 16, attributes praise to Marcella because she was the beginning of this condemnation. Jerome himself was then seeking it, and Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, unknowingly provided considerable assistance to his request.

For when that holy Doctor had sent letters against Origen to the West, and Anastasius, wishing nothing to be done precipitately, had not yet yielded to the entreaties of Jerome or anyone else, Jerome writes to Theophilus in Letter 71:

> “I think it happened by God’s providence that, at that very time, you too wrote to Pope Anastasius and, while unaware of our opinion, strengthened it.”

The same Theophilus, in a sermon addressed to certain monks, testifies that Origen was condemned by himself as well as by Anastasius, in these words:

> “Anathematizing Origen and the other heretics, following the example of ourselves and of Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, who, renowned for ancient struggles, was appointed leader of the most noble people, and whom the whole synod of the bishops of the West follows—which accepted and approved the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious man.”

The emperor Justinian praises these words of Theophilus in the letter which he wrote to Menas against the errors of Origen (*Councils*, Labbe, vol. V, p. 658).

## VII. Anastasius Did Not Condemn Rufinus by a Formal Judgment

It will be useful to examine whether Rufinus was likewise condemned by Anastasius by a formal judgment, together with Origen. Most people take this as certain, and Jerome seems to support them when he sometimes declares that Rufinus was not only accused and summoned to Rome, but also condemned. The following passage of this Doctor, in Letter 16, seems especially applicable to him:

> “The heretics, summoned by repeated letters to defend themselves, did not dare to come; and the force of conscience was so great that they preferred to be condemned in their absence rather than to be convicted in their presence.”

But in the passage cited above Theophilus mentions a single judgment pronounced against the impious man—that is, against Origen alone. Jerome can be understood conveniently as saying that the heretics were condemned insofar as, when Origen was condemned, those who were entangled in the same errors were also considered condemned.

Nor do the following words of Jerome in Book II of the *Apology against Rufinus*, where he addresses Rufinus himself, sound as though Rufinus had been condemned by Anastasius:

> “Why, when you are about to translate a heretical work, do you place before it, in defense of the heretics, a book as though it were a martyr’s, and thrust upon Roman ears what the whole world has shuddered at after it was translated? Or certainly, if you are translating it in order to accuse him as a heretic, alter nothing from the Greek, and attest this very thing—which Pope Anastasius, with the greatest prudence, expressed in his own language in the letter which he writes against you to Bishop John—acquitting me, who did this, and accusing you, who were unwilling to do it.”

Here one should note that he says “accusing you,” not “condemning you”; and he accuses him in such a way that it was still in Rufinus’s power to do what he had hitherto omitted and thus escape condemnation. Therefore no judgment had yet been pronounced against him; the matter was still pending.

Accordingly, when Jerome immediately adds to the words quoted above:

> “And lest perhaps you deny this also, I have appended a copy of his letter”—that is, Anastasius’s letter—“so that, if you do not wish to hear a brother admonishing you, you may hear a bishop condemning you,”

he does not indicate an accomplished condemnation, or a sentence already pronounced against one convicted of heresy. Rather, he indicates a hypothetical condemnation, which Rufinus had not yet undergone but would unquestionably undergo if he despised what Anastasius admonished him to do.

Indeed, when Jerome also speaks of later writings sent to the East in the following year, he says to Rufinus:

> “In them Pope Anastasius adorns you with such abundant flowers that, when you read them, you will begin to want to defend yourself more than to accuse us.”

By this he indicates that the presbyter had not yet been condemned by a formal judgment. For once a sentence has been pronounced by the supreme judge, no place remains for defense; the accused has only to endure the punishment of the judgment or correct the matter for which he was judged.

But why should I linger over arguments drawn from others, when Anastasius, in the letter appended below, consistently strives to refrain from passing judgment on Rufinus? He had not yet sufficiently discovered with what intention Rufinus had translated Origen’s books into Latin.

Certainly, if he had pronounced a judgment against him, it ought to have been announced either to Rufinus himself, or to the bishop in whose territory he lived, or publicly. Anastasius clearly indicates only this: that, in his own judgment, Rufinus is considered deserving of condemnation if he approved the doctrine of Origen’s books which he had rendered into Latin. Some further discussion of this matter will necessarily be found in the notes.

# LETTER I

## Of Anastasius I, Bishop of the City of Rome, to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, Concerning Rufinus’s Name

**[Note: In the Roman and council editions, the words “concerning Rufinus’s name” are missing. Jerome, addressing Rufinus, says that it was written not “concerning your name” but simply “against you.”]**

Consulted by John as to whether Rufinus ought to be condemned because he had translated Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) from Greek into Latin, Anastasius replies that, with all suspicion set aside, one must consider with what intention Rufinus undertook the task; that he must indeed be condemned if he translated it according to his own convictions, praising and approving it, but not if he translated it while accusing the author himself. Anastasius says that he is not troubled by groundless fear, but will take care that the churches throughout the world are not corrupted by this.

## 1. Anastasius Praises the One Who Praises Him, and Asks Him to Cease Praising Him

It is certainly a mark of approved affection that a priest should speak commendably of a priest. Therefore, for such an exceedingly abundant proclamation of praise as you have bestowed upon my merits, I thank your affection; and in turn a favorable utterance from our humility follows the splendor of your holiness and the virtues which you possess in the Lord.

**[Note: Garnerius reads “upon my unmerited merits,” although the manuscripts he used also contradict him. The reading “upon me, undeserving of it” would not be objectionable; but the reading found in the manuscripts is also sound and elegant.]**

**[Note: In the Cluniac and Bellovacian manuscripts: “and those virtues of yours”; this would be correct if “which you possess in the Lord” followed immediately.]**

For, most outstanding man of all, you shine so conspicuously with the brilliance of your praises that no discourse can equal your merits.

Yet I am so carried away by the stimulus of your titles that I shall not cease daring even what I cannot obtain. This too belongs to your praises: you praised me only for the serenity of that heavenly spirit. For the splendid order of your episcopate, radiating throughout the diverse world like a beam, has conveyed even to us the brilliance of its splendor.

**[Note: Garnerius reads “throughout the whole world … of your splendor,” against the other printed editions and the manuscripts. “The diverse world” may mean either East and West together, or simply the West, which is distinct from the region inhabited by John.]**

In me, therefore, you attribute everything to friendship and leave nothing to examination.

**[Note: In the Bellovacian manuscript: “everything then he himself.” Perhaps this should read “everything while he himself,” or “everything although he himself.”]**

Or, if you praise me justly, should you not also be praised in the same manner?

**[Note: Garnerius, with the Bellovacian manuscript, reads “you too must be praised in like fashion.” The reading of the Cluniac manuscript and the other editors seems more genuine. In those printed editions, however, the words “by me” are soon lacking; this amounts to the same thing as in the manuscripts.]**

I therefore ask, on both accounts, that you cease now to praise me to myself; for a twofold reason constrains me, lest false praise inflict pain upon the feelings of your fellow priest, or true praise kindle his embarrassment.

**[Note: Garnerius has “the reason for you.” Other editions then read “constrains this to be sought.” The expression “this to be sought,” which is absent from the manuscripts, is not foreign to Anastasius’s meaning, but is correctly understood implicitly. Although Anastasius rejects praise because even praise that is true can offend modesty and thereby provoke shame, others nevertheless do not deny that praise of the good can sometimes be useful. Augustine explains this in Letter 231, to Darius, section 4, as follows: “For if those things which you praise in me do not exist, I blush profitably and burn to make them exist. And insofar as I recognize myself in your praise, I rejoice that I possess them, and that both they and I are loved by you on account of them. But what I do not recognize in myself, I desire not only to obtain, but also to prevent those who sincerely love me from always being deceived by my praise.” With the same attitude Gregory the Great, praised by Leander, bishop of Seville, replies in Book IX, Indiction 2, in August: “What is not as it is said, let it become so because it is said, lest one who is not accustomed to lying should lie.”]**

## 2. Rufinus’s Case Is Left to God’s Judgment

But, to return to the case: Rufinus, concerning whom you have graciously deigned to consult me, has the divine majesty as the judge of his conscience; before it, with an undivided duty of devotion, he must himself see how he ought to approve himself.

**[Note: The Roman edition reads *arbitrium*, “judgment.” Baronius and Labbe read *arbitrum*, “judge.” Garnerius correctly reads *arbitram*, as in the manuscripts. Anastasius now begins to distinguish the cases of Rufinus and Origen; while suspending judgment on Rufinus, he openly sets forth his own view of Origen.]**

## 3. What Is to Be Thought about Origen

But as for Origen, whose compositions have been transferred into our language, it is not the purpose of our present undertaking to investigate either who he was or into what utterances he proceeded; I shall briefly confer with your holiness, however, about what my own concern is.

**[Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read “he did not know,” except that Garnerius entirely altered the passage according to his own judgment: “our concern did not know what the purpose of my mind is.” We do not consider such alterations permissible for an editor. But, he says, the passage, as it stands in all the manuscripts, requires an Oedipus. Granted: is it not preferable to retain the words of all the manuscripts even when they are not understood, rather than, by overturning them, to substitute an interpretation foreign to their author? Nevertheless, if I grasp Anastasius’s meaning, he intends this: Since our stated purpose, set forth at the beginning of the letter itself, concerns Rufinus’s name—and since you have consulted me only about him—it is not the purpose of this present undertaking to investigate who Origen was. Yet I shall briefly disclose to you what my concern is, what my attitude toward him is, and what judgment I hold concerning him. In fact, having digressed slightly from Rufinus in order to express his opinion of Origen, Anastasius finds the interrupted discussion of him again. Nor can it be said that Origen was wholly unknown to Latin readers before Jerome and Rufinus rendered some of his works into Latin, since Victorinus, Hilary, and Ambrose had already devoted their efforts to translating him. Hence Rufinus was also able to say in his preceding letter: “I am neither Origen’s defender nor his advocate, nor his first translator: others had undertaken this work before me; I did it afterward, as the last.” Jerome nevertheless observes in Book I of the *Apology* that it happened that the whole world burst into hatred of Origen after Rufinus’s translation, although previously it had read him without prejudice.]**

I have conceived this in my mind: that the man who, by making available to the people of our city the reading of Origen in translation, has brought it before them, has wished to dissolve the faith of the Apostles, established by the tradition of our forefathers, by winding and devious turns, after a kind of cloud of blindness had been cast over pure minds.

**[Note: The printed editions, with the exception of Garnerius, read: “that he who made known to the people of our city, through the translated works, the reading of Origen, casting over pure minds a kind of cloud, and wishing to dissolve the faith of the Apostles, etc.” Garnerius notes that the Bellovacian and Vatican manuscripts have: “that the reading made known to the people of our city”—where he has suffered a lapse of memory, for in the Bellovacian manuscript we find *lectio*—“having cast over pure minds, as it were, a cloud of blindness.” He professes to have labored greatly to restore this passage and published it as follows: “I have conceived this in my mind”—a copyist’s negligence for *concepi*—“that he who, through the works translated, has made the reading of Origen known to the people of our city, casts over pure minds as it were a cloud of blindness and wishes to dissolve, by devious windings, the faith of the Apostles, established by the tradition of our forefathers.” But who could approve a reading in which so many things have been changed contrary to the authority of the manuscripts? First, “he who” is added where it did not exist. Then “through the translated works” is substituted where the text had “through the translated reading”; likewise *lectione* is substituted for *lectio*, and *to cast* for the participle *cast*. After “faith,” the conjunction *and* is again added; finally, the word “he” before “wished to dissolve” is suppressed. Yet even with so many changes the sentence is not made entirely plain and intelligible: what is meant by “he who made known through the translated works the reading of Origen” is not sufficiently clear. Our reading, however, ought to seem preferable because it is expressed according to the authority of the ancient manuscripts, with no word added, removed, or displaced, except that in the phrase “a certain cloud of blindness cast over pure minds,” the letter *m* has been deleted; experience shows that copyists very often incorrectly added it in manuscripts. Hence some experts in grammar have observed that the accusative case was commonly used by the ancients in place of the ablative. Nor will anyone think that the letter was deleted rashly who reads below, in section 4, the statement concerning this same doctrine, which attempts to weaken devoted minds by the darkness of itself cast upon them. Moreover, both what immediately precedes and what follows require us to understand that the Origen whom Anastasius conceived as having wished to dissolve apostolic tradition is Origen, not Rufinus. Anastasius says this immediately after announcing that he will communicate briefly, as though in haste and outside his main subject, to John what he thinks about Origen. Thereafter he consistently refrains from pronouncing any judgment against Rufinus, clearly indicating that he had not yet discovered with what intention Rufinus had translated Origen into Latin, and that, until he knew this, he could make no certain judgment about him. From this it is also clear that the words “he wished to dissolve apostolic tradition” cannot be said of Rufinus. No obscurity remains if one understands that before the verb “made known” there is an implied phrase meaning “I have conceived and judged.”]**

## 4. The Intention with Which Rufinus Interpreted Origen Is Investigated

**[Note: Garnerius reads: “To say … what will he do … by this translation, and by revealing the execrable deed, he makes himself hated by the people.” The reading “to learn,” etc., should be retained with the other printed editions and the manuscripts. Anastasius is uncertain what plan Rufinus had in undertaking the translation of the books *On First Principles*; he now indicates that he wishes to discover and learn this. Jerome’s words in Book II clearly point to this: “If you are translating it in order to accuse him as a heretic, alter nothing from the Greek, and attest this very thing in your preface—which Pope Anastasius, with the greatest prudence, expressed in his own language in the letter which he writes against you to Bishop John.” A year had already passed since Anastasius wrote to John when Jerome said this; therefore no judgment had yet been pronounced against Rufinus, but only a suspicion had been raised concerning him, which it was still entirely within his power to remove. Certainly Anastasius does not condemn Rufinus, since he explicitly writes that he will approve him if he accuses the author whom he translated.]**

Here I wish to learn what this translation does in the Roman language. I approve it if he accuses the author and exposes the execrable deed to the people, so that the man whom rumor had long since bound may at last be held in just hatred.

But if the translator gives his assent to such great evils and publishes them for the people to read, he has constructed nothing by his labor except that, according to the arbitrary judgment of his own mind, he might overthrow, under the title of an unprecedented assertion, those things which alone, which first, and which among Catholic Christians have been held from the Apostles’ time down to the present as the true faith.

**[Note: The printed editions read: “gives assent to the errors of such evils and publishes impious doctrines to be read.” This has been corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]**

**[Note: Garnerius has “according to the judgment of his own will.” Our reading is found in the other books.]**

**[Note: The Bellovacian manuscripts have “by the pure faith.” The Roman and council editions read: “This faith, which alone and which first among Catholic Christians is held as the true faith …”]**

**[Note: Garnerius omits *inopinatae*, which here is equivalent to “new” or “such as had not previously entered the minds of men.” In the Bellovacian manuscript, *impiae*, “impious,” appears in place of this word.]**

## 5. Anastasius’s Vigilance against Perverse Doctrine; the Reading of Origen Prohibited by Imperial Edicts

May this be far from the Catholic discipline of the Roman Church.

**[Note: So read the manuscripts together with Garnerius. Other printed editions have: “May this never be admitted by the Catholic discipline of the Roman Church.” Anastasius now declares without circumlocution that he condemns Origen’s doctrine.]**

It will certainly never happen that I admit in any way those things which we rightly and deservedly condemn. Therefore, the providence of Christ our God, diffused throughout the whole world, will deign to demonstrate that we cannot accept at all what stains the Church, overturns approved customs, wounds the ears of those standing around, and brings about quarrels, anger, and dissensions.

Moved by this consideration, you will be able to confirm from what follows what sort of letter our littleness, with more careful attention, sent to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius.

**[Note: The Bellovacian manuscript has *moto*. The reading *mota*, referring to “our littleness,” would not be objectionable. In the Cluniac manuscript, as in Garnerius, *moti* appears, with “when we had been moved” understood. Or this verb may be construed as though *transmiserimus* followed: “our littleness, having been moved, sent.” In the Roman and council editions this passage was corruptly presented as follows: “Therefore know what sort of letter our littleness—or, in the Roman edition, our depravity—sent to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius with more careful attention, and that I have established this conscience for myself, so that I do not labor under an excessive fear or become troubled by empty anxiety.” Garnerius, suspecting a lacuna after *moti*, thought it should be filled by his own addition. Thus, changing only the typeface, he did not hesitate to add almost six lines to Anastasius’s words, introducing the pope as saying: “We have condemned Origen’s writings and errors; but since the translator has not sufficiently cleared himself, either in his preface to Origen’s books or in the apology sent to us—in fact, perhaps he really agrees with the same errors—we summoned him to Rome for judgment before the apostolic see, and, when he refused to come, included him in the same sentence. We wrote the sentence of condemnation to our brothers Venerius and Chromatius.” In the commentary appended to his edition he attempts to approve this addition on three grounds. None of them necessarily establishes what he wishes, and especially the last two rely upon words of Anastasius that are either corrupted or wrongly understood. Some, thinking that the typeface was changed in order more easily to distinguish the judgment pronounced against Origen and Rufinus, accepted Garnerius’s added words as genuine words of Anastasius. Antonius Pagius specifically fell into this error in his *Critical Work*, under the year 401, section 9. But there is now no reason for anyone to suspect that this passage of Anastasius, as we present it, is unsound or incomplete.]**

Let that man who translated it keep with himself the matter of his own conscience, and let him keep the certainty that I am not burdened by needless fear or troubled by empty anxiety.

For my part, I shall certainly not lack concern to preserve the faith of the Gospel among my peoples and, as far as I can, to address in writing the members of my body scattered throughout the various regions of the earth.

**[Note: Garnerius has “the members of the body,” omitting “my”; other editions have “the parts of my people.” The manuscripts correct both readings. Anastasius calls the churches “parts of his body” in the same manner in which Celestine, in Letter 24, calls them “his members and entrails,” and in which Siricius, in Letter I, section 21, says that he has replied to everything concerning which, as he addresses Himerius, “you have referred to the Roman Church, the head of your body.”]**

**[Note: The commonly printed editions add “spread abroad” here; this is not found in the manuscripts.]**

I shall do this so that no source of profane interpretation may creep in and, by casting its own darkness upon devoted minds, attempt to weaken them.

**[Note: Referring to this, Jerome says in Letter 8, to Demetrias, that Anastasius struck the head of the heresy which had attempted to defile and weaken the simplicity of the faith praised by the voice of the Apostle.]**

Nor could I keep silent about the circumstance that I rejoice has occurred: the responses of our most blessed emperors have been issued, by which every person serving God is recalled from reading Origen.

**[Note: The manuscripts and Garnerius read this way. Other printed editions have “the one condemned by the judgment of the emperors,” and shortly afterward “the reading of things,” not “of the guilty man.” The imperial responses mentioned here are nowhere extant. Jerome does indeed praise, in Book I of the *Apology*, the imperial writings ordering the Origenists to be expelled from Alexandria and Egypt, but he does not say that those writings prohibited the reading of Origen’s books. Indeed, around that time, when Tranquillinus consulted Jerome about Origen—whether Origen should be entirely rejected, as Brother Faustinus held, or read in part, as some thought—Jerome replied in Letter 76: “I think Origen should sometimes be read for the sake of his learning, just as Tertullian, Novatian, Arnobius, and others.” Scholars ask whether those responses should be attributed to Honorius or Arcadius—that is, to the emperor of the West or of the East. Some believe that they were issued by Honorius, at the insistence of Marcellus and others from whom the condemnation of Origen was expected. From the words of Postumianus in Sulpicius’s *Dialogue* I, chapter 3, however, it can be gathered that they came from the emperor of the East. He first says that shameful conflicts had arisen between the bishops and monks of Alexandria on this occasion: priests gathered together seemed repeatedly to have decreed in frequent synods that no one should read or possess Origen’s books. A little later he adds: “The monks were driven through various regions, so that, after edicts had been posted, they were not permitted to remain in any place.” It is highly probable that, after Origen had been condemned by Theophilus and his synod, and the reading of his works had been prohibited, the bishops of Egypt, having found that their synodal decrees achieved nothing, requested imperial edicts; and that, when the monks could not be deterred from reading Origen by the authority of those edicts—or when this was at least alleged as a pretext—they were driven into exile everywhere. It is also very likely that those rescripts prohibiting the reading of Origen were drafted according to the model and form of the edicts which the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 5, law 34, records as issued on 4 March 398, by which Arcadius and Honorius forbade the reading of the books of the Montanists or Eunomians and ordered them burned.]**

And the man whom profane reading has exposed as guilty is condemned by the sentence of the emperors.

**[Note: Garnerius published *praecesserit*, “may have preceded,” and thinks that this reading confirms his earlier view that a lacuna existed in which a sentence pronounced against Origen and Rufinus had been omitted. But not only do the other printed editions, but also the manuscripts, have *processerit*, “has proceeded,” and this is more correct. The meaning is: “I have explained thus far what ought to be done and what ought to be thought concerning the new translation of the books *On First Principles* which Rufinus has brought to light.” Here *sententia* does not mean a sentence delivered by a judge, but a response given to the questions that had been asked—as though he had said in one word: “Thus far I have explained what I think.”]**
6. But since the popular complaint against Rufinus troubles you, so that you pursue certain persons with vague suspicions, I shall restrain this opinion of yours by the example of divine Scripture, as it is written: “Not as man does God; for God sees in the heart, whereas man sees in the face” (1 Kings 16:7). [Col. 0073C]

[Note: The Roman and conciliar editions read, “so that you pursue certain persons with evil suspicions”; this opinion is corrected from the manuscripts and Garnerius. Anastasius seems here to be speaking of Jerome and Jerome’s friends, Pammachius, Oceanus, and Marcella, who in fact contributed greatly to promoting the condemnation of the Origenists. Those vague suspicions seem to fall upon the men whom Rufinus calls his rivals in the preceding letter, no. 1. Since they consisted in John’s wishing Rufinus’s accusers to be regarded as suspect of spite and envy, and since spite is an inward evil known only to God’s eyes, Anastasius rightly observes that God alone sees in the heart, whereas man sees only in the face and what appears outwardly. Nor do I think that suspicions spread about Jerome are being noted here; concerning these Pammachius and Oceanus write to Jerome himself in Letter 64: “Therefore clear away the suspicions of men and refute the accusation; for if you disregard it, you may seem to consent.”]

Therefore, dearest brother, setting aside every suspicion, consider Rufinus according to his own mind, whether he translated Origen’s statements into Latin and approved them. [Col. 0073D]

[Note: Thus Garnerius, together with the manuscripts. Other printed editions, however, read, “not as man sees, so also does God.” Immediately afterward, together with those editions, Garnerius has “man in the face,” omitting the verb “sees”; this verb is restored from the manuscripts.]

Nor is he unlike the defendant who gives assent to another’s faults. [Col. 0074B]

[Note: The Roman and conciliar edition reads, “he is unlike him.” More correctly, Garnerius, as in the manuscripts, has “he is not unlike the defendant.” Developing this argument, Jerome presses Rufinus in *Apology* II as follows: “Tell us, then, why you translated Origen’s evil works into Latin: to expose the author of the evil, or to praise him? If you expose him, why do you praise him in your preface? If you praise him, you are proved a heretic ... If all these things are judged evil, then both the author and the translator are guilty of the crime.” Such an argument would have been entirely unnecessary if Rufinus had already, from the preceding year, been convicted and condemned by Anastasius.]

Yet I want you to hold this firmly: he is regarded by our side as so alien that we wish to know neither what he is doing nor where he is. [Col. 0074B]

[Note: Thus Garnerius, together with the manuscripts. Other printed editions read, “Yet I nevertheless wish to know.” Immediately afterward, “from our side” means “from our region,” specifically from the city of Rome.]

Finally, let him himself see where he can be acquitted. [Col. 0074B]

[Note: Certainly not from a sentence already pronounced, but from the suspicions cast upon him. For when someone has been condemned by a sentence, if the judge who pronounced it is the supreme judge, he cannot be acquitted anywhere but by that one by whom he was condemned. Hence Garnerius’s argument collapses: he interprets these words as judicial acquittal and thinks that they prove Rufinus to have been condemned by a sentence pronounced by Anastasius. If the learned man had approached the matter more freely in order to correct that preconceived opinion—which others, too, had formed from corrupt copies of this letter—or had attended to the rules prescribed for editors, he would have refrained from the alterations he introduced. Certainly editors are not free to add, remove, or move any word of their own. Much less may they adapt their authors’ readings to preconceived opinions; rather, preconceived opinions must be corrected by readings that contradict them.]

## LETTER II. TO SIMPLICIANUS

[Col. 0073B]

[Note: On the date when this letter was written, see Vallarsius, volume I of Jerome, in the recension of Letters 93, 94, and 95. Col. 0074C–D.]

He praises Theophilus’s zeal and vigilance; having been informed by his letter, he announces the condemnation to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan; he also declares that he has anathematized the Origenist heresy. [Col. 0074A]

**To the Lord Brother Simplicianus, Anastasius.**

### I

A shepherd is shown to exercise great concern and vigilance over his flock. Likewise, from a high tower, a watchman carefully keeps watch day and night over the safety of the city. [Col. 0074D]

[Note: In the archetype there was the meaningless word *exultare*, which we did not hesitate to correct by conjecture with these three words, “from a high tower”; both the sequence of the sentence and the clear necessity of the sense demanded this reading. It would have been easy for an old copyist who did not understand the abbreviated signs in his exemplar to copy one word in place of three. VALLARSIUS.]

A prudent master of a ship, in a time of storm and danger, suffers great agitation of mind lest the ship be dashed upon the rocks by violent squalls and the harshest waves. [Col. 0074D]

[Note: It is astonishing how many errors occur here in so few words through the fault of an ancient copyist. In the manuscript the passage read: “A master thus far of a ship, at the hour of storm, of *ecoris* and danger, suffers great ...” We have dared to alter it only by conjecture, since no loss of meaning was involved and the reader should not be confronted with such monstrosities. We have entirely deleted *ecoris*, a word which is nothing. ID.]

With equal spirit the holy and honorable Theophilus, our brother and fellow bishop, does not cease to watch over the interests of salvation, lest the people of God, by reading Origen in the various churches, fall into great blasphemies. [Col. 0074B]

### II

In accordance with the letter mentioned, I address your Holiness, so that, just as we who are established in the city of Rome—which the glorious Peter, Prince of the Apostles, founded and confirmed by his faith—have condemned these things we have mentioned, lest anyone should read them contrary to the commandment, and have earnestly requested that the ordinances of the Gospels, which the judgment of God and Christ taught from his own mouth, [Col. 0075A] should not in any way be departed from, but that what the venerable Apostle Paul foretold and admonished should be recalled: “If anyone should preach to you a gospel contrary to what was preached to you, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1:8). [Col. 0075A]

[Note: Some words are missing here, having fallen out through the negligence of ancient scribes—for example, “let them be preserved,” and “we determined,” or something similar. Yet even though the sentence is still obstructed by many errors, the holy Pontiff’s meaning is not obscure. ID.]

[Note: The adverb *sicuti* is used here in the sense of “similarly” or “in the same way”; examples of this usage are found among ancient Latin writers. If one reads *tunc* for *ut*, and *si* for *et*, the sense also becomes perfectly clear, for almost the entire text is fragmentary through the fault of copyists. ID.]

Therefore, holding to this commandment, we have declared that whatever was once written by Origen contrary to our faith is alien to us and condemned by us. [Col. 0076A]

### III

We have written these things to your Holiness through the presbyter Eusebius, who, carrying the warmth of faith and possessing love for the Lord, presented certain chapters of blasphemy. [Col. 0075B]

[Note: Clearly this is Eusebius of Cremona. When he was in Rome, from the year 398 onward, he was the first publicly to accuse Rufinus’s Latin translation of Origen’s *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), and from it he extracted chapters containing blasphemies. When he was also in Milan—at the very time when he delivered this letter of Anastasius to Simplicianus—he recited in Rufinus’s presence a certain statement from his translation of Origen, which Rufinus himself records that he attacked in Book I of his *Invectives*. ID. Col. 0076A–B.]

We not only shuddered at them and judged them, but you should know that whatever other things have been expounded by Origen have likewise been condemned by us together with their author. May the Lord preserve you unharmed, Lord brother, deservedly honorable. [Col. 0076B]

[Col. 0075B]

# APPENDIX. TWO LETTERS WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT ANASTASIUS

(From Labbe, *Councils*, volume II.) (G, S)

[Note: **Letter.** Anastasius wrote several letters in the controversy concerning the Origenists and Donatists, including one to Ursinus concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, of which three fragments survive in the appendix to the *Breviary* of Liberatus the deacon. If this letter, as is stated at its end, was written during the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto, in the year of Our Lord 385, it must have been composed fourteen years before Anastasius’s accession. Therefore, if we wish to regard it as genuine rather than spurious, it must either be attributed to pontiffs other than Anastasius, or an error must have entered the consular dating. Suspicion of forgery is increased by the fact that most of the letter, dealing with the Manichaeans, is found in Saint Leo the Great, Roman pontiff, in his second letter written to all the bishops of Italy. Baronius placed this after Surius, under the year 402, no. 48. SEVERINUS BINIUS. Col. 0075D–0076D.]

## FIRST LETTER. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF GERMANY AND BURGUNDY

I. That all should hear the holy Gospel standing, not sitting.—II. How people from overseas are to be received into the clergy.—III. Concerning the Manichaeans found in the city of Rome. [Col. 0075C]

**Anastasius, bishop, to all the bishops of the regions of Germany and Burgundy, greeting in the Lord.**

[Note: This word itself also argues that the letter is spurious, for the Burgundians were first converted to the Christian faith under the rule of Valentinian III. LABBE. Col. 0076D.]

Your love, dearest ones, requires that, on the authority of the Apostolic See, we should answer your inquiries. And although, because of certain other occupations, we would hasten to do this not at length but briefly, nevertheless, if necessity should require it, do not hesitate to send again, charitably, as it were to the head, on account of these or other needs; for we regard your prayers as welcome both now and then. [Col. 0075D]

### I

You have informed us that certain priests sit in church when the Gospels are read, and hear the words of the Lord and Savior sitting rather than standing, and say that they received this practice from the tradition of their elders. [Col. 0076C] We command, by apostolic authority, that you permit this to happen no longer in any way. Rather, while the holy Gospels are being recited in church, priests and all the other persons present, not sitting but standing reverently bowed before the sight of the holy Gospel, should listen attentively to the Lord’s words and adore them faithfully.

### II

Likewise, concerning the people from overseas about whom you have consulted us, do not receive them into the clerical order unless they have been vouched for by the written attestations of five or more bishops, since many things commonly occur through surreptitious means. For this reason, these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care.

### III

As for the Manichaeans whom we found in the city of Rome, and their followers, do not receive them or communicate with them, or have any participation with them, before they have turned to the true faith. Otherwise the seeds of their evil growth, which are extinguished by us in the City, may be planted or sprout among you with the worst roots. [Col. 0076D]

Our investigation discovered many of them, together with the followers of their impiety and their teachers; our vigilance exposed them, and authority and judgment restrained them. [Col. 0077A] Those whom we were able to correct, we corrected. We compelled them, by a public profession in the church and by the subscription of their own hands, to condemn the Manichaean together with his preaching and teachings; and thus, after they had confessed their plunge into the abyss of impiety, we raised them up by granting them penance.

Some, however, had sunk so deeply that no remedy capable of helping them could be found. Subjected to the laws, according to the enactments of Christian emperors, lest they pollute the holy flock by their contagion, they were sent into perpetual exile by public judges. Everything profane or shameful that they possessed, whether in writings or in secret traditions, we displayed—or perhaps “made public”—with definite evidence before the eyes of the Christian people, so that the people might know what to flee and avoid. [Col. 0077A]

Indeed, the man who was said to be their bishop, detained by us, disclosed the disgraceful things he held in his mysteries—or perhaps “mystical practices”—as the sequence of the proceedings will be able to show you. [Col. 0077B]

[Note: Possibly “traitors” rather than “perverse teachers.” Justelli’s manuscript reads, “traitors”; the alternative is “destroyers.”]

[Note: Perhaps *mystical things* rather than *mysteries*.]

For your instruction we have also sent you the proceedings themselves. Once you have read them, you will be able to know everything we discovered. And because we learned that some of those whom a more severe—or perhaps more atrocious—guilt had bound so that they could not be acquitted had fled, we have sent this letter to your love, so that your Holiness, made more certain of the facts, may act with greater diligence and caution, and so that the people of the Manichaean perversity may not find among your congregations either the opportunity to do harm or teachers of this sacrilege. [Col. 0077B]

For we cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way unless we pursue, with zeal for the Lord’s faith, those who are perverse teachers—or perhaps traitors—and lost, and cut them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this pestilence spread more widely. [Col. 0077C]

[Note: The manuscript of Justellus reads *perditores*, “destroyers,” rather than *proditores*, “traitors.”]

Therefore I exhort, beseech, and admonish your love to watch with the concern that you ought and can exercise, in order to investigate them, lest anywhere they find an opportunity to conceal themselves. These men, brothers, must be guarded against with great care, lest they be able to contaminate the Lord’s flock with whatever perversities they can.

Some of them, then, appear outwardly as sheep by their clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. We must recognize them, in accordance with the word of truth, by their fruits (Matthew 7:16). When they begin to assume impiety, what was hidden within them is revealed, and every deception becomes manifest to all. [Col. 0077C]

There are also people weak in faith who thirst for the divine Scriptures and, by associating with these men, plunge themselves into destruction. For they scatter and disparage the teachings of the fathers and abandon the holy Scriptures to their own ruin. As has been said, we must foresee these things and take great care against them, lest some, occupied with their wickedness, fall from their own firmness. [Col. 0077D]

I therefore greet you, brothers, and all the churches that share your good convictions. [Col. 0078A] I also ask you, as you are now doing, to address us more often by letter and to gladden us more frequently concerning your faith, good intention, and well-being, so that we may share a common joy and faithfully serve the Lord with one accord.

Given on the Nones of October, during the consulship of the most illustrious men Arcadius and Bauto.

[Note: **Letter II.** This letter, like the preceding one, would suffer from nearly the same suspicion of forgery if the consular date added near the end were not absent from the manuscript copies. The seventh consulship of Theodosius, with Palladius as his colleague, fell in the year of Our Lord 416, fifteen years after Anastasius’s death. I do not see how Anastasius could be said to have written a letter at that time. Therefore, lest the credibility and authority of the entire letter be endangered by the manuscript copies from which this letter of Anastasius was included in the first volume of the papal letters, we have judged that the consular date added at the end should be marked with this critical stroke. SEVERINUS BINIUS. Col. 0077D–0078D.]

## SECOND LETTER. TO NERIANUS

He consoles Nerianus, a religious man, over the loss of his parents.

**To his dearest brother Nerianus, Anastasius.**

Your letters, which everywhere display your faith and goodness, provide me with much cause for rejoicing: you show such devotion toward the practice of religion and strive to assist the priests of the Lord in your region. Therefore I give thanks to God, who urges you toward this, and I beseech him to make you persevere in good works. [Col. 0078B]

Yet you ought to praise God magnificently both in prosperity and adversity, and humble yourselves beneath his powerful hand, so that in the time of tribulation he may strengthen and exalt you, according to the Apostle Peter (1 Peter 5:6).

The affliction of your brotherhood, which we have heard you suffered through the loss of your parents, caused us such grief that, since love has made us one from two, we felt our heart burning especially in your tribulations. Yet in this sorrow I was greatly consoled by the thought of your Holiness, because—perhaps “by which” (*qua*) rather than *quia*, “because”—it is fitting both to bear grief patiently and not to prolong mourning over the death of your people. [Col. 0078C]

Nevertheless, lest any further tribulation remain in your mind, I exhort you to cease from grief—or perhaps, “I exhort you to rest from grief”—because it is unfitting that you should be given over to the weariness of affection for those whom we must believe to have reached true life through death.

Perhaps those who do not know of another life, who do not trust that there is a passage from this world to something better, have a just excuse for prolonged grief. But we who know, who believe, and who teach ought not to grieve excessively for those who die, lest what appears among others as a form of piety become for us rather a fault. For it is, in a certain sense, a kind of distrust, contrary to which every preacher who loves justice complains, as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope.” [Col. 0078D]

[Note: “What each person ...” That is: “what each person preaches, while complaining of being tortured by sorrow of mind,” as the speaker says, and so forth. LABBE.]

Having therefore understood this reason, we must strive not to be distressed over the dead, as we have said, but to devote our affection to the living, for whom our piety may be useful and our love fruitful. Lay aside your grief, then, dearest one, and take up the spiritual fruit of joy for the benefit of God’s holy Church and the advancement of his servants. Strive to illuminate whatever spans of this life remain with eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may render you more illustrious throughout the ages. [Col. 0079A; Col. 0080A]

[Note: Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June. This is the consular date whose authenticity is wholly suspect and which is absent from the manuscript copies from which this letter was inserted into the first volume of the papal letters. SEVERINUS BINIUS. Col. 0079.]

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June, during the consulship of the emperor Theodosius for the seventh time and Palladius, most illustrious men.

[Col. 0079A]

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 401

### FAUSTUS THE MANICHAEAN. A BOOK AGAINST THE CATHOLIC FAITH

(This book is held and refuted by the most eminent Doctor of Grace in his thirty-three books *Against Faustus the Manichaean*; see volume VIII of the works of Saint Augustine.)

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 403

### SULPICIUS SEVERUS

(Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, volume VIII.) [Col. 0079A]

# PROLEGOMENA

### I

“The presbyter Severus,” says Gennadius, “surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man noble both by birth and learning, is reported to have flourished toward the end of the fourth century. [Col. 0079A] He was younger than Paulinus of Nola; he was liberally educated in literature, acquired a reputation for intellectual ability, and in the forum won the palm of eloquence from the others. He married a woman from a consular family and possessed great wealth. [Col. 0079B] But at last, renouncing the world, he devoted himself entirely to monastic discipline, distinguished by his love of poverty and humility.” [Col. 0079C]

[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 19.]

[Note: Paulinus, Letter 5, section 5.]

[Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume XIV, p. 724, note 9, on Saint Paulinus.]

[Note: Paulinus, cited work, section 6.]

[Note: Gennadius, cited work.]

An erudite man makes this plainly evident from various letters of Paulinus. [Col. 0079C]

[Note: Jerome de Prato, *Life of Sulpicius Severus*, section 8, p. LXI and following.]

Whether he was ordained to the priesthood, although Gennadius asserts this, is not so firmly established that no room for doubt remains. [Col. 0079C]

[Note: Jerome de Prato, *Life of Sulpicius Severus*, section 10, p. LXV; Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume XII, p. 689, note 2, on Saint Sulpicius Severus. Col. 0080C.]

He was on familiar terms with Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, and with Paulinus of Nola. The same Gennadius reports that toward the end of his life he was deceived by the Pelagians; yet the learned man just mentioned renders this account suspect. [Col. 0079C]

[Note: Jerome de Prato, cited work, section 12, p. LXIX. Col. 0080C.]

He also believes that Severus died at Marseilles at approximately the age of fifty, around the year 410. [Col. 0079C]

[Note: The same author, same work, section 15, p. LXXV. Col. 0080C.]

### II

Severus left behind many works written in brilliant language, following Sallust above all. [Col. 0080A–B] It will be useful to set out here the catalogue of his works in the words of a distinguished man who not long ago published them, with only a few exceptions, most carefully revised and elucidated. For this reason we have judged that his edition should be preferred above the others and reproduced in our printing. Thus he writes:

[Note: Jerome de Prato, cited work, section 11, p. LXVIII. Col. 0080C.]

“Severus therefore wrote the *Life of Martin*, as he had intended, although we have demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently that he did not publish it until after Martin’s death, and that this occurred around the end of the year 400. [Col. 0080C]

[Note: The same author, dissertations 1, 2, and 3, works of Sulpicius Severus, volume I, pp. 149–231.]

Three letters written on the same subject preceded it in part and followed it in part; we shall discuss them more fully elsewhere.” [Col. 0080C]

[Note: The same author, dissertation 1, sections 5 and following.]

### III

“Meanwhile, either in the year 400 or not long afterward, he undertook another work, namely, an abridgment of Sacred History, extending from the beginning of the world to Stilicho’s consulship, since Stilicho first entered upon the consulship in that very year. [Col. 0080C] He was engaged in completing this work two years later, when he asked Paulinus to explain certain chronological difficulties arising in it. We gather this from Paulinus’s Letter 28, written in the year 402, in which he replies that he had consulted Rufinus on the matter and that, if Rufinus had provided any assistance, he would inform Severus. [Col. 0081A]

“But in the year 403, having received from Paulinus the account of the discovery of the Holy Cross—which Paulinus narrates at length in his Letter 31 to Severus—he added it to his little book, expressed in almost the same words.”

### IV

“Finally, in the year 405 Severus published his *Dialogues*, which we discuss in two of our dissertations.” [Col. 0081B]

[Note: The same author, cited work, and dissertations 5 and 6, pp. 259–317.]

“Moreover, throughout that entire period he wrote a great many letters, which Gennadius mentioned first in these words: ‘He wrote some works not unworthy of notice. For he wrote many letters to his sister exhorting her to the love of God and contempt of the world; these are known—only one or another of them has survived. He also wrote two to the aforementioned Paulinus, and others to other people; but because some contain matters of private familiarity, they are not arranged.’ [Col. 0081B]

“It is certainly regrettable that even in Gennadius’s time these letters of Severus were held in lesser esteem and were not arranged—that is, scattered as they were, they were not joined into a single body—because they dealt with *τὰς φιλικὰς φιλοφρονήσεις* (*tas phil ikas philophronēseis*), ‘friendly compliments’ or the sweetnesses of friendship. For the same reason, in some manuscript books the letter to Bassula is presented in mutilated form. [Col. 0082A]

“Thus I interpret Gennadius’s words: ‘But because some contain matters of private familiarity, they are not arranged.’ For one letter of this kind, and indeed a very brief one, which was written to Paulinus and still survives, sufficiently shows how worthy the others were to be preserved in cedar—that is, to be kept permanently.

“All the matters mentioned above extend to the year 405. What Severus did afterward, where he was, how long he lived, or what in general became of him is uncertain. For in Paulinus’s letters, after those which he says in Letter 43, no. 2, that he sent to him through Victor in the following year, not a word about him occurs again.”

Thus far the learned man.

### V

Since in the new Veronese edition which we followed there were missing seven letters bearing Severus’s name, published in the preceding century, two of which are attributed to Baluzius and the other five to Dacherius, we have therefore arranged for them to be appended to the same edition. Of these, the first three are said to acknowledge our Severus as their author; the remaining four are found to have been falsely attributed to him. What care and labor we have devoted, after Clericus, to printing these letters again, anyone can easily see from the notes appended below. [Col. 0082B]
