# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SULPICIUS SEVERUS

### I

[Note: Saint Paulinus of Nola, Sulpicius Severus’s intimate friend, wrote several letters to him; only thirteen now survive. From these we have excerpted the following passages, although all of them, individually and collectively, are outstanding testimonies to Severus’s virtues. Col. 0081D.]

Saint Paulinus of Nola, Letter 5, formerly Letter 1, written in the year 395, sections 5 and 6, writes to him as follows: [Col. 0081C]

You, dearest brother, have turned to the Lord by a greater miracle, because, flourishing in age, abounding in praise, less burdened by patrimonial obligations, and no poorer in the substance of your wealth, while still dwelling in the very theater of the world—that is, in the public renown of the forum—and holding the palm of an eloquent name, you suddenly shook off the yoke of enslaving sin and broke the deadly bonds of flesh and blood. Neither the riches accumulated from your marriage into a consular family, nor, after marriage, the license to sin, nor the freedom of celibate youth could call you back from the narrow entrance of salvation and the arduous path of virtue to that soft and spacious road of the multitude ... .

You, then, are a true doer of the Law and no deaf hearer of the Gospel. Nailing your body and the world to the cross, you rejected the pleasures of youth and the evil delights of the present life as though they were poisons and sorrows. You cast away the burdens of inherited wealth as if they were dung and rightly received your holy mother-in-law as a mother eternal, more generous than any earthly parent, [Col. 0081D] because you had placed the heavenly Father before your earthly parent. Following the example of the Apostles, leaving your father in the tossing boat—abandoning him amid the uncertainty of this life with the nets of his affairs and the entanglement of his patrimony—you followed Christ.

[Note: Le Brunius observes that the word *relicto*, “leaving,” is absent from Schott’s edition; and indeed it seems redundant. Col. 0082D.]

And, receiving from men praise for intellectual ability no less than for domestic wealth, and nobly scorning empty glory, you preferred the preaching of fishermen to all the writings of Cicero and to your own literature. You fled to the silence of piety in order to escape the tumult of iniquity. You wished to become silent to mortals so that you might speak of divine things with a pure mouth, and cleanse the tongue polluted by canine eloquence through the praises of Christ and the very commemoration of his holy name. [Col. 0082C]

The same, Letter 11, formerly Letter 5, written in the year 397, to the same person, section 4:

You are not content to revisit us on every occasion unless you also send your children. You choose as messengers not only servants but also holy sons, whose blessed offspring in the Lord gladdens you, so that through their eyes we may see you and through their mouths touch you. Their feet are beautiful to us, like those of men announcing good things. For they report and bring us from you the things that belong to peace, when they recount the works of the Lord that you either perform in the word of God or write in the Spirit of the Word. [Col. 0082D]

The same, in the same letter, section 11:

Your words, as eloquent as they are holy, testify that, having conquered the law of the members and corrupted the outward man, you prepare a pure mixture and make unleavened bread for Christ without leaven—or perhaps, “that a pure mixture is prepared and unleavened bread made for Christ.” For you would not have been granted the ability to narrate Martin unless you had made your mouth worthy of sacred praise with a pure heart.

[Note: The alternative reading is *parari*, “to be prepared,” which is preferable. Col. 0082D.]

Blessed, therefore, are you, man of the Lord, who reviewed the history of so great a Priest and most illustrious Confessor in language as worthy as your devotion was just. Blessed also is he who, according to his merits, deserved an historian worthy of his faith and life, who is consecrated both to divine glory by his merits and to human memory by your writings. [Col. 0083A]

The same, in the same letter, section 13, at the end:

But in him you are accused of fleeing the sinner, not the poor man, you who are a frequent visitor to the most blessed Martin; certainly you would never have desired him if you had been willing to hunger for bodily food.

The same, Letter 23, formerly Letters 3 and 4, written in the year 401 to the same person, section 3, speaking of Victor:

In him we truly recognized the pattern of the holy blessed Martin and Clarus, whose follower, at a short interval from his illustrious master, we have learned through you that he is. [Col. 0083B]

[Note: He alludes to what Severus had written to Aurelius in Letter 2. Col. 0083D.]

Victor, the son of peace, asserted that he was the offspring of one of them in regeneration and the companion of the other on the road.

The same, in the same letter, section 4:

He scarcely allowed me to pour water over his hands. For from your book I came to love the grace of that service, so that I might taste at least a tiny drop from the sacred deeds of Martin.

The same, Letter 24, formerly Letter 2, written and sent together with the preceding letter, section 1:

Why do you dare to assign to us, as to victors who have completed the contest, the palm of perfection, because we seem to have laid down the entire burden of earthly possessions, while you groan that you are still unhappy and clinging to the mire of infernal filth because you appear not to have sold even one small estate, as you wrote?

Yet you have likewise alienated even that estate from your present ownership, as though it had been sold, so that you might be doubly devoted to God through greater fruits of faith: through different transactions but with one gain of life, being within the bounds of the same commandment both seller and giver of lands, and therefore their possessor without captivity of spirit, since even what you have retained may be possessed by the Church while you serve it. Add also what is found in sections 3 and 4. [Col. 0083C]

The same, Letter 27, formerly Letter 14, likewise written in the year 401 to the same person, section 3:

It is ineffable to me how much pleasure they poured over me when they reported your deeds and words, and your perfect heart through knowledge of divine love. They declared that in you Martin breathed in his entirety, Clarus flourished, and the Gospel ripened: humble yet exalted, poor yet rich, servant yet free, a fellow servant to servants, servant to brothers, rich to the poor in the inward parts of mercy, poor to the rich in the spirit of gentleness, humble through the virtue of piety, lofty through the sublimity of virtue, servant to God and free from mammon. [Col. 0083D]

The same, Letter 28, formerly Letter 9, written in the year 402, section 5:

Moreover, you commanded me—flattering yourself extravagantly concerning your poor friend—to teach you what would escape the annals not of one nation but of the human race, as though I were more knowledgeable. But let him blame himself for his hunger who knocks at the door of a poor friend and searches an empty storeroom. [Col. 0084A]

For I was never sufficiently interested in investigating and collecting such things. Indeed, even in former times, when I seemed to be reading things that should not be read, I wandered away from historical writers. Nevertheless, now that I am concerned with your work, in which you indicated that, for the benefit of our faith, you are occupied with examining and comparing the accounts of past times, I sought from the richer treasury of a like-minded brother what I did not possess myself. I sent to the presbyter Rufinus the very annotation which you had sent as a memorandum and which I had incorporated into my letter. [Col. 0084B]

He is the spiritual companion of the holy Melania on the way, truly holy and devoutly learned, and for this reason bound to me by intimate affection.

[Note: Thus the edition of Rosweyde and that of Le Brunius, from the manuscripts; elsewhere, however, *Melanii* is read. Col. 0083D.]

[Note: From this and other passages of Paulinus it is plainly evident that Rufinus was exceedingly dear to him. From this it is equally clear that no friendship existed between Severus and Rufinus. Norisius must therefore be corrected, since in *History of the Pelagians*, Book I, chapter 2, he wrote: “It is sufficiently clear from their letters that Paulinus of Nola and Sulpicius Severus were not only friends of Rufinus but also his eulogists.” Col. 0084D.]

If he does not publish an explanation of the causes of the gaps in the history that rightly disturb you, concerning the incompatible reckoning of years or reigns—he who is rich in both Greek and Latin scholastic and salutary writings—I fear that we shall search for such a person in these regions in vain. But if he satisfies my presumption concerning himself, I shall, at the first opportunity, if the Lord favors us, send to your unanimity whatever reply he makes to me concerning this matter.

The same, Letter 29, formerly Letter 10, written at the same time as the preceding letter to the same person, section 6:

By this I may seem in some measure to repay your illustrious book in subject and eloquence, if I praise Melania, inferior in sex but serving Christ in the virtues of Martin, and so forth. [Col. 0084C]

The same, in the same letter, section 14, speaking of the same Melania:

I did not allow you, brother, to remain unknown to her. So that she might know more fully the grace of God in you, I revealed you to her more through your own speech than through mine. I myself recited our Martin to her, since she was exceedingly devoted to such histories.

By this method I revealed you also to the venerable and most learned bishop Nicetas, who had come from Dacia and was deservedly admired by the Romans, and to many saints of God: in truth, I was not so much proclaiming you as boasting of myself. For it is my glory to be loved by you and to love you. [Col. 0084C]

[Note: Perhaps “by you.”]

Your life, in harmony with your speech, bears witness that you are a servant of truth. [Col. 0084D]

The same, Letter 32, formerly Letter 12, written in the year 403 to the same person. Among the verses which he sent to be inscribed in various places of a basilica built by Severus and painted on its walls, these occur in section 3:

Rich in wealth for Christ, poor for himself, Severus

Established these heights with sacred fountains. [Col. 0084D]

The same, in the same letter, section 5:

Most pure in body, mind, and faith, a dweller in Christ,

Severus, rejoicing, founded these buildings for God.

He himself, wholly the temple of God, flourishes with Christ as guest,

And bears within his humble heart the Lord who rejoices.

Behold, as though in a threefold name, he worships a single mind;

Thus, with a holy mind, he consecrated a threefold work. [Col. 0085A]

## II. PAULINUS

Paulinus, notary of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, writes thus at the beginning of the Life of Ambrose, which they suppose he wrote in 412 or 413, or at least in 422 [Note: See Tillemont, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, § 2], to the blessed Bishop Augustine:

> You exhort me, venerable father [Note: From these words we may rightly infer that the Life of Saint Martin written by Severus was known to Saint Augustine and held in high esteem by him. Nevertheless, I do not find it true that he ever mentioned Severus in his letters. For I attach no importance to the testimony concerning Severus which is produced in nearly all editions of his works from Letter 205: it is certain that this letter was falsely attributed to Augustine. But certain other, and by no means insignificant, writers—Labbe, Baillet, and Natalis Alexander—cite Letter 25 as his, while at the same time observing that the letter numbered 205 is spurious; they are plainly seriously mistaken. For, as far as I can discover, Augustine nowhere mentions our Severus in his letters. Indeed, in the ancient editions to which Baillet appeals, Letter XXV does not even belong to Augustine, but to Jerome.] Augustine, that, just as the blessed bishop Athanasius and the presbyter Jerome committed to writing the lives of Saints Paul and Antony, who lived in the desert, and just as Severus, servant of God, composed in lucid language the Life of Martin, the venerable bishop of the Church of Tours, so I too might set forth in my own writing the Life of the most blessed Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan. Yet I know myself unequal in speech to the merits of such men, who are the walls of the churches and the fountains of eloquence.

## III. SAINT JEROME

Saint Jerome, writing around the year 415 in his commentary on chapter XXXVI of Ezekiel:

> For we do not, in accordance with the Jewish fables which they call *deuterōseis* (δευτερώσεις), await from heaven a Jerusalem adorned with jewels and gold; nor shall we again suffer the indignity of circumcision, nor offer sacrifices of bulls and rams, nor sleep in the leisure of the Sabbath. This is promised both by many of our own writers, especially by Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Hope of the Faithful*, and by the seventh book of Lactantius’s *Institutions*, as well as by the frequent expositions of Victorinus, bishop of Pettau, and more recently by our Severus in the *Dialogue* which he entitled *Gallus*. And, to name Greeks and join the first with the last, by Irenaeus and Apollinarius.

## IV. URANIUS

Uranius the presbyter, in his letter to Pacatus, *On the Death of Saint Paulinus*, written in 441 or shortly thereafter:

> Martin, a man apostolic in every respect, whose Life is read by everyone, was a bishop of Gaul.

[Note: These words, certainly, are not different from those in the Life published by Severus.]

## V. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE

In Prosper of Aquitaine’s *Pithaean Chronicle*, which ends in the year 404, under the ninth consulship of Arcadius and Honorius:

> Severus, formed in the discipline of Saint Martin, sets forth his life in three books.

## VI. PAULINUS OF PETROCORIA

Paulinus of Petrocoria, who rendered the Life of blessed Martin in verse around the year 460, book V, verses 193 ff.:

> Severus stands forth as a remarkable witness in learned speech,  
> And, following Christ with the whole strength of his heart,  
> Distinguished by the titles of the world, but more distinguished still  
> By that virtue of holy faith with which he despised the world;  
> Powerful in nobility, yet far more greatly  
> Noble in the worship of Christ than in the origin of his blood.  
>   
> This man, compressing and writing down the Sacred Canon  
> Of an extensive history, enclosed everything in two little books,  
> Whatever had been published from the earliest ages.  
>   
> The same man, recounting anew the honors and deeds of Martin,  
> A careful investigator of truth and faithful narrator,  
> Brought before the public the marks of so illustrious a life;  
>   
> Thus preserving the just balance with even judgment,  
> So that he would assert nothing doubtful and conceal nothing certain.  
>   
> He very often remained piously attached to the Holy Man,  
> As the mind’s reflection in a mirror is accustomed  
> To join the likenesses of kindred character [Note: Read “similar.”]:  
> Hence one must believe that the witness is all the more approved  
> Who teaches what he discovered in person, when he speaks of what he saw.

## VII. GENNADIUS

Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* [Note: Collated with three manuscript codices: first, a very ancient copy of the chapter of Verona, containing the complete work of Gennadius; second, a Brescian copy; and third, a Venetian copy. In the first of the latter two this testimony concerning Sulpicius Severus precedes the *Dialogues*; in the other it follows them. Collated also with other printed books.], which he was writing around the year 494 [Note: See Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 16], under number 19:

> Severus the presbyter, surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and learning [Note: *Litteratura*: thus the Venetian manuscript reads, and thus Pastrengus read it. The Capitular and Brixian manuscripts support this, having *littera*; and this is also how it is read in the Parma edition of the works of Saint Jerome, published in 1480 [Col. 0086D]. Gennadius uses the word also of Prudentius: “A man learned in secular learning.” The Vulgate editions have *litteris*, “in letters.”], conspicuous for his love of poverty and humility, and dear [Note: The edition of Gennadius prepared at Hamburg by Johann Albert Fabricius, followed by the Veronese Hieronymian edition, has *clarus* (“illustrious”) … *notitia*, contrary to the evidence of manuscripts and printed editions. Thus Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, writes of Serapion: “Dear to Antony the monk”; and Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 9: “It is dear to God to kneel.”] also to the holy men Martin, bishop of Tours, and Paulinus of Nola, wrote works of no little value [Col. 0086C]. For he wrote many letters to his sister urging love of God and contempt of the world, and these are also known [Note: The conjunction *et*, absent from the Hamburg and Veronese editions, is found in the Capitular manuscript and in the Parma edition.]. He wrote two letters to the aforesaid Paulinus [Note: Two to the aforementioned Paulinus of Nola: so the Capitular and Brixian manuscripts, together with the Parma edition. The latter, along with the Venetian manuscript and other printed editions, prefixed *et*: “and to the aforementioned …”], and others to others. But because some of them also contain matters of personal and domestic concern, they are not arranged for publication. He also composed the *Chronicles*. He wrote, for the benefit of many, the Life of blessed Martin, monk and bishop, a man illustrious for signs [Note: “And wonders” does not appear in the Brixian manuscript.] and miracles and virtues. He also composed, in the form of a *Dialogue*, the conversation of Postumianus and Gallus, held with himself as mediator and judge, concerning the manner of life of the monks of the East [Col. 0087A], comprising it in two sections [Note: Miraeus, Fabricius, and others have “in three divisions,” incorrectly. “In two divisions” is found in the Capitular and Parma editions, supported by the Brixian and Venetian manuscripts, which also have “in two divisions”; other editions have “in three divisions.”]. In the first of these he reports that in his own time a decree was issued at Alexandria by a synod [Note: The Hamburg and Veronese editions read “at the synod.” Some other printed books incorrectly have “a decree issued at the Alexandrian synod of bishops.”], namely that Origen should be read by the wise with caution [Note: “And more cautiously.” This reading is found in the Capitular and Brixian manuscripts, the Parma edition, and others.], as a good author, but should be rejected by those of lesser understanding as evil [Note: In the Capitular and Brixian manuscripts and the Parma edition: “by those of lesser understanding.” The Hamburg and Veronese editions read “should be refuted”; the Venetian manuscript has the same reading.]. In his old age, having been deceived by the Pelagians and recognizing the fault of loquacity, he maintained silence until death, so that by silence he might thoroughly correct the sin he had contracted by speaking [Note: Thus all the books except the Hamburg and Veronese editions, which have “repenting,” from the Corbie manuscript. Its variant readings are given in volume II of the Paris edition of Saint Jerome.].

## VIII. GELASIUS

Gelasius, at the council of seventy bishops, in the decree on apocryphal Scriptures issued in 496:

> The little works of Postumianus and Gallus are apocryphal.

## IX. VIGILIUS OF TAPSA

Vigilius of Tapsa, who flourished toward the end of the fifth century—not as translator but as the author of the disputation of Athanasius against Arius—in the preface:

> But if he recalls what Sulpicius Severus of blessed memory set down in his *Chronicles*, saying, “Two Ariuses hissed like two serpents from one mouth,” he will plainly discover that there were two Ariuses.

[Note: The words quoted are not actually Severus’s own. See *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 35.]

## X. EUGIPPIUS

Eugippius the presbyter, disciple of Saint Severinus, apostle of Noricum, in the Life of Severinus, which, as he himself testifies in his letter to the deacon Paschasius, he wrote two years after the consulship of Importunus—that is, in the consulship of Felix and Secundinus—in the year of Christ 511:

> Sulpicius Severus also reports, on the account of Postumianus, that a man remarkable for great virtues and signs, in order to drive from his heart the vanity of boasting into which he had fallen, begged that the devil’s power over him might be permitted for five months, so that he might become like those whom he himself had healed.

## XI. VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS

Venantius Fortunatus, who later became bishop of Poitiers, in the Life of Martin, written before the year 570, book II, verses 467 ff.:

> Severus first sang his deeds in prose;  
> Then blessed Paulinus thundered them forth in verse.  
> Each illustrious narrator, wishing to equal him [Note: Read “wishing.”],  
> Yet both, overcome by the subject, yield even in their verse.

And book III, verses 10 ff.:

> Before, upon the Adriatic waves, I seemed to spread my sails  
> With Sulpicius as guide, from whose well-formed mouth  
> A sweet style brought forth the sacred deeds of Martin,  
> Which I now run through and close in two books of verse.

And shortly afterward:

> Yet while I seek the heights, let Gallus resound in my ear  
> The blessed deeds of the man [Note: Perhaps read “by which.”], that he may soften the swelling of the wave,  
> And lighten the road with the pleasant salt of his sweet tale.  
>   
> Behold, I am carried out upon the strait, and the shores flee from sight:  
> Let Gallus row here, and Martin guide the sails.

## XII. GREGORY OF TOURS

Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book I, chapter 7:

> Severus relates that this holocaust was offered on Mount Calvary, where the Lord was crucified.

[Note: He is speaking of Abraham’s sacrifice. But this passage is not found in Severus.]

The same author, book II of the *History of the Franks*, in the preface:

> Thus Eusebius, Severus, Jerome in their *Chronicles*, and Orosius alike wove together the wars of kings and the virtues of martyrs … Proceeding, therefore, through the histories of the aforementioned authors, we shall, by the Lord’s command, discuss what was done afterward.

The same author, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 31:

> We read that three books were written by Sulpicius Severus concerning his [Saint Martin’s] life.

The same author, book I of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*:

> There are many who have committed the virtues of Saint Martin to writing, either in verse or in prose. The first among them was that Sulpicius Severus, whose love for the holy man was so fervent that, while Martin was still living in this world, he wrote one book about the wonders of his life. After the blessed man’s death he wrote two books, which he wished to be called *Dialogues*. In them he inserted, on the report of Postumianus, certain matters concerning the virtues of hermits and anchorites. Yet he was unable to find our Martin inferior in anything; he equated him with the apostles and the earlier saints, even saying: “Happy indeed is Greece, which was worthy to hear an Apostle preaching; but neither did Christ abandon Gaul, for the Lord granted it to have Martin.”

The same author, in the letter prefixed to the four books *On the Miracles of Saint Martin the Bishop*:

> Those miracles which our Lord God has deigned to perform through blessed Martin, his bishop, while Martin was still in the body, he continues daily to confirm for the strengthening of the faith of believers. He who now adorns Martin’s tomb with miracles is the same one who worked through him when he was in the world; and he who then sent a bishop to the doomed nations now grants benefits to Christians through him. Let no one, therefore, doubt the virtues of former times when he sees the gifts of present signs being distributed, when he sees the lame raised, the blind …

> I, for my part, by introducing the testimony of the book which was written earlier about his life [Note: Either these words refer separately to Severus’s little works, or to the works of Severus, Paulinus, and Fortunatus bound together in a single volume.], shall commit to future memory the miracles of the present time, as far as I recall them, with the Lord’s command … Would that Severus or Paulinus were alive, or that Fortunatus at least were present, to describe these things—the miracles of Saint Martin!

The same author, book I of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 4, at the end:

> But if we turn to the history of Severus, at that very hour he wrote in the book of his *Life* that it had been revealed to him [Note: Others read “when he was with the book,” which is better. If we read “in the book,” this indicates the letter to Aurelius.].

The same author, book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 32:

> When we see such miracles as those we have written about taking place daily, what will those wretched men say who declare that Severus lied in the Life of the holy bishop? For I heard a certain wicked man, possessed, as I believe, by an evil spirit, saying that it could not have happened that oil increased at Martin’s blessing; nor, he claimed, could it have happened that when a flask slipped and fell upon a marble pavement, it remained undamaged [Note: These two miracles are found in *Dialogue* III, chapter 3. As we have seen, Gregory included these *Dialogues* with the Life of Saint Martin, just as he included the letters in the preceding testimony.].

The same author, in the same work, chapter 49:

> The festal day of the saint’s solemnity had arrived, and a great crowd of people had gathered … Finally, as the priests who had come proceeded to celebrate the solemn rites, and the reader whose duty it was to read had arrived, he seized the book and began to read the Life of the holy Confessor, and so forth.

[Note: Add chapter 29 of the same book II and chapter 42 of book III, in which places Severus’s book also seems to be under discussion.]

## XIII. JONAS, MONK OF BOBBIO

Jonas, a monk of Bobbio, nearly contemporary with Saint Columbanus, the abbot who died in 615, and author of whose Life he was—the Life is found in volume II of the Benedictine edition by P. Mabillon and, somewhat interpolated, in Surius—writes in the preface to that Life:

> Blessed Athanasius [wrote] of Antony; Jerome, of Paul and Hilarion, and of the others whom the practice of a good life rendered praiseworthy. Postumianus, Severus, and Gallus left to our generations the memory of Martin, that excellent shepherd. Many others [did likewise], and so forth.

## XIV. PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT PROJECTUS

In the prologue to the Life of Saint Projectus, bishop and martyr, whose death Sigebert records under the year 670, by an anonymous contemporary author:

> But, to come to the holy anchorites and confessors: blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, published the deeds of Antony; the holy and most learned man Jerome, those of Paul and Hilarion, and of the others whom the practice of a good life rendered praiseworthy. Postumianus, Severus, and Gallus published in their little writings the Life of Martin, that excellent shepherd … Jonas too, a man eloquent in our own time, most lucidly published the Life of blessed Columbanus and of his disciples Athala, Eustasius, and Bertulf.

## XV. FROM THE EPITOME OF THE CANONS

From the *Epitome of the Canons*, which Adrian, the supreme pontiff, presented to Charlemagne at Rome around the year 774 [Note: Thus in the collection of the Councils and in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, volume II. See, however, what Sirmond noted there.]

> It should be known that Hosius was an honored member among the 318 Fathers of the Council of Nicaea and was sent from the apostolic see with the presbyters Victor and Vincentius [Note: Perhaps “who remained in Spain.”], and is read to have remained bodily in Spain until the reign of Constantius. Yet at the end of his life he behaved quite foolishly, as Sulpicius Severus testifies in his *Chronicles*, asserting that the emperor Constantius had compelled the extremely numerous Council of Rimini, which he had summoned against the Catholic faith, to subscribe to the Arian heresy. Hence also, and so forth.

## XVI. FROM A HISTORICAL CHRONOGRAPHIC COLLECTION

From a historical and chronological collection drawn from Hydatius by a certain Gaul, a contemporary of Charlemagne:

> In the eleventh year of the reign of Arcadius, Martin, the bishop, full of the Holy Spirit and an apostolic man, departed to the Lord after laying aside the flesh. His life and the miracles he performed were written by Severus, a supreme man [Note: Others read “in the fifteenth year,” or *XV*. See Tillemont, *Life of Martin*, note 12, column 781.], his own disciple, who also wrote *Chronicles* different from these, beginning with Genesis, with complete clarity [Note: Vossius and others had this passage before them when they wrote that Hydatius praised Severus. Hence Tillemont writes in the place cited above: “But I have not been able to find this passage in Hydatius.”].

## XVII. RABANUS’S MARTYROLOGY

From volume II, part II, of Henri Canisius’s *Treasury of Ecclesiastical Monuments*, under the year 804:

> November 11. The deposition of blessed Martin, archbishop of Tours and Confessor, whose life and teaching, through the miracles which the Lord performed through him, are almost universally clear to the faithful. There is no need for us to mention anything further here, because Sulpicius Severus has plainly described his life, virtues, and signs in lucid speech; and Gregory, bishop of the same city, has discussed them most fully in his books of miracles.

## XVIII. ADO OF VIENNE

Ado of Vienne, in his *Chronicle*, which he brought down to the year 874:

> Severus the presbyter [Note: All this is taken word for word from Gennadius.], surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and learning and conspicuous for his love of poverty, dear also to the holy bishops Martin of Tours and Paulinus of Nola, dies. In his old age, having been deceived by the Pelagians and recognizing the fault of loquacity, he maintained silence until death, so that by silence he might thoroughly correct the sin he had contracted by speaking.

## XIX. SAINT ODO, ABBOT OF CLUNY

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, who died in 842, in Sermon 4, *On the Burning of the Basilica of Blessed Martin*, found in volume XVII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 266:

> God, who glorifies Martin in every way, as is reported of him, glorifies him also in this: that [Note: Read “all.”] all who have written about him, whether in prose, verse, or even rhythmic composition, and who are known to have been holy and learned [Col. 0091A], are understood to have set forth what they produced in language exceedingly sweet and appropriate [Note: Read “they brought forth.”].

[Note: In the same sermon he extracts much from Severus, transcribing it for the most part in the same words.]

## XX. HUGH, ARCHDEACON OF TOURS

Hugh, archdeacon of Tours, in a *Dialogue* concerning a certain miracle that occurred during the translation of Saint Martin, which Mabillon considers to have been written after 1012, in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, volume I:

> But to return to Martin: he too has excellent interpreters of his virtues, although he himself preferred to conceal them. He has, I say, Paulinus, an apostolic man; Fortunatus; Severus; and Gallus, who, like evangelical witnesses, spread Martin to the farthest boundaries of the world.

## XXI. HERMANNUS CONTRACTUS

Hermannus Contractus, in his *Chronicle*, according to the edition in Canisius’s *Ancient Lessons*, volume III, part I, which he brought down to the year 1054, under the year 397:

> Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, departed to the Lord after many virtues, in the eighty-first year of his life and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate. Sulpicius Severus published his life in excellent style.

From the same *Chronicle*, according to the manuscript of Urstisius, published by Pistorius in volume I of the *Writers of German History*, under the year 390:

> At this time Saint Martin, Ambrose the bishop, Jerome the presbyter, John Chrysostom, Augustine, and Severus, together with many other teachers, flourished.

In the same work, under the year 397:

> Saint Martin the bishop departed to the Lord in the eighty-first year of his life and the twenty-second of his episcopate [Note: Read “twenty-sixth.”], whose life and virtues Sulpicius Severus composed admirably.

## XXII. PETER DAMIAN

Peter Damian, who flourished around the year 1070, in a sermon on Saint Martin:

> That noble Confessor, the glory of priests, the jewel of bishops, the model of clerics, the light of monks, appointed a solemn day for our entire community. This is Martin, exalted by the power of miracles, who filled the whole world with the light of his knowledge. Egypt, the mother of religion and the most fruitful nurse of hermits, set Martin as an example to so many sons. The fame of his name grew immeasurably and dared to intrude even into the dignity of the apostles, whose hands handled the word of life, who proclaimed the Son of Man among the sons of men by the blessed service of their voice. The memory of so great a bishop spread throughout the whole earth, and wherever the Christian faith resounds, there the life of Martin sounds.

And shortly afterward:

> Severus, an illustrious orator, so ennobled his deeds and life by the distinction of his language that he both presented the history with a narrative full of truth and adorned it in many ways according to the laws of rhetoric.

## XXIII. SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX

Sigebert, a monk of Gembloux, in his *Chronicle*, which he brought down to the year 1112, under the year 399:

> At this time holy and learned men flourished in the Church: John Chrysostom … and, in Aquitaine, Severus, who wrote the Life of Saint Martin and many other works. In his old age he was led astray by the Pelagians and maintained silence until death, correcting by silence what he had sinned in speaking.

## XXIV. SAINT ULDARICUS

Saint Uldaricus, in the collection of the *Ancient Customs of the Monastery of Cluny*, compiled in 1110, chapter 43, concerning the Feast of Saint Martin:

> Since his Life was composed in lucid style and is so remarkable for the virtues of the man, our holy Fathers, just as on the Assumption of Saint Mary, likewise here did not wish any other Gospel to be proclaimed at his deposition, or any other homily to be read, than the Life itself [Note: That the Life of Saint Martin was formerly read in the church of Tours is established by Gregory of Tours.].

## XXV. HONORIUS OF AUTUN

Honorius of Autun, who flourished around the year 1130, book II *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 19:

> Severus the presbyter, surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and learning, wrote the Life of Martin, bishop of Tours, and of Paulinus of Nola [Note: Aubertus Miraeus notes that Honorius was mistaken when he wrote that Severus had written the Life of Paulinus.], as well as many exhortatory letters to his sister concerning love of God and contempt of the world. He also wrote two letters to Paulinus and others to other people. He flourished under Arcadius.

## XXVI. SAINT BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX

Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who died in 1153, frequently uses the words of Severus in a sermon he delivered on the feast of Saint Martin, and names him explicitly when he says:

> Hear also his gentleness, as that Sulpicius of his own writes: [Note: These words are found near the end of the Life of Saint Martin.] “He had assumed such patience toward every injury that, although he was the supreme priest, he could be injured with impunity even by the lowliest clerics; yet on that account he never removed them from office, nor, so far as it lay with him, repelled them from his own charity.”

## XXVII. SAXON CHRONOGRAPHER

The Saxon Chronographer, edited by Leibniz, who continued his annals to the year 1188 and may therefore be believed to have lived at that very time, page 84:

> In the year of the Lord 407, the ninth consulship of Arcadius and Honorius, Severus elegantly writes the Life of Saint Martin.

## XXVIII. GUIBERT MARTIN

Guibert Martin, abbot of Gembloux, who is said to have died in 1208, in his eulogy or defense of Severus, found in the *Bollandists*, January 29, page 968 ff.:

> Sulpicius Severus, at first a disciple of blessed Martin and later archbishop of Bourges, was, according to Gennadius in the book he wrote on illustrious men—and indeed, as is evident from his deeds, which I read while staying at Marmoutier—a native of the regions of Aquitaine. He shone as much in the disciplines of the liberal arts as in the nobility of his birth. Thus pre-eminent at once in the twofold glory of lineage and of wisdom and knowledge, and—what is the chief distinction among men of this kind—conspicuous for the virtue of moderation, when he had reached the mature years of manhood, he wisely judged that the world lay in wickedness and counted living or thinking according to the flesh as death and folly. Leaving home and kindred, and spending his own possessions for the use of the poor, he went to blessed Martin. Received by him with courtesy and kindness, he unhesitatingly submitted himself to Martin’s discipleship, and lived with him in the aforesaid Marmoutier in the closest familiarity until he put off the flesh.

> When blessed Martin had finally been received among the secrets of heaven, this Sulpicius Severus, who had always clung wholly to his discipleship, obtained the Father’s cell for five years by inheritance, as it were, as a devout heir and inhabitant. The clergy of Bourges then drew Sulpicius away from there, although he resisted strongly, and, moved by the holiness and learning of the man and likewise by love for his teacher, blessed Martin, elevated him to be their archbishop.

> That he strayed in any respect from the rule of orthodox faith after being deceived by the Pelagians, I have read nowhere except in Gennadius. I do not know whether he himself had read this somewhere, or learned it merely from rumor, which speaks alike of things done and things not done. Nevertheless, I firmly believe that this error of his did not diminish his merits before Christ, the merciful judge who graciously forgives the penitent, just as we see in the Church that it did not obscure the glory of his holiness. For the same author who reports that he was deceived also testifies that he was corrected, saying that he imposed penance upon himself, namely, that he should maintain silence until death, so that by silence he might thoroughly amend what he had done wrong through careless speech.

> This must seem all the more remarkable because, although he was noble by birth, exalted in rank, and a bishop by office, and therefore indebted to many, he abandoned public life and sought solitude. Condemning himself beforehand to a prison-like hiding place, and at the same time mortifying his flesh by vigils, hunger, and cold, he made satisfaction to God in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart. Who, therefore, unless he distrusts the mercy of Christ, would now dare to doubt—not merely his salvation, but his supreme holiness? “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.” Why would his heart not grow warm within him toward the love of God through that solitary silence? Why would the fire of compunction not blaze in his meditation? Why would the pain of his offense not return to him, since he had leisure for nothing else?

> Tested, therefore, by that fire in the furnace of divine trial, and sprinkled with the fountain of tears by which night after night—that is, with each recollection of the same offense—he watered the bed of his conscience, he was cleansed with the hyssop of purifying humiliation; plainly he was washed from his great transgression and made whiter than snow. Thus, passing in a manner through fire and water, he was brought out at the proper time into refreshment.

> Therefore, although this fruitful tree once passed northward when the wind of deceit stealthily carried it away, it did not fall there or remain there. Rather, when God blew again, it was driven back toward the south; there it fell, and there it will remain forever.

> But if no one believes my assertion concerning these matters, let him believe the entire holy community of Marmoutier, which every year celebrates the solemnity of his sacred deposition with festive worship. I myself, while living among them, attended this celebration once and again, and with the other brothers observed it with considerable devotion on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, as is customary.

> Let the authority of so great a church, therefore, be respected as it deserves, and let iniquity, which shamelessly strives to take away from him the confession and beauty that the Lord gave his holy and exalted servant in the word of glory, close and silence its mouth.

> I give thanks to you, almighty Wisdom, teacher of God’s ways, who conquered wickedness in him and did not abandon him when he had fallen into a pit and lain in the bonds of sin. Standing by him amid the deceit of those who sought to ensnare him, you freed him from sinners who opposed your grace and raised him to such glory that he is counted among the children of that same grace, and his portion is among the saints.

> Moreover, so that no one may be deceived through ignorance and accuse me also of having attributed one man’s holiness to another, let him know that this Sulpicius is one man and that other Sulpicius is another—the one whose feast is celebrated in some churches on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February. Both, however, were archbishops of the same city of Bourges. This one is called Sulpicius Severus to distinguish him from the other, while the other is called Sulpicius Pius.

> A diligent reckoner of years will also discover that this Sulpicius was much earlier than the other: this one lived in the days of blessed Martin, who was the third bishop of the Church of Tours; the other lived in the days of Saint Gregory, who was the nineteenth to govern that same church.

> Let our Sulpicius, then, illustrious and elegant, the writer of the studies and works of the most blessed Martin, be judged worthy not of a reproachful eulogy but of the highest proclamation of praise. Encasing the most splendid jewel in the gold of lucid eloquence, he displayed so bright and polished a mirror in the midst of the Church that all good people who carefully attend to themselves and desire to be saved in truth may see in him with perfect clarity what must be avoided, what must be sought, and by what means God may be pleased.

## XXIX. FROM THE CHRONICLE OF TOURS

From the *Chronicle of Tours*, which ends in the year 1222, in Martène, volume V of the *Ancient Writers*, page 925:

> Saint Florentius the abbot shines … Saint Maurilius, bishop of Angers, also shines … Sulpicius the Great, Gallus, Postumianus, Clarus, and Brictius, disciples of blessed Martin of Tours.

## XXX. ANONYMOUS

An anonymous author, in the Prologue to the Life of Saint Paulinus, from a Cluniac manuscript, in P. Le Brun’s *Testimonies*:

> Saint Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, Aquitanian by birth but, by the dignity of his lineage, a most illustrious senator of the city of Rome, was moved—above all by the example and preaching of blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, and of Delphinus of Bordeaux, together with Sulpicius Severus, a man equally noble and learned—to pass from lay and married life to the exceedingly rich poverty of Christian perfection. Trampling underfoot all the pomp and luxury of the world, he sold and distributed to the poor, in accordance with the Lord’s command, whatever he possessed in this world.

## XXXI. THE HISTORY OF THE SEVEN SLEEPERS

From the *History of the Seven Sleepers* in Gregory of Tours, column 1726 of the latest edition:

> No less in order to display the abundance of his charity [Martin’s], with which he had always overflowed completely, and the nobility of his origin, omitted by Severus, the first writer of his Life, than because of, etc., have we set pen in motion.

# THE TWO BOOKS OF SULPICIUS SEVERUS’S CHRONICLES, COMMONLY CALLED SACRED HISTORY (C)

## PROLOGUE

### I

I have undertaken briefly to compress the events reported in Sacred Scripture from the beginning of the world and to recount them piecemeal, with a distinction of periods, down to our own memory. Many people were earnestly demanding this of me, hastening to learn divine matters through a concise reading. Following their wishes, I did not spare my labor in collecting into two little books what had been set forth in very many volumes, striving for brevity in such a way that I removed almost nothing from the events themselves.

It seemed to me not unreasonable, since in Sacred History I had proceeded as far as the crucifixion of Christ and the deeds of the Apostles, to connect with these also what happened afterward: to speak of the destruction of Jerusalem, the sufferings of the Christian people, and then the times of peace, followed once more by the disturbance of everything through the internal dangers of the churches.

For the rest, I shall readily confess that, wherever the method required it, I used pagan historians to distinguish periods and continue the sequence of events, and drew from them what was lacking by way of supplement to our knowledge, so that I might both instruct the unlearned and convince the learned.

Nevertheless, I would not have readers pursue what I have arranged in abbreviated form from the sacred books as though I were recommending that they neglect the sources from which these matters were derived—unless, already familiar with those sources, they recognize here what they have read there. For the entire mystery of divine matters can be drawn only from the sources themselves.

Now I shall begin my narrative.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0095]

[Col. 0095C] II. The world was constituted by the Lord nearly six thousand years ago, as we shall set out in the course of this work, although those who have published investigations of the chronology agree little among themselves. Since this results either from God’s will or from the fault of antiquity, it ought to be free from reproach. Once the world had been created, man was made. The man was named Adam, and the woman Eve. But after they had been placed in Paradise and tasted the tree forbidden to them, they were expelled as exiles into this land of ours. From them Cain and Abel were then born. But the impious Cain killed his brother. He had a son, Enoch, after whom the first city was founded and named by its founder’s name. From him Irad was born, and from him Maviael. The latter had a son, Methuselah; and he begot Lamech, by whom a certain young man is reported to have been killed, although the name of the slain man is not given. Wise men judge that this had been set forth in advance as a foreshadowing of a future mystery.

Thus Adam, after the killing of his younger son, fathered Seth when he had already completed 230 years of age. He lived 930 years. Seth begot Enosh, Enosh Cainan, Cainan Mahalaleel, Mahalaleel Jared, and Jared Enoch, who is said to have been taken away by God because of his righteousness. His son was called Methuselah, who begot Lamech, from whom Noah was born, outstanding in righteousness and, more than all other mortals, dear and acceptable to the Lord. At that time, when the human race had already become numerous, the angels, whose dwelling was heaven, captivated by the beauty of women, desired illicit lusts. Degenerate from their own nature and origin, they abandoned the higher regions, whose inhabitants they were, and mingled in marriages with mortal women. Gradually sowing harmful customs, they corrupted the human race; from their intercourse, Giants are said to have been born, since the mixture of natures different from one another produced monsters.

III. Offended by these things, and especially by the wickedness of human beings, which had advanced beyond all bounds, God resolved to destroy the human race completely. But Noah, a righteous man, was exempted from the sentence decreed because of his blameless life. Warned by the Lord that a flood threatened the earth, he built an ark of immense size from timber and, having coated it with pitch, made it impervious to the waters. He was shut inside it with his wife, his three sons, and as many daughters-in-law. Pairs of birds and likewise animals of various kinds were also received within the same enclosure; everything else was consumed by the flood.

When Noah understood that the rain had ceased and that the ark was being carried over calm waters, he rightly judged that the waters were receding. He first sent out a raven to investigate, and when it did not return—because, as I suppose, it had been held by corpses—he sent out a dove. Since it found no place on which to settle, it returned. Sent out again, it brought back an olive leaf, a clear indication that the treetops were being exposed. Sent out a third time, it did not return; from this it was observed that the waters had ceased. Thus Noah left the ark. This occurred, as I determine, 2,242 years after the beginning of the world.

IV. First Noah erected an altar to the Lord and sacrificed victims from among the birds. Soon the Lord blessed him and his sons and gave him the command not to consume blood or shed human blood, because Cain, being free from this commandment, had stained the beginnings of the world. In that newly emptied age, one of Noah’s sons was Shem. For he had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. But Ham, because he had mocked his father while he lay asleep from wine, earned his father’s curse. His son, named Cush, begot Nimrod the Giant, by whom the city of Babylon is said to have been built. Many towns are also remembered as having been founded at that time, but I have not wished to pursue them by name.

As the human race multiplied and mortals occupied different regions and islands, they all used only one language, until the multitude gathered itself together in one place in order to be dispersed throughout the whole world. In accordance with human nature, they resolved to seek fame through some remarkable work before they were separated from one another. Thus they began to build a tower that would reach the sky. By God’s will, so that the workmen’s efforts might be hindered, they spoke in many languages different from their accustomed speech and unintelligible to one another. As a result they were dispersed all the more readily, since each easily abandoned the other as though he were a foreigner.

The world was therefore divided among the sons of Noah in such a way that Shem was contained within the East, Japheth within the West, and Ham within the central regions. Thus the succession down to Abram possessed nothing especially distinguished or memorable in itself.

V. Abram was born to his father Terah in the 1,070th year after the flood. Abram’s wife was called Sarah, and their first dwelling was in the land of the Chaldeans. From there he stayed with his father at Harran. At that time, warned by the Lord, he left his household, homeland, and father, took with him Lot, his brother’s son, and departed for the land of the Canaanites. He settled in a place called Shechem. Soon, driven by a shortage of grain, he went down to Egypt and returned again.

Lot, because of the great size of his household, separated from his uncle so that they might enjoy the more spacious open areas of a land then largely unoccupied, and settled in Sodom. That town is said to have been infamous for its inhabitants, with men attacking men, and therefore hated by the Lord. At that time the kings of neighboring peoples were under arms, although previously there had been no conflict among mortals. Against those who were attempting to attack the neighboring lands by war, the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, and the surrounding regions sallied forth to battle. Routed at the first assault, they yielded the victory. Sodom was then plundered by the victors and became booty for the enemy, and Lot was led into captivity.

When Abram learned this, he hastily armed his servants, numbering 318, and drove the kings, fierce with victory, from their booty and weapons and forced them to flee. Then he was blessed by Melchizedek the priest and gave him a tenth of the booty; the rest he returned to those from whom it had been taken.

VI. At about the same time the Lord spoke to Abram and promised that his offspring would be multiplied like the sands of the sea and the stars of heaven. He foretold that his offspring would be foreigners and that his descendants would endure servitude in a hostile land for 400 years, after which they would be restored to freedom.

Then his name and that of his wife were changed by the addition of one letter: thus Abram is now called Abraham, and Sarai Sarah. It is not the purpose of this work to explain the meaningful mystery of this matter. At the same time the law of circumcision was imposed upon Abraham.

He had a son, Ishmael, by a slave woman. When he was 100 years old and his wife 90, the Lord promised them a future son, Isaac; he had come to him with two angels. The angels were then sent to Sodom, where they found Lot sitting at the gate. Believing them to be men, he received them into his house and gave them supper. But the wicked young men of the town demanded that the new guests be brought out for sexual violation.

Lot offered his daughters in place of his guests; but since the men would not agree, because they desired what was unlawful even more, Lot himself was dragged out to be violated. The angels quickly rescued him from the outrage and cast blindness upon the eyes of the shameless men. Then, having been informed by his guests that the town was to be destroyed, Lot hastily departed with his wife and daughters. They were nevertheless forbidden to look back. But the woman, insufficiently obedient to the command—for such is the human fault by which forbidden things are more reluctantly avoided—turned her eyes back and is said immediately to have been changed into a mass of salt.

Sodom, however, was consumed by divine fires. Lot’s daughters, thinking that the human race had perished, desired intercourse with their drunken father; from this Moab and Ammon were born.

VII. At approximately the same time, when Abraham was also 100 years old, his son Isaac was born. Then Sarah expelled the slave woman by whom Abraham had fathered a son. She is said to have lived in the desert with her son and to have been protected by the Lord.

Not long afterward, the Lord, testing Abraham’s faith, demanded that his son Isaac be sacrificed to him by his father. Abraham did not hesitate to offer him. When he had placed the boy upon the altar and drawn his sword, a voice came from heaven ordering him to spare the boy. A ram was immediately available as the victim. When the sacrifice had been completed, the Lord spoke to Abraham, promising what he had already promised.

Sarah died when she was 127 years old. Her body was buried by her husband’s care at Hebron, a town of the Canaanites, for Abraham was living there. Then Abraham, seeing that his son Isaac was of youthful age—for he was then 40 years old—ordered his servant to seek him a wife, from that tribe and land, however, from which Abraham himself appeared to have originated. His only requirement was that, once the girl had been found, the servant should bring her to the land of Canaan, and should not suppose that he would return to his native soil for the sake of a wife. To ensure that he would diligently carry out these instructions, the servant gave an oath by touching his master’s thigh.

Thus the servant departed for Mesopotamia and came to the town of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. He entered the house of Bethuel, the Syrian, who had been born to Nahor. Seeing his daughter Rebecca, a beautiful virgin, he asked for her and brought her to his master.

After this Abraham took another wife, named Keturah, who is called a concubine in the Books of Chronicles, and had sons by her. But he gave his property to Isaac, Sarah’s son; to those whom he had fathered by his concubines he distributed gifts, and in this way separated them from Isaac. Abraham died after completing 175 years. His body was placed beside the tomb of his wife Sarah.

VIII. Rebecca, long barren, bore twins after nearly 20 years of marriage, in response to her husband’s continual prayers to the Lord. They are often said to have leapt in their mother’s womb. The Lord’s response declared that two peoples were being foretold in them and that the elder would be subjected to the rule of the younger.

The first-born was rough and hairy and was called Esau; the younger was named Jacob. At that time a severe shortage of grain had fallen upon the lands. Because of this necessity Isaac went to Gerar, to King Abimelech, having been warned by the Lord not to descend into Egypt. The possession of that entire land was promised to him, and he was blessed there. But when he had increased in flocks and every kind of property, he was driven out by the inhabitants because of their envy. Expelled, he settled at the Well of the Oath.

Now advanced in years and with his eyes clouded, Isaac was preparing to bless his son Esau. At the advice of his mother Rebecca, Jacob offered himself to be blessed in place of his brother. Thus Jacob, who was to be worshiped by rulers and nations, was preferred to his brother. Enraged by this, Esau plotted his brother’s death.

For fear of him Jacob, at his mother’s urging, fled to Mesopotamia. His father had instructed him to take a wife from the household of Laban, Rebecca’s brother. Such was their concern that, although they were living in foreign lands, he should nevertheless derive his lineage within his own family.

Jacob therefore departed for Mesopotamia. During sleep he is said to have seen the Lord. For this reason, regarding the place of his dream as sacred, he took a stone from it and vowed that, if he returned in prosperity, it would serve as a memorial of the house of the Lord, and that he would give the Lord a tenth of everything he might acquire.

From there he went to Laban, his mother’s brother. Recognizing him as the son of his sister, Laban received him kindly as a guest.

IX. Laban had two daughters, Leah and Rachel. Leah is said to have been less attractive in appearance, while Rachel was beautiful. Captivated by her beauty, Jacob burned with love for the virgin. He asked her father to give her to him in marriage and bound himself to seven years of service.

When the time had been completed, Leah was substituted for her. He was subjected to another seven years of service, and Rachel was then given to him. We are told that she remained barren for a long time, while Leah was fertile.

The names of Jacob’s sons by Leah are: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah. By Leah’s slave woman Gad and Asher were born; by Rachel’s slave woman Dan and Naphtali. Rachel, already despairing of childbirth, then gave birth to Joseph.

Jacob now wished to return to his father. His father-in-law Laban had given him a share of the flocks as payment for his service, and Jacob, thinking that Laban his father-in-law had treated him unfairly and suspecting deception on his part, departed secretly approximately 21 years after he had arrived.

Rachel stole her father’s household idols without her husband’s knowledge. Laban pursued his son-in-law because of this offense, but, failing to find the idols, made peace and returned. He earnestly warned his son-in-law not to take other wives in addition to his daughters.

After departing from there, Jacob is said to have seen angels and the camps of the Lord. Since he intended to travel through the region of Edom, which his brother Esau inhabited, he first sent messengers and gifts to test his brother, whom he suspected. Esau then came out to meet his brother, but Jacob still did not entrust himself completely to him.

On the day before the brothers were to meet, the Lord, having assumed human form, is reported to have wrestled with Jacob. Although Jacob prevailed against the Lord, he nevertheless understood that his opponent was not a mortal and asked him to bless him. His name was then changed by him, so that he was called Israel instead of Jacob.

When Jacob in turn asked him for the Lord’s name, he was told that it should not be asked, because it was wonderful. As a result of the wrestling, Jacob’s thigh became numb.

X. Israel therefore turned away from his brother’s household and moved his camp to Salem, the town of the Shechemites. There he purchased a plot of land and pitched his tent. The town was ruled by Hamor the Horrite. His son Shechem subjected Dinah, the daughter whom Jacob had by Leah, to sexual violation.

When Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, learned of this, they deceitfully killed every male in the town and promptly avenged their sister’s injury. The sons of Jacob plundered the town, and all its booty was carried away. Jacob is said to have been deeply distressed by what had happened.

Soon, warned by the Lord, he went to Bethel and there erected an altar to the Lord. From there he pitched his tent in the region of the tower of Gader. Rachel died in childbirth. The child was called Benjamin.

Isaac died at the age of 180. Esau, however, was powerful in wealth and had also taken wives from among the Canaanites. I have not thought it appropriate to insert his descendants in this work, so strictly abridged. Whoever wishes to inquire more diligently should return to the sources.

After his father’s death, Jacob remained in the land in which Isaac had lived. His sons had withdrawn some distance from him with the flocks for the sake of pasture; Joseph and the young Benjamin, however, remained at home.

Joseph was extremely dear to his father and therefore hated by his brothers. At the same time, because of his frequent dreams, it seemed to be foretold that he would become greater than them all. Thus, when he was sent by his father to inspect the flocks and visit his brothers, he became an opportunity for injury.

When they saw their brother, they formed a plan to kill him. But Reuben opposed them, since his mind recoiled from so great a crime, and Joseph was lowered into a pit. Soon Judah persuaded them to adopt a milder course, and they sold him to merchants who were then going to Egypt. The merchants handed him over to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s official.

XI. At about the same time Judah, Jacob’s son, took as his wife Shua, a Canaanite woman. By her he had three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er was joined in marriage to Tamar. When he died, Onan took his brother’s wife. Because he spilled his semen upon the ground, he is reported to have been killed by the Lord.

Then Tamar put on the dress of a prostitute and slept with her father-in-law. By him she gave birth to twins. At that birth something remarkable occurred: when a child first emerged, the midwife tied a scarlet thread around his hand to identify which would be born first; but the child drew his hand back into the womb and was born afterward. The infants were named Perez and Zerah.

Joseph, meanwhile, was treated kindly by the royal steward who had bought him for a price, and he managed his household and family. He himself was handsome and of striking appearance, and he had attracted the eyes of his master’s wife. Since she was consumed with desire for him and repeatedly solicited him without obtaining his consent, she falsely accused him of a crime and complained to her husband that he had attempted to violate her. Thus Joseph was thrown into prison.

Two of the king’s servants were held in the same custody. When they related their dreams to Joseph, he inferred the future from the dreams and declared that one of them would pay the penalty with his life, while the other would be released. And so it happened.

After two years, a dream was presented to the king. Since the Egyptian wise men could not explain it, that royal servant who had been released from prison reminded the king that Joseph was an extraordinary interpreter of dreams. Joseph was therefore released and interpreted the king’s dream: during the next seven years there would be the greatest abundance of crops, followed by years of famine.

Struck by this danger, and seeing a divine spirit in Joseph, the king placed him in charge of the grain supply, giving him authority equal to his own. Joseph therefore, while grain was abundant throughout Egypt, gathered a great supply and, multiplying the granaries, made provision against the future famine. At that time Egypt’s hope and safety rested upon him.

During the same period he had two sons by Aseneth, Manasseh and Ephraim. When he received supreme authority from the king, he was 30 years old; for he had been sold by his brothers when he was 17.

XII. Meanwhile, although affairs in Egypt had been well arranged against the famine, a severe shortage of grain was shaking the whole world. Compelled by this necessity, Jacob sent his sons to Egypt, keeping only Benjamin at home with him.

The brothers therefore approached Joseph, who held power over affairs and in whose hands lay the distribution of grain, and worshiped him according to royal custom. When he saw them, he cunningly concealed his recognition and accused them of having come as enemies and of deceitfully investigating the region. He was distressed, however, because he did not see his brother Benjamin.

The matter was therefore brought to the point that they promised to bring him. This was plainly so that it might be determined from him whether these men had entered Egypt for the purpose of spying. As a pledge of their promise, Simeon was handed over as a hostage; the others were given grain without charge.

When they returned again, they brought Benjamin, as had been agreed. Joseph then revealed himself to his brothers, not without shame on the part of those who had treated him badly. He sent them home loaded with grain and given many gifts, warning them that five more years of famine were still to come and that they should migrate to him with their father, all their descendants, and their entire household.

Jacob therefore went down to Egypt, greatly to the joy of the Egyptians and the king, and was kindly received by his son. This occurred in the 130th year of Jacob’s life; from the flood, in the 1,360th year. Moreover, from the time when Abraham settled in the land of Canaan to the time when Jacob entered Egypt, 215 years are reckoned.

Jacob, in the seventeenth year after he had come to Egypt, when illness was pressing upon him, charged his son Joseph to return his body to his own tomb. Joseph then brought his sons to his father to be blessed. After blessing them, although he placed the younger before the elder in the merit of the blessing, he blessed all his sons with a blessing.

Jacob died at the age of 147. His funeral was conducted with great magnificence, and Joseph buried his body in the tomb of his ancestors. After their father’s death, the brothers were afraid because of their guilty consciences, but he treated them kindly.

Joseph himself died in the 110th year of his life.

XIII. The Hebrews who had come into Egypt increased so rapidly in number that it is incredible to relate, and through the multiplication of their descendants filled Egypt. But when the king who had kindly cherished them because of Joseph’s merits had died, they were oppressed under the rule of the kings who succeeded him. Hard labor in building cities was imposed upon them. And because it was feared that their already abundant population might someday vindicate its freedom by arms, they were compelled by royal decree to drown their newborn infants in water. Nor was it permitted to conceal the bloody rule.

At that time Pharaoh’s daughter found an infant in the river and arranged for him to be brought up as her son. She gave the boy the name Moses. When Moses had reached manhood, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Moved by grief, he defended his brother from the outrage and killed the Egyptian by striking him with his foot.

Soon, fearing punishment for what he had done, he fled to the land of Midian. There he stayed with Jethro, the priest of that region, and married his daughter Zipporah. By her he had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer.

At about this time Job lived. Following the law of nature, he embraced both knowledge of God and every form of righteousness. He was exceedingly rich in possessions and still more distinguished because neither when these were intact was he corrupted by them, nor when they were lost was he depraved. For when, through the devil, he was stripped of his possessions and deprived even of his children, and finally afflicted with dreadful ulcers, he could not be conquered into committing sin in any part through impatience with pain. At last, having received the reward of divine testimony, he was restored to health and recovered everything he had lost twofold.

XIV. The Hebrews, oppressed by the increasing evil of their servitude, turned their complaints toward heaven and awaited help from God. Then, while Moses was pasturing sheep, a bush suddenly appeared to him to be burning, although—what was more remarkable—the flames were harmless. Astonished by this novelty, he approached the bush more closely, and God immediately spoke to him in words approximately like these:

He declared that he was the Lord of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that he desired to rescue their descendants, oppressed under the rule of the Egyptians, from their miseries. Moses should therefore undertake the journey to the king of Egypt and offer himself as leader of the people to restore them to freedom.

When Moses hesitated, God strengthened him by his power, granting him the ability to perform signs. Moses therefore departed for Egypt. After first displaying signs before his own people, he took his brother Aaron and approached the king. He declared that he had been sent by God and that, in God’s words, he commanded the king to release the Hebrew people.

But the king denied that he knew the Lord and refused to obey the command. When Moses, as a testimony to God’s orders, made a dragon from his staff, then changed all the waters into blood and filled the whole land with frogs, the Chaldeans performed similar feats. The king declared that everything done through Moses was magic rather than the power of God.

This continued until gnats were brought upon the land and it was filled with them. Then the Chaldeans confessed that these things were being done by divine majesty.

The king, compelled by the disaster, summoned Moses and Aaron and gave the people permission to depart, provided that they removed the calamity that had been brought upon the land. But once the disaster had been taken away, his self-willed spirit returned to itself, and he would not allow the Israelites to leave as had been agreed. Finally, battered and defeated by ten plagues upon his body and kingdom, he was overcome.

XV. On the day before the people left Egypt, they were instructed by the Lord’s commands, still inexperienced in such matters. They were to recognize that the month then current was the first of all months. The sacrifice of that day was to be celebrated as a festival for succeeding ages in this manner: on the fourteenth day of the month, an unblemished year-old lamb was to be slaughtered as a victim, and the doorposts were to be smeared with its blood. Its flesh was to be eaten completely, but its bone was not to be broken. For seven days they were to abstain from leaven, use unleavened bread, and hand down this rite to their descendants.

Thus the people departed rich in their own possessions and made still wealthier by the spoils of Egypt. Their number, from the 75 Hebrews who had first gone down into Egypt, had reached 600,000 men [lacuna]—in the 430th year from the time when Abraham had first entered the land of the Canaanites, and in the 1,575th year from the flood.

When they had departed hastily, a pillar of cloud went before them by day and a pillar of fire by night. But since, because of the intervening gulf of the Red Sea, the route led past the land of the Philistines, they were turned aside by God’s will and brought into the Red Sea, so that later, if the Hebrews despised the wilderness and wished to return to Egypt, no route across continuous land familiar to them would lie open.

They halted there and set up camp. When this was reported to the king—that the Hebrew people had wandered from their route and reached the sea lying before them, with no escape because of the intervening element—he was enraged. Distressed that so many thousands of people were departing from his kingdom and power, he hastily led out his army.

Already from a distance weapons, standards, and battle lines extending across the broad open fields could be seen. The Hebrews were trembling with fear and looking toward heaven when Moses, warned by God, struck the sea with his staff and divided it. Thus, as the waters withdrew to either side, a passable route lay open for the people as though across solid ground.

The Egyptian king did not hesitate to pursue those who were departing. He entered the sea where it lay open, but soon the waters closed together and he was destroyed with his entire army.

XVI. Then Moses, rejoicing in the safety of his people, the destruction of their enemies, and the power displayed, sang a hymn to the Lord; and the entire multitude, both men and women, did the same.

But after they had entered the wilderness and had already been traveling for three days, they were hard-pressed by a lack of water. What they found was unusable because of its bitterness. Then for the first time the stubbornness of the ungovernable people appeared. They were already turning against Moses when, instructed by God, he placed a piece of wood into the water. Its power was such that it gave the flowing water a sweet taste.

The people then moved on and settled at Elim, where they found twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. Again the people complained of hunger and rebuked Moses, longing for the servitude of Egypt together with full bellies.

Then a flock of quails was sent from above and filled the camp. On the following day those who had gone outside the camp observed that the ground was covered with small pods. Their appearance resembled coriander seed, and they were glacially white, as we often see the ground covered with hoarfrost laid over it during the winter months.

Through Moses the people were then informed that this bread had been sent to them as a gift from God. Each person was to take in the vessels prepared for this purpose only as much as would be sufficient for one day, according to the number of persons. On the sixth day, however, because it was not permitted to gather it on the Sabbath, they were to take twice as much.

But the people, as always, being insufficiently obedient to the command, did not restrain their greed according to human nature and stored some for the following day as well. What had been stored boiled over with a foul stench into worms; but what was reserved on the sixth day for the Sabbath remained intact.

The Hebrews used this food for 40 years. Its taste is said to have been close to honey, and its name was Manna. As a testimony to the divine gift, Moses is said to have preserved a full omer of it in a golden vessel.

XVII. From there the people moved on. When they were tested by a lack of water, they scarcely refrained from killing their leader. Then Moses, at the Lord’s command, struck a rock with his staff at a place called Horeb and produced an abundant supply of water.

When they reached Rephidim, however, the Amalekites were ravaging the people with raids. Moses led his men into battle and placed Joshua in command of the fighters. Then, taking Aaron and Hur with him as observers of the battle and also for the purpose of praying to the Lord, he climbed the mountain.

When the lines engaged with uncertain outcome, Joshua, victorious through Moses’ prayers, struck down the enemy until nightfall.

At about the same time Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came to him with his daughter Zipporah—who, having married Moses, had remained at home when her husband departed for Egypt—and his grandchildren, after learning what was being accomplished through Moses.

On Jethro’s advice Moses organized the ranks of the people. By appointing tribunes, centurions, and decurions, he handed down to succeeding generations the discipline that was necessary. Jethro returned to his homeland.

From there they reached Mount Sinai. Moses was warned by the Lord to sanctify the people, who were to hear the voice of God, and this was carefully carried out. But when God stood upon the mountain, the air was shaken by the loud blasts of trumpets, and thick clouds rolled up amid frequent flashes of lightning.

Moses and Aaron stood at the summit of the mountain beside the Lord, while the people remained around the foot of the mountain. Thus a multifaceted and comprehensive law was delivered in God’s words and repeatedly recited. Whoever is more curious about it should go to the source itself; we touch on it briefly.

“You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make an idol for yourself. You shall not take the name of your God in vain. On the Sabbath you shall do no work. Honor your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor. You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor.”

XVIII. After God had spoken these things, while the trumpets sounded all around, lamps blazed, and smoke covered the mountain, the people shuddered with fear and could not endure the words of God. They asked Moses that the Lord speak only to him and that he report to the people what he had heard.

The commands of God to Moses were as follows:

A Hebrew slave bought for money shall serve for six years; after that he shall be free. If he willingly remains in servitude, his ear shall be pierced.

Whoever kills a man shall pay the penalty with his life; whoever does so unintentionally shall properly be exiled.

Whoever strikes his father or mother, or curses them, shall be punished with the death penalty.

If anyone sells a Hebrew who has been stolen, he shall be put to death.

If anyone strikes his male or female slave and the slave dies from the blow, he shall be liable to judgment.

If anyone causes a miscarriage in a woman but does not deform the fetus, he shall be put to death.

If anyone knocks out the eye or tooth of his slave, the slave shall be freed in retaliation.
