If a bull kills a man, it shall be stoned. If its owner knew of the animal’s fault and did not take precautions, he too shall be stoned, or he may redeem himself by paying whatever amount the accuser demands.

If a bull kills a slave, thirty didrachms shall be paid to the slave’s owner.

If anyone digs a pit and does not cover it, and an animal falls into the pit, he shall pay the owner the price of the animal.

If one man’s bull kills another man’s bull, the animal shall be sold and the owners shall divide the price; they shall also divide the dead animal. But if the owner knew of the bull’s fault and did not take precautions, he shall give up the bull.

If anyone steals a calf, he shall restore five; if he steals a sheep, the penalty shall be fourfold. If the stolen animals are found alive in the thief’s possession, he shall restore double.

A nighttime thief may be killed; a daytime thief may not.

If anyone’s animals graze down another’s crops, the owner of the animals shall restore the damage.

If a deposit perishes, the person with whom the deposit was entrusted shall swear that he did nothing deceitfully. If the thief is found, he shall pay double.

An animal entrusted to someone and seized by a wild beast shall not be restored.

If anyone violates a virgin who is not yet betrothed, he shall provide her dowry and take her as his wife. If the girl’s father refuses the marriage, the violator shall pay the dowry.

If anyone has intercourse with an animal, he shall be put to death.

Let anyone who sacrifices to idols perish.

A widow and an orphan are not to be oppressed. A poor debtor is not to be harried, nor is interest to be demanded. A poor man’s garment is not to be accepted as a pledge. The ruler of the people is not to be reviled.

All firstborn things are to be offered to the Lord.

Meat taken by a wild beast is not to be eaten.

Conspiracies are not to be made for false testimony or for any kind of wrongdoing.

You shall not pass by your enemy’s straying animal; you shall lead it back. If you find your enemy’s animal collapsed under its burden, you shall raise it up.

You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous. You shall not justify the wicked for gifts. Gifts are not to be accepted.

The foreigner is to be treated kindly.

Work is to be done for six days; on the Sabbath there is to be rest.

The produce of the seventh year is not to be harvested but left for the poor and needy.

XIX. Moses reported approximately these words of God to the people and erected an altar of twelve stones beneath the mountain. Again he climbed the mountain on which the Lord stood, taking with him Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders.

Unable to look upon the Lord, they nevertheless saw the place where the Lord stood. Its wondrous form and extraordinary brightness are reported.

Moses, summoned by the Lord, entered the inner cloud that had stood around the Lord and is said to have remained there for 40 days and an equal number of nights. During that time he was instructed by God’s words concerning the construction of the tabernacle and the ark and the rite of sacrifice. Since these matters seemed exceedingly lengthy, I have not thought it appropriate to insert them in this work, which is so strictly abridged.

But while Moses remained longer than expected, spending 40 days with the Lord, the people, despairing of his return, compelled Aaron to make images. Then the head of a calf emerged from molten metals. When the people, forgetful of the Lord, had offered sacrifices to it and surrendered themselves to wine and their bellies, God looked upon this with righteous anger and would have destroyed the wicked people if Moses had not entreated him.

When Moses returned, carrying two stone tablets written by the hand of God, and found the people devoted to luxury and sacrilege, he broke the tablets, judging the nation unworthy to receive the law of the Lord.

Nevertheless, after rebuking many, he gathered the Levites to himself and ordered them to strike down the people with drawn swords. In that assault 23,000 men are reported to have been killed.

Moses then set up the tabernacle outside the camp. Whenever he entered it, a pillar of cloud was seen standing at the entrance, and the Lord spoke with Moses face to face.

When Moses asked to see the Lord in his own majesty, he was answered that the form of God could not be perceived by mortal eyes, but that he was permitted to see God’s back. The tablets that Moses had previously broken were restored. Moses is said to have remained with the Lord for 40 days during this conversation as well.

When he descended from the mountain carrying the tablets, his face shone with such brightness that the people could not look at him. But when he was about to report God’s commands, he covered his face with a veil and thus spoke the Lord’s words to the people.

At this point the construction of the inner parts of the tabernacle and of its furnishings is related. When it had been completed, a cloud descended from above and so overshadowed the tabernacle that it excluded Moses himself from entering.

These matters are contained approximately in the two books, Genesis and Exodus.

[Col. 0107B] **XX.** Next comes the book of Leviticus, in which the prescriptions for sacrifices are set forth; the commandments are also added to the law previously given, and everything is filled with priestly ordinances. Anyone who wishes to know these matters will learn them more fully there; for we, observing the limits of the work we have undertaken, pursue only the history.

Accordingly, after the tribe of Levi had been set apart for the priesthood, the remaining tribes were counted, and [the number] of men was found to be [ICC and III CIC]. When the people were living on manna as food, as we related above, they were, as always, ungrateful for God’s many and great benefits and desired the cheap dishes to which they had been accustomed in Egypt. Then the Lord brought an immense quantity of quail into the camp. As they greedily snatched them up, they died with the meat still at their lips; and on that day there was a great slaughter in the [Col. 0107C] camp, so that twenty-three thousand men are said to have perished. Thus the people were punished by the very food they had desired.

From there the army advanced and came to Paran. Moses was informed by the Lord that the land whose possession the Lord had promised them was near. Scouts were sent into it, and they reported that the region was prosperous in every respect, but that its peoples were powerful and its towns fortified with enormous walls. When the people learned this, great fear seized everyone’s minds; matters went so far that, rejecting Moses’ authority, they began to plan the appointment of a leader under whose guidance they might return to Egypt.

Then Jesus and Caleb, who had been among the scouts of the land, tore their garments and, weeping, implored the people not to believe the scouts’ alarming report. They too, they said, had been there with them and had found nothing on that soil to fear; they ought to trust God’s promises; the enemies would become prey rather than bring destruction. But the untamed nation, resisting sound counsel with ill judgment, was rushing toward their ruin. Moved by these events, the Lord exposed part of the people to be slaughtered by the enemy, after the scouts had been killed, as a warning to the multitude.

**XXI.** Their defiance was followed by that of those who, under Dathan and Abiram as leaders, tried to rise up against Moses and Aaron; but the earth swallowed them alive in its opening.

Not long afterward a revolt of the entire people arose against Moses and Aaron, to such an extent that they burst into the tabernacle, which it was forbidden for anyone but priests to enter. Then death attacked them in companies, and all would have perished in an instant if the Lord, appeased by Moses’ prayers, had not averted the destruction. Nevertheless, the number of those killed was seven hundred and fourteen thousand.

Not long afterward, as had already happened so often, a revolt of the people arose because of a shortage of water. Moses was then instructed by the Lord to strike the rock with his staff—a familiar procedure to him, since he had already done this before. He struck the rock once and again, and water flowed out. In this matter Moses is said to have been censured by the Lord, because through lack of faith he drew out the water only after striking it a second time. Finally, on account of this sin, he did not enter the land promised to him, as I shall show below.

Accordingly, Moses moved forward from that place and, when he was preparing to lead the army past Edom, sent envoys to its king to request permission to pass, judging that war ought to be avoided because of their blood relationship; for that nation was descended from Esau. But the king rejected the suppliants and refused passage, prepared to settle the matter by arms.

Then Moses turned his route toward Mount Hor, avoiding the forbidden road so as not to offer any cause for war among kinsmen. On this march also he destroyed the king of the Canaanite nation. He likewise struck down Sihon, king of the Amorites, and took possession of all their towns. He also defeated the kings of Bashan and Balak and established a camp beside the Jordan, not far from Jericho. Then war was waged against the Midianites, and they were defeated and subdued.

Moses died after having presided over the people in the desert for forty years. The Hebrews are said to have remained in the wilderness for this length of time for the following reason: they stayed until all who had not believed God’s words perished. Except for Jesus and Caleb, no one over twenty years of age who had departed from Egypt crossed the Jordan.

The fact that Moses was permitted only to see the promised land and not to enter it is attributed to his sin: when he had been commanded to strike the rock and produce water, he had doubted after all the evidence of his many virtues. He died in the one hundred and twentieth year of his age; little is known about the location of his tomb.

**XXII.** After Moses’ death, supreme authority belonged to Jesus son of Nave; Moses had appointed him as his successor, since he was a man very like him in his virtues. At the beginning of his assumption of power, he sent messengers throughout the camp to inform the people that they should prepare grain, and he announced a march within the next three days.

But the Jordan River blocked the crossing with its great force. There was neither a sufficient number of boats for the occasion nor any possibility of fording the river, which then flowed at full channel. Accordingly, he ordered the priests to carry the ark ahead and to stand in the river against its current. When this had been done, the Jordan is said to have been cut off, and the army was led across on dry ground.

In that region there was a town called Jericho, fortified with exceptionally strong walls and not easily taken either by assault or siege. But Jesus, relying on the Lord rather than on weapons or strength, attacked the city. He ordered the ark of God to be carried around the walls, with the priests going before it and blowing trumpets. When the ark had been carried around it seven times, the walls and towers collapsed, and the town was plundered and burned.

Then Jesus is said to have [lacuna]. From there an army was led against Gai. An ambush was stationed behind the city, while Jesus pretended to be afraid and gave ground before the enemy. When those in the city saw this, they came out through the open gates and pressed the retreating troops. Thus those who had been lying in ambush captured the deserted city; all the inhabitants were killed without any escape, and the king was captured and subjected to the severest punishment.

**XXIII.** When this became known to the kings of the neighboring peoples, they formed a coalition to drive the Hebrews out by force of arms. But the Gibeonites, a powerful people from a wealthy city, voluntarily surrendered themselves to the Hebrews, promising to do whatever was ordered. They were received under protection and commanded to bring wood and water.

Their surrender, however, aroused the anger of the kings of the nearby cities. Accordingly, they brought up their forces and surrounded their town, called Gibeon, with a siege. The townspeople, finding themselves in desperate circumstances, sent messengers to Jesus, asking him to come to the aid of the besieged.

He therefore hastened his march and fell unexpectedly upon them. Many thousands of the enemy were slaughtered to the point of annihilation. As the day of slaughter was drawing to an end and night seemed likely to offer protection to the defeated, the Hebrew commander, by virtue of his faith, turned night aside: the daylight continued. Thus the enemy had no means of escape. Five kings were captured and killed; in the same assault the neighboring cities were also added to the dominion, and their kings were put to death.

But since it was not my purpose to pursue all these matters in order, and since we are striving for brevity, I have thought it necessary merely to record that twenty-nine kingdoms were subjected to the authority of the Hebrews, whose territory was distributed individually among eleven tribes. No portion was given to the Levites, since they had been taken into the priesthood, so that they might serve God more freely.

Indeed, I would not pass over this example in silence, and I would gladly press it upon the ministers of the churches for their reading. For they seem to me not only forgetful of this commandment but even ignorant of it. Such a consuming desire to possess has now invaded their minds: they gape after estates, cultivate landed properties, lie upon gold, buy and sell, and pursue profit in everything. If some appear to be of better purpose, they neither possess nor trade—which is far more shameful—but sit waiting for gifts, and regard every honor of life as corrupted by payment, while they display their holiness as though it were for sale.

But I have gone on farther than I intended, while I am vexed and wearied by the condition of our times. I return to my subject.

As I said above, once the conquered land had been divided among the tribes, the Hebrews enjoyed profound peace. Their neighbors were terrified by war, and, made famous by so many victories, they were not attacked by anyone who dared to try them by force of arms.

During this period Jesus died, in the one hundred and tenth year of his age. I cannot determine much about the length of his rule; nevertheless, the common opinion is that he governed the Hebrews for twenty-seven years. If this is so, from the beginning of the world to the year of his death there are 4384 years.

**XXIV.** After Jesus’ death the people lived without a leader. But when war had to be waged against the Canaanites, Judah was chosen as military commander. Under his leadership affairs prospered: there was complete leisure at home and in the field, and the people ruled over nations either subdued or received by surrender.

Then, as commonly happens in prosperous circumstances, they forgot moral discipline and began to take marriages from among the conquered peoples, gradually adopting foreign customs and soon sacrificing to idols in profane rites. So destructive is every association with foreigners.

Foreseeing this long beforehand, God had instructed the Hebrews with a salutary command that they should put the conquered peoples to death. But the populace, eager for dominion, preferred to rule the defeated at the cost of its own ruin.

Accordingly, when they abandoned God and worshiped idols, deprived of divine assistance they were defeated and subdued by the king of Mesopotamia, and endured captivity for eight years. Then, under Gothoniel as leader, they were restored to freedom and held power for fifty years.

Again corrupted by the evil of prolonged peace, they sacrificed to idols. Punishment soon followed their sins. Defeated by Eglon, king of the Moabites, they served for eighteen years, until Aod, moved by God, killed the enemy king by stratagem and, gathering a makeshift army, recovered their freedom by arms. He ruled the Hebrews in peace for eighty years.

Semigar succeeded him. He engaged the Philistines and fought a battle with favorable outcome. Again, because the Hebrews pursued idols, Jabin, king of the Canaanites, subdued them and exercised the harshest domination over them for twenty years, until Deborah restored their former condition. So little hope was found in their male leaders that they were defended by a woman, although this event was set forth as a figure of the Church, by whose help captivity was driven away.

Under this leader, or judge, the Hebrews remained for forty years. Again, on account of their sins, they were handed over to the Midianites and held under harsh rule. Afflicted by the evil of servitude, they sought divine assistance.

Thus, whenever circumstances were favorable, they forgot heavenly benefits and prayed to idols; in adversity, they prayed to God. Consequently, when I am accustomed to reflect that a people bound to God by so many benefits, restrained by so many punishments whenever it sinned, and having experienced both God’s mercy and severity, was never corrected; and that whenever it received pardon for its error it always sinned again after pardon—I can see nothing surprising in Christ’s not having been received by them, since from the very beginning they are found so often to have rebelled against the Lord. Rather, it is more surprising that, although they were always sinning, God’s mercy was never lacking to them whenever they implored him.

[Col. 0110D] **XXV.** Accordingly, when the Midianites, as we related above, were ruling over them, the Hebrews turned to the Lord and pleaded for their customary mercy, and obtained it.

There was among the Hebrews a man named Gideon, just, dear to the Lord, and favored by him. An angel appeared to him as he was returning home from the threshing floor and said: “The Lord is with you, mighty in valor.” But he, in a humble voice, lamented that the Lord was not with them. He wept as he recalled that the people were oppressed by captivity and remembered the mighty deeds of the Lord, who had led them out of the land of Egypt.

Then the angel said: “Go in this spirit in which you have spoken, and rescue the people from captivity.” But Gideon refused, saying that his people’s strength had been broken, and that, although he himself was the least important, he could not undertake so great a burden. The angel persisted and told him not to doubt that what the Lord had spoken could be accomplished.

After completing the sacrifice and destroying the altar that the Midianites had consecrated to the idol Baal, Gideon returned from the harvest field to his people and brought camp against camp. The nation of Amalek had also joined the Midianites. Gideon, however, had assembled an army of no more than thirty-two thousand.

Before he engaged in battle, God spoke to him, saying that this multitude was too great for him to lead into battle. Because of their customary faithlessness, the Hebrews would attribute the outcome of the fight not to God but to their own valor. Therefore he should give those who wished permission to depart. When this was announced to the people, twenty-two thousand withdrew from the camp.

But of the ten thousand who had remained, at God’s instruction he retained no more than three hundred and dismissed the rest from military service. Thus, at midnight, he entered the enemy camp and ordered everyone to blow trumpets, striking them with great terror. No one had the courage to resist. They scattered in shameful flight, each wherever he could; but as the Hebrews encountered them from every side, the fleeing men fell everywhere. Gideon pursued the kings beyond the Jordan and, after capturing them, put them to death.

In that battle 120,000 of the enemy are said to have been killed and 15,000 captured. Then, by unanimous consent, the leadership of the people was offered to Gideon. He rejected it, preferring to live with his fellow citizens under the common law rather than rule over his own people.

**XXVI.** After the captivity that had held the people for seven years had been driven away, there was peace for forty years. But when Gideon died, his son Abimelech, born of a concubine, seized the kingdom after killing his brothers, with the cooperation of the worst men and especially the assistance of the leading men of Shechem.

When he had been exhausted by civil discord and was pressing his own people in war, he undertook to storm a certain tower into which the fugitives had withdrawn after losing their town. As he approached it incautiously, he was struck by a stone thrown by a woman and died, after holding power for three years.

Thola succeeded him and possessed the kingdom for twenty-two years. After him came Jair, who likewise held the leadership for twenty-two years. Then the people, abandoning the Lord, devoted themselves to idols. Because of this the Israelites were subdued by the Philistines and Ammonites and remained under their rule for eighteen years.

At that time, when they invoked the Lord, a divine answer was given to them: they should invoke their images instead; he would no longer show mercy to the ungrateful. But they confessed their guilt with tears and begged forgiveness. After casting away their idols and imploring God, they obtained the mercy that had been denied them.

Accordingly, under Jephthah as leader, they gathered in large numbers to recover their freedom by arms. First they sent envoys to the king of Ammon, asking him to be content with his own borders and refrain from war. But he did not reject battle and drew up his line.

Then Jephthah is said to have made a vow before the battle signal was given: if he fought successfully, he would offer to God as a sacrifice whoever first came out to meet him when he returned. After the enemy had been defeated, as he was returning home, his daughter came out to meet him. She had gone forth joyfully with tambourines and dances to welcome her victorious father.

Jephthah, overwhelmed with grief, tore his garments and told his daughter that he was bound by his vow. But she, with courage beyond that of a woman, did not refuse to die; she asked only for two months of life, so that she might first see her companions. When these had passed, she willingly returned to her father, and he fulfilled his vow to the Lord.

Jephthah held the leadership for six years. Esbon succeeded him and, after completing his rule amid peaceful circumstances, died in the seventh year. After him Allon the Zebulunite held power for ten years, and Abdon for eight. During the time of peace they produced nothing for history to recount.

**XXVII.** Again the Israelites turned to idols. Deprived of divine protection, they were subjected to the Philistines and paid the penalty for their faithlessness through forty years of captivity.

At that time Samson is said to have been born. His mother, long barren, saw an angel, who told her to abstain from wine, strong drink, and unclean things; she would bear a boy who would recover freedom and avenge the enemies. Thus the woman gave birth to a boy and named him Samson.

He is said to have possessed extraordinary strength while his head remained uncut, so much so that he tore apart a lion he encountered on the road with his bare hands. He took a wife from among the Philistines. When she married another man in her husband’s absence, Samson, grieving over the loss of his wife, plotted the destruction of the nation. Relying on the Lord and on his own strength, he openly inflicted disaster on the victors.

For after capturing three hundred foxes, he tied burning torches to their tails and released them into the enemies’ fields. Since the harvests were then ripe, the fields were easily set ablaze, and the vineyards and olive trees were burned.

He seemed to have avenged the wrong done to him by the loss of his wife through the great destruction of the Philistines. Enraged by this disaster, the Philistines burned the woman who had caused it, together with her household and father.

But Samson, thinking that he had not been sufficiently avenged, did not cease to press that hostile nation with every kind of affliction. Then the Jews, compelled by circumstances, bound him and handed him over to the Philistines. Once delivered, however, he broke his bonds, seized a bone of an ass, which chance had provided as a weapon, and struck down a thousand of the enemy.

When the heat intensified and he was overcome by thirst, he called upon the Lord, and water flowed from the bone that he held in his hand.

**XXVIII.** At that time Samson ruled the Hebrews; by his single strength the Philistines had been subdued. Therefore, lying in wait for his life and not daring to attack him openly, they bribed his wife—the woman whom he had later taken—to reveal her husband’s strength.

She assailed him with feminine coaxing and, after he had long deceived her and hesitated greatly, compelled him to disclose that his strength resided in the hair of his head. Then, lying in wait for him while he slept, she cut off his hair and handed him over to the Philistines; for previously, when he had been betrayed, they had often been unable to seize him.

They gouged out his eyes, bound him in fetters, and threw him into prison. But after some time his cut hair began to grow, and with it his strength began to return. Samson, now conscious that his power had been restored, was waiting only for the moment of rightful vengeance.

It was customary among the Philistines, when they held their festivals, to bring Samson out as a public spectacle and insult him as a captive. Thus one day, when they had provided a public banquet in honor of their idol, they ordered Samson to be displayed.

The temple in which the entire people and all the leaders of the Philistines were feasting was supported by two columns of extraordinary size. Samson was brought out and placed between the columns. Seizing the opportunity, he first invoked the Lord and then overturned the columns. The entire crowd was buried beneath the collapse of the building; and he himself perished together with the enemies, not without having been avenged, after having ruled the Hebrews for twenty years.

Simmichar succeeded him. Scripture records nothing further about him. I have found neither the end of his rule nor any account that the people had a leader. Therefore, when civil war arose against the tribe of Benjamin, Judah was appointed temporary commander in the war.

Many who have written about the chronology, however, have recorded one year for his rule; many others have passed him over in such a way as to place Eli the priest immediately after Samson. We shall leave the matter unresolved, since it is insufficiently known.

**XXIX.** During these times, as we have said, civil war broke out. The cause of the disturbance was as follows.

A certain Levite, traveling with his concubine, was forced by the approach of night to take refuge in the town of Gibeah, which was inhabited by Benjaminites. When an old man had kindly received him as a guest, young men from the town surrounded the visitor, intending to subject him to sexual violence.

After the old man had rebuked them strongly and urged them with difficulty to desist, they finally spared the stranger by taking his concubine’s body in his place as an object of abuse. They returned her the next day after mistreating her throughout the night.

But she—whether because of the outrage of the assault or out of shame, I cannot determine—breathed out her life when she saw her husband.

Then the Levite, as evidence of the terrible crime, cut her limbs into twelve pieces and sent them throughout the twelve tribes, so that he might stir everyone more readily through indignation at the deed. When this became known to all, the remaining eleven tribes formed a coalition for war against Benjamin.

Judah, as we have said, was commander in this war. The first two battles went badly; only in the third were the Benjaminites defeated and slaughtered to the point of annihilation. Thus the crime of a few was punished by a public disaster.

These events too are contained in the book of Judges. The books of Kings follow. But as I pursue the order of the years and the sequence of times, the history seems to me insufficiently continuous. For although Semigar was judge after Samson, and a little later the history records that the people lived without judges, Eli the priest is also reported in the books of Kings; yet Scripture has by no means stated how many years passed between Eli and Samson. I see, therefore, that there was an intervening period obscured by uncertainty.

In any case, from the day of Jesus’ death until the time when Samson died, 419 years are reckoned; from the beginning of the world, 4303 years, although I am aware that others disagree with this reckoning. I am conscious, however, that I have set out the hidden sequence of the years without negligence, until I reached these times, about which I admit that I am in doubt.

Now I shall proceed with what remains.

**XXX.** Accordingly, as I related above, the Hebrews lived without any judge or leader and were governed by their own will.

Eli was the priest. Under him Samuel was born. His father was Elcana and his mother Anna. She had long been barren, and when she asked God for conception, she is said to have vowed that, if a boy were born, he would be consecrated to the Lord. Thus, after giving birth to the boy, she handed him over to Eli the priest.

When he had grown older, the Lord spoke to him and announced his anger against Eli the priest because of the faults of his sons. They had turned their father’s priesthood into a source of profit, demanding gifts from those who offered sacrifices, although their father is generally reported to have rebuked them. But a milder reprimand had not satisfied the requirements of discipline.

Accordingly, when the Philistines invaded Judaea, the Hebrews went out to meet them. After being defeated, they prepared to reform their battle line. They carried the ark of the Lord with them into battle, and the priest’s sons went out with it, since Eli himself, weakened by age and with his eyes clouded, could not fulfill his office.

But when the ark was brought into view of the enemy, the Philistines, terrified by a certain majesty of the Lord’s presence, began to flee. Then, regaining their courage and changing their minds—not without the Lord—they engaged with all their strength.

The Hebrews were defeated; the ark was captured; the priest’s sons fell. When the evil news was brought to Eli, he was overwhelmed and breathed out his life, after having administered the priesthood for twenty years.

**XXXI.** The Philistines, victorious in the second battle, carried the ark of God, which had come into their power, into the temple of Dagon at the town of Azotus. But when the ark had been brought in, the image dedicated to the demon fell. After they had restored the idol to its place, it was found shattered the following night.

Then mice appeared throughout the entire region and, with their deadly bites, sent many thousands of men to their deaths. Compelled by this disaster, the people of Azotus, in order to avert the calamity, transferred the ark of God to the Gittites. When they too were afflicted by a similar destruction, they carried the ark to the town of the Ascalonites.

The latter, after summoning the leading men of their nation, decided to return the Lord’s ark to the Hebrews. Thus, in accordance with the opinion of their rulers, diviners, and priests, it was placed on a cart and sent back with many gifts.

The following was miraculous: although they yoked female cattle to the burden and kept their calves at home, they directed the animals toward Judaea without a guide, and the affection of the beasts did not call them back to the offspring they had left behind. The petty kings of the Philistines followed the ark as far as the borders of the Hebrews and thus performed a religious duty.

When the Jews saw the ark being brought back, they rushed eagerly from the town of Beth-shemesh to meet it with joy; they hurried, rejoiced, and gave thanks to the Lord. Soon the Levites, whose responsibility this was, performed a sacrifice to God and slaughtered the cows that had brought the ark.

But the ark could not remain in the town mentioned above. Accordingly, by God’s command, destruction raged throughout the entire city. The ark was transferred to the town of Kiriath-jearim, where it remained for twenty years.

**XXXII.** At that time Samuel the priest ruled the Hebrews. The people lived in leisure, with affairs undisturbed by war. Then peace was disrupted by an invasion of the Philistines.

As everyone trembled under the consciousness of sin, Samuel first sacrificed a victim and, trusting in the Lord, led his people into battle. At the first assault the enemy was routed, and victory remained with the Hebrews.

But once fear of the enemy had been removed, prosperity and tranquillity corrupted their counsels. Following the custom of the populace, which finds the present irksome and desires what it does not possess, the people desired a royal title, a thing almost always hateful to free nations, and plainly preferred—without any precedent except madness—to exchange freedom for servitude.

Accordingly, they crowded around Samuel and demanded that, since he himself had now grown old, he should appoint a king for them. But he gently tried to turn the people away from their insane desire with salutary speech. He explained royal domination and arrogant commands; he praised freedom and detested servitude; finally, he announced God’s anger against them, since corrupt in mind, and possessing God as their king, they were demanding a king from among human beings.

After these and similar words had been spoken in vain, and the people persisted in their decision, Samuel consulted the Lord. Moved by the madness of the senseless nation, the Lord replied that nothing should be denied to those who were asking for a king against him.

**XXXIII.** Accordingly, Saul was appointed king after Samuel first anointed him with priestly oil. He was from the tribe of Benjamin, born to Kish; he was modest in spirit and outstanding in appearance, so that the dignity of his body deservedly corresponded to the dignity of kingship.

At the beginning of his reign, however, part of the people defected from him, refusing obedience to his rule and joining themselves to the Ammonites. Saul promptly avenged this. The enemy was defeated, and pardon was granted to the Hebrews. Saul is then said to have been anointed a second time by Samuel.

After this, a savage war broke out when the Philistines invaded. Saul had appointed Gilgal as the place where the army should assemble. He waited there for Samuel for seven days so that a sacrifice might be offered to the Lord. But when Samuel delayed and the people began to disperse, the king, in unlawful presumption, performed the burnt offering in the priest’s place.

Samuel rebuked him severely, and Saul acknowledged his sin, though his repentance came too late.

Because of the king’s sin, fear spread through the whole army. The enemy camp, situated not far away, revealed the immediate danger, and no one had the courage to go out to battle. Many sought tears and hiding places. Besides the weakness of their spirits—for they believed that by the king’s sin the Lord had become alienated from them—the army was in extreme want of weapons. Indeed, apart from Saul and his son Jonathan, no one is said to have possessed a sword or spear. The Philistines, victorious in the preceding war, had deprived the Hebrews of the use of weapons, and no one had been permitted to manufacture either a weapon of war or an iron tool for farming.

Accordingly, Jonathan, with a daring plan, entered the enemy camp accompanied only by his armor-bearer. After killing about twenty of the enemy, he struck the entire army with terror. Then, by God’s will, they turned to flight. They neither carried out commands nor maintained their ranks, but placed all their hope of safety in their feet.

When Saul noticed this, he quickly led out his own men, pursued the fugitives, and won the victory. That day the king is said to have ordered that no one should eat until the enemies had been destroyed. But Jonathan, unaware of the prohibition, found a honeycomb, dipped his staff into it, and tasted the honey.

When the king learned this through the Lord’s anger, he ordered his son to be put to death; but the people rescued Jonathan from destruction.

At that time Samuel, instructed by the Lord, went to the king and announced in the Lord’s words that he should wage war against the nation of Amalek, which long ago had prevented the Hebrews who were coming from Egypt from passing through. The command also stated that he should not covet anything from the spoils of the defeated.

The army was therefore led into the enemy’s territory; the king was captured and the nation subdued. But Saul, overcome by the greatness of the booty and forgetful of the divine command, ordered that the captives be preserved and carried away. The Lord was offended by this and spoke to Samuel: he regretted having made Saul king.

**XXXIV.** The priest reported this declaration to the king. Soon, instructed by the Lord, he anointed David with royal oil. David was still a small boy, living under his father’s authority and serving as a shepherd of sheep; he was accustomed to playing the lyre frequently. For this reason Saul later took him into his service, and he was counted among the royal attendants.

At that time, while war was raging between the Philistines and the Hebrews and the battle lines stood facing one another, a certain Goliath, a Philistine of extraordinary size and strength, stepped beyond his own ranks and, hurling insults at the enemy in fierce words, challenged them to single combat.

Then the king promised great rewards and his daughter’s marriage to whoever brought back the challenger’s spoils. But no one from so great a host dared to attack him.

Accordingly, David, still a boy, offered himself for the battle. He rejected the armor, which burdened his youthful weakness, and went out to fight carrying only a staff and five stones. At the first strike, he hurled a stone from his sling and felled the Philistine. He carried away the defeated man’s head and spoils; later he placed the sword in the temple. All the Philistines, however, turned to flight and conceded the victory.

When the army returned from battle, the great favor shown to David inflamed the king’s jealousy. Fearing to kill one so beloved by everyone, lest envy and ruin follow, Saul resolved to expose him to danger under the appearance of honor.

First he made him a military commander, so that he might oversee military affairs. Then, after promising him his daughter, he broke his pledge and gave her to another man.

Soon the king’s younger daughter, named Michal, began to burn with love for David. Saul therefore proposed this condition for their marriage: if David brought back one hundred foreskins from the enemy, the royal maiden would be given to him in marriage. He hoped that the young man, undertaking a dangerous task, would easily perish.

But the result was very different from what he had expected. As Saul had proposed, David promptly brought back one hundred foreskins from the Philistines, and thus received the king’s daughter in marriage.

**XXXV.** The king’s hatred of him increased each day, inflamed by jealousy; for the wicked always persecute the good. Accordingly, he ordered his servants and his son Jonathan to prepare an ambush for David’s life.

But Jonathan had loved and valued David from the beginning. Therefore, after his son rebuked him, the king restrained his bloody command.

The wicked and the good, however, do not remain so for long. When Saul was afflicted by a spirit of error, David attended him and soothed his suffering by playing the lyre. Saul tried to strike him with a spear, and David escaped the deadly blow only by quickly dodging it.

From then on Saul prepared his death openly rather than secretly, and David no longer trusted himself to the king. First he fled to Samuel; then he took refuge with Abimelech; finally he escaped to the king of Moab. Soon, warned by the prophet Gad, he returned to the land of Judah and placed his life in danger.

At that time Saul killed Abimelech the priest because he had received David. When none of the royal servants dared to lay hands on the priest, Doeg the Syrian carried out the bloody task.

After this David went into the wilderness. Saul pursued him there as well, but labored in vain to destroy one whom the Lord protected.

There was a cave in the wilderness, opening into a vast recess, and David had thrown himself into its interior. Saul, unaware of this, entered the first part of the cave to relieve his bodily needs and there rested, overcome by sleep.

When David noticed this, and everyone urged him to take advantage of the opportunity, he refrained from killing the king. He did, however, take his cloak.

Then he came out and, from a safe place at a distance, addressed the king from behind. He recalled his services to him: how he had often exposed his own head to danger for the sake of the king’s reign, and how, even at that present moment, when the Lord had delivered Saul into his hands, he had not wished to kill him.

At this Saul confessed his guilt, begged forgiveness, shed tears, praised David’s piety, and reproached his own wickedness, calling David both king and son-in-law. He was so changed from his former fierce spirit that one would have thought he would dare nothing further against his son-in-law.

But David, who had observed and understood the wicked man’s character more deeply, judged that the king could not be trusted and kept himself within the wilderness.

Saul, foolish in spirit, since he had no opportunity to capture his son-in-law, gave his daughter Michal, who, as we related above, had been married to David, in marriage to a certain Phaltiel.

**XXXVI.** David took refuge with the Philistines. At that time Samuel died.

When Saul was facing the invasion of the Philistines, he consulted the Lord, but no answer was given him. Then, through a woman whose inward parts had been filled by a spirit of error, he summoned Samuel and consulted him.

Samuel told him that on the following day he would fall in battle with his son, defeated by the Philistines.

Accordingly, after the Philistines had established their camp in hostile territory, they drew up their battle line on the following day. David, however, was sent back from the camp, because they had not sufficiently trusted that he would remain faithful to them against his own people.

When battle was joined, the Hebrews were routed; the king’s sons fell; and Saul, having fallen from his horse, threw himself upon his sword so that he would not come alive into the power of the enemy.

We have little reliable information about the length of his reign, except that in the Acts of the Apostles he is said to have reigned forty years. I, however, think that Paul, whose preaching is being reported there, included the years of Samuel under the reign of this king.

Most writers who have dealt with chronology have nevertheless recorded that he reigned thirty years. We by no means accept this opinion. For at the time when the ark of the Lord was transferred to the town of Kiriath-jearim, Saul had not yet begun to reign. It is reported that King David later removed the ark from that town, after it had remained there for twenty years. Therefore, since Saul both reigned and died within that period, he held the kingdom for a very short time.

The same obscurity surrounds the chronology of Samuel, who is reported to have been born at the time of Eli the priest and to have exercised the priesthood at a very advanced age. Some who have written about chronology—since sacred history has truly recorded nothing about his years—report that he ruled the people for seventy years. But I have not discovered the source from which this authority was derived.

Amid such a mass of error, we shall follow the notation of the Chronicles, because we believe that it derives from the Acts of the Apostles, as we mentioned above. Accordingly, we report that Samuel and Saul exercised authority for forty years.

### XXXVII.

When Saul had been killed, David, in the land of the Philistines, is said to have wept upon receiving news of his death, in a remarkable example of piety. Then he went to Hebron, a town of Judaea. There he was again anointed with royal oil and proclaimed king. But Abner, who had been commander of King Saul’s army, rejecting David, established Ishbaal, the son of his king, as king. Thereafter the commanders of the two kings met in frequent battles. Abner was often defeated; nevertheless, while fleeing, he killed Joab’s brother, who commanded David’s army. Later, when Abner had surrendered himself to King David, Joab, moved by grief, ordered him to be slaughtered—though not without the king’s displeasure, since Joab had stained the king’s good faith with blood.

At about the same time, nearly all the elders of the Hebrews, by public agreement, transferred the kingship of the entire nation to David, for he had ruled only in Hebron for seven years. Thus he was anointed king for the third time, at about thirty years of age. He drove back the Philistines, who had invaded his kingdom, in successful battles. At that time he transferred the ark of the Lord, which, as we have related above, was in the town of Cariathjarim, to Zion. And when he intended to build a temple for the Lord, a divine response was given him that this was reserved for his offspring.

[Col. 0118C] He then subdued the Philistines in war, conquered the Moabites, brought Syria under control, and imposed tribute upon it; from the spoils he brought back an immeasurable quantity of gold and bronze. A war against the Ammonites then arose because of the wrong done by their king, Chanun. When the Syrians rebelled again—having conspired with the Ammonites for war—David entrusted supreme command to Joab, the commander-in-chief. He himself, withdrawn from the war, remained within Jerusalem.

### XXXVIII.

At that time he became involved in an adulterous relationship with a certain Bersabee, a woman of extraordinary beauty. She is said to have been the wife of a certain man who was then in the army camp. David arranged for this man to be exposed to the enemy at a dangerous point in the battle and killed. Thus, with the woman free of a husband but already pregnant from the adultery, he added her to the number of his wives.

Then, severely rebuked through the prophet Nathan, although he acknowledged his error, he did not escape the Lord’s chastisement. For he lost, a few days later, the son born from that illicit union, and many dreadful things happened to his household and family. Finally, his son Absalom took up impious arms against his father, wishing to drive him from the kingdom. Joab engaged him in battle, having been instructed by the king to spare him once he had been defeated. But, disregarding the command, Joab avenged the parricidal attempt with the sword. That victory is said to have been sorrowful for the king: such was his devotion that he wished even his parricidal son to be forgiven.

Hardly had this war seemed extinguished when another arose under a certain leader named Sheba, who had incited every wicked man to arms. But the entire movement was quickly suppressed by the leader’s death. David then fought frequent battles against the Philistines with successful results. After all enemies had been subdued in war, and both foreign and domestic disturbances had been suppressed, he possessed a most flourishing kingdom in peace.

Then a sudden desire seized him to take a census of the people, in order to measure the strength of his kingdom. Thus, through Joab, the commander of the army, 1,300,000 citizens were counted. Soon David was displeased and repentant over this act, asking the Lord’s forgiveness for having raised his mind to the point of estimating the power of his kingdom by the multitude of his subjects rather than by divine favor.

Therefore an angel was sent to him to announce three punishments and grant him the choice of one: three years of famine, three months of flight, or three days of death. Rejecting flight and famine, he chose death; and in a moment 70,000 men perished. Then David, seeing the angel whose right hand was striking down the people, begged for mercy and offered himself alone to punishment on behalf of all, declaring himself worthy of destruction because he had sinned.

Thus the punishment of the people was turned aside. At the place where he had seen the angel, David erected an altar to the Lord. Soon, weakened by age and illness, he appointed as his successor Solomon, his son by Bersabee, the wife of Uriah. Solomon was anointed with royal oil by the priest Zadok and proclaimed king while his father was still alive. David died after reigning forty years.

### XXXIX.

At the beginning of his reign Solomon surrounded the city with a wall. During sleep, the Lord seemed to stand before him and granted him the choice of asking for whatever he wished. But he asked that nothing other than wisdom be given to him, considering everything else of little value.

When he awoke and had stood before the sanctuary of the Lord, he gave proof of the wisdom granted him by the Lord. Two women, living together in one house, had given birth to children at the same time. One of the children died at night after the third day. The dead child’s mother, taking advantage of the other woman’s sleep, placed her own dead child beside her and took away the living one.

A dispute over the child arose between them, and finally the matter was brought before the king. The judgment was difficult to resolve, since both women denied the charge and there was no witness. Then Solomon, by the gift of divine wisdom, ordered the child to be killed and its body divided between the disputants. When one of the women accepted the judgment, while the other preferred to surrender the child rather than see it torn apart, Solomon inferred from the woman’s affection that she was the true mother and awarded the child to her, to the great astonishment of those present, since prudence had brought hidden truth to light.

Thus, in admiration of his intelligence and wisdom, the kings of neighboring nations sought his friendship and alliance, prepared to do whatever he commanded.

### XL.

Trusting in these resources, he undertook to build for the Lord a temple of immense size. After preparing the expenses for three years, he laid the first foundation in approximately the fourth year of his reign, about 588 years after the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt. Yet the Third Book of Kings reports that it was in the 440th year. This does not agree at all, since, according to the sequence set out above, it would more easily be the case that I have recorded fewer years rather than more.

But I have no doubt that the truth was corrupted through the negligence of copyists, especially after so many intervening centuries, rather than that the prophet made an error. We likewise believe that this will happen in this very little work of ours: through the carelessness of those who copy it, what we have arranged with care will be corrupted.

Accordingly, Solomon completed the work of the temple in his twentieth year. After sacrificing there and delivering a prayer in which he blessed the people and the temple, the Lord spoke to him, warning that, if they should ever sin and abandon the Lord, that temple would be leveled to the ground. We already see that this has long since been fulfilled, and shortly we shall set out the connected sequence of events.

Meanwhile Solomon, flourishing in wealth, the richest of all kings who had ever existed, and—such is always the order of events—sliding from wealth into luxury and vice, took foreign marriages contrary to God’s prohibition. When he already had 700 wives and 300 concubines, he established idols for them, according to the rites of their nations, so that they might sacrifice to them.

The Lord, angered by these things, severely rebuked him and announced his punishment: the greater part of the kingdom would be taken from his son and handed over to his servant. And so it happened.

### XLI.

For when Solomon died in the fortieth year of his reign, and his son Rehoboam began to hold his ancestral kingdom in the sixteenth year of his age, part of the people, offended by him, withdrew. They had asked that the levy imposed by Solomon, which had been extremely burdensome, be relaxed; but by rejecting the petitions of those who pleaded with him, Rehoboam had alienated the favor of the entire people.

Therefore, by universal agreement, rule was transferred to Jeroboam. He was of humble birth and had for some time served Solomon. But when he learned through the response of the prophet Ahijah that the kingdom of the Hebrews had been announced to him, Solomon secretly planned to kill him. Fearing this, Jeroboam fled to Egypt. There, having taken a wife from the royal line, and learning at last of Solomon’s death, he returned to his homeland and, by the will of the people, assumed power, as we have related above.

Nevertheless, two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, remained with Rehoboam. From them he raised an army of about 300,000 men. When the armies were advancing, the people were warned by God’s words to refrain from battle, since Jeroboam had received the kingdom at God’s command. Thus, disregarding the king’s authority, the army dispersed, and Jeroboam’s power grew stronger.

But because Rehoboam held Jerusalem, where the people were accustomed to sacrifice to the Lord in the temple built by Solomon, Jeroboam feared that religious observance might draw the people away from him. He therefore decided to occupy their minds with superstition. Accordingly, he set up one golden cow at Bethel and another at Dan, so that the people might sacrifice to them; and, setting aside the tribe of Levi, he appointed priests from among the common people.

A protest against this offense, hateful to the Lord, followed. Thereafter the kings fought frequent battles and held their kingdoms with uncertain success. After Rehoboam had completed the seventeenth year of his reign, he died.

### XLII.

His son Abijah succeeded him and held the kingdom of Jerusalem for six years, although the Chronicles report that he reigned for three years. His son Asa succeeded him, approximately the fifth after David, since he was his great-grandson. He was a devout worshiper of the Lord. By destroying the altars and sacred groves of the idols, he removed the traces of his father’s apostasy. He established a treaty with the king of Syria; with that king’s assistance he inflicted heavy losses on the kingdom of Jeroboam, which was then held by his son, and often returned from victory with spoils taken from the defeated enemy.

After forty-one years he died, suffering from a disease of the feet. Three sins are attributed to him: first, that he placed too much confidence in his alliance with the king of Syria; second, that he had the Lord’s prophet, who rebuked him for this very thing, thrown into chains; third, that, when his feet were painful, he hoped for a remedy from physicians rather than from the Lord.

At the beginning of Asa’s reign, however, Jeroboam, king of the ten tribes, died and left the kingdom to his son Nadab. Hateful to the Lord because of his evil deeds and because of both his own and his father’s merits, he did not possess the kingdom for more than two years; and his offspring, unworthy of sovereignty, was deprived of power.

Baasha, son of Ahijah, succeeded him, equally alienated from the Lord. He died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign. The kingdom passed to his son Elah but was not retained for more than two years. For Zimri, commander of the cavalry, killed him while he was feasting and seized the kingdom—a man no less impious toward God than toward human beings.

Part of the people then seceded. The royal title was conferred upon a certain Tibni, but Zimri reigned seven years before him and twelve years with him. In the territory of the tribe of Judah, meanwhile, after Asa’s death, his son Jehoshaphat began to reign, a man deservedly distinguished for his religious virtues. He was at peace with Omri. He died after reigning twenty-five years.

### XLIII.

During his reign, Ahab, the son of Omri, was king of the ten tribes, impious toward the Lord beyond all others. For he married Jezebel, the daughter of King Basa of Sidon, and established an altar and sacred groves for the idol Baal; he also killed the prophets of the Lord.

At that time the prophet Elijah shut up the heavens by prayer so that they would not give rain to the earth, and he announced this to the king, so that the impious man might recognize himself as the cause of the evil. Thus, while the waters were held back from the heavens and all places, scorched by the heat of the sun, provided neither food for human beings nor fodder for animals, the prophet himself withdrew into the danger of famine.

When he had gone into the wilderness, he lived with ravens providing food, while a nearby torrent supplied him with water until it dried up. Then, instructed by the Lord, he went to the town of Sarepta and stayed with a widow. When, hungry, he asked her for food, she replied that she had only a handful of flour and a little oil and that, after these were consumed, she expected death with her children.

But when Elijah promised in the Lord’s name that neither the jar of flour nor the vessel of oil would become depleted, the woman did not hesitate to believe the prophet’s request and received confirmation of his promises. For by divine increase the supplies grew by as much as was taken from them each day. At the same time Elijah restored the same widow’s dead son to life.

Then, at the Lord’s command, he went to the king. After reproaching him for sacrilege, he demanded that all the people be assembled before him. When they had quickly gathered, nearly 450 priests of the idols and sacred groves were summoned, and a dispute arose between them. Elijah proclaimed the Lord, while they asserted their superstitions.

Finally, it was agreed that a test should be made: if fire sent from heaven consumed the slaughtered sacrifice of one of them, the religion that produced this power would be accepted as genuine. The priests therefore killed a calf and began to invoke the idol Baal. Their invocations were vainly exhausted, and they silently acknowledged their master’s weakness.

Then Elijah mocked them, saying: “Perhaps he is sleeping. Cry out more loudly, so that he may awaken from the sleep that holds him.” The wretched men trembled and muttered, yet waited to see what Elijah would do.

But he placed the slaughtered calf upon the altar, having first flooded the altar with water. After invoking the Lord, while everyone watched, fire descended from heaven and consumed both the water and the sacrifice. Then the people fell prostrate and confessed the Lord and cursed the idols. Finally, at Elijah’s command, the profane priests were seized, led down to the torrent, and killed.

The prophet accompanied the king on his return. But when Jezebel, the king’s wife, plotted his death, he withdrew to more remote places. There the Lord spoke to him and declared that 7,000 men still remained who had not surrendered themselves to idols. This astonished Elijah, who had believed that he alone was free from sacrilege.

### XLIV.

At that time King Ahab of Samaria desired the vineyard of Naboth, which adjoined his own property. When Naboth refused to sell it to him, Jezebel had him killed by deceit. Thus Ahab obtained the vineyard, although he is said to have grieved over Naboth’s death.

Soon he was rebuked by Elijah in the word of the Lord. Having acknowledged his crime, he is said to have put on sackcloth and done penance; by this act he turned aside the punishment that threatened him.

For the king of Syria entered the territory of Samaria with a large army, having brought thirty-two kings into the alliance of war, and began to besiege the city together with the king. When the situation of the besieged had become desperate, he set out the terms of peace: if they surrendered their gold, silver, and women, he would spare their lives. But it seemed better to endure the utmost extremity than to accept such unjust conditions.

When the safety of all had already been despaired of, a prophet sent by the Lord approached the king. He urged him to go out to battle and strengthened him in his hesitation. Thus they made a sortie, the enemy was routed, and abundant spoils were found.

But a year later, having restored his strength, the Syrian king returned to Samaria, wishing to avenge the defeat he had suffered. He was defeated again, and 120,000 Syrians perished in that battle. The king was granted pardon, and his kingdom and former status were restored to him.

Then Ahab was rebuked by the prophet in the words of God, because he had spared the enemy delivered into his hands and had abused the divine favor. After three years the Syrian king brought war against the Hebrews. At the urging of the false prophets, Ahab went out against him, rejecting the prophet Micaiah and casting him into prison because he had warned that the battle would be fatal to him. Ahab was killed in that battle and left the kingdom to his son Ahaziah.

### XLV.

When Ahaziah was ill and had sent some of his attendants to consult the idol about his recovery, Elijah, warned by God, met them. After rebuking them, he ordered them to report to the king that his death would follow.

[Col. 0123A] The king then ordered him to be seized and brought before him. But those sent against him were consumed by heavenly fire. The king died, as the prophet had foretold. His brother Joram succeeded him and held power for twelve years.

In the territory of the two tribes, after King Jehoshaphat’s death, his son Joram held the kingdom for eighteen years. He had Ahab’s daughter as his wife, being closer to his father-in-law than to his father. After him his son Ahaziah obtained power. During his reign Elijah is said to have been taken up.

At the same time his disciple Elisha proved powerful through many signs, all of which are more familiar than to require the assistance of our pen: the widow’s son was raised by him; the Syrian was cleansed of leprosy; during a famine an abundance of all things was brought in after the enemies had been driven away; water was supplied for the use of three armies; a woman’s debt was paid from a small amount of oil through extraordinary increase, and sufficient means of livelihood was given to her as well.

In Elisha’s time, as we have said, Ahaziah was king of the two tribes, while Joram ruled the ten, as we related above. An alliance was made between them. They joined forces against the Syrians, and they also went out together to battle against Jehu, who had been anointed king of the ten tribes through the prophet. They perished in the same battle.

### XLVI.

But Jehu held Joram’s kingdom. After Ahaziah, king in Judaea, had been removed and had reigned for one year, his mother Athaliah seized power, depriving her grandson of the kingdom, although he was still a small child and was named Joash. The authority taken from him by his grandmother was restored to him after approximately eight years, when the grandmother was driven out by the priest and the people.

At the beginning of his reign Joash was extremely observant in divine worship and adorned the temple at great expense. Later, corrupted by the flattery of leading men and worshiped by them, he incurred God’s anger. For Hazael, king of Syria, brought war against him. When his fortunes declined, Joash bought peace with the temple’s gold, but he did not even enjoy that peace: hated because of his action, he was killed by his own people in the fortieth year of his reign.

His son Amaziah succeeded him.

In the territory of the ten tribes, after Jehu’s death, his son Jehoahaz reigned. He was hateful to God because of his evil deeds, and on account of them his kingdom became the prey of the Syrians, until, through God’s mercy, the enemies were driven away and the people began to recover their former condition.

When Jehoahaz died, he left the kingdom to his son Joash. Joash brought a civil war against Amaziah, king of the two tribes. After winning the victory, he transferred much booty into his own kingdom. This is said to have happened to Amaziah because of his offense: after entering the territory of the Edomites as a victor, he had taken up the idols of that nation.

He is recorded as having reigned for nine years, according to what I found in the Books of Kings. But in the Paralipomena and also in the Chronicles, it is noted that he held power for twenty-nine years. This was evidently suggested by the calculation that can easily be observed in those Books of Kings. For Joram, king of the ten tribes, is said to have begun to reign in the eighth year of Amaziah’s reign and to have held power for forty-one years. He died during the reign of Uzziah, the son of Amaziah, in the fourth year of Uzziah’s reign. In this way Amaziah’s reign amounted to twenty-nine years.

Accordingly, since we have followed this very calculation because we wish to trace the sequence of the years, we have accepted the authority of the Chronicles.

### XLVII.

Thus Uzziah, the son of Amaziah, succeeded him. In the territory of the ten tribes, Joash had died and made room for his son Joram; after Joram, his son Zechariah reigned.

We have not thought it necessary to record the reigns of these men, or of all those who ruled in the territory of the ten tribes at Samaria, since, intent upon brevity, we have omitted what was superfluous. We believe that, for knowledge of the chronology, the years of that part in particular should be followed which was later carried into captivity and had the longer period of kingship.

Uzziah, therefore, having obtained the kingdom of Judah, devoted special care to knowing the Lord and made great use of the prophet Zechariah. It is also reported that Isaiah first prophesied under him. For this reason he conducted wars against neighboring peoples with favorable results. He also defeated the Arabs.

He had already shaken Egypt with terror at the mention of his name. But, carried away by success and presuming upon what was unlawful, he offered incense to God, although only priests were permitted to do this. When the priest Azariah rebuked him and compelled him to leave that place, Uzziah grew angry and was covered with leprosy. He died afflicted by that disease, after reigning fifty-two years.

The kingdom was then given to his son Jotham. He is said to have been exceptionally holy and administered his power successfully. He defeated the Ammonites in war and compelled them to pay tribute. He reigned sixteen years, and his son Ahaz succeeded him.

### XLVIII.

Around this time the faith of the Ninevites is famously recorded. That city, founded long ago by Asshur, the son of Shem, was the capital of the Assyrian kingdom. It was then densely populated, supporting 120,000 men, and, as is usual in a great population, abounding in vices.

Moved by these things, God commanded the prophet Jonah to go from Judaea and announce the city’s destruction, just as Sodom and Gomorrah had once been consumed by divine fire. But the prophet, refusing the task of this preaching—not out of defiance, but because of his foreknowledge, since he saw that the Lord would be appeased by the people’s repentance—boarded a ship sailing toward Tarshish, in a region far away in the opposite direction.

When the ship had gone out to sea, the sailors, compelled by the violence of the storm, investigated by lot who was the cause of the disaster. When the lot fell upon Jonah, he was thrown into the depths as the pollution responsible for the storm. Received by a whale, a sea monster, and swallowed, he was cast out after approximately three days upon the shores of Nineveh. There he announced the command: namely, that the city would perish in three days because of the people’s sins.

Thus the prophet’s voice was heard without hesitation, as formerly at Sodom. Immediately, at the king’s command and following his example, the entire people—and even newborn children—abstained from food and drink. The beasts of burden and animals of various kinds likewise, driven by hunger and thirst, presented with the human beings the appearance of mourners.

Thus the impending evil was turned aside. When Jonah complained to God that faith had not followed his words, he received the answer that forgiveness cannot be denied to those who repent.

### XLIX.

In Samaria, meanwhile, a certain Shallum killed Zechariah, a very impious king whom we mentioned above as having reigned, and seized the kingdom. Menahem killed Shallum by treachery, following the example of Shallum’s deed.

Menahem held the power taken from Shallum and left it to his son Pekah. But another Pekah, a man of the same name, killed him and seized the kingdom. Soon Hosea killed him and lost the power he had acquired, by the same crime through which he had taken it.

More impious than all the preceding kings, Hosea earned for himself punishment and for his nation perpetual captivity from God. For Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, brought war against him, defeated him, and made him tributary. But when Hosea secretly prepared a rebellion and summoned the king of the Ethiopians, who at that time ruled Egypt, to his aid, Shalmaneser learned of it, threw him into prison in perpetual chains, and destroyed the city.

He carried the entire people away into his own kingdom, leaving Assyrians stationed in the hostile land as guards. From this the region was called Samaria, because in the language of the Assyrians they call guards “Samaritans.” Many of these adopted the divine rites, while the rest continued in the error of paganism.

In this war Tobias was led into captivity.

In the territory of the two tribes, King Ahaz, hateful to God because of his impiety, was often hard pressed by wars with neighboring peoples. He therefore decided to worship the gods of the nations, evidently because their assistance had made those peoples victorious in frequent battles. In this abomination of his wicked mind he died, after having been in the kingdom for sixteen years.

### L.

His son Hezekiah succeeded him, very different from his father in character. At the beginning of his reign he exhorted the people and the priests to worship God and delivered many arguments: they had often been chastised by the Lord and had more often obtained mercy; finally, the ten tribes recently led into captivity were paying the penalties of sacrilege; they must take great care lest they deserve to suffer the same things.

When everyone’s mind had thus been turned toward religion, he arranged all the Levites and priests for the celebration of sacrifices according to the law. He instituted the celebration of Passover, which had long been neglected. When the feast day approached, he sent messengers throughout the land and announced a day of assembly, so that anyone who had remained in Samaria after the deportation of the ten tribes might come together for the solemn rite.

Thus the sacred day was spent in a very large assembly and in public rejoicing, after the lawful religion had been restored by Hezekiah following a long interval.

Then, with the same diligence with which he had cared for divine matters, he administered military affairs. He repeatedly battered the Philistines in battle, until Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, brought war against him.

Entering his territory with a great army and devastating the fields far and wide, Sennacherib pressed the siege of the city, with no one resisting. Hezekiah, inferior in numbers and unwilling to engage, defended himself behind the walls. The Assyrian king attacked the gates, threatened destruction, and ordered surrender. He declared that Hezekiah trusted in God in vain; that he had taken up arms rather by God’s command; and that, as the conqueror of all nations and destroyer of Samaria, Hezekiah could not escape him unless he secured his own safety by an immediate surrender.

In this situation Hezekiah, trusting in God, consulted the prophet Isaiah. Through Isaiah’s response he was informed that there would be no danger from the enemy and that divine help would not be lacking.

### LI.

Not long afterward, Tharaca, king of the Ethiopians, invaded the Assyrian kingdom. On receiving this news, Sennacherib turned back to protect his own possessions. Roaring and shouting that victory was being snatched from him, he abandoned the war and sent a letter to Hezekiah filled with insults, declaring that, once he had settled matters at home, he would soon return to destroy Judaea.

Hezekiah, however, is said not to have been moved by these threats but to have prayed to the Lord that he would not allow such arrogance in a man to go unpunished. Thus, that same night, an angel attacked the Assyrian camp and put many thousands of men to death. The frightened king fled to the city of Nineveh, where he was killed by his sons and met an end worthy of him.

At about the same time Hezekiah was suffering from a bodily illness. When Isaiah announced to him the word of the Lord, that the end of his life was near, the king is said to have wept. By this he obtained an extension of fifteen years of life. After these had passed, he died in the twenty-ninth year of his reign and left the kingdom to his son Manasseh.

Manasseh, degenerating greatly from his father, abandoned the Lord and practiced impious worship. For this reason he was handed over to the power of the Assyrians. Compelled by misfortune, he acknowledged his error and exhorted the people to abandon the idols and worship the Lord. He did nothing worthy of remembrance. He reigned fifty-five years.

His son Amon then obtained the kingdom but held it for no more than two years. As heir to his father’s impiety and neglectful of the Lord, he was surrounded and killed by the plots of his own people. Power then passed to his son Josiah.

### LII.

Josiah is said to have been exceptionally religious and to have administered divine affairs with the utmost care, making good use of the priest Hilkiah.

When he read in the temple a book containing the word of God, which had been found by the priest, he learned that the Hebrew nation was to be destroyed because of its repeated impieties and sacrileges. Through devout prayers and continual weeping to God, he turned aside the impending disaster.

When he learned through the prophetess Huldah that this had been granted to him, he practiced the worship of God with still greater care, as one bound by divine benefits. Accordingly, he burned all the vessels consecrated by the superstitions of earlier kings to the idols. Profane rites had become so powerful that divine honors were offered to the sun and moon, and sanctuaries were even built for them from the same metals. Josiah reduced these to powder and also killed the priests of the profane shrines.

Nor did he spare even the tombs of the impious. What had once been foretold by the prophet was observed to have been fulfilled.

In the eighteenth year of his reign the Passover was celebrated. Approximately three years later he went out to battle against Necho, king of Egypt, who was bringing war against the Assyrians. Before the armies engaged one another, he was struck by an arrow. He was carried back into the city from that wound and died after reigning twenty-one years.

### LIII.

His son Jehoahaz then obtained the kingdom and held it for three months, destined for captivity because of his impiety. For Necho, king of Egypt, defeated and captured him and took him away; not long afterward he died in chains.

An annual tribute was imposed upon the Jews. Eliachim was given to them as king at the victor’s discretion; later, after his name was changed, he was called Jehoiakim. He was the brother of Jehoahaz and the son of Josiah, closer to his brother than to his father in character, and hateful to God because of sacrilege.

While he obeyed the Egyptian king, to whom he paid tribute, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, occupied the land of Judaea by force of arms and possessed it as victor for three years by the right of war. For the Egyptian king had already withdrawn, and, with the boundaries of their authority determined, it had been agreed that the Jews belonged to Babylon.

Thus, when Jehoiakim had completed eleven years in the kingdom and made room for his son of the same name, and when that son had aroused the anger of the Babylonian king—God evidently bringing about what had been determined, namely, to deliver the Jewish nation into captivity and destruction—Nebuchadnezzar entered Jerusalem with an army and leveled the city, its walls, and the temple to the ground.

He carried away an immeasurable quantity of gold, sacred ornaments both public and private, and all adults of both sexes. Those left behind were people whose weakness or age had made them contemptible in the eyes of the victors. This crowd, useless for servitude, was assigned to work and cultivate the fields, so that the land would not remain uncultivated. King Zedekiah was placed over them, though stripped of power and granted only the empty shadow of a royal name.

His son, also named Jehoiakim, however, held power for three months. He was transferred to Babylon with the people and thrown into prison. Released after thirty years and received into the king’s friendship, he shared the king’s table and counsels. He died with some consolation after his misfortune had been removed.

### LIV.

Meanwhile, King Zedekiah, placed over the useless crowd, although without strength, was treacherous in character and forgetful of God. He did not understand that captivity had been imposed because of the nation’s sins, and he was finally destined for the worst disasters. He offended the king’s mind.

Thus, after nine years, Nebuchadnezzar brought war against him, forced him to take refuge within the walls, and besieged him for three years. At that time Zedekiah consulted the prophet Jeremiah, who had already repeatedly announced that captivity threatened the city, asking whether perhaps any hope remained.

But Jeremiah, aware of the wrath of heaven, replied when questioned repeatedly, announcing a special punishment for the king himself. Zedekiah, enraged, ordered the prophet to be thrust into prison. Soon he regretted this cruel act, but, obstructed by the leaders of the Jews, whose custom from the beginning had been to oppress the good, he did not dare to release the innocent man.

At their insistence Jeremiah was lowered into a pit of immense depth, filled with mud and filth and made dreadful by a deadly stench, so that he might not even die an ordinary death. But the king, although impious and somewhat more merciful than the priests, ordered the prophet to be brought out of the pit and returned to the prison guard.
