Meanwhile the besieged were oppressed by the strength of the enemy and by scarcity. Everything that could be eaten was consumed, and famine prevailed. Thus, when the defenders had been exhausted by hunger, the city was captured and burned.

The king, as the prophet had said, had his eyes put out and was taken to Babylon. Jeremiah, through the mercy of the enemy, was removed from prison. When the royal commander Nebuzaradan was leading him captive with the others, he offered Jeremiah a choice: whether he wished to remain in his deserted and desolate homeland or go with him to Babylon and live in the highest honors. Jeremiah preferred to remain in his homeland.

After removing the people, Nebuchadnezzar placed over those who remained—those whom the conditions of war or the victors’ contempt for booty had caused to be left behind—a man of the same nation, Gedaliah, without any royal insignia or title of authority, since there was no dignity in ruling over a few and miserable people.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0127]

### I.

The period of the captivity has been illuminated by the prophecies and deeds of the prophets, especially by Daniel’s outstanding perseverance in preserving the law, by his divine judgment in the acquittal of Susanna, and by his other deeds, which we shall recount in order.

Daniel was captured and brought to Babylon under King Jehoiakim while still a very small boy. Later, because of the elegance of his appearance, he was taken into the royal service, together with Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

When the king ordered them to be supplied with more luxurious foods and entrusted this task to the eunuch Ashpenaz, Daniel, mindful of the traditions of his ancestors, asked the eunuch that they should eat only vegetables, so as not to share in the food of Gentiles from the king’s table.

Ashpenaz objected that emaciation, betraying the concealed disobedience of the king’s command, would expose them. Daniel, trusting in the Lord, promised that his face would be more handsome from vegetables than from the king’s foods. The promise proved true, so that the faces of those nourished at imperial expense were in no way comparable to theirs.

Accordingly, they were received by the king with honor and favor and, within a short time, surpassed all the king’s closest attendants in prudence and discipline.

At the same time, a certain Susanna, married to Jehoiakim and a woman of remarkable beauty, was desired by two elders. When she refused to consent to their immoral advances, they attacked her with a false accusation. The elders reported that they had caught a young man with her in a secluded place, but that he had escaped the old men’s hands through youthful agility.

Thus the elders were believed, and Susanna was condemned by the judgment of the people. When she was being led to punishment according to the law, Daniel, then twelve years old, rebuked the Jews for condemning an innocent woman to death. He requested that she be brought back to judgment and that the case be heard again.

The crowd of Jews who were present believed that, with the Lord’s assistance, a boy of such a young and despised age would not have risen to such firmness without cause. Showing him their support, they returned to the assembly.

[Col. 0129A] The trial was reopened, and Daniel was given a place among the elders. He ordered the accusers to be separated and asked one of them under what kind of tree he had caught the adulteress. The differing answers exposed the falsehood. Susanna was acquitted, while the elders who had endangered the innocent woman were condemned to death.

## II.

At that time Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream wondrous for its revelation of things to come. Since he could not work out its interpretation by himself, he summoned the Chaldeans to interpret it—men who appeared, through magical arts and the entrails of sacrificial victims, to know hidden things and foretell the future. Soon, however, fearing that, as men commonly do, they might infer from the dream not what was true but what pleased the king, he concealed what he had seen and demanded that they tell him the dream itself, if there truly were divination in it [Col. 0129B]. Only then, he said, would he trust their interpretation, if they first tested their skill by declaring the dream.

But they refused so great a task and admitted that it was beyond human ability. The king, moved because men were deceiving others through their false profession of divination, while under the pressure of the present matter they confessed that they knew nothing, ordered them punished by royal edict; and all practitioners of this art were openly put to death. When Daniel learned of this, he approached the king’s chief official and promised to disclose both the dream and its interpretation. The matter was reported to the king, and Daniel was summoned. Since the mystery had already been revealed to him by the Lord, he related the king’s vision and its explanation.

But the matter requires us to set forth the king’s dream, the prophet’s interpretation, and the confirmation supplied by what followed [Col. 0129C]. In his sleep the king had seen an image with a head of gold; its chest and arms were of silver; its belly and thighs of bronze; its legs of iron; and its feet ended partly in iron and partly in clay. Yet the iron and the clay could not join together, although they were mixed. Finally, a stone cut out without hands struck down the image; everything was reduced to dust and carried away by the wind.

## III.

According to the prophet’s interpretation, the image seen represents the shape of the world. The golden head is the empire of the Chaldeans, since we understand that it was the first and the wealthiest. The silver chest and arms announce the second kingdom: for Cyrus, after conquering the Chaldeans and the Medes, transferred the empire to the Persians. The third kingdom is foretold in the bronze belly [Col. 0129D], and we see this fulfilled: Alexander wrested the empire from the Persians and claimed it for Macedonia. The iron legs signify the fourth empire, that of Rome, the strongest of all the kingdoms that preceded it.

The feet, however, partly iron and partly clay, prefigure that the Roman empire would be divided, so that its parts would never coalesce; this too has been fulfilled. For the Roman state is now administered not by a single emperor but by several, who are always at odds with one another either in arms or in policy. Finally, the clay and the iron—materials that never unite with one another—signify the future mixtures of the human race, divided from one another. For it is evident that the Roman world, occupied by foreign peoples or rebels, or continually handed over under the appearance of peace by those who surrender, has admitted barbarian nations among our armies, cities, and provinces, and especially the Jews, who live among us without, however, passing over into our customs [Col. 0130A].

The prophets announce that these are the final times. In the stone cut without hands, which crushes the gold, silver, iron, and clay, there is the figure of Christ. For he, born not by human generation—for he was born not from the will of a man but from God—will reduce this present world, in which the kingdoms of the earth exist, to nothing, and will establish another kingdom, incorruptible and everlasting: that is, the age to come, prepared for the saints. Concerning this one matter alone the faith of certain people is still uncertain: they refuse to believe in future things, although they are convicted by past events [Col. 0130B].

Daniel, therefore, was presented with many gifts by the king and held in the highest honors as prefect of Babylonia and of the entire empire. Through his recommendation, Ananias, Azarias, and Misael were likewise advanced to the highest rank and authority.

At approximately the same time the distinguished prophecy of Ezekiel came forth, when the mystery of future events and of the resurrection was revealed to him. His book survives; it is a substantial work and must be read with care.

## IV.

But in Judaea, over which, after the destruction of Jerusalem, we have mentioned above that Godolias had been placed in charge, the Jews resented the fact that a ruler not of royal descent had been assigned to them by the victor’s decision. Under a certain Ishmael, leader and instigator of a wicked conspiracy, they set an ambush for him at a banquet and killed him.

Those who had not been involved in the crime, wishing to avenge the deed, quickly took up arms against Ishmael. But when he realized that destruction threatened him, he abandoned the army he had assembled and fled to the Ammonites with no more than eight companions. Fear then spread through the entire people that the Babylonian king would avenge the crime of a few upon the destruction of all; for, besides Godolias, they had killed many Chaldeans with him.

They therefore formed a plan to flee to Egypt. First, however, they approached Jeremiah in a large group, asking for a divine response. He urged them all in God’s words to remain in their native land: if they did so, they would be protected by God, and no danger would come to them from the Babylonians; but if they went to Egypt, they would all perish there by the sword, hunger, or some other kind of death [Col. 0130D].

But the people, accustomed to evil and unwilling to obey wholesome counsel or divine command, departed for Egypt. What afterward happened to them, the sacred writings do not say, and we have no certain knowledge.

## V.

During this period, Nebuchadnezzar, elated by his successes, set up for himself a golden statue of immense size and ordered it to be worshiped as a sacred image. Since everyone eagerly complied with this—everyone’s minds having been corrupted by flattery—Ananias, Azarias, and Misael abstained from the impious service, knowing that this honor was owed to God alone.

They were therefore brought to trial under the king’s edict. The penalty set before them was a blazing furnace, so that immediate fear might force them to worship the statue. But they preferred to be consumed by the flames rather than commit sacrilege [Col. 0131A]. Thus, with their feet bound, they were thrown into the midst of the fire.

Yet while the servants of the monstrous deed were pushing the condemned more vigorously into the flames, the fire swallowed them up. The fire did not touch the Hebrews—a wondrous thing to relate, and unbelievable to those who did not witness it—while the onlookers saw them walking about in the furnace and singing a psalm to God. A fourth figure, appearing like an angel, was seen with them in the fire. When Nebuchadnezzar looked more closely, he confessed that he had seen the Son of God.

Then, no longer doubting that divine power had been at work in the event before him, the king issued proclamations throughout his kingdom and made the miracle known, confessing that honor was owed to God alone.

Not long afterward, it is said, the king was first confronted by a dream and then warned by a voice sent from heaven. He abandoned his royal power, was removed from all human society, and sustained life only on herbs; in this condition he is said to have repented [Col. 0131B]. His empire was preserved for him by God’s will until the appointed time had been fulfilled. At last, having acknowledged God, after seven years he was restored both to his kingdom and to his former condition.

After he had conquered Zedekiah, as we said above, and transferred him as a captive to Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar is said to have reigned twenty-six years. I have not found this written in Sacred History; but perhaps, while I was examining many works, I came upon this note in a book already altered by age and lacking its author’s name, in which the periods of the Babylonian kings were recorded. I did not think it should be passed over, since it agreed with the Chronicles and allowed the chronology to fit together: according to the succession of the kings whose reigns it contained, it completed seventy years up to the first year of King Cyrus—for Sacred History reports that seventy years elapsed from the captivity to Cyrus.

## VI.

After Nebuchadnezzar, his son obtained the kingdom. In the Chronicles I find that he was called Evil-merodach. In the twelfth year of his reign he died and made way for his younger brother, who was called Belshazzar.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, when he was giving a public banquet for his princes and prefects, he ordered that the sacred vessels be brought out—those which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple of Jerusalem and which, rather than being appropriated for royal use, had been stored in the treasuries. During the extravagance and license of the royal banquet, men and women alike, including his wives and concubines, all used these vessels indiscriminately [Col. 0131D].

Suddenly the king saw fingers writing on the wall. Letters drawn in a line could be seen, but no one could be found who was able to read what had been written. Terrified, the king summoned the magicians and Chaldeans. While they whispered among themselves and gave no answer, the queen reminded the king that there was a certain Hebrew named Daniel who had once revealed to Nebuchadnezzar the dream of a hidden mystery and had already at that time been honored with the highest distinctions because of his remarkable wisdom.

Daniel was summoned. He read and interpreted the writing: because of the king’s offense in profaning the vessels sacred to God, destruction threatened him, and his kingdom had been given to the Medes and Persians. This followed immediately [Col. 0132A], for Belshazzar perished that same night, and Darius, a Mede by nationality, seized his kingdom.

Darius, following the judgment of the earlier kings, placed Daniel—whose outstanding reputation was known throughout the empire—in charge of the entire realm. Nebuchadnezzar had also placed him over the kingdom, and Belshazzar, after presenting him with a purple robe and a golden necklace, had appointed him third ruler of the kingdom.

## VII.

The men who shared power with him, stirred by envy because a foreigner from a captive nation had been placed on an equal footing with them, corrupted the king through flattery. They persuaded him to decree that for the next thirty days divine honors should be offered to him and that no one might pray to anyone but the king.

Darius was easily persuaded, through the folly common to all kings who claim divine prerogatives for themselves. Daniel, however, neither inexperienced nor unaware that prayers must be offered to God rather than to a man, was accused of disobeying the king’s edict [Col. 0132B]. Darius strongly resisted the demand, since Daniel had always been dear and welcome to him, but the princes prevailed, and Daniel was thrown into the pit.

Yet when he was exposed to the beasts, he suffered no harm. When the king learned of this, he ordered the accusers to be thrown to the lions. They did not escape in the same manner: immediately devoured, they satisfied the hunger of the beasts.

Daniel, already renowned, began to be regarded as even more renowned. The king revoked his former edict and issued a new one: abandoning errors and superstitions, people were to worship the God of Daniel.

His visions also survive. In them he revealed the sequence of succeeding ages, including the number of years within which Christ would descend to earth, as indeed happened [Col. 0132C], and he plainly set forth the coming of Antichrist. Whoever wishes to pursue the matter more diligently will find it treated more accurately there; our purpose is only to weave together the sequence of events.

Darius is said to have reigned eighteen years. At that time Astyages ruled the Medes.

## VIII.

Cyrus, his grandson through his daughter, expelled him from the kingdom by force of Persian arms. Thus supreme power was transferred to the Persians. The Babylonians also yielded to his authority and rule.

At the beginning of his reign, Cyrus issued public edicts granting the Jews permission to return to their native land. He also restored the sacred vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple of Jerusalem. Thus only a few returned to Judaea at that time. Whether the others lacked the desire or the opportunity to return, we know very little.

At that time the Babylonians possessed a bronze image of Bel, the most ancient king—whom Virgil also mentions—which human superstition had consecrated, and which Cyrus too was accustomed to worship. He had been deceived by the trickery of its priests, who claimed that the image ate and drank, while secretly consuming the daily offerings brought to the idol.

Since Cyrus was on intimate terms with Daniel, he asked him why he did not worship the image, when it was plainly evidence of a living god, consuming what was offered to it. Daniel, laughing at the man’s error, denied that it was possible for that bronze—that is, an inanimate material—to consume food or drink.

The king therefore ordered the priests to be summoned—for there were nearly seventy of them—and, having threatened them, rebuked them: who was consuming the expenditure, when Daniel, a man distinguished for wisdom, insisted that this could not be done by an insensible image [Col. 0133A]?

They then, confident in the trap they had prepared, asked the king to bring in the offerings and seal the temple, so that, unless everything were found to have been consumed on the following day, they would pay the penalty with their lives. The same condition, they said, should apply to Daniel.

The temple was therefore sealed with the king’s sign. Before this, however, Daniel had secretly scattered ashes over the floor without the priests’ knowledge, so that the footprints of those entering would reveal the hidden passages.

On the following day the king entered the temple and noticed that the things he had ordered to be set before the idol had been consumed. Daniel then exposed the hidden fraud through the footprints: the priests, together with their wives and children, had entered through a hole dug beneath the floor and devoured what had been placed before the idol [Col. 0133B].

By the king’s order they were all killed. The temple and the image were handed over to Daniel’s authority, and he demolished them as he wished.

## IX.

Meanwhile, the Jews whom we mentioned above as having returned to their homeland by Cyrus’s permission undertook to restore the city and the temple. Since they were few and poor, they made little progress. About a hundred years later, while Artaxerxes was ruling the Persians, the officials in charge of the region deterred them from building. At that time Syria and all Judaea were governed under Persian rule through magistrates and governors.

The officials therefore decided to write to King Artaxerxes that the Jews should not be granted permission to restore their city, lest, true to their rebellious character, they regain their strength and, accustomed to ruling other peoples, refuse to live under foreign rule [Col. 0133C]. The king approved the governors’ advice, and construction of the city was prohibited. The work remained suspended until the second year of King Darius.

But in order that the sequence of years may be more easily arranged, we insert here which kings ruled the Persians during this period. After Darius the Mede, whom we have stated reigned eighteen years, Cyrus held power for thirty-one years. He made war upon the Scythians and fell in battle, in the second year after Tarquinius Superbus began to reign at Rome.

Cyrus was succeeded by his son Cambyses, who reigned nine years. After attacking and subduing Egypt and Ethiopia, he was returning victorious to Persia when he accidentally wounded himself and died from the blow.

After his death, two Magi, brothers and Medes by nationality, held the Persian kingdom for seven months. Seven of the most distinguished Persians conspired to kill them. Their leader was Darius, son of Hystaspes, born of Cyrus’s paternal cousin, and the kingdom was unanimously conferred upon him. He reigned thirty-six years.

Four years before his death, he fought at Marathon in a battle celebrated in Greek and Roman histories. It occurred approximately 260 years after the founding of Rome, during the consulship of Macerinus and Augurinus—hence, if the reckoning of the Roman consuls has not deceived me, 888 years ago: for I have referred the entire period to the consulship of Stilicho.

After Darius came Xerxes. He is said to have reigned twenty-one years [Col. 0134A], although I find in many copies that his reign lasted twenty-five years. He was succeeded by Artaxerxes, whom we mentioned above.

When Artaxerxes ordered the construction of the Jewish city and temple to be halted, the work remained suspended until the second year of King Darius. But, so that the chronology may be connected right up to that point, Artaxerxes reigned forty-one years; Xerxes, two months; and after him Sucdianus held power for seven months.

## X.

Darius then obtained the kingdom, under whom the temple was restored; at that time his name was Ochus. He had three Hebrew youths of outstanding loyalty as bodyguards, and one of them, by an exhibition of wisdom, won the king’s admiration.

When he was granted the opportunity to request whatever he had conceived in his heart, he lamented the ruins of his homeland and asked for permission to restore the city. He obtained from the king authority over subordinate kings and governors, so that he might hasten the construction of the sacred building by supplying the necessary funds.

Thus the temple was completed in four years, in the sixth year after Darius began to reign. This seemed sufficient for the Jews. Since restoring the city was a major undertaking, they distrusted their strength and did not dare begin so laborious a work; they confined themselves to the temple.

At approximately the same time, nearly twenty years after the temple had been completed, Ezra, the scribe of the Law, set out from Babylonia with the permission of the second Artaxerxes—not the one between the two Xerxes, but the one who succeeded Darius Ochus. Darius had already died after ruling for twenty-one years. Many followed Ezra and reached Jerusalem with him. He also brought vessels of various kinds and gifts that the king had sent to the temple of God, accompanied by twelve Levites; for it is said that scarcely this number could be found from that tribe [Col. 0134C].

When Ezra discovered that the Jews had become mixed with the nations through intermarriage, he rebuked them severely and ordered them to renounce such marriages and expel the children born from them. Everyone obeyed the command. The people, purified, observed the rite of the ancient Law.

I find no indication that Ezra did anything concerning the rebuilding of the city. I believe that he judged it more important to reform the people, whose morals had become corrupt.

## XI.

At that time, in Babylonia, there was a royal minister named Nehemiah, a Jew by race, who was especially dear to Artaxerxes because of his meritorious service.

He asked the Jews what condition their ancestral city was in. When he learned that his homeland still lay in the same ruins, he is said to have been deeply shaken, to have prayed to God with groaning and many tears, to have reckoned up the sins of his people, and to have implored divine mercy.

When the king noticed that he was unusually sorrowful during a banquet, he asked him to explain the cause of his grief. Nehemiah then lamented the misfortunes of his people and the ruin of the city, which had lain prostrate for nearly 250 years, presenting to its enemies a spectacle testifying to its calamities. He asked for permission to go and restore it.

The king granted his pious request and immediately sent him away with a cavalry escort, so that he might travel more safely, giving him letters to the governors [Col. 0135A] instructing them to provide what was necessary.

When Nehemiah reached Jerusalem, he assigned the work of the city to the people individually. Everyone eagerly carried out the orders, and the building had already advanced to the midpoint when, inflamed by envy, the neighboring cities conspired to interrupt the work and deter the Jews from building.

But Nehemiah stationed defenses against the attackers and, entirely undaunted, carried the undertaking through. After completing the wall and finishing the gates, he measured out the city by families, assigning them houses to build within it. He judged that the population was far too small for the city: there were no more than fifty thousand people of every sex and condition. So much had been consumed in the frequent wars or held in captivity from that once enormous number.

For formerly these two tribes—the remnant of which this was—had armed 320,000 men when they were separated from the ten tribes. Given over by God to destruction and captivity because of their sin, they had declined to this small number [Col. 0135B].

But, as I have said, this was the population of the two tribes. The ten tribes, led away earlier and scattered among the Parthians, Medes, Indians, and Ethiopians, never returned to their native land; even today they remain under the rule of barbarian peoples.

The completion of the restored city is dated to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes’ reign. From that time to Christ’s crucifixion—that is, the consulship of Fusius Geminus and Rubellius—there were 398 years. From the restoration of the temple to its overthrow, which was completed under Vespasian, Augustus and consul, by Titus Caesar, there were 483 years.

Daniel had foretold this long ago, declaring that from the restoration of the temple until its destruction there would be sixty-nine weeks [Col. 0135C]. From the day of the Jews’ captivity until the restoration of the city there were 260 years.

## XII.

We believe that Esther and Judith lived during this period. I have not been able to determine easily with which kings their deeds should be connected. Esther is said to have lived under King Artaxerxes, and I find that there were two Persian kings of this name; consequently, there is considerable uncertainty as to which reign her story belongs.

Nevertheless, I have thought it appropriate to connect Esther’s history with this Artaxerxes, under whom Jerusalem was restored. For it does not seem plausible that, if she had lived under the earlier Artaxerxes, whose reign [lacuna] encompassed, he would have made no mention of so illustrious a woman—especially since, as we noted above, that Artaxerxes is known to have prohibited the rebuilding of the temple [Col. 0135D]. Nor would Esther have tolerated this, had she then been his wife. I shall now relate the events.

At that time the king was married to a certain Vashti, a woman of extraordinary beauty. Since he proclaimed her appearance to everyone, one day, while he was giving a public banquet, he ordered the queen to appear so that she might display her beauty. But she, wiser than the foolish king and modestly unwilling to present her body as a spectacle to men’s eyes, refused the order. The barbarian’s spirit, provoked by this insult, expelled his wife from the marriage and from the royal household.

When a girl was therefore sought to replace her in the king’s marriage, Esther was found to surpass the others in beauty. She was a Jew from the tribe of Benjamin, orphaned of both parents and raised by her cousin Mordecai.

When she was led to the royal marriage, she concealed her family and homeland at the command of her guardian. He had warned her not to forget the traditions of her fathers and, even though, as a captive, she was entering marriage with a foreigner, not to partake of the food of the nations.

## XIII.

After she was joined to the king, she soon, as commonly happens, completely captivated his mind by the power of her beauty. He raised her to equal authority, presenting her with royal insignia and a purple robe.

At that time Mordecai was among the king’s close associates, managing domestic affairs according to his proper share of responsibility. He had exposed a plot against the king arranged by two eunuchs. From that time he became dearer to the king and was honored with the highest distinctions.

At that time a certain Haman was especially close to the king. The king ordered him to be worshiped as his equal, according to royal custom. Mordecai alone among them all scorned to do this and thereby inflamed the Persian’s hatred against him.

Haman therefore determined to destroy the Hebrew and approached the king. He claimed that there was in the kingdom a race of people living according to wicked superstitions, hateful to God and to men, and governed by foreign laws; they were worthy of destruction. It was right, he said, to devote this entire nation to extermination, and he promised the king immense wealth from their possessions.

The barbarian was easily persuaded. An edict was issued that the Jews were to be killed, and messengers were immediately sent throughout the kingdom, from India to Ethiopia, to proclaim the decree.

When Mordecai learned of this, he tore his garments, wrapped himself in sackcloth, covered himself with ashes, and went to the royal palace. There, with much lamentation, he filled the place with his complaints: it was an outrageous deed; an innocent people was being destroyed, and no cause for its destruction had been given [Col. 0136C].

Esther was roused by the sound of his lamentation and learned the matter as it stood. She was then faced with a difficult decision, because she had no permission to approach the king. For according to Persian custom a queen was not permitted to enter the king’s presence unless summoned; nor, even when the king wished it, was she admitted except at an appointed time. It happened that Esther had been kept away from the king’s sight for the preceding thirty days.

Believing, therefore, that she must dare and attempt something on behalf of her fellow citizens, and ready to die nobly in so important a cause even though certain destruction threatened her, she first invoked the Lord and entered the king’s hall.

The barbarian, shaken by this unusual event, was gradually softened by feminine persuasion and finally led to the queen’s banquet. Haman too was with him, dear to the king and hostile to the Jewish people [Col. 0136D].

When the banquet had begun to grow warm after the meal through the many cups of wine, Esther fell at the king’s knees and begged him to spare her people. The king promised that he would refuse her nothing, whatever else she might ask.

Esther seized the opportunity and demanded Haman’s death in vengeance for the people he had desired to destroy. But the king, remembering his friend, hesitated for a while and withdrew briefly to deliberate.

When he returned, he saw Haman embracing the queen’s knees. Inflamed with anger and shouting that he had assaulted the queen, he ordered Haman to be put to death. The king also learned that Haman had prepared a punishment on the cross for Mordecai. Thus Haman was fastened to the very cross he had prepared, all his possessions were given to Mordecai, and the Jews were acquitted.

Artaxerxes reigned sixty-two years, and Ochus succeeded him [Col. 0137A].

## XIV.

I shall properly connect Judith’s deeds with this sequence of events. She is said to have lived after the captivity, but Sacred History has not identified which Persian king ruled at that time. It names the king under whom these events occurred as Nebuchadnezzar—not the one who captured Jerusalem. Yet I find that no one named Nebuchadnezzar ruled the Persians after the captivity, unless, because of his impatience and similar undertakings, the Jews called whichever king he was Nebuchadnezzar.

Most people, however, think that he was Cambyses, son of King Cyrus, because he conquered Egypt and penetrated into Ethiopia. But the same sacred history contradicts this opinion: it indicates that Judith lived in the twelfth year of that king [Col. 0137B], whereas Cambyses held power for no more than nine years.

Therefore, if it is permissible to form an opinion from history, I would believe that these events occurred under King Ochus, who was the second after Artaxerxes. I infer this also from the fact that Ochus is reported in certain secular writings to have been naturally savage and eager for war. He made war upon neighboring peoples and recovered Egypt by force, although it had revolted many years earlier.

At that time he is also said to have mocked their sacred objects and Apis, whom they had received as a god. Later, his eunuch Bagoas, an Egyptian by nationality, was angered by this and avenged the insult to his people by killing the king.

Sacred History mentions this Bagoas. For when Holofernes led an army against the Jews at the king’s command, it records that Bagoas was in the same camp. I may therefore reasonably adduce this as support for my opinion, so that the king called Nebuchadnezzar was Ochus, under whom worldly historians report that Bagoas lived [Col. 0137C].

No one should be surprised that the writers of secular literature touched upon none of the things written in the sacred books. The Spirit of God prevailed so that this history, kept uncontaminated from a corrupt mouth that mixes falsehood with truth, might remain within its own mysteries alone. Since it was separate from the affairs of the world and was to be expressed only in sacred utterances, it ought not to have been mixed with other matters as though it stood on equal terms with them. For it would have been most improper for these things to be mingled with other subjects among people engaged in different pursuits or seeking different objects.

But I shall proceed to the remaining matters and, as best I can, briefly complete the account of Judith’s deeds.

## XV.

As we mentioned above, the Jews had returned to their native land, but the affairs of the people and the city had not yet been set in order. The king of the Persians then made war upon the Medes and fought their king, named Arphaxad, in battle. After the king was killed in a successful engagement, he added the nation to his empire and did the same with the remaining peoples.

He sent ahead Holofernes, whom he had chosen as commander, with 120,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry. Holofernes ravaged Cilicia and Arabia in war, captured many cities by force, and compelled others to surrender through fear.

His army had already advanced toward Damascus and struck the Jews with great terror. But unequal to resistance and unwilling in spirit to submit—for they had already experienced the evils of captivity—they gathered in great numbers at the temple [Col. 0138A].

There, with a common groaning mingled with wailing, they implored divine aid. They said that they had paid God sufficient penalties for their sins and crimes, and begged him at least to spare the remnant recently freed from servitude.

Meanwhile, after accepting the Moabites into submission and taking them as allies in the war against the Jews, Holofernes asked their leaders on what strength the Hebrews relied when they refused to submit. A certain Achior recounted what he had learned.

The Jews, he said, worshiped God and had been instructed by their fathers in a pious tradition. Formerly they had endured slavery in Egypt; from there they had been led out by a divine gift and had crossed the dried sea on foot. Finally, after conquering all the nations, they had received the lands inhabited by their ancestors.

From that point they had flourished or declined under varying circumstances and had again emerged from their misfortunes, experiencing in turn an angry or reconciled God according to their merits. When they sinned, they were restrained by the incursions or captivities imposed by enemies; but when the divine power was favorable, they were always unconquered. If at the present time they were free from sin, they could not be overcome in any way; if they were otherwise, they could easily be defeated [Col. 0138B].

Holofernes was fierce from his many victories and considered nothing unconquerable for himself. Angered that the success of his campaign should be thought to depend specifically upon the Jews’ sin, he ordered Achior to be driven into the Hebrew camp, so that he might perish with those whom he had claimed could not be defeated.

The Jews had by then taken to the mountains. Those assigned this task reached the base of the mountains and left Achior there bound. When the Jews noticed him, they released him from his bonds and led him to a hill. When they asked the reasons for what had happened, he explained everything. He was received among them and awaited a similar outcome; after the victory he was circumcised and became a Jew.

Holofernes, learning how difficult the terrain was, saw that the heights could not be approached. He therefore surrounded the mountains with soldiers and took the greatest care to prevent the Hebrews from obtaining water. As a result, they felt the siege all the more severely.

Overcome by the scarcity of water, they all hastened to Oziash, their leader, ready to surrender. But he replied that they should wait a little and expect divine assistance, and he fixed the fifteenth day as the time for surrender.

## XVI.

When Judith learned of this—she was a widow, wealthy, distinguished in appearance, but more illustrious in character than in beauty, and was then in the camp—she judged that, in the desperate condition of her people, she must dare and attempt something even at the risk of certain death.

She arranged her hair, adorned her face, and entered the enemy camp with her maidservant as her companion. She was immediately brought before Holofernes. She spoke of the ruined condition of her people and said that she had sought to preserve her life by defecting.

Then she asked the commander for permission to leave the camp at night in order to pray. He gave the order to the sentries and the guards of the gates.

After she had established her custom of going out and returning over three days and had won the confidence of the barbarians, Holofernes was seized by the desire to abuse the body of the woman who had surrendered. Her extraordinary beauty had easily moved the Persian.

She was therefore led to the commander’s tent by the eunuch Bagoas. A banquet began, and the barbarian drowned himself in a great quantity of wine. Then, after the servants had been dismissed, he was overcome by sleep before he could use force against the woman.

Judith seized the moment and cut off the enemy’s head [Col. 0139A], carrying it away with her. When she was believed to be leaving the camp according to her custom, she returned unharmed to her own people.

On the following day the Hebrews displayed Holofernes’ head from the heights and, making a sortie, advanced against the enemy camp. The barbarians then gathered around the commander’s tent, demanding the signal for battle. When they found the headless body, they were thrown into a dreadful panic and turned to flight, exposing their backs to the enemy.

The Jews pursued the fugitives, killed many thousands, and took possession of the camp and its spoils. Judith was celebrated with the highest praise and is said to have lived 105 years.

If these events occurred under King Ochus, as we suppose, they took place in the twelfth year of his reign. From the restoration of Jerusalem to that war there were twenty-two years.

Ochus reigned twenty-three years. He was more bloodthirsty than all the others and possessed a mind more than barbarous. His eunuch Bagoas killed him with poison while he was ill.

After him his son Arses held the empire for three years; Darius ruled for four.

## XVII.

Alexander of Macedon fought against this Darius in battle. After defeating him, he deprived the Persians of their empire, which had endured for 250 years from the beginning of Cyrus’s reign.

Alexander, conqueror of almost all nations, is said to have visited the temple at Jerusalem and brought gifts. Throughout the empire that he had made subject to his authority, he decreed that the Jews living there should be free to return to their homeland.

After completing the twelfth year of his reign, and the seventh year after defeating Darius, he died in Babylonia. His friends, who had waged those great wars alongside him, divided the kingdom among themselves [Col. 0139C].

For some time they administered the portions they had received without assuming royal titles, while a certain Philip Arrhidaeus, Alexander’s brother, reigned. Since he was extremely weak, the empire seemed to have been assigned to him in name only; in reality, power belonged to those who had distributed the army and provinces among themselves.

This arrangement did not last long. All of them preferred to be called kings.

The first king in Syria after Alexander was Seleucus, with Persia and Babylon subject to him. At that time the Jews paid the king an annual tribute of 300 talents of silver. Nevertheless, they were governed not by foreign officials but by their own priests, and lived according to the tradition of their fathers.

Eventually, however, many of them were corrupted once more by a long period of peace and began to mix everything together and disturb the community with seditions, seeking the high priesthood out of lust, greed, and the desire to rule [Col. 0139D].

Source/review notes: Raw Terra review retained as complete=false; all three exact corrections were applied, including canonical *Constantino imperatore*.

### XVIII [Cols. 0140A–B]

For at first, under King Seleucus, the son of the great Antiochus, a certain Simon had been unable to remove Onias the Priest, a holy and upright man, after falsely accusing him before the king. Then, after some time had intervened, Jason, Onias’s brother, approached King Antiochus, who had succeeded his brother Seleucus, promising an increase in the tribute if the high priesthood were granted to him. Although it was an unprecedented practice and had previously been permitted to no one to hold the priesthood perpetually, the king’s mind, anxious and sick with greed, was nevertheless easily overcome. Thus Onias was expelled and the priesthood was entrusted to Jason.

He grievously tore apart both his fellow citizens and his native land. Then, when he had sent through a certain Menelaus, the brother of that Simon, the money promised to the king, the way having once been opened to ambition, Menelaus too obtained the priesthood by the same devices Jason had previously used. Not long afterward, when he had failed to pay the promised amount of silver, he was removed and Lysimachus was substituted in his place. Thereafter there were shameful struggles between Jason and Menelaus, until Jason, an exile from his homeland, withdrew.

From these beginnings of corrupted morals matters progressed so far that most of the people requested from Antiochus permission to live according to the customs of the gentiles. When the king had granted the request, every depraved man vied with the others in building shrines, worshiping idols, and profaning the Law.

Meanwhile Antiochus, returning from Alexandria—for he had then made war upon the Egyptian king, which he laid down at the command of the Roman Senate and People, when Paulus and Crassus were consuls—went to Jerusalem. When he found the people divided by the superstitions they had adopted, destroying the Law of God and favoring those who followed impiety, he stripped away all the ornaments of the Temple and devastated the place with great slaughter. This occurred in the one hundred and fifty-first year from Alexander’s death, when, as we have said, Paulus and Crassus were consuls, approximately five years after Antiochus had begun to reign.

### XIX [Cols. 0140C–0141A]

But so that the sequence of events may be connected and it may become clearer which Antiochus this was, we shall enumerate the names and reigns of the kings who ruled in Syria after Alexander. After King Alexander’s death, as we related above, his entire kingdom was divided among his friends and administered for some time under the royal title.

After nine years Seleucus was called king in Syria, and he reigned for thirty-two years. After him came Antiochus, his son, for twenty-one years. Then Antiochus, the son of Antiochus, also surnamed Theos, for fifteen years. After him came Seleucus, his son, surnamed Callinicus, for twenty-one years. Then Seleucus, the son of Callinicus, for three years.

After his death, Antiochus, the brother of Callinicus, held Asia and Syria for thirty-seven years. This was the Antiochus against whom Scipio, the brother of Africanus, fought. Defeated in that war, he was deprived of part of his empire. He had two sons, Seleucus and Antiochus, whom he had given as a hostage to the Romans.

Thus, after the death of the great Antiochus, his younger son Seleucus obtained the kingdom. Under him, we have said, Onias the Priest was accused by Simon. Then Antiochus was released by the Romans, and Demetrius, the son of King Seleucus who was then reigning, was given in his place as hostage.

When Seleucus died in the twelfth year of his reign, his brother Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome, seized the kingdom. Five years after he had begun to reign, as we have explained above, he laid waste Jerusalem. For, while paying a heavy tribute to the Romans, he was almost necessarily compelled by his immense expenses to seek money through plunder and to leave no opportunity for pillaging unused.

Two years later, when the Jews had again suffered a similar disaster, he placed a garrison in the citadel, lest they should perhaps, driven by repeated misfortunes, take up arms. Then, having undertaken to overthrow the sacred Law, he sent an edict that everyone should abandon the traditions of his ancestors and live according to the rite of the gentiles. Nor were there lacking those who willingly obeyed the profane command.

Then indeed—a shameful spectacle!—sacrifices were openly offered to the gods throughout the city, in the streets; even the sacred books of the Law and the Prophets were burned in the fire.

### XX [Cols. 0141A–B]

At that time Mathathias, the son of John, was Priest. When the royal officials compelled him to obey the edict, he displayed remarkable steadfastness: despising profanation, he publicly slaughtered before everyone a Hebrew engaged in profanation.

Only then, once a leader had been found, did the secession take place. Mathathias left the town, and when many flocked to him he formed the appearance of a regular army. All of them were resolved to defend themselves by arms against the profane government and to fall in battle rather than perform impious rites.

Meanwhile Antiochus also compelled the Jews found in the Greek cities that were under his rule to sacrifice, and subjected those who resisted to unheard-of tortures. At that time occurred the famous martyrdom of the seven brothers and their mother: when all of them were forced by punishments to violate the Law of God and the institutions of their ancestors, they preferred to die. In the end their mother accompanied them in their punishments and deaths.

### XXI [Cols. 0141B–0142A]

Meanwhile Mathathias died. He appointed his son Judas as commander in his place over the army he had prepared. Under his leadership, the royal forces were repeatedly and successfully defeated. First, he destroyed Apollonius, the enemy commander, who had come down to battle with large forces, together with his entire army.

When a certain Seron, who then governed Syria, learned of this, he multiplied his legions and attacked Judas, fierce because he had the advantage in numbers. Once the battle was joined, he was routed and put to flight; after losing approximately eight hundred men, he returned to Syria.

When Antiochus learned of this, inflamed by anger and grief—for he was distressed that his commanders had been defeated with great armies—he gathered assistance from throughout the kingdom and distributed a donative to the soldiers, after completely exhausting his treasuries. For at that time he was especially hard pressed by a serious shortage of money.

The Jews who had paid him three hundred talents of silver annually had defected from him. Moreover, because the Greek cities and many regions had been thrown into disorder by the evil of persecution—for he had not even spared the gentiles, whom he had tried to make abandon their long-established superstitions and bring them all to a single rite; they, indeed, since they had nothing sacred, readily abandoned them, but nevertheless all had been afflicted by fear and disaster—tax revenues had ceased.

Burning with these concerns—for he himself had once been wealthier than all kings but had brought poverty upon himself through his own crime—he divided his forces with Lysias and entrusted Syria and the war against the Jews to him, while he himself set out for Persia to collect the taxes.

Lysias therefore appointed commanders for the war: Ptolemy, Gorgias, Doron, and Nicanor. Forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry were assigned to them, and at their first assault they struck great terror into the Jews.

Then Judas, when everyone was despairing, encouraged his men to go down into battle with brave hearts: for those who trusted in God, nothing would be unconquerable; often before, the fewer had fought successfully against the greater number. After a fast had been proclaimed and a sacrifice celebrated, they entered the battle line, and the enemy forces were routed.

Judas took possession of the camp and found there much gold and Tyrian wealth. For merchants from Syria, having no doubt about victory, had followed the royal army in the hope of buying captives and became part of the booty.

When Lysias learned this from messengers, he prepared his forces with greater care and, the following year, attacked the Jews with an immense army. Defeated again, he withdrew to Antioch.

### XXII [Cols. 0142A–C]

After driving out the enemy, Judas returned to Jerusalem and devoted himself to cleansing and restoring the Temple, which, overthrown by Antiochus and profaned by the gentiles, presented a shameful appearance.

But since the Syrians held the citadel—which was adjacent to the Temple and, because of the nature of the site, higher and impregnable—the position below could not be approached, as they prevented access by frequent sallies. Judas set against them the strongest battle line of his men. Thus the work of the sacred building was undertaken, the Temple was surrounded with a wall, and men were appointed to maintain a permanent armed garrison.

But Lysias, returning to Judaea with a larger army, was defeated again, with great loss both to his army and to the auxiliary forces that the cities had sent to join the war.

Meanwhile Antiochus, whom we mentioned above as having set out for Persia, attempted to plunder Elymus, the wealthiest town of that region, and the temple located there, which was filled with much gold. Driven off when a multitude from every direction gathered to defend the place, he received in addition the news that matters had gone badly either for Lysias or for Lysimachus. Thus, from grief of mind, he fell into a bodily illness.

When he was tormented by internal pains, remembering the evils with which he had afflicted the people of God, he confessed that these things had rightly befallen him. Then, after a few days, he died, having reigned eleven years. He left the kingdom to his son Antiochus, whose name was Eupator.

### XXIII [Cols. 0142C–0143A]

At that time Judas was besieging the Syrians stationed in the citadel. When they were afflicted by hunger and want, they sent messengers to the king and begged for aid.

Thus Eupator came to their assistance with one hundred thousand infantry and twenty thousand cavalry, with elephants leading the battle line and causing immense terror. Judas then lifted the siege and marched to meet the king, routing the Syrians in the first battle.

The king requested peace. But because he had dealt treacherously in bad faith, vengeance followed his treachery. For Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, whom we mentioned above as having been given as a hostage to the Romans, when he heard that Antiochus had died, asked that they send him back to the kingdom. When this was denied him, he secretly fled from Rome, came to Syria, and seized the kingdom, after killing Antiochus’s son, who had reigned one year and six months.

During his reign the Jews first sought friendship and a treaty with the Roman people, and their embassy was received graciously. By decree of the Senate they were called allies and friends.

Meanwhile Demetrius waged war against Judas through his commanders. First an army was led by a certain Bacchides and by Alcimus the Jew; afterward Nicanor, placed in charge of the war, fell in battle.

Then Bacchides and Alcimus, having recovered their strength and increased their forces, fought against Judas. In that battle the victorious Syrians made very bloody use of their victory. The Hebrews chose Jonathan, Judas’s brother, in his place.

Meanwhile Alcimus, after shamefully devastating Jerusalem, died; Bacchides, deprived of his associate, returned to the king. Then, after two years, Bacchides again brought war upon the Jews. Defeated, he asked for peace, which was granted on the following conditions: that he return the deserters and captives and everything taken in the war.

### XXIV [Cols. 0143A–C]

While these things were taking place in Judaea, a certain young man named Alexander, brought up on Rhodes, claiming that he was the son of Antiochus—although this was false—came into Syria with an army, aided by the wealth of Ptolemy, the king of Alexandria. He defeated Demetrius in war and killed him, after he had reigned twelve years.

Before fighting against Demetrius, this Alexander had made a treaty with Jonathan and had given him a purple robe and royal insignia. For this reason Jonathan had assisted him with troops, and after Demetrius was defeated he was the first of all to go out and offer congratulations.

Alexander afterward did not violate the pledge he had given. Thus, during the five years in which he held power, the affairs of the Jews remained peaceful.

Accordingly Demetrius, the son of Demetrius, who had fled to Crete after his father’s death, was encouraged by Listhenes, the leader of the Cretans, to recover his ancestral kingdom by war. Because he was unequal in strength, he appealed for aid to Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, Alexander’s father-in-law, who was already hostile to his son-in-law.

Ptolemy, however, was enticed less by the suppliant’s prayers than by the hope of occupying Syria. He joined his forces to Demetrius’s and gave his daughter, who was married to Alexander, to Demetrius.

Alexander fought against them in battle. Ptolemy fell in that battle; Alexander was defeated and shortly afterward killed, after he had reigned five years—or, as I find in most authorities, nine.

### XXV [Cols. 0143C–D]

After Demetrius obtained the kingdom, he treated Jonathan kindly, made a treaty with him, and restored the Jews to their own laws.

Meanwhile Tryphon, who had belonged to Alexander’s party and was governor of Syria, [lacuna]. To oppose him by war, Tryphon went out to battle against Jonathan with a terrifying army of forty thousand.

When Tryphon saw that he was inferior, he pretended to seek peace. Having been received into friendship and invited to Ptolemais, he killed Jonathan.

After Jonathan’s death supreme authority was transferred to his brother Simon. He arranged his brother’s funeral magnificently and built those seven pyramids, a work of the highest distinction, in which he placed the bones of his brothers and father.

Then Demetrius, renewing his treaty with the Jews in consideration of the disaster inflicted by Tryphon—for after Jonathan’s death Tryphon had devastated their cities and fields by war—remitted their annual taxes forever. For until that time they had paid tribute to the kings of Syria unless they resisted by arms.

This occurred in the second year of King Demetrius. I have marked it for this reason: until this year we have followed the chronology of the Asian kings, so that the reckoning of the times might be set out clearly. Now, however, we shall arrange the sequence of events according to the times of those who were either priests or kings over the Jews, down to the birth of Christ.

### XXVI [Cols. 0144A–B]

Accordingly, after Jonathan, his brother Simon, as stated above, ruled over the Hebrews by right of the high priesthood. This honor had been conferred upon him both by his own people and by the Roman people.

When he had begun to govern his fellow citizens in the second year of King Demetrius, he was ambushed and killed after eight years by Ptolemy. His son John succeeded him. After he had fought outstandingly against the Hyrcanians, a very powerful people, he received the surname Hyrcanus. He died after holding power for twenty-six years.

After him Aristobulus was appointed high priest. He was the first of all, after the Captivity, to assume the royal title and place a diadem upon his head. After completing one year, he died.

His son Alexander then became both king and high priest. He reigned twenty-seven years; in his deeds I find nothing worthy of remembrance except cruelty.

When he left Aristobulus and Hyrcanus as young sons, his wife Salina, or Alexandra, held the kingdom for nine years. After her death there were shameful struggles between the brothers over the kingdom.

At first Hyrcanus held power. Soon, driven out by his brother Aristobulus, he fled to Pompey, who at that time, after completing the Mithridatic War and pacifying Armenia and Pontus, was victorious over all the nations he had visited. He wished to advance farther inland and add all neighboring territories to the Roman Empire, and was seeking causes for war and material for conquest.

Accordingly he gladly received Hyrcanus and, under his guidance, attacked the Jews. After capturing the city and the citadel, he spared the Temple. He sent Aristobulus bound to Rome and restored the right of the high priesthood to Hyrcanus. Having imposed a tribute upon the Jews, he placed over them a certain Antipater of Ascalon as procurator.

Hyrcanus, after holding power for thirty-four years, was captured while waging war against the Parthians.

### XXVII [Cols. 0144C–D]

Then Herod, a foreigner, the son of Antipater of Ascalon, sought the kingdom of Judaea from the Roman Senate and People, and received it.

The Jews now first began to have a foreign king. For, with Christ’s arrival already approaching, it was necessary, according to the prophecies of the prophets, that they be deprived of their own rulers, so that they would no longer expect anyone beyond Christ.

Under this Herod, in the thirty-third year of his reign, Christ was born, when Sabinus and Rufinus were consuls, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

But I shall not venture to touch upon the matters contained in the Gospels and afterward in the Acts of the Apostles, lest I diminish the dignity of the events by interrupting the intended form of the work. I shall pursue what remains.

After the Lord’s birth Herod reigned four years, for the whole duration of his reign was thirty-seven years. After him came the tetrarch Archelaus for nine years, and Herod for twenty-four years.

While this Herod was reigning, in the eighteenth year of his reign, the Lord was crucified, when Fufius Geminus and Rubellius Geminus were consuls. From that time until the consulship of Stilicho there are 372 years.

### XXVIII [Cols. 0144D–0145B]

Luke composed the Acts of the Apostles up to the time when Paul was brought to Rome during Nero’s reign. Nero was not merely the foulest of kings but the foulest of all men and even of savage beasts, and he proved worthy to be the first to begin persecution against Christians. I do not know whether he will also bring it to an end, if indeed the belief accepted by many is true that he himself is the Antichrist who is to come.

The circumstances urged me to set forth his vices more fully, if it were not too extensive for this work. I am content merely to note that in every form of filth and cruelty he advanced so far as to kill his mother; afterward he even married a certain Pythagoras in the manner of a formal wedding. An imperial wedding veil was placed upon him, together with a dowry, a bridal couch, and wedding torches; finally, everything that is observed even in women not without embarrassment was displayed.

It is uncertain whether one should be more reluctant or more ashamed to discuss the rest of his conduct.

He was the first to attempt to abolish the Christian name. For vices are always hostile to virtues, and the best people are viewed by the wicked as though they were reproaching them.

At that time the worship of God had become powerful in the city: Peter was serving as bishop there, and Paul, after appealing to Caesar from the unjust judgment of a governor, had been brought to Rome. Many people were then gathering to hear him. Having understood the truth and been moved by the virtues of the Apostles, which they displayed frequently at that time, they turned themselves to the worship of God.

For at that time occurred the famous contest of Peter and Paul against Simon. When Simon had flown up, supported by two demons and using magical arts to prove himself a god, the Apostles drove away the demons through their prayers. He fell to the ground and was torn apart before the eyes of the people.

### XXIX [Cols. 0145C–D]

Meanwhile, when the multitude of Christians had already become considerable, it happened that Rome was devastated by fire while Nero was staying at Antium. But everyone’s opinion turned the odium of the fire back upon the emperor, and it was believed that the emperor had sought glory by rebuilding the city. Nero could do nothing to prevent people from believing that the fire had been ordered by him.

Accordingly, he turned the odium against the Christians. The most savage interrogations were conducted against innocent people, and new forms of death were devised: covered with the skins of wild beasts, many were killed by the tearing of dogs; many were fastened to crosses or burned by flames; most were reserved for the purpose that, when daylight had failed, they might be burned to serve as nocturnal illumination.

This was the beginning of the persecution of Christians. Later, when laws had been issued, the religion was forbidden, and by public edicts it was not permitted to be a Christian.

Then Paul and Peter were condemned to death. One had his neck severed by the sword; Peter was lifted up on a cross.

While these things were happening at Rome, the Jews, unable to endure the injustices of their governor, Festus Florus, began to rebel. Vespasian, sent against them by Nero with proconsular authority, defeated them in many severe battles and compelled them to take refuge within the walls of Jerusalem.

Meanwhile Nero, already hateful even to himself because of his consciousness of his crimes, was removed from human affairs. It is uncertain whether he inflicted death upon himself. Certainly his body was killed.

Hence it is believed that, even if he pierced himself with a sword, he was preserved after his wound had been treated, in accordance with what is written about him: “And the wound of his death was healed” (Revelation 13:3). He is to be sent at the end of the age to exercise the mystery of iniquity.

### XXX [Cols. 0146A–D]

After Nero’s death, Galba seized the empire. Soon Otho occupied it after killing Galba. Then Vitellius, relying upon the armies over which he presided in Gaul, entered the City and, after killing Otho, usurped supreme power.

When supreme power was afterward transferred to Vespasian, he assumed the empire while besieging Jerusalem. Although the example was evil, his intention was good: to rescue the commonwealth from wicked men. As was customary, he placed a diadem upon his head and was hailed emperor by the army. He made his son Titus Caesar, assigning him part of the forces and the task of besieging Jerusalem.

Vespasian set out for Rome and was received with the greatest favor by the Senate and People. When Vitellius had killed himself, he consolidated his rule.

Meanwhile the Jews, shut up by the siege, because they were offered no possibility either of peace or surrender, eventually perished from hunger. The roads began everywhere to be filled with corpses, burial having already become impossible. Indeed, they dared every unspeakable act and did not even spare human bodies, except those which decay had taken away before they could be used as food.

Then, when the defenders were exhausted, the Romans broke in. At that time, as it happened, the entire population had gathered from the countryside and from the other towns of Judaea for the day of Passover. Clearly it had been God’s will that, at the very time when the impious nation had crucified the Lord, it should be delivered to destruction.

The Pharisees resisted fiercely for a while on behalf of the Temple, until, with minds obstinately resolved upon death, they voluntarily threw themselves into the flames.

The number of those killed is reported as 1,100,000; 100,000 were captured and sold. Titus is said, after taking counsel, first to have deliberated whether he should destroy the Temple, a building of such magnitude. For some thought that the sacred house, illustrious beyond all mortal things, ought not to be destroyed: if preserved, it would provide testimony to Roman restraint; if demolished, it would offer an everlasting mark of cruelty.

But others, and Titus himself, thought above all that the Temple ought to be destroyed, so that the religion of the Jews and of the Christians might be more completely abolished. For although these religions were opposed to each other, they had nevertheless arisen from the same founders; the Christians had come from the Jews; and once the root had been removed, the branch would easily perish.

Thus, by God’s will, when everyone’s minds had been inflamed, the Temple was destroyed 331 years ago.

This was the final destruction of the Temple and the last captivity of the Jews, who are seen wandering without a homeland and scattered throughout the world. Every day they bear witness to the world that they were punished for no other reason than the impious hands they laid upon Christ. For although on many previous occasions they had been handed over to captivity because of their sins, they had never nevertheless paid the penalty of servitude for more than seventy years.

### XXXI [Cols. 0146D–0147B]

After some time Domitian, the son of Vespasian, persecuted the Christians. At that time he banished the Apostle and Evangelist John to the island of Patmos. There, after mysterious revelations had been disclosed to him, John composed and published the book of the sacred Apocalypse, which most people reject either foolishly or impiously.

Not long afterward there was a third persecution under Trajan. When he found nothing in the Christians worthy of death or punishment through tortures and interrogations, he prohibited further violence against them.

Under Hadrian the Jews next wished to rebel, attempting to plunder Syria and Palestine. An army was sent against them, and they were subdued.

At that time Hadrian, believing that he would destroy the Christian faith by profaning the site, [lacuna], placed images of demons in the temples and at the place of the Lord’s Passion. And because Christians were thought to come chiefly from the Jews—for at that time the Church at Jerusalem had a Priest only from the circumcision—he ordered a cohort of soldiers to maintain permanent guard and prevent all Jews from entering Jerusalem.

This actually benefited the Christian faith, because at that time almost everyone who believed Christ to be God still observed the Law. Clearly this was arranged by the Lord’s ordering, so that slavery to the Law might be removed by the freedom of faith and of the Church. Thus, at that time, Marcus, the first bishop from the gentiles, was at Jerusalem.

A fourth persecution is counted under Hadrian. Nevertheless, afterward he prohibited it from being carried out, declaring it unjust that anyone should be held guilty without a crime.

After Hadrian, while Antoninus Pius was emperor, there was peace for the churches.

### XXXII [Cols. 0147B–C]

Under Aurelius, the son of Antoninus, a fifth persecution was then carried out. At that time the first martyrdoms were seen in Gaul, where the religion of God had been accepted later than beyond the Alps.

A sixth persecution of Christians followed under Severus. At that time Leonidas, the father of Origen, shed his sacred blood in martyrdom.

After an interval of thirty-eight years, there was peace for Christians, except that during the intervening period Maximinus harassed the clergy of certain churches.

Soon, under the emperor Decius, Christians were attacked in the seventh persecution. After him Valerian was the eighth enemy of the saints.

After Valerian, following an interval of approximately fifty years, an especially bitter persecution arose under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. It ravaged the people of God for ten continuous years.

At that time almost every city was stained with the sacred blood of martyrs. People rushed eagerly into glorious contests, and martyrdoms were then sought with much greater eagerness through glorious deaths than bishoprics are now pursued through depraved ambitions.

The world was never exhausted by greater wars; nor did we ever win a greater triumph than when, after ten years of slaughter, we could not be conquered.

There also survive in writing the splendid accounts of the sufferings of the martyrs of that time. I have not thought it necessary to join them to this work, lest I exceed its limits.

### XXXIII [Cols. 0147C–0148B]

But that persecution ended eighty-nine years ago, from which time Christian emperors began to rule. At that time Constantine held power, the first of all Roman rulers to be a Christian.

At that time Licinius, because he fought against Constantine for the empire, ordered his soldiers to sacrifice. He dismissed those who refused from military service. But this is not counted among the persecutions, so slight was the matter that it did not reach the wounds of the churches.

From then on we have enjoyed peace in tranquil circumstances, and we do not believe that there will be any further persecution except that which the Antichrist will exercise at the end of the age. For the sacred Scriptures have declared that the world is to be afflicted by ten plagues. Since nine have already occurred, the one that remains will be the last.

During this period it is remarkable how greatly the Christian religion has grown.

At that time Jerusalem, horrible with ruins, was adorned with numerous and magnificent churches. Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine, who reigned jointly with her son as Augusta, desired to recognize Jerusalem. When she found idols and temples there, she destroyed them. Then, using the power of the imperial government, she built basilicas at the site of the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension.

It is remarkable that the place where the divine footprints last stood, when the Lord was lifted into heaven upon a cloud, could not be joined by pavement to the rest of the paved surface. For whatever was placed against it, the unusual earth refused to receive, as though it were incapable of accepting human work; the marbles were often thrown back into the faces of those who laid them.

Moreover, the footprints of the dust trodden by God provide such enduring evidence that the impressions can be seen. Although the faith of those who come there every day eagerly snatches away the earth trodden by the Lord, the sand nevertheless shows no loss. The ground still preserves the same appearance, as though marked by impressed footprints.

### XXXIV [Cols. 0148B–C]

Through the benefit of the same queen, the Lord’s Cross was then discovered. It had not been possible to consecrate it at the beginning because of the Jews who opposed it, and afterward it had been buried beneath the ruins of the destroyed city. It deserved to be revealed only to one who sought it with such faithfulness.

After Helena had first been informed about the place of the Passion, she ordered the earth and all adjacent areas, including the immense heaps of ruins, to be excavated and cleared, with military forces brought in and all the provincials vying to show their devotion to the queen.

Then, as the reward for faith and labor, three crosses were found together, just as the Lord and the two thieves had once been fastened to them.

The difficulty of identifying the greater cross—the gibbet on which the Lord had hung—troubled everyone’s minds and thoughts, lest human error should perhaps consecrate the thief’s gibbet instead of the Lord’s Cross.

They then conceived the plan of bringing a recently deceased person near the crosses. Without delay, as though by God’s will, a dead man was being carried to his customary funeral rites. Amid the crowd, his body was taken from the bier.

After the first two crosses had been applied without result, when it was touched to Christ’s gibbet—wondrous to say!—the corpse sprang up while everyone trembled and stood among the spectators.

The Cross had been found and was consecrated with fitting ceremony.

### XXXV [Cols. 0148D–0149A]

Through these deeds accomplished by Helena, while the ruler was Christian, the world received freedom and an example of faith. But a far more grievous danger arose for all the churches during that peace.

For at that time the Arian heresy broke out and disturbed the whole world by spreading error. With two particularly fierce Arians as the authors of this treachery, the emperor too was corrupted. While he thought he was fulfilling a religious duty, he exercised the force of persecution. Bishops were driven into exile, violence was inflicted upon clergy, and laypeople who had separated themselves from communion with the Arians were punished.

What the Arians preached was as follows: the Father had begotten the Son in order to establish the world; by his own power he had been made from nothing into a new and different substance, a new and different Lord; and there had been a time when the Son did not exist.

Accordingly, because of this evil, a council was convened at Nicaea from the whole world. When 318 bishops had gathered, a complete statement of faith was written and the Arian heresy condemned.

The emperor accepted the bishops’ decree.

The Arians, daring not to retract anything openly against the sound faith, joined themselves to the churches as though assenting and holding no different opinion. Nevertheless, hatred of Catholic men remained planted in their hearts. Against those with whom they could not debate about the faith, they proceeded by means of suborned accusers and fabricated charges.

### XXXVI [Cols. 0149A–D]

Accordingly, they first attacked Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria and a jurist, who had attended the Council of Nicaea as a deacon, and condemned him in his absence.

In addition to the charges assembled by false witnesses, they added that he had perversely received Marcellus and Photinus, heretical priests condemned by the judgment of the council.

There was no doubt about Photinus: he had deservedly been condemned. In Marcellus, however, nothing then seemed to have been found worthy of condemnation. His zeal for the innocent party especially strengthened the case for him, since no one doubted that the very judges by whom he had been condemned were themselves heretics.

The Arians, moreover, did not so much wish to remove these men as Athanasius. Thus they press the emperor until Athanasius was sent into exile in Gaul.

Soon eighty bishops gathered in Egypt and declared that Athanasius had been unjustly condemned. The matter was reported to Constantine, who ordered bishops from the whole world to assemble at Sardica and the entire judgment by which Athanasius had been condemned to be reconsidered.

Meanwhile Constantine died.

When the council had assembled, under the emperor Constantine, it absolved Athanasius. Marcellus too was restored to the episcopate. The sentence against Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, however, was not rescinded, because he was also judged a heretic by our own side.

Nevertheless, this very fact weighed against Marcellus, because Photinus appeared to have been his disciple in his youth.

Yet Athanasius’s absolution was further supported by this: Ursacius and Valens, the leaders of the Arians, when they appeared to have been separated from communion after the Council of Sardica, stood before Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, and asked pardon for having condemned an innocent man. They professed that he had rightly been absolved by the judgment of the Council of Sardica.

### XXXVII [Cols. 0149D–0150B]

After some time Athanasius discovered with complete certainty that Marcellus was not sound in the faith and suspended him from communion. Marcellus showed such modesty that, marked by the judgment of so great a man, he willingly withdrew.

Nevertheless, although previously innocent and later corrupted, he could already then appear to have been guilty when judgment had been passed upon him.

The Arians therefore found an opportunity of this kind and conspired completely to overturn the decrees of the Council of Sardica. For they seemed to have some pretext: Athanasius had been judged as unjustly in his favor as Marcellus had been acquitted, even though Marcellus had now also been proved a heretic by Athanasius’s judgment.

Marcellus had been an advocate of the Sabellian heresy. Photinus, however, had already put forward a new heresy: although he differed from Sabellius concerning the Unity, he preached that Christ’s beginning was from Mary.

Accordingly, by a crafty plan, the Arians mixed the innocent man with the guilty and included the condemnation of Photinus, Marcellus, and Athanasius in the same judgment. They thereby prepared the minds of the emperors so that they themselves would not be thought to have judged wrongly concerning Athanasius, since they had judged truly concerning Marcellus and Photinus.

At that time, however, the Arians were concealing their treachery. They did not dare to preach openly the doctrines of their error; they presented themselves as Catholics, judging that nothing should be undertaken before they had removed Athanasius from the Church. He had always stood in their way like a wall, and once he was removed they hoped that the others would yield to their will.

The portion of the bishops that followed Arius obtained the condemnation of Athanasius, which it desired. Another portion, compelled by fear and faction, yielded to the purposes of the parties. A few, for whom faith was dear and truth more important, did not accept the unjust judgment.

Among these was Paulinus, bishop of Trier. When the letter was presented to him, he is said to have subscribed as follows: he gave his agreement to the condemnation of Photinus and Marcellus, but did not approve the condemnation of Athanasius.

### XXXVIII

Then, when the Arians’ stratagems had made little progress, they decided to act by force.
