For, supported by the king’s friendship—which they had bound to themselves through wicked flattery—they found it easy to dare and accomplish anything. Moreover, they were invincible because of the agreement of many: almost all the bishops of the two Pannonias, many of the Eastern bishops, and all Asia had conspired in their treachery.

The principal leaders of this evil faction were Ursacius of Singidunum, Valens of Mursa, Theodore of Heraclea, Stephen of Antioch, Acacius of Caesarea, Menophantus of Ephesus, George of Laodicea, and Narcissus of Neronopolis. They had so taken possession of the palace that the emperor did nothing without their approval. He was subject to all of them, but especially devoted to Valens.

At the time when the battle against Magnentius was being fought at Mursa, Constantius did not dare come into view of the fighting. Instead, he stayed in the basilica of the Martyrs outside the town, having taken Valens, then bishop of that place, with him for comfort. Valens, for his part, had cunningly arranged through his agents that he would be the first to learn the outcome of the battle: either to win the king’s favor if he brought the good news first, or to secure his own safety by gaining time to flee if anything went wrong.

Thus, while the few men around the king trembled with fear and the emperor was anxious, Valens was the first to announce that the enemy was fleeing. When the emperor demanded that the informant himself be admitted [the text apparently reads *indicem ipsum*], Valens, wishing to increase the respect paid to him, replied that an angel had been his informant. The emperor was easily persuaded and afterward was accustomed to say publicly that he had won through Valens’s merits, not through the army’s valor.

### XXXIX

From this beginning the Arians, encouraged by the success of their prince, grew bolder, intending to use the king’s power wherever their own authority had proved insufficient. Accordingly, when our people refused to accept the sentence they had pronounced against Athanasius, an edict was issued by the emperor that those who did not subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation should be driven into exile.

Meanwhile, councils of our bishops were held at Arles and Béziers, towns of Gaul. They demanded that, before being compelled to subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation, they should first debate the faith; and that the matter should be judged only after the question of the person had been settled. But Valens and his associates wished first to extort Athanasius’s condemnation, since they did not dare to contest the faith. As a result of this conflict between the parties, Paulinus was sent into exile.

In the meantime, a meeting was held at Milan, where the emperor was then present. The same dispute continued without either side yielding. Eusebius of Vercelli and Lucifer of Caralis in Sardinia, both bishops, were then banished.

Dionysius, the bishop of Milan, subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation, provided that the faith should be investigated among the bishops. But Valens, Ursacius, and the others, afraid of the populace, which preserved the Catholic faith with exceptional zeal, did not dare to profess their abominations openly. They therefore assembled inside the palace and issued in the emperor’s name a letter filled with every kind of wickedness.

Their purpose was plainly this: if the people received the letter favorably, they could publish what they wanted with public authority; but if it were received otherwise, all the odium would fall upon the king, and the matter itself could be excused, since he was still a catechumen and might reasonably have been thought ignorant of the sacrament of faith.

The letter was read in the church, but the people rejected it. Dionysius was expelled from the city because he had not agreed, and a bishop was immediately appointed in his place. Liberius, the bishop of Rome, and Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, were also sent into exile.

Rhodanius, bishop of Toulouse—by nature milder, and having resisted the Arians not so much through his own strength as through his association with Hilary—was subjected to the same sentence. Yet people were prepared to suspend Athanasius from communion, provided only that the faith might be investigated among the bishops; but the Arians thought it best to remove such distinguished men from the struggle.

Those whom we have mentioned were driven into exile forty-five years ago, in the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus. Liberius, however, was restored to Rome shortly afterward because of disturbances there. It is well established that the exiles were honored by the devotion of the whole world, that money was collected for their support in abundance, and that delegations from the Catholic populace of almost every province visited them frequently.

### XL

Meanwhile the Arians no longer preached the abominations of their heresy secretly, as before, but openly and publicly. They even interpreted the Council of Nicaea in their own favor, having corrupted it by the addition of a single letter, and thus cast a kind of darkness over the truth.

Where *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον) had been written—meaning “of one substance”—they claimed that *homoiousion* (ὁμοιούσιον) had been written, meaning “of similar substance.” They granted similarity while removing unity, since similarity differs greatly from unity. For example, a painting of a human body is similar to a human being, yet it does not possess the reality of a human being.

Some of them went even further, affirming *anomoiousian* (ἀνομοιουσίαν), that is, “of dissimilar substance.” The disputes progressed to such a point that the whole world became entangled in these abominations.

For Valens, Ursacius, and the others whose names we have given had infected Italy, Illyricum, and the East. Our Gauls were oppressed by Saturninus, bishop of Arles, an uncontrolled and factious man.

There was also a belief that Hosius had yielded from Spain to the same treachery. This seems astonishing and incredible, because for almost all his life he had been regarded as the most steadfast supporter of our side, and the Council of Nicaea was considered to have been completed under his direction—unless, as old age weakened him, he had become delirious. For he was more than a hundred years old, as Saint Hilary reports in his letters.

With the world thus disturbed and the churches languishing under a kind of disease, the emperor was troubled by a slower-moving but no less serious anxiety: although the Arians whom he favored seemed to have prevailed, agreement among the bishops concerning the faith had still not been reached.

### XLI

Accordingly, he ordered a council to be assembled at Ariminum, a city of Italy. He instructed the prefect Taurus not to dismiss those gathered together until they had agreed upon one faith, promising him the consulship if he brought the matter to completion.

Thus, official agents of the Master of Offices were sent throughout Illyricum, Italy, Africa, Spain, and Gaul. More than four hundred Western bishops, summoned or dispatched [the text reads *acciti aut macti*], came together at Ariminum. The emperor had ordered provisions and lodging allowances to be supplied to them all.

But this seemed improper to our Gauls—that is, the Aquitanians—and to the Britons. They rejected public funds and preferred to live at their own expense. Only three from Britain, having refused the contribution offered by the others, used public resources because of their poverty, considering it more proper to burden the treasury than individuals.

I have heard our bishop Gavidus usually mention this as though criticizing them. But I should judge it quite differently. I consider it praise that the bishops were so poor that they possessed nothing of their own and therefore accepted support from no one rather than the treasury, where they burdened no individual. Thus there was an excellent example on both sides. Nothing memorable is reported about the rest.

But I return to the narrative. After all had been gathered together, as we have said, a division arose between the parties. Our people occupied the church; the Arians took possession of another building that had deliberately been left vacant as a place of prayer. They numbered no more than eighty; the rest belonged to our side.

Accordingly, nothing was accomplished in the frequent councils: our people remained firm in the faith, while the others refused to yield in their treachery. Finally, it was decided to send ten envoys to the emperor, so that he might learn the faith and position of each party and understand that peace with heretics was impossible.

The Arians did the same, sending an equal number of envoys to oppose our representatives before the emperor. But our side chose young men, insufficiently learned and insufficiently cautious. The Arians, on the other hand, sent crafty old men of considerable ability, steeped in the poison of treachery. They easily prevailed before the king.

Our representatives, however, were instructed not to enter into communion with the Arians in any way and to leave every matter intact for the council.

### XLII

Meanwhile, following the example of the Westerners, the emperor ordered almost all the bishops of the East to assemble at Seleucia, a town of Isauria.

At that time Hilary was already spending his fourth year in exile in Phrygia. Through a deputy and the governor, permission for transportation having been granted, he was compelled to attend along with the other bishops. The emperor had issued no specific order concerning him; the judges merely followed the general command by which all bishops were ordered to be brought to the council. They wished, as I suppose, to include him among the others.

But this occurred by God’s will, so that a man thoroughly instructed in divine matters might be present when the faith was to be debated.

When he arrived at Seleucia, he was received with great favor and turned everyone’s enthusiasm and attention toward himself. He was first asked what the faith of the Gauls was, because the Easterners had been made suspicious of us by the Arians’ false reports. They had claimed that we believed, after the manner of Sabellius, in the three-named unity of a solitary God.

After explaining his own faith according to what the Fathers had written at Nicaea, Hilary gave testimony on behalf of the Westerners. Thus, when everyone’s minds had been set at rest, he was admitted into their communion and fellowship and was added to the council.

The proceedings then began. The authors of the wicked heresy were discovered and cut off from the body of the Church. Among them were George of Alexandria, Acacius, Eudoxius, Uranius, Leontius, Theodosius, Evagrius, and Theodulus.

When the council had been completed, it decreed that an embassy should be sent to the emperor to report what had been done. The condemned men also went to the king, relying confidently on the strength of their associates and on the prince’s support.

### XLIII

Meanwhile the emperor compelled the representatives of the Council of Ariminum from our side to enter into communion with the heretics. He handed them a statement of faith composed by wicked men and wrapped in deceptive language. It spoke of Catholic teaching while concealing treachery beneath it.

It abolished the word “substance” (*ousia*) as ambiguous, rashly used by the Fathers, and not derived from the authority of Scripture, under the pretext of a false argument, so that the Son would not be believed to be of one substance with the Father.

The same statement acknowledged the Son to be like the Father. But hidden within it was a fraud prepared in advance: he was to be similar, but not equal.

After the envoys had been dismissed, the prefect was ordered not to release the council until all had declared by their subscriptions that they agreed with the written statement of faith. If any resisted too stubbornly, provided their number did not exceed fifteen, they were to be sent into exile.

When the envoys returned, communion was refused, although they pleaded against the use of force by the king. Once what had been decreed became known, there was still greater confusion of affairs and counsels.

Then, little by little, most of our side were overcome—some by weakness of understanding, others by weariness from their long journey—and surrendered to their opponents, who had already gained the upper hand after the return of the envoys. The latter took possession of the church, while our people were expelled.

Once their minds had yielded, they went over in crowds to the other side, until the number of our men was reduced to twenty.

### XLIV

But the fewer they were, the stronger they proved. The most steadfast among them was our Faegadius, together with Servatius, bishop of Tongeren.

Because they had not yielded to threats and terrors, Taurus approached them with entreaties. Weeping, he begged them to consider milder measures. The bishops had now spent seven months shut up in a single city. Exhausted by the harshness of winter and by want, they had no hope of returning. What end would there be? They should follow the example of the majority; at least they should derive authority from their numbers.

Faegadius declared that he was ready for exile and for every punishment to which he might be called. He would not accept a faith devised by the Arians.

The dispute continued in this way for several days. When this produced little progress toward peace, he himself was gradually weakened and finally overcome by the terms that were proposed.

Valens and Ursacius claimed that the present faith had been formulated according to Catholic reasoning and had been issued by the Easterners with the emperor’s authority. To reject it was an abomination. What end could there be to the disagreements if what pleased the Easterners displeased the Westerners? Finally, if anything in the present statement seemed insufficiently expressed, they themselves could add whatever they thought should be added; Valens and Ursacius promised to give their assent to those additions.

This favorable declaration was received with the willing approval of everyone. Our men no longer dared resist and now wished by any means to bring the affair to an end.

The statements composed by Faegadius and Servatius then began to be published. In them Arius and all his treachery were first condemned. But the Son of God was not declared equal to the Father, nor without beginning or outside time.

Then Valens, as though assisting our side, added a clause containing a hidden deception: “The Son of God is not a creature like the other creatures.” The fraud in this statement deceived those who heard it. For by these words, while the Son was denied to be like the other creatures, he was nevertheless declared to be a creature—merely superior to the others.

Thus neither side could consider itself entirely victorious or defeated. The faith itself favored the Arians, while the statements later added favored our side, except for the clause Valens had appended. That clause was not understood at the time and was recognized only later.

In this manner the council was dismissed: begun auspiciously, it was brought to completion with a shameful outcome.

### XLV

The Arians, therefore, when affairs were proceeding far too successfully and according to their wishes, hurried to Constantinople to the emperor.

There they compelled the envoys of the Council of Seleucia, by royal force and following the example of the Westerners, to accept that wicked faith. Most of those who refused were harassed by an insulting imprisonment and by hunger and surrendered their captive consciences. Many who held out more steadfastly were deprived of their bishoprics and thrust into exile, while others were appointed in their places.

Thus, when the best priests had either been terrified by fear or led into exile, everyone yielded to the treachery of a few.

Hilary was there at the time. He had followed the envoys from Seleucia and was awaiting the emperor’s decision, without any definite order concerning himself, in case he might perhaps be ordered to return to exile.

When he perceived the final danger to the faith—that the Westerners had been deceived and the Easterners were being defeated through crime—he publicly presented three petitions and requested an audience with the king, so that he might debate the faith in the presence of his adversaries.

The Arians strongly opposed this. Finally, as though he were a seedbed of discord and a disturber of the East, Hilary was ordered to return to Gaul without any remission of his exile.

But when he had surveyed almost the whole world infected by the evil of treachery, he was uncertain and agitated by a great burden of cares. Since many thought that communion should not be entered into with those who had accepted the Council of Ariminum, he judged it best to recall everyone to correction and repentance.

Through frequent councils held throughout Gaul, and with almost all the bishops confessing their error, he condemned what had been done at Ariminum and restored the faith of the churches to its former condition.

Saturninus, bishop of Arles, a thoroughly wicked man of evil and depraved character, resisted these sound counsels. But, in addition to the disgrace of heresy, he was convicted of many shameful crimes and expelled from the Church. Thus the strength of the faction was broken when it lost its leader.

Paternus of Périgueux was equally foolish and did not refuse to profess the treachery; he was deprived of his priesthood, while the others were granted pardon.

Everyone agreed that our Gauls had been freed from the abomination of heresy through the single agency of Hilary.

At Antioch, however, Lucifer held a very different opinion. He condemned those who had been at Ariminum so severely that he separated himself even from those who had received them under conditions of satisfaction or repentance. Whether he decided rightly or wrongly, I would not presume to say.

Paulinus and Rhodanius died in Phrygia. Hilary died in his homeland six years after his return.

### XLVI

There followed the grave and dangerous times of our own generation, when the churches were polluted by an unprecedented evil and everything was thrown into confusion.

It was then that the infamous heresy of the Gnostics was first detected in Spain—a destructive superstition concealed in secret mysteries. The origin of this evil lay in the East and in Egypt. It is not easy to say by what beginnings it first took root there.

Marcus, an Egyptian from Memphis, was the first to introduce it into Spain. His pupils were a certain Agape, a woman of no obscure standing, and the rhetorician Elpidius.

Priscillian was instructed by them. He was of noble family, extremely wealthy, energetic, restless, eloquent, learned through extensive reading, and exceptionally ready in discussion and debate. He would certainly have been fortunate if he had not corrupted an excellent natural talent through misguided zeal.

In him one could see many admirable qualities of mind and body. He could remain awake for long periods and endure hunger and thirst. He was entirely free from the desire to possess and extremely sparing in the use of what he had.

Yet he was also exceedingly vain and more inflated than was proper by his knowledge of profane matters. It was even believed that he had practiced magical arts from his youth.

Once he had undertaken his destructive teaching, he attracted many nobles and still more common people into his association through the authority of persuasion and the skill of flattery.

Women eager for novelties, unstable in faith, and inquisitive by nature in every matter flocked to him in crowds. For, while he displayed an appearance of humility in speech and dress, he inspired everyone with honor and reverence for himself.

Little by little, the corruption of this treachery had spread through most of Spain. Some of the bishops were also corrupted. Among them were Instantius and Salvianus, who received Priscillian not only with their agreement but also, in a certain way, through a conspiracy.

At length Hyginus, bishop of Córdoba, who was living nearby, reported what he had discovered to Idacius, bishop of Mérida. Idacius, however, attacking Instantius and his associates without restraint and beyond what was appropriate, added fuel to the developing fire. He inflamed the wicked rather than suppressing them.

### XLVII

After many struggles between them, some worthy of remembrance, a council was assembled at Zaragoza. The bishops of Aquitaine also attended.

The heretics, however, did not dare submit themselves to judgment. A sentence was therefore pronounced against them in their absence, and Instantius and Salvianus, bishops, together with Elpidius and Priscillian, laymen, were condemned.

It was also added that anyone who received the condemned into communion should know that the same sentence would be pronounced against him.

The matter was entrusted to Ithacius, bishop of Sossuba, so that he might make the bishops’ decree known to everyone and, above all, exclude Hyginus from communion. Hyginus had been the first of all to begin publicly attacking the heretics, but later he was disgracefully corrupted and received them into communion.

Meanwhile Instantius and Salvianus, condemned by the judgment of the priests, appointed Priscillian—although a layman, he was the leader of all the evils—bishop in the town of Ávila, after he had been censured together with them by the Council of Zaragoza. They evidently thought that, if they armed an energetic and cunning man with priestly authority, they would be safer.

Then Idacius and Ithacius pressed their attack more vigorously, believing that the evil could be suppressed at its beginning. But they followed unsound counsels and appealed to secular judges, so that the heretics might be driven from the cities by their decrees and enforcement.

After many disgraceful conflicts, Idacius’s entreaties obtained from Gratian, then emperor, a rescript ordering all the heretics to depart—not merely from the churches or cities, but to be driven beyond every land.

When they learned of this, the Gnostics, despairing of their position and not daring to contest the judgment, withdrew voluntarily, at least those who appeared to be bishops. Fear scattered the rest.

### XLVIII

At that time Instantius, Salvianus, and Priscillian went to Rome to clear themselves before Damasus, then bishop of the city. Their route took them through inland Aquitaine, where they were received with great honor by the inexperienced. There they scattered the seeds of their treachery and especially corrupted the people of Elusa, who at that time were upright and devoted to religion, through their wicked preaching.

They were driven away from Bordeaux by Delphinus. Nevertheless, after spending some time in the territory of Euchrotia, they infected certain people with their errors.

They then resumed their journey in a disgraceful and shameful procession, accompanied by their wives and by other women, among them Euchrotia and her daughter Procula. Concerning Procula, people said that she had become pregnant through Priscillian’s sexual misconduct and had aborted the child with herbs.

When they reached Rome, wishing to clear themselves before Damasus, they were not even admitted into his presence.

They returned to Milan and found Ambrose equally opposed to them. They then changed their plans. Since they had failed to deceive two bishops whose authority was supreme at that time, they sought to obtain what they wanted from the emperor through gifts and influence.

Having corrupted Macedonius, then Master of the Offices, they secured a rescript ordering that the earlier decrees be disregarded and that they be restored to their churches.

Relying on this, Instantius and Priscillian returned to Spain—for Salvianus had died in the city—and recovered without opposition the churches over which they had presided.

### XLIX

Ithacius lacked not the will but the means to resist them, because the heretics had strengthened their position by corrupting Volventius, the proconsul.

Indeed, Ithacius was accused by them as a disturber of the churches and ordered to be brought before the court by a harsh enforcement. Terrified, he fled to Gaul.

There he approached Gregory, the prefect. When Gregory learned what had happened, he ordered the authors of the disturbances to be seized and reported everything to the emperor, so as to block the heretics’ efforts to exert influence.

But this was useless, because through the lust and power of a few everything there was for sale.

The heretics therefore employed their customary methods. After paying a large sum of money to Macedonius, they obtained that the investigation of Spain be taken from the prefect by imperial authority [lacuna] to the vicar (for they had already ceased to have a proconsul) [lacuna]. Officials were sent by the Master of Offices to bring Ithacius, who was then at Trier, back to Spain.

He cunningly frustrated them and afterward, protected by Bishop Pritannius, eluded them.

By then a rumor had spread that Clement Maximus had seized power in Britain and would shortly burst into Gaul. Ithacius therefore decided, although circumstances were uncertain, to await the arrival of the new emperor; meanwhile he would take no action.

When Maximus entered the town of Trier as victor, Ithacius brought forward petitions against Priscillian and his associates, filled with hatred and accusations.

Moved by these, the emperor sent letters to the prefect of Gaul and to the vicar of Spain, ordering that all those whom that pollution had involved be brought before the council at Bordeaux.

Instantius and Priscillian were accordingly brought there. Instantius was ordered to plead his case first. Since he did not sufficiently clear himself, he was declared unworthy of the episcopate.

Priscillian, however, so as not to be heard by the bishops, appealed to the emperor. Our men permitted this through their inconsistency. They ought either to have pronounced sentence against one who resisted or, if they themselves were considered suspect, to have reserved the hearing for other bishops. They should not have entrusted a case involving such manifest crimes to the emperor.

Thus all those implicated in the affair were brought before the king.

### L

The bishops Idacius and Ithacius also followed as accusers. I would not criticize their zeal in crushing the heretics if they had not pursued victory more passionately than was proper.

In my judgment, both the accused and the accusers are displeasing to me. Certainly I maintain that Ithacius had no scruples and no regard for anything sacred. He was bold, talkative, shameless, extravagant, and devoted in great measure to his belly and appetite.

His folly advanced so far that he brought charges even against all holy men who either devoted themselves to reading or had undertaken to contend through fasting, accusing them as associates or disciples of Priscillian.

That wretched man even dared at that time to cast publicly upon Bishop Martin—a man plainly comparable to the Apostles—the disgrace of heresy.

For Martin, who was then at Trier, never ceased rebuking Ithacius and urging him to abandon the accusation. He begged Maximus to refrain from shedding the blood of wretched men. It was more than sufficient that heretics judged by an episcopal sentence should be driven from the churches. It was a new and unheard-of impiety for a secular judge to judge the Church’s case.

As long as Martin remained at Trier, the investigation was postponed. When he was about to depart, he obtained from Maximus, through his outstanding authority, a promise that nothing bloody would be decreed against the accused.

But afterward the emperor was corrupted by Bishops Magnus and Rufus and diverted from his milder counsels. He entrusted the case to the prefect Evodius, an energetic and severe man.

Evodius heard Priscillian in two trials, convicted him of sorcery, and, since he did not deny that he had devoted himself to obscene teachings and had held nocturnal gatherings of depraved women and customarily prayed naked, declared him guilty and remanded him to custody until he could report to the emperor.

When the proceedings had been brought to the palace, the emperor decided that Priscillian and his associates ought to be condemned to death.

### LI

Ithacius, seeing how hateful it would be to the bishops if he remained the accuser even during the final proceedings in a capital case—for the trial necessarily had to be repeated—withdrew from the investigation, though too late: the crafty crime had already been completed.

At that point Maximus appointed a certain Patricius, an advocate of the treasury, as accuser. Through his prosecution Priscillian was condemned to death, together with Felicissimus and Armenius, who, although they had been clerics, had recently deserted the Catholics and followed Priscillian.

Latronianus and Euchrotia were also killed by the sword. Instantius, whom we have said was previously condemned by the bishops, was deported to the island of Sylina, situated beyond Britain.

The remaining cases were then taken up in subsequent trials. Asarinus and the deacon Aurelius were condemned to the sword. Tiberianus, after his property had been confiscated, was sent to the island of Sylina.

Tertullus, Potamius, and John, considered persons of lower rank and worthy of mercy because they had betrayed themselves and their associates before the interrogation, were relegated to temporary exile within Gaul.

In roughly this manner men utterly unworthy of the light of day were killed or punished by exile—a disgraceful example. What he had initially defended as sanctioned by the law of the courts and by outstanding public authority, Ithacius, habitually in disputes and finally convicted, turned against those whose orders and counsels had brought it about. Yet he alone among them was deprived of the episcopate.

Idacius, although less guilty, had voluntarily resigned his bishopric. This was a wise and modest act, had he not afterward attempted to reclaim the position he had lost.

The killing of Priscillian did not suppress the heresy that had burst forth under his leadership. Instead, it strengthened and spread it more widely. His followers, who had previously honored him as a saint, afterward began to venerate him as a martyr.

The bodies of those who had been killed were taken back to Spain, and their funerals were celebrated with great ceremony. Indeed, swearing by Priscillian was considered an act of the highest religious devotion.

Among our people a continual war of disputes had broken out. It had already been driven by shameful dissensions for fifteen years and could not be brought to an end.

Even now, when everything was seen to be disturbed and thrown into confusion above all by the disputes of the bishops, everything among them had been corrupted by hatred or favor, fear, inconsistency, envy, faction, lust, greed, arrogance, sleep, and sloth. Finally, the majority contended against the few who offered sound counsel, through insane plans and stubborn partisanship. Amid all this, God’s people and every decent person were treated as objects of disgrace and ridicule.

---

## Sulpicius Severus, One Book on the Life of Blessed Martin (C)

### The Author’s Letter to Desiderius Concerning the Book of the Life of Blessed Martin

**Severus sends greetings to his dearest Desiderius.**

Indeed, my like-minded brother, I had decided to keep the little book that I had written about the life of Saint Martin suppressed in its own manuscript and confined within the walls of my home. For, being weak by nature, I avoided human judgment, lest—as I expect will happen—my uncultivated style displease readers and I be judged deserving of everyone’s criticism for having shamelessly seized material that ought rightly to have been reserved for eloquent writers.

But I could not repeatedly refuse your request. What is there that I would not devote to your affection, even at the cost of my own modesty?

Nevertheless, I have published the little book for you with the confidence that you will reveal it to no one, since you promised this. Yet I fear that you may become its doorway, and that once released it may not be possible to recall it.

If that should happen, and you see it being read by some people, you will ask the readers’ indulgence: let them weigh the facts rather than the words, and bear with equanimity any defective style that may have struck their ears. For the kingdom of God consists not in eloquence but in faith.

Let them also remember that salvation was proclaimed to the world not by orators but by fishermen, although, if it had been useful, the Lord could certainly have supplied that as well.

When I first applied my mind to writing, I decided within myself that I would not blush at solecisms, because I considered it wrong for the virtues of so great a man to remain hidden. I have never possessed great knowledge of such matters; and if I once happened to taste something of these studies, I lost it all through the disuse of so many years.

Yet, so that we may not be burdened by such an annoying defense, let the book be published, if you think fit, without my name. To make this possible, erase the title from its front, so that the page may remain silent; or, what is sufficient, let it speak of the subject without speaking of the author.

## The Book Begins

### I

Most mortals, vainly devoted to ambition and worldly glory, have sought what they considered perpetual remembrance of their names by illuminating the lives of famous men with their writing.

This undertaking did not, of course, provide truly perpetual fruit, but it did yield some small return for the hope they had conceived. They extended the memory of themselves, though uselessly, and by presenting the examples of great men they aroused no slight emulation in their readers.

Yet their concern had nothing to do with that blessed and eternal life. What benefit did the glory of their writings bring to the authors themselves, when it would perish with the world? Or what advantage did posterity gain from reading about Hector fighting or Socrates philosophizing?

Indeed, not only is it foolish to imitate such men, but it is madness not to attack them with the greatest vigor, since they measured human life only by present actions, entrusted their hopes to fables, and their souls to tombs. They believed that they would be made immortal merely in human memory, whereas it is the duty of a human being to seek perpetual life rather than perpetual remembrance—not by writing, fighting, or philosophizing, but by living piously, holily, and religiously.

This human error, handed down through literature, has had such influence that it has found many imitators, either of empty philosophy or of that foolish form of virtue.

Therefore I seem to myself to be undertaking a worthwhile task if I write out the life of a most holy man, which will soon become an example for others. Through it, readers will be stirred toward true wisdom, heavenly warfare, and divine virtue.

In this matter we also consider our own advantage—not by seeking empty remembrance from human beings, but by expecting an eternal reward from God. For although we ourselves have not lived in such a way as to be examples to others, we have nevertheless taken care that the one who ought to be imitated should not remain unknown.

I shall therefore begin to write the life of Saint Martin, describing how he conducted himself both before becoming a bishop and as a bishop.

Although I have by no means been able to discover everything about him—for those things of which he alone was conscious are unknown, since he did not seek praise from human beings and, insofar as he could, wished all his virtues to remain hidden—I have also omitted much even from what had come to our knowledge. We thought it sufficient to record only the more outstanding matters.

At the same time, we had to consider the readers, lest an accumulation of material produce weariness. I ask those who are going to read this work to place their faith in what I say and to believe that I have written nothing except what I had discovered and verified. Otherwise, I would have preferred to remain silent rather than speak falsely.

## II

Martin was born at Sabaria, a town of Pannonia, but was brought up in Italy, at Ticinum. His parents were not of the lowest rank according to worldly status, though they were pagans. His father was first a soldier and later a military tribune. Martin himself entered the armed service in adolescence and served among the *scholares* units under the emperor Constantius, and afterward under Caesar Julian—not willingly, however, since from his earliest years his holy childhood had breathed a preference for divine service.

For when he was ten years old, he fled to a church against his parents’ wishes and asked to become a catechumen. Soon, in a remarkable way, he turned wholly toward the work of God. At twelve he longed for the desert and would have fulfilled his desire had the weakness of his age not prevented him. Nevertheless, his mind was always intent upon monasteries or the church; even in childhood he was contemplating what he later fulfilled in devotion.

But when the emperors issued an edict that the sons of veterans should be enrolled for military service, his father—who envied his son’s virtuous conduct—betrayed him. At fifteen he was arrested, put in chains, and bound by the military oath. He was content with only one servant as his companion; yet in turn he served his servant, so much so that he often removed and cleaned the man’s shoes himself. They took their meals together, though Martin more often served him.

He remained under arms for nearly three years before baptism, yet untouched by the vices in which that class of men is usually entangled. He showed great kindness toward his comrades and extraordinary charity; his patience and humility, moreover, were beyond ordinary human measure. It is unnecessary to praise his frugality, for he practiced it so rigorously that even at that time he was thought not a soldier but a monk. By these qualities he bound all his fellow soldiers to himself, so that they revered him with remarkable affection.

Although he had not yet been reborn in Christ, he lived as one preparing himself for baptism through good works: assisting those in distress, aiding the unfortunate, feeding the needy, and clothing the naked. Reserving from his military pay nothing beyond his daily food, he was already a listener to the Gospel who was not deaf to its command and did not think about tomorrow.

## III

Once, when he possessed nothing except his weapons and the simple military cloak he wore, in midwinter—which had become unusually harsh, so that its bitter cold killed many—he encountered at the gate of the city of Amiens a naked beggar. The man begged passersby to pity him, but everyone passed the wretch by. The man of God understood that the beggar had been reserved for him, since the others had shown him no mercy.

But what could he do? He had nothing except the cloak he was wearing, for he had already spent the rest on similar acts of charity. Taking the sword with which he was girded, he cut the cloak in half, gave one part to the beggar, and put the remainder on again.

Meanwhile, some of those standing nearby laughed, because his truncated garment made him look disfigured. Many others, however, whose minds were sounder, groaned more deeply, since they had done nothing similar, although they possessed more than enough to clothe the beggar without making themselves naked.

That night, after he had gone to sleep, he saw Christ clothed in the part of his cloak with which he had covered the beggar. He was commanded to look carefully at the Lord and recognize the garment he had given. Soon he heard Jesus saying in a clear voice, amid a multitude of angels standing around him:

“Martin, still a catechumen, covered me with this garment.”

The Lord truly remembered his own words—“Whenever you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me”—and declared that he had been clothed in the beggar. To confirm the testimony of so good a deed, he deigned to appear in the same garment the beggar had received.

When he saw this, the most blessed man was not lifted up into human glory. Rather, recognizing God’s goodness in his own deed, he hurried to baptism at the age of eighteen. He did not, however, immediately renounce military service, overcome by the entreaties of his tribune, with whom he maintained a close companionship. For Martin promised that, when the period of his tribuneship had ended, he would renounce the world. Thus, held in suspense by this expectation, he served for nearly two years after receiving baptism, though in name only.

## IV

Meanwhile, when barbarians had invaded Gaul, Caesar Julian assembled an army at the city of the Vangiones and began distributing a gift of money to the soldiers. As was customary, each man was summoned in turn, until Martin’s name was reached.

Then, judging that the opportunity had come to request his discharge—for he did not consider it proper to accept the gift if he was no longer going to serve—he said to the Caesar:

“Until now I have served you. Allow me now to serve God. Let your gift be received by one who is going to fight; I am a soldier of Christ, and I may not fight.”

At this statement the tyrant raged, saying that Martin was refusing military service out of fear of the battle that was to take place the following day, not for religious reasons.

But Martin, undaunted—or rather, made more steadfast by the terror directed against him—replied:

“If this is attributed to cowardice and not to faith, tomorrow I shall stand unarmed before the battle line. In the name of the Lord Jesus, protected by the sign of the cross rather than by shield or helmet, I shall enter the enemy ranks without fear.”

He was therefore ordered to be confined, so that he might prove the truth of his words by being exposed unarmed to the barbarians. On the following day the enemy sent envoys to sue for peace, surrendering themselves and all their possessions.

Who, then, could doubt that this was truly the blessed man’s victory, since he was granted that he should not be sent unarmed into battle? Although the merciful Lord could have preserved his soldier even amid the swords and weapons of the enemy, he removed the necessity of battle so that the saint’s eyes would not be violated even by the death of others. Christ could grant no other victory on behalf of his soldier than this: that, with the enemy subdued without bloodshed, no one should die.

## V

After leaving the army, Martin sought out Hilary, the bishop of the city of Poitiers, whose faith in the things of God was then widely recognized and esteemed, and remained with him for some time.

Hilary tried to bind him more closely to himself by imposing the office of deacon and to overcome him through divine service. But Martin repeatedly resisted, loudly declaring himself unworthy. The man of deeper understanding realized that Martin could be constrained only by imposing upon him an office in which there might seem to be some element of insult. He therefore ordered him to become an exorcist. Martin did not reject the ordination, lest he seem to despise it as something inferior.

Not long afterward, he was warned in sleep to visit his homeland and parents, who were still held in paganism, with religious concern. With the permission of Saint Hilary, he departed, bound by many prayers and tears from Hilary that he should return.

As they say, he undertook that journey sorrowfully, declaring to the brothers that he would suffer many adversities; subsequent events proved him right. First, while following a remote path through the Alps, he fell among robbers. When one of them had raised an axe and poised a blow at his head, another seized the attacker’s right hand. Martin was nevertheless handed over to one of them with his hands bound behind him, to be guarded and stripped of his possessions.

After taking him to a more secluded place, the robber began to ask who he was. Martin replied that he was a Christian. The robber also asked whether he was afraid. Martin then declared with complete confidence that he had never been so secure, because he knew that the Lord’s mercy is especially present in temptations. Rather, he said, he felt pity for the robber, who, since he practiced robbery, was unworthy of Christ’s mercy. Then he entered into an evangelical discussion and preached the word of God to the robber.

Why delay any longer? The robber believed, escorted Martin back to the road, and begged him to pray to the Lord on his behalf. Later, it was said, the man was seen living a religious life; indeed, the events I have related above were reportedly heard from his own lips.

## VI

Martin then continued on his way and passed Milan. On the road, the devil assumed human form and came to meet him, asking where he was going. When Martin replied that he was heading wherever the Lord called him, the devil said:

“Wherever you go, and whatever you attempt, the devil will oppose you.”

Martin answered him in a prophetic voice:

“The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.”

Immediately the enemy vanished from his sight.

Thus, as he had conceived in his mind and heart, Martin freed his mother from the error of paganism, although his father persisted in wickedness. He nevertheless saved many others by his example.

Then, when the Arian heresy had spread throughout the world and especially within Illyricum, Martin fought almost alone and with the utmost vigor against the treachery of the priests. He suffered many punishments: he was publicly beaten with rods and finally compelled to leave the city.

Returning toward Italy, he discovered that the Church in Gaul had also been thrown into confusion by the departure of Saint Hilary, whom the violence of the heretics had forced into exile. Martin established a monastery for himself at Milan. There, too, Auxentius, the author and leader of the Arians, persecuted him most severely and, after subjecting him to many injuries, drove him from the city.

Judging that he must yield to circumstances, Martin withdrew to an island called Gallinaria, accompanied by a certain presbyter, a man of great virtue. There he lived for some time on the roots of plants. On one occasion he ate hellebore, a poisonous herb, as they say; but when he felt its poison spreading through him and death already near, he drove away the danger by prayer, and all pain immediately vanished.

Not long afterward, when he learned that the king had granted Hilary permission to return from exile, he tried to meet him in Rome and set out for the city.

## VII

By the time Hilary had passed through, Martin followed his footsteps in this way. When Hilary received him with great affection, Martin established a monastery for himself not far from the town.

At that time a certain catechumen joined him, wishing to be trained in the discipline of the most holy man. After only a few days, the catechumen fell ill and was suffering severely from a raging fever. Martin happened to be away. When he returned after an absence of three days, he found the man’s body lifeless. Death had come so suddenly that he had departed from human affairs without baptism.

The body had been placed in the middle of the room, and the sorrowful brothers were crowded around it in mourning service, when Martin came running, weeping and wailing. Then, taking the Holy Spirit into his whole mind, he ordered the others to leave the cell in which the body lay. After shutting the doors, he threw himself upon the lifeless limbs of the deceased brother. Having devoted himself for some time to prayer, and having perceived through the Spirit of the Lord that power was present, he rose a little, fixed his gaze upon the dead man’s face, and fearlessly awaited the outcome of his prayer and the Lord’s mercy.

Hardly two hours had passed when he saw all the dead man’s limbs gradually begin to move and his eyes, relaxing for sight, flutter. Martin then turned toward the Lord with a loud voice and gave thanks, filling the cell with his cry. Hearing this, those who had been standing outside immediately rushed in.

It was a marvelous sight: the man whom they had left dead was alive. Restored to life, he immediately received baptism and lived many years afterward. He was the first among us to be either the occasion or the testimony of Martin’s miracles.

The man used to relate that, after being separated from his body, he had been led before the judge’s tribunal. He had been assigned to gloomy places and had received a sad sentence amid the common crowds. Then two angels had suggested to the judge that he was the man for whom Martin was praying. Through those same angels he had been ordered to return and had been given back to Martin, restored to life and to his former existence.

From this time the name of the blessed man first began to shine forth: he who was already regarded by everyone as holy was now also regarded as powerful and truly apostolic.

## VIII

Not long afterward, as Martin was passing by the estate of a certain Lupicinus, a man honored according to worldly standards, he was met by the cries and lamentation of a grieving crowd.

Concerned, he stopped and asked what the weeping meant. He was told that a young household servant had taken his own life by hanging.

When Martin learned this, he entered the cell where the body lay. After excluding the entire crowd, he stretched himself over the body and prayed for a while. Soon the dead man, whose face had been lifeless and whose eyes had withered, lifted himself and looked into Martin’s face. With a slow effort he struggled to rise; then, taking the blessed man’s right hand, he stood on his feet. He proceeded with Martin as far as the entrance of the house, while the whole crowd looked on.

## IX

At about the same time, Martin was being sought for the episcopate of the Church of Tours. But since he could not easily be drawn from his monastery, a certain Ruricius, one of the citizens, pretended that his wife was ill and, falling at Martin’s knees, succeeded in persuading him to leave.

The citizens had already arranged crowds along the road, and Martin was escorted to the city as though under guard. In an astonishing manner, an immense multitude gathered to cast its votes, not only from that town but also from neighboring cities.

There was one desire among them all, the same prayers and the same judgment: Martin was most worthy of the episcopate, and the Church would be fortunate to have such a priest.

A few men, however, including some of the bishops who had been summoned to establish the new bishop, wickedly resisted. They declared that Martin was a contemptible person, unworthy of the episcopate, a man despicable in appearance, dirty in clothing, and disfigured in hair.

The people, whose judgment was sounder, laughed at this madness of theirs. In wishing to disparage the distinguished man, they were actually proclaiming his virtues. The opposing party could do nothing except what the people, by the Lord’s will, compelled them to do.

Among the bishops who were present, a certain defender—so he is said to have been named—was especially resistant. It was therefore observed that he was gravely marked out at that moment by a prophetic reading.

For when the regular reader, whose duty it was to read that day, was prevented by the crowd from attending, the ministers were thrown into confusion while they waited for the absent man. One of those standing nearby took up a psalter and seized the first verse he found. The psalm was:

“From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, so that you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Psalm 8:3).

When it had been read, the people raised a shout and the opposing party was confounded. It was therefore held that, by divine direction, this psalm had been read so that the defender might hear testimony concerning his own deed: for from the mouth of infants and nursing children, in Martin, the Lord’s praise had been perfected, and the enemy had thereby both been exposed and destroyed.

## X

What Martin accomplished, and to what extent, once he had assumed the episcopate, it is beyond our ability to unfold. He remained exactly as he had been before. The same humility was in his heart, and the same plainness in his clothing. Thus, full of authority and grace, he fulfilled the dignity of a bishop without abandoning the discipline and virtue of a monk.

For some time he used a cell attached to the church. Then, unable to endure the disturbance caused by those who visited him constantly, he established a monastery for himself about two miles outside the city.

The place was so secluded and remote that he did not long for the solitude of the desert. On one side it was enclosed by the sheer cliff of a high mountain; the rest of the plain was closed off by the Loire River, which curved slightly around it. It could be approached by only one narrow road.

Martin had a cell woven from wood, and many of the brothers had cells built in the same way. Most had made shelters for themselves by hollowing out the rock of the overhanging mountain.

There were eighty disciples, who were being trained according to the example of the blessed master. No one there possessed anything as his own; everything was held in common. No one was allowed to buy or sell anything, as is customary among many monks.

No craft was practiced there except that of the copyists; the younger men were assigned to this work, while the elders devoted themselves to prayer. Few ever left their cells except when they gathered at the place of prayer.

After the fast, they all took their food together. No one knew wine, except one whom illness had forced to drink it. Most wore garments made from camel hair; a softer garment was considered a fault.

This is all the more astonishing because many among them were of noble birth. Raised in a very different manner, they had compelled themselves to adopt this humility and patience. We later saw many of them become bishops.

For what city or church would not desire a priest from Martin’s monastery?

## XI

But to turn to the other virtues he displayed during his episcopate: not far from the town and near the monastery there was a place that popular error had consecrated as though martyrs had been buried there. An altar was also said to have been established there by earlier bishops.

Martin, who did not rashly place confidence in uncertain matters, repeatedly demanded from the older presbyters and clerics that the martyr’s name and the time of his passion be shown to him. He said that he was deeply troubled because the memory of his predecessors had handed down nothing certain or consistent.

For some time he therefore kept away from the place. He neither detracted from religion, since he was uncertain, nor lent his authority to popular belief, lest superstition grow stronger.

One day, taking a few brothers with him, he went to the place. Standing over the tomb itself, he prayed to the Lord to reveal who had been buried there and what merit the man possessed.

Then he turned to the left and saw standing nearby a filthy, savage-looking shadow. He ordered it to declare its name and merit. The shadow gave its name and confessed its crime: it had been a robber, struck down for its offenses, and celebrated through popular error. It had nothing in common with the martyrs, since glory held them while punishment held him.

In a remarkable way, those present heard the voice speaking, although they did not see the person. Martin then explained what he had seen and ordered the altar that had stood there to be removed. In this way he freed the people from that superstition.

## XII

Later, while Martin was traveling, he happened to encounter the body of a pagan being carried to a tomb in a superstitious funeral procession. Seeing from a distance a crowd approaching, he stopped for a while, not knowing what it was. The distance was nearly five hundred paces, so that it was difficult to identify what he saw.

Nevertheless, because he observed a rustic crowd and saw linen coverings thrown over the body fluttering in the wind, he thought that profane sacrificial rites were being performed. It was customary among the rural Gauls, in their wretched madness, to carry images of demons covered with white cloth through their fields.

He therefore raised the sign of the cross toward them and ordered the crowd not to move from the place and to set down its burden. At this point, in a remarkable manner, one might have seen the wretched men first stiffen as though they were stones. Then, when they tried with all their strength to move forward, unable to advance any farther, they spun around in a ridiculous whirl until, overcome, they set down the body.

Struck with astonishment and looking at one another, they silently wondered what had happened to them. But when the blessed man learned that the gathering was for a funeral, not for sacred rites, he raised his hand again and granted them permission to depart and carry away the body.

Thus, whenever he wished, he compelled them to stand still; and whenever he pleased, he allowed them to leave.

## XIII

Likewise, when Martin had demolished a very ancient temple in a certain village and had begun to cut down a pine tree that stood near the shrine, the local priest and the rest of the pagan crowd began to resist him.

Although these same people had remained quiet while the temple was being destroyed at the Lord’s command, they would not permit the tree to be cut down. Martin earnestly warned them that there was no religious significance in a tree trunk and urged them to follow the God whom he served. He said that the tree ought to be cut down because it had been dedicated to a demon.

Then one of them, bolder than the others, said:

“If you have any confidence in your God, whom you claim to worship, we ourselves will cut down this tree. You must catch it as it falls; and if your Lord is with you, as you say, you will escape.”

Martin, trusting fearlessly in the Lord, promised that he would do so. The entire pagan crowd agreed to this condition. They readily accepted the loss of their tree if, when it fell, they could crush the enemy of their rites.

Since the pine leaned to one side, so that there was no doubt in which direction it would fall when cut, Martin was bound and placed at the discretion of the villagers precisely where no one doubted the tree would come down.

The villagers began cutting down their pine with great joy and delight. A crowd of spectators stood at a distance. The pine gradually began to sway and threaten its fall.

The monks grew pale in the distance. Terrified as the danger drew nearer, they lost all hope and confidence and waited only for Martin’s death.

But he, trusting in the Lord and awaiting the outcome without fear, raised his hand as the pine fell with a crash and, already collapsing and rushing down upon him, met it with the sign of salvation. Then, as though driven backward by a whirlwind, it fell in the opposite direction, almost bringing down the villagers who had been standing there.

The pagans then raised a shout to heaven and marveled at the miracle; the monks wept for joy; and everyone together proclaimed the name of Christ.

It was clear that salvation had come to that region on that day. For scarcely anyone among that immense pagan multitude failed, after requesting the laying on of hands and abandoning the error of impiety, to believe in the Lord Jesus.

Before Martin, very few—indeed, almost none—in those regions had received the name of Christ. Through his virtues and example it grew so strong that now there is no place there that is not filled either with numerous churches or with monasteries. Wherever he destroyed shrines, he immediately built churches or monasteries.

## XIV

At about the same time he displayed no lesser power in the same work. When he had set fire to an ancient and famous shrine in a certain village, balls of flame were driven by the wind toward the nearest house, indeed toward the house adjoining it.

When Martin noticed this, he quickly climbed onto the roof of the house and placed himself in the path of the approaching flames. Then, in a remarkable manner, one could see the fire driven back against the force of the wind, so that it seemed to be a kind of conflict between opposing elements.

Thus, through Martin’s power, the fire operated only where it had been ordered to do so.

In a village called Leprosum, when Martin likewise wished to destroy a very wealthy temple that was revered as a religious shrine, a pagan crowd resisted him so strongly that he was driven back, not without injury.

He therefore withdrew to a nearby place. There, for three days, clothed in sackcloth and covered with ashes, fasting continually and praying, he begged the Lord that, since human hands had been unable to destroy that temple, divine power might overthrow it.

Suddenly two angels, armed with spears and shields like a heavenly army, appeared before him and said that they had been sent by the Lord to scatter the rustic crowd and bring Martin aid, so that no one would resist while the temple was being demolished. He should therefore return and devoutly complete the work he had begun.

Martin returned to the village. The pagan crowds watched, but remained quiet while he destroyed the profane building down to its foundations. He reduced all its altars and images to dust.

When the villagers realized that by divine will they had been stunned and terrified, they ceased resisting the bishop. Almost all of them believed in the Lord Jesus, openly shouting and confessing that Martin’s God must be worshiped and that the idols must be disregarded, since they could not come to their aid.

## XV

I shall also relate what happened in the territory of the Aedui. While Martin was destroying a temple there, a furious crowd of pagan villagers attacked him. When one man, bolder than the rest, approached him with a drawn sword, Martin threw back his cloak and offered his bare neck to the attacker.

The pagan did not hesitate to strike. But when he had raised his right hand higher, he fell backward. Overcome with divine fear, he begged forgiveness.

A similar thing happened when someone wished to strike Martin with a knife while he was destroying idols: at the very moment of the blow, the weapon flew from the man’s hands and disappeared.

Often, when the villagers opposed him and refused to let him destroy their shrines, Martin so calmed their pagan minds through holy preaching that, once the light of truth had been shown to them, they themselves overturned their temples.

## XVI

The grace of healing was so powerful in Martin that scarcely any sick person approached him without immediately recovering health. The following example will make this clear.

At Trier a girl was suffering from a terrible paralysis, so that for a long time no bodily function served her for ordinary human purposes. Dead in nearly every part, she scarcely breathed with a faint spirit.

Her relatives stood sorrowfully, waiting only for her funeral, when suddenly word was announced that Martin had arrived in the city. When the girl’s father learned this, he ran out of his mind with grief to beg for his daughter.

Martin happened to have already entered the church. There, before the people and many other bishops, the old man came wailing and clasped Martin’s knees, saying:

“My daughter is dying from a miserable kind of illness. What is more cruel than death, she lives only in spirit, while her flesh is already dead. I beg you to visit her and bless her, for I trust that through you she will be restored to health.”

Martin was embarrassed and astonished by these words and recoiled, saying that this was not within his own power; that the old man was mistaken in his judgment; and that he was not worthy to be the one through whom the Lord would display a sign of power.

The father persisted more vehemently, weeping and begging Martin to visit the lifeless girl. At last the bishops standing nearby compelled him to go, and he descended to the girl’s house.

A great crowd waited outside to see what the servant of God would do. First he lay prostrate and prayed, using the familiar weapon he employed in such matters. Then, looking at the sick girl, he asked that oil be brought to him. After blessing it, he poured the power of the holy liquid into the girl’s mouth, and immediately her voice was restored.

Then, little by little, each of her limbs began to revive at his touch, until, her steps strengthened, she rose in the presence of the people.

## XVII

At the same time, a servant of a certain Tetradius, a proconsular man, had been seized by a demon and was being tormented by a painful death.

Martin was asked to lay his hand upon him. He ordered the man to be brought to him, but the evil spirit could not be brought out of the cell where he was in any way; it raged at those approaching with savage teeth.

Tetradius then fell at the knees of the blessed man and begged him to go himself to the house where the demoniac was being kept. Martin refused, saying that he could not enter the house of a profane pagan—for Tetradius was still entangled in the error of paganism.

Tetradius therefore promised that, if the demon were driven out of the boy, he would become a Christian. Martin laid his hand upon the boy and expelled the unclean spirit.

When Tetradius saw this, he believed in the Lord Jesus. He immediately became a catechumen and was baptized not long afterward. He always honored Martin, the author of his salvation, with extraordinary affection.

Around the same time, Martin entered the house of a certain head of a household in the same town. At the very threshold he stopped and said that he saw a horrible demon in the courtyard of the house.

When he ordered the demon to depart, it seized one of the household who was staying in the inner part of the building. The wretched man began to rage with his teeth and tear apart everyone he encountered. The house was thrown into confusion, the household was in turmoil, and the people fled.

Martin confronted the raging man and first ordered him to stand still. But when the man gnashed his teeth and threatened to bite with his mouth wide open, Martin put his fingers into his mouth and said:

“If you have any power, devour these.”

Then, as though he had taken burning iron into his jaws, the demon drew its teeth far back and avoided touching the blessed man’s fingers. When it was forced by pains and torments to flee from the possessed body, yet was not permitted to leave through the mouth, it left foul traces and was expelled through a discharge of the bowels.

## XVIII

Meanwhile, when sudden news of the movement and advance of the barbarians had thrown the city into confusion, Martin ordered a demoniac to be brought before him. He commanded the spirit to confess whether the report was true.

The spirit then confessed that there had been ten demons who had spread this rumor among the people so that, at least through fear, Martin might be driven from the town. The barbarians were thinking of nothing less than an invasion.

When the unclean spirit confessed this in the middle of the church, the city was freed from its present fear and confusion.

At Paris, while Martin was entering through the city gate with a great crowd accompanying him, he kissed and blessed a leper whose face was so dreadful that everyone recoiled. Immediately the man was cleansed of every affliction. The next day he came to the church with clear skin and gave thanks for the health he had received.

Nor should we pass over the fact that fringes taken from Martin’s garments and hair-shirt often worked healing miracles among the sick. Tied around the fingers or placed around the neck, they very often drove illnesses away.

## XIX

Arborius, a former prefect, a man of remarkably holy and faithful character, had a daughter who was burning with severe quartan fevers. By chance a letter from Martin had been brought to him. He placed it on the girl’s chest at the very onset of the fever’s attack, and the fever immediately departed.

This event had such an effect upon Arborius that he immediately vowed the girl to God and dedicated her to perpetual virginity. He then went to Martin and presented the girl to him as a living testimony to his powers, since she had been healed by him even while he was absent. Arborius would not allow her to be consecrated by anyone other than Martin, who placed upon her the habit of virginity.

Paulinus, who was later to become a man of great example, began to suffer severe pain in one eye. A dense cloud had already covered and obscured his pupil. Martin touched the eye with a small brush and restored its former health, removing all the pain.

On another occasion Paulinus fell from an upper room and, tumbling down the rough steps of a staircase, sustained many wounds. He lay lifeless in his cell and was tormented by excessive pain. During the night an angel appeared to him, washing his wounds and touching the limbs of his battered body with healing ointment. The next day he was restored to health, so completely that he seemed never to have suffered any injury.

But since it would be tedious to proceed through each case, let these few examples from among the many suffice. Let it be enough that we neither suppress the truth in matters of great importance nor create weariness by recounting too many.

## XX

And to insert lesser matters among such great ones—although, given the character of our times, in which everything has already become depraved and corrupt, it is almost a supreme achievement not to have surrendered priestly steadfastness to royal flattery:

When several bishops from different regions had gathered before the emperor Maximus, a man of fierce character and exalted by victory in civil wars, and when disgraceful flattery of every kind was being displayed around the ruler, while the dignity of the priesthood had submitted with degraded instability to royal patronage, only in Martin did apostolic authority remain.

Whenever it was necessary to plead with the emperor on someone’s behalf, Martin commanded rather than begged. He also frequently refused invitations to dine with him, saying that he could not share the table of a man who had expelled one emperor from his kingdom and another from life.

At last Maximus insisted that he had not seized the empire willingly, but had defended by arms the royal power that the soldiers had imposed upon him by divine will. God’s will, he said, did not appear hostile to him, since victory had come to him through so extraordinary an event and none of his opponents had fallen except in battle.

Finally, overcome either by reason or by entreaties, Martin came to the banquet. The emperor rejoiced remarkably that he had obtained this.

The guests had been summoned as though for a festival: the highest and most distinguished men, including Evodius, prefect and consul, a man more just than any who had ever lived; two counts endowed with supreme power; the emperor’s brother and his uncle. Martin’s presbyter reclined between them, while Martin himself sat on a small stool placed beside the emperor.

About halfway through the banquet, as was customary, a servant offered the emperor a drinking cup. The emperor ordered it to be given instead to the most holy bishop, waiting and hoping to receive the cup from Martin’s right hand.

But after Martin had drunk, he handed the cup to his own presbyter. He evidently considered no one more worthy to drink first after him, and he did not think it proper to place either the emperor himself or those closest to the emperor before his presbyter.

The emperor and everyone present admired this action so greatly that they were pleased by the very thing through which they had been slighted. It became famous throughout the palace that Martin, at the emperor’s banquet, had done what no bishop had done even at the banquets of humble judges.

Martin had also foretold to Maximus long beforehand that, if he went to Italy—as he desired to do—to make war upon the emperor Valentinian, he would be victorious at the first assault but would perish soon afterward.

We saw this prophecy fulfilled. At his first arrival Valentinian was put to flight; then, after recovering his strength about a year later, he captured Maximus within the walls of Aquileia and killed him.

### XXI

It is also established that he frequently saw angels, so that they would converse with one another in his presence; but he kept the devil so plainly visible and subject to his sight that, whether the devil remained in his own substance or transformed himself into various shapes of spiritual wickedness, Martin saw him under whatever guise he assumed. Since the devil knew that he could not escape Martin, he often assailed him with insults, because he could not deceive him by ambush.

On one occasion, holding in his hand a bloodstained ox-horn, he burst into Martin’s cell with a great roar. Displaying his bloody right hand and rejoicing in the recent crime, he said: “Where is your power, Martin? I have just killed one of your men.”

[Col. 0172B]

Then Martin summoned the brothers and reported what the devil had revealed. He ordered them to make inquiries in each monk’s cell to discover who had suffered such a misfortune. They reported that no monk was missing, but that a hired peasant, who had gone to the forest to haul wood by wagon, had not returned. Martin therefore ordered some men to go and meet him. Not far from the monastery they found him, already almost lifeless.

Nevertheless, while still drawing his last breath, he explained to the brothers the cause of his death and wound: while the oxen were yoked together, he had been tightening the loosened reins more firmly, when one of the oxen, tossing its head, drove its horn between his thighs. Not long afterward he gave up his life. Let whoever can determine by what judgment of the Lord this power was given to the devil.

In Martin this was remarkable: not only did he foresee the event related above, [Col. 0172C] but whenever many similar things occurred, he perceived them long beforehand or, when they had been reported to him, disclosed them to the brothers.

### XXII

Often, while the devil tried to mock the holy man by a thousand devices of harm, he thrust himself visibly upon him in the most diverse forms. Sometimes he appeared in the likeness of Jupiter, more often of Mercury, and very frequently he presented himself transformed into the features of Venus or Minerva. Martin, however, always remained undaunted and protected himself against him by the sign of the cross and the help of prayer.

The insults with which a crowd of demons berated him in insolent voices were also often heard. But knowing all these things to be false and empty, he was not disturbed by what was hurled against him.

Some of the brothers also testified that they had heard a demon angrily berating Martin [Col. 0172D] and asking why he had received into the monastery certain brothers who had once lost their baptism through various errors but had afterward been converted. The demon recited the crimes of each of them. Martin, resisting the devil, steadfastly replied that ancient offenses are cleansed by a life of better conduct, and that, through the mercy of the Lord, those who cease to sin must be absolved from their sins.

When the devil answered that criminals had no share in forgiveness and that the Lord showed no mercy to those who had once fallen, Martin is said to have cried out:

“If you yourself, O wretched one, would cease persecuting human beings, and if even now—when the day of judgment is near—you would repent of your deeds, I, truly trusting in the Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0173A] would promise you mercy.”

O what a holy presumption concerning the Lord’s compassion! Although Martin could not confer authority upon it, he revealed his disposition.

Since the discussion has arisen concerning the devil and his arts, it does not seem irrelevant, even though it is external to our subject, to recount what happened; for it contains a certain share of Martin’s powers, and an event worthy of a miracle will rightly be entrusted to memory as an example of caution, should anything of the kind happen anywhere in the future.

### XXIII

A certain man named Clarus, a very noble young man—later a presbyter and now blessed by a happy departure from this life—came to Martin after abandoning everything. In a short time he rose to the highest summit of faith and every virtue.

Accordingly, after he had set up a tent for himself not far from the bishop’s monastery, and many brothers were staying with him, a certain young man [Col. 0173B] named Anatolius approached him. Under the guise of a monk, he falsely assumed every appearance of humility and innocence, and for some time lived there in common with the others.

As time passed, he began saying that angels regularly spoke with him. Since no one believed him, he compelled many to believe by means of certain signs. At last he went so far as to proclaim that angels traveled back and forth between himself and God; and he already wanted to be regarded as one of the prophets.

Clarus, however, could in no way be forced to believe him. Anatolius threatened him with the wrath of God and present punishments because he did not believe a holy man. Finally he is said to have burst out with these words:

“Behold, this night the Lord will give me a white garment from heaven. Clothed in it, I shall move among you; and this will be your sign that I am God’s power, since I have been endowed with God’s [Col. 0173C] garment.”

Then everyone eagerly awaited the fulfillment of this declaration. At about midnight the whole monastery seemed to be shaken by the roar of the earth being trampled by those who were stamping upon it. The cell in which the young man was staying appeared to flash repeatedly with lights; within it could be heard the roar of those moving about and a kind of murmur of many voices.

Afterward, when silence had fallen, he came out, summoned one of the brothers, named Sabacius, and showed him the tunic he was wearing. Sabacius, astonished, called the others; Clarus himself also hurried there. After a light had been brought, they all carefully examined the garment.

It was extraordinarily soft, of remarkable whiteness, and gleamed with purple. Yet it was impossible [Col. 0173D] to determine what kind of garment it was or of what wool. When it was handled more closely with the eyes or fingers, it appeared to be nothing other than a garment.

Meanwhile Clarus urged the brothers to persist in prayer, so that the Lord might show them more clearly what the object was. Thus they spent the rest of the night in hymns and psalms.

When day dawned, Clarus wanted to seize Anatolius by the right hand and drag him to Martin, being well aware that the devil could not deceive Martin by such a trick. But the wretched man began to resist and protest, saying that he had been forbidden to show himself to Martin.
