When they compelled him to go against his will, the garment vanished between the hands of those who were dragging him. Who, then, could doubt that this too was a power of Martin’s: that the devil, when his phantom was to be thrust upon Martin’s eyes, could neither continue concealing nor disguising it?

[Col. 0174A]

### XXIV

It was also observed that, at almost the same time, there was in Spain a young man who, having established his authority by many signs, became so elated that he declared himself to be Elijah.

When many had rashly believed him, he went further and said that he was Christ. In this deception he succeeded so thoroughly that a certain bishop named Rufus worshiped him as the Lord. For this reason we afterward saw Rufus removed from the episcopate.

Several of the brothers also reported to us that at the same time there had arisen in the East a certain man who boasted that he was John. From this we may infer that, when such false prophets appear, the coming of Antichrist is near—he who is already working the mystery of iniquity in these men.

Nor should it be passed over how artfully the devil [Col. 0174B] tested Martin in those same days. One day he first surrounded himself with, and caused to shine before him, a purple light, so that he might more easily deceive Martin by the splendor of the radiance he had assumed. He was also dressed in royal clothing, crowned with a diadem of gems and gold, wearing shoes gilded with gold, with a serene expression and cheerful face—so that he might be thought anything rather than the devil. In this guise he stood before Martin as he prayed in his cell.

At first sight Martin was stunned by him, and for a long while they both remained silent. Then the devil spoke first:

“Recognize, Martin, the one you see. I am Christ. Before descending to earth, I wished first to reveal myself to you.”

When Martin remained silent and gave no answer, the devil dared to repeat his bold declaration:

“Martin, why do you hesitate to believe when you see? I am Christ.”

Then, with the Spirit revealing to him that this was the devil and not [Col. 0174C] God, Martin said:

“The Lord Jesus did not foretell that he would come clad in purple and shining with a diadem. I will not believe that Christ has come unless he bears the appearance and form in which he suffered, unless he displays the marks of the cross.”

At these words the devil immediately vanished like smoke and filled the cell with such a stench that he left unmistakable evidence that he had been the devil.

I learned that this happened as I have related it from Martin’s own mouth, lest anyone should perhaps think it fabulous.

### XXV

When in former days we had heard of his faith, life, and virtues, we burned with the desire to see him and undertook the welcome journey to visit him. At the same time, since my mind was already eager to write his life, we learned some things from Martin himself, insofar as he could be questioned, and others from those who had been present or knew what had [Col. 0174D] happened.

At that time it is impossible to believe with what humility and kindness he received me, rejoicing and giving thanks greatly in the Lord that we had thought so highly of him as to seek him by undertaking a journey.

Wretched man that I am!—I scarcely dare confess it—when he had deigned to admit me to his holy meal, he himself offered water to wash our hands; and in the evening he himself washed our feet. I had neither the firmness to resist nor the courage to object. His authority so overwhelmed me that I would have considered it a sacrilege not to comply.

His conversation with us concerned nothing other than the need to abandon the allurements of this world and the burdens of the age, so that we might follow the Lord Jesus freely and unencumbered. [Col. 0175A] He continually presented to us the outstanding example, in our own time, of the illustrious man Paulinus, whom we mentioned above. Having cast aside his great wealth and followed Christ, he had almost alone in those times fulfilled the commandments of the Gospel. “He is the one to follow,” Martin cried; “he is the one to imitate.”

He declared that the present age was blessed by so great an example of faith and virtue: in accordance with the Lord’s saying, a rich man possessing much had sold everything and given it to the poor, making possible by his example what had seemed impossible to do.

How great was the gravity and dignity of Martin’s words and conversation! How sharp, effective, ready, and fluent he was in resolving questions concerning the Scriptures! Since I know that many people are incredulous about this—for I have seen [Col. 0175B] some refuse to believe it even when I myself have reported it—I call Jesus and our common hope as witnesses that I have never heard from anyone’s mouth such learning, such intelligence, or speech so good and so pure.

Yet how small a praise this is among Martin’s virtues—except that it is remarkable that even this grace was not lacking in an uneducated man.

### XXVI

But now the book demands an end, and the discourse must be brought to a close—not because everything that ought to be said about Martin has been exhausted, but because we, like sluggish poets negligent in the final part of their work, are overcome and collapse beneath the mass of our material.

Although his deeds could somehow be set forth in words, no discourse will ever explain his inner life, his daily conduct, and his mind always directed toward heaven—this I truly confess.

His perseverance [Col. 0175C] and moderation in abstinence and fasting; his strength in vigils and prayers; the nights he spent just as though they were days; and the fact that he allowed no time to remain empty of God’s work, whether by indulging in leisure or attending to business—not even food or sleep, except insofar as the necessity of nature compelled him: truly, even if Homer himself, as they say, were to rise from the underworld, he could not describe these things.

Everything in Martin was so great that it cannot be grasped in words. Never did an hour or moment pass in which he was not either devoted to prayer or intent upon reading. Even while reading, [Col. 0176A] or if he happened to be doing something else, he never relaxed his mind from prayer.

Just as it is the custom of blacksmiths, who, while working, strike their anvil to relieve their labor, so Martin, even when he seemed to be doing something else, was always praying.

O truly blessed man, in whom there was no deceit! He condemned no one and returned evil to no one for evil. He had acquired such patience toward every injury that, although he was the highest priest, he could be harmed with impunity even by the lowest clerics. Yet for that reason he never removed them from their position or, so far as depended on him, drove them away from his charity.

### XXVII

No one ever saw him angry, no one disturbed, no one grieving, no one laughing. Always one and the same, displaying upon his face a kind of heavenly joy, [Col. 0176B] he seemed to be beyond ordinary human nature.

Never was there anything in his mouth except Christ; never was there anything in his heart except devotion, peace, and mercy. He often used to weep over the sins of those who appeared to be his detractors, men who attacked him with their venomous tongues and poisonous mouths while he remained remote and tranquil.

We ourselves have encountered some who were envious of the virtues and life of this man—those who hated in him what they did not see in themselves and could not imitate.

And—O shameful thing, to be lamented and bewailed!—almost the only persecutors he had, although very few, were nevertheless generally bishops. There is no need to name anyone, although many of them barked all around us. It is enough that if one of them reads these words and recognizes himself, [Col. 0176C] he may blush. For if he becomes angry, he will admit that the words are about him, even though perhaps we intended them of others.

Nor do we refuse to have men of this kind hate us along with such a man. I confidently believe that this little work will be pleasing to all holy people. For the rest, if anyone reads these things without faith, he himself will sin. I am conscious that I wrote this because I was impelled by faith in the facts and love of Christ; I have set forth what was evident and spoken what was true. I hope that God will grant a reward—not to everyone who reads, but to everyone who believes.

[Col. 0175C]

## Three Letters of Sulpicius Severus (C)

### Letter I. To the Presbyter Eusebius

Against the rivals of the virtues of blessed Martin.

[Col. 0175D]

Yesterday, when several monks had come to me, during a continuous exchange and lengthy conversation the subject of my little book arose—the one I published about the life of the blessed man Martin—and I was delighted to hear that many people read it eagerly. [Col. 0176D]

Meanwhile I was informed that someone, stirred up by an evil spirit, had said: “Why was Martin, who had raised the dead and driven flames away from houses, recently himself burned and subjected to a dangerous ordeal?”

O wretched man, whoever he is! We recognize in his words the faithlessness and the sayings of the Jews, who rebuked the Lord as he hung upon the cross with these words: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42). [Col. 0177A]

Indeed, whoever you are, if you had been born in those times and had been able to say this of the Lord, you would have spoken in the same way as one who now blasphemes the Lord’s saint by a similar example.

What, then? Is Martin therefore powerless and therefore not holy because he was endangered by fire? O blessed man, and in every respect like the Apostles, even in these insults!

The Gentiles are also said to have spoken thus of Paul when a viper bit him: “This man must be a murderer; though saved from the sea, fate does not allow him to live” (Acts 28:4). But Paul shook the viper off into the fire and suffered no harm.

They expected him suddenly to fall and die; but when they saw that no harm came to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

Otherwise, by the example of these men, [Col. 0177B] you, most wretched of all mortals, ought yourself to have exposed your faithlessness. If it had scandalized you that Martin seemed to have been touched by the flame of fire, you should instead have referred this very encounter to his merit and power: surrounded by flames, he did not perish.

Recognize, wretched man—recognize what you do not know: almost all the saints have been made more illustrious by the virtues displayed in their dangers.

I see Peter, powerful in faith, walking upon the sea despite the opposition of nature and pressing the unstable waters beneath his bodily footstep. Yet for that reason the preacher to the nations does not seem lesser to me—the one whom the waves swallowed and whom the water restored after he had emerged from the depths after three days and as many nights. Indeed, I do not know whether it was greater to live in the depths or to pass over the depths of the sea. [Col. 0177C]

But you, as I suppose, foolishly, had not read these things or, though you had read them, had not heard them. For the blessed Evangelist would not have set forth such an example in the sacred writings without divine purpose, unless it were so that the human mind might be instructed by them: that shipwrecks and encounters with serpents—as the Apostle relates, boasting of nakedness, hunger, and dangers from robbers—and all such things are indeed common to holy men and to all human beings as things to be endured; but that in enduring and overcoming them the righteous have always possessed a special virtue, since, patient through every trial and always unconquered, they conquered more strongly the more grievously they suffered.

Thus, what is called an infirmity in Martin is full of dignity and glory, [Col. 0177D] since he was tested by a most dangerous accident and overcame it.

No one should be surprised that I omitted this in the little book I wrote about his life, since I stated there that I had not included all his deeds. Had I wished to pursue everything, I would have produced for readers an immense volume. The things he did are not so few that they could all have been included.

Nevertheless, I will not allow this matter, about which the question arose, to remain hidden. I will relate the whole event as it happened, lest we appear to have omitted through deliberate design something that could be brought forward to Martin’s discredit.

When Martin had come, in accordance with the customary practice, to a certain diocese—for bishops customarily visit their churches—in the middle of winter, the clerics prepared lodging for him in the church’s sacristy. They built up a large fire beneath a floor already rough and very thin, [Col. 0178A] and made him a bed piled high with straw.

After Martin had lain down, he recoiled from the unfamiliar softness of the bed, which offered him a treacherous comfort. He was accustomed to lie upon the bare ground with only a hairshirt thrown over him. Therefore, as though moved by the injury he had received, he threw all the straw away.

By chance, part of the straw he had removed came to rest upon the furnace. Martin himself, as was his custom, rested upon the bare ground, compelled by the weariness of the journey.

Around midnight, through the broken floor, the burning fire caught the drying straw. Martin awoke from sleep, overtaken by the unexpected event and the double danger—especially, as he himself related, because the devil was lying in wait and pressing the attack—and he fled more slowly than he should have to the aid of prayer.

As he tried to get outside [Col. 0178B] and struggled for a long time with the bolt he had fastened across the door, he felt a very great fire around him, so much so that the flames consumed the garment he was wearing.

At last, coming to himself, he knew that protection lay not in flight but in the Lord. Taking up the shield of faith and prayer, he turned wholly toward the Lord and fell down amid the flames. Then, by divine intervention, the fire was pushed aside, and Martin prayed within a circle of flames that caused him no harm.

The monks who were outside the door, hearing the crackling and tumultuous roar of the fire, broke open the barred doors. After moving the fire aside, they carried Martin out from the midst of the flames, although they had thought that he must already have been completely consumed by such a long-lasting fire.

The Lord is my witness to the truth of what I say: Martin himself told me this and confessed with a groan that he had been deceived by the devil’s art. Startled [Col. 0178C] from sleep, he had not had the presence of mind to resist the danger through faith and prayer. Finally, the fire raged around him for as long as, confused in mind, he tried to break out through the door.

But when he had taken up again the help of the cross and the weapons of prayer, the flames withdrew from his midst, and he then felt them sprinkling him with dew, though he had previously experienced them as burning him.

From this, whoever reads these words may understand that Martin was indeed tested by that danger, but also proved by it.

## Letter II. To the Deacon Aurelius

On the death and apparition of blessed Martin.

Sulpicius Severus sends greetings to Aurelius the deacon.

After you had departed from me in the morning, I was sitting [Col. 0178D] alone in my cell. Those thoughts that often occupy me had come upon me: hope of the future, disgust with the present, fear of judgment, dread of punishments; and, as naturally followed and from which the whole thought arose, the recollection of my sins had made me sad and exhausted.

Then, after I had laid my limbs upon the little bed, wearied by anguish of mind, sleep crept over me—as it often does in sorrow. Just as sleep at the first light of morning is always lighter and more uncertain, so it spreads suspended and doubtful through the limbs, so that, unlike what happens in deeper sleep, you almost feel yourself sleeping while awake.

Suddenly I seemed to see the holy bishop Martin: he wore a white-bordered toga, his face was fiery, his eyes were starry, and his hair was purple. He appeared to me in the bodily condition and form in which I had known him, so that—something almost impossible for us to express—he could not be looked upon, though he could be recognized. [Col. 0179A]

Smiling at me slightly, he held in his right hand the little book I had written about his life. I embraced his holy knees and asked for his blessing, according to custom. I felt his hand placed upon my head with the gentlest touch, while amid the solemn words of blessing he repeatedly spoke the familiar name of the cross with his lips.

Soon, as I gazed intently at him and could not have enough of the sight of his face and presence, he was suddenly lifted up and taken from me into the heights. When he had crossed the vastness of the air, although our eyes followed him as he was carried by a swift cloud, he could no longer be seen, received into the open sky.

Not long afterward I saw the holy presbyter [Col. 0179B] Clarus, his disciple, who had recently departed this life, ascending by the same path as his master. Shamelessly wishing to follow, while I struggled and strained to make great strides, I awoke.

When I had awakened from sleep, I began to rejoice over the vision. Then a familiar servant entered, sadder than usual, with a face that spoke of grief as much as of speech.

“Why,” I asked, “do you seem so sad that you wish to speak?”

“Two monks,” he replied, “have just arrived from Tours, announcing that the lord Martin has died.”

I collapsed, I confess, and, as tears welled up, I wept profusely. Even now, as we write these things to you, brother, the tears are flowing, and I admit no consolation for my unbearable grief.

When this was announced to me, I wanted you, who were my companion in love, to share my mourning. Come to me at once, then, so that together [Col. 0179C] we may mourn the one whom together we love.

Yet I know that we ought not to mourn that man to whom, after conquering and triumphing over the world, the crown of righteousness has at last been restored. Nevertheless, I cannot command myself not to grieve.

I sent ahead a protector, but I have lost the consolation of my present life. Even if grief allowed reason any room, I ought to rejoice. He has been joined to the Apostles and prophets and—to speak with due respect for all the saints—has, as I hope, believe, and trust, been added to the flock of the righteous, second to no one, especially those who washed their robes in blood. Pure from every stain, he follows the Lamb as his leader.

Although the circumstance of the time could not grant him martyrdom, he will not lack the martyr’s glory, because by his resolve and virtue he both could have been a martyr and desired to be one. [Col. 0179D]

If he had been permitted to fight in the times of Nero and Decius, in that conflict which then took place, I call the God of heaven and earth to witness that he would willingly have mounted the rack, freely have committed himself to the flames, and, made equal to the Hebrew boys, would have sung the Lord’s hymn in the furnace amid the balls of fire.

If his persecutor had happened to prefer the punishment inflicted upon Isaiah, he certainly would never have feared having his limbs cut apart by saws and blades, unequal to the prophet. If impious fury had preferred that he be made to pass through jagged rocks and broken mountains, I confidently give my testimony to the truth: he would have fallen willingly.

If, following the example of the teacher of the nations, he had been assigned to the sword and led [Col. 0180A] among other victims—as often happens—he would have been the first of all to seize the palm of blood, even forcing the executioner to act.

Against all the punishments and torments before which human weakness usually yields, he would have stood so immovable in his confession of the Lord that, joyful and rejoicing in his wounds, he would have laughed amid any tortures.

Although he did not undergo these things, he nevertheless fulfilled martyrdom even without bloodshed. What sufferings of human pain did he not endure for the hope of eternity—hunger, vigils, nakedness, fasts, the insults of the envious, the attacks of the wicked, care for the sick, concern for those in danger? For whose suffering did he not suffer? At whose scandal was he not burned? At whose destruction did he not groan?

Besides these were his daily struggles against the various forms of human and [Col. 0180B] spiritual wickedness. Though he was assailed by various temptations, the strength to overcome, the patience to wait, and the equanimity to endure always prevailed in him.

O truly ineffable man! His devotion, mercy, and charity—although these grow cold each day even in holy men as the world grows cold—continued in him to the end, increasing day by day.

I myself enjoyed this goodness of his in a special way, since he loved me uniquely, though I was unworthy and undeserving. Look: again the tears flow, and groans burst from the depths of my breast.

In what man will I find a similar rest hereafter? In whose love will there be consolation? Wretched and unhappy that I am! If I live longer, will I ever be able not to grieve that I survive Martin? Will life hereafter be pleasant to me? Will there be a day or hour [Col. 0180C] without tears? Or, dearest brother, shall I ever be able to mention him with you without weeping? Will I ever speak with you of anything other than him?

But why do I move you to tears and weeping? Behold, now I wish to console you, although I myself cannot be consoled.

Believe me, he will not be absent from us—he will not be absent. He will be present when we speak of him and will stand beside us when we pray. And what he has deigned to grant us already today, he will often allow us to see him in his glory, and, as he did a little while ago, will protect us with continual blessing.

In accordance with the order of the vision, he showed heaven opened to those who followed him and taught us by what path he was to be followed. He instructed us where our hope should be directed and toward what goal our mind should turn.

But what will become of me, brother? I know myself: I shall not be able to climb that difficult road or penetrate within. [Col. 0180D] So burdensome a load weighs me down, and, pressed beneath the weight of sin and denied ascent to the stars, my wretched self is driven fiercely into Tartarus.

Yet hope remains—the only hope, the last hope—that what we cannot obtain through ourselves, we may at least deserve through Martin’s prayers on our behalf.

But why do I detain you, brother, any longer with such a talkative letter, and delay your coming? The page is already full and can receive no more.

My reason for extending this discourse at such length was that, since the letter was bringing you news of grief, the same sheet might provide you consolation through a kind of conversation between us.

## Letter III. To Bassula, His Mother-in-Law

How blessed Martin passed from this life to immortality.

[Col. 0181A]

Sulpicius Severus sends greetings to the venerable Bassula, his mother-in-law.

If it were permitted to summon parents before the court, we would drag you before the praetor’s tribunal, with justified indignation, as guilty of plunder and theft.

For what complaint could I not make about the injury I suffer from you? You have left me no little sheet of paper at home, no little book, no letter. You steal everything; you publish everything. [Col. 0181B]

If I have written something familiarly to a friend; if, while we were joking, I happened to dictate something that I nevertheless wished to remain secret, everything reaches you almost before it has been written or dictated.

Clearly you have bribed my secretaries, through whom our foolishness is made public to you. Yet I cannot be angry with them if they obey you, since they came into our service chiefly through your generosity and still remember themselves to be yours rather than mine.

You alone are guilty; you alone are blameworthy. You lie in wait for me and trick them by fraud so that things written familiarly, sent off carelessly, composed late at night, and wholly unpolished are handed over to you.

To say nothing of the rest, tell me, I ask, how could that letter reach you so quickly which we recently wrote to the deacon Aurelius? I was in Toulouse, while you were staying at Trier, separated from your homeland by the son who keeps you unsettled. By what opportunity, then, did you steal that familiar [Col. 0181C] letter?

For I received a letter from you in which you write that, in the same letter in which I mentioned the death of the lord Martin, I ought to have explained the holy man’s passing itself.

As though I had published that letter for anyone other than the person to whom it appears to have been sent to read! Or as though I were assigned to so great a task that everything which ought to be known about Martin must become known chiefly through my writing!

Therefore, if you desire to hear about the death of the holy bishop, learn it rather from those who were present. I had resolved to write nothing to you, so that you would not make me public everywhere. Nevertheless, if you promise that you will let no one else read it, I will satisfy your wish in a few words. Thus I will make you a participant in what I have learned.

Martin therefore foresaw his death long beforehand [Col. 0181D] and told the brothers that the dissolution of his body was approaching.

Meanwhile an occasion arose for him to visit the diocese of Condat. The clergy of that church were quarreling among themselves, and Martin, wishing to restore peace, did not refuse to set out for such a purpose, although he knew that the end of his days was near. He considered it a good completion of his virtues if he left peace restored to the church.

Having set out with his usual numerous and most holy company of disciples, he saw cormorants on the river pursuing prey and driving their rapacious appetites by continual captures.

“This,” he said, “is the form of demons: they lie in wait for the unwary, seize those who do not know, devour those whom they have caught, and cannot be satisfied by what they have devoured.” [Col. 0182A]

Then, by the powerful force of his words, he commanded them to leave the pool in which they were swimming and seek dry and deserted regions. He exercised this authority over the birds in the same way that he was accustomed to drive away demons.

Thus, gathering into a flock, all those birds came together in one body, left the river, and made for the mountains and forests. Many people were astonished to see such power in Martin that he even commanded birds.

After staying for some time in that village, or in the church to which he had gone, and restoring peace among the clergy, he was already considering returning to the monastery when his bodily strength suddenly began to fail.

He summoned his disciples and announced that he was already dissolving.

Then there was mourning and grief among them all, and one voice from all who lamented:

“Why do you leave us, father? To whom do you leave us [Col. 0182B] in our desolation? For ravenous wolves will attack your flock; and who will keep them from their bites once the shepherd has been struck down? We know that you long for Christ; but your rewards are secure, and delay will not diminish them. Rather, have mercy on us, whom you are abandoning.”

Moved by these tears—for, as always, he overflowed entirely with the Lord’s compassionate mercy—he is said to have wept. Then he turned to the Lord and replied to those who were weeping with these words alone:

“Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor. Let your will be done.”

Placed, as it were, between hope and love, he almost hesitated over what he preferred: he did not want to abandon them, nor did he wish to remain separated from Christ any longer. Yet he placed nothing in his own desire or left anything to his own will, but entrusted himself wholly to the Lord’s judgment and power. [Col. 0182C]

Would he not seem to say to you in these few words:

“Indeed, Lord, the struggle of bodily service is burdensome, and it is enough that I have fought thus far. But if you command me still to stand in the same labor for the defense of your people, I do not refuse, nor will I complain of my failing age. Devoted, I will fulfill your duties; beneath your standards I will serve as long as you yourself command.

“Although discharge after labor is desirable for an old man, my spirit is victorious over the years and does not know how to yield to old age. But if you now spare my age, it is good for me, Lord: let your will be done. You yourself protect those for whom I am afraid.”

O ineffable man, conquered neither by labor nor to be overcome by death! He inclined toward neither side, feared neither to die nor refused to live.

For several days he was held by the violence of fevers, [Col. 0182D] yet he did not cease from God’s work. Spending the whole night in prayers and vigils, he compelled his failing limbs to serve the spirit, lying upon his noble bed in ashes and a hairshirt.

When the disciples asked him at least to allow poor straw to be placed beneath him, he replied:

“It is not fitting, my sons, for a Christian to die except in ashes and a hairshirt. If I leave you any other example, I have sinned.”

His eyes and hands always directed toward heaven, he did not relax his unconquered spirit from prayer. When the presbyters who had gathered around him asked him to relieve his body by turning onto his side, he said:

“Allow me, brothers, allow me to look toward heaven rather than earth, so that the spirit, already about to travel its own road to the Lord, may be directed toward him.”

Having spoken these words, [Col. 0183A] he saw the devil standing nearby.

“Why do you stand here?” he said. “Bloody beast, You will find nothing in me, deadly one. Abraham’s bosom will receive me.”

*(From the Verona Capitular Codex.)*
[Note: From these words almost to the end of the letter, greater divergences from the Vulgate occur than anywhere else in the Capitular manuscript, and from them a more coherent and simpler sense emerges. Indeed, I have long suspected that the latter part of this letter, as it is read in the Vulgate, was interpolated by someone. Therefore we present the two texts opposite one another, so that the reader may see at a glance what is redundant in the Vulgate and may judge more correctly which reading is to be preferred. EDITOR OF THE VERONA MANUSCRIPT.]

With these words, therefore, he returned his spirit, wearied by divine works, to heaven. Those who had been present testified to us that, once the man’s body was lifeless, they had seen him glorified. His face shone brighter than light, while not even the faintest blemish discolored the rest of his limbs; in the other limbs also—and, in him alone, in parts not unseemly [reading uncertain]—there appeared, as it were, the grace of a seven-year-old boy. Who would ever have believed that this man, covered with a hair shirt, could have been wrapped in ashes? Thus he was shown purer than glass, whiter than milk, already displaying something of the glory of the future resurrection and of a nature transformed in the flesh.

As for the attendance at his funeral, it is impossible to believe how great a multitude of people gathered. The whole city rushed out to meet the body; everyone came from the fields and villages, and many also from neighboring cities. O what mourning there was among all, and especially what lamentation among the grieving monks! Nearly two thousand are said to have gathered on that day—a particular glory of Martin, through whose example so many branches had flourished in the service of the Lord.

The deceased shepherd was surely leading his flocks before him: the pale crowds of that holy multitude, the cloaked ranks, either old men worn out by their completed labors or novices sworn to Christ’s military oath. Then the chorus of virgins, abstaining from tears out of modesty, felt that they ought rather to rejoice for him whom the Lord had now cherished in his own bosom, than conceal in holy joy the grief they felt; for faith forbade them to weep, while affection forced a groan from them. Indeed, their exultation over his glory was as holy as their sorrow over his death was devout. You would forgive those who wept and congratulate those who rejoiced, because it is devout both to rejoice over Martin and to weep for Martin, while each person does what is fitting for himself in grieving and what he owes to Martin in rejoicing.

Thus a melodious crowd accompanied the body of the blessed man with heavenly hymns all the way to the place of burial. If you wish, compare with it that secular pageantry—not, I say, of a funeral but of a triumph: what can be compared with Martin’s obsequies? Let them lead captives bound behind their chariots; Martin’s body is accompanied by those who, under his leadership, had conquered the world. Let the madness of the crowd honor them with confused applause; Martin is applauded with divine psalms. Martin is honored with heavenly hymns. Let them, after their triumphs, be thrust into the savage underworld; Martin is joyfully received into Abraham’s bosom. Martin, poor and humble here, enters heaven rich. From there, I hope, he watches over us and looks upon me as I write these words and you as you read them.

[Col. 0183A] With these words, therefore, he returned his soul to heaven. Those who had been there testified to us that they had seen his face like the face of an angel. His limbs appeared white as snow, so that they said: “Who would ever have seen this man covered with a hair shirt? Who would have believed him wrapped in ashes?” [Note: Read: *esset* (“would have been”).] For he already appeared as though he had been shown in the glory of the future resurrection and in the nature of transformed flesh.

[Col. 0183B] As for the attendance at the funeral, it is impossible to believe how great a multitude gathered. The whole city rushed out to meet the body; everyone came from the fields and villages, and many also from neighboring cities. O what mourning there was among all, and especially what lamentation among the grieving monks! Nearly II [as printed; the extent denoted by the numeral is uncertain] are said to have gathered on that day, a particular glory of Martin, since so many branches had flourished in the service of the Lord through his example. [Note: In the manuscript: *frutecaverant* (“had sprouted”).]

The shepherd was surely leading his flocks before him: the pale crowds of that holy multitude, the cloaked ranks, either old men of completed [supply: “labors”] labors or novices sworn to Christ’s military oath. Then the chorus of virgins, abstaining from tears out of modesty—by what holy joy it concealed what it mourned! For faith forbade weeping, yet affection elicited a groan. Indeed, as holy was its exultation over his glory [the editor supplies: “and”] as devout was its sadness over his death. You would forgive those who wept; congratulate those who rejoiced [Note: Perhaps *congratularere* (“you would congratulate”).], while each person both grants himself leave to grieve and owes it to him to rejoice.

Thus a melodious crowd accompanied the body of the blessed man with heavenly hymns all the way to the place of burial, and so forth.

[Col. 0183C]

## The Dialogues of Sulpicius Severus (C)

### Dialogue I

[Col. 0183D] I. When our friend Gallus and I had met in one place—he was especially dear to me both because of Martin’s memory (for he had been one of Martin’s disciples) and because of his own merits—my Postumianus came to us. He had returned from the East, where he had gone three years earlier after leaving his homeland for that purpose.

We embraced this most beloved man and kissed his knees and feet. After walking about for some time, almost stunned and weeping for joy, we spread our hair shirts on the ground and sat down. Then Postumianus, looking at me first, said:

“When I was in the remote parts of Egypt, I wished to go as far as the sea. There I came upon a merchant ship that was preparing to set sail for Narbonne with a cargo of goods. That same night you seemed to me to be standing beside me in a dream, placing your hand upon me and pulling me aboard that ship. As soon as dawn broke through the darkness and I rose from the place where I had rested, I reflected on my dream by myself and was suddenly seized by such longing for you that, without hesitation, I boarded the ship. On the thirtieth day I landed at Marseilles, and from there I arrived here on the tenth day. So favorable a voyage attended my loving desire.

“Now you, for whose sake we have crossed so many seas and traveled so much land, give yourself wholly to be embraced and enjoyed by us, with everyone else excluded.”

“But I,” I replied, “even while you were staying in Egypt, was always wholly with you in spirit and thought. As I thought of you day and night, your affection possessed me entirely. How much more should you not imagine that I could be absent from you for even a moment now, when I am hanging upon your love and looking at you, listening to you, and speaking with you, with absolutely no one admitted into our private meeting, which this more secluded cell provides for us.

“For I suppose you will not find the presence of our friend Gallus burdensome. As you see, he is rejoicing at your arrival just as I myself am.”

“Certainly,” said Postumianus. “This Gallus will be retained in our company. Although I know him only slightly, since he is so dear to you he cannot fail to be dear to me, especially since he belongs to Martin’s school. Nor shall I object to conversing with you at whatever length you desire, since I have come here for this very purpose: to devote myself, even with many words, to the longing I feel for my Sulpicius.” As he said this, he embraced me with both hands.

### II

“Indeed,” I said, “you have sufficiently shown how powerful devoted love can be: for our sake you have crossed so many seas and traversed so much land, coming, so to speak, from the rising of the sun all the way to its setting. Come, then. Since we are alone together and not otherwise occupied, and since we ought to give our attention to your conversation, I ask you to tell us the whole story of your journey: how the Christian faith flourishes in the East; what sort of repose the saints enjoy there; what customs the monks observe; and by how many signs and miracles Christ works in his servants. For certainly, since life itself has become burdensome to us in these regions and amid the circumstances in which we live, we shall gladly hear from you whether Christians can live even in the desert.”

To this Postumianus replied: “I shall do as I see you desire; but first, I ask to hear from you whether all those priests whom I left here are such as we knew them to be before I departed.”

“Do not ask about that,” I said, “for either you know it as well as I do, or, if you do not know it, it would be better for you not to hear it. This much I cannot conceal: not only have those about whom you ask become no better than you knew them, but one man, formerly fond of us, in whom we used to find relief from the attacks of the others, has proved harsher toward us than he ought to have been.

“Nor shall I say anything more severe about him, because I honored him as a friend and loved him even when he was thought to be an enemy. Yet as I silently ponder these things, I am deeply pierced by the pain of having been almost deprived of the friendship of a wise and religious man: that one who was once so friendly to us could have become so bitter toward us.

“But let us leave these matters, which are full of sorrow. Let us hear you instead, as you promised a little while ago.”

“Let it be so,” said Postumianus. After he had spoken, we all remained silent for a little while. Then he moved the hair shirt on which he had been sitting closer to me and began as follows:

### III

“Three years ago, Sulpicius, when I left here and said farewell to you, we set sail from Narbonne and entered an African harbor on the fifth day. So favorable was the voyage by God’s will. I desired to visit Carthage, to see the places of the saints, and especially to pray at the tomb of the martyr Cyprian.

“On the fifteenth day we returned to the harbor and, putting out to sea on our way to Alexandria, were driven almost into the Syrtis by a contrary south wind. The experienced sailors, taking precautions against this, stopped the ship by casting anchors. The mainland was visible before our eyes. We went ashore in small boats and, seeing everything empty of human cultivation, I proceeded farther than the others in order to explore the region more carefully.

“About three miles from the shore I saw a small hut among the sands. Its roof, as Sallust says, was like the keel of a ship: adjoining the ground and built of fairly strong planks—not because any force of rain was feared there (indeed, it was said that no rain had ever been heard there), but because the force of the winds is such that, if a breeze begins to blow even under a somewhat gentle sky, it causes greater shipwreck in those lands than anywhere at sea.

“No plants grow there, and no crops spring up, since the unstable ground consists of dry sands that yield to every movement of the winds. But where certain headlands, torn away by the sea, resist the winds, the earth is somewhat firmer and produces sparse, bristly grass. This provides sufficiently useful fodder for sheep.

“The inhabitants live on milk. Those who are more industrious—or, so to speak, wealthier—use barley bread. That is the only crop there, and because of the rapidity of its growth it usually escapes, by the nature of the soil or climate, the destructive effects of the winds. For it is said to ripen on the thirtieth day after the seed is sown.

“The reason people remain there is simply that they are all exempt from tribute. It is, in fact, the outermost region of Cyrene, adjoining that desert which lies between Egypt and Africa, through which Cato once led his army while fleeing from Caesar.”

### IV

“When I reached the hut I had seen in the distance, I found an old man in a garment of skins, turning a millstone by hand. He received our greeting kindly.

“We explained that we had been cast ashore there and were detained by the calmness of the sea, so that we could not immediately resume our journey; that, having landed, as is the custom of human nature, we had wished to learn about the character of the region and the way of life of its inhabitants; that we were Christians; and, above all, we wished to know whether there were any Christians among those solitudes.

“At this he wept for joy and fell at our knees. He kissed us again and again and invited us to pray. Then he laid rams’ skins on the ground and made us recline. He set before us a truly sumptuous meal: half a barley loaf.

“There were four of us, and he was the fifth. He also brought in a bundle of herbs, whose name has slipped my memory. It resembled mint, was abundant in leaves, and had the flavor of honey. We delighted in and were completely satisfied by its very sweet taste.

“At this I smiled at my Gallus and said: ‘What do you think, Gallus? Do you approve of a meal consisting of a bundle of herbs and half a loaf for five men?’

“He, being extremely modest, blushed slightly. Taking account of my weariness, he said: ‘You are acting in your usual manner, Sulpicius. You never let any opportunity offered to you pass without reproaching us for gluttony. But you act inhumanely by forcing us Gauls to live like the angels—even though, in my eagerness to eat, I believe I could eat the angels themselves. For I am afraid even to touch that half-barley loaf by myself.

“‘Let that Cyrenian be satisfied with it, for whom hunger is either a necessity or a natural condition; or, finally, let those be satisfied who, I suppose, had been made to fast from food by the tossing of the sea. We are far from the sea, and, as I have often assured you, we are Gauls. But let him proceed instead to tell the story of his Cyrenian.’”

### V

“Indeed,” said Postumianus, “from now on I shall be careful not to praise anyone’s abstinence, lest the example prove altogether too difficult for our Gauls. I had intended also to recount the Cyrenian’s dinners—or rather, the feasts that followed, since we stayed with him for seven days—but I must refrain, lest Gallus think himself worn out.

“On the following day, however, when some of the inhabitants began to gather to visit us, we learned that our host was a presbyter, something he had concealed from us with the greatest discretion.

“Then we proceeded with him to the church, which was nearly two miles away and hidden from our view by an intervening mountain. It was woven from cheap branches and was not much more elaborate than our host’s hut, in which no one could stand upright.

“As we inquired into the customs of the people, we noticed this remarkable fact: they neither bought nor sold anything. They do not know what fraud or theft is. They neither possess nor desire gold and silver, which mortals regard as the first of all things. For when I brought that presbyter ten gold coins, he refused them, declaring with loftier understanding that the Church is not furnished with gold but rather destroyed by it. We gave him a small amount of clothing.”

### VI

“When he had received this kindly and the sailors called us back to the sea, we departed and reached Alexandria on the seventh day with a favorable voyage. There we found ugly conflicts being waged between bishops and monks. The occasion or cause was that the priests, gathered together in councils, seemed repeatedly to have decreed that no one should read or possess the books of Origen, who was regarded as a most accomplished interpreter of the sacred Scriptures.

“But the bishops cited certain passages in his books that had been written in a more insane manner. His defenders did not dare to defend them, but said instead that they had been deceitfully inserted by heretics. Therefore, they argued, the remaining works should not be condemned on account of passages that deserved criticism; readers’ faith could readily distinguish between them, so that it would not follow what had been corrupted while retaining what had been discussed in a Catholic manner.

“They also argued that it was not surprising if heretical fraud had operated in books that were recent and newly written, since in certain places it had not hesitated to cut into the truth of the Gospel.

“Against this, the bishops resisted with greater obstinacy. By their authority they compelled people to condemn everything sound along with what was corrupt and with the author himself, arguing that the books received by the Church were more than sufficient; any reading that would harm the foolish more than it benefited the wise was to be utterly rejected.

“As I examined some of Origen’s books with particular curiosity, I found very much that pleased me. But I also detected certain passages in which it is beyond doubt that he held erroneous opinions, though his defenders insist that these passages have been corrupted.

“I am astonished that one and the same man could have been so unlike himself: in the portion in which he is approved, he has no equal after the Apostles; in the portion that is rightly censured, no one can be shown to have erred more deformedly.”

### VII

“For when many excerpts from his books were read by the bishops, and were clearly written against the Catholic faith, one passage above all was preparing the way for hostility. It was stated there that, just as the Lord Jesus had come in the flesh for the redemption of humanity, had endured the cross for human salvation, and had tasted death for humanity’s immortality, so, following the same order of suffering, he would also redeem the devil. This, it said, was consistent with his goodness and compassion: since he had restored fallen humanity, he would also free the fallen angel.

“When the bishops brought forward these and similar statements, a sedition arose from partisan rivalries. Since it could not be suppressed by the authority of the priests, by a sinister precedent a prefect was appointed to enforce the discipline of the Church. By his intimidation the brothers were dispersed and the monks driven into various regions, so that, after edicts had been posted, they were not permitted to remain in any one place.

“What greatly troubled me was that Jerome, a man most Catholic and highly learned in sacred law, was thought at first to have followed Origen, whereas now that same Jerome especially—or rather, entirely—condemned all his writings.

“I did not dare to judge anyone rashly. Nevertheless, the most distinguished and learned men were said to disagree in this dispute. But whether, as I think, the matter is error, or, as is believed, heresy, it could not be suppressed by the many punishments inflicted by the priests. Indeed, it could never have spread so widely if it had not grown through controversy.

“When I arrived in Alexandria amid such disturbances, the city was in turmoil. The bishop of that city received me very kindly, better than I had expected, and tried to keep me with him. But I had no desire to remain where hostility over the recent disaster suffered by the brothers was still burning. For even if they may perhaps seem to have been obliged to obey the bishops, it was nevertheless not right that so great a multitude living under the confession of Christ should have been afflicted, especially by bishops.”

### VIII

“Accordingly, I departed from there and went to the town of Bethlehem, which is six miles from Jerusalem and sixteen stages from Alexandria. The presbyter Jerome governs the church there, for it is a parish of the bishop who holds Jerusalem.

“From my earlier journey I had already come to know Jerome, and he easily persuaded me that I should regard no one as more worth seeking. For, apart from the merit of his faith and the endowment of his virtues, he is so learned not only in Latin and Greek but also in Hebrew literature that no one would dare compare himself with him in any field of knowledge.

“I am surprised if you have not also come to know him through the many works he has written, since he is read throughout the entire world.”

“But we know him all too well,” said Gallus. “Five years ago I read one of his little books in which the entire nation of our monks is fiercely attacked and criticized by him. Our Belgian friend sometimes becomes very angry because he said that we are accustomed to eat until we vomit.”

“But I forgive that man,” I said, “and I think that he was speaking about the monks of the East rather than those of the West. Among the Greeks gluttony is a vice of the throat; among the Gauls it is nature.”

Then I said: “You are defending your nation learnedly, Gallus. But tell me, does that book condemn only this one fault among monks?”

“Certainly not,” he replied. “He omitted nothing that he did not criticize, tear apart, and expose. He attacked avarice especially, and vanity no less. He discussed pride at length and superstition in no small measure. To tell the truth, he seems to me to have painted the faults of many people.”

### IX

“Moreover, how truthfully and forcefully he argued about the familiar relationships of virgins and monks, and even of clerics! For that reason some people—whom I do not wish to name—are said not to love him. Just as our Belgian friend is angry that we have been branded for excessive gluttony, so those others are said to rage when they read in that little work: ‘The virgin spurns her celibate blood-brother and seeks a stranger as brother.’

“To this I said: ‘You are going too far, Gallus. Take care lest someone who recognizes these things overhear you and begin not to love you along with Jerome. Since you are a learned man, I shall appropriately remind you with a verse from that comic poet: “Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.”’

“Rather, Postumianus, let us have you continue, as you began, with your account of the East.”

“As I was beginning to say,” he replied, “I spent six months with Jerome. His continual struggle and unending battle against the wicked had stirred up the hatred of the lost. Heretics hate him because he never stops attacking them; clerics hate him because he pursues their way of life and their crimes.

“But all good people admire and love him. Those who think he is a heretic are insane. I would truly say that the man’s Catholic learning is sound doctrine.

“He is always wholly occupied with reading, wholly occupied with books. He does not rest by day or night; he is always either reading something or writing.

“If I had not fixed in my mind and promised before God that I would visit the desert I had set before me, I would not have wished to leave such a great man even for the briefest moment.

“To him, therefore, I entrusted and committed all my possessions and my entire household, which had followed me against my will and kept me entangled. Thus, as though relieved of a heavy burden, completely freed, I returned to Alexandria. After visiting the brothers there, I proceeded from there to the upper Thebaid, that is, to the farthest regions of Egypt. The vast, open solitudes of the desert were said to contain a great many monks.

“It would take too long to recount everything I saw. Nevertheless, I shall touch briefly on a few things out of the many.”

[Col. 0190B] ### X

“Not far from the desert, along the Nile, there are many monasteries. In most cases a hundred men live in one place. Their supreme rule is to live under the authority of an abbot, to do nothing according to their own judgment, and in everything to depend on his command and power.

“If any of them conceive in their minds a greater virtue, so that they wish to go into the desert to lead a solitary life, they do not depart except with the abbot’s permission. This is their first virtue: to obey another’s authority.

“Once they have gone into the desert, bread or any other food is supplied according to the arrangement of the abbot. It happened during the days when I had arrived there that the abbot sent bread by two boys to a man who had recently withdrawn into the desert and had set up a hut for himself no more than six miles from that monastery. The older boy was fifteen years old; the younger was twelve.

“As they were returning from there, an asp of extraordinary size came toward them. They were not at all frightened by its approach. When it came before their feet, it lowered its blue neck, as though enchanted by spells.

“The younger boy seized it with his hand and began carrying it wrapped in his cloak. Then he entered the monastery like a victor and, while all the brothers watched, unwrapped the captive beast and set it down, not without a swelling of ostentation.

“But while the others praised the children’s faith and courage, the abbot, with a higher purpose, beat both of them with rods so that their weak age would not become insolent. He rebuked them severely for having revealed what the Lord had worked through them. It had been the work not of their faith but of divine power. They should learn instead to serve God in humility, not to glory in signs and miracles, because awareness of weakness was better than the vanity of powers.”

### XI

“When the monk heard this, and learned that the young boys had been endangered by the serpent’s approach and had moreover earned many blows after overcoming the serpent, he begged the abbot that henceforth no bread or food whatsoever should be sent to him.

“By then the eighth day had passed, during which this man of Christ had shut himself up within the danger of hunger. His limbs were drying up from fasting, but his mind, intent upon heaven, could not fail. His body was wasting from lack of food, but his faith remained firm.

“Meanwhile, the abbot was inwardly prompted by the Spirit to visit his disciple. Wishing, out of devout concern, to discover what substance of life sustained the faithful man who had refused to have bread supplied by human hands, he himself set out to look for him.

“When the disciple saw the old man coming from a distance, he went to meet him, gave thanks, and led him to the cell. When they had entered together, they saw a palm basket hanging from a post by the doorway, piled high with warm bread.

“First the smell of warm bread was perceived; by touch it was shown to be as though it had only shortly before been taken from the fire. Yet the form of Egyptian bread could not be recognized.

“Both men, astonished, recognized the heavenly gift. The disciple acknowledged that it had been granted on account of the abbot’s arrival, while the abbot attributed it instead to the disciple’s faith and virtue. Thus both of them broke the heavenly bread with great rejoicing.

“When the old man later returned to the monastery and recounted this to the brothers, such ardor was kindled in everyone’s hearts that they hurried eagerly, one after another, to the desert and its holy solitudes, confessing themselves wretched for having remained any longer in a community of many people, where human interaction had to be endured.”

### XII

“In this monastery I saw two old men who were said to have lived there for forty years, never having departed from the place. Their story should not, I think, be passed over, since I heard their virtues celebrated both in the testimony of the abbot himself and in the speech of all the brothers: the sun had never seen one of them eating, and it had never seen the other angry.

“At this Gallus looked at me and said: ‘If that man of yours were here now—I do not wish to mention his name—I would very much like him to hear this example. We have often found, in the cases of many people, that he becomes excessively angry. Yet since, as I hear, he recently forgave his enemies, if he heard this he would be strengthened all the more by the example and would be convinced that it is a splendid virtue not to be moved to anger.

“‘I shall not deny that he had just causes for anger. But where the struggle is harder, the crown is more glorious. Accordingly, if you recognize the man, I think he should rightly be praised because, when his ungrateful freedman deserted him, he pitied rather than persecuted the man who was leaving—and he is not angry even with the person by whom he seems to have been led away.’

“But I said: ‘If Postumianus had not disclosed this example of overcoming anger, I would be seriously angry at the departure of the runaway. But since it is not permitted to be angry, the whole recollection of these matters, which pierces us, must be abolished. Let us hear you instead, Postumianus.’”

“I shall do what you command, Sulpicius,” he replied, “since I see how eager you are to listen. But remember that I am depositing this conversation with you at interest: I gladly provide what you ask, provided that shortly afterward you do not refuse what I shall ask.”

“But we have nothing,” I replied, “with which we can repay you, whether with or without interest. Nevertheless, whatever you think appropriate, command us, so long as you satisfy our desires as you began to do. Your conversation gives us great pleasure.”

“I shall not defraud your eagerness,” said Postumianus. “And since you have recognized the virtue of one beginning his life as a hermit, I shall tell you a few more things out of the many.”

### XIII

“When I first entered the desert, we came to a certain old monk who lived at the foot of a mountain, about twelve miles from the Nile. I had one of the brothers as my guide, a man familiar with the region.

“There was a well there, something extremely rare in those places. The old man had one ox, whose entire labor consisted in drawing up water by means of a wheel-driven mechanism, for the well was said to be almost a thousand feet deep, or even more.

“There was also a garden rich in many vegetables. This was contrary to the nature of the desert, where everything is dry and scorched by the heat of the sun, and no seed ever produces even a small root. But the holy man’s labor, shared with the animal, and his own industry made this possible. For the frequent watering gave such richness to the sand that we saw the vegetables in that garden growing green and bearing fruit in a truly marvelous way.

“The ox lived on these vegetables together with its master. The holy man also gave us supper from this supply.

“There I saw something that you Gauls may perhaps not believe: a pot of vegetables that had been prepared for our supper boiling without fire. So great is the power of the sun that it would suffice for any cook, even for the stews of the Gauls.

“After supper, as evening was already approaching, he invited us to a palm tree whose fruit he sometimes used. It was nearly two miles away, for these are the only trees found in the desert, although they are rare.

“Whether resourceful antiquity arranged for them or the nature of the soil itself produces them, I do not know—unless God, foreseeing that the desert would one day be inhabited by saints, prepared these trees for his servants. For most of those who live within those solitudes, since no other plants grow there, are nourished by the fruits of these trees.

“When we reached the tree to which the kindness of our host was leading us, we encountered a lion there. At the sight of it, my guide and I trembled, but the holy man approached without hesitation. Though frightened, we followed him.

“The beast withdrew a little, as though you could see that it had been commanded by God, and stood still while the holy man plucked fruit from the lower branches. When he held out a hand full of dates, the animal ran up and accepted them as freely as any domestic creature. After it had eaten, it went away.

“As we watched this, still trembling, we could readily assess how great was the power of faith in him and how great was the weakness in us.”

### XIV

“We saw another man equally remarkable, living in a small hut in which only one person could fit. It was said of him that a she-wolf customarily stood beside him while he ate. The beast was seldom deceived about the proper time for his meal: it would come to him at the appointed hour and wait outside the door until he offered it the bread left over from his little supper. It was accustomed to lick his hand and then depart, as though its duty had been fulfilled and consolation had been provided.

“But it happened that the holy man, while escorting a brother who had come to visit him, was away for a longer time and did not return until after nightfall.

“In the meantime the beast arrived at its customary mealtime. Finding the cell empty and sensing that its familiar benefactor was absent, it entered and searched carefully to discover where the inhabitant was.

“By chance, a small palm basket containing five loaves was hanging nearby. The wolf took one of them and devoured it; then, having committed the offense, it departed.

“When the hermit returned, he saw that the basket had come undone and that the number of loaves was no longer complete. He understood that his household had suffered a loss, and near the threshold he recognized the fragments of the eaten bread. There was no uncertainty, however, about what creature had committed the theft.

“Accordingly, when the beast did not come on the following days as usual—for, conscious of its bold deed, it pretended not to approach the man whom it had wronged—the hermit suffered painfully from being deprived of the consolation of his fosterling.

“Finally, recalled by the hermit’s prayer, it appeared on the seventh day, as it had done before, beside him at supper. But, as you could easily see from the shame of the penitent, it did not dare to come closer. With its eyes cast down toward the ground in profound embarrassment—for this could plainly be understood—it was asking for some forgiveness.

“The hermit, moved by compassion for its confusion, ordered it to come closer and gently stroked its sorrowful head with his hand. Then, doubling its portion of bread, he fed the guilty creature.

“Having thus obtained pardon, it laid aside its sorrow and resumed its customary duty.

“Consider, I beg you, the power of Christ even in this matter: before him everything brute has understanding, and everything savage is gentle. The she-wolf performs its duty; the she-wolf acknowledges the crime of theft; the she-wolf is overcome with conscious shame. When called, it comes; it offers its head; and it understands that pardon has been granted to it, just as it displayed shame over its error.

“Yours is this power, O Christ; yours are these miracles, O Christ. For the things your servants perform in your name belong to you. And in this we groan: the wild beasts perceive your majesty, but human beings do not revere it.”

### XV

So that this may not perhaps seem incredible to anyone, I shall relate greater things. The faith of Christ is present as my witness that I invent nothing and do not report tales circulated by unreliable authorities; rather, I shall explain what I learned from trustworthy men.

Many live in the desert without any shelters; they are called anchorites. They live on the roots of plants. They never remain in any fixed place, lest they be visited by human beings; wherever night compels them, there they have their dwelling.

Two monks from Nitria therefore went to visit a certain man who lived according to this custom and under this rule. Although he lived in a distant region, they went to him because he had once been dear and familiar to them in the common life of the monastery, having heard of his virtues. After searching for him long and diligently, they finally found him in the farthest part of that desert adjoining Blemmis, where he was staying. He was said to have inhabited those solitudes for twelve years already.

Although he avoided the company of all human beings, he did not shun those whom he recognized, and he did not refuse his dearest friends for three days. On the fourth day, as he had gone forward a little way and was accompanying them as they departed, they saw a lioness of extraordinary size coming toward him.

Although the beast had found three men, she was not uncertain whom she sought. She threw herself at the anchorite’s feet and, falling down with something like weeping and lamentation, showed the feeling of one who was at once groaning and making a request. This moved everyone, but especially the man who understood that he was the one being sought.

They followed her as she went ahead. Since she went before them, then repeatedly stopped and repeatedly looked back, it could easily be understood that she wanted the anchorite to follow wherever she was leading.

What more need I say? They reached the beast’s cave, where she was nourishing five already-grown cubs, born prematurely and in poor condition. Since they had emerged from their mother’s womb with their eyes closed, they were afflicted with perpetual blindness. The mother brought them out one by one from the rocky place and laid them before the anchorite’s feet.

Only then did the holy man understand what the beast was asking. Calling upon the name of God, he touched the cubs’ closed eyes with his hand; and immediately, their blindness being driven away, the long-denied light became visible to the beasts’ opened eyes.

After visiting the anchorite whom they had desired to see, those brothers returned with a very fruitful reward for their labor. They had been admitted as witnesses of so great a virtue, and had seen the faith of the holy man and the glory of Christ, which was to be attested through them.

I am about to relate something extraordinary: five days later the lioness returned to the author of so great a benefit and brought him, as a gift, the hide of that unusual beast. The holy man often wore it wrapped around himself like a cloak, and he did not disdain to accept a gift through the beast whose true author he understood to be another.

### XVI

There was also a man of great renown among the anchorites in those regions, who lived in that part of the desert which is at Syene. When he had first withdrawn into the desert, intending to live on herbs and the roots of herbs—for the sand sometimes produces plants of very sweet and excellent flavor—he was ignorant of how to distinguish the edible ones and usually plucked harmful plants.

It was not easy to distinguish the strength of the roots by their taste, because all were equally sweet; but many, by their more hidden nature, contained a deadly poison. When the inward force of the poison therefore tormented him as he ate, and every vital organ was shaken by immense pains, while frequent vomiting, amid intolerable suffering, dissolved the very seat of life as his stomach was already failing, he became utterly afraid of everything that might be eaten and spent the seventh day in fasting, his spirit failing.

Then a wild animal called an ibex came to him. Standing close by, it threw down before him a bundle of herbs that it had gathered the day before, but which he had not dared to touch. The beast, however, scattering with its mouth those that were poisonous, selected those it knew to be harmless.

Thus the holy man, taught by its example what he ought to eat and what he ought to reject, both escaped the danger of hunger and avoided the poisons of the herbs.

But it would take too long to relate everything we learned or heard about all who inhabit the desert. I spent a whole year and almost seven months in the solitudes, more an admirer of another’s virtue than capable of attempting so arduous and difficult a way of life myself. Nevertheless, I often lived with that old man who had a well and an ox.

### XVII

I visited the two monasteries of the blessed Antony, which are still inhabited by his disciples. I also went to the place where the most blessed Paul, the first hermit, had lived.

I saw the Red Sea. I climbed the ridge of Mount Sinai, whose highest summit, almost touching heaven, cannot be reached. Somewhere amid its recesses, an anchorite was said to live. Although I sought him for a long time and with great effort, I was unable to see him. He had been withdrawn from human society for nearly fifty years, it was said; he used no clothing, but was covered by the bristles of his own body, and in this divine gift he did not know that he was naked.

Whenever religious men wished to approach him, he fled through trackless places and avoided human encounters. He was said to have presented himself to only one man, about five years earlier; and I believe that the other, by the power of his faith, deserved to obtain this. When that man asked him many questions, including why he avoided human beings so completely, he is said to have replied that one who was frequented by human beings could not be frequented by angels. Hence, in accordance with the widespread belief, rumor had rightly circulated that the holy man was visited by angels.

After leaving Mount Sinai, I returned to the River Nile. I surveyed both its banks, which are thickly lined with monasteries. I often saw, as I said earlier, a hundred men living in one place; but it was also known that two or three thousand lived in the same villages.

Nor should you suppose that the virtue of those who live among a multitude of monks is any less than that of those who have withdrawn from human gatherings. Their chief and primary virtue there, as I have already said, is obedience. A newcomer is not received by the abbot of a monastery except as one who has first been tested and proved, and who will never refuse any command of the abbot, however arduous, difficult, or unworthy of endurance it may be.

### XVIII

I shall relate to you two very great miracles of astonishing obedience, although I have more to recall. But for arousing emulation in virtue, much will not benefit one for whom a few examples do not suffice.

When a certain man, having renounced the affairs of the world, entered a monastery of strict discipline and asked to be received, the abbot began to set many things before him: the labors of this discipline were severe, and his own commands were harsh, such as no one could easily fulfill with sufficient endurance. He should seek another monastery where life was governed by easier rules; he should not attempt what he could not complete.

The man, however, was not moved at all by these threats. Rather, he promised such complete obedience that, if the abbot ordered him to enter a fire, he would not refuse to go in. When the master heard this profession, he did not hesitate to test the man who had made it.

By chance, an oven stood burning nearby, kindled with a great fire and being prepared for baking bread. Flames poured out from its gaping furnaces, and the fire raged with all its force inside the hollow chamber of the kiln.

The master therefore ordered this newcomer to enter it. He did not delay in obeying the command: without hesitation he entered the midst of the flames, which were immediately overcome by so bold a faith and yielded before him, just as they once did before those Hebrew boys.

Nature was conquered; the fire fled. The man who was thought likely to burn found, to his own amazement, that he was as though drenched with cool dew.

But what is surprising if that fire did not touch your novice, Christ, so that the abbot would not regret issuing a harsh command, nor the disciple regret obeying it? On the very day on which he had arrived, while being tested in weakness, he was found perfect—rightly fortunate, rightly glorious: tested by obedience, glorified by suffering.

### XIX

In the same monastery, the following event was said to have happened within living memory.

Another man had likewise come to be received by the same abbot. When the first law of obedience was laid down for him, and he promised perpetual endurance in everything, even in the extremest circumstances, the abbot happened to be carrying in his hand a storax branch that had long since dried up. He planted it in the ground and imposed upon the newcomer this task: he was to supply the little branch with water for irrigation until, against all nature, the dry wood should become green in the parched soil.

The newcomer, subjected to the command of this harsh rule, carried water every day on his own shoulders. He had to fetch it from the River Nile, almost two miles away. Even after a year had passed, the labor of the worker did not cease, although there could be no hope of any result from his work. Nevertheless, the virtue of obedience endured in the labor.

The following year also mocked the labor of the already exhausted brother. At last, as the third successive period of time was passing, while that water-carrier did not cease his work either by night or by day, the branch blossomed.

I myself saw from that little branch a small tree which still remains in the monastery courtyard, with green branches, as a kind of testimony. It shows how much obedience achieved and how much faith can accomplish.

But the day will fail before I do, if I must finish the various miracles that have come to my knowledge concerning the virtues of the saints.

### XX

I shall relate two more outstanding examples to you. One will be an excellent example against the inflation of wretched vanity; the other, a considerable lesson against false righteousness.

There was a certain holy man endowed with an incredible power for driving demons out of possessed bodies, and he performed unheard-of signs every day. He cured possessed bodies not only when present and not merely by a word, but sometimes even when absent, by sending pieces of the fringe of his hair-shirt or letters.

He was therefore visited in an extraordinary manner by crowds coming to him from every part of the world. I say nothing of lesser people: prefects and counts, and judges of various authorities, often lay prostrate before his doors. Even most holy bishops, laying aside their priestly authority, humbly asked to be touched and blessed by him. Whenever they touched his hand or garment, they rightly believed themselves sanctified and illumined by a divine gift.

He was said to abstain permanently and completely from every drink, and to sustain himself on no food except—let me whisper this in your ear, Sulpicius, so that the Gaul does not hear it—seven dried figs a day.

Meanwhile, just as honor arose from virtue for the holy man, so vanity began to creep in through honor. As soon as he was able to sense this evil advancing within him, he tried for a long time and with great effort to drive it away. But, although his virtue continued, it could not be wholly expelled, even by his silent awareness of the vanity.

Everywhere the demons acknowledged his name, and he could not exclude the crowds who flocked to him. Meanwhile, a hidden poison crept through his heart; and the man by whose command demons were driven from other bodies could not cleanse himself of the secret thoughts of vanity.

He is therefore said to have turned to the Lord with all his prayers and asked that, after the devil had been granted power over him for five months, he might become like those whom he himself had cured.

Why delay with more? That powerful man, that man renowned throughout the whole East for signs and virtues, that man to whose thresholds crowds had once streamed and before whose doors the highest powers of the world had prostrated themselves, was seized by a demon and held in chains. After suffering everything that the possessed usually endure, he was finally cleansed in the fifth month—not only of the demon, but also, what was more useful and more desirable for him, of vanity.

### XXI

As I repeat these things, our own unhappiness and weakness come before me. For which of us is there who, if one humble little man greets him or one woman praises him with foolish and flattering words, will not immediately be lifted up by pride and instantly puffed up by vanity?

Even if he has no awareness of holiness, nevertheless, because he is called holy—whether through the flattery or perhaps the error of fools—he will think himself most holy.

If frequent gifts are sent to him, he will claim that he is being honored by God’s generosity, since necessities are supplied to him while he sleeps and relaxes. If even some small signs of virtue should come from him, he would think himself an angel.

But when he is distinguished neither by deed nor by virtue, if he has become a cleric, he immediately enlarges his fringes, rejoices in greetings, is puffed up by encounters, and himself runs everywhere. Though previously accustomed to go on foot or on a little donkey, he rides proudly on a foaming horse.

Previously content to live in a small and humble cell, he raises lofty ceilings, builds many rooms, carves doors, paints cupboards, rejects coarser clothing, desires soft garments, and assigns these tasks as tribute to dear widows and familiar virgins: to one that she weave a stiff *byrrhus*, to another a flowing *lacerna*.

But let us leave the more biting description of these matters to the blessed Jerome; let us return to our subject.

“But,” said my Gaul, “I do not know what you have left Jerome to discuss.
