You have so briefly summed up all the practices of our people that, if they receive and patiently consider these few words of yours with equanimity, I think they will profit greatly from them and will not afterward need to be restrained by Jerome’s books.

“But instead, go through what you had begun, and produce the lesson you promised to give against false righteousness. For, to confess the truth, we suffer from no more destructive evil within Gaul.”

“So I shall,” said Postumianus. “Nor will I keep you waiting any longer.”

### XXII

A certain young man from Asia, exceedingly rich in possessions and illustrious by birth, had a wife and a little son. When he was a tribune in Egypt and, during frequent expeditions against the Blemmes, had come near certain parts of the desert, he had also seen many shelters of the saints and received a word of salvation from the blessed John.

Without delay, he scorned the useless military life and its empty honor, entered the desert resolutely, and soon shone forth as perfect in every kind of virtue. Powerful in fasting, conspicuous for humility, firm in faith, he had easily matched the ancient monks in his zeal for virtue.

Meanwhile, a thought entered his mind, planted by the devil: it would be more right for him to return to his homeland and save his only son, his whole household, and his wife. This would certainly be more pleasing to God than, content merely to rescue himself from the world, impiously to neglect the salvation of his own family.

Overcome, then, by this appearance of false righteousness, after nearly four years he abandoned his cell, his way of life, and the desert. But when he came to the nearest monastery, which was inhabited by many brothers, he confessed the reason for his departure and asked their advice.

Although everyone opposed him, and especially the abbot of that place, the decision fixed in his evil mind could not be removed. Thus, tearing himself away in wretched obstinacy, he departed from the brothers amid everyone’s grief.

He had scarcely gone out of their sight when he was filled by a demon. Spitting bloody foam from his mouth, he tore his own flesh with his teeth. He was then carried back to the same monastery on the shoulders of the brothers. Since the unclean spirit could not be restrained within him, necessity compelled them to bind him with iron chains; his feet and hands were fastened together. It was a punishment not undeserved for a deserter: since faith had not restrained him, chains restrained him.

At last, after two years, he was freed from the unclean spirit through the prayers of the saints. He immediately returned to the desert from which he had departed, now both corrected himself and destined to become an example to others, so that no one might be deceived either by the shadow of false righteousness or compelled by uncertain fickleness and useless levity to abandon what he had once begun.

Let this be sufficient for you to know about the virtues of the Lord, which he has worked in his servants either for imitation or for fear.

But since I have satisfied your ears—or perhaps have been more verbose than I ought—I ask you now”—and he was speaking to me—“to pay the debt you owe, so that we may hear you, as is your custom, relate more about your Martin, whom my long-standing desires have been burning to hear about.”

### XXIII

“What?” I said. “Is my book about Martin not enough for you—the book you yourself know that I published about his life and virtues?”

“I certainly acknowledge it,” said Postumianus, “and that book never leaves my right hand. For, if you recognize it”—he opened the book that had been hidden beneath his clothing—“here it is.

“This was my companion by land and sea, my associate and comforter throughout my entire journey. But I shall tell you how far this book has penetrated and how scarcely any place exists in the whole world where the material of so fortunate a history is not widely known.

“Your devoted friend Paulinus first brought it to the city of Rome. Then, when the whole city eagerly snatched it up, I saw the booksellers rejoicing because they had nothing more profitable to sell; for nothing was offered more readily or sold more dearly.

“This book, having gone far ahead of my voyage, was already being read throughout Carthage when I arrived in Africa. Only that presbyter of Cyrene did not possess it, but he copied it when I gave him the opportunity. For why should I speak of Alexandria, where it is almost better known to everyone than to you?

“It passed through Egypt, Nitria, the Thebaid, and all the regions of Memphis. In the desert I saw an old man reading it. When I told him that I was your friend, he and many brothers entrusted me with this commission: if ever I reached those lands with you still alive, I was to compel you to supply what you had professed in your book about the virtues of the blessed man but had passed over.

“Come, then. Since I do not desire to hear those things that the written work sufficiently covers, explain those matters which, as I suppose, you omitted because of the readers’ weariness, while many are now asking you, together with me, to relate them.”

### XXIV

“Indeed, Postumianus,” I said, “while I have been listening attentively to you for some time as you spoke of the virtues of the saints, I was returning in silent thought to my Martin. I rightly perceived that everything the individual men had done in different ways could easily be accomplished by this one man.

“For although you have related lofty deeds—which I may say with the indulgence of the saints—I have heard nothing at all in which Martin was inferior. But just as I openly declare that no one’s virtue can ever be compared with that man’s merits, so we must also observe that it is unfair to compare him with hermits or even anchorites.

“They, free from every hindrance and having only heaven and the angels as witnesses, are plainly said to perform marvelous deeds. He, however, stood firm in the midst of crowds and public life, among quarrelsome clergy and raging bishops. Although he was pressed on every side by almost daily scandals, he nevertheless remained established in an unconquerable virtue and performed deeds as great as those accomplished by the men whom we have heard from you to be, or to have been, in the desert.

“And if they had performed equal deeds, what judge would be so unjust as not to judge this man superior in merit? Imagine that he was a soldier who fought in an unfavorable position and nevertheless emerged victorious, while they too were soldiers, but fought from an equal or even a superior position. What then? Even if the victory of all is one and the same, the glory of all cannot be equal.

“Yet although you have related glorious deeds, you have not mentioned anyone who raised a dead man to life. In this one respect, at least, you must necessarily confess that no one can be compared with Martin.”

### XXV

“For if it is admirable that the Egyptian was not touched by flame, Martin too often commanded fires. If you recall that the ferocity of beasts yielded and submitted to the anchorites, Martin likewise restrained both the rage of beasts and the poisons of serpents through familiar contact.

“If you compare with him the man who cured those possessed by unclean spirits through the command of his word and even through the power of his fringes, there are many proofs that Martin was not inferior in this respect either.

“If you turn also to the man who, thought to be clothed in the bristles of his own body instead of a garment, was believed to be visited by angels, angels spoke with Martin every day.

“Against vanity and boasting, he bore himself with such an unconquerable spirit that no one despised those vices more strongly. He often cured from a distance those afflicted by unclean spirits, and he commanded not only counts and prefects but even kings.

“This is a small matter among his virtues; but believe me, no one resisted vanity—and even the causes and occasions of vanity—more strongly.

“I shall relate something small but not to be passed over, because the man who possessed the highest power is also worthy of praise for showing so religious a desire to honor the blessed man.

“I remember that the prefect Vincent, an outstanding man, superior within Gaul to everyone in every kind of virtue, repeatedly asked Martin, while passing through Tours, to give him a banquet in his monastery. In this he was following the example of the blessed bishop Ambrose, who was said at that time to entertain consuls and prefects from time to time. But Martin, a man of higher understanding, did not wish to do so, lest vanity and inflation should creep in through it.

“You must therefore confess that Martin possessed the virtues of all those whom you have listed, while they did not possess all the virtues of Martin.”

### XXVI

“What is this?” said Postumianus. “Why do you speak to me as though I did not always think and have always thought the same as you?

“As long as I live and retain my understanding, I shall praise the monks of Egypt, commend the anchorites, and marvel at the hermits; but I shall always make an exception for Martin. I would not dare to compare any monk with him, and certainly no bishop.

“Egypt acknowledges this, Syria acknowledges it, Ethiopia has learned it, India has heard it, Parthia and Persia know it, and Armenia is not ignorant of it. The excluded Bosporus has learned it; and finally, if anyone inhabits either the Fortunate Islands or the icy ocean, he knows it.

“How wretched is our own region, which, although it possessed so great a man nearby, did not deserve to know him! Yet I shall not involve the common people in this accusation: only the clergy, only the priests, do not know him.

“Nor did the envious wish to know him without reason. For if they had known his virtues, they would have recognized their own vices.

“I shudder to say what I recently heard: some unhappy man said that you had lied about many things in your book. That is not a human voice but the devil’s. Nor is Martin disparaged in this matter alone; faith in the Gospels is undermined. For when the Lord himself testified that deeds of the sort Martin performed are to be done by all the faithful, anyone who does not believe that Martin did these things does not believe that Christ said them.

“But those unhappy, degenerate, sleepy men are ashamed that deeds they themselves cannot perform were accomplished by him. They prefer to deny his virtues rather than confess their own indolence.

“But let us leave all memory of such men behind as we hasten to other matters. You, as I have long desired, continue the remaining deeds of Martin.”

“But I think,” I said, “that this should rightly be requested from Gallus, since he knows more—for a disciple could not have failed to know the deeds of his master—and since he owes this service not only to Martin but also to us. I have already published a book, and you have thus far related the deeds of the Easterners; let Gallus now unfold this necessary history of our conversation. As I said, he owes us his turn to speak, and I believe he will also grant his own Martin the favor of recounting his deeds without reluctance.”

“Although I am unequal to so great a burden,” said Gallus, “I am nevertheless compelled by the examples of obedience that Postumianus related above not to refuse this task you impose upon me. But when I consider that I, a Gaul, am going to speak among Aquitanians, I fear that a rustic speech may offend your excessively refined ears.

“Nevertheless, you will hear me as a man of Gurdus, speaking without cosmetic or high tragic style. For if you grant that I am Martin’s disciple, grant me this also: that, following his example, I may despise empty rhetorical flourishes and verbal ornaments.”

“You may speak,” said Postumianus, “either in Celtic or, if you prefer, in Gaulish, provided that you now speak of Martin.

“I declare that even if you were mute, words would not be lacking to you with which to speak of Martin, however eloquent your speech might be—just as Zachariah’s tongue was loosened in the name of John.

“Besides, since you are a scholar, you artfully pretend to excuse your lack of skill, because you overflow with eloquence. But it is not fitting for a monk to be so cunning, nor for a Gaul to be so clever.

“Rather, begin and explain what awaits you. We have already spent too much time on other matters; and now the lengthening shadow of the setting sun warns us that little of the day remains before night approaches.”

Afterward, when we had all been silent for a little while, Gallus began as follows:

“I think I must be especially careful not to repeat what Sulpicius here recorded in his book about Martin’s virtues. Therefore I shall pass over his first deeds while he was still serving as a soldier, and shall not touch upon what he did as a layman and a monk. Nor shall I relate things heard from others rather than those which I myself witnessed.”

## DIALOGUE II

But rather, the second part of Dialogue I.

### I

When, therefore, I had first left my studies and joined the blessed man, a few days later we were following him as he went to the church.

Meanwhile, a poor man, almost naked, met him during the winter months and begged that clothing be given him. Martin then summoned the archdeacon and ordered him to clothe the freezing man without delay.

Afterward he entered the sacristy. When he was sitting alone, as was his custom—for the freedom granted to the clergy allowed him this solitude even in the church—he remained there. In another sacristy the presbyters sat, either occupied with greetings or engaged in hearing business. Martin’s solitude, however, held him until the hour when custom required the sacred rites to be performed for the people.

I shall not omit the fact that, while sitting in the sacristy, he never used a chair. No one ever saw him sitting in the church. By God, I recently saw someone sitting on a lofty throne, as though on a royal tribunal, and I was not without shame at the sight.

Martin sat on a rustic stool, such as are used by servants. We rustic Gauls call these *tripetiae*; you scholars—or at least you who come from Greece—call them *tripods*.

The poor man, having sought out this private place of the blessed man, burst in when the archdeacon delayed giving him a tunic. He complained that the cleric had ignored him and lamented that he was cold.

Without delay, the saint, while the poor man did not see, secretly drew a tunic from beneath his *amphibalus*, covered the poor man with it, and ordered him to leave.

A little later the archdeacon entered and reminded him that the people were waiting in the church according to custom and that he ought to proceed to conduct the sacred rites.

Martin replied that the poor man—he was speaking of himself—ought first to be clothed; he could not proceed to the church unless the poor man received clothing.

The deacon understood nothing, because from outside Martin was dressed in the *amphibalus* and the deacon could not see that he was naked underneath. At last he complained that the poor man was nowhere to be found.

“Bring me the garment that has been prepared,” Martin said. “There will be no shortage of a poor man to clothe.”

At last, compelled by urgent necessity and already stirred to anger, the cleric seized from the nearest shops a short, rough *bigerrica*, bought for five silver pieces, and angrily laid it at Martin’s feet.

“There is the garment,” he said; “but the poor man is not here.”

Unmoved, Martin ordered him to wait a little outside, obviously arranging for privacy while he put the garment on his naked body. He was exerting all his strength to conceal what he had done.

But when are such things hidden in holy men? Whether they wish it or not, everything is disclosed to those who seek it.

### II

Wearing this garment, he proceeded to offer sacrifice to God.

On that day—I shall relate something extraordinary—when he was already blessing the altar, as is customary, we saw a ball of fire leap from his head. Rising upward, it produced a very long lock of flame.

Although we saw this on a most celebrated day and before a great multitude of people, only one of the virgins, one of the presbyters, and three of the monks saw it. Why the others did not see it cannot be for us to judge.

At nearly the same time, my uncle Evanthius, a man occupied with worldly affairs but nevertheless a very devout Christian, began to be afflicted by a grave illness and was in extreme danger of death. He summoned Martin.

Martin hastened without hesitation. Yet before the holy man had covered half the distance, the sick man felt the power of the one who was coming. He immediately recovered his health and himself came out to meet us.

The next day, when Martin wished to return, Evanthius detained him with earnest entreaty. Meanwhile, a serpent struck one of the household’s boys with a deadly blow. Evanthius himself carried the boy, already lifeless, on his shoulders and laid him before the feet of the holy man, confident that nothing was impossible for him.

The evil serpent’s poison had already spread through all his limbs. Everyone could see the skin swollen along every vein and the vital parts stretched like a wineskin.

Martin extended his hand and examined every part of the boy’s body. He fixed his finger close to the tiny wound through which the beast had injected its poison.

Then—I shall relate something extraordinary—we saw the venom drawn back from every part of the body and run toward Martin’s finger. Through the small opening of the wound, he then forced out the poison together with the blood, so that it streamed in a long line of abundant fluid, just as milk flows from the udders of goats or sheep when shepherds press them with their hands.

The boy rose unharmed.

We, astonished at the miracle of so great a deed, confessed what the truth itself compelled us to confess: that under heaven there was no one who could imitate Martin.

### III

At a later time, we were likewise traveling with him while he visited the dioceses. We had been delayed by some necessity or other, and he had gone a little ahead.

Meanwhile, along the public roadway, a state wagon full of soldiers was approaching. But when they saw Martin beside them, dressed in a rough garment and wrapped in a black, hanging cloak, the animals nearest him drew back in fright toward the other side.

Then, becoming entangled in the ropes and in the extended traces by which, as you have often seen, those wretched animals are harnessed together, they threw the ranks into confusion. While the soldiers struggled to disentangle them, they caused a delay for those who were hurrying onward.

The soldiers, angered by this affront, leapt down to the ground and attacked. They began to assail Martin with whips and clubs. He remained silent and, with incredible patience, offered his back to those beating him. This provoked still greater madness in the wretched men, who became all the more furious because he seemed not to feel the blows and treated them with contempt.

We followed immediately and found him lying lifeless on the ground, horribly bloodied and lacerated over every part of his body. We at once placed him on his little donkey and, cursing the place of his beating, hurried away.

Meanwhile, the soldiers returned to their wagon. Their fury having been satisfied, they ordered the animals to be driven on toward the place where they had begun to go.

But the animals stood fixed to the ground as though they were bronze statues. Although their masters raised their voices, and whips resounded on every side, they were completely unmoved.

Then all of them rose together to beat the animals. The punishment inflicted on the mules wore out the Gallic whips. The entire neighboring woodland was stripped; the animals were struck with logs. But the savage hands accomplished absolutely nothing. The beasts remained fixed in one place, immobile images.

The unhappy men did not know what to do. They could no longer conceal from themselves that, however brutish their minds, they recognized that they were being held by divine power.

At last, coming to their senses, they began to ask who the man was whom they had beaten in that same place a little earlier. By questioning passersby, they learned that they had so cruelly beaten Martin.

Then the cause became clear to everyone. They could no longer fail to understand that they were being held because of the injury they had inflicted upon that man.

They therefore pursued us at a rapid pace. Conscious of their bold deed and overwhelmed by deserved shame, they came weeping and with their heads and faces covered in the dust with which they had defiled themselves. They threw themselves at Martin’s knees, begging forgiveness and asking him to permit them to leave.

They said that their own consciences alone had already inflicted sufficient punishment upon them, and that they had understood well enough how the earth might have swallowed them alive, or how they themselves, deprived of their senses, ought rather to have stiffened into the immobility of stone, just as they had seen the animals fixed in the places where they had stood.

They prayed and begged him to pardon their crime and grant them permission to depart.

Before they arrived, the blessed man had already perceived that they were being held, and he had told us so earlier. Nevertheless, he mercifully granted them forgiveness and allowed them to leave, after their animals had been restored.

[Col. 0204A] **IV.** I have often noticed, Sulpicius, that Martin used to tell you that in his episcopate he had by no means possessed that abundance of power for working miracles which he remembered having had before. If this is true—or rather, since it is true—we can infer how great those deeds must have been which he performed as a monk, and which he carried out alone, with no witness, when we have seen him perform such mighty signs in his episcopate before the eyes of everyone. Many of his earlier deeds became known throughout the world and could not be concealed; but countless others, it is said, he concealed while avoiding display and did not allow to come to human notice. For, having surpassed human nature, and trampling the world’s glory underfoot through awareness of his own virtue, he enjoyed the testimony of heaven.

We can judge that this is true even from the things that have come to our knowledge and could not remain hidden. Before his episcopate, he restored two dead men to life, as your book has described more fully; but during his episcopate—as I am surprised that you omitted this—he raised only one. I am a witness to this, if indeed you have no doubts about a witness of lesser standing. I shall explain to you how it happened.

Some matter had arisen which required us to go to the town of Chartres. Meanwhile, as we were passing through a village densely populated with inhabitants, an enormous crowd came out to meet us, and it was entirely pagan. No one in that village knew a Christian; yet the fame of so great a man had drawn together a multitude that covered all the broad fields around us. Martin sensed that he had work to do, and, as the spirit announced it to him, he trembled all over. With a voice that sounded not human, he preached the word of God to the pagans, repeatedly lamenting that so great a multitude did not know the Lord and Savior.

Meanwhile, since an incredible crowd had surrounded us, a woman whose son had died shortly before began to offer his lifeless body to the blessed man with outstretched hands, saying: “We know that you are a friend of God. Restore my son to me, for he is my only child.” The rest of the crowd joined her and cried out in support of the mother’s prayers.

Then Martin, seeing—as he himself later told us—that he could obtain this power for the salvation of those who were waiting, took the dead boy’s body in his own hands. After kneeling while everyone watched, he rose when his prayer was finished and restored the child, alive, to his mother.

Then the whole crowd raised a shout to heaven and confessed Christ as God. Finally, they all began to rush in groups to the knees of the blessed man, earnestly asking him to make them Christians. Without hesitation, there in the middle of the field, he laid his hand upon them all and made them catechumens. At that point he turned to us and said that it was not unreasonable for catechumens to be made in a field where martyrs were accustomed to be consecrated.

**V.** “You have conquered,” said Postumianus. “You have conquered, Gallus—not me, certainly, for I am Martin’s advocate rather, since I have always known and believed all these things about that man; but you have conquered all hermits and anchorites. None of them, like this Martin of yours—or rather, ours—has commanded the dead. Sulpicius rightly compares him with the apostles and prophets, for the strength of his faith and the works of his virtues testify that he resembles them in every respect.

“But continue, I beg you. Although we could hear nothing more magnificent, continue nevertheless, Gallus, to unfold whatever remains to be said about Martin. My mind is eager to recognize even his smallest and most ordinary deeds, because no one doubts that his smallest deeds are greater than other men’s greatest.”

“So I shall,” said Gallus. “But I did not see the event I am about to recount. It happened before I joined that man; nevertheless, it is famous, having been spread abroad by the account of faithful brothers who were present.

“It was approximately the time when he was first made bishop. He had to go to the imperial court. Valentinian then held supreme power. When he learned that Martin was asking for things he was unwilling to grant, he ordered him to be kept away from the palace doors. His wife, an Arian woman, had indeed gained influence over his savage and arrogant mind and had turned him completely away from the holy man, so that he would not show him the reverence due to him.

“Thus, when Martin had tried once and again, but in vain, to approach the arrogant emperor, he returned to his familiar defenses. He wrapped himself in sackcloth, sprinkled himself with ashes, abstained from food and drink, and continued in prayer day and night.

“On the seventh day an angel appeared to him and ordered him to go confidently to the palace. The royal doors, though closed, would open of their own accord; the emperor’s proud spirit would be softened.

“Strengthened by the speech of this present angel and relying on his assistance, Martin went to the palace. The doors stood open; no one resisted him. At last, with no one preventing him, he reached the emperor.

“When the emperor saw him approaching from a distance, he angrily demanded why Martin had been admitted. He did not deign to rise for the man standing before him, until fire enveloped the imperial chair and burning heat scorched the emperor himself on the part of his body where he was seated.

“Thus the arrogant man was driven from his throne, and he rose unwillingly for Martin. After embracing at length the man whom he had previously resolved to despise, he confessed, now more corrected, that he had experienced divine power. Without waiting for Martin’s prayers, he granted everything before Martin had even asked.

“He frequently invited Martin to conversation and banquets. Finally, when Martin was departing, he offered him many gifts, but the blessed man, as always, the guardian of his poverty, rejected them all.”

[Col. 0205D] **VI.** Since we have entered the palace once, let me connect events that occurred in the palace at different times. In discussing the wonder inspired by Martin, we must certainly not omit the example of the faithful empress.

“Emperor Maximus governed the state. He was a man deserving praise throughout his life, if only he had been permitted either to reject the diadem unlawfully imposed upon him by a mutinous army or to abstain from civil war. But a great empire could neither be refused without danger nor held without arms.

“He repeatedly summoned Martin and received him inside the palace, honoring him reverently. Their entire conversation concerned present things, future things, the glory of the faithful, and the eternity of the saints.

“Meanwhile, day and night, the empress hung upon Martin’s lips. Following the Gospel example, she washed the saint’s feet with her tears and dried them with her hair. Martin, whose body no woman had ever touched, could not escape her continual attention—or rather, her servitude.

“She thought neither of the wealth of the kingdom, nor of the dignity of imperial power, nor of the diadem, nor of the purple. Lying prostrate on the ground, she could not be torn away from Martin’s feet.

“Finally, she asked this of her husband, and then both of them pressed Martin to allow her to prepare a meal for him alone, with all attendants removed. The blessed man could not resist so obstinately.

“The chaste meal was arranged by the empress’s hands. She herself spread the little seat, brought up the table, and supplied water with her own hands. She set before him food that she herself had cooked. While he sat, she herself stood motionless at a distance, fixed to the ground according to the discipline of servants, displaying in every respect the modesty and humility of one who serves. She mixed his drink and handed it to him.

“After the little meal had ended, she gathered up the fragments of bread and the crumbs, placing those relics with sufficient faithfulness above imperial banquets.

“Blessed woman! In the devotion of such piety she is rightly to be compared with the woman who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon—if we follow the simple historical account. But if the faith of queens is to be compared—something I may say while setting aside the majesty of the mystery—she sought to hear a wise man, whereas this woman was not content merely to hear the wise man but also deserved to serve him.”

**VII.** “For some time now,” said Postumianus, “Gallus, as I have listened to you speak, I have greatly admired the empress’s faith. But what becomes of the claim that no woman was ever said to have stood close to Martin? Here is an empress who not only stood near him but also served him. I fear that those who willingly associate with women may use this example to defend themselves somewhat.”

“What?” said Gallus. “Do you not see what grammarians customarily teach: place, time, and person? Picture before your eyes Martin, held at the emperor’s palace, besieged by prayers, compelled by the empress’s faith, and constrained by the needs of the time to free those shut up in prison, restore those sent into exile, and return confiscated property. How costly do you think this must have been for a bishop, so that for all these things he relaxed, even slightly, the strictness of his purpose?

“Nevertheless, since you think some will make bad use of this example, those people will be fortunate if they do not depart from the discipline of the example. Let them observe that Martin was served only once in his life, when he was already seventy years old—not by a free widow, not by a flirtatious virgin, but by a woman living with her husband, while the husband himself was likewise entreating Martin. The empress served and waited upon him.

“She stood beside him while he ate; she did not recline at table with him. She did not dare to share the meal but offered him service.

“Learn the discipline, then: let a married woman serve you, not command you; and let her serve without reclining at table. Martha served the Lord in this way, yet she was not invited to join the meal; rather, the woman who listened to the word was preferred to the one who served.

“But in Martin’s case this empress fulfilled both roles: she served like Martha and listened like Mary. If anyone wishes to use this as an example, let him observe the example in every respect: the same kind of circumstance, the same kind of person, the same kind of service, the same kind of meal—and only once in an entire life.”

**VIII.** “Your speech,” said Postumianus, “admirably restrains these men of ours, so that they do not go beyond Martin’s example. But I confess to you that these words will fall on deaf ears. If we followed Martin’s ways, we would never speak of cases involving kisses, and we would be free of every reproach arising from a depraved reputation. Yet, just as you customarily say when accused of gluttony, ‘We are Galluses,’ so in this matter we confess that we shall never be corrected either by Martin’s example or by your arguments.

“Nevertheless, while we have been discussing these things for some time, why are you so silent, stubborn Sulpicius?”

“I am not merely silent,” I replied, “but long ago resolved to keep silent about such matters. Since I rebuked a certain wandering, stylish, extravagant widow for living too licentiously, and likewise a virgin who clung indecorously to a young man dear to me—although I had often heard her rebuking others who did such things—I aroused such hatred against myself among all women and all monks that both armies have sworn to wage war against me.

“So, I beg you, be silent, lest even what you are saying now be attributed to my unpopularity. Let all mention of those matters be left to you. Let us return instead to Martin. You, Gallus, explain the work you began.”

“Indeed,” he said, “I have already told you so much that my speech ought to have satisfied your eagerness. But since I cannot refuse your wishes, I shall speak for as much of the day as remains. For certainly, when I look at the straw laid out for our beds, I am reminded that a miracle was also performed through the straw on which Martin had lain.

“The event happened as follows. Claudiomagus is a village on the border of the Bituriges and the Turones. There is a church there renowned for the sanctity of its religion and no less celebrated for its multitude of holy virgins.

“As Martin was passing through, he stayed in the church’s sacristy. After he had departed, all the virgins rushed into that sacristy. They kissed each place where the blessed man had either sat or stood, and they divided among themselves the straw on which he had rested.

“A few days later, one of them hung around the neck of a possessed man, whom the spirit of error was tormenting, a portion of the straw that she had gathered for herself as a blessing. Immediately, faster than one can say it, the demon was expelled and the man was cleansed.”

**IX.** At approximately the same time, as Martin was returning from Trier, a cow came toward him, driven by a demon. Abandoning its herd, it charged at human beings and had already gored many of them in its violent frenzy.

“When it began to approach us, those who were following it from a distance began loudly warning us to be careful. But when it came nearer, raging with wild eyes, Martin raised his hand toward it and ordered the animal to stop. At once it began to stand motionless at his word.

“Meanwhile Martin saw a demon riding on its back. Rebuking it, he said: ‘Depart, deadly one, from the cow, and stop tormenting this harmless animal.’

“The evil spirit obeyed and withdrew. The heifer’s understanding did not fail to recognize that it had been freed. Having recovered its calm, it fell at the feet of the saint; then, at Martin’s command, it returned to its herd and mingled with the rest, gentler than a sheep.

“This was the occasion when Martin, placed amid flames, felt no burning. I do not think this needs to be recounted, because Sulpicius has described it more fully—not in his book, where he passed over it, but later in a letter that he wrote to Eusebius, then a presbyter and now a bishop. You, Postumianus, have either read that letter, I believe, or, if it is unknown to you, you have access to it whenever you wish from that archive. We are recounting what he omitted.

“On another occasion, while he was traveling around the dioceses, we came upon a hunting party. Dogs were pursuing a hare. The little animal had already been worn out over a great distance, and, since there was no escape anywhere across the wide-open fields, it was delaying its imminent death, now almost within reach, by repeatedly darting this way and that.

“Moved by compassion for its danger, the holy man ordered the dogs to stop pursuing it and to allow the fugitive to escape. At the first command of his speech they immediately halted. You would have thought them bound—or rather fixed in place, clinging to their tracks.”

**X.** Thus the little hare escaped unharmed while its pursuers were restrained. It is worthwhile also to recall some of Martin’s familiar remarks, seasoned with spiritual wit.

“He happened to see a sheep that had recently been shorn. ‘This sheep,’ he said, ‘has fulfilled the Gospel command: it had two tunics and gave one of them to the one who had none. You too must act in this way.’

“Again, when he saw a shivering swineherd almost naked beneath a sheepskin garment, he said: ‘Behold Adam, expelled from paradise, tending pigs in a garment of skin. But let us put off that old Adam who still remains in this man, and instead put on the new Adam.’

“Cattle had grazed part of a meadow, and pigs had rooted up another part. The remaining portion, which had been left unharmed, bloomed in spring like a picture composed of different flowers.

“‘That part,’ he said, ‘represents marriage. Although the part grazed by cattle has not entirely lost the beauty of its grasses, it retains none of the dignity of flowers. The part rooted up by unclean animals, the pigs, presents the foul image of fornication. But the portion that suffered no harm displays the glory of virginity; fertile in grasses, it flourishes luxuriantly, its hay yielding abundant fruit, and, distinguished beyond every other appearance, it shines adorned with flowers like glittering gems.

“‘Blessed and God-worthy beauty! Nothing can be compared with virginity. Those who compare marriage with fornication therefore greatly err; and those who judge marriage to be equal to virginity are utterly wretched and foolish.

“‘Yet this distinction must be maintained by the wise: marriage belongs to forgiveness; virginity looks toward glory; fornication is assigned to punishment unless it is cleansed by repentance.’”

**XI.** A certain soldier had cast aside his military belt in the church and professed himself a monk. He had built himself a cell some distance away in a remote place, intending to live like a hermit.

“Meanwhile the crafty enemy agitated his dull heart with various thoughts, so that he would change his mind and prefer to have his wife live with him, although Martin had ordered her to remain in a monastery for women.

“The brave hermit therefore approached Martin and confessed what he had in mind. Martin strongly refused, saying that it was unreasonable for a woman to be joined again to a man who was now a monk rather than a husband.

“At last, when the soldier persisted, asserting that this intention would cause no harm—that he merely wished to enjoy his wife’s companionship, and that there was no fear of their returning to their former vices, since he was a soldier of Christ and she too had sworn the same oath of that same service—the soldier asked that the bishop permit them, holy and ignorant of their sexes by the merit of faith, to serve together.

“Then Martin—and I shall give you his very words—said: ‘Tell me: have you ever been in battle? Have you stood in the battle line?’

“He replied: ‘I have often stood in the battle line and have frequently taken part in war.’

“Martin then said: ‘Tell me, therefore: in that battle line prepared for combat, armed for war, or already fighting a hostile army hand-to-hand with swords drawn, did you ever see a woman standing or fighting?’

“Only then did the soldier, confused, blush. He gave thanks that he had not been allowed to persist in his error and that he had been corrected not by harsh verbal rebuke but by a true and reasonable comparison appropriate to a soldier’s identity.

“Martin then turned to us—for a large crowd of brothers surrounded him—and said: ‘Let no woman enter the camp of men. Let the battle line of soldiers stand apart. Let the woman remain at a distance in her own tent. An army is made contemptible if a crowd of women is mixed with the companies of men.

“‘Let the soldier fight in the battle line; let the soldier fight in the field. Let the woman keep herself within the defenses of the walls. She too has her glory if she preserves her chastity while her husband is absent. This is her first virtue and her complete victory: not to be seen.’”

[Col. 0209C] **XII.** I believe, Sulpicius, that you remember the feeling with which, when you too were present, he praised that virgin to us—a virgin who had withdrawn herself so completely from the eyes of all men that she did not even admit Martin himself when he wished to visit her as a matter of duty.

“As he was passing by her little estate, where for several years she had restrained herself in chastity, Martin heard of her faith and virtue and turned aside, so that as bishop he might honor a girl of such distinguished merit with a religious duty.

“We who followed thought that the virgin would rejoice, since she would have this as testimony to her virtue: a priest of such great renown had come to her, setting aside the strictness of his purpose. But she did not relax the strong bonds of her resolve even out of consideration for Martin. Thus the blessed man, receiving from another woman a praiseworthy excuse, departed joyfully from the door of one who had not allowed herself to be seen or greeted.

“O glorious virgin, who did not permit even Martin to see her! O blessed Martin, who did not regard that rejection as an insult to himself, but magnified her virtue with delight and rejoiced in an example so unusual, at least in those regions!

“Because approaching night forced us to remain not far from that little estate, the same virgin sent a gift of hospitality to the blessed man. Martin did what he had never done before—for he had never accepted anyone’s hospitality or anyone’s gift: he rejected nothing that the venerable virgin had sent, saying that a priest must not reject her blessing, since she was superior to many priests.

“Let virgins, I beg, hear this example, so that if they wish to resist evil, they may close their doors even to the good, and so that, to prevent wicked men from having free access to them, they may not hesitate to exclude even priests.

“Let the whole world hear this: the virgin did not permit herself to be seen by Martin. She did not reject just any priest from her presence; rather, the girl did not come into the sight of a man whose sight was salvation for those who saw him.

“What other priest besides Martin would not have regarded this as an insult to himself? What anger and resentment would he have conceived in his mind against the holy virgin! He would have judged her a heretic and decreed that she must be anathematized.

“How much would he have preferred those virgins to that blessed soul who repeatedly present themselves everywhere before the priest, arrange lavish banquets, and recline at table together with him!

“But where is my speech leading me? This somewhat freer manner of speaking must be restrained, lest it perhaps offend certain people. Words of rebuke will not benefit the faithless, but the example will satisfy the faithful.

“Yet I shall praise this virgin’s virtue in such a way that I do not thereby think I detract from those women who often came from distant regions to see Martin. For the blessed man was also frequently visited by angels, moved by affection.”

**XIII.** “What I am about to say, Postumianus, I properly affirm to you with this man as witness”—and he was looking at me—“one day Sulpicius and I were keeping watch outside his door. For several hours we had been sitting there in silence, in great dread and trembling, as though we were carrying out assigned guard duty before an angel’s tabernacle. The door of his cell was closed, and he did not know that we were there.

“Meanwhile we heard the murmur of people speaking, and soon we were surrounded by a kind of dread and astonishment. We could not fail to recognize that something divine was taking place.

“After approximately two hours Martin came out to us. Then Sulpicius—for no one spoke more familiarly with him—began to ask him earnestly to tell us, since we were making our request piously, what that divine experience of terror had been which we both confessed to having felt, or with whom he had been conversing in his cell. For, although faintly and scarcely intelligibly, we had heard the sound of people speaking inside.

“Martin hesitated for a long time and at length. Yet there was nothing Sulpicius could not wrest from him, even against his will. I shall perhaps say things that are incredible, but with Christ as my witness I do not lie—unless someone is so sacrilegious as to think that Martin could have lied.

“‘I shall tell you,’ he said, ‘but please do not tell anyone.’

“‘Agnes, Thecla, and Mary were with me.’

“He described to us the face and appearance of each of them. Nor did he confess that they had visited him only on that day; he said that they frequently came to visit him. He did not deny that the apostles Peter and Paul also often appeared to him.

“As for the demons, whenever one of them came to him, he rebuked it by its own name. Mercury especially harassed him. Jupiter, he said, was brutish and dull-witted.

“These things seemed incredible to many even within that same monastery, and I can hardly expect that everyone who hears them will believe them. For unless Martin had led a life and practiced virtue beyond all reckoning, he would never have enjoyed such glory among us. Yet it is hardly surprising if human weakness has doubted Martin’s works, since even today we see many who have not believed even the Gospels.

“We have both often sensed and experienced that angels were familiarly seen by Martin. I shall tell a very small matter, but I shall tell it nevertheless.

“A synod of bishops was being held at Nîmes. Martin had not wished to attend it, but he wanted to know what had been done. By chance Sulpicius was sailing with him. As always, he sat alone at a distance from the others, in a remote part of the ship.

“There an angel announced to him what had taken place at the synod. Later, when we carefully inquired about the time at which the council had been held, we learned with certainty that it had been held on that very day and that the bishops had decreed there precisely what the angel had announced to Martin.”

**XIV.** When we asked him about the end of the world, he told us that Nero and the Antichrist would come first.

“Nero would rule in the western region after subduing ten kings, and would carry out persecution to such an extent that he would compel the worship of the idols of the nations.

“The Antichrist, however, would first seize control of the East. He would have Jerusalem as the seat and capital of his kingdom. He would restore the city and the Temple. His persecution would be such that he would compel people to deny Christ as God, affirming instead that he himself was Christ. He would order everyone to be circumcised according to the Law.

“Finally, Nero would be killed by the Antichrist, and the whole world and all nations would be brought under the Antichrist’s power until the impious one was crushed by the coming of Christ.

“There was no doubt, he said, that the Antichrist, conceived by an evil spirit, had already been born and was now in childhood, destined to assume power when he reached the proper age.

“It is now eight years since we heard these things from him. Judge for yourselves how near to fulfillment the things that are feared may already stand.”

While Gallus was saying these things and had not yet finished recounting what he had decided to tell us, a household boy entered and announced that the presbyter Refrigerius was standing outside.

“We began to wonder whether it would be better to continue listening to Gallus or to go out to meet the man we most desired to see, who had come to us on official business.

“Then Gallus said: ‘Even if this speech did not have to be abandoned because of the arrival of so holy a priest, night itself compels us to bring our prolonged conversation to an end here. But since it has been impossible to unfold all the virtues of Martin, let it be enough for you to have heard these things today. Tomorrow we shall tell the rest.’

“Thus, having accepted Gallus’s promise, we rose together.”

# DIALOGUE III

*Which nevertheless ought to be called the Second.*

[Col. 0211]

**I.** “It is becoming light, Gallus; it is time to rise. For, as you see, Postumianus is pressing us, and this presbyter, who missed yesterday’s gathering, is waiting for you to unfold what you postponed until today—what you promised to explain about our Martin.

“He is not ignorant of any of the things worth remembering; but it is sweet and welcome knowledge even for one who rereads what he already knows. Nature has arranged matters in such a way that one rejoices with a better conscience when one knows that what one knows is not uncertain, having been confirmed by the testimony of many.

“This man too has followed Martin from early youth and knows everything, but he gladly learns again what he already knows. I shall confess to you, Gallus, that I have often heard of Martin’s virtues, since I have also committed much about him to writing. Yet, through admiration for his deeds, the things about him that are repeated—even though heard many times—are always new to me.

“Therefore we rejoice all the more that Refrigerius has been added to our audience, since this Postumianus, who is eager to carry these things to the East, will more readily receive from you a truth sealed, as it were, in the presence of witnesses.”

While I was saying this, and Gallus was already prepared to speak, a crowd of monks rushed in: the presbyter Evagrius, Aper, Sebastianus, and Agricola. A little later our presbyter Aetherius entered with the deacon Calupio and the subdeacon Amator. Last of all came my very dear presbyter Aurelius, who had traveled a longer road and hurried along.

“Why,” I asked, “have you run here so suddenly and unexpectedly, from such different regions, and so early in the morning?”

“We learned yesterday,” they replied, “that this Gallus had spent the entire day recounting Martin’s virtues and had postponed the rest until today because night had overtaken him. Therefore we hastened to form a large audience for one who was about to speak on so great a subject.”

Meanwhile, we were told that many laymen were standing outside. They did not dare enter but were begging to be admitted.

“These men should certainly not be mixed with us,” said Aper. “They have come to listen out of curiosity rather than devotion.”

I was embarrassed on behalf of those whom he thought should not be admitted. At last I managed with difficulty to obtain admission for Eucherius, a former vicar, and Celsus, a former consul. The others were turned away.

Then we seated Gallus in the middle. After he had maintained silence for a long time with his characteristic noble modesty, he finally began as follows:

**II.** “You have gathered to hear me, holy and eloquent men; but, as I think, you have brought ears that are religious rather than learned, since you are going to hear me speak as a witness of faith, not with an orator’s eloquence.

“I shall not review what was said yesterday. Those who did not hear it may read it again from the written account.

“Postumianus is expecting something new, which he will announce to the East, so that it will not place itself above the West in comparison with Martin.

“First, my heart desires to explain what Refrigerius has just whispered in my ear.

“The event occurred in the city of Chartres. The head of a household began to offer Martin a twelve-year-old girl who had been mute from birth, asking that the saint, by his merits, release her bound tongue.

“Martin deferred to the bishops who happened at that time to be standing around him, Valentinus and Victricius, saying that he was unequal to so great a task. Yet he acknowledged that nothing was impossible for them, as though they were more holy.

“They joined their devout prayers with those of the suppliant father and begged Martin to grant what was hoped for.

“He did not delay any longer—thus displaying both virtues, humility by not claiming the power and compassion by not postponing the deed. He ordered the surrounding crowd to withdraw. With only the bishops and the girl’s father standing beside him, he prostrated himself in prayer in his customary manner.

“Then he blessed a little oil with the introductory words of an exorcism. Holding the girl’s tongue with his fingers, he poured the consecrated liquid into her mouth.

“The result of the saint’s power did not disappoint. He asked the girl her father’s name, and immediately she answered.

“The father cried out, embracing Martin’s knees with joy and tears alike, and, to everyone’s astonishment, confessed that this was the first voice he had ever heard from his daughter.

“And so that no one might perhaps regard this as incredible, let the present Evagrius testify to you that it is true, for the event took place in his presence.”

**III.** “The little matter I recently learned from the account of the presbyter Harpagius may seem insignificant, but it should not be passed over.

“The wife of the comes Avitianus sent Martin some oil so that he might bless it for various medical purposes, as is customary. The glass flask was of the following kind: it widened into a round belly, with an elongated neck, but the hollow part of the projecting mouth was not filled. For it is customary to fill such vessels in such a way that the upper part is left free for sealing with a stopper.

“The presbyter testified that he saw the oil increase under Martin’s blessing until, overflowing in abundance, it ran out over the top. He also testified that, while the vessel was being carried back to the mistress of the household, the oil continued to seethe with power. In the hands of the boy carrying it, the oil overflowed so continually that the entire garment was covered by the abundance of the liquid that had spilled over.

“The matron received the vessel so full to the very brim that the presbyter still declares that there was no room in the glass for the stopper by which vessels intended for careful preservation are customarily closed.

“Another wonder, which I remember happened to this man”—and he was looking at me—“is the following. He placed the glass vessel containing the oil Martin had blessed on a somewhat elevated windowsill. An inattentive household boy, unaware that the flask was there, pulled away a cloth laid over it.

“The vessel fell onto the marble pavement spread beneath it. Everyone was terrified that the blessing might have been lost, but the flask was found just as unharmed as if it had fallen upon the softest feathers. This event must be attributed not to chance but to Martin’s power, for his blessing could not perish.

“What shall I say of the event performed by a certain man whose name will be suppressed because he is present and has forbidden that he be identified? Saturninus was also present on that occasion.

“A dog was barking at us most annoyingly. ‘In the name of Martin,’ he said, ‘I order you to become silent.’

“The barking stuck in the dog’s throat; its tongue became silent, as though you might have thought it had been cut out.

“Thus it is not enough that Martin himself performed miracles. Believe me: others too have performed many things in his name.”

**IV.** You knew how savage Avitianus, once a comes, was—barbarous beyond measure and bloodthirsty above all others.

“When he entered the city of Tours with a raging spirit, with ranks of prisoners following him in miserable condition and chained together, he ordered various kinds of punishments to be prepared for their destruction. He planned to proceed with this dreadful work on the following day, while the terrified city looked on.

“When this became known to Martin, he went alone, shortly before midnight, to the palace of that beast. But when, in the deep silence of night, everyone was asleep and no entrance was open through the barred doors, he prostrated himself before the bloody threshold.

“Meanwhile Avitianus, buried in deep sleep, was shaken when an angel attacked him. ‘The servant of God lies at your threshold, and you are resting?’

“When he heard this voice, Avitianus was thrown into confusion and jolted from his bed. He summoned his servants and cried out in agitation that Martin was outside. ‘Go at once and unbolt the doors, lest the servant of God suffer injury.’

“But the servants, as is the nature of all servants, had scarcely gone beyond the first threshold when they mocked their master for having been deceived by sleep. They denied that anyone was outside, reasoning from their own experience that no one could remain awake at night—much less that a priest could be lying in the terror of that night before another man’s door. Avitianus was easily persuaded of this.

“Again he sank into sleep. But soon, shaken with greater force, he cried out that Martin was standing outside and that for this reason he was being allowed no rest either in body or in mind.

“When the servants delayed, he himself advanced as far as the outer threshold. There he found Martin, just as he had sensed.

“Struck by the sheer manifestation of such power, the wretched man said: ‘Lord, what have you done to me? You need say nothing. I know what you desire; I see what you require. Go away as quickly as possible, lest heavenly anger consume me because of the injury I have done you. I have suffered enough punishment already. Believe me, it was no small matter for me to come out myself.’

“After the saint’s departure, he summoned his officials and ordered all the guards to be released. He then departed at once himself.

“Thus, when Avitianus had been driven away, the city rejoiced that it had been liberated.”

## V.

When these things had become learned from many people on Avitianus’s report, and recently the priest Refrigerius, whom you see before you, heard them from Evagrius, a trustworthy man and former tribune, under invocation of the divine majesty—who swore that Avitianus himself had related them to him—I do not want you to be surprised that today I am doing what I did not do yesterday: attaching to each individual virtue the names and persons of witnesses whom anyone who is incredulous may approach, since they are still alive. The unbelief of many demands this, for they are said to waver over certain matters mentioned yesterday. Let them therefore accept as witnesses people who are still safe and living, whom they may believe more readily because they doubt our good faith. Yet if they are so unbelieving, I declare that they will not believe even those witnesses.

I am astonished that anyone possessing even the slightest sense of religion should wish to commit so great a sacrilege as to think that anyone could lie about Martin. Let such a suspicion be far from anyone who lives under God: Martin does not need to be defended by lies. Nevertheless, before you, Christ, we affirm the truth of our entire account: that we have said, and will say, nothing except what we ourselves saw or learned from manifestly reliable authorities, and for the most part from Martin himself as he related it.

Although we have adopted the form of a dialogue, so that the reading might be varied to relieve weariness, we solemnly affirm that we are preserving the truth of history. The unbelief of certain people has compelled me, not without pain, to insert these external assurances. But let the narrative return to our gathering. Seeing myself listened to so attentively, I must confess that Aper acted firmly when he drove away the unbelievers, judging that only those who believed ought to listen.

## VI.

Indeed, believe me, I am carried away by the spirit and am wholly beside myself with grief: Christians do not believe the miracles of Martin, which demons themselves acknowledged!

The monastery of the blessed man was two miles distant from the city. But if you had seen what happened whenever he was about to come to the church and set his foot beyond the threshold of his cell, you would have seen the possessed throughout the church roaring, and the hosts destined for condemnation trembling as though a judge were approaching. Thus the groans of the demons announced the bishop’s arrival to the clergy, who did not know that he was coming.

I saw a man, as Martin approached, seized and suspended in the air with his hands stretched upward, so that his feet did not touch the ground at all. Whenever Martin undertook the work of expelling demons, he touched no one and rebuked no one with words, as the torrent of words is commonly poured forth by clerics. Instead, after the possessed had been brought in, he ordered the others to leave. Once the doors had been bolted, he prayed in the middle of the church, wrapped in a hairshirt, sprinkled with ashes, and lying prostrate on the ground.

Then you would see the wretched sufferers driven by different means toward their end: some hanging, as it were, from a cloud, with their feet raised high, yet with their clothing not falling over their faces, lest the naked parts of their bodies cause shame; elsewhere you would see others, tormented without questioning, confessing their crimes. They even disclosed their names without being asked: one confessed that he was Jupiter, another Mercury.

Finally, you would see all the devil’s ministers tortured together with their author, so that we may acknowledge that in Martin was fulfilled what is written: “For the saints will judge angels.”

## VII.

A certain village in the Senonian territory was devastated by hail every year. Driven to the extremity of their misfortunes, the inhabitants asked Martin for help, sending through Auspicius, a prefect and a man of sufficiently trustworthy character, a reliable delegation. His fields in particular were accustomed to suffer a storm more severe than that of the others.

But after Martin had prayed there, he completely freed the whole region from the approaching plague, so that for the twenty years during which he afterwards remained in the body no one in those places suffered hail. And lest anyone think that this had happened by chance rather than through Martin’s intervention, in the year in which he died the returning storm again descended. The world itself felt the departure of the faithful man so keenly that it mourned his death, just as it had rightly rejoiced in his life.

If an even weaker listener should demand witnesses to prove what we have said, I will produce not one man but many thousands, and I will summon the entire Senonian region to testify to the virtue it experienced.

And yet you, priest Refrigerius, surely remember that recently we discussed this matter with Romulus, the son of that Auspicius, an honored and religious man. He reported these things to us as though they were unknown to him, and, trembling over the crops to come because of the constant losses, mourned with great sorrow—as you yourself saw—that Martin had not been preserved for these times.

## VIII.

But to return to Avitianus—who, although in every place and every city he produced unspeakable memorials of his cruelty, was harmless only at Tours: that beast, who was nourished by human blood and the deaths of the unfortunate, presented himself as gentle and tranquil in the presence of the blessed man.

I remember that Martin came to him one day. When he entered Avitianus’s private chamber, he saw behind him a demon of extraordinary size sitting there. Martin expelled it from a distance—though, because it is necessary, let us use a somewhat un-Latin expression—and Avitianus, thinking that Martin was expelling him, said: “Why, holy man, do you treat me in this way?”

Martin replied: “Not you, but the one who foully weighs upon your neck.”

The devil withdrew and abandoned his familiar seat. It is well established that from that day Avitianus became gentler, either because he understood that he had always been carrying out the will of the devil who sat beside him, or because the unclean spirit, driven away by Martin from its seat beside him, was deprived of the power to rage: the servant was ashamed of the author, and the author no longer drove the servant on.

In the village of Ambatia—that is, in the ancient fortress now thickly inhabited by the brothers—you know that an idol-shrine had been built on a grand scale. A tower-like mass had risen from highly polished stones; extending upward into a cone, it preserved the superstition of the place through the dignity of its workmanship.

The blessed man had often instructed Marcellus, the priest stationed there, to destroy it. After some time he returned and rebuked the priest for allowing the structure of the shrine still to stand. Marcellus offered as an excuse that such a great mass could scarcely be overthrown even by military force and the power of a public multitude, much less easily dealt with by feeble clerics or weak monks.

Then Martin returned to his customary resources and kept vigil in prayer throughout the night. At dawn a storm arose and cast the idol’s temple down to its foundations. But let these things be accepted as reported on the testimony of Marcellus.

## IX.

With Refrigerius supporting my testimony, I report another miracle of his, similar to this one and performed in a similar matter.

Martin was preparing to overthrow a column of immense size on which an idol stood. But there was no means by which he could accomplish this. He then turned, according to his custom, to prayer. It is certain that a column somehow like it was seen to fall from heaven; striking the idol, it dissolved the entire impregnable mass into dust. It would have been little enough if he had used the powers of heaven invisibly, unless those very powers were visibly seen to serve Martin before human eyes as well.

The same Refrigerius is my witness that a woman suffering from a flow of blood was healed in an instant when she touched Martin’s garment, after the example of that woman in the Gospel.

A serpent was crossing the river and was swimming toward the bank on which we were standing. “In the name of the Lord,” he said, “I order you to return.” At once the evil beast turned back at the holy man’s word and crossed to the farther bank while we watched. When we all saw this with no little astonishment, Martin groaned deeply and said: “Serpents listen to me, and human beings do not listen.”

## X.

He was accustomed to eat fish during the days of Easter. A little before the hour of the meal he asked whether any was available. Then the deacon Cato, who was responsible for the administration of the monastery and was himself skilled at fishing, said that he had caught nothing throughout the entire day, and that the other fishermen, who were accustomed to sell fish, had likewise been unable to accomplish anything.

“Go,” Martin said, “cast your line; a catch will come.”

As Sulpicius here described it, we had our dwellings next to the river. We all went out—for it was a holiday—to watch the fisherman, with everyone eagerly hoping that the attempt would not prove fruitless, since, at Martin’s command, a fish was being sought for Martin’s use.

At the first cast, the deacon pulled an enormous pike from a very small net and joyfully hurried back to the monastery, plainly, as some poet—I do not know which—said, for we are using a schoolroom verse since we are chatting among schoolmen:

> And he brought the captive sow, to the amazement of Argos.

Truly this disciple of Christ, an imitator of the virtues performed by the Savior and displayed as examples for his saints, showed Christ working in himself. Christ, glorifying his saint in every way, gathered into one man the gifts of diverse graces.

Arborius, a former prefect, testifies that he saw Martin’s hand, as he offered the sacrifice, clothed, as it were, in the noblest jewels, shining with a purple radiance; and he heard the clash of the gems striking one another as the right hand moved.

## XI.

I shall come to the matter which, because of the notoriety of the circumstances, he always concealed, but which he could not conceal from us. The miracle here is that an angel spoke with him face to face.

The emperor Maximus—otherwise a good man—was corrupted by the counsels of priests. After the death of Priscillian, he protected by royal power Ithacius, the bishop who had accused Priscillian, and the others associated with him, whose names need not be mentioned, so that no one might charge him with having condemned a man of whatever character at their instigation.

Meanwhile Martin, compelled to go to the imperial court by many serious cases involving those who were suffering, encountered the storm of the whole tempest. The bishops had gathered at Trier and, communicating daily with Ithacius, had made his cause their common cause.

When it was unexpectedly announced to them that Martin was present, they were shaken in their hearts and began to mutter and tremble. The previous day the emperor had already decided, on their advice, to send heavily armed tribunes possessing supreme authority to Spain to search out heretics; once they had been discovered, they were to deprive them of life and property.

There was no doubt that this storm would also destroy a great multitude of saints, with little distinction among the various classes of people. For at that time people were judged merely by what met the eyes: someone was considered a heretic on the basis of complexion or clothing rather than faith.

The bishops understood that Martin would by no means approve this. But, since their consciences were troubled, they were especially anxious that he might abstain from their communion upon his arrival, for there would be no shortage of people who would follow the constancy of so great a man, once his authority had been set before them.

They consulted with the emperor and arranged that, by sending the Master’s officials to meet him, Martin should be forbidden to approach the city unless he declared that he was arriving in peace with the bishops stationed there.

He cleverly frustrated them, declaring that he would come in the peace of Christ. Finally, he entered at night and went only to the church for the sake of prayer. On the following day he went to the palace.

Among many requests, which it would take too long to unfold, he had these principal ones: he pleaded for the count Narses and the governor Leucadius, both of whom had belonged to Gratian’s party and had incurred the victor’s anger through especially persistent political activity, the details of which are not relevant here.

His chief concern was that the tribunes should not be sent to Spain with the legal authority of the sword. For Martin’s devout concern was not only to free the Christians who would be harassed on that pretext, but also the heretics themselves.

But the crafty emperor delayed him for the first and second day, either to give greater weight to the matter, or because he was excessively hostile to him, or because, as most people then thought, avarice opposed it—for he had his eyes fixed upon their property.

It is said that this man, endowed with many good qualities and deeds, took too little care against avarice. Unless perhaps he may be excused by the necessities of government: since the treasury of the state had been exhausted by earlier emperors and he was almost constantly on campaign and prepared for civil wars, he could easily be excused for securing resources for the empire by whatever opportunities arose.

## XII.

Meanwhile the bishops whose communion Martin did not join hurried to the emperor, complaining that they had already been condemned. They claimed that their entire position was finished if Martin’s authority armed the obstinacy of Theognistus, who alone had publicly condemned them with a formal sentence.

The man ought not to have been received within the walls. He was no longer a defender of heretics but their avenger. Priscillian’s death had achieved nothing if Martin were to carry out his vengeance.

Finally, prostrate with tears and lamentation, they implored the imperial power to use its force against one man. The emperor was not far from being compelled to mingle Martin with the lot of the heretics.

Yet although he was excessively bound to the bishops by favor, he knew that Martin surpassed all mortals in faith, holiness, and virtue. He therefore prepared to overcome the saint by a very different path.

First he summoned Martin privately and addressed him courteously. He said that the heretics had been condemned lawfully, according to the procedure of public courts rather than through the persecution of priests; that there was no reason to suppose that the communion of Ithacius and his party should be condemned; that Theognistus had broken communion out of hatred rather than for a valid cause; and that he alone had so far separated himself from communion, while nothing had been changed by the others. Indeed, a synod held only a few days earlier had declared Ithacius free of guilt.

When Martin was little moved by these arguments, the emperor was inflamed with anger and tore himself away from his presence. Immediately executioners were sent against those for whom Martin had pleaded.

## XIII.

When Martin learned of this at night, he burst into the palace. He promised that, if they were spared, he would communicate with the bishops, provided that the tribunes already sent to Spain to destroy the churches were also recalled.

There was no delay: Maximus granted everything.

The next day the ordination of Bishop Felix was being prepared. He was certainly a most holy man, plainly worthy of becoming a priest in better times. Martin joined in the communion of that day, judging it better to yield for the moment than to fail to protect those over whose necks the sword was hanging.

Nevertheless, although the bishops exerted every effort to make him confirm that communion by his signature, they could not force him to do so.

On the following day, as he hurried away from there, he sighed sadly while traveling, saying that he had been mixed, even for an hour, with a harmful communion. Not far from a village called Andethanna, where vast forest solitudes offer their secluded places, he went a little ahead of his companions and sat down. As thought alternately accused and defended the cause of his grief and his action, he turned the matter over in his mind.

Suddenly an angel stood beside him.

“Rightly are you troubled, Martin,” he said, “but you could not have escaped by another path. Restore your strength; recover your steadfastness, lest you now incur danger not to your glory but to your salvation.”

From that time onward he took great care not to join in the communion of the Ithacian party.

Nevertheless, whenever he healed some of the possessed more slowly than usual and with less grace, he repeatedly confessed to us with tears that he felt his power diminished because of the evil of that communion, with which he had mixed himself for a moment through necessity, not in spirit.

He lived for sixteen years thereafter. He attended no synod and withdrew from every gathering of bishops.

## XIV.

But, as we ourselves have experienced, he repaired the grace diminished for a time by a manifold recompense.

I later saw a possessed man brought to the forecourt of the monastery itself and healed before he reached the threshold.

I recently heard a man testify that, while sailing on the Tyrrhenian Sea along the route toward Rome, a sudden storm arose and placed everyone in the utmost danger of death. A certain Egyptian merchant, who was not yet a Christian, cried out in a loud voice: “God of Martin, save us!” At once the storm was calmed, and he maintained his desired course in the complete stillness of a tranquil sea.

Lycontius, a trustworthy former vicarius, sought Martin’s help by letter when a deadly plague was afflicting his household and, in an example of unheard-of calamity, sick bodies were lying throughout the entire house.

At that time the blessed man promised that the matter would be difficult to obtain, for he perceived in spirit that the house was being struck by divine power. Nevertheless, he did not cease until he had obtained what he had undertaken to ask for, continuing to pray and fast for seven full days and as many nights.

Then Lycontius, having experienced the divine benefits, rushed to him, announcing and giving thanks at the same time that his household had been freed from every danger. He also offered one hundred pounds of silver. The blessed man neither rejected nor accepted it; before that weight reached the monastery threshold, he immediately assigned it to the redemption of captives.

When the brothers suggested that he reserve some of it for the monastery’s expenses—for food was scarce for everyone and many lacked clothing—he replied: “Let the Church feed us and clothe us, provided that we do not appear to have sought anything for our own needs.”

At this point the great miracles of that man come to mind, which we can more easily admire than recount. You surely recognize what I mean. Many of his works cannot be explained, such as the following, which I do not know whether we can describe as it happened.

One of the brothers—you know his name, but the person must be concealed, lest we bring shame upon the holy man—found a supply of coals beside Martin’s little furnace. He placed a small stool for himself and, sitting over the fire with his legs spread and his groin exposed, remained there.

Immediately Martin perceived that an injury had been done to the sacred covering, and cried out in a loud voice: “Who is polluting our dwelling with his groin exposed?”

When that brother heard it and recognized from his conscience what was being rebuked, he immediately ran to us, as though lifeless, confessing his shame without denying Martin’s miraculous power.

## XV.

Likewise, one day, while he was sitting in the little wooden seat familiar to you all, in the courtyard that surrounded his very small dwelling, he saw two demons standing on the lofty rock rising above the monastery. From there, lively and delighted, they uttered a cry of encouragement: “Come on, Brictio! Come on, Brictio!”

I believe they saw the wretched man approaching from a distance, aware of the fury the spirits had stirred up in him.

There was no delay. Brictio burst in, and, full of madness, poured a thousand insults upon Martin. The previous day Martin had rebuked him for keeping horses and buying slaves, although he had never possessed anything before becoming a cleric—he had been raised in the monastery by Martin himself. For by that time many people were accusing him of having bought not only barbarian boys but also girls with attractive faces.

Moved by these matters and by an insane bitterness—and, as I believe, especially driven by the prompting of those demons—he attacked Martin so violently that he could scarcely restrain his hands. The saint, however, with calm expression and tranquil mind, restrained the unfortunate man’s madness through gentle words.
