But the evil spirit surged through him so powerfully that his own mind, however greatly deceived, did not even obey him. With trembling lips and a shifting expression, his face discolored by rage, he hurled forth words of sin, asserting that he was holier, since he had grown up from his earliest years in the monastery amid the sacred disciplines of the Church, under Martin’s instruction.

Martin, he claimed, had been sullied from the beginning by military activities, which he himself could not deny; and now, through empty superstitions and the ridiculous phantoms of visions, he had grown old amid sheer delusions.

After he had poured forth many such things, and others even more bitter which it is better to leave unmentioned, he finally departed, satisfied by his fury, as though he had completely avenged himself, and hurried back along the path by which he had come.

Meanwhile, I believe that through Martin’s prayers the demons had been driven from his heart. Restored to repentance, he soon returned and threw himself at Martin’s knees. He asked forgiveness, confessed his error, and admitted that he had not been in his right mind and had not been without a demon.

It was no difficult task for Martin to forgive one who was asking forgiveness. The saint then explained to Brictio and to all of us how he had seen him being agitated by demons and had not been moved by his insults, which had harmed the man who uttered them more than the one against whom they had been spoken.

Afterwards, although Brictio was often burdened by many serious accusations before him, Martin could not be compelled to remove him from the priesthood, lest he appear to be pursuing his own injury. He often recalled the saying: “If Christ tolerated Judas, why should I not tolerate Brictio?”

## XVI.

At this Postumianus said: “Let our friend who is nearby hear this example. Although he is wise, he forgets the present and forgets the future; if offended, he becomes insane and is no longer master of himself. He rages against clerics, attacks laymen, and stirs up the whole world to avenge him.

“For three years he has remained continually engaged in this struggle, calmed neither by time nor by reason. What a pitiable and lamentable condition for a man—even if he were afflicted by this single incurable plague of evil!

“Yet, Gallus, you ought often to have recounted to him these examples of patience and tranquility, so that he might learn not to grow angry and might learn to forgive.

“If he should happen to recognize that this brief passage of my speech was directed at him, let him know that I have spoken no less from the heart of a friend than from the mouth of an enemy. For if it could be so, I should prefer him to be said to resemble Bishop Martin rather than the tyrant Phalaris.

“But let us pass over this man, whose mention is scarcely pleasant, and return, Gallus, to our Martin.”

## XVII.

Then I, sensing that evening was already approaching with the setting sun, said: “The day has passed, Postumianus; we must rise. At the same time, dinner is owed to listeners so eager to learn.

“As for Martin, you must not expect any limit to the telling of his deeds. He extends more widely than any speech can encompass.

“For the present, carry these accounts of that man to the East. As you return, and pass through different regions, places, harbors, islands, and cities, scatter Martin’s name and glory among the peoples.

“Above all, remember not to pass by Campania. Even if your route is greatly out of the way, do not consider any expense of delay, however long, too great for you to visit there the illustrious man praised throughout the world, Paulinus.

“I beg you, first unroll for him the volume of our conversation, whether that which we completed yesterday or that which we have spoken today. You will report everything to him and recite everything to him, so that through him Rome may soon learn the sacred praises of the man—just as he formerly spread our first little book not only throughout Italy but through all Illyricum as well.

“He, who is not jealous of Martin’s glory and is a most devout judge of holy virtues in Christ, will not refuse to compare our bishop with his Felix.

“If by chance you cross over to Africa, report what you have heard at Carthage. Although, as you yourself said, it has long known the man, let it now learn more about him in particular, lest it admire there only its martyr Cyprian, even though that city has been consecrated by his holy blood.

“If, after turning a little toward the left side of the Gulf of Achaea, you enter Greece, let Corinth know, and let Athens know, that Plato was not wiser in the Academy, nor Socrates braver in prison.

“Happy indeed is Greece, which deserved to hear the Apostle preaching; but the Gallic lands were by no means abandoned by Christ, since he granted them Martin.

“When you reach Egypt, although it is proud of the number and virtues of its saints, let it nevertheless not disdain to hear that Europe, in the single person of Martin, has not yielded to it or to all Asia.”

## XVIII.

“Moreover, when from there you set your sails to the winds again, intending to travel to Jerusalem, I entrust you with a task arising from our grief. If you ever reach the shore of that illustrious Ptolemais, diligently inquire where our Pomponius lies buried, and do not disdain to visit foreign bones.

“There shed many tears, both from your own affection and from the depths of our hearts. Although it is an empty gift, scatter over the ground purple flowers and sweet-smelling grasses.

“Yet speak to him—not harshly or bitterly, but in a compassionate address rather than a reproachful epitaph. Say that, if he had once been willing to listen to you, or had always been willing to listen to me, and had imitated Martin rather than the man whom I do not wish to name, he would never have been separated from me so cruelly, covered by the sand of an unknown shore.

“He would not have suffered death in the middle of the sea, like a shipwrecked pirate, and only barely found burial on a distant shore.

“Let all those who wished to harm me through his departure look upon the work they have done. Let them see their glory, and, now that they have been avenged, let them cease their attacks upon me.”

While we were uttering these words in a deeply mournful voice, stirring everyone’s tears through our lamentations, we departed amid great admiration for Martin, but no less grief arising from our own tears.

# Appendix to the Veronese Edition of the Works of Sulpicius Severus, Containing Seven Letters Previously Published (C, G, S)

## First Letter: To Claudia, His Sister. On the Last Judgment

### I.

After reading your letters, I could not restrain my feelings, which were deeply stirred, from breaking into tears. I wept from joy because, from the very language of your letter, I could recognize that you were living according to the commands of the Lord our God. Yet, because I longed for you, I could not help grieving that I was separated from you through a very great injury on your part, if you had not sent a letter.

[Note: “Through a very great injury on your part.” Perhaps Severus had placed the words “on your part” after the word “injury.” For the ear can scarcely tolerate such a transposition. Clericus.]

Would I then not enjoy such a sister?

I call your salvation to witness that I have often wished to come to you, but until now I have been prevented by the one who is accustomed to obstruct such plans. I was eager to satisfy my longing by seeing you, and I thought that, in passing, we might perform the work of our Lord among ourselves, living by consoling one another after trampling down the burden of the world.

But I no longer set a day or time for coming, because whenever I have done so I have been unable to fulfill it. I shall await the Lord’s will, and I hope that, through my desires and your prayers, he will enable us to receive the fruit of our perseverance.

[Note: “Perseverance.” Read “presence” (*praesentia*), Baluzius. A little earlier I wrote, with Baluzius, “I shall await” (*opperiar*), for which Clericus has “I await” (*opperior*).]

### II.

Moreover, since in all the letters I have sent you, when I desired to give you instruction concerning your life and faith, I have now exhausted my words through the constant repetition of my writing, I cannot now write anything new to you that I have not written before.

And indeed, by God’s favor, you no longer need admonition. You have brought your faith to completion from its beginnings and show yourself devoted in Christ.

Yet I give you one warning: do not retrace what you have passed beyond; do not desire what you have rejected; do not, after putting your hand to the plow, turn back and look behind you (Luke 9:62).

If this fault should return in you, the furrow must necessarily lose its proper order, and the cultivator will not receive his reward. Otherwise he will not obtain even a portion of the prize if he ceases before completing the work.

For just as one must flee from sin toward righteousness, so one who has entered upon righteousness must take care not to leave an opening for sin. It is written concerning the righteous person that on the day when he goes astray, his righteousness will not benefit him (Ezekiel 18:24, 26).

We must therefore stand firm in this and labor at this: having escaped our sins, we must not lose the rewards prepared for us.

The enemy stands ready against us, so that, once the shield of faith has been stripped away, he may immediately strike us. The shield must not therefore be cast aside, lest our side be exposed. The sword must not be lowered, lest the enemy begin to fear us no longer. But when he sees us armed, he will depart.

We do not fail to recognize that it is hard and difficult to fight daily against the flesh and the world. But if you consider eternity, if you contemplate the kingdoms of heaven—which the Lord will surely deign to grant us, even though we are sinners—what suffering could possibly be worthy of earning such rewards?

The struggle in this world lasts only a short time. For even if death does not come, old age will come. The years slip away and time flows onward. And, as I hope, the Lord Jesus will swiftly call us to himself as people whom he desires.

### III.

Oh, how blessed will be our departure, when Christ receives us into his dwelling, cleansed from the stain of sin through the conduct of a better life!

The martyrs and prophets will meet us; the apostles too will be filled with joy; the angels will rejoice, and the archangels will be glad. Satan, defeated, will grow pale, even with his bloodstained mouth—for he will have lost the sins which he had prepared for himself in us.

He will see the glory granted through forgiveness and the merits honored through glory. We shall triumph over the conquered enemy, while the wise men of this world will be laughed at. There the greedy man, the adulterer, the impious man, the drunkard, and the slanderer will be recognized.

What will those wretched people say in their defense?

“We did not know you, Lord; we did not see that you were in the world. You did not send prophets; you did not give the age a law. We did not see the patriarchs; we did not read the examples of the saints. Your Christ was not on earth; Peter was silent; Paul did not wish to preach; the Evangelist did not teach; there were no martyrs whose examples we might follow.

“No one foretold your future judgment. No one commanded us to clothe the poor. No one ordered us to restrain lust. No one persuaded us to resist greed. We fell through ignorance; we did what we did without knowing.”

[Note: “To restrain.” Perhaps “to curb” (*cohibere*).]

[Note: “Cleansed from the stain of sin.” Related are the words of Severus in *The Life of Blessed Martin*, chapter 13: “To cleanse former sins through the conduct of a better life.” H. de Prato.]

[Note: “They will be touched.” This is an instance of *apo koinou*: they will be filled with joy.]

[Note: “Where then.” Clericus’s edition mistakenly reads “where now.”]

### IV.

In reply, from that choir of saints the righteous Noah will be the first to proclaim:

“I, Lord, both preached the flood that was to come upon account of human sins and, after the flood, offered myself as an example to the good, so that, while the wicked perished, the good might not perish; so that these people might recognize both the salvation of the innocent and the punishment of sinners.”

After him faithful Abraham will stand forth:

“I, Lord, established, almost at the midpoint of that world’s age, the faith by which the human race would believe in you. I was chosen as the father of nations, whose example they might follow.

“I did not hesitate, Lord, to offer Isaac, still a little child, to you as a victim, so that these people might recognize that nothing must be withheld from the Lord, since they understood that I had not spared even my only son.

“At your command I abandoned my land and my kindred, so that these people too might have an example of abandoning the wickedness of the world and the sins of the age.

“I was the first to recognize you, Lord, though bodily and under a visible form. I did not hesitate to believe in the one whom I saw, although you appeared to me in another substance, so that these people might understand that judgment is made not according to the flesh but according to the spirit.”

Blessed Moses will support him:

“I delivered the law, Lord, to all these people at your command, so that those whom free faith did not hold might at least be restrained by the law that had been given.

“I said, ‘You shall not commit adultery’ (Exodus 20:14), so that I might restrain the license of fornication.

“I said, ‘You shall love your neighbor’ (Leviticus 19:18), so that charity might abound.

“I said, ‘You shall serve the Lord alone’ (Deuteronomy 6:13), so that these people might not sacrifice to idols or permit temples to exist.

“I decreed that false testimonies should not be spoken, so that I might close their mouths against every lie.

“I explained the deeds and words from the beginning of the world, with the spirit of your power working in me, so that knowledge of the past might provide them with instruction for the future.

“I proclaimed that you, Lord Jesus, would come, so that it would not be unexpected for them to recognize the one whose coming I had foretold.”

[Note: “Knowledge of the past.” For the same thought, see above, *Sacred History*, Book II, chapter 8.]

[Note: “Unexpected.” Thus correctly in the first edition of Baluzius. The Leipzig edition mistakenly reads “expected.” Clericus thought one should read “not having expected,” but the passage requires no emendation.]

### V.

After him a man worthy of his Lord’s lineage, David, will stand forth:

“I proclaimed you, Lord, in all things. I cried out that you alone should be served.

“I said, ‘Blessed is the man who fears the Lord’ (Psalm 111:1). I said, ‘The saints will exult in glory’ (Psalm 149:5). I said, ‘The desire of sinners will perish’ (Psalm 112:10), so that these people might recognize you and cease from sinning.

“Although I possessed royal power, I cast a hairshirt over myself, placed dust beneath me, laid aside the garments that marked my splendor, and prostrated myself, so that these people might be given an example of gentleness and humility.

“I spared my enemies who wished to kill me, so that I might prove to these people that they ought to imitate my mercy.”

After him Isaiah, worthy of the Spirit of God, will not remain silent:

“I warned them, Lord, with you speaking through my mouth: ‘Woe to those who join house to house’ (Isaiah 5:8), so that I might impose a limit upon greed.

“I testified that your anger had come upon sinners, so that, if hope of rewards did not restrain them from their evil deeds, at least fear of punishment might hold them back.”

[Note: “Upon greed.” Clericus incorrectly reads “of greed.”]

[Col. 0226B] **VI.** After these and many others who have rendered us the services of instruction, the Son of God himself will speak as follows:

“I, indeed, exalted upon a lofty throne, holding heaven in my palm and the earth in my fist (Isa. XL, 12), diffused within and without, interior to all things that are born and exterior to all things that move, infinite through the immeasurable power of my nature, invisible to sight, incomprehensible to touch, became, in order that I might exist among you as the least of your number for the purpose of subduing the hardness of your hearts and softening your faithlessness by saving instruction, willing to be born in the flesh. Having laid aside the glory of God, I assumed the appearance of a servant, so that, by sharing bodily weakness with you, I might once again admit you into fellowship with my glory through obedience to the saving commandment.

“I restored health to all who were sick and weak, hearing to the deaf, sight to the blind, speech to the mute, and the use of their feet to the lame, so that I might move you by heavenly signs [Col. 0226C], and so that you might more easily believe in me and in the things that I had proclaimed. I promised you the kingdoms of heaven. Moreover, that you might have an example of pardon, I placed in paradise the thief who, at the hour of his death, confessed me, so that you might follow the faith of one who had deserved to have his sins forgiven. And so that you yourselves also might be able to suffer for yourselves according to my example, I suffered for you, lest a human being doubt that he ought to suffer for himself what God had endured for humanity.

“I showed myself after the resurrection, so that your faith might not be shaken. Through Peter I admonished the Jews; through Paul I preached to the Gentiles. Nor am I sorry. There is fruit in good works. The good understood my work, the faithful completed it, the righteous fulfilled it, the merciful brought it to perfection; and a great number are martyrs, a great number saints. Certainly these people too were in the same body and in the same world. Why do I find no good work at all in you, offspring of a viperous stock? You did not repent of your evil deeds even on the final day of your end. But what does it avail that you worship me with your lips, if in your deeds and actions you deny me? Where now are your riches, where your honors, where your power, where are your pleasures? I impose no new sentence upon you. You have the judgment that I foretold beforehand.”

[Note: [Col. 0226D] *Move you.* Here the Cleric criticizes Baluzius for having printed *promoverem* (“I might advance”), but unjustly. Baluzius’s exemplar properly gives *permoverem* (“I might move”). The blame should instead be attributed to the Cleric’s copyist, who often made errors while copying Baluzius’s edition, as we show more fully below.]

**VII.** Then the Evangelist will recite this to those wretched people:

“Go into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII, 13; XXV, 30).

O wretched people whom these things do not move! They will see their own punishment and the glory of others. Let them make use of the world, since they will not enjoy that eternity which has been prepared for the saints. Let them abound in riches and brood over gold, while there they are found destitute, there impoverished.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] *Let them abound in riches.* Two related expressions occur in Sulpicius, *Sacred History*, book I, ch. 23: “They gape after possessions, cultivate estates, brood over gold.” H. DE PRATO.] Let them be rich in this world, while in eternity they are poor—of whom it is written: “The rich have become needy and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII, 11). Scripture then added concerning the good: “But those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.”

Therefore, sister, although these people mock us, although they call us foolish and unhappy, let us rejoice more happily in the reproaches by which glory is heaped upon us and punishment upon them. Nor should we laugh at their folly; rather, let us grieve over their unhappiness, because a great part of our own people are among them. If we can win them over, our glory is increased. But let them conduct themselves as they wish; let them be to us as Gentiles and publicans. Let us, however, safeguard ourselves in safety and salvation. If they now rejoice in our grief, later we shall rejoice in their grief.

Farewell, dearest sister and most beloved in Christ.

# EPISTLE II. TO THE SAME WOMAN. On Virginity

[Col. 0227C] **I.** Apart from the testimonies of Scripture, we are also taught by the custom of the Church how great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heaven, because we learn that a special merit belongs to it, whose consecration is distinctive. For although the entire throng of believers receives equal gifts of grace, and all glory in the same sacramental blessings, these women possess something proper beyond the others: they are chosen by the Holy Spirit from that holy and spotless flock of the Church, as if holier and purer offerings, according to the merits of their will, and are offered upon God’s altar by the high priest.

Truly the offering of so precious a living creature is an offering worthy of the Lord, and no offering is more pleasing than that of his own image. I think the Apostle said especially of such women: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. XII, 1).

Virginity therefore possesses both what others have and what others do not have: it possesses both a common and a distinctive grace, and rejoices, so to speak, in the privilege of its own consecration. Ecclesiastical authority also permits us to call virgins brides of Christ, since the Church consecrates and veils them to the Lord in the manner of brides, showing that those who have avoided bodily union will especially possess a spiritual marriage. And rightly are those spiritually joined to God by comparison with marriage who, for the sake of his love, have rejected human marriages. In them above all is fulfilled the Apostle’s saying: “He who clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17).

[Note: [Col. 0227D] *Because we learn.* The Cleric incorrectly has *qua dicimus* (“which we say”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227D] *While he consecrates brides, etc.* Holsten in the *Appendix to the Codex Regius*, p. 10, reads: “While, in the manner of brides whom he consecrates to the Lord, he veils them,” and so on, showing that they have been consecrated. The Cleric has it very poorly as *velut ostensas* (“as though displayed”).]

**II.** It is a great and immortal achievement, almost beyond bodily nature, to overcome lust, to extinguish by strength of spirit the flame of desire kindled by the torches of youth, to exclude by spiritual exertion the force of innate pleasure, to live contrary to the law of the human race, to despise the consolations of marriage, to scorn the sweetness of children, and to count as nothing, in hope of future blessedness, whatever advantages the present life may offer. These, as I have said, are great and admirable virtues, and not undeservedly are they destined for an immense reward in proportion to the magnitude of their labor.

“I will give the eunuchs,” says God, “and in my house and within my walls a named place better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall not fail” (Isa. XVI, 5). Concerning these eunuchs the Lord repeats in the Gospel, saying: “For there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 12).

The labor of chastity is indeed great, but greater is its reward; its guardianship is temporal, but its recompense is eternal. Blessed John the Apostle also speaks of these, saying that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes. I think this is to be understood in the sense that no place in the heavenly court will be closed to them, but that all the dwelling places of God will be opened to them.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] *To surpass … the fiery desire.* Holsten more correctly reads “to lull … the fiery desire.” The context confirms this restoration.]

[Note: [Col. 0228D] *I will give to the eunuchs, says God.* Holsten has: “I will give, says the Lord, to my eunuchs.” *My* is absent in Isaiah. Against the evidence of the exemplar, the Cleric has, as often elsewhere: “I will give, says God, to the eunuchs, and in the house,” and so on. Shortly afterward Holsten has: “a better name than sons … which shall not fail.” Nor does the sacred text read otherwise.]

**III.** But so that the merit of virginity may shine more brightly, and so that it may be understood more clearly how worthy it is of God, let us consider that when the Lord and our Savior, God, deigned to assume humanity for the salvation of the human race, he chose no other than a virgin womb, thereby showing that this state was especially pleasing to him and making known to both sexes the excellence of chastity.

He had a virgin mother, remaining himself a virgin. In himself he offered an example of virginity to men, and in his mother to women. Thus it is shown that blessed integrity has acquired the fullness of divinity in both sexes, since whatever was in the Son was present in the mother.

But why should I labor to reveal the excellent and sublime merit of chastity and to display the glory of virginity, when I know that many have spoken at length on this subject and proved its blessedness by the clearest arguments, and when it cannot be doubtful to any wise person that the matter requiring the greater labor possesses the greater merit? For whoever considers chastity to be without reward or of little worth clearly either does not understand it or does not willingly endure its labor. Hence those who always disparage chastity are those who either do not possess it or are compelled to possess it unwillingly.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] *And in his mother.* So too Holsten. The Cleric has *but in his mother*.]

[Note: [Col. 0228D] *Had.* Read, with Holsten, *was present*. Shortly afterward, in the same place, read *satago* (“I labor”) instead of *satisago*.]

**IV.** Now, therefore, since, although briefly, we have shown both the labor and the merit of integrity, we must keep watch more diligently, lest a matter established by great virtue and destined for an immense reward be deprived of its fruit. For the more precious any object is, the greater care is taken to guard it.

And since there are many things that lack their own proper quality unless they are supported by the aid of other things—for example, honey, which unless it is preserved, or rather nourished, by the protection of wax and the cells of the honeycombs, loses its natural sweetness and cannot exist by itself; and likewise wine, which, unless it is maintained in a vessel of good fragrance and frequently repaired with pitch, loses the wine’s native sweetness

[Note: [Col. 0229D] *Vasis* (“vessels”). I would prefer, with Holsten, *vas* (“vessel”); a little later he reads *rebus nec* (“nor things”) for *viribus nec* (“nor powers”).]—we must therefore provide more attentively, lest virginity too should require certain necessities without which it can in no way suffice to bear fruit. Otherwise such great labor will accomplish nothing, while what is possessed without the necessary strength is mistakenly believed to be useful.

For, unless I am mistaken, integrity of chastity is preserved for the sake of the reward of the heavenly kingdom; and it is certain that no one can attain that reward without the merit of eternal life. Eternal life, however, can be earned only through the observance of all the divine commandments, as Scripture says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX, 17).

Therefore he does not possess life unless he has kept all the commandments of the law. And whoever does not possess life cannot be an heir of the heavenly kingdom, in which not the dead but all the living will reign. Virginity alone, therefore, will accomplish nothing for one who hopes for the glory of the heavenly kingdom, unless she also possesses that other thing to which eternal life is promised, through which the reward of the heavenly kingdom is possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Holsten reads *illud* (“that thing”) for *aliud* (“another thing”). Shortly afterward, in the same place: *mandatorum sunt custodienda praecepta* (“the precepts of the commandments must be observed”).]

Above all, therefore, those who preserve chastity and integrity and hope for its reward from God’s justice are commanded to keep the commandments, lest the labor of glorious chastity and continence be rendered void. No wise person is unaware that virginity is above the commandment or precept of the law, since the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice” (I Cor. VII, 25).

Since, therefore, he gives advice, not a commandment, for the attainment of virginity, he has declared that it is above commandment and precept. Accordingly, whoever preserves virginity does more than is commanded. Doing more than one is ordered will then be of greater benefit, if one does what is ordered.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] *Ex lege* (“from the law”). This is better than Holsten’s *et legens* (“and reading”).]

[Note: [Col. 0229D] *For how will you boast … if you have not done something less?* The careless copyist omitted this in Holsten. Shortly afterward, in the same place, the erroneous reading is *remuneratio mandatorum* (“the reward of commandments”).]

For how will you boast of having done more, if you have not done something less? Desiring to fulfill the divine counsel, keep the commandment above all. Wishing to obtain the reward of virginity, embrace the merit of life, so that your chastity may be rewarded. For just as observance of the commandments bestows life, so, conversely, their transgression produces death. And whoever has been consigned to death through transgression will not be able to hope for the crown of virginity, nor expect the reward of chastity while established under punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] *Had been in death.* It seems that, with Holsten, it should read: “has been consigned to death.”]

**V.** There are three forms through which one enters into possession of the heavenly kingdom. The first is chastity, the second contempt of the world, and the third justice. Just as these, when joined together, greatly benefit those who possess them, so when divided they can scarcely be beneficial, since each is required not only for its own sake but also for the sake of the others.

First, therefore, chastity is sought so that contempt of the world may more easily follow, because the world can be despised more readily by those who are not held by the bonds of marriage. Contempt of the world, however, is demanded so that justice may be preserved, and those who are entangled in desires for secular goods and the pursuits of worldly pleasures can scarcely fulfill justice.

Whoever possesses the first form, chastity, but does not obtain the second, contempt of the world, possesses the first almost without reason, since he lacks the second for whose sake the first was sought. And if he possesses the first and second but lacks the third, which is justice, he labors in vain, since the first two are sought chiefly for the sake of the third.

For what does it profit to possess chastity for the sake of contempt of the world, yet not possess that for the sake of which you have chastity? Or for what purpose should you despise the world if you do not preserve justice, for whose sake you ought to possess both chastity and contempt of the world? For just as the first form exists for the sake of the second, so both the first and the second exist for the sake of the third; and if the third is absent, neither the first nor the second will be beneficial.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] *For what purpose.* So Baluzius, that is, “to what advantage?” Holsten has: “why should you despise worldly things?”]

**VI.** Perhaps you will say: “Teach me, then, what justice is, so that if I know it I may more easily be able to fulfill it.” I shall tell you briefly, as best I can, and shall use the simplicity of ordinary speech, because the matter with which we are dealing is such that it ought not to be obscured by the more elaborate language of eloquence, but rather unfolded in the narratives of simpler expression. A matter necessary to everyone in common should be explained in common speech.

Justice, therefore, is nothing other than not sinning; and not sinning is observing the precepts of the law. The observance of the commandments is maintained in two ways: by doing nothing that is forbidden and by striving to fulfill everything that is commanded. This is what the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII, 15).

I do not want you to think that justice consists in this alone, that you do not do evil, since failing to do good is itself evil, and transgression of the law is contained in both. For the one who said, “Turn away from evil,” also said, “and do good.” If you turn away from evil and do not do good, you are a transgressor of the law, which is fulfilled not only in the rejection of evil deeds but also in the completion of good works.

You are not commanded merely not to strip the clothed of their garments, but to clothe the stripped with your own; not merely not to take away the bread of one who has bread, but willingly to give your own to one who has none; not merely not to drive a poor person from your hospitality, but to receive into your own lodging one who has been driven out and has nowhere to stay.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] *Neque ut solum.* Read with Holsten *neque solum ut*. A little earlier, read *spoliatum* (“the stripped person”) for *spoliatos* (“the stripped persons”), so that it corresponds to the preceding *vestitum* (“the clothed person”).]

For we have been commanded to weep with those who weep (Rom. XII, 15). How do we weep with them if we share in none of their needs and offer them no assistance in the matters over which they shed tears? God does not seek the unproductive moisture of our weeping. Rather, because tears are an indication of grief, he wants you to feel another person’s distress as your own. And just as you would wish to be helped if you were in such tribulation, so you yourself should help another, in accordance with this: “Whatever good things you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII, 12).

For to weep with one who weeps, while contributing nothing to the one who weeps although you are able to contribute something, is a sign of mockery, not compassion. Thus our Savior wept with Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, and displayed the feeling of his immense mercy by the testimony of his tears. The works of true compassion immediately followed, when Lazarus, for whose sake the tears had been shed, was restored alive to his sisters. This was to weep piously with those who weep: to remove the occasion of their weeping.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] *Vivus redditur* (“is restored alive”). Holsten omits *vivus*, and it is indeed redundant, since Lazarus has already been said to have been raised.]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] *But who is able? you will say. But not even …* Holsten has: “But as though he were able, you will say, he did it. But neither is anything impossible for you,” and so forth. I have no doubt that this reading should be restored here.]

“But who is able?” you will say. Yet nothing impossible is commanded of you. He has fulfilled everything who did what he could.

**VII.** But, as we had begun to say, that it is not sufficient for a Christian to abstain from evil unless he also fulfills the duties of good works is proved above all by that testimony in which the Lord threatens that those will be guilty of eternal fire who, although they have done no evil, have not done everything that is good. He says:

“Then the King will say to those who are on his left: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,’” and so forth (Matt. XXV, 41).

He did not say, “Depart from me, accursed ones, because you committed murder, because you committed adultery, or because you committed theft,” but they are condemned because they did not do good. They are consigned to the eternal punishments of Gehenna, not because they committed what had been forbidden, but because they were unwilling to fulfill what had been commanded.

Hence one must consider what hope those can have who still do some of the things that are forbidden, when even those are guilty who have not done what is commanded. I do not want you to flatter yourself on this point if you have not done certain things, since it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James II, 10).

Adam sinned once, and he died. Do you think that you can live while repeatedly committing the act that killed another when he had committed it only once? Or do you think that he committed a great crime, for which he was rightly and justly condemned? Let us therefore see what he did. Against the commandment, he ate from the fruit of the tree.

What then? Did God condemn the human being to death because of the fruit of a tree? Not because of the fruit of the tree, but because of contempt for the commandment. The issue, therefore, is not the quality of the sin but the transgression of the commandment.

The one who told Adam not to eat the fruit of the tree has commanded you not to curse, not to lie, not to slander, and not to listen to slanderers; not to swear at all; not to covet; not to envy; not to be lukewarm; not to be greedy; not to return evil for evil; to pray for those who accuse and persecute you; to offer the other cheek to one who strikes you; not to litigate in a secular court; if someone wishes to take away your property, to relinquish it gladly; not to admit into your heart the evil of anger or jealous resentment; to flee the crime of greed; to avoid every evil of boasting and pride; and to live humbly and gently after the example of Christ.

You are to avoid the company of the wicked to such an extent that you do not eat with fornicators, or greedy people, or those who curse, or the envious, or slanderers, or drunkards, or robbers. If you have despised him in any respect, will he spare you, if he spared Adam? Indeed, Adam deserved greater mercy, because he was still inexperienced and newly created, and had no example before him of anyone who had sinned and died because of his sin. But after so many lessons, after the law, the prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles, if you wish to sin, I do not know how you can be forgiven.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] *But because they did good.* Before these words Holsten has: “For they are condemned not because they had done evil, but because they had not done good,” and so forth. That these words were carelessly omitted from Baluzius’s exemplar is suggested by the words that occur shortly afterward in the same sense: “not because they had done what was forbidden … but because,” and so forth.]

**VIII.** Do you boast to yourself about the privilege of virginity? Remember that Adam and Eve sinned while virgins, and that bodily integrity did not benefit those who sinned. A virgin who sins should be compared with Eve, not with Mary.

We do not deny the remedy of repentance in the present time; but we urge them rather to hope for a reward than for forgiveness. It is disgraceful for those who await the palm of virginity to ask indulgence for wrongdoing, and for those who have castrated themselves even from what is permitted to incur something unlawful.

For it is permitted to enter into marriage. And just as those women are worthy of praise who, for the love of Christ and the glory of the heavenly kingdom, have rejected marital union, so those who, not yet devoted to God, make use of the apostolic remedy for the sake of the pleasure of incontinence are not to be condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] *Of incontinence.* Baluzius correctly has this. Holsten corruptly has “of innocence.”]

Therefore, as we have said, those who abandon marriage reject not what is unlawful but what is lawful. But if such women swear, curse, slander, are known to listen to slanderers, return evil for evil, incur the crime of covetousness with regard to the property of others or of greed with regard to their own, possess the poisons of jealousy and resentment, speak or think anything indecent contrary to legal and apostolic regulations, go out adorned and beautified in the desire to please the flesh, and commit the other things that are customarily done unlawfully, what will it profit them to have rejected what was permitted and to practice what is not permitted?

If you wish what you have despised as lawful to benefit you, take care that you do none of the things that are unlawful. For it is foolish to have feared what is lesser and not to fear what is greater, or not to avoid the things that are forbidden while fleeing what is permitted.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] *Therefore, as we said.* The Cleric has it very poorly: “Therefore, as we said, those who despise lawful marriages as though they were unlawful,” and so forth. He then adds that if such women swear, curse, covet what belongs to others, listen to slanderers, return evil for evil, commit the crime of greed in their own affairs, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0233D] *Which they have avoided.* Holsten has “if they avoid.” Shortly afterward, following the Apostle’s words, some interpolated material is known to occur.]

For the Apostle says: “The unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (I Cor. VII, 34). He says, “She thinks about the things of the Lord,” not the things of the world, not the things of human beings, but she thinks about the things of the Lord.

What, then, are the Lord’s things? The Apostle says: “Whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report, if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline” (Phil. IV, 8). These are the Lord’s things, which truly holy apostolic virgins meditate upon and think about day and night.

The kingdom of heaven is also the Lord’s; the resurrection of the dead is the Lord’s; the incorruptibility of immortality is the Lord’s; the splendor of the sun that is promised to the saints is the Lord’s; the many dwelling places in heaven are the Lord’s; and the thirtieth-, sixtieth-, and hundredfold fruit is the Lord’s. They think about these things, and they think about by what works they may obtain the Lord’s things.

The law of the New and Old Testament is also the Lord’s, in which his holy praises shine forth. If virgins meditate upon these without interruption, they think about the Lord’s things, and the prophetic saying is fulfilled in them: “Eternal foundations established upon the earth, and the commandments of the Lord in the heart of a holy woman” (Ecclus. XXVI, 24).

[Note: [Col. 0233D] *In which his.* Read, with Holsten, “in which the holy praises of his mouth shine forth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0233D] *The splendor of the sun, which, etc.* The Cleric’s text is badly punctuated and corrupt: “The Lord’s is the splendor, the sun’s things that are promised to the saints.” The author is referring to Matt. XIII, 43: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”]

**IX.** The Apostle continues: “How she may please the Lord”—the Lord, I say, not human beings—“so that she may be holy in body and spirit.”

He did not say, “so that she may be holy in one member or in body alone,” but “so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” A member is one part of the body, whereas the body is the entire structure of its members. Therefore, when he says that she should be holy in body, he testifies that she must be sanctified in all her members. The sanctification of the other members will not profit if corruption is found in even one. The body, which is composed of all the members, will not be holy if it has been polluted by the defilement of even one.

But so that what I am saying may become clearer and more explicit, suppose that a woman has been purified by the sanctification of all her members, and only her tongue sins, blasphemes, or gives false testimony. Will all the members free the one, or will the others be judged because of the one? Therefore, if the sanctification of the other members is of no benefit when one is at fault, how much less, when all are corrupted by various sins, will the integrity of one be of any profit!

[Note: [Col. 0233D] *That she should be holy.* The Cleric incorrectly has “already holy.” Shortly afterward Holsten reads: “And she will no longer be holy in body.”]

[Note: [Col. 0233D] *Let it be, let there be whatever.* The Cleric, in his customary manner, corruptly has “whatever there may be,” omitting *let it be*. Shortly afterward: “How much more, therefore, without the sanctification of the other members.”]

**X.** Therefore, virgin, I beg you, do not flatter yourself on the ground of chastity alone, nor place your confidence in the integrity of a single member. Rather, following the Apostle, preserve the holiness of your body for God alone.

Cleanse your head from every defilement, because after the sanctification of chrism it is a serious insult to be soiled by the color or powder of saffron or any other pigment, or by gold, gems, or the appearance of any earthly creature. For preference given to worldly and secular adornment is a great insult to divine grace.

Cleanse your forehead, so that it may blush at human works, not divine ones, and receive that shame which produces not sin but the grace of God, as divine Scripture says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings the grace of God” (Ecclus. IV, 25).

Cleanse your neck, so that it may not wear necklaces woven with gold and hanging from the hair, but rather carry those ornaments of which Scripture says: “Mercy and faithfulness shall not fail you; hang them around your neck” (Prov. III, 3).

Cleanse your eyes by withdrawing them from every desire, never turning them away from the poor, and preserving them free from all cosmetics in the sincerity of the things made by God.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] *So that she may not wear necklaces woven with gold …* The Cleric corruptly has: “so that she may not wear a golden ornament in her hair and hanging necklaces.” Holsten has: “but hang those things in your heart as though around your neck.”]

[Note: [Col. 0234D] *You preserve them in regard to the things made by God.* This is the reading of Baluzius’s exemplar, which the Cleric copied unfaithfully: “you preserve them by the works of God.” Holsten’s reading is preferable: “and preserve them free from all cosmetics in the sincerity of the things made by God.”]

Cleanse your tongue from lying, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11); from slander, swearing, flattery, and perjury. Do not think that the order is reversed because I have said that the tongue ought to be cleansed from swearing before perjury. You will more easily avoid perjury if you do not swear at all.

Let this saying be fulfilled in you: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. XXIII, 14). And remember the Apostle’s saying: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14). But also recall more frequently this: “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil or curse for curse; instead, bless, because you were called for this purpose, that you might possess the inheritance of blessing” (I Pet. III, 9). And this: “If anyone does not offend his brother in word, he is perfect” (James III, 2).

[Note: [Col. 0234D] *In you.* The Cleric omits these words.]

It is impious that those lips by which you confess, entreat, bless, and praise the Lord should be polluted by the filth of any sin. I do not know with what conscience anyone prays to the Lord with a tongue by which he either lies, curses, or slanders.

The Lord hears holy lips, and quickly assents to the prayers that an unstained tongue utters.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] *Utters.* The Cleric preferred *nuntiat* (“announces”). Shortly afterward he again preferred to rewrite the text as “with holy and true words,” contrary to the Baluzius exemplar represented here. Holsten also has this latter reading. Shortly afterward, however, the Cleric agrees with Holsten in reading “or hear anyone disparaging another.”]

Cleanse your ears, so that they may give hearing only to holy and serious words, so that they may never receive obscene, shameful, or worldly speech, and so that they may not listen to someone slandering another, in accordance with what is written: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclus. XXVIII, 28). Thus you may have a share with the one of whom it is said that he was just in hearing and sight (II Pet. II, 8)—that is, he did not sin either with his ears or with his eyes.

Cleanse your hands, so that they may not be extended for receiving while folded for giving (Ecclus. IV, 36); let them not be ready to strike, but readily prepared for every work of mercy and compassion.

Cleanse your feet, so that they may not travel along the broad and spacious road that leads to the splendid and costly banquets of the world, but may rather walk the steep and narrow path that tends toward heaven. For it is written: “Make straight paths for your feet” (Prov. IV, 26; Isa. LVII, 14; LXII, 10).

Recognize that your members were formed by God the Creator not for vices but for virtues. When you have cleansed all your limbs from every stain of sin and have been sanctified in your whole body, then understand that chastity will profit you, and confidently await the palm of virginity.

**XI.** I think I have explained briefly but fully what it means to be holy in body. Now we must understand what follows, “and in spirit”: namely, that what it is wicked to do in deed must not even be conceived in thought.

She is holy in body and spirit who sins neither in mind nor in flesh. Knowing that God is the examiner of the heart, she takes care in every way to keep her soul as well as her body pure from sin, knowing that it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23). And: “For the Lord loves holy hearts, but the blameless are acceptable to him” (Prov. XI, 20). And elsewhere: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

I think this is said of those whose conscience reproves them for no fault of sin. John also seems to have spoken of them in his epistle: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God; and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (I John III, 21).

Do not think that you have escaped the guilt of sin if the will is not followed by the act, since it is written: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). Do not say: “I did think about it, but I did not carry it out,” because it is also wicked to desire what constitutes a crime when it is done.

For this reason blessed Peter also commands, saying: “Sanctify your souls” (I Pet. I, 22). If he had known of no defilement of the soul, he would not have desired it to be sanctified.

We must also consider more attentively the passage in which it is written: “These are the ones who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV, 4). We must ask whether they are joined to the divine company and move through all the tabernacles of heaven solely by merit of bodily integrity and chastity, or whether there are other qualities by which virginity, when joined to them, obtains the glory of such blessedness.

But how can we know this? From what follows, unless I am mistaken, where it is written: “These were purchased from among all as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb, and no falsehood was found in their mouth; they are without blemish before the throne of God” (ibid.).

You see, therefore, that it is not those who cling to the Lord’s footsteps in only one member who are referred to, but those who, in addition to virginity, have lived an unstained life, free from every sinful thought.

This is especially why a virgin should reject marriage: so that, being more secure, she may more easily keep herself from every sin—which is also required of married women—and fulfill all the commandments of the law. For if she does not marry but nevertheless does the things from which married women too are commanded to remain free, what benefit will it have been not to marry?

And although no Christian is permitted to sin, and all who are cleansed by the sanctification of the spiritual washing ought to live an unstained life, so that they may be incorporated into the inner being of the Church, which is described as being without stain, wrinkle, or any such defect (Eph. V, 27), a virgin must fulfill this all the more. Neither a husband nor children nor any other necessity prevents her from fulfilling divine Scripture; and if she sins, she will not be able to defend herself by excuse.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] *In one member only.* The Cleric has “in one virgin,” but this introduces the word *virgins* improperly into the text. The following verb refers to those about whom the preceding passage from Revelation speaks.]

## XII

O virgin, preserve the commitment entrusted to you and appointed for a great struggle. The virtue of virginity and chastity is highly esteemed before the Lord, provided that it is not weakened by other falls into sin and stains. Recognize your state, recognize your position, recognize your commitment. You are called the bride of Christ. Take care not to admit anything unworthy of the one to whom you appear betrothed. He will quickly write a bill of repudiation if he sees even a single act of adultery in you.

Therefore, any woman who is betrothed by the pledges of human marriage [Note: *Obarrhatur*: Holstenius, *subarrhatur*.] immediately asks carefully and diligently of the bridegroom’s household, relatives, and friends what sort of character the young man has, what he especially loves, what he accepts, how he lives, by what habits he governs himself, what foods he uses, and in what matters he most delights and rejoices. Once she has learned these things, she so regulates herself in everything that her obedience, cheerfulness, affection, diligence, and life accord with the bridegroom’s character.

[Note: “And you also who…” The relative *quae* is omitted by Clarius, who consequently, and imprudently, presents the passage as: “And you also have Christ as your bridegroom.”]

And you also, who have Christ as your bridegroom, inquire of his household and familiars about the character of your bridegroom, and investigate earnestly and diligently what especially pleases him and what arrangement of clothing he desires in you. Let his most intimate associate Peter tell you. He permits even married women not bodily adornment but spiritual adornment, as he writes in his Epistle:

“Women likewise should be subject to their own husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe your chaste conduct in fear. Let yours be not outward hair-braiding, or putting on gold, or the adornment of clothing, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, which is precious in the sight of God” (1 Peter 3:1–4).

Let the other blessed apostle, Paul, also speak to you. Writing to Timothy, he bears witness to the same discipline for believing women:

“Women likewise should adorn themselves in respectable clothing, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but—as is fitting for women who profess chastity—through good conduct” (1 Timothy 2:9–10).

## XIII

But perhaps you say: Why did the apostles not command these things to virgins? Because they did not consider it necessary, lest such an admonition to virgins appear rather an insult than a correction. Nor did they ever suppose that virgins would be so reckless as to presume upon the bodily ornaments not even granted to married women.

Indeed, a virgin ought to adorn and arrange herself. For how will she be able to please her bridegroom unless she comes forth arranged and adorned? Let her certainly be adorned, but with inward ornaments; let her be arranged spiritually, not bodily, because the Lord desires in her not the beauty of the body but that of the soul.

Therefore you also, whoever you are who desire that your soul be loved and inhabited by God, arrange it with every care [Note: *Come*. Thus Baluzius correctly; Holstenius has *compone*. Clarius incorrectly has *comple*, who shortly before writes *habitari* for *inhabitari*.] and adorn it with spiritual garments. Let nothing indecorous, nothing foul, appear in it. Let it shine with the gold of justice, sparkle with the gems of holiness, and flash with the most precious pearl of chastity. Let it be clothed, instead of fine linen and silk, with the garment of mercy and piety, according to what is written:

“Therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on the inner organs of mercy, [Note: “Kindness.” Greek: χρηστότητα (*chrēstótēta*). Clarius inserted “goodness”; he also soon prints, “Let it seek not the beauty of another pigment,” omitting the words concerning white lead.] kindness, humility, etc.” (Colossians 3:12).

Let it not seek the beauty of white lead or another cosmetic, but possess the whiteness of innocence and simplicity; let it possess the rose-colored complexion of modesty [Note: “And let it possess the purple color of shame and the blush of modesty.” This is also found in Jerome, in the cited edition of Victorius, vol. IX, p. 55. H. But with Holstenius it should be read: “and let it possess the purple color of shame and the blush of modesty.”] and the shame of blushing and modesty.

[Note: “Let it be washed with the heavenly soda of teaching and with cleansing agents.” So reads Baluzius’s sole edition of 1678, *Miscellanea*, book I, p. 349, which I have before me. It is therefore surprising that Cotelerius, in *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. II, p. 541, read *abluatur et lamentis* (“let it be washed and with lamentations”), a reading which Clarius is also said to have followed. From this Cotelerius takes occasion to conjecture that the reading should be *abluatur et lomentis* (“let it be washed and with cleansing agents”). Holstenius, however, has *coelesti et lamentis*; the latter perhaps fits less well with the verb *emundetur* (“let it be cleansed”). In the passage of the Jerome cited by Victorius, *lavamentis* appears. Nevertheless, with Cotelerius I would prefer *lomentis*, which also comes closer to the Baluzius edition. Clarius shortly afterward has the erroneous reading “Nothing evil in it”; and a little later, “But even your own.”]

Let it be washed with the heavenly soda of teaching and cleansed with spiritual cleansing agents [*lumentis*]. Let no stain of wickedness, no stain of deceit, remain in it. And lest it ever smell foul with the odor of sin, let it be drenched with the ointment of the sweetest wisdom and knowledge.

## XIV

God seeks adornment of this kind, and desires a soul arranged in this manner. Remember that you are called God’s daughter, according to the words: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Psalm 44:11). But you too, whenever you call God your Father, testify that you are God’s daughter. Therefore, if you are God’s daughter, take care not to do anything that is unsuitable for God the Father; but do everything as God’s daughter.

Observe how the daughters of the nobles of this world conduct themselves, what habits they adopt, and by what disciplines they train themselves. In some there is such modesty, such dignity, such restraint that, out of regard for their natural nobility, they surpass the customary conduct of other people [Note: “And never strive to disgrace their honorable parents by their downfall.” Clarius rightly suspected an error here. Read, with Holstenius: “and never strive to bring any disgrace upon their honorable parents.”], never branding their honorable parents with the mark of disgrace through their fall, and thus, in a manner of speaking, making for themselves a second nature of habitual conduct among human beings.

You too, therefore, look to your origin, consider your lineage, and reflect upon the glory of your nobility. Recognize that you are not merely the daughter of a human being but also the daughter of God, adorned with the nobility of divine birth. Conduct yourself so that heavenly birth may be revealed in you and divine nobility shine forth. Let there be in you new dignity, admirable honor, astonishing modesty, remarkable patience, a virgin’s bearing, and the manner of true chastity [Note: “Of true chastity.” Clarius wrongly has “the manner of the chastity of life,” and, with several words inserted, “This is not a discipline of mortal human instruction.”].

Let your speech always be modest and uttered at the proper time, so that whoever sees you may admire you and say:

“What is this new dignity of patience among human beings, this modesty of shame, this restraint of honor, this maturity? This is not a human institution or a mortal discipline. Something heavenly shines upon me in an earthly body. I think that God dwells in certain human beings.”

And when he recognizes that you are a daughter of Christ [Note: “A daughter of Christ.” Jerome likewise has this in the cited edition of Victorius, p. 56b. But, following Holstenius, correct it to “a handmaid of Christ.” The restoration is confirmed by what follows: “what sort of Lord he is whose such a handmaid she is.”], he will be struck with even greater wonder and will consider what sort of Lord he is whose handmaid is such a woman.

## XV

If, therefore, you wish to have a share with Christ, you must live according to Christ’s example. He was so removed from every wickedness and evil that he did not repay even his enemies in kind, but rather prayed for them [Note: “He prayed.” Clarius has *rogabat* (“he asked”), and shortly afterward, contrary to the evidence of his exemplar, printed “with the whole heart of conscience, before the testimony of God.” Yet the Baluzius edition is entirely sound: “with the whole heart and conscience … before the testimony of God,” etc. At least he should have written, as in Holstenius’s exemplar: “with the whole heart and conscience before God’s testimony.”].

I do not want you to consider Christian those souls which, not to say hate brothers or sisters, do not love their neighbors with their whole heart and conscience, with God as witness. For Christians must love even their enemies in imitation of Christ.

If you desire fellowship with the saints, cleanse your breast from every thought of wickedness and evil. Let no one deceive you; let no one seduce you with deceitful speech. The heavenly court will receive only the holy, just, simple, innocent, and pure [Note: “Will receive.” So also Holstenius. Clarius has “receives,” and shortly afterward omits the word *tam* (“so”).]. Wickedness has no place with God. Anyone who desires to reign with Christ must be free from every evil and deceit.

Nothing is so contrary, nothing so detestable to God, as to hate one person and wish to harm another; nothing is so praiseworthy as to love everyone. The Prophet testifies to this in anticipation, saying:

“You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Psalm 96:10).

## XVI

Take care not to love any human glory [Note: “Lest your portion also be among those.” Clarius absurdly has, “lest that portion also be among them.” Shortly afterward, in the Johannine text, read with the Vulgate and Holstenius, *ab invicem* (“from one another”).], lest your portion also be counted among those of whom it was said:

“How can you believe, when you seek glory from one another?” (John 5:44).

And of whom it is said through the Prophet:

“Add evils to them; add evils to all the glorious ones of the earth” (Isaiah 26:15, according to the Septuagint) [Note: Holstenius has: “Add evils to them, add evils to the glorious ones of the earth.” The first passage, according to the Septuagint, occurs at Isaiah 26:15: Πρόσθες αὐτοῖς κακά, πρόσθες κακὰ πᾶσι τοῖς ἐνδόξοις (“Add evils to them; add evils to all the glorious ones”). The second likewise occurs according to the Septuagint at Jeremiah 12:13: Αἰσχύνθητε αἰσχύνην ἀπὸ καυχήσεως ὑμῶν, ἀπὸ ὀνειδισμοῦ ἔναντι Κυρίου (“Be ashamed with shame because of your boasting, because of reproach before the Lord”). This reading should be restored here from Holstenius’s exemplar in the Baluzius edition.].

And:

“Let them be confounded by your glorification and by reproach before the Lord” (Jeremiah 12:13, according to the Septuagint).

I do not want you to look to those virgins who belong to the world, not to Christ; nor to those who, forgetful of their commitment and profession, rejoice in luxuries, delight in wealth, and glory in the nobility of bodily birth. If they truly believed themselves to be daughters of God, they would never, after their divine birth, admire human nobility, nor glory in some honored father, if they felt that they had God as their Father.

Why, foolish woman, do you flatter and indulge yourself? [Note: Holstenius has: “Why do you flatter yourself in the nobility of your lineage?” This reading appears to be demanded by the context.] In the beginning God made two human beings, from whom the whole forest of the human race descended. Worldly nobility is not granted by the equality of nature but by the ambition of desire. No distinction can exist among those whom a second birth has generated, through which both rich and poor, free and enslaved, noble and ignoble become children of God; and earthly nobility is overshadowed by the splendor of heavenly glory.

It now disappears entirely, while those who previously were unequal in secular honors are clothed equally with the noble dignity of heavenly and divine glory. There is no place there for ignobility; nor is anyone degenerate whom the sublimity of divine birth adorns—except among those who do not think that heavenly things should be preferred to human things.

Or, if they do think so, how foolish it is for them to prefer themselves in lesser matters to those whom they acknowledge as their equals in greater matters, and to regard as beneath themselves on earth those whom they believe to be their equals in heaven.

But you, whoever you are who are Christ’s virgin and not the world’s, flee all the glory of the present life, so that you may attain the glory promised in the future.

## XVII

Avoid contentious speech and the causes of hostility; likewise shun the occasions of discord and lawsuits. For if, according to the Apostle’s teaching, the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, how much more must this be true of God’s handmaid, whose sex is more modest [Note: “Her sex is more modest.” *Sexus* is absent in Clarius, who also shortly afterward has “lest anything which,” omitting *quid*. Immediately afterward he has the erroneous “Blessed, therefore, such as lips” instead of “such lips”; and a little later, “destroy the hearers,” where one should follow the reading “in divine matters.”] and whose spirit ought therefore to be more restrained!

Restrain your tongue from evil speech, and place the reins of the law upon your mouth. Then, if you happen to speak when silence would be sinful, take care not to say anything that could rightly be condemned. A word spoken is a stone cast forth; therefore it must be considered for a long time before it is uttered. Blessed indeed are the lips that never let anything escape which they might wish to recall.

The speech of a chaste mind ought to be chaste, always building up rather than at some time destroying its hearers, according to the Apostle’s command:

“Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such speech as is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29).

Precious to God is the tongue that knows how to form words only about divine matters, and holy is the mouth from which heavenly utterances are always brought forth.

By the authority of Scripture deter those who slander the absent, as though they were malicious people; for the Prophet also counts this among the virtues of a perfect person (Psalm 14:4): that before the sight of the just person the malicious one who has spoken unacceptable things against his neighbor is brought to nothing.

You may not patiently listen to another’s disparagement, since you do not wish your own to be received by others. Whatever is done against the Gospel of Christ is unjust, if you allow another to suffer what would trouble you if someone else did it to you.

Accustom your tongue always to speak of good things, and direct your hearing more toward praise of the good than toward condemnation of the wicked.

See that everything you do well, you do for God’s sake, knowing that from the Lord you will receive as great a reward for that deed as you have accomplished because of fear and love of him.

Strive to be holy rather than to appear holy, because it is useless to be esteemed as something you are not, and it is a double guilt both not to possess what is believed about you and to pretend to possess what you do not have.

## XVIII

Take greater delight in fasts than in banquets, remembering that widow who did not leave the temple, serving God with fasts and prayers day and night. And if such was a widow, and indeed a Jewish one, what kind of virgin ought a virgin of Christ now to be?

Love rather the banquet of divine love, and desire to be filled with spiritual foods. Seek those foods by which the soul, more than the body, is refreshed. Flee the appearances of flesh and wine as fuel for heat [Note: “Of heat.” Clarius incorrectly has “of color”; shortly before he has “let it be refreshed,” and shortly afterward “use” instead of “make use of.”] and incitements to lust. If necessity should at some point compel you because of excessive stomach pain and bodily weakness, then use only a little wine.

Conquer anger, restrain hostility, and whatever it may be that, after it has been done, brings remorse as though for a grave crime [Note: “As though for a very serious crime.” These words are absent from Holstenius’s exemplar, apparently rightly. Clarius begins chapter 30 with: “Avoid the abomination of the crime of your neighbor,” thus breaking the continuity of the text.], avoid the abomination of a neighbor’s wrongdoing.

A mind that desires to be God’s dwelling ought to be sufficiently quiet and tranquil, free from every disturbance of fury. God testifies through the Prophet and says:

“Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

Believe that God is the observer of all your acts and thoughts, and take care neither to do nor to think anything unworthy of the divine eyes. When you desire to celebrate prayer, conduct yourself as one who is about to speak with God.

## XIX

When you recite a psalm, recognize whose words you are speaking, and take greater delight in the compunction of the soul than in the sweetness of a ringing voice. For God approves the tears of one who sings psalms more than the charm of the voice, as the Prophet says:

“Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11).

Where there are fear and trembling, there is not elevation of the voice but a sorrowful and tearful prostration [Note: “Prostration.” Clarius preferred *dilectio* (“love”), contrary both to the sense and to the truth of the exemplar.].

Show diligence in all your actions, because it is written:

“Cursed is the one who does the works of the Lord negligently” (Jeremiah 48:10).

Let grace increase in you with the years, let justice increase with age, and let faith appear more perfect the older you become. For the Lord Jesus, who left us an example of how to live, advanced not only in bodily age but also in wisdom and spiritual grace, before God and human beings (Luke 2:52).

Consider every period in which you have not found yourself better to have been lost.

Preserve the commitment to virginity that you have conceived until the end; for it is a mark of virtue not merely to have begun but to have completed, as the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

Take care, therefore, not to give anyone an occasion for desire, because your bridegroom is a jealous God. An adulteress of Christ is more culpable than an adulteress of a husband.

Therefore be an example of life to everyone; be a model. In conduct, go before those whom you surpass in the sanctification of chastity. Show yourself a virgin in everything. Let no corruption be brought against your head. Let the conduct of one whose body is intact be inviolable.

And since, as we stated at the beginning of the Epistle, you have been made God’s sacrifice [Note: “Made.” Clarius has the neuter *factum*, whereas the context requires the feminine *factam*. Shortly afterward he has “from them,” contrary to the context.], which certainly also imparts its holiness to others, so that whoever worthily partakes of it becomes himself a participant in sanctification, so also through you, as through a divine offering, let the other women be sanctified. Conduct yourself in all things so that whoever encounters your life, whether by hearing or by sight, may feel the power of sanctification and understand that so much grace is transferred to him from your conduct that, while he desires to imitate you, he too may be worthy of God’s sacrifice.

# EPISTLE III. TO THE HOLY BISHOP PAULINUS

Severus sends a cook suitable for preparing the monks’ food.

[Note: “After I learned,” etc. Paulinus’s Epistle 23 is a reply to this letter of Severus.]

After I learned that all your cooks had resigned from your kitchen [Note: “Afterwards,” etc.], I suppose they were ashamed to provide service with cheap stews. We have sent you a boy from our workshop, sufficiently skilled at cooking pale beans, seasoning humble beets with vinegar and sauce, and bringing cheap porridge to the hungry throats of monks; ignorant of pepper, unacquainted with laserwort, familiar with cumin, and exceptionally skilled at vigorously working the clamorous mortar with sweet-smelling herbs.

He has one fault: he is not a civilized enemy of every garden. Thus, if he is admitted, he will cut down everything nearby with his sword and will never be sated by the slaughter of mallows.

As for the wood supplied to him [Note: “He will not be a calumniator to you.” Clarius has “to himself”; shortly afterward he incorrectly has “because you are not ashamed.”], he will not be a calumniator to you: he will burn everything in his path; he will cut wood and will not hesitate to lay hands upon roofs or to remove ancient beams from household shrines.

We therefore wish to give you this man, endowed with such habits and virtues, not as a slave but as a son in place of a slave, since you are not ashamed to be the father of the least of men.

I would have wished to serve you in his place; but if the will to act is itself a part of the deed, then make sure that amid your happy lunches and dinners you remember me. For it is more fitting to be your servant than the master of others.

Pray for me.

# EPISTLE IV

Although my lord and brother asked, on the strength of your honor, that you should be willing to make the secure entirely secure, nevertheless there was no reason to commend the same man in writing, so that through a doubled petition he might be made safer. For the childish fault and error of an uncertain age would have harmed him, since it stained the beginning of his years; but because he did not yet know what was owed to good morals, he sinned almost without guilt.

For when he turned toward a sound mind and reflection, he understood that a theatrical life ought to be condemned by better judgment. Yet full purification could not come to him unless, through the approach of divinity, he washed away his offenses. For, transformed by the remedy of the Catholic religion, he rejected the practice of the shameful place and rescued himself from the eyes of the populace.

[Note: “Of the Lord, as above.” Since the inscription of this letter is missing, not even Apollo himself could have divined to whom it was written—unless one understands that it was sent to the decurions of some city. They were dragging back unwillingly onto the stage a certain young man, whose name is hidden at the beginning beneath the word *tutum*, which is undoubtedly corrupt, although he had renounced the stage after being purified by the sacred waters. Dacherius. I doubt whether this letter is by our Severus, whose style seems better to me. Clarius.]

How, then, could both divine laws and the faithful civic body permit sanctified persons to offer dishonorable entertainments and stage vulgar pleasures—especially since it would somehow seem an injury to chaste devotion if someone renewed through holy baptism were recalled to his former wantonness?

It is fitting that your praiseworthiness should favor good intentions [Note: Clarius has “your praiseworthiness,” singular, contrary to the evidence of the exemplar. The common reading is confirmed by what follows: “Nevertheless, the judgment of all of you.”], so that the man who has obtained the pious gift through God’s favor may not be forced to fall into the theatrical pit.

Nevertheless, he does not reject the judgment of all of you if you impose other appropriate duties according to the needs of the common fatherland.

# EPISTLE V. TO SALVIUS

He complains that peasants are harassed and that the rights and properties of others are usurped.

## I

The boastfulness of the law court ought to burn through the exercise of the forum; for it is fitting that the muscles of industry, struggling daily, should have movements that inspire terror. But when sonorous eloquence has sounded the retreat and withdrawn into idle groves and pleasant retreats [Note: “It withdrew.” Clarius rewrites this as *remigravit* (“returned”), apparently correctly.], it ought to cast aside its inert roar and cease making ineffective threats.

For we know that the palm-bearing teams, once they have withdrawn from the circus, stand quietly in their stalls. They are disturbed neither by the yoke nor by uncertain victory; finally, fixed in peaceful mangers, they no longer know fear of the driver, taking sweet forgetfulness of seditious rivalry.

It is also pleasant for the glorious soldier, when his service has been completed, to hang up his trophies and bear old age patiently.

## II

I do not quite understand whether it is your desire to terrify wretched farmers; nor do I recognize why you wish to press my peasants with the fear of public proceedings. As though I did not know how to console them, withdraw them from fear, and teach them that the fear is not as great as you yourself pretend.

I confess that, while the field received us, I was often terrified by your eloquence [Note: “Eloquence.” So we read with Clarius, instead of the printed *eloquia*. Dacher. Shortly afterward Clarius incorrectly has “that he wishes to lead back.”], but I frequently repelled the recurring wounds as best I could.
