With you, certainly, I learned by what law and in what order colonists are summoned, to whom an action belongs, and to whom the outcome of an action does not belong.

“You say,” you repeatedly groan in anger, “that you intend to lead back the Volusianenses,” and you threaten that you will drag my peasants back from my little tower. You, who—as I hope and desire—are joined to me by an ancient relationship, recklessly threaten to proceed against my people without observing the proper summons.

I ask your distinguished prudence whether advocates have one law, men in the toga another, whether what is equitable at Rome is one thing [Note: “One thing for the Mataritans.” The Mataritan plebs in Africa is mentioned in the *Collationes Carthaginenses* (Day 1, chapter 133). Dacher.], and at Matarita another.

## III

Meanwhile, I do not know that Volusius was ever the owner of the estate. For Dionysius is said to have preserved the rights of that property, and his heirs did not fail him; while he lived, he directed poisonous barbs in many directions in matters concerning naval affairs.

At that time there was a certain Porphyrius, born of Zibberinus; yet he was not properly called the son of Zibberinus. He too was overturning the question of his lineage through military service, and, to drive the cloud from his brow, he performed acts of obliging favor and cheerful service.

He spent much time with me both at home and in the forum, using me more than once as an advocate before his father and as a patron before the judge. At one point I even restrained Dionysius, because he ought not to stir up naval quarrels over twenty *jugera* on Porphyrius’s account.

## IV

Here, then, is the reason why your distinguished prudence threatens my estate agents [Note: “Twenty *jugera*.” Clarius has “twenty *jugera*,” perhaps from Dacher’s first edition, which is not at hand. Shortly before, Clarius likewise has, “and if you are Porph—.”], although you are not the owner of the place, and why you speak everywhere of my colonists.

But if you declare yourself Porphyrius’s successor, you should know that the narrow extent of even a single *jugerum* cannot be worked by one cultivator; or, if you are ashamed to call yourself Porphyrius’s heir, as one mindful and protective of your own dignity, it is certain that the person who possesses the power of presenting a claim may present it, so that he may proceed against those who possess nothing from that same land.

But if you examine the matter carefully, the claim for recovery can most properly be brought by me. Therefore, my praiseworthy lord and brother, you ought to rest, become reconciled with me, and deign to come to a private conversation.

Please cease disturbing the inactive and frightened, exercise your boastfulness far away, and suppose that I rejoice in your arrogance rather than being offended by it. For we are neither harsh nor uneducated.

At least let Maximinus make you gentle.

# EPISTLE VI

The faith and devotion of souls certainly remain, but they must be made known through the evidence of letters, so that the increase of affection may grow through greetings.

For just as a fertile field cannot raise abundant crops if cultivation ceases, and the goodness of the earth perishes through the idleness of one who rests, so I think that love and favor of the heart can grow sluggish unless those who are absent are visited by the presence of letters.

Thanks be to God. Amen.

[Note: Epistle VII. This is Epistle II among the five that Dacherius first published under the name of Sulpicius Severus. Our Hieronymus de Prato formed the following judgment about it in the preface to his edition of the works of Sulpicius Severus, vol. I, p. 32:

“ I find that it was addressed not to Paulinus but to Augustine, and not by Sulpicius Severus but in the name of the people of Cirta; to them Augustine evidently replies in the letter that is listed as no. 144 in the Maurist edition of the Fathers. Let both letters, I beg, be carefully compared with one another, especially in the example of Polemo; and everyone will acknowledge that what I say is true. For now it is enough that I have indicated this. Moreover, this letter, wrongly attributed to Severus, appears mutilated both at the beginning and at the end.”

So wrote that learned man. To make his judgment more fully evident, we have arranged for the other letter of Saint Augustine just mentioned to be placed after this Epistle 7.]

# EPISTLE VII. OF THE PEOPLE OF CIRTA TO SAINT AUGUSTINE

Published under the false name of Sulpicius Severus. Augustine is praised for the wisdom and gentleness he employs in his exhortations.

## I

The faithful interpreter of holy religion orders everything so that no further place can remain for sins. For what else do you promise through such great holiness of conduct than that we should lead a blessed life once errors have been removed?

In this I see the greatest praise agreeing with your virtues: you change an unlearned mind through pious exhortations and draw it toward the best course of life [Note: “I see.” Either *vides* (“you see”) or *videmus* (“we see”) should be restored. Throughout the letter the plural number is used; this is the correction of the same distinguished man just mentioned.].

Otherwise it would not seem so remarkable if you had strengthened educated minds by pouring in wisdom. Prudence has a natural kinship with devotion among wise men, and rusticity is not readily compatible with credulity [Note: “Rusticity with credulity.” Dacherius preferred this emendation, since the earlier reading was *crudelitati* (“with cruelty”). Clarius retained the manuscript reading *crudelitati*, explaining the word as “severity,” and claimed that the following context supported this sense. I would not adopt his view.].

Thus those who carve figures of animals from stone undertake the more difficult work, when they strike the hardest rocks with iron tools. But those who take on trials involving softer material find that their hands are aided by the ease of shaping [Note: “Of painting.” I suspect an error entered Dacher’s edition, which I use; accordingly I prefer Clarius’s *fingendi* (“of shaping”).]. It is considered fitting that the craftsman’s arduous labor should be counted worthy of the highest honor.

So for you, lord, preaching must be presented in a singular manner: you have freed rough and unpolished country minds from the darkness of sin, made them capable of human understanding, and taught them to know divine things.

## II

That Xenocrates too deserves no less praise—the most learned by far of the philosophers—who by stern exhortations brought luxury under control. For when a certain Polemo, weakened by wine, was wandering publicly from a banquet that had begun before dawn, and when it was the time at which listeners were gathering at Xenocrates’ gymnasium, he entered as well and sat shamelessly among the students in the same clothing in which he had left the banquet.

His head was covered with a flowering crown, and he was not ashamed to appear unlike all the others, although prolonged drinking had truly turned his head—the dwelling place of health—upside down [Note: “Whose head, the dwelling place of health, prolonged drinking had truly turned upside down.” Clarius has: “who had truly turned his head, the dwelling place of health, upside down through prolonged drinking.” The passage seems not to require this emendation.].

While the others were then murmuring indignantly because an untimely student had intruded into a crowd of learned men, that teacher was not moved in the least. Rather, he began to discuss the discipline of conduct and the laws of modesty. The authority of the teacher had such power that it drove the young man’s insolent spirit toward love of shamefastness.

At first, Polemo, confused, laid down the crown from his head [Note: “Confused, he laid it down.” Dacherius corrected the reading, where the text had *exposuit* (“displayed it”). Clarius did not depart from the manuscript reading.], and declared himself a disciple. Finally, he bent himself so completely toward the duty of dignity and shaped himself entirely toward modesty that a glorious reform corrected the habits of his former life.

This is precisely what we admire in your instructions: without threats and without any terrors at all, you have turned deranged minds toward the worship of God, so that the confused mind might believe it far more right to live well and happily with everyone than to think unjustly with a few.

# LETTER 144 OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

Augustine congratulates the people of Cirta, converted from the faction of the Donatists to fellowship with the Catholic Church, and admonishes them to attribute this to the divine gift.

To the honorable lords, deservedly to be welcomed, most beloved and most longed-for brothers of every rank of honor, the people of Cirta: Augustine, bishop.

## I

If that which was causing us deep sorrow in your city has been removed; if the hardness of the human heart, resisting the most evident and in a certain sense public truth, has been overcome by its power; if the sweetness of peace is pleasing, and the charity of unity no longer strikes wounded eyes but enlightens and strengthens healthy ones, these are not our works but God’s.

I would not attribute these things to human works at all—not even if, while we were with you, so great a conversion of the multitude had come about through our speaking and exhorting.

He does this and brings it about who, through his ministers, admonishes people outwardly by signs of events, but through the events themselves, by himself, teaches outwardly [Note: “Or inwardly?”].

Therefore we ought not to be slower to hurry to visit you because whatever praiseworthy thing has been done in you was done not by us but by him who alone works wonders (Psalm 71:18).

Indeed, we ought to hasten much more eagerly to behold divine works than our own, because if we are anything good, we too are his work, not the work of human beings.

Hence the Apostle said:

“Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

## II

Xenocrates, as you write, and we too remember from those letters [Note: [Col. 0246D] The printed editions read “from his [letters]”; the manuscripts have “from those [letters].” BB.], converted Polemo, while discussing the fruit of temperance, not merely from a drunkard, but from a man who was drunk at that very moment, suddenly to a different way of life. Although, therefore, as you prudently and truthfully understood, he was not won for God, but merely liberated from the domination of lust, nevertheless I would attribute even that improvement in him not to human work but to divine work. For whatever good qualities belong to that very body of ours, which is weak—such as beauty, strength, health, and anything of that kind—come from none other than God, the creator and perfecter of nature; how much more, then, can no one else bestow the goods of the soul! [Col. 0247A] What more perverse or ungrateful thought could human folly entertain than to suppose that, while God makes a human being beautiful in body, a human being can make him chaste in soul? This is written in the book of Christian wisdom: “Since I knew,” he says, “that no one can be continent unless God grants it—and this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was” (Wisdom 8:21).

If, therefore, Polemo, having been made continent from a man of lust, had known whose gift this was in such a way that, after casting aside his superstitions, he worshiped him piously, he would have become not only continent but also truly wise and healthily religious; and this would have benefited him not merely for the honorableness of the present life, but also for the immortality of the life to come.

How much less, then, ought I to claim for myself this conversion of yours, or of your people, which you have just announced to us—something which, without my speaking, and indeed without my even being present, was unquestionably accomplished by divine power, wherever it was truly accomplished! [Col. 0247B] Recognize this above all; think upon it piously and humbly. Give thanks to God, brothers—to God. Fear God, lest you fail; love him, that you may advance.

## III

But if the love of a human being still secretly separates some, and human fear deceitfully gathers them together, let those who are such observe that they neither deceive God, before whom the human conscience lies naked, nor escape him as judge.

If anything concerning the question of unity troubles them out of concern for their salvation, let them exact from themselves, as I think is entirely just, that concerning the Catholic Church—that is, the Church spread throughout the whole world—they believe rather what the divine Scriptures say [Col. 0247C] than what human tongues utter in denunciation.

As for the very dissension that has arisen among human beings—whatever sort of people they may have been, they certainly do not prejudice the promises of God, who said to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 26:4), a promise that was believed when it was heard in prophecy and denied when it was seen to have been fulfilled—let them meanwhile consider only this brief point, which, unless I am mistaken, is unanswerable: either this case was tried in an ecclesiastical tribunal overseas, or it was not tried.

If it was not tried there, the fellowship of Christ throughout all the overseas nations is innocent, and we rejoice in communion with that fellowship; consequently, they are separated from those innocent people by a sacrilegious division.

But if this case was tried there, who does not understand, who does not feel, who does not see that those whose communion has been separated from there were defeated in it? [Col. 0248B] Let them choose, then, whether they prefer to believe what the ecclesiastical judges pronounced or what the defeated litigants mutter.

Consider carefully, with the prudence that is yours, how nothing sober can be answered to this argument—so brief to state and so easy to understand—and yet the wicked Polemo is more thoroughly overthrown by the drunkenness of his long-established error.

Forgive, perhaps, this letter, longer than it is agreeable, but, as I think, more useful than flattering, honorable lords, brothers worthy of respect, most dear and most earnestly desired. As for our coming to you, may God fulfill the desire of both sides. We cannot express in words how ardently the fire of charity kindles us to visit you, but we do not doubt that you will kindly believe us.

[Col. 0247C]

## In the Year of Our Lord 405

## In the Year of Our Lord 407

### SAINT CHROMATIUS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA

*(Edition prepared by Braida, Udine, 1816.)*

[Col. 0247]

[Col. 0247C]

## EDITOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0247D] [V] We are bringing nothing new to the republic of letters by presenting here the surviving WRITINGS—or, if you prefer, the OPUSCULA—of SAINT CHROMATIUS, bishop of Aquileia. Ever since 1528, when the writings of Chromatius first saw the light of publication at Basel, they have been printed several times, sometimes separately but chiefly in collections of the Fathers; most recently they received a place in volume VIII of Andrea Gallandi’s *Bibliotheca Patrum Scriptorumque Ecclesiasticorum*, published at Venice, and certainly in a better and more suitable form than they had ever previously possessed. Nevertheless, we trust that our plan for establishing a new, special edition of the writings or opuscula of Chromatius will be approved by fair-minded judges of these matters, if they weigh carefully the general and particular considerations that impelled us to undertake it.

It is established first of all that in collections of the Fathers—not only the older ones but also those produced through more recent care and labor—quite a few things relevant to the elucidation of authors and works are lacking. This is either because the compilers set themselves the task of deliberately omitting much, for the sake of brevity, that learned men had written at greater length; or because nothing of scholarly value had yet actually emerged that deserved to be reprinted there; or finally because the compilers, intent upon editing the works of the Fathers and as though overwhelmed by the multitude of works and opuscula, were content to gather the more common materials and meanwhile to safeguard the integrity of the texts—which was certainly always the principal concern in labors of this kind.

Moreover, certain works, especially those consisting of few pages, have scarcely ever been published outside the libraries of the Fathers or other collections of ancient monuments; and when they have occasionally been printed separately, the editions themselves are scarcely accessible. Meanwhile, acquiring those libraries or collections of several volumes, whatever their title, has always been within the reach of very few.

Finally, many works or opuscula of the holy Fathers have been inserted into libraries and other collections and have scarcely ever been published separately, although they confer no little honor and glory both upon provinces [VI] and regions, and upon cities and other places in which their authors became famous during their lifetimes. All those places therefore have an interest in seeing such works become more widely known, at least among their own people, and more generally used.

Add to this, above all, the religious consideration, particularly in the case of those holy Fathers who flourished in the early centuries of the Church, through whose care and labor the Christian cause in those regions, provinces, cities, and other places either began or later grew and prospered. No one who loves the religion of Christ with the love it deserves would fail to see with the greatest pleasure, with his own eyes if he wished, or at least readily to understand from others who have seen it, what his ancestors once heard from those most holy men, their superiors in Christian discipline, who were the first—or lived not far from the first—to speak the Word of God among them. Through their instruction and labor, therefore, he too, by the favor of divine grace, remains firm and unharmed after so many centuries in the deposit of faith received from them.

Who, then, would deny that for many reasons it can often happen that a person who proposes to give new and separate illumination to any writings or opuscula of the holy Fathers, even though they have already been published in collections and libraries, is not wasting his labor but rather deserves praise and gratitude?

[Col. 0250A] To apply these observations to the writings of our Chromatius, they have almost always appeared in the libraries and older collections either naked or clothed in very slight garments. Finally, the most distinguished Gallandi himself, who could certainly have presented these same writings of Chromatius with much embellishment—as he did many other works of even smaller size—being fond of a certain concision, admirable though it is to observe in him the man’s intelligence and diligence, allowed quite a few things to remain wanting which not only scholars but, so to speak, all readers would gladly have seen collected and suitably arranged in one place.

Indeed, with the manifold learning in which he was so highly accomplished, he could also have drawn much from his own store, by which this edition of the writings would have shone more brightly and become more agreeable and useful.

For what are we saying when we name Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia? We mean a man outstanding among the bishops of the West in his own age, whose holy mind Saint Ambrose admired for its study of the divine utterances; whom Saint Jerome—upon whom the charge of flattery certainly cannot be imposed—called the holiest and most learned of bishops; whom Rufinus called a second Beseleel of his own time; to whom Saint John Chrysostom himself, writing to him, attributed a most vehement and fire-filled charity, and a sincere tongue suffused with immense freedom and confidence, together with an adamantine steadfastness; and to whom, finally, we owe very much because Saint Jerome himself, the greatest teacher given by God to his Church for expounding the sacred Scriptures, labored over them so intensely, as is known to all.

Chromatius was therefore worthy to emerge in this literary light adorned with every form of cultivation, although otherwise only a few things survive concerning him. Yet as soon as those few works burst forth from the darkness, the most learned men always valued them highly, both for the brilliance of their style, the weight of their subject matter, and the excellence of their learning, and for the materials they everywhere supply for strengthening Christian instruction and confirming Catholic doctrines.

As for us, since we are people of Aquileia and rightly glory in so great a man, praised so highly by the most commendable men both of his own and of later ages; and since we were privileged to have him, after Saint Valerian, as our sacred bishop, teacher of religion, guide of Christian life, and vigorous defender of the faith handed down by the apostles during the closing years of the fourth century and the opening years of the fifth—since, I say, this is our concern, it was certainly no longer permissible for us to tolerate his remaining hidden, as it were, in the libraries of the Fathers and other ancient collections of similar monuments, while those to whom it was granted to possess such volumes were forced to seek here and there the materials relevant to his elucidation.

Moreover, although matters contributing to the elucidation of our Chromatius have also been treated by other learned men, especially Tillemont and Ceillier, they can nevertheless be sought nowhere more fully and clearly than from our own writers: namely, the most distinguished men, endowed with every kind of learning, Fontanini and De Rubeis. In their works they wrote about Chromatius deliberately and with a vast apparatus of material, and with the utmost care and labor clarified everything relating to his age, homeland, episcopate, virtues, merits, and writings. The two do not always agree with each other on every point; but this will not be inconvenient for readers—indeed, it may sometimes be pleasant to have them appointed, as it were, judges between such eminent men when they differ on some matter concerning the same subject.

Here, then, kind reader, is what we present to you in this volume. We offer the surviving writings or opuscula of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. We have called them “writings” or “opuscula,” but not simply “opuscula.” For apart from the first Sermon—or Tractate, or Homily, as you may call it—on the Eight Beatitudes, which is truly a complete and finished opusculum, all the rest are not in reality one or several opuscula, but rather the remains of one substantial Work that was intended to constitute a Commentary on the whole Gospel of Matthew, as will be said below. Therefore, rather than simply calling them opuscula, we have more suitably, as we think, named the materials we now possess concerning this same holy bishop “writings or opuscula.”

Observe, however, in what order and with what presentation we are having them appear.

After this preface of ours, in which we also discuss in their proper place certain matters that either escaped the diligence of our scholars or exceeded their period, there appear first, at the outset, selected Testimonies of the Ancients concerning Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. In them you will especially enjoy seeing what Saint Jerome wrote either about Chromatius or to Chromatius, what Saint Ambrose wrote, what Rufinus of Aquileia wrote, and what Saint John Chrysostom wrote. What men they were, and men of what authority!

In second place you will receive the Proper Lessons composed by the distinguished Count Francesco Florio, superior of our sacred Order, and approved by the Apostolic See. They are recited in the diocese of Udine at Matins on the feast of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, on 2 December. Until now they had been available only in the proper little book of the Saints of the Diocese; they are now made accessible to scholars, who will gladly welcome them both for the excellence of their diction and for the history of the holy man, drawn from the purest sources and condensed into a brief account.

In third place comes the title-page of the first edition of the writings of Saint Chromatius, produced at Basel in 1528, together with its exceedingly rare edition and the dedicatory letter of John Sichardus. From that letter we learn how highly these writings were valued from the very first moment when they were discovered and given to the public light.

In fourth place comes Andrea Gallandi, who in the Prolegomena to volume VIII of his *Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*, etc., in which the writings of our Saint Chromatius are included, discussed that holy man carefully and learnedly, drawing from what our two distinguished men mentioned above, Fontanini and De Rubeis, wrote at much greater length.

These are the materials that precede the writings or opuscula of Saint Chromatius in our edition. They proclaim the merit both of those materials and of their author, and kindle ever more strongly the desire to read them.

The writings themselves that have reached us follow. We have decided to take them from no other source than the cited volume VIII of Gallandi’s *Bibliotheca*, where they first appear divided into as many Tractates as there are Doxologies, or Glorifications, found in them. Previously they had been divided either into only two parts, as in their first Basel edition, or into three, as in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers* [Col. 0252B] and perhaps other earlier editions.

We have gladly retained in each case the title “Tractate” that Gallandi imposed upon them, even though, as will become clear below, we believe that all of them except one were not written by the holy man for use in preaching.

The singular Tractate, which is first in our edition and which we have also called a Sermon under the title *On the Eight Beatitudes*, was in fact delivered by the holy bishop before a gathered audience. In the Basel edition mentioned above it was called, quite incongruously both with respect to its subject matter and its manner of expression, a *Declamation*. All the others, published there continuously, are called, somewhat less improperly but still with a less suitable designation, a *Dissertation on chapters 5 and 6 of Matthew*.

[Col. 0252C] Although we have retained the term “Tractate” used by Gallandi, we were nevertheless compelled to depart from the order these Tractates occupy in his *Bibliotheca*. Apart from the singular Tractate, or Sermon, on the Eight Beatitudes—which we placed first, as Gallandi himself did, but separated from the number of the others and placed entirely outside their sequence, since it has nothing in common with them except its subject matter, which, because the explanation of the Gospel requires it, is in one other Tractate almost the same, though expressed in a different manner, style, and use of connections—we began the remainder with the Tractate that is number 17 in Gallandi, calling it the first *On chapter 3 of the Gospel of Saint Matthew*.

We called the second *On chapter 3 of Saint Matthew*, which in Gallandi is number 18 and the last. We called the third *On chapter 5 of Saint Matthew*, which there is numbered second. We proceeded similarly with the remaining Tractates in the same order, through chapter 5 and chapter 6, up to Tractate 17, which is the last in our edition and is number 16 in Gallandi, who had placed our first two Tractates last.

The reason for our decision is the text of the Gospel itself. We judged that the expositions on chapter 3 of Matthew, whatever their condition—whether mutilated or interrupted from the rest by some lacuna—ought properly to precede those on chapters 5 and 6.

Gallandi could hardly have failed to notice this, but [X] he perhaps attributed too much authority—or rather too much weight to the error—of the preceding editions, especially the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, where our first two Tractates had in fact been compressed into one and placed last under the title *Fragment*.

For the rest, Sixtus of Siena, whose article on Saint Chromatius is read in the Lyons *Library*, had reviewed these writings of his excellently. He mentioned first what we possess of this holy bishop on chapter 3 of Matthew; second, what survives on chapters 5 and 6; and third, the homily on the Eight Beatitudes, which he rightly also calls elegant.

This ought to have warned the editor of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers* to preserve at least this arrangement himself in organizing the writings or opuscula of Chromatius that he inserted into his collection.

We, however, preferred to begin with the singular Tractate or Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes, both so that we might begin with the holy man’s more excellent and complete work and so that we might avoid beginning with something in a sense truncated at its head, as is the Tractate that, as we have already said, is presented as number one in our edition.

In this edition we devoted our care especially to presenting the writings of our Saint Chromatius in as corrected a form as possible. This was accomplished chiefly by collating those writings with the first Basel edition mentioned above, which, now that manuscript copies are lacking, serves as a manuscript of the highest value; and also with the edition of John Grynaeus in his *Orthodoxographia*, *Monuments of the Holy Fathers*, Basel, 1569, volume II, [Col. 0254A] p. 1192.

In this work of correction we achieved what was most desirable: restoring to its genuine and correct reading the notable text of this holy bishop concerning the mystery of the Trinity, found in Tractate 2, number 2 of our edition. It is read in a thoroughly corrupt form and with an erroneous meaning both in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers* and likewise in Gallandi’s latest edition, although Gallandi himself testifies that he labored considerably, chiefly with the help of the Combefisian excerpts, to correct even the defective readings of other copies in the writings of Chromatius.

The aforementioned first Basel edition, as well as the subsequent edition of John Grynaeus, opened the way for us to restore this text to its integrity. Thereafter Alcuin, or Flaccus Albinus, supplied us with helping hands: he had reproduced the same text, together with texts of many other holy Fathers, in his little book against the heresy of Bishop Felix.

We used both the text reproduced by him, which appears among the works of Alcuin in the edition of the distinguished Abbot Frobenius, volume I, part II, p. 767, and the text that the distinguished Fontanini extracted from a manuscript codex of Alcuin in the Vatican and inserted into his *Aquileian Literary History*, book III, chapter 4, no. 2, where he discusses Saint Chromatius appropriately. The reader will be able to see him below in his proper place.

Here, then, is the text itself, both corrupted and complete, so that anyone may recognize through comparison what has hitherto been read in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers* and also in Gallandi’s latest edition, and what ought rather to have been read, as we provide it for reading in this edition.

### The celebrated text of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, on the most holy mystery of the Trinity

[Note: [Col. 0253] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

*(From the Lyons Library of the Fathers and from the latest edition of Andrea Gallandi.)* [Col. 0253C]

“Therefore, what sort of testimony of the Father concerning the Son is it when he says, ‘This is my Son’? His own, certainly—not by the adoption of grace, nor through the religion of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the property of his kind and the truth of his nature.

“For many of the saints are called sons of God, and are so called; but this one, ‘without compassion’ (*sine compassione*; perhaps a corrupt reading for ‘without comparison’), is the one only-begotten, true, and proper Son of God the Father, born from no one other than the Father. For the true Father is Father and is God; likewise the true Son is shown as Son of the Trinity, since the Father testifies that Christ our Lord and God is his Son; and the Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a mystery of faith, so that we might believe in the true Father, the true Son, and also the true Holy Spirit: three persons, but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance.”

*(Restored to its integrity in our edition.)* [Col. 0254C]

“Consider, therefore, what sort of testimony of the Father concerning the Son it is when he says, ‘This is my Son.’ His own, certainly—not by the adoption of grace, nor through the religion of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the property of his kind and the truth of his nature.

“For many of the saints are called sons of God, and are so called; but this one, without comparison, is the one only-begotten, true, and proper Son of God the Father, born from no one other than the Father. For the true Father is as truly Father as he is true and God; just as the true Son is as truly Son as he is true and Lord.

“Therefore the perfect faith of the Trinity has been revealed, since the Father testifies that Christ our Lord and God is his Son; and the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a mystery of faith, so that we might believe in the true Father, the true Son, and also the true Holy Spirit: three persons, but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance.”

[Col. 0253D] [XII] Having restored this text of Saint Chromatius, which provides a most clear testimony to his faith concerning the most sacred mystery of the Trinity, and having made a few other corrections of lesser importance here and there, we also took from Gallandi all the notes appended to the Tractates of Chromatius. We placed them at the bottom of the pages and added one or two of our own.

These, then, are the matters that the reader needed to know about the writings or opuscula of Saint Chromatius that we are now publishing anew, so that the rationale of our undertaking might not remain hidden from him.

After the writings of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, we judged it useful to present two of his very brief but highly significant Statements, which he delivered at the Council of Aquileia held in 381 under Saint Valerian, bishop, against the Arian bishops Palladius and Secundianus, when he himself was still a presbyter of that same Church of Aquileia.

Even the briefest statements of great men must be regarded as being of the greatest importance. These statements, in fact, already showed Chromatius the presbyter to possess such virtue, faith, and apostolic strength that he would be fully worthy to succeed Valerian in the episcopate.

Chromatius spent eighteen years, or even nineteen, in the episcopate of Aquileia, according to the common reckoning. We therefore reasonably believe that he wrote much for the instruction of the flock entrusted to him, much for the defense of the faith against the especially prevalent errors of the Arians and others, and also against the superstition of the pagans, which still extended widely.

What he himself wrote, beyond what we possess, may not be asserted without testimony and without adequate grounds. Meanwhile, testimony exists, and adequate reasons are not lacking, which affirm and suggest that he also wrote other specific works that have perished. We therefore append, after the works that have been published, at least a brief list of those lost writings.

What has happened more than once to great men, especially those of the earliest antiquity and of the age immediately following it—that writings appear under their names which were the productions of obscure persons and wholly unworthy of enjoying such authority—happened also to our holy Chromatius.

Under his name, and at the same time under that of Saint Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum, who was joined to Chromatius by the closest friendship, two letters appeared addressed to Saint Jerome, together with two replies by Jerome himself to them. These letters were published repeatedly and in many places; they were at times even regarded as genuine, but now, and for some time already, by the common judgment of scholars they are listed among the spurious works both of Chromatius [XIII] and of Jerome.

Nevertheless, we have thought it worthwhile to present these letters here, together with the fictitious replies of the same Saint Jerome and with the critical observations of two illustrious men, placing them last, so that nothing might be lacking from this Chromatian edition that is ordinarily desired and supplied in the latest editions of the holy Fathers.

This concludes what we have to say about the writings of Chromatius presented in this volume, and about the apparatus and order in which they appear.

But what of the life of Saint Chromatius—of the period in which he flourished, of his deeds, of the years of his life and episcopate; what of the condition of the Church of Aquileia at that time and other similar matters, which are usually investigated and ought to be elucidated in the case of every ancient author by the person who undertakes the edition of his works?

Our two most learned fellow countrymen, men of the first rank among the writers of the immediately preceding age, undertook to adorn this field: Justus Fontanini, archbishop of Ancyra, and Bernard Maria De Rubeis, of the Order of Preachers.

[Col. 0256A] We therefore trust that our decision will be approved by gracious readers: in place of what our weakness might have been able to provide on this subject, we present the complete studies of these distinguished men. Although they were previously published among the works of each author, which deal with broader subjects, they will nevertheless rejoice to be reprinted here, as though in their proper place, namely after the writings of the Holy Bishop whom they specifically discuss.

First, then, we give the study of the distinguished Fontanini, which he wrote while living in Rome in 1713, as he himself testifies, and which appears in book III of his *Aquileian Literary History*. That work itself, however, did not see the light until after his death, when it was printed at Rome in 1714.

After Tillemont, Fontanini was the very first to undertake to treat the subject of Saint Chromatius in every respect, with a vast apparatus of learning and criticism. He brought the matter to such a point that, for the period in which he wrote, nothing more complete or more careful could have been desired. This is also the judgment of Andrea Gallandi in the brief piece about Chromatius that we mentioned above and shall append below.

Nevertheless, we have been compelled to place a considerable number of our notes beneath this study by Fontanini, both to explain certain matters that the distinguished man perhaps did not express with sufficient clarity, and to record others that did not satisfy scholars of a later age; finally, also, to correct certain things in reality—either matters that he could not have known when he wrote or matters that, being occupied with other very serious concerns, he failed to notice.

The distinguished De Rubeis treated this same subject of Saint Chromatius after Fontanini, but before Fontanini’s *Aquileian Literary History* was published, from chapter 10 through chapter 13 of his *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, which were published at Strasbourg—or Venice—in 1740.

We have therefore appended these chapters to Fontanini’s study, as a second study by this learned man on the same subject. In it you may indeed miss much concerning Chromatius that Fontanini gathered with a more extensive scholarly apparatus, but you will also find much that De Rubeis completed more precisely, especially matters relating to the vicissitudes of Origen’s works [Col. 0256D] and to the person of Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, who was so fiercely harassed because of those works, although our Saint Chromatius honored him with the greatest devotion throughout his life.

To these chapters of the *Aquileian Monuments* we added something else from De Rubeis: namely, what he wrote as numbers 5 and 6 of chapter 18 of his *Dissertations of Varied Learning*, etc., which appeared at Venice in 1762, after he had read Fontanini’s work, the *Aquileian Literary History*. There you will understand his observations on what Fontanini had written both concerning the ordination of Chromatius as bishop of Aquileia and concerning the title of Roman bishop bestowed upon Chromatius in the first Basel edition of his writings.

Here, then, kind reader, is an outline of our edition of the writings or opuscula of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. Here also are the reasons that may perhaps show that our labor in preparing this edition was not useless, and may indicate that we have in some sense contributed something new, even if we have not produced new materials.

This preface of ours could end here. But lest this subject appear to have been left entirely untouched by us, and because after what Fontanini and De Rubeis contributed to its elucidation there remain some matters that deserve to be considered and illuminated in one way or another, do not be displeased if, although we are far from equal to the great men who preceded us in this undertaking, we too seize upon something—whether it escaped their diligence or, given the time in which they wrote, could not be treated by them sufficiently or at all.

To begin with the family of Chromatius: there were only two brothers, Chromatius and Eusebius, with no third anonymous brother such as Fontanini had proposed. What should be thought about Eusebius, who is known to have been a deacon of Aquileia while Chromatius was a presbyter and who was afterward raised to the honor of the episcopate?

Rufinus testifies to this in book I, no. 4, of his *Apology for Saint Jerome*, writing:

“About thirty years ago I …, having been regenerated by the grace of baptism, received the seal of faith through the holy men Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, men of the highest reputation and proven excellence in the Church of God, of whom one was then a presbyter under Valerian of blessed memory, another an archdeacon, and the other a deacon; and at the same time he was my father and teacher in the Creed and the Faith.”

Rufinus wrote this around the year 400 or 401, according to De Rubeis in his dissertation on Rufinus, chapters 3 and 4. Accordingly, the event of his baptism, which he says took place at Aquileia about thirty years earlier, at the time when Eusebius, the brother of Chromatius, then a presbyter, was a deacon, belongs—as De Rubeis correctly calculated—to the year 371 or 372.

After this event, therefore, since Eusebius too was made a bishop, according to Rufinus himself, of what see or place should he be regarded as bishop?

That Saint Eusebius, bishop of Bologna, took part in the Council of Aquileia held under Saint Valerian, bishop, in 381 against the Arian bishops Palladius and Secundianus, at which Chromatius also was present, still a presbyter of Aquileia, is established by the Acts of that council, which appear in volume II of the Paris Maurist edition of the works of Saint Ambrose and in the collections of councils.

Was, then, the bishop of the Church of Bologna, Eusebius, the brother of our Chromatius? If the chronology is taken into account, Tillemont says in his *Memoirs to Serve the Ecclesiastical History*, etc., volume XI, note 1 on Saint Chromatius, there is nothing to prevent this from being believed. He nevertheless thinks that the Eusebius who was the brother of our Chromatius was by no means Eusebius, bishop of Bologna. He is led to this conclusion by the consideration that Eusebius, bishop of Bologna, may at some time have been married, as can be inferred from Saint Ambrose; whereas this cannot be said of Eusebius, the brother of our Chromatius, since these two brothers are called by Saint Jerome “the twin Samuels raised in the temple,” in Letter 7 of Vallarsi’s edition, addressed to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, which is assigned to the year 373.

The learned Benedictine editors of the works of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, count two Bolognese Eusebiuses of the same period: one a noble married citizen with children, with whom the holy Doctor himself maintained close relations, and the other the bishop of Bologna.

On this hypothesis Tillemont’s difficulty would disappear, and Eusebius, bishop of Bologna, could be Eusebius himself, the brother of our Chromatius. But who could assert on this single foundation [Col. 0258B] that he really was the bishop of Bologna?

Restoration notes: All canonical column locators from 0258C through 0268D and the missing printed boundaries XVIII, XIX, XX, XXV, and XXVII were restored at their associated translated passages.

Our most distinguished Count Francesco Florius, whom we mentioned above, showed a certain inclination to recognize Eusebius, the brother of our Chromatius, in Eusebius, bishop of Bologna. In a certain Note to the *Bachiarius* edited by him at Rome in 1748, p. 57, he writes:

> “Chromatius, presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, and Eusebius, his brother, distinguished by the office of deacon . . . . both . . . . attained episcopal dignity: the former, certainly, succeeded our Valerian; the latter, however, most holily governed a Church of uncertain name (unless it was Bologna).”

[Col. 0258C] Indeed, from his papers that remain with the nobleman Count Filippo Flori, the son of that same brother and heir to his learning—whom, out of respect and gratitude, we name here—we plainly understand that he later extended that inclination of his so far that he almost took it as certain that Eusebius, the brother of our Chromatius, was Eusebius himself, bishop of Bologna. For he left the following written in his own hand:

> “It has occurred to me to make known an ornament of the Church of Bologna, although she is already very rich in ancient and modern ones. At the same time, however, everyone will see that, without offending the truth, I am, so to speak, serving my own cause and fulfilling an act of piety toward that most noble Church which for a long time was my mother and which nourished me while she lived. In a few words I shall propose my conjecture. [Col. 0258D] Saint Eusebius, bishop of Bologna, is that Eusebius, deacon of Aquileia, of whom, as we shall see, Saint Jerome and Rufinus speak with great praise. There is nothing that opposes this conjecture, and many observations combine to make it highly probable.”

Here, then, is the opinion of that most distinguished man, disclosed in writing and presented in such a way that he sufficiently declared that he had already weighed the matter thoroughly and had nothing left but to set forth the arguments that had led him to embrace the same view. He did not do so, doubtless because he was hindered by other concerns—unless we should rather say that the work he had undertaken on this subject has perished.

[Col. 0259A] We too gladly embrace the opinion of so great a man, without separating it in the least from the moderation with which he himself proceeded, calling it a conjecture. Meanwhile, we congratulate both our Chromatius and ourselves on the sanctity of this Eusebius, likewise ours; and also on the veneration which he enjoys among the people of Bologna on 26 September. Concerning this veneration, Prosper Lambertini, later Benedict XIV, wrote very learnedly—although saying absolutely nothing about this holy man’s Aquileian origin—in his *Annotations on the Acts of Certain Saints whose Office and Mass are celebrated, for the most part without proper Lessons, in the Diocese of Bologna*, etc., Bologna, 1740. This work was also rendered into Latin; it may be found in vol. X of the works of the same Pope Benedict XIV, Rome, 1751.

[Col. 0259B] Nevertheless, since the opportunity presents itself, we may not pass over in silence the dates assigned there by the aforementioned Lambertini to this holy Eusebius, according to what he calls a more accurate chronology: namely, that Eusebius began his episcopate at Bologna in the year of Christ 370 and died in the year 400.

Our Aquileian documents, to speak frankly, do not agree very well with these dates. For Eusebius, the brother of Chromatius, was a deacon of the Church of Aquileia not only in the year 371, or even 372, when Rufinus received baptism at Aquileia under his ministry, as we have seen, but also in the year 373, when Jerome wrote to him, Chromatius, and Jovinus, all residing at Aquileia, without mentioning any episcopal dignity. Moreover, Eusebius of Aquileia—who later became a bishop, as Rufinus testifies—had already died in the year 396, as appears from another letter of Jerome to Bishop Heliodorus, likewise belonging to that year. [Col. 0259C] In all these references we consistently cite the edition and chronology of Vallarsius. How, then, can the episcopate at Bologna of our Eusebius of Aquileia, the brother of Chromatius, be reconciled with this difference in dates, so that the Eusebius of Aquileia who was bishop of Bologna may be one and the same person?

Yet this difference in dates is not, in truth, so great as it seems to us that it could overthrow the conjecture of our most distinguished Florius, which we have embraced, or drive us from the opinion we have formed in its favor. [Col. 0259D] For where monuments are lacking, we are always in uncertainty when we attempt to assign the years of Christ to events or persons of the first five and more centuries, as everyone knows.

Lambertini, moreover, produces no monuments in the work cited in support of the dates attributed to Saint Eusebius of Bologna. Meanwhile, the fact that these dates—370 and 400—are absolute and, so to speak, round numbers, assigned even by very exact chronologists without the addition or subtraction of any other number at either point, readily gives rise to the presumption that the chronologists themselves were uncertain when assigning these dates.

[XVIII] Our own very firm monuments in no way prevent Eusebius, the brother of Chromatius, from having been appointed bishop of Bologna after the year 373 of Jerome’s letter to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius—or even during that same year in which the letter was written. [Col. 0260A] Those same monuments also warn us to regard Eusebius, the brother of Chromatius, as already dead by the year 396. What, then, should be inferred from this?

That more accurate chronology which Lambertini mentions, perhaps lacking its own reliable and invincible documentary evidence, may indeed have been careful to assign at least approximately the period of Eusebius of Bologna’s episcopate—namely, a period extending between the years 370 and 400—without wishing to assert strictly and precisely that these were truly and properly the exact years in which his episcopate began and in which his death occurred.

And behold, unless we are mistaken, the chronological difficulty—which is perhaps the chief difficulty in this matter—can be removed in a brief and easy way, entirely consistent with circumstances that are for the most part uncertain. [Col. 0260B] We may therefore be more inclined to recognize in Eusebius of Bologna that very Eusebius who was the brother of our Chromatius. This would certainly be exceedingly pleasing and honorable to us Aquileians, and most welcome to the people of Bologna themselves. They would thereby receive this further glory: that they might rightly believe their bishop, Eusebius by name, renowned for holiness in the fourth century of the Church, to have come from the clergy of the Church of Aquileia, so greatly praised by Saint Jerome, and to have had as his brother the bishop of that same Church, Chromatius, whose name alone is the highest possible praise.

[XVII]

[Col. 0260C] Meanwhile, why should the very name of Eusebius, borne by the brother of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, not also indicate a family of Eusebii—and indeed an Aquileian family, from which both brothers originated?

Fontaninus most firmly asserted that our Chromatius was Aquileian by birth. De Rubeis did not depart very far from his view when he readily made him either Romatinus or Concordianus—two places that at that time belonged properly to the diocese of Aquileia and were situated not far from the city of Aquileia.

After those two men had written about Chromatius’ homeland, several distinguished monuments came to light from the most fertile ruins of Aquileia. These monuments now make their first mention of a certain Eusebian family, unquestionably Aquileian. They were recently illustrated [XIX] and published by the most distinguished Angelo Maria Cortinovi, provost of this college of Saint Paul at Udine, who has lately died among us.

[Col. 0260D] From these monuments taken together, Cortinovi argues that a certain—and indeed distinguished—family of Eusebii existed at Aquileia in the fourth and fifth centuries of Christ. He also readily conjectures that our Chromatius and his brother Eusebius belonged, at least in some manner, to this same family.

For at that time names were propagated from grandfathers and fathers to sons and grandsons, and they already constituted something like family surnames. Although our Eusebius is named after Chromatius by Saint Jerome in Letters 7 and 8 of Vallarsius’ edition because Chromatius was then a presbyter of Aquileia while Eusebius was only a deacon, Eusebius nevertheless appears to have been older than Chromatius. [Col. 0261A] He therefore bore the name of the Eusebian family, since in the year of Christ 381 he was already bishop of Bologna at the Council of Aquileia, as we infer from what was said above, while Chromatius was still only a presbyter of Aquileia.

Eusebius also died before Chromatius, as we learn from the same Jerome, Letter 60, no. 19, to Heliodorus, which, as we have already said, belongs to the year 396.

From this Aquileian Eusebian family, itself especially distinguished, as the same monuments teach us, we readily believe that our Chromatius came forth. From this he derives no small praise: he adorned the distinction of his origin with holiness of life, splendor of doctrine, and every virtue worthy of a bishop, together with his brother Eusebius.

[Col. 0261B] The monuments of the Aquileian Eusebian family were published in print by Cortinovi in his dissertation written in Italian, entitled *On a Greek Inscription of Aquileia*, or rather in the dedicatory letter prefixed to it and addressed to the Most Eminent Cardinal Borgia, Bassano, 1792. They were also published in another dissertation, likewise written in Italian, entitled *On a Bas-relief of Constantius and Julian*, which appeared in the literary fascicles entitled *Memoirs for the Service of Literary and Civil History*, Venice, at the press of Pasquali, 1799, March and April, p. 3 and following.

Another matter now presses upon us, one that concerns Chromatius himself, about whom we are writing: namely, his writings, or *Opuscula*, which we are issuing in this new edition. First of all, are the works published under his name, and now published again, genuinely his?

[Col. 0261C] We must admit, with Tillemont, Ceillier, and others, that the ancient writers who deliberately left us information about authors of their own or [XX] earlier ages, and who recorded their writings—whether universally known, lost, or concealed—are completely silent about all the works written by Chromatius.

Nor can it be concealed that our Chromatius first became known to the literary world as having left something in writing when his works emerged at Basel in 1528 from an ancient manuscript, through the good judgment and labor of Johann Sichard. Nevertheless, Blessed Albinus Flaccus, or Alcuin, abbot, had mentioned these writings much earlier in his booklet against the heresy of Bishop Felix.

[Col. 0261D] Tillemont, in the work and volume cited above, p. 539 of the Venetian Pitterian edition, and likewise in note 2, p. 653, although candidly admitting that the writings attributed to our Chromatius are worthy of his reputation, and that no other known Chromatius exists to whom they could more suitably be assigned, nevertheless adds:

> “It would be desirable to have stronger proofs that they are his than the title of the manuscripts that attribute them to Chromace, Roman bishop.”

[Col. 0262A] Our Fontaninus understood the force of these words of Tillemont. He therefore devoted himself entirely to the *Study on Chromatius* which we publish after the *Writings*, or *Opuscula*, in order by every possible means to confirm that they correspond most closely to the name they bear—that of our Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia—and to refute the objections that someone might wish to press on the basis of the silence of the ancients, especially Jerome.

Whether or not Ceillier saw the arguments of our Fontaninus—an author otherwise sufficiently well known even in France—he writes in his *General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. X, chap. 3, in terms not very different from Tillemont:

> “We find nothing of the writings of Saint Chromace in any of those who have left us catalogues of ecclesiastical writers. Nevertheless, there are some manuscripts in which the name of Chromace is found at the head of three discourses that have been printed in the *Library of the Fathers* . . . . [Col. 0262B] The best that can be said is that the writings bearing the name of Saint Chromace are not unworthy of him, and that no bishop of this name is known to whom they could be attributed with greater justice.”

Here, then, is Ceillier’s reproduction of what Tillemont had supplied, so that even in his view it is still not certain and established that those writings circulating under the name of our Chromatius are in fact his—especially because they are not mentioned in the catalogues of the ancients.

[XXI]

[Col. 0262C] We therefore reply to Ceillier with what Fontaninus left written concerning Tillemont’s observation. Although the catalogues of the ancients who listed the works of ecclesiastical writers are silent, we nevertheless hold it to be indubitable and certain that our holy Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, is truly the author of the writings published under his name.

Whatever may be said about the title “Roman bishop,” with which they were labeled from the first Basel edition—concerning which both Fontaninus and De Rubeis have spoken at length, and to which we too intend to add something below—nothing further need be investigated or desired. It is not as though, because the ancient catalogues are silent, the case concerning the writings of Chromatius were still undecided, or as though no other rule of criticism could compensate for the deficiency of those catalogues in recognizing the truth, as Fontaninus has fully demonstrated.

[Col. 0262D] The acute critic Johann Clericus recognized the authority of ancient catalogues in judging the genuineness of works. In his *Critical Art*, part III, section 2, chapter 3, no. 1, he established the following aphorism:

> “Writings of which there is no mention in ancient catalogues, and which were not mentioned by any writer of the immediately succeeding centuries, ought for the most part to be judged fictitious, or at least regarded as suspect.”

But here is what he himself added in no. 15:

> “Although the authority of our aphorism generally remains unimpaired, we nevertheless cannot deny that several excellent writers survive, whose contemporaries—those, at least, who have survived—made no mention of them.”

That critic was therefore convinced that ancient catalogues do not always possess such weight that, even when they are silent, the truth cannot be discovered by other rules of criticism when judging the genuineness of works attributed to an author in manuscript codices.

[Col. 0263A] In the same place Fontaninus produced examples of authors and works known throughout the Church, about which critics have no doubt, although neither Gennadius nor Isidore nor other foreign cataloguers remembered them. Clericus, in the passage recently cited, also adds among ecclesiastical authors the famous Athenagoras, whose name and works, as he himself says, were nevertheless unknown to Eusebius and Jerome.

Let us add one point on this matter, demonstrating the occasional carelessness and negligence of the authors of literary journals, even the more celebrated ones—much to the inconvenience of scholars and to the detriment of the literary world, although such journals were established precisely to assist it.

[Col. 0263B] In the famous journal of French literature entitled *Journal des Scavans*, in March 1745, there appeared a synopsis or summary of the tenth volume of the work of Remy Ceillier mentioned above. In chapter 3 Ceillier discusses Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, and his writings.

[XXII]

Here is what the author of that journal—or rather of that article in the journal—writes about Ceillier’s opinion concerning the writings of our Chromatius:

> “Dom Remy Ceillier once again finds himself in contradiction with M. Fontanini. In the work we have just cited, in which he shows himself very zealous for the glory of the writers of Aquileia, this scholar attributes to Saint Chromace eighteen homilies on Saint Matthew, and endeavors to prove that M. de Tillemont is mistaken in doubting that they are by Saint Chromace, although he believed them to be by an ancient and learned author. [Col. 0263C] Dom Remy Ceillier, on the contrary, among the eighteen homilies finds only three that can be attributed to this saint; and even then he shows that it is highly uncertain whether he is their author.”

So writes the author of this French journal, or rather of this article in the journal.

But how could anyone write in this way who had carefully read both Fontaninus and Ceillier himself, and who had at least looked at the writings of Chromatius as they appear in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, to which Ceillier was referring?

Ceillier certainly did not dream of selecting from the eighteen homilies mentioned by Fontaninus only three that could be considered the genuine offspring of Saint Chromatius. [Col. 0263D] Without even mentioning Fontaninus—whom he perhaps never knew in connection with what he wrote about Chromatius—and without indicating the number of homilies first proposed by Fontaninus himself, Ceillier reviewed all the surviving writings of Chromatius in three parts, exactly as they appear in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*. He gave his judgment concerning them as they appear there, and these works, taken as a whole, constitute Fontaninus’ eighteen homilies. He made no separation whatever of any part of these writings.

But this is incidental. We mention it so that no one, on the basis of this false and utterly inept report in the French journal, may unfairly accuse Ceillier of excessive critical hostility toward the writings of our Chromatius that we possess.

[Col. 0264A] Meanwhile, we also consider it useful to know that the founders of another well-known and outstanding literary work, the Trevoltians, were extremely accurate in this matter and wrote entirely in accordance with Ceillier’s view. Their work was entitled *Memoirs for the History of the Sciences and of the Fine Arts*. They published their account in November of the preceding year, 1744. Had the author of the aforementioned article in the French journal, *Journal des Scavans*, consulted their genuine and straightforward synopsis of Ceillier’s chapter on Chromatius of Aquileia, he perhaps would never, in March of the following year, 1745, have departed so far both from the truth and from Ceillier’s meaning.

[XXIII]

We must now investigate the writings themselves, or *Opuscula*: what they really are, why and in what order they were composed, and on what occasion our holy Chromatius produced them.

[Col. 0264B] The oldest indication of these writings is found in Blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, abbot, in his booklet against the heresy of Bishop Felix. There, taking all these writings together, he calls them *Chromatius’ Book on the Eight Beatitudes*.

Perhaps this was the title borne by the manuscript codex of Chromatius that Abbot Alcuin used. Yet the work Chromatius appropriately wrote *On the Eight Beatitudes* is one thing, and the passage cited by Alcuin among the other testimonies of the holy Fathers against the heresy of Bishop Felix is another.

The first edition of these writings, which, as we have seen, was published at Basel in 1528, divided them into two parts. It called the first a *Dissertation on Chapters V and VI of Matthew*, although at the end it continuously included what Chromatius had written on the third chapter. The second it called simply a *Declamation* of the same kind.

[Col. 0264C] Who does not see at least the obscurity, if not also the inappropriateness, of the titles in this Basel edition?

[Col. 0264D] We cannot say in what order the writings of our Chromatius appeared, or under what title they were listed, in Martin Lipsius’ *Micropresbyticon of Certain Brief Theologians*, first published at Louvain in 1546 and then at Basel in 1550, p. 412; nor in Johann Herold’s *Orthodoxographia of Sacred Theology*, Basel, 1555, vol. I, p. 430; nor in Laurentius Cumdius’ *Library of Homilies*, Lyons, 1588, vol. II, p. 1170.

Fontaninus mentions these collections in his most learned *Study*. We have not been able to see them today, especially after the recent, most grievous, and more-than-Vandalic destruction that drove so many libraries of the regular religious communities of this city from their homes.

We have, however, seen at least Johann Grynaeus’ *Monuments of the Holy Fathers, Orthodoxographia*, printed at Basel in 1569. There, in vol. II, p. 1192, we observed the writings of our Chromatius divided into two parts.

The first consists of the discourse that also occupies the first place in our edition and bears there a sufficiently appropriate title: *An Elegant Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes*. In the upper part of the page the word *declamation* also appears, since that was the term this sermon had borne in Sichard’s earlier edition.

[Col. 0265A] The second part consists of the remainder of what we possess from Chromatius, under the title: *Several Treatises on the Fifth Chapter of Matthew and Part of the Sixth, Equally Distinguished for Learning and Piety*. To this is appended, without a separate division, what remains on the third chapter, under the simple designation *A Fragment of Another Treatise Not Yet Published in Its Entirety*. Here too, in the upper part of the pages, the word *dissertation* is added, taken from Sichard’s earlier edition.

[XXIV]

In the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, the writings of Saint Chromatius are presented in three parts. The first two are initially designated under one title, *Two Sermons on the Eight Beatitudes*. The second then bears its own title, namely, *A Sermon on the Fifth Chapter of Matthew and Part of the Sixth, Equally Distinguished for Learning and Piety*, although both are always entitled *On the Eight Beatitudes* in the upper part of the pages.

[Col. 0265B] The third is called *A Fragment of a Treatise on the Saying, “I Must Be Baptized by You,” etc., Matthew III, 4*.

Finally, in the latest *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, etc., of Andrea Gallandi, these writings are called, more suitably and accurately than ever before, although still not adequately for the matter itself, *Eighteen Treatises on the Gospel of Saint Matthew*. Fontaninus had earlier called them eighteen homilies in his *Study on Saint Chromatius*, which we publish below.

After indicating these various titles—which we have judged neither unpleasant nor useless to record—let us now say what the writings of Chromatius that we are reprinting actually seem to be.

[Col. 0265C] The treatise that Gallandius listed first among the eighteen, which we too have placed first, although we have not called it “the first,” is a separate treatise, or sermon, or discourse. It is in fact elegant, as Sixtus of Siena and Johann Grynaeus called it. It should properly bear the separate title *On the Eight Beatitudes*, and in no way forms part of the other treatises.

This was certainly delivered orally by the holy bishop on the occasion of some market at which a large gathering of people was present, as can be gathered clearly enough from its wording. Nothing more distinguished survives among the writings of the holy bishop, whether one considers the aim of the discourse, its style, or its opening, development, and conclusion. It may also rightly be counted among the more distinguished writings of Fathers of the same age and genre.

What, then, should be thought about the remaining works?

[Col. 0265D] With Tillemont and others, we hold that the remaining treatises—which in our edition number not eighteen but seventeen—are not separate homilies, nor even distinct treatises, but rather appear to be the surviving portions of [XXV] a complete Commentary which Chromatius wrote on Matthew.

We also hold that Chromatius wrote this Commentary not for use in preaching to the people, as he wrote the Treatise or Discourse on the Eight Beatitudes, but especially for the pious and fruitful reading of the faithful.

We infer this from his own words, found in our Treatise 5, elsewhere numbered 4, no. 2, where he writes:

> “And many similar things which we have passed over, lest we cause weariness to the readers.”

[Col. 0266A] As far as we know, this point has not been considered by others who have written about Chromatius. Why did the holy bishop not express his mind more clearly on this matter in the beginning of his Commentary, which, together with other parts of it, is missing?

If we may also conjecture the occasion that perhaps led Saint Chromatius to prepare this nourishment of reading for his people, I should say that it was no other than the one that moved him to compel Rufinus of Aquileia, his presbyter, to render Eusebius’ Greek *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin.

For Alaric’s invasion of Italy through the territory of Aquileia, in the year of Christ 400, devastated fields, herds, and men far and wide, as Rufinus himself says in his preface to Chromatius to the Latin *History of Eusebius* that he had produced. It threatened the peoples entrusted by God to the holy bishop with deadly destruction.

[Col. 0266B] Therefore, in order to seek some remedy for the afflicted people—by which, as Rufinus adds, sick minds might be withdrawn from the contagion of the approaching evil and kept occupied with better pursuits—Chromatius instructed his presbyter Rufinus to translate Eusebius’ *Ecclesiastical History* from Greek into Latin. By listening to it, the minds of the hearers, captivated while avidly seeking knowledge of past events, would in some measure receive forgetfulness of the evils then occurring.

[Col. 0266C] Why, then, should the holy bishop Chromatius not also have wished to contribute his own labor toward this same end, according to the distinction of doctrine and holiness in which he excelled? Why should he not therefore have undertaken a work worthy of a bishop—namely, a Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew—which he could at that very time place before the faithful for reading, especially because the Latin Church, at least, was then greatly lacking in works of this kind?

Moreover, although in the year 400 of Christ the faithful living in the western regions did not possess an abundance of Latin explanations of the Gospel—and perhaps most of them scarcely knew even Hilary of Poitiers’ work on Matthew or Ambrose of Milan’s commentaries on Luke—it is useful to recall here that the Church of Aquileia already possessed commentaries on the Gospels, the work of Fortunatianus, bishop of that Church before Saint Valerian.

[Col. 0266D] Saint Jerome had asked Paul of Concordia to send these works to him in the East, calling them “a pearl of the Gospel,” in Letter 10, no. 3, of Vallarsius’ edition, belonging to the year 373. Saint Jerome himself mentions them in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 97, stating that Fortunatianus wrote commentaries on the Gospels, arranged under headings, but in a brief and rustic style—or, as he says elsewhere, briefly and in a rustic style. These works have long since perished.

Fortunatianus has a bad reputation among the common people, accused of Arian doctrine and of the weakened constancy of Liberius, the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0267A] But after our most distinguished Fontaninus had already admirably cleared him of both charges in *Literary History of Aquileia*, book III, chapter 2, the most learned Zaccaria recently purified and defended him eloquently in his dissertation *On the Fictitious Fall of Liberius*, which is the seventh dissertation in vol. I of his *Latin Dissertations on Matters Relating to the History and Antiquities of the Church*, Foligno, 1781.

At the same time, our own most diligent and industrious Johann Peter von Stua did likewise in a special dissertation written in Italian, *Whether Fortunatianus, Bishop of Aquileia, Should or Should Not Be Counted among the Arians*, printed in 1782 in Calogerian—or rather Mandellian—*New Collection of Scientific and Philological Opuscula*, vol. XXXVII.

[Col. 0267B] Nothing, therefore, could Chromatius have provided his Aquileian people at that time more desirably than an Evangelical Commentary composed by himself. In it they could profitably exercise themselves in a subject of doctrine and piety that was already in some sense familiar to them, while nevertheless desiring to be instructed in it with fuller and more polished expression because of the brevity and inarticulate style of the older work.

[XXVI]

This observation enables us readily to conclude that our holy Chromatius not only began his Commentary at the very beginning of Matthew’s Gospel and carried it without interruption to the passage in the sixth chapter where our seventeenth treatise ends, but also proceeded beyond that point and actually provided a Commentary illuminating the whole Gospel of Matthew. Tillemont, following Sixtus of Siena and others, likewise held this view.

[Col. 0267C] The same reasoning that undoubtedly persuades us that he began the Commentary at the very beginning of the Gospel and carried it to the place where the aforementioned seventeenth treatise now ends likewise compels us to believe that the holy bishop did not leave his work unfinished.

This is especially so because the need to instruct the people and [XXVII] raise them up amid so many adversities was pressing, and because he does not seem to have lacked time to complete the work he had begun—even if we suppose that he undertook it only in the year 400, when Alaric invaded Italy.

Why the complete Commentary has not come down to us, we cannot say. So many other works of the holy Fathers and of other ancient authors have reached us mutilated. Moreover, the extremely harsh fate that Aquileia and the whole Aquileian region suffered after Chromatius is too well known to require explanation here. Perhaps this prevented Chromatius’ writings from surviving intact, just as it did so many other works undoubtedly left by the bishops who preceded and followed him.

[Col. 0267D] But what are we to say about the doxologies, or glorifications, read at the end of the individual homilies or treatises?

From these, Fontaninus in particular, and also De Rubeis, attempted to infer that these were genuine homilies, either brought together into one work or cut out from an already existing work and adapted for preaching.

Neither view appeals to us, since we have already stated that these remnants seem to us to be portions of a complete Commentary on Matthew, which Saint Chromatius deliberately wrote so that it might be read by the faithful.

[Col. 0268A] Nor are we moved by the doxologies, frequently repeated at the end of each treatise or homily, such as:

> “The only-begotten Son of God, who is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.”

Or:

> “Through Christ our Lord, who is blessed for ever.”

Or simply:

> “Through Christ our Lord.”

Or:

> “To whom be praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

Or finally the longer form:

> “To whom belong honor, praise, and glory, together with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.”

We do not think that such doxologies constitute the completion or conclusion of a homily or treatise in our Chromatius.

[Col. 0268B] For the holy bishop, most learned in the Scriptures, certainly knew how often Saint Paul the Apostle, as well as Peter, used such doxologies in their letters. Both of them employed them throughout the course of their epistles, as an outpouring of the soul toward God, the Creator of all, and toward the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior. They are not signs of the completion either of the letters or even, on more than one occasion, of some particular subject being discussed in the letter.

[XXVIII]

Thus we read in Romans 1:25:

> “They served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.”

Yet the Apostle does not there conclude either his letter or even his discourse on the empty wisdom of the ancient philosophers, which was his subject.

Similarly, in Romans 9:5, we have:

> “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.”

Nor does he thereby conclude either his letter or his discourse concerning the promises made to Abraham, about which he is speaking there.

[Col. 0268C] Another doxology may be seen in Romans 11:36. Although the subject discussed there comes to an end, the letter certainly does not. Another appears in 2 Corinthians 11:31, where neither the letter nor the subject comes to an end. Finally, other examples may be indicated in 1 Timothy 6:16; 2 Timothy 4:18; Galatians 1:4; and 1 Peter 4:11.

What else, then, can the doxologies used by Chromatius in his Commentary—which he composed for the sake of reading—be understood to be, except certain outpourings of his soul and of his most fervent charity, uttered in the course of writing for the praise of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as the apostles Peter and Paul regularly did in their letters?

[Col. 0268D] Nor are examples of this kind of doxology lacking before the end of letters, treatises, or sermons in the works of the ancient Fathers. You can therefore readily understand them as outpourings of the souls of those holy men in the course of writing, rather than simply as conclusions of speech or writing.

One need only consult Letter 1 of Saint Pope Clement to the Corinthians. Frequent doxologies are found throughout the course of that lengthy letter, namely in numbers 20, 22, 38, 43, and 50, in addition to two others at the end of the letter, numbers 58 and 59.

In Cotelerius’ *Apostolic Fathers*, where this letter of the holy pontiff appears in volume I, one may also see a learned note that clarifies this matter. It is found there as note 4, p. 161, of the Amsterdam edition of 1724.
