Another explanation of the use of such doxologies, which we have inferred by conjecture, may preferably be proposed in the case of our Chromatius [Col. 0269A], although it does not exclude the former. Since, as was previously stated and confirmed, the holy Bishop wrote his Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Matthew for the devout reading of the faithful, why should he not have placed doxologies here and there, as though also admonishing the reader either to pause at each one or even to bring the reading to an end for that occasion, lest, burdened by excessive reading, he lose the fruit of his reading? Indeed, the doxologies used by Chromatius are arranged in such a way that a sufficient portion of reading lies between one and the next, and none of them interrupts the order of the discourse or divides its subject matter. Moreover, lest the subject matter in some way be divided, he made two sections in the remains we possess of his Commentary [Col. 0269B] that are more than twice as long, without any intervening doxology: the first is the section that constitutes our third treatise, in which the eight Beatitudes are discussed according to the order of the sacred text. A doxology certainly concludes it, but he wished to separate it with none inserted within it. The other is the section comprising our fourteenth treatise, which is an outstanding exposition of the Lord’s Prayer. It too ends with a doxology, as do the others, but none at all is inserted within it.

The doxologies themselves used by Chromatius, however, require some observation on our part. Some refer to God, without any particular mention of the Persons, as in treatise 13: “reaching God, who is accustomed to hear the prayer of the one praying, who is blessed for ever. Amen.” Others are directed to Christ [Col. 0269C], our Lord and Savior, as in treatise 12: “before our Lord and Savior, who is blessed for ever. Amen.” Finally, some distinctly name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as in treatise 2: “and to be endowed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit: through whom praise and glory are due to the Father and to the Son for ever and ever. Amen”; and again in treatise 14: “the Lord (Jesus Christ) clearly manifests: to whom honor, praise, and glory are due, together with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now, and always, and for ever and ever. Amen.”

What, then, is the meaning of this diversity of doxologies in Saint Chromatius, and in one and the same writing of his? Perhaps it will not be unreasonable to conjecture that the holy Bishop did this deliberately, so that the faithful might learn from him various formulas of glorification, which they too might use in ordinary speech, especially when conversing about divine matters. We may also reasonably suppose that he did this so that at one time he might profess faith in the one Godhead, against the folly of the pagans by whom Christ’s faithful were still surrounded; at another, the divinity of the Son, against the Arian heretics, who at that time did not cease attacking the Catholic faith; at another, the Trinity of Persons, against the Sabellians, whose errors had not yet entirely fallen into disuse; and finally, the divinity also of the Holy Spirit, against the Macedonian heretics who had arisen in his own age and had been condemned by the general Council of Constantinople in the year 381.

[Col. 0270A] With regard to the last of these, it is especially pleasing to us to recall a man of outstanding and universal learning, Stephen Anthony Morcelli. In one of his most learned annotations [XXX] to his edition, printed at Venice in Greek and Latin, of Saint Gregory of Agrigentum’s Explanation of Ecclesiastes, on page 42, while discussing the clausulae, or doxologies, with which the ancient Fathers used to conclude their letters and other writings, he says that they scarcely ever did so in any other way than by invoking Jesus Christ alone, with mention of the Father made rarely and of the Holy Spirit more rarely still. “But from the time,” he continues, “when Macedonius the heresiarch began to rave and undertook to spread that wicked and impious doctrine concerning the Holy Spirit; while the holy bishops everywhere protested, it gradually became customary for everyone, as a mark of Catholic profession, to conclude his books, prayers, and homilies with the invocation of the three divine Persons.” As examples he then cites the clausulae of the Greek Fathers Saints Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Basil; and finally concludes: “You will now find similar clausulae throughout the writings of the other Fathers who followed these.”

Behold, then, among those “other Fathers,” Chromatius of Aquileia also, who perhaps with the same intention, and certainly with the same faith as they, mentions the Holy Spirit twice in the doxologies of the surviving fragments of his Commentary on Matthew. This concludes our general discussion of the writings, or works, of Chromatius.

Certain particular matters must now be examined, which may serve as an appendix, especially to the points presented by Fontaninus and De Rubeis in their studies. And, so as not to delay the Reader at length, let us begin with Ceillier, who noticed in Chromatius something overlooked by Tillemont and likewise not indicated at all by Fontaninus or others—something nevertheless worthy of being recorded in an author of such importance, namely, a man of the latter part of the fourth century, a friend of Jerome, and a most devoted student of the divine Scriptures. “He cites,” says Ceillier, “the History of Judith, without expressing any doubt about the authenticity of the book in which it is reported.” Thus Saint Chromatius writes in treatise 15, no. 2:

“For the most holy Judith, when she was afflicted with great sorrow for the people, after the solemnity of a three-day fast, with her head anointed and her face washed, concealed the sadness of her inward distress in such a way that, by feigning joy, she appeared to rejoice before her enemies, etc.”

Here, moreover, not merely one but three points in Chromatius’s words deserve notice, especially because they oppose the positions of the heterodox: namely, the celebrated widow’s holiness is proclaimed, the truth of her history is affirmed, and the divine authority of the Book of Judith is asserted—a book which heretics place among the apocrypha, whereas in the Catholic Church it is numbered among the canonical books.

Whatever theologians and interpreters may dispute—even among Catholics—about the propriety of the words and actions employed by that heroine to accomplish the task she had undertaken; and whatever they may further debate about the truth of the event, namely, whether it is a fabrication and parabolic composition devised piously but only later in order to raise the spirit of the Jewish people amid tribulations, perhaps those endured in the time of Antiochus, or rather a true and genuine account of a miraculous event, as Catholics commonly hold, wherever it must finally be placed in Jewish history: this testimony of our Chromatius can certainly deservedly be counted among the many other testimonies of the holy Fathers and ancient writers by which Catholic theologians have hitherto defended the divine character of this deuterocanonical book against the heretics.

Immediately after mentioning Judith, Chromatius also names Esther, saying:

“Likewise the most holy Esther, when, with her face washed and her head anointed, she was able to make herself known to the king after the three-day fast, killed that utterly wicked enemy of her people, Haman.”

The heterodox also count the Book of Esther among the canonical books, except for the final seven chapters of our Vulgate, beginning with verse 4 of chapter 10. Nevertheless, as the most distinguished Joannes Franciscus Marchinius writes in *On the Divinity and Canonicity of the Sacred Books*, part II, article 9, certain Lutherans and Anabaptists assert that the history of Esther contained in this divine book is a tragedy and a parabolic composition lacking dignity.

Here, then, we have Chromatius of Aquileia, who acknowledges both the divine character of this book and the truth of Esther’s history, thereby increasing the number of those who, in addition to recognizing the book’s canonicity, have also recognized the truth of this history from the earliest centuries of the Church, after the Synagogue.

But what are we to say about the final seven chapters of this book, which the heretics call by the offensive name “additions” and which they likewise number among the apocryphal writings? From the words of Chromatius just cited we may reasonably conclude that he too recognized these final chapters, or additions, as part of the same Book of Esther and therefore as possessing the same divine authority as the preceding chapters. For what he says—that Esther, with her face washed and her head anointed, could be understood by the king—could in no way have been derived from the first nine or ten chapters of that book, where there is absolutely nothing about such preparation of the face and head. Rather, he clearly derived it from the additions themselves, which the heterodox reject—namely, from chapter 14 of our Vulgate, where verse 2 says that, having heard of the danger threatening Esther’s Jewish nation and wishing to pour out her prayers to the Lord for its safety, she had removed her royal garments for the sake of humility [Col. 0271D] and, instead of perfumes, filled her head with ashes and dung. It follows naturally that, when on the third day, after pouring out her prayers to the Lord, she was to approach the king in order to plead for her people, and therefore had again put on her royal garments, as the text says in chapter 5, verse 1, she first washed her face, which had been soiled by the filth falling from her head, and, after shaking off the ashes and dung, anointed her head with various perfumes, as was fitting for a queen approaching the king’s throne.

What we have observed in Chromatius concerning the Books of Judith and Esther warns us to say something also about two other books that the heretics likewise do not regard as canonical, namely, the Books of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus.

Our Chromatius cites the Book of Wisdom only once in the writings that survive from him, namely, in treatise 10, no. 2. Yet he cites it as constituting a part of divine authority and sacred Scripture, for he says:

“Perjury and lying are condemned to punishment by divine judgment, as Scripture says: ‘The mouth that lies kills the soul’”—

which is found in Wisdom 1:11.

The Book of Ecclesiasticus, however, is cited by the same Chromatius not merely once or twice but very frequently in the writings we possess, and is always regarded as possessing divine authority. Thus its words are sometimes called the words of the Lord and sometimes those of the Holy Spirit, as may be seen in treatise 3, no. 5; treatise 6, no. 2; and frequently elsewhere. How true, then, is what Marchinius asserted about the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the work cited above, part II, article 16: among the deuterocanonical books, “certainly there is no book of Sacred Scripture whose authority the Fathers support more strongly, although the universal Church had not yet sanctioned it by a public decree.”

It is indeed true that our Chromatius believed that the Book of Ecclesiasticus had Solomon as its author, as he frequently writes when he cites passages from that same book. Other holy Fathers also held this opinion. Or perhaps we should say instead that Chromatius himself, and the other Fathers who wrote in the same way, called the Book of Ecclesiasticus Solomon’s because its author imitated Solomon, and because Ecclesiasticus also contains certain things that Solomon himself had long before taught in his own books, especially Proverbs and Ecclesiastes.

Let us now proceed to other matters, still under Ceillier’s guidance.

Speaking of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Chromatius has the following in treatise 1, no. 3:

“John indeed baptized our Lord and Savior, but rather he was baptized by Christ: for the one sanctified the waters, while the other was sanctified by the waters; the one bestowed grace, while the other received it; the latter laid aside sins, while the former forgave them . . . . John needed baptism, because he could not be without sin.”

Two, or even three, points must here be noted in Chromatius’s words: according to Chromatius, Saint John the Baptist was baptized by Christ the Lord; and he genuinely needed baptism because he could not be without sin—whether Chromatius intended this to refer to original sin or to some actual sin by which even the Lord’s Forerunner might have been bound. Let us examine each point.

That Saint John the Baptist was baptized by Christ the Lord is expressly asserted among the Greek Fathers by Saint Gregory of Nazianzus in Oration 39, p. 633, Paris edition of 1609; and among the Latins by Saint Augustine in Sermon 293, § 12, in the Maurist edition. Yet Saint John Chrysostom, in Homily 12 on Matthew; Saint Jerome, on chapter 2 of the same Gospel; Saint Maximus of Turin, in Homily 31, which is on the Baptism of Christ, part 3, p. 92 of the latest Roman edition; and others deny this, or at least express doubt.

The matter may be debated in either direction without impiety. It may perhaps seem more probable, and also more consistent with the Gospel text, that the Baptist himself was baptized by Christ the Lord immediately after he had baptized Christ, as some interpreters especially infer from those words of the same Lord to the Baptist, “Let it be so now,” Matthew 3:15, spoken in response to the Baptist’s statement, “I need to be baptized by you.” From these words, I repeat, some interpreters draw that conclusion.

In the meantime, following Nazianzen and Augustine, we also have our Chromatius as an advocate of the affirmative position, namely, that John received baptism from Christ the Lord. It is enough to have stated this.

But how did Saint John need baptism because he could not be without sin, as Chromatius says? For it is one thing for John to have been baptized, and another for him to have needed baptism. The law of Christian baptism had not yet been established at that time; indeed, before Christ promulgated such a law, the Baptist had already died a martyr. As for original sin, all Jews at that time were cleansed from it, whether through the faith of their parents in the One to come or through circumcision. Therefore no one will deny that the Baptist had long since been cleansed from the original stain that he had contracted at conception by at least one of these means.

Yet who would say that John the Baptist needed those same ancient means in order to be cleansed from original sin, when he had been filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, as the angel Gabriel foretold to his father Zechariah, Luke 1:15?

Some holy Fathers indeed seem to have doubted whether the grace of sanctification with which John was endowed in the womb was also the grace of regeneration—by which, once the fault of original sin had been wiped away, he would have been reborn in Christ, having died in Adam according to the law of carnal conception. Among these is Saint Augustine, in his letter to Dardanus, 187, formerly 57, nos. 31 and 32; and Saint Bernard, in Letter 174, addressed to the canons of Lyons. It is worthwhile to quote his words:

“Most certainly,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, with whom he was filled, sanctified him. But to what extent this very sanctification availed against original sin, whether in the case of this Saint John, or of Jeremiah, or of anyone else similarly preceded by grace, I would not rashly assert. I would nevertheless have no doubt in calling those sanctified whom God sanctified, and in saying that they emerged from the womb with the same sanctification that they had received in the womb. Nor would I say that the guilt which they contracted at conception had any power to impede or take away the blessing already granted at their birth. Yet who would say that a son filled with the Holy Spirit nevertheless remained a son of wrath, and that, if he had happened to die in the womb, he would have paid the penalties of condemnation with that fullness of the Spirit? It is a difficult thought. Nevertheless, I would by no means dare to define anything on this point according to my own judgment.”

Such are the words of Saint Bernard.

Nevertheless, very many of the holy Fathers speak so magnificently of John the Baptist’s sanctification in his mother’s womb [Col. 0274A] that they leave no room for doubt that he was then suffused with a holiness that immediately cleansed him from every stain of the ancient transgression.

“The soul of blessed John was holy; and while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, and destined to come into the world, he knew, as though through the experience of his senses, what Israel did not know”: so Origen, Homily 10 on Luke.

“John . . . that one who, while still in his mother’s womb, was filled with divine grace”: so Saint Cyprian, Letter 73 to Jubaianus, near the end.

Saint Athanasius agrees in Sermon 4 Against the Arians; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem in Catechesis 3; Saint Ambrose in Book II on Luke; Saint Maximus of Turin in Sermon 56, on the Nativity of Saint John, part 5, p. 554 of the aforementioned edition; and Saint Gregory the Great in Book III, chapter 5 of the *Moralia*.

The blessed Peter Damian expressed the understanding of all the holy Fathers concerning John’s sanctification in his mother’s womb most magnificently [XXXV] in Sermon 1, on Saint John the Baptist, speaking as follows:

“We read that no mortal was ever sanctified within his mother’s womb except John the Baptist and Jeremiah. But Jeremiah’s sanctification was far less than John’s. The former was sanctified in his mother’s womb; the latter is known to have been filled with the Holy Spirit. For it is much more excellent to be filled with the Holy Spirit than to be sanctified. In the one case sanctification signifies cleansing; in the other, fullness signifies overflowing.

“Finally, even the Apostles, who handled with their own hands the Word of life, when they had received the Holy Spirit through the breath of the Savior, could scarcely reach that degree until the fiftieth day after the Resurrection at which it could be said of them: ‘They were all filled with the Holy Spirit.’ And although the Holy Spirit then filled the hearts of believers with a more abundant gift, John is nevertheless read to have attained in the womb what the apostolic dignity was eventually able to obtain only after a longer interval.”

Thus Saint Peter Damian.

Therefore, with respect to original sin, from which the Hebrews were cleansed either through the faith of their parents in the One to come or through circumcision—neither of which was lacking in John—and especially through the sanctification received in his mother’s womb, John could not have been infected when he was to be baptized by Christ the Lord, and therefore could not have needed that baptism for this reason. For it is absolutely certain that no one can at once be endowed with holiness and remain held by original sin; become a friend of God by grace and remain at the same time a child of wrath through original sin; become a participant in the divine nature and at the same time be enslaved to the devil.

These matters are discussed more fully by the distinguished Jacobus Hyacinthus Serry, *Exercises, etc., on Christ and His Virgin Mother*, exercise 28, nos. 10 and 11, from whom we have borrowed some of what we have said.

Hence, if our Chromatius said that John the Baptist needed baptism because he could not be without sin, we must certainly acknowledge that he did not mean this because he believed the Baptist still stained by original sin, but rather because, as a human being, he was not without some stain of actual fault.

Nor does this conflict with the holiness of so great a man [Col. 0275A], nor does it contradict that fullness of the Holy Spirit which he received in his mother’s womb. Saint Augustine said in the *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, chapter 64:

“Except for the gift of baptism, which was given against original sin . . . apart from this great indulgence, by which the renewal of the human being begins, in which every guilt, both inherited and added, is dissolved, the rest of life, even at an age already capable of reason and however greatly it may abound in righteousness, is not lived without the remission of sins. For as long as the children of God live mortally, they struggle with death. And although it is truly said of them, ‘All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God,’ they are nevertheless so stirred by the Spirit of God and advance toward God as sons of God that, even by their own spirit—especially when the corruptible body weighs them down—they may, like sons of men, fail through certain human impulses and therefore sin.”

“I need to be baptized by you,” the most holy John said to Jesus, who came to him to receive John’s baptism: “I need to be baptized by you.”

“But why,” adds the same Saint Augustine in the previously cited Sermon 293, no. 12, “why would he say, ‘I need to be baptized by you,’ if he were wholly clean from every fault, if there were nothing in him to be healed, nothing in him to be cleansed? . . . ‘I need to be baptized by you,’ he says: it is necessary for me; I require it. And this was granted to him there.”

Explaining these same words of the holy Forerunner, the distinguished Estius wrote:

“I need to be baptized by you—that is, to be washed, cleansed from sins. From this it is rightly inferred that John the Baptist was not without venial sins, in accordance with the statement of the other John, 1 John 1:8: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.’ Hence Augustine also wishes John to be included among those righteous who do not live without sins.”

Here, then, is what our Chromatius means when he asserts that Saint John the Baptist needed the baptism of Christ because he could not be without sin. Anyone who wishes to learn more about this matter should consult the Catholic and non-Catholic writers on Saint John the Baptist and matters pertaining to him, whom the distinguished Paulus Maria Paciaudius, with his extensive learning, lists in the preface to his *Christian Antiquities on the Cult of Saint John the Baptist*, Rome, 1755, pp. 2–3.

Another subject, and a particularly joyful and edifying one, is presented to us by Chromatius, under Ceillier’s guidance, in that part of his Commentary in which he explains the Lord’s Prayer with great eloquence and devotion—namely, treatise 14 in our edition, no. 5—where he discusses “our daily bread.”

After distinguishing two ways in which those words of the Lord’s Prayer, “Give us this day our daily bread,” are to be understood, and after speaking of daily bread in the literal sense, necessary for sustaining the present life, he turns to the spiritual meaning of those words [XXXVII]. From this we also draw an excellent indication of a practice that then flourished in the Church of Aquileia itself, namely, the very frequent, indeed even daily, Communion of the faithful—a practice from which, alas, we are now so far removed, not without disgrace to the Christian cause and harm to the spiritual life.

“We must understand,” he says, “that this has been commanded to us spiritually, so that we may ask for daily bread: that is, that heavenly and spiritual bread which we receive daily for the healing of the soul and the hope of eternal salvation, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘The heavenly bread is my flesh, which I will give for the life of this world.’ And therefore we are commanded to ask for this bread daily: that is, that, through the Lord’s merciful provision, we may deserve to receive the bread of the Lord’s body every day. For the holy Apostle says: ‘Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of the Lord’s bread and drink from the cup.’ And again: ‘Whoever eats the Lord’s bread unworthily and drinks the cup will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.’ Therefore it is not without reason that we ought always to pray that we may deserve to receive this heavenly bread every day, lest, through the intervention of some sin, we be separated from the Lord’s body.”

Thus Saint Chromatius.

We know that among the faithful of the earlier centuries of the Church it was customary to receive the Lord’s body daily, or at least very frequently. Writers on liturgical matters and ecclesiastical discipline gather many testimonies from both the Greek and Latin Fathers confirming that this most excellent practice flourished in both the Eastern and Western Churches, especially, as regards Italy, in the Roman and Milanese Churches.

No one, so far as we know, has produced anything concerning the Church of Aquileia, which was close to Milan and in antiquity and renown by no means inferior to it or to the other Churches of the West. Here now is our Chromatius, appearing as a new witness to this most holy discipline of the ancient centuries in the West, and at the same time transmitting to us the practice of his own Church—that is, of our Mother Church—in the closing years of the fourth century and the opening years of the fifth. He says:

“which we receive daily for the healing of the soul and the hope of eternal salvation”; likewise, “that, through the Lord’s merciful provision, we may deserve to receive the bread of the Lord’s body every day”; and again, “that we may deserve to receive this heavenly bread every day.”

These words undoubtedly indicate the practice of those to whom, or for whom, he was writing.

Similar statements may be seen in Cyprian’s work *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 209 of the Paris edition of his works by Baluze. I am pleased to quote them here, both so that you may understand that our Chromatius wrote on the same subject in agreement with so great a teacher, and so that you may observe that the same discipline which then prevailed in the Church of Carthage during the persecutions continued to be practiced in Aquileia in a time of peace, almost two centuries after Cyprian.

“We ask that this bread be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily as food for salvation may not, if some more serious offense intervenes, be kept away from the heavenly bread while abstaining and not communicating, and thus be separated from Christ’s body, since he himself proclaims and warns: ‘I am the bread of life who came down from heaven. If anyone eats of my bread, he will live for ever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.’

“When, therefore, he says that whoever eats of his bread will live for ever, just as it is evident that those live who touch his body and receive the Eucharist by right of communion, so on the other hand we must fear and pray that, while someone is kept away and separated from Christ’s body, he may remain far from salvation, since he threatens and says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’

“And therefore we ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not depart from his sanctification and body.”

Thus Saint Cyprian.

While our Chromatius was writing these things concerning the daily Communion of the faithful at Aquileia, Saint Augustine among the Africans was also sending those two letters in response to Januarius’s inquiries, which the Maurist editors of his works assign to the year 400. From the first of them, which in their edition is Letter 54, formerly 118, chapter 3, we learn that among those who at that time were upright and devout practitioners of Christian life, especially perhaps among those living in the African regions, there was a certain diversity of opinion concerning the daily use of Eucharistic food. Yet this diversity proceeded on both sides from faith and religious devotion.

Some defended daily Communion as necessary nourishment and medicine for the soul each day; others rather advised against daily Communion, because, as they said, days should be chosen on which a person might live more purely and continently, so as to approach so great a sacrament with greater worthiness.

The holy teacher settled the question beautifully and appropriately, as was his custom, commending both positions in the matter under discussion and writing the following. Because of the importance and dignity of the subject, we think it will be neither unpleasant nor wholly useless for readers to quote it here:

“Perhaps the dispute is more rightly settled among them by someone who urges them above all to remain in the peace of Christ, while each person does what he devoutly believes ought to be done according to his faith. For neither of them dishonors the body and blood of the Lord; rather, they vie with one another in honoring the most health-giving sacrament.

“For Zacchaeus and that centurion did not quarrel among themselves, nor did either place himself above the other, when one joyfully received the Lord into his house, while the other said, ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.’ Both honored the Savior in different and almost contrary ways; both were wretched because of their sins, and both obtained mercy . . . . For the one, by honoring him, does not dare to receive him every day; the other, by honoring him, does not dare to omit receiving him on any day.”

Such are the words of Saint Augustine.

That no disagreement of this kind had arisen among the people of Aquileia in the time of Chromatius—that is, at approximately the same time when Augustine was writing this letter—we infer from Chromatius himself. For this would have been a particularly suitable occasion to instruct the Christian people concerning both ways of honoring the most sacred sacrament of the Eucharist, whether by daily use or rather by abstention on some days.

It therefore appears that daily Communion, or at least very frequent Communion, was entirely customary there, as we maintained, without any diversity of opinion; nor were the faithful themselves there held back by the reproaches of an impaired conscience, as we understand from Chromatius’s own words.

But what of those faithful who approached the sacred table daily, or at least several times a week? Did they also precede each reception by confessing their sins to penitential priests?

We raise this question here because Chromatius himself, in the words cited above, is relevant to it, as is Cyprian, with whom Chromatius agrees. Both expressly teach that the Eucharist ought to be received only by those who are clean from sins.

We reply that such a practice would certainly have been extremely burdensome, and that, because of the multitude of the faithful communicating, daily or even very frequent reception of the Eucharist could not in any way have taken place. Therefore the faithful of those centuries who received the Eucharist daily or very frequently did not in fact precede it with that confession which we call sacramental, unless they happened at some point to feel themselves bound by a sin that was grave, or at least feared to be grave, and that consequently could be expiated only after sacramental confession and the reception of penance.

This is apparently indicated by the very words of Chromatius that we quoted [XL], where he said:

“Therefore we ought always to pray that we may deserve to receive this heavenly bread daily, lest, through the intervention of some sin, we be separated from the Lord’s body.”

We ought always to pray, that is, that our conscience may be clean every day, and thus that we may deserve to receive the heavenly bread daily; lest, through the intervention of some sin that separates us from divine grace, we be obliged to abstain from that daily participation until we have obtained cleansing from the sin committed through the sacrament of penance.

Compare with this the words of our Chromatius and of Cyprian that we added above. The lesser sins, therefore, which, through the weakness of human nature, almost daily creep in, and which we call venial sins, from which even the righteous and men of proven virtue do not remain wholly free—these, I say, did not prevent, any more than they prevent today, the Eucharist from being received daily, even without prior sacramental confession.

For the expiation of these sins, it was sufficient, as it is today, either to make a private and humble confession before God—one that was especially elicited before participation in the sacrament, both from laypeople and from the clergy and priests themselves, in those prayers that were then therefore called “prayers in silence”—or to use a certain public formula of general confession and repentance. The institution of the latter still survives today in that solemn prayer called the *Confiteor*, which is always used before receiving the Eucharist.

We have already said that the ancient faithful who communicated daily, or at least very frequently, did not customarily make sacramental confession beforehand unless they happened at some point to feel themselves bound by a sin that was grave, or at least feared to be grave. To make this still clearer, we shall cite another passage from the Cyprian mentioned above, from his book *On the Lapsed*, p. 186 of the aforementioned edition.

There Saint Cyprian rebukes those who, deceived by the excessive ease and leniency of certain ministers, did not hesitate to receive the Eucharist without prior and public penance, although they had recently been defiled in the Decian persecution by the public and monstrous crime either of sacrifice or of producing a certificate of sacrifice, and although, as he put it, they returned from the altars of the devil and approached the Lord’s holy [body] with dirty hands polluted by foul stench.

By contrast, on page 190 he wonderfully praises those “who, although”—here are his words, worthy of notice—“although they were bound by no crime of sacrifice or certificate, nevertheless, because they had even thought of such a thing, sorrowfully and plainly confessing this very fact before the priests of God, make an exomologesis of their conscience, lay open the burden of their soul, and seek healing for their wounds, even though small and slight.”

Here, then, are the more serious and especially public offenses that kept people from Communion until they had been cleansed by confession and also by public penance according to the gravity of their offenses; and here are the lesser offenses, even hidden ones, which did not at all prevent daily Communion, but concerning which those Christians nevertheless sometimes felt anxious fear because of the importance of the matter and the severity of the times, and on account of which they did not dare approach Communion without an exomologesis of conscience.

But another monument is available for illuminating the same matter, one that concerns the very period of our Chromatius and therefore must by no means be passed over. For in the place cited above from the letter of Saint Augustine to Januarius concerning inquiries, that group of Christians which commended the daily use of the Eucharist opposed the other group, which, as we have seen, recommended not daily Communion; that group, I say, relying unquestionably on the common doctrine then prevailing and approved, argued in favor of its position [Col. 0279D] that “if sins are not so great that someone ought to be judged excommunicated, he ought not to separate himself from the daily medicine of the Lord’s body.” This must therefore be understood of grave and so-called mortal sins, which alone required sacramental confession and, according to the measure of guilt, penance, so that a person might approach the Eucharist. Hence it followed that those Christians necessarily had to interrupt that daily Communion from time to time if they were burdened with sins of this kind. The ancient faithful therefore freely approached Holy Communion, either daily or at least very frequently, without sacramental confession, unless they sometimes felt themselves bound by some sin [Col. 0280A] that was grave, or at least feared that it might be grave, just as we asserted above. This, then, concerns the notable passage of Chromatius in which daily, or at least very frequent, Communion of the faithful—at that time also prevailing in the Church of Aquileia—is discussed.

Ceillier now points us to another text of Saint Chromatius, one that concerns marriage; and the reason why I shall mention it here is that certain civil laws concerning marriage, enacted in France during these past years and soon brought here as well, have compelled us in a certain sense to do so, since they prevailed with the gravest injury to religion and the indignation of all good people. The text is as follows:

“For he himself [the Lord] says: ‘Therefore what God has joined together, let no man separate . . .,’ clearly [XLII] demonstrating [Col. 0280B] that the person acts against God’s will who dares to violate a marriage joined by God through an illicit separation by divorce. Hence let them not be unaware how grave a crime of condemnation before God they incur who, through the unrestrained pleasure of lust, dismissing their wives, wish, apart from the cause of fornication, to dismiss their wives and enter into other marriages. They believe that they may commit this with impunity because it appears to be permitted by human and secular laws, not knowing that they offend more seriously and grievously in this respect because they place human laws before divine ones, so that they believe something to be lawful which God has established as unlawful merely because it has been freely permitted by man.”

Thus Saint Chromatius, in treatise 10 of this edition, no. 1. This text has two parts: the first, in which Chromatius simply expounds [Col. 0280C] the teaching of our Savior in Matthew 5:31–32: “But I say to you: Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery”; and the second, in which he censures those who, under the pretext of human laws, were dissolving the divine ordinance concerning the sacred character of marriage, thereby also aggravating their guilt because they preferred human laws to divine sanctions.

There is nothing that needs to be said about the first part of this text. Tillemont, followed by Fontaninus and, most recently, Ceillier, observed that Chromatius by no means spoke there as though he thought that a new marriage could be contracted after dismissing an adulterous wife; rather, he added nothing to the Evangelist’s words and expressed no opinion of his own on this matter. The question whether a marriage might be dissolved on account of adultery had perhaps not yet been raised. Concerning the second part, however, something must be said, now that the sanctity of marriage has been violated by the latest laws of the Franco-Italian domination.

Saint Chromatius was speaking of the ancient laws—whether of the Roman Republic or of the Roman Empire—when he wrote: “They believe that they may commit this with impunity because it appears to be permitted by human and secular laws.” These laws, as experts in Roman law know, permitted the dissolution of marriage, for example, also on account of the civil or fictitious death of one party, such as was said to occur when someone was reduced to captivity or slavery. They also permitted dissolution on account of deportation, as though the deported person had become a slave under sentence. Furthermore, they permitted the dissolution of marriage by mutual consent of the parties; this dissolution was said to take place *bona gratia*, “by mutual goodwill,” to distinguish it from other dissolutions said to take place *ex causa*, “for a stated cause.”

When the Christian religion found such laws, enacted by pagan rulers who did not know God, in force throughout the Roman Empire, the governors of the Christian flock were undoubtedly wholly intent on ensuring that those who bore the name of Christ would regard the civil laws concerning marriage as subordinate and would themselves contemplate the divine origin of indissoluble marriage, which Christ the Lord had also endowed with the new dignity of a sacrament precisely because it cannot be dissolved.

[Col. 0281B] Accordingly, the Apostle warned the Corinthians who had come to the Church from paganism concerning the marriage bond, on the basis of the teaching of Christ the Lord and contrary to what the civil laws of the pagans permitted, in 1 Corinthians 7:10–11: “To those who are joined in marriage I command—not I but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she has departed, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not dismiss his wife.”

Accordingly, writing to Polycarp, the martyr Ignatius likewise prescribed in his genuine letter, no. 5, in Cotelerius, *Patres Apostolici*, vol. II, p. 41 of the edition cited above, Amsterdam 1724:

“Tell my sisters to love the Lord and to be content with their husbands in flesh and spirit. Likewise command my brothers, in the name of Jesus Christ, to love their wives [Col. 0281C] as the Lord loves the Church . . . . It is fitting that brides and bridegrooms enter marriage with the approval of the bishop, so that the marriage may be according to the Lord and not according to desire.”

Regarding this latter judgment of Ignatius, Tertullian also wrote elegantly in book II *To His Wife*, no. 8:

“How shall we be sufficient to recount the happiness of that marriage which the Church brings together, the offering confirms, the blessing seals, the angels announce, and the Father ratifies?”

In the *Apostolic Constitutions*, commonly attributed to Clement of Rome, but in fact ancient and possessing authority of their own, these instructions concerning the indissoluble bond of marriage are found under the name of the Apostles in book VI, chapter 14, in the cited Cotelerius, *Patres Apostolici*, vol. I, p. 346 of the same edition:

“We signify to you . . . that marriage ought to be contracted lawfully; for such a marriage is free from guilt, since the wife is joined to the husband by the Lord . . . . Therefore after the wedding it is not permissible to cast out an innocent wife . . . . For the Lord says: ‘What God has joined together, let no man separate.’ For the wife is a partner in life, united by God from two into one body. But whoever divides what is one again into two is an enemy of God’s creation and an adversary of divine providence.”

From this basis Saint Justin Martyr did not fear to write openly even to pagan rulers hostile to the Christian religion and persecutors of Christ’s faithful. In *First Apology*, no. 15, p. 52 of the Maurist Paris edition of 1742, after first citing the Gospel law in Matthew 5:32 and 19:9—“Whoever marries a woman repudiated by another man commits adultery,” or, as our Vulgate has it, “Whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery”—he wrote that “even those who enter into a second marriage according to human law”—that is, those who dismiss their first wife and marry another, as those Roman laws permitted—“are sinners in the sight of our Teacher.”

From these facts, then, we understand that Christians of the earlier centuries who had come from paganism and had long been accustomed to Roman legislation were thoroughly instructed by their pastors concerning the dignity of Christian marriage and its principal laws, which certainly could not stand together with the laws either of the Roman Republic or of the Empire.

It is therefore already sufficiently clear what our Chromatius intended when he warned the Christians of his own age how grave a crime of condemnation before God they incurred who, through the unrestrained pleasure of lust, dismissed their wives and wished to enter into other marriages; and who believed that they might do this with impunity because it appeared to be permitted by human and secular laws, not knowing that they offended more seriously and grievously in this respect because they preferred human laws to divine ones, so that they believed something lawful merely because it had been freely permitted by man, although God had established it as unlawful.

Here we consider it worthwhile to note one point: shortly before Chromatius wrote these words for his Aquileian people [Col. 0282C], the bishop Ambrose, a friend of Chromatius and, as is reported, the one who initiated him into the dignity of the episcopate, had taught the same congregation entrusted to him at Milan concerning the same Roman laws relating to marriage. In addition to the matters mentioned above, those laws also contained this provision contrary to divine law: a married man who had intercourse with an unmarried woman was not subject to judgment for adultery, even though the married woman who received an unmarried man was condemned for adultery.

“I warn you,” he says, “men, especially those who are striving for the grace of the Lord, not to mingle with an adulterous body . . . . Let no one flatter himself because of human laws. Every sexual violation is adultery, and a man is not permitted what is not permitted to a woman. The same chastity is owed by the husband as by the wife. Whatever is committed with a woman who is not a legitimate [Col. 0282D] wife is condemned as adultery. Therefore you have understood what you must avoid, lest anyone make himself unworthy of the sacraments.”

Thus the holy Doctor, *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 4, no. 25. According to the Maurist editors, this work was written around the year 387.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] In the edition we are reprinting, four leaves, without page numbers, were inserted in a second revision. On the front of the first leaf appears this note: “Pages XLIV of the preface to Saint Chromatius, after [Col. 0282D] the last line ending with the words ‘written around the year 387,’ are to be added as follows.” We enclose this interpolation in brackets. EDITOR.]

[These matters are sufficient for illustrating our Chromatius concerning what he wrote about Christian marriage, taking the occasion from the Gospel reading that he was explaining. Nevertheless, the seriousness of the subject requires us to add more here, as does the fear that, because of the French legislation mentioned above, to which we were subject, some may still be deceived into asserting for rulers who profess the Christian religion and the Catholic faith a right over the marriages of Catholic subjects such as the Roman laws claimed for themselves.

To continue the argument, after the ancient testimonies cited above, by which we showed the care taken by our teachers in instructing the faithful in what divine law taught contrary to what the pagan laws had decreed concerning marriage, it is useful first to observe that, so far as we know, there are no examples from the first three centuries—or even from the greater part of the fourth—showing any Christian who knowingly and willingly, by force of the secular laws mentioned above, and therefore on the pretext of captivity, slavery, deportation, or mutual consent, dissolved a marriage once contracted lawfully and in the Christian manner, or attempted to do so, and presumed to enter into a new one.

Saint Jerome indeed reports in his letter 77 in Vallarsi’s edition, addressed to Oceanus, the case of Fabiola, the noblest of Roman women. Toward the end of the fourth century she had dismissed a most criminal husband and, while he was still alive, married another, likewise with the favor of those worldly laws that permitted it:

“Because,” he says, “she had persuaded herself and thought that she had lawfully dismissed her husband, and she did not know the force of the Gospel, in which every pretext for marrying is cut off from women while their husbands are alive.”

But this lapse of Fabiola, arising more from ignorance than from depravity of mind, ultimately turned to the benefit of the Church because of the public and solemn penance performed by this woman before the eyes of the whole city of Rome. The holy Doctor wrote about it so splendidly in the cited letter, composed after her death and belonging to the year 399. On that occasion, speaking also about Christian marriages in relation to Roman law, he uttered the famous statement that on this matter “the laws of the Caesars are one thing, the laws of Christ another; Papinianus commands one thing, our Paul another.”

Thus, abuses in Christian marriages appear to have gradually crept in at a later time. Our Chromatius may have been the first, or at least one of the first, to mention and rebuke those who, with the support of those laws, perhaps in the cases referred to by them, believed that they could with impunity dismiss their wives and hasten into new marriages.

It is probable that some at that time very easily rushed to this opinion because they saw that those ancient laws, once enacted by pagan rulers, had not been abolished by Constantine the Great and the other Christian emperors. Meanwhile, they paid no attention to the fact that human laws can do nothing against the law of God, and likewise that the old human laws concerning marriage, which still remained in force under Christian emperors, affected at that time only those who were entangled in pagan superstitions and who, long after the peace of the Church in the Roman Empire, both in East and West, continued to prevail in authority and numbers.

As time passed and the fervor of Christian instruction grew cold, while barbarian forces poured into the Roman Empire—especially in the fifth century of the Church—and calamities simultaneously broke upon the whole world, that chastity of conduct which had distinguished the faithful of earlier times became a thing of the past. The sanctity of marriage in particular began to be undermined here and there. Consequently, bishops throughout the world complained of violations of the Gospel laws in this matter, and the Roman pontiffs more than once had to fight with apostolic strength for the divine law concerning the indissoluble permanence of marriage.

Thus, at the very beginning of the fifth century, we find Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, asking Saint Innocent I what should be thought of those who, after a divorce permitted by human laws, joined themselves to another in marriage. And we find the Roman pontiff himself replying to this request in the following words, in letter 6, chapter 6, in Coustant, *Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum*, cols. 794–795; the letter is assigned to the year 405:

“Your affection also inquired about those who, after a divorce had taken place, joined themselves to another in marriage. It is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. Those, however, who, while their wife was still alive—although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved—hastened to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons joined to them appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery’; likewise, ‘Whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.’ Therefore all are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful [Col. 0284C]. But concerning their parents or relatives, nothing of this kind can be decreed unless they are discovered to have encouraged the illicit union.”

Saint Augustine had taught this doctrine somewhat earlier as well, in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapters 7 and 8—a work which, according to the Maurist editors, he wrote around the year 401—and he mentioned there also the laws of the Gentiles, which were different from the Gospel commands:

“By the intervention of divorce,” he said, “the marriage alliance is not abolished, so that the spouses remain married even when separated; and they commit adultery with those to whom they have been joined after their repudiation, whether the woman with a man or the man with a woman. Yet such is the case with a wife only in the city of our God, on his holy mountain. Who does not know that the laws of the Gentiles operate differently, where, after a divorce has been interposed, without incurring any punishment under human law, the woman marries whomever she wishes and the man takes whomever he wishes?”

The same holy Doctor, in book II *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 8—works which, as the same Maurist editors note, he wrote in the year 419—rebuked those Christians who, as he said, “choose, and especially in this matter”—namely, the matter he was then discussing, the dismissal of wives on account of adultery—“choose above all to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to Christ, because civil laws seem not to bind men by the same bonds of chastity by which they bind women.”

And in book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 10—a work belonging, according to the same authorities, to that same recently mentioned year—he taught the following concerning divorce on account of a wife’s sterility:

“This is preserved in Christ and the Church: that one living spouse is not separated from another living spouse by any divorce for eternity. Such is the observance of this sacrament in the city of our God, on his holy mountain—that is, in the Church of Christ—among all married believers, who are undoubtedly members of Christ, that, although women marry or wives are taken for the purpose of bearing children, it is not lawful to abandon a barren wife in order to take a fertile one. If anyone does so, not under the law of this world, where, after a divorce has been interposed, it is permitted without guilt for one person to join another in marriage . . . but under the law of the Gospel, he will be guilty of adultery; and likewise she, if she marries another.”

Nor did only some Christians weak in faith and badly behaved make the abuse of divorce and a new marriage lawful to themselves under the laws of the world, whether on the grounds of adultery or sterility. At times they also hastened to new marriages with the support of those same laws if one of the parties had been carried into captivity.

A case of this kind also came before the aforementioned holy Pope Innocent, as we gather from his letter in Coustant, no. 36, cols. 909–910. That letter is there said to be of uncertain date, although perhaps it should more accurately be called a letter of uncertain year, because of the date of the barbarian storm mentioned there—namely, apparently, the invasion of Italy by Alaric and the sack of the city of Rome. These two calamities occurred in the years 409 and [Col. 0285C] 410, and the letter was probably written after them, because of the case that readily arose on that occasion.

Here is how the holy Pontiff wrote about this matter to a certain Probus, who appears to have held secular authority and perhaps had been summoned as judge by the injured party in this affair, and who certainly had the greatest interest in knowing the facts:

“Innocent to Probus. The violence of the barbarian storm has brought an incident before the capacity of the laws. For when a well-established marriage had been contracted between Fortunius and Ursa, the attack of captivity would have inflicted a blemish, unless the sacred statutes of religion had provided otherwise. For while the aforementioned woman Ursa was held in captivity, the aforesaid Fortunius is known to have entered into another marriage with Restituta. But when, by the Lord’s favor, Ursa returned, she approached us and, with no one denying it, proved that she was the wife of the aforementioned man. Therefore, most illustrious lord and deservedly honored son, with the Catholic faith lending its support, we have decreed that the marriage which was first founded by divine grace is the true marriage; and that the union with the second woman, while the first survived and had not been dismissed by divorce, can in no way be legitimate.”

This is the complete letter of Pope Innocent I concerning this event. Here you see that human laws—that is, the legislation of the Roman Empire—gave Fortunius the power to enter into another marriage with Restituta while his wife Ursa was being held captive. You see that his earlier marriage with Ursa is called by the holy Pontiff well established and founded by divine grace—that is, confirmed by divine law and strengthened by divine grace, namely the sacrament—so that it could not be dissolved by any human ordinance. Finally, you see that the statutes of religion and the rules of the Catholic faith silence the laws of the world, and that the Pontiff’s authority declares illegitimate what those laws approved.

Another barbarian storm later brought another case before the Apostolic See under Saint Leo the Great. This was the catastrophe caused by Attila, which Aquileia, the leading city of Venetia, suffered in the year 432; as a result, a multitude of Aquileians were led into captivity by the barbarians.

What Fortunius had done earlier by the authority of worldly laws because his wife Ursa was captive, certain Aquileian women who had their husbands in captivity thought they ought to do: compelled by loneliness and encouraged also by the favor of the ancient laws, they chose other husbands for themselves in place of those held captive. Some of those husbands, however, when circumstances turned for the better, returned and sought to reclaim their wives, although the women had been joined to other men.

The novelty of this case in the Church of Aquileia, together with its circumstances, undoubtedly led Saint Nicetas, who was then bishop of Aquileia, to propose that the Apostolic See should be consulted. He did so both through Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church who was then present at Aquileia, and through his own letters or some other written communication, as we argued conjecturally when discussing the writings of Nicetas.

What did Saint Pope Leo reply? “Because,” said the holy Pontiff, “we know that it is written that a woman is joined by God to a man; and again we recognize the command that what God has joined, man must not separate, we must believe that the bonds of lawful marriage are to be restored, and, once the evils inflicted by hostility have been removed, each person must be restored to what he lawfully possessed. Every effort must be made so that each person receives what is his own.”

Then, after not judging culpable—given the singularity of the case and the circumstances described in the petition, as is evident from the reply—those who had taken the place of husbands who were thought no longer to exist, and after likewise declaring that, for the same reason, the matter was excusable in the women who had acquired new husbands, he added the following concerning those women whose husbands had returned and were calling them back into their former marital partnership:

“But if some women have been so captivated by love of their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to the lawful marital partnership, they are rightly to be censured, so that they may even be deprived of ecclesiastical communion. They chose contamination by guilt in a matter that was excusable, thereby showing that, through their lack of self-restraint, they preferred what a just remission could have expiated. Let marriages therefore return to their former state by voluntary restoration; and in no way let what necessity forced be turned into a reproach of ill will. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection begun by God are rightly to be praised.”

Thus Saint Leo the Great, in his letter to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, which is letter 159 in the edition of the Ballerini brothers [Col. 0287A] and belongs to the year 458, the sixth year after the destruction of Aquileia.

These things, too, were decreed in accordance with the prescription of divine law and the Gospel teaching, contrary to what the laws of the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire, so highly celebrated, had at times sanctioned.

Afterward the Roman laws became silent concerning the freedom to dissolve marriages, especially when the Christian religion, idolatry having finally been extinguished, became the sole religion throughout the Roman world. The Christian emperors themselves after Constantine the Great, even while pagan worship survived, placed some restriction, according to the circumstances of the times, on the ancient license of repudiations and divorces arising from Roman legislation. Finally, when that license had been overthrown, the laws themselves became obsolete, being left solely to the learning of jurists and the ingenuity of scholars.

After the fall of the Roman Empire, when so many dominions and kingdoms arose on every side, and when others in turn fell and still others emerged, and when rulers framed laws for themselves—especially drawing on Roman law as though from an ancient and celebrated source of equity and justice in matters belonging merely to human law—there was no Christian, and especially no Catholic, dominion that caused the teachings of the ancient Roman legislators concerning the dissolution of marriages by repudiation and divorce, or on account of captivity, slavery, deportation, or mutual consent of the parties, to revive against the law of God and the Gospel doctrine.

It was reserved for our late age that, from the most recent domination—which, by the just judgment of God permitting the vicissitudes of affairs, had raised itself from small beginnings to immense power, and which proclaimed itself Christian and Catholic in order to deceive men’s aspirations—we should receive a code of laws commonly called by the ruler’s name, NAPOLEON, and imposed upon almost the whole of Europe by force, by blandishments, and by negotiation. In it, divine law was subordinated and the Gospel ordinances neglected, while the ancient laws of the Romans, who did not know God, affecting the sanctity of marriage were restored to use after so long a period of disuse.

Who did not shudder, who did not groan, when he learned that this code, for example, made the penalty of infamy, called civil death, a cause for dissolving the marital bond, and also made the adultery of either party such a cause; indeed, even mutual and constant consent of the spouses? We omit the other provisions established by that same code on this matter, contrary to the divine laws and the teaching of the Catholic Church, which we could add here if we wished to pursue each point or if the nature of our work permitted it.

That anti-Catholic code had few Catholics who wished to use it under that law to violate the sanctity of marriage. Those who did were either among the number of people who may be called utterly depraved because of their dissolute morals and their complete expulsion of religion from their hearts, or among those who, through a certain lightness of intellect and mind, are easily deceived and drawn away from the right path—not indeed of their own accord, but rather by the perverse counsels of the impious and cunning.

To these wretched people, who prostituted the sanctity of marriage not through wickedness of mind and heart but because they had been seized by deception, our Chromatius in this age also would most appropriately have said:

“They believe that they may commit this with impunity because it appears to be permitted by human and secular laws, not knowing that they offend more seriously and grievously in this respect because they prefer human laws to divine ones, so that they believe something to be lawful which God has established as unlawful merely because it has been freely permitted by man.”

But at last let immortal thanks be rendered to God, the Most Good and Most Great, our savior and avenger: in the years immediately past, 1814 and 1815, he summoned together, by his divine power, the forces of all Europe once and again, wonderfully uniting the wills of all rulers and peoples—although separated by nation, language, customs, religion, and interests—toward the same goal. Thus he finally crushed, overthrew, and completely destroyed that insolent domination which had most proudly raised itself against God and his most holy laws, and against the Catholic Church, defender of the divine laws.

This may serve as an example for all ages of the truth of what is written: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30); and that “the Lord frustrates the plans of the nations, but he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and rejects the counsels of rulers” (Psalm 32:10). “And now, therefore, understand, you kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth”; thus the most holy King, inspired by the divine Spirit, admonished all the kings of the earth who would be in future ages (Psalm 2:10). But enough on this subject.]

[XLV] After the statements of Saint Chromatius that we have examined, we must not now pass over in silence the eulogy with which the presbyter Rufinus adorned that same holy prelate in the Prologue to Chromatius himself, prefixed to Origen’s *Treatise on the Book of Joshua*, and which we have placed among the Testimonies of the Ancients concerning Chromatius.

Saint Jerome had repeatedly called our Chromatius “holy pope” and “venerable pope,” following the common manner of speaking and writing in those times when bishops were being discussed. He also called him—something that was not common—“the most learned of bishops,” indeed “the holiest and most learned of bishops,” as may be seen in the same ancient testimonies.

Rufinus himself, however, had called Chromatius “the venerable Father,” and, together with his brother Eusebius and Jovinus, “a most renowned and highly esteemed bishop in the Church of God,” as in the cited Testimonies.

But Rufinus also gathers together at once many and great merits of Chromatius, and at the same time shows what were in a certain sense his principal merits in the Prologue cited above, when he simply compares him to the Israelite Bezalel and calls Chromatius the Bezalel of his own time.

No one, of course, is unaware that Bezalel, in Exodus 31, was called by God and filled with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of work, to devise whatever could be skillfully made from gold, silver, bronze, marble, precious stones, and various kinds of wood in the construction [Col. 0289A] of the Tabernacle, whose construction God himself had commanded Moses.

Rufinus therefore understands these things in a spiritual sense of Chromatius when he calls him the Bezalel of his own time. What praise of Chromatius, then, may we draw from this eulogy of Rufinus?

What Rufinus wrote about Chromatius in the Prologue to Origen’s *Treatise on the Book of Joshua*, Saint Gregory Nazianzen wrote about Saint Basil the Great in his Oration in Praise of Basil, p. 346 of the Paris edition of Morellus, 1609, likewise calling him Bezalel in a spiritual sense and beginning his discourse in this way:

“Then, because an action without speech is equally an imperfect thing, and speech removed from action is likewise imperfect, he [Basil] added the support of action to his speech: approaching some, sending embassies to others; summoning some, admonishing, accusing, rebuking, pursuing with threats, assailing with reproaches; undertaking the struggle on behalf of nations, cities, and even individual persons; devising every kind of means of salvation and applying medicine to the disease from every source. He was that Bezalel, that—yes, that divine craftsman of the Tabernacle—fitting every material and every art to the work, weaving everything together [XLVI] into the outstanding beauty and harmony of a single work.”

Thus Nazianzen spoke of Basil under the figure of Bezalel.]

We may therefore rightly infer that Rufinus intended to praise these very qualities in Chromatius when he called him the Bezalel of his time. There are indeed certain facts about Bishop Chromatius that are sufficiently well known and that Fontaninus and De Rubeis examined, and which Tillemont and Ceillier also recalled; from these we understand our Chromatius to have been fully worthy of comparison, in a spiritual sense, with that ancient Bezalel, the craftsman of the divine Tabernacle.

Such, certainly, were the things he did while he was a presbyter under Bishop Valerian, above all at the Council of Aquileia in 381 against the Arian bishops Palladius and Secundianus. Such also were the things he did after Valerian, as bishop of Aquileia himself, both by word and by example. Testimony to this survives in the Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes and in the remains of the Commentary that he had written on Matthew—not to mention other works that he undoubtedly composed but which, through the injustice of the ages, have perished.

We may add the assistance he himself provided to Jerome, including financial support, so that Jerome might continue his studies of the books of Sacred Scripture for the benefit of the whole Church. We may also add the encouragement he gave Rufinus, whom he himself wished to enroll, on his return from the East, among his Aquileian presbyters, so that Rufinus might render Eusebius’s Greek Ecclesiastical History in Latin letters, and might also bring from the resources of the Greeks other materials for the building of the divine Tabernacle, such as Origen’s homilies, or little discourses, on the book of Joshua.

The patronage undertaken by our Chromatius on behalf of John Chrysostom showed the fervor of his piety and the strength of his faith: no distance between places restrained him, no difficulties wore him down, and no harshness of temporal power broke him, so as to prevent him from defending the rights of justice and promoting everywhere the welfare of the Church and the honor and glory of God.

These, then, are the celebrated and public merits of our Chromatius in the construction of the divine Tabernacle. But I do not think that Rufinus had regard only to these when he called him the Bezalel of his time. Thus Rufinus wrote while he was staying at Aquileia with Chromatius, as De Rubeis explains in his dissertation on Rufinus; and for that reason he himself was a witness of Chromatius’s entire public and private life. He saw, beyond what was publicly known—indeed, he saw what Chromatius worked for the construction of the divine Tabernacle, as though in the hidden recesses of his workshop, even without witnesses. He saw Chromatius’s labors by day and by night, his daily diligence, and his concern for his exceedingly extensive diocese; how he received the weak in faith, how he helped the feeble, how he entreated and admonished, how he reproved and rebuked, just as Nazianzen said of Basil.

All these things taken together made our Chromatius, in the Church of Aquileia, the Bezalel of his time in the building of the divine Tabernacle. And Rufinus undoubtedly had all these merits of Chromatius in view when he called Chromatius the Bezalel of his time.

If credence is to be given to the Anonymous and ancient author of the little work entitled *The Origin of Ecclesiastical Chants and Offices*, whose text we placed last among the testimonies, and concerning whom Fontaninus also wrote in his study, then we should say that our Chromatius had rendered good service to ecclesiastical liturgy as well in the Church of Aquileia, and that for this reason too he was rightly called by Rufinus, his presbyter, the Bezalel of his time. It is enough to have indicated this.

Another subject of discussion now awaits us. It has exercised the ingenuity of many, and Fontaninus and De Rubeis wrote about it especially in the studies that we append to the writings of Chromatius: namely, why this Chromatius of ours, bishop of Aquileia, was called a Roman bishop in the first Basel edition of his surviving works, published in 1528; and why, long before that edition, the blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin the Abbot, likewise called him the bishop of the holy Roman Church in his little work against the heresy of Bishop Felix, § 26, where he quotes Chromatius’s text concerning the most holy mystery of the Trinity.

The entire difficulty seems to lie in Alcuin’s nomenclature. John Sichard, who prepared that Basel edition, gave Chromatius the title “Roman bishop”—or at least accepted it as authoritative in his own manuscript—because he found Chromatius called this by Abbot Alcuin. But I should by no means think that Alcuin had spontaneously called Chromatius a Roman bishop, or the bishop of the Roman Church. Rather, he did so because he found him so designated in the manuscript of Chromatius’s writings or little works that he was using.

What, then, should be thought about this designation?

Scholars have diverged in their views on this matter, as may be seen in the cited writings of our two authors. What they thought, however, you may learn briefly.

Fontaninus understood the designation “Roman bishop” to mean the bishop of the Latin Church, in contrast to the bishops of the Greek or Eastern Church. De Rubeis, however, in his *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, considered it probable that Chromatius had been called a Roman bishop through the error of copyists or others, and that he ought rather to have been called and written “bishop of Romatium” or “bishop of Romatinum”—from the homeland, namely, that Chromatius may have had at Portus Romatius or Romatinus, then in the diocese of Aquileia and not very far from Aquileia.

Since this illustrious author had published his *Monuments* before Fontaninus’s posthumous work appeared, he later wished, having learned the learned prelate’s opinion, to weigh in his own subsequent dissertations all the arguments of learning by which Fontaninus had supported his view, and to show that they were inadequate to sustain it. He immediately added, where necessary, another hypothesis: namely, that by the designation “Roman bishop,” which was most likely attached to Chromatius’s writings during his lifetime or not long after his death, one should understand a Catholic bishop, in contrast to the Arian bishops, who were then numerous, including in Italy, after the barbarian Goths, who professed Arianism, had invaded it.

The most recent editor of Alcuin’s works, the distinguished Abbot Frobenius, likewise, in a note on the passage of Chromatius quoted by Alcuin in his little work against the heresy of Bishop Felix—and placed here among the testimonies of the ancients—although he said that it was uncertain in what sense the manuscript copies containing Chromatius’s writings called the Aquileian Chromatius a Roman bishop, nevertheless added his own conjecture, which had also occurred to our De Rubeis: namely, that the copyists may perhaps have been misled in the designation “Roman bishop” because Saint Jerome had called this same Chromatius “bishop,” “holy pope,” both once and again.

“But that old and everywhere familiar form of honorific address could have deceived no one,” said the distinguished Vallarsius, making the same observation in his notes on the Aquileian Rufinus. There he further observes that our Chromatius was called not merely a Roman bishop and bishop of the Roman Church, but truly and absolutely “supreme pontiff” in Rufinus’s Preface to Chromatius, prefixed to his own Latin translation of the *History of Eusebius of Caesarea*, according to the edition of Renatus Laurentius de la Barre—and undoubtedly from the manuscript copy of Rufinus that this editor used.

“For,” as Vallarsius writes, “the antiquaries were deceived: they did not understand by what method or in what sense Chromatius was called both a Roman bishop and bishop of the Roman Church, and they supposed that these forms of expression properly denoted the bishop who held the city of Rome and occupied the chair of the Roman Church. They therefore did not hesitate to interpolate their copies so as to call Chromatius also the supreme pontiff.”

See the works of Rufinus of Aquileia in Vallarsius’s edition, column 209 and following, in the learned scholar’s appended notes. If desired, one may also consult our observations on Fontaninus’s study, which we append to the writings of Chromatius, where the title “supreme pontiff” attributed to Chromatius is discussed.

What, then, are we to make of all this?

We have always approved—and approve once again in this highly uncertain and disputed matter—the hypothesis devised by the distinguished and much-praised Bernard Maria De Rubeis in his *Monuments*: namely, that in the words “Roman bishop” or “Roman prelate” we should suspect an error by copyists, who could very easily have written *Romanum* where they ought to have read and transcribed *Romatium* or *Romatinum*. At the same time, however, we are no longer equally persuaded by what he adds: that Chromatius could easily have been called the bishop of Romatium or Romatinum because he had Portus Romatinus, or the city of Concordia not far away, as his homeland.

Why, then, could our Chromatius have been called a Romatian or Romatinian bishop, when he was beyond doubt the bishop of Aquileia? We have explained this matter at length in our work on Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. Nicetas likewise is called the bishop of the Roman city in a manuscript of Gennadius indicated there, and also in the very ancient—indeed, the first and exceedingly rare—edition of Gennadius’s work, a copy of which is held by the distinguished Mauro Boni, who recently communicated this information to us with the greatest kindness. In those sources he is called the bishop of the Romatian, Romatitian, and Romatician city.

There is no reason here, however, to appeal to the custom of auxiliary bishops that prevailed in the Church at that time, as was done in the case of Saint Nicetas. For Chromatius is said to have been ordained bishop of the Aquileians by the holy Ambrose of Milan immediately after the death of his predecessor, Saint Valerian. Certainly there is no mention or indication of Chromatius’s episcopal rank, nor even any occasion or necessity for conjecture about it, before he became bishop of the see of Aquileia.

We therefore suppose that our Chromatius, once established in the episcopal chair of Aquileia, sometimes resided—not at Aquileia, but at Portus Romatius or Romatinus, which at that time belonged to the bishop of Aquileia and then stood at the mouth of the river Romatius or Romatinus, as we learn from Pliny. For this reason he could very easily have been called a Romatian or Romatinian bishop rather than an Aquileian one, named after the place where circumstances and changing events may have required him to be present, perhaps repeatedly, and to remain for long periods.

Let us demonstrate this probable explanation as briefly as possible, especially on the basis of what we have said elsewhere about Chromatius himself in connection with Saint Nicetas.

It is useful to state first that, in Chromatius’s time, the places of episcopal residence had not yet everywhere been fixed and, so to speak, established as they were in later centuries. Bishops were therefore then free, even after leaving their principal residence, to go wherever they wished within the boundaries of their own dioceses and to remain there as long as they wished. This was especially customary wherever some reason existed that actually impelled them to adopt such a course.
