After Valerian’s death, our Chromatius assumed the helm of the Church of Aquileia in the closing months of 388, as De Rubeis conjectures in his *Monuments* and confirms in his *Dissertations of Varied Learning*. That same year was the year in which the city of Aquileia endured a siege by the army of Theodosius the Great Augustus, who was pursuing the tyrant Maximus. Maximus had entered Aquileia with his forces and was captured there shortly afterward by the victorious Augustus himself and condemned to death.

Chromatius’s inauguration at Aquileia probably took place after the victory of Augustus and the death of Maximus, once peace had been restored. But not long after Maximus’s fall, Eugenius seized the tyranny. The same Theodosius, returning to Italy in 394 with a large force of soldiers, reached the territory of Aquileia, where a battle was fought that brought destruction and death upon the new tyrant.

In 400, the sixth year after Eugenius’s annihilation, Alaric, leader of the Goths, invaded Italy. The region of Aquileia was the first of all to lie open to the greed of the barbarians, who had come at that time not so much to acquire dominion as to carry off plunder. After Alaric had then been driven from Italy, another Gothic leader, Radagaisus, entered Italy with the same wicked intention, in 404 or the following year, and likewise attacked the territory of Aquileia. After devastating many places, he eventually perished in Tuscany.

What, then, was Bishop Chromatius of Aquileia to do amid such straits? There is certainly nothing surprising in his withdrawing from the city and territory of Aquileia once, twice, and again, and especially in prolonging his stay for a considerable time on the two latter occasions in the place that he had chosen as a residence. Thus he may in some manner have appeared to be the bishop of that place rather than of the city of Aquileia.

Anyone, I think, who knows the Roman roads that were then famous will easily understand that the Port of Romatium or Romatinum, on the river of that name, was in reality a suitable place for Chromatius’s retreat at that time. Whether we understand by the name of that port the place that is now Portus-Gruarius above Concordia, or another place beyond Concordia mentioned by Pliny at the mouth of the river of the same name, where it flows into the lagoon—the latter seems more probable—that place, I say, was well suited to Chromatius’s withdrawal both for avoiding the military disturbances of the Romans and for evading barbarian incursions.

This is particularly clear in view of the road—whether one calls it the Flaminian or the Postumian—which led from Aquileia through Venetia and Aemilia to the chief cities of Italy and finally to the very metropolis of the world. Both the Port of Romatium or Romatinum and the river of the same name lay to the left of this road for travelers coming from Aquileia, almost unknown, or at least less desirable to the barbarians, who were then heading elsewhere.

From this Port of Romatium or Romatinum, then, to which our Chromatius probably went repeatedly to avoid military disturbances and barbarian incursions, and where he perhaps remained for some time, he acquired the name “bishop of Romatium” or “bishop of Romatinum.” Some less-informed copyist could very easily have changed this—whether by removing one syllable or changing one of them into a single letter—into the title “Roman bishop,” thereby giving later scholars the cause of so much dispute.

No one should think that this was an isolated example in the case of Bishop Chromatius, as though he alone could have acquired another designation in place of “bishop of Aquileia”—namely, “bishop of Romatium” or “Romatinum”—because he may at some time have stayed in the old Port of Romatium or Romatinum in order to secure a more peaceful and safer residence.

The Church of Aquileia itself offers us an outstanding and indisputable argument for this. It is certain that the bishops of Aquileia, after leaving Aquileia because of the unhealthy climate, had a permanent seat for a long time in the city of Forum Julii, especially in the eighth and ninth centuries, as De Rubeis demonstrates in his *Monuments*, chapter 36.

Yet because of this Forum-Julian residence of the Aquileian bishops, those same bishops were themselves, at that time and even in public documents, called Forum-Julian bishops rather than Aquileian bishops. The Church of Aquileia itself consequently acquired the designation “Church of Forum Julii.” See the documents of this matter in our work on Saint Nicetas, chapter 6, page 133 and following.

There is also another living example in the former province of Aquileia, which is now the province of Udine, after that patriarchal Church was divided into two archiepiscopal sees. The episcopal city of Concordia, subject to the metropolitan of Udine, possesses an ancient cathedral and episcopal buildings situated near it. Yet it sees its bishop only rarely, and at fixed times of the year rather than on fixed days. He has his permanent and stable residence and fixed episcopal see in the nearby city of Portus-Gruarius, where there is another sacred building serving as a cathedral, as well as a bishop’s residence, an episcopal curia, a college of canons, and a seminary for clerics.

In public acts the bishop is always called the Bishop of Concordia. But in ordinary speech and writing, both among the inhabitants and among outsiders, as though the designation “Bishop of Concordia” had become obsolete, he is commonly called the Bishop of Portus-Gruarius.

What, then, is surprising if Bishop Chromatius of Aquileia, as the fourth century was ending and the fifth beginning, after withdrawing once, twice, and even a third time from the city of Aquileia under the pressure of the gravest necessities, retired to the Port of Romatinum or Romatium, a place suited to safety and repose and then situated within his diocese, and remained there for some time? What, I say, is surprising if he could consequently have acquired the name “Bishop of Romatium” or “Romatinum,” which could easily have been prefixed to the writings or little works that he left behind?

But what if Chromatius himself also ended his days in this Port of Romatium or Romatinum? That would certainly have furnished a still stronger common basis for this designation.

In 407 or 408, Chromatius exchanged mortal life for heavenly glory, according to De Rubeis in his *Monuments*, printed in 1740. He supported this with a weighty conjecture, as he himself confirmed in his *Dissertations of Varied Learning*, chapter 9, page 199, published in 1762—contrary to what he had said in his dissertation on Rufinus, published in 1764, where on pages 144 and 147 he had placed the year of Chromatius’s death in 406.

In that very year, 407 or 408, the Gothic leader Alaric, whose forces had been restored, again descended into Italy and once more shook the territory of Aquileia with terror. He nevertheless passed by Aquileia and the other cities of Venetia, making straight for Rome, which he finally captured and plundered in the following year, 409 or 410.

Nothing, therefore, is more probable than that Chromatius withdrew with the greatest haste to that same place, as he had been accustomed to do, during this new and terrifying barbarian invasion. There, perhaps more severely seized by the illness from which he had previously suffered—as we learn from Chrysostom’s letter of 406—he may have surrendered his soul.

This, then, concerns the title “Roman bishop,” which the writings or little works of Chromatius of Aquileia bore before the Abbot Alcuin and in their first Basel edition.

The mention of the year of Bishop Chromatius’s death, which the opinions of our two authors do not extend beyond 408 of the common era, now reminds us to say something about a recent discovery that has not yet seen the light of publication. From this discovery, if nothing stood in the way, the life of our Chromatius would have to be extended at least to the year 420.

This discovery is an old lead seal, or medallion, which we reproduce below. When the distinguished Mauro Boni, whom we praised above, recently discovered it in Venice among several old monuments of this kind, he most kindly communicated it to us as soon as possible, so that, when the opportunity arose, we might write something about it as well.

> **Note:** Concerning this and other more recent discoveries of antiquities—not only Venetian ones, but also those belonging to Aquileia and Grado—the same highly deserving Mauro Boni also informed the Venetian Athenaeum, in accordance with its purpose, of which he is a distinguished member. There is in print an Academic Report on this discovery by Boni, delivered at a public session of the same Athenaeum on 28 May of the preceding year, 1815, by the distinguished Francesco Aglietti, likewise one of its eminent members. We refer the reader to it.

Here you see both sides of this ancient piece of lead, the front and the back. There can be no doubt that the Chromatius who is inscribed on the front as bishop of Aquileia is in fact our Chromatius, the subject of our discussion.

But what does the year 420 signify on the back, marked there together with a pastoral staff? Can one infer from it either that Chromatius exchanged his life for heavenly glory in that same year, or at least that he was still living in that year—as though, in either interpretation, this leaden numerical mark together with the whole medallion could be considered a work of that very year?

It is sufficiently established among scholars that in the year of Christ 420 it was not yet customary to mark dates by years counted from Christ’s incarnation or birth. Indeed, this practice began much later, even in ecclesiastical matters, and became widespread later still, at least in the West.

Learned writers on chronology have treated this matter abundantly, most recently the Maurist authors of the excellent work *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, in the preliminary dissertation, part I, § 2, in the Paris edition of 1770. So too have the masters of diplomatic studies, among whom we mention here the distinguished Tiraboschi, in his *History of Nonantola*, volume II, page 16. He observes there that among the Italians this same practice scarcely began before the end of the ninth century in the dating of documents.

In the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome and continued down to his own age, those little panels in which the years of the Lord, counted from his birth, are marked along the margin of the pages are absent from the older manuscript copies. In the judgment of scholars they are additions of a much later period and were therefore wholly unknown to Eusebius and Jerome themselves.

See the Eusebian *Chronicle* in the edition of Saint Jerome’s works prepared by Vallarsius, volume VIII, column 635, note a; and also the notes and corrections of Arnaldo Pontaco on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, printed at the end of the same volume of Jerome, columns 230–231.

By this statement alone concerning the year 420, therefore, we reject the Chromatian lead medallion as belonging to that year. It must be a work of a later age and consequently possesses no contemporary authority whatsoever for proving that our Chromatius lived at least until the year 420, contrary to what those two learned countrymen of ours, Fontaninus and De Rubeis, wrote. After properly weighing the most reliable contemporary monuments, they did not extend his life beyond, at most, the year 408 of that same century.

But what if it may further be suspected that this lead medallion or seal was probably made even after the year 1000 of Christ, especially at a time when historical chronicles were being written everywhere throughout the cities of Italy? Such chronicles are generally not mistaken in assigning the years of their own times, but, as is sufficiently well known, they often produced by chance many errors when referring events of earlier ages to the Christian era. Later scholars, applying the rules of criticism, were compelled to correct these errors only with considerable tedium and labor.

The letters themselves, or rather the forms of the letters visible on this lead monument, give us reason to suspect this of the Chromatian piece—especially the letters A, E, M, and R. Their forms resemble, either entirely or nearly so, those that we can see—since we now prefer to cite our own examples rather than foreign ones—on the coins of the patriarchs of Aquileia. All of those coins were struck after the year 1000, and they are reproduced in De Rubeis’s first dissertation on the coins of the patriarchs of Aquileia and in Liruti’s *The Coinage That Circulated in Friuli*, and so forth.

We do not deny that the forms of the letters C and O on this lead medallion or seal are unusual. The former, on the front as a letter and on the back as a numerical mark, consists of two straight angles placed back to back; the latter consists of four angles forming a perfectly square figure.

But this very peculiarity of the two letters excludes from this medallion the antiquity of the beginning of the fifth century and indicates a later period, whatever period it must finally be judged to be.

The first letter, C, drawn in the manner that appears on our lead, is displayed on a small Venetian silver coin reproduced by the cited Liruti, plate VI, no. 60. He himself thinks that it belongs to the Lombard period, perhaps to the earlier part of the eighth century, as he learnedly argues there on pages 140 and following.

The same letter had also been seen at Rome, carved in exactly this manner on a fragment of Latin stone in the pavement of Saint Agatha of the Goths near the Subura, by the celebrated Antonius Maria Lupi. Although the fragment had no intelligible meaning, he nevertheless wished to display it because of the unusual form of this letter in his most learned dissertation on the epitaph of the martyr Severa, page 104 of the Palermo edition of 1734.

The name of the Goths attached to the church of Agatha seems sufficiently to indicate the origin of that meaningless broken stone. We should therefore no longer be surprised that the Latin letter C had also, among that people, in some way departed from its Roman form, and we may finally conclude that a form so degenerate from the ancient one cannot belong to the beginning of the fifth century.

Moreover, Dom Vainesius of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur asserts in his *Reasoned Dictionary of Diplomatics*, volume I, page 213, Paris edition of 1774, that this form of the third Latin letter was very common in inscriptions of the eleventh century.

That the same form of this third Latin letter also appeared on coins of the eleventh century—as we pass over other contemporary monuments—is sufficiently demonstrated by coins bearing the name of the Emperor Henry. These were recently discovered at Venice in the ark where the sacred remains of Saint Mark the Evangelist were deposited in 1094. They therefore probably belong to Henry Augustus IV, who was still reigning at that time, and certainly cannot be later than him.

The types of these coins are accurately engraved in copper in the excellent study by the noble Leonardo Manin, Count and Venetian Patrician, entitled *Historical-Critical Memoirs concerning the Life, Translation, and Discoveries of Saint Mark the Evangelist, Principal Protector of Venice*, Venice, 1815.

As for the letter O, which on this lead is formed as a perfectly square outline, it is true that on certain very ancient Greek coins the Greek letters omicron and omega appear formed in this way, as the distinguished Franciscus Neumanus observes in *Ancient Unpublished Coins of Peoples and Kings*, part I, page 221, Vienna, 1779.

Nevertheless, we must admit that nothing of this kind has come before us in published ancient Latin monuments that we have been able to consult.

Instead, however, there is abundant evidence in the lead pages or tablets recently discovered at Venice by the distinguished Mauro Boni. They came from an ancient literary society of the Correr family, hitherto unknown to all writers, which, as we have learned from trustworthy and highly learned men, already existed there in the eleventh century.

Among other concerns, this society took particular care to transfer onto lead plates—in either Latin or the vernacular Venetian language of their time, and in the script then in use—whatever ancient memories and documents it could obtain and investigate from writings on parchment. Thus, when those parchment documents later decayed through their fragility or perished altogether, the more durable material of lead would preserve all those things for posterity.

> **Note:** The distinguished and greatly devoted Camaldolese abbot of Saint Michael of Murano in Venice, Placidus Zurla, first brought us news of this most auspicious discovery in a letter sent to us on 27 July 1814. In it he also transmitted to us a most faithful specimen, not only of the script of those lead plates but also of certain matters contained in them. He wrote as follows:
>
> “You will find various things in different languages, everything faithfully and with indescribable patience transcribed from certain little lead plates formerly owned by a patrician Correr family. That family had in its house, from as early as the eleventh century, an Academy of Scholars. As various indications show, this Academy took care to have the ancient records that had long existed on parchment and were gradually perishing engraved on lead. Boni also succeeded in finding some of those original parchment documents, and the number of these lead pieces is exceedingly large. They record events of the homeland from the foundation of Venice down to about 1300.
>
> “The discovery of these lead pieces caused a great stir when it was made public in a report delivered at this Athenaeum last May by the aforementioned Boni. Some strongly opposed it, denying its authenticity on the principal grounds that neither Foscarini nor anyone else knew of them, and because they contain certain phrases said to have come into use only later, and so forth.”

When the distinguished Boni had heard these and other objections, and in the meantime, with fortune favoring him, had discovered many other Venetian monuments of various kinds—lead, parchment, and stone, as well as seals, coins, and niello work—which both revealed facts hitherto unknown to writers on Venetian affairs and supported especially the genuineness of those lead plates through their remarkable agreement with them in dates, events, and names—he presented all these materials in the following year, 1815, at the same Royal Venetian Athenaeum. Taken together, they constitute an almost immense collection of such antiquities, which he confidently called the *Neography of Venice*.

At the urging of the same Venetian Athenaeum, the learned man had resolved to clarify all these matters in a printed work. But shortly afterward, remembering the vow he had made to the Society of Jesus, recently restored and formerly his own, and having fulfilled that vow, he once again entered the Society. May someone else, among the many distinguished students of Venetian affairs, undertake to adorn this field.

In the meantime, let the reader consult the printed Academic Report that the aforementioned Francesco Aglietti delivered on this matter at the Venetian Athenaeum on 12 June 1814, as well as another report by the same author, mentioned above, delivered on 28 May of the following year, 1815.

In these tablets—which, as we hope, will one day also enjoy the light of public attention—whenever the letter O occurs, whether in Latin or in the vernacular Venetian language of that time, it is always perfectly quadrangular, just as it appears on the Chromatian medallion or seal. The other letters there are likewise angular, although in different ways, apparently because of a certain angular style of writing that seems to have been in use there at that time, perhaps for the sake of a particular elegance.

Vainesius, likewise, in his cited *Diplomatic Dictionary*, volume II, page 141, displays this square form of the Latin letter O as used in inscriptions. He nevertheless considers it, together with certain other distinctive forms of the same letter, to belong not to the earlier centuries, either before or after Christ, but absolutely and without distinction to the broadly extended period of the Middle Ages.

Nothing, therefore, is more probable than that the Chromatian lead medallion was made even after the year 1000 of Christ. Consequently, the numerical mark 420 on its reverse should be regarded as no more significant than the dates that later historical writers attached to events and deeds of the earlier centuries after Christ, when they wished to refer those events to the Christian era, even though in those centuries they were not dated by years of Christ.

In such calculations of years, therefore, greater confidence must be placed in our critics and chronologists, who have examined each matter with the utmost care and have consulted especially the many contemporary monuments that later ages have brought to light and the art of printing has made common to all—monuments that could not have been available to those ancient, otherwise deserving, writers.

Let that numerical mark on our Chromatian lead medallion or seal, then, be regarded as worthless concerning the life or death of our Chromatius; and let us rather accept the accounts, differing little from one another, established by Fontaninus and De Rubeis. What, meanwhile, should we think about the medallion or seal itself, which was undoubtedly made, as we conjectured, after the year 1000? We are entering upon a purely conjectural matter when we ask for what reason it was struck—or rather embossed—or to what use it was dedicated. Yet we are far from suspecting that the makers of this medallion or seal wished to deceive posterity.

[Col. 0299C] We have no doubt that Chromatius possessed his episcopal seal, with which he would seal his writings and letters whenever necessary. For ancient monuments teach us that this practice was current among the bishops of that and even earlier ages; Ducange, in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, and Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Book II, chapter 15, §1, demonstrate this learnedly. It is clear from the same Mabillon that such seals were of various kinds, and that each one in particular often bore the name of the bishop to whom it belonged. We readily believe, too, that bishops generally placed the sign of the life-giving Cross on their seals together with their own name. In former times they placed this sign before their personal name when they subscribed acts or charters, as Mabillon likewise shows in chapter 22, §12. Why, then, should we not suppose that the seal of Chromatius of Aquileia was precisely of the form which our lead medallion bears on its obverse, with the Cross set in the middle and his own name together with that of his city inscribed around it?

[Col. 0299D] Yet although our medallion has the form of a seal, it cannot be the genuine and proper seal used by Chromatius, both because of all the considerations given above, which led us to judge it a work made after the year 1000, and also because its reverse lacks the loop or attachment with which seals were equipped to make them easy to use. What, then, should we conjecture after this? Let those who at some time after the year of Christ 1000 were devoted to literary studies and antiquities—and perhaps also the members of the Corrarian society itself at Venice—have seen some impression of the Chromatian seal still surviving, formed in wax, plaster, or chalk. Let them, I say, have considered the fragility of the material and the danger that, with the passage of time, both the surviving impression and the memory of the seal might perish. They therefore decided to commit its form to lead for posterity: the form of the seal that they had before their eyes, with the Cross introduced in the middle of the little field and the words **CHROMATII- EPISCO-AQUIL-** placed around it, while employing a form of lettering characteristic of their own age. And behold, as we conjecture, the natural and obvious origin of the obverse of this lead Chromatian medallion—or, more truly, seal.

[LIX] As for the reverse, on which there is an episcopal crozier together with the Roman numeral **CCCCXX**, we judge without hesitation that it was wholly and entirely the arbitrary invention of those who attended to the object at that time, namely after the year 1000. Wishing somehow to cover the vacant part of that leaden plate, they thought they would do something pleasing to posterity in good faith if they marked there some indication of time according to the then-current Christian era, within which, in their own opinion, Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, had lived; and if, in accordance with the custom then introduced, they also added the emblem of his pastoral episcopal rule, namely the crozier.

Who, moreover—if we may touch on this subject here—has ever seen, or read mentioned by contemporary authors, an episcopal crozier on the seals of bishops of the fourth century or of the beginning of the fifth? Everyone will readily recognize that the form of the crozier expressed on our lead plate is not primitive, nor one belonging to the fourth or fifth century, but rather the form that we know to have been in use after the year 1000, and that we especially observe on the coins of the patriarchs of Aquileia.

Enough, then, has been said about the recently discovered Chromatian lead medallion or seal.

Another investigation now presents itself to us, one that likewise offers something new in the study of antiquity: the route by which the people of Aquileia traveled to the Portus Romatium or Romatinum, as though by a direct and shorter road. For we do not consider it wholly useless or unpleasant to investigate which route Chromatius probably took when he turned from Aquileia toward the Portus Romatium or Romatinum.

This investigation was occasioned by an Aquileian stone, very beautiful indeed, which was recently found, in the year 1806, near Aquileia in a wooded place known among the inhabitants as Roncato and also Tombola. It was therefore unknown to all the interpreters of Aquileian antiquities and deserved to be examined, elucidated, and brought into its true light by some scholar of the first rank in antiquarian studies.

Here, then, excellent reader, is the stone as it was first published for the public by Giovanni Labus, a doctor of Brescia, in his learned letter written in Italian, entitled *Sopra una colonna letterata di Maguzzano* [*On an Inscribed Column at Maguzzano*], Brescia, 1812, p. 10. The most courteous author later communicated it to us by letter with all its notes and measurements, with the greatest care; and finally we ourselves received it from the same upright and knowledgeable men who had diligently attended its original discovery.

[Note: [Col. 0301D] Among these we name Leopold and Sanctus Zucculo, brothers, our excellent fellow citizens, devotees of the painter’s art and ardent lovers of the antiquities of Aquileia, which they have often examined with their own eyes. They themselves repeatedly insisted that the inscription of this stone, first printed by the most distinguished Labus, was genuine in every respect: nothing had been added to it, nothing removed, and nothing corrupted in it through the fault either of the transcriber or of the printer.

We considered it worthwhile to record this here for the reader’s guidance, because in the *Journal*, that is, the *Giornale dell’Italiana letteratura*, printed at Padua, volume XXXII of the complete series and volume II of the new series, no. 4, July and August 1812, pp. 249–250, the following less favorable judgment was expressed concerning this inscription: “It seems that, in the form in which the author (Mr. Labus) gives it, it cannot stand; and certainly, through an error either of the copyist or of the printer, some word was added or altered.” We, on the contrary, see nothing at all wrong with this inscription—apart from the name of the emperor, which was erased in antiquity—that would prevent it from being judged complete and perfect in meaning.

What happened to the stone bearing the inscription after its discovery, where it now exists, or what fate it has undergone, we do not know. Indeed, to tell the truth, we searched for it in vain recently at Aquileia so that we too might compare the original inscription with the published one. In any case, after the authority of Doctor Labus that we have cited, and after the testimony of eyewitnesses that we have mentioned, no prudent doubt remains either about the discovery of the stone or about the genuineness of the inscription.]

[Col. 0302B] We shall not say much here about this stone, but only what concerns the matter before us, and what may at the same time stimulate the studies of others to illuminate the question more fully. Its dimensions are as follows: height, 4 feet 9 inches; width, 2 feet 5 inches; thickness, 9 inches.

[LXI] This stone is headless, because the entire first line and the earlier and larger part of the second were erased with a chisel or hammer. There stood the name of the emperor, to whose memory it had been dedicated, because he had restored the Via Annia mentioned there.

I now produce another Aquileian stone, long known, likewise headless after its first two words. It can nevertheless shed some light on the preceding stone, since it apparently refers to it; and it is regarded as complete, namely with its lacuna represented by lines, in Bertoli, *Le Antichità d’Aquileja*, p. 284, and in Basilio Asquini, *Ragguaglio*, etc., of Monfalcone, p. 9. This lacuna had previously been absent in Gruter and others who had printed the same stone, and hence the inscription was falsely attributed, from its opening words, to Caesar Augustus.

The inscription is therefore reported in the following form by both of the cited local writers, who examined the stone itself with their own eyes at Aquileia. We have here adopted the more accurate form in which the very diligent and equally learned Angelo Maria Cortinovius, whom we mentioned above, recorded it in his papers after repeated comparisons with the stone itself; and we ourselves recognized at Aquileia, by sight and touch, that this form was true and genuine.

[Note: [Col. 0304D] This stone, which in the time when our Bertoli was writing was seen in the pavement of the sacred building of the nuns then at Aquileia of the Order of Saint Benedict, now stands a little distance from that place in the residence of the Counts de Cassis Pharaon. There, in the picture gallery, it occupies the foremost place among the ancient monuments of Aquileia.]

[LXII]

[Col. 0303C] The dimensions of this second stone are as follows: its height is 5 feet 4 inches; its width is 2 feet 1½ inches. Its thickness is concealed by the wall into which the stone is inserted.

These two stones appear to have been set up for one and the same emperor, on account of two works of the same kind carried out for the benefit of the people of Aquileia: namely, the restoration of the Via Annia, as in the first stone, and the fortification and restoration of the Via Gemina, as in the second. The first stone, to which the second referred by the connective word *quoque* (“also”), had until now been unknown. For the second clearly indicated, besides the Gemina, another road restored by the same emperor, which we now know to have been the Annia.

Moreover, the second stone agrees very well with the wording of the first, in which that most provident emperor is said to have conferred upon the people of Aquileia numerous benefits. For, on account of those many benefits—and certainly because he restored both the Via Annia and also the Via Gemina mentioned there—the same emperor is rightly called the restorer of the Aquileians and, in a certain sense, also their founder, in accordance with the not uncommon flattery that peoples of those times directed toward their rulers.

[LXIII] Who this emperor was, whose name has been erased in both places, I shall state plainly. Bertoli, cited above, who was elucidating the second stone, believed him to be Diocletian; but Asquini, who immediately after Bertoli discussed this same stone in the place cited above, more probably maintained that he was Hadrian. Whatever Bertoli himself later wrote against this opinion in the pamphlet he published against Asquini in the first Calogerian collection, *Opuscoli scientifici e filologici*, volume XXVI, p. 501, is beside the point here.

The distinguished man recently praised above, Cortinovius, an expert in all antiquities and especially in those of our Aquileia, likewise adopted Asquini’s opinion. I possess his learned memorandum in manuscript concerning this same second inscription. In it he ingeniously supplied in the margin the lacuna of three lines, which he had accurately taken from the stone itself at Aquileia—not marked by a continuous succession of little lines, as in Bertoli and Asquini, but distinguished by intervening blank spaces, as we have presented it here—on the basis of several other complete inscriptions of the emperor Hadrian, undoubtedly also taking into account the capacity of the space to admit all the words and abbreviations.

**Imp. Caes. DIVI. TRAIANI. PARTHICI F. DIVI. NERVAE N. TRAIANVS. HADRIANVS Invictus Aug. etc.**

The most learned Filiasi recently also subscribed to the opinion of the illustrious Cortinovius that this was Hadrian rather than Diocletian, in *Memorie storiche dei Veneti Primi e Secondi*, volume II, chapter 25, p. 224, Venice, 1796. Yet there he reports the Aquileian inscription of the Via Gemina exactly in the manner of Bertoli and Asquini: the lacuna of three lines is indicated by a continuous series of dots, without any indication of intervening spaces. It is therefore clear that he knew and approved Cortinovius’s opinion, which he had adopted, but had not understood the restoration of the lacuna. For that reason we now publish it for the first time from Cortinovius’s papers, after testing and confirming it at our own risk.

[LXIV] I myself once thought that the Roman emperor whose name had been erased might have been the emperor Trajan, Hadrian’s father: first, because his Italian homeland is mentioned on the stone; then because he himself carried out numerous and distinguished works both at Rome and in the principal cities of the empire; and especially because he restored almost all the roads of Italy, as I had learned from a chance reading of the physician Galen, who wrote in Book IX, chapter 8 of *The Method of Healing*:

“Since all the roads in Italy were in such a condition”—that is, in a worse condition—“that Trajan restored them. Wherever they were wet and muddy, he paved them with stones or raised them by means of constructed embankments; wherever they were overgrown with thorn bushes and rough, he cleared them; rivers that could not be crossed he joined by bridges; wherever the road appeared longer than necessary, he cut out another, shorter one; wherever it was difficult because of a steep hill, he diverted it through gentler places; and if it was blocked by wild animals or deserted, he transferred it from there and led it through inhabited regions; then he leveled the rough places.”

Thus Galen, about the second century after Trajan’s reign, speaks of the roads of Italy restored by that emperor.

But who would say that Trajan’s name had been erased from stones intended to preserve the memory of roads restored by him, when he had received the title of “best emperor” by decree of the Senate, and his memory remained so dear to everyone even after his death that the Roman people became accustomed to acclaiming new emperors after him: “May you be more fortunate than Augustus, better than Trajan”? This was as though no Roman emperor before or after him had reached Trajan’s goodness, just as no one had surely reached Augustus’s good fortune.

I was therefore compelled, especially for this reason, to defer to Asquini and Cortinovius, and with them to recognize Hadrian in this second stone, and consequently also in the first, which, according to what was said above, may be called the elder brother of the second.

Indeed, Hadrian too was Italian by birthplace or origin. He was Trajan’s cousin, later regarded as his adopted son, and his successor in the empire. Once established in power, he left everywhere numerous monuments of his generosity and beneficence. Moreover, at Aquileia Hadrian founded a building of immense size and remarkable construction, called for that reason the Hadrianaeum. It was undoubtedly then dedicated to the profane worship of the gods, but in the fourth century of the Church, when that century had matured, it was adapted and devoted to Christian worship. Its foundations and notable ruins were finally discovered not many years ago, when small dwellings were being erected for settlers brought there from parts of Greece under inauspicious circumstances; they consequently remained there only briefly. This may be learned from the Filiasi mentioned above, in the same cited volume II, chapter 22, p. 212, and chapter 24, p. 225.

[LXV] This distinguished work of the emperor Hadrian, undertaken for the benefit of the Aquileians and for the adornment of the city of Aquileia, whose memory has come down to us, was one of the many monuments of his beneficence toward the Aquileians of which the first stone speaks. On account of these works he was called on the other stone the restorer and founder of the Aquileians. Other such monuments, perhaps still lying hidden beneath the earth, may in time be brought to light.

Furthermore, in both inscriptions we observe the title **Invictus** (“Unconquered”). This title was once attributed only to the gods and was not bestowed even upon Trajan himself; it first began to be given to Hadrian among the emperors on inscriptions, as our Bertoli observed while arguing his case for Diocletian, on p. 286 of the cited work *Le Antichità d’Aquileja*.

What of the fact that Hadrian also assumed Trajan’s name, placing it before his own, as we see on stones and coins: **IMP. CAESAR. TRAIANUS. HADRIANUS. AUG.**? Before him Trajan himself had likewise placed the name of his predecessor Nerva before his own: **IMP. CAESAR. NERVA. TRAIANUS. AUG.** Perhaps, then, the physician Galen, when he simply wrote “Trajan,” intended Trajan-Hadrian, although it is certain that Trajan too busied himself, as I said, with constructing works here and there. In ancient and uncertain matters, who can forbid an occasional conjecture?

Let these two local stones, then, be attributed to the emperor Hadrian. But why was the name of this Augustus erased on both stones at Aquileia? After the many praises with which he is exalted there—as the most provident emperor, giver of numerous benefits to the Aquileians, and restorer and founder of Aquileia—did Hadrian later deserve so ill of the Aquileians that his name was cut from the stones?

Hadrian certainly deserved as well of the Aquileians as, broadly speaking, of all the regions and cities of the Roman world, because of the benefits he bestowed everywhere. He traversed the Roman Empire on continuous journeys, accompanied by what was almost an army of architects and craftsmen of every kind, as Aurelius Victor in the *Epitome* and Spartianus in his *Life of Hadrian* report.

“Hadrian,” says Aurelius Victor, “undertook immense labor, for he traveled on foot through all the provinces, preceding the company that followed him, while restoring every town and enlarging its public buildings. For, after the model of military legions, he had organized into cohorts and centuries craftsmen, surveyors, architects, and every kind of worker concerned with constructing or adorning walls.”

“In almost every city,” says Spartianus, “he both built something and staged public entertainments.”

But Hadrian, as it were, stained all these good deeds with blackness and even obliterated them: first by the excessively permissive manner of his life, through which he was hated by everyone; then by a certain unrestrained ambition to surpass everyone in every discipline of literature and the liberal arts, so that he never tolerated anyone’s being preferred to him with impunity; and also by the violent savagery of his spirit, through which he treated many innocent people, especially learned men whose intellectual distinction aroused his jealousy, with the indignation of all good men, and removed them with the greatest severity and cruelty. We learn this from the cited Spartianus and from Dio Cassius, Book LXIX.

What is more, toward the end of his life, made still more cruel by the force of the illness with which he was grievously afflicted, he raged especially against the Senate itself, ordering a large part of that most illustrious order to be killed, as the cited Aurelius Victor reports in the same passage and in *On the Caesars*. Consequently, the Senate itself wished after his death to invalidate his acts and refused to call him divine, as custom required, unless his son Antoninus intervened with the most earnest entreaties. For this reason too he acquired the surname Pius, as we learn from the same Spartianus and from Julius Capitolinus in his *Life of Antoninus Pius*.

Here, then, are the offenses of the emperor Hadrian on account of which his name was undoubtedly erased after his death from stones—not by public authority, perhaps, but nevertheless through the private judgment of those most concerned—not only at Aquileia but perhaps elsewhere as well. Such was the Roman custom toward emperors who had become hated, especially because of cruel actions, as we learn from Dio, Suetonius, and other historians of Roman affairs. Our learned Bertoli likewise notes this in the cited work *Le Antichità d’Aquileja*, p. 285, where he thinks the lacuna in the second stone belongs to Diocletian, the most savage enemy of the Christians.

[Col. 0307B] What, then, are we now to say about the Aquileian Via Annia, which we see on the first of these stones and on account of which chiefly we are writing this? We do know the Roman Via Annia, although we have no information about it in the ancient writers and only a little in a few inscriptions.

This Via Annia is mentioned only four times in Gruter’s *Thesaurus Inscriptionum*. Pitiscus mentions it, but briefly and inadequately, in the *Lexicon of Roman Antiquities*, volume III, p. 704, The Hague edition of 1737, citing two of Gruter’s inscriptions in which the Via Annia is mentioned.

Nicolaus Bergier also mentions it in *On the Public and Military Roads of the Roman Empire*, in Graevius’s *Thesaurus*, etc., volume X. He first mentions it in Book I, section 4, §7, where he presents a Gruterian inscription in which one curator is responsible for several roads at once: the Annia, and also the Clodia, Cassia, Cimina, the Three Traianae, and the Amerina. From this we understand the proximity of all these roads, entrusted to one and the same curator, and likewise the distance of all of them from the region of Aquileia, including the Annia mentioned there.

He mentions it again in Book III, section 22, §9. There, however, he also lists the Annia among those public roads of Italy that did not extend beyond the Po and therefore had no connection whatever with Aquileia:

“From here,” he says, “follow the roads Annia, Augusta, Cimina, Amerina, Sempronia, and Posthumia, which are inserted into and connected with the Via Flaminia at various places and extend from it in different directions; that is, like branches, they run through the regions of Italy between Rome and the Eridanus, or Po.”

As far as we know, therefore, no one has written about this Via Annia mentioned in our Aquileian inscription—namely, the road that would have been directed toward Aquileia, that would have lain near Aquileia, and whose restoration could therefore be called a benefit granted to the Aquileians through the emperor’s generosity.

The most diligent interpreter of Aquileian antiquities, Bertoli himself, makes no mention of any Via Annia belonging to the Aquileians. Only on p. 291 of his frequently cited and most learned work does he indicate that certain traces of two ancient Roman roads still appear in the territory of Aquileia. He says that in certain old documents, dating, as he himself claims, from three or four centuries ago, one of them was called the Via Appia in certain old documents of the chapter of Aquileia, of which he himself was a canon. Unless, rather, *Annia* ought to have been read, since there is no other mention of an Appia among us; this newly discovered stone, with its uncorrupted letters, now offers a torch to the letters of the old documents, whose antiquity not infrequently deceives even the eyes of antiquarians and scholars.

Meanwhile, let others investigate this Aquileian Via Annia: who laid it out, and at what time; from whom it received its name; whether it belonged in some way to the well-known Roman Via Annia beyond the Po, or should be considered an entirely different road and judged peculiar to Aquileia, like that Gemina mentioned in the second inscription. Such matters belong to antiquarians. For the moment we wholly refrain from harvesting in this field of scholarship, preferring to await from them what we ought to think about these questions.

We merely observe that on this recently discovered stone our Via Annia is said to have been destroyed by the inflowing marsh waters, so that it had become impassable for travelers; and that it was therefore restored for the benefit of the Aquileians through the generosity of the most provident emperor.

From this we learn that it was a road lying over marshy waters and therefore separated from the other land routes; that it was near Aquileia, indeed almost the private road of the Aquileians, and extremely useful to them; and finally, that it was like an embankment laid across the marshes, providing the Aquileians with an easier and shorter passage to the coastal regions of the estuary, while avoiding the higher and longer land routes lying farther from the waters and marshes.

The inhabitants of Aquileia still point out a certain road situated to the south of that once vast and wealthy city, now abandoned and most wretched, toward Concordia and covered by marsh waters. When those waters occasionally recede, stones and rubble appear at their bottom—the remains of an ancient road—as well as a very large iron ring still fixed in a stone. This ring was undoubtedly placed beside the edge of the same road and served for fastening small boats near it.

What, then, if our Chromatius used this very Via Annia, restored for the Aquileians by the emperor Hadrian, to travel immediately from Aquileia to the Portus Romatium or Romatinum, and then to return from that port to Aquileia, as the circumstances and changing conditions of those times required? We have judged that this final investigation concerning Chromatius, prompted by this Aquileian stone recently brought to light, is neither wholly foreign to our purpose nor unpleasant for our readers.

These, finally, are the matters that we wished to set forth by way of preface at the beginning of the writings or minor works that survive and that we are presenting in this new edition of the holy Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. We did so both to explain to our readers the reason for our undertaking and the care we have taken, so that the writings might appear both more correct and arranged in a more suitable order, and also adorned with a considerably better finish than before; and so that, after the labors of the most distinguished men, we might ourselves seem to contribute something that could in any way serve to illuminate the subject.

You will therefore, excellent reader, judge these matters favorably and generously. We shall always have done enough—and more than enough—if you approve at least our intention and effort, and kindly pardon our errors, while expecting from others, after our attempt, things better, fuller, and more accurate.

[Col. 0309A]

## Selected Testimonies of the Ancients Concerning Saint Chromatius

[Col. 0309A]

[LXXI] **Saint Jerome, Letter 7, to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius**, §§1 and 6, A.D. 373; preserved in his *Works*, volume I, columns 17 and following, in the Veronese edition of Domenico Vallarsi.

A sheet of paper ought not to divide those whom mutual love has joined; nor should the duties of my correspondence be distributed among individuals, since you love one another so much that charity joins three of you no less than nature has united two. Indeed, if the nature of the matter permitted it, I would enclose your undivided names beneath the single tip of my little letter, since your letters also provoke me to think of three as one and of one as three . . . .

We greet your common mother—with whom you share holiness, though she precedes you in this respect because she gave birth to such children, so that her womb may truly be called golden—with the honor you know. We also embrace all the sisters who are to be received together, women who have overcome both their sex and the world, and who, having abundantly prepared oil for their lamps, await the coming of the Bridegroom.

O blessed household, in which dwell the widow Anna, the virginal prophetesses, and the twin Samuel nurtured in the Temple! O happy dwelling, in which we behold a martyred mother crowned with the crowns of the Maccabean martyrs! For although you confess Christ daily by keeping his commandments, this public and open confession has been added to your private glory: through you, the poison of the Arian doctrine was once excluded from your city.

**The same, Letter 8, to Niceas, subdeacon of Aquileia**, A.D. 373; preserved in the same edition of his *Works*, volume I, column 21.

Behold, blessed Chromatius, who is related to the holy Eusebius not more by nature than by equality of character, has challenged me through the duty of correspondence.

**The same, Letter 60, to Heliodorus**, §19, A.D. 396; preserved in the same edition, volume I, column 345.

Let us be joined in spirit, bound together in affection, and imitate in our son the strength of mind that blessed Pope Chromatius displayed at the death of his brother.

[LXXII] **The same, Letter 81, to Rufinus**, §2, A.D. 399; preserved in the same edition, volume I, column 508.

My brother Paulinianus has not yet returned from his homeland, and I think that you have seen him at Aquileia with the holy Pope Chromatius.

**The same, Book II against Rufinus**, §22, cited *Works*, volume II, column 515.

Who are these people who are accustomed to dispute at length in the Church? Who are accustomed to write books? Who speak and write about Origen everywhere? Who, because they do not want their own thefts to be recognized and are ungrateful toward their teacher, therefore deter simple people from reading him? You ought to name them explicitly and identify the men themselves.

Are, then, the blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, and Chromatius, together with the entire synod of Catholics of both East and West—who with one and the same judgment, because they share one and the same spirit, denounce him to the peoples as a heretic—to be judged thieves of his books? And when they preach in the churches, do they recall not the mysteries of the Scriptures but the thefts of Origen?

**The same, Book II against Rufinus**, §27, cited *Works*, volume II, column 521.

I shall also offer another testimony, lest you now say that, compelled by the necessities of the case, I have changed my opinion. In the *Book of Times*, that is, the *Paralipomenon*, which is called in Hebrew *Dabre Jamin* [“Words of the Days”], I used the following preface addressed to the holy Pope Chromatius: “If the edition of the Seventy,” etc. See the remainder below.

**The same, Book II against Rufinus**, §31, cited *Works*, volume II, column 526.

I also translated from Hebrew the books of Solomon, which I had formerly rendered into Latin according to the Septuagint with obeli and asterisks, and dedicated them to the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus. At the end of my preface I added the following:

“If anyone prefers the edition of the Seventy translators, he has it from us as formerly corrected. For we do not forge new things in such a way as to destroy the old.”

[LXXIII] **The same, Book III against Rufinus**, §2, cited *Works*, volume II, column 533.

I call Jesus, the witness of my conscience, to witness that he will judge both this letter and yours: at the urging of the holy Pope Chromatius I wished to remain silent, to put an end to our quarrels, and to overcome evil with good. But because you threaten me with destruction unless I remain silent, I am compelled to reply, lest by keeping silent I appear to acknowledge the crime, and lest you interpret my gentleness as a sign of a bad conscience.

**The same, in the Prologue to Book I of the Commentaries on the Prophet Habakkuk**, cited *Works*, volume VI, column 587.

First, Chromatius, most learned of bishops, we must know that among the Greeks and Latins the name of the prophet is read corruptly as *Ambacum*. Among the Hebrews he is called *Abacuc*, and the name is interpreted as “embrace,” etc.

**The same, in the Prologue to Book II of the Commentaries on the Prophet Habakkuk**, cited *Works*, volume VI, column 631.

A second work, my dear Chromatius, venerable Pope, we are writing on the book of Habakkuk, dedicating to his song a work of its own and undertaking with all our strength an epic discourse composed in the manner of the psalter—that is, in lyric style.

Let the viper hiss, then, and let Sardanapalus jeer, more shameful in his vices than in his name. Let us pursue the path we have begun; and with your prayers, you who have conquered the flesh by virtue, let us expound in the eighth prophet—that is, in the number of the Lord’s Resurrection—the clearest prophecy concerning Christ.

**The same, Preface to the Books of Solomon**, cited *Works*, volume IX, column 1293.

Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops.

Let a letter join those whom the priesthood joins; indeed, let paper not divide those whom the love of Christ binds together. I would have written the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi, which you request, if my health had permitted it. You send financial support; you sustain our secretaries and copyists, so that our talent may labor especially for you.

And behold, from the side comes a large crowd of people asking for different things—as though it were fair for me, while you are hungry, to labor for others, or as though, in the accounting of what is given and received, I were indebted to anyone besides you.

And so, broken by a long illness, I did not wish to remain entirely silent this year or mute toward you. I consecrated a work of three days to your name: namely, a translation of the three books of Solomon—*Masloth*, which the Hebrews call *Parables* and the common Latin edition calls *Proverbs*; *Coeleth*, which in Greek is called *Ecclesiastes* and which in Latin we may call “Preacher”; and *Sir Assirim*, which in our language is translated *Song of Songs*, etc.

[LXXIV] **The same, Preface to the Books of Paralipomenon**, cited *Works*, volume IX, column 1405.

If the pure edition of the Seventy translators, as it was translated by them into Greek, had remained intact, you would be urging me in vain, my dear Chromatius, most holy and learned of bishops, to translate the Hebrew books into Latin. What had once occupied the ears of men and strengthened the faith of the nascent Church deserved also to be confirmed by our silence.

But now, since different copies are circulated according to the variety of regions, and since that genuine and ancient translation has been corrupted and violated, you think it belongs to my discretion either to judge among several copies which reading is true, or to forge a new work within an old one and, as the saying goes, to prick the eyes of crows while the Jews mock us, etc.

**The same, Preface to the Book of Tobit**, cited *Works*, volume X, columns 1–2.

To Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, Jerome the presbyter sends greetings in the Lord.

I never cease to marvel at the urgency of your demands: for you require me to render into Latin style a book written in the Chaldean language—namely, the Book of Tobit, which the Hebrews, cutting it away from the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, have consigned to those writings they call apocryphal. I have satisfied your desire, though not my own preference. For the studies of the Hebrews accuse us and charge us with transferring such material to Latin ears contrary to their canon. But, judging it better to displease the Pharisees’ judgment and to obey the commands of bishops, I persisted as best I could. And because the Chaldean language is close to the Hebrew tongue, after finding an eloquent man thoroughly skilled in both languages, I undertook a single day’s labor: whatever he expressed to me in Hebrew words, I, having summoned a secretary, set forth in Latin speech. I shall repay this work with your prayers, once I learn that it has pleased you that I have completed what you deigned to command.

### [LXXV] Saint Ambrose, Letter 50, to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, on the Prophecy of Balaam, §16, A.D. 390

Published in the works, volume II, column 996, Paris edition of the Benedictines of Saint-Maur, 1686–1690.

I have sent this little gift to your holy mind, because you wish me to put into writing something from the interpretations of ancient authors. For my part, I have undertaken to append letters in a familiar style, redolent of something of the conduct of the Fathers; if you approve their taste, I shall not be embarrassed to send you more of this kind hereafter. For I would rather ramble with you about heavenly matters in the words of old age—what the Greeks call ἀδολεσχῆσαι, “to chatter”—[lacuna]—I would rather, I say, ramble with you in the words of old age, lest I seem to have abandoned the art of uttering, in more hurried language, something no longer suited either to our studies or to our strength. Farewell, and love us; indeed, I love you.

### Rufinus, priest of Aquileia, Preface to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, to his own Latin History and that of Eusebius of Caesarea

Published in the works, column 209, the Veronese edition of Domenico Valtarsius.

The learned say that it belongs to physicians, whenever they see general diseases threatening cities or regions, to provide some medicine or kind of drink by which people, having been fortified, may be protected from the approaching destruction. You too, venerable father Chromatius, performed this kind of medical service when, at the time that the barriers of Italy were burst open by Alaric, leader of the Goths, a pestilential disease spread through the land and devastated fields, herds, and men far and wide. Seeking some remedy for the deadly destruction among the peoples entrusted to you by God, by which sick minds might be withdrawn from the contagion of the impending evil and kept occupied with better studies, you instruct me to translate into Latin the Ecclesiastical History that the most learned Eusebius of Caesarea composed in Greek, so that, while the minds of those listening were held captive by its reading and eagerly sought knowledge of past events, they might in some measure receive forgetfulness of the evils then taking place.

### The same, Apology for Saint Jerome, book I, §4

Published in the cited edition of the works, column 310.

As he himself and everyone knows, I had already been established in a monastery for almost thirty years; regenerated through the grace of Baptism, I received the seal of faith through the holy men Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, most renowned and approved bishops in the Church of God. One of them was then a priest under Valerian of blessed memory, another an archdeacon, and the other a deacon, and at the same time a father and teacher to me in the Creed and the faith.

### The same, Prologue to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, to Origen’s Treatise on the Book of Joshua

From volume II, page 396, of the Paris edition of Origen’s works in Greek and Latin by Charles Delarue, O.S.B., of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, 1733.

In the divine books it is related that, for the construction of the temple—or, alternatively, for the construction of the tabernacle—each person offered according to his ability: the powerful and the leaders of the people, gold, silver, precious stones, bronze, and others, incorruptible wood; some also scarlet, purple, fine linen, and others linen, these too destined to be useful for the priests’ garments and the high priest’s robe. The poorer, however, and those who offered red skins and goats’ hair, were not rejected. For this reason that Bezalel is said to have been filled by God with every wisdom: so that, understanding the uses to which each of these things was suited, he might reject nothing from the devotion of those offering.

Since, therefore, you too, my ever-venerable father Chromatius, instruct and command us to contribute something toward the building and construction of the divine tabernacle from the resources and wealth of the Greeks, we have explained for you in Latin, according to the smallness of our ability, the twenty-six little homilies on Joshua that the old Adamantius delivered extemporaneously in the Church, translating them from Greek. Let it be the task of the Bezalel of our own time—your judgment—to assess what we offer: even if no pure gold is found here that may benefit the altar, nor silver that may form the bases of the Church’s columns or adorn their capitals; if none of these stones can be found in which a jewel set into the breastplate might adorn your pontifical and divine-aware heart; at least see whether some purple, some royal splendor, or scarlet, the color of mystical blood, is woven into them; whether anything imitates the purity of fine linen and the strength of linen, and possesses something worthy of priestly garments; finally, whether you find among us red skins, representing modesty of the forehead; and, lastly, whether you find at least goats’ hair with which we may cover our poverty or cleanse by repentance whatever faults we have incurred.

Let all of this, then, depend upon your judgment. If there is anything that can please, let it belong to the author; for we do not think it right to seize what others have gained through labor and apply it to our own praise. But if the force of the meaning is made harsh by an unpolished style, attribute this either to me—or, if I may say so with your permission, to you yourself, who seek from the unlearned a work that ought to have been entrusted to the learned.

### [LXXVII] Saint John Chrysostom, Letter to Pope Innocent, A.D. 404

From the Greek and Latin Dialogue of Palladius of Helenopolis on the Life, etc., of Blessed John Chrysostom, chapter 2, in volume VIII of the Library of the Ancient Fathers, etc., of Andrea Gallandi, page 262; and from the edition of Peter Coustant of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, Paris, columns 771 and following.

I think that your piety heard, even before receiving our letter, what injustice has dared to do here. For the magnitude and gravity of the events are such that scarcely any part of the world has been left that has not heard this mournful tragedy, etc.

At the end he closes as follows:

“This same letter was also written to Venerius, Bishop of Milan, and to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia. Farewell in the Lord.”

[Note: In the Benedictine edition of the works of Saint John Chrysostom, Greek and Latin, volume III, page 515, this letter appears; but on page 520, where it ends, without any mention of Venerius of Milan or Chromatius of Aquileia, it closes as follows: “Farewell always, and pray for me, most reverend and holy lord.” Nevertheless, the former conclusion displayed by Palladius, and retained by Coustant, seems preferable. On this matter see Coustant himself in the note that he adds to this passage, column 787 of the cited edition.]

### The same, Letter to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, A.D. 406

Number 155 among the works of the Holy Doctor, Greek and Latin, in volume III, pages 689 and following, of the Benedictine edition of Saint-Maur.

The very clear trumpet of your fervent and sincere charity has spread its sound all the way to us, breathing something great and long-lasting across so vast a distance and reaching even to the ends of the earth. Although otherwise so far separated, we too have experienced no less than those who are present your most vehement and fire-filled charity, your sincere tongue steeped in immense freedom and confidence, and your adamantine zeal. For this reason, it would have been greatly in our wishes to enjoy your presence and meeting. But since that solitude in which we are now confined as though by fetters has also taken this from us, having found my most revered and devout lord the priest, we fulfill our desire as far as we can by writing and sending greetings, and by offering you our greatest thanks for the devotion that you have displayed throughout this long period with such great earnestness of spirit.

We ask and entreat you that, when he returns, and moreover whenever messengers who come to this solitude are encountered, you write to us about your health. For you know how much pleasure we shall derive from hearing more frequently of the good health of people who love us so ardently.

### [LXXVIII] Honorius Augustus, Letter to his brother Arcadius Augustus, A.D. 406

From Palladius of Helenopolis’ Dialogue on the Life, etc., of Blessed John Chrysostom, Greek and Latin, chapter 3, in volume VIII of Gallandi’s Library of the Ancient Fathers, etc.; and from the Paris edition of Peter Coustant’s Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, column 806.

For the third time I am now writing to your gentleness, asking that the proceedings undertaken by agreement against John, Bishop of Constantinople, be corrected; and, as it seems, this has not yet been accomplished. Therefore I have written again through these bishops and priests, being very concerned about ecclesiastical peace, through which our empire also obtains peace, so that you may deign to order the bishops of the East to assemble at Thessalonica, etc.

So that you may know what the Westerners’ opinion is concerning Bishop John, from all the letters that have been written to me I have appended two which contain the same position as the others: one from the Roman bishop, the other from the Bishop of Aquileia, etc.

Accordingly, when the holy Aemilius, Bishop of Beneventum, and Cythegius and Gaudentius, together with the priests Valentinian and Boniface, had received letters from the emperor Honorius, from Innocent, and from the Italian bishops Chromatius of Aquileia and Venerius of Milan, as well as from others, together with the memorandum of the council of the whole West, they set out for Constantinople by public conveyance with the bishops Cyriacus, Demetrius, Palladius, and Eulysius.

### Blessed Flaccus Albinus, or Alcuin, abbot, Against the Heresy of Bishop Felix, §26

From volume I, part II, page 767, of the edition of Abbot Frobenius, Regensburg, 1777.

Chromatius too, bishop and head of the holy Roman Church, says the following in the little book that he wrote on the Eight Beatitudes:

[Note: This passage is found not in the little book On the Eight Beatitudes, but in a fragment of Chromatius on Matthew 3:4, in volume V of the Library of the Fathers, Lyon edition, page 990. This Chromatius was Bishop of Aquileia, not of Rome, although in manuscripts containing his writings he is also called a Roman bishop, though it is uncertain in what sense. Perhaps the copyists were misled by the fact that Saint Jerome called him “holy pope” in Letter 81 to Rufinus, volume I, and in Book II Against Rufinus, volume II of the Verona edition, page 521. See volume XI of D. Tillemont’s Memoirs, page 534, and D. Ceillier, General History of Ecclesiastical Authors, volume X, page 82. Thus Abbot Frobenius.]

> “For in the mystery of Baptism, the Son too [Note: Others add: ‘remaining.’] appears in a body; and the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove; and the Father’s voice is heard from heaven, so that the unity of the Trinity may be declared, because neither can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Son be known without the Holy Spirit. See [Note: Alternatively: “Hence.”], therefore, what kind of testimony the Father gives concerning the Son when he says: ‘This is my Son.’ His, certainly, not by adoption of grace, nor by the status of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the propriety of his origin and the truth of his nature. For many of the saints are called sons of God, and are so; but this one, without comparison [Note: Alternatively: “without compassion.”], is the one only-begotten, true, and proper Son of God the Father, born from no other source than the Father; for he is as truly Father as he is truly God; just as the Son too [Note: Alternatively: “as.”] is as truly Son as he is truly Lord. The perfect faith of the Trinity has therefore been revealed, since the Father testifies that Christ our Lord and God is his Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Paraclete—is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a mystery of faith, so that we may believe without hesitation in a true Father, a true Son, and a true Holy Spirit: three persons, but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance.”

### [LXXX] Anonymous author of the booklet entitled The Origin of Ecclesiastical Chants and Offices

Published from a very ancient manuscript by Henry Spelman in volume I of the Councils of Britain, page 177; also found in David Wilkins, Councils of Great Britain, etc., London, 1737, volume IV, Appendix, pages 741–742; mentioned by Mabillon, On the Gallican Office, §1, in his work On Gallican Liturgy, page 380, and by our Fontaninus below, book III of his Literary History of Aquileia, chapter 4, number 7.

There is also an Eastern Office, issued by Saint Chromatius and Heliodorus and by blessed Paulinus, or also by Bishop Athanasius, which is not found in the custom of the Gauls. Saint Macarius chanted it; that is, through twelve hours, one hour at a time.

### [LXXXI] Proper Lessons for the Second Nocturn, for the Office of Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia

From the booklet entitled Proper Offices of the Saints, to be recited by the clergy of both dioceses of Udine by indult of the Apostolic See.

#### December 2: Feast of Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia

##### Lesson IV

Chromatius, together with Eusebius—his brother not so much by nature as by similarity of character—was enrolled in the clergy of Aquileia from his earliest years. Adorned with outstanding virtues, he devoted himself entirely to God and to ecclesiastical studies, in which he advanced so far that among the clergy of Aquileia he stood out for learning and holiness. To their private glory, as Saint Jerome writes, there was added this public and open testimony: through them the poison of the Arian doctrine was excluded from the city of Aquileia. Ordained priest by Saint Valerian, he succeeded him and is said to have been consecrated by Saint Ambrose.

##### Lesson V

After becoming bishop, he defended the Nicene faith and ecclesiastical discipline with the greatest vigor. He himself condemned, with the same judgment as Saint Anastasius, Roman Pontiff, the Origenist errors proscribed by every Catholic council of both East and West. When discord consequently arose between that greatest teacher and the priest Rufinus, he took the greatest care to bring it to an end through silence. But Saint John Chrysostom especially recognized the pious concern of this most holy prelate; Chromatius undertook to defend John’s cause before the Emperor Honorius with such faith and religious devotion that Chrysostom, astonished by his sincere and fervent charity toward him, warmly congratulated him in a letter sent to him.

##### Lesson VI

He always added study of the Sacred Scriptures to the other duties worthy of a pastor. In the judgment of Blessed Jerome, he was the holiest and most learned of bishops. At his particular urging, that same holy Doctor translated the Hebrew books into Latin and illuminated the books of the Prophets with commentaries, some of which he inscribed with Chromatius’ name. Chromatius himself also published treatises on the Gospel of Matthew, distinguished by learning and piety. Finally, after governing the Church of Aquileia with great holiness for eighteen years, he departed to heavenly life on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

### [LXXXIII] Title of the First Edition of the Writings of Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia

Together with the dedicatory letter of Johannes Sichardus.

**A Dissertation by Chromatius, the Most Learned Roman Bishop, on Chapters Five and Six of Matthew, and a Declamation in the Same Genre.**

Now discovered for the first time and published. Basel, by Adam Petri, in the month of March, with permission and privilege.

### Dedicatory Letter

**Johannes Sichardus to Sigismund Ilsung, Patrician and Dean of the Church of Saint Maurice at Augsburg**

I do not belong to the number of those, most courteous Ilsung, who measure friendship chiefly by the obligation of correspondence. Otherwise, long ago I would have sent you a message, since, after the closest intimacy had been most pleasantly maintained between us in complete agreement of mind and counsel, you could not finally restrain yourself from informing me of the most flourishing increase of your fortunes—the sort of thing that those who love even lightly are accustomed to do, considering it no small fruit of prosperity if it becomes known to as many people as possible. For how little do riches differ from the very rags of obscurity?

But after you departed from here for Padua together with Servatius of Scibolsdorf, that most distinguished young man, you did not meanwhile say a word to me even about common affairs. Although I do not wish to interpret this too harshly, it seems to me that it is your responsibility not to allow a friendship, strengthened by great benefits freely exchanged on both sides, to break apart through that persistent silence.

For my part, as far as I am concerned, I still kiss the sweetest character and intellect of you in your absence, so that I scarcely persuade myself that anything is lacking for solid happiness as much as the companionship of someone like you. This Chromatius of ours, the most learned of bishops not only in my judgment but also in that of Saint Jerome, we dedicate to you by name, both to overcome the design of your long silence and so that at least in some measure you may know the course of my life, since we consider no concern more important than that which toils wholly at recovering the writings of the ancients.

In this field, I shall speak grandly, but truthfully: may I perish if this Chromatius is not worthy not only of being read by the learned but also of being learned by heart. So great is the elegance of his language and the dignity with which he treats this subject. He deals divinely with almost everything that is currently being called into controversy concerning Baptism and the oath.

In this matter you will certainly owe much to Matthias of Saraecastro, official of Trier, a man of singular learning and piety, who, so that I might publish it, sent me the text copied from a most ancient manuscript in recent months and also pressed me to hasten its publication.

If you think that some gratitude ought also to reach us, I do not object; for I am not one whose heart is made of horn. Yet I want you to convince yourself that you will repay me abundantly if, under the auspices of your name, you undertake to read and defend this newly published booklet. We believe that it will for this very reason be exposed to the slanders of certain faultfinders: namely, because he was a Roman prelate, a circumstance that now seems to some the most convenient single handle by which anything ever thought or said by this class of men may be attacked.

For a long time we hesitated because it was not sufficiently clear whether this was the Chromatius whom Jerome honored so often. But Albinus removed that scruple for us in his booklet Against the Heresy of Felix, where he expressly reviews a large part of this work together with a highly honorific preface by Chromatius, the Roman bishop.

Farewell, most courteous and dearest Ilsung.

Basel, from our house, in the month of March, A.D. 1528.

### [LXXXV] On Saint Chromatius — Andrea Gallandi

From the Prolegomena to volume VIII of the Library of the Ancient Fathers and Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter XV, page XXVIII.

#### I

Chromatius, distinguished among the bishops of the West for holiness and learning, succeeded Valerian in the see of Aquileia; Valerian had died in the year 388 [Note: Bernard M. de Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, chapters 7 and 10, pages 64 and 89.]. His ordination was carried out by Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, whom Paulinus reports to have been present at Aquileia at that time [Note: Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, §21]; this was conjectured by the great Baronius [Note: Baronius, under the year 388, §84.]. We find this opinion, though not approved by Fontaninus [Note: Fontaninus, *Literary History of Aquileia*, book III, chapter 3, §2, page 125], asserted by a learned man [Note: Bernard M. de Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, chapter 10, §1, page 90.].

Among the praises of the new prelate, one should especially note that he entered into bonds of friendship with the greatest men of his age: Ambrose, Jerome, John Chrysostom, Heliodorus, and Rufinus. From Ambrose, indeed, Chromatius, burning with the greatest zeal for the study of Sacred Scripture, first requested that something excerpted and explained from the divine books be sent to him. The Bishop of Milan complied and arranged for an exposition of the prophecy of Balaam to be delivered in the form of a letter [Note: Ambrose, Letter 50, works, volume II, pages 993 and following.] around the year 390.

What of Jerome? In that same year, at the entreaties of Chromatius and Heliodorus, Bishop of Altinum, who was working together with the Bishop of Aquileia in cultivating Sacred Scripture, Jerome prepared a Latin version of the Book of Tobit from the Chaldean language [Note: Jerome, Preface to the Translation of Tobit.]. Then, at the urging of both bishops, in the following year, 391, he sent them his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—serving, as it were, in place of the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi that he says he would have written for them at their request if his health had permitted [Note: The same, Preface to the Translation of Proverbs, etc.].

In 392 he dedicated two books of commentaries on the prophet Habakkuk to Chromatius alone, who had requested from him the historical and literal sense of that prophet [Note: The same, Prologue to Book I of the Commentaries on Habakkuk.]. Finally, urged by the Bishop of Aquileia to translate the Hebrew books into Latin [Note: The same, Preface to Chronicles], Jerome sent him in 397 the translation of the Books of Chronicles.
