“These are surely,” to use the words of the most distinguished man [Note: Bernard M. de Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, chapter 1, §3, page 92], “the splendid testimonies to the learning in which Chromatius excelled. From them we learn that he was Jerome’s principal encourager in undertaking the outstanding labor of translating the Hebrew books into Latin and in placing the final hand upon the work once begun.”

#### II

To continue with the remaining principal deeds of Chromatius: in 404, when John Chrysostom was expelled from the see of Constantinople and driven into exile, our Aquileian prelate stood out among the Western bishops who labored most earnestly for his restoration. He wrote letters to Chrysostom himself, as Palladius of Helenopolis reports [Note: Palladius, *Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom*, chapter 2], and in turn received a letter from that Bishop of Constantinople [Note: John Chrysostom, Letter 155; works, volume III, page 689, Benedictine edition.] in 406. In it Chrysostom professes that Chromatius had spoken out for his cause and against his adversaries more loudly than a trumpet; he also gives thanks for the diligent service rendered to him and declares that he greatly desired to enjoy Chromatius’ presence.

Nor should this especially be omitted: when the Emperor Honorius intended to inform his brother Arcadius of the opinion of the Western bishops on this matter, he sent him, among the other letters written to him, two above all—the one from Innocent, Roman Pontiff, and the other from Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia.

Palladius, cited above, quotes the letter of Honorius in these words [Note: Palladius, cited work, chapter 3]:

> “For the third time I am now writing to your gentleness, asking that the proceedings undertaken by agreement against John, the bishop, be corrected . . . . For you to know what the Westerners think concerning Bishop John, from all the letters that have been written to me I have appended two expressing the same judgment as the others: one from the Roman bishop, the other from the Bishop of Aquileia.”

“What, then, do the Westerners think concerning Bishop John? From all the letters written to me I have appended two, equal in force to all the others: the letter of the bishop of Rome and that of the bishop of Aquileia.”

The Augustus wrote this in the year 405. When that most holy man understood how zealously Chromatius had labored in his defense, he sent him a letter from exile in the following year, 406, the letter just mentioned.

#### III

Moreover, Chromatius counted Rufinus among the beloved priests of the Church of Aquileia and honored him, as the learned man repeatedly cited against Noris demonstrates at greater length [Note: Bernard M. de Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, chapter 12, §2, page 106.]. Therefore, when a dispute arose between Rufinus and Saint Jerome, Chromatius endeavored, according to his ability, to restore to Christian harmony such great men, who had previously been joined by friendship for so many years. With this purpose, he tried to turn Rufinus’ mind and pen in another direction and instructed him to render Eusebius’ Greek History into Latin ears.

Rufinus enlarged it by his own labor in two books and dedicated it to Chromatius in the year 400. Later he also dedicated to him the twenty-six Homilies of Origen on the Book of Joshua, which he had translated into Latin at Chromatius’ urging.

After these and other distinguished deeds, our holy prelate is thought to have died around the year 408, having governed the Church of Aquileia prudently and energetically for eighteen years. This is the view of the distinguished man, explained at greater length [Note: The same, same work, chapter 13, §§1 and 3, pages 111 and 115], although later he changed his mind [Note: The same, *Dissertation on Rufinus*, chapter 19, §3, pages 144 and 147] and assigned the year of Chromatius’ death to 406. Fontaninus agrees [Note: Fontaninus, *Literary History of Aquileia*, book III, chapter 3, §9, page 132.]. Tillemont, taking a middle position between the two opinions, assigned the year 407 [Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume XI, page 538.]. The memory of Saint Chromatius is commemorated both in the ecclesiastical calendars and in the Aquileian records on December 2.

#### IV

We saw above that Chromatius, especially devoted to the study of Sacred Scripture, consulted the most learned men for that reason—Ambrose, I mean, and Jerome—and requested from them either expositions or translations of the divine utterances. It is also found that he himself diligently devoted his efforts to cultivating and explaining those same Holy Scriptures.

Eighteen Homilies survive under his name. They appear to be a Commentary, or fragments of a Commentary, on the Gospel of Saint Matthew. Johannes Sichardus first published them from a very ancient manuscript at Basel in 1528. Later Martin Lipsius compared them with other ancient manuscript copies, repeated them in various places, and they were finally incorporated into the Libraries of the Fathers.

Because of the carelessness of librarians or copyists, so many homilies had been joined together and compressed into only three little works. They could easily have been distinguished by the frequently repeated doxology, which ends with these or similar words: “through Christ our Lord, who is blessed forever.” It is therefore by its guidance that they are recognized as eighteen. This observation is owed to Tillemont [Note: The same, same work, page 653, note 2, on Saint Chromatius.].

We have accordingly decided to restore this number in our copy of the homilies, while also retaining the order that had hitherto prevailed in the earlier printed editions—an order, to be sure, misplaced and plainly contrary to the author’s intention. In addition, we have prefixed to these homilies the title “Treatises”:

> “For this designation,” to speak with learned men [Note: Ballerini, Preface to the Sermons of Saint Zeno, §16, page XVIII], “is proper to ancient ecclesiastical usage and is found employed very frequently. Although in former times *treatises* were called bishops’ discussions concerning some matter of the Church, as is clear from Cyprian [Note: Cyprian, Letters 51 and 52], nevertheless, just as *to treat*—which, according to Optatus, is a function of bishops [Note: Optatus, book VII Against Parmenianus]—is first used by Cyprian [Note: Cyprian, Letter 56] and afterward frequently by others in the sense ‘to preach’ in public assemblies of the Church, so the word *treatise* became established as a formal designation for an episcopal sermon to the people. In the same sense it is prefixed in many places to the sermons of numerous ancient Fathers, as we learn from the manuscripts of Saints Gaudentius, Augustine, Leo the Great, and others, and from several editions accurately prepared according to the manuscripts.”

Fontaninus had previously thought that Chromatius’ homilies should be entitled in the same way [Note: Fontaninus, *Literary History of Aquileia*, book III, chapter 4, §1, page 133.].

We have not only divided them into various sections according to the practice of our institution, but also compared them with the excerpts of Combefis [Note: Combefis, *Library of Councils*, volume II, pages 22 and 94; volume V, pages 202 and 424; volume VIII, pages 344 and 346, and elsewhere]. Through this comparison we corrected corrupt readings in other copies and filled one or two gaps, while adding notes in certain places in which we proposed conjectural restorations of several doubtful passages.

#### V

Nor should this be omitted: in Sichardus’ first edition, from which the others derive, these homilies—or, if you prefer, treatises—were given the following title: “Of Chromatius, Roman Bishop.” For this reason, many learned men have thought that these little works should be denied to Chromatius of Aquileia.

But two learned men have shown with sufficient precision in what sense that title, attributed to our holy Father, should be understood [Note: Fontaninus, cited work, §2, pages 134 and 138; Bernard M. de Rubeis, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, chapter 10, §2, page 90 and following]. The same homilies are in fact a genuine and complete work of Chromatius; this is established at length by the learned Fontaninus, whom we have repeatedly cited [Note: Fontaninus, cited work, §§3 and 8, pages 138 and following]. He also demonstrates their value, defends them against the calumnies of the Magdeburg Centuriators, and explains the author’s style and purpose. Nor does he fail to point out writings falsely attributed to Chromatius. The reader should therefore consult him; for we know no one who has fulfilled this task more successfully.

### Treatise of Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia

A separate treatise [Note: In Gallandi: “Treatise I, on the Gospel of Saint Matthew.”], or sermon, on the Eight Beatitudes. (C)

[Col. 0323C] **3 I.** Brothers, this gathering of the people and the bustle of the marketplace provide us with an opportunity to set forth an evangelical sermon. For worldly things are accustomed to serve as examples of spiritual things, and earthly realities to offer an image of heavenly ones. For the Lord and Savior frequently admonishes us concerning heavenly things through earthly ones, when he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea” (Matt. 13:47). Or again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls” (ibid., 45). If, then, this marketplace itself has the purpose that each person, for his own advantage, either sell what is superfluous to him or buy what he lacks, I too shall not ineptly offer for sale the merchandise that the Lord has entrusted to me—namely, heavenly preaching. For he has chosen even me, though the least and unworthy, from among those servants [Col. 0323D] to whom the Lord distributed talents for trading and making profit. Nor, indeed, will there be any lack of merchants where there are such and so many hearers through the grace of God. Rather, heavenly profit must be sought where earthly advantage is not neglected.

Dearest brothers, I desire to offer you those precious pearls of the beatitudes from the holy Gospel. Open, therefore, the treasures of your hearts; buy them, receive them eagerly, and possess them happily. Our Lord and God, the only-begotten Son of the Most High Father, who deigned to become man from God and teacher from the Lord, when a great crowd gathered from various regions, took his disciples—that is, his apostles—and “went up onto a mountain, and, opening his mouth, taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth,’” and so forth (Matt. 5:1–3).

The Lord [Col. 0324D] and Savior lays out, as it were, certain very firm steps made of precious stones, by which holy and faithful souls may climb and ascend to that highest good, namely, the kingdom of heaven. Briefly, therefore, dearest brothers, I wish to demonstrate the character of these steps. Let your whole mind and soul be attentive, for the things that belong to God are not insignificant.

**II.** “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” What a remarkable beginning, brothers, for heavenly teaching! It does not begin with terror, but with blessedness; it does not produce fear, but rather desire. For, in the manner of a director of the games or a distributor of prizes, he sets before the contestants in this spiritual stadium a great reward, so that, while they look upon the prize, they may neither fear the labors nor dread the dangers.

“Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He did not simply or indiscriminately call the poor blessed, but added, “the poor in spirit.” For not every poverty [Col. 0325B] is fortunate: it often arises from necessity, sometimes from the worst conduct, and sometimes even from divine indignation. Blessed, therefore, is spiritual poverty—namely, that of people who make themselves poor in spirit and will for God’s sake, renouncing the goods of the world and freely distributing their possessions. He rightly calls them blessed: “the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” For through voluntary poverty they attain the riches of the heavenly kingdom.

Then he says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (ibid., 4). Remarkably, after the first step a second is shown: “Blessed,” he says, “are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” But just as it is impossible to stand on the second step out of order unless one has first climbed the first, so no one can be meek unless he has first become poor in spirit.

How, then, can a mind situated amid riches, cares, and worldly anxieties—from which business dealings, lawsuits, provocations, anger, and bitterness continually arise—how, I say, can such a mind be meek and gentle unless, by renouncing them, it has first cut away from itself all causes of anger and occasions of quarrels? The sea does not become calm unless the winds cease; fire is not extinguished unless one removes the fuel and the thorny branches that feed the blaze. So, too, the mind will not be meek and tranquil unless the things that rouse and inflame it have been cast off. The step is therefore rightly joined to the step, because the poor in spirit already begin to become meek.

**III.** A third step is added: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (ibid., 5). What kind of mourning are we to understand as salutary? Certainly not that which arises from the loss of possessions, nor that which arises from the loss of loved ones, nor that which arises from the forfeiture of worldly honors—for one who has already become poor in spirit will not grieve over any of these things.

This is the salutary mourning that is undertaken for sins and in remembrance of the divine judgment. For previously, with the mind situated amid the countless occupations and hardships of the world, it could not think about itself. Now, having become secure and meek, it begins to look more closely at itself and examine its deeds by day and by night. Thus the wounds of past crimes begin to appear, and then salutary mourning and tears follow—so healing that heavenly consolation immediately comes to meet them. For truly he spoke who said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

**IV.** Let us approach the fourth step, brothers. “Blessed,” he says, “are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (ibid., 6). Indeed, after repentance, after mourning and tears for sins, what other hunger and thirst arise except those for righteousness? Just as one who has passed through the darkness of night already longs for the approaching light, and one who has digested bitter bile craves food and drink, so the mind of a Christian, [Col. 0326A] after it has digested its sins through mourning and tears, now hungers and thirsts for the righteousness of God alone. And rightly so: it will rejoice in the satisfaction of what it desires.

**V.** Let the fifth step also come before us: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (ibid., [Col. 0326B] 7). No one can benefit another unless he has first benefited himself. Therefore, after he has obtained mercy for himself and the satisfaction of righteousness, he begins to grieve for the wretched and to pray on behalf of other sinners. Having become merciful even toward his enemies, through such piety he will prepare for himself a greater accumulation of mercy at the Lord’s coming. Therefore it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

**VI.** Behold, the sixth step is present: “Blessed,” he says, “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid., 8). Truly they are now pure in heart; truly they will be able to see God—those who are poor in spirit, meek, mournful over sins, refreshed by righteousness, and merciful—even toward their adversaries. They bear so sincere and clear an eye of the heart [Col. 0326C] that they may behold the inaccessible brightness of God without impediment and without the eye of malice making them bleary. For purity of heart and cleanness of conscience will tolerate no cloud obstructing the sight of the Lord.

**VII.** It follows, brothers: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (ibid., 9). Great is the dignity of those who pursue peace, since it is reckoned to them as the title of sons of God.

This reconciliation too, which takes place among brothers who quarrel over worldly possessions, or over empty glory, or because of mutual hostilities, is certainly good; but its reward is small. For the Lord said, as an example for us: “Who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12:14). He had already said: “From one who takes away your goods, do not demand them back” (Luke 6:30). And elsewhere: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another?” (John [Col. 0326D] 5:44).

We must therefore understand a more valuable and sublime peacemaking: that by which pagan people, who are enemies of God, are led to peace through persistent instruction; by which sinners are corrected and reconciled to God through repentance; by which rebellious heretics are corrected; and by which churches in disagreement are formed into unity and peace. Truly, those who are peacemakers in this way are not merely blessed, but deservedly will be called sons of God. For, imitating Christ, the Son of God himself, who is proclaimed by the Apostle as “our peace” (Eph. 2:14) and our reconciliation, they receive a share in his name.

**VIII.** “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. [Col. 0327A] 5:10). There is no doubt, brothers, that envy always accompanies a good deed. For, despite the cruelty of persecutors, as soon as you begin to uphold strict righteousness, to strike back at insolence, and to summon unbelievers to the peace of the Lord; as soon, finally, as you begin to differ from worldly and misguided people, persecutions immediately arise. It is necessary that hatreds rise up and jealousy tear one apart.

Thus Christ finally leads his hearers to that highest step, to the very summit and pinnacle—not merely so that they may endure through suffering, but also so that, by dying, they may rejoice together.

**IX.** “Blessed are you,” he says, “when they persecute you, revile you, and speak every evil against you falsely on account of righteousness. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (ibid., 11).

It is perfect virtue, brothers, after carrying out every work of righteousness, to endure reproaches from people for the sake of truth, to be afflicted by torments, and finally to be put to death without being terrified. We have been given the example of the prophets, who, torn apart in various ways for the sake of righteousness, were deemed worthy to be conformed to Christ’s sufferings and reward.

This is the higher step, at which Paul, looking toward Christ, said: “But one thing: forgetting what is behind and stretching myself toward what is in the first place, I pursue the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:13–14). And still more openly he says to Timothy: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4:7). As though he had climbed all the steps, he added: “I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (ibid., 8).

For truly, when the entire course had been completed, this remained: that Paul, rejoicing through tribulations and sufferings, should reach the more sublime step of martyrdom. Rightly, therefore, the Lord urges his servants: “Rejoice,” he says, [Col. 0328A] “and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5:12); and he clearly shows that they increase through the successive growth of persecutions.

The eight evangelical steps have been shown, brothers, constructed, as I said, from precious stones. That ladder of Jacob has been shown (Gen. 26:12), whose top reached from earth to heaven. Whoever climbs it finds the gate of heaven; entering through it, he will stand joyfully forever in the presence of the Lord, praising the Lord with the holy angels for eternity.

**X.** This is our marketplace; this is our spiritual fair. Let us give, blessed ones, what we possess. Let us offer poverty of spirit, so that, according to the promise, we may receive the abundance of the heavenly kingdom. Let us offer meekness, so that we may possess the earth and paradise. Let us mourn our sins and those of others, so that we may deserve consolation from the Lord’s [Col. 0328B] goodness. Let us hunger and thirst for righteousness, so that we may be nourished more abundantly. Let us give mercy, so that we may obtain true mercy. Let us live as peacemakers, so that we may be called sons of God. Let us offer a pure heart and a chaste body, so that with a clear understanding we may be able to see God. Let us fear persecutions for righteousness’ sake not at all, so that we may become heirs of the heavenly kingdom. If reproaches, torments, and finally death should come, let us joyfully and gladly embrace them for the sake of God’s truth, so that an abundant reward may be granted to us in heaven with the prophets and apostles.

And so that the conclusion of our words may correspond to the preface: if merchants rejoice over present and perishable profits, let us all rejoice and be glad together much more, because today we have found such pearls of the Lord, with which none of the goods of the world can be compared.

That we may deserve to acquire, obtain, and possess them, we must ask help and grace, together with strength, from the Lord himself, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0327]

**TREATISES OF SAINT CHROMATIUS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA, WHICH SURVIVE, ON THE GOSPEL OF ST. MATTHEW. (C)**

**13 TRACTATUS I** [Note: [Col. 0327D] In Gallandius: *Tractatus XVII, on the Gospel of St. Matthew*.], On chapter 3 of the Gospel of St. Matthew. *(The beginning is missing.)*

**I.** … Therefore the Lord Jesus, answering, said to him: “Let it be so for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

Jesus, therefore, in order to complete all the mysteries of the Law, descended from Galilee into the Jordan to be baptized by John. But John, recognizing his God through the Holy Spirit—whose sandals he had professed himself unworthy even to carry—excuses himself from fulfilling what he was commanded. For he did not believe that baptism was necessary for one whom he knew had come for the purpose of removing the sins of the world through his baptism. Therefore he declares that he ought rather to be baptized by him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you; and you come to me?” (ibid., 14).

It was as though he were saying: “I am a human being; you are God. I am a sinner, because I am human; you are without sin, because you are God. Why do you wish to be baptized by me? I do not refuse obedience, but I do not understand the mystery. I baptize sinners for repentance. Why do you wish to be baptized, since you have no cause of sin? Or rather, why do you wish to be baptized as a sinner, when you have come to take away sins?”

What, then, is the meaning of John’s statement: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” [Note: [Col. 0329D] *Quidnam* is read here. Other copies have *quidem* or *quidam*; but in any case the passage is defective, it seems. The same reading is found in the first Basel edition and likewise in Grynaeus’s second edition.]

What faithful service of his servant, and what mystery of his dispensation, did he indicate by saying: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness”? He showed that this is the whole of righteousness: that the Lord and teacher of our salvation himself should complete the sacrament.

The Lord did not therefore come to be baptized for his own sake, but for ours, in order to fulfill all righteousness. For it is right that whoever teaches another to do something should be the first to begin doing it. Since the teacher and Lord of the human race had come, he wished by his example to teach what had to be done, so that the disciples might follow the Teacher and the servants the Lord.

Since he was about to give a new baptism for the salvation of the human race and the forgiveness of sins, he himself first deigned to be baptized—not to lay aside sins, since he alone had committed no sin, but to sanctify the waters of baptism for washing away the sins of believers. For the waters of baptism could never have cleansed the sins of believers unless they had been sanctified by contact with the Lord’s body.

He, therefore, was baptized so that we might be washed from sins. He was immersed in water so that we might be cleansed from the filth of transgressions. He received the bath of rebirth [Col. 0329C] so that we might be born again from water and the Holy Spirit, as he himself says elsewhere: “Unless one is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

**II.** The baptism of Christ, therefore, is the washing away of our transgressions and the renewal of saving life. Hear the Apostle himself demonstrate this when he says: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). And he adds: “You were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so you too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4).

Through baptism, therefore, we die to sin but live together with Christ; we are buried with our former life but rise to a new life; we strip off the error of the old man but receive the clothing of the new man. [Col. 0329D] Thus the Lord also fulfilled all righteousness in baptism, because he wished to be baptized for this purpose: that we might be baptized. For this purpose he received the bath of rebirth: that we might be reborn into life.

**III.** John did indeed baptize our Lord and Savior, but rather John was baptized by Christ: for Christ sanctified the waters, while John was sanctified by the waters; Christ bestowed grace, while John received it; John laid aside sins, while Christ forgave them—for John was human, but Christ was God. For it belongs to God to forgive sins, as it is written: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Luke 5:21).

Therefore John says to Christ: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” John needed baptism, because he could not be without sin; but Christ could not need baptism, because he had committed no sins. Thus in that baptism our Lord and Savior first cleansed John’s sins and thereafter those of the whole world.

Therefore he says: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” The grace of this baptism had long before been shown symbolically, when the people were led through the river Jordan into the promised land. Just as then the Jordan was the way for the people going to the promised land, with the Lord going before them, so now, through the same waters of the river Jordan, the first path on the heavenly way has been opened, by which we are led to that blessed promised land—that is, to the promise of the heavenly kingdom.

For them, Joshua son of Nun was the leader in the Jordan; for us, Jesus Christ the Lord became, through baptism, the leader of eternal salvation: the only-begotten Son of God, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

**TRACTATUS II** [Note: [Col. 0329D] In Gallandius: *Tractatus XVIII, on the Gospel of St. Matthew*.], On chapter 3 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

**I.** Next follows: “And when Jesus had been baptized, immediately he came up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove. And behold, a voice from heaven said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3:16–17).

Just as at the Lord’s bodily birth, so also at his baptism things worthy of all wonder and befitting his majesty appeared. After the Lord had risen from the waters following his baptism, the heavens were opened. [Col. 0330C] The Holy Spirit descended in bodily form under the appearance of a dove, bearing the Father’s testimony concerning the Son. The Father’s voice too was immediately heard from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

David had also foretold the hearing of this sacred voice over the waters, saying: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered” (Ps. 28:3)—namely, in this event, in which the voice of the Father’s majesty, bearing witness to the Son, sounded like a kind of thunder.

**II.** What place, then, is left here for heretics against the faith? What opportunity for blasphemy remains in this confession of the Father, when the sacrament of the perfect Trinity has been shown even through the explicit precision of the words? In the mystery of baptism, the Son is seen remaining in the body, the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice is heard from heaven, so that the unity of the Trinity may be declared. For neither can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Son known without the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0329D]

In the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, *Vide* (“See”) is read here instead of *Unde* (“Therefore”), volume V, page 990, and likewise in Gallandius, volume VIII, page 352. In the note immediately below, however, he wrote hesitantly: “Should *Vide* be read?”

We have confidently placed *Vide* here instead of *Unde*, since the sense of the sentence requires it, relying also on the authority of Abbot Alcuin, who quoted this entire text of Chromatius in his little book against the heresy of Bishop Felix. See it above among the ancient testimonies concerning Saint Chromatius, bishop. We rely likewise on the authority of the first edition of Chromatius, published at Basel in 1528, which we have at hand, and on the authority of an ancient codex of the Palatine Library of the Vatican. From this codex the illustrious Fontaninus extracted the entire text of Chromatius from the aforesaid work of Alcuin. Fontaninus also inserted it in its entirety in book III, chapter 4, section 2, of his *Literary History of Aquileia*.

Moreover—and this is certainly astonishing—the whole of this text of Chromatius, which concerns the mystery of the Trinity, appears badly corrupted in the cited Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, to the point that it even conveys an erroneous meaning. The distinguished men mentioned above, Fontaninus and De Rubeis, did not notice this; and the text appeared in the most recent edition of Gallandius polluted by precisely the same errors.

For this reason, in our present edition we have restored the entire text of Chromatius to its integrity, correcting it in no fewer than six places by comparing it with the same text as it appears in Alcuin in Frobenius’s most recent edition. From there we inserted the text itself among the ancient testimonies. We also took into account the cited first Basel edition of Chromatius’s *Writings*, or *Minor Works*, of 1528, as well as the second Basel edition of 1569, in John Grynaeus’s *Orthodoxographia of the Monuments of the Holy Fathers*, and an ancient Alcuinian codex of the Vatican Library, as we explained at the appropriate place in the Preface.]

See, then, what kind of testimony the Father gives concerning the Son when he says: “This is my Son.” His own Son, certainly—not through the adoption of grace, nor through the religion of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the distinctiveness of his origin and the truth of his nature.

Many holy people are called sons of God, and are so; but this one, without comparison, is the one and only-begotten, true, and proper Son of God the Father, born from no other source than the Father. For the Father is as truly Father as he is truly God; likewise, the Son is as truly Son as he is truly Lord.

Thus the perfect faith of the Trinity has been displayed: the Father testifies that Christ our Lord and God is his Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Paraclete—is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a sacrament of faith, so that we might believe in the true Father, the true Son, and also the true Holy Spirit: three persons, but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance. These things have been said briefly concerning the mystery of the Trinity.

**III.** But because we recognize that everything the Lord did for us was manifested as a sacrament of our salvation, the fact that the heavens were opened when the Lord was baptized likewise shows that the kingdoms of heaven would be opened to those reborn in baptism. The Son of God first opened them for us when, in the body, he ascended to heaven.

Therefore, in the fact that the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and the Father’s voice was heard from heaven, saying, “This is my Son,” the order of this heavenly mystery and of our salvation is revealed: through the saving baptism of water we would become sons of God and be endowed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Through him be praise and glory to the Father and to the Son forever and ever. Amen.

**TRACTATUS III** [Note: [Col. 0332D] In Gallandius: *Tractatus II, on the Gospel of St. Matthew*.], On chapter 5 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

**I.** “When Jesus saw the crowds,” he says, “he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matt. 5:1–2), and the rest that follows.

As the Lord was about to lead his disciples from earthly and humble things to those that are high and exalted, he climbed a mountain—specifically, the Mount of Olives—so that through the significance of its name he might show the gift of his divine mercy. The Lord therefore ascended the mountain so that, with his disciples now leaving earthly things behind and seeking heavenly ones, as though already placed on high, he might give them the commandments of heavenly precepts and bestow the blessings long ago promised through the divine gift, in accordance with what David had previously testified, saying: “For he who gave the law will give a blessing” (Ps. 83:8).

And to show more clearly both the grace given to the apostles and the author of so great a blessing, he added: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion”—namely, the Son of God, who bestowed blessings upon the apostles in Zion.

It was the same one who gave blessings to the apostles on this mountain who had long before given the Law to Moses on Mount Sinai. He thereby proved himself to be the author of both laws, in accordance with what the Lord himself declares through Jeremiah: “I will give them a new covenant, not like the one I formerly gave to their fathers when I led them out of the land of Egypt. But this is the covenant that I will give them: I will write my laws in their hearts, and I will write them in their understanding” (Jer. 31:31–32).

And formerly, when the Law was given (Exod. 19:21), the people were forbidden to approach the mountain. But now, when the Lord speaks on the mountain, no one is forbidden; rather, everyone is invited to listen. For in the Law there is severity, but in the Gospel grace; there terror is inflicted upon unbelievers, here the gift of blessings is poured into believers.

If you too wish, therefore, to receive a blessing from the Lord, leave behind your earthly way of life and seek the heavenly life. Climb the height of faith as though it were a mountain, so that you may rightly deserve to be blessed by the Lord. But let us now see what the actual words of the blessings are.

**II.** “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

We certainly know many poor people, but they are not blessed merely because they are poor. For it is not the necessity of poverty that makes any one of us blessed, but the devout faith of poverty. We know many who indeed lack the resources of the world, yet do not cease from sins and are alienated from faith in God. It is obvious that such people cannot be called blessed.

We must therefore inquire who these blessed people are of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He means that those poor are blessed who, despising the riches of the world and rejecting worldly possessions, wished to become poor to the world so that they might become rich toward God.

Such people appear poor in the world, but they are rich toward God; needy in the world, but wealthy in Christ. The apostles themselves first offered us an example of this blessed poverty. They despised every possession and, immediately following the Lord’s call, deserved to become his disciples.

We find such poor people also in the times of the apostles: the first believers, who sold all their goods and possessions and, under this devout poverty, sought the riches of the Lord. Therefore the Apostle shows that heavenly riches are present in such poverty when he says: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (1 Cor. 6:10).

Thus Peter, when he was going up into the temple and a lame man asked him for alms, said: “I have neither silver nor gold; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6).

O truly blessed poverty, which, possessing nothing from the resources of the world, gives so much from heaven! It does not give silver or gold, but—what is greater than all riches—it restores health to the body. Peter did not possess an image of Caesar on a coin to give, but he restored the image of Christ in a human being.

The Lord speaks in the present passage about such poor people, concerning whom David also testifies in many places, saying: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and their hearts shall live forever and ever” (Ps. 21:7). And again: “He shall judge the poor of the people, and he shall save the children of the poor” (Ps. 71:4). “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33:7).

The Lord therefore teaches that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such poor people, who have made themselves poor to the world for the sake of religion and faith, in order to possess the Holy Spirit in abundance.

Or certainly he calls those poor blessed who are inflated by no pride of the devil and raised up by no ambition of the world, but preserve humility of spirit together with devotion to the faith. Hence David says in the Psalm: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). Such, then, are the poor in spirit who are blessed before God.

**III.** Then he says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

As above he spoke of the poor, so here he speaks of those who mourn. He does not call blessed those who grievously mourn the death of a beloved spouse, or the loss of dear relatives, children, and offspring. Rather, he signifies that those are blessed who either strive to expiate their own committed sins by continual weeping of tears, or who, out of love for the Law, do not cease to mourn the world’s iniquity and the offenses of sinners.

To those who mourn so holily, the Lord promises, not undeservedly, the consolation of eternal joy. The holy David, awaiting this, even drenched his bed with continual tears, saying: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6:7). And again: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. 41:4). And again: “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10). [Col. 0334A] And again: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 79:6).

Do you wish to know the devout mourning of the saints? Hear what is said of the prophet Samuel: that he mourned King Saul until the day of his death (1 Sam. 15:35). Jeremiah too, when he lamented the sins of the people, said: “My eyes have poured forth streams of water over the destruction of my people” (Lam. 3:48). And again: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep for this people day and night?” (Jer. 9:1).

Daniel also was afflicted with profound mourning for the sins of the people, as he himself testifies, saying: “I was mourning for three weeks of days, eating no bread and drinking no wine” (Dan. 10:3).

The holy Apostle likewise mourns certain Corinthians with similar grief, saying: “I will come to you, so that I may mourn over many of those who previously sinned and did not repent of the impurity and fornication they had practiced” (2 Cor. 12:21).

The Lord compensates such mourning with the consolation of perpetual joy, in accordance with what Isaiah reported, saying: “Give to those who mourn in Zion glory instead of ashes, the oil of joy to those who mourn, and a garment of glory instead of a spirit of sadness” (Isa. 61:3). David says: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Ps. 29:12).

**IV.** Then he says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance.”

The graces of the divine promises are different, because the degrees of merit are different. He therefore says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

The meek are gentle, humble, and modest people, simple in faith and patient under every injury. Instructed by the evangelical commandments, they imitate the example of the Lord’s meekness, who says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:19).

For this reason Moses long ago found the greatest favor with God: he was meek. It is written of him: “Now Moses was meek beyond all people who were upon the earth” (Num. 12:3). Hence David says in the Psalm: “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 131:2).

The Lord therefore shows such meek people to be blessed. He promises them possession not in the present life but in the future—the possession of that happy land of which we read in the Psalm: “But the meek shall possess the earth, and shall delight in the abundance of peace” (Ps. 38:11). And again: “Those who wait for the Lord shall possess the earth as an inheritance” (Ps. 68:36).

The Holy Spirit also testifies concerning this land through Solomon, saying: “For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the holy shall dwell in it” (Prov. 11:21). The Lord therefore shows those meek people to be blessed who, following the gentleness of the Lord’s meekness, will enjoy the inheritance of that blessed land in perpetual possession.

Above all, however, he is speaking of the earth of our body, in which the saints, transformed into glory, will reign in eternal happiness, according to the Apostle.

### V

Then he says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” He teaches that righteousness is not to be sought by an easy desire or a light ardor of longing. Rather, he declares blessed those who burn with the inward desires of hunger and thirst in order to attain it. For if each of us longs for it with a hungry and thirsty desire, he cannot continually think of anything other than righteousness and seek righteousness; since one who is hungry and thirsty must long for what he thirsts and hungers for.

Rightly, therefore, to those who hunger and thirst in this way he promises, as the satisfaction of that perpetual refreshment, him who is the heavenly bread and the fountain of living water, saying: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” This is surely the righteousness of faith, which belongs to God and Christ, concerning which the Apostle also says: “But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ, for all and upon all who believe in him” (Rom. III, 20).

Or certainly he means our Lord and Savior himself, who, according to the Apostle, “was made for us righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I, 30). The blessed always burn with desire for him as though for food and drink, according to what the Lord himself testifies through Solomon, speaking in the person of Wisdom: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Eccli. XXIV, 29).

Therefore we too must always hunger and thirst for this righteousness, so that we may deserve to be satisfied with the food of perpetual refreshment. Appropriately, the present passage adds: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” For those who hunger not for righteousness but for unrighteousness—that is, those who desire gold and silver, who covet the riches or honors of the world, and who are never satisfied with earthly wealth or the desires of the flesh—such people are not blessed but wretched, because they are owed not the hope of the promised glory but the punishment of condemnation.

### VI

Then he says: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them.” In very many testimonies, both in the Old Testament and also in the New, we are urged by the Lord to show mercy. But, for the sake of brevity in the faith, we think that what the Lord himself declares in his own voice in the present passage is sufficient and more than sufficient: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them.”

The Lord of mercies declares the merciful blessed, showing that no one can merit God’s mercy unless he too has been merciful. Hence elsewhere he says: “Be merciful, therefore, just as your Father who is in heaven is merciful” (Luke VI, 36).

Then he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” He signifies that those are pure in heart who, having laid aside the filth of sin, have cleansed themselves from every defilement of the flesh and have pleased God through works of faith and righteousness. Thus David testifies in the Psalm, saying: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain” (Ps. XXIII, 3–4).

David also rightly knew that God can be seen only by the pure in heart, and so he prays in the Psalm: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. L, 12).

The Lord therefore declares those pure in heart blessed who, living in faith in the Lord with a pure mind and an undivided conscience, will deserve to behold the God of glory in the future heavenly kingdom—not now “through a mirror and in an enigma,” but “face to face,” as the Apostle reports (I Cor. XIII, 12).

For now, although we contemplate God with the eyes of faith, we cannot see his splendor because of the weakness of the flesh. Then, however, transformed into heavenly glory after receiving immortality, we shall see him when we begin to behold the immortal God with immortal eyes. Then what is written will truly be fulfilled in us: “As we have heard, so also have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts” (Ps. XLVII, 9).

Not without reason, when the same David was revealing the glory of the future age in which the saints will dwell with God, he said: “Yet the righteous shall give thanks to you, and the upright shall dwell in your presence” (Ps. CXXXIX, 14).

### VII

Then he says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Peacemakers are those who, separated from the scandal of dissension and discord, preserve the love of fraternal charity and the peace of the Church in the unity of the catholic faith. The Lord especially commends this peace to his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV, 27).

David had already testified that the Lord would give this peace to his Church, saying: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me, for he will speak peace to his people, and to his saints, and to those who turn to him” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9).

The Apostle also admonishes us to preserve this peace, saying: “In all things preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV, 3). And again: “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your bodies from evil” (Phil. IV, 7).

For nothing is so necessary to the servants of God, nothing so beneficial to the Church, as preserving charity and loving peace. Without it, the Apostle teaches in the Epistle to the Hebrews, God cannot be seen: “Above all, love peace, without which none of us will be able to see God” (Heb. XII, 14).

Therefore it is fitting for us to preserve the peace of the Church with every effort and devotion, and, insofar as it lies within us, to recall those who disagree with peace to the charity of the Church through devotion to peace and faith, following the example of the Prophet who says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CXIX, 7).

Rightly also, in the Gospel, amid the rejoicing of the angels announcing the Lord’s birth, this holy voice is heard: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

David also spoke of this peace: “There is abundant peace for those who love you, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. CXVIII, 165). Isaiah likewise says: “I will place your children in abundant peace, and you shall be built in righteousness” (Isa. LIV, 13).

Since the Son of God deemed it worthy to assume flesh and suffer for this purpose—that he might reconcile us to God through the blood of his cross (Col. I, 20)—we ought, according to the Apostle’s teaching, to be peaceful in all things, so that we may truly deserve to have the God of peace within us (Rom. XV, 33). For it is written: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV, 3).

Thus we shall truly be not only sons of God but also heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ. For the Apostle says: “If sons, then heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17).

### VIII

Then he says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” It was not without reason that the Lord earlier spoke of hungering and thirsting for righteousness: we ought to thirst for it so greatly that for its sake we should despise both the persecution of the world, the punishments of the body, and even death itself.

The martyrs are especially revealed in this sense. For the sake of righteousness, faith, and the name of Christ, they endure persecutions in this world, and a great hope is promised them—that is, possession of the kingdom of heaven. The Apostles were the leaders in this blessedness, as were all the righteous who, afflicted by various persecutions for the sake of the righteousness of the Law, rightly attained the heavenly kingdoms by the merit of their faith.

### IX

Then he says: “Blessed will you be when people persecute you, and reproach you, and speak every evil against you. Rejoice on that day and exult, for I say to you: your reward is great in heaven; for this is how their fathers treated the Prophets.”

Everything that impious persecutors, during a persecution for the name of Christ, can devise against the righteous—whether inflicting various reproaches or imposing punishments upon the body—we must not merely endure patiently but also receive with joyful exultation, on account of the glory that is to come.

This is why he says: “Rejoice on that day and exult; I tell you, your reward is great in heaven.” How glorious is the endurance of this persecution, whose reward the Lord says is stored up in heaven! Therefore, considering the reward of the glory set before us, we must be prepared in devoted faith for every endurance of suffering, so that we may deserve to become companions in the glory of the Prophets and Apostles, through Christ our Lord, who is blessed forever.

## TREATISE IV

*[Note: In Gallandi: Treatise III, on the Gospel of St. Matthew.]*

On chapter V of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

### I

Then he says: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has become tasteless, it is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people” (Matt. V, 13).

The Lord calls his Apostles the salt of the earth. Let us see what the Lord wants us to understand about his Apostles under this comparison. To grasp this more fully, we must first carefully inquire what this salt is, what earth is meant, and toward what purpose and usefulness it proceeds. We must also examine the nature and use of salt itself, so that, once these matters are understood, we may more easily attain the force of the Lord’s saying through spiritual understanding.

The nature of salt consists of water, the heat of the sun, and the breath of the wind; and from what it was, it is generated into another form. In the same way, the Apostles and all believers, through the water of baptism, through faith in Christ—who is called, by way of comparison, the sun of righteousness—and through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, were reborn to God and passed from an earthly birth into a heavenly one.

Therefore the holy Apostles are rightly called by the Lord the salt of the earth. And whose earth? It is easy to recognize: the earth of our body, which they once salted, when it was foolish and insipid through the perception of vanity, with the wisdom of evangelical preaching.

They themselves became the salt of our earth, because through them we received the words of wisdom and, through heavenly birth, were changed into a spiritual nature. Just as this salt—that is, the salt of the earth—is needed indiscriminately by everyone, by kings and the powerful, by the rich and the poor, by servants and masters, so also the word of heavenly wisdom preached through the Apostles is necessary for everyone unto life. For, according to the Apostle, “all have need of the grace of God” (Rom. III, 23).

Just as we cannot live this present life without the use of salt, so we cannot attain that eternal life without the gift of divine wisdom.

### II

But since the nature or grace of salt has already been discussed above according to spiritual understanding, let us now also consider the power of salt itself. “You,” he says, “are the salt of the earth.”

Therefore, just as salt, when it acts upon any flesh, does not allow corruption, removes foul odors, cleanses impurities, and does not permit worms to be generated, so the heavenly grace and faith given through the Apostles works in us in a similar way. It removes the corruption of carnal desire, cleanses the filth of sins, excludes the odor of evil conduct, and does not permit the worms of sins to be generated—that is, it prevents lustful and deadly pleasures from arising in the body. It also preserves our bodies from that immortal worm which torments sinners with unceasing punishment, concerning which it is written: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Mark IX, 43, 45, 47; from Isa. LXVI, 24).

And just as salts are applied from outside but work inwardly through the power of their nature, so the heavenly grace penetrates the external and internal parts of a person and preserves the whole person intact and uncorrupted by sin.

That those who are seasoned with the salt of heavenly wisdom are worthy of God was also shown earlier through a preceding figure of the Law, because every sacrifice offered to God was salted with salt (Lev. II, 13). The Evangelist recalled this very point, saying: “Every sacrifice shall be salted with salt” (Mark IX, 48), showing that a person truly becomes a sacrifice worthy of God when infused with the power of heavenly wisdom.

Therefore, not without reason, when the Lord rebuked Jerusalem—or rather, the Synagogue—through the prophet Ezekiel, he said among other things: “You were not washed with water, nor salted with salt” (Ezek. XVI, 4), foretelling that it would receive neither the grace of saving baptism for washing away its sins nor the faith of heavenly wisdom.

If anyone makes use of this heavenly salt, he will be seasoned; but whoever refuses it will become tasteless. The Apostle also rightly admonished us that our speech should always be seasoned with the salt of grace (Col. IV, 6).

### III

We find the grace and power of this salt foreshadowed also in the Books of Kings (IV Kings II). When there were waters at Jericho that were harmful and caused barrenness, the holy prophet Elisha was summoned to provide those waters with a saving remedy.

Then the holy Elisha, who was not ignorant of the heavenly mystery, ordered a clay vessel to be brought to him and salt to be put into it. He came and cast the salt into the sources of the waters; and thus the barren nature of the waters was healed and changed into fertility. We understand that this was done as a sacrament of the future truth, for a clear reason.

The Apocalypse explicitly reported that peoples are signified by waters, saying: “The waters that you saw are peoples, and nations, and crowds, and races” (Apoc. XVII, 15). They could not otherwise be healed or receive a saving remedy unless salt were put into a clay vessel—that is, unless the Wisdom of God assumed a human body.

After it came to the sources of the waters—that is, to the outcome of human death—for the sake of our salvation, then the nature of all believers, which had been barren of the fruit of the seed, was changed into the fertility of faith and righteousness.

Therefore the Lord rightly calls his Apostles the salt of the earth, for he filled them from himself with divine and heavenly wisdom. He testified that they were the salt of the earth just as they were also the light of the world (John VIII, 12).

For although he himself declared that he was the light of the world, he nevertheless wished his disciples also to be called by this name—not taking away from himself what is his own light, but bestowing it. For he bestows the true and eternal light that belongs to him without any diminution of his own nature.

We certainly know that some salts are generated from the earth; but this comparison too suits the persons of the Apostles. Although they appeared to have been born from the earth of the human body, they had already begun through faith in Christ to be something else, so that they were no longer regarded as earth but as the salt of the earth. For they had been changed from carnal to spiritual, made capable through faith of seasoning the insipid hearts of believers.

### IV

“You,” he says, “are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has become tasteless, with what will it be seasoned? It is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people.”

He shows that those become tasteless who, once instructed through faith and heavenly wisdom, ought to remain faithful and steadfast, but, abandoning faith and divine wisdom, either fall into heresy or return to the folly of the pagans.

And therefore he says: “But if the salt has become tasteless, with what will it be seasoned?” For such people, made tasteless through the devil’s deception, lose the grace of faith and vanish away. Although they could have seasoned others who did not yet believe and were still estranged from the faith with the word of divine preaching, they became useless even to themselves.

Finally, Judas Iscariot had been one of such salts. But after he rejected divine wisdom and became an apostate from the Apostles, he was not only unable to benefit others; miserable and useless, he became so even to himself.

For this reason the Lord added: “It is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people.” Such people are no longer faithful members of the household; rather, cast out from the Church, they are to be regarded as outsiders and enemies of the faith. Thus Judas, from being a member of the household of faith, became an enemy of the truth.

When such people have been cast outside the Church, they must be trampled underfoot by various vices of the flesh and diverse pleasures of the world. This is what he says: “It is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people.”

What it means to be trampled underfoot by people Solomon also reported in his book when speaking of a prostitute: “A promiscuous woman,” he says, “is trampled by people passing by like dung in the road” (Eccli. IX, 10).

Since we have already been seasoned with apostolic salt, we must remain in such a great seasoning of spiritual grace, so that we too may deserve to be called the salt of the earth by Christ our Lord, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## TREATISE V

*[Note: In Gallandi: Treatise IV, on the Gospel of St. Matthew.]*

On chapter V of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

### I

Then he says: “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matt. V, 14–15).

The Lord called his disciples the salt of the earth because they seasoned with heavenly wisdom the hearts of the human race, which had been made tasteless by the devil. Now he also calls them the light of the world, because, illuminated by him who is himself the true and eternal light, they too became light for those in darkness.

For since he himself is the sun of righteousness, he rightly also calls his disciples the light of the world. Through them, as through rays that flash forth, he poured the light of his knowledge over the whole world. They drove the darkness of error from human hearts by displaying the light of truth.

Illuminated through them, we too have been made light from darkness, as the Apostle says: “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. V, 8–9). And again: “You are not children of night or of darkness, but you are children of light and children of day” (I Thess. V, 5).

The holy John also rightly testified in his Epistle, saying: “God is light” (I John I, 3), and whoever remains in God is in the light, just as he himself is in the light. Therefore, since we rejoice that we have been freed from the darkness of error, we must always walk in the light as children of light.

### II

And he added: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14). Here he signifies the Church, concerning which the divine Scriptures testify in many places and of which David speaks especially, saying: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 3).

And again: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5). And again: “As we have heard, so also have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God: God founded it forever” (Ps. XLVII, 9).

To show clearly that the Holy Spirit was speaking of this city, he also mentioned the mountain itself, saying: “In the city of our God, on his holy mountain.”

Through Isaiah the Lord speaks of it, saying: “Behold, I will prepare for you a carbuncle stone, your foundations of sapphire, your battlements of jasper, your gates of crystal stone, your whole circuit of precious stones, and all your children taught by God” (Isa. LIV, 11–12, according to the Septuagint).

There are many similar passages that we have omitted lest we weary our readers, especially since what has been said is more than sufficient to establish this city.

He therefore shows that the city set upon a mountain is the Church, established in the heavenly glory upon faith in our Lord and Savior. Through spiritual action it surpasses all the moisture [Note: “Humiditatem” (“moisture”). Or “humilitatem” (“humility”), as in the first Basel edition?] of earthly weakness and has become glorious and visible to the whole world. It is no longer overshadowed by the proclamation of the Law but is seen openly through evangelical preaching.

### III

And he added: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Matt. V, 15).

Let us therefore examine the meaning of this saying of the Lord. We know that a lamp is lit so that it will not be covered by a bushel or by some other covering; if this were done, its use would benefit no one. Rather, it is lit and placed upon a lampstand so that, set in a lofty place, it may drive away the blindness of the dark night and grant the use of its light to those in the house.

The Lord recalls this so that we might know that we too have been kindled by the grace of faith and illuminated by the light of the Spirit for this purpose: that we ourselves might shine spiritually, like a lamp, through works of faith and righteousness, and that, once the night of ignorance has been driven away, we might illuminate those who are placed in the darkness of error with the light of truth itself.

Hence the Apostle says: “Among whom you shine like lights in this world, holding the word of life” (Phil. II, 15–16).

If we do not do this, we shall appear to cover and obscure, by our unbelief as by a kind of veil, the benefit of such necessary light, to the harm both of ourselves and of others. For this reason we know and read that the man who preferred to hide the talent he had received for the profit of heavenly commerce rather than give it to the money-changers incurred the punishment due to him (Matt. XXV, 28–30).

### IV

Therefore that spiritual lamp, which has been lit for the use of our salvation, must always shine within us. We have the lamp of the heavenly commandment and spiritual grace, concerning which David said: “Your commandment is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths” (Ps. CXVIII, 105).

Solomon also says concerning it: “For the commandment of the Law is a lamp” (Prov. VI, 23). Through the prophet Zephaniah the Lord also testifies concerning it: “I will search Jerusalem with a lamp” (Zeph. I, 12).

In this lamp he displays the unquenchable light of his Law and grace. It must not be covered or obscured by any veil of a blind mind, as the Jews or heretics do, who strive to cover and conceal the clear light of divine preaching with perverse interpretations, preaching treachery instead of faith and veiling the light of truth with the darkness of error.

Therefore this lamp of the Law and faith must not be hidden from us but must always be placed in the Church, as upon a lampstand, for the salvation of many, so that we may enjoy the light of truth itself and all believers may be illuminated.

The Holy Spirit also exhorts us through Isaiah to contemplate this light, saying: “Come, let us walk in the light of the Lord. For he has dismissed his people, the house of Israel” (Isa. II, 5–6, according to the Septuagint).

The blessed Peter also testified concerning this light in his Epistle, saying: “He rescued us from darkness and called us into his marvelous light” (I Pet. II, 9).

The prophet Zechariah, wishing to reveal the mysteries of this spiritual light and heavenly lampstand, which was shown in the figure of the Church, testified that among the things displayed to him according to the merit of his prophecy he saw a golden lampstand with its lamps (Zech. IV, 2).

In the tabernacle of witness, too, as an example of the future truth, the lampstand with its lamps shone upon the people with unfailing light (Exod. XL). The meaning of this was hidden to the Jews, as were all the mysteries of the Law, but it is now manifest to us.

For we know that in that lampstand a type of the true and eternal light was shown: namely, the Holy Spirit, who through his manifold grace continually illuminates the whole body of the Church.

Therefore, in the Gospel, among other things, the Lord exhorts his disciples to have lamps burning in their hands, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII, 15). This command of the Lord must certainly be understood not in a bodily sense but according to spiritual reason.

For since the commandment of God, or the light of the Law, is signified by the lamp, we are commanded to carry a lamp in our hands so that, illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may shine through works of righteousness and faith, according to what Solomon reports: “The ways of the righteous will shine like light; they proceed and give light until the day is corrected” (Prov. IV, 18, according to the Septuagint).

*[Note: “Corrigat” (“is corrected”). The Septuagint has κατορθώσῃ, “may direct.” Nevertheless, Lucifer of Cagliari also reads “corrigat,” as Nobilius notes at that passage. The first Basel edition has “decurrat,” “runs its course.”]*

### V

Rightly, therefore, when the Lord had mentioned the lamp in the present passage, saying: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house,” he added: “So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

God is glorified in us among unbelievers and faithless people if we live according to the divine commandments and shine through good works. Hence the holy Apostle says: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20).

The blessed Peter likewise admonishes us in his Epistle: “So that when they speak evil of you, the works of righteousness may glorify our God” (I Pet. III, 16).

This may also be understood in another way, since spiritual understanding is manifold: we may recognize that the Lord himself is signified by the lamp, on account of the humility of the body he assumed.

In accordance with the glory of his divinity, he is called not only the sun of righteousness, but, according to the mystery of the body he assumed, he is also shown as a lamp. For although he was the God of glory and eternal majesty, he appeared humble in this world like a lamp.

And not without reason like a lamp, since a lamp commonly shines through the night. Therefore he appeared humble in this world like a lamp in order to drive away from our hearts the darkness of error and the night of ignorance, for we live in this world as though placed in the night.

This lamp—that is, the incarnation of Christ, displayed by the Law and the Prophets—is no longer read as obscure preaching of the Law, hidden beneath a bushel, nor is it covered, as though by a vessel of treachery, by the unbelief of the Scribes and Pharisees. Rather, placed upon the cross as upon a lampstand, it illuminates the entire house of the Church.

According to the mystery of the incarnation, he is a lamp; according to the glory of his divinity, he is the sun of righteousness. Finally, upon the lampstand of the cross he shone like the sun, when, through the preaching of the Apostles as through certain rays, the Lord and our Savior brought the most radiant light of his knowledge to the whole world. He is blessed forever.

## TREATISE VI

*[Note: In Gallandi: Treatise V, on the Gospel of St. Matthew.]*

On chapter V of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

### I

Then he says: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matt. V, 17).

The Son of God, who is the author of the Law and the Prophets, did not come to destroy the Law or the Prophets. For he himself gave Moses to hand on the Law to the people, and purified the Prophets by the Holy Spirit for the preaching of future things.

“Therefore,” he says, “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill.”

He fulfilled the Law and the Prophets in this way: he himself brought to completion the things that had been written in the Law and the Prophets. Therefore, when he had drunk the vinegar offered to him on the cross, he said: “It is fulfilled” (John XIX, 30), clearly showing that everything written about him in the Law and the Prophets had been completed, even to the drinking of vinegar.

He fulfills the Law in every way when he completes, through the sacrament of his passion, the mystery of the Passover or the lamb formerly displayed in a figure. Hence the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V, 7).

He fulfills the Law when, by receiving a body, he completes in the reality of truth the sacrifices of the Law and all the examples prefigured in himself.

Or certainly he fulfills the Law when he confirms the commandments of the Law that he had given by the supplement of his evangelical grace.

What Law he came to fulfill he demonstrates in what follows, saying: “Until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to be” (Matt. V, 18).

From this we recognize how true and divine the preaching of the Law is, since the Lord makes clear that not even one iota or one stroke can pass from it. Yet in this iota or stroke of the Law the mystery of the cross may also be understood, since the iota and the stroke display in themselves a certain image of the cross, which, having been proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets, could in no way be passed over.

### II

Then he says: “Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 29).

If it is impious to abolish the least commandments, how much more the great and greatest ones. Hence the Holy Spirit bears witness to this same point through Solomon, saying: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccli. XIX, 20).

Therefore nothing is to be abolished from the divine commandments, nothing mutilated, but everything must be preserved and taught with faithful and devoted minds, lest the glory of the heavenly kingdom be lost. For what the judgment of unbelievers or worldly people considers least and small is not small before God but necessary.

The Lord shows that whoever teaches and does the commandments will be great in the kingdom of heaven. Therefore we must work not only in words but also in deeds—not merely teach, but do what we have taught.

Let us hear the Lord himself rebuking such teachers in the Gospel, those who say but do not do: “Woe to you,” he says, “Scribes and hypocritical Pharisees, because you load people with burdens that cannot be carried, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with your finger” (Matt. XXIII, 4).

Hence the Apostle says: “Those who hear the Law are not righteous before God, but those who do the Law will be justified” (Rom. II, 13). If he says this even about hearers, what must we understand concerning teachers?

Solomon also says: “Do not be hasty with your tongue, and do not be sluggish and remiss in your works” (Eccli. IV, 34).

Therefore the one who teaches must provide from himself an example of pure faith through the integrity of his conduct, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: “Be an example of the faithful” (I Tim. IV, 12). And again: “Showing yourself as an example of good works, in righteousness, in chastity, in sobriety, through sound doctrine” (Tit. II, 7–8).

The Son of God himself, who is the teacher and Lord of the Law, likewise wished to fulfill in deeds, for our example, everything that he taught.

### III

And he added: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20).

The righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees is censured because they sought not faith in the divine promise but human praise and worldly glory. We have an example of this in that proud and arrogant Pharisee who, as he saw it, setting forth the merits of his righteousness, shamelessly boasted before God with an exalted mind and proud words (Luke XVIII, 11).

The Scribes and Pharisees therefore retained the appearance of righteousness not in order to please God but to seek the reputation of human glory and acquire earthly profits and temporal advantages.

Therefore the Lord exhorts us to surpass this celebrated [Note: “Famosam” (“celebrated”). Or “fumosam” (“smoky”), as in Grynaeus’s margin.] righteousness of human praise through works of heavenly righteousness and the merits of faith, through Christ our Lord.

## TREATISE VII

*[Note: In Gallandi: Treatise V, on the Gospel of St. Matthew.]*

On chapter V of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

### I

Next comes: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you: if anyone is angry with his brother, he shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 21–22).

This is what the Lord meant when he said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.” This is to add what was lacking: namely, to reform the commandments of the Law for the better.

Hence the holy Apostle says: “Do we then destroy the Law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the Law” (Rom. III, 31).

To a crude and hard people the commandments of righteousness were given through the Law; but to a perfect and faithful people the evangelical commandments of consummate faith and heavenly righteousness are given.

The Law commanded that one must not kill, but the Gospel commands that one must not even be angry, in order to remove from our hearts the entire root of sin, since through anger one can proceed even to murder.

Therefore blessed Job rightly testified in his book, saying: “Anger kills the fool, and jealousy slays the deluded” (Job V, 2).

David likewise says: “Be angry, and do not sin; speak within your hearts, and be pierced with remorse upon your beds” (Ps. IV, 5).

The holy Apostle interpreted this testimony, saying: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger, and do not give place to the devil” (Eph. IV, 26–27).

If anger is therefore not permitted, how much less is it permissible to admit the crime of murder. And if anger is held liable in the future judgment, what punishment do we suppose the perpetrator of the crime itself will have?

## II

“But whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; but whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22). Thus the Lord teaches us to be perfect in every respect, so that we may not be held guilty at the future judgment even for slight or empty words. For he forbids a brother to be called *raca*, that is, “empty” and “vain”; for one who is filled with faith and the Holy Spirit ought not to be called empty and vain. Nor should one be called a fool who, by believing in Christ, has obtained the grace of divine wisdom.

Accordingly, when the Holy Spirit spoke through Solomon about the evangelical man, he testified as follows: “Blessed is he who has not fallen by the word of his mouth and has not been pierced by the sorrow of sin” (Ecclus. 14:1). For this reason Solomon also says elsewhere: “Make bolts for your mouth, and make a balance for your tongue and your words” (Ecclus. 28:18). And again: “Cut away from yourself a crooked mouth, and put wicked lips far from you” (Prov. 4:24). And again: “Do not accustom your mouth to undisciplined speech; for there is in it the sorrow of sin” (Ecclus. 23:17).

Hence David also says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140:3). And again, in another psalm, he said: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue’” (Ps. 38:1). For, as Solomon says: “The lips of the imprudent will tell foolish things, but a balance is applied to the word of the prudent” (Ecclus. 21:28).
