Therefore the Lord testified in the Gospel that we shall also give an account for an idle word (Matt. 12:36).

For this reason the Apostle likewise exhorts us, saying: “Let no evil speech come out of your mouth, except what is good for the building up of faith” (Eph. 4:29). And again: “Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4:6). For this reason we ought to be cautious in all things, lest through familiarity with useless words we acquire harm to our salvation.

## III

Then he says: “If you offer your gift before the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24). From this very point we recognize how highly the Lord esteems brotherly love: he shows that a gift offered to God cannot be acceptably presented unless the one offering the gift first reconciles himself to his brother, setting anger aside.

Finally, we find that Cain’s offerings were rejected by God for this reason (Gen. 4:5): because, failing to observe the laws of charity, he retained anger against his brother in his heart. Hence, in many places in the Gospel, the Lord indicates that brotherly love must be guarded above all, saying: “I give you a new commandment, that you should have love for one another” (John 13:34). And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid., 35).

Nor without reason does the Lord speak similarly through the prophet Zechariah: “Judge a just and peaceful judgment, and do not retain the malice of your brother in your hearts” (Zech. 8:16). Through David also he testifies in the same way: “Cease from anger and forsake indignation” (Ps. 36:8). Likewise the Holy Spirit speaks through Solomon, saying:

> “A man keeps anger against another man and seeks healing from God? He himself has no mercy on a man like himself, and yet he entreats God for his sins? Though he is flesh, he retains anger and seeks propitiation from God? And who will pray for his offenses?” (Ecclus. 28:3–5).

And he added: “Remember the last things, and cease from enmity” (ibid., 6).

Thus the holy David, not ignorant through the Holy Spirit of the evangelical commandment, testified about himself as follows: “If I have seen iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. 65:18).

For what is so pleasing to God, so necessary for our salvation, as what the Lord commands: not to retain anger, to offer a gift to God with a peaceful spirit and a clear conscience, as Abel the first offered it? Therefore his gifts were accepted by God, while Cain’s were rejected: Abel offered his gifts to the Lord with a pure and simple mind, whereas Cain held anger against his brother in his heart.

Accordingly, if we want our gifts to please God, we must drive anger from our heart, kill the malice conceived against our brother, maintain brotherly peace, preserve charity, love unity, and guard concord, so that we may deserve to appease the Lord, who is blessed forever.

# TREATISE VIII

[Note: In Galland: “Treatise VII on the Gospel according to St. Matthew.”]

On chapter 5 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

After this comes the following: “Agree with your adversary while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Amen, I say to you, you will not come out from there until you pay the last quadrans” (Matt. 5:25–26).

Some think that this saying of the Lord should be understood in the following way. They assert that such an adversary—one who has become an enemy through his own fault or that of another—should quickly be recalled to peace and friendship while we are with him on the way, that is, in the course of the present life. Otherwise, when one has departed from the world, each person, as one forgetful of charity and guilty of enmity, might begin to be brought before God the judge and handed over by the judge to the officer, that is, the overseer of punishments, so that, cast into the prison of Gehenna, he might pay the penalties due for his sin.

But this assertion does not seem to possess a complete rationale. For what if one of the brothers should become an adversary on account of the faith? Is agreement to be granted to his infidelity, lest religious disagreement remain with such a person? We also have adversaries among the Gentiles who oppose our faith and who sometimes, during persecution, compel us to abominable sacrifices. Is this therefore also to be done for such adversaries, so that we grant sacrilegious agreement to their will lest they remain enemies? Their sacrilegious persuasion must not merely not be accepted; it must be resisted with unconquerable faith.

## II

Some also plainly think that the devil is to be understood here as the adversary; but I do not see on what grounds they establish this. In what respect ought agreement to be granted to the devil, whose work it is to persuade, urge, and extort everything against the faith, against salvation, and against divine religion?

Unless perhaps it should be understood in this sense: if some hostile persecutor, or the devil—because he is the author of persecution—should wish to inflict death upon a Christian for the sake of the name of Christ, the Christian should willingly grant agreement, so that he may be handed over to death for Christ. Otherwise that same devil, who is our accuser, might establish us as guilty before God of treachery against the faith and make us liable to punishment. For although the devil is the author of every crime, he is also the accuser.

We read that this was said about him in the Apocalypse: “And the Dragon, the accuser of our brothers, who accused them before our God day and night, was thrown down” (Rev. 12:10). He himself is the tempter and the accuser: he tempts in order to deceive; he accuses in order to condemn.

## III

Others, however, whose assertion seems to me clearer [Note: Alternatively, “fuller” (*plenior*)], think that the Holy Spirit is to be understood here as the adversary. He opposes vices and the desires of the flesh, as the Apostle makes clear when he says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you may not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

The Spirit desires heavenly things; the flesh desires earthly things. The Spirit rejoices in spiritual gifts; the flesh delights in bodily vices. Hence the Apostle also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

I believe that the Lord commanded us to obey this adversary of sin and human error in all things—the one who urges what is just and holy—while we are with him on the way, that is, in the course of the present life, so that we may be able to have eternal peace and perpetual fellowship with him.

But if someone refuses to obey the will of the Holy Spirit and proves contrary to it, there is no doubt that, after the departure from this life, such a person must be brought before the Son of God, who is judge of the living and the dead. He will be handed over by him to an officer, that is, an angel of punishments, and sent into the prison of Gehenna. He will not be released from there unless he also pays the last quadrans, that is, pays the full penalty of his debt, down to the very last sin.

It is therefore understood that the Lord speaks in the present passage about this adversary: the one who opposes our sins and desires our salvation, who therefore wishes us to be in agreement with him, so that we may deserve both to escape the punishments of hell and to obtain the heavenly kingdoms.

Solomon also seems to testify about this in his book when he says: “There is one, and there is not a second; indeed, he has neither son nor brother, and there is no end to all his labor” (Eccles. 4:8). And:

> “Two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labor; because if one falls, the other raises up his companion. Woe to the one who is alone when he falls, because he has no one to raise him up” (ibid., 9–10).

This shows that the flesh which has deserved to possess the harmony and fellowship of the Holy Spirit, when it falls into death, is raised by that same Spirit to life and everlasting glory.

Therefore he said, “Woe to that one who is alone,” because when he falls he has no one to raise him up—that is, because the flesh which, through its own unbelief, has not deserved to have fellowship with the Spirit is not raised to eternal life, but is awakened to everlasting punishment by him who is judge of the living and the dead. To him be praise and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# TREATISE IX

[Note: In Galland: “Treatise VIII on the Gospel according to St. Matthew.”]

On chapter 5 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you: Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27–28).

The holy David rightly says: “You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly” (Ps. 118:4). Exceedingly indeed, because not only adultery but also desire is held guilty of the crime. The Law condemns adultery, but the Gospel also punishes desire, which is the root of adultery.

Hence, in many places, the Holy Spirit bears witness through Solomon to this same matter, saying: “Do not follow your desires, and restrain yourself from your pleasure; for if you give your soul its desire, it will make you a joy to your enemies and to those who envy you” (Ecclus. 18:30–31). And again:

> “Do not give your soul over to prostitutes in any way, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance. Do not look around in the streets of the city, and do not wander through its squares. Turn your face away from a well-dressed woman, and do not gaze upon the appearance of another” (Ecclus. 9:6, 8).

Afterward he added: “Many who admired the appearance of another man’s wife have been rejected; for her conversation burns like fire” (ibid., 11).

He rightly said, “It burns like fire,” because in conversation with such a woman the desire of lust is kindled like fire. Therefore you must avoid such a woman, lest the flame of desire consume you.

For this reason Solomon also says: “Let not desire for beauty overcome you, nor be captured by your eyes, nor be carried away by your eyelids” (Prov. 6:25, according to the Septuagint). And again he says: “Take away from me the desire for intercourse of the belly, and let not the desire of intercourse seize me; and do not hand me over to an irreverent and unrestrained soul” (Ecclus. 23:6).

[Note: In the Basel editions, the first and second of Grynaeus have “desire of the belly.”]

[Note: “Unbridled.” The Vulgate has “a soul … without restraint.” Shortly before, in the Septuagint at Prov. 6:25, μηδὲ συναρπασθῇς ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῆς βλεφάρων, “nor be carried away by her eyelids.” Thus also the Vulgate.]

Let us also hear the blessed Job, who showed himself in all things an evangelical man and fulfilled the Lord’s command before hearing it. He testifies about this very matter concerning himself when he says:

> “If my foot has turned aside from the way, and my heart has followed my eye; if my hands have touched gifts, let others eat my fruits; if my heart has followed another man’s wife, or if I have been constant with her, then let my wife also please another man. For this is the fury of anger and an unclean spirit: to defile another man’s wife; it is a burning fire” (Job 31:7, 12).

Since adultery is a grave sin, therefore, in order to uproot the root of that sin and prevent our conscience from being defiled, he also forbade desire, which is the source of adultery, in accordance with what blessed James reports in his Epistle: “Desire gives birth to sin, and the desire of sin produces death” (Jas. 1:15).

For this reason the Holy Spirit also speaks through David about this very matter: “Blessed is he who will seize them and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:9). He presents as blessed, and truly evangelical, the man who kills the desires and lusts of the flesh, born through human weakness, immediately before they grow, at the very beginning of their birth, through faith in Christ, who is called the Rock (1 Cor. 10:4).

## II

Then he says: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna. And if your hand,” he says, “causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna” (Matt. 5:29–30).

He does not mean the eye or hand of the human body, but the eye or hand of the heart. That is, he commands that the perception of evil desire and carnal longing be cut away from our hearts. The Lord himself reveals in the Gospel that all evils proceed from there, saying: “For from the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, blasphemies, false testimonies, and the other things that defile a person” (Matt. 15:19–20).

But cutting off the body accomplishes nothing toward correcting an evil mind, in which the whole chasm of vices lies. Indeed, we see many people deprived of their eyes or weakened in body who nevertheless do not cease from their vices.

Therefore the Lord commands us, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, to cut away rather these members of vice, of an evil mind, and of depraved thought, lest, when vices rule, both body and soul—that is, the whole person—be made liable to eternal fire.

Some think that this should be understood of sons or close associates, who are dear and beloved to us like the eyes of our head. If some such people, being opposed to our faith and hope, should create a stumbling block, they are to be rejected by us and regarded as enemies of salvation, lest, when each of us is associated with such faithless and blasphemous people, we be condemned to the same punishment.

## III

But since mention has been made of the body, it can more correctly be understood of the body of the Church. In it, the eye, as a precious member, is recognized as signifying the bishop, who illuminates the whole body with the light of the divine commandment.

Accordingly, the saying is rightly understood in this way: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.” If such an eye—that is, a bishop—should become a stumbling block to the Church through perverse faith and shameful conduct, the Lord commands that he be torn out, that is, rejected from the body of the Church, lest the people be held guilty for his sin.

For it is written: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (1 Cor. 5:6). And again: “Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (ibid., 13).

The hand, however, is understood to signify the presbyter. If he too, holding perverse faith or not living rightly, should become a stumbling block to the people, the Lord commands that he be cut off, that is, rejected, lest the Church be defiled by his sin, since, according to the Apostle, the Church ought to be holy and without blemish (Eph. 5:27), through Christ our Lord, who is blessed forever. Amen.

# TREATISE X

[Note: In Galland: “Treatise IX on the Gospel according to St. Matthew.”]

On chapter 5 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then follows: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.’ But I say to you: Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matt. 5:31–32).

In all things our Lord and Savior reforms the provisions of the ancient Law for the better. Long ago, because the Jewish people lived unlawfully and served their own pleasures, Moses seemed to have granted them permission to issue a divorce for any reason. This was not because the rationale of the Law demanded it, but because the unrestrained desire of the carnal people could not, according to the strictness of discipline, keep the justice of the Law.

This permission was therefore granted, as the Lord himself makes clear elsewhere in his response, when they continued to question him. For when they asked why Moses had permitted a bill of divorce to be given, the Lord answered: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to give a bill of divorce; but from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. 19:8).

Thus now, not without reason, our Lord and Savior, removing that permission, restores the commands of his ancient ordinance. For he orders the chaste marriage of matrimony to be preserved under an unbreakable law, showing that the law of marriage was first instituted by him.

He himself says: “Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.” By this saying he condemned both the wicked license of the Jews and the foolish and wretched presumption of the Manichaeans, who deny that marriages are from God. [Note: The text’s *passivam* is erroneous; read perhaps *pessimam* (“most evil”) or *pravam* (“depraved”).] He pronounced that a wife may not be dismissed except on account of fornication, plainly demonstrating that anyone who presumes to violate a marriage joined by God through an unlawful separation acts against God’s will.

Therefore let those who, through the unrestrained pleasure of lust, dismiss their wives and wish to enter into other marriages without the cause of fornication know what a grave crime of condemnation they incur before God. They believe that they may commit this with impunity because it seems permitted by human and secular laws, not knowing that they sin more gravely in this respect because they prefer human laws to divine ones. Thus they believe something to be lawful merely because it has been freely permitted by human beings, although God has established it as unlawful.

But just as it is not lawful to dismiss a wife who lives chastely and purely, so it is permitted to dismiss an adulterous wife, because she has made herself unworthy of her husband’s fellowship by sinning against her own body and daring to violate the temple of God.

## II

Then he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely; but you shall render your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ Whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. 5:33–37).

Through the grace of evangelical teaching, the Law given through Moses has advanced. In the Law it was commanded that one must not swear falsely; in the Gospel, one must not even swear.

The Holy Spirit formerly anticipated giving this very command through Solomon, saying: “Do not accustom your mouth to oaths” (Ecclus. 33:9). And again: “Just as a slave who is continually flogged is not freed from his bruises, so everyone who swears and [Note: *negotians*; Greek ὀνομάζων, “naming.” Shortly before, in place of *flagellatus*, the Greek has ἐξεταζόμενος, “questioned.” The text and the Vulgate do not otherwise differ.] names things will not be cleansed from sin” (ibid., 11).

Therefore it is wholly unsuitable for us to swear. What need does any one of us have to swear, since we are absolutely forbidden to lie, and our words ought always to be so true and so trustworthy that they are accepted as an oath?

For this reason the Lord forbids us not only to swear falsely but also to swear, lest we seem to speak the truth only when we swear. He does not want us, whom he has established as truthful in every word, to think that it is lawful to lie without an oath.

The reason for an oath is that everyone who swears does so in order to declare what is true. Therefore the Lord wants there to be no difference between an oath and our speech: just as there must be no faithlessness in an oath, so there ought to be no falsehood in our words. Both perjury and lying are condemned to the punishment of divine judgment, as Scripture says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

Therefore whoever speaks the truth swears, since it is written: “A faithful witness does not lie” (Prov. 14:3). Hence Scripture often and rightly records that our God swears, because whatever is spoken by God, who is truthful and unable to lie, is regarded as an oath, since everything he says is true.

Indeed, we find God swearing on several occasions, but this was because of the faithlessness of the Jews, who think that every truth rests only upon the assurance of an oath. Therefore God also wished to swear, so that those who did not believe God when he spoke might believe him at least when he swore.

## III

The Lord therefore says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King.”

In these sayings of the Lord, by which he forbids us to swear by such elements, there is a twofold meaning.

First, he wished to remove from us both the practice of swearing and the custom arising from human error, lest any one of us, swearing by these elements, should hold a creature in the honor of divine veneration, or believe that he possessed impunity for perjury if he swore by the elements of the world, although it is written: “He has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor” (Ps. 23:4).

In this he also condemns the error both of Jewish faithlessness and of the human race, which, abandoning the Creator, has held the creature under divine veneration, as the Apostle reports: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1:25).

The saying can also be understood in another way: when one swears by heaven and earth, one swears by him who established heaven and earth, as the Lord himself made clear elsewhere when he said: “Whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by all that is upon it; and whoever swears by the throne of God swears by it and by all that is upon it; and whoever swears by the throne of God swears by it and by him who dwells in it” (Matt. 23:20).

[Note: “By the throne of God … by the throne of God.” The text and the Vulgate have a different reading.]

“Nor,” he says, “shall you swear by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King”—that is, the type of the body of Christ, which is that spiritual and heavenly Church.

“Nor,” he says, “shall you swear by your head,” because, according to the Apostle, “the head of a man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3). Therefore whoever swears by these things swears by the one who is the author of them all.

“Let your speech,” he says, “be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ Whatever is more than this is from evil.” He teaches that every speech uttered by us ought to contain nothing other than what is true, since every lie—that is, whatever is more than this—is traced back to the devil as its author, who has always been a liar from the beginning and is also its father (John 8:44).

Therefore we must always speak and meditate upon what is true, so that we may show ourselves to be disciples of him who is the truth, who is blessed forever.

[Note: In Galland: “Treatise X on the Gospel according to St. Matthew.”]

# TREATISE XI

On chapter 5 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then follows: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you: Do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also; and to anyone who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well” (Matt. 5:38, 40).

Through the evangelical commandments the Lord forms us according to every example of patience and humility. Long ago it had been commanded in the Law that if anyone, moved by the fury of anger, tore out another person’s eye or tooth, he too should be subjected to a similar punishment and the same loss.

In this command the justice of the Law was displayed, and the rashness of an insolent people was restrained by such fear, so that, because they had no fear of the future judgment, at least the penalty of present vengeance might prevent them from crime.

Those who live according to evangelical faith, however, do not seek this repayment of vengeance; for them every hope of repayment and vengeance is reserved for the future. Therefore in the Gospel the Lord not only does not command us to return an injury, but commands that those struck on the right cheek offer the other also, if the anger of the one striking demands it.

For this is what he says: “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the left also.” This is [Note: The text has *vere* (“truly”); perhaps *vera* (“true”)? No alteration is made.] truly to live by faith: not to seek present vengeance, but future retribution from him who says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19).

Jeremiah clearly presents such an evangelical man, who, when struck on the cheek, willingly offers the other, when he says:

> “It is good for a man when he bears a heavy yoke in his youth. He will sit alone and be silent, because he has borne a heavy yoke. He will give his cheek to be struck, and he will be filled with reproach” (Lam. 3:27–29).

In this he plainly shows as blessed the man who, living under the yoke of the evangelical Law, does not turn away from any injury inflicted by a persecutor.

Such practice of endurance leads to the suffering of martyrdom. A person will easily be able to endure bodily punishments even in a time of persecution if, having first been trained in peace, he receives such injuries calmly and willingly.

Nor is it fitting for a Christian to return an injury, lest he be judged like the one to whom he returns it. For if it is evil to inflict an injury, the one who repays evil in kind is not free from guilt; and therefore the person who imitates evil cannot be considered good.

## II

The Lord commands not only that the cheek be offered to the one who strikes, but also that losses be endured. For he adds: “And to anyone who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well.”

After the endurance of bodily injury, the Lord also wishes us to despise worldly possessions and to be so removed from every lawsuit or legal dispute that, if some slanderer or tempter should bring a suit to test our faith, wishing to take what is ours, the Lord commands us willingly to offer not only what he unjustly demands but also what he does not ask for.

For if someone, because of the slanderous lawsuit, despises these small possessions, he will, trained through such an exercise, easily be able also during persecution to despise all such things as belong to this world. [Note: The text has *hujusmodi* (“such things”); *hujusmundi* (“of this world”) appears to be the intended reading.]

This is perfect faith and perfect victory over the one who inflicts injury: to offer even those things he does not demand.

## III

Then he says: “Whoever compels you to go one thousand paces, go with him another two” (Matt. 5:41). The Lord commands us to be energetic and ready for every work of devotion.

He wants our goodness to arise not so much from necessity as from our own will [Note: Perhaps *promptae* (“ready, willing”) should be read instead of *propriae* (“one’s own”)], so that, while we do more for others than they ask of us, we may attain the glory of a greater reward.

It is the duty of complete charity and perfect devotion to provide willingly more than one has asked.

Some have also believed that this meaning should be understood spiritually: whoever is compelled to go one thousand paces should go with him another two. That is, if some unbeliever, or someone who has not yet attained knowledge of the truth, mentions the one God the Father, creator of all things, as though entering by way of the path of the Law, you should go with him another two—that is, after his confession of the Father, lead this same person by the way of truth onward to knowledge of the Son and the Holy Spirit, showing him that not only the Father but also the Son and the Holy Spirit must be believed in.

## IV

Finally follows: “And to the one who asks from you, give” (ibid., 42). That is, after knowledge of the Trinity, we should bestow the gift of heavenly grace with a ready spirit.

Or certainly, let us give mercy to those who ask according to our ability, so that, preceded by this merit, we may more easily obtain from God what we ask, from him who says: “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matt. 7:7).

But if we despise those who ask us, with what confidence do we believe that God will grant us what we ask? Scripture says: “Take care not to turn your face away from any poor person; then the face of God will not be turned away from you” (Tob. 4:7).

“And from everyone,” he says, “who wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away” (Matt. 5:42).

We are commanded in all things to preserve the religion of piety and faith, to count another’s need in affliction as our own, and not to value possessions more highly than a brother.

Therefore, whether brothers ask or request a loan in their need, we ought to share with a religious spirit and pious affection, awaiting the reward of eternal repayment, according to what David says: “The man is gracious who shows mercy and lends; he will order his words in judgment” (Ps. 111:5). And again: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever” (ibid., 9).

Hence the holy Job, whose example we ought to follow, recalls that he fulfilled these very evangelical commands, saying:

> “If I sent away the needy empty-handed, to go out from my door with a bare bosom; if I held anyone’s bond and did not tear it up; if I lent and took nothing from the debtor; or if the earth ever groaned on my account, or its furrows wept together; or if I ate its fruits alone without payment; or if I grieved the soul of the lord of the land by deceiving him” (Job 31:34–40, according to the Septuagint).

Job faithfully fulfilled all these things because he was awaiting a reward from him who repays eternal goods. To him be praise forever. Amen.

# TREATISE XII

[Note: In Galland: “Treatise XI on the Gospel according to St. Matthew.”]

On chapters 5 and 6 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then follows: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who slander and persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:43–45).

In all things the Lord wants us to be perfect in his commandments. Long ago, indeed, it was commanded in the Law: “Love your friends and hate your enemies” (Lev. 19:18). But these commands, like the one that says, “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. 21:23; Lev. 24:20; Deut. 19:20), were given for a temporal purpose to an earthly and carnal people.

Now the commands of heavenly and perfect righteousness are delivered to the evangelical people: that we should love our enemies, love those who hate us, and pray for those who slander and persecute us, so that we may truly deserve to be sons of God, who in his mercy indiscriminately bestows upon good and evil, just and unjust, the heavenly benefits and gifts of the present life.

The Holy Spirit also exhorts us through Isaiah to keep such evangelical commands: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who fear his name. Say to those who hate and abhor you, ‘You are our brothers’; let the name of the Lord be glorified, and let him appear to them in their joy, and let them be put to shame” (Isa. 66:5).

Hence David rightly testifies in the Psalm, saying: “Lord my God, if I have done this; if I have repaid those who rendered evil to me, then may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:4).

Blessed Job also recalls the same thing, saying: “If I rejoiced at the misfortune of my enemy, or said in my heart, ‘It has been done well,’ then let my ear hear a curse” (Job 31:29–30, according to the Septuagint).

These commands of evangelical grace, now given for the salvation of human beings, we find represented through the commands of the Law in the case of animals, when it says: “If you see your enemy’s ox fallen under its burden, you shall not pass by, but you shall raise it up with him” (Exod. 23:5; Deut. 22:4). Thus, already in the Law of Moses, each person was to learn from animals what he would one day do for a human being according to the Gospel.

## II

And rightly he follows up: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet your brothers only, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this? Therefore you must be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:46, 48).

The Lord shows that we cannot possess the reward of perfect love if we love only those whom we know will return our love in kind, since we know that such love is common even to Gentiles and sinners. Therefore the Lord wishes us to surpass the common law of human affection through the law of evangelical love, so that we may show the feeling of our love not only toward those who love us, but also toward enemies and those who hate us; thus, in this respect, we may imitate the example of true piety and paternal goodness.

## III

And he added: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 6:1).

The Lord wishes us to be strangers to every boastfulness of empty glory and human ambition, so that we may perform the work of our righteousness not with the aim of pleasing people, but God alone, from whom we expect the reward of our merit. For the merit of righteousness before God is lost by the person who wishes to live righteously for the purpose of acquiring the glory of human praise. Hence the Apostle says: “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Col. 1:10).

## IV

Then he says: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do, who love to stand in the synagogues and in the streets so that they may be honored by people. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you” (Matt. 6:2–4).

In all things the Lord shapes us through heavenly teaching toward the glory of perfect faith. Above he taught that the work of righteousness must be done not for people but for God. Now also, when giving alms, we are commanded not to sound a trumpet—that is, not to publicize what we do—because it is not the mark of a devout mind to do something in God’s affairs for the purpose of expecting human praise. Many people give something for the use of the poor precisely so that they may purchase empty human praise and worldly reputation with their resources. The Lord makes clear that such people have received the reward of their work in this world, because while they seek the glory of this world, they lose the reward of the future promise.

## V

And for this reason the Lord added: “So that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.” He wished the work of mercy to be not public but hidden; that is, we should act not for human praise but solely for God, from whom we expect the glory and reward of future blessing.

Solomon, praising the Church, once proclaimed this almsgiving, the work of faithful devotion, under the silence of religious discretion, saying: “Your cheeks are beautiful, apart from silence” (Song 6:6). He means that silence of which the Lord says: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 6:3).

But here the Lord is not speaking of the hands of the human body, which possess no faculty of seeing or speaking. Rather, by the right or left hand either a work or people are signified. Indeed, we read in the Books of Kings that people are signified by the hand, when it says: “Are there not ten hands of mine in Israel?”—that is, the ten tribes of Israel.

Therefore there is no doubt that the righteous are signified by the right hand, while sinners are understood by the left, according to what Solomon reported: “The right-hand paths the Lord knows; but the crooked are those that are on the left” (Prov. 4:27).

The Lord makes the meaning of this right and left hand most clearly known in the Gospel, when he declares that the righteous are to be placed on the right, but sinners on the left. Accordingly, when this right hand of the righteous does anything according to the Lord’s command, it is ordered that the left hand not know—that is, that we should not boast before sinful and faithless people about what we perform religiously and faithfully.

Yet if we were to do something faithfully, not for the sake of human praise, even in the presence of devout brothers, the work of devotion and faith cannot be judged as boastfulness by those brothers before our Lord and Savior, who is blessed forever. Amen.

# TREATISE XIII

[Note: In Galland: **TREATISE XII on the Gospel of St. Matthew**.]

On chapter 6 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then he says: “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, enter your room, and after closing the door pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you” (Matt. 6:5–6).

The Lord instructs us toward every perfection of heavenly righteousness and faith. For he wishes us to fulfill every work of divine religion without hypocrisy and without any desire for human praise. We are forbidden, after the manner of hypocrites, to display our prayers boastfully before everyone, lest we lose the reward of grace. The Lord seeks not a simulated and boastful prayer, but a simple and faithful one.

Therefore, after closing the door—that is, within the secret place of the heart and conscience—we are commanded by the Lord to pray, so that from him who knows secrets and hidden things we may receive the reward of hidden prayer.

For it belongs to a religious mind to pray to God not with shouting or the sound of the voice, but with devotion of spirit and faith of heart, as David testifies in the Psalm, saying: “Speak in your hearts, and be pierced with remorse upon your beds” (Ps. 4:5).

Finally, we find in the Books of Kings that the most holy Hannah fulfilled the commandments of this evangelical teaching (1 Sam. 1:13). For when, without any sound of the voice, she poured out the prayers of her desire in the secret of her heart, praying faithfully in the presence of the Lord, she immediately deserved to be heard by the Lord.

So also, when Daniel and the three youths were always praying secretly, the Lord granted them knowledge of the interpretations of dreams and the secrets of revelations (Dan. 1:17). Cornelius too, although he had not yet been instructed in the evangelical commandments, while praying secretly and faithfully in his room, deserved to hear the voice of the holy angel speaking (Acts 10:2–3).

What shall we say of Jonah, who, shut up not merely in a room but in the belly of a sea-monster, prayed so earnestly that he deserved to be heard and to emerge unharmed and alive from the depths of the sea and from the belly of so immense a beast (Jonah 2)?

He was heard by God not because he cried out with his voice, but because he cried out with faith. Therefore in prayer to God there is no need for a cry of the voice, since we know that he looks upon the secrets of the heart; what is needed is the cry of faith and the devotion of a religious mind.

## II

Therefore, not without reason, the Lord says in what follows: “When you pray, do not say many words, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Do not be like them, then, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. 6:7–8).

The Gentiles think that through a multitude of words they can more easily obtain from the Lord what they ask. But the Lord does not expect this from us. Rather, he wishes us to commend our prayer not by verbal loquacity, but by faith of heart and the merits of righteousness—to him, certainly, who knows better everything that is necessary for us and recognizes all that we are going to ask before we speak.

Finally, in that Pharisee and the tax collector we have an example of how far a talkative prayer differs from a humble and simple one. The prayer of the Pharisee, who boasted in his abundance of words, is rejected; but the humble and submissive tax collector, asking forgiveness for his sins, went down more justified than the boastful Pharisee (Luke 18:10).

In him we find fulfilled what is written: “A humble prayer pierced the clouds” (Ecclus. 35:21), reaching God, who is accustomed to hear the prayer of the one who prays, who is blessed forever. Amen.

# TREATISE XIV

[Note: In Galland: **TREATISE XIII on the Gospel of St. Matthew**.]

On chapter 6 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then he says: “Thus, therefore, you shall pray” (Matt. 6:9).

Our Lord, who is accustomed to hear those who pray to him, shows us with what words we ought to pray. O how faithful and blessed for us is this prayer, whose order the teacher of life and heavenly master established for us! How blessed we too can be if we preserve these words of the Lord’s Prayer not merely in the duty of the lips, but in the most faithful conduct of our lives!

Accordingly, the Lord established this form of prayer for his disciples as a hope of human salvation, saying: “Our Father who are in heaven” (ibid.).

How great is the Lord’s love toward us! How great is his mercy and piety, which has granted us the gift of such grace that we dare freely to call our Lord and God “Father,” although we are servants! By this title he shows that we are no longer merely servants but also children of God.

And although it would have been more than sufficient for grace if we had merely deserved to be called servants, the love of God overflowed to such an extent that we are called not only servants but also children of God by adoption.

John shows in the Gospel the grace of this name, granted through faith to those who believe in Christ, saying: “As many as believed in him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name; who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:12–13).

Hence the Apostle also says: “Because you are children of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6).

Since, therefore, we have received the grace of so great a gift, so that we have been made not only servants but also children, we ought to act and live as children of God, so that by spiritual conduct we may prove ourselves to be what we are called.

Accordingly, John says in his Epistle: “Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because God’s birth preserves him, and the devil does not touch him” (1 John 5:18). “But whoever commits sin is not of God, but is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning” (1 John 3:8).

And therefore, guarding the sacrament of our heavenly birth, we ought to be strangers to every sin, so that we may truly deserve to be called—or to be—the children of God.

The holy Prophets also know the grace of this divine mercy, through which we have been permitted to call God “Father,” as Isaiah says: “For you are our Father, because Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not know us; but you, Lord, are our Father; from the beginning your name is upon us” (Isa. 63:16).

Malachi likewise testifies in his book, saying: “For there is one Father of us all” (Mal. 2:10).

How great is the Lord’s mercy! Once, by our own will, we had adopted the devil as our father; now, reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, we have begun to have God as our Father.

God himself is the one Father for us, who regenerates by his Spirit those whom he makes children for an eternal inheritance. And therefore we ought to walk as children of God, lest, acting in a manner unworthy of God’s children, we be held guilty for usurping so great a name.

## II

He therefore says: “Our Father who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.”

This does not mean that God’s name can be sanctified by anyone, since he himself sanctifies all things, the one who says through the Prophet: “Be holy, just as I also am holy, says the Lord” (Lev. 11:44; 19:2).

Rather, we ask that his name be sanctified so that it may be sanctified in us through works of righteousness, through the merit of faith, and through the grace of the Holy Spirit. To receive this sanctification through such gifts, the help of his mercy is necessary.

Yet he who is the source of eternal holiness does not need any sanctification.

## III

Then he says: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10).

Here too we are not asking God to reign, since he is the King of the eternal ages, whose kingdom has neither beginning nor end. Rather, we ask that the kingdom—that is, the heavenly kingdom—which he promised us may come.

But it is a mark of great confidence and a sincere conscience to desire confidently that the Lord’s kingdom come. And therefore, since we always pray that the kingdom of God may come, we ought to present ourselves in the faith of the Lord and in his commandments in such a way that we may be worthy of the future kingdom.

## IV

Then he says: “Let your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” (ibid.).

Here too the principle of interpretation is the same. No one can resist or oppose God so as to prevent him from doing what he wills, since all things in heaven and on earth subsist by his will. Rather, we pray that his will may be done in us.

The will of God is that, believing in him with our whole heart, we fulfill the things that he commands to be done. Concerning this will of God the Apostle testifies, saying: “The will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from carnal desires” (1 Thess. 4:3).

The Lord also spoke of this will in the Gospel, saying: “This is the will of my Father who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life” (John 6:40).

Therefore, when we say, “Let your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” this is what we pray: that just as God’s will is faithfully kept by the angels in heaven, so also it may always be observed by us on earth with religious and faithful devotion.

For this will to be rightly fulfilled in us, we must ask without interruption for the help of divine favor.

[Note: We have restored this very corrupt passage—indeed, in Gallandi’s edition, as well as in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyon and in Grynaeus, it was virtually without meaning—to its proper form from the first Basel edition.]

Or certainly: “Let your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” so that just as in heaven—that is, among holy and heavenly people—God’s will is fulfilled, so also on earth—that is, among those who have not yet believed—we may pray that God’s will may be done through the assent of faith and knowledge of the truth.

## V

Then he says: “Give us today our daily bread” (Matt. 6:11).

We understand this saying of the Lord in two ways. First, so that we ask for nothing other than daily sustenance. For we are not commanded to ask for riches or an abundance of worldly goods, but for daily bread, which is all that Christians who live by faith need for the present life, as the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” (1 Tim. 6:8).

Solomon also clearly indicates the same thing: “The use of a human being,” he says, “is bread, water, and clothing” (Ecclus. 29:28).

But when we say “today,” we are taught to think only about the present day, not about the whole duration of life, lest our mind be occupied with worldly anxiety. The Lord himself openly demonstrates this elsewhere, saying: “Do not think about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself” (Matt. 6:34).

We must understand that this command has also been given to us spiritually, so that we ask for daily bread—that is, that heavenly and spiritual bread which we receive daily for the healing of the soul and the hope of eternal salvation. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “The heavenly bread is my flesh, which I will give for the life of this world” (John 6:52).

Therefore we are commanded to ask for this bread daily—that is, that, through the Lord’s mercy, we may deserve daily to receive the bread of the Lord’s body.

For the holy Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of the Lord’s bread and drink from the cup” (1 Cor. 11:28). And again: “Whoever eats the Lord’s bread unworthily and drinks the cup will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (ibid., 29).

Therefore we ought rightly to pray always that we may deserve to receive this heavenly bread daily, lest, through some intervening sin, we be separated from the Lord’s body.

## VI

“And forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

This is plainly a just and necessary utterance for everyone. First, so that we confess that we are sinners; then, so that we ask God to forgive our sins in the same way that we ourselves forgive those who sin against us.

If we do not do this, we make ourselves guilty before God by our own words, as Scripture says: “A strong snare for a man is his own lips” (Prov. 6:2, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore Solomon too, not ignorant through the Holy Spirit of the form of this prayer of the Lord, warned beforehand, saying: “You shall not lie in your prayer” (Ecclus. 7:15).

For who would dare—or how could anyone—lie to God in prayer? Unless perhaps it is the person who, asking God for forgiveness of sins according to the Lord’s Prayer, himself refuses to forgive those who sin against him, failing to retain the divine saying: “A person keeps anger against another person, and seeks healing from God? He has no mercy on a human being like himself, and asks God for his sins” (Ecclus. 28:3–4).

The Lord himself makes this most clearly known elsewhere, when he presents the example of that servant who owed a great debt, whose master, when entreated, had forgiven the entire debt. But when, after his debt had been forgiven, he himself was unwilling to forgive his fellow servant who owed him, he was handed over to prison and condemned to punishment (Matt. 18:23 ff.).

## VII

Then he says: “And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

There are two kinds and different causes of this temptation, because for some people temptation is brought through sin for correction, for others for the testing of faith, and for still others for glory, as blessed James testifies in his Epistle, saying: “Blessed is the one who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him” (Jas. 1:12).

For we do not pray that we should entirely refuse temptation, which we know to be useful, since holy David says: “Test me, Lord, and tempt me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. 25:2).

We also know that holy Abraham attained the glory of perfect faith through temptation, and we read that the blessed Apostle was handed over to temptations for the advancement of his faith. When he asked the Lord that the author of temptation might be driven away from him, he received the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Therefore we do not pray that we should not be tempted at all, but that we should not be handed over to temptation beyond what the strength of faith can bear. The same thing is clearly shown in another book of the Gospel, for it is written: “And do not bring us into temptation” (Luke 11:4)—that is, temptation which we cannot endure.

The Apostle also, to show the same thing, testifies as follows: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

And therefore we do not ask that the temptation which may be useful be taken away from us, but that temptation which exceeds the measure of our weakness and leads to the overthrow of our faith be removed.

For this reason, suitably and necessarily, at the end of the prayer we also ask to be delivered from evil (Matt. 6:13). The author of every sin does not cease to attack our faith daily, and we rightly pray every day that we may be delivered from him, lest, hindered by his assaults, we be altogether unable to fulfill the divine commandments.

[Note: From the margin of Grynaeus’s edition, if you approve, correct as follows: **“he does not cease to attack us daily, from whom we…”**]

Thus everything necessary for our faith and salvation is contained in the brief prayer of the Lord: when we confess the profession of the Father’s name; when we ask that the meaning of that name be present in us; when we ask that the kingdom of God come; when we entreat that his will be done in us; when we daily ask for earthly or heavenly bread for the hope of our salvation; when we implore forgiveness of sins; when we ask that grievous temptation be taken away from us; and finally, when we continually ask the Lord to deliver us from evil, which is the author of every sin.

The Holy Spirit had long before foretold through Isaiah that this would happen, saying: “For the Lord will make a brief word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:23).

Therefore it rightly follows: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14–15).

To our prayer, “Forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors,” there follows the Lord’s just judgment, in which he says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you.”

And therefore, so that we may confidently pray to the Lord for our sins to be forgiven, let us first forgive those who sin against us. Hence Solomon also says: “Forgive your neighbor’s sins, and your own sins will be forgiven you” (Ecclus. 28:5, according to the Septuagint).

But if, with faithless spirit and hardened mind, we retain the sins committed against us by those who offend us, the Lord plainly shows that we too do not deserve to receive forgiveness of sins.

To him be honor, praise, and glory, together with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now, and always, and throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# TREATISE XV

[Note: In Galland: **TREATISE XIV on the Gospel of St. Matthew**.]

On chapter 6 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then he says: “When you fast,” he says, “do not become like the hypocrites, who are gloomy; for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who is in secret, will reward you” (Matt. 6:16, 18).

As in the preceding commandments, so also concerning the observance of fasting the Lord instructs us by the commands of his teaching toward the merit of perfect faith, so that we may fast not for human glory, as the hypocrites do, but for future hope, for the Lord alone, from whom we expect the reward of this devoted humility.

Those who fast in such a way that they wish to please people more than God do indeed have the labor of bodily affliction, but they cannot have the reward of their labor before God through empty glory. For although they ought to do this solely for the sake of religion and faith, they prefer to seek the glory of human praise. And therefore the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

The purpose of fasting appears to be one and the same both for the person who fasts with a devoted mind for God alone and for the person who fasts while wishing to please people. But the grace of those who fast is different. Although the purpose of both may appear similar and the labor of fasting the same, the fruit and the recompense of merits are not the same.

There is a great difference between the person who fasts for God and the one who intends to fast for people. For the latter receives, as the reward of labor, a return of human praise; for the former, on account of the devotion of humility, the merit of glory is reserved in the future.

The same is true of the conduct of those who pray. In intention it may not seem different, but according to the faith of the mind and the disposition of the spirit there is a great difference in merits.

[Note: Here too, from the first Basel edition and from the second edition of Grynaeus, we have inserted the complete line and restored the text to its proper reading.]

For it is one thing, as was said above, to pray in expectation of human praise; it is another to pray solely in order to await from God, the giver of reward, the recompense of one’s prayer. The same principle applies to every observance of divine religion.

## II

Therefore, not without reason, the Lord, wishing every desire for praise and every human boastfulness to be absent from us, teaches us how to please him with a religious spirit and devoted mind, saying:

“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret.”

Thus, if it can be done, he wishes us to cover the work of fasting and the affliction of body and soul with a cheerful appearance.

We also read that examples of this were displayed beforehand in the saints of former times, even according to the historical account. For when the most holy Judith was afflicted with great sorrow on behalf of the people, after the solemnity of a three-day fast, with her head anointed and her face washed, she concealed the sadness of her inner affliction in such a way that she appeared to her enemies to rejoice with feigned gladness. Thus, while she concealed her fast through the joyfulness of her face, she carried away a victorious triumph over the enemy (Judith 12:6–10).

[Note: From the first Basel edition and likewise from the second edition of Grynaeus, we have restored this text to a more accurate reading.]

Similarly, when the most holy Esther, with her face washed and her head anointed after a three-day fast, was able to be recognized by the king, she brought about the death of Haman, that most wicked enemy of her people (Esther 4:16).

What shall we say of Daniel and the three youths, who, amid such great abstinence and among so many young men who were fed royal foods, alone were found more pleasing in appearance than the others (Dan. 1:12, 15)?

## III

But since we have spoken of this according to the literal sense, we must also consider what should be understood spiritually.

We know that mercy is signified by the anointing of the head. Therefore, to anoint the head means to show mercy to one’s neighbor. When this mercy is shown to a poor person, it is referred to the Lord, who is understood according to the Apostle as the head of the man, the Lord himself saying: “As long as you did it for one of these least, you did it for me” (1 Cor. 11:3; Matt. 25:40).

In return for this mercy, through divine recompense we are drenched, as it were, with a kind of heavenly oil by him who says: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. 5:7).

Holy David also knows this anointing of heavenly oil upon the head, when he says: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard” (Ps. 133:2).

In the washing of the face, the cleansing of the body and the purity of a sincere conscience are understood to be signified. Therefore, to wash the face means to present both the face of our heart and our conscience cleansed from every filth of sins and stain of wrongdoing, so that we may truly possess within us the joy of heavenly gladness and the cheerfulness of the Holy Spirit.

And so it comes about that, while under this devotion of faith we fast for God rather than for people, we receive from God, who knows what is hidden, the reward of recompense.

This is what the Lord says: “Do not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who is in secret, will reward you.”

Therefore, if you wish always to carry an anointed head and to have a clean face of heart, faithfully devote yourself, according to the Lord’s saying, to works of mercy; devote yourself to the devotion of fasting, so that you may deserve to please the Lord, to whom be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# TREATISE XVI

[Note: In Galland: **TREATISE XV on the Gospel of St. Matthew**.]

On chapter 6 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal. For where your treasure will be, there also will your heart be” (Matt. 6:19–21).

The Lord forbids us to store up treasures on earth, where everything is weak and perishable. For it is contrary to faith and salvation to seek these earthly treasures, to pursue the riches of the world, and to chase after worldly possessions, which moths can corrupt, rust consume, and thieves carry away.

For whoever wishes to store up treasures more on earth than in heaven cannot possess those treasures of eternal and heavenly life, as the Lord himself says: “For a rich person will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty” (Matt. 19:25).

The Apostle says similarly: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9).

Let us remember that rich man who placed all his glory in the treasures of the world and in the abundance of his revenues. When, because of the abundance of his crops, he was considering enlarging his barns and promising his soul the pleasures of wealth and the security of a long life, I will not say that he lost what he had gathered because of a thief’s theft; rather, on that very night he lost his own soul, for which he was storing up treasure (Luke 12:16–20).

Therefore David himself rightly testified, saying: “He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Ps. 39:7).

Let us also consider that young man who, although he had fulfilled nearly all the commandments of the Law, because he possessed earthly treasures more than heavenly ones, was unable to obtain the treasures of eternal life (Matt. 19:21).

And therefore David rightly says: “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder; if riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 62:10).

## II

Therefore the Lord wishes us to store our treasures not on earth, where they can perish, but in heaven, where no adversities hold sway, where thieves do not break in—that is, the devil and his angels—nor does rust destroy—that is, sins hold dominion.

The Lord himself reveals in the Gospel how we ought to place this treasure in heaven, when he says to that young man: “Go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

Accordingly, we are commanded to store up such treasures, which are eternal and incorruptible and cannot perish, in heaven through works of righteousness and through the merits of piety and mercy.

Whatever, according to the faith of Scripture, is faithfully distributed for the use of the poor is stored up in heaven, as Scripture says: “Whoever gives to the poor lends to God” (Prov. 19:17).

Hence we find that believers in apostolic times, mindful of this command of the Lord, stored up treasures for themselves in heaven, because, after selling all their possessions, they transferred their earthly treasures to the heavenly kingdoms (Acts 4:34).

## III

And therefore the Lord added, saying: “Where your treasure will be, there also will your heart be” (Matt. 6:21).

When we continually store up treasure in heaven through good works, where all our hope and salvation are, where eternal life is laid up for us, although we are placed on earth, we nevertheless always have our heart in heaven.

But the person whose desire for the world has seized him, and who has preferred to store up treasure for himself on earth, cannot have his heart in heaven.

The holy Apostle also rightly exhorts the rich of this world concerning how they may obtain this heavenly treasure, saying: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who supplies us abundantly with all things for enjoyment. Let them do good, let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share, storing up for themselves for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19)—from him who is the author of life and eternal immortality.

To him be praise and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# TREATISE XVII

[Note: In Galland: **TREATISE XVI on the Gospel of St. Matthew**.]

On chapter 6 of the Gospel of St. Matthew.

## I

Then he says: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matt. 6:22–24).

The lamp of the body is understood as the perception of the mind and the faith of the heart. If this is pure and bright in us, it undoubtedly illuminates our whole body.

The lamp is compared with faith because, just as a lamp illuminates the steps of those traveling at night so that they do not fall into pits or stumble against various obstacles, so in this night of the world the radiance of faith illuminates all the steps of our life, with the light of truth going before us, lest we fall either into the pits of sins or against the obstacles of the devil.

This, therefore, is what the Lord says: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness.” He shows that if this faith of ours, signified by the lamp or eye of the body, is blinded in us either by the darkness of sins or by the obscurity of faithlessness, without doubt our whole body is made dark and shadowed.

St. John demonstrates the same thing, saying: “God is light.” And: “Whoever loves his brother is in the light; but whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 1:5; 2:10–11).

And if this is understood, according to John’s saying, of the person who hates his brother, we must consider in what darkness the heretic remains, who, having lost the light of catholic truth, exists as faithless and blasphemous.

And therefore the Lord says: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” This applies to the person who has changed truth into falsehood and faith into faithlessness.

## II

In another sense, we understand the bodily eye—which is more beautiful and precious than all the other members—to signify the bishop, who, through the clear proclamation of his faith and teaching, illuminates the body of the Church like a certain eye. If, through simple faith and holy conduct, he proves to be a Catholic and faithful teacher, the people over whom he presides can always remain in the light of truth, following the example of his teaching and character. But if he who seems to provide light for the others proves to be a wicked and faithless teacher through perverse faith or disgraceful conduct, he can undoubtedly make the whole body dark through the example of his life and faithlessness. Hence the Lord not undeservedly says of such an eye: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be!” That is: if a teacher of this kind, who ought to provide the light of faith from himself to others, becomes blinded by heresy and turns dark, we must consider how great the darkness of sins may be among that people.

## III

And he added: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

The Lord plainly declares that none of us can serve two masters—that is, God and the devil. God, indeed, although he is Lord of all, since all things were created by him and he rules in all things by power, might, and nature, nevertheless deigns especially to be the Lord of those who recognize him as their Lord and God, the Creator of the universe, and faithfully preserve his commandments in service to him.

The devil, however, is understood to be the lord of those whom he leads astray through sin from the true Lord and Father, subjecting them to his most wicked service, and over whom he exercises unlawful dominion through the works of their iniquity. For this reason he too is called “lord” in his own sphere, because through sin he rules over foolish people of this sort. Accordingly, it is written: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).

But since, by God’s mercy, we have now been visited and freed from the devil’s dominion, and have recognized the true Lord by whom we were created and redeemed, we are forbidden to serve our former master—that is, the devil, who ruled over us in tyrannical fashion—or rather, avarice and greed, which he calls Mammon and which sometimes even habitually takes captive religious minds. Therefore we must flee and avoid the desire for money and worldly avarice, lest we subject ourselves to its unworthy slavery, or to the devil, who is the author of avarice.

## IV

And this is what the Lord says: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will tolerate the one and despise the other” (Matthew 6:24). For whoever loves the Lord and his God with all his heart must necessarily hate the devil together with his works, since, in the love of God, it is evident that the devil is always held in abhorrence.

But whoever loves Mammon or the devil through the wicked works of sins, by doing his will, cannot love God, whose commandments he despises. Therefore he who loves God cannot be called the devil’s slave, since God himself already rules over him through faith in heavenly grace.

[Note: [Col. 0367C] Here we have preferred the clearer reading of the Basel first edition and of Grynaeus.]

Likewise, whoever serves sins and subjects himself to the devil’s dominion does not deserve to have God as his Lord. Therefore the Lord says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon,” showing that we cannot serve both God and the devil—that is, God, the author of mercy, and the devil, the ruler of Mammon and avarice.

The Apostle also makes this clear when he says: “What fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Mammon—that is, the devil, who is the author of Mammon—leads us toward avarice, whereas God leads us toward mercy; the one toward life, the other toward death; the one toward salvation, the other toward destruction. Which of the two should we obey? Surely the one who invites us to life, not the one who hands us over to death . . . . The remainder is wanting.

# 95. Sayings of Saint Chromatius, While He Was Presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, at the Council Held at Aquileia in the Year 381 under Saint Valerian, Bishop of Aquileia, against the Arian Heretics Palladius and Secundianus

(From the Acts of the same Council of Aquileia, among the works of Saint Ambrose, Paris edition of the Benedictine Maurists, 1686–1690, volume II, column 798, §45, and column 800, §51.) (C, S)

[Col. 0367D] Palladius said: “Do you now want a complete examination to be held, or not?”

Chromatius the presbyter said: “You did not deny that he is a creature; you denied that he is powerful. You denied everything that the Catholic faith professes.”

[Col. 0368D] Palladius said: “Let the hearers come forward.”

Chromatius the presbyter said: “Subject to priestly condemnation; indeed, let the supporters of Palladius also now be read out in full.”

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Roman edition: “let them also now be heard.” The other manuscripts and Tell. read as in the text.]

# 97. Appendix: Lost Writings of Saint Chromatius

Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, undoubtedly wrote treatises or commentaries on the Gospel of Saint Matthew, beginning with the very opening of that sacred text and extending at least to chapter 6, verse 24, where the last surviving treatise on that Gospel ends. Since our holy bishop wrote these treatises or commentaries for private reading and the devout exercise of the faithful, as we inferred in the Preface from the very words of the holy Prelate found in Treatise 5, section 2, we may rightly conclude that he began his treatises or commentaries at the beginning of that Gospel and carried them through in their entirety, without any gap, at least as far as the last treatise that we possess, which in our edition is Treatise 17. We may even reasonably conjecture that he continued the work farther, perhaps all the way to the final verse of the entire Gospel history of Matthew, as we explain more fully in the Preface.

The first works rightly considered lost, therefore, are those that Saint Chromatius wrote from the beginning of the Gospel of Saint Matthew up to verse 15 of chapter 3, where the treatise that is first in our edition begins, although Gallandius, reversing the order entirely, numbers it 17.

The second lost works are those that Saint Chromatius wrote from verse 17 of chapter 3 of the same Gospel up to the beginning of chapter 5, where the treatise begins that is numbered 3 in our edition and incorrectly designated 2 by Gallandius.

These, at the very least, are the portions that are rightly and properly missing from Saint Chromatius’s work on the Gospel of Saint Matthew.

Third, several letters are lost, which we know that the holy Prelate sent to Saint Ambrose, to Saint Jerome, to Saint John Chrysostom, and also to the emperors Honorius and Arcadius, as is clear from the studies of the distinguished men Fontanini and de Rubeis, which we append.

# 99. Writings Falsely Attributed to Saint Chromatius

## Notice Concerning the Following Letters

From the *Holy Library* of Sixtus of Siena, book II, page 138 of volume I of the Neapolitan edition of Fr. Pius-Thomas Milante, 1742.

Matthew the Evangelist is falsely presented as the author of two books, one entitled *On the Origin, or Lineage, of Mary*, and the other *On the Infancy of the Savior*. These are fabrications of the Valentinians and Gnostics. Certain foolish men, wishing to establish the authority of these books, added prefaces under the names of Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, addressed to Jerome, and a fictitious reply from Jerome to them. These prefaces were intended to testify that both works had been translated from a Hebrew volume of Matthew by Jerome for the benefit of those bishops and purged of the falsifications of heretics.

But since the same childish tales now appear in these books as those which Irenaeus refutes in the first book of his work against the Valentinian heresies, and Epiphanius refutes in the first book of the *Panarion*, section 3, from those same volumes, the deception of the impostors is plainly evident. Gelasius, in distinction 15, rejects both books among those condemned by the Church.

## Letter I

Under the names of Saints Chromatius and Heliodorus, addressed to Saint Jerome, concerning two apocryphal books—namely, *On the Origin of Mary, the Queen and Virgin*, and *On the Infancy of the Savior*—with a twofold reply by Pseudo-Jerome appended.

(From John Albert Fabricius’s *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, volume I, page 7 and following, second edition, Hamburg, 1719; and from volume XI of the works of Saint Jerome, the Verona edition of Domenico Vallarsi, column 279 and following.)

To our most beloved brother Jerome the presbyter, Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0369D] We found the origin of Mary, the virgin queen, and likewise the birth and infancy of our Lord Jesus Christ, in apocryphal books. Since we find in them many writings contrary to our faith, we believe that all of them must be rejected, lest, under the pretext of Christ, we hand joy over to Antichrist.

As we were considering these matters, there appeared men of God, Armenius and Virinus, who said that Your Holiness had found a Hebrew volume written by the hand of the most blessed Matthew the Evangelist, in which the infancy both of the Virgin Mother and of the Savior had been written. For this reason we earnestly request your charity, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, that you translate it from Hebrew for Latin ears—not merely so that the glorious deeds of Christ may be understood, but also so that the cunning of the heretics may be excluded. For, in order to establish an evil teaching, they mingled Christ’s good birth with their own falsehood, so that after the sweetness of life they might conceal the bitterness of death.

It will therefore be an act of the purest piety, whether you heed us as brothers who are making a request, or receive what you judge appropriate from bishops who demand the debt of charity. Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us.

## Letter II. Jerome to the Bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus

To the holy and most blessed lords, the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, Jerome, the least of Christ’s servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

He who digs up earth rich in gold does not immediately seize whatever the torn-up ground has poured forth. Before he lifts the gleaming weight with the blow of his flashing iron, he pauses meanwhile to turn over and suspend the clods—and especially when he has not yet increased his profits.

A difficult task is imposed upon me, since Your Blessedness has commanded me to do what even Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist did not wish to have written openly. For if this matter had not been secret, he would certainly have added it to the Gospel that he published. Instead, he sealed this little book in Hebrew letters, and he published it to such an extent that a book written in his own hand and in Hebrew letters is possessed by deeply religious men, who also received it from their predecessors through the succession of the ages.
