Yet they have never handed this very book over to anyone for translation; they have related its contents in different ways.

But it happened that, when this book was published by a disciple of Mani named Seleucus—who also falsely composed an account of the acts of the Apostles—it provided material not for edification but for destruction. It was found to be such in a synod to which the ears of the Church rightly should not be open.

Let the bites of the barking critics now cease. We have not added this little book to the canonical Scriptures; rather, to expose the deception of heresy, we are translating the writings of an Apostle and Evangelist. In this work we obey not so much pious bishops who command us as we oppose impious heretics.

It is therefore Christ’s love that we are satisfying, believing that those who, through our obedience, have been able to reach the holy infancy of our Savior will assist us with their prayers.

## Letter III. The Same Pseudo-Jerome to the Same Addressees

In another letter prefixed to the translation of the book *On the Nativity of Mary*.

You ask me to write back to you and tell you what I think about a certain little book that some people regard as being about the birth of Saint Mary. I therefore want you to know that many falsehoods are found in it.

A certain Seleucus, who composed the passions of the Apostles, produced this little book. But just as he spoke truthfully about their virtues and the miracles performed through them, while lying about much of their teaching, so here too he fabricated many untrue things from his own heart.

Accordingly, I shall strive to translate it word for word, as it is found in the Hebrew. It is certainly clear that the holy Evangelist Matthew composed this same little book and placed it, sealed in Hebrew letters, at the beginning of his Gospel. Whether this is true I leave to the author of the preface and to the writer’s credibility. For, just as I declare these matters doubtful, I do not positively assert that they are false.

I do freely state this, however, which I think no believer will deny: whether these things are true or were fabricated by someone, the most sacred birth of Saint Mary was preceded by great miracles and followed by still greater ones. Therefore, without injury to the faith, they may be believed and read by those who believe that God is able to do such things, without danger to their souls.

Finally, insofar as I can remember, following the writer’s meaning rather than his words, sometimes proceeding along the same path without following the same footprints, and sometimes returning to that path by certain byways, I shall attempt the style of the narrative [Note: [Col. 0372C] More probably, “I shall shape or regulate it.” Same source.]. I shall say nothing other than what was either written there or could consistently have been written.

## Notice Concerning the Following Letters

From Cardinal Baronius’s discussion *On the Roman Martyrology*, chapter 7.

As for the letter written under the name of the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus to Jerome, you can easily detect the imposture from its very address, if you take account of the manner of speech of those times. In it the aforesaid bishops—or rather, the synod itself, for they profess to write in the name of the synod they invoke—call Jerome the presbyter “Father.” Yet among the writers of those times you will find absolutely no example of this designation: in the writing of a bishop, or of a synod itself, a presbyter of whatever merit is not called “Father,” whereas they customarily called even the bishops of the most distinguished sees and patriarchs only “brothers.”

The same letter mentions a council of all the bishops of Italy convened at Milan in the presence of the emperor Theodosius. You should have no doubt that this is a fabrication. For how could so celebrated a synod have disappeared so completely from the records of writers and been buried in such silence that no writer of those times—whose number was certainly not small—mentions it even by name?

These matters will become still clearer if an exact account is taken of the chronology of Jerome’s works. When, I ask, do they want that synod to have been convened at Milan before Theodosius? Was it when he first came from Constantinople to Italy in the tenth year of his reign, intending to fight the tyrant Maximus? Certainly this cannot be said, since Jerome’s own writings strongly contradict it. In his book *On Illustrious Men*, at the end, when he lists all the works he had composed up to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, he does not say a word about a book on the Martyrs that he had written or translated, although the letters quoted there indicate that it was written immediately after that synod. It is therefore sufficiently clear that the alleged synod cannot be referred to Theodosius’s first arrival at Milan.

If they say that the same synod was held at Milan on his second arrival—when he came down from the East to Italy to defeat the tyrant Eugenius, since it is certain that he came to Italy only twice after obtaining the imperial power—the chronology certainly contradicts them.

Theodosius came into Italy with an army in the sixteenth year of his reign, which was also the last year of his rule. He fought Eugenius and defeated him on the sixth day of September, then proceeded to Milan. What he did there from that time until 17 January, when he departed this life, is described exactly by Ambrose in the speech he delivered at his funeral, as well as by other writers of those times. It is therefore clear that no time remained for convening such a council.

From these facts the entire fabrication concerning letters issued from the aforesaid synod, and the other matters contained in the same letters, is exposed in the clearest light. The same is true of the statement in them that Bishop Gregory of Córdoba celebrated morning and evening Masses. For Augustine, who lived at the same time, seems to testify that this was customary in the Catholic Church only on the Thursday of Holy Week, on the Lord’s Supper, when he writes to Januarius in Letter 118, chapter 5.

We know, of course, that in the time of Cyprian a morning and evening sacrifice was offered in Africa, as Cyprian himself testifies in his letter to Caecilius, Letter 63 in Pamelius’s edition. Sozomen states that this custom continued only among the Egyptians, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 7, chapter 19.

We also know that, according to the more recent reading, the Council of Agde mentions morning and evening Masses, and that from it this is cited in chapter 13 of distinction 15. We do not object to these matters, since we know that the customs of ecclesiastical rites differed among different peoples.

An imposture is also detected in the matter concerning Gregory, when he is said to have celebrated the festivals of Martyrs even during a time of fasting. The ancient canons testify that the custom of the Church was different, as in the Council of Laodicea, canon 51, in Martène’s collection, canon 48, and in 33.1, “It is not permitted during Lent.”

Moreover, both in the aforesaid letter of the bishops and in the letter said to have been returned to them in Jerome’s name, Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea is commended with the title of sanctity. This is monstrous. For although formerly the title “holy” may have been more broadly used—not merely, as today, for Christians who have died and reign with Christ in heaven, but also for any believers of especially praiseworthy life—no one can rightly say that it was ever given to a heretical man.

But let us hear Jerome himself with what titles he customarily named Eusebius. Writing to Pammachius in Letter 65, he says of him: “He is the most outspoken champion of Arius’s impiety,” and much else in the same vein appears at the end. In *Apology against Rufinus*, book 1, he says of the same man: “Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, once standard-bearer of the Arian faction.” In book 2 he calls him “the leader of the Arians.” Likewise, in his letter to Ctesiphon, speaking of Eusebius’s writings, he says: “No one is unaware that he was an Arian.” And in Letter 152 to Minerius, he explicitly testifies that Eusebius had erred in the truth of doctrine.

These, then, are the titles by which Jerome calls Eusebius, and they are very different from the praise of sanctity found here. From this alone you can clearly recognize that the author of that letter was someone entirely different from Jerome. Even if there were no other evidence, anyone reading the letter can easily recognize from its style of expression that its author was far removed from Jerome.

So much for the wording. If you investigate the matters recorded in it, you will understand the imposture even more clearly. If the things that the same author recounts as having taken place between the emperor Constantine and Eusebius are true, how could Eusebius have shown such modesty—he who always appeared to be an outstanding herald of his own praises—that he passed them over in silence, when he had frequent opportunities to repeat them whenever he discussed the book on the Martyrs that he himself had written?

He was accustomed to recount and exalt the things he had done with Constantine, and to repeat them frequently, as in *The Life of Constantine*, book 2, chapters 44 and 45; book 3, chapters 57, 58, 59, and 60; and book 4, chapters 33, 34, and 35.

Finally, the author objects in the same letter to the Kalends of January, as though no martyr had suffered on that day. Consult what is noted below under 1 January B to see how false and frivolous this objection concerning the Kalends is.

We believe that these points are already sufficient, even though others could also be added, to refute the falsity of the aforesaid letters.

## Letter IV

Likewise under the names of Saints Chromatius and Heliodorus, addressed to the same Saint Jerome, concerning the commemorations of the saints, or the compilation of a Martyrology; with a reply by Pseudo-Jerome likewise appended.

(From Cardinal Baronius’s discussion *On the Roman Martyrology*, and from volume XI of the works of Saint Jerome, the Verona edition of Domenico Vallarsi, column 473 and following.)

## Letter V. Chromatius and Heliodorus, Bishops, to the Blessed Jerome

Concerning the compilation of a Martyrology.

To the holy lord Father Jerome, Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0373B] When the most devout emperor Theodosius had entered the city of Milan and invited all the bishops of Italy to him, and was conducting an inquiry because of certain bishops who had stained their souls with the dregs of Arianism, it happened that our small selves were also present at that same council.

When everything that had to be said had been said and everything that had to be decided had been decided, the most Christian Prince began to praise Saint Gregory, bishop of the Church of Córdoba, because every day, when he was not fasting, he celebrated morning Masses, and when he was fasting, evening Masses, commemorating the names of very many of those martyrs whose commemorations were being celebrated.

It consequently happened that we all resolved to write to your charity, asking you to search out from the archives of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, the most renowned ferial records and send us the feasts of the martyrs, so that through your holy diligence we might render this service to the martyrs more fully and perfectly, to the honor of God.

# 106. Letter VI. The Blessed Jerome to the Same Addressees

A reply concerning that same matter.

[Col. 0374B] To Chromatius and Heliodorus, holy bishops: Jerome the presbyter.

It is established that our Lord Jesus Christ receives every day the triumphs of his martyrs, whose sufferings we find recorded by Saint Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea. For when the emperor Constantine had entered Caesarea and told the aforesaid bishop to request any benefits that would advance the interests of the Church of Caesarea, Eusebius is said to have replied that the Church, enriched by its own resources, was compelled by no need to request benefits.

Nevertheless, he said that he had an unshakable desire that whatever had been done throughout the Roman state against the holy judges of God should be carefully investigated by those who succeeded those judges throughout the Roman world, by examining the public records; and that from the archives themselves they should send to Eusebius, at the emperor’s command, information about which martyrs, under which judge, in which province or city, on what day, and through what perseverance in their passion had won the palm.

Thus it came about that, being a competent narrator, he both rewove ecclesiastical history and, as a diligent historian, displayed the triumphs of nearly all the martyrs of all the Roman provinces. In this way, while offering sacrifice to God every day, people might commemorate their names, honoring those who on the very day on which the sacrifice was offered had proved victorious over the devil and, enriched and exulting in the triumph of their martyrdom, had reached Christ their King.

For this reason we have written down the feasts of the individual months and of the individual days, as you commanded, believing that the memory of our lowliness would endure when the holy names of the saints had been celebrated festively every day through so many years.

And since on each day the names of more than eight hundred or nine hundred martyrs from different provinces and different cities have been recorded—so that there is no day on which a number within five hundred cannot be found listed, with the exception of the day of the Kalends of January—I considered that the reader’s mind might grow weary amid innumerable crowds within a single month. To prevent this from happening, I have briefly and concisely mentioned above all the others those who are commemorated in the places of their greatest festival, so that, with weariness removed, a single written booklet might suffice for all.

In the first part of the booklet we have recorded the feasts of all the blessed Apostles, so that differing days might not seem to divide those whom the single dignity of the apostolate made exalted in heavenly glory.

# From the Literary History of Aquileia by Justus Fontanini, Archbishop of Ancyra

Published at Rome in 1742.

# 109. Book III, Chapter III

1. Chromatius, a native of Aquileia.  
2. He succeeded Valerian.  
3. Praised by great men.  
4. At his request Jerome translated various books of the Bible into Latin.  
5. He endeavored to reconcile Rufinus and Jerome.  
6. He supported the cause of John Chrysostom.  
7. John Chrysostom’s letter to Chromatius.  
8. Blondel’s fabrications.  
9. Chromatius died and was entered in the calendars of the saints.

## I

We have now reached those who entered the fifth century, the age of achieved salvation. Their company is led by Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, whom Dandulus, in *Chronicle* book 1, chapter 14, made Spanish by nationality; Marianus Victorius, in the preface to Jerome’s Letter 43, a Dalmatian; and Sixtus of Siena, in *Library* book 4, a Roman.

Yet I would contend, even with a wager, that they are all mistaken and that he was a citizen of Aquileia. For he lived continually at Aquileia, where Saint Jerome—his close associate and an expert on Aquileian affairs—reports that he had a mother, sisters, and brothers. Jerome wrote Letter 7, otherwise 43, to Chromatius while he was still a presbyter, and likewise to Jovinus and Eusebius, Chromatius’s brother. In that letter he says that he is sending a single letter to all three because they love one another so deeply that their affection joins three no less than nature joined two.

Those two are Chromatius and Eusebius, whom nature again calls brothers in Letter 8, otherwise 42, written to Nicetas, a subdeacon of Aquileia: “Behold,” he says, “the blessed Chromatius has challenged me to a literary duty together with holy Eusebius, his brother not more by nature than by equality of character.”

Chromatius was therefore not the brother of Jovinus, as Baronius wrote under 22 June, but the brother of Eusebius; yet our Henry Palladius, book 9, page 158, joined one Jovinus to him.

Chromatius had another brother, still unnamed, whose courage Jerome greatly praises at his death in Letter 35, otherwise 3, to Heliodorus [Note: [Col. 0375D] This other brother of Chromatius, still unnamed, was introduced solely by the distinguished Fontanini. Bernard Maria de Rubeis does not agree with him; he recognized only Eusebius as Chromatius’s brother. See his *Dissertation on Rufinus*, chapter 2, pages 13–14.].

Since this letter was written in A.D. 396, as will later be established, Tillemont, volume 11, page 536, Martianay in his notes, and Adrian Baillet in the *Lives of the Saints* under 2 December must therefore be mistaken when they say that the brother of Chromatius about whose death Jerome speaks was Eusebius. Eusebius, however, was still alive four years later, distinguished by episcopal rank, just as were Jovinus and Chromatius, as Rufinus testifies in his first *Apology*, written in A.D. 400 [Note: [Col. 0375D] In this first *Apology*, which Fontanini cites here and which belongs to the year 400 or 401, as de Rubeis also agrees, Rufinus mentions Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius. Nearly thirty years earlier, as he himself says, while Valerian was bishop of Aquileia, one had been a presbyter, another an archdeacon, and another a deacon; later they too were advanced to the episcopal dignity. For this reason he honorifically calls them highly esteemed and most approved bishops in the Church of God. From this designation it by no means follows, as Fontanini believes, that in the year 400 or 401, when Rufinus wrote of them in this way, each of them—and therefore Eusebius also—was still alive. He could have written this even if they had all already died by that time. Nothing therefore follows from it against Tillemont, Martianay, and Baillet, who quite rightly assert that the brother of Chromatius whose death Jerome discusses in the letter belonging to the year 396 was Eusebius. See the article on Rufinus’s *Apology*, to which Fontanini refers, among the ancient testimonies that we have supplied after the Preface.]

On the basis of this opinion—namely, that Eusebius’s life extended at least to the year 400—Fontanini was compelled to devise and, as it were, create in writing a third, completely unknown brother of Chromatius, and for that reason to call him still unnamed. He claimed that it was this man, rather than Eusebius, whose death Jerome discussed in 396. But, as de Rubeis explains more fully in the place cited above, this was entirely gratuitous on the part of Fontanini, otherwise a most learned man and one who deserved great credit concerning the subject of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia.]

The same Letter 43 also teaches us that Chromatius had a widowed mother and virgin sisters. In it Jerome asks that they be greeted, commending the care of his sister to them in these words:

“We greet our common mother, who shares holiness with you and has surpassed you in this respect: she gave birth to such children that her womb may truly be called golden. We greet her with the honor you know. We also greet all the sisters, who have overcome their sex together with the world; they have abundantly prepared oil for their lamps and await the Bridegroom’s arrival.

“O blessed household, in which Anna the widow dwells, prophetic virgins, and the twin Samuel nourished in the temple!”

These twin Samuels are Chromatius and Eusebius.

So that no room for doubt about their homeland should remain, Jerome calls Aquileia their city and native place: “Through you the poison of the once-Arian doctrine has been expelled from your city.”

These facts explain why Jerome, in the Eusebian *Chronicle* as expanded by him, under Olympiad 280, A.D. 376, corresponding to the ordinary year 374, adorned the pupils of our Church with this notable and memorable praise: “The clergy of Aquileia are regarded as a choir of the blessed.”

Chromatius, who, as was stated above in the discussion of Fortunatianus—and will be stated again—was still a deacon in A.D. 371 [Note: [Col. 0378D] Here too de Rubeis contradicts Fontanini. De Rubeis asserts that Saint Chromatius was already a presbyter when Rufinus received baptism at Aquileia in 371 or 372; he also maintains that Rufinus received baptism from Saint Chromatius. See the same *Dissertation*, in the same place, pages 11–12.], instructed Rufinus, then newly reborn through the grace of baptism, in Catholic doctrine.

Later, as the presbyter of Bishop Valerian, he vigorously pleaded the cause of the Son of God against Palladius the Arian at the council held there in A.D. 381, and showed that Palladius had denied everything that the Catholic faith professes. When Palladius appealed to lay hearers, Chromatius briefly checked the man’s boldness: “Subject,” he said, “to priestly condemnation.”

See the acts of the council in Ambrose, volume II, page 798, §45, and page 800, §51.

These facts refute the Magdeburg fabricators, who wrote that Chromatius flourished in A.D. 335 and conflated Valerian of Aquileia with the bishop of Calagurris of the same name, whom Prudentius praises, *Century* IV, chapter 10.

As for the name Chromatius, it occurs among both Latins and Greeks. Libanius wrote a letter to a certain Chromatius, not yet published, which I once translated into Latin. Chromatius, prefect of the city, is mentioned in the Acts of Saint Sebastian under 20 January in Bollandus, volume II, page 271. Among the fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine who declared Pelagius Catholic at the Council of Diospolis in A.D. 415, there was a Chromatius of uncertain see, in Baluzius, page 361.

## II

We must now inquire in which year of Christ our Chromatius began to occupy the Aquileian see, left vacant by Valerian. For from this point the errors of recent historians will be corrected: John Candidus, book 2, folio 9; Panvinio, *Chronicle*, page 35; Wolfgang Lazius, *Commentaries*, book 12, section 5, chapter 8, page 1014; Leander Alberti, *Description of Italy*, folio 439, second edition, part I, year 1550; Henry Palladius, book 8, page 129; Philip Ferrari, *Catalogue of the Saints*, page 733; and Godefridus Hermannus, *Life of Ambrose*, book 5, chapter 12.

For, while all these writers attempt to establish Chromatius’s successor, they fall into enormous errors: one inventing two Fortunatianuses and just as many Valerians; another assigning the place between Valerian and Chromatius to Benedict; another to Januarius.

Now, as I have already said, the anonymous writer of Treviso and Dandulus, in chapter 13 of book 1, testify from ancient records that Valerian succeeded Fortunatianus in the Aquileian see in A.D. 366 and held it for nineteen years. He therefore died toward the end of A.D. 386, and Chromatius succeeded him at the beginning of A.D. 387.

The ancient codices of the Martyrologies that give 26 November as the day of Valerian’s death are the following.

1. Atrebatensis, in volume II of the Bollandist *March*, p. 39.  
2.  
3. Aquisgranensis and Augiensis.  
4. Baluzianus, in Dacherianus’s *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII, p. 13, § 6.  
5. Barberinus, in volume II of the Bollandist *March*, p. 39.  
6. Blumanius, ibid.  
7. Sancti Cyriaci, in volume III of the Bollandist *February*, p. 282, col. 2.  
8. Gellonensis, in *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII, p. 418.  
9. Hieronymianus, ibid., vol. IV, p. 684, and volume III of the Bollandist *February*, p. 282, col. 2, where *Valentinus* is read instead of *Valerianus*.  
10. Laetiensis, in volume II of the Bollandist *March*, p. 39.  
11. Lucensis, in Florentinius, p. 999.  
12. Sancti Maximini, in volume III of the Bollandist *February*, p. 282, col. 2.  
13. Rabanus Maurus, in Canisius, vol. VI, p. 594, where, as elsewhere, through a scribal error *Valentinus* is read instead of *Valerianus*.  
14. Sangermanensis, in *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII, p. 13, § 6.  
15. Sanremigianus, ibid.  
16. Tornacensis, in volume II of the Bollandist *March*, p. 59.  
17. Vaticanus, ibid.  
18. Rosweyde’s *Usuardus*, in Sollerius, p. 702.

Such agreement among so many ancient records reveals the error of Usuard’s Brussels codex, in Sollerius, p. 711, where the following is read for the day before the Kalends of December: “At Aquileia, the deposition of Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor.” Whether he could have been buried 112 days after his death is for others to investigate. The day of his deposition is perhaps more correctly given by Baronius as the fifth day before the Kalends of December, on the basis of the Martyrology of Saint Cyriacus.

The same Baronius, under A.D. 388, § 84, having read that Ambrose was established at Aquileia after Maximus had been overthrown by Theodosius, thought that Ambrose had gone there, as was customary, for the creation of a new bishop, since, after Saint Valerian, bishop of that city, had died, Saint Chromatius had been substituted in his place. Thus Baronius.

The words of the deacon Paulinus, who recounts that journey in chapter 22 of his *Life of Ambrose*, are these:

“After Maximus had been extinguished and the emperor Theodosius had been installed at Milan, while Bishop Ambrose was at Aquileia, in a certain fortress in the East, the synagogue of the Jews and the grove of the Valentinians were burned by Christian men, because the Jews or Valentinians were insulting the Christian monks.”

But Candidus, book II, fol. 9, 2, and Palladius, book IX, p. 156, in order to provide a pretext for Ambrose’s journey, have invented that this sort of burning took place at Aquileia, although Paulinus expressly stated that it occurred “in the East,” namely at the fortress of Callinicum. This fortress stood not in Venetia but in Mesopotamia, on the bank of the Euphrates, as is shown by Ammianus, book XXIII, chapter 3, and by Procopius, *Persian War*, book I, chapter 18, book II, chapters 11 and 21, and *Secret History*, chapter 3 at the end.

Our own historians could also have learned this from Ambrose’s letter 40, written at Aquileia, in which the holy man remonstrates with Theodosius because he had ordered by edict that the synagogue should be restored by the bishop of Callinicum and that the monks should be punished.

Idacius, in the *Labbean Fasti*, volume II of the *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, testifies that the tyrant Maximus was defeated at the third milestone from Aquileia on the fifth day before the Kalends of August in A.D. 388. He should be believed rather than Socrates, a foreign writer, who in book V, chapter 14, assigns that defeat to the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

After the enemy had been routed—Maximus, whom, as Jerome says in the *Epitaph for Nepotianus*, disgraceful servitude pierced before the enemy’s sword did—Theodosius remained for some time at Aquileia in order to revoke Maximus’s acts. For Law 6, title 14, book XV of the *Theodosian Code*, issued there on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, concerns the annulment of honors conferred by Maximus.

Sixteen days later, on the sixth day before the Ides of October of the same year, 388, he enacted a similar measure at Milan. He was still residing in that city on the third day before the Nones of May and the sixth day before the Kalends of December of the following year, 389, when he published laws 17 and 19 concerning heretics, title 15, book VI.

Thus we find Theodosius staying at Aquileia on September 26 and at Milan on October 10, A.D. 388. In the interval between these dates, after Maximus had been extinguished and Theodosius had been installed as emperor at Milan, Ambrose, as Paulinus says, hastened to Aquileia. Otherwise, while in one or the other city, he would have remonstrated with the emperor face to face, not by letter, concerning the rescript issued at Milan against the Christians.

See the authors of the *Admonition concerning the order of Saint Ambrose’s Letters*, § 40, and Pagius under A.D. 388, § 12. But since, as we have seen, Valerian died on November 26, it follows that Ambrose went to Aquileia before, not after, Valerian’s death, and therefore for a reason other than the substitution of Chromatius for Valerian, since Valerian had not yet departed this life.

But how much more must this eminent man be judged to have been mistaken about the reason for Ambrose’s journey if Valerian had died two years earlier, as the monuments of Venetia report? The authors of the new edition of Saint Ambrose’s works therefore rightly said in his *Life*, chapter 98, that the reason for such a journey was unknown and that no evidence could be produced in support of Baronius’s opinion.

If Ambrose traveled to Pannonia to ordain Anemius bishop of Sirmium, as Paulinus testifies in chapter 11, I do not see why that same careful recorder of Ambrose’s deeds would have concealed the reason for his journey to Aquileia if it had concerned the ordination of Chromatius.

[Note: Baronius’s conjecture, which the distinguished Fontanini does not approve here, is defended by Bernardus Maria De Rubeis, no. 5 of chapter 18 of the *Dissertationes Variae Eruditionis*, etc.; we give his discussion below.]

### III

Chromatius was the most renowned among the Western bishops for holiness and learning, as the praises bestowed upon him by distinguished men openly attest. For he enjoyed the friendship of great figures: John Chrysostom, Jerome, Ambrose, Heliodorus, and Rufinus.

In A.D. 389, Ambrose was asked by Chromatius to share with him, in an exchange of familiar letters, something he had discussed from the sacred books. He therefore interpreted the history of Balaam the false prophet from the Book of Numbers in Letter 50, promising to add other discussions, which the injustice of the times has taken from us. See the *Admonition concerning the order of Ambrose’s Letters*, § 5, and the *Life*, chapter 108.

Later we learn that Chromatius, having lost a brother whose name is unknown, gave a great example of Christian courage and of meeting adversity with an unconquered spirit. For Jerome concluded the *Epitaph for Nepotianus*, which is Letter 35, elsewhere numbered 3, written from Syria to Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum, with these words:

“Let us be joined in spirit, bound together in affection, and let us imitate in the son the strength of mind that blessed Pope Chromatius displayed at the death of Germanus.”

Peter Francis Chiffletius shows from what follows that this letter was written in A.D. 396, in the second part, chapter 10, of his *Paulino Illustrato*:

“Behold: last year wolves were sent against us from the remotest crags of the Caucasus—no longer wolves of Arabia but of the North—and within a short time they traversed vast provinces.”

This was the incursion of Alaric, king of the Goths, into the Eastern Empire, through the treachery of the patrician Rufinus, when Olybrius and Probinus were consuls in A.D. 395.

The words of Jerome that precede those just quoted confirm the date even more strongly:

“For twenty years and more Roman blood has been shed daily between Constantinople and the Julian Alps.”

He is referring to the first incursions of the Quadi and Marcomanni into our Venetia, after they had broken through the Julian Alps. At that time Aquileia was besieged and Opitergium destroyed, as Ammianus testifies in book XXIX, chapter 5. Henry Valesius observes that these events occurred during the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the third time and Equitius, A.D. 374. With the same destruction threatening Italy, the elder Valentinian had arranged for the bridge over the Liquentia in the territory of Opitergium to be repaired in A.D. 370, by Law 2, title 10, book XI of the *Theodosian Code*.

### IV

When the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus requested that the Chaldean Book of Tobit be rendered into Latin, Jerome complied through a day’s labor, with a man skilled in that language dictating the book to him in Hebrew, as his Letter 110, written in A.D. 390, informs us:

“I cannot cease to marvel at the urgency of your demand. For you require me to bring a book written in the Chaldean language into Latin style.”

And shortly afterward:

“I have satisfied your desire, though not my own inclination. For the studies of the Hebrews accuse us and charge us with transferring these things into Latin ears contrary to their canon. Yet, judging it better to displease the Pharisees’ judgment and to serve the commands of bishops, I persisted as best I could.”

Finally he concludes the letter with these words:

“I shall repay your prayers with the reward of this work when I learn that it is pleasing to you that I have fulfilled what you deigned to command.”

In addition, at the urging of both bishops, who generously supplied money for distribution to the copyists so that he might illuminate certain prophets with commentaries, Jerome, pleading ill health, sent them his Latin explanations of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, completed in three days:

“Let the letter,” he says in the preface, “join those whom the priesthood joins; indeed, let the page not divide those whom Christ’s love binds together. I would have written the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi that you request, if my health had permitted it. You send assistance for expenses; you support our shorthand writers and copyists so that our talent may labor especially for you. And behold, from the side comes a large crowd of people asking for different things—as though it were fair for me, while you are hungry, to work for others, or as though, in the reckoning of what has been given and received, I were indebted to anyone besides you. Therefore, broken by a long illness, so that I might not remain entirely silent this year and be mute before you, I consecrated a work of three days to your name—namely, the interpretation of the three books of Solomon.”

Hardly had he completed these works when, in A.D. 392, he presented Chromatius with his commentary on Habakkuk, divided into two books. In the prologue to book I he calls Chromatius “the most learned of bishops.” In the prologue to book II he commends him with praise as a venerable pope and declares that he surpassed the flesh by virtue.

Later, when asked to translate the remaining books of Scripture from the Hebrew language, he sent Chronicles to Chromatius in A.D. 397. In the preface to that book, extolling him with magnificent praise, he calls him “the most holy and most learned of bishops.”

Sixtus of Siena, having quoted this praise in book IV of his *Bibliotheca*, adds the following words of his own: “something rarely found.” Yet this perhaps belonged to the age of Sixtus, not to that of Chromatius.

In book II of his *Apology*, which we shall show was written in A.D. 400, Jerome recalls the translations of the sacred volumes he had made as follows:

“In the Book of Chronicles, that is, *Paralipomenon*, I used a little preface addressed to Saint Chromatius.”

And shortly afterward:

“I also translated the books of Solomon into Latin from the Hebrew, books that I had formerly rendered into Latin with the addition of obeli and asterisks, and dedicated them to the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus.”

Each of these prefaces, prefixed to the same books, likewise survives together with Jerome’s letters in the order of Marianus Victorius: 107, 110, and 115.

Finally, Pope Sixtus V, in the preface to the Bible printed at Rome in the Vatican press in A.D. 1590, places Chromatius among the most holy bishops who consulted Jerome about passages of Scripture.

### V

The great teacher, in Letter 42, elsewhere numbered 66, written to Rufinus in A.D. 399, speaks as follows of his brother Paulinianus, whom he had ordered to cross over to Dalmatia:

“My brother Paulinianus has not yet returned from his homeland, and I think that you have seen him at Aquileia with Saint Pope Chromatius.”

Two years earlier, Rufinus had returned from the East with Melania and was staying at Aquileia with Chromatius, after presenting Origen’s books *On First Principles* to the city of Rome. From this arose serious disputes between him and Jerome.

In book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*, Jerome testifies that Chromatius—whom he joins, after Anastasius, bishop of Rome, with the great metropolitans of East and West, Theophilus of Alexandria and Venerius of Milan—had denounced Origen’s errors to the people subject to him in the assembly of his metropolitan church:

“Therefore,” he says, “are the blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, and Chromatius, and the entire synod of Catholics of both East and West, who with one judgment, because with one spirit, denounce that man as a heretic to the peoples, to be judged thieves of his books?”

Pope Anastasius, in his letter to John of Jerusalem, cited by Baronius under A.D. 403, § 26 and following, says that he wrote a letter concerning Origen’s condemnation to his brothers Venerius and Chromatius.

[Note: These words are by no means found in Anastasius’s letter at the place cited in Baronius. The distinguished bishop should rather have observed—as he expressly does in this same *History of Aquileian Literature*, book V, chapter 19, no. 2—that John Garnerius interpolated the holy Pope’s Letter to John of Jerusalem at this point, although without any intention of deception. Thus some have wrongly accepted as genuine words of the holy pontiff the words that Garnerius inserted as a supplement. Moreover, this letter contains no mention whatever of the transmitted condemnation of Origen or of Chromatius—not in Coustant’s *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, Paris edition, col. 728; not among the works of Saint Jerome in the Verona edition of Domenico Vallarsi, vol. II, col. 580; and not among the works of Rufinus of Aquileia edited by the same Vallarsi, col. 411. See in both places the editors’ learned notes on this same passage.]

I shall discuss this letter and that assembly of Chromatius more accurately in book V, chapter 19.

Nevertheless, Chromatius never withdrew from Rufinus’s fellowship and affection. He remained so attached to Jerome that, always devoted to both and dear to both, he earnestly sought, as far as he could, to restore such great men to Christian harmony. He admonished Jerome to put an end to his bitter dispute and moved Rufinus, who was staying with him at Aquileia, to another task, ordering him to adapt Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin.

Jerome himself acknowledges the first point in *Apology* 2, book III, where he says:

“I call Jesus, the judge of my conscience, as witness that, at the urging of Saint Pope Chromatius, who will judge both this letter and yours, I wished to remain silent and put an end to our disputes.”

Rufinus, in the preface to his Latin translation of Eusebius’s *History*, which he expanded by two books, addresses Chromatius as “the supreme pontiff,” as he calls him honorifically:

[Note: This designation, “supreme pontiff,” attributed to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, certainly did not proceed from Rufinus’s pen. Rufinus therefore did not call him “supreme pontiff” as an honorific title, as Fontanini maintains. See the note of the distinguished Vallarsi on this passage, col. 209 of the works of Rufinus edited by him, as well as the following note, col. 211.

With respect to what Vallarsi observes in the passages cited here, it is also worth adding that in the archive of the distinguished collegiate church of Cividale, in this diocese of Udine, which arose from the Aquileian diocese, there exists a parchment codex unknown even to Vallarsi while he was working on his edition of Rufinus. It appears to belong to the twelfth century and contains Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, translated into Latin by the presbyter Rufinus. We recently saw it with great pleasure through the favor and work of the excellent canon Michael della Torre, count of Valle-Saxina, the prefect of the archive; we wish to name him here in his honor.

It would not be implausible to say that this codex, brought forth in that century, was copied from another very ancient codex of the same former Aquileian region, in which Rufinus certainly lived for several years under Bishop Chromatius and in which, and for which, at Chromatius’s command, he prepared that translation. Unless, rather, it should be thought that for this very reason it was copied from Rufinus’s own autograph codex, which may still have survived at that time, or certainly from one of its earliest copies, which Rufinus himself and Chromatius had then distributed throughout the entire extensive diocese in accordance with the purpose of the work they had undertaken.

In this codex, which, whatever the truth of the matter, may and should possess considerable authority, Rufinus’s preface to Chromatius is stated simply as follows:

“Here begins the prologue of Rufinus the presbyter to Chromatius the bishop, concerning the *Ecclesiastical History*.”

It is therefore far from the truth that Rufinus actually called Chromatius “the supreme pontiff” in the preface to his Eusebian *History*, and did so as an honorific, as Fontanini believed.

It is also worth observing that during the lifetime of Rufinus of Aquileia, and especially in the year of Christ 400 or the first or second year thereafter, when Rufinus was writing this work to Chromatius, the absolute and literal title “supreme pontiff”—which the ancient Roman pagans used for the chief hierarch of their sacred rites, and which pagan emperors later assumed as appropriate to their supreme dignity—had not yet been transferred to Christian usage.

Certain Christian rulers, too, had not infrequently received this title from their pagan subjects, particularly while paganism still prevailed, even though they themselves may easily have wished otherwise, down to approximately the year 382. This is evident from Baronius under the year 312, from Pagius in the same place, from De la Bastie in volume XV of the *Mémoires de Littérature de l’Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres*, and from other sources as well.

I say that this title, “supreme pontiff,” in its pure and proper sense had not yet been transferred to Christian use, since it still seemed to carry too strong a scent of idolatrous worship. Consequently, it was not attributed even to the Roman bishop, although by that time the bishop of the chief apostolic see enjoyed many highly honorific titles, entirely similar to that designation and peculiar to him alone.

Nor does the title “supreme pontiff,” with which Tertullian presented an edict or decree of the holy Pope Zephyrinus in *On Modesty*, chapter 1, in the year 216, as Baronius holds, create any difficulty.

For this title—asking Baronius’s pardon, since in the same place, no. 8, he would have it be the true and genuine title of that decree, prefixed to it by the decree’s author, and likewise asking pardon of the distinguished scholars after Baronius who assert that the use of this title had already been introduced into the Church at that time on the basis of Tertullian’s designation—Tertullian himself deliberately borrowed from paganism. In that passage, owing to the malice of his disposition, he used it not as an honorific but as an insult and mockery, indeed as a means of directing envy against the pontiff.

He was by then a man devoted to the Montanist sect and hostile to the Roman bishop, as Rigaltius and others observe on this passage, and as is readily apparent to anyone who weighs the context. Thus nothing can be extracted from this single passage, in support of the title “supreme pontiff” having already been transferred to Christianity at that time, even though it represents the whole of antiquity down to at least the fourth century.

For this reason, too, it appears still less probable that the presbyter Rufinus called Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, “the supreme pontiff,” and did so as an honorific, as Fontanini asserts.]

Rufinus addresses him in these words:

“Experienced physicians, they say, when they see that general diseases are threatening cities or regions, take care to provide some medicine or kind of potion by which people, once fortified, may be protected from the impending destruction.

“Likewise you, venerable father Chromatius, carrying out this kind of medical service, at the time when, after the barriers of Italy had been broken open by Alaric, leader of the Goths, a pestilential disease spread through the fields, devastated herds and men far and wide, and you were seeking a remedy against deadly destruction for the peoples entrusted to you by God—a remedy by which sick minds, withdrawn from the contagion of the advancing evil, might be kept occupied with better studies—you command me to translate into Latin the *Ecclesiastical History* that the most learned Eusebius of Caesarea composed in the Greek language.”

Learned men agree that in A.D. 400 the Goths, under the leadership of Alaric and Radagaisus, first burst through our Julian Alps, which Rufinus calls “the barriers of Italy” and Nicephorus Callistus, book XII, chapter 39, calls “the gates of Italy.” See Norisius, *Pelagian History*, book I, chapter 2; Pagius under A.D. 400, § 25; and Tillemontius, *History of the Emperors*, vol. V, pp. 524, 803.

At that time Aquileia, the capital of all Venetia, suffered a barbarian siege. For Jerome says in *Apology III against Rufinus*, who was then staying there:

“You flee the judgment of the Roman city so completely that you prefer to endure a barbarian siege rather than the sentence of a peaceful city.”

Our unfortunate year 1713 vividly represents the pestilential disease then introduced by the Goths into our Venetia. It spread first among the herds and afterward among human beings, as Rufinus testifies, devastating far and wide.

[Note: Thus in the year 1713 our Fontanini was writing this study of Saint Chromatius. It is therefore not surprising that this most learned man, and one highly skilled in bibliography, does not list the extensive works or editions of works that appeared afterward, up to the year 1736, when he ended his life on April 17, nor up to the year 1742, when his posthumous *History of Aquileian Literature* finally saw the light of day.

For this reason Fontanini could not have seen Vallarsi’s edition of Rufinus from the year 1745, in which the addition “supreme pontiff” to Chromatius’s name in the prologue to Eusebius’s *History* is rejected as the work of ignorant copyists.]

Thus the cattle plague, spreading from Pannonia into Italy already overwhelmed by disasters, infected it, while the same calamity advanced against human beings through Austria and the rest of Germany and threatened us from afar—would that it had not come near!

Rufinus dedicated to Chromatius not only Eusebius’s *History* but also his Latin translation of twenty-six homilies of Origen on Joshua, or Jesus son of Nun, which Chromatius had asked him to undertake. In the prologue he falsely presents Jerome as the author among the works of Origen in Erasmus’s edition, Basel, Froben, 1557, vol. I, p. 318.

Rufinus addresses Chromatius there in these words:

“Since, therefore, you too, my ever-venerable father Chromatius, charge and command me to contribute something from the resources and riches of the Greeks toward the edification and construction of the divine tabernacle, I have explained for you in Latin, to the modest extent of my abilities, twenty-six brief homilies on Jesus son of Nun, which the aged Adamantius delivered extemporaneously in the Church.”

Let us now proceed to other matters.

### VI

John Chrysostom, unjustly driven from the see of Constantinople in A.D. 404 and compelled to go into exile, sought assistance from Innocent, the Roman pontiff, and from the principal metropolitans of the West. In addition to Venerius of Milan, he informed Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, of his sufferings, writing the same single letter to each of them. Palladius of Helenopolis quotes it in his *Life of Chrysostom*, chapter 2, pp. 10, 22.

For in ancient times it was customary that, after the supreme pontiff, the principal metropolitans should be informed about the Church’s major affairs. This is demonstrated by Chrysostom’s action by Jerome Aleander the Younger, *On the Suburban Regions*, dissertation 2, chapter 3, p. 130.

The example of Theodoret confirms this as well. After being deposed from his bishopric, he appealed to Saint Leo the Great in Letter 113, and Letter 112 to the lord of Antioch shows that he wrote to the bishops of Milan, Aquileia, and Ravenna concerning the matter, as the principal metropolitans of the West.

How much Chromatius’s authority assisted Chrysostom’s cause before the emperors, Honorius himself testified in a letter to his brother Arcadius. When he wished to communicate the judgment of the Western bishops, he sent him two letters written above all others for his consideration—those of Innocent and Chromatius—as Palladius records in chapter 3, p. 30:

“To show what the judgment of the Westerners concerning Bishop John is, from all the letters that have been written to me I have appended two that express the same judgment as the others: one from the Roman bishop and the other from the bishop of Aquileia.”

Just as Sabinus, the Milanese deacon and legate of the Roman council under Damasus in the grave matter of confirming the Nicene faith and the divinity of the Holy Spirit, carried to Saint Basil the Great, in addition to synodical letters, other letters as well—especially one from Saint Valerian, metropolitan of Aquileia and predecessor of Chromatius, as Basil’s Letter 324, written to that same Valerian, testifies—so too Aemilius, bishop of Beneventum, and the legates Cythegius and Gaudentius, together with the presbyters Valentinianus and Boniface, carried to Constantinople in A.D. 406, for the emperor Augustus Arcadius, not only the memorandum of the Western synod but also letters from the emperor Honorius, Innocent, and the Italian bishops, including Chromatius of Aquileia and Venerius of Milan, as well as others. The same Palladius testifies to this in chapter 4, p. 31.

From these facts we conclude that Chromatius wrote not only to Honorius but also to Arcadius concerning Chrysostom’s case. It is therefore clear how highly he was regarded, both as a man distinguished for holiness and learning and as metropolitan of Aquileia.

### VII

Baronius, under A.D. 405, § 17, observes from the surviving letters of Chrysostom to Chromatius, Venerius, and Gaudentius of Brescia that these bishops communicated with the great man not only by peaceful letters but also by formal letters. Those letters, however, have perished.

I wish to transfer here Chrysostom’s complete Letter 105 to Chromatius from volume IV, p. 784, of the *Opuscula*, in the edition of Fronto Ducaeus, because it magnificently adorns the most holy man:

“The most renowned trumpet of your fervent and sincere charity has spread its sound all the way to us, breathing forth something great and enduring for a very long time from so great a distance, and reaching even to the furthest ends of the earth.

“Although we are otherwise so far separated, we have nonetheless experienced no less than those who are present your most vehement and fire-filled charity, your sincere tongue overflowing with immense freedom and confidence, and your adamantine zeal. For this reason we would greatly desire to enjoy your presence and your meeting as well.

“But since the solitude in which we are now confined, as though by fetters, has also taken this from us, we have therefore found my most reverend presbyter lord, and through him we fulfill, as we can, our desire, writing to you and sending you greetings. We also offer you the greatest thanks for the devotion that throughout this long period you have shown with such great exertion of mind.

“We also ask you that, when he returns, and further, if messengers should appear who come to this solitude, you write to us about your health. For you know how much pleasure we shall derive when news of the health of people who love us so ardently is brought to us more frequently.”

Thus far Chrysostom.

### VIII

This passage requires us to refute what David Blondel, in his *Historical Treatise on Primacy*, pp. 262, 266, 283, and 1265, has tried to derive from what has been said in support of his sect.

Since Chrysostom informed not only Innocent I, the Roman pontiff, but also Venerius of Milan and Chromatius of Aquileia about his unjust deposition, Blondel falsely argues that he appealed equally to all of them and did not recognize the Roman see as the supreme tribunal of the Church.

He adds that Chrysostom was not merely recounting events historically, as the great Cardinal Perron had written in his repeated reply to James I, king of Britain, p. 118, but wrote to each of them equally as an appellant.

You are mistaken, Blondel; you are mistaken.

Boniface I, in his Letter to Rufus and the other bishops of Macedonia, which Lucas Holstenius recovered from the treasures of sacred antiquity in the first part of his *Roman Collection*, p. 77, says that Innocent I, his predecessor—not Chromatius or Venerius—had withdrawn from communion with the Easterners in the matter of Chrysostom. The Easterners later sought peace through legates from the apostolic see—not from Aquileia or Milan:

“A short time ago,” says Boniface, “that is, under my predecessor, Innocent of blessed memory, the bishops of the Eastern Churches, grieving that they had been separated from the communion of blessed Peter, sought peace through legates, as your Charity remembers. At that time the apostolic see readily forgave everything.”

Nicephorus Callistus, book XIII, chapter 33, quotes letters in which Innocent I devoted the Constantinopolitan clergy, Arcadius, Atticus, and Theophilus of Alexandria to dreadful curses—not as one among the Western bishops, but as the greatest pontiff of all and head of the universal Church. No one is recorded to have done this among the others.

In his Letter 19 to Acacius of Beroea, cited by Labbeus, vol. II, p. 1270, Innocent likewise says, as the supreme guardian of the Church, that responsibility for ensuring that he found nothing crooked or defective in anyone rested upon him.

When Arcadius replied to Innocent through Michael Glycas, *Annals*, part IV, p. 260 of the Royal edition, after attempting to defend his actions against Chrysostom, he recognized the Roman pontiff as the sole and supreme judge of Chrysostom’s case and concluded as follows:

“Therefore, I earnestly beg you, for what remains, to free us from separation and not punish us in many ways.”

This is further confirmed by the eloquent Hermianensis, who lived for a long time at Constantinople. In book IV, chapter 1, of his *Defense of the Three Chapters*, he testifies that Chrysostom was condemned without a judgment from the apostolic see. In book VI, chapter 5, concerning Cyril of Alexandria, who followed the judgment of his predecessor Theophilus, he reports the following:

“Against the judgment of the apostolic see, which through the most blessed Pope Innocent had released the condemnation of the aforesaid holy John, who was in exile, he prohibited his name, after his death, from being recited among God’s priests in the sacrifice.”

Finally, Gelasius I, in Letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania, speaking of Innocent’s judgment against Chrysostom’s unjust condemnation, says:

“The apostolic see, even by itself, because it did not consent, absolved him.”

Do you see, Blondel, that one and only one apostolic see is mentioned in this judgment, never the see of Aquileia or Milan?

It is equally far from the truth to say that, when Innocent refused to admit Alexander and Atticus to communion because Chrysostom’s name had not yet been restored to the sacred Diptychs, he was merely giving the reason for his own separation without any authority over the churches of other dioceses, and that, by analogy, he could have demanded the same from Venerius and Chromatius.

But why, then, did they not demand it? Why did the Roman see alone demand it and alone pronounce judgment in the case of Chrysostom’s condemnation and absolution?

These remarks are offered against Blondel as the occasion requires.

IX. Concerning the year in which Chromatius, full of merits, died, no firm determination has hitherto been reached. For we have discovered that Panvinio in his *Chronicle*, p. 39, Sixtus of Siena in *Bibliotheca*, book IV, Antonio Possevino in *Apparatus*, vol. I, and Henry Palladius, book X, p. 178—some of whom thought that he died in A.D. 410, others later—departed from the truth. Philip Labbe, in his notes on Bellarmine’s *Catalogue*, vol. I, p. 223; François Combefis, in his *Review of the Authors of the Preaching Library*, vol. I, p. 8; and Natalis Alexander, century IV, chapter 3, article 34, to avoid the reefs, used a broad and ambiguous formula, reporting that he lived “at the end of the fourth century of Christ and the beginning of the fifth,” while leaving the year of his death unknown.

But Chrysostom, who died on 14 December A.D. 407, in thanking Chromatius for benefits conferred upon him, twice states in the letter cited above, written in A.D. 406, that he was anxious about Chromatius’s health, because Chromatius had written to Chrysostom that he was ill. Certainly, no mention whatsoever of Chromatius as still alive is found beyond A.D. 406. Therefore, I do not doubt that in this same year, after occupying the see for eighteen years and nine months, he exchanged this mortal life for the eternal on 2 December, according to Andrew Dandolo in his *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 14, worn out by old age, leaving the see of Aquileia not to Nicetas, as Baronius, Ughelli, and others have it, but to Augustine. For Dandolo, unquestionably the most accurate of all historians who have written about our affairs, affirms in book II, chapter 1, under A.D. 407, that Augustine was appointed Chromatius’s successor.

Chromatius’s sanctity is commended by the fact that in the parish of Aquileia he is venerated on the same day, 2 December, with the rite called double. On that day he is recorded in the Roman Martyrology, as well as in the *Catalogue* of Peter Equilinus, book VII, chapter 48, and likewise in the *Catalogue* of Philip Ferrarius, p. 746. These last two writers are wholly mistaken when they report that Heliodorus of Altinum was ordained bishop by Chromatius. For at the Council of Aquileia in A.D. 381, Heliodorus was present as bishop, while Chromatius was present as presbyter, not bishop. Consequently, there can be no doubt that Heliodorus was ordained by Chromatius’s predecessor, Valerian.

When Jerome addressed letters to both men, he placed Chromatius before Heliodorus—not as though he were the younger, but because Heliodorus was attached to his metropolitan see. This circumstance, perhaps not understood, led the authors mentioned above into error.

Although I have not seen Chromatius’s name in the more ancient Martyrologies, I nevertheless find that his cult is extremely ancient, contrary to Baillet. For he is invoked in the greater litanies, said to have been collected from Jerome’s book *On the Birthdays of the Saints* in the works of Alcuin, p. 281. I think that Walafrid Strabo praises these litanies in chapter 28 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*. He is also invoked in the more extensive manuscript litanies following the Psalter in a twelfth-century codex of the Passionean Library.

Claudius Castellanus, a Parisian canon and a man who rendered outstanding service to the saints—devoting his life to recovering and restoring their names from antiquity—lists Chromatius in his *Universal Martyrology* on 2 December, p. 612. He believed that before Gregory XIII Chromatius had appeared in no Martyrology. “Then,” he says, “Baronius inserted him into the Roman Martyrology.”

Yet long before that, Chromatius was included not only in the *Catalogue of the Saints* prepared by Bishop Equilinus in A.D. 1370, but also, before Baronius, by John, Bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, in his *Topography of the Saints* appended to Maurolycus’s Martyrology; indeed Maurolycus himself had inserted him in his Martyrology on 11 August. Before Maurolycus, Peter Natalis also mentioned him in his *Catalogue of the Saints*.

In the Martyrology of Usuard, published at Cologne by Hermann Grever, a Carthusian, from the press of John Roelhoff of Lübeck in A.D. 1490, our Chromatius is listed on 17 August; see Soller, p. 461. This was certainly for a reason other than his death.

# BOOK III, CHAPTER IV

I. The eighteen homilies of Saint Chromatius gathered into one work.  
II. Why, and by whom, he was called a Roman bishop.  
III. That he is unquestionably the author of those homilies.  
IV. Learned men praise them.  
V. They are vindicated from the calumnies of the Magdeburg Centuriators.  
VI. Their style and purpose.  
VII. Writings falsely attributed to Chromatius.

## I

Among the writings that won Chromatius praise for piety and learning, there still survive eighteen homilies, or sermons, on the Gospel of Saint Matthew. In them this man, renowned for piety and learning—as Sixtus of Siena calls him—strives to implant in the minds of the faithful voluntary poverty, purer doctrine, and Christian perfection.

John Sichard first published these little works, together with the *Apology of Pope Symmachus*, from a very ancient codex belonging to Matthew of Saracastro of Trier, as he testifies in his preface, under the following title:

*Dissertation of Chromatius, the most learned Roman bishop, on chapters V and VI of Matthew, together with a declamation of the same kind: now for the first time recovered and published.*

Basel, at the press of Adam Petri, March 1528, octavo.

Martin Lipsius caused this first edition of Sichard to be corrected and supplemented from an ancient codex of the Library of Saint-Trond and from another obtained from the Laurentian scholars near Liège. It appeared in his *Micropresbyteric of Certain Ancient Brief Theologians*, first published at Louvain in A.D. 1546 and subsequently at Basel by Henry Petri in 1550, p. 412.

Afterward John Herold inserted all this material in the *Orthodoxographia of Sacred Theology*, published at Basel by Henry Petri in 1555, vol. I, p. 430. John Grynaeus likewise included it in his *Monuments of the Holy Fathers*, the *Orthodoxographia*, printed there in 1569, vol. II, p. 1192.

Lipsius therefore was not the first to bring Chromatius’s homilies to light, although Aubert Miraeus seems to have believed this in his *Eulogies of the Distinguished Writers of Belgium*, p. 73 of the first edition.

> **Note:** D. Remigius Ceillier mentions another separate Louvain edition of these little works of Saint Chromatius, from the year 1646, in *General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. X, chapter 3, no. 7.

I would not add these very minor details if I did not observe that they are passed over by writers of literary history, so that, in a certain sense, the glory of discovery is lost to those who first brought Chromatius from parchments and hiding places into the light.

It is surprising that no critic has hitherto noticed that this same *Dissertation of Chromatius*, as Sichard called it—or *Little Work*, *Declamation*, or *Fragment of a Commentary*, as others, following Bellarmine and Labbe, vol. I, p. 223, have preferred to call it—is nothing other than eighteen homilies gathered into one. They may also conveniently be called treatises, in the sense in which François Bernardinus Ferrarius observes that ancient ecclesiastical writers used the term to designate homilies and sermons, in book I, chapter 2 of *On the Rite of Sacred Sermons*.

Indeed, whenever these words, or similar ones, occur in Chromatius—“who is blessed forever”—the individual homily is brought to an end. Ferrarius, following Erasmus in the brief preface to volume II of Origen’s works, observes in book I, chapter 31 that this kind of formula, familiar in homilies, which always conclude with a doxology (*doxologia*), was customarily used to bring sacred sermons to an end.

Laurentius Cumdius inserted Chromatius’s homilies, divided into only three parts, in the *Library of Homilies* edited by Gerard Mesan at Lyon by the Junta press in A.D. 1588, vol. II, p. 1170. François Combefis translated them, divided into six parts, into his *Preaching Library*, published at Paris by Antoine Bertier in A.D. 1662: vol. II, pp. 22 and 94; vol. V, pp. 202 and 224; vol. VIII, pp. 344 and 346.

They appear joined together in the second Paris edition of Margarino de la Bigne’s *Library of the Fathers*, A.D. 1589, vol. II, p. 792; likewise in vol. II, p. 151 of the fourth Paris edition, A.D. 1624; and finally in vol. V, p. 976, of the Lyon edition printed by Anisson in 1677.

It was easy for so many homilies to coalesce into one through the laziness of copyists, since each and every one dealt with an exposition of the Gospel of Saint Matthew. Let us therefore follow the customary division.

In the first little work there is only one homily. In the second little work there are fifteen homilies, the end of the last of which is partly missing; it was likewise missing in the manuscript codices of Sichard and Lipsius. In the third little work, which is acephalous, there are two homilies.

Of all these, only the first and the second concern the Eight Beatitudes.

> **Note:** Strictly and properly speaking, only one of Saint Chromatius’s homilies or treatises can be called *On the Eight Beatitudes*. We too therefore give it first place in this edition, outside the order of the other treatises.  
>   
> The other treatise—which is third in our edition—although it deals with the Beatitudes, is not by its nature properly a treatise *On the Eight Beatitudes*. Rather, it is a continuation of the Commentary on Matthew, and it too ends with the customary doxology, just as do the other sections that precede and follow it. Nevertheless, it has neither an opening nor a conclusion or epilogue that would make it a treatise properly so called *On the Eight Beatitudes*, as does the earlier treatise of which we spoke.  
>   
> The same reasoning applies to the homily or treatise that is number 14 in our edition, which is wholly devoted to explaining the Lord’s Prayer. Yet no one has called it a treatise or homily *On the Lord’s Prayer*, because it too is a continuation of the Commentary on Matthew, without either an opening or a conclusion that would constitute it as a distinct treatise deserving a special title.

The remaining homilies are also commonly given that title, but improperly.

## II

In Sichard’s first edition, from which the others derived, Chromatius is called a Roman bishop.

> **Note:** See the title of this edition together with the dedicatory letter of John Sichard, after the completed preface, following the Testimonies of the Ancients and the Proper Readings, and so forth.

This designation “Roman” has hitherto tormented the ingenuity of critics exceedingly. Sixtus of Siena, in book IV of his *Bibliotheca*, derives the designation from the city of Rome, which he considers Chromatius’s homeland. But Baronius, under 22 June and 2 December, and with him Henry Palladius, book V, p. 74, and book IX, p. 157, together with others who followed them, derive the origin of the surname from the title of the second Rome—that is, the Roman or Romatian city—which they do not doubt was attached to Aquileia.

I shall have to investigate this matter later in the discussion of Nicetas.

> **Note:** The distinguished Fontanini intended to investigate what is here promised, but later, hindered by other scholarly labors and finally overtaken by death, was unable to complete it. His *Literary History of Aquileia* did not reach Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia.  
>   
> Nevertheless, from his papers, which we saw in the Library of the town of San Daniele, where not a few manuscripts of the distinguished prelate are preserved and which are known to have belonged to the completion of his *Literary History*, we can sufficiently infer that he adhered to the more common opinion of learned men, which in this matter is by no means favorable to Baronius. See, if you wish, our extended discussion of this subject in chapters 5 and 6 of our *Dissertation*, which we published together with the surviving little works of Saint Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia, in 1810.

Far removed from these views, Paschasius Quesnellus, in his commentary on letter 129 of Saint Leo the Great, § 4, after boldly calling into question whether such an inscription truly concerned our Chromatius, recalls the origin of the patriarchate of the Church of Grado from that of Aquileia. He then asserts that the bishop of Grado was sometimes called Roman, so that he might be distinguished from the bishop of Aquileia, who was subject to the Lombards.

In support of his position he cites the words of Paul the Deacon, who writes in book IV, chapter 34 of *The History of the Lombards*:

> “At Grado also Candidianus was ordained bishop for the Romans. When he had died,” he says, “the bishops who were under the Romans ordained Epiphanius patriarch.”

Baronius, under A.D. 605, § 4, thought that these “Romans” should be understood as Catholics.

But Quesnellus, and following him Pagi under A.D. 396, § 6, as well as Tillemont, vol. XI, p. 647, understand them to be the actual Roman Italians: either the inhabitants of old Aquileia who had gone to Grado and obeyed the Roman Italians, or else, since those bishops were under the Romans.

Quesnellus has no doubt that all this is entirely true. Hence he readily believes that the designation “Roman” was attached by scribes, through an anachronism, to our Aquileian Chromatius after the seventh century—namely, if we follow him, as a title which those scribes knew was commonly given to the bishops of Aquileia in their own age.

Thus Quesnellus, wishing to present certain facts on the basis of frivolous conjectures, not to say mere inventions, proceeds as though no mortal had ever called the metropolitans of Aquileia or Grado “Romans,” either before or after the seventh century. Yet the bishops by whom, according to the Deacon’s account, the patriarch of Grado was ordained were just as much under the Romans as Grado itself was, according to that same Deacon.

The patriarch of Grado, therefore, was no more Roman on this account than the other bishops who ordained him.

These facts sufficiently, indeed more than sufficiently, warn us that we must investigate whether something else lies hidden in the origin of the word.

Grado and the cities of the province of Istria then attached to that ecclesiastical metropolitan see were subject not to our true Romans, as Quesnellus thought through ignorance of Italian affairs, but to the Greek Empire. We learn from letter 57 of the Carolingian Codex that Istria still obeyed that empire shortly before the end of the eighth century.

I shall set printed books, rather than unpublished ones such as the *Annals of Andrew Dandolo*, against the critic of Leo. Finally, Charlemagne subdued Istria, as Einhard testifies in chapter 15 of his *Life of Charlemagne*; Cointius thinks this should be assigned to A.D. 789.

Now, if the people of Ravenna were subject to the imperial exarch, as is clear from Paul, they were certainly subject to the empire of the Greeks, not to Roman Italian rulers. The same must be said of the Istrians and the people of Grado.

Therefore these Romans are Greeks.

We learn this not only from Paul the Deacon, who frequently uses the same designation in his *Miscellaneous History*, but more clearly from Liutprand in his embassy to Nicephorus Phocas, p. 139 of the Plantin edition. According to him, it is certain that the Greeks of Byzantium had appropriated the name “Romans” as their own.

This is also clear from other authors cited by Cangius in both of his Glossaries. In the Greek volume, vol. II, p. 1312, Cangius observes from Justinian’s Novella 21 that in the time of that emperor, who assumed the Empire in A.D. 527, it had not yet entirely become established that the Byzantine Greeks should be called Romans as their accepted designation.

After Justinian this usage became so widespread that eventually, among Westerners, the name “Roman” was a reproach, says Liutprand.

Jordanes, both in his little book *On Gothic Affairs* and in another *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, and Isidore in his *Chronicle*, under the year 446 of the era, generally called those subject to the Empire, as well as the Empire itself, “Romans” and “Romania.”

Others have taught the same from Greek writings, and long ago John Baptist Cotelier did so in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, vol. I, p. 752.

For this reason the Greeks called Constantinople the seat of the Greek Empire, New Rome, and the head of Romania. Indeed, the Italian region in which the exarchs of the Byzantine court ruled—after the Goths had been completely expelled by Narses the Patrician, the general of the Emperor Justinian—received from this the name of Romania, commonly Romagna. Blondus and other later writers chatter foolishly against this.

David Blondel, in his book *On the Primacy*, p. 539, excellently explained Paul the Deacon’s phrase “the bishops who were under the Romans” as referring to those who obeyed the Greek Empire, contrary to Quesnellus.

But later, on p. 612, he erred with Blondus when he stated that the name Romania had been given to the exarchate of Ravenna and that it had passed into the jurisdiction of the Roman Church through the agency of Pepin and Charlemagne. He had written the same on p. 125, falling into error there more than once. For the passage cited from Paul, as well as others to be cited shortly, plainly refers to times earlier than Pepin and Charlemagne themselves.

In the Palatine manuscripts of Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 47, Janus Gruterus noted at the end of volume II, p. 170, of his *Latin Writers of Augustan History*, that the people of Ravenna are called Romans without a conjunction. In the printed editions of Paul, however, the reading is “with the Ravennates and Romans,” with the conjunction wrongly inserted.

The same Paul says in book VI, chapter 46:

> “Faroald, leader of the Spoletans, invaded Classis, the city of the Ravennates. But by order of King Liutprand it was restored to the Romans”—namely, to the Ravennates just mentioned.

The people of Grado, therefore, were no more Romans than the Ravennates, whose exarchs they obeyed.

I have not written these things because I think that Chromatius was called Roman in this sense, but in order to demonstrate that Quesnellus’s opinion cannot be maintained in any way.

Indeed, it is obvious that Chromatius, a writer of the fourth century, ought not above all others to have been called Roman in this sense. At that time not only the Greeks, but equally all those subject to the Roman Empire, were regarded as Romans; and the Roman Church itself was called the metropolis of Romania, as we learn from Athanasius, *History of the Arians*, p. 364, and from the Council of Aquileia, in the Theodosian appendix published by Sirmond, vol. I of his works, p. 743.

Thus Epiphanius, book I, heresy 69, § 11, says that Arius, by his perverse doctrine, occupied “all Romania” (*πᾶσαν τὴν Ῥωμανίαν*, *pasan tēn Rhōmanian*).

Similarly, Possidius, in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter 30, calls the Vandals, who were devastating Africa, “the destroyers of Romania.”

It is therefore clear that the surname “Roman,” attached to Chromatius, must be explained from another source.

Sichard, in his dedicatory letter to Sigismund Islungus, testifies that Chromatius was praised in highly honorable terms and that a large part of his work was quoted by Albinus in his *Little Book against the Heresy of Felix*.

Later, on folio 59, p. 2, beside the passage concerning the divinity of the Son of God, he wrote in the margin of the book:

> “This passage is cited by Albinus against Felix from Chromatius’s *Little Book on the Eight Beatitudes*.”

Martin Lipsius afterward added this note to his own edition.

After I had searched in vain for this passage among the printed works of Albinus, also called Alcuin, I finally found it in an unpublished codex, number 290 among the Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library. It is entitled *Albinus against the Heresy of Felix* and appears to have been written seven hundred years ago.

Among other testimonies of the Latin Fathers, it recites the following on folio 12:

> “Chromatius also, bishop of the holy Roman Church, says the following in the little book that he wrote on the Eight Beatitudes:
>
> ‘For in the mystery of baptism the Son also is seen in bodily form, and the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father is heard from heaven, so that the unity of the Trinity may be declared, because neither can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Son be known without the Holy Spirit.
>
> “Consider, therefore, what kind of testimony the Father gives concerning the Son when he says: “This is my Son.” His own Son, certainly—not through the adoption of grace, nor through the religion of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the propriety of his origin and the truth of his nature.
>
> “Many saints are called sons of God, and they are. But this one, without comparison, is the one and only-begotten, true, and proper Son of God the Father, born from no one other than the Father; because he is as truly Father as he is true God, just as he is also as truly Son as he is true Lord.
>
> “The perfect faith of the Trinity is therefore manifested, since the Father testifies that Christ the Lord, our God, is his Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Paraclete—is joined to the Father and the Son in so great a sacrament of faith that we do not hesitate to believe in the true Father, the true Son, and the true Holy Spirit: three Persons, but one divinity of the Trinity and one substance.”’

I have brought forward this illustrious passage all the more gladly because the same words are read in the final homily of Saint Chromatius, which concerns the Baptism of Christ, on p. 990 of the Anissonian edition that I use.

> **Note:** This illustrious passage of Chromatius, cited by Alcuin, is by no means found in precisely the same words, as Fontanini asserts, in the final homily of Saint Chromatius in the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*. Nor is it found thus in the newest library of Andrew Gallandi, which faithfully copied the passage from the Lyon edition. In both places the passage is so corrupt—on a matter of such importance as the mystery of the Trinity—that it could easily trouble the ingenuity of theologians. This is true not for the purpose of establishing the Catholic faith concerning so great a mystery, which is already supported by almost innumerable testimonies of the Fathers, but certainly for determining the correct thought of Saint Chromatius, which appears here to deviate somewhat from orthodox faith if one adheres to the words presented to us in both libraries.
>
> We therefore present this passage in our edition restored to its integrity in Treatise 2, no. 2, exactly as it unquestionably proceeded from Chromatius’s pen.
