We relied especially—as was stated in the annotation there—on this same passage cited by Fontanini from the Vatican Codex; we also consulted Chromatius’s first Basel edition of 1528 and the second edition of 1569, among the *Monuments of the Holy Fathers* and the *Orthodoxographia* of John Grynaeus. We likewise consulted the very passage that we have included among the Testimonies of the Ancients from the Frobenian edition of Alcuin.

Alcuin, therefore, who, in his customary manner, often speaks poetically, after praising the letters of Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, written to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, in defense of the Catholic faith, immediately opposed to Felix of Urgell the doctrine of Chromatius of Aquileia, along with that of Augustine, Isidore, and Leo, prominent Fathers of the Roman—that is, Latin—Church. By calling him “bishop of the Roman Church,” he intended to indicate not his homeland or his see, but the Western or Latin Church.

For this reason Sichard bestowed upon the same Chromatius the surname “Roman.”

I would not suppose that Alcuin, the most learned man of his age, was so ignorant of ancient formulas and pontifical history that he believed Chromatius to have been supreme pontiff on account of the title “holy and venerable pope,” with which Jerome honored him in the preface to the book of Chronicles and at the beginning of his Commentary on Habakkuk.

With precisely the same understanding, Jerome, who was a Dalmatian, says in letter 58 to Damasus, speaking of three Antiochene bishops who were then demanding from him a confession of three hypostases:

> “A new name is being demanded from me, a Roman man.”

Understand “Latin” in place of “Roman.”

In the same way Gelasius of Cyzicus, in book I of *The Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, chapter 1, and the Second Council of Nicaea, session 1, as well as Photius in codex 89, called Rufinus, a presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, “Roman.”

Are we therefore to understand our Rufinus as Roman—that is, subject to the Romans—with Quesnellus? Or are we to understand him as Roman in the strict and proper sense? Certainly not.

Nor is there any other Latin bishop named Chromatius, distinguished for doctrine and holiness, to whom the praised works can rightly be attributed, except our own Chromatius. Jerome, so great a man, honorifically called him, in the preface to the books already mentioned, “the most learned of bishops,” and again “the holiest and most learned of bishops.”

Peter Castellanus, in his *Hagiological Lexicon* preceding Aegidius Menagius’s *Gallic Origins*, does indeed mention Saint Chromatius, bishop of Metz, but testifies that this man flourished in the sixth century.

I wish the Bollandist writers had kept silent about Chromatius in volume IV of the June *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 246, § 10. For what could be more trivial than to say that the title “Bishop” could have been attached to a truly Roman man, or that “Comanian” could have been changed by scribes into “Roman”?

There were two cities of Comana with episcopal sees: one in Lesser Armenia, the other in Pontus, both in Cappadocia. They also introduce a Comania on the Danube. Yet this Comania, or Cumania, or Comm ania, of which Cangius speaks in his notes on Villehardouin, p. 336, is a region forming part of Wallachia, not an episcopal city.

Pius, in his notes on Antonio Panormita’s *Sayings and Deeds of King Alfonso*, book IV, chapter 32, calls the peoples of Hungary “Comani.”

Yet if these things were true, Chromatius ought to have written not in Latin but in Greek.

Away with such frigid conjectures, unworthy of such great men! Unless I am mistaken, these matters sufficiently reveal that what often causes trouble for first-rate critics is, when examined more closely, entirely ordinary and straightforward.

## III

There can be no doubt that the writings which we maintain to be those of our Chromatius are ancient and belong to a most trustworthy author. Tillemont judges so in volume XI, p. 539; he also considers them wholly suited to the name of Chromatius and agrees with Sixtus of Siena, who commends them for their abundance of learning and piety.

Their antiquity is confirmed by many considerations.

### 1

The testimonies of Sacred Scripture are quoted there, following the custom of the ancient Fathers, with great frequency—not indeed from Jerome’s Vulgate version, but from the old Itala. In the Old Testament the author follows the Septuagint interpreters, as Martin Lipsius likewise observed on p. 412.

### 2

The author speaks of the Gentiles as adversaries who still existed. Thus, in the first little work, p. 977, he says that the words “Blessed are the peacemakers” are to be understood of that peace by which Gentile peoples, who are enemies of God, are brought through the persistent application of teaching to peace; and by which sinners are corrected and reconciled to God through repentance.

> **Note:** The distinguished Fontanini always cites Chromatius’s passages from volume V of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*. For the convenience of readers, we have transferred the cited passages in these Notes to our edition. See, therefore, the cited passage in the Treatise or Sermon *On the Eight Beatitudes*, which we present first, no. 7.

In the second little work, p. 982, he says:

> **Note:** That is, in our edition, Treatise 8, no. 1.
>
> “We have adversaries and Gentiles who oppose our faith; they sometimes compel us, during the time of persecution, to participate in wicked sacrifices.”

Likewise, on p. 985, in commenting on Matthew 5:41, “Whoever forces you to go one mile, go with him another two,” he explains:

> **Note:** That is, in our edition, Treatise 11, no. 3.
>
> “That is, if any unbeliever, or anyone who has not yet attained knowledge of the truth concerning the one God the Father, creator of all things, has not mentioned him, as though entering upon the journey of the law, you should go with him another two.”

Moreover, Severinus converted the Noricans, who bordered the region of Aquileia and were still unbelievers or Gentiles, to the Christian faith approximately fifty years after Chromatius. For this reason he was honored in the Roman Church’s calendars with the title “Apostle of the Noricans” on 8 January.

Rufinus, a contemporary of Chromatius, who dedicated his *History* to him, speaks in his *Exposition of the Creed* of Gentiles or pagans as enemies of the Christian religion who still existed at that time:

> “But the pagans are accustomed to mock us.”

Furthermore, while Chromatius was still alive, Sisinnius and his companions, overcome by Gentiles, suffered martyrdom in the ecclesiastical province of Aquileia near Trent in A.D. 397. See the *Acts* of Ruinart, p. 608.

Nicetas, a subdeacon of Aquileia of the same age, and later bishop of the Romatian city in Dacia, published a book *On the Errors of Paganism*, according to Gennadius in his *Catalogue*, chapter 22.

> **Note:** Nicetas, certainly a bishop of Aquileia, published a book *On the Errors of Paganism*, as Gennadius says in the cited passage. But this is not the Nicetas—or rather Niceas—who was a deacon of Aquileia and about whom Saint Jerome wrote to him; nor should he be confused with another Nicetas who was bishop in Dacia and whose praises were sung by Saint Paulinus of Nola. See our dissertation cited above, where these matters are explained more fully.

### 3

At the end of the final homily, p. 990, the divinity of the Son of God is vigorously defended against the Arians, the heretics of that age, in the words cited above from Alcuin.

> **Note:** That is, in our edition, Treatise 2, no. 2.

These things fit no Chromatius except our own, whom we observed to have disputed against the Arian Palladius at the Council of Aquileia in A.D. 381, and of whom Jerome says, in letter 7, formerly 43, that he drove the poison of Arian doctrine from the city of Aquileia.

### 4

The beginning of the first homily, recited before a large crowd, is as follows:

> **Note:** This is the beginning, in our edition, of the Treatise or Sermon *On the Eight Beatitudes*, which we placed first.
>
> “This gathering of the people and the crowds at the marketplace, brothers, gives us an opportunity to set forth an evangelical sermon.”

How well this corresponds to Aquileia may be inferred from the fact that frequent fairs were customarily held there because of the neighboring peoples who gathered at that place for purposes of trade. Aquileia was at that time the metropolis of Venetia, as Jordanes testifies in chapter 42 of *Gothic Affairs*, and Paul the Deacon in book II, chapter 14 of *The History of the Lombards*.

For this reason it is called by the Emperor Julian, in Oration 1, “the wealthy marketplace of the Italians,” and by Liutprand, in book III, chapter 2 of his *History*, “exceedingly rich.” Mela, in book II, chapter 4, had long before celebrated it as “wealthy,” and Ammianus, in book XXI, chapter 11, as renowned for its riches.

Labbe’s argument from Jerome’s silence for rejecting Chromatius’s homilies is extremely weak. For, apart from the fact that Jerome did not compose his *Catalogue* after Chromatius, but while Chromatius was still alive, in A.D. 392—

> **Note:** Vallarsi also holds this opinion in his preliminary notice to the holy Doctor’s book *On Illustrious Men*.

—that year being the fourteenth of Theodosius, as Pearson proves against Scaliger and Valesius in part I, chapter 6 of his *Vindication of the Letters of Saint Ignatius*, it is wholly unreasonable to suppose that this great man, while composing his brief catalogue, had all the works of all authors available to him. He himself says so in the preface:

> “If any of those who have continued writing to the present day have been omitted by me in this volume, they will have themselves, rather than me, to blame. For since they concealed their writings, I could not know what I had not read; and what may perhaps be known to others was unknown to me in this remote corner of the earth. Certainly, when they become famous through their writings, they will not greatly lament the loss caused by our silence.”

Jerome wrote these words when he was wholly unaware of Chromatius’s homilies—although Chromatius was his friend—perhaps because they had not yet been published or even written.

The same judgment applies to Gennadius, Isidore, and other foreign cataloguers, who did not mention either Marius Mercator, a friend of Saint Augustine, or Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia and a contemporary of Chromatius, or Peter Chrysologus. Yet who does not know that their genuine works have come down to us?

Let us now consider the opinions of distinguished men concerning Chromatius’s labors.

## IV.

Sichardus, in his letter to Islungus, says: “May I perish if this Chromatius is not worthy to be read not only by the learned, but also to be learned by heart: such is the elegance of his language and the excellence of his treatment of this subject! He deals admirably with almost everything that is nowadays disputed concerning Baptism and the Oath.” Martinus Lipsius agrees with Sichardus in these very words in his *Micropresbyticon*, p. 412: “Receive Chromatius, now as if restored anew to the world; for, to pass over other matters for the moment, he writes so clearly and devoutly concerning those Eight Beatitudes in Matthew that he is truly worthy not merely to be read by cultivated lovers of piety, but also to be learned word for word; such is his skill and incisiveness in treating the subject.”

Heroldus, in his account of the authors on whom his *Orthodoxographa Theologiae Sacrosanctae* is based, no. 27, says: “Chromatius—whether he was a pope (for that title was given in that age to elders and ecclesiastical superiors) or a bishop—certainly wrote distinguished commentaries, notable both for learning and piety, on the Eight Beatitudes and on the Lord’s Prayer.” Again, on p. 433, he commends his homilies as equally distinguished for learning and piety.

Joannes Jacobus Grinaeus, in the preface to the *Monumenta Sanctorum Patrum Orthodoxographa*, says that Chromatius expounded the Eight Beatitudes in an elegant *δημηγορία* (*dēmēgoría*, that is, a speech addressed to the people).

Nicolaus Serarius, in his notes on the first letter of Saint Boniface the Martyr, p. 292, places Chromatius at the head of the fifth and sixth chapters of Matthew among the ancient Fathers who make not Jesus son of Sirach but Solomon the author of the ecclesiastical book.

Caspar Barthius valued these writings of Chromatius so highly that he devoted his ingenuity to elucidating several passages in them. For in his *Adversaria*, book XXXII, chapter 4, while uncovering verses that had accidentally escaped authors unawares, without their having deliberately aimed at composing them, he found the following in *Opusculum* I, p. 977:

> Here  
> Our market, this spiritual fair.

[Note: That is, in our edition, *Treatise* or *Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes*, no. 10.]

In book XXXV, chapter 13, he observes that Chromatius, in *Opusculum* II, p. 978, column 20, used *misereri* with the dative case; other Christian writers also used it without hesitation, as Saint Cyprian did in his letter to Demetrianus, quoting the Prophet: “Do not spare the old or the young.” Corippus and Petrus Pictavensis likewise occur in the same place in Barthius.

Nor should we pass over in silence what Barthius brings forward in book LIV, chapter 4, concerning the word *Mammon* in Matthew 6:24. After citing the opinions of various writers who interpret Mammon as wealth, he adds:

> It seems to me, however, that no one has explained the Evangelist’s passage better than Chromatius, whose words are these: “The Lord says: You cannot serve God and Mammon,” showing that we cannot serve both God and the Devil—that is, God, the author of mercy, and the Devil, Mammon. Mammon, that is, the Devil, who is the author of Mammon.

These words appear in Chromatius, *Opusculum* II, p. 989.

[Note: That is, in our edition, *Treatise* 17, no. 4.]

Barthius further remarks that Gennadius of Constantinople takes Mammon to mean the Devil in these words of the Synodal Letter:

> For it cannot happen that things which cannot come together should be joined, or that God should agree with Satan, or that those who serve him should also serve God. For this too is indisputably the Lord’s saying: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

The same Barthius, in his notes on Phoebadius, bishop of Agen, *Sermon against the Arians*, p. 51, observed in the same way that Chromatius’s *Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes* was called a *Book*, and was improperly entitled a *Declamation* by Sichardus.

Let us proceed from Barthius to Sixtus of Siena. In his *Bibliotheca Sancta*, comparing several passages of Chromatius with the opinions of the ancient Fathers that appeared difficult to understand, he explains them lucidly. Such is the passage in *Opusculum* II, p. 984, concerning the law of marriage. After saying that it is not lawful to dismiss one’s wife except on account of fornication, he adds:

> But just as it is not lawful to dismiss a wife who lives chastely and purely, so it is permitted to dismiss an adulterous wife, because she has made herself unworthy of her husband’s companionship: by sinning against her own body, she has dared to violate the temple of God.

Dupinius, in volume three of his *Bibliotheca*, thinks that Chromatius here speaks of divorce as though he believed that a new marriage could be contracted after an adulterous wife had been dismissed. Tillemontius, however, in volume XI, note 2, concerning Chromatius, p. 647, observes that Chromatius adds nothing to the Evangelist’s words, since perhaps the question had not yet arisen at that time.

Sixtus comes closer to the truth in book VI, annotation 81, where he observes that most of the ancient Fathers agree with Chromatius: Hilary, Chrysostom, Augustine, Euthymius, and Theophylact. They grant husbands—and sometimes even prescribe—that they drive away and repudiate adulterous wives, especially those who reject correction; but they neither recommend nor permit taking a new wife.

A little farther on, Chromatius appears not to approve of swearing.

[Note: The same place, no. 2.]

“Therefore,” he says, “it is altogether unfitting for us to swear. For what necessity is there for any of us to swear, when we, whose words ought always to be so true and so utterly faithful that they may be regarded as an oath, are altogether forbidden to lie? And for this reason the Lord forbids us not only to perjure ourselves but also to swear, lest we should then seem to speak the truth only when we swear; lest, having been established as truthful in every word, we should think it lawful to lie without an oath.

“For this is the reason for an oath: everyone who swears swears in order to speak what is true. Therefore the Lord wishes there to be no difference between an oath and our speech; for just as there ought to be no treachery in an oath, so there ought to be no falsehood in our words, since both perjury and lying are condemned by the punishment of divine judgment.”

Thus Chromatius speaks. Sixtus examines his words in book VI, annotation 26, together with similar statements of the holy Fathers, who hold that it is not lawful to swear without necessity, or even to become accustomed to swearing, and that the practice should be despised.

[Note: Here it is fitting to repay the kindness of the most distinguished Francis Florio, provost of the metropolitan church of Udine, who used this passage of our Chromatius to elucidate a similar manner of speaking concerning the use of oaths, or rather concerning abstention from oaths, in his *Bachiarus*, published at Rome in 1748, p. 94, note 1. Receive, therefore, the words of Bachiarus in his book addressed to Januarius, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, no. 17, in the same place. They may also serve as an addition to the similar sayings of the holy Fathers cited by Sixtus of Siena in his *Bibliotheca Sancta*, cited here by Fontanini:

> “See, brother, how permission to swear is forbidden us. If you believe anything concerning my lowliness, I promise, according to the mercy of the Lord, that I wish to share in this labor which I recommend.”]

Ambrose aptly says in his *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 11:

> One should not swear readily, because many circumstances usually arise that prevent us from fulfilling what we have sworn. Whoever does not swear certainly does not commit perjury. Whoever swears must at some time fall into perjury, because every human being is a liar. Therefore do not swear, lest you begin to perjure yourself.

## V.

What I have said thus far reminds me not to forget to vindicate Saint Chromatius from the calumnies of the Magdeburg heretics. They did not hesitate, under the leadership of Illyricus—of whom it has been reported that he never did anything good except when he departed this life for hell—to malign his ancient and truly Christian teaching, since it opposed the novelty of their doctrines.

Thus, in *Centuria* IV, chapter 10, they babble that he speaks inappropriately and dangerously concerning certain parts of doctrine because he asserts that human beings merit righteousness by their works. Robert Bellarmine, however, thoroughly discussed this matter in volume IV of the *Controversies*, book V, *On Justification*, chapter 2. Therefore, lest I repeat what has already been done, I refer the reader there.

They are also displeased that Chromatius excessively exalts and presses voluntary poverty, as though through it we obtain the riches of the heavenly kingdom, since he interprets “the poor in spirit” as those who freely renounce worldly goods and distribute their possessions.

But the Lord Christ himself commends this very thing in Matthew, chapter 19: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” In the same passage the Apostles say: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.”

It is true that the passage in chapter 5, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” is also interpreted by the holy Fathers in another sense, namely, as referring to humility of spirit, as by Saint Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 72, chapter 24, and in *Sermon* 53, chapter 1, on Matthew.

But the others more frequently explain it literally as referring to voluntary poverty, as Saint Jerome does: “Blessed are the poor, who are poor by their will for the sake of the Holy Spirit.”

Gregory of Nyssa, speaking of the Beatitudes in *Oration* 1, volume I of his works, p. 771 of the Paris edition of 1638, says:

> Do you wish to understand who is poor in spirit? He is the one who exchanges bodily wealth for the riches of the soul; who is needy for the sake of the spirit; who has shaken off and cast away earthly riches as though they were a burden.

Basil the Great, in the *Rule for Monks*, Question 125, in Rufinus’s translation, explains Matthew in the same way:

> These are the poor in spirit who are poor for no other reason than the teaching of the Lord, who says: “Go, sell everything you possess and give it to the poor.”

Augustine also teaches in *Against Petilianus*, book II, chapter 104, that voluntary poverty belongs to Christian perfection, and he likewise extols it in book V, chapter 18, of *The City of God.

Besides these, Bellarmine gathers other Fathers who agree in the same opinion in volume IV of the *Controversies*, book II, *On Monks*, chapter 20; among them he names Chromatius.

For this reason Nicolaus Zegerus rightly approves the interpretation concerning voluntary poverty above all others, both because Luke 6:20 does not add the word “spirit,” and because in both passages the word is *πτωχοί* (*ptōchoi*), which properly designates beggars.

Accordingly Erasmus rashly rebukes Bede and others for interpreting the passage as referring to voluntary poverty—not, as he himself says, in a forced and alien manner, but in its proper sense—and asserts that it should be understood only of humility or modesty. Chromatius’s teaching therefore corresponds entirely to the Gospel, and differs from none of the teaching that the doctors of the Church have always transmitted with one voice from the mouth of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The Magdeburg heretics utter similar nonsense against Chromatius when he compares the degrees of the Beatitudes, which he calls evangelical, to Jacob’s ladder, by which whoever ascends finds the gate of heaven.

That no criticism could be more foolish or absurd will be clear from the following words of Chromatius, *Opusculum* I, p. 976, column 1:

> In a certain manner the Lord and Savior lays out very firm steps made from precious stones, by which holy and faithful souls may creep and ascend to that supreme good, namely, the kingdom of heaven. In brief, therefore, dearest brothers, I wish to demonstrate the qualities of the steps.

After explaining each of the Beatitudes, he concludes on p. 977, column 1:

> Brothers, the eight evangelical steps have been shown, constructed, as I said, from precious stones. That ladder of Jacob has been shown, whose summit reached from earth to heaven; by it whoever ascends finds the gate of heaven, and, entering through it, will stand joyfully forever in the presence of the Lord.

Who does not recognize that the wisest Bishop is speaking here in a truly evangelical language?

The Sectarians, however, again grow angry with Chromatius because, in the statement “The upright shall dwell in the land, and the holy shall dwell in it,” he understands the land to mean the transfigured body of the saints.

For in *Opusculum* II, p. 978, column 2, explaining who the meek are in Matthew, he argues as follows:

> Accordingly, he shows those to be blessed who are meek, to whom he promised possession not in the present life but in the future of that happy land, concerning which we read in the Psalm: “But the meek shall possess the land, and shall delight in the abundance of peace.” And again: “Those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the land.” Concerning this the Holy Spirit also testifies through the Savior, saying: “For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the holy shall dwell in it.” The Lord therefore shows as blessed those meek persons who, following the gentleness of the Lord’s meekness, will enjoy the inheritance of that blessed land forever.

He is speaking especially of the land of our body, in which the saints, transfigured into glory according to the Apostle, will reign in eternal happiness.

What in this explanation is contrary to true faith and religion? Yet the Magdeburgers still do not spare Chromatius. They add the following:

“In his exposition of the statement, ‘Be reconciled quickly with your adversary,’ he says that he adopts the opinion of those who taught that the adversary is the Holy Spirit.”

This is a censure suggestive of unsound faith, but it should not be accepted before Chromatius’s actual words have been considered. In *Opusculum* II, p. 982, column 2, when explaining Matthew 5:25—“Be reconciled quickly with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be thrown into prison”—he reports various opinions of authors concerning the word “adversary.” Some understand it as an enemy who must be recalled to peace; others take it as the Devil.

After reporting these views, he immediately adds:

> Others, however, whose assertion seems fuller to me, think that the adversary here should be understood as the Holy Spirit, who opposes vices and the desires of the flesh, as the Apostle makes clear when he says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. The spirit desires heavenly things; the flesh covets earthly things. The spirit rejoices in spiritual gifts; the flesh delights in bodily vices. Hence the Apostle also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” I believe that the Lord commanded us to obey this adversary of sin and human error, who urges what is just and holy, while we are with him on the way—that is, in the course of the present life—in order that we may be able to have eternal peace and perpetual fellowship with him.

Thus Chromatius embraces the opinion of other interpreters in this explanation, in which there is certainly nothing un-Catholic.

Saint Paulinus of Nola, in letter 36, formerly 20, to Amandus, shows that he understood the passage from Matthew in the same way as Chromatius, in these words:

> Let our mourning not exceed seven days, if on the way of this life we agree with our Adversary, that is, with the Spirit and the Word of God, which opposes us when we sin.

## VI.

What I have said makes it clear that Chromatius’s homilies were composed according to the rules of completely sound faith and in a truly apostolic spirit.

Let us say something also about their style. He does not use a lofty manner, but one that is plain, proper, even, harmonious, and by no means commonplace—precisely the style appropriate to a bishop speaking to his own people. His diction is select and polished; his reasoning is highly suited to the subject under discussion. Thus Natalis Alexander rightly and deservedly called Chromatius’s writings most elegant in *Saeculum* IV, chapter 3, article 33.

His reflections are highly useful; his explanations are directed chiefly toward morals and are literal, for he seems to have devoted himself to them more than to allegorical interpretations. He explains the Lord’s Prayer; he commends voluntary poverty, love toward one’s neighbor, almsgiving, fasting, and the other virtues concerning which the Savior spoke on the mountain.

In the final *Opusculum*, or Homily 18, he speaks of the efficacy of the baptism of Jesus Christ.

[Note: In our edition this is *Treatise* 2.]

The homilies of the first *Opusculum* are superior to the others in clarity and moral teaching.

[Note: There is a single homily of the first *Opusculum* in the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and here it constitutes the *Treatise* or *Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes*.]

This is substantially the view of Dupin in volume III of his *Bibliotheca* and of Tillemontius in volume XI, pp. 539 and 647. Franciscus Lucas frequently uses Chromatius among the Latin Fathers in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 5, pp. 62, 63, 65, 66, and 79.

Hadrianus Baillet, in his *Lives of the Saints*, 2 December, believes that Chromatius’s style was more suited to instruction than to moving the emotions; but everyone can see that both qualities appear in his homilies.

## VII.

Do not judge Chromatius by the letters to Jerome concerning the birthdays of the saints, which have circulated under the names of Chromatius and Heliodorus, together with Jerome’s reply to them, from the time of Walafrid Strabo onward, as he himself suggests in chapter 28 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*:

> The Litany of the names of the saints is believed to have been adopted later for use. Jerome composed a Martyrology, following Eusebius of Caesarea, throughout the annual cycle, having been asked by the Bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus to compile it on this occasion: the religious Emperor Theodosius had praised Gregory, bishop of Córdoba, at a council of bishops because, while celebrating Masses every day, he mentioned many of the martyrs whose birthdays were being commemorated.

Walafrid seems to have drawn this from letters that, in ancient manuscripts of Usuard, bear the names of Chromatius, Heliodorus, and Jerome.

Erasmus long ago suspected that these letters were false. At the end of his index of what he calls the pseudepigraphical books of ignorant writers, he says:

> We have found Jerome’s Martyrology, prefaced by a preface of Jerome and written in Lombard letters, but in another language—Spanish, I think—its words mostly twisted and corrupted into another form.

Joannes Molanus rejected both letters in chapter 2 of *On Martyrologies*, as did Baronius in chapters 6 and 7 of his *Roman Martyrology*. Franciscus Maria Florentinus, however, defended the same letters in the preliminary admonitions to the ancient Martyrology that he edited.

Since Baronius considers the council of Milan mentioned in Chromatius’s letter to be fictitious—a council to which Theodosius is said to have invited all the bishops of Italy because certain bishops had stained their souls with Arian filth—Florentinus attempts on p. 60 to persuade us that it was the council that Baronius reports as having been held at Milan in A.D. 390, section 7.

But the learned man failed to observe that this council dealt not with Arians but with Priscillianists, and with bishops formerly driven from their sees by heretics, as Pagius notes under A.D. 390, section 10.

Nor could the council have dealt with several bishops stained by Arian filth if Saint Ambrose had long before cleansed the Italian region of this plague, as Jerome testifies in his *Chronicle*, under Olympiad 388 and A.D. 376 according to Eusebius. After the death of the Arian Auxentius and the establishment of Ambrose as bishop of Milan, Jerome writes:

> All Italy is converted to the true Faith.

Ambrose confirms the same thing in letter 14, written to Theodosius in A.D. 382, volume II of his works, p. 818:

> We even thought that this labor should be imposed upon us, not on behalf of Italy, which long ago has been quiet and secure from the Arians and has not been troubled by any disturbance of the heretics.

The same author, in his commentary on Luke, book IX, chapter 32, volume I, p. 1501—a work written in A.D. 386 according to Pagius under A.D. 376, section 3—says:

> All the heats by which the people of Italy were once scorched by the fires of Jewish violence and, more recently, of Arian violence are now tempered by a tranquil breeze.

When he says that the people of Italy, once scorched by the fires of Arian violence, were then being cooled by a tranquil breeze, he clearly shows that by the same A.D. 386 those fires had been utterly extinguished, not only throughout all Italy, which was the Milanese ecclesiastical province, but also throughout the entire West. Arnaldus Pontacus concludes that, apart from Auxentius, there were very few followers of that impiety, in his notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, pp. 742 and 745.

Hence Saint Basil, in letter 70 to the bishops of Italy and Gaul, says:

> For this evil of heresy is devouring everything, and there is danger that, after our churches have been devastated, it may spread even to the healthy part of your dwelling-place.

Florentinus is therefore wrong to consider it uncertain on p. 59 whether the rest of Italy had been cleansed of these impurities, even though Saint Valerian of Aquileia had labored to expel Arianism from the boundaries of his Church.

The same letters are also plainly disqualified from belonging to Chromatius by their solecisms and their dense concentration of linguistic blunders in a few words: for example, *feriales* for *calendaria*, *perquirere causam* for *in crimen inquirere*, and *ex faece inquinare*, along with other wholly barbarous expressions.

I am astonished that Florentinus, in order to fasten these blemishes upon Chromatius, was not afraid to write that the holy Bishop had applied himself less carefully to the purity of the Latin language because he used *mercatus* for *nundinae*. Yet nothing more truly Latin could be brought forward with that word, if Serenus and Varro in Nonius under *mercatus*, Plautus in *Paenulus* I.ii.126, and in *Asinaria* II.iii.17 genuinely know Latin.

I pass over the rest, since Florentinus himself is finally forced to admit on p. 69 that the letters are by no means genuine, although he again errs in declaring everything contained in them to be true. The falsity of that opinion is apparent from what has already been said.

I think the origin of the fraud was taken from Cassiodorus, chapter 32 of *On the Institution of Divine Letters*, where he praises a letter of Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus in which the sufferings of the martyrs were read. Some trifler attached to that lost letter letters composed by himself. Cassiodorus’s words are these:

> Therefore, remembering future blessedness, read constantly the lives of the Fathers, the confessions of the faithful, and the sufferings of the martyrs—these, among other places, you will undoubtedly find in the letter of Saint Jerome addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus—who flourished throughout the entire world, so that holy imitation, prompting you, may lead you to heavenly things.

Do you see that martyrs were listed in Jerome’s letter itself? Therefore it was different from the Martyrology, and considerably longer, appended as it was to a very short letter, as happens today.

For this reason I do not think that the single letter of Jerome praised by Cassiodorus is the letters of Chromatius, Heliodorus, and Jerome that now survive. Tillemontius nevertheless held this view, together with Henricus Valesius, in volume XII, pp. 354–355.

Bede, in his commentary on Mark, book II, chapter 26, and in chapter 6 of his *Retractation* on the Acts of the Apostles, praises Saint Jerome’s Martyrology. But Joannes Mabillon, in the preface to the fourth-century, part II, of the *Acta Sanctorum Benedictina*, p. LXXXV, considers it uncertain whether Jerome wrote any Martyrology.

The opinions of Cassiodorus and Bede nevertheless seem to be supported by the Litany collected from the book that Blessed Jerome wrote concerning the birthdays of the saints throughout the year, among Alcuin’s works, p. 280, although certain saints more recent than Jerome may have been added there by copyists, as was customary.

Valesius, in his dissertation on Rosweyd’s Martyrology, thinks that the Hieronymian Martyrology is mentioned by Gregory the Great in book VII, letter 21.

Jacobus Usserius, in the conclusion of chapter 2 of his *Sacred Chronology*, does not doubt that Jerome translated Eusebius’s Martyrology into Latin, just as he translated the *Chronicle*. He believes that this Martyrology, later expanded by Usuard, Ado, and others, always retained on 25 December the number of years established by Eusebius from the creation of the world to the Nativity of Christ.

From this, the use of Eusebian chronology spread throughout the entire Western Church, without any loss of Hebrew truth; for in the *Chronicle* itself Eusebius had carefully recorded the calculation of the Hebrew manuscripts alongside his own and had set forth the sequence of the years of the world as reckoned by the Hebrews through fifty Jubilees.

This is more or less Usserius’s view.

Learned men have observed that three manuscripts of the Hieronymian Martyrology survive, although they were expanded after Jerome himself.

Bollandus praises the first in volume I of the January acts, p. 46. The second, which Mabillon judged to have been written eight hundred years ago in his *Italian Journey*, p. 188, was published by Florentinus at Lucca in A.D. 1666. The third, from the Corbie manuscript, was published by Lucas Dacherius in the *Spicilegium*, volume IV, p. 617.

At this point it should not be left unmentioned that the Anonymous author of *On Ecclesiastical Courses*—by which name our forefathers designated the fixed prayers of the Church that must be run through and recited each day under the name of the Breviary—is said by Anonymus, in Henricus Spelmannus’s *Councils of Britain*, volume I, p. 177, to have attributed the origin of the Eastern Course to Chromatius and Heliodorus.

Holstenius, writing in the margin of Spelmannus’s copy in the Angelica Library, noted from Usserius that the manuscript of this Anonymous author was nine hundred years old.

Mabillon, in his inquiry into the Gallican Course, p. 380, inferred from the style that the author was a Briton or Scot, and judged that he confused the Course with the liturgy.

Nothing else concerning this Course of our Chromatius is found anywhere.

## VIII.

Other letters of Chromatius and Heliodorus to Jerome, and of Jerome to them, must also be assigned to the same category of false wares. Idle men sought through their authority to give value to the little works *On the Origin or Lineage of Mary* and *On the Infancy of the Savior*, which Pope Gelasius I formerly listed among the apocrypha.

We have defended Gelasius’s decree concerning books to be received elsewhere and have published it in an authentic form.

Joannes Albertus Fabricius included these same letters, covered with critical notes, in the first volume of his *Codex Apocryphorum*, printed at Hamburg in A.D. 1703. They are also found among the works of Saint Jerome in the Roman edition of A.D. 1572, volume IX, p. 398, and in volume V, p. 444, of the Paris edition of Joannes Martianaeus, published in 1706 by Claudius Rigaud.

Vossius likewise rejects them in book II, chapter 11, of *On Latin Historians*.

It is worth hearing the judgment of the most distinguished Melchior Cano from book XI, chapter 6, of *On Theological Places*:

> Of this kind is also that silly and equally barbarous fable, *On the Nativity of Saint Mary*, addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops.

Sixtus of Siena, in book II of the *Bibliotheca*, while discussing Matthew, wholly denies the work to Jerome; Baronius does the same in his *Apparatus*, section 44.

Finally, consult Christophorus a Castro, *History of the Virgin Mother of God*, p. 704 of the Mainz edition of 1610; and Rosweyd, in his *Lex Talionis for Baronius*, p. 106, against Casaubon, *Exercitation* I, chapter 15. Rosweyd does indeed list the work among the fabulous writings, but considers it different from the work that ancient heretics fabricated on the same subject. This matters little, provided it is not attributed to Jerome; certainly no person of sound judgment attributes it to him.

Petrus Wastelius, in volume II, book II, pp. 419 and 423, of his *Vindications of John of Jerusalem*, contends that ninety homilies of Chromatius lie hidden among the works of John Chrysostom in the Latin editions—the Basel edition of Erasmus and the Paris edition of Chevallon.

For the moment Wastelius offers no proof stronger than the contracted word “Chr.” that supported his claim. This abbreviation, first written in the margins of manuscripts, was later applied by copyists to designate Chrysostom, a Greek and therefore more celebrated figure, instead of Chromatius, a Latin writer. Hence the ignorant attributed Chromatius’s homilies to Chrysostom.

This is the whole basis of Wastelius’s opinion. But the good man failed to notice that these homilies on Matthew really are Chrysostom’s, translated into Latin by Annianus, a Pelagian deacon of Celeda, with a letter added to Orontius, a bishop expelled from Italy on account of the same heresy and later condemned at the Council of Ephesus.

Georgius Trapezuntius later published them after interpolating them. Annianus also translated Chrysostom’s letter to the Neophytes and seven homilies on the praises of Paul, which he dedicated to Evangelius, a Pelagian presbyter. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, volume VII, p. 645.

## 137. Works of Saint Chromatius

### I. Extant

Eighteen homilies on Matthew.

### II. Lost

Letters to the holy Ambrose, Jerome, and John Chrysostom, and to the Augusti Honorius and Arcadius.

[Note: Fontanini mentions these only among the lost works of Saint Chromatius. In our list of lost works, however, we have mentioned above, on the basis of substantial conjectures, several others as well, p. 97.]

### III. Spurious

Two letters to Saint Jerome.

*(Thus far Fontanini.)*

## 139. From the Monuments of the Church of Aquileia, Illustrated in a Commentary

By Fr. Bernardo Maria de Rubeis of the Order of Preachers. Strasbourg (or Venice), 1740.

## Chapter X

Valerian dies; Chromatius is chosen: was he ordained by Saint Ambrose? His homeland is investigated. He obtains from Ambrose an interpretation of Balaam’s prophecy, and Jerome dedicates to him and to Heliodorus of Altinum a Latin translation of several books of Sacred Scripture and commentaries. Rufinus returns from his journey in the East to Rome, where he translates Origen’s *On First Principles* into Latin. A quarrel begins with Jerome; Rufinus requests Aquileia. Chromatius induces him to translate Eusebius’s history into Latin. The first invasion of Italy by Alaric, king of the Goths.

### I.

We have reached the time when Valerian, exhausted and weakened by the very many labors he had undergone for Aquileia and the universal Church, exchanged mortal life for eternal life. The memory of this most holy prelate is celebrated on 27 November in the calendars of the Church.

Dandulus assigns the year of his death as 388 in his *Chronicle*. In the same work he reports that Chromatius succeeded him in these words:

> Chromatius is consecrated bishop of Aquileia in the year of the Lord 388. By birth he was a Spaniard; he had been ordained deacon by his predecessor Valerian, later ordained presbyter, and educated in Catholic disciplines. With the acclaim of clergy and people, he obtained this see.

The ancient records by which this chronology could be confirmed with certainty are lacking. But we know that Ambrose was staying at Aquileia at the end of that year, or even at the beginning of 389. From this one may conjecture that the most holy Bishop went to that city for the election of the new bishop.

Paulinus first informs us of this in his *Life of Ambrose*, no. 21:

> After Maximus had been destroyed, Theodosius had been established as emperor at Milan, while Bishop Ambrose was staying at Aquileia. Ambrose himself sent a letter to the emperor—which in the Nourrian edition is letter XL—to recall him from his decision concerning the rebuilding of a certain Jewish synagogue by the bishop of Callinicum Castrum, and concerning the punishment of the monks who, after being provoked by an insult, had burned a shrine of the Valentinian heretics.

From the Theodosian Code we can establish with certainty that the Emperor Augustus Theodosius had not yet departed from Aquileia on 20 September 388, and that he had already arrived at Milan on 10 October of the same month. He remained in that city until the following May.

Thus Ambrose was staying at Aquileia at the end of 388, or at the beginning and opening of 389, and there he sent the aforementioned letter to the Emperor Theodosius.

Reflecting on this, Baronius says under the year 388, no. 84:

> Since Ambrose was being detained at Aquileia, although there is no record that a council was held there at this time, I believe that he went there, as was customary, for the creation of a new bishop, when Saint Chromatius was substituted in that city for Valerian, its deceased bishop.

I do not consider this conjecture groundless.

That an ancient custom was ordinarily observed in the ordination of a bishop both at Aquileia and at Milan is shown by Pope Pelagius I in a fragment of his first letter, written in A.D. 557 or the following year to Narses, which Lucas Holstenius published in these words:

> It was an ancient custom that, because the distance or difficulty of the journey made it burdensome for them to be ordained by the Apostolic See, the bishops of Milan and Aquileia should ordain one another. In this way the election of the person to be ordained could be recognized more properly and easily by the present ordaining bishop, with the consent of the universal Church over which he was to be placed; and the person who was to be promoted to the episcopate, although he was not to be subject to his ordainer, could be ordained in his own Church.

But did this custom, which Pelagius I calls ancient a full century and a half later, perhaps originate in this period? We know that Ambrose went to Aquileia, and no other reason for his journey presents itself except the election and ordination of the new Bishop.

## II.

Dandulus calls Chromatius, the new bishop of Aquileia, Spanish by birth. Saint Jerome, in a letter addressed to Chromatius himself, Jovinus, and Eusebius, speaks to them as follows:

> “Through you the poison of the formerly Arian doctrine has been expelled from your city.”

The city meant is Aquileia, where, at that time, Chromatius was a presbyter under Bishop Valerian, Jovinus an archdeacon, and Eusebius a deacon. He calls it “your” city when addressing them because they were occupied with sacred offices in the Church of that city. Why should he not also be indicating their place of origin? In the same letter Jerome commends the household, family, mother, and sisters of Chromatius. He therefore knew them well, and it seems unlikely that he could have known them elsewhere, or have enjoyed their companionship, except at Aquileia or in its immediate vicinity.

Marianus Victorius thinks that Chromatius’s homeland was a place not far from Stridon, Jerome’s native city. I propose another conjecture, based on the title prefixed to Chromatius’s works in certain editions. They are there entitled, “The minor works of Chromatius, Bishop of Rome.” Others think that we should read, “Bishop of Cumae,” and they search in various provinces of the world for a place bearing that name where this Chromatius—whom they consider different from the Aquileian Chromatius—might have held a see.

To Baronius, “Roman” and “Aquileian” bishop are equivalent. In his notes on 22 June and 2 December in the Martyrology, he holds that Aquileia was at times called the Roman, Romacian, or Romanician city. We shall reject this view below. Finally, there is Portus Romatius, concerning which Pliny writes in Book III, chapter 18, under Venetia, the tenth region of Italy:

> “The colony of Concordia, and the river and harbor Romatium.”

We also read of Portus Romatinus, a town—today called Porto Gruaro by its inhabitants—on the river Romatium, commonly called the Lemene, near the destroyed city of Concordia. Why, then, should Chromatius not have been called Romanus, or rather Romatius and Romatinus from his homeland, while being bishop of Aquileia?

### III.

Chromatius took the greatest pleasure in the study of the Sacred Scriptures, which he himself illuminated with commentaries. He also consulted the highly learned men Ambrose and Jerome and induced them to prepare commentaries and a new Latin version. He asked Ambrose to send him, in the course of their friendly correspondence, some discussion drawn from the sacred books. The bishop of Milan complied, choosing a subject from the prophecy of Balaam.

He therefore sent Chromatius Letter 50 in the Nourrian edition. In section 16 we read these words:

> “I have sent this little gift to your holy mind, since you wish me to put something into pages concerning the interpretations of the ancient writers.”

Ambrose remembers his advanced age:

> “I prefer,” he says, “to speak with you in senile words about heavenly matters,”

that is, to speak and write things slight and far inferior. Nourrius thinks that this letter was sent by the aged Ambrose around the year 390.

In the same scholarly undertaking Chromatius had as his companion Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum. Around the same time both of them urged Jerome to work out a new Latin version of Tobit. Jerome reveals the prayers and prompting of both men in the preface to that version:

> “I cannot cease to marvel at the persistence of your demands. For you require me to bring into Latin style a book written in the Chaldean language—the book, of course, of Tobit. . . . I have satisfied your desire.”

Not long afterward, around the year 391—I follow Tillemont’s calculations—the same bishops requested commentaries on the prophecies of Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi, supplying the money necessary for the expenses. In place of these Jerome sent them, and dedicated to them by name, a Latin version of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

The words of the most holy teacher are these:

> “You request commentaries on Hosea, Amos, and Zechariah, and also on Malachi. I would have written them, if illness had allowed it. You send assistance for the expense. . . . Therefore, broken by a long illness, lest I remain entirely silent this year and be mute before you, I consecrated to your name a work of three days: namely, the interpretation of the three books of Solomon, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.”

We also read that Jerome dedicated to Chromatius two books of Commentaries on the Prophet Habakkuk. He begins the prologue of the first book with these words:

> “First, most learned of bishops, Chromatius, we must know, and so forth.”

The beginning of the second is:

> “We are writing a second book on Habakkuk, my venerable father Chromatius.”

Chromatius himself had requested the historical and literal sense of this prophecy, as Jerome testifies in the prologue to the first book:

> “You forcibly demand from me that I interpret the history for you . . .”

Jerome lists these books among his works in the final chapter of *On Illustrious Men*, where he records the works he had written up to the present year, that is, the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius. The fourteenth year of Theodosius falls in the common era year 392 and begins on 19 January, according to Pagius. The date of the Commentaries on the Prophet Habakkuk can therefore be determined.

Finally, at Chromatius’s request Jerome prepared a Latin version of the *Paralipomenon* [Greek: τῶν, “of the”], and dedicated it to him as bishop of Aquileia. In the preface he addresses him as follows:

> “If the pure edition of the Seventy Interpreters, as it was translated by them into Greek, had remained intact, you would be urging me in vain, most holy and learned of bishops, Chromatius, to translate the Hebrew books into Latin.”

In the same place the holy Father says that he had recently written a book *On the Best Kind of Translation*. That epistolary work, addressed to Pammachius, belongs, according to Tillemont, to the year 396. This book, therefore, described as recently written, was followed in the same year or the next by the version of the *Paralipomena*.

These are the illustrious testimonies to the learning in which Chromatius flourished. We also learn that he was Jerome’s principal encouragement to undertake the outstanding labor of producing a Latin version of the Hebrew books and to place the finishing hand upon the work already begun.

Jerome himself celebrates Chromatius as a man of lofty spirit in the epitaph for Nepotianus, written to Heliodorus around the year 396. There we read that Eusebius, Chromatius’s brother, had died; and that, at his death, Chromatius displayed the strength of mind which Jerome proposes for Heliodorus to imitate.

### IV.

After leaving the East, Rufinus came to Rome. While he was living there, urged on by the advice and prayers of Macarius, a man devoted to learning, he translated Origen’s *Apology* from Greek into Latin and published it under the name of the martyr Pamphilus.

In works subsequently written against Rufinus, Jerome openly withdrew what he had earlier written in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. He insisted that the work should be attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea, or to another of Origen’s followers. Nevertheless, this opinion could not persuade certain critical scholars, who regard most of the *Apology* as the unquestionably genuine product of the martyr Pamphilus. This took place in the year 397.

In the following year, at the urging and under the advice of the aforementioned Macarius, Rufinus rendered into Latin the books *On First Principles* [Greek: περὶ ἀρχῶν], with a preface in which he adorns Jerome with extraordinary praise. He warns the reader that in his Latin version he has entirely omitted whatever he had judged in those books to be corrupted or foreign, or else has rendered it according to the rule which he had frequently found Origen himself establishing in his other works. Finally, he says that several passages expressed obscurely by the author have been explained in clearer language.

From this arose the apple of discord, which inflamed the once very close friendship between Jerome and Rufinus. It also moved Chromatius, who was deeply attached to both men, to reconcile them by restoring their bond of friendship.

### V.

I shall now relate the beginning of the disagreement, by which these highly celebrated men were provoked to fall into quarrels and to attack one another in published letters and pamphlets.

Their mutual affection had already grown cold in the East. Jerome had begun to reject as hostile to the Christian faith the doctrines of Origen, which John of Jerusalem and Rufinus seemed to value highly. A certain Aterbius was persecuting Rufinus in Jerusalem on this account. The holy Father himself, who was being judged a heretic because of his friendship with Rufinus, wished to profess his orthodoxy openly and publicly by condemning the doctrines of Origen—whose learning and devotion to Scripture he had formerly praised in his youth, before he had come to know the heresy more fully.

At the same time Epiphanius, who had come to Jerusalem, rebuked John, the bishop of that city, because he offered support to Origen’s teaching and maintained his friendship with Rufinus. Taking this opportunity, Jerome quarreled with both men. The disagreement, however, did not grow. He restored his former friendship with Rufinus, and the two joined hands. Jerome himself relates all this in Book III against Rufinus.

The smoldering fires of the disagreement were fanned by Rufinus’s Latin translation of the books *On First Principles*, which he had prepared at Rome. Most people detested the work because they feared that it would become a stumbling block to others, and they accused the Latin translator.

At that time Jerome says in the *Epitaph for Marcella*, addressed to Principia, that Rufinus had brought into the Roman harbor a ship full of blasphemies. To avoid the complaints of his opponents—including Eusebius of Cremona, Pammachius, and Marcella—Rufinus decided to go to Aquileia. He obtained from Pope Siricius an ecclesiastical letter by which, according to the custom of that age, testimony was given concerning the orthodox faith of those traveling in distant lands. Jerome, for his part, thought that Rufinus had deceived the simplicity of Siricius.

Siricius died in the year 398, on 26 November, as Pagius and others establish. Rufinus therefore had withdrawn from Rome shortly before that date. He passed through Milan, where Simplicianus governed the Church. There, Rufinus himself testifies in Book I of his *Invectives against Jerome*, he had a dispute with the aforementioned Eusebius concerning a certain proposition in the books *On First Principles*.

At last he reached Aquileia either at the end of 398 or at the beginning of 399. Jerome, informed of all this more reliably by his friends, sent a letter to Pammachius and Oceanus. In it he clearly explains with what disposition he had read and praised Origen, refutes the slanders of his rivals, dispels people’s suspicions, and exposes many of Origen’s errors.

He sent another letter to Rufinus, whom he gravely and seriously admonishes that he does not wish to be praised because of Origen, whose evil doctrines he detested, and that it would be better for Rufinus to preserve the laws of their restored friendship. Finally, the holy Father undertook a new Latin translation of the books *On First Principles*, so that a careful and faithful new version might expose the errors which the author had taught.

Rufinus was driven into a fury. In that same year he began composing two books of *Invectives* against Jerome. In them he attempts not only to refute, with a sharper pen, the letter addressed to Pammachius and Oceanus, a copy of which he had received from his friend Apronianus, but also to assail the commentaries of the outstanding teacher on Holy Scripture with barbed criticisms.

### VI.

Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, was distressed that men very dear to him, whose bond of affection had kept them united for so many years, had broken their alliance and, moved by anger, rushed into mutual conflict.

He tried to turn Rufinus’s mind and pen toward another subject, and he assigned him the task of translating Eusebius’s Greek history into Latin.

Rufinus obeyed. The following words from his preface deserve attention:

> “It is said to be the characteristic of skilled physicians that, when they see general diseases threatening cities or regions, they provide some kind of medicine or drink by which people, having been fortified, may be protected from the impending destruction. You too, venerable Father Chromatius, carrying out this kind of medical treatment, at a time when, after the barriers of Italy had been broken through by Alaric, leader of the Goths, a pestilential disease had spread and devastated fields, herds, and people far and wide, sought some remedy for deadly destruction for the peoples entrusted to you by God. Through it, diseased minds might be withdrawn from the contagion of the threatening evil and kept occupied with better studies. You therefore impose upon me the task of translating into Latin the ecclesiastical history which the most learned Eusebius of Caesarea composed in Greek. By reading it, the minds of the audience would be captivated while they eagerly sought knowledge of past events and would in some measure receive forgetfulness of the evils then taking place.”

Rufinus completed the task assigned to him, adding two books to Eusebius’s history, which he composed by his own effort. Yet, while preparing this work, he did not become gentler toward Jerome. He was laboring at the same time over the books of *Invectives* that he had begun to compose, and he published them in the year 401.

### VII.

Rufinus’s words present the first invasion of Italy by Alaric, king of the Goths, and disclose the time and year when Rufinus himself was working on his translation of Eusebius’s history.

Prosper, in his chronicle, under the consulship of Stilicho and Aurelian, who began the year 400 of the Christian era, writes:

> “The Goths entered Italy under the leadership of Alaric and Radagaisus.”

Likewise, under the fifth consulship of Arcadius and the fifth of Honorius, in the year of Christ 402:

> “A fierce battle was fought against the Goths at Pollentia, with the defeat of both sides. Pollentia was a town of Liguria. Alaric then migrated into Pannonia.”

Many deny that Radagaisus invaded together with Alaric. Others think that Alaric returned to Pannonia in the advanced part of the year 401 and invaded Italy again in the following year. They also defer the battle at Pollentia to the year 403 and assign Radagaisus’s entry to the following year, so that he too might test the regions of Italy.

But, by general agreement against Baronius, Alaric’s first invasion is now usually assigned to the year 400 of the Christian era. Jordanes describes it in *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 29, in these words:

> “As soon, therefore, as the aforementioned Alaric had been made king, he deliberated with his people and urged them to seek a kingdom through their own labor rather than remain subject to others in idleness. Having gathered an army, he entered Italy through Pannonia, when Stilicho and Aurelian were consuls, passing through Sirmium on the right, as though through a land empty of men. The first region to suffer his fury was lower Venetia, which was afterward called the province of Forum Julii. There the Gothic king devastated fields, herds, and people far and wide, and threatened the peoples entrusted by God to Chromatius with deadly destruction.”

Thus, in the year 400, at the command of Chromatius, Rufinus undertook and completed a Latin version of the ecclesiastical history composed by Eusebius.

# CHAPTER XI

## On the condemnation of Origen, and Rufinus himself being accused, writes an apology. Theophilus of Alexandria, Anastasius of Rome, Venerius of Milan, and Chromatius of Aquileia condemn Origen’s doctrines. The pontiff distinguishes Origen’s case from Rufinus’s and reserves Rufinus for divine judgment. Jerome’s statements are explained. The pamphlet of recantation published under Rufinus’s name is taken away from him. A conjecture concerning its author.

### I.

For a long time a question had been under discussion in the East against Origen’s teaching, and Theophilus of Alexandria was pressing for its condemnation. The same case was being pursued at Rome, where it had been provoked by the Latin version of the books *On First Principles* which Rufinus had prepared.

Rufinus himself was being accused. Then witnesses were brought forward—Jerome’s words in the *Epitaph for Marcella* are these—who had first been instructed by Rufinus and his followers and afterward had been seized by heretical error. A multitude of deceived persons was exhibited, people who, being insufficiently cautious, read the books translated into Latin. The impious volumes of *On First Principles* were also brought forward, shown as corrected by the hand of the scorpion—that is, Rufinus.

So that the crime, if there was one, might not go unpunished, the heretics—this is the name applied to Rufinus and his followers—were summoned to Rome by repeated letters, but did not dare to come. Indeed, Rufinus himself fled the judgment of the Roman city so completely—these are Jerome’s words in Book III against Rufinus, section 21—that he preferred to endure a barbarian siege rather than the sentence of a peaceful city. Jerome means Alaric’s invasion, when Alaric entered Italy, occupied the fields of Aquileia, and laid them waste.

Because Rufinus was distressed that his faith was being blackened, and because, having been summoned to Rome, he either could not or would not set out, he sent Anastasius, the Roman pontiff, a lengthy apology together with an explanation for his absence:

> “I have heard,” he says, “that when certain persons were raising controversies before Your Beatitude, whether concerning the faith or concerning I know not what other questions, they also mentioned my name. Your Holiness, however, instructed as you are from your very beginnings by the rules of ecclesiastical tradition, did not lend an ear to those who were slandering an absent man whom you knew well both in faith and in the charity of God.
>
> “Nevertheless, since the report of the reputation they were attacking has reached me, I thought it right that, since I myself have been restored to my parents after almost thirty years, and since it would be harsh and inhuman to abandon so quickly those whom I had revisited so late—and also because the hardship of so long a journey has made me more fragile for undertaking further labors—I should satisfy Your Beatitude by my letter. I do not do this to wipe away a stain of suspicion from your holy mind, which, like a sanctuary of God, admits nothing unjust, but to offer you, against those who bark at me out of rivalry, a kind of staff of my confession with which they might be driven away.”

He then gives an exposition of his faith and declares in eloquent language what he believes concerning the Trinity, the Incarnation of the Word of God, the Resurrection, the judgment of the devil, and the origin of souls. Finally, he professes that he is Origen’s translator, not his defender, although he had rendered certain of Origen’s works into Latin.

### II.

Meanwhile Theophilus of Alexandria had prohibited the faithful from reading Origen’s books, and Anastasius had done the same at Rome. We learn both facts from the pontiff’s letter to Simplicianus, certainly the bishop of Milan, which Dominicus Vallarsius was the first to publish, previously unknown, in his Veronese edition of the works of Saint Jerome.

We read:

> “Theophilus, our brother and fellow bishop, does not cease to watch over the interests of salvation, lest the people of God, by reading Origen in various churches, fall into great blasphemies. . . . We too, being placed in the city of Rome . . . have condemned what we have mentioned, so that no one may read it contrary to our command. Holding to this command, we have judged whatever was written long ago by Origen contrary to our faith to be alien to us and subject to punishment.”

The Milanese records place Simplicianus’s death on 15 August of the year 400. The date of the letter can therefore now be determined.

In the same year, at a synod convened by Theophilus at Alexandria, a more solemn condemnation of Origen was issued. It is contained in the encyclical letters addressed to the bishops of Palestine and Cyprus. The aforementioned Vallarsius published them from a very ancient manuscript in the Ambrosian Library at Milan, formerly belonging to Saint Columbanus of Bobbio. After examining several difficulties, he reconciles calculations that seem to conflict with the chronology.

Anastasius, moved with equal fervor against Origen, proscribed Origen’s doctrines and sent the sentence of condemnation to Venerius, who had succeeded Simplicianus in the see of Milan. Anastasius himself testifies to this in a letter which he sent to John of Jerusalem in the year 401:

> “Moved by this matter, you will be able to establish from what follows what sort of letter our littleness sent to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius, written with the greatest care.”

That letter has been lost or still lies hidden in the shelves of libraries.

That Chromatius of Aquileia also approved, in spirit, the sentence of condemnation pronounced against Origen together with Anastasius and Venerius is most clearly attested by Jerome in Book II against Rufinus, section 22:

> “The blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, and Chromatius, and every Catholic synod of both East and West . . . with one judgment, and therefore with one spirit, declare him [Origen] a heretic before the peoples.”

### III.

When John of Jerusalem had received this information, he consulted Anastasius by letter as to whether Rufinus should be condemned because of the often-mentioned books *On First Principles*, which he had translated from Greek into Latin.

Anastasius replied to John in the year 401. He distinguishes Origen’s case from Rufinus’s and reserves the latter for divine judgment. I gather the pontiff’s meaning from the same letter, which Petrus Constantius carefully examined and elucidated in volume I of *The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, rejecting the edition and interpretation of Joannes Garnerius.

In sections 2 and 3 it reads:

> “Rufinus, concerning whom you have deemed it worthy to consult me, has the divine Majesty as judge of his conscience. Before that Majesty he must himself see, with the whole duty of his devotion, how he ought to approve himself. But who Origen was, and into what statements he proceeded, the fact that his writings have been rendered into our language does not concern our present purpose.
>
> “Since, however, I shall briefly discuss with Your Holiness the disposition of my mind concerning this matter, I have conceived the following thought, which the reading of Origen’s translated works has disclosed to the people of our city: that he wished, as though a fog of blindness had been cast over pure minds, to dissolve the faith established by the tradition of the Apostles and our forefathers, as if through winding and devious paths.”

That is, Anastasius teaches that Origen’s case is one thing and Rufinus’s another. He considers it necessary to leave it to Rufinus’s conscience before the divine Majesty to decide how he translated Origen into Latin; thus Anastasius suspends judgment concerning Rufinus.

The following words concerning Origen convey this sense:

> “Since our subject concerns the name of Rufinus, about whom alone you have consulted me, it is therefore not our purpose to investigate who Origen was. Nevertheless, I shall briefly disclose the disposition of my mind, my feeling toward him, and my judgment concerning him. The reading of his translated books has made clear that he wished, by casting a fog of blindness over pure minds, to dissolve the faith which the tradition of the Apostles and our forefathers confirms.”

Thus the man whom Anastasius says wished to dissolve the Christian faith is Origen, not Rufinus. At this point, as though in passing and outside his immediate subject, he indicates to John of Jerusalem what he himself thinks of Origen.

In section 4 Anastasius returns to Rufinus:

> “At this point it is useful to learn what this translation [the translation of Origen’s books prepared by Rufinus] contributes to the Roman language.”

Receive the pontiff’s judgment:

> “I approve it if it accuses the author and exposes his detestable deed to the peoples, so that he may at last be held by a just hatred, since reputation had long ago bound him. But if the translator gives his assent to such great evils and publishes them for the peoples to read, he has built nothing by his labor except this: that, as though by the judgment of his own mind, he might overthrow under the title of an unexpected assertion that faith which alone, which first, and which among Catholic Christians has been held true from the Apostles down to the present time.”

Here Anastasius again condemns without ambiguity the doctrines of Origen that were being exposed in Rufinus’s Latin translation. But no absolute condemnation of Rufinus appears. The Roman pontiff speaks hypothetically. He approves Rufinus if the translator condemns the author and detests his wicked doctrines; he pronounces anathema if Rufinus gives his assent to Origen’s doctrines rendered into Latin.

Anastasius uses the same strategy in section 5, where he first condemns Origen for manifold error and shows himself less concerned about Rufinus’s conscience and intentions:

> “Far be this from the Catholic discipline of the Roman Church. It will certainly never happen that we admit in any way those things which we justly and deservedly condemn. Therefore, through the providence of Christ our God spread throughout the whole world, he will deign to approve that we cannot accept at all things which stain the Church, overturn approved customs, wound the ears of those around us, and arrange quarrels, anger, and dissensions. These are the detestable kinds of Origen’s doctrines.
>
> “Moved by this matter, you will be able to establish from what follows what sort of letter our littleness sent to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius, written with the greatest care.”

The letter sent to Venerius is said to have been written with greater diligence, so that it may be distinguished from the shorter letter which Anastasius had sent to Simplicianus. In both letters, however, we know that Origen was condemned and that the faithful were forbidden to read his works.

Anastasius then returns to Rufinus:

> “Therefore, let him who translated it keep with himself whatever conscience he has; I do not labor under needless apprehension or trouble myself with empty fear.”

But the pontiff continues to declare his concern regarding Origen’s doctrines:

> “For my part, I shall certainly not lack concern to guard the faith of the Gospel among my peoples, and, as far as I can, to address by letter the members of my body scattered through the various regions of the earth, lest some origin of profane interpretation creep in and, having spread its darkness, attempt to shake devout minds.”

He had fulfilled his pastoral office both by prohibiting the reading of Origen and by condemning Origen’s doctrines. At the same time he was vigilant lest darkness introduced through the Latin translation shake simple and devout minds:

> “For this reason I could not remain silent about the further matter which I rejoice has occurred: that replies have come from our most blessed emperors, by which everyone serving God is recalled from reading Origen, and he whom the reading of profane things has exposed is condemned by the sentence of the emperors.”

The replies of Honorius and Arcadius followed the earlier prohibition issued by Theophilus of Alexandria and Pope Anastasius. Those imperial responses, however, have either been lost or remain unpublished.

Coustantius considers it probable that, after Origen had been condemned by Theophilus and his Alexandrian synod and the reading of his works had been prohibited, imperial edicts were issued at the request of the orthodox Fathers in order to deter the Origenists more forcefully.

Anastasius continues:

> “Thus far the form of my judgment has proceeded.”

As if he were saying: “Thus far I have explained what I think.”

Finally, in section 6 he says:

> “But since the complaint of the common people concerning Rufinus troubles you, so that you persecute certain persons more on the basis of suspicions, I shall restrain this opinion of yours by the example of divine Scripture, as it is written: ‘Man is not like God, for God sees the heart, while man sees the face.’”

Anastasius warns John not so readily to suspect of envy and ill will those who were accusing Rufinus’s Latin translation, since envy is an inward evil known only to the eyes of God:

> “Therefore, dearest Brother, putting aside every suspicion, consider Rufinus according to his own mind, whether he translated Origen’s statements into Latin and approved them; for he is not unlike the accused who gives assent to the vices of another.”

Just as in section 4 he had left the entire matter of Rufinus’s conscience unresolved, and before reaching any decision concerning him had wished to learn whether Rufinus accused the author whose translator he was or embraced the author’s errors by giving his assent, so now he urges John, freed from every suspicion, to strive to discover Rufinus’s intention:

> “I nevertheless want you to hold firmly that he is regarded by our side [by our region and the city of Rome] as foreign and distant—he was living at Aquileia—to such an extent that we neither wish to know what he is doing nor where he is.”

He had already said above that he did not wish to be anxious or concerned about Rufinus’s mind and intentions:

> “Let him himself see where he may be acquitted.”

This does not mean acquitted from a sentence already pronounced—there is no trace of such a sentence anywhere in the letter—but from the suspicions that were being circulated about him.

### IV.

Nothing, therefore, can rightly and justly be identified in Anastasius’s letter as signifying Rufinus’s condemnation. Nor should this letter be cited as an anathema pronounced against him according to the edition of Garnerius, since Coustantius warns that Garnerius introduced several alterations at his own discretion and adapted variant readings to a preconceived opinion.

If, therefore, Jerome says in the heat of debate that Rufinus had been condemned, his statement must be explained in a milder sense, in accordance with Anastasius’s intention, who wished judgment in this matter to remain suspended.

Jerome says in Book III against Rufinus, section 15:

> “How did Italy accept what Rufinus boasted that Rome had rejected? How did the bishops accept what the apostolic see had condemned?”

The holy Father says this concerning the apology that Rufinus had offered to Anastasius. Yet the apology is said to have been condemned because it was disregarded; and Pope Anastasius disregarded it because, in his letter to John of Jerusalem, he made no mention of it and did not wish to take any account of it.

The following words of Jerome are also brought forward, which we read in Book II against Rufinus, section 13:

> “If you do not wish to hear a brother admonishing you, hear a bishop condemning you.”

Likewise, in the *Epitaph for Marcella the Widow*, section 10:

> “The heretics—he means Rufinus and his followers—were summoned by repeated letters to defend themselves, but did not dare to come. Such was the force of conscience that they preferred to be condemned in their absence rather than be convicted in person.”

All these statements, and any similar ones, signify only this: after Origen had been condemned by Anastasius, all those who were entangled in his errors were regarded as struck by the same anathema. Jerome suspected this of Rufinus and his followers.

His intention is made clear by the words found in the same section 13 of Book II against Rufinus:

> “Why, when you are about to translate heretical works, do you place before them, in their defense, a book supposedly written by a martyr [Pamphilus]? And why do you thrust upon Roman ears what the whole world, once it had been translated, shuddered at? Or, if you translate it for the purpose of proving him a heretic, do not alter anything from the Greek, and testify to this very fact. Pope Anastasius, in the letter which he writes against you to Bishop John, most wisely expressed this in his own words: he acquits me, who did the work, and accuses you, who were unwilling to do so.”

Jerome is indicating the condemnation found in Anastasius’s letter—not an absolute condemnation, but a hypothetical one. In this, however, Jerome differs from Anastasius: Anastasius suspended judgment and transferred the interpretation Rufinus had made to the judgment of Rufinus’s own conscience; Jerome turns this into an unfavorable meaning and inclines toward a judgment of a guilty conscience.

### V.

Henricus Norisius produces, from the Vatican Library, a pamphlet of recantation in Book I, chapter 3 of his *Pelagian History*.
