In it Rufinus rejects some errors which he had asserted himself and others which had been attributed to him. Norisius thinks that Rufinus himself sang this recantation at Rome, after the death of Anastasius, before Innocent I, who was installed in his place and see in the year 401.

The title of the pamphlet is:

> “Beginning: For the faith.”

Its opening words are:

> “For the sake of reverence for the holy places, Jerusalem and Bethlehem, we came there, and we learned that several brothers were scandalized by us because they had heard that we professed many heretical doctrines and things contrary to the faith of the Church. Therefore, in the presence of God, we testify that the matters written below were partly held by us through error and are condemned by us at the present time; that in other matters, with which we are falsely defamed, we neither said nor say them; and that we have asserted and condemned the contrary of those things which we suspect in others.”

Twelve anathematisms follow, by which Origen’s doctrine is rejected and the heresies that arose from that source—those of Paul of Samosata, Arius, Apollinaris, and Photinus—are condemned. The pamphlet ends with these words:

> “The end: concerning the faith, in the name of Rufinus.”

Joannes Garnerius published the same pamphlet among the works of Marius Mercator, appended to the letter sent by Anastasius to John of Jerusalem. Its opening words are given as follows:

> “For the sake of reverence for the holy places, we came to Jerusalem and Bethlehem, and we learned that several brothers were scandalized by us.”

This is undoubtedly the sound reading; the earlier reading of Norisius cannot yield any coherent meaning. Yet Dominicus Vallarsius, in a report to the Ballerini brothers, also testifies that these words are read in the same form in the Vatican manuscript used by Norisius. At their request, Vallarsius carefully examined that manuscript while staying in Rome.

How, then, could Rufinus have written this pamphlet at Rome before Pope Innocent, in order to regain the favor of the apostolic see? The author of the pamphlet is said to have come to Jerusalem and Bethlehem for the sake of reverence for the holy places, and there to have condemned errors partly asserted by himself and partly attributed to him, in order to satisfy the brothers who were scandalized. This in no way fits Rufinus of Aquileia.

Two other men named Rufinus occur in the letters of Saint Jerome. One of them is the person concerning whom the holy Father writes in a letter addressed to Rufinus of Aquileia in the year 399:

> “My brother Paulinianus has not yet returned from his homeland, and I think that you saw him at Aquileia with the holy Pope Chromatius. We also sent the holy presbyter Rufinus to Rome and Milan for a certain matter, and we asked him to visit you as a representative of our mind and affection.”

This Rufinus was a disciple of Jerome, sent from the Bethlehem retreat to Italy to conduct some business.

A letter to another Rufinus of the same Jerome is extant; Dominicus Vallarsius establishes by several arguments that it was given in the preceding year, 398. In very many manuscript codices the heading reads “To Rufinus, a Roman presbyter”; and the words read in section 6 sufficiently prove that he had only recently become Jerome’s friend. For Jerome says:

> While lying sick in bed [Col. 0419B] and exhausted by a long illness, we dictated these very words to be written rapidly by a secretary, not to provide a complete treatment, but lest, when you were making some request of me at the beginning of our friendship (for you had asked for an exposition of Solomon’s Judgment), we should seem to refuse you.

If some Rufinus published the little book of recantation under discussion, he was perhaps not the other but rather the first of those whom we have seen sent by Jerome to the West. Nevertheless, we must admit that the opening words of the same little book do not fit him well or appropriately: they portray a man setting out for Jerusalem and Bethlehem out of veneration for the holy places. Can that Rufinus be called Jerome’s disciple who, sent from the Bethlehem retreat which he had long inhabited with Jerome in order to conduct some business in the West, was to return to that same retreat?

## VI.

John Mabillon reports in his *Italian Journey* that the same little book, discovered in the library of the Monastery of Bobbio, was found with this title:

> An abridgment of the Catholic faith, expounded by St. Jerome so that certain persons who had fallen into heresy might be corrected.

No one would say that the work is to be attributed to Jerome. But from the different title found in the manuscript codices, I could easily infer that it was not truly published by any Rufinus, but rather fabricated and falsely attributed by someone else who, in his leisure, had taken pleasure in gathering together Jerome’s teaching against the doctrines of Origen.

If you examine the anathemas of the little book with closer attention, you will recognize that it adopts a doctrine which Jerome approved, although in that age it was not regarded as certain by other Fathers of the Church [Col. 0419D]. The twelfth anathema reads:

> Let him be anathema who says that souls existed before they were born and are not made daily by God together with the body, after the example of the first man.

Jerome always adhered to this view: that individual rational souls are newly created when human beings are born. Rufinus of Aquileia, in his *Apology to Anastasius*, reports differing opinions on this subject:

> I hear, he says, that questions are being raised also about the soul . . . I have read that some say that, just as the body, the soul too is diffused through the transmission of human seed . . . Others assert that, once bodies have been formed in the womb, God makes souls daily and infuses them. Others say that souls were made long ago—that is [Col. 0420A], when God created all things from nothing—and that he now assigns them to bodies according to his judgment.

He testifies that he himself is doubtful and perplexed:

> But after reading all these opinions, I declare before God that, up to the present, I have no certain or definite position on this question.

No one is unaware of Augustine’s perplexity—or rather, of his sufficiently strong inclination toward the propagation of souls through transmission. Bellarmine thinks that this opinion was retracted by the holy Doctor in his letter to Optatus. He is plainly mistaken, since he admits in section 2 that Augustine never dared to offer a defined judgment on this question. In section 18 Augustine indeed accuses those who defend the propagation of souls of inconsiderate rashness—not because he thought that they were defending an erroneous opinion contrary to Scripture, but because they defended it more stubbornly [Col. 0420B] than was proper.

Meanwhile, Jerome held with the utmost constancy in *Against John of Jerusalem*, section 22:

> God fashions souls daily;

and in book 3 of *Against Rufinus*, section 28, he calls this an ecclesiastical dogma. The person who composed the aforementioned anathema defended this doctrine of Jerome’s and proposed that anathema should be pronounced against those who held the contrary view.

The first anathema also deserves attention. It reads:

> Let him be anathema who says that the Devil, demons, and the impious—that is, pagans, Jews, Samaritans, and all heretics—should at some time be spared and that their punishments are not eternal (with the exception of Christians who follow the true faith and are sinners).

The exception concerning Christians [Col. 0420C] who follow the true faith and nevertheless die in mortal guilt is contrary to Christian doctrine. It is sufficient to observe here that the aforesaid anathema, whether one considers its doctrine or merely its wording, has been taken from Jerome’s works. For in the final chapter of his *Commentary on Isaiah* he says:

> Just as we believe that there are eternal torments for the Devil and for all deniers and impious persons who said in their heart, “There is no God,” so we judge that the sentence of the Judge concerning sinners and impious persons who are nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified by fire, is measured and mingled with clemency.

[Col. 0420D] He writes similarly in *Dialogue 1 against the Pelagians*, section 28:

> But if Origen says that all rational creatures are not to be destroyed and attributes repentance to the Devil, what is that to us? We say that the Devil, his satellites, all the impious, and transgressors perish forever; and that Christians, if they have been overtaken in sin, are to be saved after their punishments.

I do not wish to debate Jerome’s meaning; if anyone wishes to interpret his words in a Catholic sense as referring to purgatorial punishments, I willingly and gladly agree. Nevertheless, I have established that the anathema under discussion was drawn from the doctrine and words of that same holy Father.

Why, then, could one not conjecture that someone, observing in book 3 of Jerome’s *Against Rufinus*, section 23, that the holy Father himself had once been judged a heretic by Aterbius because of his friendship with Rufinus, and that he had sufficiently satisfied Aterbius by condemning Origen’s doctrines [Col. 0421A], took this as an occasion to write a little book in which Jerome’s doctrine would be set forth and contrary doctrines struck down by anathema? Perhaps the idle author thought that Jerome could not have satisfied Aterbius in any other way than through a book of recantation containing the condemnation of Origen’s doctrines. Hence it was easy for the same little book to be attributed either to Jerome, as in the Bobbio Codex, or to Rufinus—whether Rufinus of Aquileia or Jerome’s disciple—as in other codices.

# CHAPTER XII

Augustine laments the rupture of the friendship between Jerome and Rufinus. Chromatius urges Jerome to silence. He favors Rufinus after enrolling him in the list of the Aquileian presbyters. Paulinus of Nola maintains a friendship with the same Rufinus. Rufinus dedicates his works to Chromatius, Gaudentius of Brescia, and others [Col. 0421B]. Chromatius energetically defends in the West the cause of John Chrysostom, driven from the see of Constantinople.

## I.

Meanwhile Rufinus and Jerome were fighting in written pamphlets. Rufinus published in 401 the two books of *Invectives* which he had begun in 399, against Jerome. Before reading them, but having heard portions of them only from the mouths of friends, the holy Father published a response in the following year, likewise divided into two books, entitled *Apology*. Rufinus replied with a letter and at the same time sent the books of invectives, to which Jerome opposed a third book of his *Apology*.

Augustine grieved over the rupture of their friendship. In letter 73 [Col. 0421C], otherwise 15, written around 404, he censures Rufinus’s barbed books and sets forth to Jerome the gentle sentiments of his own heart. He says in section 6:

> I do not know what malicious writings (Rufinus’s books of invectives) concerning your name have reached Africa. We have nevertheless received what you deigned to send in response to those insults. After reading it, I confess, I grieved greatly that such a great evil of discord had arisen between persons so dear and familiar, joined by the bond of friendship known to almost all the churches . . . Who would not fear a friend as a future enemy, if what we lament could have arisen between Jerome and Rufinus?

And in section 10:

> This is a great and sad wonder: that such friendships should have led to such enmities. It will be joyful, and a much greater wonder, if such enmities should return to their former concord.

## II.

Chromatius of Aquileia tried to instill a gentler disposition in Jerome; and by his admonition [Col. 0421D] he obtained that both men should refrain from new writings by which they might attack one another. He pressed Rufinus, who was present, by his authority to put an end to the quarrel; and Rufinus certainly did not reply to the third book of the *Apology* which Jerome had published. By letters also sent to Jerome, Chromatius secured the end of the conflict which he desired most vehemently.

The most holy man has left the matter attested in book 3 of *Against Rufinus*, section 2, where he gives as the reason for writing that book the fact that he had disregarded Chromatius’s admonition:

> I call Jesus as my witness that, at the admonition of the holy Pope Chromatius, I wished to remain silent, put an end to the quarrel, and [Col. 0422A] overcome evil with good. But because you threaten me with destruction unless I remain silent, I am compelled to reply, lest by keeping silent I seem to acknowledge the crime and lest you interpret my gentleness as a sign of an evil conscience.

Thereafter Jerome abstained from quarrel and writing, although when occasion arose he wrote about Rufinus not without contempt, whether Rufinus was still alive or already dead.

## III.

Chromatius never denied his communion and friendship with Rufinus; he counted and honored him among the beloved presbyters of the Aquileian Church. I explain this matter somewhat more fully because Henry Noris denies it. Rufinus, devoted to the monastic way of life and still a layman, departed from Aquileia after receiving baptism in 371 or the following year. According to Tillemont’s calculations, he had not yet been ordained presbyter in 386 [Col. 0422B], when Palladius, author of the *Lausiac History*, visited him, Jerome, and Melania in Jerusalem and Bethlehem. For Palladius says in chapter 3:

> With the elder Melania there also lived the most noble Rufinus, very like her in character and exceedingly courageous, from the city of Aquileia in Italy, who was later deemed worthy of the presbyterate [πρεσβυτερίου εἰς ὕστερον καταξιωθεὶς]; among human beings no one was found either more learned or gentler.

In the letter of St. Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem, which was given in 394 and translated into Latin by Jerome, we read that Rufinus was called a presbyter. Perhaps John, who held him in high esteem, ordained him presbyter. I have no doubt that he was ordained with the title of a monastery. This explains why the aforementioned Epiphanius writes in the same letter [Col. 0422C] that Paulinianus, the monk and brother of St. Jerome, was consecrated by him as a presbyter to celebrate the divine mysteries in the Bethlehem coenobium, because the holy presbyters Jerome and Vincentius, out of modesty and humility, were unwilling to perform the sacrifices owed to their rank. Christian Lupus discusses the various titles of ordination at length and with great distinction in his notes on canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon.

From Gennadius, an ancient writer, we can infer that after 398, when Rufinus had returned to his homeland and the city of Aquileia, Chromatius incorporated him into the Aquileian clergy outside the monastery’s enclosure. In chapter 17 of *Illustrious Men* Gennadius calls him “Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia.” Noris denies this. His words in book 1 of his *Pelagian History*, chapter 2, are [Col. 0422D]:

> Nor does he seem to have been enrolled in his clergy by Bishop Chromatius after his return; for shortly afterward he departed from there again, intending to return to the East.

I believe that this learned man is mistaken. It cannot be proved that Rufinus left Aquileia before 407, as will be explained below. Moreover, Tillemont demonstrates by the example of Paulinus of Nola that in that age clergy could be enrolled in the register of a church even if they did not maintain a permanent residence there. Paulinus says in letter 3, otherwise 45, to Alypius, section 4:

> Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, wished to claim me for his clergy, so that, although I lived in different places, I would be regarded as his presbyter.

## IV.

Not only Chromatius, but also many of the holiest men flourishing in that age [Col. 0423A], granted Rufinus ecclesiastical communion. They did not at all regard him as condemned by Anastasius, and they maintained their friendship with him. Several letters of Paulinus of Nola to him are extant. Here we may examine the one given by Lebrun as number 28, otherwise 9, to Sulpicius Severus. From it we learn that Severus had sent Paulinus a memorandum concerning several difficulties which he had encountered while composing his *Sacred History* and wished to have resolved; and that Paulinus had in turn forwarded this memorandum to Rufinus, so that Rufinus might explain Severus’s difficulties with the learning in which he excelled.

Paulinus celebrates Rufinus with this very ample eulogy [Col. 0423B]:

> Moreover, you ordered me—flattering yourself too lavishly about your poor dependent—to teach you what had escaped you from the annals not of one nation but of the human race, as though I were the more knowledgeable . . . Yet what I did not possess from my own resources, I sought from the richer treasury of my like-minded brother; and the very annotation that you had sent in place of a memorandum, inserted into my letter, I forwarded to Rufinus the presbyter, the spiritual companion of the holy Melania in her life, truly holy and devoutly learned, and for that reason joined to me by intimate affection. If he does not explain the causes of the incongruous reckoning of years or reigns which rightly trouble you—he who is rich in both scholarly and salutary letters, sacred and humane, in Greek as well as Latin—I fear that we shall seek in vain for anyone else in these regions [of Italy] who can do so.

The mention of the elder Melania, with whom Rufinus had spent several years pursuing the spiritual life in Egypt and Jerusalem [Col. 0423C], seems to indicate the return of that most devout widow to Italy. In the following letter to the same Severus, Paulinus pursues Rufinus’s praises at great length and relates that he had received her as a guest when she returned from Jerusalem after five lustra. Here Paulinus counts twenty-five years of her residence in Jerusalem, whereas Palladius in the *Lausiac History* counts twenty-seven.

The Benedictine editors of St. Augustine’s works, volume 2, in their preface; Lebrun in his new edition of the works of St. Paulinus of Nola; and Tillemont in note 2 to the *Life of St. Melania* assign Melania’s return to the year 402. We know that Pagi opposed them; his view is that Rufinus, together with Melania, both undertook the journey to the East and migrated back to Italy. We accept the calculations of the earlier *Chronography*, which Peter and Jerome Ballerini, Veronese presbyters, vigorously defend and establish with several arguments in book 1 of their *Observations on the Work of Henry Noris*, chapter 2, section 5 [Col. 0423D].

Accordingly, Paulinus adorns the aforementioned Rufinus with this eulogy after the great disturbances that had been stirred up against him at Rome. Confirmation is supplied by the date of the composition of Sulpicius Severus’s *Sacred History*. Severus had intended to carry it down to the consulship of Stilicho, that is, to the year 400 of Christ, as he says in book 2. In that year, therefore, Severus was preparing his history and completed it one or two years later; and at approximately the same time Paulinus sent Rufinus the memorandum concerning the difficulties Severus had encountered [Col. 0424A], so that he might resolve the doubts troubling the mind and spirit of their mutual friend.

## V.

Rufinus devoted his labor and his life to translating Origen’s homilies on Sacred Scripture into Latin and to composing other works on his own initiative. He dedicated these works to distinguished men whose friendship and companionship he enjoyed. He presented Chromatius of Aquileia with his Latin translation of the homilies on the book of Joshua. In the dedicatory letter—which is falsely attributed to Jerome in printed editions—he addresses him in these words:

> Since you too, then, my ever-venerable father Chromatius, charge and command us to contribute something from the resources and riches of the Greeks toward the edification and construction of the holy tabernacle, I have rendered into Latin, according to the smallness of my abilities, the twenty-six little discourses on Jesus Nave which the elder Adamantius delivered extemporaneously in church [Col. 0424B].

He compares Chromatius himself to Bezalel, whom Divine Scripture in Exodus chapter 31 relates to have been filled with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every work for the construction of the tabernacle.

We also possess works dedicated by the same Rufinus to Heraclius, whom he calls his brother: a Latin translation of Origen’s commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans. In the concluding section, which Cotelerius proves from manuscript codices to have been wrongly attributed to Jerome in printed editions, he mentions another work which he had undertaken at the request of Bishop Gaudentius of Brescia [Col. 0424C]:

> After this, indeed, a work calls us—one that was once assigned to us but is now being pressed upon us more insistently by Blessed Bishop Gaudentius: namely, the books of Clement, the Roman bishop, companion and successor of the apostles, *The Recognitions*, to be translated into Latin . . . If the Lord permits me to complete it, we shall return to them [the books of Adamantius, to be published in Latin translation] and to your wishes, so that, God permitting, we may say something about the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.

He complied with Gaudentius, later fulfilling his pledge to Heraclius. In the preface to *The Recognitions* he says:

> To you, Gaudentius, distinguished glory of our teachers . . . the work which the virgin Silvia, of venerable memory, once commissioned us to undertake, namely, to render Clement into our language, and which you afterward claimed by hereditary right, we have at last restored, although after many delays.

In the aforementioned conclusion to his commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, he lists Origen’s works [Col. 0424D] which he had already translated into Latin:

> The homilies or little discourses on Genesis and Exodus . . . and on the book of Leviticus . . . and on Jesus Nave, and on the book of Judges, and on the thirty-sixth, thirty-seventh, and thirty-eighth Psalms.

We shall mention his other works dedicated to Paulinus of Nola, the abbot Urseius, and Donatus in the following chapter.

## VI.

Our discussion returns to Chromatius, whose concern was especially conspicuous during this period in the grave case of John Chrysostom, who had been driven by force and injustice from the see of Constantinople. At the instigation of the proud Empress Eudoxia and through the evil machinations of Theophilus of Alexandria and the bishops who had conspired with him [Col. 0425A], the most holy man was condemned in 403 at the pseudo-synod held in the suburb of Chalcedon, at the Oak, and the Augustus Arcadius ordered him into exile by his decree. After a great earthquake and with the populace tending toward revolt, he was recalled from exile. Eudoxia did not relinquish her impotent anger until Chrysostom, overcome by his adversaries at a synod held at Constantinople in 404, was again deported into exile. During that exile he completed his most holy course of life on 14 September 407. The see of the outstanding bishop who had been driven into exile was first occupied by Arsacius and then by Atticus.

While Chrysostom was suffering exile after being unjustly driven from his see, he sent letters to Innocent I, the Roman pontiff [Col. 0425B] who had succeeded Anastasius in 401 on 4 December—or, as others prefer, in the following year, 402, on 27 April. Palladius reproduces these letters in his dialogue on the life of Chrysostom and likewise testifies [Note: [Col. 0425D] Palladius by no means testifies that similar letters were written by John Chrysostom to Venerius of Milan and to Chromatius of Aquileia. Rather, it is Chrysostom himself who writes this, closing his own letter. Constantius rightly infers and persuasively argues as much on more than one ground in the note which he appends to this passage among the letters of the Roman pontiffs, col. 787 of the Paris edition. See the complete closing of that letter of Chrysostom among the ancient testimonies which we have collected at the beginning of this volume, after the preface.] that similar letters had been written by him to Venerius, bishop of Milan, and to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia.

Intending to lend Chrysostom aid in accordance with his authority and dignity, Innocent sent letters to the Emperor Honorius. Moved by these, the piety of the Augustus—these are Palladius’s words—ordered a synod of the Westerners to be convened, and when they had reached one common judgment, ordered it to be referred to his piety. Palladius likewise recounts that the bishops of Italy assembled. A synod was held at Rome. The Fathers petitioned in supplicatory memoranda submitted to the emperor that he himself write to his brother and partner in the empire, Arcadius [Col. 0425C], ordering a synod to be held at Thessalonica, so that both parts of the East and West might more easily render a certain and unquestionable judgment concerning the case of John Chrysostom.

Chromatius energetically defended the cause of the most holy man. Honorius selected his letter, together with the letter of the Roman pontiff, so that he might send them to Arcadius. These events belong to the year 405. Honorius says in his letter to Arcadius:

> What the judgment of the Westerners concerning Bishop John is can be seen from all the letters written to me. I have appended two of them: one from the Roman bishop and the other from the Bishop of Aquileia.

The legates of the Roman Church, having received the letters of the Emperor Honorius, of Innocent, and of the Italian bishops—Chromatius of Aquileia, Venerius of Milan [Col. 0425D], and others—as well as the memorandum of the synod of the entire West, traveled by public conveyance to Constantinople. I think that these letters of Chromatius were different from those which Honorius mentions as having been sent, together with his own, to Arcadius [Col. 0426A]. They may perhaps have been addressed to Chrysostom himself [Note: [Col. 0426D] From these words of Palladius, on the basis of which De Rubeis conjectures that letters may perhaps have been sent by Chromatius to Chrysostom himself, Fontaninus inferred earlier, in chapter 3, section 6, that Chromatius had written in Chrysostom’s case not only to Honorius but also to the Augustus Arcadius. Ceillier likewise agrees with Fontaninus. Why should Chromatius not have written to both—namely, to Arcadius and to Chrysostom—on that occasion?].

Chrysostom learned in exile of the efforts which the Bishop of Aquileia had made with the greatest diligence on his behalf; and for that reason he received from Chrysostom in 406 an ample eulogy and many thanks. For Chrysostom says in a letter sent to him:

> The most famous trumpet of your fervent and sincere charity has spread its sound all the way to us . . . Although otherwise separated by so great a distance, we have come to know no less than those who are present the most vehement and fiery charity, the sincere tongue filled with immense freedom and confidence, and the adamantine struggle.

He gives the warmest thanks for the diligent care which Chromatius had shown in his cause with great exertion of spirit, and asks him [Col. 0426B], if messengers should arrive who have come to his solitude or place of exile, to write about his health:

> For you know how much pleasure we shall derive from this, when news of the good health of men who love us so ardently is brought to us more frequently.

The matter having failed, the legates returned, Theophilus having prevented a synod from being held in which, once his deceptions had been exposed, Chrysostom’s innocence would have become clearly evident. A miserable and unjust exile was ended by the death of the most holy man; but the memory of our outstanding Chromatius’s charity and concern for him will never perish.

# CHAPTER XIII

Chromatius dies; his works are reviewed. Augustine ascends the see of Aquileia. Rufinus leaves Aquileia. *(The remainder of this chapter is omitted because it does not concern Chromatius.)*

## I.

[Col. 0426C] At last Chromatius completed his most holy life and his many distinguished labors for the universal Church and for the Church of Aquileia. His memory is celebrated in the church calendars on 2 December. Dandulus assigns the end of his life to the year of Christ 407. That this epoch is indicated by Paulinus of Nola in a letter to Rufinus will be explained below. Dandulus adds that Chromatius held the Church of Aquileia for eighteen years, while Italy was already greatly disturbed by the incursions of the barbarians. Alaric first invaded Italy in 400, ravaging the Aquileian fields far and wide; nor did he withdraw into Pannonia until after the battle at Pollentia, a town of Liguria. Radagaisus, another king of the Goths, later attempted the same region in 404 or the following year; after devastating many places [Col. 0426D], he fell in Tuscany. The second invasion of Alaric will be discussed shortly.

Several little works circulate in print which are commonly attributed to Chromatius. We have mentioned several letters sent by him to Pope Innocent [Col. 0427A], Ambrose, Jerome, and John Chrysostom, which have perished. Baronius, in chapter 5 of the preface to the *Roman Martyrology*, reproduces a letter to Jerome in the names of Chromatius and Heliodorus. In it, the most approved bishops are said to request that, after searching the famous calendars from the archive of St. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, he send them the festivals of the martyrs. The father of the annals rightly and deservedly rejects this letter, together with Jerome’s reply, as spurious material.

A letter to Jerome in the names of the same Chromatius and Heliodorus, together with Jerome’s reply to them concerning the apocryphal books—namely, *On the Origin of Mary, Queen of the Virgin*, and likewise *On the Birth of Mary, Queen and Virgin, and likewise *On the Nativity and Infancy of Our Lord Jesus Christ*—also appeared among Jerome’s works. All critics regard these writings as falsely attributed and spurious. Finally, the Carmelite Peter Wastelius, in his *Vindication of John of Jerusalem*, attributes ninety homilies to Chromatius; they were published among the works of Chrysostom, but we cannot add them to our reckoning. Henichius also presents his *Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer* in part 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, as Gottfridus Olearius reports in his *Library of Writers*. This work will be mentioned again below.

Other works—or rather fragments of works—are also circulated, often published under his name [Col. 0427C]. They are listed in volume 5 of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers* in the following order:

1. *On the Eight Beatitudes*, or on the fifth chapter of Matthew.
2. *On the entire fifth chapter of the same Matthew and part of the sixth chapter*.
3. *On the third chapter of Matthew*.

The first little work is a homily delivered on the occasion of a market fair. It begins:

> This gathering of the people and the abundance of the market give us, brothers, an opportunity to offer a Gospel sermon.

Christ’s sermon in Matthew on the Eight Beatitudes is selected. It ends:

> But so that the conclusion may agree in words with the preface: if merchants rejoice because of present and passing profits, let us all rejoice and be glad still more, because today we have found such pearls of the Lord, with which no goods of this world can be compared. In order that we may deserve to acquire, obtain, and possess them, let us ask help and grace with strength from the Lord himself, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Note the doxology.

The two works that follow are fragments of a commentary [Col. 0427D] on the Gospel of Matthew. The doxology mentioned above, by which the homily on the Eight Beatitudes is concluded, is more frequently read in the two remaining fragments, either in the same words or in similar ones. For example:

> To him be praise and glory forever and ever. Amen;

or:

> To him be honor, praise, and glory, together with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now and always, and forever and ever. Amen;

or:

> Who is blessed forever;

or:

> Who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

The words “Through Christ our Lord” also occur at the end.

Two conclusions follow from this. First, the commentaries appear to have been divided into homilies, which, according to the number of repeated doxologies, are divided into seventeen or even eighteen sections. We owe this observation to Tillemont. Second, all the aforementioned homilies appear to be by the same author, since they employ doxological formulas in the same manner.

[Col. 0428A] Among the homilies on the fifth and sixth chapters of Matthew there is an *Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer*. Whether this is the same as the work presented by Henichius, those who possess his *Ecclesiastical History* may determine. In some editions these same works are titled “of Chromatius, bishop of Rome.” For this reason most learned men think that they should be denied to our Chromatius. We discussed this title in chapter 10, section 2.

## II.

Augustine succeeds Chromatius. The beginning of his tenure of the see, his homeland, and his excellence in character and learning [Col. 0428B] are described by Dandulus in his *Chronicle*:

> Augustine, Bishop of Aquileia, was enthroned in the year 407 from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, because the Catholic people, greatly shaken by the invasion of the barbarians, together with the clergy, chose this orthodox man, a native of Beneventum and sufficiently learned in the Divine Scriptures, as their bishop for the strengthening of their faith.

The very brief eulogy found in the *Aquileian Chronicle* reads:

> Augustine the patriarch succeeded Chromatius. After nineteen years from his ordination, with the people of God increased, he rested in peace with all the saints.

The beginning of his tenure depends on the year of Chromatius’s death, which will be designated below. At that time Arcadius still held the Empire of the East; the younger Theodosius succeeded him in 408 after the Kalends of May [Col. 0428C]. Honorius ruled the western regions, which the barbarian hordes were ravaging with plunder and fires. Dandulus calls Augustine a native of Beneventum, but reliable and ancient records of this fact are lacking. The *Aquileian Chronicle* counts nineteen years of his tenure; the chronicler Venerus adds another nine:

> Augustine, Bishop of Aquileia, died in the twenty-eighth year of his enthronement.

Ughellus, in *Sacred Italy*, places Nicetas immediately after Chromatius, not Augustine. The error of this man, who otherwise rendered excellent service to the churches of Italy, is demonstrated by the chronicles cited above, to which agrees the Forojulian catalogue, which we mentioned as having been composed according to the form of the diptychs and which we give first in the appendix [Col. 0428D]. We shall produce other and very certain arguments for the error when Nicetas is discussed.

## III.

Rufinus, grieving excessively over the death of Chromatius, was uncertain whether he should remain in Aquileia or seek a see elsewhere. Although he had considered going to Rome, this was not yet a settled decision in his mind; he was uncertain whether he should seek a residence elsewhere. We think that this is the meaning of the words of Paulinus of Nola found in his letter 46, otherwise 47, to Rufinus:

> Now, amid the heat of anxiety and the uncertainty of your sojourn, you have decided that you should go to Rome.

What other cause could there have been for Rufinus to be troubled by such heat of anxiety and to waver, uncertain and undecided, about where he should stay, except the death of Chromatius [Col. 0429A]? He did not wish to remain in Aquileia after the death of the most holy bishop, whom he had found to be a most loving father. He had decided to depart for Rome, but even this was not a firm decision. Paulinus continues:

> May the Lord grant that we may as soon as possible be gladdened by the Lord concerning our undertaking . . . And yet let us begin to hope for the fruit of your presence, if you begin to be certain of your decision or of the Lord’s will concerning you.

Rufinus, therefore, had not yet determined which see he would choose.

The year in which Paulinus wrote this letter must be investigated. A chronological indication seems to be suggested in the same letter, where we read:

> Although, because of your affection for us, it may be presumptuous to assume that, when you return to the East, you will not endure to leave without visiting us; [Col. 0429B] nevertheless, there is fear because of our sins, lest even the daughter of Babylon, though so close to us, should turn you away.

We learn that Rufinus had by then already resolved in his mind to return to the East. No other person can be understood there as the Daughter of Babylon except Rome. Paulinus himself explains the meaning in letter 29, otherwise 10, where, speaking of the elder Melania, who had left Jerusalem and migrated to Italy and Rome, he says:

> Thus far the daughter of Zion [Jerusalem] possessed her and longs for her; now the daughter of Babylon [Rome] possesses and admires her.

Paulinus therefore asks Rufinus, who was about to depart for the East, not to leave without visiting him; yet he also fears that Rome, although close to Paulinus living at Nola, might turn Rufinus aside.

The cause of the fear which Paulinus expresses [Col. 0429C] is readily understood as the new invasion of Alaric, king of the Goths, which would prevent Rufinus from undertaking the journey to Rome and proceeding from there to Nola. After Stilicho, who had invited the Goths into Italy, was killed on 23 August 408, Alaric occupied the city’s port; and toward the end of the same year he surrounded Rome in his first siege, as the most skilled authorities in chronology infer from Zosimus. Again, in the following year, 409, the Gothic king advanced to besiege Rome; and finally, for the third time, in 410 he besieged, captured, and most miserably ravaged it [Col. 0430A]. Many very learned men hold and prove that the city was captured in that year; we embrace their opinion, although Pagius thinks it happened in the preceding year. Thus Paulinus’s letter to Rufinus must have been given late in 408 or at the beginning of 409.

This dating is approved by Tillemont and Lebrun, who prepared a new edition of the works of Saint Paulinus, embellished with very extensive notes. At the same time, they judge that, in the same year 409, when it had begun and was not yet far advanced, Paulinus had not yet been raised to the episcopal insignia of Nola; for Rufinus, in the dedicatory letter of Book II of *The Benedictions*, which we shall say was composed after the letter just mentioned, calls him by no other title than “confident brother,” nor does he use any expression indicating his pastoral care or dignity. [Col. 0430B] They present and resolve objections that seem to argue against them. It is permissible to examine briefly what Pagius says for the year 403, no. 10, which they omit.

He quotes the words of Pelagius, writing in 417 to Pope Innocent—whose death he did not know—namely: “Let them read the letter which nearly twelve years ago we wrote to the holy man Paulinus, bishop.” Augustine cites this fragment of the letter in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35. If those twelve years are counted backward, the year of Christ 405 is obtained, in which Pelagius was writing to Paulinus the bishop. So it is indeed: there is no doubt about the time and year in which the letter was written. But when, in 417, Pelagius declares that he had written to “the holy man Paulinus, bishop,” he is indicating the dignity which Paulinus possessed in the year in which Pelagius was writing to Innocent, not the year in which he wrote to Paulinus.

Since it has been worthwhile to mention this in passing, it may now finally be concluded that Chromatius died about the year 408, or even earlier, as Dandulus maintains, and that Rufinus consequently judged that, amid the turmoil of his anxiety and the uncertainty of delays, he should make for Rome; yet he was not certain about the decision he had formed.

*(The material that follows does not concern Chromatius; and therefore we conclude this chapter here.)*

[Col. 0429]

# From the *Dissertations of Varied Learning* of Fr. Bernardo Maria de Rubeis, of the Order of Preachers

Venice, 1762.

## Chapter XVIII, sections V and VI

The most holy man Valerian died after the Church of Aquileia had been cleansed of the stains of heresy which his predecessor Fortunatianus had introduced, together with the neighboring Arians, and after that Church had likewise been enlarged by metropolitan jurisdiction.

[Note: [Col. 0429D] Perhaps the most illustrious man would now think differently about Fortunatianus of Aquileia; on this matter, see what was said in the Preface. [Col. 0430D]]

His memory is commemorated on 27 November in the Roman Martyrology and in two other manuscripts, those of Saint Cyriacus and Saint Maximinus, cited by Bollandus and Henschenius. The ancient Martyrology published by Florentinius, and the Corbie manuscript cited by him, the Hieronymian and Gellonense Martyrologies cited by Dacher, the Labbean Martyrology and the *Auctarium* of Usuard, and Bede’s Martyrology as published by the continuators of the aforementioned Bollandus, have the preceding day, 26 November. The Antuerpiense and Rabban Martyrologies, cited by Florentinius, and the second Richenoviense Martyrology published by the same Bollandists, give the name Valentinus, evidently a corrupt form of Valerianus.

As for the year of his death and the succession of Chromatius to the see of Aquileia, I argued as follows in the *Monuments*, chapter 10, no. 1:

> “We know that Ambrose was staying at Aquileia at the end of the year 388, or at the beginning of 389. Hence one may conjecture that the most holy bishop had gone to that city for the consecration of the new bishop. Paulinus first informs us of this in the *Life of Ambrose*, no. 21, where he says: ‘Maximus having been extinguished, and the Emperor Theodosius having been established at Milan, while Ambrose the bishop was stationed at Aquileia, Ambrose himself sent a letter to the emperor,’ numbered 40 in Nourry’s edition, in order to recall him from his decision concerning a certain synagogue of the Jews that was to be rebuilt by the bishop of Caster Callinicum, and concerning the monks who had burned the shrine of the Valentinian heretics after being provoked by their insults, and were to be punished.
>
> “Yet we gather with certainty from the Theodosian Code that the emperor Theodosius had not yet departed from Aquileia on 12—or 10—Kalends of October, that is, on 20 or 22 September, in the year 388, and that he had already arrived at Milan on the sixth Ides of the same month, where he remained until May of the following year. Therefore Ambrose was staying at Aquileia at the end of 388, or at the beginning of 389, when he sent the aforementioned letter to the emperor Theodosius.
>
> “Baronius, considering this carefully under the year 388, no. 84, says: ‘But since Ambrose was detained at Aquileia, although there is no record of a council having been held there at this time, I believe that he went there, as was customary, for the creation of a new bishop; for when Valerian, the bishop of that city, had died, Saint Chromatius was appointed in his place. I do not think the conjecture unfounded.’”

The archbishop of Ancyra, Justus Fontaninus, rejects this, and Joan. Josephus Liruti follows his lead in the work cited above, *Notices of the Lives and Written Works of the Learned Men of Friuli*, in the Life of Chromatius. In Book III, chapter 3, no. 2, of his *Literary History of Aquileia*, he reports the following:

1. That Saint Valerian died on the sixth Kalends of December, that is, on 26 November.

2. That the tyrant Maximus was defeated three miles from Aquileia in the year 388, on the fifth Kalends of August, that is, on 27 July, according to Idacius in Labbe’s *Fasti*; but according to Socrates, on the sixth Kalends of September, that is, on 27 August.

3. That after the enemy had been defeated, Theodosius remained for some time at Aquileia; for Law X, concerning the invalidation of acts carried out under tyrants, was issued there on the sixth Kalends of October, that is, on 26 September.

4. That only sixteen days later, a similar law, Law VII in the Theodosian Code, was enacted at Milan on the sixth Ides of October, that is, on the tenth day of that month.

5. That in the same city of Milan Theodosius himself issued Law XVII, *On Heretics*, on the sixth Nones of May, that is, on 5 May of the following year, 389, and also Law XIX, *On Heretics*, on the sixth Kalends of December, that is, on 26 November.

From this Fontaninus concludes that Theodosius remained at Aquileia on 26 September 388 and was likewise at Milan on 10 October of the same year.

> “During this interval,” he says, “Ambrose, after Maximus had been extinguished and Theodosius had been established as emperor at Milan, as Paulinus says, hurried to Aquileia; otherwise, in one or the other city, he would have remonstrated with the emperor in person, not by letter, concerning the rescript issued at Milan against the Christians.”

He then advises that the authors of the Sammaura edition be consulted, in the *Admonition concerning the order of Saint Ambrose’s letters*, §11, and finally says:

> “But since, as we have seen, Valerian died on 26 November, it follows that Ambrose went to Aquileia before, not after, Valerian’s death; and therefore for another reason than that of replacing Valerian with Chromatius, who had not yet departed from this life.”

I do not think that the interval during which Ambrose hurried to Aquileia should be understood as the period between 26 September and 10 October; and thus Fontaninus’s entire argument seems to collapse. The Sammaura editors of Saint Ambrose’s works, whom he orders us to consult on this matter, do not, as far as I understand from their words, contradict us:

> “It must therefore be established that this letter”—the aforementioned Letter XL—“was written at the time when the emperor, after Maximus had been overthrown, returned to Milan. Yet from the Theodosian Code it is understood that on 12 Kalends of October, that is, 22 September, in the year 388, he had not yet departed from Aquileia, but on the sixth Ides of the same month, October, that is, on the tenth, he had already arrived at Milan, where he remained until May of the following year. From this it is clear that during this very interval the holy bishop, who had gone to Aquileia on his own business, wrote to Theodosius concerning the revocation of the aforesaid edict.”

I understand these most learned men to have calculated that interval from 10 October 388, after the emperor had returned to Milan, until May of the following year.

The words of Paulinus in the *Life of Saint Ambrose* favor our interpretation. In no. 22 he says:

> “Maximus having been extinguished, Theodosius having been stationed at Milan, and Ambrose the bishop having been stationed at Aquileia”—notice that Ambrose is said to have been stationed at Aquileia after Theodosius had been stationed at Milan—“in the regions of the East, in a certain fortress, the synagogue of the Jews and the grove of the Valentinians were burned by Christian men.… But concerning this deed the governor of the East sent a report to the emperor; and when the emperor had received it, he ordered that the synagogue be rebuilt by the bishop of the place.… But when the wording of this order reached the ears of the venerable bishop Ambrose, he sent a letter to the emperor, because he himself could not hasten there at the proper time; in it he urged him to revoke what had been decreed by him.”

From this passage we learn clearly that, after Aquileia had been left behind and Theodosius had already been established at Milan, the emperor was informed by the governor of the East about the burning of the synagogue; and that at that time Ambrose, stationed at Aquileia, sent letters to the emperor concerning the revocation of the edict. There is therefore room for Baronius’s conjecture that Ambrose went to that city even after 26 November, the date of Valerian’s death, in order to ordain Chromatius as bishop.

Moreover, the Theodosian Code gives the law cited above, Law VI concerning the invalidation of such acts, as having been issued at Aquileia—not on 12 Kalends of October, as the Sammaura editors have it, nor on the sixth Kalends of October, as Fontaninus reports, but on 10 Kalends of October, under the consulship of Theodosius II and Cynegius, in the year 388.

## VI

Joan. Sichardus was the first to publish the minor works of our Chromatius, together with the *Apologeticus* of Pope Symmachus, from a very ancient manuscript, under this title: *Of Chromatius, the Most Learned Bishop of Rome, etc.*, Basel, at the press of Adam Petrus, March 1528, octavo.

The designation “Roman” creates a difficulty. Sixtus of Siena thought that it indicated his homeland. Dandulus calls Chromatius a Spaniard; but without any proven authority it is asserted either that he was Roman by origin or Spanish by nationality. Baronius, in the *Martyrology*, in his notes on 22 June and 2 December, observes that Aquileia was sometimes called a Roman city; accordingly, to call Chromatius a Roman bishop would be equivalent to calling him a bishop of Aquileia.

Quesnellus, in his note on Letter 129 of Saint Leo, §4; Pagius, under the year 396, no. 7; and Tillemont, in volume XI of the *Ecclesiastical Historical Memoirs*, explain the expression “Roman” [Col. 0433C] to mean Catholic, or even a bishop of a Church situated within the Roman Empire. Amid so many conjectures, I may also advance the one that occurred to me, in chapter 10, no. 2, of the *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*: namely, that the word indicated Chromatius’s homeland, which may have been Concordia, of which Pliny says in Book III, chapter 18: “The colony of Concordia, the river and harbor Romatium.” Thus Chromatius ought rather to have been called Romatius, or Romatinus, by origin, and afterward bishop of Aquileia.

The posthumous *Literary History of Aquileia* of Justus Fontaninus appeared in Roman type in 1742. In Book III, chapter 4, no. 2, he considers the difficulty and thinks it should be resolved by saying that Chromatius was called Roman, that is, the father and bishop of the Latin or Western Church. Joannes Josephus Liruti adopts this interpretation.

I add some observations to the arguments that are advanced. Saint Jerome is called as a witness. In his letter to Damasus—Letter XV in the Verona edition—he says: “A new name is being demanded from me, a Roman man,” in the controversy then being stirred in the East concerning whether there was one or three *hypostases* in God. The example may seem less suitable. Jerome calls himself a Roman man not merely because he was born in the West and was a man of the Latin language, but because he was especially devoted to the Roman See and professed the faith which the Roman See taught concerning that question. Hence he had first said that, in this dispute, the See of Peter should be consulted, and he praised the faith commended by the apostolic mouth. Again he says that he is joined in communion with the See of Peter, and finally adds: “Let this be far from the Roman faith.” Jerome therefore did not call himself a Roman man merely because he was a man of the Latin or Western Church.

They add as witnesses Gelasius of Cyzicus, in the Preface to Book I of the Council of Nicaea; the Fathers of Nicaea, in Act I; and Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 89, who called Rufinus Roman. But was their testimony appropriate? In the Greek text of Gelasius of Cyzicus and of the Nicene Fathers, I read Rufinus πρεσβύτερον Ῥώμης, “presbyter of Rome.” These words indicate that they believed Rufinus to be Roman—not merely a Latin presbyter and presbyter of the Western Church, but Roman by homeland and birth. Perhaps Photius too was misled by this error when he calls Rufinus τοῦ Ῥωμαίου, “of the Roman.” It would not be surprising, however, if Greek writers called Rufinus Roman, that is, a Latin and Western Church writer. What is surprising is that among the Westerners themselves Chromatius should be called Roman, that is, Latin and a bishop of the Western Church.

Finally, as an especially authoritative testimony, they cite Albinus, surnamed Alcuin, who, in an unpublished booklet against the heresy of Felix preserved among the Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library, cites, among the sayings of the Latin Fathers—Augustine, Isidore, and Leo—the opinion of Chromatius in these words:

> “Chromatius also, bishop of the holy Roman Church, in the booklet which he entitled *On the Eight Beatitudes*, etc.”

It is important to observe that the words of Chromatius cited by Albinus or Alcuin occur in the aforementioned booklet published by Sichardus. Sichardus appended this note in the margin of the book:

> “This passage is cited by Albinus against Felix from Chromatius’s booklet *On the Eight Beatitudes*.”

From this it must be concluded that, in this passage of Alcuin, Chromatius was called a Roman bishop in Sichardus’s edition of his works not on the basis of another manuscript.

Yet it seems less likely that by this expression, or by the words “bishop of the holy Roman Church,” Alcuin intended to signify merely that Chromatius was a Western and Latin bishop. Why would he not have marked Augustine and Isidore with the same title, since they were undoubtedly Latin and Western bishops whose testimonies he extracts?

The bishops of Gaul and Germany who were Alcuin’s contemporaries, in the synodical letter to the bishops of Spain against Felix and Elipandus, preserved in the Council of Frankfurt, cite Jerome, Augustine, and Cassiodorus as Fathers of the Latin and Western Church; yet they do not call them Romans, or bishops and Fathers of the Roman Church. Later, however, they apply that title to the deacon Paschasius and Gregory the Great: “Paschasius, deacon of the holy Roman Church,” they say, “and Gregory, Roman pope.” Why, again, would he have used the title “bishop of the holy Roman Church” in the less obvious sense, one so well suited to misleading readers?

[Col. 0435A] I would not wish to suppose that Alcuin was the author of this title. He may have read in the manuscripts either “bishop of the holy Roman Church” or “Roman bishop.” I cannot say in what sense he understood these words.

The seven bishops who celebrated the sacred rites in the Lateran Church, each in turn during the week assigned to him, are customarily called by writers Roman bishops, Roman pontiffs, bishops of the Roman Church, and cardinal bishops of the Roman Church. The first mention of such bishops is found in Baronius under the year 769. Was Chromatius perhaps considered one of these? Or did an ignorant and inexperienced scribe, noticing that Jerome calls Chromatius “venerable pope” in the prologue to Book II of his Commentaries on the prophet Habakkuk, and “most holy of bishops” in the Preface to the Latin translation of the *Paralipomena* (‘Things Omitted,’ i.e. Chronicles)—believe him to have been the supreme pontiff, and, while copying his works, mark him with the title “Roman bishop” or “bishop of the holy Roman Church”?

Yet the title itself may be entirely sound. Is another, more probable interpretation available?

Theoderic Ruinart, in note 49 to the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, observes that Catholics were designated by the name “Romans” both by the heretics themselves, as in the present passage, and by Catholic authors. The passage occurs in Book I, no. 14, where the words of the Arian presbyter Jocundus to Theodoric, the king’s son, are reported:

> “If you kill him with the sword”—Armogastes—“the Romans will begin to proclaim him a martyr.”

Ruinart cites Mabillon discussing this matter in the Preface to the *Gallican Liturgy*, no. 11. His words are as follows:

> “Among Gregory of Tours, the bishop, Catholics are more than once called Romans. There is one passage in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 25, where Gregory, speaking of fountains in Lusitania violated by heretics and of heavenly vengeance upon those who violated them, adds:
>
> “‘Finally, when Theodegisilus, king of that region, had seen this miracle that was taking place at these fountains consecrated to God, he reflected within himself, saying: “It is the ingenuity of the Romans”—for they call the people of our religion Romans—“that this should happen, and it is not the power of God.”’
>
> “In chapter 80 of the same book he likewise reports a miracle performed in confirmation of the Christian faith involving a Catholic presbyter against an Arian presbyter. Gregory calls the Catholic presbyter a man of our religion, while the heretics call him a Roman.
>
> “Indeed, even before that time Catholics themselves understood ‘Roman faith’ as Catholic faith. Thus Jerome says in his first *Apology against Rufinus*: ‘Which faith does he call his own? The faith by which the Roman Church is strong, or that which is contained in the volumes of Origen? If he answers, “Roman,” then we are Catholics.’”

Ruinart adds to this the fact that the emperor Theodosius II, in a letter to Acacius and other bishops and anchorites reported in the Council of Ephesus, exhorted them to show themselves approved priests of the Roman religion.

I add from Ducange’s *Glossary* the earlier testimony of Lucifer of Cagliari, in his *Book to the Emperor Constantius on Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*:

> “Therefore, when you say that he is not the Son of God.… But we Romans say that he is of one substance with the Father.”

Finally, receive the very worthy observation of the aforementioned Ruinart in the same place:

> “This custom of calling Catholics Romans became especially prevalent when barbarians devoted to the Arian sect ravaged the provinces of the Roman Empire.”

We therefore possess evidence of the use of “Romans” for Catholics from a remote period. That period corresponds to the time when Chromatius governed the Church of Aquileia, as is clear from Lucifer of Cagliari. It is likewise known that under Chromatius the incursions into Venetia and Italy began of the Goths, who were infected with Arian error.

Why, then, would Chromatius not have wished to describe himself in the title of his work as a Roman bishop, that is, a Catholic bishop, or a bishop of the Roman Church, that is, of the Catholic Church, as a profession of the true faith? Why would someone who copied his works in a later age not rather have called him a Roman bishop in praise of his faith, and why would the scribes or copyists of later ages not have retained this designation as his distinctive title?

In Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 34, where the election of two patriarchs of Aquileia is related—one a schismatic, the other a Catholic and a venerator of the Fifth Ecumenical Council—we read:

> “In those days”—about the year 607—“when Severus the patriarch had died, John the abbot was ordained patriarch at Old Aquileia with the consent of the king”—of the Lombards—“and of Duke Gisulf. At Grado, Candidianus was likewise ordained bishop for the Romans.… When Candidianus too had died, Epiphanius was ordained patriarch at Grado … by the bishops who were under the Romans.”

We explained the force of this word in our *Monuments*, chapter 33, no. 3.

Ruinart, in the cited place, note 199, commenting on this passage in Book V, no. 18, of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, says:

> “However many gifts you lavish upon the barbarians.… They know nothing else except to envy the Romans; and as far as their will is concerned, they always desire to obscure the splendor and nobility of the Roman name, and do not desire any Roman at all to remain alive.”

He continues:

> “After various barbarian invasions, when in most provinces of the Empire, especially in the West, barbarians and the ancient peoples whom the Romans had previously subjected were mingled together, the custom arose that some were called Romans and others barbarians.… Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy, issued laws for the barbarians, that is, for men of his own nation, and for the Romans, namely, the ancient inhabitants of Italy. See further examples of this matter, if you wish, in Hadrian Valesius, Book VI of the *History of the Franks*, roughly in the middle.”

The various meanings of the same word are evident. Tillemont, in volume XI of the *Ecclesiastical Historical Memoirs*, note 2 on Saint Chromatius, understands the word “Romans” in Paul the Deacon’s passage in this sense; and perhaps he also indicates that Chromatius was called Roman in the same sense. Quesnellus holds the same opinion in his notes on Letter 129 of Saint Leo, no. 4:

> “Candidianus is said to have been ordained for the Romans, namely for those inhabitants of Old Aquileia who had crossed over to Grado and were subject to the Romans.”

Fontaninus very rightly refutes this empty conjecture in the place cited.

# In the Year of Our Lord 408

# Saint Victricius, Bishop of Rouen

[Col. 0437]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0437A] Saint Paulinus seems to indicate that Victricius was born somewhere within the limits of the empire when he says (*Epistle* 18, no. 4) that the Lord brought him forth into the light for his people “from the farthest edge of the world.” From these words the learned Lebeuf conjectures that he may have been British by nation.

Of an age different from blessed Martin, who was born in the year 316 or 317, Victricius first enlisted in the secular army and embraced the Christian faith while serving there. Later, when he released himself from his military oath in order to devote himself entirely to Christ, the tribune was roused to fury; Victricius was led out for a beating, battered with huge clubs, and finally condemned to death. But when the executioner of the holy confessor was just about to cut off his head, his eyes were suddenly struck and he was afflicted with blindness. Victricius himself, freed from his bonds, escaped unharmed. For this reason Paulinus calls him a living martyr.

It is not entirely known where he withdrew afterward. It is more certain that he subjected the fierce peoples of the Morini and Nervii to the yoke of Christ. Since his zeal for the faith and religion consequently became widely renowned, he was summoned to govern the Church of Rouen.

This must have occurred before the year 390, when Paulinus of Nola, still involved in the concerns of this world, saw him at Vienne among the Allobroges, in the company of Saint Martin. Nor should one omit what Sulpicius Severus relates: namely, that Victricius was so distinguished by a reputation for holiness that when a mute girl from birth was brought to blessed Martin at Chartres so that he might release her bound tongue by his merits, Martin transferred the honor of curing the illness to Victricius or Valentinian, who at that time happened to be accompanying him.

Paulinus further praises him for the daily singing of psalms established among the people of Rouen through numerous churches and monasteries, in places where formerly foreign barbarians or resident bandits haunted the deserted and equally unsafe forests and shores.

In the year 394 or 395 he went to Britain, summoned by the bishops of that kingdom to bring about peace, which the new Pelagian heresy was disturbing, as he himself testifies. Then, at the end of 403, he made for Rome; the aforementioned Paulinus mentions this journey.

Why he undertook such a journey is readily apparent: he had evidently been accused before the Roman pontiff of holding an incorrect view concerning the faith. At the beginning of the following year, while Victricius was still staying in Rome, he received from Pope Innocent I the notable letter which is called the *Book of Rules*, as the distinguished Coutant has learnedly demonstrated. It is so called because, after a brief preface, the most blessed pontiff proceeds to set out many points of ecclesiastical discipline.

Soon afterward Victricius returned from Rome to Rouen. That same year he sent a brief letter to Paulinus of Nola through Candidianus, one of his own pupils. For this reason Paulinus addressed a second letter to the bishop of Rouen; it is numbered 36.

The writers of *Gallia Christiana* discuss that Pauline letter as follows:

> “The learned Bollandists appear to think that Paulinus’s last letter was not written until after he had become bishop of Nola. For, they say, his earlier letter, from the year 399, is addressed ‘To the Most Blessed Father Victricius,’ while the later one, from the year 404, is addressed ‘To Victricius, his United Brother.’ But the word ‘brother’ is of little importance in Paulinus. In the years 394 and 395, long before he became a bishop, he wrote Letters 4 and 6, both addressed to Augustine, his brother.
>
> “Certainly Paulinus was not raised to the episcopate until the year 409. In that year, writing to Saint Augustine, he lists the most distinguished bishops of the Gallican Church then living: Exsuperius of Toulouse, Simplicius of Vienne, Amandus of Bordeaux, Diogenianus of Albi, Dinamius of Angoulême, Venerandus of Auvergne, Alithius of Cahors, and finally Pegasius of Périgueux; but he says nothing about Victricius. Hence it seems that the holy bishop of Rouen had then ceased to live.”

*(You will find fuller documentation in the following Preface of Joan. Lebeuf.)*

[Col. 0437]

# Preface of Joan. Lebeuf to the Following Book, *On the Praise of the Saints*

[Col. 0437D] The occasion for the work which I am bringing to light was provided by the reception of the relics of the holy Apostles and Martyrs. Anyone who considers the work carefully will readily attribute it to the industry of some bishop of Rouen.

These words, which are read in paragraph 3—“Twice the Saints come to the city of Rouen”—immediately indicate that the relics were received in the city of Rouen. What is written near the end of paragraph 6—“But what do I, poor Victricius, your worshiper, fear concerning the character of the place?”—clearly shows that the author of this little work was Saint Victricius, who held the bishopric of that city toward the end of the fourth century and the beginning of the fifth.

The style of this work has the greatest similarity to the style of Saint Paulinus, between whom and Saint Victricius there was a very close bond. The passages taken from Sacred Scripture are drawn from the Latin version then in use. D. Martianay, from a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, reported several passages in which a similar translation of Saint Matthew is found—the translation on the authority of which the Fathers cited testimonies from Scripture before the time of Saint Jerome.

A question could arise here whether the work is a sermon which Victricius recited before the people of Rouen, or a booklet which he composed for the instruction of the people. From two passages in the work, I would judge it to be a booklet rather than a sermon.

“But we,” he says in paragraph 9, “fill a book with the tumult of questions amid such great rejoicing.” And near the end of paragraph 9: “If our speech should be displeasing to anyone, our zeal will certainly not displease him, if he sees that we have written the book in simple faith, and ourselves in words.”

Indeed, the confession of faith which he calls a confession of faith in paragraph 4, and the repeated invocations of the holy Apostles and Martyrs whose relics had recently arrived in the city, find a more suitable place in a book than in a speech.

If the time of death of Theodulus and Eustachius, bishops of the province of Milan, whom he mentions in paragraph 2, were known as securely as the time of Saint Ambrose’s death, we could more easily assign the year in which those relics were brought to Rouen.

Only this can be held as certain: since Saint Ambrose was among those who stripped their churches for the sake of Saint Victricius, and since, when Victricius names the saints who cure diseases, he mentions Saint Nazarius of Milan, that translation must be assigned to the period between the discovery of the bodies of the saints Nazarius and Celsus and the death of Saint Ambrose.

Since Ambrose did not discover the bodies of those saints before the death of Theodosius, which occurred on 17 January in the year of Christ 395, and since Ambrose himself died in the year 397, on 4 April, it follows that this reception of the relics among the people of Rouen took place about the year 396.

Concerning the bishops and Theodulus—if indeed Victricius is speaking of bishops—it is established that their names were subscribed to the letter of the Council of Milan of the year 390, at least according to Labbe’s edition, volume II of the *Councils*, column 1027; for in other copies one reads Theodorus, not Theodulus.

A considerable difficulty arises concerning Theodulus himself: namely, whether he was the secretary of blessed Ambrose about whom the presbyter Paulinus wrote in the Life of Ambrose in the year 417 as follows:

> “When Ambrose was going to the palace, and we were following him in accordance with the duty of our office, Theodulus was then a notary; afterward he governed the Church of Modena with the greatest favor,” etc.

For if Victricius is speaking of a bishop, it is clear that this man is distinct from Theodulus, bishop of Modena, since Theodulus had not yet ascended the see of Modena when the relics of the saints were assigned to him. From the passage of Paulinus cited above it is certain that in 395, after the death of Theodosius, he was still performing the duties of a notary under Saint Ambrose.

Ughellus writes that the memory of this bishop—whom he incorrectly calls Theodorus—appears in the monuments of Modena under the year 397, at which time Ambrose may have died and Victricius’s little work may already have been written.

Since the letter of the Council of Milan to Pope Siricius in the year 390 names another Theodulus, Victricius probably indicates this Theodulus instead. What see he held can be inferred from the subscriptions of the Council of Aquileia of the year 381, which are repeated in the Roman copy of the subscriptions of that same Council of Milan. In them Theodulus—incorrectly called Theodorus—is assigned the see of Octodurum.

Since the bodies of the Agaunian Martyrs rested in his territory, if Theodulus was sending anything concerning the relics of the saints to Victricius, he would certainly have placed in the little capsule intended for the bishop of Rouen some earth stained with the blood of those Martyrs, which was then also being preserved with the greatest reverence.

The profound silence concerning the relics of Saint Mammas therefore requires us to understand that the material reported in the treatise of Saint Victricius concerns a different Theodulus from the bishop of Octodurum.

Whatever bishop or minister of the Church may have written it, this booklet which I offer the reader deserves veneration, both because of its antiquity—more than fourteen hundred years—and because of the author whose name it bears. For Saint Victricius, after the letters he had written to Saint Paulinus of Nola were lost, repairs that loss and illuminates several passages of Paulinus’s letters to Victricius.

Furthermore, if some who shed light on Gallic and Frankish authors are displeased that, in the dissertation published above, I removed Honorius, commonly called of Autun, from the number of our writers, let them observe that I have substituted for Honorius a man distinguished both by rank and by an antiquity worthy of the highest commendation.

The many digressions with which this writing is filled seem to confirm the opinion of the recent author of the *Life of Saint Victricius* [Note: [Col. 0439D] De Brun des Marettes] concerning the accusations brought against him, as though he had erred in certain articles of faith.

They believe that he had previously gone to Italy to clear himself, and that from there he was able to bring relics, to which he joined those he later received—unless, however, others had obtained them earlier.

There is a church in the suburb of Rouen dedicated to Saint Gervasius. I would not unreasonably believe that it occupies the site where Saint Victricius had built a temple, the one of which he speaks at the end of this work.

So great is the reputation of its antiquity that it is said that the body of Saint Mellonus, the first bishop of Rouen, was buried there. I suspect that it was built outside the Roman city, where, according to the laws, it was permitted to bury bodies in the earth, and that it was the first place at Rouen to possess the right of a cemetery. The faithful frequented it especially because of the relics and tombs of the saints.

Many other matters that invite investigation concerning this manuscript will be read in the notes inserted below the pages of this edition.

I have omitted the remaining scholia which a certain monk of Saint Gall, perhaps of the ninth or tenth century, observed, because it is plainly acknowledged that this monk—whether he was Notker or Ekkeard—was somewhat unsophisticated. For example, he said that the city of Rouen was a city of Britain; and in place of Victricius, whom he did not know, he perhaps thought that *Vicarius* should be read. He was misled because a scribe had believed Saint Ambrose to be the author of this work, since the manuscript he held contained some writings of the holy Doctor.

Here the account of the life of St. Victricius would appropriately be inserted, if anyone happened to be unfamiliar with it. It was excellently written by Jean-Baptiste Le Brun, an acolyte of Rouen, according to what is related about Victricius in the letters of St. Paulinus. [Col. 0441C] The Bollandists published it again in the second volume for August. There it is reported that Victricius served in the army from his youth. Then the desire to worship God led him to lay down his arms at the tribune’s feet and request his discharge. The tribune ordered him to be beaten with rods and thrown into prison. The commander of the military force, before whom Victricius was brought, condemned him to death. The executioner was already about to cut off his head when he was suddenly struck blind and the bonds were loosed. When the commander saw this, he sent Victricius back to the emperor, by whom he was released.

It is uncertain where he withdrew, but after Peter’s death the people of Rouen elected him bishop around the year 385. Later, around the year 389, Paulinus saw Victricius at Vienne with St. Martin of Tours. His reputation for holiness, however, was so great that when a mute girl was brought to blessed Martin at Chartres for healing, Martin transferred to him—or to Bishop Valentinian—the honor of curing her illness; both of them declined it. Victricius taught his people with simplicity and always placed example before precept. He built monasteries in the city and diocese of Rouen. Many people observed continence in marriage at his admonition; still more brought him their possessions so that he might distribute them as alms. Among [Col. 0442A] the Morini and Nervii he preached the Gospel.

Paulinus heard all this from Paschasius the deacon at Nola. Victricius had sent Paschasius to Italy with the catechumen Ursus, and Paschasius later reported Paulinus’s letter to Victricius. On his return from the Morini, Victricius found weeds sown in his field. He fought against his adversaries for the purity of his teaching, and this perhaps was the reason why he went to Rome around the year 403. When he had returned, he wrote to Paulinus, asking pardon because he had not directed his journey to him. He sent him Candidianus, one of his own pupils, who was conducting some business with the Roman pontiff. From Candidianus, Paulinus learned everything concerning Victricius, and he gave him a second letter to the bishop of Rouen.

In the documents that Victricius was sending to the pope, he indicated that he was troubled by certain scruples concerning the regulations observed by the Roman Church regarding conduct, for the punishment of violators of the canons. Innocent gave him the *Book of Regulations*—that is, a book containing the canons of the Roman Church. These are all that is known about the life of St. Victricius; to them must be added the circumstances supplied by this work.

His body was later transferred to the castle of Brana in the district of Soissons. The Bollandist associates thought that it had been reduced to ashes by the Calvinists when they plundered that district. But this rumor—which is also circulated concerning the relics of certain saints of Gaul—rests on a false foundation with respect to the intact body of St. Victricius. Indeed, five of the larger bones of the holy bishop’s body have been preserved at Brana, beneath the altar of the parish church of St. Nicholas, even since the time of those wars, in a wooden sarcophagus: namely, the thighbone, the shinbone, the bone called the fibula, as well as a shoulder blade and a hipbone. Some portions of the same sacred body were also preserved in the abbey church of St. Evodius in that town; but not the entire body, as Ballet had supposed. Add to these an arm, which had already been transferred at the beginning of the twelfth century to the Monastery of Charity above the Loire.

The five bones mentioned above were solemnly transferred on 5 May 1733 into a new reliquary by the hands of the Reverend Father in Christ, D. François Le Febvre de Laubrière, bishop of Soissons. As I learned from the official record, he decreed that henceforth this translation should be commemorated every year in the said church of St. Nicholas with a semi-double rite.

For the rest, in publishing this little work of Victricius, I intend to preserve the very division of the numbers found in the manuscript of St. Gall, so that nothing may be lost from a manuscript of such great antiquity, and so that the reader may be certain that everything has been faithfully collated with the venerable codex.

I wrote this in Paris in the month of August of the year 1737.

[Col. 0443]

# BOOK OF ST. VICTRICIUS, BISHOP OF ROUEN, ON THE PRAISE OF THE SAINTS

From a manuscript codex of St. Gall, more than a thousand years old. (C)

[Col. 0443A]

## I

Beloved brothers, we are reminded that we belong to the mercy of God and to the omnipotence of the Savior even by the present abundance of spiritual blessings. We have seen no executioner; we know no sword empty of its sheath; we approach the altars of the divine powers. No bloodstained enemy is present today, yet we are enriched by the passion of the Saints. No torturer now presses upon us, yet we bear the triumphal trophies of the Martyrs. No blood is currently being shed, no persecutor pursues us, yet we are filled with the joy of triumphs.

We must therefore be immersed in tears, and great joys must be dissolved into abundant weeping.
