[Note: [Col. 0443C] Because of joy.] Behold, the greater part of the heavenly army deigns to visit our city, so that we must now dwell among the throngs of the Saints and the renowned powers of heaven. It is no small alleviation of our sins to have with you those whom you instruct, to have with you those whom you appease. Indeed, from the present joy I measure how much I have lost until now.

I ask you to pardon my impatience: excessive joy does not know how to weigh its words. I grieve, and in a certain human way I am saddened, that the inhabitants of our breast have come so late; they would have found fewer sins had they come earlier. Therefore, dearest ones, let this be our first petition to the Saints: that they excuse our sins by the mercifulness of their advocacy, rather than investigate them with the mind of a judge.

And as for me, holy and venerable Martyrs, so far as I think, my excuse for delay is pardonable in your sight. For the fact that I went to Britain, and that I remained there, was the result of carrying out your commands. The priests who are my fellow ministers summoned me to establish peace. [Note: [Col. 0443C] The complaint of the Church, or of the faith, is the complaint of the Martyrs of the whole Church, and especially of the Apostles. In this sense Victricius could say that, in obeying the commands of those whose relics were being brought to him, he had crossed over to Britain, since among them were the relics of St. John the Baptist, St. Andrew, and St. Thomas, whom he names below.] I could not refuse this, since I was serving you. To obey commands is not to fail in obedience. I rightly know that you are everywhere by your power, for no earthly distance deprives heavenly glory of its presence.

You should therefore pardon me because I came almost belatedly to meet you only at the fortieth milestone. Within Britain [Note: [Col. 0443D] Perhaps Victricius was British by birth, and this is the sense in which what Paulinus wrote to him in Letter 18 should be understood: “The Lord brought you forth into the light for his people from the farthest—or outermost—part of the world.”] I was obeying you, and although separated by the surrounding ocean, I was nevertheless detained by your service. This delay [Note: [Col. 0443D] The fortieth milestone seems to indicate that, on his return from Britain, he did not meet the relics of the Saints until he was only fifteen leagues from the city of Rouen. For one of our present-day leagues contains nearly three miles of the ancients.] injured my desire, but did not abandon my obedience.

Yet I attribute everything to your majesty, [Note: [Col. 0444C] The title “majesty,” which occurs more than once among the ancients, was formerly applied not only to God but also to Saints and emperors and kings, to certain bishops, and to others holding positions of dignity, as may be seen in Cange’s *Glossary*.] because you are the body of Christ, and the divine Spirit dwells in you. It is your doing that I was absent; it is your doing that I returned.

It remains, therefore, to set forth the grounds of my excuse. You are the authors of the peace of the Lord, whose judgment you appointed me to interpret. I carried out this salutary command of the Lord Jesus and of you within Britain—not as I ought, perhaps, but as I was able. I infused love of peace into the wise; I taught it to the teachable; I impressed it upon the ignorant; I forced it upon the unwilling, according to the Apostle, insisting in season and out of season. Through teaching and persuasion I reached their souls.

But whenever the place and human frailty tested me, I implored the protection of your spirits. I did what those who sail do in the midst of a great storm: they do not appeal to the skill of the helmsman, but to the mercy of heavenly majesty. For it is Jesus, who is in you, who can calm the waves and impose restraint upon the winds; earthly skill does not know how to do this.

Nor do I now need to labor concerning those who have completely fallen away from the bond of discipline. I have the presence of your majesties. Where the attendant of religion offers an excuse, let the authority of your power complete it.

## II

With what reverence shall I now embrace you, blessed Ambrose? With what affection shall I kiss you, Theodulus? With what inward arms shall I join you, Eustachius, to my understanding? With what devotion of a renewed mind shall I honor you, Carion? [Note: [Col. 0444D] I have already noted that the names Theodulus and Eustachius are found in the subscriptions to the Council of Milan of the year 390. The name Carion is not found elsewhere.] With what admiration shall I look up to you? Surely I do not know—before such great merits, I do not know—what I can repay.

There is only one thing that can answer your benefits: if you ask from the holy Apostles and Martyrs what is owed to us, so that those whom you wished to be with us may not be lacking to you.

To your devoted diligence also, dearest brother Aelianus, [Note: [Col. 0444D] Aelianus was perhaps one of the church custodians of Milan, the bearer of the relics.] and likewise to your expectation, I give thanks. But the Apostles and Martyrs have already paid you the reward for your labor and service: they have been with you for a long time.

Give, then, give—why do you delay? Bring forth the shrines of the Saints. I wish to act, not to speak. For if the Savior’s fringe, lightly touched, healed, [Col. 0445A] then without doubt the dwellings of suffering that have embraced him will heal.

Moreover, this labor does not feel fatigue. By faith we carried our Apostles and Martyrs before us. Twice the Saints come to the city of Rouen. [Note: [Col. 0445D] From this passage it is clear that, not finding the holy bishop Victricius at Rouen, the bearer had already turned his journey toward Britain with the relics; and that, when Victricius met him, they returned together to Rouen. It is also clear that the chest or casket of relics was not very large, perhaps similar to the one that St. Germanus of Auxerre carried around his neck.] Long ago they entered our breast; now they celebrate the Church of the City.

Behold, every age pours itself into your service, each striving to surpass the others in religious devotion. Hence priests, deacons, and every minister familiar to you come forward in daily service. The services of those who are known are more pleasing: it is not that one begins to be loved who was not known, but that he gains an increase of love. [Subaud.: “the one who is known.”]

## III

Furthermore, a known and long-established service wins more favor with the Lord. An increase of service is an increase of fear. For the one who has something to lose through offense is more fearful.

Thus a soldier tested over time in your service, worn out by vices, approved by labor and vigils, comes forward. [Note: [Col. 0446D] He alludes to what he had formerly suffered for Christ.] Such, I say, is eager to serve: one who turns labor into desire, who knows nothing of the name of fortune, who measures this life not by its present brevity but by the blessedness of eternity. Finally, his state of mind is such that whenever his hands are laden with the relics of the Saints, he considers himself enriched by enormous interest.

Hence the company of monks, refined by fasts, is gathered densely; hence the ringing joy of innocent children resounds. Hence the choir of devoted and undefiled virgins bears the emblem of the cross. [Note: [Col. 0446D] He says more about the state of widows and virgins in order to refute the disciples of Jovinian, who had recently been condemned by the holy bishops at the Council of Milan, and to display the unanimity of the teaching.] Hence a multitude of the continent and of widows, wholly worthy of such service, is assembled.

Their life is more splendid in proportion as the condition of human fate has been more difficult. For it is a severe struggle to resist familiar pleasure. If you do not know it, ignorance itself defends you through nature. If you do know it, knowledge itself attacks you through desire.

The chill of her dead husband has extinguished this fire, and every desire embraces a gloomy tomb. The surviving husband preserves these loves, caressed by the promise of eternity. In unequal circumstances there is an equal palm of virtue. The former condemned sexual union with horror and modesty while the marriage still endured; the latter commended it after the husband’s death.

Nor is such devotion to religion without reason. For where there is no thought of pleasures, there is the dwelling of chastity. A good conscience willingly serves the Saints. It makes no difference whether rumor tears one apart or the silent injury of thought torments one. The display of modesty is the sustained abstinence of one who serves.

No one here wears Tyrian clothing that pours forth its ardor; no waves of crackling silk are curled by the fashionable movement of those who walk; no jewel, no circle of gold is seen. Human things are filthy where divine things are valued. As the Apostle teaches: “I have considered all these things as dung, that I might gain Christ.”

They walk radiant, burning with the intoxication of chastity. They walk crowned with the divine gifts of adornment. Their breasts are filled with the riches of the Psalms. There is no night of vigils in which such a jewel does not gleam. There is no place of religion in which such a precious inlay does not shine. The joy of the Saints is a throng of the chaste.

The multitude of widows and the continent is an irritation to the powers of this world. Hence the tears of old men and mingled joys pour forth; hence the vows of mothers. May these joys also touch the minds of infants. Finally, hence arises the single affection of the whole people around your majesty.

## IV

Therefore have mercy, have mercy! You have something for which to forgive; we confess God the Father, we confess God the Son, we confess God the Holy Spirit. We confess that the three are one.

I said “one,” because from one—as the Son is from the Father, so the Father is in the Son—while the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son. Thus both the Father and the Son are in the Holy Spirit. One divinity, one substance, because there is one principle and one eternity: whether before all things or through whom all things exist, true God from true God. For just as one is from another, so one is in another: living from the living, perfect from the perfect, light from light, and light in light.

Thus the divinity of this Trinity, remaining from one and in one, is one. The Father is Father, the Son is Son, the Spirit is Spirit. Three in names, three from one principle, three in one perfection, three in one divinity, three in one light, three in one power, three in one operation, three in one substance, three in one eternity; for just as the three are from one, so unity is in the three.

Thus we confess, because thus we believe, the undivided Trinity, before which nothing can be fabricated or conceived by the mind; through which all visible and invisible things exist, whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers. “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” He descended from on high for the salvation of the human race, was incarnate from the Virgin Mary and put on humanity, suffered, was crucified, was buried, rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead.

And we believe in the Holy Spirit, because Christ himself established this sacrament in the Apostles, saying: “When I have ascended to my Father and your Father, I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, because he remains with you and is in you” (John 14:16–17). And elsewhere: “When they set you before the authorities of this world, do not be anxious about what you shall say; the Spirit of your Father will speak in you” (Matthew 10:19).

In this unity we confess the lights of your venerable sufferings. In the Gospel we read that you are the lights of the world (Matthew 5:14). This we proclaim in danger; this we proclaim in joy.

May this confession benefit sinners, for he obtained this who asked, as the Lord says in the Gospel. When the thief hanging on the cross asked the Savior to remember him, the Savior said: “Amen I say to you, today you shall be with me in Paradise.” Let no one examine our sins; we ask for pardon.

## V

Come now, dearest brothers; let us sip the words of the Psalms, softened with honey and milk by the most sacred relics. Let sobriety, made drunk by vigils and fasts, seek the washing away of sins. Let us draw toward us the favor of the Saints while their coming is still warm.

Their dwellings are indeed above, but let us pray as guests. Sometimes it is beneficial to conceal what you know. Let them know their own secret. Those who guard the mysteries and do not seek out hidden things obtain more easily.

You also, sacred and inviolate virgins, sing the Psalms—sing them—and beat with your feet upon the paths and by the dances through which one ascends to heaven. [Note: [Col. 0447D] He speaks metaphorically.] Tread those paths, I say—the paths which those who truly rejoice in the bright light of Paradise, troubled by no clouds, tread; wear them out with your assaults.

## VI

But let no one complain of error: the mercy of the Savior has added other guides for us. For what else, dearest ones, is a Martyr but an imitator of Christ? One who subdues raging pleasure, tramples ambition, longs for death, despises riches, restrains lust, and persecutes excess? One from whom avarice has never snatched the scepter of prudence, nor desire the right to avenge itself?

Through these steps of virtue the Savior ascended from the place to which he had descended, as the Apostle teaches: “He who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens.” Finally, through these steps he raised with himself those whom he predestined, saying: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me.”

Prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance are the heavenly way. The Savior opened this way, saying: “I am the way and the truth.” The merchant of heavenly pearls and eternity wore it smooth. The prophets show it to Christian travelers; the Apostles frequented it. Neither cold contracts it nor heat inflames it. It is declared in the Psalms: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.”

Therefore let us pray, dearest ones, let us pray, that if the mass of our sins prevents us from ascending, we may at least warm with closer kisses the footprints of those who ascend.

These are the venerable ones; these are the holy ones who brought death upon death. As we read: “Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, shall live.” O how precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his Saints, to whom the threatening persecutor gave even greater distinction! The torturer was terrified; the condemned man laughed beneath the questioning; the executioner trembled, and the one about to die supported the trembling hand of the man who struck him.

The wild beast refused, but the one exposed provoked it—not because nature had lost physical suffering, but because the Savior, the champion of so great a contest, brandishing the palm, displayed the victory of immortality.

Although these things are so, nevertheless in that passion the bodies of the members endured the struggle with you. Therefore, lying prostrate on the ground and watering it with tears, let us cry out with one voice: you who always possess the sacred relics, purify our bodies. Nor will our offering seem filthy to you, venerable ones. It is a worthy dwelling, inhabited by so many victors.

Here you will find John the Baptist—him, I say, who stood bloodstained in the common contest, [Note: [Col. 0447D] The manuscript reads *studio*, “zealously,” but incorrectly.] but ascended crowned to heaven, whom the Lord himself declares superior among those born of women. Here you will find Andrew, here Thomas, here Gervasius, here Protasius, here Agricola, here Euphemia, who, with her spirit once burned, did not blanch as a virgin beneath the executioner.

Finally, so great is the multitude of heavenly citizens here that, at the arrival of your majesties, we would have to seek another place for ourselves unless your secret and the unity of your power joined you to us.

These commands are yours: not to rival charity, not to seek the things that are one’s own. [Note: [Col. 0448D] He seems to indicate that the Church of Rouen already possessed some relics.] Hence I do not doubt that, according to human standards, the insult of a lowlier place affects you. Human beings weigh such matters far too narrowly. Divinity rejects rank; it is defined neither by place nor by time. Unity has no subordination.

Nor is it surprising that nothing in earthly substance is difficult for you, since everything is shared among you in the light of the Spirit. Yet the glory of your powers will be greater if you defend those who labor, if you protect those subject to enemies. Let arms cover those whom they wish; your battle lines and your standards will guard us. There is no enemy if you grant pardon for sins. The restraints of our life are held in your hands. Forgive our offenses, and no wars will disturb us.

But why should I, poor Victricius, your worshiper, fear concerning the quality of this place? You have come from yourselves to yourselves. Here you will find those whom you left ministering around the altars of the Lord Jesus Christ. With arms outstretched, John the Baptist awaits you. You, Thomas; you, Andrew; Luke and the rest of the heavenly multitude call you into their embrace with equal longing. No new host will receive you. These are the ones with whom you serve in the army of heaven.

Yet their joy will be especially great if those who were joined in spiritual glory are joined also in their relics.

## VII

For, as Scripture suggests, we gather together into one mass of bodily substance. What person could be found so brutish by nature or so devoid of reason that he would deny that woman received her origin from the sides of man? From this it follows that we understand the beginnings of flesh to have been derived from flesh. Nature itself was so constituted that, if someone diligently applies his mind and investigates genus as it were through genus, he discovers Adam made a genus from a species.

For that cannot fail to be a genus from whose material and formation the offspring of the whole human body has been diffused and grown. Therefore, holiest brothers, we must first know this: human beings differ among themselves not by nature, but by place and time, by action and thought. For diversity is foreign to unity. Unity spreads widely without diminishing itself.

And if the eyes of reason have discerned that all human beings constitute one body, it follows that, by the same reasoning, we should believe that those living in Christ and in the Church possess one substance—of flesh, blood, and spirit—through the gift of adoption.

The beginning of the new law is the washing away of former sins. The Savior, although he belonged to the earlier covenant, nevertheless came as the guarantor of the better covenant. It is therefore necessary that there be one power in those who possess one perfection of the sacraments.

The Apostle says: “You are the body of Christ and members of it, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.” Since, according to the teaching of Scripture, we are assured that through the divine sacrament of Baptism we can be joined to the Spirit, and since by the same reasoning we say that our bodies too are bound to the members of the Son by the bond of a confession that endures, and that nothing is lost to unity through grace, what doubt remains that our Apostles and Martyrs also earned perfect and complete concord?

For the Spirit is God, and God is the Son, Christ, who by equal power rejects the notion of an injurious subordination; who by the venerable triumph of his members left no space for death; who refuses the name of singularity; who perceives neither an end nor a beginning in any part of himself.

The Apostles, moreover, and the Saints, both through the sanction of the spiritual mystery and through the sacrifice of the body and the reckoning of blood and the sacrifice of suffering, ascend to the throne of the Redeemer. He himself says in the Gospel: “When the Son shall sit on the throne of his glory, you also shall sit upon twelve tribunals, judging the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). And again: “Whose sins you remit, they are remitted; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

It follows, then, that they are wholly with the whole Savior. For those who differ in nothing in their profession share everything in the truth of the Godhead. Through justice they become the Savior’s companions; through prudence, his rivals; through the use of their limbs, fellow-members of the body; through blood, kindred; through the completion of the sacrifice, sharers in the eternity of the cross.

For it is written: “I ascend to my Father and your Father.” If, therefore, the Father is common, the sons also are common; if the sons are common, the inheritance is common; if the inheritance is common, eternity is common.

The Saints, having been granted immortality through victory, still require that the authority of their wills be not divided but one. The Lord himself declares this before the Father: “Father, sanctify them in truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world. And for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth. I ask not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me and that I send them.

“The glory that you gave me, I have given them, so that they may be one as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected in one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me.”

For saving authority is seized by the worthy man, whoever has raised aloft the insignia of sacred confession.

## VIII

There is one kind of immortality, dearest ones, which is eternal without any conception of frailty. There is another, which is granted through generosity. We cannot deny that immortality was given to the Apostles and Martyrs. But we maintain this: after divinity has been attained, there is nothing that separates the Trinity from the offering of the Saints, since the very Truth of the Trinity brought them forth.

For we must confess that the nature of God is full and perfect. Otherwise an injury is done if we deny this, since the Lord says: “Whoever denies me and my words before human beings, I also will deny him before my Father and his Angels.”

Moreover, fullness admits nothing beyond itself. But blood, after martyrdom, glows with the reward of divinity. Therefore let the injury of distinction be banished, since the bond of glory is the same.

“I go,” he says, “to my Father and your Father.” You see, then, beloved ones, that what belongs to the Father and the Son by the property of nature belongs to the Saints through the unity of the gift they have received.

God is diffused far and wide, and lends his light without diminishing himself. In whatever part he is present, he is wholly present in sense, wholly in sight, wholly in the consciousness of himself. Therefore the one who is perfect in the whole cannot fail to be perfect in the Apostles.

Perhaps someone might cry out at this point and say: “Then is the martyr the same as the first virtue, the absolute and ineffable substance of the Godhead?” I say that he is the same by gift, not by property; by adoption, not by nature. And thus it happens that when the great day arrives, the one who received the authority does not appear to have acquired anything, nor the one who gave it to have diminished anything.

It is the mark of a merciful and good disputant to proclaim beforehand what one should beware of. Behold, as though by the light of their relics set before us, they show us the path of truth. They teach reverence, faith, prudence, justice, fortitude, concord, continence, and chastity, while in the bodies they possess they punish what is contrary to these virtues and remove the stains of vices.

But they possess this mercy, this desire to teach, these riches of relics, and these fiery rays of light even when they begin to weigh our sins. It is the mark of a good king to judge without favor. Pure truth is found where the judge’s mind does not incline to either side.

But we are assisted by those very benefits that we now enjoy from them. Therefore all the goodness of the Saints, now dispersed, will be gathered together as though into one heap, so that they may hold the scepter of judgment without favor and without the injustice of appeal.

Sins are darkness; innocence is light. Therefore the prison of darkness must appear when what is of the light begins to return from itself to itself.

## IX

The benefits of the sun are widespread: it fills and illumines the eyes of all dwellings throughout the earth, yet its abundant supply does not withdraw from itself. It pours forth its gift and receives it back, and possesses within itself as much as it had previously bestowed. It gives, yet is found to be the master of the things given.

In the same way, dearest ones, before the day of judgment the splendor of the righteous is poured into all basilicas, into every church, and finally into the breast of every faithful person, only to return to itself when it assumes the person of the judge.

If this comparison seems paltry to anyone, let him understand that its majesty, not its error, lies in the fact that we compare corruptible things with divine realities and small things with great ones. Beginnings that are without a genus cannot be defined.

The substance of the Godhead, inclined toward itself, retains the dignity of its own likeness. No quality and no quantity can be found equal to the Trinity. The heavenly principle is taught, not compared; suggested, not embellished.

The example of the sun has therefore taught us about the Godhead. Yet it has not mingled itself with unity. Now it is clear to everyone that God made from nothing what did not exist; hence the poison (*virus*) of the dialecticians is often crushed. [Note: [Col. 0451D] The monk of St. Gall noted that *virtus* (“power”) should perhaps be read, and rightly so. This is against atheists.]

For if God, the author of things, fashioned this spiritual vessel and its members from what was empty, why could he not transfer an animated body, compacted as it were by the ferment of blood, into the substance of his own light?

But amid such great rejoicing we fill the book with the tumult of questions. Nor is this without reason, for the investigation of truth is the pleasure of the one who searches.

Thus God is recognized; thus the Savior is recognized; thus triumph is found extending its saving arms; thus eternal splendor is acquired for bodies. We understand by heavenly discourse that the Angels contain the spirit of fiery majesty, for thus we read: “He makes his Angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire.”

Therefore, if there is blood in the body, and if that blood itself is mingled with heavenly fire, nothing remains to be questioned: we must conclude that the blessed possess one and the same harmony with the whole.

Now, dearest ones, this suspicion must be wiped and erased from our minds, lest anyone, deceived by a common error, should think that in the small portions of the righteous and in this apostolic consecration the reality of the whole bodily passion does not remain.

But we proclaim with complete faith and authority that nothing in the relics is incomplete. For the limbs are whole where the healing is whole. We say that the flesh is held together by the bond of blood; we affirm that the spirit too, moistened with the dew of blood, has drawn the fiery heat of the Word.

Since this is so, it is certain that our Apostles and Martyrs have come to us with their powers intact. We are reminded that this is so also by the benefits presently bestowed. For when we acknowledge that the right of translation has been granted at their own will, we understand that they do not inflict loss upon themselves by their own dispersal, but, enriched by unity, scatter benefits.

A flame pours forth its brightness and gives it away, yet does not suffer loss through its generosity. Thus the Saints are munificent without damage, full without addition; thus they have reached us without the weariness of exile.

In the relics, therefore, there is a reminder of perfection, not an injury caused by division. Whatever is formed from an unequal conception and is not drenched with the liquid of the first spring must necessarily be perishable. The sun and the stars, the earth, and the remaining names of vanities receive corruptibility because they do not possess a spiritual origin.

But the suffering of the Saints is an imitation of Christ, and Christ is God. Therefore division must not be inscribed upon fullness; rather, in the very division that lies before the eyes, the reality of fullness must be adored.

[Col. 0452B] **X.** Why, then, do we call them relics? Because they are verbal images and signs of realities; blood and clay are placed before the eyes. We designate this by the name “relics,” since we cannot otherwise do so, as though by the impression of a living utterance. But now, by speaking of the whole in the part, we open not the barriers of bodily eyes but the eyes of the heart. For realities do not serve words; words serve realities. Therefore, once the snares of language have been removed, let reality contend with reality and reason with reason.

Every part that is called a species must receive within itself the force and definition of its genus. For when I say that an animal is an animate substance and a sensible substance, I have at the same time stated the definition of human beings, oxen, and the other living creatures. How, then, can anyone who does not perceive the things that are God’s be a human being? But if, in the definition of the genus, the characteristics of the species are also taken into account, how can it be that in relics there is not the fullness of the flesh, when the same principle applies spiritually?

We have therefore shown that the whole can be present in the part. We can no longer complain of smallness; for when we have said that nothing is lost from the sacred bodies according to the likeness of a genus, we have certainly established that what is divine cannot be diminished, because the whole is in the whole. Wherever something is present, the whole is present. And from divine teaching we gather that the body is made eternal through the infection—[or: infusion]—of the spirit. It follows, then, that nothing more should be desired where fullness is perceived.

For the sake of instruction, let us remain with that easy and widely known example. We speak of the ray of fire; we speak of its color; yet, by nature’s command, the one is divided from the other only by a distinction of names. Light gives birth to radiance, yet there is no separation between light and radiance. A human being, insofar as he is human, forms one fellowship with all others through the common condition of birth. Bronze, gold, and the remaining kinds of metals, although greed snatches them apart with hooked claws, nevertheless possess the quality of an indivisible substance.

It is therefore clear that a species must be referred to its nature. It is therefore clear that in relics there is perfection of the members, because communion is present in spiritual consecration. For as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones. If we were to say that the relics had been divided from the spirit, then indeed every connection and solidity of the inward parts would rightly be sought. But since we recognize that the substance is united, it is beside the point to seek the whole in the whole. An inquiry into a greater power is an injury to unity. This is deception of the eyes; the lights of reason are clearer.

We see small relics, a little blood. But truth perceives that these small fragments are brighter than the sun, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “My saints will shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father”; and then the sun itself will shine more brightly and more clearly than it does now.

[Note: Since he received only particles of congealed blood from several saints, he nevertheless indicates that these small relics are to be regarded as greatly precious. Here and above he gathers much concerning the intercession of the saints, and proposes further matters concerning the prerogative of blood, which he calls “the fragments of the saints.”]

**XI.** To this is added the fact that healing is no less present in the parts than in the whole. Do they otherwise extend medicine to the afflicted in the East, at Constantinople, Antioch, Thessalonica, and Naissus, than in Rome and Italy? Are suffering bodies otherwise relieved?

[Note: Naissus is here reckoned among the principal cities. It was situated in Thrace and is said to have been the birthplace of Constantine the Great. Among the letters of Pope Innocent I, one is addressed to Martianus, bishop of Naissus.]

The Evangelist John heals at Ephesus and, moreover, in many other places. We have received him from the breast of Christ, and we understand that he did not depart before his consecration; his medicine is present among us as well. At Bologna Proculus and Agricola heal, and here too we behold their majesty. Antoninus heals at Piacenza. Saturninus and Trajan heal in Macedonia. Nazarius heals at Milan. Mutius, Alexander, Datysus, and Chindeus pour forth the grace of salvation with abundant power.

[Note: Mutius, perhaps from Byzantium, in the year 211.]

[Note: Datysus, perhaps Dathus, bishop of Ravenna, who died on 3 July, probably around the year 190.]

[Note: Chindeus, perhaps a presbyter and martyr in Pamphylia under Diocletian, on 2 July. Further investigation remains concerning the others.]

Rogata [Note: The manuscripts read “Ragota,” which seems to be a copyist’s error.], Leonida, Anastasia, and Anatoclia heal, as the Apostle Paul says: “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,” by one and the same Spirit, who works all things in all.

Tell me: is the healing of the saints mentioned above one among us and another among others? If whatever belongs to the saints everywhere defends, purifies, and protects their worshipers with equal devotion, then their worship is to be increased, not their majesty examined. Even if the full weight of power were not present in relics, it would nevertheless not be sound-minded to detract anything from such dignity. For it is not useful to know, but to fear. For it is written: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin.” Whoever is without fear can nowhere be justified.

Countless matters present themselves, but we pursue the channels and paths of pure liquid. The hypothetical and categorical forms of syllogisms do not entangle me; the empty sophistries of philosophers do not deceive me. Truth itself discloses its face; faith spits out arguments; guilt seeks hiding places, innocence the open public.

With my hand, then, I point out what is sought; I touch the sores; I affirm that in these relics grace is perfect and power is perfect. If the matter had to be unfolded by a clash of words, I would say that it is the same in genus, species, and number. The faithless slanderer doubts this—perhaps he is not one who doubts, but one who does not love. But since I hold the whole by faith, I think that for the present we should dispense with superfluities: these things must be seen, not investigated.

Behold, the torturer of an unclean and polluted spirit presses upon him, yet the one who tortures does not appear to the eyes. There are no bonds, yet the sufferer is bound. The heavenly anger possesses a brazen rack.

There is no claw, yet such are the crimes confessed; no wound appears, yet the gnashing of teeth is heard; there is no questioning by an interrogator, yet permission to depart follows.

Surely no one—no one—is so poor in understanding as to say that fullness is lacking when he sees that nothing is lacking for examination. For undoubtedly God is whoever is the torturer and judge of invisible things. An imperfect nature does not know how to wound the spirit. No one judges inward things except the one who heals. No one commands the elements except the one who treads upon the scepter. No one possesses the Trinity except the one who is entire in the parts and whole in the whole; the first sense needs no addition.

The Apostles and saints, moreover, not only seek no additions, but also bestow the benefits of health and salvation.

There is therefore one sense, one spirit, and one mingling of these with truth. The one who heals lives; the one who lives is in the relics. The Apostles and martyrs heal and cleanse. In the relics, therefore, they are bound by the bond of the whole of eternity. Every division is darkened by the cloud of death. We have sufficiently, indeed more than sufficiently, declared that the saints do not know the losses of division.

It remains, then, for us to understand that what the righteous lavish upon all is a matter of mercy, not of inquiry. The one who loves believes; the one who believes searches out faith in the disputant and priest, not words. Therefore, if our speech should seem distasteful to anyone, our devotion will certainly not displease him. He will see that we have written the book in simple faith, not in words; in worship, not in arguments; in veneration, not in curiosity. Whoever offers reverence is a lover of truth; whoever raises a question is its hater.

**XII.** Therefore, beloved, while the throng of the saints is still fresh, let us apply ourselves and bring forth sighs from the deepest veins of our bodies. The advocates are present; let us unfold the record of our offenses in prayer. The judges are favorable; they can soften the sentence—those to whom it was said: “You shall sit upon twelve tribunals, judging the twelve tribes of the children of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). They are always judges, because they are always Apostles.

But it was not so much eagerness to speak as the duty of faith that drew me farther; excessive joy does not know how to be silent. It is a loss to joy if there is no hearer. Therefore, if I had been able to remain silent amid such a celebration of those who rejoice, I would have incurred the charge of sorrow. The Apostles and martyrs are coming; it is not fitting for a bishop to be silent.

Altars are being raised; let the people take their beginning from the joy of the priest. Who, I ask, is so brutish, so profane, so ignorant of law and religion that he would not feel these joys? If one of the secular princes were now to visit our city, at once every space would laugh, bound with garlands; mothers would fill the roofs; the gates would stir a flood of people; every age, divided in its enthusiasm, would sing praises and martial deeds; it would marvel at the flames of the military cloak and Tyrian purple; it would be astonished at the price of the Red Sea and the frozen tears of beasts. And indeed such things are wondrous if you look at them, contemptible if you consider them. In the end they are called stones; yet these things, I say, would hold the gaping crowd spellbound.

But when the triumph of the martyrs and the procession of their virtues enter our homes, why should we not dissolve in joy? There is no lack of what we may admire. In place of royal clothing, the garment of eternal light is present. Here are the purple robes; here are the free togas of the saints; here are diadems distinguished by the varied brightness of gems—wisdom, understanding, knowledge, truth, counsel, fortitude, endurance, temperance, justice, prudence, patience, and chastity. These virtues are represented and inscribed in the individual stones.

Here the Savior, the artisan, has adorned the crowns of the martyrs with spiritual gems. Let us spread the sails of our souls toward these gems: there is nothing fragile in them, nothing that diminishes what is greater, nothing that suffers loss. They flower more and more in their appearance. Even the blood shows that the insignia of eternity have been set forth, for it still marks the fire of the Holy Spirit in the bodies themselves and in the relics of the members.

We rejoice, beloved, whenever we see darkness driven away by light. Why should we not rush forth more abundantly into joy when we see the radiance of lights that bring salvation and eternity conveyed to us? The day seems to me to have taken up the joy of a brighter serenity. And not without reason: as I have said, the martyrs are seven times brighter than the sun.

But now, beloved, we must pray, not deliver a speech—“pray,” I say [the manuscript lacks “pray” here]—that every assault of the devil may be driven away from us, for he enters our breast by a hidden slide. Therefore, saints, strengthen your worshipers; strengthen them, and equip our breast with the cornerstone.

The enemy is dangerous and strong; he examines every approach and every entrance. But there is nothing to fear: a great multitude of saints is coming to meet him. Since such a number of soldiers and kings has come to us from the heavenly camp, let us seize the weapons of justice and prudence; let us protect ourselves with the shield of faith; let us fortify our breasts not with the scales of armor but with the plates of temperance and chastity. Let us always brandish in our right hands the weapons of faith and patience. Let us strike at once if any enemy knocks.

Such weapons the Apostles once carried, such weapons. Equipped with them, they broke the necks of intemperance, wantonness, greed, ambition, anger, and pride.

The Savior’s mercy has denied us nothing—not weapons, not defenses. We must therefore take the greatest care lest the torpor of vices overtake us as though we were drowsy; lest unbelief, hostile to faith, steal upon us; lest anger delay us, greed harass us, or ambition struggle against us.

Our martyrs will gladly dwell with us if we bring them a pure conscience in their service. If this warfare should seem hard and inescapable to anyone, let him not throw away his spear before the trumpet sounds, nor let the chill of death overtake him before the battle. Let no one abandon the standards of the Savior. He gave the example; he sends reinforcements.

Victory is certain when one fights with such comrades-in-arms and with Christ as commander. Then, surely, the priest’s helmet will shine upon me, if your love sees me in the battle line. To fight while you watch and follow is a blaze of glory.

A secure station and the most fortified harbor of salvation are unshaken faith and spiritual steadfastness. A good life is of no benefit if you do not know for whom you live. The storm of winds will carry away a light and unbelieving mind.

Faith is what carried the saints to heaven. Faith is what changed flames into dew and infused saving coolness into the spheres of fire. Faith is what solidified the liquids of tossing waves beneath the feet of those who walked upon them. Faith is what presents the martyrs, consecrated, as an example of death. Faith is what fortified the souls of confessors in the struggle of suffering. Faith is what feeds upon fasting, vigils, and dry food in humility. Faith is what guards virginity, widowhood, and continence with modest integrity. Faith is what removed bodily desire and instilled love of heavenly rule. Faith is what joins immortality to the Lord through the death of the cross.

Through the world’s hatred, faith presents to the Lord those who can die together with him. It comforts confessors in prisons, enclosed in the most dreadful horror of darkness; while they are tossed about amid squalor and filth and pierced by the very beds of the earth, deprived of sleep, they obtain only a little rest for a short time. While each day they are mangled by every kind of torture, while at last they are pressed by punishments of many forms, their virtue advances toward the crown.

Faith is what, amid all these struggles, offers God a beloved unity and repays Christ by dying for him. Just as the head died for the members of the body, so the members die for the head, so that, as the head lives, the members may also be made alive with the head. Blessed Paul confirms this: “If we die with Christ, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him.”

It remains, beloved, that the confession of our sins should follow. Not that the divine powers do not know the departures and secrets of souls, but an unforced confession readily draws forth the mercy of the judge.

Let there be no day, dear brothers, on which we do not recall in these stories: that martyr did not grow pale beneath the torturer; that one outstripped the executioner’s delay by his eagerness; that one eagerly drank the flames; that one was cut apart but stood unharmed; that one called himself fortunate because he was granted torture; that one, among the hands of executioners, ordered the river to return more quickly, lest any delay impede his haste.

One woman grieved at her father’s tears as a daughter but despised them as a martyr. Another, eager for death, provoked the lion’s anger by goading it. Another, while her son fasted, offered breasts full of milk to the wild beasts. Another, a virgin, submitted her neck to the executioner, adorned with the necklaces of eternity.

There are thousands, dear brothers, of examples of virtue that the sacred page commemorates. But for the sake of exhortation rather than instruction, we have selected a few from many. For a few things suffice for the faithful; many things benefit the unbelieving not at all.

The desires of the saints must not be delayed. Why do we linger? Let the divine hall be opened to the martyrs [the manuscript has an uncertain reading, represented by “y”]; let the relics be joined; let graces also be joined; let the beginnings of the first resurrection come together. Meanwhile, let our confession steal forward. The rejoicing of the powers is forgiveness of sins.

Not without reason, dear brothers, in my eagerness as a builder I seized the space of the basilica. The arrival of the saints excuses my eagerness. By the hidden intention of my desire, they themselves ordered a hall to be prepared for them. So it is, truly so. For we laid foundations, extended the walls lengthwise, and today we learn by what works the purpose of our labor was growing.

Therefore, every delay has been driven away by correction; nothing sluggish or slow delights me. It pleases me to turn the work with my hands and carry great stones upon my shoulders. May the earth drink my sweat—and would that it might drink my blood for the name of the Savior! For the present, let the earth drink my sweat as it prepares to receive the altars. If our faithful Apostles and martyrs see us, they will invite others.

[Col. 0457]

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 417**

**PAMMACHIUS AND OCEANUS. SOME LETTERS**

[Col. 0457A] See these letters among the Hieronymian letters, volume XXII of our *Patrologia*, under numbers XLVIII, XLIX, LVII, LXVI, LXIX, LXXXIII, LXXXIV, and XCVII.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 417**

**POPE INNOCENT I**

[Col. 0457]

## Prolegomena

### Biographical Notices

**I.**

From the *Liber Pontificalis*, in Labbe, *Collection of the Councils*, volume II.

Innocent, by nationality an Albanian, the son of Innocent, sat for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. He issued a decree concerning the whole Church, the rules of monasteries, the Jews, and the pagans. He found many Cataphrygians, whom he banished into the exile of a monastery. He found Pelagius and Caelestius to be heretics and condemned them. He also decreed that whoever had been born of a Christian woman ought to be born again through baptism—that is, to be baptized—which Pelagius condemned.

At the same time he dedicated the basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, in accordance with the disposition of the will of a distinguished woman named Vestina. The presbyters Ursicinus and Lopardo and the deacon Libyanus directed the work. The woman mentioned above arranged the text of her will in such a way that a basilica of the holy martyrs would be built from its ornaments and pearls, sold at fair valuations. It was constructed to completion.

In that place, the blessed Innocent, by authority delegated by the distinguished woman Vestina, established a Roman title. In the same building he offered two silver patens, each weighing twenty pounds; two silver *amae* [vessels], each weighing twenty pounds; twelve silver crowns, each weighing fourteen pounds; one *pharus-cantharus* [lamp or vessel], weighing twenty-two pounds; four silver *cerostrata* [lampstands or candle-bearing vessels], each weighing twenty-five pounds; a silver tower with a paten; and a gilded dove weighing thirty pounds.

For the decoration of the baptistery he offered a silver stag pouring out water, weighing fifteen pounds; a silver vessel for chrism oil, weighing five pounds; another vessel for exorcised oil, weighing five pounds; two patens for chrism, each weighing three pounds; an embossed silver cup weighing ten pounds; another silver cup weighing ten pounds; five silver chalices, each weighing three pounds; three silver baptismal chalices, each weighing one pound and two ounces; silver water vessels weighing sixteen pounds; sixteen bronze *phara-canthara*, each weighing ten pounds; and twenty bronze *phara-canthara cerostrata* in the basilica, each weighing forty pounds.

He also gave houses beside the basilica in the Libyan district, yielding eighty-five solidi and one tremissis; a bathhouse in the same district beside the temple of Mamuri, yielding thirty-two solidi; houses on the Clivus Salutis Balneatae, yielding seven solidi and one tremissis; the estate of Sarras in the territory of Clusium, yielding seventy-one solidi and one tremissis; the estate of Corbiana in the territory of Clusium, yielding seventy-nine solidi; the estate of Fundanensis in the territory of Fundanum, with fifteen adjoining plots, yielding 181 solidi and one tremissis; the estate of Figlina in the territory of Casinum, yielding fifty-eight solidi and one tremissis; the estate of Amandinus, which the distinguished woman Vestina had given to her cousin in the territory of Veii, yielding forty-six solidi and one tremissis; the estate of Antoniana in the territory of Clodius, yielding sixty-two solidi; and the houses of Emeritus on the Clivus Mamuri, between the city of Rome and the basilica, yielding sixty-two solidi.

He also gave houses on the Clivus Patricius, whose value was assessed; houses beside the basilica on the Long Street, called “at the Lake,” yielding eighty-two solidi; houses at the stone chair of Florianus, yielding fifty-eight solidi; a bakery on the Long Street, called “of Castorianus,” yielding sixty-one solidi; and a bathhouse on the Long Street, called “the Temple,” yielding forty solidi … [lacuna] siliquae … three … ounces … at the Nomentan Gate, yielding twenty-two solidi and a half.

He decreed that fasting should be observed on Saturday, because the Lord was placed in the tomb on Saturday and the disciples fasted. He established that the basilica of Saint Agnes the martyr should be carefully and appropriately administered, roofed, and decorated by the presbyters Leop ardus and Paulinus. By Vestina’s arrangement, the presbyters of the title mentioned above were granted authority.

He held four ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: thirty presbyters, fifteen deacons, and fifty-four bishops for various places. He was also buried in the cemetery of Priscilla, at the Bear with the Cap, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. His episcopate ended on the twenty-second day.

### Notes of Severinus Binius

Innocent. After the pontifical see had been vacant for twenty-one days following the death of Anastasius, Innocent the Albanian was elected Roman pontiff on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year of Christ 402, the eighth year of Arcadius and Honorius.

At the beginning of his pontificate Martin, bishop of Tours, departed this life for heaven. Chrysostom, banished through the efforts and machinations of Theophilus from the council held at the Oak and recalled with difficulty by the emperor Arcadius, was ordered into exile a second time because he had spoken publicly against the secular games celebrated with the permission of the emperor Honorius and against the pagan rites at the dedication of the silver statue of the empress Eudoxia.

For this reason Eudoxia, again inflamed with the greatest severity, arranged through Theophilus of Alexandria that Chrysostom, after being restored to his see, should once more be deposed and banished by the emperor Arcadius—even though, having been deposed by a synod, he ought to have been restored only by a synodal judgment, according to canon twelve of the council of Antioch.

In the third year of his exile, he was sent farther away by order of Arcadius, at the request of his adversaries. Struck by fever, he departed to the Lord in the year 407, the sixth year of Innocent’s pontificate. The emperor Arcadius, the empress Eudoxia, and the other persecutors of Chrysostom experienced the indignation of the offended deity and were removed prematurely from life a few months after Chrysostom’s death.

When that great invasion of the city occurred, brought about by the indignation of God through Alaric, the pontiff was being kept at Ravenna by hidden divine providence, like righteous Lot withdrawn from Sodom, so that, as the blessed Orosius says in book VII, chapter 39, the holy man would not see the destruction of the sinful people.

During his time the famous conference in Africa between Catholics and Donatists took place. It had long been desired and often attempted, but never completed because the Donatists repeatedly withdrew. Saint Augustine describes it at length in the *Breviarium*.

The arch-heretics Pelagius and Vigilantius arose under this pontiff and, by his judgment, received a rightful sentence of condemnation. He correctly maintained against Pelagius that children born of faithful parents must be baptized with no less necessity for salvation than those born of unbelieving parents. Yet he did not establish this sufficiently well by the argument that the Eucharist must likewise be received by all infants with equal necessity for salvation. See the notes on letter 25 below.

He sat for fifteen years and two months. The beginning and end of his pontificate show that he held it for fifteen years, one month, and ten days. It is clearly gathered from the twenty-sixth letter of Innocent and from certain letters of Zosimus, dated to the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, that he departed this life in the year 417, the twenty-third year of Honorius and the tenth of Theodosius.

Since the aforementioned consuls held office in the year of Christ 417, and Innocent’s death is recorded on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, calculation from the beginning of his see to that point will yield the stated number of years, months, and days. Baronius, year 417, no. 4.

“He issued a decree concerning the whole Church.” That is, a decree pertaining to the universal Church. I think this is the decree that Gennadius describes in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 43, in these words: “Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a decree issued by the Western and Eastern churches against the Pelagians; his successor, Pope Zosimus, later promulgated it in Latin.” His other decrees, concerning the rules of monks, the Jews, and the pagans, are lacking. Baronius, no. 5.

“Pelagius and Caelestius, etc.” Concerning this condemnation, Saint Prosper, in *Against the Collator*, reports the following from the words of Pope Zosimus: “We decree that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Caelestius by the venerable Innocent from the see of the blessed Apostle remain in force until they openly confess the grace of God,” and so forth.

“To be baptized, which Pelagius condemned.” In his letter written to Innocent, as Augustine reports in *On Original Sin*, chapter 17, Pelagius complained that he was being falsely defamed in this matter: “He says,” Augustine writes in the passage cited, “that he is defamed by people because he denies the sacrament of baptism to little children and promises the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption.”

Therefore, what is said here—that Pelagius denied baptism to infants—must be understood in the sense that, even if not in words, he could nevertheless appear to have condemned it in fact, since he denied original sin, on account of which baptism is necessary for infants.

This is what Saint Augustine adds in the same place: “But these charges are not brought against them in the form in which he presented them; for they neither deny the sacrament of baptism to infants nor promise the kingdom of heaven to anyone without Christ’s redemption. Thus, in stating the matter about which he complains that he is defamed, he put it in such a way that he could easily answer the charge brought against him while preserving his own doctrine.”

The charge brought against them, however, is that they refuse to confess that unbaptized infants are subject to the condemnation of the first man and that original sin has passed into them, to be cleansed through regeneration. Baronius, year 417, no. 5.

“He decreed that fasting should be observed on Saturday.” Understand this not as though Innocent, by the authority of this decree, were the first to institute Saturday fasting, but as meaning that he wrote about it in his reply to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, who had written to him asking to be informed of the reason for this fast. Baronius, year 417, no. 6. See the notes on Apostolic Canon 65.

**II.**

From Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, volume I.

Immediately after the death of Anastasius, Innocent was appointed in his place by the unanimous consent of the bishops, clergy, and people. Antonio Pagius thinks that this occurred on 21 December in the year 401.

He was rightly adorned with praises by both Greeks and Latins. Socrates, book VII, chapter 9, records that he was the first to persecute the Novatians and to deprive them of many churches. He acquired singular glory through his steadfast defense of John Chrysostom. He then increased that glory considerably through the reconciliation and peace of the church of Antioch and the other Eastern churches, and finally crowned it by the solemn condemnation of the Pelagians.

Since it is established by the evidence of his own letters that he carried this out at the end of January 417, and since it is no less certain from the letters of this pope that Zosimus was administering the Roman Church before April of that same year, it remains that Innocent’s death must be assigned to the year 417, specifically to the interval between January and April.

It cannot therefore be reconciled either with 28 July, as Baronius believed by following the ancient pontifical books, or with 21 December, as Bollandus preferred on the authority of certain martyrologies. Cardinal Norisius learnedly approved and confirmed its placement on 12 March in his *History of the Pelagians*, page 71, as did Antonio Pagius for the year 417, numbers 5 and 6.

The authority of the martyrologies of Bede, Ado, Usuard, and others is clear on this matter. But nothing more evident or certain against the opinions of Baronius and Bollandus can be desired than the testimony of Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, bishop in Sicily. Writing to Pope Leo in letter 3, he expressly teaches that Zosimus held the pontificate of the Roman Church in the year 417, while Easter was being celebrated.

**III.**

From Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, volume VIII.

**1.** At the end of the year 401, Innocent succeeded Anastasius. He was, as Saint Jerome says, “the successor and son of Anastasius in the apostolic chair and in the same office.”

Prosper calls him “most worthy of the see of Peter.” Theodoret rightly calls him *ἀνὴρ ἀγχινοίᾳ καὶ συνέσει κοσμούμενος*, “a man adorned with remarkable intelligence and prudence.” For he accomplished marvelous things in the government of the universal Church, whether in defending the Catholic faith, restoring ecclesiastical discipline, or preserving the unity of the churches; in all these matters he acted vigorously and manfully.

Tillemont, as is his custom, carefully wove together his distinguished deeds above all others. Coustantius summarizes them as follows:

Socrates records that Innocent was the first to persecute the Novatians and to deprive them of many churches. He acquired singular glory through his steadfast defense of John Chrysostom. He then increased it considerably through the reconciliation and peace of the church of Antioch and the other Eastern churches, and finally crowned it by the solemn condemnation of the Pelagians.

Therefore, to conclude with Pagius, God summoned him to heaven soon after so outstanding a deed, by which he acquired such fame that no further addition to his reputation seemed possible, “lest after that divine and immortal act he should perform anything mortal.” These are words of Pliny, used by Pagius.

For the rest, the most learned Norisius vindicates Innocent’s commendation of Saint Augustine’s doctrine against the Pelagians from the distorted interpretations of more recent writers.

[Notes: Jerome, Letter 130 to Demetrias, §16; Prosper, *Against the Collator*, ch. 5, §3; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, V.24; Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. X, p. 627 ff.; Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 737; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.9; Pagi, under the year 417, §4; Pliny, *Panegyric of Trajan*, ch. 10; Noris, *Vindication of Augustine*, ch. 6, *Works*, vol. I, p. 1157.]

**2.** Nor should the following, which Orosius relates as having happened to Innocent, be passed over without remembrance. In the year 409, the chief pontiff was sent by the Romans as an envoy to the emperor Honorius in order to establish peace with Alaric. But when the embassy failed, and while the holy pontiff was still staying at Ravenna, the Gothic king besieged Rome in the following year, 410, and devastated it.

On this subject the praised Orosius writes:

“It also happened, so that it might be proved that the city’s invasion was brought about more by the indignation of God than by the strength of the enemy, that the blessed Innocent, bishop of the Roman Church, was then kept at Ravenna by the hidden providence of God, like righteous Lot withdrawn from Sodom, and did not see the destruction of the sinful people.”

Speaking of the same siege of the city, Zosimus, the most hostile enemy of Christians, says that Innocent permitted the pagans, when Alaric was already threatening Rome, to drive away the barbarian enemy by vows publicly made to their gods. But the great Baronius refutes the slander brought by Zosimus against the Roman pontiff on the basis of Sozomen.

For learned observations concerning the date of this embassy of Innocent, see the Ballerini brothers.

[Notes: Orosius, *History*, VII.39; Zosimus, *New History*, V, p. 356, Oxford ed. 1679; Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.6; Baronius, under the year 409, §7; Ballerini, notes on Noris’s *Works*, vol. IV, pp. 851 ff.]

**3.** Finally, after Innocent the pontiff had condemned the Pelagians at the end of January 417, as is proved by the authority of his letters, he was soon afterward summoned to heaven, on the fourth day before the Ides of March of the same year.

His day of death is established on the authority of the martyrologies of Bede, Ado, Usuard, and others. The month and year, however, are established beyond dispute by the testimony of Paschasinus of Lilybaeum in Sicily, once a client of Pope Zosimus, who succeeded Innocent.

For in a letter written to Saint Leo, he expressly teaches that this pontiff held office at Easter in the year 417, saying:

“In the time of the blessed memory of my lord Zosimus, your predecessor in the apostolate, in the eleventh consulship of the emperor Honorius Augustus and the second of Constantius—for then, when it was being reckoned that Easter Day would be observed on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, it was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

This chronological notation was first observed and explained by a man most eminent both in rank and learning, whom others subsequently followed. [Note: Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, I.11, *Works*, vol. I, p. 3.]

Finally, the following unusual fact must not be omitted: in the *Fasti* of the ancient marble calendar of the Neapolitan Church, the memory of Saint Innocent is celebrated with a martyr’s commendation and, contrary to custom, is recorded on 24 April, whereas in other liturgical books it is entered either on 12 March, 28 July, or 21 December.

The learned Mazochius discusses both difficulties with his customary erudition; we refer readers to him. [Note: Mazochius, *Commentary on the Ancient Marble Calendar of the Neapolitan Church*, vol. I, pp. 229 ff.]

## 4.

Moreover, the letters of so great a pontiff—forty-two in number, with another seven interwoven with them, written to him or concerning his actions—were diligently reviewed and elucidated with learned notes by the distinguished scholar Coutantius. Accordingly, as often elsewhere, we have reproduced his edition in print. Since mention of Innocent’s writings has arisen again, it is useful to bring forward what Gennadius reports in these words [Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, book, chapter 43]:

> Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a decree issued against the Pelagians by the Western and Eastern Churches, which his successor, Pope Zosimus, later promulgated more fully.

Concerning this passage Norisius observes as follows [Note: Norisius, loc. cit., p. 114]:

> “I do not know,” he says, “what the Eastern Church decreed against the Pelagians before Innocent’s decree. Their case was debated only in the Synod of Diospolis, in which Pelagius was acquitted, although in fact he was compelled to anathematize the errors alleged against him—a fact which Augustine reproaches the Pelagians with hundreds of times. Certainly Innocent did not wish to approve the proceedings of the Palestinian synod. Hence,” he says [Note: Innocent, letter 31, § 4, below, p. 605b], “we can neither condemn nor approve their judgment, since we do not know whether the proceedings are genuine; or, if they are genuine, whether it is not clear that he”—that is, Pelagius—“rather evaded the charge than cleared himself entirely by the truth.”

> Photius writes [Note: Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex LIV] that the Pelagians were condemned in the East by the Church of Alexandria: “Those who held such opinions,” he says, “were expelled from the Church as heretics in the time of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and Innocent, bishop of Rome.”

> Photius is mistaken. Theophilus, seized by lethargy, died in the consulship of Honorius IX and Theodosius V, on 15 October, according to Socrates [Note: Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 7], that is, in the year 412. But in that year the Pelagian heresy was still concealed and had broken out nowhere except at Carthage. Furthermore, when Valerian, a Pelagian servant, withdrew to Alexandria, Eusebius warned Cyril, Theophilus’s nephew, not to provide a place for the heretic, since the Pelagians were being expelled by the other Easterners:

> “How is it now,” he says, “that, when Innocent of blessed memory condemned Pelagius and Caelestius [Col. 0464B] together with their leaders, and all the Easterners rejected them, the Church of Alexandria has received them into communion—although it alone, and first among its neighboring churches, ought to have rejected such men?”

> He says nothing here about any sentence pronounced by Theophilus against the Pelagians. Yet this ought to have been pressed upon his nephew, who clung so stubbornly to his uncle’s decrees that he even used them as grounds for censure in the case of Chrysostom. It is therefore clear that the Eastern Church pronounced nothing against the Pelagians in Theophilus’s time. Vossius was consequently misled [Note: Vossius, *History of the Pelagian Controversy*, book I, chapter 39] when he counted Theophilus among those who condemned Pelagius—misled by Photius’s testimony.”

The very learned author inserts this and much more into the passage of Gennadius. However, concerning what Norisius here reports about Photius’s testimony and Eusebius’s letter to Cyril of Alexandria, the learned Ballerinii must be consulted [Note: Ballerinii, *Observations on Noris’s Works*, vol. IV, book I, chapter 5, §§ 4–5, p. 866]. They demonstrate that Photius was not mistaken and, following Tillemont, call into question the authenticity of that letter of Eusebius.

# [LETTERS AND DECREES]

[Col. 0463]

## LETTERS AND DECREES OF SAINT INNOCENT I, POPE. (C,S)*

[Note: These are among the letters which Helstenius published as inserted into the acts of the Roman synod under Boniface II, in the first part of the *Roman Collection*. Since Innocent calls these letters the first fruits of his episcopate, which he began immediately after the death of Anastasius, we may reasonably conclude that they were written around May of the year 402.]

## LETTER I, OF POPE INNOCENT I, TO ANYSIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

Innocent confirms to Anysius the authority over the churches of Illyricum which Anastasius and his predecessors had granted him.

[Col. 0463D]

### INNOCENT TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHER ANYSIUS

Since our God Christ deigned to call to himself, though swiftly, Anastasius, the bishop of blessed memory [Col. 0464D], reckoning his merits to be so great and such that they had already surpassed the fellowship of human life and this age, on account of the purity of his life and the abundance of his learning, by which he governed God’s people with the full rigor of ecclesiastical authority; and since, so that his Church might not remain even briefly without the governance of a ruler, God in his mercy immediately ordained me in his place, with the holy priests, the entire clergy, and the people consenting in peace—that peace which God, returning to heaven, deigned to grant to his Church—it was fitting, dearest brother, that you should learn [variant: “know”] that I had been appointed in his place, and that I should promptly announce my first fruits to none other than a man of the highest excellence, always laboring faithfully in God [Note: This same Anysius is praised by Palladius in his *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*, chapter 3, with the encomium “of the good old man” (*τοῦ καλογήρου*). There it is also mentioned that he gave his own letters to Eulysius, bishop of Apamea in Bithynia, who was carrying to Rome letters from fifteen bishops on behalf of Chrysostom.].

To him, moreover, my predecessors, such great and eminent men—the bishops Damasus and Siricius, and the man mentioned above—showed such deference that they entrusted to your holiness, which is full of justice, the knowledge of everything that was being done in those regions. You ought to recognize that I hold the same judgment and have the same will. For it was not right either that I should attempt to act against the judgment of such good men, whose place I am recognized to have succeeded, or that anything should seem to be taken away from your merit, to which those distinguished men appear to have granted so great a share of this authority. I therefore openly acknowledge that this too has been reserved for my insignificance: that, with the same judgment and in like manner, I should grant to both good men and your charity what you deserve.

# NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

### 1. Its authenticity is not rendered doubtful by the passages transcribed from Siricius

Much of Siricius’s fourth letter is reproduced in this one. But, as Tillemont observed, this should by no means seem surprising, since Innocent, when Victricius asked him to provide the rules customarily observed in the Roman Church, could not have fulfilled the request more effectively than by copying the decrees of his predecessors. There is therefore no adequate reason for rejecting either the aforesaid letter as Siricius’s or this one as Innocent’s. Nor are the grounds for assigning this letter to Innocent weaker than those for assigning the other to Siricius. It is cited under Innocent’s name by the Second Council of Tours, canon 20; frequently by Cresconius in his *Brief Summary of the Canons*; and by Pope Zacharias in Sirmond’s first volume of the *Councils of Gaul*, letter 9, chapters 14 and 20. Moreover, among the many ancient collections which we have examined, it is missing from none and appears in none without being assigned to Innocent. It is attributed to him by the Corbie exemplar copied in the time of Pope Vigilius; by the larger Colbert manuscript written in Lombard capitals; by the ancient Code of Canons published by Quesnellus; by the exemplars of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections; and also by the Hispana, Isidoriana, and several other collections.

### 2. It should not be assigned to the year 405

In all these collections—except the Dionysian, in which the consular notation is omitted—the ending of the letter is exactly the same, and with complete agreement it is assigned to the consulship of Honorius Augustus VI and Aristenetus. Thus no room remains for the conjecture of the learned man who suspects that this consular notation was added by someone else to Innocent’s letter, or at least that one ought to read “after the consulship of Honorius,” and so forth. Even if we grant that the words “after the consulship,” ordinarily represented by the initial letters P. C. by copyists, might easily have dropped out, nevertheless, in at least one old manuscript the wording would have been retained as “of Honorius and Aristenetus,” not “to Honorius and Aristenetus”; nor should the abbreviation *conss.* have been added in any manuscript.

Nor are we compelled to concede more to that conjecture if we examine why he thinks the letter was written in 405 rather than 404. He is moved solely by the words in section 5, in which Innocent mentions what he endured concerning the curials while the emperor was present and Victricius was staying with him. Hence he thinks it follows that the letter was written not only after the emperor had come to Rome, but also after Victricius had returned from Rome to Rouen.

He says that the emperor Honorius came to Rome only in December 403 and had not come there earlier, as may be gathered from Claudian’s poem. Victricius, however, could not have returned from Rome to Rouen in so short an interval—the period extending from the emperor’s arrival in the city to 15 February 404—and then sent a letter to Innocent which would have reached him beforehand. From this he concludes that the letter was sent not during the consulship of Honorius Augustus, but after the consulship of Honorius Augustus, that is, in 405 rather than 404.

But if, on account of an event of which there is no certain record, we are permitted to reject the testimony of so many, so diverse, and so ancient titles, what certainty will remain in history? Let us grant, then, that Honorius came to Rome toward the end of 403 and that Victricius was at that time in the city. Even if we agree that this same bishop had returned to Rouen before receiving Innocent’s letter, what compels us to do so? Innocent mentions neither anyone sent to him in Victricius’s name nor any letter of his delivered to him.

The learned man replies that the word *misi* (“I sent”), which Innocent uses at the beginning, indicates that Victricius was absent. But even if it indicates absence, it does not necessarily mean that Victricius had returned to Rouen or had left Rome. What prevents Victricius, while preparing to depart from Rome and saying farewell to Innocent, from asking him for a book of ecclesiastical rules, and Innocent, not then having the book at hand, from arranging for it to be prepared as soon as possible and delivered to Victricius before his departure from the city?

Nor is it necessary that those to whom we are said to send something be far from us. Every day friends send one another small gifts, books, letters, and so forth, even while remaining within the walls of the same city. Damasus and Jerome provide an example of this above, pp. 579 and following.

### 3. The book is called a book of rules. The division into chapters

Moreover, the aforementioned book of rules seems to be none other than this very letter, since in it Innocent, after a brief preface, explains numerous chapters of discipline by which the Churches are to be governed. These chapters, although not in every manuscript, are displayed summarily in most manuscripts with headings placed before them. Yet even in those manuscripts the division or summary of the chapters is not uniform; it varies according to the skill and discretion of those who collected the pontifical letters.

The division found in the exemplars of the Code published by Quesnellus is more extensive than the others. We would therefore have been content to reproduce that one here, unless it seemed worthwhile to add another from the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, with which the Hispana—and through it the Isidoriana—agrees almost everywhere. Since Cresconius and other collectors of canons commonly cite the decrees of the Roman pontiffs according to the division of headings arranged by Dionysius, it is necessary to know what that division is if their citations are to be understood.

Dionysius Exiguus encompasses in twenty-nine headings all the decrees he collected from Innocent. Among them the first place is occupied by this pope’s letter to Decentius, divided into eight headings. This letter to Victricius follows it and is divided into twelve headings. Accordingly, Dionysius calls the first decree of this letter heading 9 and the last heading 20, as may be seen below.

### 4. The laws that prohibited curials from leaving the curia

Among those decrees, the matter discussed chiefly in chapter 11 concerning the curials—because the same subject will repeatedly arise in the letters of other pontiffs—requires somewhat fuller explanation here than is possible in the annotations.

Curials, or decurions, were those who performed municipal magistracies and offices. The emperor Majorian, at the beginning of Novel 1, speaks of them as follows:

> “No one is unaware that the curials are the sinews of the commonwealth and the entrails of the cities; antiquity rightly called their assembly the lesser Senate.”

But, as the same emperor observes, provincial judges or governors reduced many people by their unjust exactions to the point of abandoning their homeland.
