The curials were responsible for the administration of taxes, buildings, public duties or games, and similar matters. Consequently, the emperors enacted severe laws by which no one was permitted to be released from the curia unless he had fulfilled all the offices of his curia.

The emperor Constantine decreed [Theodosian Code, book XII, title 1, law 11]:

> “Let no judge attempt to grant any curial exemption from civic duties, or release anyone from the curia at his own discretion.”

He also ordered that, even among those who abandoned their curiae and sought refuge in military service,

> “all who are not yet found bound to the office of *primipilus* shall, once released from military service, return to the curia” [law 1].

He likewise established [law 12], as the commentator Annianus explains:

> “Whoever among the curials wishes to pass from the city in which he was born to another shall in no way be able to escape the condition owed to the curia, nor, under any pretext of necessity or by claiming the services of his city, evade it merely because he wished to change cities.”

By another law [law 20] he ordered:

> “No curial may assume the office of curator or defender unless all the duties of the curia have been performed in their proper order”—Annianus adds, “those owed to the homeland.”

Nor were the emperors more indulgent toward those who moved from the curia into the clergy. Ambrose, in letter 41 to the emperor Theodosius, section 29, thought it appropriate to protest to him on this matter as follows:

> “How shall I excuse myself before the bishops, who now grieve deeply because certain presbyters who have held their rank for thirty and more years, or ministers of the Church, are being dragged away from sacred office and assigned to the curia?”

That protest was all the more equitable because Constantine had previously ordered [law 13] that the curiae should be warned to do the following from then on:

> “Let them drag back to the curia only those whom they find, within twenty years of service in office, either to have evaded their origin or, having rejected nomination to military service, to have inserted themselves into it.”

Indeed, Julian later decreed [law 56]:

> “Those who, being curials by birth, have desired military service shall, once ten years of service have been completed, be exempt from the curia by the authority of our commands.”

### 5. Under what condition curials were permitted to enter the clergy

Curials were not so excluded from the clergy that every access to it was closed to them. Valentinian and Valens permitted them to enter the clergy under a certain condition, which they explained in a law issued on 10 September 364 [law 59]:

> “Whoever chooses the Church must either make a curial in his place by transferring his own property to a close relative, or surrender his resources to the curia which he has left; otherwise, the person who has done neither is to be recalled by necessity.”

That is, whoever transferred neither his property to a relative nor to his own curia was to be recalled to the curia without exception.

There is also a constitution on the same subject, issued by Theodosius on 7 November 384 [law 104]:

> “Curials who prefer to serve the churches rather than the curiae, if they wish to be what they pretend to be, must despise the possessions which they withhold. For we do not free them in any other way than by their despising their patrimonies.”

Ambrose had this in mind when he wrote in letter 18 to Valentinian, section 13:

> “If a priest seeks the privilege of avoiding the curial burden, he must surrender possession of his homeland, his ancestral property, and all his resources.”

Constantius had been somewhat more indulgent. For on 29 August 361, he first decreed, in favor of bishops [law 49]:

> “No one shall compel a bishop to transfer his possessions to the curia, as had previously been established.”

He then wished those who had attained the rank of presbyter, and also of deacon, subdeacon, or other clerical orders, to enjoy the same privilege, provided that the curia assisted and the judge, observing the matter, expressed consent—especially if they were sought by the voices of the entire people.

Otherwise, he ordered them to assign two portions of their property either to relatives substituted for them in curial service or to the curia; but he reserved the third portion for them.

The following provision at the end of the same constitution seems to concern those who failed to meet the conditions mentioned above:

> “If the superintendents of warehouses, those who are about to undertake a magistracy, and also the superintendents of the peace or collectors of various commodities should believe that they ought to aspire to the Church”—that is, to the ministry of the Church—“after they have begun the offices of the responsibility or honor imposed upon them, the bishops themselves must first resist them under the authority of the heavenly law; and, with the bishops first exerting themselves, they must be recalled to the same duties. If the bishops neglect this, the men are to be drawn back by the curials, with the judgment of the office lending its support.”

Moreover, Arcadius, derogating from his father’s law, issued a constitution dated 27 July 398, reproduced in the Justinian Code, book I, title 3, law 12. By it he ordered that a curial who had been ordained a cleric should immediately be restored after the prescribed agreement:

> “For we no longer permit the law to benefit clerics which, after the surrender of patrimony had taken place, did not forbid decurions to be clerics.”

That this was said only of minor clerics is proved by what the same emperor established toward the end of 399 [law 163]:

> “If any persons, abandoning the curia after the second consulship of our father, have devoted themselves to the company of clerics, and have already deserved to be bishops, presbyters, or deacons, let them indeed remain in the sacred and more secret mysteries; but let them be compelled either to provide substitutes for the curia or, in accordance with the law previously enacted, to transfer their resources to the curia. All the rest—readers, subdeacons, or clerics to whom the privileges of clerics are not due—are to be presented immediately for the duties owed to their homeland.”

There was therefore no shortage, amid so many and such diverse laws, of opportunities for judges to reclaim importunately the curials who had been admitted to the clergy and thereby cause trouble for the bishops of the Churches.

# LETTER II

From the ancient Colbert manuscript, note 932.

I. No bishop may dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.

II. After the remission of sins, no one who has chosen to bear the military belt may be admitted to the clergy.

III. All disputes or cases arising among clerics of any order are to be settled before the provincial bishops, that is, their own bishops. More serious cases are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment.

IV. A cleric may take a virgin as his wife.

V. A layman who has taken a widow as his wife, whether before baptism or after baptism, is not to be admitted to the clergy.

VI. One who has taken a second wife is not to be ordained a cleric, even if he contracted that marriage before baptism.

VII. No one may usurp the right to ordain a cleric from another Church.

VIII. Those baptized by the Novatians or Montanists who come over are to be received by the laying on of hands alone.

IX. Priests and Levites are not to have intercourse with their wives.

X. If a monk wishes to strive for the clerical order, he must not depart from the earlier purpose which he undertook as a monk.

XI. Whoever wishes to enter the clergy after having been corrupted must promise that, according to the rule of the ancients, he will not take a wife.

XII. Curials and those occupied in any public functions are not to become clerics.

XIII. Consecrated female servants of God, if they marry publicly or secretly give themselves to sexual corruption, are not to be admitted to penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has withdrawn from the world.

XIV. Female servants of God who have not yet been consecrated, if they later wish to marry, are to be received into penance.

[Col. 0469A]

From the ancient manuscripts of the collection of Dionysius Exiguus:

IX. That a bishop is not to be ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan.

X. [Note: In the Hispana collection and in Isidore: II, “Concerning those who, after baptism, have taken up the belt of secular military service: they are not to be admitted to the clerical order.” III: “Concerning clerical cases which are not justly concluded in the province: they are to be settled by the apostolic see.” In the very ancient Corbie exemplar, IV: “Concerning those who, after the remission of sins, have borne the belt of secular military service.” V: “That no one may summon another to a different Church.”]

Those who cannot be admitted to the clergy. And that clerical cases are to be settled by their own bishops.

XI. [Note: Isidore, together with the Hispana collection, IV: “Concerning the wives of clerics: that they be joined to virgins and not take a second wife.” Corbie manuscript, VI: “Concerning clerics: that they not take women as wives.” VII: “Concerning those who take women as wives,” understanding by the term “woman” one who is not a virgin. We have seen the same meaning of the word used by Siricius in letter 1.]

That a cleric is not to take a widow as his wife.

XII. That if a layman has married a widow, he is not to become a cleric.

XIII. Whoever has had a second wife is not to be a cleric.

XIV. No bishop is to usurp the right to ordain another’s cleric.

XV. Those who come to the Church from the Novatians or Montanists are not to be rebaptized.

XVI. That priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with women.

XVII. That if a monk has become a cleric [Note: Thus the pure Regius exemplar of Dionysius. Other copies are subsequently expanded; Isidore and the Hispana collection agree in requiring him to preserve his original purpose.], he is not to take a wife.

XVIII. That a cleric is not to be made from among the curials, because he is compelled to provide the entertainments invented by the devil.

XIX. Concerning veiled virgins [Note: In the Hispana collection and in Isidore: “Concerning consecrated virgins, if they should fall.” In the very ancient Corbie manuscript: “Concerning monastic girls: how they ought to be veiled.”], if they go astray.

XX. Concerning virgins who are not veiled, if they go astray.

## INNOCENT TO VICTRICIUS, BISHOP OF ROUEN, GREETINGS

[Note: In some manuscripts, “Victorius”; in certain others, as in Merlin, “Victoricius”; in others, “Victoricius”; in the Regius manuscript, “Victorit ius”; in the rest, “Victricius.” Paulinus, bishop of Nola, commended this Victricius’s great merit to memory in two letters written to him.]

### 1.

Although, dearest brother, in accordance with the merit and honor of the priesthood in which you are pre-eminent, all the rules of ecclesiastical life and teaching are known to you, and there is nothing from the sacred readings that seems to have been gathered by you less fully [Note: One Colbert manuscript and another Fossat manuscript, together with the Roman and Quesnellian editions, read, as in Crab’s margin, “according to the ecclesiastical rules,” contrary to more than twenty other manuscripts. The meaning is: “Although you know all the precepts of teaching and living contained in ecclesiastical rule.”]; nevertheless, because you earnestly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church [Note: In the very ancient Corbie manuscript, and from it in Sirmond and Labbe, “the norm for authority,” a reading not to be despised, with nearly the same sense as in the Council of Carthage below, letter 26, section 1, where the council writes to Innocent that it refers its statutes to him so that they may also receive the authority of the apostolic see], I have readily complied with your wish and sent with my letter an arranged set of disciplines for life and approved conduct. Through these, the peoples of the Churches in your region may learn by what matters and rules the life of Christians is to be ordered in each person’s calling, and what discipline is maintained in the churches of the city of Rome.

It will be your duty, through the neighboring congregations and through our fellow priests who preside over their own churches in those regions, diligently to commend this book of rules, as a teacher and admonisher, so that they may both learn our practices and, through diligent instruction, shape the conduct of those who flock to the faith. For either they will recognize their purpose from this harmonious reading of ours, or, if anything is still lacking, they will easily supply it by good imitation.

### 2. The beginning of the apostolate and episcopate from Peter

Let us begin, therefore, with the assistance of the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ took their beginning [Note: Merlin, Crab, and the Roman edition, together with only the Hispana and Isidorian manuscript collections, read “with the assistance of God and the holy apostle of God.” What Innocent teaches here as a certainty was expressed by Caesarius of Arles in a letter to Pope Symmachus, letter 14, section 2: “Just as the episcopate took its beginning from the person of the blessed apostle Peter, so it is necessary that your holiness clearly show each Church what it ought to observe according to the appropriate disciplines.”].

Since many cases have often arisen which in some instances were not cases but crimes, let every priest henceforth be concerned to maintain such care in his own Church as the apostle Paul proclaims (Ephesians 5:27): that the Church is to be presented to God in such a way that it has neither spot nor wrinkle, lest our conscience be defiled and violated by the breath of some diseased sheep.

For the sake, therefore, of those who, through ignorance or negligence, do not observe ecclesiastical discipline and presume many things that ought not to be presumed, you rightly requested that in those regions the form maintained by the Roman Church should be observed. This is not because any new commands are being imposed, but because we wish all to observe what the negligence of certain persons has allowed to be neglected, although these things have been established by apostolic and patristic tradition.

For it is written to the Thessalonians, at Paul’s admonition (2 Thessalonians 2:14):

> “Stand firm and hold to our traditions which I delivered to you, whether by word or by letter.”

This in particular ought to rouse your mind more forcefully: that, free from every stain of this age, you may be found secure before the sight of God. For to whom much has been entrusted, from him more will be demanded (Luke 12:48)—the interest of punishments [Note: These words, “the interest of punishments,” are absent from the Colbert, Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispana, and Isidorian manuscripts, as well as from most editions and from Siricius. They appear in Sirmond, Labbe, and Quesnellus, as well as in two older Colbert manuscripts, one Corbie manuscript, the Fossat manuscript, and in the later revision of the Coislin manuscript together with the Hispana collection.].

Therefore, since we are compelled to render an account not only for ourselves [Col. 0471A] but also for Christ’s people [Note: In Siricius, “for the people entrusted to us,” a reading preferred in the Roman edition after Crab, contrary to the other books], we must teach the people the divine discipline [Note: Thus the ancient Corbie manuscript together with the Fossat manuscript. In two Corbie manuscripts: “the Lord’s discipline.” Another Colbert manuscript, together with the Regius and the Dionysian collection and the Roman edition: “divine discipline.” In Crab: “therefore we ought to sanctify and instruct the people with God’s divine discipline.” In the Hadrianic manuscript collection: “sanctifying discipline,” corruptly. Hence in the second revision of the Corbie manuscript it was changed to “to sanctify by discipline,” which also prevailed in the Hispana and Isidorian manuscript collections. It is therefore clear that Merlin’s reading, which Quesnellus also adopted—“therefore we ought to sanctify and instruct the people by God’s discipline”—is not genuine.].

For some have arisen who, not holding to the statutes of their forefathers, violate the Church’s chastity through their presumption, pursuing the favor of the people and not fearing God’s judgment.

Therefore, lest by our silence we appear to give them our consent, since the Lord says (Psalm 49:18) [Note: In the Corbie manuscript, in the Hadrianic collection, the words “through the prophet” were added by an early hand; they were subsequently adopted in the Hispana and Isidorian collections and by Merlin, Crab, and Quesnellus]:

> “You saw a thief, and you ran with him.”

These, then, are the matters which, in view of the divine judgment, every Catholic bishop ought henceforth carefully to guard.

# CHAPTER I

### 3. First: no one is to dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop

(Decree, distinction 64, chapter 5.) [Note: In the Roman edition, and in the editions of the Councils and Quesnellus, following the Hispana and Isidorian manuscript collections, the word “a bishop” is added here. That word is absent from the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections and from the other older manuscripts, as also from Siricius. In only one of those ancient manuscripts we read “the metropolitan bishop” in place of “the metropolitan bishop’s.” We have already observed that Innocent borrows Siricius’s words in such a way as to adapt them to discipline in Gaul; what Siricius prescribed for the Italians—“that no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the apostolic see”—he does not likewise impose upon the Gauls.]

For a judgment confirmed by the opinions of many is valid: [Note: Sirmond, Quesnellus, and several manuscripts read, “Let no one.” Other editions then have, “Let no bishop presume to ordain a bishop.” The final word is absent from many of the more important manuscripts. Here, as above, it is understood. This twofold part of the decree is required by the standard of Nicene canon 4.] no single bishop is to presume to ordain, lest the benefit conferred appear to have been stolen. For this too was established and defined at the Council of Nicaea.

# CHAPTER II

### 4.

Likewise (Decree, distinction 56, chapter 61), if anyone, after the remission of sins [Note: In the Colbert manuscript written in Lombard letters, opposite this decree in the margin is written, “Concerning penitents.” The person who added this, believing that the passage concerns not the remission of sins received through baptism but that granted after the completion of penance, interpreted the decree as referring not to the baptized but to those who had completed penance. It was observed above, in the note on Siricius’s letter 5, p. 654, note d (in our *Patrology*, vol. XIII, col. 1158, note d), that it must be understood otherwise. Accordingly, the Hispana collection more accurately summarizes this decree as follows: “Concerning those who, after baptism, have taken up the belt of secular military service.”], has borne the belt of secular military service, he is under no circumstances to be admitted to the clergy.

# CHAPTER III
5. But if any disputes or contentions, whether among clergy of the higher order or also of the lower order, arise (3, q. 6, c. 14), so that, according to the Council of Nicaea, the dispute may be brought to an end after the bishops of the same province have assembled, no one may—without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, whose reverence must be preserved in every case—abandon those priests who by God’s will govern the Church of God in that province and flee to other provinces. If anyone should presume to do so, let him be judged by all both removed from clerical office and guilty of wrongdoing.

[Col. 0471D] The older editions of the Councils, and only the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, together with Isidore, add here “or among laymen.” The passages that follow, however, indicate that only clergy are meant here. This addition was prompted by canon 5 of the Council of Nicaea. Indeed, Peter de Marca thinks that this fifth canon and the sixth are explained throughout this passage (*De Concordia*, book I, chapter 6, no. 10). Hincmarus, in his *Opusculum* 47, or letter to John VIII, chapter 12, p. 773, supports him to the extent that he considers the decree of the Council of Sardica, canon 7, to be recalled by the qualification “without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church,” etc. Paschasius Quesnellus, in his notes on Leo’s fifth letter, no. 4, believes that reference is made here to the canons of the Council of Sardica alone. Yet those canons establish nothing here concerning cases involving clergy of lower rank, except canon 16, where they are permitted to appeal to neighboring bishops.

Nor is it obscure that Innocent here recalls the canon which the Africans, who were unfamiliar with the Council of Sardica, mention in their third letter to Celestine in these words: “The Nicene decrees most clearly entrusted both clergy of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans” [Col. 0472C]. Of the three opinions, therefore, the more probable seems to be the one Hincmarus explains in the cited passage: namely, that when Innocent says, “so that, according to the Nicene Council, after the bishops of the same province have assembled, judgment may be brought to an end concerning cases that have arisen,” he is explaining chapter 5 of the Council of Nicaea; and that when he forbids anyone “to flee to any other provinces” from the ecclesiastical order, he is explaining another chapter—namely, chapter 6—of the Council of Nicaea, which orders that throughout each province the privileges of its own churches be preserved. Certainly, the words “according to the Nicene Council,” which are omitted in the Langobard manuscript of Colbert, refer not to the exception enclosed in parentheses but only to what precedes it.

[Col. 0472A] The words “whose reverence must be preserved in every case,” which Nicholas I, in letter 40, or elsewhere numbered 40, does not read (whether the manuscripts have *debet* or *debetur*), are also absent from the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections and from many other ancient codices. Quesnellus, relying on their authority, deleted them, although they were not absent from the Oxford copy of the codex that he published. The learned man attempts to argue, in Dissertation 12, chapter 4, no. 5, that the Roman Codex editors—that is, the editors of the codex he published—added them. But two copies of that same codex, which he calls Roman, older than the Oxford one should have prevented him from persuading himself of this: namely, the Pithoean and Colbert manuscripts, in which the words do not occur.

They are found, however, in the Langobard Colbert manuscript and in another Colbert manuscript, no. 3368, containing an ancient collection of canons, as well as in the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and also in Hincmarus, *Opusculum* 45, chapter 12, and the *Book of Fifty Chapters*, chapter 28. I say nothing of Gratian and others. Finally, in a very ancient Corbie exemplar, they were added by an old hand—one precisely like the hand that usually supplies omitted words. Whether they are thought to be Innocent’s or someone else’s, everyone should be convinced that the pope’s meaning is not rashly explained by them, since they rest on the words of Hosius at the Council of Sardica, canon 4: “If it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter,” etc.; and also on what Gaudentius adds in the same place, canon 5, concerning a bishop who, after being deposed by the judgment of neighboring bishops, declares that his case must be conducted in the city of Rome.

6. If more serious cases have been brought forward, they must, as the Council has established and blessed custom requires, be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment.

[Col. 0473B] This is how the Roman edition and the older editions of the Councils read, together with the Oxford manuscript, the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and Hincmarus, *Opusculum* 45, chapter 12. But in the Dionysian codices and almost all our other manuscripts, followed by Sirmond, Labbe, and Quesnellus, the words “blessed custom requires” are lacking. Conversely, in the Langobard Colbert manuscript and another, no. 3368, the reading is “as ancient custom requires,” while the preceding words “the synod has established,” etc., are omitted.

This reading is supported by what Innocent writes either in letter 29, to the Council of Carthage, no. 1: “By preserving the examples of ancient tradition and remembering ecclesiastical discipline, you have rightly strengthened the vigor of our religion no less now in seeking advice than formerly, when you pronounced judgment, since you approve that matters be referred to our judgment”; or in letter 30, to the people of Milevis, no. 2: “You diligently and appropriately consult the secrets of apostolic honor … concerning what judgment must be maintained in anxious matters, following the ancient rule which you know has always been preserved with me throughout the whole world.”

Cyril likewise supports it when he says to Celestine in letter 8, no. 1: “The ancient custom of the churches advises that matters of this kind be communicated to Your Holiness.” So too does Leo, in letter 5, no. 5, where he asks that more serious cases be referred to him in accordance with the tradition of the ancient institution and the due reverence owed to the apostolic see.

Isidore Mercator, copying this passage of Innocent in a letter which he falsely attributed to Pelagius, alters it as follows: “But greater and more difficult questions, as the holy synod has established and blessed custom requires, must always be referred to the apostolic see.” By the words “as the holy synod has established,” we think reference is made not to canons 3, 4, or 7 of the Council of Sardica, by which appeal to the Roman bishop is permitted, but to the letter of that same council to Julius, in which the synod declares that it is best and most fitting for the priests of the Lord in each province to refer all matters to the see of the apostle Peter.

Nor does Innocent here reserve the judgment of major cases to himself; rather, he requires that the report of cases judged by an episcopal council customarily be sent to the apostolic see. For this reason Hincmarus’s interpretation (*vol.* II, p. 774) is not satisfactory: he takes the passage to mean that, if major cases—including the appeal of a judged bishop—have been brought forward, they should, as the Sardican Synod established and ancient custom requires, be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment. Here, however, there is no discussion of an appeal by a judged bishop. The only command is that what bishops have judged concerning more serious matters be referred to the apostolic see. Recall what we explained more fully on this subject in the general preface.

## CHAPTER IV

7. A cleric must not take a woman as his wife, because it is written (Leviticus 21:13–14; Ezekiel 44:22): “Let the priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow” [Col. 0474B], “not one who has been cast out.” Certainly, he who strives toward the priesthood by his own labor and uprightness of life must take care lest, obstructed by this impediment, he be unable to attain it.

[Col. 0473D] The Roman edition, following Dionysius, reads “that he not take a widow.” Quesnellus, following the earlier editions of the Councils and the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, reads “that he not take a widowed woman.” We prefer, with Sirmond, Labbe, and the other ancient books, “that he not take a woman.” Siricius also wrote this way in letter 5. Likewise, in Hilary’s synodal decree following his letter 14, no. 14, Tiberius, bishop of Sabina, says: “If in my church I should discover any of the clergy … to have taken a wife, or a woman [to have been taken].”

[Col. 0474B] One of the Colbert manuscripts, together with the ancient Corbie manuscript, reads “not a divorced woman.”

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0474A]

8. A man who, even while a layman, has taken a woman as wife—whether before baptism or after baptism—must not be admitted to the clergy (Dist. 34, c. 13), because he appears to be excluded by the same fault.

[Col. 0474B] Sirmond and Labbe, with the more authoritative manuscripts, read “a woman.” Others, following the Dionysian, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, read “a widow”; Siricius also uses this word here.

For in baptism sins are forgiven; the union with a wife already taken is not annulled.

## CHAPTER VI

9. A man who has taken a second wife must not become a cleric, because it is written (1 Timothy 3:2), “the husband of one wife” [Col. 0474B]. And again: “Let my priests marry only once.” And elsewhere (Titus 1:6): “My priests shall not marry again.”

[Col. 0474B] The Langobard manuscript and another Colbert manuscript read “the husband of one wife.” The words “and lest some,” with the intervening material omitted, seem to have been deliberately suppressed by some scholar, who would more readily have believed them an addition because the cited testimonies do not offend against Sacred Scripture; indeed, in Jerome’s letter 83 to Oceanus he would read: “Just as the Law permitted the people to beget children through many wives, so the priests themselves also possessed this license.”

The testimonies that Innocent cites here are nevertheless expressly cited from the Law by Tertullian. The first occurs in *On Monogamy*, chapter 7, where he says: “Meanwhile, as concerns the Law … that same Law forbids priests to marry again.” The second occurs in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 7, where he says not only: “It is prescribed in Leviticus: ‘Let my priests not marry more than once,’” but adds: “I can say that even that is ‘more’ which is not once.”

[Col. 0474C] The Roman edition reads “And lest some think,” a reading which Crabbe noted in the margin; below, however, all the other books are sufficiently mistaken.

And lest anyone think that, if a man happened to have taken a wife before baptism and, after she had departed from this world, took another, the first marriage was dismissed in baptism, he is seriously mistaken regarding the rule [Col. 0474C], if he thinks that this is dismissed in baptism. Sins are forgiven; the number of wives taken is not abolished. For a wife is certainly taken in accordance with the precept of the Law, to such an extent that when the parents of the human race were joined together in paradise, they were blessed by the Lord himself (Genesis 1:28); and Solomon says (Proverbs 19:14), “A wife is prepared for a man by God.”

The practice of the Church itself also shows that all priests must observe this rule. It is quite absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not counted after baptism, when the blessing imposed by the priest upon those marrying teaches not that the material for wrongdoing was given, but that the form of the law instituted by God from ancient times was maintained.

[Col. 0474C] This is how the ancient Corbie codex and one Colbert manuscript read. Others have: “because sins are forgiven in baptism, not …” Innocent here and in the preceding decree copies Siricius’s words in such a way that in both places he necessarily decides what should be held concerning wives taken before baptism, about which Siricius had said nothing. A recent controversy on this matter demanded such a decision.

Carterius, bishop of Spain, to whom, Jerome says in letter 83 to Oceanus near the end, “his rivals could allege nothing apart from the marital bond—and that bond contracted before baptism,” had taken another wife after the death of his first wife. Oceanus thought that Carterius had been ordained contrary to the apostolic precept. Jerome, however, vigorously defended the legitimacy of his ordination in the cited letter 83 and said that the whole world was full of such ordinations.

Before writing that letter, however, Jerome does not conceal that at Rome he had met “a most eloquent man” who opposed his own opinion. He met others not long afterward. Certainly Rufinus, while Siricius was still alive, charged him with this opinion. Jerome replied to Rufinus at the end of book I of his *Apology*, while Siricius was not yet dead, and moderated his former position: he no longer said that the world was full of such ordinations, but testified that there were some such priests in the Church. He added that he was not bound by this question but allowed each person to abound in his own judgment.

“We were asked by the brethren,” he says, “what we thought, and we replied, prejudicing no one: let each follow what he wishes, and let us not overturn another’s decree by our own opinion.”

The Council of Valence I, held in the year 374, had already defined in canon 1 that after this synod—by which relief was provided, even if belatedly, for such illicit unions—no one who was a digamist or the husband of a woman previously married to another could be ordained a cleric. Nor should it be asked whether those who had defiled themselves with this unhappy condition had received the divine sacraments or were pagans, since the form of the divine command is chaste.

Ambrose approves the same opinion (*On the Duties*, book I, chapter 50, no. 2, and letter 63 to the people of Vercellae, no. 63); Augustine, in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18, where he also explains the mystical reason for this discipline; and Leo, in letter 45.

[Col. 0475A] The man who thinks this is dismissed in baptism is far from the rule: “sins are forgiven; the number of wives taken is not abolished.” For a wife is certainly taken according to the precept of the Law, to such an extent that even in paradise, when the parents of the human race were joined together, they were blessed by the Lord himself (Genesis 1:28); and Solomon says (Proverbs 19:14), “A wife is prepared for a man by God.”

The Church’s own practice also demonstrates that all priests must observe this form. It is indeed quite absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not counted after baptism, when the blessing imposed by the priest upon those marrying teaches that the blessing did not furnish the material for wrongdoing but preserved the form of the law instituted by God from ancient times.

And if (Dist. 34, c. 13) a wife taken before baptism is not thought to count, then [Col. 0475B] neither will children born before baptism be regarded as children [Col. 0475C].

[Col. 0475C] The Dionysian Regium exemplar reads “will be regarded.” The old Corbie manuscript, with Fossat and two Colbert manuscripts, reads “would be regarded.” Quesnellus has “must be regarded”; the other printed and manuscript witnesses have “are regarded.”

## CHAPTER VII

10. No one may presume to ordain a cleric from another church (Dist. 71, c. 2), unless his bishop, prevailed upon by entreaties, is willing to grant permission.

[Col. 0475D] “By entreaties” is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from another Colbert manuscript. The Council of Nicaea, canon 16, and the Council of Sardica, canon 19, forbid an outsider cleric to be ordained without the consent of his own bishop and without his will.

In the African church’s canonical code, chapter 54, Bishop Epigonius, after stating that many councils had enacted that no bishop should seize another’s cleric for himself, contrary to the will of the bishop whose cleric he was, complains to Julianus that Julianus had appropriated his own cleric and ordained him a deacon without consulting him. Bishop Numidius replies: “If Julianus appears to have done this without asking or consulting your dignity, we all judge that it was unjustly and improperly done.” He then decrees that Julianus must be separated from office unless he makes satisfaction by returning the cleric.

The Nicene Synod also established this (canon 17): that one church must not receive a cleric rejected by another.

## CHAPTER VIII

11. Those who come from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received by the laying on of hands alone, because, although baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in the name of Christ—except those who, if they happened to pass over from us to them, were rebaptized.

[Col. 0476C] Quesnellus reads “were baptized,” as do the Corbie manuscript and another Colbert manuscript. Yet these same manuscripts, in Siricius’s fifth letter, whose words Innocent follows, prefer “were rebaptized”; the other codices retain that reading here as well, and the context of the sentence itself requires it. We explained in the relevant passage of Siricius who are called Montenses and demonstrated that the practice of rebaptizing was familiar to them, as it was to the Novatians.

If these people, coming to their senses and reflecting upon their ruin, should prefer to return, they are to be admitted after a long satisfaction of penance.

[Col. 0476C] The word “penance” is absent from two manuscripts. The Council of Valence I, chapter 3, established that access to satisfaction should not be denied to those who, after the one holy washing, had polluted themselves with an impious washing; but it wished them to perform penance until the day of death.

## CHAPTER IX

12. Moreover, the Church must preserve in every way what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of their ministry.

[Col. 0476A] A Colbert Langobard manuscript reads “must not have intercourse, because of their daily ministries.” The reading “daily ministries” is not objectionable, especially since in Siricius one reads “daily necessities.”

For it is written (Leviticus 11:44), “Be holy, because I also am holy, the Lord your God.” If in ancient times the priests did not leave the temple of God during the year of their service (Leviticus 21:12), as we read concerning Zechariah, nor touched their houses at all—although marital intercourse had been relaxed for them because of the succession of offspring, since no one from another tribe and outside the seed of Aaron was commanded to approach the priesthood (Numbers 18:7)—how much more must these priests or Levites preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry is without succession and no day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism!

[Col. 0476D] Crabbe added “than” here in smaller type; later printed editions retained it, although Merlin and the manuscripts resist it. Shortly afterward, with two Corbie manuscripts and one Colbert manuscript, we restore “no one had been commanded,” whereas other books have “no one had been prescribed.”

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 7:5), saying, “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer”—and this he certainly commands laymen—how much more must priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, always abstain from such intercourse?

If a priest has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to sacrifice? Or with what conscience or merit will he believe himself able to be heard, when it is said (Titus 1:15), “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

[Col. 0476D] The Langobard Colbert manuscript, together with the Roman and later editions, reads “to be able to be heard.” The word “able” is absent from the other manuscripts and from the older editions of the Councils.

But perhaps he thinks this permissible because it is written (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6), “the husband of one wife.” This was said not of one remaining in the desire to beget, but with a view to future continence.

[Col. 0476D] Quesnellus reads “not concerning the one who remains”; Labbe has in the margin “not for the sake of remaining”; the Roman edition, following Merlin and Crabbe, has “not remaining.” The Fossat manuscript has “not remaining.” As in Siricius’s letter, so here all the other manuscripts consistently read as we do. Ambrose, in letter 63 to the people of Vercellae, no. 62, observes that the cited words do not dissolve a marriage, but neither do they permit marital intercourse; and that a second marriage is forbidden.

For he did not reject men who were bodily intact when he said (1 Corinthians 7:7), “I wish that all were as I myself am.” And he declares the matter more plainly when he says (Romans 8:8), “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not now in the flesh, but in the Spirit.”

## CHAPTERS X AND XI

13. Concerning monks who, after remaining for a long time in monasteries, later advance to the clerical order: they must not depart from their former purpose.

[Col. 0477B] Quesnellus, with one Colbert manuscript, reads “strive to attain.” Shortly afterward, the Langobard Colbert manuscript has “or let him be as he was in the monastery,” a reading not to be despised. Innocent here takes care that a monk who has been advanced to those clerical orders in which marriage is not forbidden should not think himself permitted to abandon his former purpose of celibacy. Accordingly, Dionysius summarized this chapter in the title index, following the Regium exemplar: “That if a monk becomes a cleric, he must not take a wife.”

Either he must remain as he was in the monastery, and, having preserved that state for a long time, he must not abandon it after being placed in a better rank; or, if, having been corrupted and then baptized, he should wish, while remaining in the monastery, to advance to the clerical order, he can in no way have a wife. For a man already corrupted cannot be blessed with a bride.

[Col. 0477B] Several editions and manuscripts read “already corrupted before baptism.” Caesarius of Arles confirms the rule mentioned here by Innocent, in Augustine’s appendix, volume V, sermon 289, in these words: “He who wishes to take a wife should desire to find her a virgin; so let him himself remain a virgin until the wedding. For if he has not been one, he will not deserve to receive the blessing with his bride.”

This explains the reason for the ancient rule which commanded that anyone who had been corrupted before baptism and afterward wished to become a cleric should promise that he would never take a wife: so that the disgrace by which he was judged unworthy of the nuptial blessing would not return upon the clerical order itself. If any cleric is kept from taking a wife by this impediment, how much more a monk!

For the same reason Siricius, in letter 1, no. 13, wished a cleric being advanced to a higher rank to be content with one woman only, and with one whom he had received as a virgin through the common blessing of the priest.

This form is observed among clerics, especially since an ancient rule states that anyone who, having been corrupted, was baptized and wished to be a cleric should promise that he would never take a wife.

## CHAPTER XII

14. Moreover, some of our brethren frequently strive to make clerics out of men occupied with civic offices (Dist. 51, c. 3) or with any public functions. Later, when the emperor orders something concerning their recall, a greater sorrow arises for them than the gratification arising from having recruited someone.

[Col. 0477C] Two manuscripts add here “or honors.” Quesnellus, like the Roman edition, reads “of those recruited,” whereas all the manuscripts have “of one recruited.” Crabbe has the worse reading “of one summoned.” The words that follow—“pleasures invented by the devil,” which curiales were often compelled to provide—explain why many Christians also avoided those offices. Against them the apostate emperor Julian, in the Theodosian Code, book XII, title 1, law 50, decrees: “Decurions who avoid their duties as Christians are to be recalled.”

It is clear that in these very offices they also provide entertainments, which were certainly invented by the devil, and either preside over or participate in the arrangements of games and public spectacles.

Let the concern and sorrow of the brethren that we have often endured serve as an example—when, in the emperor’s presence, we repeatedly pleaded on their behalf, as you yourself, being present with us, recognized.

[Col. 0477D] Paulinus of Nola mentions that Victricius came to Rome in letter 37, no. 1, addressed to Victricius himself, as follows: “From there we had drawn the bitterness of sorrow because you had not come to us from the city as we had hoped, though you had reached the city after crossing such vast stretches of land.”

He hints that Victricius had gone there to clear himself of a charge falsely brought against him in these words: “Your holiness not only possesses glory in the abuse of lawful things … but, as I have learned, also in the multitude of adversaries and in enduring temptations: for unjust witnesses rose up against you, and wickedness lied to itself.” Yet “a knot in a reed” and “a blemish in the light” could not be found.

There was great distress that not only lower-ranking clerics from the curiales, but also those already established in the priesthood, should be restored.

[Col. 0478B] Sirmond, Labbe, and Quesnellus, with the ancient Corbie manuscript, Fossat, and two Colbert manuscripts, read “was impending.” The others read “was threatening,” with no difference in meaning. The language of this whole chapter is somewhat perplexed. Innocent wishes to persuade his audience that curiales should not be ordained. The primary reason is the one he touches on in passing: “It is clear that in these very offices they also provide entertainments,” etc. Yet he does not press this point; he returns more quickly to the other reason he had introduced, namely that greater sorrow arises for the bishops who ordain them.

He then proves this by his own example, of which Victricius was a witness: “Let the concern and sorrow serve as an example,” etc. Thus the final words—“great distress was impending that they should be restored”—are to be understood as follows: while great distress was impending for me, those who had been ordained from among the curiales had to be restored—not only lower-ranking clerics, whom the law of Arcadius cited in the *Monitum* commanded to be recalled, but also those established in the priesthood.

## CHAPTER XIII

15. Likewise, those women who have spiritually married Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly defile themselves, must not be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from this world.

[Col. 0478C] The ancient editions of the Councils, as well as the Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, read “marry and are veiled by a priest.” In Siricius’s tenth letter, no. 3, we read that a virgin who has publicly professed her integrity and, after prayer has been offered by the priest, has received the veil of blessing is called veiled.

Ambrose, in book III *On Virgins*, chapter 1, inserted a sermon delivered by Pope Liberius when his sister Marcellina marked her profession of virginity at the nativity of the Savior before the apostle Peter, also by changing her clothing, with many other maidens of God and others standing by. The pope’s sermon to Marcellina begins: “You have desired a good marriage, daughter. See how great a multitude has gathered for the birthday of your Bridegroom, and no one goes away unfed.”

The canons wished maidens to be veiled or consecrated only at a mature age. In the year 381, the Council of Saragossa, canon 8, decreed that virgins who had vowed themselves to God were not to be veiled unless they had been proved to be forty years old. The emperor Majorian and the Council of Agde, canon 19, later confirmed the same. In the year 397, however, the Third Council of Carthage, to which the Second Council of Arles, canon 52, also seems to give support, enacted in canon 4 that before the age of twenty-five neither deacons were to be ordained nor virgins consecrated.

Subsequently, the Second Council of Milevis, held in the year 416, canon 26—or chapter 126 of the African church’s canonical code—decided that if any bishop, because of the danger threatening a woman’s chastity, had veiled a virgin, or had veiled her before the age of twenty-five, this should not count against him because of the Carthaginian council’s decree concerning that age.

The capitularies of our kings, the Aachen capitulary of 789, chapter 45, and the Frankfurt capitulary of 794, chapter 44, accept the constitution of the said Council of Carthage with the Milevitan exception. It must nevertheless be observed that these precautions concern only solemn profession, since even earlier maidens were permitted to undertake the purpose of virginity.

[Col. 0479A] Older editions of the Councils read “if afterward they marry,” and then “or if they have been corrupted publicly or secretly,” moving the words “publicly” and “secretly” from their place contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts. The Langobard Colbert manuscript, as well as the other Hispanic and Isidorian collections, has “or if they have been secretly corrupted.” Quesnellus prefers “or if they have been corrupted in a hidden corner,” and conjectures that the phrase may once have been *clanculo*, as if derived from *clam in angulo*, “secretly in a corner.” But in the copies of the codex published by him—the Thuan or Colbert, Pithoean, and others—as well as in Dionysius, Hadrianus, and the Corbie and Fossat manuscripts, we read “if they have secretly corrupted themselves.” His conjecture therefore appears to have no authority.

They are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from this world.

[Col. 0479B] Most and best manuscripts read “to whom she had joined herself”; Quesnellus supplied some words of his own. Dionysius and Hadrianus read “has departed from the world”; the Langobard Colbert manuscript, along with the Hispanic and Isidorian collections and the ancient editions of the Councils, reads “has departed from this life.”

We think this double reading was substituted for the genuine one from a marginal note. Since the expression “has departed from the world” seemed ambiguous and could be interpreted either as withdrawal from the world into a monastery or as departure from this world and mortal life, the ambiguity was removed by a marginal gloss explaining that “from the world” meant “from this life.” This annotation is supported by what follows concerning a woman who, while her husband was alive, married another.

How this assists those who think that Innocent disapproved of marriages contracted by consecrated virgins but did not dissolve them is unclear to us. Or they must prove that this pope, and the earlier lawmakers of the canons, judged that the later marriage of a woman who married another while her first husband was alive ought not to be dissolved.

Innocent’s meaning is illuminated by the First Council of Toledo, held in the year 400. Canon 16 first states that a woman devoted to God who sins is not to be received into the Church unless she ceases to sin and, after ceasing, performs suitable penance for ten years. It then adds: “But if she has taken a husband, she is not to be admitted to penance unless she begins to live chastely while that husband is still alive, or after he has died.” How can she live chastely unless she can be shown to have separated from the adulterer?

The fathers of that same council explain this more plainly in canon 19. Concerning the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who, having been devoted to God, sinned and took a husband, they establish that she is not to be admitted to communion unless she performs penance after her husband’s death; but if she separates from him while he is alive and does penance, then, if she fails at the end, she is to receive penance.

The Second Council of Tours, canon 20, clearly understood Innocent to command the dissolution of such a marriage. It first quotes his words and then professes that it may not depart from his decrees. Finally, adding canon 52 of the Second Council of Arles and several others, it decrees concerning the consecrated virgin who has married and the man whom she has married: “They are to be destroyed by the sword of the mouth and deprived of communion if they refuse to observe the decrees of the elders assigned to them, despise hearing their pastor, and refuse to be separated.”

“Those who persist in this obstinacy and prefer to remain in the mire of evil conduct rather than separate themselves from the forbidden marriage are to be condemned to perpetual excommunication.” For if the expression “the decrees of the elders” refers to the decrees cited there, especially Innocent’s words—and this cannot be denied—since it judges that those who refuse to separate themselves from the forbidden marriage despise them, it follows that the council judged Innocent to have commanded the dissolution of such a marriage.

The Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19, agrees with this, as does the First Council of Mâcon, canon 12. It permits such persons to be restored to the grace of communion only on condition that they heal their fault by separation. That union, which in the judgment of the Council of Mâcon is adultery rather than marriage, is called incest by Siricius in letter 10, no. 3; and no name other than the false name of husband can be imposed upon the adulterer.

Innocent, together with the same pope, also considers consecrated virgins truly married, since they have joined themselves to an immortal Bridegroom. It follows that, because their Bridegroom never ceases to live, the law of marriage begun with him can never be dissolved.

The Second Council of Tours, citing the Theodosian Code, title 25, law 2, praises the law by which the emperor Jovian decrees: “If anyone should dare not merely to seize consecrated virgins, but even to attempt, for the purpose of contracting marriage, either consecrated virgins or unwilling women, he shall be struck with capital punishment.”

[Col. 0480C] Merlin and Crabbe, with the Langobard Colbert manuscript and other Hispanic and Isidorian codices, read “chose to pass over.”

For if this rule is observed in all cases—that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is regarded as an adulteress and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of the two has died—how much more must it be observed concerning a woman who had previously joined herself to an immortal Bridegroom and afterward passed over to human marriage!

## CHAPTER XIV

16. But those women who have not yet been consecrated with the sacred veil …

[Col. 0480C] Two manuscripts read “consecrated,” the word also used by Leo in letter 5 to Rusticus, chapter 15, where the same girls are under discussion. Our reading is supported by Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*:

> There are also exceedingly beautiful rewards for our virgins,
And modesty, and a face veiled beneath a sacred covering.”] [Note: [Col. 0480C] The older editions of the councils, together with the Dionysian, Hadrian, Spanish, and Isidorian manuscripts, consistently read *se simulaverunt permanere* (“they professed themselves to remain”). Quesnel, with the old Corbie manuscript and one Colbertine manuscript, has *se permanere simulaverant*. Fossat has *semper manere simulaverant*. Sirmond and Labbe have *semper manere promiserant*. The Roman edition has *semper se permanere promiserant*. Our preference for the reading, found in two Colbertine manuscripts, *se promiserant permanere* (“they had promised themselves to remain”), is supported by what follows, where the engagement, stipulated promise, and earlier undertaking of these same girls are mentioned. Certainly the passage concerns girls who had bound themselves to God to preserve virginity and who are therefore said by Siricius, Letter 10, no. 3, not to have kept the precept of the heavenly marriage, but who lacked solemn consecration.] Though covered, they had nevertheless [Col. 0480A] promised to remain in their virginal vocation, although they were not veiled. If, perchance, they should marry, they must do penance for some considerable time, because their pledge was held by God. [Note: [Col. 0480D] Crabbe and the later editions of the councils read *sponsio earum* (“their pledge”). Merlin and all the manuscripts read *sponsio ejus* (“her pledge”), with the implied words “which is of this kind.” Below, Crabbe and the Roman edition read *pepigerunt* (“they made a compact”), whereas Sirmond, restoring the manuscript reading, has *pepigit* (“she made a compact”) and added *virgo* (“the virgin”) on his own authority; Labbe and Quesnel subsequently retained it.] For if among human beings a good-faith contract is ordinarily dissolved on no account, how much more must this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment! [Note: [Col. 0480D] In the manuscripts of the Dionysian, Hadrian, Spanish, and Isidorian collections, as in the older editions of the councils, the reading is *non poterit* (“will not be able to be dissolved”).] For if the Apostle Paul said that those who departed from their determination to remain widows incurred condemnation because they had invalidated their first pledge (1 Tim. 5:12), how much more will virgins who break faith with their prior promise incur it! [Note: [Col. 0480D] The Roman edition, together with the Colbertine and Langobard manuscripts, reads: “who have in no way kept faith with their agreement.” Merlin and Crabbe, following the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, read: “who have in no way kept faith with their earlier promise.” Dionysius and Hadrian have: “who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise.” Quesnel, as in one Colbertine and one Pithoean manuscript, reads: “who have endeavored to break faith with their earlier promise.” In place of *nisae*, Sirmond and Labbe substituted *visae*. We follow the ancient Corbie manuscript and Fossat.]

### 17.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] The learned man who prepared the most recent edition of the works of Saint Paulinus of Nola thinks, in Dissertation 4 at the end of chapter 4, that what follows was excerpted from certain other sources and does not cohere with what precedes. But what he immediately adds shows how slight the foundation of his opinion is, unless the whole letter is understood to concern this rule. For it is beyond doubt that by the name “rule” is meant the body of decrees contained in the whole letter, and that what at the beginning had been called a “book of rules” is now more simply called a “rule.” Thus it is evident that this concluding clause coheres most fittingly with the opening and the rest of the letter. The author who in the opening praised Victricius for strongly demanding the norm and authority of the Roman Church, and who promised him a book of rules by which he might learn what discipline was observed in the churches of the city of Rome, now, having set out that discipline most fully, fittingly concludes that peace and concord are preserved in the Church by careful observance of that same rule or discipline, and consequently that schisms and heresies, and so forth, are avoided. Finally, since among all the manuscript and printed codices none presents this letter without this conclusion, the sacred authority of general consensus assigns it an unquestionable authenticity.] 

Therefore, this rule, dearest brother, if it is observed with complete vigilance by all the priests of God, ambition will cease, dissension will be stilled, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no opportunity to rage, unanimity will remain, iniquity, once conquered, will be trampled underfoot, truth will blaze with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will accord with the will of the soul. The Apostle’s saying will also be fulfilled (Phil. 2:2–3): that we should remain of one mind and like-minded in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through rivalry or empty glory; pleasing not human beings but our God and Savior, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [February 15, A.D. 404], during the sixth consulship of the Emperor Honorius and the consulship of Aristenetus. [Note: [Col. 0482D] Merlin and Crabbe, following the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, read *Aristo*. Crabbe added *Aristoneto* in the margin, which the Roman editor adopted. The ancient Corbie manuscript and one Colbertine manuscript prefer *Aristineto*. Another Colbertine manuscript, together with the Pithoean, has *Aristhineto*. Another Colbertine has *Aristinio*. Sirmond and Labbe read *Aristaeneto*, “the most illustrious man.” These last two words, in place of which the Roman edition has *viris clarissimis* (“the most illustrious men”), are absent from all the manuscripts and also from the ancient editions of the councils. The entire consular or chronological notation is absent only from the collection of Dionysius, whether in its original or expanded form, as we have explained above.]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

### 1. This letter is shorter in some books and longer in others. Who abridged it?

Some books present this letter in a shorter form, others in a longer one. It was first published in its shorter form by Jacques Merlin; it was then reprinted in the same form both in collections of papal letters and in various editions of the councils, until Jacques Sirmond found it complete in ancient books and decided that it should be made public for the common benefit. In the copies of the Spanish Collection preserved in the libraries of Laon, Noyon, and Beauvais, as well as in all the copies of Isidore Mercator, it is found only in mutilated form. We therefore suspected that it had first been truncated by the compiler of the Spanish collection.

That suspicion was later dispelled by Colbertine manuscript 408, written more than seven hundred years ago and containing *On the Instruction of Clerics*, and by another similar and no later manuscript, the Coislinian. Although these were compiled solely from the monuments of the Spanish Collection, they nevertheless preserve the chapters of this letter that are missing from the shorter copy. Finally, when we learned that authentic and genuine copies of the Spanish Collection still existed in the churches of Urgell, Girona, and Ripoll, in which this letter is read in full, we became entirely convinced that it had been mutilated not by the compiler of that collection but by someone else.

Since, however, it is found in every copy of Isidore Mercator only in mutilated and abridged form, who, one may ask, should be regarded as the author of this deed? Nor is it surprising that a man who felt no scruple about fabricating many things, interpolating others, and altering still more in various ways should not have been afraid to suppress certain passages as well. Content to copy Innocent’s general decrees, he removed the rest, as more remote from his purpose, insofar as it concerned particular persons or cases.

The Laon, Noyon, and Beauvais books mentioned above do not contradict this view. Although they were copied from the Spanish Collection, it is clear from Pope Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus that the person by whom they were written and dictated also possessed the collection of Isidore and sometimes, though rarely, preferred it to the Spanish collection. Moreover, this complete letter of Innocent is preserved not only in genuine copies of the Spanish Collection but also in the very ancient Corbie manuscript and in the Fossat manuscript, now Colbertine. Since this is so, and since nothing should remain wanting for the reader, we now present it in full, following the authority of the more reliable manuscripts; at its end we shall also indicate how it was published by Mercator.

### 2. It was addressed to the bishops of the Council of Toledo, not of Toulouse

In both groups of copies a misleading title is prefixed to it. In the preliminary index of the Corbie manuscript it is given this title: “Letter of Pope Innocent to all the bishops of the Church of Toulouse concerning all heresies or concerning the ordinations of bishops, and the rest to be sought in the letter.” [Col. 0482B] At the head of the letter itself this heading is placed before it: “Innocent to all the bishops assembled in the Council of Toulouse.” The same title is found in the Fossat manuscript, except that in it *diversis* (“various”) is substituted for *universis* (“all”). In most copies both of the Spanish and of the Isidorian collection it is likewise addressed “to all the bishops assembled in the Council of Toulouse.” Merlin did not alter this title. Jacques Sirmond also retained it and, on that account, assigned the letter a place among the councils of Gaul.

“Concerning this matter,” he says in the preliminary Notice, “although I understood that it could not unreasonably be doubted, it nevertheless seemed preferable, especially since it has hitherto been mutilated, that it should appear here complete, even in a foreign place, rather than perhaps be missing in its proper place.”

Later, however, he added in his notes that it did not seem doubtful to him “that it was written to the bishops of Spain after the Council of Toledo, indeed, concerning matters dealt with in that council or occurring afterward. Therefore,” he says, “I think the ancient title of the letter should be restored, so that it may read ‘in the Council of Toledo.’” He calls it ancient because it had already been restored by Crabbe and retained by those who reprinted either the councils or the letters of the Roman pontiffs. Previously, too, it was found in at least some manuscripts. Among various copies of Isidore’s collection we found one from Navarre, written at least six hundred years ago, and another belonging to the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, both of which have “in the Council of Toledo.” The genuineness of this reading, which the evidence we are about to present will confirm, should not be doubted. From the comparison of various manuscripts one may also infer how the other reading entered the tradition.

### 3. How it came to be entitled “In the Council of Toulouse”

Although the Noyon copy addresses this letter to “all the bishops assembled in the city of Toulouse,” in its general index it is headed “to all the bishops of Toledo.” There, the fact that *Tolotanos* is written for *Toletanos*, not for *Tolosanos*, is demonstrated by the German manuscript, no. 424, containing a canon collection compiled eight hundred years ago. Whenever a Council of Toledo is cited in it, it is consistently called *Tolotana*.

Accordingly, when the scribes of this book had also written *Tolotana* for *Toletana*, antiquarians more readily thought that *Tolosana* should be restored, since they saw Innocent’s letter to Exsuperius of Toulouse and, in the text of this letter, no. 3, found *Galliarum* or *Gallorum* corruptly written where *Galliciarum* or *Gallaecorum* should have stood.

Furthermore, below, in no. 6, where the Colbertine copy gives us the reading that Rufinus asked pardon for his error “in the Council of Toledo,” the Corbie manuscript has “in the Council of Toulouse.” Everyone will agree that the same error could have entered the title with equal ease.

### 4. It was written to the fathers of the First Council of Toledo

It is disputed which council Innocent is addressing here and when it was held. In the first edition of his *Annals*, Baronius took two points as certain: first, that this letter of Innocent had been written to the First Council of Toledo; and second, that this council had been celebrated during Stilicho’s second consulship, that is, in the year 405 of Christ.

In the latest edition, however, he changed his view. Convinced that the First Council of Toledo should be assigned to Stilicho’s first consulship, and therefore to the year 400, he judged that this letter belonged to some later Council of Toledo. Several others, especially Antonio Pagi, have adopted this opinion.

The earlier view, which postponed the First Council of Toledo until Stilicho’s second consulship, cannot be defended at all. But there also appears to be no reason to distinguish from the First Council of Toledo the council whose bishops Innocent is addressing here. To make this clearer, it will be worthwhile to examine what has been published under the name of the First Council of Toledo.

### 5. The three parts published under the name of the First Council of Toledo

Three parts must be distinguished in this council. The first consists of a preface, twenty canons, and the subscriptions of the bishops.

The second contains a rule of faith and eighteen chapters against heresies, under this heading: “Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica composed and sent, together with the command of Pope Leo of the city of Rome, to Balconius, bishop of Galicia.”

The last part bears this title: “Here begin copies of the professions made at the Council of Toledo against the sect of Priscillian, in the Spanish era 438.” It is then preceded by this preface:

“After the council had been held on the Kalends of September, on the third day before the Nones of September, after the various proceedings then conducted, on the eighth day before the Ides of September the professions of the lord Symphosius and the lord Dictinius, bishops of holy memory, and of the lord Comasius, then a presbyter, were excerpted from the full acts. Among the others, they had made these professions in the Council of Toledo concerning the condemnation of Priscillian or his sect, as follows: After some matters, and among the matters conducted at that time, Bishop Dictinius said,” and so forth—that is, the rest of Dictinius’s profession. After it has been transcribed, the profession of Comasius follows, preceded by this preface or interlocution:

“In the same era, on the third day before the Ides of September, the professions of the bishops of holy memory, the lord Symphosius and the lord Dictinius, and of Comasius of holy memory, then a presbyter. Comasius said.”

Finally, Comasius’s profession is followed by “a copy of the definitive sentence transcribed from the acts. On the same day the bishops said: ‘Let the sentence be read.’ And he read,” and so forth.

### 6. The council is presented as having been held in the year 447

No one, so far as I know, has yet explained how these three parts fit together or can be referred to one and the same council. Scholars agree only that the middle part belongs to the council which Leo, writing to Turibius in 447, ordered to be convened, and therefore does not belong to the First Council of Toledo. For this reason, following Baronius, Binius notes that it was inserted among the other two parts through the compiler’s error.

Nor can the last part be referred more conveniently to the First Council of Toledo. The bishops who speak in it indicate that they are holding a synod, although Symphosius, Dictinius, and Comasius were already dead. At the time of the First Council of Toledo, they were still alive and, indeed, are known to have been present at that very council and to have condemned the heresy of Priscillian.

The three parts fit together most appropriately, however, if they are referred to the general council of Spain convened at the command of Pope Leo. Thus, at that council, the twenty canons of the First Council of Toledo were first read and confirmed; eighteen new canons were then established in a rule of faith; and finally certain excerpts from the full acts of the First Council of Toledo were recited.

Accordingly, what is commonly called the First Council of Toledo would more properly be entitled: “The Council of Spain, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica celebrated at Leo’s command on the Kalends of September in the year 447,” prefaced by the twenty canons of the First Council of Toledo, held in the year 400, and followed by certain excerpts from that same council, transcribed from its full acts.

### 7. A council was held at Toledo in the year 400

We thus restore that council to the year 447 without denying that another council was held at Toledo in the year 400; rather, we establish the latter all the more clearly. Concerning this Council of Toledo, Idacius says in his *Chronicle*, under the year 400:

“In the province of Carthage, in the city of Toledo, a synod of bishops is assembled. In it, as is contained in the acts, Symphosius and Dictinius, together with other bishops of the province of Galicia, followers of Priscillian, condemn his most blasphemous heresy, along with its author, by subscribing their own profession. Certain matters concerning the discipline of the Church are also established for observance, with Bishop Ortygius participating in the same council; he had been ordained at Celenis.”

Now the council held at Leo’s command in 447 first lists the disciplinary canons that the Council of Toledo issued during Stilicho’s consulship—that is, in the year 400. Subsequently, from the acts of that same council, dated according to Spanish custom by the era 438, equivalent to the year 400, it presents not only the professions of Symphosius, Dictinius, and the others who condemned the heresy of Priscillian together with its author, but also the sentence of that council, which preserves their honor and concludes in Ortygius’s favor with these words:

“But we declare that our brother Ortygius’s churches, from which he had been expelled, must be restored to him.”

The agreement between those acts and the Chronicle of Idacius is therefore evident. Moreover, the sentence of the Council of Toledo just mentioned refers to Simplicianus as the one then governing the Church of Milan. Simplicianus succeeded Ambrose only in 397, and before the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 401, as is clear from the Council of Carthage inserted in chapter 56 of the *Code of the African Church Canons*, he had Venerius as his successor. This, too, confirms the date at which the Council of Toledo was held.

### 8. To what extent the following letter can be said to have been written to this synod

Once these points have been established, and once it is certain beyond dispute that the Council of Toledo whose canons and acts are reported in the council of Spain mentioned above was held in the year 400, no controversy seems to remain concerning whether the following letter of Innocent was addressed to that Council of Toledo.

First, in the letter, as may be read in sections 6 and 7, the acts and decrees of this council are repeatedly praised. Second, in section 10 Innocent observes that he is addressing bishops “who have decreed, in accordance with the Nicene rules, that ordinations must be carried out by judgment.” The bishops of the First Council of Toledo had first decreed in its very preface that “the enactments of the Council of Nicaea must be observed perpetually and that no departure must be made from them”; they then proceeded to establish what was to be observed in ordinations.

Innocent should not, however, be understood as writing to the Council of Toledo while it was still assembled, but rather to the bishops who had gathered in it. Unless one prefers to understand “the Council of Toledo” here as meaning the bishops belonging to the Council of Toledo. Certainly, in section 6 the pope mentioned above speaks of the First Council of Toledo as a council already completed. Nor does the venerable Patruinus of blessed memory, whose place Innocent says Gregory occupied in section 9, appear to be anyone other than the man who is recorded as having first subscribed the canons of the First Council of Toledo.

Finally, the principal aim of Innocent’s efforts in this letter is to suppress and settle the schism that arose from the reception, with their honors preserved, of Symphosius, Dictinius, and others in the Council of Toledo, and that was spreading more widely each day. It is therefore clear that some interval elapsed between this letter and that synod. How long the interval was cannot be determined with certainty. We may only infer that the letter was written before Spain was disturbed by military upheavals, and therefore before the year 408, when Constantine wrested that province from Honorius.

Whether this letter is earlier or later than the preceding one we do not know. Nevertheless, since the matters defined in both concerning the ordination of clerics are related, it will be agreeable and convenient for the reader to have both letters placed close together. Nor is it now of great importance to know precisely when this one was written, provided that one knows with whom, on what occasion, and for what purpose it was written.

Someone may perhaps wonder how the same pontiff can now praise and approve so earnestly the indulgence shown by the Council of Toledo toward the followers of Priscillian, while later he so consistently denied that clerics ordained by Bonosus should retain their honors. But a wise priest must distinguish leprosy from leprosy and investigate when the severity of discipline should be maintained and when it should be relaxed.

Although the holy leaders of the churches are animated by the same Spirit, they nevertheless established different rules at different times concerning clerics returning to the Church from heresy or schism. In canon 8, the fathers of Nicaea wished the Novatians to remain in the clergy. According to the testimony of the Africans, a council beyond the sea, in the time of Siricius and Ambrose, prohibited clerics coming from heresy from retaining their honors. The Council of Toledo, however, in the year 400, judged that this indulgence should be extended to the followers of Priscillian; and Innocent now approves its decision in the interest of unity, although in the year 414 he will vigorously defend the strictness of ecclesiastical discipline toward the Bonosians.

The Council of Carthage, held in 401, judged that the following moderate course should be adopted: when the return of clerics produces some compensation for unity, their honors should be preserved; when no such compensation exists, they should be denied (Code of the African Church Canons, chap. 68).

# LETTER III

Concerning dissension and the corruption of the discipline of the Churches of Spain. [Note: [Col. 0485D] We have taken this title and those that follow from Sirmond, not from the manuscripts.]

I. That certain bishops wrongly separate themselves from others because they have received converts from heresy.  
II. Concerning bishops ordained by Rufinus and Minicius in churches not their own, contrary to the canons.  
III. That the case of Bishop John, and of others who refused fellowship in communion, be examined.  
IV. Concerning the defective ordinations of many: what has hitherto been usurped should be tolerated in such a way that it may be prohibited in the future.
