V. That the complaint of Gregory, bishop of Emerita, be investigated.  
VI. Whom it is permissible to admit to the clerical order, and what sort of men are to be chosen. Also, that a woman who was a wife before baptism makes a man a bigamist.

INNOCENT, to all the bishops assembled in the Council of Toledo, his dearly beloved brothers, greeting in the Lord.

### 1. Schism in Spain and contempt for the canons

The excessive concern that often kept me anxious over the dissension and schism of the Churches, which, rumor reports, is spreading more widely through Spain each day and advancing at an ever-swifter pace, has brought about a necessary moment at which so great a correction could no longer be delayed and an appropriate remedy had to be provided.

For our brothers, the fellow bishop Hilary and the presbyter Elpidius, moved partly by love of unity and partly aroused, as was proper, by the disaster afflicting the province, came to the apostolic see. With sorrow and lamentation they reported that, within the very bosom of the faith, peace had been violated throughout the province, the order of discipline thrown into confusion, many things committed against the canons of the fathers with due procedure disregarded and rules neglected, churches usurped, and the concord on which the entire stability of our faith rests rendered impossible to preserve. These matters are preserved in the records of the presbyteral assembly and can be shown to you by reading. [Note: [Col. 0486D] That is, of the Roman clergy, this designation being repeated from the more dignified rank. In cases of this kind, bishops staying in Rome were also regularly summoned to the same assembly.]

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Even before the First Council of Toledo, a certain disagreement concerning the ordination of clerics had arisen among the Spaniards. Accordingly, Bishop Patruinus says in the preface to that council: “Since each of us has begun to do different things in our churches, and from this have arisen such great scandals that they reach even to schism, if it pleases you, let us decide by common agreement what all bishops should follow in ordaining clerics.” But after the council just mentioned, another cause was added to this schism: although that synod had received into Catholic communion, with their honors preserved, those who had converted from the Priscillianist heresy, some bishops admitted them while others rejected them and argued that they should be excluded. Innocent now attempts to remedy the causes of this twofold evil.]

## CHAPTER I

### 2. The bishops of Baetica separate themselves from the others because the Galicians have been received

First, concerning the faith itself, dissension has arisen because the bishops of Baetica or Carthage have withdrawn from the peace of all on account of communion with the Galicians. [Note: [Col. 0486D] Thus the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts. Sirmond has *dissederunt* (“they dissented”). It would rather be necessary to restore *discesserunt* (“they withdrew”). In the Corbie manuscript the earlier reading is *Galliarum*, and in the Colbertine *Gallorum*, perhaps in place of *Gallicorum* or *Gallaecorum*. As we heard above from the Chronicle of Idacius, Symphosius, Dictinius, and the others who condemned the heresy of Priscillian, together with its author, by their subscription at the Council of Toledo, were bishops of Galicia. It is therefore not surprising that the bishops of Baetica and Carthage took offense at their being received into peace and consequently withdrew from communion with the others. Gregory, bishop of Eliberis, had sown the seeds of the Luciferian error deeply in the province of Baetica. It is not astonishing that these seeds continued to produce an unhappy harvest in Innocent’s time.]

This dissension is not merely diminishing; rather, it increases day by day through the zeal for contention, since, with each person determined to obtain what he has chosen, they have made an endless cycle of evil and a kind of circle out of such hostility. Yet in matters of this kind it is better for every good person to be defeated than, by an evil custom, to secure the perverse intention once adopted.

For what other cause, even in earlier times, apart from the obstinacy of that Lucifer, held him back from concord with those who had condemned the Arian heresy through a prudent conversion? [Note: [Col. 0487B] The manuscripts read *cum illorum* (“with those of them”). The sentence would be more complete in this form: “both with those who had condemned the Arian heresy through a prudent conversion and with those who had received their satisfaction.” Sulpicius speaks of the same matter in book 2: “Lucifer condemned those who had been at Rimini to such an extent that he separated himself even from the communion of those who had received them after their satisfaction or penance.” Augustine likewise says in Letter 185.47: “He who disliked such indulgence fell into the darkness of schism, having lost the light of charity.” Since Innocent, Sulpicius, and Augustine in these passages reproach Lucifer only with schism, the error by which his disciples—not Lucifer himself—dared to rebaptize seems to be attributed to the disciples alone.]

With the same zeal, although Priscillian’s detestable sect had rightly been condemned by the unanimous agreement of all, we have learned that some people took it very badly that those who had been converted through sounder counsel were received into the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0487B–C] Sirmond and Labbe add: “after the detestable sect of Priscillian had been condemned by the detestation of all.” The preposition *post* is absent from the manuscripts, in which *consensione* is at times more harmonious than *detestatione*. This accords with Jerome’s statement to Ctesiphon that Priscillian was condemned by the authority of the whole world.] It is revealed that they disliked both this beneficial act and the peace of the churches itself.

For although Symphosius and Dictinius themselves, with the intention of unity, condemned the depraved heresy and were received, once such persons had been removed, so that the innate dissension might be utterly extinguished, there were found people who disliked the correction itself, though it had been rightly made. And now the churches are divided, concealing from one another, with no small hostility, their mutual resentment. [Note: [Col. 0487B] The Colbertine manuscript reads *Symposius*. He should not be identified with Symposius, who subscribed the Council of Saragossa held against the Priscillianists in 380. How Symphosius, Dictinius, and their associates, after confessing their error and professing the faith, were admitted to Catholic communion is explained in the acts of the Council held under Pope Leo, in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. 2, pp. 1229ff., from the acts of the Council of Toledo.

In the sentence passed by the fathers of Toledo concerning them, it should be noted that, while permitting Paternus to retain the church in which he had been established, they add that they will also receive him into their communion when the apostolic see has sent its reply. Concerning the other bishops of Galicia, who had always persisted in communion with Symphosius, they likewise decreed that they should await, on the same model, what the present pope, Saint Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and the other leaders of the churches might write.

It may incidentally be observed that the Roman bishop is designated simply by the title “pope.” The fathers of Toledo continue: “Let the aged and religious Symphosius, concerning whom we have written above what he did, remain in his church … He will await communion from there”—that is, from the pope and the bishop of Milan—“from where he had previously received hope of future peace.” They decree that the same should be observed for Dictinius and Anterius.

Immediately afterward they state: “But we establish that, before communion is restored to them through the pope or through Saint Simplicianus, they are to ordain neither bishops, nor presbyters, nor deacons.”

Why did they issue a judgment concerning all those bishops in such a way that they wished the communion of the Roman and Milanese bishops to be awaited until it was restored to them by letters from the apostolic see and from the bishop of Milan? Similar decrees shed light on this question: those of the Council of Carthage held on June 18, 401, and of another held on September 13 of the same year. As may be seen in chapter 65 of the *Code of the African Church Canons*, the Africans decided to send representatives to Anastasius, the Roman pontiff, and Venerius, the bishop of Milan, so that, with their permission, they might promote to the clergy infants baptized by the Donatists and receive into their former honors clerics who wished to pass from the Donatists to Catholic unity, whenever this seemed beneficial to Christian peace. They explain that this was because the matter had been prohibited by those sees.

The fathers of Toledo plainly teach that they established that the communion of the Roman and Milanese bishops should be awaited for the aforesaid bishops because some kind of judgment concerning them had already proceeded from those sees, insofar as Ambrose and Siricius had prescribed certain conditions of peace for them in letters. Hence the more complete sentence of the Spaniards concerning Vegetinus reads as follows: “But Vegetinus, against whom no sentence had specifically been pronounced beforehand, having submitted the profession accepted by the synod, we establish that he is to be restored to our communion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0488C] Dictinius had not only followed Priscillian’s teachings but had also defended them in books. Later, however, at the Council of Toledo, he rejected and condemned everything he had previously thought or written wrongly, saying: “I accuse and condemn all my presumption concerning my writings.” Shortly afterward he added: “Again I repeat: whatever I wrote in my earlier understanding and at the beginnings of my conversion, I reject with all my heart … Except for the name of God, I anathematize everything … I condemn everything found contrary to the faith, together with its author.”

His writings were nevertheless not suppressed so carefully that many people did not continue to read them with reverence even in the time of Pope Leo. In Letter 17.19, that pope advises such people that they should love Dictinius’s restoration more than his fall.]

If correction through conversion cuts away the errors themselves while preserving the dignities, what reason is there for refusing, through stubbornness, to retain the path of righteousness and the road leading to salvation?

### 3. Some resent that their honors were preserved

Why, I ask, were they distressed that Symphosius and Dictinius, and others who had condemned the detestable heresy, were then received into the Catholic faith? [Note: [Col. 0488D] Sirmond, together with the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts, reads *Numquidnam aliquid* (“Did they perhaps lose anything?”). The Bona Vallis manuscript has *Nam quod non aliquid*. By restoring *num* from the first two witnesses and *quod non* from the last, a complete and clear reading is obtained. Augustine uses the very examples by which Innocent now proves that clerics may retain their honors after penance, for the same reason, in Letter 185.45: “For holy David,” he says, “did penance for deadly crimes and yet remained in his honor; and blessed Peter, when he shed the bitterest tears, certainly repented that he had denied the Lord, and yet remained an apostle.”]

Did they perhaps lose any of the honors they possessed? If this wounds or provokes anyone, let him read that the Apostle Peter, after his tears, remained what he had been; let him consider that Thomas, after that doubt, lost nothing of his former merits; finally, let him observe that the eminent prophet David, after his manifest confession, was not deprived of the merits of his prophecy.

If correction through conversion both cuts away the errors and preserves the dignities, what justification is there for refusing, through stubbornness, to retain the course of righteousness and the path that directs one toward salvation?

### 4. The power of unity and the danger of schism

Therefore your affection must devote itself to this, and good priests must strive to ensure that, with teaching going before, all who are scattered may be gathered into the unity of the Catholic faith; and that one unconquerable body may begin to exist. If it is divided into parts, it will lie exposed to every injury of laceration and will suffer an internal plague, when the very bond that holds it together struggles against itself. [Note: [Col. 0489C] By this teaching, the perversity of schism or heresy and the rectitude of the Catholic faith are demonstrated, so that the light of truth may drive away the darkness of error. Augustine says this in Letter 93.3. The Church should thus appear to receive the corrected rather than the perverse.]

But let all priests accept these general statements concerning the restoration of unity as though they had been written to each individually. Thereafter let your affection direct its attention in particular to all the matters that will be proposed.

## CHAPTER II
### 5. Rufinus and Minicius usurped the right to ordain in churches not their own

For it could not remain hidden that the bishops Rufinus and Minicius, contrary to the canons of Nicaea, usurped the right to ordain bishops in churches not their own. We must now at least providently ensure that no one dare claim these provisions for himself (Nicaean Canons 4, 6, and 16), lest, through shameless usurpation, connivance grow worse and what does not proceed from the discipline itself prescribed in writing become established as a rule by custom.

[Note: It would be expressed more clearly: “lest shameless usurpation grow worse through connivance.”]

In this matter, the complaint of our brother and fellow priest Hilary should first be heard. He asserted that Rufinus had engaged in every kind of attack against the peace of the churches, and that long ago, at the Council of Toledo, he had asked pardon for his error. Yet now, although the priestly ordination was owed to the metropolitan bishop, he ordained a bishop in a remote place, against the will of the people and contrary to the rule of discipline, and embroiled the churches in scandals.

[Note: The text is so found in the Colbertine manuscript, where the Corbie and Toulouse manuscript has a different reading. It should be remembered here that the acts of the Council of Toledo have by no means come down to us complete and intact, but only in fragments recited at a later council, insofar as they were then useful; nor were all the acts recited at that council, but only those concerning the Priscillianists. Rufinus, however, belonged rather to those bishops about whom Patruinus complains in the preface to the First Council of Toledo: namely, those who undertook unlawful ordinations and thereby stirred up scandals that went as far as schism—not to those who had been followers of Priscillian. The same should be understood of Minicius. Hence the portion of the acts of the Council of Toledo that concerned them was omitted at the aforesaid council.]

[Note: Sirmond and Labbe read *sacerdotis* (“of the priest”); the manuscripts more correctly read *sacerdotes* (“priests”). The Council of Laodicea, canon 12; the Council of Nicaea, canons 4 and 6; and the Council of Antioch, canon 19, forbid the ordination of bishops of any province without the metropolitan’s consent. See also Ferrandus, *Breviarium*, canon 4. The creation of bishops in remote places, moreover, conflicts with canon 6 of the Council of Sardica.]

Next, the case of the bishops of Tarragona must be considered. They likewise complained that Minicius had ordained a bishop in the church of Girona; and, in accordance with the Nicene canons, judgment must be pronounced on such usurpation.

[Note: The Council of Nicaea, canon 6, declares that one who has been ordained in this way ought not to be a bishop. The Council of Antioch, canon 13, confirms this and further imposes the penalty of deposition on the authors of the usurped ordination.]

A full investigation must also be made of those bishops who were ordained by Rufinus or Minicius contrary to the rules, so that, since they were improperly made, they may understand that they cannot continue to possess what they obtained through a defective beginning.

### CHAPTER III

### 6. John is to be deposed if he does not cease resisting the decree concerning the reception of those returning to the Church, to which he had subscribed

With regard also to Bishop John, whose agreement concerning the reception of Symphosius and Dictinius was given through legates at the Synod of Toledo, and to whom that correction appeared reasonable, let the events that followed be examined. And, in every case in which cessation of communion has been called into question, let a full inquiry be conducted, so that, in accordance with the decree of the Synod of Toledo, either they may be joined in the fellowship of communion, to abolish the suspicion of schism, or, if any are found who reject concord and the decisions that were agreed upon, they may, by the judgments of Your Charity, be excluded from the communion of the Catholic faith.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “who deny.”]

Thus the contagion of the schismatics’ manifest profession may be avoided—not an internal evil that, while concealed, does not always remain silent.

[Note: Labbe and Sirmond read, “which does not cease to creep,” whereas the manuscripts have, “which does not always remain silent,” perhaps instead of “which does not always keep itself silent.” Innocent, unwilling that anyone should be avoided on account of any suspicion of internal evil, but only when its profession is manifest, gives a suitable reason: internal evil does not always remain concealed or confined within, but eventually breaks out and usually reveals itself in words or deeds. In this way he carefully avoids the serious danger into which the schismatic Ithacians had fallen—or those who, at their instigation, had been sent into Spain by the emperor Maximus to investigate the Priscillianists. Of them Sulpicius wrote: “There was no doubt that that storm would devastate the greater part of the saints, with little distinction among the classes of people. For at that time judgments were made with the eyes alone, and someone was considered a heretic because of his pallor or clothing rather than his faith.”]

### CHAPTER IV

### 7. Certain ordinations contrary to the canons are to be tolerated for the sake of peace; thereafter, however, they are to be invalid, and their authors deposed

As for the ordinations that we know the Spanish bishops celebrate through the fault of a bad custom, something ought to have been established in accordance with the tradition of our predecessors, unless we had considered that we would stir up very many disturbances in the churches.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads this way, and the Colbertine, retaining “very many,” adds “churches.” Sirmond, however, substitutes “very many churches.” Augustine, animated by the same spirit as Innocent, writes in *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, book III, section 14: “When the same disease has seized very many, nothing remains for the good except grief and groaning.” A little later he says: “For then plans of separation are both empty and pernicious and sacrilegious, because they become impious and proud, and disturb good people who are weak more than they correct bad people who are bold.” Accordingly, in section 16 and elsewhere, in Letter 64, now 22, section 5, he explains how cautiously a multitude must be rebuked. Although this was properly said of a multitude of the people, it can appropriately be applied to every multitude of offenders.]

We rebuke their action in such a way that, because of the number of those who must be corrected, we do not call into question what has been done in whatever manner, but rather leave it to God’s judgment. For how many of those who, after receiving grace, practiced forensic advocacy and took up the determination to prevail have we discovered to have been admitted to the priesthood? Rufinus and Gregory are said to belong to this number.

[Note: Here actors in legal cases seem to be meant: although they sometimes undertake unjust causes, they nevertheless strive to win them by force of eloquence and persistent effort.]

How many from military service, who necessarily obeyed the authorities and carried out their commands! How many from the civil administration, who, while obeying those in authority, did what they were ordered to do!

[Note: Some copies add *severa* (“severe”); the more reliable copies lack it. The same idea is expressed here as shortly afterward, where it says that they “carried out the commands” and “did what was ordered of them.” In both places the meaning is that those bound to military and civil service were accustomed to being compelled to perform actions that barred them from the clergy. In Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 51, canon 4, canon 8 of the First Council of Toledo appears in the following interpolated form: “If anyone has served in the army after baptism and has taken up the military cloak or belt for killing the faithful”—the final three words do not occur in the manuscripts of the Council of Toledo—“even if he has committed no graver offense, if he has been admitted to the clergy, he shall not receive the dignity of deacon.” The same preconceived opinion that provided the occasion for this interpolation of the canon seems also to have caused the addition of the word *severa* here.]

How many who celebrated pleasures and public entertainments for the people have attained the honor of the high priesthood!

[Note: From the preceding letter, section 15: supply “of games or spectacles.”]

Yet none of all these ought even to have reached membership in the clerical order. If we were to order each case to be investigated individually, we would introduce into the Spanish provinces—whose troubles we wish to remedy—not insignificant disturbances or scandals in our zeal for correction.

For this reason, we think these matters should rather be allowed to pass. But to ensure that similar things are not committed hereafter, Your Charity’s maturity must take care that, at least now, a necessary end be imposed on so great a usurpation. Let this, namely, be established: if anyone hereafter attempts to enter either the ecclesiastical order or the priesthood itself contrary to the canonical forms, he shall be deprived, together with those who created him, of the order and honor in which he is found.

[Note: In the Isidorian copies there is added here: “so that whoever has been ordained in this way shall be deposed together with his ordainers.” This is merely a marginal gloss or summary chapter explaining Innocent’s text. In the same books, *ordinatoribus* (“ordainers”) is substituted shortly afterward for *creatoribus* (“those who created him”).]

### CHAPTER V

### 8. The complaint of Gregory of Mérida is to be heard

The complaint of Gregory, bishop of Mérida, who was ordained in the place of Patruinus of venerable memory, should also be heard, if there is one; and, if he has suffered an injury contrary to his merit, let him be vindicated against those who begrudged another’s honor. And henceforth let the spirit of faction rise against none of the good.

[Note: Those who thought that Patruinus—whose name occurs in the preface to the First Council of Toledo and who subscribed to it first—was bishop of Toledo are corrected here. Gregory appears to have had Antoninus as his successor; Hydatius, in his *Chronicle*, Olympic year 306, section 21, reports that Antoninus governed the church of Mérida at the time when Turibius governed the church of Astorga, that is, in the age of Leo.]

### CHAPTER VI

### 9. The Nicene rule is to be observed in ordinations; those who are to be barred from the orders

Although the Nicene rule is known to Your Charity, dearly beloved brothers, and according to it you decree that ordinations are to be carried out, I nevertheless thought that a portion of the provisions concerning ordinations should be inserted, so that ordinations may hereafter be celebrated according to it and no one be left free to interpret the matter otherwise.

[Note: The sequence of the sentence requires *secundum* (“according to”) here. Copyists frequently omit *ut* in place of *et*, and conversely *et* in place of *ut*. This is an old error. In an attempt to repair it, Isidore Mercator added, after *celebrandas*, the words *esse sciamus* (“we know to be celebrated”). The same addition was transferred from his copies into the Noviomese manuscript of the Spanish collection, but not into the Laon copy of the same collection.]

First, the prohibitions are set out. No one who has served in the army after baptism is to be admitted to the clerical order; nor anyone who has practiced as an advocate after receiving baptism; nor anyone who, after receiving God’s grace, has administered public affairs. Nor may anyone from the civil administration enter the ecclesiastical order if, after baptism, he has been crowned or has held the office called a priesthood and celebrated public spectacles.

[Note: These were the solemnities that arose from pagan rites, in which magistrates were compelled to represent a priesthood devoted to the worship of demons. This is relevant to Tertullian, *On the Crown*, chapter 10: “You have the crowns of all the priestly colleges under Claudius”; as is mentioned in chapter 7, Claudius had a work *On Crowns* that taught their origins, causes, forms, and solemnities.]

For this too must be guarded against in the case of men from the civil administration: those who have belonged to that class must not at some time be reclaimed by their former administrations, as we frequently see happen. All these things, reasonably prohibited, ought by every means to be observed.

### 10. Who are to be chosen; the baptism of wives is not annulled

What sort of men are to be chosen for the clerical order is clearly set forth: namely, those who were baptized from early childhood and associated with the office of lector; or, if they are older, who, once they have received God’s grace, immediately dedicate themselves to the ecclesiastical orders.

[Note: Labbe reads, “and assigned to the office of the elect”; this is corrected from other books. That reading is confirmed by Siricius, Letter 1, section 13: “Whoever has devoted himself to the services of the Church from infancy … ought to be joined to the office of lector”; and section 14: “But whoever is already advanced in age … at the time he is baptized shall immediately be enrolled among the lectors or exorcists.”]

And if they have had wives, it must be asked whether they took a virgin as wife, because it is written in the Old Testament: “Let the priest take a virgin as wife” (Leviticus 21:13); and elsewhere: “Let my priests marry only once.” Nor may a man who has had two wives be admitted (see the preceding letter, section 9), because the apostle Paul says: “The husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2).

Nor should the claim be admitted that some put forward in defense of their perverse error: that a wife taken before baptism ought not to count, because everything is remitted in baptism. They do not understand that in baptism sins alone are remitted, and that the number of wives is not abolished.

For if, as it is written, a wife is prepared for a man by God (Proverbs 19:14), and “what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6; Genesis 1:28), and the very founders of the human race are blessed by the Lord at their origin, how can this be believed capable of being remitted among sins?

But if, according to those who think this, the claim is true, then all the righteousness performed by catechumens before baptism will be taken away through baptism. Let no one, therefore, think or admit anything of this sort against the Apostle; rather, let him faithfully understand that the expression “husband of one wife” refers to a man who has had one wife either before baptism or after baptism.

For if a wife taken before baptism is not counted, neither can the children born from her be counted among his children. How absurd and alien this is, Your Prudence will judge better.

Therefore no one may interpret the divine Scriptures otherwise than right reason permits, lest, while preparing unlawful remedies as excuses for themselves, they be judged to have corrupted the law and overturned the rules.

What must be maintained, however, is what the sequence of the divine Scriptures contains and what the priests have established for good reason.

[Note: The Spanish and Isidorian manuscript collections add here, “a certain person.”]

And with another hand: Farewell, dearly beloved brothers.

## THE SAME LETTER

Such is the abbreviated form found in the old copies of Isidore Mercator, as also in the Noviomese, Laon, and Beauvais manuscripts of the Spanish collection, and as it appears in the Roman edition of the papal letters and in the old printed editions of the councils.

I. On the rebuke of the Spaniards who irregularly appoint clerics.  
II. That lawyers, civil officials, and those devoted to secular military service are not to be admitted to the clergy.  
III. That whoever has been ordained in this way is to be deposed together with his ordainers.  
IV. What sort of men are to be chosen for the clerical order.  
V. That a man who had a wife before baptism and another after baptism is not to become a cleric.

Innocent sends greetings in the Lord to all the beloved bishops assembled at the Synod of Toledo.

Often, and with excessive anxiety, I have been kept concerned about the schism of dissension among the churches, which rumor reports as advancing day by day more widely through the regions of Spain by stages of separation. A necessary moment has now arisen in which so great a correction cannot be postponed and a suitable remedy ought to be provided.

For concerning the ordinations that the Spaniards, through the fault of a bad custom, and the rest thereafter—as in the preceding example from section 8 to the end—[the text continues], except that the contents of section 9 are also omitted here. Thus, while only the general decrees are retained, the rest, concerning particular cases or persons, has been suppressed.

## LETTER IV

[Note: In the edition of the councils, this is number 27. It was transmitted to us by Palladius in his *Dialogue on the Life of Saint John Chrysostom*. From there it was first published at Rome among the letters of the Roman pontiffs in the Latin translation of Ambrose of Camaldoli, and later printed in Greek at the head of the letters of Chrysostom with a new Latin translation. Finally, in 1680, through the work of Emeric Bigot, it appeared in a more carefully corrected and elegant form together with the whole dialogue of Palladius. We have collated it in full with the Coslinian and Hamburg manuscripts. It was written soon after the violence inflicted on the Church of Constantinople by Chrysostom’s opponents during the Easter vigil, and therefore around April of the year 404.]

### Of John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, to Pope Innocent

[Column 0494]

How unjustly he was expelled from the city and his church through the faction of Theophilus, and how many evils were perpetrated both then and afterward.

(This letter is properly included among the other letters of Saint Chrysostom; see volume III of the works of the holy Doctor.)

## LETTER V

[Note: In the edition of the councils, number 31; what was formerly number 5 is now number 38. It was inserted without title or heading by Palladius, to whom alone it is owed, on page 24 of the *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*. It was printed in Latin at Rome among the papal letters from the translation of Ambrose of Camaldoli and was subsequently reprinted in editions of the councils. Palladius himself explains the occasion and date of its composition in the same work as follows: A few days after Innocent had received a letter from Theophilus through an Alexandrian lector and had sent him a reply, Peter, Theophilus’s presbyter, and Martyrius, a deacon of the Church of Constantinople, came to Rome again in Theophilus’s name, bringing another letter from Theophilus together with certain acts against John. After reading them, Innocent, finding that the accusations were not serious, sent the new legates back with this second letter. It follows that this letter was written not long after the preceding one.]

### Of Pope Innocent I to Theophilus, bishop of the Alexandrian Church

He cannot withdraw from communion with John unless John is condemned by a lawful judgment. Theophilus is summoned to a canonical synod.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Brother Theophilus, we regard both you and our brother John as sharing our communion, just as we made our mind clear in our earlier letters.

[Note: These letters are no longer extant.]

And even now, without abandoning the same resolve, we write the same things to you again. Whenever you send us a reply, it is plainly impossible for us, unless a proper judgment follows concerning matters conducted in mockery, to withdraw without reason from communion with John.

Therefore, if you trust in your judgment, present yourself at the synod that has been convened according to Christ; and, having laid out the accusations there, before the witnesses of the canons of Nicaea—for the Roman Church accepts no other canon—you will possess security free from contradiction.

[Note: Bigot, preferring *cogitur*, appears to follow the reading of George of Alexandria in the *Life of Chrysostom*, which gives γινομένῃ (“being held”) for γεγενημένῃ (“having been held”). Ambrose of Camaldoli translates: “hasten to the synod soon to be held in Christ,” which shows that he read γενουμένῃ. Tillemont thinks that Innocent speaks of the future synod as certain because Honorius, then at Rome, had promised that he would request it from Arcadius. But even if this pope ever held that hope as certain, he did not hold it long. For around May of this year, 404, he replied to John and his companions that powerful persons were obstructing him in evil, preventing him from being able to bring them aid more quickly. Therefore we understand that Innocent means nothing else here than to summon Theophilus to a lawful synod, saying that another irreproachable synod of Westerners and Easterners ought to be convened, as Palladius says on page 23.]

[Note: Ambrose of Camaldoli interprets this as: “and there contend there according to the Nicene canons and decrees.” Innocent is warning Theophilus that he relies in vain on the canons of Antioch, as will be explained more suitably in Letter 7.]

#### Greek text

Brother Theophilus, we know both you and our brother John to be in communion with us, just as in our first letters we made our mind clear. Even now, without departing from the same purpose, we write the same things to you again; and whenever you send us a message, unless a fitting judgment follows concerning matters carried out in jest, it is impossible for us without reason to withdraw from communion with John. Therefore, if you have confidence in the tribunal, come to the synod convened according to Christ; and, having exposed the accusations there before the witnesses of the canons of Nicaea—for the Roman Church accepts no other canon—you will have security that cannot be contradicted.

## LETTER VI

[Note: In the edition of the councils, number 3; what was formerly number 6 is now number 39. It is found in all kinds of ancient collections, such as those of Isidore, the Spanish collection, Hadrian I, Dionysius Exiguus, and the codex published by Quesnel. It is likewise found in the sixth-century Corbie codex, the Colbertine codex written in Lombard capitals, and others. Moreover, it is cited by canon 9 of the Council of Agde in the year 506. Accordingly, an educated man rightly laughs at, and considers unworthy of refutation, a certain heterodox writer who wishes to deny this letter to Innocent for the sole reason that Siricius is cited in it—as though it were unworthy of a pope to confirm his own decree by the decrees of his predecessors. Innocent was also faced with a question that necessarily required him to mention Siricius’s constitution, so that he could moderate his judgment with equal discrimination toward those who had sinned either knowingly or unknowingly.]

[Column 0495A]

I. [Note: We have transcribed these headings from Dionysius Exiguus, though what is first for us is number 21 for him, and what is seventh for us is number 27 for him. In an old copy of the Colbertine library, this letter is entitled: “Letter of Pope Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, in which he explains to him, under six headings, the matters of his questions and the decrees of his answers”; it then adds a summary of the divine books of the Old and New Testaments.]

On the sexual misconduct of priests or Levites.

II. [Note: The edition of the councils, as well as the Spanish and Isidorian collections, following the old Corbie codex, reads: “Concerning those who, after baptism, have been devoted to sexual misconduct throughout their lives and seek penance at the very end.”]

On final penance.

III. [Note: The Corbie manuscript, together with Isidore, reads: “Concerning those who, after baptism, have administered throughout their lives and exercised cruel tortures.” The old editions of the councils read: “Concerning administrators or secular judges.”]

Concerning administrators.

IV. That husbands are not to have intercourse with adulterous wives.

V. That those who dictate petitions or criminal indictments are to be considered exempt.

VI. That those who, after a divorce obtained through repudiation, have undergone divorce and joined themselves to other marriages are shown to be adulterers.

VII. Which books are to be received into the canon.

Innocent sends greetings to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse.

[Note: Most manuscripts have this form, rather than the *Exuperio* of the printed editions. Many copies of good authority omit *salutem* (“greetings”), which seems first to have been added by Dionysius. Jerome praises Exsuperius’s merits in more than one place. In his Letter 11, to Ageruchia, he writes: “I cannot mention Toulouse without tears, since the merits of the holy bishop Exsuperius have ensured that it has not fallen even to this day”; and at the end of Letter 4, to Rusticus, among other things: “No one was richer than he, who carried the Lord’s body in a wicker basket and his blood in a glass vessel.”]

### 1

When you consulted me, dearest brother, about what I thought should be observed concerning each of the matters you proposed, I answered, according to the capacity of my understanding, what seemed appropriate: what ought to be followed, what a teachable reason persuaded, what the authority of the reading showed, or what the preserved sequence of times demonstrated.

[Note: The Lombardic Colbertine codex and another manuscript read “or a clearer reason.”]

Your Charity, following the practice of prudent men, preferred to refer to the apostolic see what ought to be observed concerning doubtful matters, rather than, through presumed usurpation, to obtain whatever might seem right to you in each individual case.

For why should we consider it more shameful to learn something than to be entirely ignorant? I too gain teachability from discussion, since I am compelled to answer the questions after examining the arguments; and thus the person who is asked to teach always learns something.

[Note: The older manuscripts read “after carefully examining” and below “the one who is asked to teach.”]

I shall therefore set out each matter and append the answer.

### CHAPTER I

### 2

You asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministries of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, have been shown by the children they fathered to be, or to have been, sexually incontinent (Distinction 82, canon 2; Ivo, part 6, canon 57; Council of Agde, canon 9).

Concerning such men, the discipline of the divine laws is clear, and the explicit admonitions of Siricius, bishop of blessed memory, have been handed down, so that those placed in such offices who are incontinent are deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and are not permitted to approach the ministry that ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

[Note: Merlini and Crabbe, as in the manuscript collections of Dionysius, the Spanish collection, and Isidore, read “such a ministry.” Other books more correctly omit *such*.]

For there is a very ancient authority of sacred law, observed from the beginning, namely that priests were commanded to dwell in the temple during the year of their service (Luke 1).

[Note: Six ancient manuscripts read “in the temples.” Four others read “during the year of their turn.”]

Thus, while serving the sacred offerings, they might claim for themselves divine ministries pure and cleansed from every stain.

[Note: Merlini, Crabbe, and most manuscripts read “mysteries.” We retain, with the Pithoean manuscript, the Roman edition, and others, “ministries.” Siricius, in Letter 1, section 11, decrees that incontinent priests and Levites can never touch the divine mysteries; but there he speaks of priests and Levites of the New Law. In what follows, Gratian, Distinction 31, canon 6, quotes the passage in this form: “Let those be admitted to the sacrifices who do not perform carnal intercourse even with a wife.” Since Innocent’s judgment has been corrupted, this reading is rightly demanded.]

Nor is it lawful to admit to the sacrifices those who engage in carnal intercourse even with a wife, because it is written: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus 11:44 and 20:7).

For them, on account of the succession of offspring, marital intercourse had for that reason been relaxed, because no one from another tribe had been commanded to approach the priesthood. How much more, then, must these priests or Levites preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession and no day passes on which they are not occupied either with divine sacrifices or with the ministry of baptism!

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7:5)—and he certainly commanded this to laypeople—how much more must priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, always abstain from such intercourse?

If a priest has been polluted by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit will he believe that he is heard, when it has been said: “Everything is pure to the pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus 1:15)?

### 3

But perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written, “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2).

[Note: Crabbe and the Roman edition read *ad permanentem*; Labbe, *de permanente*; Quesnel, *propter manendum*; one Colbertine manuscript, *propter permanentem*; the Noviomese and Laon manuscripts with Merlin, *permanenti*. More than twelve other manuscripts, and the older ones, read *permanentem*; the following note confirms that this is the reading required.]

He did not say this of one who remains in the desire to beget children, but with a view to future continence.

For he did not exclude men who were physically intact when he said, “I wish that all were as I myself am” (1 Corinthians 7:7); and he declares this more clearly when he says, “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9).

And he said “having children” (1 Timothy 3:4), not “begetting them.”

[Note: Again, the Roman edition, following Crabbe, adds *et ad habentem* (“and to one having”), improperly inserting the preposition *ad*. Ambrose, Letter 63, to Vercellae, section 22, illustrates the same meaning with the Apostle’s words: “For he said ‘having children,’ not ‘begetting them.’” Earlier editions, following Merlin, read “which he also declares more clearly,” adding *quod* contrary to the manuscript evidence.]

### 4

But the judgment is plainly different and divided.

[Note: The Roman edition and later editions of the councils read *diversa* (“different”), a reading found in only one manuscript, the Pithoean. We restore *divisa* (“divided”) from the other books, that is, divided into two parts: one concerning those who sinned in ignorance because they did not know the decrees of Siricius sent to the provinces, and the other concerning those who knew them.]

For if that rule of ecclesiastical life and discipline which was sent by Bishop Siricius to the provinces is shown not to have reached some persons, the pardon of ignorance shall be granted to them, provided that from now on they begin entirely to abstain.

They shall retain the ranks in which they are found, but in such a way that they may not climb to higher ones. They should regard it as a benefit that they do not lose even the position they now hold.

But if some are discovered to have known the rule of life sent by Siricius and nevertheless not to have immediately cast away their lustful desires, they must by every means be removed: after learning the admonition, they preferred pleasure to what ought to have been placed first.

[Note: The printed editions, except Quesnel’s, read “after the admonition, because”; the manuscripts do not support *because*.]

### CHAPTER II

### 5

This question was also raised: what ought to be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of sexual incontinence and, at the very end of their lives, seek both penance and restoration to communion?

[Note: 23rd Cause, question 4, canon 45.]

6. On these matters, the earlier practice was stricter; the later, with mercy intervening, more lenient. For the earlier custom maintained that penance should be granted but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times, lest the easy granting of communion make people secure about reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling away, communion was rightly denied while penance was granted, so that everything would not be wholly refused; and the circumstances of the time made the remission more severe. But after our Lord restored peace to his churches, now that fear had been driven away, it was decided that communion should be given to those departing, [Col. 0498C] both because of the Lord’s mercy, as a viaticum for those about to depart, and lest we appear to follow the harshness and severity of the heretic Novatian, who denies pardon. Therefore, together with final penance, communion will be granted, so that people of this kind, even at the end of their lives, may—with the permission of our Savior—be rescued from perpetual destruction.

[Note: Thus Lab., Sirm., and several more and better manuscripts. Other printed editions read *obeuntibus* (“to those who are dying”), and below, with Dionysius and Isidore, *subsequi* (“to follow”) instead of *sequi*. That stricter discipline, mentioned by Innocent, is found especially in the Council of Elvira, canons 6, 7, 8, and so forth. It had also prevailed earlier in Africa, but only among certain bishops. These bishops did not think that peace should be granted to adulterers, and they closed the entire avenue of penance against adulteries; nevertheless, they did not withdraw from the fellowship of their fellow bishops who held a different opinion and granted them peace, as Cyprian relates in Epistle 52, to Antonianus. A further example of this severity appears in the commonly circulated work of Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, where, in chapter 8, section 38, the following statement is addressed to her: “Cling to penance until the end of your life, and do not presume that pardon will be granted to you by human judgment; for he deceives you who wishes to promise you this. Since you sinned specifically against the Lord, it is fitting that you await from him alone, on the day of judgment, the remedy.” Although Cyprian proves at length in the aforementioned letter that neither penance nor indulgence should be denied to those who have fallen, nevertheless, toward its end he decrees the following: “Those who do not undertake penance, nor testify with their whole heart and by an open confession of their lamentation to their grief over their sins, we have judged must be entirely excluded from the hope of communion and peace if they begin to plead for them in illness and danger. For it is not penance for sin but the warning of impending death that compels them to make their request; and he is not worthy to receive consolation in death who has not considered that he would die.” If this judgment is to be considered somewhat too severe, as Pamelius thinks, the same must be said of canon 22 of the First Synod of Arles: “Concerning those who apostatize and never present themselves to the church, nor even seek to do penance, and afterward, seized by illness, ask for communion: it has been decided that communion is not to be given them unless they recover and perform worthy fruits of penance.” In truth, they held this opinion not because they greatly distrusted God’s clemency, but because they greatly distrusted the genuineness of such penance. Indeed, toward the end of his book *To Demetrianus*, Cyprian teaches that no penance is too late for one who still remains in this world, and that no one should be deterred from it either by sins or by years; pardon is to be granted to the one who confesses, and through death itself one passes into immortality. Although he is speaking principally of the grace of baptism, there is no doubt that he holds the same view concerning every penance undertaken after baptism, provided that it is genuine. Hence, as may be seen in his Epistles 13, 14, 15, and others, he always took great care that someone should be available to grant peace and communion to those who had fallen, if they began to be weighed down by illness or danger, after making their confession. What Innocent now defines was afterward expressly confirmed by Celestine in Epistle 4, to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, section 3, and by Leo in Epistle 100, to Theodorus, section 5. Earlier, the Roman clergy had prescribed the same thing to the Carthaginian clergy through Cyprian, Epistle 3, in these words: “If those who have fallen into this temptation begin to be seized by illness, and do penance for their deed, and desire communion, they must certainly be helped.” Jerome, above, p. 550, notes that the example of the thief was set before us so that no one might ever think conversion too late. But there he asks for conversion and change.]

## CHAPTER III

7. It was also asked about those who, after baptism, held office and either employed torture alone [Note: The Pith. manuscript reads *tormenta sua* (“their tortures”). Other manuscripts more correctly read *sola* (“only”), meaning those by which death is not inflicted upon the accused. The purpose of this question may be supplied and explained from Ambrose’s Epistle 25, to Studius. He too had asked whether someone, after a capital sentence had been pronounced, ought to abstain from communion in the sacraments. Ambrose replies in section 2: “There are some—although they are outside the Church—who do not admit to communion in the heavenly sacraments those who have judged that a capital sentence should be imposed upon certain persons.” He immediately adds: “Many also abstain voluntarily, and are indeed praised; nor can we fail to commend them, since we observe the Apostle’s authority to the extent that we do not dare deny them communion.” Finally, in section 9 he explains what the earlier authorities thought about the matter in these words: “And therefore our predecessors preferred to be more indulgent toward judges, so that, while their sword was feared, the fury of crimes might be restrained rather than incited; whereas, if communion were denied, the punishment of criminals would appear to have been vindicated. Our predecessors therefore preferred that abstinence should lie more in the will of the one abstaining than in the necessity imposed by law.”] or even pronounced a capital sentence.

8. We read that the earlier authorities defined nothing concerning these matters. For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that it had been given as God’s avenging minister in such cases [Col. 0499B] (Romans 13:1, 4). How, then, could they condemn an act which they saw had been granted by God’s authority? Accordingly, concerning them we hold to what has hitherto been observed, lest we either overturn discipline or appear to act against the Lord’s authority. Their deeds, however, will all be taken into account when they render an account.

## CHAPTER IV

9. It was also desired to know why men who remain in communion do not live with adulterous wives, whereas wives seem, by contrast, to remain in the company of adulterous husbands.

10. In this matter (32, q. 6, c. 23; Ivo, p. 8, c. 214), the Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not have punishment. Men, however, are accustomed more freely to report adulterous wives to priests; and therefore communion is denied to women once their crime has been exposed. But, when the offense of men remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicions. He will certainly be removed if his disgrace is discovered. Since the case is therefore the same, the administration of punishment sometimes rests when proof is lacking.

## CHAPTER V

11. You also wished to inquire (23, q. 4, c. 46; Ivo, p. 10, c. 94) [Note: In the margin of the Colb. Langob. manuscript is noted this summary of the chapter: “Concerning advocates who pronounce sentences in accordance with the crime.” But the question concerns rather those who seek capital sentences—or rather who compose petitions for those seeking them—than those who pronounce such sentences. This question, like that proposed in chapter 3, makes clear how greatly the Church abhors bloodshed. Yet Innocent does not deny communion to those who, after baptism, have either held office or composed petitions for persons seeking capital sentences; nevertheless, in Epistle 37, section 5, he teaches that they must be excluded from the clergy.] whether those who dictate petitions may freely ask the rulers, after the regeneration of baptism, for someone’s death or for blood on account of guilt. The rulers never grant this without investigation; rather, they always refer the actual cases or crimes to judges, so that [Note: The old edition of the councils and several manuscripts read *causae cognitae* (“the cases having been examined”). The Royal exemplar, collated with Dionysius and with Colb. Langob., reads *causa cognita vindicetur* (“it may be punished after the case has been examined”). In the second reading found in other books, *crimina* (“crimes”) is understood before *vindicentur*. See the Theodosian Code, book II, title 18, law 1, and book XIX, title 40, law 1.] the case may be punished after it has been examined. Once these matters have been delegated to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the affair. And while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the one who dictated the petition will remain immune.

## CHAPTER VI

12. Your affection also inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves to another in marriage. It is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. But those who, while their wife is still alive—even though the marriage may appear to have been dissolved—hurry into another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons joined to them appear themselves to have committed adultery, in accordance with what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; likewise, whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (Matthew 19:9). And therefore all are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful. [Note: Early editions here add *tales* (“such persons”), which is absent from the manuscripts. Six reliable manuscripts then add: “all are to abstain from communion.” But after *abstinendos* (“are to abstain”), the phrase *esse manifestum est* (“it is clear”), which Innocent expressed at the beginning of this response, is understood. There is therefore no reason, with Quesnel, to substitute *abstinendi*, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.] [Note: In the old Corb. manuscript and another Colb. manuscript, *moechatur* (“commits adultery”) is absent here. The integrity of the sentence would remain intact if *moechantur* (“they commit adultery”) were supplied afterward.]

Concerning their parents or relatives, however, no such judgment can be made unless they are found to have been instigators of the illicit union.

## CHAPTER VII

13. Which books are to be received in the canon is shown by the brief appended list. [Note: Dionysius here added *scripturarum* (“of the Scriptures”), and the author of the Spanish collection subsequently prefixed *sanctarum* (“holy”) to that word. Isidore adopted both, but the other manuscripts have neither. Moreover, *brevis* here means a catalogue. The same sacred books, though not in the same order, are listed among the canonical Scriptures in canon 47 of the Third Council of Carthage, held in 397. The cited canon of that council is read inserted in the *Codex of the African Ecclesiastical Canons*, chapter 24, with this addition: “Let this also be made known to our brother and fellow priest Boniface, or to the other bishops of those regions, for the confirmation of this canon: for we have received from the fathers that these books are to be read in the church.” Hence it has been conjectured that the decree of the Third Council of Carthage concerning the sacred books was recited at another Council of Carthage, held in 419 under Pope Boniface, and confirmed by the clause just mentioned.]

These are the matters concerning which you wished to be instructed by voice: the five books of Moses—that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—and Joshua son of Nun; one book of Judges; four books of Kingdoms, together with Ruth; sixteen books of the Prophets; five books of Solomon; the Psalter.

Also among the historical books: one book of Job, one of Tobit, one of Esther, one of Judith, two of Maccabees, two of Ezra, [Col. 0502A] and two books of Chronicles.

Also of the New Testament: four books of the Gospels; fourteen epistles of the apostle Paul; three epistles of John; two epistles of Peter; the epistle of Jude; the epistle of James; the Acts of the Apostles; [Note: The Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 633, seems to have referred to this when it said in canon 13: “The authority of many councils and the synodal decrees of the holy Roman bishops prescribe that the book of the Apocalypse belongs to John the Evangelist and is to be received among the divine books.” From this it may also be inferred that this epistle was synodal.] and the Apocalypse of John.

But the other writings, whether under the name of Matthias or of James the Less, or under the names of Peter and John, which were written by a certain Leucius, [Note: The material enclosed in brackets is omitted by Quesnel and is found only in copies collated with Dionysius, the Spanish collection, and Isidore. Shortly afterward, the same Quesnel, together with one Colb. manuscript and another Pith. manuscript, prefers *et si qua sunt talia* (“and if there are any such writings”), where the other books read *alia* (“others”).] [or under the name of Andrew, written by the philosophers Nexocharides and Leonidas], or under the name of Thomas, and any others of this kind, you should know are not merely to be rejected but also to be condemned.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of March [Note: February 20, 405. In Merlin and Quesnel, as in the two manuscripts just mentioned, *secundo* (“second”) is lacking; in the other copies it is correctly included, as is confirmed by the accompanying name of the colleague-consul, Anthemius.], in the consulship of the illustrious men Stilicho for the second time and Anthemius.

## EPISTLE VII

[Note: In the edition of the Councils this is Epistle 29; what was Epistle 7 is now 18. It was copied from Sozomen, who, having obtained it and the following Epistle 12 translated from Latin into Greek, published both in book VIII, chapter 26. Nicephorus Callistus later took both from there and inserted them into book XIII, chapter 32 of his *History*. By this letter Innocent replied to letters sent to him by the same clergy through Germanus and Cassian, and thus received after some progress had been made in the year 405. For, as Palladius relates on pp. 26–27, Germanus and Cassian arrived in Rome after Palladius; Palladius, however, arrived a month after Cyriacus, bishop of Synnada, who had begun to flee from the East to Rome after the law promulgated at Constantinople on November 18, 404. In Sozomen and Nicephorus nothing precedes the heading “Innocent, bishop,” etc. Consequently, the title prefixed in the editions of the Councils, in which the name ἀρχιερεύς (*archiereus*, “high priest”) is given to Innocent, is wholly without authority and proves nothing about the use of the word ἀρχιερεύς at that time. The same must be said of Epistle 12, in whose title the editors of the Councils on their own authority call both Innocent ἀρχιερεύς and John ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (*archiepiskopos*, “archbishop”).]

### TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0501] Innocent consoles them in accordance with their own conviction; he deplores the unjust substitution of another bishop in the place of John while he was alive. He then declares that only the Nicene canons are to be received and that others opposed to them are to be rejected. Finally, he signifies that he is concerned that an ecumenical synod be assembled. [Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0501B] Innocent, bishop, to the presbyters and deacons, and to all the clergy and people of the church of Constantinople who are under Bishop John, beloved brethren: greeting.

1. There is one consolation of patience for the things that they suffer. From the letter of your charity, which you sent through Germanus the presbyter and Cassian the deacon, I learned with anxious concern the spectacle of evils which you set before my eyes; and, by reading it repeatedly, I perceived by how many calamities and afflictions the faith is oppressed. This matter can be healed by the consolation of patience alone. For our God will shortly put an end to such great tribulations, and it will be helpful to have endured these things.

Indeed, at the beginning of the letter of your charity we recognized this necessary consolation itself, praising your purpose, confirmed by many testimonies exhorting you to patience. For you yourselves, by your letter, anticipated the consolation which we owed you by ours. For our Lord is accustomed to grant this patience to those who suffer, so that the servants of Christ may console themselves even in tribulations, reflecting that the things which they suffer had already happened to the saints. Yet we too may draw consolation for ourselves from your very letter. For we are not removed from sharing your sorrow, since we are afflicted in you.

2. How unjustly a bishop was substituted while John was alive. [Col. 0503B]—For who could endure what is done by those [Note: That is, Acacius, bishop of Beroea; Theophilus of Alexandria; Antiochus of Ptolemais; and Severian of Gabala, whom the Constantinopolitans expressly named in their letter as the authors of the sufferings which they endured.] whose foremost duty was to be devoted to tranquility, peace, and concord? But now, by an inverted practice, innocent priests are driven from the sees of their own churches. This was first suffered unjustly by our brother and fellow priest John, your bishop, when he had received no hearing whatever. No charge is brought, nor is he heard. And what is this ruinous plan? So that no appearance of a trial may exist or be sought, others are substituted in the places of living priests—as though those who began with such an offense could be judged to possess or to have done anything right.

For we have never learned that such things were done by our fathers, but rather that they were forbidden, since no one has been granted permission to ordain another in the place of one who is alive. [Col. 0503C] For a reprobate ordination cannot take away a priest’s rank, since he who is unjustly substituted cannot be a bishop at all. [Note: That is, by canon 4 of the Council of Sardica, which, for the benefit of a bishop who has appealed to the Roman see, decrees: “Another bishop shall by no means be ordained in his see after the appeal of him who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been decided by the judgment of the bishop of Rome.” Yet John was expelled even while appealing to a synod, as he himself testifies above in Epistle 4, section 3. Ignatius the patriarch cites that canon in somewhat different words in his letter to the pope and the Roman council, in Baronius under the year 861. What the Synod of Sardica expressly forbids may also seem forbidden by Nicene canon 9, which provides that two bishops are not to be approved as existing in one city.]

3. Which canons are to be received or rejected.—As regards the observance of canons, we say that only those defined at Nicaea are to be obeyed; the Catholic Church ought to follow and acknowledge these alone. [Note: Paschasius Quesnel, *Dissertation* 12 at the end of Leo’s works, chapter 2, says that Innocent received, besides those, the Sardican canons too, but regarded them as Nicene and adorned and clothed them with that name. Yet from the fact that this pope immediately adds the Synod of Sardica condemning the Antiochene canons, it is plain that he received what was done at Sardica. But since he praises those acts by the proper name of the Sardican synod, it is no less plain that he received the Sardican canons as distinct from the Nicene, not as if they were taken for Nicene and clothed with that name. We therefore understand Innocent to proclaim that the Nicene canons alone are to be followed, not so as to reject or despise those which agree with them, but only those which disagree with them. For Leo too says in Epistle 96, to Pulcheria, section 2: “Nothing is ever permitted to be attempted against the enactments of the fathers’ canons, which were founded many years ago in the city of Nicaea by spiritual decrees; so that, if anyone wishes to determine anything different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupts them.” Certainly the Sardican synod may be regarded as an appendix to that of Nicaea, since Hosius presided over it—he who had sat at Nicaea either as chief or among the foremost bishops—and since the same faith was established and the same heresy overthrown there. Under Pope Damasus, as we observed above, p. 591, section 3, following Athanasius, in order that the Arians, who invented various names of synods, might deceive no one, councils were held at Rome and elsewhere which decreed that thereafter no synod should be named in the Catholic Church except the one at Nicaea. How greatly it concerned Athanasius that the authority of the Sardican synod should not be diminished is known to everyone.]

But if others are produced by some persons who dissent from the Nicene canons and are shown to have been composed by heretics, these are rejected by Catholic bishops. For what has been devised by heretics may not be appended to Catholic rules. By contrary and unlawful opinions, they continually strive to undermine the judgment of the Nicene fathers.

We therefore say that these canons are not merely not to be followed, but are to be condemned together with heretical and schismatic doctrines, just as they were already condemned in the Sardican synod by the bishops who preceded us. [Note: Not indeed by opposing canons or decrees, but by contrary acts: they admitted Athanasius and other bishops to communion and restored them to their sees without taking account of any of the aforesaid canons. We do not invent this explanation ourselves; Palladius supplies it on p. 78, where, after citing canon 4 of the Council of Antioch, he adds: “This canon, issued by impious men as impious, was abrogated at the Council of Sardica by the Romans, Italians, Illyrians, Macedonians, and Greeks, when Liberius or Julius—Julius then presided over the church—admitted Athanasius and Marcellus of Galatia to communion under Constans, for whose sake this canon too had been made.”]

For it would be preferable that things badly done—or, as the Greek apparently requires, things “not rightly done”—should be condemned [Note: The Greek should apparently read κακῶς or οὐ καλῶς, “badly” or “not rightly”; accordingly the text should here be restored as *quae male* (“things badly done”) or *quae non recte acta sunt* (“things not rightly done”).] than that things done contrary to the canons should obtain any validity, most dear brethren.

4. One ecumenical synod can heal these evils.—But what are we to do against such things at present? A synodal investigation is necessary, and we have long said that one should be convened. For it alone can calm the agitations of storms of this kind. In order that we may obtain it, it will be useful meanwhile to await the remedy for these evils from the will of the great God and Christ himself our Lord. Everything now disturbed through the devil’s envy for the testing of the faithful will be brought to peace. Through firmness of faith we must despair of nothing from the Lord.

For we too have long and earnestly considered how an ecumenical synod may be convened, so that, by God’s will, the turbulent disturbances may at last be calmed. Let us therefore wait a little, fortified by the rampart of patience, and hope that all things will be restored by the help of our God. Moreover, we learned by careful inquiry from our fellow bishops who fled to Rome at different times and are with us—namely Demetrius, Cyriacus, Eulysius, and Palladius—all the things which you said that you endure. [Note: Palladius notes on pp. 10 and 26 the different times at which those bishops fled to Rome; from this we designated above the date of this letter.]

[Col. 0502B] Innocent, bishop, to the presbyters and deacons and to all the clergy and people of the church of Constantinople, beloved brethren who are under Bishop John: greeting.

[Col. 0502B] From the letter of your love, which you sent through Germanus the presbyter and Cassian the deacon, I learned with anxious concern the spectacle of evils which you set before my eyes; and, by repeatedly reading it, I saw by how many hardships and sufferings the faith is wearied. This matter is healed by the consolation of patience alone. For our God will shortly give an end to such great afflictions, and it will be beneficial to have borne these things.

But we recognized this necessary consolation itself, placed at the beginning of the letter of your love, while commending your purpose, as containing many testimonies urging endurance. For by your letter you anticipated the consolation which we owed to write to you. For our Master is accustomed to grant this patience to those who suffer, so that Christ’s servants, even while in afflictions, may console themselves, considering within themselves that the things which they suffer had happened earlier to the saints. And we too can bring consolation to ourselves from your very letter. For we are not strangers to suffering pain with you, since we too are chastened in you.

2. For who will be able to endure the offenses committed by those [Col. 0504B] who especially ought to be zealous for calm, peace, and concord itself? Now, by an altered practice, innocent priests are expelled from the presidency of their own churches. This our brother and fellow minister John, your bishop, first suffered unjustly, having received no hearing whatever. No accusation is brought, nor is he heard; and what is this forbidden design? So that no pretext for judgment may arise or be sought, others are installed in the places of living priests, as though those who set out from such an offense could be judged by anyone to possess or to have done anything right.

For we have never known that such things were dared by our fathers, but rather that they were forbidden, because no one has been given authority to ordain another in the place of one who is alive. For an unapproved ordination cannot take away the honor of a priest, since he who is unjustly substituted cannot be a bishop.

3. Concerning the observance of the canons, we write that those defined at Nicaea must be followed, [Col. 0506A] and that the Catholic Church ought to follow and recognize these alone. But if others are brought forward by some persons which differ from those at Nicaea and are demonstrated to have been compiled by heretics, these are rejected by Catholic bishops. For things invented by heretics cannot be attached to Catholic canons. For by contrary and unlawful measures they always seek to lessen the authority of those at Nicaea.

Therefore we say not only that these must not be followed, but rather that they themselves are to be condemned with heretical and schismatic doctrines, just as previously occurred at the Synod of Sardica through the bishops before us. For it is more fitting that things well done should be condemned than that things done openly contrary to the canons should possess any validity, most honorable brethren.

[Col. 0506B] 4. But what shall we now do in the present circumstances against such things? A synodal determination is necessary, and we said long ago that it must be assembled. For it alone can suppress the movements of such storms. In order that we may obtain it, it is useful meanwhile to defer the remedy to the will of the great God and of Christ himself our Lord. All the things now disturbed by the devil’s envy for the testing of the faithful will be calmed [Lab.: “will be consoled”]. We must not despair of anything from the Lord through firmness of faith.

For we too are considering much how an ecumenical synod might be assembled, in order that, by God’s will, the turbulent disturbances may cease. Let us therefore wait for the present and, fortified by the wall of patience, hope that all things will be restored by the help of our God. And all the things which you said you endure, we had already learned by full inquiry from those who had arrived earlier, although at widely different times—namely Demetrius, [Col. 0508A] Cyriacus, Eulysius, and Palladius—who are with us.

## EPISTLE VIII, OR A COPY

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, after Epistle 31. It first appeared in the Roman collection of papal letters from an ancient book in the Vatican Library. Nor was it without reason placed among Innocent’s letters, since he was the principal author of its composition. For, as Palladius testifies on p. 28, when holy bishops and other religious men came together at Rome from every side, bringing letters from various churches or synods concerning the unhappy condition of the church of Constantinople, the devout pope, no longer able to endure it, informed Emperor Honorius about the matters reported severally by those letters. Moved by these, Honorius warned Arcadius by letters once, twice, and indeed a third time what needed to be done. Of those three letters the first has perished; this second exists only in Latin; Palladius preserved the third in Greek, and we shall place it after this one. Baronius assigns this to the year 404; but the sequence of events which, according to Palladius, preceded it requires that it belongs to the year 405, already drawing to a close.]

### THE IMPERIAL LETTER OF HONORIUS AUGUSTUS SENT TO ARCADIUS, RULER OF THE EAST

[Col. 0507] Honorius laments what was perpetrated at Constantinople on Easter Day. The burning of the venerable temple and of the senate-house is the first indication of divine wrath. Other things are to be feared unless God is appeased. He cannot be silent about this, lest silence be taken for assent. The holy bishops were driven into exile with undue haste while episcopal judgment was awaited. From this, a disturbance of religion has been introduced and wide scope opened to heresies and schisms.

[Col. 0507B] 1. Although concerning the female image [Note: Namely the silver statue of the Empress Eudoxia, erected on a porphyry column and placed, with popular games, on the south side of the church of St Sophia, separated only by a street, as Count Marcellinus in his *Chronicle*, Socrates, book VI, chapter 18, and Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 20, record. Baronius dates this event to the year 404, but Pagius, vol. II, p. 60, thinks it occurred about the end of the year 310.] newly set up, and concerning the report of detractors circulated [Note: When Baronius refers *circumlata* (“circulated”) to the image, he interprets this passage to mean that Eudoxia’s statue was not only displayed for veneration at Constantinople but also carried through the provinces, just as pagans of old were accustomed to carry about Cybele’s image; and he thinks this the truer reason why John was so greatly stirred against Eudoxia. But this interpretation is opposed both by the silence of ancient writers about so profane a rite and by their statement that the female image was erected, placed, and dedicated, not carried about. The natural meaning of these words is that the report of detractors concerning the affair was circulated through the provinces and spread throughout the world.] and spread throughout the whole world, I had warned you by another letter, so that through repentance for such a deed and abandonment of the project the hostile rumor might grow old and might have nothing which public speech could censure in the conduct of the times; although we also disclosed to you, with pious feeling, our grief over the ruin of perishing Illyricum—why you had not wished us to learn of these losses of the commonwealth and why they were announced by other informants rather than by letters from Your Piety [Note: The sequence of the sentence requires *nos* (“us”), not *vos* (“you”). Honorius is reproaching Arcadius because he wished the losses of the commonwealth to be unknown to him, concerning which Arcadius had not deigned to write anything to him.]—nevertheless, we may not conceal even this from Your Serenity: that recently, in matters divine, something occurred, not without fear of public danger, as the swift report, ever the herald of evils, has not kept silent.
