And, as human nature is, always aroused by novel events to slander, when an opportunity to criticize is offered, it exercises its malice upon the times by a passion for cruel talkativeness.

For it has recently been reported (see Palladius, pp. 82–83) that at Constantinople, on the most sacred and venerable day of Easter, when religion, to be celebrated with more restrained ceremony in the presence of the emperors, had gathered almost all the people of neighboring cities into one place, the Catholic churches were suddenly closed and priests thrust into custody. This was done, plainly, so that at the very time when the principal indulgence [Note: In Sirmond’s appendix to the Theodosian Code, pp. 17 and 19, there is a twofold constitution of Theodosius which, for the festival of Easter, restores to their former status all persons released from prison custody except those whom the enormity of five crimes does not permit to be released. There, on p. 19, this clemency is proclaimed as enjoined and handed down by the ancestors.] opens the gloomy prisons of the guilty, a cruel prison might shut up the ministers of the holy law and peace; and all the mysteries might be disturbed as in war, some persons killed in the very sanctuaries of the church, and such violence rage around the altars that venerable bishops were thrust into exile and human blood—to say which is abominable—stained the heavenly sacraments.

Upon learning this suddenly, I confess that we were disturbed. For who, amid so bloody a crime, would not fear the wrath of almighty God? Or how could anyone think that the supreme danger lay outside the Roman world and all mortals, when almighty God himself, the author of our Empire and governor of the commonwealth entrusted to us, was believed to be angered by these utterly dreadful and execrable offenses, most venerable lords, holy brother and nephew Augustus? [Supply: “who.”]

If any matter concerning religion was in dispute among bishops, there ought to have been episcopal judgment. [Note: Ambrose, Epistle 21 to Valentinian the Younger, section 2, praises an edict of Valentinian I which decreed that, in a case involving the faith or any ecclesiastical order, judgment ought to belong to one neither unequal in office nor unlike in right; that is, Ambrose says, he wished priests to judge priests. Indeed, even if a bishop were accused in other matters and his conduct had to be examined, he wished this also to belong to episcopal judgment.] For the interpretation of divine matters belongs to them; religious obedience is incumbent upon us. [The ancient usage of *exspectat* is “is incumbent upon.”]

But let it be granted that the imperial concern presumed somewhat further authority in mystical and Catholic questions: [Col. 0509A] was the aroused indignation to proceed so far as the exile of priests and the killing of men, so that where chaste prayers, sincere vows, and unblemished sacrifices are offered, there the sword—scarcely to be drawn even against the throats of the guilty—should be unsheathed?

## 2

The facts themselves finally show what the divine majesty thought about these matters. This present upheaval was indeed the first judgment—and may it be the only one! For human trembling, conscious of having perpetrated so great a crime, causes us to fear that something even more serious may follow, though almighty God avert it, after the experience of such a terrible vengeance.

I hear [Palladius, pp. 91 and 93] that the most holy church, exposed to the resources of so many emperors [perhaps: “polished/refined” (*expolitam*)], renowned for its costly adornments, and made most august by the prayers of princes who supplicated there, burned; and that the one unique light of the city of Constantinople collapsed into ashes and smoked, since God did not prevent it. (He seems to be cursing the defiled mysteries and to have turned his eyes away from the place which blood had already polluted, lest anyone attempt to implore heavenly mercy beneath bloodstained altars.) Buildings also, no less distinguished by their divine splendor, were consumed when the flames spread more widely in the violence of the raging fire; and the ornaments which our ancestors had carefully fashioned to adorn the public appearance of the city were burned as though in a kind of funeral of the city.

[Note: That is, the very spacious senate-house, which Palladius says was some distance away, opposite the church to the south. That fire crossed the intervening crowd of people as though by a bridge and consumed it. Zosimus laments this loss. Socrates, Book VI, chapter 18, reports that the fire occurred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, under the consulship of Honorius VI and Aristaenetus; the Alexandrian Chronicle adds that it was on the second day of the week, at the sixth hour.]

[Note: Baron prefers *indicium* (“sign”) here. Nevertheless, *judicium* (“judgment”), that is, the punishment and vengeance of God the judge, should be retained.]

## 3

Although, assailed by repeated injuries, I ought to have kept silent about these matters and not so faithfully admonished my most closely connected brother and partner in the kingdom, nevertheless, placing the duty of our blood relationship before the impulse toward silent grief, I urge and advise you that, if possible, these things be corrected for the future by reforming your conduct, and that the divine anger—which the event shows to have been aroused to a considerable degree—be appeased by assiduous prayers.

Receive from me the highest indication of sincerity. I therefore thought that this should be brought to the attention of your Clemency, lest my silence itself make me suspected by anyone of concealing some secret congratulation, or lest anyone believe that I approve such actions and that, although I had often warned that they should not occur, I did not grieve after they had been committed.

[Note: In the Roman edition, *judicium* (“judgment”) is read. The reading found here with Baron, *indicium* (“indication” or “sign”), is preferable.]

## 4

For who could be free from grief who remembers that he is a Christian, when so great a sudden disturbance has been introduced into religion that the entire condition of the Catholic faith must inevitably waver?

There was a dispute among the bishops which ought to have been settled after consultation and deliberation together.

[Note: Baron reads “after a council had been convened and deliberation undertaken” (*contractoque concilio … tractatoque consilio*). The preceding word *collato* supports the Roman edition’s preferable continuation, “and after deliberation had been undertaken” (*tractatoque consilio*).]

[Note: Baron substitutes *missis … legatis* (“after envoys had been sent”). According to Palladius, p. 9 and elsewhere, envoys were sent to Rome from both sides: first, from Theophilus’s side, an Alexandrian lector bearing a letter from Theophilus; then the presbyter Peter, also sent by Theophilus, together with Martyrius, deacon of the church of Constantinople, who delivered another letter from Theophilus together with certain documents to Pope Innocent; and finally Paternus, who claimed to be a presbyter of the church of Constantinople, bearing a letter from the bishops Acacius, Paul, Antiochus, Severianus, and several others, in which they accused John as though he had burned the Church of Hagia Sophia.

From John’s side—leaving aside the others who later arrived in large numbers—four bishops first came to Rome: Pansophius, Pappus, Demetrius, and Eugenius. They delivered three letters: one from John, another from forty bishops concerning their communion with him, and a third from his clergy. Palladius, p. 22, specifically testifies that John’s letter to Innocent had also been written to Venerius, bishop of Milan, and Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. Hence Honorius could say that those envoys had been sent to the priests of the eternal city and of Italy.]

Envoys from both sides had been sent to the priests of the eternal city and of Italy. A decision based on the authority of all was awaited, one that would establish the rule of ecclesiastical discipline. Nothing ought to have been altered while a carefully deliberated judgment was proceeding. Meanwhile, however, an astonishing precipitate rush of haste broke out, so that, without awaiting the letters of the priests who had been consulted through the mutual embassies of the parties, and without examining the facts, the bishops were driven into exile and condemned to punishment before they had undergone the judgment of an episcopal tribunal.

In the end, the matter itself proved how premature that condemnation had been. For those whose authority had been awaited, after peaceable communion had been granted [Baron: “previously granted”] to Bishop John, judged that concord should be established and thought that no one should be excluded from fellowship before judgment.

[Note: The emperor here attributes this action to several persons, whereas Palladius attributes it to Innocent alone. He says on p. 22: “Then blessed Pope Innocent sent letters of communion to both parties, disapproving the judgment which had been made by Theophilus.” That communion was granted to both parties by Innocent is attested by his Letters 4 and 5. But who could persuade himself that Innocent settled so important a matter without a synod, especially since we read in Letter 3, no. 1, that Innocent, adhering to the custom of his predecessors, ordered that the Spanish bishops, who showed him some deference, should be heard in the presbyteral council?]

## 5

What else now remains except that schisms, divided and separated in different directions, tear apart the Catholic faith; that heresies, always hostile to communion, arise from such a bewildering variety of events; and that the people should scarcely be blamed if they happen to withdraw into opposing parties through the diversity of sects? For the material of discord has been supplied by public authority, and a certain fuel for nurturing sedition has been kindled.

To prevent this from flaring up again to the great destruction of the human race, we must pray that God, patient toward human failings, may prosper and favor the badly managed affair. For, as far as depends on us, we can fear what has been done; but as regards God, who is always ready to be appeased by piety, the immunity granted will not be an impunity deserved, but forgiveness.

# LETTER

[Note: When Honorius, prompted by Innocent’s letters, had already written twice to Arcadius concerning John’s case without accomplishing anything, he asked Innocent to send him five bishops, two presbyters, and one deacon to carry a third letter to his brother. Those sent were Aemilius, bishop of Beneventum; Cythegius; Gaudentius, perhaps bishop of Brescia; and the presbyters Valentinianus and Boniface, apparently the same man who later succeeded Pope Zosimus. Palladius does not give the names of the others, but he reports that Cyriacus, Demetrius, Palladius, and Eulysius traveled to Constantinople with them.

We owe this letter to Palladius alone, who inserted it in his *Dialogue*, p. 29. Baronius had its Latin translation, taken from Ambrose of Camaldoli, reprinted under the year 405. It appears to have been written around the spring of 406.]

## IX. Honorius the Emperor to Arcadius Augustus

*He orders that a synod be convened at Thessalonica and that Theophilus go there.*

[Col. 0511]

I am now writing for the third time to Your Mildness, asking that the measures undertaken by agreement against John, bishop of Constantinople, be corrected; and, as it appears, this has not yet been accomplished. Therefore I have written again through these bishops and presbyters, being very deeply concerned for ecclesiastical peace, through which our empire also enjoys peace, asking that you deign to order the bishops of the East to assemble at Thessalonica.

For the bishops of our West, having chosen men who do not know how to turn aside toward evil and falsehood, have sent five bishops, two presbyters, and one deacon of the great Roman Church. I ask that you honor them with every distinction, so that, if they become convinced that John was justly expelled, they may instruct me to withdraw from communion with him; or, if they prove that the bishops of the East are acting with an evil intention, they may cause you to withdraw from communion with them.

[Note: The Greek word *ἐθελοκακοῦντας*, properly used of soldiers who deliberately do not exert their strength so that the adversary may prevail, is rightly applied to those bishops who, although they could have opposed Theophilus by means of the canons, voluntarily yielded so that he could oppress John unjustly.]

For you may learn what the Westerners’ opinion concerning Bishop John is: from all the letters that have been written to me, I have appended two containing the same substance as the rest, one from the bishop of Rome and the other from the bishop of Aquileia.

[Note: I have supplied the words enclosed in brackets so that the sentence would not remain ambiguous. The text is not fuller in Ambrose of Camaldoli, who adds here: “From nearly all the letters which they sent me frequently, I appended two which contained the same thing as the others.” Palladius, p. 28, reports that, after receiving various letters, Innocent wrote to Honorius, “setting out in order the force of the letters,” and then individually explained what those letters contained. This suggests that he expressed merely the substance or summary of each letter. But from this passage it can be inferred that not only the substance of the individual letters, but the letters themselves or copies of them, were sent to him at the same time.]

[Note: Palladius, p. 31, writes that letters were handed to the same envoys not only from the Emperor Honorius, Innocent, bishop of Rome, and Chromatius of Aquileia, but also from Venerius of Milan and others. Honorius was content to mention the writings of Innocent and Chromatius previously sent to him, not those which they were sending anew to Arcadius, nor those which he himself was dispatching in his own name, nor those which others had added to them on that occasion.]

Above all, I ask Your Clemency to order Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, who is said to be the author of all these evils, to appear, even against his will. Thus nothing may prevent the synod of the bishops who are present from establishing the peace appropriate to our times.

## Honorius the Emperor to Arcadius the King

I am writing for the third time to Your Mildness, asking that the measures undertaken against Bishop John of Constantinople be corrected; and, as it appears, this has not been accomplished. Therefore I have written again through the bishops and presbyters, being deeply concerned for ecclesiastical peace, through which our empire also enjoys peace, asking that you deign to order the bishops of the East to assemble at Thessalonica.

For the bishops of our West, having chosen men unwavering toward evil and falsehood, have sent five bishops, two presbyters, and one deacon of the great Roman Church. Deign to honor them with every distinction, so that, if they become convinced that Bishop John was justly expelled, they may instruct me to withdraw from their communion; or, if they prove that the bishops of the East are deliberately acting wickedly, they may cause you to withdraw from their communion.

For, so that you may know what the Western bishops think concerning Bishop John, from all the letters written to me I have appended two equivalent to them all: the letter of the bishop of Rome and that of the bishop of Aquileia.

But above all I ask Your Mildness to compel Theophilus of Alexandria, even against his will, to appear, since he is said to be chiefly responsible for all these evils. Thus the synod of the bishops who have assembled, impeded by nothing, may establish the peace appropriate to our times.

# LETTER

[Note: This letter appears under title 38 among the decrees of Innocent in Dionysius, as well as in the Spanish and Isidorian collections. It was carried by Germanus, who, together with Cassianus, had delivered to Rome at the beginning of 405 the letters of the clergy and people of Constantinople to which Innocent replied in Letter 7.

It is probable that Innocent, either in 405 itself or rather in the following year, used the services of this same Germanus to greet Aurelius and Augustine, and that on this occasion Germanus related to the Africans how great and how undeserved were the sufferings endured by John, and what disagreement had arisen between Innocent and Theophilus for this reason.

Certainly the Council of Carthage, held on 13 June 407 and recorded in African Ecclesiastical Canon 101, decreed that a letter should be written to Innocent so that peace might be arranged between the Roman and Alexandrian churches. It is no less certain that Aurelius, around the same time, displayed his devotion to John; concerning this, John gives him thanks in a letter.]

## X. A salutatory letter full of charity from Pope Innocent I to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and Augustine, bishop of Hippo

[Col. 0511C]

### Innocent to Aurelius and Augustine, bishops

The return of our fellow presbyter Germanus, so dear to me, ought not to have been empty of service to our office. For it seems natural and fitting to us, in a certain way, to send greetings to those dearest to us through those who are dear.

Therefore, beloved ones, we desire that Your Brotherhood rejoice in the Lord, and we ask you to return to God prayers equal to ours on our behalf; for, as you well know, through common and reciprocal prayers we accomplish more than through prayers that are individual or private.

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads *respondere* (“to reply” or “return”).]

# LETTER

[Note: This letter is taken from the edition of Chrysostom’s works, where it precedes his letters, and was reprinted by Baronius under the year 406, as well as by the editors of the papal letters and councils. We have checked it against an old Hamburg manuscript. Chrysostom testifies in section 4 that he wrote it in the third year of his exile, therefore in 407.

It also follows that it was written before July, if Chrysostom reckons the first year of his exile from the day on which he was brought to Cucusus through the corresponding day of the following year, rather than calling it the third year according to the commonly published reckoning based on the three changes of consuls.]

## XI. John Chrysostom, bishop, to Pope Innocent

*He praises Innocent’s paternal affection toward him and his supreme vigilance in times of affliction, and repeatedly implores him not to relax this concern.*

(You can find this letter, like another letter of Chrysostom mentioned above, in volume III of the works of that same Doctor.)

# LETTER XII

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, this is Letter 28. What was formerly Letter 12 is now Letter 14. We owe this letter, as well as the preceding Letter 7, to Sozomen alone. He introduces both in Book VIII, chapter 24, as follows: “When Innocent was attempting to convene an ecumenical synod, he wrote to John and separately to the clergy of the city of Constantinople.”

These words may indicate either that both letters were sent at the same time or, at any rate, that this letter was not later than Letter 7. But it is not unusual for this writer to combine and confuse events that occurred at widely separated times.

Since this letter is entirely silent about the convening of the synod in which Innocent had placed all his hope, this is a strong argument that it was written after that hope had failed. It is not inconsistent with the truth to suppose that Innocent, moved by John’s preceding letter, wrote this one to console the holy prelate in the troubles which he had learned were afflicting him. If so, it could scarcely have reached John while he was still alive.]

## Pope Innocent to John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople

*He consoles John by placing before him the commendation of endurance.*

### Innocent to his beloved brother John

Although an innocent man ought to expect all good things and ask mercy from God, nevertheless letters appropriate to the occasion have also been sent by us, who recommend endurance, through the deacon Cyriacus, lest insult prove stronger in crushing you than a good conscience in raising your hopes.

For you, teacher and shepherd of so many peoples, do not need to be taught that the very best are always and repeatedly tested, to see whether they remain steadfast in the vigor of endurance and do not succumb to any hardship or distress.

Indeed, conscience is a firm defense against everything that happens unjustly. Unless someone overcomes such things through endurance, he gives grounds for an unfavorable suspicion concerning himself. For the person who relies first on God and then on the confidence of his conscience ought to endure everything.

A good and honorable man may certainly be exercised in endurance, but he cannot be overcome, since the divine Scriptures fortify and protect his mind. Sacred readings abound in examples which we pass on to the peoples; they testify that nearly all the saints were afflicted in various ways and tested as though in an assay, and that they thus reached the crown of endurance.

Therefore, most revered brother, let your conscience itself console Your Charity, since in afflictions it possesses the consolation of virtue. For, while the Lord Christ looks on, a pure conscience stands in the harbor of peace.

[Note: Valesius rendered this passage in Latin as follows: “which in calamities is accustomed to be the consolation of virtue.” We adhere to the Greek wording, in which it is not conscience that is proclaimed as the consolation of virtue, but rather virtue as the consolation of conscience. Innocent asserts this more confidently than the Orator, who expressed it somewhat more cautiously: “Punishments undertaken with virtue possess some consolation in themselves.” By “virtue,” Innocent chiefly understands endurance. In Letter 7 to the clergy and people of Constantinople, after describing their calamity, he writes: “This matter can be healed only by the consolation of endurance.”]

## To the beloved brother John, Innocent

Although the innocent man ought to expect all good things and ask mercy from God, nevertheless, since we advise endurance, the appropriate letters have been sent through Cyriacus the deacon, so that insult may not be more powerful in crushing than good conscience is in hoping. [Editorial addition: *ἤ*, “than.”]

For you, teacher and shepherd of so many peoples, ought not to need instruction that the best men are always and repeatedly tested, to determine whether they remain in the full strength of endurance and do not fall under any labor of suffering.

And conscience is truly a firm thing against everything that happens unjustly; unless someone conquers such things by enduring them, it produces evidence of an unfavorable suspicion.

For the one who trusts first in God and then in his own conscience ought to endure everything. When the good and honorable man can be trained especially for endurance, he cannot be defeated, because the divine Scriptures guard his mind.

The divine readings which we transmit to the peoples overflow with examples. They testify that almost all the saints were afflicted in various ways and continually, and that they were tested as though in an examination, and thus reached the crown of endurance.

Let conscience itself console Your Charity, most honored brother, since in afflictions it possesses the consolation of virtue. For, while the Lord Christ watches over it, the conscience, having been purified, will stand in the harbor of peace.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

# LETTER

[Note: This letter was formerly read in the Roman synod under Boniface II and was later praised by Nicholas I in Letter 2. It was subsequently published by Luca Holstenius together with the other records of that Roman synod.

The time at which it was written is indicated by the consular date. But the distinguished Tillemont, vol. X, p. 829, believes that the date contains an error and that Honorius VII and Theodosius II should be restored in place of Honorius IX and Theodosius V. From this it would follow that the letter was written in 407.

He attempts to establish this opinion by the following argument. First, he assumes that this is the first of the letters which Innocent wrote to Rufus and that it was given to him as soon as Innocent learned of Rufus’s ordination; this need not be denied. He then adds that the Rufus to whom Innocent is now writing does not appear to be anyone other than the man whom the same pope says in Letter 17 to Marcianus that he had already written about the clergy of Naissus.

Granting this as well, he continues: “But Innocent wrote that letter to Marcianus while residing at Ravenna, where he arrived at the beginning of 409 and where he was still staying in August 410; nor is there any trace in history from which we might infer that he returned to the same city thereafter.” From this he thinks it follows that neither Rufus’s ordination nor this letter should be placed later than 408.

But since not everything that happened was committed to writing, and someone who had once gone to Ravenna could have gone there a second and third time; and since, as the distinguished man himself admits, the occasion and reason for doing so were not lacking in 413, when Heraclianus prevented grain from being transported to Rome, it is hardly safe to replace a certain date with an uncertain conjecture.

Indeed, the scribal error would be very unusual if, when mistakes had been made in expressing the years of two consuls who had held the same dignity several times, the error nevertheless happened to fit so neatly in designating their consulships that Honorius’s ninth consulship was paired with Theodosius’s fifth—not his fourth or third—and conversely Theodosius’s fifth with Honorius’s ninth—not his seventh or any other.]

## XIII. To Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica

*The administration of various provinces is entrusted to him; he is appointed Innocent’s vicar and first among the primates.*

### Innocent to his most beloved brother Rufus

#### 1

The Lord entrusted everything to the most excellent and glorious Moses for the liberation and governance of Israel, to such an extent that he expressly commanded him, after receiving the report, to follow the counsel of his father-in-law Jethro (Exodus 18): namely, to appoint men equal in rank to the dignity of judges, who would settle among the people the multitude of cases according to the place entrusted to them, while he himself would devote himself chiefly, or even entirely, to divine consultations.

[Note: In old books, where the sequence of the speech requires the word *consultation*, we have often—and indeed usually—found *consolation* being read. We suspect the same error here and think that the text should be restored as: “while he himself would devote himself chiefly or even entirely to divine consultations.” Innocent is referring to Exodus 18:19 and 22: “Be you for the people in those matters which concern God, that you may refer to him what is said … Whatever matter is greater, let them refer to you, and let them judge only the lesser matters.”]

The pattern of the Apostles was promulgated in no other way (Acts 6:2–3): once they had been appointed leaders of the Gospel, they entrusted the handling and performance of the causes and duties of other matters to their disciples. Finally, as we learn from the reading of the sacred letters, Paul, marvelous in all his compassion, entrusted Titus with what he should take care of in Crete (Titus 1:5), and Timothy with what he should arrange throughout Asia (1 Timothy 1).

#### 2

Therefore, as this grace proceeds from God, divided among churches separated from me by such long intervals, let them learn to seek counsel in such a way that, with the Lord Christ’s approval, they deem it proper to entrust to your prudence and gravity the care and the cases, if any arise, of the churches throughout Achaea, Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus, Crete, Mediterranean Dacia, Ripensian Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalitana.

[Note: Those whose suggestion caused Justinian to write Novel 11 evidently imposed upon the emperor the belief that the dignity of vicar had been assigned to the bishop of Thessalonica only in the time of Attila, that is, after the year 440.]

[Col. 0516A]

For we impose this responsibility upon the foresight and virtue of your most excellent sincerity in accordance with the sacred commands of the Lord—not establishing this arrangement for the first time, but imitating our apostolic predecessors, who wished these duties to be assigned, according to their merits, to the most blessed Acholius and Anysius.

[Note: We observed in the note to Damasus’s Letter 8 that this responsibility had been imposed upon Acholius at least as early as 380, contrary to Haller’s opinion.]

For it is entirely just that those who have deserved well should be adorned with honors in such a way that the arrogant, as necessity requires, may be restrained. Therefore, let there be a reward for the good and a mark of censure for the less good; for thus the one is corrected and the other ennobled.

[Note: *Censio* ordinarily signifies a mark imprinted by a censor. The metropolitans of the provinces named above are meant by the title “primates.”]

#### 3

Take up, therefore, most beloved brother, in our place, the care of the churches mentioned above, without prejudice to their primacy. As first among the primates themselves, let them not request anything that they must send to us without your judgment.

For we command that either everything in question be settled through your experience, or that it be brought to us through your counsel. Know also that, with the favor and permission of the apostolic see, it is permitted to your Brotherhood that, whenever some ecclesiastical matter must be discussed and investigated either in your own province or in those mentioned above, you may choose from whatever churches you wish those bishops as associates whom you will take with you. With their trustworthiness and moderation, you will direct whatever necessity or case demands as the best and chief arbiter, and you will determine it as the principal intercessor, since you have been chosen by us.

We have ordered that the entire documentation of the archives concerning this matter be prepared with the presbyter Senecio, a man of very mature judgment.

[Note: Holstenius reads *archivorum*, not *Achivorum*, as Tillemont reads it. Both what precedes and what follows persuade us that the subject here is documents and archives. The truth of the documents by which the office of vicar had been delegated to the bishop of Thessalonica appears to have been called into doubt by some at that time.

Accordingly, although Innocent had just said to Rufus, “since you have been chosen by us”—which suggests that the authority was conferred upon him not so much by a prerogative of the see as by the act of the one who chose him—he nevertheless does not deny that it was supported by custom. Therefore he advises Rufus to review both his earlier letter and other letters sent for this reason by his predecessors.]

[Note: In the edition of the Councils this is Letter 11. What was formerly Letter 14 is now Letter 23. Perhaps this is the same Senecio who is said by Siricius in Letter 9, no. 5, to have been given to Bishop Bassus as an associate in governing the church.]

Thus, by carefully reviewing both our earlier letter and these documents, recognize what you must do. For we have made our will sufficiently clear, as was fitting, in letters to each province.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July—that is, June 17, 412—during the consulships of the Augusti Honorius IX and Theodosius V.

# LETTER

[Note: In the Roman edition of the papal letters this is marked as copied from Cresconius. It might more suitably have been marked as copied from Dionysius. In his collection it forms title or chapter 50 among the decrees of Innocent. From there both the author of the Spanish collection and Isidore borrowed it.

Everyone agrees that this letter discusses the celebration of Easter in the year 414, and therefore most place its composition in 413. Tillemont, however, weighing everything with his customary subtlety, observes that Innocent does not yet prescribe the observance of Easter here, but wishes first to have his opinion on it reviewed in an African synod and then reported back to him; from this he judges that the letter should be assigned to 412.

He considers this especially likely because, as he says, Aurelius generally held both a provincial council around the end of June and a plenary council of Africa around the end of August, at which, in accordance with canon 41 of the Third Council of Carthage, the date of the following year’s Easter was to be announced.

Unless, therefore, we suppose that some synod was held in Africa outside those customary periods, the learned man’s opinion seems to deserve acceptance. Otherwise it is not apparent how Innocent could conveniently learn the African synod’s judgment on this question and then announce the date of Easter to the bishops of the entire West.

Moreover, Pope Leo, likewise concerned about the date of Easter in 455, sought to be informed about it by several letters not in 454, when that date had to be prescribed and announced to the churches, but from 453.]

## XIV. Concerning the calculation of Easter in the year 414

[Note: In the manuscripts of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections: simply “concerning Easter,” or “concerning Easter, in which matter he is mistaken,” that is, whether Innocent is mistaken in prescribing its date or not. In the Spanish collection: “concerning the announcement or prescribed dates of Easter.”]

### Innocent to Aurelius

The duty of our charity is not interrupted by any interval, even if no written page carries our words. For spiritual grace lives reciprocally in our hearts, and the priestly fellowship itself nourishes our love.

Take care, as is fitting, to preserve the unity of the Church; and let us all likewise both think and proclaim the same thing, dearest brother.

[Note: We emend the text with the help of the Royal manuscript, which reads, “Take care, as is fitting.” This is supported by the Coislin manuscript, which reads, “Therefore take care, as is fitting.” Other books read, “Why, then, is it unfitting?” and, shortly afterward, the printed editions alone have *custodiri* (“to be preserved”). In the Coislin manuscript the text continues, “and may all of us, dearest brothers …”]

I have therefore prescribed in this letter the calculation of Easter for another—that is, the coming—year. Since the moon is almost full on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April (for it falls slightly short), and since the twenty-third day occurs on the fourth day before those same Kalends, I judged that the Easter festival should be celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends, since we know that Easter had never previously been celebrated on the twenty-third day of the moon.

[Note: The word “another” may refer either to the year after the year in which the date of Easter is to be celebrated or to the year after the year in which it is to be announced. If the latter is accepted, this letter must be dated to 412; if the former is preferred, it must be assigned to 413. Nevertheless, below he rather clearly indicates that he is writing in the second year after the year in which the date of Easter was to be announced.]

I have explained and declared the tenor of my opinion. Now it will be your responsibility, my associate brother, to review this very matter in a most devout synod with our unanimous fellow priests, so that, if nothing results contrary to our arrangement, you may write back to us fully and openly, in order that we may prescribe at the proper time the Easter date already determined and previously announced in writing, as is customary, for observance.

[Note: In the Coislin manuscript: “who agrees with me.”]

[Note: The practice of the Roman pontiff’s sending letters concerning the date of Easter to everyone is attested by the Council of Arles, held in 314, and its use is confirmed by Leo in Letter 88 to Ravennius. The whole of this passage of Innocent suggests that the time when he had to satisfy this custom had not yet arrived.]

Although I know that you will receive our fellow presbyter Archidamus most willingly and according to your customary practice, nevertheless, as an additional precaution, I ask you to deign to keep him among your own clergy.

[Note: All the manuscripts have the additional phrase “as an additional precaution.”]

# LETTER

[Note: In the edition of the Councils this is Letter 13; what was formerly Letter 15 is now Letter 20. Dionysius Exiguus did not consider this letter unworthy of inclusion among Innocent’s decrees. He placed it under title or chapter 39 immediately before the preceding letter. It occupies the same place in the Spanish and Isidorian collections.

Perhaps it was sent together with the same letter. Baronius believes that it was written in 413, thereby indirectly refuting Pelagius’s book written to Demetrias, the daughter of Juliana. Letters 169 of John Chrysostom and 150 of Augustine were written to the same Juliana, as were Augustine’s and Alypius’s Letter 188. Augustine dedicated his work *On the Good of Widowhood* to her in 414. Jerome also mentions her in Letter 8, to Demetrias, her daughter.]

## XV. An exhortation from Pope Innocent to Juliana, a noblewoman

A singular member of the Church, the greatness of your religious devotion is clearly manifest to all and is held by us in the highest reverence. At the very summit of nobility, you devote yourself to the Church with a devotion much nobler still; rejoicing more greatly in the knowledge of Christ, you obey his commands, and you exult in faith rather than boast in the splendor of so distinguished a lineage.

It is the mark of supreme virtue to have conquered the glory of the flesh; and it is a great grace of Christ, noble lady and daughter, to have surpassed nobility by your character.

[Note: Baronius rightly observes that this was not said without purpose, but as an antidote by which the poison concealed in Pelagius’s words to Demetrias—words which displeased Alypius and Augustine so greatly—might be driven out: “No one apart from you will be able to bestow spiritual riches upon himself; in these you are rightly praised, in these you are deservedly preferred to others, for they can exist only from you and in you.”

The conclusion of the letter is no less opposed to Pelagius’s words. Innocent does not say, “Since you have made yourself distinguished, make yourself brighter through the ages for him,” but refers all of this to God’s gift. Certainly, if this letter preceded Pelagius’s aforementioned work, it must be admitted that, not without God’s prompting, Innocent so aptly anticipated Juliana’s mind against that poisonous doctrine.]

Therefore, being certain, dearest daughter, strive to illuminate whatever spans of this life you possess with eternal divine duties, so that he who made you distinguished may render you brighter for himself throughout the ages.

# LETTER

[Note: In the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, this letter constitutes Decree L of Innocent. The title prefixed to it by Dionysius Exiguus himself is cited by Cresconius in chapter 58. The Spanish and Isidorian collections also transmit it. Innocent states that he was at Ravenna when he wrote it. Zosimus (*History*, book V), Sozomen (*History*, book IX, chapter 7), and Orosius (*History*, book VII, chapter 39) report that he went to that city around the beginning of 409 and was there when Rome was captured by Alaric in 410. Hence some think that the letter was sent during that interval. Others consider it much later, in 414, since at its beginning they believe the subsequent letter to Rufus, Marcianus, and the other bishops is mentioned. Perhaps for this reason it was placed after the following letter in the Roman edition, although Dionysius places it before that letter. In the following letter, however, the subject is not the admission of the clergy of Naissus who had been ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation, but the expulsion from the clergy of those whom the same condemned heretic had ordained. Accordingly, nothing certain can be established concerning the date on which this letter was written. It is nevertheless appropriately placed here, following Dionysius: not only because it is plausibly believed to be earlier than the letter appended to it, but also because the order of events requires that Innocent’s judgment first concerning those ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation, and then concerning those ordained by him after his condemnation, be explained.]

## XVI. On receiving the clergy whom Bonosus is known to have ordained before his condemnation

## Innocent to Bishop Marcianus

[Note: So most manuscripts read. Some, as in Merlin, have “to the bishop of Naissus.” The Roman edition after Crabbe has “to the bishop of Naxos.” Crabbe himself added “to the bishop of Naresis” in the margin; this reading was preferred in later editions of the councils. In the pure Regius manuscript of the Dionysian collection, this entire heading is absent.]

## To Marcianus, bishop of Naissus

In an earlier period, if I remember correctly [Note: The manuscripts of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections read “I think.”], I recall sending letters of this kind both to Your Charity and to our brothers and fellow bishops Rufus and the others concerning the clergy of Naissus [Note: Merlin has “of Naisus”; Crabbe and the Roman edition, “of Naxus”; later editions of the councils, following Crabbe’s marginal reading, “of Naresis”; the Navarre manuscript, “of Naisis”; the other manuscripts, “of Naissus.” Those who maintain that Bonosus was bishop of Naissus rely on this passage, reasoning that he could not have ordained clergy of Naissus unless he had presided over the church of Naissus. Their opinion would certainly not be rejected if it were established that this heretic had confined himself to the rules of ecclesiastical discipline. But, as is shown in the following letter, §12, he indiscriminately and without any investigation performed illicit ordinations. Nothing therefore prevents us from adhering to the authority of Marius Mercator, who calls Bonosus bishop of Sardica.]—namely, concerning those who claimed that before Bonosus’s condemnation they had been ordained by him both as priests and as deacons—so that, if after abandoning and condemning his error they wished to be joined to the Church, they might willingly be received, lest those who were worthy of recovering salvation should perhaps perish in that same state [Note: The printed editions add “error”; this is absent from the manuscripts and is correctly understood implicitly].

But now, while I am residing in the city of Ravenna because of the frequent needs of the Roman people [Note: Only the Roman edition reads *Germanus*. Merlin and Crabbe read *Germanium*, and subsequently *Lupentinum*; here the later editions of the councils prefer *Lupentinus*, rejecting in the margin *Lupentius*, which is the reading of the manuscripts], Germanus, who claims to be a priest [Col. 0520A], and Lupentius, who says that he is a deacon, having undertaken what was almost an embassy on behalf of many such men, poured out their pleas and eagerly expressed their personal grief [Note: The verb “asserting,” omitted in Crabbe and the subsequent printed editions, is restored from Merlin and the manuscripts. What the clergy ordained by Bonosus were then asserting—that Marcianus had allowed them to retain their churches while denying them his communion—is illustrated by the acts of the First Council of Toledo, Labbe, vol. II, p. 1231. There, certain people departing from the sect of Priscillian are allowed to retain their churches, but communion is not granted to them until it has been restored by the Roman bishop. These clergy, who were allowed to retain their churches, had not been ordained again. Accordingly, the bishops of Macedonia had not been persuaded that, if the Bonosians were to be allowed to remain in the clergy, this could be granted to them only by repeated ordination. This should meanwhile be noted against the opinion of Paschasius Quesnellus, which will be discussed in the note to the following letter].

They said that they did indeed retain the churches situated in the parishes of Your Charity, but had not been able to merit your communion, for the following reason: a certain man named Rusticius had received the priesthood through repeated ordination. And this creates no small impediment, since either they grieve that such a man is being retained in the Church, or he supposes that the same sin ought to be committed against others which he acknowledges to have been committed against himself [Note: In our manuscripts, as in the printed editions, the reading is *peccare* (“to sin”); but the following *esse peccatum* (“to be a sin”) necessarily requires *peccari* (“that sin be committed”). Those familiar with the practices of people who wear out old books know how frequent the interchange of *i* and *e* is. Further, editions after Crabbe, following the Regius manuscript, read *debere in alio* (“ought to be committed against another”), whereas the other books more correctly read *debere in alios* (“ought to be committed against others”), with “ordained by Bonosus” understood. The Dionysian and Hadrianic collations then give *arbitretur quem in se*, “he should regard as committed against himself,” rather than *quemadmodum in se*, “in the same way as against himself”; the latter is more correctly found in the Spanish and Isidorian manuscript collations].

Although my earlier letters, which I mentioned above, contain a fuller treatment of this matter, we have nevertheless thought it necessary to admonish Your Fraternity again now: if it is truly established that some men were ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation and afterward wished, or now wish, to return, we judge that they ought to be received. This is especially so since the men mentioned above assert that they were ordained so long ago that Cornelius, a man of holy memory and bishop of the city of Sirmium, as well as our brother Nicetas and several others, were present [Note: He is thought to be the Nicetas called bishop of Romatiana by Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*. Geographers place that city in inland Dacia, or Upper Moesia, between Naissus and Sardica], when they were advanced to the honors which they say they possess [Note: Later editions after Crabbe read *faterentur* (“they confessed”); the Regius manuscript has the corrupt reading *nihil agerentur*; the others read *augerentur* (“were advanced”). Innocent calls them “advanced to the honors” in the same manner in which Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book X, §11, says that those who received Christ were advanced into the sons of God: just as those who become sons of God receive an accession of dignity, so do those who are ordained].

Therefore, dearest brother, if their assertion is accepted as true, you ought not to hesitate to receive those whom you have allowed for so long to retain the churches entrusted to them.

# EDITORIAL NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

### 1

This letter is found in the Corbie manuscript written around the middle of the sixth century, in the Colbert manuscript written in Lombard script, in the old copies of the Codex published by Quesnellus, and in the collections of Dionysius, Hadrian, the Spanish collection, Isidore, and others. Dionysius divided it into seven chapters, placing them among Innocent’s decrees so that he calls the first of these chapters Innocent’s Decree LI and the last LVIII. In the Corbie manuscript, however, it is divided into twelve titles, which we have set out at the beginning of the letter itself.

A shorter title is prefixed to the letter in the ancient copies of Quesnellus’s Codex, as follows:

> “Rescript of Pope Innocent to the Macedonian bishops concerning the inquiry into three headings.  
> I. That one who takes a widow as wife is not to be admitted to the clergy.  
> II. That one who had a wife before baptism, and, after her death, married another after baptism, is to be regarded as a bigamist and is not to be admitted to the clergy.  
> III. That those who, after withdrawing from the Catholic Church, receive priestly ordination from heretics are not to be counted among the clergy until they wish to return.”

Indeed, the letter chiefly discusses those three questions. Referring to the first two, Innocent says in §1:

> “Concerning these matters I remember having written long ago; but the repeated inquiry contained in your report compels me now to restate the rule with clearer arguments.”

He had evidently written concerning the first in Letter 2 to Victricius, chapter 5; in Letter 3 to the Council of Toledo, chapter 6; and in Letter 6 to Exsuperius, §1; and concerning the second in the letters to Victricius and to the Council of Toledo cited above.

The fact that those letters are not general ones does not stand in the way. When the Roman pontiffs replied to questions submitted by individual bishops or churches, they commonly shared with them whatever might be useful to other churches as well. But when Innocent reaches the third question, he acknowledges that its difficulty requires a longer discussion, thereby sufficiently indicating that it was a new matter which he had not previously treated.

### 2

That new question arose on account of those whom Bonosus ordained after his condemnation. There was no difficulty concerning those ordained by him before his condemnation. The Council of Capua had judged that they should be received in the offices they held. Approving that judgment, Innocent had written specifically to Rufus and the other Macedonians concerning the clergy of Naissus “who asserted that before Bonosus’s condemnation they had been ordained by him both as priests and as deacons,” saying that, “if after abandoning and condemning his error they wished to be joined to the Church, they should willingly be received” (*Letter* 17, §1).

The dispute, therefore, concerned only those clergy whom Bonosus ordained after he had been condemned. When this question was referred to Innocent, he observes that a distinction must be made between those who were baptized in heresy and come to the Church, and those who pass from the Catholic Church into heresy and then return from there to the Catholic Church from which they had departed.

The former were immediately joined to the faithful through the laying on of hands alone. The others, however, were admitted to communion only after a long period of penance. “Hence,” he says (§11), “it is clear that those who passed from the Catholic Church to condemned Bonosus, and allowed or desired themselves to be ordained by him, ought not to have received the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination,” since “the canons themselves, by their authority, do not permit them to become clergy even after penance.”

Accordingly, he reproaches the Macedonians (§8) because “those who passed from the Catholic Church into heresy not only do not perform penance among them, but are also heaped with the honor of the clergy.” Concerning the others, Innocent notes that “there were ancient rules, handed down by the Apostles or apostolic men, which the Roman Church preserves and commands those who have heard them to preserve,” and which prescribe that “those coming from heretics who were baptized there are to be granted only lay communion through the laying on of hands, and that none of them is to be elevated even slightly to clerical honor.”

### 3

Nevertheless, he readily admits that the needs of the Church have sometimes prompted a departure from this last rule. For this reason the Council of Nicaea had judged that the Novatians should be received in the offices they held. The same was afterward the judgment of Anysius and his colleagues concerning those who had been ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation. In the year 400, the First Council of Toledo likewise granted the same kind of concession to those who had received ordination from followers of Priscillian.

Innocent not only approves the decrees of the Council of Nicaea concerning the Novatians, and of Anysius and his colleagues concerning those who had adhered to Bonosus; he also vigorously rebukes and refutes those who were displeased by the Council of Toledo’s indulgence toward the followers of Priscillian (*Letter* 3, chapter 1).

Thus that pontiff, who was especially devoted to equity, admits and approves those exceptions, but insists forcefully that, where such necessity is absent, the Church’s general rules must be followed. In attempting to establish this, he cites canon 8 of Nicaea in the following form:

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, the Pure, and who sometimes come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should thus remain in the clergy.”

A new question therefore arises concerning the genuine meaning of this canon, which it will be useful to explain here.

### 4

The ancient Code of Canons which Paschasius Quesnellus considers to have been used by the Roman Church reports this canon in no other words, in chapter 22 of this letter of Innocent, although in chapter 1 of the same Code, where the Nicene canons are presented together, it is expressed as follows:

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, the Pure, if any come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy council that they be ordained and thus remain in the clergy.”

Since this interpretation belongs properly to the Codex, it ought to have been common to those who used that Codex, and therefore to Innocent himself, if—as is claimed—the aforementioned Codex was used by the Roman Church in his time.

In the interpretation followed by Innocent, however, although the order of the words is different, there is this great distinction: where the Codex mentioned above has “that they be ordained,” Innocent prefers “after receiving the laying on of hands.” It follows that this pope used an interpreter of the Council of Nicaea who had read canon 8 as **χειροθετουμένους** (*cheirothetouménous*, “those receiving the laying on of hands”), not the Codex of Quesnellus, in which the interpretation of a man who mistakenly read **χειροτονουμένους** (*cheirotonouménous*, “those receiving ordination”) instead of **χειροθετουμένους** had been inserted.

Feeling that this substantially conflicted with his view of the Codex, the learned author mentioned above devised the following explanation in Dissertation 12, chapter 7:

> “When Pope Innocent was responding to the objection of the Macedonians, he wished either to write or to translate the canon that had been cited, word for word from their letter, not from his own Codex.”

But in making this response, he is shown not to have considered Innocent’s words carefully enough. For the pope had first said:

> “That earlier canon established by the fathers must be set forth, so that we may observe, and so forth.”

He thereby clearly declares that he is presenting the canon first, not copying or interpreting it from someone else’s letter.

Moreover, it is known that in his own copy of the Council of Nicaea Innocent read **χειροθετουμένους**, not **χειροτονουμένους**, in canon 8, and that in the same copy **χειροθετουμένους** had been rendered into Latin not by a term for ordination but by a term for the laying on of hands.

For when he gives a summary of this Nicene canon in Letter 2, §11, following Siricius, Letter 4, chapter 8, he prescribes “that those coming from the Novatians or Montenses be received through the laying on of hands.” Nor does Siricius confirm this only in the passage just cited; he also confirms it in Letter 1, §2, where, in response to Himerius’s question whether those coming from the Arian heresy ought to be baptized again, he writes:

> “Those whom, together with the Novatians and other heretics, as the synod has established, we join to the assembly of Catholics through the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit, by the laying on of the episcopal hand.”

No prudent person will deny that the Council of Nicaea is meant there by “the synod,” and that its canon 8 is being cited. It is therefore clear that Siricius and Innocent read that canon as “after receiving the laying on of hands,” not “that they be ordained.”

Leo likewise follows in their footsteps and responds similarly in Letter 2, in answer to Rusticus’s inquiry 18:

> “Through the laying on of hands, after invoking the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics, they are to be joined to the Catholics.”

The Corbie manuscript, written in the middle of the sixth century, agrees with this. It gives the Nicene canon as follows:

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, the Pure, if they should at any time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that, receiving the laying on of hands, they should thus remain in the clergy.”

But the manner in which the laying on of hands required there is to be understood is a matter of no small importance.

### 5

In the Dissertation 12 mentioned above, chapter 7, the learned author takes two propositions as certain, although it would have been worthwhile to prove them. First, he says:

> “The Macedonians readily admitted that ordination was signified there [in Nicaean canon 8, by the laying on of hands].”

He then adds that the Macedonians and Innocent agreed that, if the Bonosians were to be allowed to remain in the clergy, this could be granted to them only through repeated ordination.

As for the Macedonians, if it is permissible to infer what an entire province or region thought from what one man did, even though others disapproved of his action, it must be conceded that they were not far from the opinion attributed to them by that learned man.

In the preceding letter we saw that a certain Rusticius, returning from the company of Bonosus to the Catholic Church, “received the priesthood through repeated ordination,” and that this was a great impediment to others who wished to return, “since either they grieve that such a man is being retained in the Church, or he supposes that the same sin ought to be committed against others which he acknowledges to have been committed against himself.”

But who would wish to judge from the individual sin of one man, which horrifies the others, what practice had been accepted throughout the province? On the contrary, from the fact that the Macedonians allowed Germanus, Lupentius, and several others to retain their churches without repeated ordination, it is clear that they did not hold the opinion that those ordained by Bonosus could remain in the clergy only through repeated ordination.

In the words cited concerning Rusticius, who allowed himself to be ordained a second time, Innocent likewise indicates that he shared this view with the Macedonian clergy: namely, that Rusticius had committed a sin, and indeed such a sin that it did not permit him to be retained in the Church or counted among the clergy.

Neither that pope, therefore, nor the Macedonian clergy, nor the bishops of the same province were at all of the opinion that, if the Bonosians were permitted to remain in the clergy, this would have to be granted to them through repeated ordination. But let us trace the matter further back.

### 6

The Church has always maintained the rule that those who come from heresy to the Church, whether clergy or laity, are received through the laying on of hands. We have proved above, on page 240 and following, by the testimony both of Pope Stephen himself and of the councils of Africa under Cyprian, as well as of Eusebius and others, that this custom was already in force before the Council of Nicaea, indeed before the time of Pope Stephen and Cyprian.

It is clear from those same testimonies that the hand was then laid upon them for penance, not in order that they might be ordained. Anyone who maintained that laypeople were ordained by this laying on of hands would make himself an object of universal ridicule.

Who, then, would agree that the Nicene fathers spoke of the laying on of hands in another sense when they decreed concerning the Novatians:

> “It has pleased the holy and great council that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should thus remain in the clergy”?

Siricius himself gives us authority not to suppose that they spoke in another sense. In the passage already cited, Letter 1 to Himerius, chapter 1, he testifies that Arians and other heretics were joined at Rome to the assembly of Catholics through that same laying on of hands by which the Council of Nicaea prescribed that the Novatians should be received, and that this practice was observed throughout both East and West.

It follows that what the Nicene canon prescribed concerning receiving the laying on of hands was understood, by the common tradition, to have been commanded for all heretics throughout East and West; but what it adds—“and thus let them remain in the clergy”—was granted, according to Innocent’s own interpretation, only to the Novatians.

If, in the case of Arians and other heretics, that laying on of hands was not repeated ordination, then neither was it so in the case of the Novatians. Moreover, below (§8), Innocent openly teaches that he adheres to the law of his Church, which required the laying on of hands for those coming from heresy, but that this laying on of hands did not confer ordination, since he simultaneously affirms (§9) that through it only lay communion was granted.

Therefore, when he says:

> “This was the firm decision of our former brother Anysius and the other fellow priests: that those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received as ordained, so that they would not remain with him and a considerable scandal arise,”

he does not understand *ordinati* (“ordained”) to mean that they had to be ordained again before being received. Rather, because Bonosus had ordained them, they were to be regarded as ordained and received in the rank and order which they had received.

### 7

Nevertheless, as the same pope warns (§8), a legitimate order must be distinguished from usurpation. And not without reason may we call those ordained by the condemned Bonosus guilty of usurped dignity (§12), because they thought themselves to possess what had not been granted to them by any regular procedure.

Although what had been given remained in them, it nevertheless remained—as Augustine puts it, *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book II, §29—as a punishment for the usurper, both for the one who illicitly gave it and for the one who illicitly received it. They must truly be said to have received nothing insofar as they could not lawfully exercise the power which they had acquired for themselves contrary to the rules.

Augustine says the following (§30):

> “Concerning those who have been separated from the unity of the Church, there is now no question that they both possess and can give [baptism and ordination], and that they possess and transmit them perniciously outside the bond of peace.”

A little earlier (§28) he says:

> “Each is a sacrament, and each is given to a person through a certain consecration: the one when he is baptized, the other when he is ordained. Therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Just as they possess in baptism what can be given through them, so also in ordination they possess the right of giving. Both, indeed, are to their own destruction so long as they do not possess the charity of unity. But it is one thing not to possess, another to possess perniciously, and another to possess beneficially.”

These statements carry all the greater weight in illustrating and proving Innocent’s position because Augustine explained them around the year 400, before Innocent wrote to the Macedonians. Yet Augustine asserts that he was defending not merely his private opinion, but “what has been discussed and considered within the unity of the whole world, and completed and defined” (*ibid.*).

He certainly would not have said that this had been “defined within the unity of the whole world” if the Roman Church had not agreed in the same doctrine. The embassies and letters which the Africans sent to Siricius, Anastasius, and Innocent himself testify how carefully, especially at that time and in matters of this kind, they guarded against differing from the decrees of that Church.

If we consider where the definition praised by Augustine was issued, the first evidence that meets us is what the Africans write in the *African Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, chapter 48:

> “We further report that a mandate has been given to us, which also appears to have been established in the plenary Council of Capua: that rebaptisms and reordinations may not be performed.”

No one can deny that in so celebrated a council nothing was done except according to Siricius’s judgment, and certainly nothing that he himself had not approved.

Although the learned man mentioned more than once, in Dissertation 12 on Leo, chapter 7, asserts:

> “The question between the Macedonians and Innocent was not whether the Bonosians ought to be ordained again in order to remain in that clerical order which they had held under Bonosus; on that point both sides agreed. The question was whether they should be allowed to remain in the clergy after repeated ordination,”

we may rightly appeal against his opinion to Augustine’s words:

> “Concerning those who have been separated from the unity of the Church, there is now no question that they both possess and can give [baptism and ordination]. Therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church.”

Hence, he says, when “it was judged necessary that those coming from the party of Donatus should perform the same offices which they had performed, they were not ordained again; rather, just as baptism remained intact in them, so ordination remained intact.”

### 8

If we go even to the source itself—that is, to the Greek text of the Council of Nicaea—it will become clear that the fathers of that council did not wish ordination to be repeated except for those whose baptism they judged invalid and therefore requiring repetition.

Certainly, when canon 8 grants that the Novatians, whose baptism it accepted, should remain in the clergy **χειροθετουμένους** (*cheirothetouménous*), that is, after receiving the laying on of hands, canon 19 does not allow the clergy of the Paulianists, whose baptism it rejected, to be admitted into the clergy unless they had first been baptized and ordained:

> **ἀναβαπτισθέντες χειροτονηθήτωσαν**  
> “After being rebaptized, let them be ordained by a bishop of the Catholic Church.”

They do not use the same word in those two places without reason. The first are admitted to the clergy as **χειροθετούμενοι** (*cheirothetouménous*), a term that simply means “receiving the laying on of hands”; the others as **χειροτονούμενοι** (*cheirotonouménous*), which properly means “receiving ordination.”

It is therefore clear that the interpretation of the Nicene canon used by Innocent in this letter is more suitable and more consistent than the one found in Quesnellus’s Codex.

Perhaps the author of that interpretation, when he encountered **χειροτονηθήτωσαν** in canon 19 concerning the Paulianists, was led from this to judge that in canon 8 concerning the Novatians the Greek should be read as **χειροτονούμενοι**, and the Latin as *ut ordinentur*, “that they be ordained.” From this faulty interpretation appears to have arisen, above all, the opinion that clergy coming from heresy to the Church were admitted to the clergy only through repeated ordination.

Yet although there have repeatedly been some who doubted whether sacraments were effectively conferred by bishops who had been condemned, the Church’s judgment in this matter was never uncertain or ambiguous.

At the end of the fifth century, when some held the opinion that, “after the judgment issued by Pope Felix II against Acacius, he had afterward acted ineffectively in the sacraments which Acacius had usurped,” Pope Anastasius replied in Letter 1, chapter 8:

> “Since the condemned man claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head; for it was not the people, who thirsted for his gift in the mysteries, who were excluded, but only that soul which had sinned and was subject by just judgment to the penalty of its own fault.”

This is truly said of one who seeks the sacraments with a simple soul, not of one who abuses the occasion of schism to serve his ambition.

In the ninth century a similar controversy arose concerning clergy ordained by Ebo after he had been deposed from the episcopate. But the Third Council of Soissons, in 866, decreed concerning them that they should “be received in their orders, in accordance with the indulgence of the Council of Nicaea concerning those whom the condemned Meletius ordained, and in accordance with the tradition of the African council” concerning the Donatists.

See also the Second Council of Nicaea, Labbe, volume VII, pages 66–78.

Thus the Nicene fathers judged that the Meletians and Novatians should be received in their offices; the Africans did the same for certain Donatists; the Council of Capua and Innocent did so for those ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation; and Anastasius II did so for those whom the condemned Acacius ordained.

Moreover, Gregory I, in the letter formerly numbered 61, to Quiricus, written in July of the fourth indiction, judged that Nestorians likewise should be received in the offices they held. We pass over in silence similar judgments and decrees of others.

# LETTER XVII

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, this is numbered 22. What was formerly numbered 17 is now numbered 19.]

## From Dionysius Exiguus

I. That if a priest or anyone from the clergy marries a widow or a divorced woman, he is to lose his office.

II. That if a catechumen had a wife and, after her death, married another after baptism, he is not to be a cleric.

III. That those ordained by heretics are not to be received into the clergy.

IV. That people should not rightly believe that crimes or vices are removed through ordination.

V. That those ordained by the heretic Bonosus were received for this reason: so that no scandal might remain in the Church.

VI. That the people’s sin is customarily allowed to go unpunished in the Church.

VII. That something was fraudulently imposed upon the Apostolic See, and that it changed its judgment for the better.

## From the ancient Corbie manuscript

I. Concerning those who are said to have taken two wives.

II. That a man who had and lost a wife while a catechumen ought not to be called a bigamist.

III. How crimes are remitted in baptism.

IV. Concerning children who were born before baptism.

V. Concerning catechumens who devoted themselves to holy virtues.

VI. How heretical clergy ought to be reconciled.

VII. That sacrilegious persons and adulterers ought not to be admitted to the clergy.

VIII. And how heretics are to be received.

IX. Concerning those who call themselves Cathars and the Pure.

X. Concerning those returning from the Novatians and heretics.

XI. Concerning Catholic clergy who pass into heresy.

XII. Concerning the reception of Fontinus and Eustasius.

## Innocent

[Note: In the ancient Corbie manuscript this heading is given as follows: “Innocent to Eustasius, Eugenius, Polychronius, Hilary, Zosimus, Hermogenes, Terentianus, Rufus, Claudius, Gerontius, Sophronius, Macedonius, Profuturus, Vincentius, Herodianus, Eusebius, Maximianus, John, Flavianus, Calicratus, Nicetas, Asialogus, Marcianus, the Macedonian bishops and deacons: greetings in God.” The other Colbert manuscript agrees with it. It is therefore clear that no firm argument can be constructed from the order in which bishops occur in such headings to establish their rank or antiquity. Dionysius Exiguus, content to name two of these bishops, abbreviates the entire heading as follows: “Innocent to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other Macedonian bishops and deacons: greetings in the Lord.” The author of the Spanish collection and Isidore afterward followed him.]

To Rufus, Eusebius, Eustasius, Claudius, Maximianus, Eugenius, Gerontius, John; Polychronius, Sophronius, Flavianus, Hilary, Macedonius, Calicratus, Zosimus, Profuturus, Nicetas [some manuscripts: Nicetius], Hermogenes, Vincentius, Asialogus, Terentianus, Herodianus, and Marcianus, Macedonian bishops and deacons: greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0527A]

1. I was filled with great joy when, after so many perils of the whole world, so to speak, Vitalis, the archdeacon and bearer of your letters, sent from those regions all the way to us, arrived. When we saw him, we immediately—as was proper—inquired about your situation. But when we learned that you were faring as you wished, we gave abundant thanks to our God, because he both protects his servants who serve his altars amid adversity and deigns to govern them in prosperity.

When he had delivered the letters, I ordered them to be read through immediately. In them I saw many things that would produce astonishment in our minds [Note: In the Corbie manuscript and one Colbertine manuscript, *reperivimus* (“we discovered”).], and would make us doubt considerably whether we should understand them otherwise, or whether they had actually been written as they sounded. When I had them read through repeatedly, I perceived that some injury was being done to the apostolic see, to which the report had been sent—as to the head of the churches—and whose judgment was still being left in uncertainty [Note: The better manuscripts restore here the word *aliquam* (“some”), which had previously been missing. Innocent had already forbidden, in Letters 2.7–8 and 3.11, that anyone be admitted to the clergy who had married either a widow or a second wife, even if he had taken his first wife before baptism. It is probable that, following the example of Siricius, he took care that letters and decrees of this kind should circulate through the provinces, so that no one could plead ignorance, as he himself says in Letter 6.2. Certainly the matter which he testifies that he had written about earlier concerns the two points mentioned above, not the other two that are dealt with subsequently.]. Therefore, the repeated inquiry into your report compels me now to restate, with clearer arguments, the form of what I remember having written long ago [Note: In the manuscripts of Dionysius, Hadrian, and the Hispanic collection, *relationis vestrae* (“of your report”) is missing. In the Langobard Colbertine manuscript, *relationis* is present; in another Colbertine manuscript and the old Corbie manuscript, *relegationis* appears, without *vestrae*. All those manuscripts then add the repeated phrase *geminata percontatio vestra* (“your repeated inquiry”). Merlin printed *gemina percontatio vestra*. The reading of the vulgate editions is preserved by the old copies of Quesnel’s codex.].

## Chapter I

2. I have learned that those who are said to have taken widows as wives [Ivo, p. 8, c. 503] not only became clerics, but even advanced to the insignia of the highest priesthood—a practice which no one is unaware is contrary to the commands of the law. For when Moses the lawgiver loudly declares, “A priest shall take a virgin as his wife” (Lev. 22:13–14), and lest anything in this command be thought ambiguous, he adds: “not a widow, nor one who has been divorced.” Against this command, submitted under divine authority [Note: So the better manuscripts. Other books read *subnixum* (“supported by”), and Pithoeus has *subnexum* (“attached to”).], no defense based on another command is offered except your custom. Yet, as you yourselves admit, it was established through ignorance—to speak more modestly—not through apostolic tradition and sound reasoning.

Let your love know that we, and all the churches throughout East and West, absolutely do not permit this; nor do we permit such men to be admitted even to the lowest rank of the ecclesiastical order [Note: Agreeing with the first part of this decree, the Council of Valence I, in 574, canon 1, decreed that thereafter no one could be ordained a cleric if he were a bigamist or the husband of a remarried woman, whether he had entered bigamy before baptism or afterward. Yet it did not dare remove those who had already been ordained. Gallican councils later relaxed this severity somewhat. The Council of Orange I, canon 25, and the Council of Arles II, canon 45, were content to forbid such men from being promoted beyond the subdiaconate. Nor were the Spaniards, Moors, or Italians more observant of the apostolic rule in this matter, as witnesses Letter 1 of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, section 12; Leo’s Letter 1 to the Moors, sections 3 and 5; and his Letter 4 to the bishops of Campania, Picenum, and Tuscany, section 3.]—and, if any are found there, we remove them.

## Chapter II

3. It is then stated [Distinction 26, c. 3; Ivo, p. 1, c. 292, and p. 8, c. 303] that a man should not be called a bigamist if, while a catechumen, he had had and lost a wife, and after baptism had taken another; and that the first wife should be considered the one joined to the new man, because that former marriage had been washed away, together with the other sins, through the sacrament of baptism. But if this is said of one wife, then certainly, if while still in the old man he had had three wives, the woman who is fourth after baptism will, according to this interpretation, be his first; and she will receive the name of virgin, although she was taken as the fourth wife [Note: Quesnel prints “the name of the first virgin,” contrary to the manuscripts and to Innocent’s meaning. Other editions likewise have *prima*, with *virginis* as a noun. Most manuscripts read *virgini aeque nomen* (“an equal name with a virgin”).]. Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, who says that a priest must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6)?

4. But it is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man has been released. Tell me—speaking with your indulgence—are only crimes forgiven in baptism, or also those acts which are fulfilled according to the commands of the Law and God’s institutions [Note: So the better manuscripts. Merlin, Crabbe, the Roman edition, and the manuscripts of Dionysius and Isidore read “the Lord’s commands.” Our reading is supported by the phrase closing section 5, “what the Law commanded and God joined.”]? To take a wife: is it a crime, or is it not a crime? If it is a crime, then—let me say this with the forgiveness already mentioned—the author will be at fault who blessed them in paradise in order that they might commit crimes, when he himself joined them in this way.
