But if it is not a crime, since it would be impious to call a crime what God joined together (Gen. 1:28), and Solomon added, “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 19:14), how can it be believed that what is recorded as completed by God’s authority was forgiven among crimes?

5. What is to be decided about the children of such persons (28, q. 1, c. 3)? Are those who were born from the woman who was his wife before baptism not to be admitted to a share in the inheritance? Are they to be called either natural children or bastards, because there is no legitimate marriage except, as you think, the one assumed after baptism [Note: The manuscripts of Dionysius and several others read *assumetur* (“will be assumed”).]?

When the Lord was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, and explained that this ought not to be done, he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). And lest anyone think that he was speaking of those whom they take after baptism [Note: So, with broad manuscript agreement. Crabbe and the Roman edition read *qui* (“who”). The verb *sortiuntur* is to be understood passively, as though *accipiuntur* (“are received”) were present.], let them remember that this was asked by Jews and answered to Jews.

I ask—and I ask anxiously—if the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and afterward a believer is one and the same, and if he had children by her while he was a catechumen and afterward had others while he was a believer: are they to be called brothers, or, after their father’s death, are those children to have no share in dividing the inheritance because spiritual rebirth is believed to have taken away the name of “children” from them? Since it is absurd to think and judge this, what reason—alas—is there for defending and proclaiming this empty opinion rather than strengthening it by some authority, when what the Law commanded and God joined cannot be counted among sins [Note: Several manuscripts read *jungit* (“joins”). One Colbertine manuscript has *indulget* (“permits”), while Pithoeus and Quesnel have *injungit* (“commands”). The reference to Christ’s words, “What God has joined,” is clear. Yet no authority supports the addition of “and the Law joined” in Merlin, or “and the Law joins” in Crabbe and the Roman edition.]?

6. If a catechumen devoted himself to virtues, followed humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued those condemned to death by whatever means, abhorred adulteries, and preserved chastity, does he lose these things when he becomes a believer, because baptism is thought to remove everything the old man did? I ask this.

Let us look at the gentile Cornelius, who was devoted to prayers and almsgiving and saw a revelation and Peter himself [Note: One manuscript, the Colbertine, reads: “devoted to prayers and almsgiving, summoned Peter through a revelation, and saw him himself.” Quesnel took from this *devoted to prayers*, and then, from Crabbe and the later editions, added “and devoted to almsgiving, through a revelation of the Angel and Peter.” Merlin had earlier printed, “through a revelation of the Angel and Peter, devoted to prayers and almsgiving.” Our reading is that of all the manuscripts except the Colbertine mentioned above.]. Were these things taken away from him through baptism, on account of which baptism seemed to have been granted to him [Note: Six reliable manuscripts read *abluta* (“washed away”). This may be understood to mean that, just as stains commonly disappear when washed away, so the merits of his prayers and almsgiving were considered to have perished when washed away. In this sense, above in section 3, we heard that the marriage was “washed away” through the sacrament of baptism together with the other crimes. But if *abluta* is not contrary to Innocent’s meaning, neither does *ablata* (“taken away”) seem more foreign to it, as is suggested by what we read immediately afterward: “because through baptism everything the old man did is thought to be taken away.”]?

If this is believed, believe me, it is a considerable error. For whatever has been done well and preserved according to the commands of the Law cannot perish for the person who did it [Note: The editions following Dionysius and Isidore add, “cannot perish for those who do it.” Since the union of marriage is accomplished by God’s command, it cannot perish: this is confirmed by the manuscripts, which are usually more reliable.]. Since it is accomplished by God’s command, it cannot be called sin; and what is not sin absolutely ought not to be released among sins [Note: Crabbe added *credi* (“to be believed”) here. The later editors adopted the word, although it is absent from the manuscripts.]. It will therefore remain wholly valid to judge that the title of the former wife cannot be abolished, since it was not dismissed on account of sin, but was completed according to God’s will.

## Chapter III

7. We have come to the third question, which, because of its difficulty, requires a longer discussion (I, q. 1, c. 17; Ivo, p. 6, c. 59). We say that those ordained by heretics have a wounded head through that laying on of hands. [“And where the wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that it may receive healing. Yet the healing that follows a wound cannot be without a scar.”] And where the remedy of penance is necessary, there the honor of ordination cannot have a place [Note: The word *decernimus* (“we decree”), which was added here in the Roman edition and later councils, is found in not a single manuscript, nor in Merlin, Crabbe, or the others. At the beginning of this discussion it is useful to note the distinction between *ordinatio* (“ordination”) and *honor ordinationis* (“the honor of ordination”). Innocent does not deny that ordination can be conferred by heretics; rather, he argues that the honor of ordination conferred by them cannot have a place. Indeed, in the preceding letter 3 he asserts at greater length that, when the welfare of the Church requires it, such ordination can retain its honor.].

For if, as we read, “whatever an unclean person touches will be unclean” (Num. 19:22), how will what purity and cleanness customarily receive be granted to him? On the other hand, it is asserted that one who has lost honor cannot give honor, and that the recipient received nothing, because there was nothing in the giver that he could receive.

We agree, and it is true. Certainly, because he could not give what he did not possess, he gave through a corrupt laying on of hands the condemnation that he did possess. And I cannot discover how one who has become a sharer in condemnation should be able to receive honor [Note: The old Corbie manuscript and another Colbertine manuscript, supported by two others, read *comparticeps factus est* (“has become a sharer”), while Pithoeus has *factus est*. Other books read *qui particeps effectus est damnato* (“who has become a participant in the condemned man”). Long before this, the Council of Laodicea, canon 32, had decreed: “One must not receive the blessings of heretics, for these are curses rather than blessings.” Moreover, whoever becomes a sharer in condemnation is not free from blame; therefore, according to the apostolic judgment, he is judged unworthy of the honor of ordination.].

## Chapter IV

8. But it is said that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every defect inflicted by a corrupt person. If this is so, then let sacrilegious men, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be brought to ordination, because through the blessing of ordination their crimes or defects are thought to be removed. Let there be no place for penance, since ordination can accomplish what lengthy satisfaction is accustomed to accomplish.

But this is OUR LAW OF THE CHURCH: to those coming from the heretics who were nevertheless baptized there, to grant through the laying on of hands only lay communion, and to promote none of them, even to the smallest ecclesiastical office [Note: The law referred to had been enacted—or rather confirmed as handed down from the Apostles or apostolic men—by the council of Italy mentioned in the *Codex canonum ecclesiae Africanae*, chapter 56. The Africans, although acknowledging the equity of this law, nevertheless resolved to send a delegation to Anastasius, Innocent’s predecessor, asking that something be relaxed from its severity because of the shortage of clergy from which their churches suffered. Augustine, observing the same law, wrote to Possidius in Letter formerly 73, now 245, section 2: “Concerning ordaining one who was baptized in the party of Donatus, I cannot authorize you,” although he immediately adds: “For it is one thing to do something when compelled, and another to advise that it be done.” The Africans’ letter to John II, Letter 8, must also be read in full. In it they ask how the priests of the Arians ought to be received into the Catholic faith—whether in their offices or in lay communion. They then add: “From the silent feelings of all our colleagues, we have perceived that no one approves their being received in their offices.” Further below they ask: “We consult you not only about priests but also about the little children baptized among them, whether they customarily or ought, if they ask, to be admitted to the clergy.” Cyprian’s position on this matter in Letter 72 to Stephen is: “It is enough that forgiveness be granted to such persons when they return; yet faithlessness must not be promoted in the house of faith.”]. But those who have passed from the Catholic Church to heresy, whom it is proper to receive only through penance, among you not only do not perform penance but are even loaded with honor.

## Chapter V

9. But the supreme deliberation of Anysius, formerly our brother, and the other fellow priests was this: those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received with their ordinations, so that they would not remain with Bonosus and a serious scandal would not arise [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, together with the old Corbie manuscript, reads: “But before the twelve brothers, formerly ours,” corruptly. We had already learned from Siricius’s Letter 9.1 that the Council of Capua had delegated the examination of Bonosus’s case to Anysius and the other bishops of Illyricum, especially the Macedonians. We are now told what their judgment in the matter was. By approving it, Innocent indicates that he is far from thinking the ordinations of heretics invalid and entirely null.].

We have, I think, overcome the ambiguity [Note: The same manuscripts read *Vicensimus* (“we have conquered”), corruptly; another Colbertine has *Vicibus*, perhaps with ambiguous meanings. The issue was whether the honor of ordination should always be preserved for those ordained by a heretic, or always denied. Innocent resolves and surpasses this ambiguity by answering that it is to be denied in such a way that, when necessity requires or serious scandal is feared, it is to be preserved. He praises the judgment of Anysius and his colleagues, who, after separating Bonosus, allowed those ordained by him to retain their offices so that they would not remain with him.].

Therefore, what was established as a remedy and necessity of the times was not originally the rule; rather, there were ancient rules, handed down by the Apostles or apostolic men, which the Roman Church preserves and commands to be preserved by those accustomed to listen to her. But the necessity of the times urgently demanded that this be done. Therefore, what necessity discovered as a remedy must, when the necessity has ceased, likewise cease, since one thing is the legitimate order and another is the usurpation which the circumstances of the time temporarily compel.

10. But the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done with regard to the Novatians. The canon instituted by the Fathers must first be set out, so that we may observe what they understood and in what manner they understood or commanded it.

“Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, Pure Ones, and who at some time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy” (Council of Nicaea, canon 8).

I can say that this was commanded only concerning the Novatians and does not apply to the clergy of other heresies. For if they had truly defined it concerning all, they would have added that those returning from the Novatians and other heretics ought to be received in their own order [Note: The editions read “into their own order.” Quesnel then adds *suscipi* (“to be received”), which is not supported by the manuscripts or by Innocent’s meaning. Innocent first says, “I can say that this was commanded only concerning the Novatians”; then, to prove that he can in fact say this, he correctly adds, “That this is so.” The manuscripts of Dionysius or Hadrian have substituted, very badly, “If this were so,” from which the editors based on the Hispanic collection, Isidore, and Merlin derived that reading. In the Langobard Colbertine manuscript, a marginal note is written opposite this passage: “He speaks of the Novatians: when they have returned to the Catholic Church and been received through the laying on of hands, let them remain in the clergy. When the clergy of other heresies have returned, let them receive only lay communion.”].

That this is so can be confirmed especially by what was said about the Paulianists: those coming from them are even commanded to be baptized. When they command that those coming from the Paulianists be baptized, will all who return from heretics be baptized according to this example (Council of Nicaea, canon 19)? Since no one dares to do this, reason itself shows that the command concerns only them.

Finally, those rightly baptized by the evangelist Philip are completed by Peter and John through the laying on of hands alone. But those whom the Apostle Paul found baptized with John’s baptism, and whom he asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit, ordered to be baptized when they confessed that they had not even heard of that name (Acts 8:17; 19:2 ff.). You therefore see that those rightly baptized cannot have that gift repeated for them, whereas those washed with water in another manner plainly need to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is clearly shown that the command concerned the Novatians alone. The evident reason why this was distinguished between those two heresies is that the Paulianists do not baptize at all in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (I, q. 1, c. 53), while the Novatians baptize with those same terrifying and venerable names. Among them the question of the unity of divine power—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—has never arisen. Therefore, after all the others had been excluded, they alone were chosen as those to whom this was believed capable of being granted, because they did nothing wrong in the sacrament of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [Note: Several manuscripts, with Dionysius, read *de omnibus* (“concerning all”). The reading *omnibus*, with “heresies” understood, is preferable, as in the vulgate editions, the Corbie manuscript, and two Colbertine manuscripts. Through the examples of the Novatians, whose baptism is accepted because they do nothing wrong in conferring this sacrament, and of the Paulianists, whose baptism is rejected because they do wrong in it, the Council of Nicaea gave us a model for determining whose baptism should be admitted and whose rejected.].

11. But if someone passing from the Catholic Church to heresy, or returning to apostasy from the faith [Note: Isidore, followed by the Hispanic collection and subsequently by the Roman editions and councils, adds “returning and repenting from apostasy.”], wishes to return in repentance, will he be permitted to enter the clergy by the same reasoning, when the offense committed by him can be abolished only through lengthy penance? Nor do the canons, by their own authority, permit a person to become a cleric after penance.

Therefore it is clear that those who passed from the Catholic Church to Bonosus after he had been condemned, and who endured this or desired to be ordained by him, ought not to have assumed the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination. They abandoned the common judgment of all the churches and decided that their own particular error in following Bonosus should be followed [Note: This means, after Bonosus had been condemned at the council of the bishops of Illyricum, to which his case had been referred by the Council of Capua. It is therefore clear that the whole of this third question concerns only clergy ordained by Bonosus. The issue was not whether those whom that heretic had ordained before the Council of Illyricum were to be received. At that council Anysius and his colleagues condemned Bonosus and decreed that those whom he had ordained should be received in their offices so that they would not remain with him; Innocent approves this decree above, in section 9. The matter concerned those who were ordained by him after Bonosus had been condemned by the judgment of Anysius and the Macedonians.].

12. But it is clear that many suffered force and were drawn against their will, and, while resisting, were ordained by him. Let whoever believes this answer me, I ask: if, after ordination by Bonosus, he did not take part when Bonosus celebrated the sacraments; if he did not participate in his communion; if he immediately departed from his most wicked assembly and returned to the Church—such a man may have some semblance of an excuse [Note: Quesnel alone has *Bonoso* (“after Bonosus”). The other books have *Bonosi* (“of Bonosus”), that is, “conferred by Bonosus.”].

But whoever returned to the Church after a year or even months is understood to have gone to him because, knowing that in the Catholic Church he could not be admitted to ordination on account of his vices, he went to one who indiscriminately and without any examination performed unlawful ordinations. They believed that through this institution they could find in the Catholic Church a place from which they had previously despaired [Note: The vulgate editions have “or a month … we understand those who, in the Catholic Church …” Quesnel below reads *reperire locum* (“to find a place”), while Merlin and Crabbe have *recipere locum* (“to receive a place”), although the other books retain *invenire locum*. Innocent here gives a new reason why he is reluctant to admit to the clergy those ordained by heretics. He observes that most heretics had the custom of receiving into their ranks any Catholics who crossed over to them, even if their morals were corrupt and depraved, and sometimes even if they had been expelled or degraded by the Church for crimes. They not only received such people without penance or satisfaction but sometimes heaped new honors upon them. The devil, father of heretical sects, is not concerned with moral purity. The Church, however, is never glad to have a multitude of hypocrites or evildoers. Certainly, a person proves that he loves himself rather than God when he honors those devoted to him without caring that they be good.].

Now I ask about what remains: if someone who returned after a month or more, conscious that he had been ordained a presbyter by Bonosus, neither celebrated the sacraments, nor distributed them to the people, nor completed Masses according to custom, what do you judge concerning such men? I ask you to state it more openly.

In sum, those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of usurping a dignity: they claimed for themselves the authority to celebrate the sacraments, or did not claim it [Note: In the vulgate editions, as in the Noviomagus manuscript, the words *aut non vindicaverunt* (“or did not claim”) are missing; they are found with strong agreement in the other manuscripts. This gives Innocent’s statement greater fullness and integrity, since he is pronouncing generally concerning those unlawfully ordained by Bonosus: whether they claimed or did not claim authority to celebrate the sacraments, they are guilty of usurped dignity, since they received no regular and legitimate power. Therefore they wrongly thought themselves to be what had not been granted to them by any regular procedure. Quesnel omits *regulari* (“regular”), although it appears in all the printed and manuscript books, except that one Colbertine manuscript corruptly has *relaxandi*, and Pithoeus has *relaxari*.], and thought themselves to be what had not been granted to them by any regular procedure.

## Chapter VI

13. Let your love therefore understand that such things have been tolerated up to now, and observe that what necessity compelled—as you yourselves say—must certainly not be presumed upon by churches already established in peace [Note: Quesnel, with two manuscripts, reads *non posse praesumere* (“cannot presume”). If anything were to be supplied, *debere* (“ought”) would be more suitable than *posse*. Innocent teaches that churches established in peace must not presume upon what necessity compelled churches in turmoil to do. Here too he plainly admits that he would grant the Bonosians the honors which he now denies if the same necessity existed.].

But, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd sins, because it is impossible to exact punishment from everyone on account of their numbers, it is customary for the matter to pass unpunished [Note: Four manuscripts, with Quesnel, read *solere* (“to be accustomed”); several others, with Merlin and Crabbe, read *soleat* (“is accustomed”). These two editors, as well as Quesnel, then add *transire* (“to pass”). The preceding words therefore belong together. Our reading is that of the more carefully corrected manuscripts. Innocent remains consistent with what he taught in Letter 3.4 concerning offenses that should either be treated or tolerated more mildly, or restrained and punished severely. Augustine writes similarly in Book 3 against the Letter of Parmenian, section 14: “Correction by many cannot be salutary unless the one corrected has no multitude as his companion.” After a short interval he writes: “If the contagion of sin has seized a multitude, the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary; for plans of separation are empty, pernicious, and sacrilegious.” But, as he first says in section 13, “when someone’s crime is so well known that he has either no defenders at all or none through whom schism can arise, the severity of discipline must not sleep. Correction of depravity is more effective when the preservation of charity is more diligent.” Thus the prudent shepherd regulates discipline according to the varying conditions of the times: toward some ordained by Bonosus he is more indulgent, considering it sufficient to leave them to God’s judgment; toward others he is stricter, judging that they must be punished according to the prescription of tighter discipline.].

I say that the earlier matters should be left to God’s judgment, and that from now on the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.

## Chapter VII

14. I shall now come to the great subject, as it were, of Photinus, a matter anxious and extremely difficult for me, and I shall review the judgments of my predecessors (36, q. 9, c. 5). Concerning him too, something more severe had indeed been established, as you yourselves also remember. But because, as you assert, you show that this was introduced to this see through a false report and procured by intrigue, and because the matter has turned toward salvation, we even, yielding to your efforts, substitute this pardon after the condemnation pronounced by the voice of the apostolic see; and we judge that, in the face of so many assertions from persons so good and dear to us, not to grant consent would be harsher than every hardship [Note: The particles *et vel* (“and even,” or “or even”), first suppressed by Dionysius and afterward omitted in the Hispanic collection and by Isidore, are restored from six more reliable manuscripts. With their help Innocent softens and removes the reproach implied by the word *veniam* (“pardon”), as though he were saying: Photinus, whom you attest not to be guilty, does not need pardon; but if he had been guilty, I consider it harsh not to confirm the pardon you granted him.].

Therefore, dearest brothers, in accordance with your approval, judgment, and request, deem it permissible to establish Photinus as bishop in the manner for which you plead; and accept our judgment, changed for the better through your effort or testimony, as participants in the fulfillment of your wish [Note: Crabbe and many manuscripts read *votis* (“wishes”), with the final letter improperly doubled, from which the following word begins. Where other manuscripts have *Eustasium*, others *Eustachium*, *Eustatium*, or *Eustathium*, and all exhibit *comprobatum* (“approved”), Quesnel substituted “Eustathius … approved,” apparently to make the syntax conform to grammatical rules. Here Innocent begins asking the Macedonians to pardon and remit the sentence they had pronounced against Eustathius, just as, at their request, he himself had pardoned and remitted the sentence that the apostolic see had pronounced against Photinus.].

15. And do not expect that Eustathius, whom I have very often approved [Col. 0536B], should be stripped of the dignity of the diaconate. For I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation (II Cor. 2:10); but I do not readily permit action even against a head, should that be necessary. To whomever you extend your hand, I extend mine with you; to whomever I extend mine, extend yours with mine. For this was the apostolic kindness declared toward the Corinthians: that, in one spirit, they should always follow without distinction the sentence that had been pronounced and recalled [Note: [Col. 0536D] In the printed editions and in several manuscripts, *ductam* (“led”). In the old Corbie manuscript and one Colbert manuscript, *ducta ac reducta sententia* (“the sentence led and recalled”). I prefer the reading in another Colbert manuscript, *dictam* (“the sentence pronounced”). Innocentius is referring both to Paul’s words in I Cor. 5:4, where he speaks of the sentence against the Corinthian guilty of incest, and to II Cor. 2:6, where he recalls and revokes the sentence.].

For I confess that this consideration first makes me favorably disposed toward the deacon Eustathius: I have recognized neither that he said anything against the faith, nor that he admitted anyone who did so, nor that he ever committed, whether alleged or fabricated, any crime deserving death. And one who is safe in these respects, if in some way he lacks a lovable manner of life, ought to be regarded as temporarily less loved, not as an enemy [Note: [Col. 0537C] The word *aestimatur* (“is regarded”) was omitted by Quesnel. In the other editions there is instead *aestimatus* or *existimatus* (“regarded”). From this it may be inferred that Eustathius was not merely deprived of the dignity of the diaconate but also struck with an anathema: for it would be exceedingly harsh to act so against a man of whom no one has ever alleged or fabricated either that he said anything against the faith or that he committed a crime deserving death.], who is to be handed over to the devil forever.

I recognize that, amid those quarrels and storms, he held an opinion different from the efforts of many—I do not say what sort—and that, since the circumstances and calamities themselves have now been corrected, this commendation of the subdeacons Dizonianus and Cyriacus has not been able to revive among you [Note: [Col. 0537C] The Roman edition and the editions of the councils, following Dionysius of Spain and Isidore, read “the correction to revive.” The present reading is restored on the authority of six manuscripts of better quality.]. Extinguish, I ask, in him and in the others whom you see, whatever passionate and unjust rivalries [Note: [Col. 0537C] Thus one Colbert manuscript and another Pithoean manuscript, together with Quesnel. Other manuscripts read *animos ac* (“spirits and”).] there are, so that he may be unimpaired among us and, among you, restored together with his companions [Note: [Col. 0537C] The printed editions, following Dionysius and Isidore, read: “restored, may he deserve peace, discerning a love that is not feigned.” The fuller form is corrected with the aid of better manuscripts, in three of which *charitati* occurs instead of *charitatis*. The sentence would be more complete if one read *charitatisque vinculis* (“and by the bonds of charity”).], may encounter all of you, individually and collectively, with profound peace and discern a love that is not feigned; and, joined with you forever in the Lord by bonds of charity that Christ can never in any way dissolve, may he rejoice.

Given on the Ides of December (13 December 414), in the consulship of Flavius Constantius, a man of illustrious rank.

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0537D] In the edition of the councils, this is number 7. The letter that was formerly XVIII is now XXIV. It appears not only in the collection of Mercator but also in those of Spain and Dionysius the Younger. In the latter it occupies position 35 among Innocentius’ decrees. We place it here both so that matters concerning Macedonia may not be separated too far from one another and especially because there is a plausible basis for thinking that it was written when the peace of the church of Antioch was being negotiated, and therefore around the year 414. For below Innocentius states in Letter XXII that Maximianus, one of the Macedonian envoys, took part in this important affair. This was perhaps the principal reason why this Maximianus and his companion remained in the City longer than had been expected.]

Concerning Bubalius and Taurianus, condemned by the provincial bishops, whose sentence the apostolic see undertook to reconsider.

### INNOCENTIUS TO RUFIUS, GERONTIUS, SOPHRONIUS, FLAVIANUS, MACEDONIUS, PROSDOCIUS, AND ARISTEAS, BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT MACEDONIA

[Note: [Col. 0538C] Thus the better manuscripts. Navarre reads *Aristeo*, and another manuscript, together with the printed editions, *Oristeo*. The names Aristeas and Prosdocius do not appear in the inscription of the preceding letter, where we read the names of the others mentioned above. It may therefore be conjectured that the preceding letter addresses neither only nor all the Macedonian prelates, whereas this one addresses both all and only the bishops of that province, with their envoys added in the body of the letter.]

1. The delay—or rather the untimeliness—of our fellow bishops Maximianus and Eumenius [Note: [Col. 0538C] In the next letter, as also in Chrysostom’s Letter 165 addressed to the Macedonians, Eugenius is associated with Maximianus. Hence there is reason to suspect that *Eumenii* has crept in here in place of *Eugenii*.] caused you to renew your complaint concerning Bubalius and Taurianus [Note: [Col. 0538C] The Regius manuscript of Dionysius’ genuine collection reads here *Thariano* and below *Tariano*. Another manuscript of Hadrian’s collection has *Tariano* here but *Tauriano* below; the manuscripts of the Spanish and Isidorian collections have *Tauriano* in both places.], and caused us once again to rise up against utterly depraved men. But, as I can, I shall measure the summary of such great evils in a few words and briefly reconsider what I have seen in the volume of your letters.

It ought not to have seemed burdensome [Nicolaus I, Letter 32, no. 12] to your most devout minds that anyone’s judgment should be reconsidered: for truth, repeatedly tested, shines more brightly in the light; and a pernicious matter, brought back for judgment, is condemned more severely and without repentance [Col. 0538B] [Note: [Col. 0538D] That is, without the repentance of the person who previously judged, as is also noted in Labbe’s margin. It may therefore be inferred that Bubalius and Taurianus, having been judged by the Macedonians, appealed to the apostolic see, and that the Macedonians resented the reconsideration of their own judgment.]. For it is a divine fruit, dearest brothers, that justice should be reviewed repeatedly.

2. Yet I see what has disturbed your minds: Bubalius, often caught in many deceptions, produced copies of letters supposedly forged as though they were from us, although, in keeping with the man’s usual character, nothing he could produce now seemed sufficiently trustworthy. But let all murmuring about such a matter now be silenced, and let the very breathings of the convicted devil be restrained.

We have appended to these the earlier letters [Note: [Col. 0538D] These letters are no longer extant.] that we had sent through the bishops mentioned above. In them the whole judgment of our thoughts was set out so clearly that, when you reread them, you will not afterward return to this case with anything ambiguous or anything still requiring clarification.

Send this little document of ours to the bishops of Crete for more careful rereading [Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscripts of Hadrian’s collection read *credentibus* (“to those believing”), to which the author of the Spanish collection added *sibi* (“to themselves”); this reading subsequently prevailed in Isidore and in the printed editions. The genuine Regius copy of Dionysius’ collection supplies the true reading. Among the churches to which Innocentius entrusts his representation to Rufus in Letter XIII, no. 2, Crete is also listed.], so that they may know fully what has been decreed concerning Bubalius, Taurianus, and the others; and let those who are worthy of ecclesiastical administration [Note: [Col. 0539D] “And let them observe” would be preferable. In place of *administration*, which we restore from the excellent Regius manuscript, other copies have *admonition*. A Noviomagus manuscript reads *ne talibus sortiantur*, from which the printed reading *ne talibus socientur* was formed. The reading to be retained with the better manuscripts is *ne talia sortiantur*, that is, so that, knowing what was judged concerning Bubalius and Taurianus, they may beware of doing such things and thereby incur an equal punishment. What that punishment was is understood from the words “who are worthy of administration”; this is expressed by antiphrasis, since Bubalius and Taurianus had been removed from the administration of the churches.] beware of such things, lest they incur such a fate.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTERS

1. Dionysius the Younger preserved all these letters for us. From his collection they passed into the Spanish and Isidorian collections. It is undisputed that they were written on the occasion of the peace of the church of Antioch. Regarding that peace, Theodoretus, in Book V, chapter 35 of his *History*, recorded the following; to summarize his words:

Alexander, outstanding in an austere way of life, devotion to wisdom, contempt for wealth, eloquence, and innumerable other virtues, succeeded Porphyrius. By his persuasive gentleness of speech and his frequent exhortations he joined to the body of the Church the Eustathians, whom Paulinus and, after him, Evagrius had formerly refused to allow to be united with the others. For this reason he instituted a festival of a kind no mortal had ever seen.

After this, the same writer adds concerning Alexander: “He was the first of all to enter the name of the most excellent John in the ecclesiastical registers.”

According to the same author, Book III, chapter 5, the division of the church of Antioch “continued for eighty-five years,” up to Alexander. From this it would be possible to recognize and establish with certainty the time when that peace was concluded and the following letters were written, if scholars agreed about the beginning of the aforementioned division.

Baronius, under the year 308, thinks that it should be reckoned either from the day on which Meletius professed the consubstantial faith or from the day on which Lucifer ordained Paulinus—that is, from the year 361 or 362. He is therefore forced to reject Theodoretus’ calculation as false.

Tillemontius, however, reckoning the beginning of the Antiochene division from the deposition of Eustathius, which he believes occurred in 430 or 431, observes that those eighty-five years end in the year 413 or 414. Eutychius, although otherwise not sufficiently accurate, supports this computation when he reports that Porphyrius, whom he calls Barchus, presided over the church of Antioch for ten years. Palladius, in the *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*, p. 141, states that Porphyrius was appointed in place of Flavianus around the beginning of the year 403.

Furthermore, Theodoretus, Book V, chapter 35, teaches that the reconciliation of the church of Antioch took place while Cyrillus, the successor of Theophilus, was bishop of the church of Alexandria. But Theophilus, according to Socrates, Book VII, chapter 7, died on 15 October 412. Consequently, this reconciliation cannot have been recorded earlier than the year 413. There is no difficulty, however, if it is assigned to the year 414 or even 415.

2. The reconciliation of the parties in disagreement within the church of Antioch was followed, after no long interval, by the embassy through which Alexander, its bishop, hastened to obtain communion with the Roman see [Col. 0540A]. The father of the *Annals* thought that Alexander did not obtain this immediately; consequently, he devised two embassies: one by which Alexander requested Innocentius’ communion, and for which Innocentius prescribed the conditions of peace; and another by which Alexander testified that he had fulfilled the prescribed conditions.

But no reason for this double embassy appears. Ever since the death of John Chrysostom—that is, since the year 407—Innocentius had made these conditions sufficiently well known when he denied his communion to the bishops of the East until they had entered John’s name in the sacred diptychs. Theodoretus, Book V, chapter 34, speaks as follows:

“After the death of the great Teacher, the bishops of the Western world—clearly with the agreement and at the direction of Innocentius—did not admit the bishops of Egypt, the East, the Bosphorus, and Thrace to communion until they had entered the name of that divine man together with the other bishops who had died.”

Nor was Alexander so ignorant of affairs that he would not know this, nor so thoughtless as knowingly to send an unnecessary embassy. Indeed, when Innocentius, in Letter XXII, recalls that Alexander had fulfilled the conditions of peace and requires Atticus to make a similar “profession concerning the fulfillment of all the conditions,” he does not say “which we prescribed after Alexander’s embassy had been sent back,” but “which we previously stated at various times.”

3. Nor can we agree with the learned Tillemontius, who thinks that Letter XX was sent first and Letter XIX somewhat later. We think that both were sent at the same time, together with Letter XXI, addressed to Acacius.

The earlier one—that is, Letter XIX—was synodal and shared by Innocentius with the twenty bishops who signed it; this is revealed by the note added at its end. The other—that is, Letter XX—we consider private and familiar. Both letters mention the proceedings of the synod that had been appended to the first.

## LETTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 0540D] In the edition of the councils, this is number 17. The letter formerly numbered XIX is now XXI. In the Roman edition it is identified as copied from Cresconius. More accurately, it should be said to have been copied from Dionysius, where it appears under the title XLIV of Innocentius’ decrees.]

### OF POPE INNOCENTIUS I TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

Concerning peace.

[Col. 0540C] Recalling what was done at Antioch for the sake of peace, Innocentius, having obtained the fulfillment of his chief wishes, willingly grants communion and offers it to Acacius, provided that Acacius also fulfills the same requirements.

1. The grace of apostolic favor has shone upon us with the great splendor of peace; it has shed so much light and joy upon the faithful that, while giving God the greatest praises, we confess that we ought to give Him still greater ones. We have been made glad by God all the more because, after examining every aspect of the actions of your Fraternity, we have learned that everything was conducted with such devotion and patience that in all things we praise the Lord.

We see that the success itself was granted to your labors because, being wholly a lover of peace, you sought it, found it, and preserved it when found with the greatest charity—toward everyone, but especially toward those who had formerly been counted under the name of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius. I have obtained the chief of my wishes: that the cleansing of the ancient stain should be granted in your time and through your merits.

I also judged that those of the same name who had received the dignity of the clerical office in Italy should retain the grace already bestowed upon them, for the sake of the tranquility that is good. And because our fellow presbyter Cassianus said that it would be pleasing to your Dignity if, on my advice, they were regarded as holding the clerical order in your city, I decided, because of your goodwill and on the promise of the aforesaid man, that they should be counted among the other priests and ministers who are in the city, dearest brother [Note: [Col. 0541B] Merlonius and Crabbe, together with the Regius and Noviomagus manuscripts and one Colbert manuscript, read *duxit* (“he said”). This Cassianus is thought to be the author of the *Collations*, who, as Palladius relates in the *Life of Chrysostom*, p. 27, came to Rome while still a deacon toward the end of 404; afterward he was honored with the rank of presbyter. The whole passage may seem obscure to some, since the speaker is expressing intense feeling and is concerned less with arranging his words than with expressing his emotion. For its interpretation one must remember that the church of Antioch had been divided into two parties: the party of Paulinus, succeeded by Evagrius, and that of Flavianus, in whose place Alexander was installed after Porphyrius, once Evagrius had died. Since the West favored Paulinus and then Evagrius, some of their adherents had withdrawn to Italy and there attained clerical rank. Ecclesiastical discipline required that, if the dignity conferred upon them was to be preserved, they should be counted as clergy of the city by whose bishops they had been ordained or promoted. Innocentius first judged that the clerical dignity of clergy ordained or promoted in Italy by the party of Paulinus or Evagrius should be preserved; then, at Cassianus’ suggestion, he decreed that they should be numbered among the other priests and ministers who were in the city of Antioch. The same point is confirmed and expressed somewhat more clearly below in Letter XXIII. It should incidentally be noted that the word “priests,” beyond the usual ancient usage, signifies presbyters, not bishops. Jerome also uses the term in this sense in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 48, when he censures the arrogance of deacons who, ignorant of the humility proper to their order, swell with pride beyond the priests—that is, beyond the presbyters. And in his letter to Evangelus he says: “If a presbyter is ordained from a deacon, let him know that he is lower in possessions but higher in priesthood.” Innocentius writes in Letter XXV, no. 6, that presbyters are “second priests.”].

I was also glad to learn concerning the bishops Elpidius and Pappus that they had recovered their churches without dispute. I carefully investigated the matter, as the proceedings appended to the letter testify [Note: [Col. 0541D] The printed editions, as in Isidore, read *subscrīpta* (“written below”). The manuscripts of the Dionysian, Hadrianic, and Spanish collections have the better reading *subjecta* (“appended”). Innocentius did not confirm the peace until he had heard Alexander’s envoys in a public assembly and carefully questioned them about what had been done at Antioch. Since he had ordered the proceedings to be drawn up, he had them appended to this letter.], to determine whether all the conditions had been fulfilled in the case of the blessed and truly God-worthy priest John. When the envoys’ assertion acknowledged that everything had been completed according to our wishes, I gave thanks to the Lord and received your Church into communion in such a way as to make clear that the fellow disciples of the apostolic see were the first to give the others a path of peace. In that peace, once you and we have been established, the kindness of the Lord Christ will embrace and strengthen us so that henceforth no pretext [Note: [Col. 0542B] A Colbert manuscript has *titulamento*, which may appropriately be understood as “a title,” “pretext,” or “color.” Shortly before, the Antiochenes are called fellow disciples of the apostolic see because the church of Antioch was founded by the same Apostle-teacher as the Roman Church.] or embarrassment arising from even the slightest contention will disturb us.

2. We received the letter of the bishop Acacius [Note: [Col. 0542B] The council edition, together with one Colbert manuscript and the Noviomagus manuscript, reads *Attici*. Labbe wrote *Acacii* in the margin instead; this is the reading supplied by the manuscripts of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections and by the Roman edition, and it must be retained, as Letters XXI and XXII clearly demonstrate. In this passage Innocentius testifies that he had received no letter from Atticus. The editor who inserted the name Atticus reveals his own error at the beginning of Letter XXI, which in the same manuscripts is addressed to Atticus, bishop of Beroea. But Atticus was not bishop of Beroea; Acacius was. Palladius regularly lists this Acacius first among the enemies of John Chrysostom and among the principal actors in the tragedy raised against him. For this reason he deserved to be suspended by Innocentius. This should be understood as meaning that Innocentius’ communion with him was suspended, not that Innocentius deprived him of his office. The same pope explains his meaning more clearly in Letter XXII.], since it had been sent together with yours, so that he who had formerly been suspended by us would not be rejected through an insult to you. Nevertheless, in the proceedings we clearly established—please take care to reread them graciously—what must be observed in his case, so that, if he should ask to share fully in your holy counsels and actions, the favor of communion and of letters from us may be granted to the old man through your favor and our judgment [Note: [Col. 0542C] He is rightly now called an old man. Even his nostrils had very long gray hairs when he came to Rome carrying the decree concerning John’s ordination as bishop—that is, before the year 402—as Theodore the deacon relates in Palladius’ *Dialogue*, p. 39. According to Baluzius, *New Collection of Councils*, p. 763, he had also taken part in the Roman synod under Pope Damasus. We have shown above, pp. 491–492, nos. 3 and 4, that this occurred in the year 378.].

Twenty Italian bishops signed.

[Note: [Col. 0542D] This is supported by the strong consensus of the manuscripts. Merlin reads: “Twenty bishops signed, twenty-four from Italy.” Crabbe then removed the numeral XX and retained XXIV, and that reading subsequently prevailed. The error arose from manuscripts of the Spanish collection, in which, after the words “twenty bishops signed from Italy,” XXIV is added—not to indicate the number of subscribing bishops but to indicate the order occupied by the following letter among the letters in that collection.]

## LETTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0543C] In the edition of the councils, this is number 15. The letter formerly numbered XX is now XLI. This letter too is identified in the Roman edition as copied from Cresconius. It was more probably copied from Dionysius, who calls Innocentius’ decree XLII.]

### OF POPE INNOCENTIUS I TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

Concerning peace.

[Col. 0543A] Innocentius testifies, by sending the proceedings, that the embassy dispatched to him by Alexander, bishop of Antioch, was most welcome to him.

### INNOCENTIUS TO BISHOP ALEXANDER

How welcome, devout, and necessary the embassy sent to us from your Holiness, dearest brother, has been, you will learn from the repetition of the proceedings themselves. For our fellow presbyter Cassianus wished this little document of our friendship to be written as the first fruits of our peace through our fellow presbyter Paulus, the deacon Nicolaus, and the subdeacon Petrus, our sons.

I therefore greet both your kinship with me in Christ and the entire Church that agrees so well with you. I ask you, as you do us, to address us more frequently by letter and to gladden us more often with news of your welfare. For I trust that the Lord will allow us to make good all the losses of the past through the most loving exchange of letters [Note: [Col. 0543C] The printed editions read *recompensare* (“to compensate”); the manuscripts reject this reading.].

## LETTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0543C] In the edition of the councils, this is number 19. The letter formerly numbered XXI is now XVII. We received it from Dionysius, not, as the Roman edition states, from Cresconius; it appears under the title XLVIII of Innocentius’ decrees. The fact that it was sent together with the two preceding letters to Alexander is clear from Letter XIX. It is equally clear that Merlin and Crabbe incorrectly address it, as do the manuscripts of the Spanish collection, to Atticus, bishop of Beroea. For Atticus was bishop of Constantinople, not of Beroea. The summary prefixed to it by Dionysius, and thence in other collections and old editions of the councils—“Concerning the holy John, bishop of Constantinople”—is not sufficiently accurate. It is known from Palladius in many places, from Socrates, Book VI, chapter 18, and from Sozomenus, Book VIII, chapter 20, that Acacius, to whom it is addressed, played a principal role in Chrysostom’s deposition. Thinking himself neglected by John, he said in anger, according to Palladius, p. 49: “I am cooking a pot for him.” Later Palladius, p. 82, reports that Acacius said together with Antiochus: “Emperor, let John’s deposition fall upon our heads.” Hence, as Theodore the deacon says in the same place, p. 39, he was regarded both as the author of the sedition and as the leader of those whose crime had stirred up revolutionary activity at Constantinople. He therefore needed a mediator and guarantor whose influence with Innocentius would be no less than Alexander’s. This is why Innocentius sent the letters indicating communion not to Acacius himself but to Alexander, to be delivered to Acacius only under specified conditions.]

### OF POPE INNOCENTIUS I TO ACACIUS, BISHOP OF BEROEA

The condition on which Innocentius grants communion to Acacius.

[Col. 0543C] From your letters we have learned that your brotherhood rejoices at the reception of the clergy and peoples of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius and of the restoration of our fellow bishops Elpidius and Pappus; and, setting aside all contention, we have recognized that you cherish, even if late, the grace of the peace received.

Therefore we have sent this letter to your unanimity, to be delivered to our distinguished brother and fellow bishop Alexander, namely on the condition that, if every hostility and every rivalry concerning both the name of the holy and remarkable bishop John and all those who share his communion has departed from your animosity, you receive this letter of our fellowship, dearest brother—provided that you confess before our kindly mediator Alexander, in person and as one who shares communion, all that has been confirmed in the proceedings here [Note: [Col. 0544C] The council edition, together with one Colbert manuscript, reads “what has been enacted in these proceedings.” Here the acts performed in the Roman synod, in which at least twenty Italian bishops took part, are meant.].

For just as this cause of unanimity and charity is venerable to us, so it remains vigilant lest anything crooked or residual be found to remain in anyone [Note: [Col. 0544C] The printed editions, except Merlin, read *cognoscat* (“may he recognize”); the reading is corrected from the written copies. Acacius’ sincerity throughout this affair becomes highly suspect from what is written about him in Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapters 26–27, both in Atticus’ letter to Cyrillus and in Cyrillus’ letter to Atticus.].

## LETTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 0544C] In the edition of the councils, this is number 16. The letter formerly numbered XXII is now XVI. In Dionysius, from whom we have this letter first—not from Cresconius, as the Roman edition states—it appears under title XLIII of Innocentius’ decrees. There seems no doubt that the Maximianus to whom this letter is addressed is the same Maximianus whom Chrysostom, in exile, thanks in Letter 163, together with the other Macedonian bishops, for having steadfastly remained on his side, and who is listed above among the Macedonian bishops in Letter XVII. He also appears to be the same Maximianus, the Macedonian envoy, who is said in the preceding Letter XVIII to have remained in Rome longer than expected. The probable reason for this delay was that he wished to attend the Roman synod and to testify to everything that had been done in the reconciliation of the church of Antioch. Then, moved and encouraged by his recollection of what he had heard at that synod, as soon as he was able to reach Constantinople he did not cease pressing Atticus to follow the example of the bishop of Antioch. Once he had obtained Atticus’ assent in some measure, he could not endure delay without writing to Innocentius in Atticus’ favor. This provided the occasion for Innocentius to write the present letter. Its date may be inferred from this straightforward account. It was evidently written neither at the same time as the preceding three letters nor much later; rather, one must allow between this letter and those only the interval required for Maximianus to travel from the Roman synod to Constantinople and for his letter in Atticus’ favor to reach Innocentius. How Alexander, on coming to the imperial city, obtained from Atticus what Innocentius desired is related by Atticus himself in Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 26.]

### CONCERNING ATTICUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0544B] Communion is not to be restored to him unless he first requests it through a solemn embassy and himself fulfills what was done at Antioch—that is, restores John’s name to the sacred diptychs.

### INNOCENTIUS TO BISHOP MAXIMIANUS

We are surprised, prudent brother, that you request for Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, in your own petition and by the written memorandum appended below, what you regard as something to be granted to one who has not brought us or your synod even a single letter from himself. You judge that it should be granted to one who does not ask, simply because you see it granted, after examination of the matter, to those who do ask.

Communion is restored to one who demonstrates that the causes for which it had been suspended have now been removed and who professes that the conditions of peace have been fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0545C] Communion between Innocentius and Atticus had been suspended because Atticus, as Palladius testifies on p. 95, the architect of all the plots against John, had seized John’s place. Thus the bishops of the East and the people of Constantinople recoiled from communion with him, and he was scarcely able, even by an imperial rescript, to compel them to communicate with him, however unwillingly. More specifically, according to Theodoretus, Book V, chapter 34, the bishops of the West had decided after Chrysostom’s death to admit none of the eastern bishops to communion until they had entered the name of that great Teacher in the sacred diptychs. Innocentius first wishes this cause of the suspended communion to be removed, so that he may be able to communicate with Atticus.]. As I have said, Atticus has not wished either to say or to demonstrate through any of his representatives, either before you or before us, that this has been accomplished, as our brother and fellow bishop Alexander of the church of Antioch both presented and proved it by a worthy embassy.

Since you graciously took part in all these matters, you learned how I examined one by one everything that our earlier letters had set out concerning the cause of our most blessed former bishop John [Note: [Col. 0545D] One Colbert manuscript reads *discusserint* (“they examined”), a reading that had once seemed preferable because it appeared that the matters to be fulfilled should be examined by those whose task it was to fulfill what was required. But after Letter XIX, no. 1, was reread, it became clear that Innocentius had examined in his synod whether the conditions that he had prescribed at various times and in various letters for obtaining peace had been fulfilled. In the printed editions one reads *ut quae*; *utque* should be read instead, meaning “and how.” A Regius manuscript has *nuntiaverint* (“announced”) in place of *monstrarint* (“demonstrated”), and some editions have *ostenderint* (“shown”).], and how they demonstrated to him with complete clarity that everything that ought to have been done at Antioch had been completed.

Having embraced their peace, we gave them our pledge of faith and showed to all who were asking for that same peace the great path [Note: [Col. 0545D] Merlin corruptly reads *eamdem quam praestolaris* (“the same peace that you await”). Although Innocentius appears not to have been content with the written requests of those seeking peace but also to have required a solemn embassy, he did not require each person to send envoys in his own name. As Maximianus’ example makes clear, it was enough if someone offered Innocentius his written requests through envoys sent by anyone. In Atticus’ case, however, who had been installed after Arsacius in John’s place, the validity of his ordination was also then at issue. As observed above, p. 598, no. 21, the practice had begun whereby the Roman pontiffs did not consider the ordination of the bishop of the imperial city valid until they had been informed of it by a solemn embassy.], provided that they themselves should at some point demonstrate that they had done or completed, in their own capacity, what had been examined and completed, and that, like these men, they should solemnly request through an embassy that communion be restored to them.

We therefore await both the profession of the aforesaid man concerning the fulfillment of all the conditions that we previously stated at various times, and his request for communion, so that we may restore it rightly to one who both asks for it and proves himself worthy of it, dearest brother. For you received long ago a very full letter concerning all these matters addressed to the holy synod of our brothers [Col. 0546A] [Note: [Col. 0546C] The letters mentioned here are no longer extant.].

## LETTER XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0546C] In the edition of the councils, this is number 14. The letter formerly numbered XXIII is now III. Dionysius arranged it under title XLI of Innocentius’ decrees, and the Roman edition, as with the preceding letters, identifies it as copied from Cresconius. The Bonifacius to whom it is addressed seems, not without reason, to be the presbyter of the Roman Church who, together with another presbyter and five bishops, is said in Palladius’ *Dialogue*, p. 31, to have been sent by Honorius to Arcadius, and who later succeeded Zosimus as Innocentius’ successor. At this time he may have been serving as an envoy to Theodosius on behalf of the apostolic see. From the final words, in which he is ordered to instruct those who regularly intervene on behalf of Atticus, it is clear that this letter is not earlier than the one just written to Maximianus. We may reasonably suppose that both were sent together. Dionysius and Isidore prefix to this letter the simple summary: “Concerning the church of Antioch.”]

Concerning the peace granted to the church of Antioch.

### INNOCENTIUS TO THE PRESBYTER BONIFACIUS
The Church of Antioch, which blessed Peter the Apostle illuminated by his presence before he reached the city of Rome, as the sister of the Roman Church, did not permit itself for a long time to remain alienated from that Church [Note: Crabbe and the subsequent editions read “from the same [church].” Concinnius and Merlin, as in the manuscripts, read “from the same [feminine],” that is, the Roman Church.]. For it sent envoys and requested and obtained peace in such a way that it would receive the Evagrians in their orders and offices, with the ordination they had received from the aforesaid [Note: Evagrius is to be supplied. For Innocent proceeds as though he had previously said not “the Evagrians,” but “the clerics of Evagrius.” In the manuscripts the reading is “they would receive,” although in the same manuscripts “would gather and assemble” follows. Both expressions can be understood so that “they would receive” refers to receiving them into the Church, and “would gather” to gathering them to Alexander. Moreover, in place of the word “promising,” which is expressed in the epistolary style then customary, a grammarian would prefer: “He further promised.”], and would gather and assemble into one the clerics or laypeople of John of holy memory, the bishop of that city, my brother Alexander [see Letter 19, no. 1], promising that, even if someone should come to them from us or from elsewhere after the later ordination, he would receive him without controversy and recite the name of the aforementioned bishop (John) among the bishops who rest.

Know, dearest brother, that we have given our hands to this arrangement and received them into our own heart, so that members which had sought healing might not long be regarded as alienated from the unity of the body. My son the deacon Paul, bearer of this letter, will be able to recount to Your Love everything that was done in due order, so that you may share our common joy and inform those who are accustomed to intervene on behalf of Atticus.

## LETTER XXIV

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, this is Letter 18; the letter that was formerly 24 is now 29. In the Roman edition this letter, like the preceding ones, bears the common note, “From Cresconius.” Cresconius himself, in the *Breviary*, chapter 53, cites it according to the division introduced by Dionysius. He divided it into three titles, or decrees—XLV, XLVI, and XLVII—each decree being prefaced by a summary, which the author of the Spanish collection and Isidore copied in the customary manner. Here we reproduce the same division, together with the summary prefixed by Dionysius to each title or chapter. Although this letter bears no indication of time, it nevertheless does not seem to be separable from the preceding letters, especially since it is probable that Alexander, invited by Innocent in Letter 20 to refresh him more frequently by his letters, did not delay to cultivate the friendship that had been offered and to make the concerns that troubled him useful to himself as soon as they had been presented.]

### TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

I. That the first see of blessed Peter is said to have been at Antioch.—II. That, according to the decrees of the emperors, there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops.—III. That Arian clerics are not to be received in their offices, although the Church confirms the baptism administered by them, which is known to be Catholic.

[Note: Thus read the copies of Dionysius in the general index. Within the body of the letter, however, the title is repeated with this alteration: “although the Church confirms their baptism, which is known to be Catholic”; Isidore and, following him, the editions of the Councils placed this wording first.]

**INNOCENT TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP.**

### CHAPTER I

1. The burden and honor imposed upon us by Your Fraternity have brought forward the matters requiring necessary discussion, so that we may reply to your letter or memorandum, as the grace of the Holy Spirit grants. Accordingly, as we review the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which [Canon 6] expresses the one mind of all priests throughout the world, we recognize that it judged concerning the Church of Antioch that all the faithful—not to say all priests—must carefully preserve the arrangement by which that Church was established over its aforesaid diocese, not over a single province [Note: That is, it established that Antioch should preside not over one province but over the entire Eastern diocese, which consisted of fifteen provinces. Jerome vindicates and explains this right of the see of Antioch over the East, asserted by the Council of Nicaea, in Letter 61 to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem, in these words: “You who seek ecclesiastical rules and appeal to the canons of the Council of Nicaea, answer me: what connection have you with the bishop of Alexandria in Palestine? If I am not mistaken, this is what is decreed there: that Caesarea is the metropolis of Palestine and Antioch of the entire East. Therefore you ought either to have referred the matter to the bishop of Caesarea or, if judgment had to be sought from farther away, to have directed your letters rather to Antioch.” Jerome is referring there to Canons 6 and 7 of Nicaea. The Council of Nicaea did not so much establish Antioch over its diocese as recognize an arrangement already established, and it wished this prerogative to remain unimpaired.] We therefore observe that this was attributed to it not so much because of the magnificence of the city as because it is shown to be the first see of the first Apostle [Note: In the Regius manuscript, *primi* is absent. In one Colbert manuscript the reading is: “the first apostolic see.” This passage makes clear why Innocent calls the Antiochenes “fellow disciples of the apostolic see” in Letter 19, no. 1.], where the Christian religion also received its name, and which merited having the Apostles’ most celebrated assembly take place in its midst [Acts 11] [Note: Gregory, bishop of Pisinuntum, also praises the assembly of the Apostles held at Antioch in the Second Council of Nicaea, volume VII of Labbe’s *Councils*, p. 63; indeed, he derives from it a canon concerning images. Learned scholars, however, judge that no assembly of the Apostles was held there. On this matter see Tillemont, volume I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 525. Yet this passage of Innocent at least shows that the writing praised by the aforementioned bishop as an account of a council held at Antioch by the Apostles was not recently composed, and therefore that the authority he derived from it concerning images should not be dismissed—not because that canon is truly to be attributed to the Apostles, but because it may plausibly be thought to be no later than the fourth century.], and which would not yield to the see of the city of Rome except that Rome earned its distinction in passing, whereas Antioch rejoices that what it received was completed in its midst [Nicholas I, Letter 8].

Therefore, dearest brother, we judge that just as you ordain metropolitan bishops by your singular authority, so you should allow the other bishops to be appointed only with your permission and knowledge. In this matter you will rightly observe the following rule: you should decree by letters that those who are far away be ordained by the men who now ordain them solely at their own discretion; but those who are nearby, if you judge it appropriate, you should arrange to come to the laying on of hands by Your Grace. For those whose care especially pertains to you ought particularly to merit your judgment [Note: Nicholas I, applying this passage to his own see, says in Letter 42, no. 9: “We are certainly bound by the care of all who constitute the Church, and all—perhaps ‘everyone’—whose greatest concern awaits us ought especially to obtain our judgment, just as Innocent says to Alexander,” and so forth. In another letter, no. 1 of the appendix to Letter 2, where he reports Innocent’s words themselves, he adds: “Therefore, since the care of the whole Church awaits us.” It follows that Nicholas understood the verb *exspectat*, “awaits,” here in the sense in which it commonly sounds, namely, “is incumbent upon” or “belongs to.” Nevertheless, we are convinced that here it is used in its ancient sense, “looks to,” and that “the care awaits you” means nothing other than “the care pertains to you.” This interpretation would have been much more suitable to Nicholas’s purpose.].

### CHAPTER II

2. As for what you ask—whether, when provinces are divided by imperial decision so that two metropolises are created, two metropolitan bishops ought accordingly to be appointed—this has not truly been judged to be the case [Note: The printed editions, the Spanish collection manuscripts, and Isidore read, “it was not truly judged”; Nicholas I and the Hadrianic collection manuscripts read, “therefore it was not judged.” The wording is corrected with the aid of the Regius copy of Dionysius, which has “it has not been judged.” Innocent’s judgment differs from what the Council of Chalcedon decreed in Canon 17: if any city has been renewed by imperial authority, or is thereafter renewed, the ecclesiastical order should follow the civil and public arrangements. The same council, in Canon 12, decrees only against those who, contrary to ecclesiastical statutes, divide one province into two by imperial letters, so that as a result two metropolitan bishops appear to exist in one province; anyone who thereafter attempts this is to be punished by loss of his proper rank.], that God’s Church should be changed according to the shifting necessities of worldly affairs, or suffer honors or divisions which the emperor may judge necessary for his own purposes. Therefore metropolitan bishops ought to be counted according to the former custom of the provinces [Note: Thus read the manuscripts. The printed editions have “ought to be appointed.”].

3. You assert that the Cypriots, once wearied by the power of Arian impiety, did not maintain the Nicene canons [5 and 6] in the ordination of their bishops, and have continued to presume to ordain at their own discretion, consulting no one. We therefore urge them to take care, in accordance with the Catholic understanding of the canons [Note: Although Crabbe rashly repeated the word *fidem* here, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, that repetition was retained in the subsequent editions. The issue here is not faith, but the discipline established by the rules of the canons and received by the practice of the universal Church. Innocent urges the Cypriots to take care to understand the canons in accordance with Catholic teaching. Not only Alexander but also his successors claimed for themselves the ordination of the Cypriot bishops; the Cypriots, however, consistently protested. On this controversy see the seventh act of the Council of Ephesus. There, when Zeno, bishop of Carpasia in Cyprus, had said, “They can never show from the holy Apostles that anyone from Antioch came and ordained, or ever shared with the island the grace of ordination,” the holy council replied: “Let the holy council remember the canon of the holy fathers assembled at Nicaea [namely, Canon 6], which preserves to each his ancient dignity.” See also what precedes and follows. In this matter Innocent, the Cypriots, and the Council of Ephesus agree that all wish the Nicene canons to be preserved. Nor did Innocent authorize the Cypriots to allow themselves to be ordained by the bishop of Antioch except insofar as, on Alexander’s testimony, he took it as certain that they had usurped this right for themselves contrary to ancient custom.] to understand correctly and to share one mind with the other provinces, so that it may be evident that they too, like all the Churches, are governed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

4. **CHAPTER III**

Furthermore, concerning Arians [I, question 1, chapter 73] [Note: The manuscripts read *caeterosque* (“and all other [such plagues]”).], and other such plagues: since we receive their laity, converted to the Lord, under the appearance of repentance [Note: The meaning of the phrase “under the appearance of repentance,” repeated again at the end of the letter, is questioned. The word “appearance” recurs in the following letter, no. 7, where the appearance of the Lord’s Day and of Friday—on which Christ suffered and rose again—is said to be renewed each week. Another passage, in Letter 29, no. 2, better illuminates the present one: Pelagius and Celestius are introduced as disputing under the appearance of Catholic faith, instructed—or rather destroyed—by the subtleties of perverse words. Just as “the appearance of Catholic faith” there means something that presents a certain semblance of Catholic faith, so here something that presents a certain appearance of repentance is called “the appearance of repentance.” Nor was it without reason that Innocent called the laying on of hands, by which heretics formerly corrected were immediately joined to the faithful, “the appearance of repentance”: this laying on of hands evidently contained a kind of profession of repentance. Accordingly, Augustine, in Book II of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, aptly expresses the mind of this pope: “If the laying on of hands were not administered to those coming from heresy, they would be judged to be entirely without guilt. But for the sake of the bond of charity, which is the greatest gift of the Holy Spirit, without which all other holy things in a person are unable to bring salvation, hands are laid upon heretics who have been corrected.” This laying on of hands, however, did not include the substance of penitence—that is, dirty garments, frequent fasts, and the other mournful labors and preparations of repentance to which those separated from the assembly of the faithful were subjected and after which alone, following a long satisfaction, they were admitted again. Thus it was merely a shadow and appearance of that repentance.

“Furthermore, Siricius, Innocent, and Pope Vigilius distinguish two classes of heretics returning to the Church: one consists of those baptized among heretics—such as Novatians, Donatists, or Arians—who return to the Church; the other consists of those who, after receiving baptism in the Catholic Church, allowed themselves to be rebaptized by those heretics. They prescribe the laying on of hands for both groups, but in the first it presents only the appearance of repentance, while in the second it embodies repentance itself. Concerning the first group, Siricius says in Letter 1, no. 2: ‘Those whom, together with the Novatians and other heretics, as was established in the [Nicene] council, we join to the assembly of Catholics by the simple invocation of the sevenfold Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands.’ Concerning the same people he says again in Letter 4, chapter 8: ‘Those coming from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received by the laying on of hands.’ He distinguishes others from these by the following exception: ‘except those whom they rebaptize.’ Our Innocent explains Siricius’s meaning in Letter 2, no. 11, where he likewise orders: ‘Those coming from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received by the laying on of hands,’ but adds the exception more explicitly: ‘except those who, if they have passed from us to them, have perhaps been rebaptized. If, having come to their senses and considering their ruin, they prefer to return, they are to be admitted only after a long penitential satisfaction.’ Thus the first were received under the appearance of repentance, because hands were laid upon them to receive the Holy Spirit, without any penitential satisfaction following. The others, however, were admitted not under the appearance but under the reality of repentance, because communion was granted to them only after a long penitential satisfaction, which preceded the laying on of hands. Pope Vigilius, clearly distinguishing the two kinds of laying on of hands, illustrates and confirms our explanation in Letter 2 to Profuturus—or, as the printed editions corruptly circulate it, to Etherius—no. 4. Concerning those who had been rebaptized, he likewise declares: ‘Their reconciliation, however, is accomplished not by that laying on of hands which operates through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, but by that through which the fruit of repentance is obtained and restoration to holy communion is completed.’] and by the sanctification of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, it does not seem that

their clerics should be received with the dignity of the priesthood or of any ministry. For when we permit only their baptism to be valid—which is certainly performed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit [Note: The copies of the Hadrianic collection read *promittimus* (“we promise”). Dionysius and the other manuscripts and editions more correctly read *permittimus* (“we permit”).]—we do not think that they possess the Holy Spirit from that baptism and those mysteries. When the authors of their faith departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received. They cannot bestow the fullness of the Spirit, which operates especially in ordinations, since through the treachery of their impiety—or, rather, through what I should call their faithlessness instead of faith [Note: The printed editions read “through faith.” The manuscripts, more harmoniously, omit the preposition *per*. The point is that the faith of heretics is rightly called faithlessness, because, as Hilary observes in Book I of *Against Constantius*, “whatever is beyond the one faith is faithlessness, not faith.”]—they lost it.

How could we consider their profane priests worthy of Christ’s honors [Note: This relates to what the Donatists, to whom the preservation of clerical honor was promised, object in Augustine, Letter 185, no. 44: “If, then, we ought to repent that we were outside the Church and against the Church, how do we remain clerics or even bishops among them after this repentance?” Augustine replies: “This would not happen, since, in truth, it ought not to happen, unless it were healed by compensation for peace itself. It ought not to happen because those who are not free from blame are not worthy of Christ’s honors.”], when, as I have said, we receive their imperfect laity so that they may obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit under the appearance of repentance?

Therefore let Your Gravity bring this to the knowledge of your fellow bishops, either through a synod, if possible, or through the reading of this letter, so that what you have so necessarily inquired about and we have answered so carefully may be observed by the common agreement and zeal of all.

## LETTER XXV

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, this is Letter 1; the letter that was formerly 25 is now 30.
