This letter is preserved in the Corbie manuscript written in the sixth century and in the Codex published by Quesnel, as well as in the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, Hadrian, the Spanish collection, and Isidore. Dionysius calls it a “regular letter,” and places it before all of Innocent’s decrees under eight titles, namely I through VIII. It is cited without Innocent’s name by the Second Council of Seville, held in 619, chapter 7, and by the Sixth Council of Paris, held in 829, Book 2, chapter 27; with his name, by Isidore of Seville in Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 26, by the Council of Meaux, held in 845, chapter 44, and by Nicholas I, Letter 2 of the appendix, no. 2.]

**From Dionysius Exiguus**

I. On giving the kiss of peace after the mysteries have been completed.—II. On not reciting names before the priest’s prayer.—III. That those who have been baptized should be signed only by the bishop.—IV. That fasting should rightly be observed every Saturday.—V. On the fermented bread that is to be sent only to the priests of the city.—VI. On baptized demoniacs.—VII. On penitents.—VIII. On the Letter of the holy Apostle James, in which prayer for the sick is commanded.

[Note: Instead of the titles appended below, which are copied from the Dionysian copies and the codex published by Quesnel, the old Corbie manuscript gives the following: I. How peace ought to be given in the Church. II. On the recitation of names. III. On signing infants. IV. On the fermented bread. V. On baptized persons who are afterward afflicted by a demon. VI. On anointing the sick.]

**From Colbert Manuscript 932**

I. That, after the mysteries have been completed, those who are to share in peace in the Church should give it to one another.—II. That the names of those making offerings should be recited not beforehand but during the mysteries.—III. On signing infants: only bishops may give the consecrated oil.—IV. That on the holy day of Easter the fermented bread should be given only to those priests who are within the city.—V. On the Saturday fast.—VI. On those who are seized by a demon after baptism.—VII. On penitents: what rule should be observed concerning them around the holy day of Easter.—VIII. That holy oil may be used for anointing not only by priests but by all Christians in their own need and that of their families.—IX. That holy oil, like the other sacraments, should not be granted to penitents during the time of their penance.

**INNOCENT SENDS GREETINGS TO DECENTIUS, BISHOP OF EUGUBIUM** [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “Capua.” Other reputable copies have “Eugubium.” In the copies of Dionysius, where “Eugubium” is read, *salutem* (“greetings”) is added, and from there it also appears in the printed editions.]

1. If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve the ecclesiastical institutions exactly as they were handed down by the blessed Apostles, there would be no diversity or variation in the rites and consecrations themselves. But since each person judges that what seems right to him, rather than what has been handed down, must be observed, different practices appear to be maintained or celebrated in different places and Churches. This creates scandal among the people, who, because they do not know that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, suppose either that their Churches do not agree with one another or that contradiction has been introduced by the Apostles or apostolic men [Distinction 5, chapter 11] [Note: The Corbie manuscript, together with one Colbert manuscript, reads “by the Apostles.” Three others have “by apostolic men,” not “by the men themselves.” Another Colbert manuscript reads “contrary practices and practices not to be used have been introduced.” Above, in Letter 17, no. 9, we heard Innocent commending the ancient rules which the Roman Church preserves as handed down by the Apostles or apostolic men.].

2. Who, indeed, is ignorant or fails to recognize that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, the prince of the Apostles, and is preserved even to the present day, ought to be observed by everyone, and that nothing lacking authority should be superimposed or introduced, or appear to have been received from elsewhere? This is especially clear since it is evident that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands [Note: “And lands” is to be supplied. Hilary, writing his *Book on the Synods* to those united with the Gauls by one communion and fellowship of faith, lists with them the bishops of First and Second Germany and of Britain. If the various provinces of Illyricum are added—the provinces which Innocent lists in Letter 13, no. 2, when entrusting Rufus with his responsibility for them—this provides a sufficiently accurate enumeration of the dioceses belonging to the Roman patriarchate. Among the Churches named by this pope, some think that Lyons should be excepted, since they believe that it received its first priest neither from Peter nor from his successors. Elsewhere, however, the author of this opinion admits that he does not know by whom Pothinus, the first bishop of that Church, was either ordained or sent.], no one established Churches except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read whether, in these provinces, another Apostle is found to have taught or is recorded as having taught. If they cannot read this because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, from which it is beyond doubt that they received their beginning; otherwise, while pursuing foreign assertions, they may appear to neglect the source of their institutions.

3. There is no doubt that Your Love has often come to Rome, met with us in the Church, and learned what practice is observed either in consecrating the mysteries or in conducting the other sacred rites. We would regard this as sufficient for the instruction of your Church—or its reform, if your predecessors observed something less or something different—unless you had thought that we should be consulted about certain matters [Note: The verb *arbitrarer* is added here in the ancient editions of the Councils, as it is in the manuscripts.]. We therefore answer these questions not because we believe that you are ignorant of anything, but so that you may instruct your own people with greater authority, and, if anyone departs from the institutions of the Roman Church, either admonish him or not delay to inform us, so that we may know who introduces novelties or considers the custom of a Church other than the Roman Church to be the one that must be observed.

### CHAPTER I

4. You report that some require peace to be given to the people before the mysteries have been completed [On the Consecration, distinction 2, chapter 9], or that priests give it to one another, whereas after everything that I ought not to disclose, peace must necessarily be proclaimed [Note: Merlin and several manuscripts read “necessary.” The practice of the Churches was not uniform on this point. In the *Apostolic Constitutions* published under the name of Clement, Book II, chapter 61, the kiss of peace follows the offering. Indeed, according to Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2 to Antoninus Pius, the kiss of peace preceded the offering itself. “When we have finished the prayers,” he says, “we greet one another with kisses. Then bread and a cup of water and wine are brought to the one who presides over the brothers.” The Council of Laodicea expresses the rite in Canon 19 as follows: “After the bishop has given the presbyters the kiss of peace, then the laypeople shall give peace to one another, and thus the holy offering shall be celebrated.” In the Mozarabic Missal for the Sunday of Advent, peace is prescribed to be announced and offered to the people before the *Illation*, or, as we say, the preface, so that they may be fit to participate in the most holy mysteries of God. For the same reason, in certain other rites—for example, that of the Church of Salisbury—the priest is ordered to offer the kiss of peace to the deacon and subdeacon so that they may be fit for the ministry of the Lord’s most holy altar, and therefore before the sacred mysteries are celebrated. The ancient Gallican Order supports this practice, since the collect for peace, or the collect after peace has been given, is commonly placed before the *Illation*. Innocent’s caution and reverence are noteworthy: even when writing to a bishop, he speaks of the mysteries “which I ought not to disclose.” This certainly leaves no room for the later heterodox view of those mysteries.], by which it may be clear that the people have given their consent to everything performed in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that, once everything is finished, this is shown by the seal of the concluding peace.

### CHAPTER II

5. As for the recitation of names [On the Consecration, distinction 1, final chapter] before the priest says the prayer and commends in his prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, Your Prudence itself recognizes how superfluous it is to mention the name of someone whose offering you have not yet offered to God, although nothing is unknown to Him. The offerings, therefore, must first be commended, and then the names of those to whom they belong must be proclaimed, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other things that we set forth beforehand in order to open the way for the prayers that will follow within the mysteries themselves [Note: Merlin reads: “For the offerings must first be commended, and then the names must be proclaimed.” In one Colbert manuscript, after “must be commended,” there follows: “And the names of those making offerings must not be recited beforehand, but only within the mysteries. Then their offerings are to be proclaimed, so that among the sacred rites…” This is plainly a marginal note by a scholiast who, in his copy—as in another Colbert manuscript—read “whose offerings are to be proclaimed” instead of “whose names are to be proclaimed.” That reading would support the practice criticized by Jerome in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 18, in these words: “We see many who oppress others by force or commit theft so that they may give a small amount to the poor from much, and glory in their crimes; and publicly the deacon recites the names of those making offerings: ‘So much that woman offers; so much that man has promised,’ and they please themselves to the applause of the people.” It is clear, however, that Innocent does not approve such ostentation, since he wants the offerings of the faithful to be commended to God, not to the people, and not by the deacon’s public recitation but by the priest’s silent prayer. The Council of Frankfurt renewed this command in 794, issuing a decree that names should not be recited before the offering was made. What that council calls the “offering,” Innocent above calls the “prayer.” By both terms he means what we call the Canon. Thus Gregory the Great, in the same letter to John—otherwise Letter 64, Indiction 2—after first stating that some had complained because he had ordered the Lord’s Prayer to be said immediately after the Canon, adds: “For this reason we say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer.” Socrates, Book VII, chapter 25, also calls this same part of the sacred mysteries *εὐχαί* (*prayers*). Accordingly, Innocent and the Council of Frankfurt do not approve those who, following the practice of the Eastern Church, recited the names before the Canon, or, as Cyprian says in Letter 10 to his clergy, “offered the names.” The practice they disapprove, however, was later also received in Gaul and Spain, as is attested by the ancient Gallican Order and the Mozarabic Missal.].

### CHAPTER III

6. As for signing infants, it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop [On the Consecration, distinction 4, chapter 119]. For although presbyters are second-ranking priests [Note: The printed editions omit *secundi* (“second-ranking”); we restore it on the authority of the ancient Corbie manuscript and two others. Relevant here is the statement of Optatus in Book I: “Why should I mention deacons in the third priesthood and presbyters in the second priesthood? The bishops themselves are the summit and chief of all?”], they do not possess the summit of the episcopate [Ivo, Book 1, chapter 265]. This right, belonging exclusively to bishops, whether for signing [Note: The manuscripts just mentioned read this way. Other books have: “But this is owed to bishops alone, so that they may sign.” Theologians ordinarily interpret Innocent’s statement as referring to ordinary ecclesiastical law. Jerome, in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, teaches that the practice by which one baptized in the Church does not receive the Holy Spirit except through the bishop’s hands was instituted rather in honor of the priesthood than from the necessity of the law. The same Doctor seems not only to assert the right of signing for presbyters but also to indicate in his letter to Evangelus that it was sometimes permitted to them, where he says: “What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do?” Chrysostom likewise writes concerning bishops in Homily 2 on the First Letter to Timothy: “They are superior only in ordination, and seem to possess nothing more than presbyters except this.” Gregory, in Book IV, Letter 9, to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia, writes: “Presbyters should anoint those to be baptized on the chest, so that afterward the bishops may anoint them on the forehead.” Yet in another letter to the same man, Letter 24, he writes: “It has also come to our attention that some have been scandalized because we prohibited presbyters from touching with chrism those who are to be baptized.” He first replies: “We acted according to the ancient custom of our Church”; then he adds: “But if some are greatly troubled about this, we grant that where bishops are absent, presbyters too may touch those to be baptized on the forehead with chrism.” Nor does this conflict with Gelasius, who in Letter 12, chapter 6, commands presbyters not to usurp for themselves the power either of making chrism or of administering the episcopal signing. For it is one thing to usurp such power and another to use an authority that has been granted. In the commentaries published under Ambrose’s name on Ephesians, chapter 4, we read: “In Egypt presbyters sign when the bishop is not present.” The ancient author of the *Questions on Both Testaments*, preserved among Augustine’s works in the appendix to volume III, chapter 101, agrees: “In Alexandria and throughout Egypt, if a bishop is absent, the presbyter consecrates”—more correctly, the Colbert manuscript reads, “signs.” This practice still obtains among the Greeks. Nor does the First Council of Toledo appear to oppose it when, in Canon 20, it decrees that a deacon may not chrismate, but a presbyter may do so in the bishop’s absence, and, when the bishop is present, if he has ordered it. Nor do the First Council of Orange, Canon 11, and the Council of Epaon, Canon 16, oppose it when they wish heretics at the point of death who desire to become Catholics to be signed by presbyters, with blessing and chrism, if a bishop is absent. As for Innocent, both this passage and the preceding decrees, as well as the preface of the entire letter, show that he was especially concerned to prevent Churches that had received the faith from Rome from turning aside to rites foreign to the custom of that Church. Following his practice, the Second Council of Seville, held in 619, chapter 7, determined that presbyters may neither make chrism nor sign the foreheads of the baptized with chrism. In imitation of it, Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, concludes in Book 17 of *On Baptism*: “That presbyters may anoint the baptized with chrism but may not impart the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands is an ancient custom handed down from the Apostles”—that is, handed down through the example of the Apostles recorded in Acts. The Sixth Council of Paris, held in 827, Part II, chapter 27, and the Council of Meaux, held in 843, chapter 44, deny this power not only to presbyters but also to chorepiscopi. Accordingly, Isaac, bishop of Langres, decrees in title XI, canon 30: “If anyone has been confirmed not by a bishop but by a chorepiscopus, he must be confirmed again with other blessings.” The Capitulary of 803, in Baluze, p. 381, also decrees the same, supported by the authority of Leo III, who had previously been consulted.], or for imparting the Spirit who is the Paraclete, is due to bishops alone. This is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which says that Peter and John were sent to impart the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized. For presbyters may anoint baptized persons with chrism, whether they baptize outside the presence of a bishop or in his presence—but the chrism must have been consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that oil, since this belongs to bishops alone when they impart the Spirit who is the Paraclete.

I cannot state the words that are spoken, lest I seem to disclose more than to answer the inquiry [Note: From this it is clear that the sacrament of Confirmation was completed not only by the anointing of the forehead but also by prescribed verbal formulas. Yet by deliberately keeping these words silent, Innocent makes plain how great was the reverence of the ancients for concealing the mysteries of the sacraments. There are many further examples of this when they speak of the Eucharist.].

### CHAPTER IV
### 7. (De consecr., dist. 3, c. 13.)

That fasting should indeed be observed on Saturday is demonstrated by the clearest reasoning. For (Ivo, part 4, chapter 28), if we celebrate the Lord’s Day, on account of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, not only at Easter but also throughout each weekly cycle, and if we regularly commemorate the image of that day, while we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s passion, we ought not to omit Saturday, which appears to be enclosed between the sorrow and the joy of that time. For it is certainly established that during those two days the Apostles were both in grief and concealed themselves through fear of the Jews. There is no doubt that they fasted during those two days to such an extent that the tradition of the Church holds that during those two days the sacraments were not celebrated at all.

[Note: In the manuscripts, *qui* is enclosed; Quesnel adds *dies* to these words. If you wish, consult Quesnel’s special Dissertation on the Saturday fast in the Roman Church at the end of Leo’s works.]

[Note: In *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 430, where it is stated, “Since the canons command that during these two days the sacraments ought not to be celebrated,” we may reasonably conjecture that this passage is being referred to. The Council of Rouen in 1072, chapter 22, records that this very custom had been prescribed in the *Pontifical Book*.]

[Note: Supply, “of the fast observed by the Apostles.” For the following discussion of the sacraments not being celebrated during the two days before the Lord’s resurrection is mentioned only in passing, being added solely to establish the Saturday fast; and the very course of the argument confirms this. Socrates indeed says, book V, chapter 22: “While all churches throughout the world celebrate the sacred mysteries every week on Saturday, the Alexandrians and Romans, following an ancient tradition, decline to do so.” But the liturgies of Gregory and Gelasius suggest otherwise, since they prescribe Masses even on the Saturdays of Lent. Nor would Jerome, in letter 28 to Lucinius, have written, “Concerning the Saturday about which you ask, whether one ought to fast; and concerning the Eucharist, whether it should be received daily, as the Roman Church is reported to observe,” unless the sacred mysteries from which the Eucharist is received had been celebrated daily. Augustine likewise attests the practice of receiving the Eucharist daily in letter 54 to Januarius, section 4; from which it follows that the divine mysteries too were celebrated daily. For ordinarily the Eucharist was not received apart from their celebration, except by the sick. Perhaps Socrates said what we have just cited because the Romans and Alexandrians, having transferred the Saturday solemnity to Sunday, declined to celebrate both days with equal religious observance.]

This practice, then, is to be maintained every week because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated. But if they think that one should fast only once, on a single Saturday, then Sunday and Friday too will necessarily be celebrated only once, at Easter. If, however, the image of Sunday and of Friday is to be renewed every week, it is madness to observe the custom of the two days while omitting Saturday, since it has the same reason as Friday: namely, that on Friday the Lord suffered and descended to the underworld, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding two days of sorrow.

[Note: One manuscript has “Sunday … to be celebrated.” But in Merlin and Crabbe the reading is very poor: “Sunday … to be celebrated.”]

We therefore do not deny that one should fast on Friday; but we say that this must also be done on Saturday, because both days imposed sorrow upon the Apostles, and upon those who followed Christ. Having been gladdened on Sunday, they wished not only to make that day especially festive, but also judged that it ought to be observed throughout all the weeks.

### Chapter V

#### 8.

As for the *fermentum* which we send on Sunday to the titular churches, you wished to consult us about something unnecessary, since all our churches are situated within the city. Their presbyters cannot meet with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them; therefore they receive from us, through the acolytes, the *fermentum* which we have prepared, so that they may not think themselves separated from our communion, especially on that day.

[Note: In one Corbie manuscript, the words “prepared by us” are lacking. By the term *fermentum*, some understand blessed bread which takes the place of the Eucharist, while many more understand the Eucharist itself here. Indeed, our Mabillon observes that in the Roman *Ordo* the Eucharist is frequently designated by the term *fermentum*. Nor need we fear that this latter interpretation supports the opinion of those who think that in former times the Eucharist was made in the Latin Church from leavened bread. The argument drawn from this in support of that opinion is very weak. For that venerable sacrament, in accordance with the custom of those times—when they were eager to conceal the mystery of sacred things from profane persons—was appropriately called *fermentum* when it was sent to the churches. Just as leaven, when put into and mixed with flour, binds the whole mass together, so the term signified that it was a certain bond of mutual unity and communion for them.

For this reason Christ himself is also called *fermentum* outside the sacrament of the Eucharist, in the collection of the encyclical letters sent to the emperor Leo, letter 37, volume IV of Labbe’s *Councils*, page 920. For this reason the Council of Chalcedon praises the bishops of maritime Phoenicia because they destroyed those who, monstrously believing that Christ was not from the Virgin Mother of God, believe him to be “leaven” (*FERMENTUM*).

But that we should not think Innocent understood *fermentum* to mean merely a *eulogia*—a blessed loaf—is shown by the reasoning he adds below. He teaches that this custom of sending the *fermentum* applies neither to the church of Gubbio nor to other churches that do not have several titular churches within one city, because the sacraments do not have to be carried a long distance. If anyone denied that a *eulogia*, or blessed bread, could be carried farther without distinction, he would be refuted by the letters of Paulinus of Nola to Augustine, letters 24, number 6; 25, number 5; and 32, number 3, as well as by Augustine’s letter formerly numbered 34 and now 31, number 9. In these we read that those holy men sent one another blessed loaves from Italy to Africa and back again as a symbol of their mutual unity or communion.

The custom of sending the *fermentum* to the churches, which was perhaps peculiar to the city of Rome, is attributed to Melchiades, as was observed above, on page 339, where we also discussed the matter more fully.]

I do not think that this ought to be done for the parish churches, because the sacraments do not have to be carried a long distance—and we do not send them through the various cemeteries to presbyters established there—and because their presbyters have the right and permission to consecrate them.

[Note: Quesnel, following the old editions of the councils and the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, reads, “and their presbyters.” Two manuscripts read, “by their prayers”; Pithou, “and by their prayers.” The subsequently current reading is sounder and more polished. Having first taught that sacraments ought not to be carried to parish churches, Innocent now adds a second reason, showing that this is unnecessary.]

[Note: The printed editions read *parochias*; in the copies of Dionysius and Hadrian, *paroecias* or *parroecias*; in the very old Corbie manuscript, *proicias*, unquestionably standing for *paroicias*. From this it may be inferred that it was not originally so, but that only in the course of time did it become customary for copyists to write *parochias* or *parrochias*. By this name Innocent here understands churches situated outside the episcopal city. No one is unaware that Roman cemeteries too were situated outside cities, since the Romans regarded burying bodies within the walls as religiously improper.]

### Chapter VI

#### 9.

Concerning those baptized persons who are afterward seized by a demon, when some vice or sin has intervened, your affection is concerned to know whether they can or ought to be [ritually] marked by a presbyter or deacon.

[Note: Thus several manuscripts of good authority. But the manuscripts of Pithou, Dionysius, and Isidore read, “your affection has inquired.”]

[Note: Thus the old Corbie codex, together with the ancient copies of the edition published by Quesnel, and another manuscript of good authority from the Colbert collection. Dionysius also appears to have read this way; his Regius copy is still cited in support of it. In the other books *consignari* is found. The Roman edition then reads, “which, unless to bishops, this is not permitted to command.” Quesnel has “which, unless,” suppressing *hoc* contrary to the agreement of all the manuscripts. The sentence will be complete if before *quod* the verb *censeo* is supplied, or if, with the Regius manuscript of Dionysius and certain others, one prefers: “that this may not be commanded except by a bishop.”

John Morinus thinks in a certain posthumous work that Innocent here granted deacons the power to administer Confirmation when necessity pressed. But his editor Moretus correctly observes that there is no discussion here of that sacrament. The learned man was misled by the verb *consignari*, by which the sacrament of Confirmation is designated above.

The question plainly concerns baptized persons—that is, the faithful—not those who were seized by a demon at the very reception of baptism, but those who were seized afterward. Neither the learned Morinus nor anyone acquainted with antiquity is unaware that in this age the sacrament of Confirmation was customarily conferred upon those who had emerged from the sacred bath of baptism. This is taught by Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapters 7 and 8; Cyprian, letter 73 to Jubaianus; Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, chapter 7; Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*; Augustine, Sermon 324; Pope Leo, Sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord; and much later by Magnus, bishop of Sens, in the little work on the mystery of baptism which he composed at the command of Charlemagne, as well as by our Edmund Martène, who published it in *The Ancient Rites of the Church*, volume I, page 160. In that work we read: “When all the sacraments of baptism have been completed, finally, through the imposition of hands by the high priest, they receive the Holy Spirit of sevenfold grace.”

Moreover, throughout this entire chapter there is not a word about the Holy Spirit, although Innocent is not usually silent about him when speaking of the sacrament of Confirmation. Finally, the man who in the preceding chapter, 3.6, asserted that the right to mark or to impart the Holy Spirit belonged to bishops alone, and denied this power to presbyters, was far from granting it to deacons.

It is therefore evident that the rites by which a person seized by a demon is assisted are explained here. Our Edmund Martène discusses these rites at length in *The Ancient Rites of the Church*, book III, chapter 9. In particular, among those which he transcribes from the old Regius codex 3866 and another from Vendôme, ibid., page 366, it is prescribed that the priest to whom the possessed person is brought receive the confession of all his sins, place his hand on the top of the sick person’s head, make the sign of the cross three times, and, after many prayers, sign him on the forehead, eyes, ears, nostrils, breast, mouth, feet, and both hands, applying to each member its proper blessing. There is therefore scarcely any room for doubt that Innocent denotes this last rite by the word *designari*.

Nevertheless, I do not object to retaining *consignari*, nor do I deny that the following supports this reading: in the codices cited from our Martène, page 520, a double formula for signing is given, and the latter is entitled: “Another consignation of the head and eyes, or of all the members.” Care must be taken, however, not to suppose that the word *consignandi* is used here in the sense in which it is used above in chapter 3. Perhaps Innocent used above the word *consignandi* and here *designandi* in order to distinguish the two matters. But whether here you prefer *designari* or *consignari*, neither seems to mean anything other than simple signing.]

“Marked” (*designari*). This is not permitted unless a bishop has ordered it. For hands must absolutely not be laid upon them unless the bishop has authorized it. For it to be done, it belongs to the bishop to command that hands be laid upon them either by a presbyter or by the other clergy.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “hands be laid upon them.” This imposition of hands was a certain form of penance. Whatever concerns public penance was always subject in the Church to the authority of bishops. When a bishop was present, hands were laid upon penitents both by him and by his clergy.

Thus Cyprian writes to his clergy in letter 10, complaining that although sinners in lesser offenses do penance for a long time, and in accordance with the order of discipline come to confession, and receive the right of communion through the imposition of the hands of the bishop and clergy, “now, in this rash time … before penance has been performed, before confession has been made, before hands have been laid upon them by the bishop and clergy, the Eucharist is given to them.”

But when the bishop was absent, and no urgent necessity compelled him, he permitted this same act to presbyters or even to deacons. Accordingly, Cyprian also writes to his clergy in letter 13: “If they are overtaken by some illness and danger of weakness, without awaiting our presence, they may make confession of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter is found and death begins to press, even before a deacon, so that, hands having been laid upon them for penance, they may come to the Lord in peace.”

This is relevant to what Regino, book I, chapters 295 and 296, and Burchard, book X, chapters 155 and 156, quote as being from the Roman *Penitential*: “For just as bishops and presbyters alone ought to offer sacrifice, so no others ought to usurp the judgments of penitents. But if necessity arises and no presbyter is present, let the deacon receive the penitent for holy communion.”

Those statements concern the reconciliation of a penitent when the danger of death is imminent. But Innocent determines that in the case of the possessed a certain authority may be granted by the bishop which appears to belong not only to presbyters or deacons, but also to the other clergy, among whom the lowest order is that of exorcists. This must be understood in such a way that the lower clergy omit those rites which are permitted only to priests.]

For how could it be done without great difficulty, if a possessed person living far away had to be brought to the bishop, when, if such a case occurred on the journey, he could neither easily be carried to the bishop nor taken back home?

### Chapter VII

#### 10.

As for penitents who are doing penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones, the custom of the Roman Church shows (De consecr., dist. 3, c. 17; Ivo, p. 15, c. 40; Isaac of Langres, c. 15) that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. The priest is responsible for judging the gravity of the offenses, so that he may consider the penitent’s confession, as well as the weeping and tears of the person correcting his life, and then order him to be released when he sees that his satisfaction is adequate.

[Note: Thus two Colbert manuscripts. But the other books read “his satisfaction.” How concerned the ancients were that penitents should not be absolved before making adequate satisfaction, or depart from this world without reconciliation and communion, is shown—to mention no others—by Cyprian in the passages cited shortly above. There that holy martyr also speaks of penance performed for lesser sins; but, since these are compared with more serious offenses, we may reasonably suppose that they are called lesser and lighter, although they too were deadly.]

Or if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.

### Chapter VIII

#### 11.

Since your affection wished to consult us about this matter, as about the others, my son the deacon Caelestine also added in his letter that your affection had raised what is written in the letter of the blessed Apostle James:

“If anyone among you is sick, let him call the presbyters, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the suffering person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed a sin, it will be forgiven him” (James V, 24).

[Note: Thus six of the better manuscripts, which in expressing this passage almost entirely agree with the old Italian version. But the printed editions have, “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church,” except that the word “of the Church” is absent from Merlin, as it is from the other manuscripts. Two Colbert manuscripts add, “and let them pray for him”; Pithou has, “and let them pray for him.”]

[Note: One Colbert manuscript, together with Pithou and the cited copy of the Italian version, reads “in faith”; and then, together with the older witnesses, “will save the suffering person,” whereas the printed editions have “will save the sick person.”]

[Note: The printed editions read, “if he has been in sins, they will be forgiven him.” This is corrected on the authority of the better manuscripts, three of which have, “if he has committed sins.” Dionysius then has “it will be forgiven him,” as it is also read in the old copy of the Italian version.]

There is no doubt that this is to be understood of sick believers, who may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism. This oil, having been prepared by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but also by all Christians, for use in their own need or that of their household.

[Note: Crabbe and the later printed editions have “which was prepared by the bishop”; Merlin and the manuscripts oppose this reading. The Greek Christians, as our Edmund Martène proves in volume II of *The Ancient Rites of the Church*, page 114, also customarily prepare this oil through presbyters.]

[Note: Quesnel has *ungendo*, “for anointing”; the Roman edition has *ad ungendum*, “for anointing”; the others have *inungendo*. The manuscripts more correctly have *ungendum*, or, as it is written in most of them, *unguendum*. Nor is it unusual among grammarians to use a verb with an accusative, as can be seen in Plautus: “the other things which we use.”

Those who think that Innocent here grants to all Christians the right to anoint themselves and their own people with holy oil, and declares all the faithful ministers of this sacrament, depart from Innocent’s meaning. He refutes only the opinion of those who may at that time have persuaded themselves that the use of holy oil was so proper to the priests who prepared it that no one else was to be anointed with it. He teaches that it is prepared by them not so that they alone may be anointed from it, but so that all Christians may be anointed.

For at this point he is not yet discussing the minister of anointing, but only the person to whom it may be conferred. He then proceeds to the second question: namely, whether administering this sacrament is so proper to presbyters that bishops may not confer it. He refutes the false opinion of certain people concerning this matter, about which Decentius had thought it necessary to consult him. This question of Decentius clearly shows how far removed from the faith of those times was the belief that every Christian could anoint the sick with holy oil.]

But we see that it is superfluous to add that there should be doubt about the bishop, since it is beyond doubt that this is permitted to presbyters.

[Note: The Roman edition and the councils after Crabbe, together with one Colbert manuscript, read “about presbyters.” Merlin, together with the other manuscripts, has “presbyters,” which we understand with *licere*—“to presbyters, because … it is permitted.” Quesnel’s reading, *presbyteros*, is also unobjectionable, with the sense: “For this reason James said *presbyters*, supplying ‘let him call.’”]

For this reason presbyters were mentioned: because bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot visit all the sick. But if a bishop either can or considers it proper to visit someone himself, he may without hesitation both bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one responsible for preparing the chrism.

[Note: Quesnel has “and anoint.” Although above, in section 6, we read “it is permitted to anoint the baptized with chrism,” here we find *tangere*—“to touch”—in no old manuscript. In two manuscripts *tangere* is absent; in one of them, instead of *chrismate*, we find *chrismare*, “to chrism.” This reading agrees with canon 2 of the First Council of Toledo, where it is decreed that a deacon is not to chrism. Gregory uses the expression *chrismate tangere*—“to touch with chrism”—once and again in book IV, letter 26, to Januarius.]

For he may prepare the chrism. But it cannot be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For how can one kind be thought capable of being granted to those to whom the other sacraments are denied?

[Note: One Colbert manuscript has *sacramentorum*, “of the sacraments.” This is supported by the old Corbie manuscript, which reads *sacratorum*. That reading is certainly corrupt, and it is clear from what follows that Innocent counts the anointing of the sick not merely among sacred rites but also among the sacraments.

When he denies this sacrament to penitents to whom the other sacraments are denied, he plainly shows that it was then customary for it to be granted to other faithful persons suffering outside the danger of death. For above, in section 10, he orders that when penitents fall into desperate illness, the other sacraments also be conferred upon them without delay.

According to Peter Arcudius, book V, chapter 4, the Greeks proceeded so far that they anointed not only the sick who were suffering from no dangerous illness, but also healthy penitents, using the sacramental form, just as they did with the sick.]

### 12.

Therefore, dearest brother, we have taken care to answer, as best we could, all the matters that your affection wished us to explain, so that your Church may be able to observe and preserve the Roman custom from which it derives its origin. As for the remaining matters which it was not lawful to commit to writing, when you are present we shall be able to state them in answer to your questions.

It will belong to the power of the Lord also to bring it about that you instruct well both your Church and our clergy, who under your episcopate serve in the divine offices, and that you provide others with a model which they ought to imitate.

[Col. 0561B] Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, March 19, in the year 416, in the consulship of the emperor Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and of Palladius, a man of the highest rank.

[Note: The printed editions have “most illustrious men.” The manuscripts more correctly have *v. c.*, that is, “most illustrious man,” which applies to Palladius alone. When notaries wish to express “most illustrious men,” they double the abbreviation in this form: *vv. cc.*; this is then understood to refer to two consuls.]

## Notice concerning the following letters

### 1.

The following six letters are represented by a great many old manuscripts reviewed in the latest edition of Augustine. They are displayed, together with the following letter 32, not only in the collection of Isidore, but also in the Hispanic collection and in the copies of the codex published by Quesnel.

Augustine himself mentions them individually in letter formerly numbered 106 and now 186, section 2, in these words:

> “Reports concerning this matter were therefore sent from the two councils, Carthaginian and Milevitan, to the apostolic see … We also wrote to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, in addition to the reports of the councils, a personal letter in which we dealt with the matter at somewhat greater length. He replied to everything in the manner in which it was right and proper for the apostolic see.”

More specifically, concerning Innocent’s letters, he says this in book I of *Against Julian*, chapter 4:

> “For what could that holy man have answered the African councils except what the apostolic and Roman see has held from ancient times and what the rest of the Church perseveringly holds?”

Then, after quoting certain statements which Innocent had drawn from those letters, he presses Julian in these words:

> “Answer him—or rather answer the Lord himself, whose testimony that bishop used.”

Likewise, in book II of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 4, section 6, after presenting some words from letter 29, he exclaims:

> “What could be clearer than this judgment of the apostolic see?”

And again, in section 7, after placing other words from letter 30 in the middle of his discussion, he adds:

> “What does the ungrateful man say to this?”

Thus he calls Caelestius, whom in the same place, section 5, he accuses of deceit, since he afterward falsely claimed before Zosimus that he agreed with these letters of Innocent.

With so many and such evident testimonies, Henry Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, page 74, refutes Vossius’s criticism, in which, following Erasmus, he had called into question “whether these letters were worthy of so great a bishop,” and at the same time he refutes the opinion of a more recent writer who likewise appears to doubt their authenticity.

We pass over Prosper, Pope Caelestine, and other writers who expressly attribute those letters to Innocent. Nor is it necessary to explain at length why he did not elaborate more fully on a subject so abundant and extensive, since he himself supplied the reason for this.

### 2.

The Africans themselves did not conceal the reason why they wrote to Innocent. They testify that they desired, amid the grave crisis which Pelagius and Caelestius had provoked, to become more certain of the truth of the faith, and that their own judgment should be confirmed by Innocent’s decision. In this way, they hoped, the authority of the apostolic see would be added as a firm support to their own decrees.

Finally, they indicate that they hoped those who held such perverse and destructive opinions would more readily submit to the authority of that see, since it was “drawn from the authority of the holy Scriptures” (letter 27, section 3).

### 3.

The Africans clearly demonstrate in their letters how much deference they considered due to the apostolic see. Innocent therefore seized the opportunity to exalt it. If anyone thinks that he exceeded the proper measure in this, Augustine will refute him, since, as we have seen above, Augustine judged that Innocent “replied to everything in the manner in which it was right and proper for the bishop of the apostolic see.”

Are Augustine and the other Africans to be thought to have approved only what Innocent judged concerning Pelagius, Caelestius, and their associates, but not what he stated beforehand in letters 29 and 30 concerning the prerogative of his see? That these matters too were approved by them may be inferred from what their successors wrote at the beginning of the letter sent by the three councils of Africa to Pope Theodore and later read at the Lateran Council under Martin I. There they repeat in their own name everything that Innocent asserts concerning the dignity of the Roman Church in letter 29, using nearly the same sentences and almost entirely the same words (Labbe, volume 6, page 118).

But nothing more illustrious could be desired to commend the excellence of the apostolic see than what Augustine openly proclaimed after receiving Innocent’s letters, in Sermon 131, section 10:

> “For already two councils have sent their decisions concerning this matter to the apostolic see; from there replies have also come. The matter is finished—if only the error would at some time be finished!”

That is, the Pelagian matter had been carefully discussed and judged in two African councils. Since the judgment of the apostolic see agreed with theirs, the matter, decided by the judgment of three authorities of such weight, is rightly considered finished.

### 4.

Augustine spoke in this way while he was still uncertain whether the Pelagians would abide by those replies, or not, and therefore while the replies had only recently arrived in Africa. In the new edition of Augustine it has been observed that the sermon is marked in an old manuscript as having been “delivered on Sunday, the ninth day before the Kalends of October,” and that in the year 417 the ninth day before the Kalends of October fell on a Sunday. From this it is also established that the replies were not later than September of the year 417.

Their precise date, however, remains securely preserved in manuscripts of excellent authority. They record that the replies were dated “the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Junius for the fourth time, men of the highest rank,” that is, January 27 of the year 417.

Nor does this date become doubtful because of the other form found in certain manuscripts: “the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius and Constantius, men of the highest rank.” For in fact Honorius and Constantius held the consulship in the year 417.

We may reasonably think that this alteration occurred either through the work of a copyist who wrote in the margin, in place of the consuls of the previous year, the consuls of the current year—whom Innocent perhaps did not yet know—or through the simplicity of a scribe who, removing the original reading, transferred that marginal note into the text.

Of the seven letters that follow, the first was written somewhat before letters 27 and 28, but was transmitted along with them, as the year 416 was drawing to a close, by the same African bishop Julius. The next four were given on one day and carried by the same bishop Julius. That these letters were returned to the Africans before October of the year 417 is established by the note prefixed to Augustine’s Sermon 131, as we have already indicated.

### 5.

Peter Marca, book VII of *On Agreement*, chapter 12, section 5, and John Garnerius, *Dissertation on the Synods Held in the Pelagian Controversy*, assert that Innocent replied to the Africans on the basis of some Roman synod. But Antonius Pagi, under the year 416, section 19, denies this and confirms his own opinion with the words of Augustine, book IV of *To Boniface*.

The two opinions can be reconciled without much difficulty. For when the Pelagians boasted that the doctrines of Pelagius and Caelestius had been condemned without a synodal gathering, Augustine, in book IV of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 12, section 31, did not deny this to them. Yet in the same work, book II, chapter 3, when those heretics accused the Roman clergy of betrayal, the same Doctor answered:

> “If—God forbid—it had then been judged concerning Caelestius or Pelagius in the Roman Church that their doctrines, which Pope Innocent had condemned in them and together with them, ought to be approved and maintained, then the mark of betrayal would more properly have been branded upon the Roman clergy.”

But there would have been no basis for blaming those clergy if Innocent had written against Pelagius and Caelestius without their knowledge. Therefore that holy pope composed these letters without a synodal assembly of bishops summoned from different provinces, but not without an assembly of the Roman clergy. In this way the opinions which appear to conflict are reconciled, and the enduring custom is confirmed—a custom which, as we have hitherto seen, required the Roman pontiffs, when consulted by the churches, to reply only after at least gathering a body of their own clergy.

## Letter XXVI of the Carthaginian Council to Innocent

So that the authority of the apostolic see may be added to their judgment by which they condemned the impieties of Pelagius and Caelestius. And finally, if they deny that these opinions are their own, an anathema is decreed against any supporters of them.

To the most blessed and most honored lord, holy brother, Pope Innocent: Aurelius, Numidius, Rusticianus, Fidentinus, Evagrius, Antonius, Palatinus, Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tutus, Pannonius, Victor, Restitutus, another Restitutus, Rusticus, Fortunatianus, Ampelius, Ambivius, Felix, Donatianus, Adeodatus, Octavius, Serotinus, Majorinus, Posthumianus, Crispulus, Victor, another Victor, Leucius, Macianus, Fructuosus, Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, Maximus, Megasius, Rusticus, Rufinianus, Proculus, Severus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetextatus, Sixtus, Quodvultdeus, Pentadius, Quodvultdeus, Cyprianus, Servilius, Pelagianus, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus, Bizacenus, Germanus, Germanianus, Invenitus, Majorinus, Invenitus, Candidus, Cyprianus, Aemilianus, Romanus, Africanus, and Marcellinus, and the others who were present at the council of the Church of Carthage.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way except for one, which has Fidentianus. The printed editions have Fidentius, supported by the Carthaginian Collation, in which three bishops bearing the name Fidentius are recorded.]

[Note: In Crabbe’s margin: Antonius; the manuscripts here also have that form. But the letter with which Innocent replied to him is addressed in the Corbie and German manuscripts to Antonio, not Antonino.]

[Note: The Roman edition has Pantonius, contrary to the manuscripts. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 126, Pannonius, bishop of the people of Puppitana, is recorded.]

[Note: In the Corbie and German manuscripts this bishop’s name is missing. In the reply of Innocent in those same manuscripts he is called Ambivius, and in the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 133, he is identified as bishop of Pisitana. In Quesnel, as in the Pithoean, Colbertine, and Isidorian manuscripts, he is Avivius; in Merlin, Crabbe, and the Roman edition, Avinius.]

[Note: One manuscript has Majorianus. The Roman edition, following Merlin, then has Porturianus; the same edition has Trispulus; Merlin and Crabbe, together with the Isidorian manuscripts, have Crispolis. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 123, Posthumianus, bishop of the people of Tagora, and in chapter 128, Crispulus, bishop of the church of Volitana, are mentioned.]

[Note: In the Navarrese manuscript and the Isidorian Collation: Leucianus. Two Colbertine and the Corbie manuscripts, as in Merlin: Leutius. Another Colbertine manuscript: Lucius; the Carthaginian Collation supports this reading. The Vatican has Leontius; the German manuscript, Eleutius. The Roman edition then has Macinus; Merlin, Marinus; Crabbe, Marinianus. In the Carthaginian Collation two bishops named Marianus are recorded.]

[Note: Quesnel and two Colbertine manuscripts have Magerius; another Colbertine, Magarus; the Pithoean, Megarius; the Capuchin Isidorian Collation, Magorus; Merlin, Crabbe, and the Roman edition, Magarius. On the authority of the Corbie and German manuscripts, as well as the Augustinian edition, we restore Megasius.]

[Note: The manuscripts read this way, except that one Colbertine has Rufianus, as does Quesnel. Crabbe and the Roman edition have Sufinianus.]

[Note: Garner’s conjecture, by which he thinks Proculianus should be read, is supported by none of our manuscripts. From the Corbie and German manuscripts, and from the new edition of Augustine, the name Severus is supplied; it is absent from the other manuscripts and editions.]

[Note: In one manuscript, as in Quesnel, item is placed here first; in five others, as in Augustine, it is absent. In the Roman edition, Crabbe, and Merlin, Quodvultdeus is missing here. Indeed, the same name is also omitted earlier in the Isidorian manuscripts.]

[Note: Augustine has this form, as do the Corbie and German manuscripts. Other books, however, have Pelagius.]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has Bazathinus; another Vatican manuscript, Bizatenus; two other Colbertine manuscripts and the Pithoean, together with the Roman edition and Quesnel, Bazacenus; Merlin and Crabbe, Bazecenus; Isidore, Batecenus. We follow Augustine, whose reading agrees with the Corbie and German manuscripts.]

[Note: Augustine has Inventius. The Roman edition, Quesnel, Crabbe, and Merlin, following the Pithoean manuscript, have Juventius. Isidore has Viventius. Other manuscripts have Invenitus.]

[Note: The printed editions and the manuscripts just mentioned, with which Isidore now agrees, retain here as well Inventius or Juventius, and Quesnel prefixed item to the name. The Corbie manuscript here reads Juventinitus, but in the reply it has the name Invenitus; this is also retained here by two Colbertine manuscripts and the German manuscript.]

[Col. 0564B]

[Note: The first printed edition of Augustine, on the authority of the Corbie and German manuscripts, added here and the others.]

[Col. 0564C] 1. When, as was customary, we had solemnly come to the Church of Carthage, and a synod had been assembled from among us for various reasons, our fellow presbyter Orosius gave us a letter from our holy brethren and fellow priests Heros and Lazarus, whose text we have decided should be appended here. After it had been read, we recognized that Pelagius and Coelestius, authors of an utterly criminal error, must be accused and anathematized by all of us.

[Note: The manuscripts of Isidore have Nerotis or Anerotis. The council editions have Averothis. The individuals were Heros, bishop of Arles, and Lazarus, bishop of Aix. Both, driven from their sees, presented to Eulogius of Caesarea, after reaching Palestine, a written accusation against Pelagius and Coelestius. By his authority the Synod of Diospolis was subsequently convened in 415. The letter of those bishops mentioned here has been lost.]

Accordingly, we asked that a review be made of what had been discussed here at the Church of Carthage nearly five years earlier concerning the name of Coelestius. When this had been read, as your holiness will be able to perceive from what follows, although the judgment was manifest and it might have seemed that at that time this single wound had been cut out of the Church by episcopal judgment, nevertheless, after common deliberation, we judged that the authors of such a persuasion—even though Coelestius himself is also said afterward to have attained the presbyterate—ought to be anathematized unless they most openly anathematized these teachings themselves. Thus, if their own healing could not be secured, at least the healing of those who had been or might be deceived by them could be secured, once they had learned the judgment issued against them.

[Note: We supply the verb “were accused,” which was previously lacking, with the Augustinian edition on the basis of the Corbie and German manuscripts. From the same sources, and from the Pithoean manuscript, we restore “to be anathematized” instead of “to be anathematized” in the alternative form.]

We have therefore thought that this action should be reported to your holy charity, so that the authority of the apostolic see may be added to the decrees of our humble body, for the protection of the salvation of many and also for the correction of the perversity of some.

2. For these men are engaged in this by their damnable arguments: not by defending free will, but rather by exalting it in sacrilegious pride, they leave no place for the grace of God, by which we are Christians and by which the faculty of our will itself truly becomes free, when it is liberated from the domination of carnal desires. As the Lord says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). This assistance is obtained by the faith that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

[Note: The sentence “which faith, in Christ Jesus our Lord, obtains as assistance” is omitted in the Corbie and German manuscripts.]

But these men assert, as we have learned from brethren who have also read their books, that God’s grace is to be understood in this respect: that he established and created human nature in such a way that, through its own will, it can fulfill the law of God, whether that law was naturally written in the heart or given in written form. They likewise say that the same law belongs to grace because God gave it to human beings as an aid.

But they are entirely unwilling to acknowledge that grace by which, as has been said, we are Christians—the grace of which the Apostle is the herald when he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22–25)—although they do not dare openly to attack it either (1 Corinthians 2:14).

3. But what else are they doing when they persist in persuading animal human beings, who do not perceive the things of God’s Spirit, that human nature alone is sufficient for working out and perfecting righteousness and fulfilling God’s commandments? They pay no attention to what is written: “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Romans 8:26); and: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16); and that we are one body in Christ Jesus, while individually we are members of one another, possessing different gifts according to the grace given to us (Romans 12:5); and: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10); and: “Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57); and: “Not because we are competent to think anything as coming from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5); and: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be God’s and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7); and countless other passages which, if we wished to gather them from all the Scriptures, would not fit into a single volume.

[Note: Augustine has tempus, “time,” as do the Corbie and German manuscripts. We retain tomus, “volume,” with the other books. Among the ancients this word commonly denoted a synodal letter. Thus Athanasius entitled the letter of the Alexandrian Synod to the Antiochenes a tomus, and the Council of Constantinople called the letter of the Antiochene council to Damasus, in its letter 13, section 4, a tomus. The synodal letter of Damasus itself is designated by the same council, in canon 5, by the name tomus. The word is used in this sense frequently in the Council of Chalcedon—for example, in the edition of Labbe, volume IV, pages 187d, 264d, and 494e. Leo’s famous letter to Flavian is also commonly called a tomus. Sometimes tomus means a summary of a longer discourse, and it is used in that sense in the preface of the Eighth Council of Toledo. Literally, however, it means a section. As for the Africans, they seem to mean here only that they would exceed the customary length of a letter if they collected all the testimonies relevant to their case.]

And we fear that, by mentioning these very things to you, we may seem to be acting improperly, since you proclaim these things with such greater grace from the apostolic see.

[Note: The Roman edition and the council editions, following Crabbe, have “with greater grace”; the other books more fittingly read “with which greater grace.”]

But we do so because, the weaker each of us is, the more attentive each is thought to be in preaching the word of God in every direction; and consequently we endure them everywhere rising up more frequently and more boldly.

4. Therefore, even if Pelagius, according to the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East at the Synod of Diospolis, seemed rightly absolved to your veneration, nevertheless the error and impiety itself—which already has many advocates scattered in different places—must be anathematized by the authority of the apostolic see.

Let your holiness consider, and sympathize with us in our pastoral compassion, how pestilential and destructive to Christ’s sheep is what necessarily follows from these men’s sacrilegious arguments: that we ought not to pray that we enter not into temptation, although the Lord both instructed his disciples to do so and included it in the prayer he taught (Matthew 6:13); or that our faith should not fail, although he himself testified that he had prayed this for the Apostle Peter (Luke 22:32).

For if these matters have been placed within the power of nature and the choice of the will, who would not see that they are vainly requested from the Lord and deceptively prayed for, when in prayer people ask for what is already obtained by the sufficient powers of nature as it was created? The Lord Jesus ought not then to have said, “Watch and pray” (Matthew 24:41), but merely, “Watch, lest you enter into temptation.” Nor ought he to have said to blessed Peter, the first of the Apostles, “I have prayed for you,” but rather, “I warn you, or command and order you, that your faith should not fail” (Luke 22:32).

The contention of these men also contradicts our blessings, so that we seem to say over the people in vain whatever we ask from the Lord for them—that by living rightly and piously they may please him—or what the Apostle prays for the faithful when he says: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit” (Ephesians 3:14–16).

If, therefore, in blessing the people, we wish to say: “Lord, grant that he may be strengthened with power through your Spirit,” their argument contradicts us, asserting that free will is denied if we ask God for what lies within our power. For, they say, if we wish to be strengthened with power, we can do so by that capacity of nature which we did not receive now but received when we were created.

5. They also deny that infants should be baptized for the salvation given through Christ the Savior. Thus, by this deadly doctrine, they kill them eternally, promising that even if they are not baptized they will possess eternal life, and that they do not belong among those of whom the Lord says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

For, they say, these infants were not lost, and there is nothing in them to be saved or redeemed at so great a price: nothing in them has been corrupted, nothing is held captive under the devil’s power, and Christ’s blood was not poured out for them—the blood which, as we read, was poured out for the remission of sins.

[Note: The Pithoean manuscript has “would have been poured out”; Isidore, together with the Roman and council editions, has “to have been poured out,” omitting the following “which was poured out.” We restore the text from the better manuscripts. Christ’s blood, which was to be poured out for the remission of sins, is read at Matthew 26:28.]

Nevertheless, Coelestius has already confessed in a written statement at the Church of Carthage that through Christ’s baptism redemption also takes place for infants.

[Note: The Roman edition, following Merlin, wrongly adds dicunt, “they say,” here. Augustine expresses this same matter concerning Coelestius in Letter 157, section 22: “He was compelled to confess, on account of the baptism of infants, that redemption is necessary for them also.” Although, he says, Coelestius did not wish to speak more explicitly about original sin, nevertheless, by the very term “redemption,” he imposed a considerable obligation upon himself.]

But many who are said or are known to have been their disciples do not cease to affirm, by every means at their disposal, these evils by which they are attempting to overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith.

[Note: The Roman and council editions have “by every possible cunning.” On the authority of all the manuscripts, we remove the word “cunning.”]

[Col. 0568B] 6. Therefore, even if Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or say that they have never held these views, and deny that any writings produced against them are theirs, so that there is no way of convicting them of falsehood, nevertheless anyone who teaches and asserts that human nature is sufficient for overcoming sins and carrying out God’s commandments by its own power, and in this way proves to be an adversary of the grace of God—a grace displayed most clearly in the prayers of the saints—and anyone who denies that infants are liberated from perdition through Christ’s baptism and receive everlasting salvation: let him be anathema.

[Note: In the first hand of the Corbie manuscript: “for supporting”; in a later correction, “for avoiding.” This reading is also preferred in the German manuscript and in Augustine’s edition. We nevertheless retain “for overcoming,” both on the authority of the greater number of manuscripts and because later, in Letter 28, section 13, five bishops again write that Pelagius defended the capacity of nature for overcoming sins and fulfilling commandments. For this reason he had also been compelled at the Synod of Diospolis to confess that, when we fight against temptations and unlawful desires, victory comes not from our own will but from God’s assistance.]

As for whatever other charges are brought against them, we do not doubt that your veneration, when you have examined the episcopal proceedings of the Palestinian synod, said to have been conducted in the East concerning this same matter, will judge in such a way that we may all rejoice in God’s mercy. Pray for us, most blessed lord Pope.

## LETTER XXVII. OF THE COUNCIL OF MILEVIS TO POPE INNOCENT

That by his authority he may restrain as quickly as possible the pernicious heresy of the enemies of Christ’s grace.

To the most blessed, deservedly venerable, and honored in Christ, Pope Innocent: Silvanus, an elder, Valentinus, Aurelius, Donatus, Restitutus, Lucianus, Alypius, Augustine, Placentianus, Severus, Fortunatus, Possidius, Novatus, Secundus, Maurentius, Leo, Faustinianus, Cresconius, Malchus, Litorius, Fortunatus, Donatus, Ponticanus, Saturninus, Cresconius, Honorius, Lucius, Adeodatus, Processus, Cresconius, Secundus, Felix, Asiaticus, Rufinianus, Faustinus, Servus, Terentius, Cresconius, Sperantius, Quadratus, Lucillus, Sabinus, Faustinus, Cresconius, Victor, Gigantius, Possidonius, Antoninus, Innocentius, Praesidius, Crescentius, Felix, Antoninus, Victor, Honoratus, Donatus, Petrus, Praesidius, Cresconius, Lampadius, and Delphinus, from the council of Milevis, send greetings in the Lord.

[Note: The Roman and Augustinian editions omit senex, “elder,” although the word appears in all our manuscripts. The same Silvanus is called an elder of the Church of Summensis by Augustine, at the end of Letter 128, and is subscribed as of the first see of the province of Numidia at the end of Letter 129. Among the Africans, senex and primas are equivalent, because primacy was conferred upon the one who was senior by ordination.]

[Note: Merlin and Crabbe, with one manuscript, have Lictorius. Other council editions, following the Roman edition, have Victorius. The remaining books have Litorius or Littorius. In the Carthaginian Collation, chapter 133, Litorius is called bishop of Suavis.]

[Note: The Pithoean manuscript and one Colbertine have Ponticianus. Two others, together with Merlin, Crabbe, and Quesnel, have Pontianus.]

[Note: The Roman and Augustinian editions have Christonius. Other printed editions, as well as all our manuscripts, have Cresconius. That the name Cresconius or Crisconius was familiar among the Africans is shown by the Carthaginian Collation, where several bishops of different sees are recorded under that name.]

[Note: Five of our manuscripts, together with Merlin, Crabbe, and Quesnel, have Rufinus.]

[Note: Quesnel, Labbe, Crabbe, and Merlin once again have Sabinus in place of Faustinus, as it is repeated in the Isidorian copies; the better manuscripts disagree.]

[Note: Augustine has Gignantius. The names of this bishop and the nine following him are omitted in the council editions through the customary scribal error caused by the repeated name Victor.]

[Note: The Isidorian manuscripts and two other Colbertine manuscripts, together with the Pithoean, have Innocentius and Felix, omitting the names Praesidius and Crescentius.]

1. Since the Lord has placed you in the apostolic see as a special gift of his grace, and has granted you to our times in such a way that, if we kept silent before your veneration about matters that ought to be brought forward for the Church, this would count against us as negligence more than you could receive them either with disdain or carelessness, we ask that you deign to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers threatening the weakened members of Christ.

2. For a new and exceedingly pernicious heresy, arising from the enemies of Christ’s grace, is attempting to raise itself up. By their impious arguments they are even trying to take away from us the Lord’s Prayer.

For when the Lord taught us to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), these men say that a person can attain in this life, once he knows God’s commandments, such perfection of righteousness through the mere choice of free will and without the help of the Savior’s grace that it is no longer necessary for him to say, “Forgive us our debts.”

As for what follows—“Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13)—they say that it should not be understood as though we ought to ask for divine assistance, lest, when tempted, we fall into sin. Rather, they say, this lies within our power, and the human will alone is sufficient to fulfill it—as though the Apostle had said in vain, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16); and, “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

The Lord also would have said in vain to the Apostle Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), and to all his own, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 24:41), if all this lies within human power.

[Note: The Roman and council editions have “if they are instructed by no,” a reading supported by the manuscripts. Garner and Augustine have “are renewed.” The reading “although they receive no Christian-grace sacraments” is supported by the statement in the preceding letter, section 5: “promising that even if they are not baptized, they will possess eternal life.” It is therefore clear that the sacraments of Christian grace here mean baptism.]

They contend, with a presumption that is by no means Christian, that little children will possess eternal life even if they receive none of the sacraments of Christian grace,

[Note: In place of nequaquam, “not at all,” Garner substitutes nequam, “wickedly”; this was then transferred into the Augustinian edition. The ambiguity disappears if one reads praesumptione nequaquam Christiana, “not at all with Christian presumption.”]

thereby nullifying what the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12); and elsewhere: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

To pass over their many other arguments against the holy Scriptures, how can faithful hearts endure these two things by which they are attempting entirely to overthrow all that makes us Christians: that God should not be asked to be our helper against the evil of sin and for the working of righteousness, and that the sacrament of Christian grace should not assist little children in obtaining eternal life?

[Note: Garner has “cannot endure,” adding a negative particle contrary to the authority of the ancient manuscripts and without necessity.]

3. In making these matters known to your apostolic heart, we have no need to say much or to exaggerate such great impiety in words. Without doubt, these things will move you so deeply that you cannot altogether disregard correcting them, lest they spread more widely and contaminate—or rather destroy—many, while under Christ’s name they utterly estrange them from Christ’s grace.

[Note: Quesnel and Augustine have “may move you in this way.”]

The authors of this most pernicious error are said to be Pelagius and Coelestius. We prefer that they be healed within the Church rather than cut off from the Church with their salvation despaired of, if no necessity compels otherwise.

One of them, Coelestius, is also said to have attained the presbyterate in Asia.

[Note: Marcellinus Mercator relates the matter as follows in the Commonitorium, chapter 1, edition of Baluze, page 133: “Coelestius, accused in the Carthaginian council on six charges and ordered to condemn them, refused in every way to comply and was deprived of ecclesiastical communion. He believed that an appeal should be made from this sentence to the judgment of the Roman bishop. But, soon disregarding the same appeal, he went to Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there dared, by stealth, to seek the presbyterate.” Earlier, toward the end of 411, according to Augustine, Letter 157, section 22, while staying at Carthage, he had already begun to insinuate himself into the honor of the presbyterate in the church of that city. But because of these very arguments against Christ’s grace, the brothers, with the most faithful freedom, brought him before episcopal judgment. A letter of Nestorius to him is preserved in Marcellinus Mercator, page 131, addressed “to the honorable and most religious presbyter Coelestius.”]

As for what happened concerning him a few years ago, your holiness is better informed by the Church of Carthage.

[Note: That is, because the Church or synod of Carthage had appended to the preceding Letter 26 the proceedings of another council held at Carthage nearly five years earlier concerning Coelestius. Since both this letter of the Council of Milevis and the Carthaginian letter were delivered to Innocent together by the same bishop Julius, there was no need for Garner to replace the reading with “so that he may be better informed.”]

Pelagius, however, as letters sent by some of our brethren report, is said to be deceiving certain people while staying at Jerusalem. Nevertheless, many more who have been able to investigate his views more carefully are fighting against him on behalf of Christ’s grace and the truth of the Catholic faith, especially your holy son, our brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.

But we believe that, with the help of the mercy of our Lord God, who deigns both to direct you when you consult him and to hear you when you pray, by the authority of your holiness—an authority drawn from that of the holy Scriptures—it will be easier for those who hold such perverse and pernicious opinions to yield, so that we may rejoice more in their correction than grieve at their destruction, most blessed lord.

[Note: The Isidorian manuscripts have “drawn from the clear,” arising from the ignorance of a scribe who had read de scarum in his exemplar, that is, de sanctarum, “from the holy.” The Capuchin manuscript, in a later correction, has “drawn from the declaration of the holy Scriptures.” The Roman and council editions consequently read “drawn from the clear light of the Scriptures.” The better manuscripts supply the more genuine reading. Here the fathers of the Council of Milevis indicate that the authority of the Roman pontiff is itself supported by the authority of the Scriptures.]

Whatever they themselves may choose, your venerability sees that we must urgently and speedily provide at least for the many others whom they can entangle in their snares if they are left unchallenged.

We have sent these words to your holiness from the Council of Numidia, imitating the Church of Carthage and our fellow bishops of the province of Carthage, whom we have learned to have written to the apostolic see, which you, blessed one, glorify, concerning this matter.

[Note: The Roman edition and Garner omit “the Church of Carthage”; those words are restored from the other books.]

(And in another hand:) May you, most blessed, deservedly venerable, and honored in Christ, holy Pope, increase in God’s grace, remembering us.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: Augustine mentions this letter in On Original Sin, chapter 9, and in Letter formerly 47, now 215, section 12, as having been written by five bishops. Accordingly, it was not improperly entitled “of the five bishops” in the council editions.
