The same Doctor, in Letter formerly 106, now 186, section 2, calls it, in contrast with the preceding synodal letters, a private letter.]

OF THE FIVE BISHOPS TO POPE INNOCENT

They expose and refute the heresy of Pelagius, by which he contended that human nature alone, through free will, was sufficient for subduing desires, overcoming temptations, and fulfilling God’s commandments. They show that wherever he preached grace, he understood by it either free will, or the remission of sins, or the commandment of the law, while the faithful understand something else by the proper name “grace.” They also explain in what sense his statement that a person can be without sin if he wishes may be true, and in what sense it may be said tolerably, even if not without error.

To the most blessed and deservedly most honored brother, Pope Innocent: Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius send greetings in the Lord.

1. From the two councils of the provinces of Carthage and Numidia we have sent letters, subscribed by a considerable number of bishops, to your holiness against the enemies of Christ’s grace. They trust in their own strength and, in a certain sense, say to our Creator: “You made us human beings; we made ourselves righteous.” They say that human nature is free precisely so that they need not seek a liberator; it is sound precisely so that they may judge a savior unnecessary.

For they say that nature is so powerful that, by the powers once received at the origin of its creation, it can, through free will and without any further help from the grace of the one who created it, subdue and extinguish every desire and overcome every temptation.

Many of them rise up against us and say to our soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm 3:3). But Christ’s household, which says, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10),

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “then I am stronger,” which another manuscript also seems originally to have read.]

and to which its Lord says, “I am your salvation” (Psalm 34:3), awaits the Lord’s assistance with a heart suspended in fear and trembling, also through the charity of your veneration.

2. For we have heard that in the city of Rome, where Pelagius lived for a long time, there are some who favor him for various reasons: some, evidently, because he is said to have persuaded them of such things;

[Note: Quesnel reads this way from the Oxford manuscript, and the new Augustinian edition follows him. The words that Innocent writes in reply agree with this. Merlin and Crabbe have: “who are said to have persuaded us of such things”; Crabbe added in the margin, “who are said to have persuaded you,” and the Roman and other council editions consequently read, “because you are said to have persuaded them of such things.” The manuscripts offer similar readings, except that most have perhibentur, “are said,” instead of perhibent, “they say,” and one Colbertine and one Vatican have perhibetur, “it is said.” The Vatican also reads quia vobis, “because to you.” A suitable reading could therefore be constructed as: “because he is said to have persuaded you of such things.” For the Pelagians, according to Possidius, chapter 18, attempted by their ambition to persuade the holy see of their false belief. What they had been unable to accomplish, they falsely boasted that they had accomplished. Among those whom they boasted they had persuaded at Rome of their perverse doctrines, the chief was Xystus, then a presbyter and later supreme pontiff. After the slander had been exposed, Augustine congratulates him in Letter formerly 104, now 191, section 1, as follows: “For what could be more pleasant to read or hear than so pure a defense of grace against its enemies from the mouth of one who was being proclaimed a significant patron of those same enemies?” See also his Letter 194, section 1.]

but more favor him because they do not believe that he holds such views, especially since ecclesiastical proceedings are said to have taken place in the East, where he resides, by which he is thought to have been cleared.

If the bishops there pronounced him Catholic, this must be thought to have happened for no other reason than that he said he confessed God’s grace and that a person could live righteously by his own labor and will, while not denying that God’s grace helped him to do so.

Upon hearing these words, the Catholic bishops could not have understood any other grace of God than that which they were accustomed to read in God’s books and preach to God’s peoples—namely, the grace of which the Apostle says: “I do not nullify the grace of God; for if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21)—without doubt, the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness, not the grace by which we were created with our own will.

For if those bishops had understood him to be speaking of the grace that we share even with the ungodly, with whom we are human beings, while denying the grace by which we are Christians and children of God, which Catholic priest, we ask, would not have heard him patiently, but would have kept the matter before his eyes?

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts alone have “before his eyes,” with somewhat greater emphasis. Augustine explains how Pelagius confessed God’s grace at the aforesaid synod in On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapters 6 and 7, and afterward, in chapter 10, explains how he detected that Pelagius had there deceitfully confessed God’s grace.]

Therefore the judges are not to be blamed, because they heard the word “grace” according to ecclesiastical custom, not knowing what such people habitually disseminate either in the books of their teaching or into the ears of their followers.

### 3

The issue is not one Pelagius, who perhaps has by now been corrected—would that it were so!—but so many others, whose loquacious arguments drag along weak and uninstructed souls as though [Note: Merlin has *conjunctas* (“joined together”); the Roman edition, the more recent editions of the councils, and Garner have *convictas* (“overcome”); the new edition of Augustine has *vinctas* (“bound”). With Crabbe and the better manuscripts, we prefer *convictas*, as though they were bound together at the same time. *Devinctas* (“deeply bound”) would not be objectionable, in view of what Innocent writes in Letter 31, §2: “If, then, there are some whom such great perversity has bound in its defense.” The word found in Isidore’s examples, *pervinctas*, is also close to this.] defeated, and weary by the very controversy those who are firm and steadfast in faith. Everything is already filled with such cases.

Therefore either he must be summoned to Rome by Your Reverence and carefully questioned about what grace he means—if indeed he now acknowledges any grace—by which he admits that human beings are helped to avoid sin and live justly; [Col. 0573C] or this very matter must be discussed with him by letter. When he is found to mean the grace taught by ecclesiastical and apostolic truth, he must then be absolved without any scruple on the Church’s part and without any hiding-place for ambiguity; then indeed we should rejoice at his purification.

### 4

For whether he says that grace is free will, or that grace is the remission of sins, or that grace is the commandment of the law, he says none of the things that, through the supply of the Holy Spirit, pertain to overcoming desire and temptations—[Col. 0574A] through the supply of the Holy Spirit, whom he who ascended into heaven poured out most abundantly upon us, “taking captivity captive and giving gifts to human beings” (Tit. 3:6).

For this reason we pray that we may be able to overcome the temptation of sin (Eph. 4:8), and that the Spirit of God, from whom we have received the pledge, may help our weakness (Rom. 8:26). But whoever prays and says, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13), certainly does not pray that he may be a human being, which he is by nature; nor does he pray that he may possess free will, which he already received when nature itself was created; nor does he pray for the remission of sins, since that has already been said: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12); nor does he pray that he may receive a commandment. Rather, he plainly prays that he may carry out the commandment.

For if he is led into temptation—that is, if he fails in temptation—he certainly commits the sin that is contrary to the commandment. He therefore prays that he may not sin, that is, that he may do nothing evil. This is what the Apostle prays for the Corinthians when he says: “We pray to the Lord that you do nothing evil” (2 Cor. 13:7).

It is therefore sufficiently clear that, although free choice of the will undoubtedly exists, its power is nevertheless insufficient for not sinning—that is, for doing no evil—unless weakness is helped. The prayer itself, then, is the clearest testimony to grace. Let him acknowledge this, and we shall rejoice in him, whether he has become sound or has been corrected.

### 5

Law and grace must be distinguished. The law knows how to command; grace knows how to help. Nor would the law command if there were no will; nor would grace help if will were sufficient.

We are commanded to have understanding where it says, “Do not be like the horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9); yet we pray to have understanding where it says, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:125).

We are commanded to have wisdom where it says, “Fools, become wise at last!” (Ps. 93:8); yet we pray to have wisdom where it says, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given him” (Jas. 1:5).

We are commanded to have self-control where it says, [Note: Thus Merlin, Crabbe, Garner, and our manuscripts. It is nevertheless clear that something is missing here. For this reason the Roman editor added the following in brackets and in another typeface: “[Something of this sort is missing: Let your loins be girded; and yet we pray that it be given to us, where it says …]” This addition was retained in some later editions. Quesnel substituted for it: “Turn away from your pleasures, and yet we pray to have self-control, where it says …” Neither supplement is satisfactory. The manner in which the passage should be restored can be learned from another similar passage in Augustine. In Letter 147 to Hilary, §9, treating the same argument, the Doctor writes: “When the Law says, ‘You shall not desire,’ what else does it seem to command except self-control from unlawful desires? … and yet we pray to have self-control, where it says, ‘When I knew that no one could be self-controlled unless God gave it …’” He then concludes: “God therefore commands self-control and gives self-control.” The present passage will therefore be complete according to Augustine’s meaning if we restore it as follows: “We are commanded to have self-control where it says, ‘You shall not desire’; yet we pray to have self-control where it says, ‘When I knew …,’ and so forth.” The repetition of nearly the same words immediately afterward, a fertile source of lacunae, occasioned this difficulty.]

“When I knew that no one could be self-controlled unless God gave it—and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was—I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wis. 8:21).

Finally, so that it may not be too lengthy to go through everything, we are commanded not to do evil where it says, “Turn away from evil” (Ps. 36:27); yet we pray not to do evil where it says, “We pray to the Lord that you do nothing evil” (2 Cor. 13:7).

We are commanded to do good where it says, “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27); yet we pray to do good where it says, “We do not cease praying and asking for you” (Col. 1:9), and among the other things for which he prays for them, he says: “That you may walk worthily of God in every pleasing work, in every good work and word” (Col. 1:10).

Therefore, just as we recognize the will when these things are commanded, so let him recognize grace when they are requested.

### 6

We have sent Your Reverence a book given by certain religious and honorable young servants of God, whose names we shall not conceal: they are called Timasius and James. As we have heard—and as you also know—they abandoned the hope they had placed in the world at the exhortation of Pelagius himself, and now serve God in continence.

When, through some work of ours inspired by the Lord, they had at last been freed from the same error, they produced the book, saying that it belonged to Pelagius, and earnestly requested that a reply be made to it. This was done: the reply itself was sent back to them (*Augustine’s Book on Nature and Grace*); they wrote back with thanks (*Letter preserved in Augustine, now Letter 168*).

We are sending both: the work to which the reply was made and the reply itself. And, so that we might not be excessively burdensome, we have marked the places where we ask you not to consider it onerous to examine how, when the charge was brought against him that he denied the grace of God, he answered in such a way that he said grace was nothing except the nature in which God created us.

### 7

But if he denies that this book is his, or denies that the passages in the book are his, we do not press the matter. Let him anathematize them and openly acknowledge the grace that Christian teaching demonstrates and proclaims to belong properly to Christians—a grace that is not nature, but by which nature is saved. [Note: This passage was restored in the latest edition of Augustine from a Vatican manuscript, supported also by two Colbertine manuscripts. In the other books, except Merlin’s edition, the words “which … nourishes nature” are lacking. Quesnel retained only the first of those three words. In the same books, as well as in Merlin’s edition, the words “just as a planter and irrigator” occur; Quesnel removed the particle *sicut* (“just as”).]

This grace does not nourish nature by teaching that merely sounds in the ears, or by some visible assistance, like a planter and irrigator working externally; rather, it does so through the supply of the Spirit and hidden mercy, “as God does, who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

For although it may be said, in a certain unobjectionable sense, that the grace of God is the grace by which we were created, so that we might exist at all—and not exist in the manner of a corpse that does not live, or a tree that does not feel, or an animal that does not understand, but as human beings who exist, live, feel, and understand, and are able to give thanks to our Creator for so great a benefit—[Note: The Roman edition has *agere debeamus* (“we ought to give thanks”), which is corrected from the other books.] and although this may rightly be called grace because it was bestowed not on account of the merits of any preceding works but from God’s gratuitous goodness, there is nevertheless another grace by which we are called predestined, justified, and glorified, so that we may say: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:31–32).

### 8

The question concerned this grace when those whom Pelagius was seriously offending and disturbing told him that he was attacking it in his arguments, by which he asserted that, for both doing and completing the divine commandments, human nature was sufficient for itself through free will.

Apostolic teaching not without reason calls this grace by that name, the grace by which we are saved and justified through faith in Christ. [Note: Merlin, Crabbe, and the edition of Augustine add *non immerito* (“not without reason”) here.] Of this it is written: “I do not nullify the grace of God; for if justification is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21).

Of this it is written: “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen away from grace” (Gal. 5:4).

Of this it is written: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. 11:6).

Of this it is written: “To one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt; but to one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4:4–5).

There are many other passages, which you yourself can remember better, understand more wisely, and proclaim more eloquently.

But although we understand that the grace by which we were created as human beings may not improperly be called grace, it is nevertheless surprising if we read it called by that name in any legal, prophetic, evangelical, or apostolic writings.

### 9

Since, then, the question put to him concerned this grace, so well known to Christian and Catholic believers, so that he might cease attacking it, what is one to make of the fact that, when he himself had raised this very charge against himself in his book, as though from the person of an opponent, in order to clear himself by his answer, he replied with nothing other than that the grace of the Creator should be referred to the nature of the created human being? [Note: Quesnel alone has *naturam creati referri ad gratiam creatoris* (“that the nature of the created [human being] should be referred to the Creator’s grace”). *Referre* here means to exhibit or represent something in oneself. Augustine transcribes and reports Pelagius’s own words (*On Nature and Grace*, ch. 51) as follows: “The very possibility of not sinning lies not so much in the power of free choice as in the necessity of nature. Whatever is placed in the necessity of nature is undoubtedly attributed to the author of nature, namely God. How, then, can that be thought to exist without God’s grace which is shown to belong properly to God?” Augustine immediately says that the hidden opinion has been expressed there. Pelagius attributes the possibility of not sinning to God’s grace because God is the author of the nature into which he says the possibility of not sinning has been inseparably implanted.]

Is this how he says that righteousness can be fulfilled without sin through free will [Col. 0576D] with the help of divine grace—that God gave this to human beings in the very possibility of nature?

### 10

The proper answer is therefore: “Then the offense of the cross has been abolished” (Gal. 5:11). “Then Christ died for nothing” (Rom. 4:25). [Note: The Roman edition and the editions of the councils have *Non enim* (“For not”). Merlin and Crabbe subsequently have *nec ascendisset in altum et captivans* (“nor would he have ascended on high and, taking captive”); the Roman edition and Labbe have *nec ascendens in altum, captivans* (“nor, ascending on high, taking captive”).]

For if he had not died on account of our sins and risen on account of our justification, and had not ascended on high, taking captivity captive and giving gifts to human beings, would this possibility of nature that he defends not have existed in human beings (Eph. 4:8; Ps. 67:19)?

Or was God’s commandment perhaps lacking, and did Christ therefore die? On the contrary, it was already holy, just, and good (Rom. 7:12). It had already been said, “You shall not desire” (Exod. 20:17); it had already been said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18). The Apostle says that the whole law is fulfilled in this saying (Rom. 13:9).

And because no one loves himself unless he loves God, the Lord says that the whole law and the Prophets depend upon these two commandments (Matt. 22:40). These two commandments had therefore already been divinely given to human beings.

Or had the eternal reward of righteousness not yet been promised? Pelagius himself does not say this, since in his writings he asserted that the kingdom of heaven had also been promised in the Old Testament.

If, then, the possibility of nature through free will already existed for doing and completing righteousness; if the holy, just, and good commandment of God’s law already existed; and if the eternal reward had already been promised, then Christ died for nothing.

### 11

Therefore righteousness comes neither through the law nor through the possibility of nature, but from faith and the gift of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, the one mediator between God and human beings.

If he had not died in the fullness of time on account of our sins and risen on account of our justification (Rom. 4:25), surely the faith of the ancients, as well as ours, would be abolished. But once faith is abolished, what righteousness remains for a human being, since “the righteous person lives by faith” (Heb. 10:38; Rom. 1:17)?

Since through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12), clearly no one was or is liberated from this body of death, where another law opposes the law of the mind (Rom. 7:21, 24), by his own possibility, which, having been lost, needs a redeemer and, having been wounded, needs a savior. [Note: Some manuscripts incorrectly have *suae possibilitas*. This gave an antiquarian occasion, in a second revision of the Navarrese edition and perhaps elsewhere, to add *naturae*. Hence the printed editions, except Augustine’s, have *suae possibilitas naturae*. Below, in Innocent’s Letter 29, §3, we shall read, apparently from our possibility altogether—*ex nostra in totum simus possibilitate perfecti*—without the word *naturae*. See below, Letter 30, §4.]

Rather, liberation comes through the grace of God, through faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), who, although he was God, made man and, remaining God, having become man, himself restored what he had made.

### 12

I think he is unaware that the faith of Christ, which later came into revelation, existed secretly in the times of our fathers. Through it, nevertheless, all those were liberated by the grace of God who, throughout all the ages of the human race, were able to be liberated—by God’s hidden judgment, though not one deserving blame.

Hence the Apostle says: “Having the same spirit of faith” [namely, the same one that they also had], “according to what is written” (2 Cor. 4:13): “I believed, and therefore I spoke; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (Ps. 115:1).

That is why the Mediator himself says: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

That is why Melchizedek, having brought forth the sacrament of the Lord’s table, knew how to foreshadow his eternal priesthood (Gen. 14:18).

When the Law had then been given in writing—the Law which, as the Apostle says, entered in so that the offense might increase (Rom. 5:20), and of which he says, “If the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise”—what, then, is the purpose of the Law?

“It was added because of transgressions” [Note: Quesnel and Augustine, following the Pithoean manuscript, have *proposita est* (“was appointed”).], until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, “ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one party, but God is one. Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would indeed be from the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:18–22).

Is it not sufficiently shown that the Law was given so that sin might be recognized and increased through transgression? “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). Thus, against the victory of sin, people would flee to divine grace, which is contained in the promises.

In this way the Law would not be against the promises of God, because through it the knowledge of sin comes about, and through transgression of the Law the abundance of sin, so that God’s promises might be sought for liberation—which is the grace of God—and righteousness might begin to exist in a human being, not his own righteousness but God’s, that is, righteousness given as God’s gift.

### 13

Even now some, ignorant of God’s righteousness, as was formerly said concerning the Jews, and wishing to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3).

They imagine that they are justified through the Law, since free will is sufficient for them to keep it—that is, their own righteousness, arising from human nature, rather than righteousness bestowed from divine grace, for which reason it is called God’s righteousness.

Thus it is also written: “Through the Law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:20–21).

When he says, “has been manifested,” he shows that it existed then also, but was hidden at that time as the rain obtained by Gideon was hidden, as it were, in the fleece, whereas now it is manifest as upon the threshing floor (Judg. 6:37).

When, therefore, the Law without grace could not have been the death of sin but its strength—for it is written, “The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the Law” (1 Cor. 15:56)—just as many now flee from the face of reigning sin to grace, which is exposed as upon the threshing floor, so at that time few fled to it, as though it were hidden in the fleece.

This distribution of the ages pertains to the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, concerning which it is said: “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

### 14

Therefore, if both before the time of the Law and during the time of the Law the righteous fathers who lived by faith were justified not by the possibility of weak nature—[Note: The Roman edition, the editions of the councils, and many manuscripts have *indignae* (“unworthy”), arising from *indiguae*; for the ancients liked to write the word *indigae* in that form.] needy, corrupted, and sold under sin—but by God’s grace through faith, and if that same grace, now brought into the open and revealed, justifies us, let Pelagius anathematize his writings in which he argues against it—not through defiance, but through ignorance—by defending the possibility of nature for conquering sins and fulfilling the commandments.

Or, if he denies that these writings are his, or says that passages which he denies to be his were inserted into his writings by his enemies, let him nevertheless anathematize and condemn them, at the paternal exhortation and by the authority of Your Holiness.

If he wishes, then, let him learn to remove the scandal that is burdensome to himself and harmful to the Church. [Note: The Pithoean manuscript has *Ecclesia* (“the Church”), incorrectly. Quesnel published the whole passage as follows: “If he does not wish to learn that it is burdensome and harmful to himself to remove the scandal of the Church, which his hearers …” This is contrary to all the manuscripts and to Innocent’s meaning. The reading he judged less correct fits extremely well with what precedes and follows. The five bishops urge Pelagius to learn how to remove the scandal, which is burdensome to him and harmful to the Church. Nor do they doubt that it will be removed as soon as his disciples learn that the book published under his name has been condemned by Pelagius himself.]

His hearers and those who perversely love him do not cease spreading this scandal everywhere. For if they learn that the same book, which they either think or know to be his, has been anathematized and condemned by the authority of the Catholic bishops, and especially by Your Holiness—whose greater weight with him we have no doubt about—we do not think they will thereafter dare to disturb faithful and sincerely Christian hearts by speaking against the grace of God revealed through the passion and resurrection of Christ.

Rather, with the help of the Lord’s mercy, and with your prayers, which contend alongside us and burn with charity and piety, they will trust not in their own strength but in that same grace, so that they may be not only blessed forever but also just and holy. [Note: Quesnel adds *conari* (“to strive”); it is more correctly absent from the other books.]

Accordingly, we thought that the letter written to him by one of us—to whom he had sent certain writings as records of his purification through a certain Eastern deacon who was also a citizen of Hippo—should instead be directed to Your Blessedness, judging and requesting that you yourself would deign to send it to him. [Note: Quesnel also had no need to add *causa* (“for the sake of” or “on account of”) here. The passage is illuminated by another version in Augustine’s *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, ch. 32: “In the written statement of his defense, which he sent to me through our fellow citizen of Hippo, Charus, who was an Eastern deacon, he did something that differs from what is contained in the episcopal proceedings. But what the proceedings contain is much better, firmer, and clearer in defense of Catholic truth against the plague of that heresy.” It is therefore clear that Pelagius called the writings or proceedings concerning his purification—namely, the falsified proceedings of the Synod of Diospolis that he had sent to Augustine—his “purification.” Augustine speaks again in the same work, ch. 29: “Whatever proceedings of his purification he may produce.” It is no less clear from this that the five bishops refer, under the name of one of their number, to Augustine, whose letter sent at that time has been lost and has not reached us.]

[Note: Quesnel, with one Colbertine manuscript and the Pithoean, has “that you yourself may send it.” The reading of the other books is sounder.] [Note: Quesnel, with one Colbertine manuscript and the Pithoean, has “that you yourself may send it.” The reading of the other books is sounder.] In this way he will prefer to read it rather than reject it, attending more to the person who sent it than to the person who wrote it.

### 15

As for what they say—that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes—although it seems more tolerable when they add that this occurs through the help of grace, which was nevertheless revealed and given through the incarnation of his Only-Begotten Son, it can nevertheless understandably provoke the question of where and when grace accomplishes this in us, so that we are entirely without sin: whether in this life, when the flesh desires against the spirit, or in the other life, when the saying that is written will be fulfilled (Gal. 5:17): “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15:55).

This must be examined more carefully on account of certain others who have held and committed to writing the view that even in this life a human being can be without sin—not from the beginning of birth, but by turning from sins to righteousness, and from a wicked way to a good life (Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke* 1:6). [Note: Garner and Augustine have *a vita* (“from life”). Pelagius at one time adopted the opinion of those under discussion. Augustine reports that Pelagius wrote to him as follows (Letter formerly 252, now 179, §7): “We did not say that anyone can be found who has never sinned from infancy to old age, but that, having turned from sin through his own labor and with the help of God’s grace, he can be without sin.” In the same letter, §8, the same Doctor proves that Pelagius did not always remain in this opinion.]

They understood what is written about Zechariah and Elizabeth—that they walked in all the commandments of the Lord without reproach (Luke 1:6)—in this way. They took the words “without reproach” to mean “without sin,” not denying but rather piously confessing what is found in other passages of their writings: the help of the grace of our Lord, not through the natural spirit of human beings but through the principal Spirit of God.

They seem not to have considered sufficiently that Zechariah himself was certainly a priest. At that time, all priests necessarily had to offer a sacrifice first for their own sins and then for the people, according to God’s law (Lev. 9:7; Heb. 7:27).

Therefore, just as now we are shown by the sacrifice of prayer not to be without sin, since we are commanded to say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), so then, through the sacrifices of animal victims, the priests were shown not to be without sin, since they were commanded to offer sacrifices for their own sins. [Note: One of the Colbertine manuscripts has “through the prayers of sacrifices.”]

If the matter is as follows—that through the grace of the Savior we make progress in this life, desire diminishing and charity increasing, but are perfected in the other life, desire having been extinguished and charity completed—then certainly the statement, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9), [Note: The same manuscript has “Whoever is from God.” Another Colbertine manuscript, together with the Pithoean, has “From God,” omitting “who has been born.”] was spoken with reference to charity itself, which alone does not sin.

For the birth that is from God pertains to charity’s being increased and perfected, not to the desire that must be diminished and consumed. Yet, so long as desire remains in our members, it opposes the law of the mind according to its own law (Rom. 7:20).

But one who is born of God, neither obeying its desires nor presenting his members as weapons of unrighteousness for sin (Rom. 6:13), can say: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:20).

### 16

However this question may stand—for even if no human being is found to be without sin in this life, it is nevertheless said that this can happen through the help of grace and the Spirit of God, and one must strive and ask that it may happen—anyone who is mistaken in this matter is tolerably mistaken.

It is not diabolical impiety but human error to affirm and desire that what one cannot demonstrate may nevertheless be possible. For he believes that something can happen which it is certainly praiseworthy to wish for.

For us, however, it is enough that no one in the Church of God, whatever his progress in excellence and righteousness, is found who dares say that he has no need of the prayer of the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), and says that he has no sin, lest he deceive himself and the truth be absent from him, even though he may already live without reproach (1 John 1).

For it is not every sin arising from human temptation, but grave sin, that brings reproach. [Note: Merlin and Quesnel, with one Colbertine manuscript and the Pithoean, have “whatever the human temptations may be.” The reading of the other manuscripts is more correct: those who are said to live without reproach are to be understood as free from grave sins, but not likewise from lesser sins, which we contract through temptation or human weakness.]

### 17

As for the other matters charged against him, Your Blessedness will undoubtedly judge them according to how he is seen to have defended himself in the proceedings.

The gentleness of your most tender heart will surely pardon us for having sent Your Holiness a letter perhaps longer than you wished. For we are not pouring our little stream back into your abundant fountain in order to increase it; rather, amid this not insignificant trial of the times, from which may he deliver us to whom we say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” we wish you to approve that even our small stream flows from the same source of waters from which your abundant stream also flows, and to be consoled by your replies through our common participation in the one grace. [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts have “not with a small [trial].” The others have *non comparva*. Augustine has “not, however, a small [trial].” Merlin and Crabbe, after the preceding word *refundimus* (“we pour back”), immediately add “but even our own, although small,” omitting the intervening words.]

## LETTER XXIX

[Note: In the edition of the councils, this is Letter 24. What was formerly Letter 29 is now Letter 7.]

Innocent, replying to the bishops of Carthage, praises and confirms their doctrine and judgment against the Pelagian heretics.

## INNOCENT

[Note: The printed editions, except Augustine’s, following the old exemplars of Quesnel’s codex and of Isidore, read: “To Aurelius and all the holy bishops, or others present at the council of the church of Carthage,” omitting the individual bishops’ names, which are listed in the more reliable manuscripts.]

To Aurelius, Numidius, Rusticianus, Fidentianus, Evagrius, Antonius, Palatinus, Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tuto, Pannonius, Victor, Restitutus, another Restitutus, [Note: From this it is clear that the other Restitutus is also missing from the address of Letter 26.] Rusticus, Fortunatianus, Ampelius, Ambivius, Felix, Donatianus, Adeodatus, Octavius, Serotinus, Majorinus, Posthumianus, Crispulus, Victor, another Victor, Leucius, Marianus, Fructuosus, Proculus, Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, Maximus, Megasius, Rusticus, Rufinianus, Proculus, Severus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetentatus, Sixtus, Quodvultdeus, Pentadius, Quodvultdeus, Cyprianus, Servilius, Pelagianus, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus, Bizacenus, Germanus, Germanianus, Invenitus, Majorinus, Invenitus, Candidus, Cyprianus, Romanianus, Aemilianus, Africanus, Marcellinus, and the other beloved brothers in the Lord who were present at the Council of Carthage: greetings.

1. In [Note: The Council edition has “Inquiring into these matters.” Garner, Quesnell, and Augustine have “In investigating these matters.” The Roman edition and several manuscripts read “In matters to be investigated.” The more correct reading is found in the manuscripts of Remigius, Corbie, and Germanus: “In investigating the matters of God.” This reading is confirmed by the Africans’ letter to Pope Theodore at the Lateran Council under Martin I, act 2, tome VI of Labbe’s Councils, p. 128. Its opening, as we have already noted, is expressed in Innocent’s words and ideas, and it will be useful to reproduce it here. It begins as follows:

“No one can doubt that there stands at the Apostolic See a fountain from which great and unfailing streams flow abundantly for all Christians. From it rivulets issue forth in abundance, most generously irrigating the entire Christian world. To this See, too, in honor of the most blessed Peter, the decrees of the Fathers have assigned every special reverence, IN INVESTIGATING THE MATTERS OF GOD, which ought to be examined entirely and diligently, and above all justly, by that very apostolic summit of the bishops, whose ancient duty it is both to condemn what is evil and to approve what deserves praise. For the ancient regulations have decreed that whatever may be done, even in distant or remote provinces, must not be dealt with or accepted before it has been brought to the knowledge of your venerable See, so that by its authority a just decision might be confirmed; and that from there the other churches might take the beginning of their preaching, as from their native fountain, and that throughout the various regions of the whole world the mysteries of the faith and salvation might remain pure and uncorrupted.”]

In investigating the matters of God, which ought to be handled with every diligence by priests, and especially by a truly just and catholic council, while preserving the examples of ancient tradition and mindful of ecclesiastical discipline, you have confirmed the force of your religious commitment no less now in seeking advice than formerly when you pronounced judgment. For you approved that the matter should be referred to our judgment, knowing what is owed to the Apostolic See, since all of us assembled here desire to follow the Apostle himself, from whom the episcopate itself and the entire authority of this title have arisen. Following him, we know how to condemn what is evil and approve what deserves praise.

Indeed, you do not consider that the institutions of the Fathers, which you preserve in the exercise of your priestly office, should be trampled underfoot—institutions which they established not by a human but by a divine decision: namely, that whatever might be done, even in distant and remote provinces, they should not regard as concluded before it reached the knowledge of this See, so that by the authority of this See the just decision that had been reached might be confirmed. From there the other churches would take their beginning—as all waters proceed from their native fountain—and throughout the various regions of the whole world pure waters would flow from an uncorrupted source.

[Note: The Roman and Council editions, as well as Quesnell, read “pure waters of the source”; Merlinius has “uncorrupted,” Crab has “uncorruptly,” and the remaining witnesses have “uncorrupted.” The latter reading is restored from Augustine’s edition and the manuscripts of Corbie and Germanus. The substance of this opening was chiefly taken by Innocent from what the five bishops had written to him at the end of the preceding letter: “For we do not pour our stream back into your abundant fountain … whether our own, although small, stream also flows from the same source from which yours, abundant as it is, flows forth—we wish this to be approved by you.”]

What should they command [Perhaps read: should command] [Note: The manuscripts of Germanus and Corbie have this reading. Many others, together with the Roman and Council editions, read “what they should command.” In the manuscript of Germanus follows “whom to absolve,” whereas the others have “whom to wash.” Quesnell and Augustine have “what they should command, whom they should wash.” Garner, indulging his own ingenuity too freely, edited the whole passage as follows: “From where the other churches might draw waters, as from their native fountain from which all things proceed, and throughout the various regions of the whole world the waters of the uncorrupted source might flow; from where he might receive those whom, as if stained with mud, etc.” Our reading, supported throughout by the authority of the ancient manuscripts, will be complete if after the words “whom to wash” we understand “they ought.” Nor should we rashly deny that three classes of people presenting themselves for the Church’s judgment are distinguished here, together with three corresponding forms of judgment, derived from the three properties of water. Like clean water, the Church readily receives the innocent and undefiled as pure streams; those who are soiled but repentant she washes; but the uncorrected, who could defile her, she wisely avoids and rejects.]

whom to wash; whom the water, worthy of clean bodies, would avoid as though they were stained with uncleansable mud.

2. I therefore rejoice, dearest brothers, that you have sent letters to us through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. In caring for the churches over which you preside, you show your concern for the benefit of all; and throughout all the churches of the whole world you request that what is beneficial to everyone alike should be decreed, so that the Church, established upon its own regulations,

[Note: The Roman edition and the more recent Council editions, beginning from this point and then agreeing with the older witnesses, read: “which, strengthened by decretal decisions of just judgment, takes care that it cannot be open to such men.” Merlinius has “seek”; Crab has “be open”; the Roman edition and those following it have “fear.” Garner, cutting out “which takes care that,” retained: “strengthened by decretal decisions of just judgment, it should fear.” Our reading is that of Quesnell, Augustine, and the better manuscripts, except that Quesnell deletes “this,” while Augustine, as in the manuscripts of Corbie and Germanus, has “obey” instead of “be open.” The meaning is as though Innocent were saying: “You request that I decree that the Church, already established by its ancient regulations, now also strengthened by this new decree of a just judgment, by which she is ordered to avoid those heretics mentioned above, may no longer be open to such men, but may remain forever closed to them.”]

and this decree, by which it avoids them, having been confirmed as a just judgment, may not be open to such men—men instructed, or rather destroyed, by perverse subtleties of speech, who argue under the appearance of catholic faith and, breathing out a poisonous virus, seek to corrupt the hearts of those who think rightly and to overthrow the entire discipline of true doctrine.

The disease must therefore be healed more swiftly, lest a loathsome sickness creep farther into people’s souls.

[Note: One manuscript of Cologne has “lest it creep into the detestable habits of their souls”; another has “lest it creep into detestable diseases of the soul.” The verb “creep in,” retained by the Roman and Council editions and several other manuscripts, is better represented by the manuscripts of Germanus and Corbie as “insinuate itself.”]

Just as a physician, when he sees some weakness in this earthly body, considers it a great proof of his art if, through his intervention, one who was thought beyond hope quickly recovers; or when he sees a festering wound, he applies remedies and whatever else may cover the wound that has arisen; and if it cannot be healed while it remains, lest it corrupt the rest of the body with its rottenness, he cuts away with the knife what was harmful, so as to preserve what remains whole and untouched—so this must be cut away, what has crept like a wound into a pure and healthy body, lest, when it is cleansed too slowly, the refuse of this evil settle almost in the very entrails, where it cannot afterward be drained away.

3. For what sound judgment can we hereafter form of people who think they owe their goodness to themselves and do not consider the one whose grace they receive every day? But these people, being what they are, receive no grace from God: they confidently believe that they can attain without him as much as even those who ask him scarcely deserve to receive.

[Note: The Roman and Council editions, together with the manuscripts of Pithou and Isidore, read “and receive.” One Cologne manuscript has “so that they receive,” which led Quesnell to prefer “so that they may receive.” Augustine, as in the manuscript of Corbie, has “to receive,” without the preceding “and,” which is retained by Germanus and other witnesses. The sentence is clearly arranged in this way: “as much as even those who ask deserve scarcely to receive.”]

For what could be so unjust, so barbarous, so ignorant of the whole of religion, so hostile to Christian minds, as to deny that you owe to him whatever you obtain through daily grace, when you yourself confess that you owe to him the fact that you were born? Will you therefore be better able to provide for yourself than the one who made you exist?

[Note: Garner has “if you think you owe it to him.” Other editions have “and although you think you owe it to him.” Pelagius is being criticized here without being named. He distinguished “being able,” “willing,” and “being”; he assigned “being able” to nature, “willing” to free choice, and “being” to inclination. He granted that the ability properly belongs to God, the author of nature, but insisted that willing and being—or acting—must be attributed to human beings. He taught that it belongs solely to God that a person can will and accomplish the good; but that the person wills to accomplish it, actually accomplishes it, and therefore wills to be good and perfect, or even is good and perfect, he declared to belong to the person himself. He did not deny that human beings are always assisted by the help of grace, but located that help in this: that God never fails to grant the possibility of willing and acting. His own words may be seen in Augustine, On the Grace of Christ, chapter 4.]

And if you think you owe to him the fact that you live, how can you not think you owe to him the fact that, by obtaining his daily grace, you live in this way? And you who deny that we need divine help, as though we were altogether perfect by our own ability, how can we fail to draw his help upon us, when we can also become such people by ourselves?

[Note: The word “his” is restored from the manuscript of Germanus and Augustine’s edition. Garner alone presents the passage as follows: “Tell me, how do we truly call upon his help among us, when we can also become such people by ourselves?” The person who denies God’s help, I would ask again, ought to be questioned why he says that we do not deserve it.]

4. For I would ask the person who denies God’s help what he means: that we do not deserve it, or that God cannot provide it, or that there is nothing for which each person ought to ask for it?

That God can provide it, the works themselves testify. Nor can we deny that we need daily help. For whether we live well, we call upon it so that we may live better and more holily; or whether, thinking wrongly, we turn away from what is good, we need his help all the more so that we may return to the right path.

[Note: The manuscripts and the older Council editions have this reading. The Roman edition and the more recent Council editions, together with Garner, have “we pray.”]

For what could appear more deadly, more headlong toward ruin, more exposed to every danger than this: if, thinking that the free choice we received when we were born is sufficient for us, we seek nothing further from the Lord—that is, if, forgetting our author, we renounce his power in order to display ourselves as free—as though the one who made you free at your birth no longer had anything that he could give? We do not know that unless grace is invoked upon us through earnest prayers, we shall in no way be able to strive against the errors of earthly corruption and the body of this world, since it is not free choice but only God’s help that can make us equal to resisting them.

[Note: Garner has “in vain”; and below, “David cries out,” instead of “For if he cries out.”]

5. For if free choice were of greater benefit to anyone, he who cries out that he needs divine help would not rightly seek it; for although he was a blessed man and already chosen by the Lord, he would need nothing. Yet he nevertheless entreats God in these words: “Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior” (Psalm 26:9). We say that the free choice with which we are born is sufficient for us; he asks God to be his helper.

[Note: The Roman edition has “We therefore say plainly, ‘For what purpose should we pray to God?’” Garner has “We say plainly, ‘For what purpose should we pray to God?’” and below “David therefore,” instead of “For David.”]

Do we not plainly learn what we ought to pray for, when that blessed man, as we said above, earnestly desires not to be despised? Those who affirm those teachings must necessarily bring these charges against him. For David must then be accused as ignorant of prayer and unaware of his own nature: although he knows that so much is present in his own nature,

[Note: The Roman and Council editions have “in his nature.” Garner has “he calls upon a helper and it is not enough for him to call upon him continually”; other books, however, show that the noun “helper” is governed by the verb “desires.”]

he nevertheless desires God as his helper, and as his continual helper; indeed, continual help is not enough for him—he prostrates himself in prayer and asks that God never despise him. Throughout the entire body of the Psalter he both proclaims and cries out for this. If, then, he knew this to be so great a matter that he said it continually, and confessed it to be so necessary that he taught it,

[Note: Several manuscripts, together with Quesnell and the Roman and Council editions, have: “knew it to be so great that he said it continually.” Augustine has: “was so great as continually to say it.” Garner has: “if this seemed so great to him that he said it continually, and confessed it to be so necessary.” We retain the reading found in the more numerous and older manuscripts. We would nevertheless prefer: “he knew it to be so great that he continually said it, and so necessary that he confessed it.”]

how do Pelagius and Coelestius, setting aside the whole testimony of the Psalms and rejecting such teaching, trust that they will persuade anyone that we neither ought to seek nor need God’s help, when all the saints testify that they can do nothing without it?

6. For when that man was once permitted free choice, he used his goods too incautiously, fell, and was plunged into the depths of transgression; nor did he find any way by which he could rise from there. Deceived forever in his freedom, he would have lain crushed beneath the ruin of this fall,

[Note: The manuscripts, as in the editions of Merlinius and the Roman edition, have “would have lain concealed, crushed beneath the ruin,” or “crushed beneath it”; Pithou has “under the crushing,” and in Corbie an ancient hand restored “would have lain.” This correction is supported both by Augustine, Book II to Boniface against Two Letters of the Pelagians, no. 6, and by Pope Celestine’s Letter 21, chapter 4, where these words are quoted. Yet even in those two places there are manuscripts reading “would have lain beneath the crushing.” Crab and the Council editions have “would have lain crushed beneath this ruin”; Garner and Quesnell have “would have been crushed beneath this ruin.”]

unless Christ’s coming had raised him up through his grace.

[Note: The manuscripts agree with Augustine’s edition in reading “through his grace”; other editions have “by his grace.”]

Through the cleansing of a new birth he purified every past fault by the washing of baptism; and, strengthening the condition in which he might proceed more rightly and securely, he nevertheless did not deny him his grace for the future. For although he had redeemed humanity from past sins, knowing that it could sin again, he preserved many means for restoring it, by which he might correct it even after these sins. He provides daily remedies; unless we rely upon them and strive with confidence in them, we shall in no way be able to overcome human errors. For we must necessarily be overcome if the one by whose help we conquer does not again help us.

7. But I could say more, if it were not clear that you have said everything. Whoever therefore appears to agree with the opinion that we do not need divine help declares himself an enemy of the catholic faith and ungrateful for God’s benefits.

[Note: The conjunction “for” is restored from Merlinius, Crab, Augustine, and many manuscripts. In the Isidorean manuscripts “our” is absent. The Roman and Council editions, together with some manuscripts, have “Thus indeed,” whereas with the other books we prefer “For they themselves.” Garner, judging the passage mutilated, suggested in a marginal note that it might be repaired as follows: “You therefore condemned Pelagius and Coelestius, whom you recognized as the authors of an utterly wicked error, one to be anathematized by all, by a just judgment: nor are they worthy of our…” But the words of the Carthaginian Fathers at the end of their preceding Letter 26 do not indicate that they pronounced a sentence against Pelagius and Coelestius by name: “If Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or say that they never held these views, and deny that any writings produced against them are theirs, and there is no way to convict them of lying, nevertheless let there be a general anathema against the doctrines whose authors they are considered to be, whoever is found to defend them.” Nor does anything in this passage of Innocent’s appear to require the judgment that it is mutilated.]

For they themselves are not worthy of our communion, which they have polluted by preaching in this way. Of their own accord, by following the doctrines they proclaim, they have fled farther from true religion. Since our entire profession consists in this, and since in our daily prayers we do nothing except seek how we may obtain God’s mercy, how can we endure people who boast such things?

Who, I ask, has so great an error blinded their hearts that, if they themselves feel no grace of God because they are neither worthy of it nor deserve it, they do not even consider what divine grace bestows daily upon each of the others? Such people are indeed most deserving of total blindness, since they have not even left themselves the possibility of believing that they can be recalled from their errors by divine help.

For by denying that help, they have taken it away completely—not from others, but from themselves. They must be torn away farther and removed far from the bosom of the Church, lest, unpunished for a long time and gaining hold of many, the error grow incurable.

[Note: The editions, except Augustine’s, have “lest, while many things remain unpunished for a long time.” Augustine, as in the manuscripts of Corbie and Germanus, more coherently has “lest many things remain unpunished for a long time.” Hence the following sentence follows appropriately: “For if they remain for a long time in this IMPUNITY…”]

For if they remain for a long time in this impunity, they will necessarily lead many into the depravity of their own mind and deceive the innocent—or rather, the unwary—who now follow the catholic faith.

[Note: Garner’s reading, also found in the manuscripts of Corbie and Germanus, is approved by Quesnell, although he retains the common reading of the Roman and Council editions, namely “do not follow.” In Augustine, the particle “now” has been omitted through a copyist’s carelessness.]

For they will think that those whom they still see remaining in the Church think rightly. Let the incurable wound therefore be separated from the healthy body; and, once the breath of the raging disease has been removed, let what is sound be preserved with greater caution, and let the purer flock be cleansed from the contagion of this diseased sheep. Let the perfection of the entire body remain undefiled. We have learned that you follow and maintain it in this judgment against them, and together with you we preserve it by equal agreement.

8. But if they should nevertheless call upon some help of God—which up to now they have denied—and recognize that they need his help in order to be freed from the stain into which they fell through the crookedness of their hearts, and, as though dragged into the light from a foul darkness, should condemn the things they have held until now, removing and rejecting everything by which their entire vision was defiled and darkened so that they could not see the truth,

[Note: Quesnell and Augustine have “so that they might see.”]

and should at last submit their minds to sound discussions, having been corrected to some degree from this stain, and entrust and subject themselves to true counsels for healing,

[Note: Garner has “healing councils.” The preceding word, “for healing,” which Quesnell removed, is preserved by all our manuscripts.]

then it will be within the power of the bishops to assist them to some extent and to provide some care for such wounds—a care which the Church ordinarily does not deny to those who have fallen when they repent—so that, recalled from their own precipices,

[Note: Merlinius omits the word “recalled.” The Roman edition and the later Council editions substitute “removed” for it.]

they may be brought back within the Lord’s fold. Otherwise, remaining outside and excluded from the protection of the fortress of faith,

[Note: Quesnell has “excluded from the protection and strength of the fortress”; Garner has “excluded from the protection of the faithful fortress.” The latter reading is less objectionable.]

they will be exposed to every danger, to be devoured and tormented by the teeth of wolves, against which they cannot resist by the perverse doctrine with which they have provoked them against themselves.

9. But enough. Your admonitions have been shown to have been answered by such abundant examples from our law. We judged that nothing remained for us to say, since nothing has been omitted or suppressed by you by which they might be refuted and shown to have been utterly convicted. Therefore we offer no testimonies, because your account is complete, and it is sufficiently clear that so many highly learned priests have said everything. Nor is it right to believe that you have passed over anything that could contribute to the case.

And in another hand: “Farewell, brothers.”

And beside it: “Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February” (January 27, in the year 417), after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Junius Quartus, a man of clarissimus rank.

[Note: The manuscript of Corbie has “Luni Quarti.” Germanus has “after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus VII and Lucius Quartus, most illustrious consuls.” This arose from the copyist’s ignorance: he did not understand that the earlier note, “after the consulship,” was to be retained, and therefore substituted “Theodosius Augustus” for it; nor did he understand that the later note, “V. C.,” should be rendered by the words “most illustrious consuls.”]

## LETTER XXX. OF POPE INNOCENT TO THE COUNCIL OF MILEVIS

[Note: In the Council edition this is Letter 25; what is now Letter 30 was formerly placed in the appendix.]

Innocent praises the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, both because they judged that obstinate heretics should be separated and that those who had been corrected should be received, and because, following the canons accepted everywhere, they sought the judgment of the Apostolic See in matters of anxiety. He then proves that the heresy which maintains that a human being can suffice for himself without God’s grace, and denies that baptism is necessary for infants to attain eternal life, fights against the Scriptures. He orders that its authors and their followers be cut off from the Church, but that they be received if they condemn their errors.

INNOCENTIUS to Silvanus the elder, Valentinus, [Note: It is more probable that in this heading Innocent addressed the individual bishops who had been named at the beginning of the council’s letter because the only surviving copies of this reply likewise, in the preceding letter, indicated the remaining bishops under a general formula after Aurelius had been named.] and the other beloved brothers who were present at the synod of Milevis, greetings in the Lord.

1. Among the other cares of the Roman Church and the occupations of the Apostolic See, in which we deal with the consultations of different people through faithful and sound discussion, our brother and fellow bishop Julius unexpectedly brought me the letter of your charity, which you sent from the Council of Milevis with heightened concern for the faith,

[Note: In certain copies of Isidore’s collection, and consequently in Merlinius and Crab, the reading is “from the Council of Milevis convened by our authority,” a gloss worthy of Mercator and rightly removed from the Roman edition. It would imply that Innocent said that letters from a council convened by his own authority had been unexpectedly thrust upon him.]

adding to it the similar written complaint of the Council of Carthage. The Church surely rejoices to see pastors displaying such care for the flocks entrusted to them that they not only do not allow any of them to fall into error, but, if some have been led astray by the grass of a more savage delight,

[Note: Merlinius has “or”; Crab has “of savage [grass]”; other Council editions after the Roman, together with Garner, have “obscene.” The remaining books more correctly have “savage,” a reading also noted in the margin by Labbe. The manuscripts of Isidore then have “your charity.”]

and if they persist in error, either wish them to be completely separated or, while avoiding what they previously sought unlawfully, protect them with the vigilance of their former custody. In both respects, they are acting with prudent concern, lest by receiving such people the rest of the sheep be led astray by a similar example, or, by despising those who return, they appear to have exposed them to the bites of wolves. This is a very prudent and thoroughly catholic policy.

[Note: Garner has “consolation.” The Roman and Council editions, together with the manuscripts of Isidore, have “a desire for consultation.” One Cologne manuscript has “indeed, consultation,” but lacks “desire.” Quesnell has already observed that “consultation,” though a less Latin word, is more suitable than the other Cologne manuscript’s reading “consult.” It refers to the course by which they act with concern in both respects: neither admitting the obstinate nor despising those who return.]

For who could tolerate one who remains in error, or refuse to receive one who corrects himself?

[Note: Augustine has “one who corrects himself.”]

For just as I consider it harsh to show indulgence to sinners, so I judge it impious to deny a hand to the converted.

2. You therefore consult carefully and appropriately the mysteries of apostolic honor—

[Note: Garner, together with the Roman edition, has “you consult the apostolic honor, honor.” Quesnell, following one Cologne manuscript, has “you consult the secrets of apostolic honor, honor.” Another Cologne manuscript differs only in reading “secret” instead of “secrets.” The Isidorean manuscripts have “you consult the honors of apostolic secrecy, honor.” One Vatican manuscript has “you consult the mysteries of the burden of the apostolic office.” The more sincere reading is the one presented here after the Council edition and Augustine. The meaning is: “you consult the Apostolic See, whose mysteries it is your task to disclose.” Boniface I uses the same expression in Letter 5, no. 1: “what is the mystery of this See which you consult.” Hence it is clear that Crab incorrectly wrote “ark” in the margin here in place of “mysteries.”]

—over matters of anxiety, asking what judgment must be maintained (II Corinthians 11:28), following the form of the ancient rule which, as you know, has always been observed with me by the whole world.

But I pass over these matters, for I do not believe that your prudence is unaware of them.

[Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts. Merlinius has the equivalent: “which you have also confirmed by action, unless you know.” The Roman and Council editions, after Crab, have “what you have also confirmed by action,” omitting “unless.” Quesnell likewise omits it, preferring “which you have also.” Augustine has “which you have indeed confirmed by action.” Garner has “why you have indeed confirmed by action.” If anyone thinks that the claim that answers are always sent from the apostolic fountain to those who seek them throughout all the provinces is exaggerated, he should recall what Jerome wrote to Damasus in Letter 110, now 91: “When I was assisting Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, with ecclesiastical documents, I answered the synodal consultations of the East and West.”]

Why else did you confirm this by your action, unless you knew that answers always flow from the Apostolic Fountain to those who seek them throughout all the provinces?

Especially (24, question 1, chapter 12), whenever the matter of faith is being debated, I think that all our brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer to Peter, the author of his own name and honor,

[Note: That is, to Peter, “from whom the episcopate itself and the entire authority of this title have arisen,” as Letter 29, no. 1, states; or, as Siricius says in Letter 5, no. 5, “through whom the beginning of the apostolate and episcopate in Christ was established.” Our Innocent also copies this in Letter 2, no. 2.]

just as your charity has now referred it, so that it may benefit all the churches throughout the world collectively.

For they must become more cautious when they see that the authors of evil, upon the report of a twofold synod, have been separated from ecclesiastical communion by the statutes of our judgment. Your charity will therefore enjoy a double benefit: you will possess the grace of the canons that have been preserved, and the whole world will make use of your good service.

[Note: The Roman and Council editions have “will be protected.”]

For what catholic man would wish to continue discussing with the adversaries of Christ? Who would wish even to share the light of life in communion with them?

[Note: One manuscript adds “with them” here.]

The authors of this new heresy must plainly be avoided.

3. For what more bitter thing could they have devised against the Lord than to abolish divine assistance and remove the reason for daily prayer? This is to say: “Why do I need God?” The hymn-singing prophet rightly says against them: “Behold, the men who did not set God as their helper” (Psalm 52:9).

Therefore, while denying God’s help, they say that a human being can suffice for himself and has no need of divine grace. Deprived of this grace, he must necessarily perish entangled in the snares of the devil, while striving by freedom alone to fulfill all the commandments of life. O perverse doctrine of utterly depraved minds!

[Note: The older Council editions, as in Augustine, have “Let him finally perceive this.” Other editions and two manuscripts have “Perceive this at last,” and the latter is supported by Celestine’s Letter 21, chapter 7, where the passage is quoted as: “Perceive at last, O doctrine of utterly depraved minds.” Although the order of Innocent’s words is altered there, we might favor retaining “perceive” because of that ancient authority, were it not for the sequence of the sentence, in which the manuscripts read not “hear,” as Garner and Quesnell printed against them, but “let him hear.” It is therefore preferable to follow some manuscripts in reading “perceiving,” or “attending.”]

Let him finally perceive that freedom itself so deceived the first man that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumptuous transgression,

[Note: Quesnell, with one Cologne manuscript, has “through the presumption of transgression.” Merlinius and Crab, with the Isidorean manuscripts, have “into the presumption of transgression.”]

and could not be rescued from it until the coming of the Lord Christ, through the providence of regeneration, restored the condition of his former freedom.

[Note: Quesnell alone has “through his coming.”]

Let him hear David saying: “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 123:8); and: “Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior” (Psalm 26:9). He would have spoken these words in vain if what he so pathetically asked from the Lord had depended solely upon his own will.

[Note: Garner has “if everything depended upon it.”]

4. Since these things are so, and since throughout all the divine writings we read that God’s help alone must be joined to free will, and that free will can do nothing when deprived of heavenly assistance, how do Pelagius and Coelestius, as you report, stubbornly defend this possibility as belonging to free will alone, and persuade many to accept it—though it is even more grievous and worthy of common sorrow that they persuade themselves?

[Note: Quesnell has “more grievous and more worthy”; Garner substitutes “a common grief.”]

We could use many examples to destroy such teaching, unless we knew that your holiness fully understands all the divine Scriptures—especially since your report is filled with such great and weighty testimonies that by these alone the present doctrine can be overthrown, and there is no need for hidden arguments, since they neither dare nor can oppose the things you have set forth, which readily present themselves.

So they are trying to take away God’s grace, which we must seek even after the condition of our former freedom has been restored, since we can avoid no other snares of the devil except with that same grace helping us (Augustine, Book II to Boniface, chapter 4, no. 7).

5. But what your fraternity asserts that they preach—that infants can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of baptism—is utterly foolish. “Unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves” (John 6:54).

Those who defend the possibility of infants possessing this life without regeneration seem to me to wish to abolish baptism itself, since they teach that infants possess what, as they believe, can be conferred upon them only through baptism. If, therefore, they do not wish the failure to be reborn to cause any harm, they must confess that the sacred waters of regeneration are likewise of no benefit.

But so that the perverse doctrine of superfluous people may be cut away by the swift reasoning of truth,

[Note: This is the reading of Quesnell and two Cologne manuscripts. Merlinius, with another Cologne manuscript, has “distinguished,” which is erroneous. The other books have “cut apart,” but that reading is no better. Silius likewise says, “to cut away deceits by reason.”]

the Lord proclaims this in the Gospel, saying: “Let the infants come, and do not prevent them from coming to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Luke 18:16).

### 6.

Accordingly, we decree that Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, inventors of new expressions which, as the Apostle says, habitually produce nothing conducive to edification but rather utterly empty questions (2 Tim. 2:23)—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion by the authority of apostolic vigor, until they recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will [Note: One manuscript has “captured.”]; and that meanwhile they are not to be received into the Lord’s fold, which they themselves chose to abandon after following the path of a perverse road [Note: The Roman edition and the Councils read: “until they wish to abandon the path of the perverse way” (Merl.: “after following the path”; others: “which they followed”). These readings are corrected from the manuscripts.]. For those who trouble you and wish to overturn the Gospel of Christ must be cut off (Gal. 5:12). At the same time we decree that whoever attempts with similar obstinacy to defend this position is to be restrained by an equal punishment; for not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them (Rom. 1:32) [Note: “An equal punishment ought to restrain them” must be supplied. Quesnell adds here, “they are worthy of punishment,” though I do not know whether this has any authority. Merl. and Augustine, from two Vatican manuscripts, have instead “they are worthy of death.” Garnerius presents these words as though they were Scripture: “Not only are those who do these things worthy of death, but also those who consent to those who do them.” These three readings all the more suggest the work of an interpolator, since in our manuscripts, as in the Roman, Crabbe’s, and other editions, only the Apostle’s words appear. It was sufficient to point these out to bishops familiar with Scripture.], because I do not think that there is much difference between the mind of one who commits an act and the favor of one who consents to it. I add something further: often the person who has no one’s consent ceases to err.

Let this sentence, therefore, dearest brothers, remain fixed concerning the men mentioned above: let them be absent from the Lord’s courts, and let them lack at least pastoral guardianship [Note: The particle *duntaxat* (“at least”) is absent in Augustine. Garnerius not only omitted it, but also altered Innocent’s sentence to read: “Let pastoral vigilance beware.” The pope praises at the beginning of this letter those shepherds who, avoiding sheep formerly attacked unlawfully—that is, sheep converted to better conduct—do not disdain to protect them with the vigilance of their former guardianship. Here he wishes those sheep that persist obstinately in error to lack pastoral guardianship, that is, to be separated from the flock entrusted to the shepherds’ care.], lest the grievous contagion of two sheep perhaps spread through an unwary populace, and the wolf, ravenous at heart, rejoice within the Lord’s fold to see such great herds of sheep scattered, while the wound of two is negligently overlooked by their guardians.

Therefore care must be taken lest, by allowing wolves to remain, we appear rather to be hirelings than shepherds. We decree, certainly—for Christ our Lord has declared in his own words that he does not desire the death of the one who is dying, but only that he turn back and live (Ezek. 33:11; 2 Pet. 3:9)—that, if they should ever return to soundness after laying aside the error of their wicked doctrine, and should condemn the things by whose transgression they themselves condemned themselves, the customary remedy, that is, their restoration to the Church, is not to be denied them [Note: Garnerius has *propria voluntate significavit*, “declared by his own will.” The word *significavit* was subsequently transferred into Augustine.].

Thus, lest perhaps, by preventing them when they return, they truly remain outside the fold and are swallowed by the rabid jaws of the waiting enemy—jaws which they have armed against themselves with the darts of evil disputation [Note: Quesnell, as one Colbertine manuscript, has *velut* (“as it were”) for *vere* (“truly”). In place of this word Garnerius substitutes *oves* (“sheep”). Augustine, from Vatican manuscripts, has “remaining and waiting”; Merl. has “of the swift enemy”; other editions of the Councils, with the Roman edition, “of the swift enemies.” Garnerius omits *rabidis* (“rabid”) without supplying any substitute. Note: One Colbertine manuscript lacks *ad sanum* (“to soundness”); another has *sano* instead. Quesnell has *sanum*; Garnerius, *sani*. Note: Garnerius: “which they have armed against themselves.” Quesnell, following an old Colbertine exemplar: “by which they have armed certain spiritual men against themselves” (the Colbertine manuscript has “certain men”).].

Farewell, brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February (27 January 417), in the consulship of the most illustrious men Honorius and Constantius [Note: The manuscripts of Isidore have “Constantius.” Merl. has “Constantine.” Other editions of the Councils and the Roman edition read “Constantius, most illustrious men,” with one Colbertine manuscript having the abbreviation “v. v. c.” Garnerius has “Honorius XI and Constantius II as consuls.” For the consular notice to be exact, it should read: “Honorius Augustus XI and Constantius, most illustrious man,” not “most illustrious men.” Yet the consular notices in Letters 29 and 31, which have come down to us from better manuscripts than this one, require that this notice be emended. There seems no doubt that Innocent dated all three letters at the same time and in the same manner, after the consulship of Theodosius VII and Junius Quartus.
