But since Honorius and Constantius were invested with the same dignity after that consulship, it is conjectured that some ancient copyist added in the margin “in the consulship of Honorius and Constantius,” and that this marginal note was transferred into the text.].

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, Letter 26. What was Letter 39 is now 5.]

Innocent writes back to five bishops that he has already made sufficiently clear what he thought of their judgment and of Pelagius’s perfidy; that the supporters of this heretic, if they are in Rome, should remain hidden, but wherever they may live they must be condemned and their salvation attended to; that he is highly suspicious of Pelagius’s clearing of himself in Palestine, though he neither blames nor approves his judges; that there is no need to summon him to Rome, and that his book is certainly filled with blasphemies; that if Pelagius himself anathematizes his errors, those whom he led astray will more readily be recalled; but that provision must at least be made for these men.

**INNOCENT, to the bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius, greetings** [Note: In the Corbie manuscript: “Innocent to his dearest brothers Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius.”].

[Col. 0594A]

### 1.

I received with the greatest pleasure the letters of your fraternity, full of faith and strengthened throughout by the vigor of Catholic religion, sent from two councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. Their entire tenor and composition consist in a sound consideration of God’s daily grace and in the correction of those who think otherwise: so that the letters may both remove every error from those men and, by providing a suitable example of our law, offer them a teacher worthy of imitation [Note: Garnerius has *contextio est*, “the composition is,” and below *integra relatio ita consistit*, “the complete account thus stands,” rather than “the composition of the letters.” The Corbie manuscript previously had *correptione*, “correction,” instead of *correctione*. Quesnell, like the Pithou manuscript, has *possint* (“may be able”) rather than *possit* (“may be able”), correctly referring to the composition of the letter. The Roman and Councils editions read *idoneo dato cuivis*; older Councils editions retain *quovis*. Garnerius has *idoneum cuivis, dato legis*.].

But I think we have already said enough about this above, when, in replying to your reports, we wrote back what we thought both of their perfidy and of your judgment. Yet something continually comes to our aid and supplies what may be said against them; nor can there ever be anything capable of prevailing, since what is so miserable and impious is more completely overcome by the strength of our faith and by the truth itself [Note: Merl., Crabbe, Garnerius, and Augustine, following the Vatican manuscripts, read *deesse*, “be lacking.” Other books have *esse*, “exist,” which seems preferable: “Nor can it ever happen that a doctrine so miserable and impious should prevail, since it is more completely overcome by the power of our faith and by truth itself.”].

For the one who rejects and despises every hope of life, confusing his heart with a hostile and condemnable argument, who believes that there is nothing to receive from God and nothing left to ask for in order to heal himself—what has he left for himself after taking this away?

### 2.

If, then, there are some whom so great a perversity has bound in their own defense [Note: Merl. has *defixit*, “fixed”; Garnerius *devinxerit*, “bound.” Below, Crabbe and Labbe have *oberrans*, “wandering,” and the Roman edition *aberrans*, “straying,” instead of *abhorrens*, “shrinking from” or “abhorrent.”], who surrender and attach themselves to this doctrine, hoping that it belongs to Catholic teaching, although it is shown to be wholly and utterly opposed to it, and who, led astray by the affection, admonitions, and words of those men, have been induced to fall, they will hasten to return to the straight path of the road, lest an error that has long occupied their minds and has, as it were, fed upon their perceptions invade them [Note: The printed editions have *infecti*; the Vatican manuscript *infectis*. The reading is corrected from an old Colbertine exemplar. These words correspond to the five bishops’ statement in §14: “which scandalized hearers and caused his perverse lovers everywhere to spread it continually. For if they should learn…”].

For if Pelagius, wherever he has appeared, has deceived by this assertion the minds of those who would readily or simply believe his disputation—whether those people are in this city, which we cannot disclose or deny because we do not know [Note: One Colbertine manuscript and the first hand of the Corbie manuscript read *seu hic illi*, “whether those people are here.” Another, as in Quesnell, has *seu hic aliqui decepti sint*, “whether some who have been deceived are here.”]—even if they are here, they remain hidden and never dare, in the presence of one of us, either to defend these things while he preaches them or to boast of such doctrines; and amid so great a multitude of people no one can easily be detected or recognized anywhere [Note: One manuscript has *quolibet nostrorum*, “in the presence of any one of us.” Garnerius reads: “nor can it be known where he may be hiding.” Manuscripts of inferior quality have: “nor can anyone easily be detected, anywhere.”], or whether they live in any place on earth, we trust in the mercy and grace of our God that they will readily be corrected when they hear the condemnation of the man who is found to have persisted in and resisted this doctrine. It makes no difference where such men have been, provided that wherever they can be found, they may be healed.

[Col. 0595B]

### 3.

Nevertheless, we cannot be persuaded that he has been cleared, although the proceedings have been brought to us by I know not what laymen, by which he believed himself both heard and acquitted [Note: Garnerius, from old editions of Augustine, restored “by some of our laymen.” The proceedings of the Council of Diospolis are mentioned here.]. We doubt whether these things are true because they have not come through any official account of that council, nor have we received from those before whom he pleaded this case any letters concerning it [Note: Merl. and Crabbe have *executione*, “in an official account”; Garnerius, *innotuerint*, “have become known.” Other books oppose these readings.].

If he had been able to rely upon his own clearing, we believe that he would have done what would have been much more credible: he would have compelled them to indicate in their letters what they had judged [Note: Quesnell has “what they judged,” as does the Navarre manuscript in its second recension; that manuscript and other copies of Isidore have “what they judged.” Later editions of the Councils have “who judged.” Augustine has “what they discerned.” The Roman edition, like the Colbertine, Pithou, and Corbie manuscripts, reads “what they had judged.” The reading restored from Merl., Crabbe, and others is “what they had discerned.” Garnerius has “what they had judged,” in the ecclesiastical sense, but this appears to be a gloss.].

But since there are matters recorded in the proceedings which he partly suppressed by avoiding the charges brought against him, and partly confused in complete obscurity by turning many words back upon himself, and since in some matters he cleared himself, as could be seen for the time, more by false arguments than by true reasoning, denying some things and distorting others by a false interpretation [Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “which he did for a time.” Garnerius gives the entire passage as follows: “He cleared himself by denying some things, interpreting others falsely, rather by false arguments than by true reasoning, so that he could not even for a time appear acquitted,” with words omitted, added, or displaced contrary to the testimony of the other books. From Innocent’s account it may be suspected that the proceedings of the Council of Diospolis sent to him were not genuine, but had been adulterated by Pelagius—those which he called the written document of his defense—and that he had sent similar material to Augustine. Certainly Augustine suspects that Pelagius worked to circulate the adulterated proceedings everywhere. In *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, book 1, §57, he says: “Who would not believe that this had been arranged so that, as if in place of an abridgment of those proceedings, this document of his might circulate everywhere?” We may reasonably suppose that the unknown men who brought the writing were devoted to Pelagius and delivered to Innocent what they had been persuaded would favor their teacher. Innocent therefore rightly says above that he doubts whether those proceedings are true, and repeats the point below.].

[Col. 0596A]

### 4.

Would that he might now—what is most to be desired—turn from the error of that path of his to the true way of the Catholic faith, and desire and wish to be cleared, considering God’s daily grace and recognizing his assistance, so that he may truly appear and be approved by all as corrected by evident reason, not by the evidence of the proceedings, but by a heart converted to the Catholic faith [Note: Augustine has *verum*, “truly,” as do the manuscripts. Labbe, followed by the Roman and Merl. editions, has *gestorum judicio*, “by the judgment of the proceedings,” incorrectly.].

For this reason we can neither approve nor condemn the judgment of those men, since we do not know whether the proceedings are genuine; or, if they are genuine, it is clear that he evaded the matter rather than cleared himself with complete truth. If he is confident and knows that what he now says is not deserving of condemnation by us, or that he has already refuted this whole matter which he formerly said [Note: Quesnell, having first inserted “If he is confident in himself,” adds: “to confirm that what he says is true, or even all this,” a mere gloss not found in the ancient manuscripts of the edition published by him. In the Roman edition the conjunction *aut* (“or”) before *jam hoc totum* is absent. Garnerius, and subsequently the new edition of Augustine, print the passage as: “But if he is confident and knows that he is deserving of condemnation by us, let him now refute everything he said” (Augustine has “has refuted”). Our reading is preferable because it follows the ancient manuscripts and is fuller and more complete. Innocent means that if Pelagius is confident that what he now says and teaches is not worthy of condemnation, or that he has already refuted, retracted, and rejected what he formerly said and taught, he should hasten to Rome, assured of his acquittal.], he ought not to be summoned by us; rather, he himself should hasten so that he may be acquitted.

For if he still thinks in this way, when he knows that he is to be condemned by our judgment, how will he entrust himself to our judgment when summoned by letters of any kind [Note: The printed editions have *acceptis*, “having received”; the Pithou manuscript has *acceptus*, “received.” The Corbie manuscript more fittingly has *accitus*, “summoned.” Shortly before, the Vatican manuscript has *acciri* instead of *accersiri*, “to be summoned.”]? If he had to be summoned, it would be better done by those who are closer to him and are not separated by a great distance across the earth. Yet care will not be lacking if he provides material for a remedy. He can condemn what he formerly believed and, by sending letters, request pardon for his error, as is proper for one returning to us, dearest brothers.

### 5.

We carefully examined a book said to be his, which your charity sent to us. In it we read many things written against God’s grace, many blasphemies, nothing that pleased us, and almost nothing that did not thoroughly displease us—material to be condemned and trampled underfoot by anyone, such as no one other than the man who wrote it would admit into his mind or hold as his opinion [Note: The words “we read many things written against God’s grace,” together with the nearly preceding wording, have been restored from Augustine’s edition and the Vatican and Corbie manuscripts, since they were absent from others.].

At this point we did not think it necessary to discuss the law at greater length, as though Pelagius were present and resisting, since we are speaking with you, who know the whole matter of the law and rejoice in agreement with us [Note: The Roman edition and the Councils have *totam rem*; the Corbie manuscript *totum*. The other printed and manuscript books more correctly have *totam*, meaning “the whole law.” As Quesnell noted, Innocent alludes to the Apostle’s words in Rom. 7:1: “I speak to those who know the law.” Likewise, later, in addressing the Council of Ephesus, Celestine says in Letter 17, §4: “Having briefly encouraged you in all these matters, because, as the Apostle says, I speak to those who know the law.”]. For these examples are better brought forward when we are dealing with those who are known to be inexperienced in such matters [Note: Three manuscripts, like the edition of the Councils, have *prudentes*, “wise.” Other books more correctly have *imprudentes*, that is, inexperienced and uneducated, less familiar with the law. Hence the following word is better understood as “more fitting and more appropriate.”].

Who would not find it exceedingly fruitful to discuss the possibility of nature, free will, the whole grace of God, and daily grace, provided that he thinks correctly? Let him, therefore, anathematize the things he believed, so that those who had fallen through his speeches and instructions may finally learn what true faith contains. They will more readily be recalled when they perceive that these things have been condemned by their own author.

But if he should obstinately persist in this impiety, action must be taken so that help may be given to those whom not their own error but rather his error led into it [Note: Garnerius has: “so that help may be given to those whom not crime but rather error led into this,” an incorrect reading. Here the author of the error is distinguished from those whom he led astray.], lest the remedy be lost even for those for whom he refuses and does not seek such treatment.

*(By another hand:)* May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February (27 January 417) [Note: Quesnell has, as do the Roman and Councils editions and most manuscripts, the words that follow omitted. Garnerius substitutes: “in the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II.” The scribe who copied the Corbie manuscript, unless this is an older error, had the genuine reading before him but corrupted it through ignorance: “The day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most glorious Theodosius, who is also Junius Quartus Palladius, most illustrious man.” As was observed in the latest edition of Augustine, he displaced *post consulatum* (“after the consulship”) and joined it to *VI Kalendas*, thereby making “the day before the Kalends”; and he read *Theodosii qui* instead of *Theodosii VII Augusti*. A comparison with Letter 29 makes both errors evident and restores the text. The same heading appears in a Vatican manuscript as: “Given on the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus and Junius Quartus Palladius,” with the two numerical designations omitted.], after the consulship of the most glorious Theodosius Augustus VII and Junius Quartus Palladius, most illustrious man.

## LETTER XXXII

Innocent returns Aurelius’s greeting as a friend [Note: In the edition of the Councils, Letter 27. What was formerly Letter 32 is now 35. In the ancient manuscripts of Quesnell’s edition and in copies of Isidore’s collection, it is titled, with broad agreement, “a familiar letter.” It was written at the same time as the three preceding letters and sent through the same bishop Julius.].

**INNOCENT TO AURELIUS, bishop of Carthage.**

True affection consists in familiar correspondence. For the duties of charity secure their claim more firmly when they are performed separately [Note: The Roman edition and the Councils read *melius se orsa mercantur*, which is corrected from the manuscripts. Immediately afterward, *extrinsecus missae* means “sent separately,” that is, written independently.]. Therefore I was eager to reply through our brother Julius to the letters sent separately, lest there perhaps remain with me the offense of having denied you a personal greeting, dearest brother [Note: An old exemplar of Quesnell reads: “we preferred to reply,” omitting *mox* and *frater charissime* (“immediately” and “dearest brother”).].

Accordingly, I return the aforesaid brother to your affection, together with the judgments of the apostolic see in response to the report of the two councils [Note: In the old editions of the Councils and the Roman edition, the word *dignum* is incorrectly added here, contrary to the manuscripts. Innocent calls the responses of the apostolic see “judgments” because they indicate the see’s decision concerning matters referred to it. We shall see elsewhere that *judicatum* and *constitutum* are synonyms in Pope Vigilius and Gregory.]. It remains for the Lord, entreated by us, to grant that every stain of his Church may be wiped away through our unceasing labors. May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [Note: The consular notice is omitted here and must be supplied from the preceding letters.].

## NOTICE ON THE THREE FOLLOWING LETTERS

### 1.

The three following letters were first published at Rome among the papal letters from an old book of the Vatican library; afterward Baronio reprinted them, having compared them with another manuscript, under the year 416. The first editor explains as follows what he thought had occasioned their composition:

“Since John, bishop of Jerusalem, followed the errors of Origen, Jerome, who was living at Bethlehem, and many others abstained from communion with him. For this reason many evils were inflicted upon them through John’s agency.”

We have learned a more accurate account of their cause from what Augustine relates at the end of his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, in these words:

“But concerning the things said to have been perpetrated after that judgment—the judgment held at Diospolis in Palestine—there by some unknown band of wretched men who are reported to have strongly supported Pelagius in his perversity, with incredible audacity, so that the servants and handmaids of God who belonged to the care of the holy Jerome were afflicted with the most criminal slaughter, a deacon was killed, the monastery buildings were burned, and scarcely a fortified tower protected Jerome himself, by God’s mercy, from this attack and assault of the impious: I think we ought rather to remain silent about these things and await what our brother bishops there judge should be done concerning such great evils. For who could believe that they could overlook them?”

It is clear that the evils described in the letters that follow were suffered by Jerome not from the Origenists but from the Pelagians.

### 2.

From the same account we learn that the invasion of the monastery entrusted to Jerome’s care occurred after the Council of Diospolis. It follows that it did not occur at the time when Jerome was abstaining from communion with John. For the Palestinian, or Diospolitan, council was held toward the end of December 415. Learned authorities establish that John was reconciled with Jerome through the agency of Theophilus of Alexandria in the year 397 [See Tillemont, vol. XII, p. 199].

It is likewise clear from this that the following letters were certainly not written before 416. But John’s death, dated to 417, persuades us that they were not written much later than 416. Baronio assigns them to the end of 416. Yet he himself would have had to infer from Letter 33 that they should be assigned to 417.

For he judges that Aurelius, to whom this letter is addressed, and through whom Jerome wished his letters to be delivered to Innocent, while Innocent in turn wished the letters he wrote to Jerome to be returned to him, was the Carthaginian bishop, and no one contradicts him on this point. But while this Aurelius, together with his colleagues, was writing to Innocent against Pelagius and Coelestius at the beginning of 417, he did not know that Jerome had suffered anything from the agents of these heretics. At that time it was merely being widely reported in Africa that Pelagius, established at Jerusalem, was deceiving many there, but that many more—among whom Jerome is named in the letter of the Council of Milevis—were “fighting against him on behalf of the grace of Christ and the truth of the Catholic faith.”

Certainly, if knowledge of so atrocious a crime had reached Africa, this passage required that the suffering inflicted by the impious upon the new defender of Christ’s grace also be added. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that Jerome’s fierce conflict against Pelagius was the true reason why he was treated so cruelly. Thus, although Eustochium and Paula concealed both the cause and the author of the violence inflicted upon their monastery, it was not difficult for Innocent, who had already been informed about Pelagius’s activities at Jerusalem, to detect the matter.

### 3.

That pope rebuked John of Jerusalem in letters so threatening not only because it was his duty either to restrain or to punish such great crimes, but also because there may have been some suspicion that he had favored them. The old hostilities between John and Jerome on account of Origen, although long since quieted, were not unknown. Rumor had also reported how greatly Pelagius was loved by John.

Accordingly, Augustine addresses John himself in Letter 179, §1, as follows:

“But our brother Pelagius, your son, whom I hear you love greatly…”

And in §5:

“If you love Pelagius, let him also love you—or rather, let him love himself more—and not deceive you.”

### 4.

Finally, we observe that Innocent’s letter to this John has a Greek turn of phrase. Thus this pope either wrote in Greek, or at least arranged for what he had written in Greek to be translated into Latin; and only a Latin interpretation closely adhering to the Greek text has come down to us. Certainly, one or two passages that at first sight appear obscure or even incomplete become immediately clear and complete when they are examined according to the Greek phrasing.

## LETTER XXXIII

Innocent sends a letter to Aurelius to be delivered to Jerome [Note: In the edition of the Councils, Letter 34. What was formerly Letter 33 is now 34.].

[Col. 0600A]

**INNOCENT TO HIS DEAREST BROTHER AURELIUS.**

Our fellow presbyter Jerome rightly believed that you had a most devout desire to come to us [Note: Some, following Baronio, persuade themselves that Jerome’s letters to Innocent, like those of Eustochium and Paula, were delivered by Aurelius himself. Here, however, Aurelius is said to have had a desire to come to Rome, not to have arrived. Nor, if he had been present, would these letters have been necessary. We should therefore judge it more likely that he arranged for them to be delivered by one of his own people.].

We sympathize with a member of our flock, and we have swiftly carried out what we judged ought to be done, or what we were able to do. Let your fraternity, dearest brother, hasten to deliver the letter to the man mentioned above [Jerome].

## LETTER XXXIV

Innocent consoles Jerome for what he has suffered and declares what he judged ought to be done for the time being and what he has already done [Note: In the edition of the Councils, Letter 32. What was formerly Letter 34 is now 33.].

**INNOCENT TO HIS DEAREST SON, THE PRESBYTER JEROME.**

[Col. 0600B]

The Apostle testifies that contention has never accomplished anything good in the Church; and therefore he commands that corrections of heretics be made first rather than through a prolonged process of disputation [Note: We had judged that this should be corrected, since it had been printed with a meaning that was not only null but contrary to Innocent’s thought; the conjecture was strengthened by examination of the Vatican archetype, and we learned that the error arose from a mere copyist’s incompetence in reading old books. Innocent refers to Paul’s words in Titus 3:10: “After a first and second admonition, avoid a heretical person.” He is speaking especially of a pertinacious and deceitful heretic such as Pelagius, who was more eager to deceive and conceal his heresy than to seek the truth.]. When this rule is carelessly considered [Note: Baronius, rejecting *aspicitur* at the margin of the book—here equivalent to “is considered”—substituted *accipitur* (“is received”) in the text.], the evil that ought to be avoided is not avoided but increased.

Yet because your grief and lamentation shake our inmost parts so greatly that there is no reason not to treat and consider the matter [Note: The Vatican manuscript lacks *ratio*. Some other word is required to complete the sentence. It would be more complete if it read: “so that there is no reason for not treating and considering the matter.”], I first address the faithfulness of your steadfastness. Whoever is struck by injury or, as you say, by danger on behalf of the truth expects blessedness; you have often explained this to many, and we remind you that you are well mindful of your own preaching [Note: The Councils edition, following Baronius, has *qui exspectat*. The Roman edition, with the Vatican manuscript, more correctly has *quia exspectet*, “because he expects.” The sentence is more elegantly constructed as follows: “Whoever is struck by injury or danger on behalf of the truth, because he expects blessedness, as you have often explained to many.” It follows that such a man, being blessed through hope, is less to be mourned.].

Therefore, stirred by the spectacle of such great evils, we hastened to invoke the authority of the apostolic see to suppress every outrage [Col. 0600C]; but we read that the person against whom we should rise has not been named, nor has any charge been specified. We therefore grieve with you as far as we can.

If you set forth an open and explicit accusation against particular men, I shall either appoint competent judges, or, if anything more urgent and more careful can be done by us, I shall not delay, dearest son. Nevertheless, I have written to my brother Bishop John that he should act with greater circumspection, lest anything of this kind should still happen in the Church entrusted to him—something which it was his duty to foresee and prevent, lest it happen or happen again, and which would afterward be most troublesome even to him [Note: This passage would be more complete if read: “lest, if anything of this kind should still happen concerning the Church entrusted to him, such as he ought to have taken care that it did not happen or should not happen.” Innocent recalls here what he writes at the beginning of the following letter to John: “It was necessary for your fraternity to guard and more carefully provide for his flock, lest anything of this kind should arise,” as well as other words with which he closes that letter. These words should be compared with Augustine’s account in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §66: “For such impious doctrines of these men must be refuted by any Catholics, even those who live far from those lands, lest they be able to do harm anywhere they may reach. But impious deeds, the correction of which belongs to episcopal discipline, must be punished where they are committed, especially by those who are present or nearby, with pastoral diligence and pious severity. We, therefore, situated so far away, ought to desire that such an end be given to these matters there that it will not be necessary for them to be judged elsewhere.” There Augustine distinguishes impious doctrines from impious deeds: he teaches that impious doctrines may be challenged by any Catholic anywhere, but that impious deeds cannot likewise be punished by everyone. Innocent, however, holding a different view of the authority of his see, did not doubt that he had the right to punish impious deeds committed in a territory no less distant from him than from Augustine, either by appointing competent judges or by some other means. Nevertheless, he agrees with Augustine in saying that competent judges should be appointed by him. By this expression he may reasonably be understood to mean bishops established either in the same province or in a neighboring one.].

## LETTER XXXV

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, Letter 32.]

Innocent tells John, bishop of Jerusalem, that he ought to have protected Jerome, so that Paula and Eustochium would not have been overwhelmed by the many and great evils inflicted upon them; and that, unless such things are henceforth corrected or restrained, John will have to give an account for them.

**INNOCENT TO HIS DEAREST BROTHER JOHN.**
The most noble holy virgins Eustochium and Paula, of the utmost clemency, lamented that the devil had perpetrated plunderings, massacres, fires, and every crime in places belonging to your Church; [Note: At one time, following Baronius and the edition of the Councils, we approved “madness”; but afterward it seemed to us that the holy virgins are rather praised here as being of the utmost clemency, because they concealed the name of the hostile man and the cause of the hatred; and therefore one must adhere to the reading of the Roman edition.] for they concealed the man’s name and the cause. Although it is not [Note: Suspicion for this crime fell upon Pelagius.] ambiguous by whom it was committed, your brotherly care nevertheless ought to have guarded, and [Note: So Baronius. But the Roman edition reads “of the flock.” This is the first passage from which we conjectured that this letter had been translated from Greek. For if the Greek τῷ ποιμνίῳ ἑαυτοῦ or αὐτοῦ is rendered in Latin not literally as “that flock,” but, as Latin usage requires, “his flock,” the initially defective and obscure sequence of the sentence becomes complete and clear.] to have provided more diligently for that flock, lest something of this kind should arise, which, through the danger to others, your negligence provokes [Note: The Roman edition and the edition of the Councils read “to lose the flock,” arising from an erroneous reading in old books, in which *ammittere* is commonly written for *admittere*. The reading is corrected from Baronius, though in the latter there is afterward an even more serious error, [Col. 0602C] where one reads “and such lambs, whom you strip naked by fire . . .,” as though *nudas* were the second person of the verb *nudo*. On that reading, John, contrary to the entire sequence of the letter, is proclaimed the author of these crimes.] to admit into the Lord’s flock; and we have scarcely heard that such ewe-lambs, stripped bare, weakened by fire, weapons, and persecutions, after the slaughter and deaths of their own people, are hardly still alive. Does that piety [Note: This other passage also gives off the scent of Greek speaking Latin according to the custom of its own language. Since the Greek text had τὴν εὐσέβειαν, the translator thought that the article τὴν should be expressed in Latin by the word “that.” Moreover, a Latin speaker would have said “such great power” rather than “of such great power.”] of your priesthood feel no indignation that such great power of the devil has been admitted against you and yours? Against you, I say; for it utterly condemns the dignity of a priest that so great a crime has been completed in the Church. Where are your provisions? Where, certainly, if such disasters occurred, are the assistance or consolations, [Col. 0602A] when they say that they still fear more than they complain they have suffered? I would judge the matter more gravely if they had spoken with me more openly about it. See, brother, the snares of the ancient enemy, and keep watch with the spirit of a good ruler, so that these things, which have been reported to us more by rumor than by an overt accusation, may either be corrected or restrained; lest ecclesiastical law compel the person who has not defended the injured parties to render an account [Note: The printed editions read *causis*, but we had already conjectured that *causam*, that is, “an account,” should be restored; afterward we learned that *causas* is in the archetype. Furthermore, *jus ecclesiasticum* is here stated in the nominative case.] for the damaged causes.

## LETTER XXXVI

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, 9. Dionysius Exiguus assigns this letter the place 37 among the decrees of Innocent. The compiler of the Hispana collection took it from there, and Isidore, as usual, copied it from him. Cresconius cites it in chapter 226. It bears no indication of the time when it was written. We are therefore forced to relegate it to the class of letters of uncertain date.]

If a husband whose wife had been carried into captivity has taken another wife, when the first returns, the second woman must be dismissed.

**INNOCENTIUS TO PROBUS.**

[Note: This Probus seems to have been the son of the prefect Probus and of Proba Faltonia, that distinguished matron about whom Jerome writes to Demetrias in Letter 8 as follows: “That Proba, whose name was more illustrious than all dignities and the entire nobility in the Roman world, whose holiness and goodness toward everyone was venerable even among barbarians, was not worn out by the ordinary consulships of her three sons, Probinus, Olybrius, and Probus; and when houses in the City have been burned and plundered and captivity has occurred, she is now said to be selling her estates.” Ursa is readily believed to have been carried off in that captivity which occurred when Rome was captured by Alaric in August of the year 409, but when she returned is unknown.]

The disturbance of the barbarian storm has brought calamity upon the security of the laws. For a well-established marriage between Fortunius and Ursa would have suffered a blemish through the incursion of captivity, unless the holy statutes of religion had provided for it. Since the aforesaid woman Ursa was being held in captivity, the aforementioned Fortunius is known to have entered another marriage with Restituta (34, q. 1 and 2, c. 2; Ivo, p. 8, c. 245). But, by the favor of the Lord, Ursa returned and approached us; and, with no one denying it, she proved fully that she was the wife of the aforementioned man. Therefore, my lord and deservedly illustrious son, with the Catholic faith lending its support, we have decreed that the marriage which was originally [Note: We rightly believe that the marriage which the Catholic faith regards as founded by divine grace is a sacrament. For a similar reason, a similar response was later given in Leo’s Letter 149, no. 2. Cresconius also indicates the responses of both pontiffs under one canon, chapter 226. Earlier, Tertullian, in *To His Wife*, book II, no. 8, had praised Christian marriage as follows: “Whence shall we suffice to recount the happiness of that marriage which the Church brings together, and the offering confirms, and the blessing seals, which the angels report and the Father ratifies?”] founded by divine grace is the marriage; and that the union with the second woman, while the first survives and has not been expelled by divorce, can in no way be legitimate.

## LETTER XXXVII

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, 4. Dionysius Exiguus divided this into five headings or decrees, XXVIII, XXIX, XXX, XXXI, and XXXII. Cresconius cites it more than once. It also appears in the Hispana, as in the collection of Isidore.]

1. If anyone willingly amputates a part of his body, he cannot be a cleric; but if he did so unwillingly, he can.  
2. That bigamists cannot be admitted to the clergy.  
3. Which laymen must not be promoted to the clergy.  
4. Which laymen may become clerics. Here concubinage is expressly forbidden.  
5. The periods to be spent in the orders of the clergy.

**INNOCENTIUS TO FELIX, BISHOP OF NUCERIA.**  
[Note: So the Royal manuscript; in others, “to the bishop of Nucerianus.”]

### 1

We cannot be surprised that your affection follows the institutions of our ancestors and refers to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, everything that may admit some doubt, so that, after consultation, the apostolic see may pronounce from those doubtful matters something definite that must be done [Note: The printed editions read *faciendum pronuntiet*, omitting the conjunction, which is restored from the manuscripts.]. We gladly accept this, and we approve your affection as mindful of the canons.

You have therefore written that, through the fervor of faith with which you are endowed and your love for the holy people, you have either restored the churches of God or built new ones; but that among those whom you appoint as clerics, some are mutilated and some are twice-married. We were astonished that a prudent man wished to consult us about matters which are clearly established for everyone. We do not speak as though you were ignorant; rather, perhaps occupied with other matters, we say that you have forgotten this.

### CHAPTER I

3. Whoever willingly cuts off part of any finger from himself is not admitted by the canons to the clergy (Dist. 55, c. 6; Council of Tribur, c. 33; Council of Nicaea, c. 1). But if this happens to someone accidentally [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “through some mishap.”], while he is attending to agricultural work or, while doing something, strikes himself unintentionally, the canons command that such men both be made clerics and, if they are found among the clergy, not be expelled. In the former, the will [Note: In the same codex: “the will which dared to cut itself with iron,” with *judicata* omitted. That word is equivalent to “condemned,” since pardon is immediately set against it. The reason for this judgment is that such a person is judged unlikely to hesitate to commit the same act against others, or to commit without scruple against another what he had committed against himself. Hence we do not approve the reading found shortly afterward in the printed editions, *dubitari*. The Royal manuscript has *possint*; there is no objection to accepting this word as referring to those whose will is being condemned, not to the will itself.] has been judged, since it dared to apply iron to itself, and therefore could not hesitate to do the same to others [Col. 0604A]; in the latter, the accident has earned pardon.

### CHAPTER II

4. Concerning the twice-married, no consultation was needed, since the Apostle’s teaching is clear: a man of one wife must be admitted to the priesthood or the clergy, and even this wife must have been a virgin when he took her (1 Tim. 3:2). For a woman who had previously had a husband, even if he has died, if she is afterward joined to a cleric, the cleric who takes her cannot be one, because the law has prescribed that a priest may not have as his wife a widow or a rejected woman (Lev. 21:13) [Note: The Labbe edition reads *bigamis*, as does the Royal manuscript. Other books more elegantly read *digamis*.].

### CHAPTER III

5. Concerning laymen, your religious office has consulted us as to which ones the canons prohibit from being ordained (see the Council of Sardica, c. 13). It is indeed certain that ecclesiastical rules contain this provision; but it has not been defined in such a way that it applies to all laymen. For men cannot be born clerics rather than become clerics; but categories have been designated from which one cannot reach the clergy—that is, if a Christian has served in the army, if a Christian has pleaded cases, that is, [Note: This word designates an advocate who asks judges to impose penalties on defendants, just as the voice of “administering,” shortly afterward, indicates a judge, whose duty it is to impose such penalties and punishments, or even pronounce a capital sentence. Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, once also doubted concerning both of them whether they should be admitted to communion. When consulted about this, Innocent replied to him in Letter 6, chapters 3 and 5.] has demanded such a sentence; if a Christian has administered an office. Concerning members of the municipal council, the reason is clear: even if men of this sort are found who ought to become clerics, since they are frequently summoned back to the council, one must beware of them [see above, Letter 2, no. 14] because of the trouble that often comes to the Church through them.

### CHAPTER IV

6. Laymen who were baptized while having wives, and who have so conducted themselves that their reputation has not wavered in any respect, whether they have been attached to clerics or have remained in monasteries from the time they were baptized, and who, if they have not known a concubine or mistress, have been vigilant in all good works [Note: The word *omnibus* was first deleted by Crabbé and was not afterward restored; it is recovered from Merl[inus] and the manuscripts.], are not prohibited from being admitted to the clerical lot.

### CHAPTER V

They must, however, observe the periods established by our ancestors (see Siricius, Letter 1, no. 13, and Zosimus, Letter 9, no. 5). Let no one quickly become a reader, quickly an acolyte, quickly a deacon, quickly a priest; for if they remain for a long time in the lesser offices [Col. 0605A], and both their life and their service are approved, they may afterward come to the priesthood after completing the merits of their periods of service, and must not seize in advance what an approved life deserves to receive [Note: The Royal exemplar reads “in all offices.” From this passage it is evident how frivolous is the claim of a recent writer who, having persuaded himself that Roman pontiffs customarily ordained only once a year, in December, maintains that those who had been ordained were required by necessity alone to wait until the following year before being advanced to a higher grade.].

7. Since it has therefore been shown by a definite ruling who ought to be admitted and who rejected, you must choose from all those whom your dignity sees cannot be rejected those whom you will make clerics. For if we wish to grant no favor or benefit at all to men, we can find such candidates that, in taking them up, we will neither incur scandal nor have cause for shame.

## LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, 5. This letter occupies a place in the Dionysian collection, from which it was copied into the Hispana and Isidorian collections, and is inscribed as Innocent’s title or decree XXVIII.]

That those who have begotten children while in the presbyterate must be removed from office.

**INNOCENTIUS TO MAXIMUS AND SEVERUS, BISHOPS AMONG THE BRUTTII.**

The norm of the ecclesiastical canons ought to be unknown to no priest; for it is sufficiently disgraceful for a pontiff not to know these things, especially when religious laymen both know them and consider that they must be observed. Recently, what sort of complaint our son Maximilianus, an *agens in rebus* [Note: The printed editions, compared with the Hispana and Isidorian manuscripts, read *in rebus hujusmodi qualem querelam*. This is corrected from the Dionysian and Hadrianic exemplars.], brought forward is shown by the sequence of his petition appended below. Led by zeal for faith and discipline, he does not tolerate the Church’s being polluted by unworthy priests whom he asserts have fathered children while in the presbyterate. I would explain that this is unlawful, if I did not know that your prudence is acquainted with the whole law. Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the substance of the appended petition, you shall order those who are said to have committed such acts to be brought before you; and, after investigating the charges brought against the priests themselves, if they can be convicted, you shall remove them from priestly office [Note: So the Dionysian and Hadrianic manuscript collections. Other books, with the printed editions, read “if they are convicted,” and afterward *tractare* instead of *tentare*. I am not unaware that the African Code of Ecclesiastical Canons, canon 4, which decrees that a bishop, priest, and deacon, or anyone who “handles the sacraments,” must guard chastity and abstain from their wives, may seem to favor the final reading. Nevertheless, we judged that we should in no way depart from the manuscripts we have found more reliable, especially since here only priests are under discussion, and by “holy things” are meant not one particular sacrament of the body and blood of Christ but whatever pertains to the ministry of priests. Therefore the word *tentare*, being more general, is also more suitable for expressing this matter.], because those who are not holy cannot handle holy things; and let them be made strangers to the ministry which they have polluted by living unlawfully [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “which they pollute.”]. But we are astonished that bishops conceal such things, so that they may be judged either to connive at what is unlawful or not to know it.

## LETTER XXXIX

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, 6. It is included in the Hispana and Isidorian collections according to Dionysius Exiguus, who placed it under title XXXIV of Innocent’s decrees.]

That after penance no one can be admitted to the clergy.

[Col. 0606A]

**INNOCENTIUS TO AGAPITUS, MACEDONIUS, AND MARIANUS, BISHOPS IN APULIA.**

Many reports from different people and very trustworthy submissions have informed us that numerous practices contrary to the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of our ancestors are being usurped throughout the province. These could easily be cut away if bishops were not found to be their authors—bishops who, while trying to show favor either to friends or to those who obey them, violate religion and corrupt the orders. Thus it happens that all sorts of unworthy men receive ecclesiastical honors and are admitted to the clergy, although they would not deserve to hold a respectable place even among the laity. This has been demonstrated in the petition recently delivered to us: a certain Modestus, entangled in many crimes, for which he is also said to have performed penance, has not only been made a cleric, which is unlawful, but is even striving toward the summit of the episcopate; whereas the canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices [Note: Not indeed in those exact words, but because the fathers of that council enact a rule from which this consequence is understood. Indeed, when in canon 10 they profess to follow the ecclesiastical rule concerning this matter, they presuppose that it had already been established. This reasoning also applies to all who have been contaminated by some serious stain of sin: Cyprian, in Letter 72, excludes and removes from the clergy those who return to the Church from heresy or schism, with the common consent of the brethren: “For priests and ministers who serve at the altar and in sacrifices ought to be whole and unblemished.” The laws which the Church sanctioned from the beginning agree in this: no one is to be promoted to the clergy unless, from baptism onward, he has led an innocent life, pure from every stain of any crime. If a previously hidden fault is afterward discovered, the Nicene canons 2 and 10 require that the convicted man be deposed. See above, Letter 16, no. 11.] (Dist. 50, c. 60; Council of Nicaea, c. 10). Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the petition, you shall order him to be presented; and if he is truly found to be such as the petition asserts, you shall remove him not only from his ambition [Note: Crabbé and later printed editions read “from ambition for the episcopate,” against Merl[inus] and all the manuscripts. Modestus is not merely barred from the episcopate but from every grade which he had not yet attained and from which he was striving toward the summit of the episcopate.] but also from the office of the clergy.

## LETTER XL

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, 8. It is found in the collections of Isidore, the Hispana, and Dionysius. In the latter it is called decree XXXVI of Innocent.]

That it is unlawful to invade another’s parish or to do anything in it without consulting its bishop.

**INNOCENTIUS TO FLORENTINUS, BISHOP OF TIBUR.**

[Col. 0606C] Sacred Scripture repeatedly cries out that the boundaries established by our fathers must not be moved, because it is a sacrilege for one person to invade what another has always possessed; and our brother and fellow bishop Ursus asserts that you have committed this very act. For he complains with sorrow that you have invaded the Nomentan or [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “Felician parish.” Moreover, the word *parish* here does not mean a collection of several churches subject to a bishop, which is how it was commonly understood in ancient times, but denotes a single church assigned to one presbyter. Innocent himself uses it in the same sense above, Letter 25, no. 8.] Felician parish, belonging by ancestral right to his [Col. 0607A] diocese, and celebrated the divine mysteries there without consulting him and without his knowledge [Note: Paschasius Quesnel, in his note on Leo’s First Letter, note 4, taking it as certain that the word *diocese* was scarcely used at that time by Roman or Eastern bishops for a provincial parish subject to a bishop, cites this passage of Innocent and says that the word seems to him to mean an administration, although he acknowledges that the term was already familiar in that sense to Africans and, after Leo’s time, to Gauls. But since at that time there were only two dioceses in Italy in the sense of an administration—namely, the Roman, over which the Roman bishop presided, and the Italian, which was subject to the bishop of Milan—the Nomentan parish belonged in that sense to the Roman bishop’s, not to the diocese of Ursus or Florentinus. The term *diocese* was also used for an episcopal territory by Hilary, Leo’s successor, as well as by Gelasius, Vigilius, and others. The same usage appears both in Augustine’s Letter 209, no. 8, and in canon 20 of the First Council of Toledo: “It has been decided from this day that no one except a bishop shall consecrate chrism and send it throughout the DIOCESE.”]. If this is true, you should recognize that you have incurred no slight offense [Note: Crabbé added *culpam* here on his own. That word would require *non levem*, not *non leviter*. Nevertheless, it was not corrected afterward. Moreover, *incurrere* and *offendere* are synonyms in Cicero.]. Therefore, if you wish to avoid the ill repute of so great a usurpation, it is appropriate to admonish you by our letters to abstain. Certainly, if you believe that something is supported by justice, with everything intact and remaining in its former condition, you must appear after the venerable days of Easter, so that you may respond to the complaints of the aforementioned man [Note: The printed editions after Crabbé read *memoratis*. Merl[inus] and the manuscripts more harmoniously read *memorati*, that is, of Ursus. *Intentiones* means the complaints; among the ancients *intentio* commonly meant a dispute, complaint, or lawsuit.], and, with both parties placed before us, we may inquire into what antiquity or truth requires.

## LETTER XLI

[Note: In the edition of the Councils, 20. It has come down to us through the three or four collections frequently mentioned. In Dionysius it is prefaced as Innocent’s decree XLIX, concerning the Bonosians, that they are to be compared with the Jews. This summary was copied from there by other compilers of canons and prevailed both in all manuscripts and in the earliest printed editions of the Councils and of Rome. Indeed, from this summary and another from the preceding Letter 16, joined together, Cresconius composed chapter 58 of his abridgment as follows: “Concerning the heretics called Bonosians, that they are to be compared with the Jews. And concerning the clerics whom the same Bonosus ordained before he was condemned. From the decrees of Pope Innocent, titles XLIX and L.” Hence Merlin, placing that double title before this letter, appended the preceding Letter 16 to it as though it were its second chapter. As we observed in the preliminary note to Siricius’ Letter 9, no. 7, the heresies of Bonosus and Photinus were related; nevertheless, there is no reason to depart from the wording of our letter, in which the followers of Photinus, not Bonosus, are mentioned. Indeed, if this letter was written to the bishop of Senia in Croatia—or, as it was formerly called, Liburnia—not to the bishop of Sena in Etruria, it is beyond dispute that Photinus, not Bonosus, is designated in it. Furthermore, since Photinus was bishop of Sirmium in Pannonia, near Liburnia, no one is unaware that he infected those provinces with the poison of his heresy. Finally, Innocent speaks of a heresy which he implies was spread through almost the whole world; this fits the Photinian heresy more than the recently arisen Bonosian one. Its author is said to be Marcus, not because he invented it, but because he displayed greater zeal in propagating it.]

That Laurentius should take care that those who follow the poison of Photinus be expelled.

**INNOCENTIUS TO LAURENTIUS, BISHOP OF SENIA.**  
[Note: Some manuscripts read “of Sinia”; Merl[inus] has “of Symena.”]

We have long been astonished, after reading your affection’s letters, that heretics following the poison of Photinus are not merely present in your territory but are also publicly preparing meeting places for themselves on certain people’s estates, since nowhere in almost the whole world have so many chosen to live as among you. Marcus, the author of their wicked doctrine, long ago expelled from the City, has been driven by such audacity that he claims the first place among them. But lest they retain the opportunity to rage any further and drag simple people and the unlearned [Note: The Roman edition reads “rustics.” Other books more correctly read *rusticanorum*, a word designating not inhabitants of the countryside but people lacking education.] with them into the Gehenna to which they are destined, action has been taken against them by the defenders of our Church [Note: If I remember correctly, the name and office of the defenders of the Roman Church is here mentioned for the first time in the letters of the supreme pontiffs. But Innocent does not speak of the office as though it had only recently been instituted. They will be mentioned again at the end of Zosimus’ Letter 9 to Hesychius.], so that they may be expelled: for those who deny that Christ God was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages may share condemnation with the Jews, who denied and still deny his divinity. It is your duty, dearest brother, to carry out the commands without slackening, lest through dissimulation you lose the people entrusted to you and begin to render God an account for those who have been lost.

## LETTER XLII

Or fragments of the letters of Pelagius written to Pope Innocent after his death, though Pelagius did not know that he had died.

1. In these writings, according to Augustine (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 30), Pelagius says that there are matters for which people try to defame him: one, that he denies the sacrament of baptism to infants and promises the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption; the other, that he says a person can avoid sin in such a way as to exclude God’s assistance, and trusts so greatly in free choice that he rejects the help of grace.

2. Augustine continues [same work, chapter 31]: After he had mixed in spiteful complaints against his enemies, he came to the point in these words: “Behold, before your Blessedness let this letter clear me, in which we say plainly and simply that we possess an unimpaired free choice for sinning and not sinning, and that in every good work it is always assisted by divine aid.”

3. Then, says Augustine [same work], after inserting certain remarks about the condition of man and his natural capacity for sinning and not sinning, he added: [Col. 0609A] “We say that this power of free choice exists generally in everyone—in Christians, Jews, and Gentiles. In everyone free choice is equal by nature; but among Christians alone it is assisted by grace. In the others the good of their condition is naked and unarmed; but in those who belong to Christ it is fortified by Christ’s help. The others are to be judged and condemned because, although they have free choice by which they could come to faith and merit God’s grace, they use the freedom granted to them badly [Note: Augustine comments on these words: “Clearly,” he says, “he means that grace is given according to merits, whatever sort or quality of grace he signifies; yet he does not express this openly.”]. But those are to be rewarded who, using free choice well, merit the Lord’s grace and keep his commandments.”

4. Likewise, he challenged his opponents to read the books which he had formerly written, in these words [same work, chapter 35]: “Let them read that letter [Note: Augustine adds: “I read this letter, and found that he dwelt almost throughout only on the power and possibility of nature, and established God’s grace almost only there. He touches on Christian grace so briefly that he seems to have feared nothing so much as remaining silent about it.”] which we wrote nearly twelve years ago to the holy bishop Paulinus, a letter of perhaps three hundred lines which confesses nothing other than God’s grace and assistance, and that we can do absolutely no good without God. Let them also read the letter [Note: Augustine testifies that he was unable to find this letter: “But if it is not unlike the others,” he says, “it too does not contain what we seek.”] to the holy bishop Constantius, where I briefly but clearly joined God’s grace and help to man’s free choice. Let them also read the letter which we wrote in the East to the holy virgin of Christ, Demetrias [Note: Concerning this, the same Doctor says: “I certainly read it, and it had almost persuaded me that he confessed the grace at issue. But when other writings came into my hands, which he composed later and at greater length, I saw how he could even there name grace while concealing what he thought beneath ambiguous generality, using the word ‘grace’ to blunt resentment and avoid offense.” In this work Augustine exposed the hidden poison in Letter 143, now 188, to Juliana. At the end of that letter he plainly refers to this letter of Pelagius to Innocent, and even to this very passage, when he says: “In one of his letters, the same Pelagius, where he openly gives his name and does not conceal the name of the holy virgin, says that he wrote to her and tries by the testimony of that same work of his to prove that he most openly confesses the grace of God which, he is said either to conceal or to deny.”] (same work, chapter 37); and they will find that we praise human nature in such a way that we always add the help of God’s grace. Let them also read my recent little work [Note: Augustine’s judgment concerning this work is as follows: “There are four books of this work, and I read them . . . But in all four books, whatever he seems to say in favor of grace—the grace by which we are helped to turn away from evil and do good—he says in such a way that he never departs from an ambiguity of words which he could explain to his disciples so that they would believe in no help of grace by which the possibility of nature is assisted, except in law and teaching.” After a short interval he adds: “But he thinks that this assistance of law and teaching also existed in the prophetic period, while the assistance of grace, which is properly called grace, exists in Christ’s example; and you see that this too belongs to teaching, which is preached to us as evangelical.”] (same work, chapter 41), which we were recently compelled to publish in defense of free choice; and they will recognize how unjustly those who wished to defame us by denying grace have acted, since throughout almost the whole text of that work we confess both free choice and grace perfectly and completely.”

5. But from these letters he also wishes the reader to proceed to the book of his faith, which he had appended to them (same work, chapter 32). This book of faith is reproduced in full in one of Augustine’s sermons *On Time*, 191, now Appendix 236, nos. 2 and following; it was also published separately in the appendix to volume X of the new edition of that saint’s works, page 96, as also in Jerome, to whom it had formerly been attributed.

6. Moreover, in those letters “which,” Augustine says (*On Original Sin*, nos. 19–21), “he sent to Rome to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, and since they did not find him alive, they were delivered to the holy Pope Zosimus and sent on to me”—that is, in the same letter—he complained that people defamed him because he denied the sacrament of baptism to infants and promised the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption [Note: Augustine says at the cited place: “These charges are not made against them in the form in which he stated them. For they do not deny the sacrament of baptism to infants, nor promise the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption . . . What is charged against them is that they do not wish to acknowledge that unbaptized infants are subject to the condemnation of the first man.”]. And after saying that he had never heard even an impious heretic say this concerning infants, he added: “For who is so ignorant of the evangelical reading that he would not only attempt to affirm this but could even lightly say or think it? Moreover, who is so impious as to wish infants to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, while he forbids them to be baptized and reborn in Christ [Note: Before bringing forward these words of Pelagius, Augustine prefaces them: “See how the hiding places of ambiguity prepare refuges for falsehood by casting darkness over the truth, so that even we, when we first read these words, almost rejoiced as though they were correct or corrected. But his longer discussions in the books where, however much he conceals himself, he is often forced to reveal himself, made even these statements suspect to us, so that, examining them more carefully, we might discover their ambiguities.”], and forbids him who was born for uncertain life to be reborn for perpetual and certain life [Note: Concerning the meaning of these words, Augustine adds, after explaining how much labor he had expended: “They are so ambiguous that they can provide hiding places for his doctrine, from which the heretical meaning may spring forth to lay its snares.”].”

7. Together with the aforesaid letters of Pelagius and his book of faith sent to Innocent, and likewise delivered to Innocent’s successor Zosimus, there was also a letter from Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem. From Zosimus we learn only this about it: Praylius, John’s successor, intervened as a most energetic supporter of Pelagius’ case (Letter 3, no. 2).

8. Whoever reads the aforesaid fragments of Pelagius’ letters, and carefully considers the observations appended by Augustine, who thoroughly understood all the cunning devices and evasions of that crafty heretic, and at the same time hears that Pelagius had been approved and praised with the commendation of the bishop of Jerusalem, will be less surprised that Zosimus, accepting his words simply as they sounded, could have been deceived by him.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING FRAGMENT

(*Spicilegium of Mai, volume III*)

In the preceding published letters of Innocent I, we have often appended a more extensive passage from his unpublished letter to Severian, bishop of Gabala. Indeed, in the Arabic manuscript “Haiala,” not “Gabala,” is written; this reading gains some support from the fact that Aila is an episcopal city of Palestine, according to Lequien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, p. 758. Nevertheless, among the very few bishops of that city known to Lequien, Severian is not listed. I therefore immediately thought of Severian, bishop of Gabala, likewise a city of Syria, who was a contemporary of Innocent; and, more importantly, from the notice of Innocent’s lost letters preserved by Constantius, p. 921, we learn that letters had been exchanged between Severian and Innocent. Moreover, a little farther below the Arabic manuscript likewise contains a fragment of Severian, where his episcopal see is called not Haiala but Gabala. The error in the Arabic manuscript therefore arose from the similarity of the letters. Let us consequently gratefully receive this fragment of an epistle of Innocent, preserved for us by an Arab.

## LETTER XLIII, OR FRAGMENT OF A LETTER WHICH INNOCENT, ONE OF THE FIRST BISHOPS OF ROME, WROTE TO SEVERIAN, BISHOP

[Col. 0611C] When the divine Word came from heaven and dwelt in the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, from whom he took flesh, he did not bring his body with him from heaven, nor did he acquire his divinity on earth; rather, he himself was God, and he himself fashioned his body in the Virgin’s womb. In forming his body he had no associate, but he alone formed it.

We confess that in everything accomplished through his humanity, the divinity was its companion, and that it was never separated from the humanity, even for the briefest moment. We also confess that, at the very time when our Savior came from heaven and descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary, he united divinity with humanity; these were never divided in any matter or action, since they were indivisible. And just as his divinity has no end, so also his humanity remains forever after the resurrection.

He suckled milk from a woman; nevertheless, divinity and humanity constituted one [Christ]. Let no one suppose that, when the divine Word came on earth to receive baptism from John, that was the beginning of his divinity, namely, when John heard the Father’s voice coming from heaven. The matter is certainly not so. Rather, at the very moment when he descended into the Virgin’s womb, he became one indivisible being with body and divinity; the divinity became the companion of the body and, in an unchangeable and inseparable manner, became a single unity.

The divinity was not separated from the humanity. While Christ was on the cross, the divinity did not withdraw from his humanity. He ascended into heaven with the body that he had taken from the Virgin Mary, and sat at the right hand of his most excellent Father.

This is our faith. Those who do not believe thus are expelled by the Catholic Church; indeed, God himself, its author, excommunicates them.

Praise be to God forever! Amen.

[Col. 0611]

# APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF SAINT INNOCENT I, POPE  
## NOTICE OF THE LETTERS THAT NO LONGER EXIST BUT CONCERN INNOCENT

*(D. Coust.,* Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum, *vol. I.)*

[Col. 0611D] **1. In the year 404, in April. Theophilus’s letter against John Chrysostom.**—Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, reported in a letter written to Innocent and delivered by an Alexandrian reader that he had deposed John. When the blessed Pope Innocent had read this letter, says Palladius, *Dialogue*, ch. 1, p. 9, “he came very near condemning Theophilus’s rashness and arrogance, since he had written alone, had not sent a clear account of the matter, and had not indicated why or with whom he had deposed John.”

This was the first of the letters that Innocent received concerning John’s case after John had been removed from the episcopate. It should therefore rightly be judged to have been written immediately after John’s deposition, following the disturbance raised in the Church of Constantinople on Holy Saturday—that is, in April of the year 404.

What Palladius writes on p. 151 concerning Theophilus should apparently be referred either to this letter or to the other one of which we shall speak under no. 4: “In his letter to Pope Innocent, while censuring the blessed John, he calls Epiphanius ‘most holy,’ whom, he says, he had previously reviled as a heretic or schismatic.”

**2. At the same time. Three letters on John’s behalf.**—Three days after Theophilus’s preceding letters had been delivered to Innocent, says Palladius, pp. 9–10, “four bishops from John’s party, religious men—Pansophius of Pisidia, Pappus of Syria, Demetrius of Second Galatia, and Eugenius of Phrygia—delivered three letters [to Innocent]: one from John the bishop, another from forty bishops concerning communion with John, and a third from John’s clergy. All agreed with one another and reported the disturbance caused by certain undisciplined men.”

Of those three letters, only John’s—that is, the fourth letter above—has come down to us. But if the three agreed with one another, then from what we still read in John’s letter it is not entirely obscure what was asserted in the other two.

**3. In the year 404, about June. Innocent’s letters of communion to both parties.**—At that time Innocent, judging that peace must be safeguarded until the opportunity to establish it more firmly should appear, wrote two letters: one to Theophilus and those attached to him, and another to John and his associates. By these letters he granted his communion to both parties.

Regarding them Palladius, ch. 3, pp. 22–23, preserved only this statement: “In response, the blessed Innocent sent equal letters of communion to both parties, disapproving the judgment that had apparently been rendered by Theophilus. He said that another, irreproachable synod of Westerners and Easterners ought to be convened: first with the friends of that assembly withdrawing, and then its enemies as well; for, generally speaking, a sound judgment does not proceed from either side.”

The letter written to John’s party was carried by Demetrius, metropolitan bishop of Pisinuntis in Second Galatia, who had most recently come to Rome with Pansophius, Pappus, and Eugenius. Palladius, p. 27, relates that Eugenius traveled through the East on this occasion and, by displaying these letters of Pope Innocent, established the communion of the Romans with Bishop John.

These letters were sent by Innocent shortly after he received the preceding letters, whether from Theophilus or from John and his party.

**4. About the same time. Theophilus’s letter against John.**—After this, Innocent received a further letter from Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning which Palladius says the following: A few days after Innocent had written the letters just mentioned, “a certain Peter, a presbyter of Theophilus, arrived with Martyrius, a deacon of the Church of Constantinople. They delivered Theophilus’s letter together with certain acts, in which John appeared to have been condemned by thirty-six bishops, twenty-nine of them Egyptians and seven from other regions.”

After these acts had been read, Innocent learned, according to the same Palladius, “that the accusations were not serious, that John had not been present, and that he had not been reproved in his presence.” What this pope replied to that letter can be read in his fifth letter.

**5. In the year 404, in June. Letter on John’s behalf.**—Innocent had scarcely dismissed Peter and Martyrius, who had brought Theophilus’s preceding letter, when he received letters from twenty-five or slightly more bishops who belonged to John’s synod. For, says Palladius, p. 24, “a short time afterward Theotecus, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, arrived, delivering letters from John’s synod of twenty-five or somewhat more bishops. They reported that John had been driven from the city by armed force, that he had been sent into exile at Cucusus, and that the church had been set on fire.”

This fire is recorded as having occurred on June 20 of the year 404. It follows that those letters were written toward the end of that month. In the *Theodosian Code*, book XVI, title 2, law 37, there is a law dated August 29 which states that, when many of John’s clerics had been committed to custody because of this fire, and after an investigation no one had been found guilty, Arcadius ordered them released.

**6. At the same time, John’s adversaries write.**—Shortly afterward, a certain contemptible fellow named Paternus brought to Innocent the letters of Acacius, Paul, Antiochus, Severian, and a few others (Palladius, p. 25), “in which they slandered John as though he had set the church on fire.” Innocent did not deign to reply to them.

**7. At the same time, the Africans commend their legates to Innocent.**—The letters of the Council of Carthage, held in the year 404 on June 26, to Pope Innocent also belong to this period; they are mentioned near the end of ch. 93 of the *African Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*. When this council had decreed that a delegation should be sent to the emperors to request laws for restraining the insolence of the Donatists, it immediately added: “Letters should also be sent to the bishop of the Roman Church for the commendation of the legates.”

The designated legates were Theasius and Evodius, and four letters were given to them, which Possidius lists in the catalogue of Augustine’s letters in this continuous sequence: “To Bishop Innocent, to the emperors, to Stilicho, and to the prefects of Italy.” From this it is inferred that those letters were composed by Augustine.

**8. About August, Innocent replies to the bishops of John’s synod.**—Innocent returned to Theotecus, who had brought him the letters of John’s synod of bishops, a letter for John and the other participants in his communion. In it he “exhorted them with tears to remain of good courage, since he could not bring them assistance because powerful persons stood in the way of doing good.”

Innocent spoke thus because the manifest disagreements between Honorius and Arcadius prevented the convocation of a council in which a remedy for the Church’s troubles might be sought. Theotecus had set out from Constantinople for Rome after June 24, intending to carry the letters of John’s synod of bishops to Innocent. Consequently, Innocent’s reply could not have been delivered to him before the following August.

**9. In the year 404, about November. Porphyrius’s letter to Innocent.**—While John Chrysostom was living in exile in Armenia, Flavian, bishop of Antioch, died (Palladius, p. 144). Porphyrius was then ordained in his place by Acacius, Severian, and Antiochus, and immediately informed Innocent of his ordination. Yet, according to Palladius, p. 141, he was not considered worthy of a reply from Innocent. The same Palladius explains at length, p. 142 and following, how depraved his conduct was.

From the constitution of Arcadius inserted in the *Theodosian Code*, book XVI, title 4, law 6, it is clear that Porphyrius was ordained in the year 404, before November 18.

**10. In the year 405, Innocent replies to the Africans, and his letter is read at the council.**—At the Council of Carthage held on August 23, 405, Innocent’s letter was read; it warned that bishops should not readily travel overseas (*African Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, ch. 94). This letter is believed to have been brought from Rome to Africa by Theasius and Evodius, who had been sent as legates to the emperor in June of the year 404 with letters to Innocent.

When the aforementioned letter of Innocent was read, “this very matter,” which it prescribed, “was confirmed by the judgment of the bishops.” Earlier, at the Council of Sardica, canon 8, chiefly on account of the Africans, it had been decreed “that bishops should not go to the imperial court, unless perhaps those who had been invited or summoned by letters of the most religious emperor,” when Gratus, bishop of Carthage, had complained that his own advice on this matter was being disregarded.

Nevertheless, so that the common interests of the churches might not thereby be neglected, the same synod added in canon 9 that, if bishops had petitions to present on behalf of widows, orphans, or others oppressed by unjust force, they should not carry them personally, but “send them through their deacons.”

Accordingly, the council at which Innocent’s letter was read decreed “that, for giving thanks and excluding the Donatists, two clerics of the Church of Carthage—not two bishops—should be sent to the imperial court.”

**11. About the beginning of the year 405. Exsuperius’s letter.**—The letter of Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, which contained various questions answered by Innocent in his sixth letter, appears to belong to the beginning of the year 405.

**12. Letter of fifteen bishops to Innocent.**—About the same time Innocent received a letter from fifteen bishops of John’s synod, which Palladius, p. 26, recalls in these words: “After Cyriacus, Eulysius, bishop of Apamea in Bithynia, arrived, delivering a letter from fifteen bishops of John’s synod, in which they described both the earlier and the present plundering of all Constantinople.”

Immediately before this, Palladius states that Eulysius, bishop of Sinnada, had fled to Rome, bringing no letters but being well qualified to recount what had happened. He had been moved by the injustice of the imperial order, which proclaimed: “If anyone does not communicate with Theophilus, Arsacius, and Porphyrius, let him be excluded from the episcopate and at the same time lose whatever property in money he appears to possess.”

From this it is possible to determine the time when that letter was delivered to Innocent. Either the order mentioned there is the one issued by Arcadius “concerning those who dissent from communion with Arsacius, Theophilus, and Porphyrius, the most reverend bishops of the sacred law, and who are therefore unquestionably to be expelled from the Church” (*Theodosian Code*, book XVI, title 4, law 6), or it was some later order in which a monetary fine was added to the earlier penalty.

Now Arcadius’s constitution addressed to the provincial governors is recorded as having been issued on November 18 at Constantinople, during the consulship of Honorius and Aristenaetus—that is, in the year 404. It therefore follows that the aforesaid letter of the fifteen bishops cannot have been delivered to Innocent before the beginning of 405, although it may be considered to have been written toward the end of 404.

**13. Letter of Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica, to Innocent.**—The same Eulysius also brought Innocent a letter from “Anysius, a most excellent old man,” as Palladius says, p. 27, “who wrote that he stood by the judgment of the Roman Church” in John’s case.

**14. Edict against clerics who communicated with John.**—A month after the arrival of Cyriacus, bishop of Sinnada, Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis and author of the *Lausiac History*, likewise came to Rome, bringing a copy of an edict. The other Palladius expresses it in the *Life of Chrysostom*, p. 27, as follows: “Whoever entirely conceals a bishop or cleric who communicates with John, let his house be confiscated.”
