We believe that these words indicate and briefly summarize the decree which Arcadius enacted on August 29, 404, in the following form: “Nor shall houses escape the danger of confiscation if it is established that they have received foreign bishops or clerics after the publication of the edicts and the addresses of Our Serenity. The same rule is to be observed if any houses receive citizens who are clerics and who hold new and tumultuous gatherings outside the church” (*Theodosian Code*, book XVI, title 2, law 37).

**15. Letter of the clergy of Constantinople to Innocent.**—After Palladius’s arrival in the City, “Germanus the presbyter and Cassianus, religious men, also arrived, delivering to Innocent a letter from all John’s clergy” (Palladius, p. 27). In it they wrote that their own Church had suffered violence and tyranny, its bishop having been expelled by armed force and driven into exile through the faction of Acacius, bishop of Beroea, Theophilus of Alexandria, Antiochus of Ptolemais, and Severian of Gabala.

At the beginning of this letter those devout clerics cited many testimonies from Scripture, declaring that they found consolation in them. Then, after explaining the violence of the bishops who opposed John, as well as the canons by which they attempted to defend their crimes, they asked what judgment ought to be formed concerning those canons. Innocent replied to them, and his letter—the seventh, namely—has come down to us.

**16. Some time later, letters from the bishops of Caria and from the presbyters of Antioch are delivered.**—After traveling through the East, Demetrius, bishop of Pisinuntis, is said by Palladius to have returned to Rome again after the arrival of Germanus and Cassianus, bringing both a letter from the bishops of Caria, “in which they embraced communion with John,” and one from the presbyters of Antioch, “in which, in maintaining communion with that same John, they followed the discipline of the Romans and deplored the ordination of Porphyrius as contrary to law and right” (Palladius, p. 28).

For, as Palladius relates, pp. 145–146, Porphyrius had secured, by sending money to the imperial court and to powerful bishops, that Constantius, who stood out among the other presbyters, should be exiled as a disturber of the peoples. He also arranged for other presbyters and clerics to be placed in custody.

Then, on the first day of the celebration of the Olympic games, when the entire city had gone out to the suburbs to watch the athletes, he burst into the church. There, together with the bishops Acacius, Severian, and Antiochus—whom he had concealed with him—and a few clerics, “he was secretly ordained with the doors shut and with such haste that they did not even complete the prayer, fearing that they might be detected.”

**17. As the year 405 was already drawing to a close, Innocent writes to Honorius concerning the wretched condition of the Churches.**—Afterward Domitian, presbyter and steward of the Church of Constantinople, and Vallagas, a presbyter of Nisibis, who also reported the affliction of the monasteries of Mesopotamia, delivered to Innocent the records of the prefect Optatus. These records stated that respectable women of the Church of Constantinople, deaconesses of consular families, were compelled either to be brought before him, to communicate with Arsacius, who had been substituted in John’s place, or to pay two hundred pounds of gold to the treasury (Palladius, p. 28).

Then Innocent, no longer able to endure so many and such great evils, wrote a letter to the Emperor Honorius. In it he explained point by point what was contained in the letters he had received from various persons concerning the wretched condition of the Church of Constantinople and of the other churches.

**18. Shortly afterward a synod of the bishops of Italy is convened.**—As soon as Honorius received this letter of Innocent, he ordered, to use Palladius’s words (Palladius, p. 29), “that a synod of the Westerners be convened and that, after they had delivered a single common judgment, they should refer it to his piety.”

Soon afterward, “the bishops of Italy assembled and asked the Emperor to write to his brother and fellow emperor Arcadius, so that he might order a synod to be held at Thessalonica. In this way both sides of East and West might more easily come together, and the synod, established not so much by the number of its bishops as by the weight of its judgment, might issue a certain and undisputed decision.”

A synod was indeed then held, but Palladius does not indicate where. We know only that its decision was entirely consistent with what Innocent had consistently judged from the beginning of this disturbance and thereafter, as may be seen above under no. 3 and in letters 5 and 7. It therefore follows either that he presided over this synod or that nothing was done in it except according to his judgment.

**Toward the end of the year 405, Honorius writes to Innocent.**—Following the decree of the preceding synod, Honorius wrote once and then a second time to Arcadius. When he accomplished nothing and was considering sending a third letter to him, he also wrote to Innocent, asking him to “send five bishops, two presbyters of the Roman Church, and one deacon to carry it” (Palladius, p. 29). How Innocent complied with his request has been explained in the first annotation to his ninth letter.

**19. In the year 406, Innocent writes to Arcadius.**—Innocent not only supplied Honorius with the legates he had requested—Aemilius, bishop of Beneventum; Cythegius and Gaudentius, likewise bishops; together with the presbyters Valentinian and Boniface; and one deacon of the Roman Church whose name is not given—but also entrusted them with a letter to deliver to the Emperor Arcadius.

The same legates received, together with the letter of Honorius that we still possess, letters from Chromatius of Aquileia, Venerius of Milan, and other bishops of Italy to the same emperor.

The time of this embassy may be inferred from the words of the legates. After relating that they had arrived at the imperial city, had immediately been detained in a suburb, and three days later had been released and confined in a coastal fortress of Thrace, they add: “The following day they sent someone to us—we do not know whether he was a court official or Atticus, for he himself was said to have invaded the throne of the Church—who gave us three thousand coins, asking us to communicate with Atticus.”

Arsacius had therefore already died, and Atticus had been appointed in his place. The legates indicate this in the words just quoted, since they say that they first began to hear of it when they approached the imperial city.

Now Socrates, book VI, ch. 20, relates that Arsacius died on November 11, in the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and of Anthemius—that is, in the year 405. He likewise records that Atticus was appointed under the consulship of Arcadius for the sixth time and Probus, and indeed, as Sozomen, book VIII, ch. 27, reports, after the see of Constantinople had been vacant for four months. Thus Atticus must have been substituted for Arsacius in March of the year 406.

It follows that Innocent’s letter with which we are concerned was written about the beginning of the year 406.

**20. At the same time, a memorandum is given to the legates.**—The legates were also given a memorandum of the entire Western synod (Palladius, p. 31), “which stated that John ought not to enter into judgment unless both the church and communion had first been restored to him, so that, once the reason for declining judgment had been removed, he might voluntarily enter the assembly.”

A similar provision was made by the Council of Lampsacus held under Damasus, according to Sozomen, book VI, ch. 7: “that bishops who had been deposed by those who asserted that the Son was unlike the Father should recover their sees by restoration, since they had been unjustly deprived of them; and if anyone should afterward wish to accuse them, he should do so under threat of equal condemnation.”

In that case, the sees of bishops unjustly deprived and expelled are restored to them first, and only afterward is an opportunity granted to accuse them.

In imitation of decrees of this kind, Isidore Mercator fabricated many similar documents, both in the name of Pope Symmachus in the fictitious Fifth Roman Synod under that pope and in the names of more ancient pontiffs; he did not hesitate to repeat them again and again.

**21. In the year 407, in June, the Africans attempt to reconcile Innocent with Theophilus.**—The Council of Carthage, held on June 13, 407, issued the following decree concerning letters to be written to Pope Innocent (*African Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*, ch. 101): “It was also resolved that a letter be written to the holy Pope Innocent concerning the disagreement between the Roman and Alexandrian Churches, so that each Church might maintain within itself the peace which the Lord commanded.”

This disagreement was none other than the one that had been aroused by the case of John Chrysostom, since Innocent had been unable to approve Theophilus’s violence against him.

**22. On June 17, 412, Innocent writes to the bishops of Illyricum.**—In his thirteenth letter, no. 3, Innocent himself mentions letters to the bishops established throughout Macedonia, Achaia, Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus, Crete, Mediterranean Dacia, Riparian Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalitana. They were sent together with that same letter—that is, on June 17, 412—and informed them that he had entrusted the care of those provinces, in his place, to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica.

**23. In the year 413, he writes to Augustine.**—Augustine, in his letter formerly numbered 259 and now 151, to Caecilianus, formerly prefect of Italy, no. 2, mentions that “a letter was sent to me by the brothers from the holy Pope Innocent, venerable for his outstanding merits; as is shown by reliable evidence,” he says, “it was delivered to me through your excellence.”

We know nothing else about this letter. Since Augustine’s aforementioned letter to Caecilianus is shown to have been written after September of the year 413, but not long afterward, we infer that this writing of Innocent belongs to that same year, 413.

**24. In the year 414, the Macedonians ask Innocent to grant them five concessions.**—In the following year Innocent received a letter from Rufus and the other Macedonian bishops consisting of five chapters. In the first they asked that, according to the custom of their province, they might promote to the clergy and even to the highest priesthood those who had taken widows as wives.

In the second they asserted “that a man should not be called twice-married if, while a catechumen, he had had and lost a wife, and after baptism had taken another; for that former marriage had been cleansed, together with the other sins, through the sacrament of baptism.” Accordingly, such a man should not be excluded from the clergy.

Their third question concerned those who had been ordained by heretics, specifically by Bonosus after his condemnation: whether such persons should be received in their offices. They persuaded themselves that this was permitted by the indulgence shown both by the Fathers of Nicaea toward the Novatians and by Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica, toward the Bonosians themselves.

Fourth, they asked Innocent, by revising the judgment against Photinus—which had been obtained from the Apostolic See through a false report and extracted from his predecessor by deceit—to permit them to establish this man as bishop.

Finally, they asked him, while confirming their own judgment against the deacon Eustathius, to strip him of the dignity of the diaconate and consign him forever to the devil.

In his fifteenth letter, written toward the end of the year 414, Innocent replied to each of these chapters.

**25. About the year 414, the Macedonians’ letter to Innocent. Innocent replies to it. A letter falsely attributed to Innocent. A second letter from the Macedonians.**—About the same year, 414, Bubalius, Taurianus or Tarianus, and others condemned by the Macedonians appealed to the Apostolic See. Accordingly, Rufus and his associates sent Maximianus and Eumenius, or Eugenius, to Rome with letters in which the crimes of Bubalius and Taurianus were set forth.

After examining the case, Innocent gave the Macedonian legates a letter in which, after first presenting a complete exposition of his views, he confirmed the condemnation of Bubalius, Taurianus, and their associates.

While the legates delayed on their return journey, however, Bubalius forged a letter in Innocent’s name and presented it to the Macedonians. They, having repeatedly experienced his deceptions, placed no confidence at all in this new fabrication and decided to repeat their earlier complaint in a second letter. They did not conceal that they found this kind of freedom to appeal gravely troublesome and burdensome.

Innocent replied to that second letter in his eighteenth letter. We should regret the loss of this letter less than the loss of the other one, in which he explained the entire affair and his judgment concerning it fully and openly.

**26. Innocent’s letter to the synod of the East.**—The fullest letter of Innocent to the synod of the East, concerning everything that should be required of the Easterners who sought peace, may be referred to this period. Innocent speaks of it as having been sent some time before peace was restored to the Church of Antioch (letter 22).

By the name “synod of the East,” the Churches subject to the bishop of Antioch are ordinarily understood.

**27. In the year 414, an embassy and letters concerning the ordination of Alexander and the peace of the Church of Antioch. Acacius’s writings.**—Alexander, bishop of Antioch, who had been substituted in the place of Flavian, sent an embassy to Innocent with letters in which he announced that he had been lawfully ordained; that, with the schism extinguished under which the Church of Antioch had so miserably suffered for so many years, peace had happily been restored to that Church; that he had received with the greatest charity those who had formerly been enrolled under the names of Paulinus and Evagrius; that Elpidius and Pappus, who had been expelled because of the case of John Chrysostom, had recovered their Churches without any dispute; and finally, that John’s name had been inscribed in the sacred diptychs.

He therefore earnestly requested that the Roman Church grant him its communion (Innocent, letter 19).

Acacius, bishop of Beroea, also appended writings to these letters. He too asked Innocent to restore the communion which, because of John, he had thus far denied him.

**28. About the year 415, Innocent holds a synod at Rome concerning the same matter.**—On the occasion of the Antiochene embassy, a council was assembled at Rome, attended by twenty bishops. After Alexander’s letters had been read and the legates heard—their leader appears to have been the presbyter Cassianus—the matter was carefully examined: whether all the conditions previously required for peace had been satisfied at Antioch.

In consequence, Innocent sent Alexander both a private letter and a common letter signed by the twenty bishops, together with the acts of the synod, and writings addressed to Acacius, carried by Paul the presbyter, Nicholas the deacon, and Peter the subdeacon (Innocent, letter 19).

We still possess those three letters, but the signatures of the twenty Italian bishops and the acts appended to them have been lost. We learn from letter 23 only that Maximianus, bishop of Macedonia, attended this synod. From this it may be conjectured that, as was customary, other bishops of other provinces who happened to be in the City at the time were also summoned to it.

**29. Some time later Maximianus writes on Atticus’s behalf.**—After witnessing the peace granted by Innocent to Bishop Alexander and the Church of Antioch, Maximianus, bishop of Macedonia, returned to the imperial city and appears to have advised Atticus himself to seek peace without delay.

Whether Atticus indicated that he was not at all opposed to this course and asked Maximianus to obtain this favor for him, or whether Maximianus undertook it of his own accord, driven by an overhasty desire for unity, he sent a letter with a memorandum to Innocent and requested from that pope a letter of communion for Atticus of Constantinople.

Innocent replied to this letter of Maximianus in his twenty-second letter.

**30. About the year 415, Alexander presents certain questions to Innocent.**—After sending a memorandum, Alexander asked Innocent, first, what authority the bishop of Antioch possessed in the ordinations of bishops in the diocese of the East; then, “whether, when the provinces had been divided by imperial decision so that there were two metropolitan cities, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be appointed.”

Third, he complained that the Cypriots, who belonged to the diocese of the East, having formerly been harassed by the power of Arian impiety, had not observed the canons of Nicaea in the ordination of bishops, but had their own bishops ordained without consulting anyone. He asked what conduct ought to be maintained toward them.

Finally, he asked whether clerics of the Arians, when returning to the Church, should be received “with the dignity of a priesthood or of any ministry.”

Innocent’s response to each question is found in letter 24.

**31. About the beginning of the year 416, Decentius and Caelestine consult Innocent concerning various rites.**—Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, likewise consulted him concerning various customs by which some Churches differed from the Roman Church:

1. Concerning the peace which, in some churches, is either imposed upon the people before the mysteries have been completed or exchanged among the priests themselves;

2. Concerning the names recited before the canon;

3. Concerning infants, whether presbyters may sign them on the forehead;

4. Concerning fasting on Saturday;

5. Concerning the fermented bread, whether it should be sent on Sunday through each parish, as it is sent in Rome through the titular churches;

6. Concerning the possessed, whether presbyters or deacons may lay hands upon them;

7. Concerning penitents, when they should be absolved.

At the same time Decentius had sent another letter to Caelestine, then a deacon, in which he asked him three further questions: first, whether only priests, or other Christians who were ill as well, might be anointed with the holy oil of chrism; next, whether only presbyters, or bishops also, might anoint the sick with chrism; finally, whether that oil should be poured upon penitents.

In letter 26 Innocent answers all these questions.

**32. In the year 416, several writings concerning the case of Pelagius are sent from Africa to Innocent.**—The letters that the Africans composed for Innocent in the year 416 mention several documents sent to him concerning the case of Pelagius and Caelestius (letter 26, no. 1).

First, the Council of Carthage indicates that it appended to its letter the letters of the bishops Heros and Lazarus against Pelagius and Caelestius.

[Col. 0622B] Next, the same council states, in an appendix to that letter, that it attached the acts of another Council of Carthage held nearly five years earlier, by which Caelestius had been cut off by episcopal judgment.

It had also appended, as may be gathered from the final words of the letter itself, the acts of the Council of Diospolis, by which Pelagius boasted that he had been acquitted—that is, in the form in which they had been falsified by this heretic. For no other version had then reached Africa.

Shortly afterward Augustine, writing to Innocent together with four companions (Innocent, Letter 28, no. 6), indicates that he appended to his letter the book of Pelagius sent to him by Timasius and James, disciples of that heretic, as well as the work he had composed to refute it, *On Nature and Grace*, concerning which James and Timasius themselves had written him a letter in thanks; he also appended the letter Augustine judged should be written to Pelagius, who had sent him the proceedings of the Palestinian synod—altered by Pelagius—“as writings of his acquittal.” Of these documents, only Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace*, together with the letter of James and Timasius to Augustine, has come down to us. What Innocent thought of Pelagius’s book he makes clear in Letter 31, no. 5.

### 33. The Letter of Eustochium and Paula to Innocent

Not long afterward Eustochium and Paula sent a letter to Innocent, in which they lamented the most serious persecution inflicted upon them with such restraint that they even withheld the name of its author.

### 34. Jerome’s Letter to the Same

Jerome likewise wrote another letter [Col. 0622D], in which he did not conceal the danger to which his life had been exposed, unless the protection of a strongly fortified tower had saved him from the attack of the impious. On this occasion he informed him that Bishop Aurelius had conceived the desire to visit Innocent.

### 35. At an Uncertain Date, Felix of Nuceria Consults Innocent

Felix, bishop of Nuceria, testified in a letter written to Innocent that, following the institutions of his predecessors, he referred everything that raised any doubt to him as to the head and summit of the episcopate, so that he might learn from him what he ought to do. He stated that he had either built new churches of God or restored those that had fallen into ruin; but he indicated that he lacked clerics whom he could appoint in them, while some mutilated men or men with two wives were available. Finally, he asked to be instructed which persons from among the laity the canons prohibited from being ordained. Innocent satisfies his consultation in Letter 37.

### 36. A Petition against Incontinent Presbyters

Maximilianus, *agens in rebus* in Bruttium, sent Innocent a petition against certain presbyters of that province, whom he accused of having fathered children while in the presbyterate. This occasioned Innocent’s Letter 38.

### 37. A Petition against Modestus, a Cleric Made from a Penitent

Innocent mentions another petition delivered to him (Letter 39), but says nothing of where he received it. It reported that a certain Modestus, involved in many crimes for which he had performed penance, had not only been made a cleric in Apulia but was also striving toward the summit of the episcopate [Col. 0623B].

### 38. A Petition against a Bishop Who Had Celebrated the Divine Mysteries in Another Parish

Another petition was given to the same pope (Letter 40), in which Ursus complained that Florentinus, bishop of Tibur, had celebrated the divine mysteries in the Nomentine parish, which belonged to his diocese, without his knowledge [Col. 0624A].

### 39.

Finally, the letter of Laurentius, bishop of Siena, to Innocent is lacking. In it he reported that followers of Photinus were living in his territory and publicly preparing meeting places on the estates of certain persons.

### 40.

Moreover, if the *Pontifical Book* is to be trusted, Innocent “issued a decree concerning the whole Church, concerning the rules of monasteries, and concerning Jews and pagans.”

### 41. Spurious Letters

Amid so many genuine writings of the holy prelate, Isidore Mercator was not at all afraid to insert a counterfeit product of his own ingenuity and attribute it to so great a name. But we shall restore that spurious letter, which was addressed to Aurelius and stood as number 12 in the edition of the councils, to its parent in the following volume. The appendix to this volume, if the volume permits it, will present four other false letters: two bearing the names of Innocent writing to Arcadius, and two others bearing the names of Arcadius replying to Innocent.

[Col. 0623]

## Decrees Extracted from the Letters of Saint Innocent I

*(Collection of the Councils, Mansi, vol. III.)*

### Notice

[Col. 0623C] In that old Lucensian collection, about which I have spoken more than once, there occurs, in an epitome of numerous councils and certain decretal letters, an excerpt from a letter of Pope Innocent taken from the Council of Nicaea. No prudent person would doubt that this letter belongs to Pope Innocent I, since the age of this codex surpasses that of every other pontiff named Innocent by at least nine hundred years. What this letter of Innocent is, however; from which codex it was copied; whether Innocent issued a separate letter concerning the Nicene canons, or whether he cited and repeatedly emphasized them on various occasions in his letters, after which the author of this epitome joined them into a single series of canons, I frankly do not know. Although nothing new is presented here, it is nevertheless worthwhile to publish it in whatever form it may have, since this is the most ancient Latin edition of the Nicene canons. The edition that names Dionysius Exiguus as its author is certainly later than Innocent I. As for the version found in the collection of Isidore Mercator, it has not yet been determined whether it is earlier or later. The version of Rufinus, finally, is approximately as old as Innocent himself [Col. 0623D].

## From a Letter of Pope Innocent I Taken from the Council of Nicaea

I. Let one who has castrated himself not enter the clergy.

II. A pagan who has been converted and baptized shall not be promoted secretly into the clergy.

III. A bishop or other clerics shall not live with unrelated women.

IV. A bishop shall be ordained by all the bishops, or by three with the consent of the metropolitan.

V. A bishop shall not receive another bishop’s cleric, nor one who has been excommunicated. Councils shall be held twice a year because of the complaints of different persons [Col. 0624C].

VI. The Alexandrian and Roman popes shall have primacy.

VII. Presbyters shall be chosen with the consent of many bishops, especially with the consent of the metropolitan. *(Perhaps, however, the text reads “bishops.”)*

VIII. The bishop of Jerusalem shall have primacy, without prejudice to the privilege of the metropolitan.

IX. The Cathari—that is, converted Novatians—shall be received into the clergy. A bishop, however, shall be received into the place of a presbyter.

X. There shall not be two bishops in one city.

XI. If someone is discovered after priestly ordination, he shall be deposed; the same applies to the lapsed.

XII. The lapsed shall perform penance for seven years without tortures.

XIII. If someone is converted after military service and serves again, let him perform penance for thirteen years.

XIV. If he has received Communion in necessity and survives, let him observe penance [Col. 0625A].

XV. If catechumens have fallen, let them perform penance for three years.

XVI. A bishop, or members of the other orders, shall not go from one city to another.

XVII. A wandering cleric shall not be received into communion by another.

XVIII. No one shall promote a cleric from elsewhere to an office of honor.

XIX. Clerics shall give neither interest nor *renovum* [sic].

XX. Deacons shall not be preferred to presbyters or sit in their place, nor shall they administer the Eucharist to presbyters; but in the presbyters’ absence they shall distribute it.

XXI. Paulianists shall be baptized [sic].

XXII. Deaconesses shall be counted among the laywomen [sic].

XXIII. Easter shall be observed by the bishops on one day.

## Dissertation on the Following Epitome of Innocent’s Letter

Although I have no new letters of Innocent I to bring forward, I nevertheless think that I ought to share with my readers what our abbreviated collection of canons exhibits in a manuscript codex from Lucca that is nine hundred years old. It contains canons extracted from several letters of Innocent and reduced to an epitome.

In the epitome drawn from the letter to Exsuperius, canon 3 is absent: it concerns those who, after baptism, held public office and pronounced sentence in a capital case. I can think of no other reason for this omission than that the Pontiff judged that nothing needed to be decreed on this matter. The canon that follows, canon 4—which is canon 3 in our epitome—has been badly expressed. Married men are not deprived of communion if they commit adultery; rather, the innocent spouse is separated from the adulterer. The rest agrees with the letter. The addition concerning the Lamentations of Jeremiah should not be overlooked: it is supplied by one of our manuscripts and is not found in the printed editions.

This epitome is followed by another letter of Innocent to the bishops of Toledo. Several points in it plainly deserve attention. First, in our breviary, just as in all the ancient codices, according to Hardouin’s testimony, the reading is *Tolosanos*, not *Toletanos* [Col. 0625D].

Next follows a synopsis of Innocent’s letter to Victricius—our codex has *Victorius*—in which everything is clear and agrees with the printed editions, except for the second part of canon 3. In the printed letter, Innocent rules that ecclesiastical cases are to be heard in their respective provinces, without prejudice to an appeal to the Roman Church, or unless the seriousness of the case requires that judgment be referred to the apostolic see. This is the printed text. The manuscript codex, however, reads differently: “Roman clerics shall not dare to state their cases before other bishops.” These two readings are so far apart that they appear to have been taken from different codices. Nevertheless, no one can reasonably doubt that the words found in the printed editions belong to Pope Innocent I, since Nicholas I praises them as coming from Innocent in a pair of letters to be read at the Seventh Roman Council, in Labbe, vol. X. Since Nicholas does not say that he took them from the letter to Victricius, and since our epitomator is not always successful in conveying the sense of the canons, one of two conclusions is necessary: either this canon, in the form found in the printed editions, was badly stitched onto Innocent’s letter to Victricius from another letter of Innocent—as is known to have happened with the letters of other ancient pontiffs—or our anonymous epitomator entirely failed to grasp the Pontiff’s meaning [Col. 0626A].

In the epitome of canon 8, a rule is issued that monks are not to be admitted into the clergy. But Innocent does not command this; rather, he warns that those promoted to a higher rank should not cast aside the modesty and other virtues they had cultivated in the monastery. Our epitomator’s negligence therefore requires correction.

The synopsis of Innocent’s letter to Decentius is thoroughly barbarous, but its first chapter expresses an ancient liturgical practice which the printed editions do not mention, although in sense it agrees with them. In canon 1 the Pontiff forbids the peace to be given before the end. Our anonymous epitomator expressed this as follows: “The order of Mass: to give the peace after the fourth prayer.” I believe that “the fourth prayer” here designates what the old Roman order, in Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum*, vol. II, calls the *oration ad complendum*, the prayer for completion. In the Mass, the first prayer was the one read before the Apostle, that is, before the Epistle. Another followed over the offerings. Then the Lord’s Prayer occupied the third place; finally, the fourth prayer was the *oration ad complendum*. Thus our epitomator is reconciled with Innocent.

I can assign no other reason why the fifth canon of this letter was divided into two, especially since both parts amount to one and the same thing, except the negligence of our epitomator. The remainder is clear.

Finally, an epitome of Innocent’s letter to Bishop Aurelius—certainly Aurelius of Carthage—is read. In the Labbean collection, no. 12, there is a letter of Innocent to Aurelius to which the matters contained in this synopsis may be referred.

## I. From Innocent’s Letter to Exsuperius

[Col. 0626C]

I. Incontinent presbyters and deacons shall be deposed.

II. Those who are continent shall receive the viaticum at all times, and Communion through mercy.

III. Married persons who commit adultery shall be excommunicated.

IV. It is permitted to accuse a murderer.

V. Whoever divorces his wife and marries another shall be excommunicated; likewise the woman.

VI. The books that are to be received:

The five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy; Joshua son of Nun, one book; Judges, one; Kings, four; Ruth, one; the Prophets, sixteen; Solomon, five; the Psalter, one; Job, one; Tobit, one; Esther, one; Judith, one; Maccabees, two; Ezra, two; *Chenib*, that is, the Lamentations of Jeremiah; Chronicles, two.

Of the New Testament: the four Gospels; fourteen letters of the Apostle Paul; four of John; two of Peter; one of James; the Acts of the Apostles; the Apocalypse of John.

## II. From Innocent’s Letter to All the Bishops in Toulouse

A bishop shall not ordain bishops in another church [Col. 0627A]. He shall remove Spaniards from secular military service and not hastily ordain them to the priesthood; nor shall he ordain curials who ought not to be clerics. Those who have engaged in forensic practice, or who have come from military service or from the curial class, disparage the Spaniards in order that they may enter the priesthood or the minor offices.

## III. Innocent to Bishop Victorius

I. A bishop shall not be ordained without the consent of the metropolitan.

II. Whoever has worn the belt of secular military service shall not enter the clerical office.

III. A bishop shall hear cases among the clerics. Roman clerics shall not dare to state their cases before other bishops [Col. 0627B].

IV. A cleric shall not take a widowed woman as his wife.

V. No one shall receive a cleric from elsewhere.

VI. Novatians or Montenses shall be received by the laying on of hands. Those of our people who went over to them and are recalled shall perform prolonged penance.

VII. Deacons shall not associate with a wife.

VIII. A monk shall not enter the clergy, nor take a wife.

IX. Curials shall not be ordained as clerics [Col. 0627C].

X. If a veiled woman goes astray, she shall not receive penance.

XI. Consecrated women who are not veiled, if they marry, shall perform penance.

## IV. Innocent to the Bishop [sic]

I. No cleric who has married twice shall be ordained.

II. Whoever had a wife before baptism and married another after baptism is a man married twice.

## V. Innocent to Decentius

[Col. 0628A]

I. The order of Mass: give the peace after the fourth prayer.

II. The names shall be recited after the commendation of those making the offerings.

III. Presbyters shall not sign infants [with the sign of the cross] except bishops.

IV. Let there be a fast every Saturday.

V. Presbyters shall hold Mass in the city when the bishop is present.

VI. Without the bishop’s order, a presbyter shall hold Mass in the city when the bishop is present [Col. 0628B].

VII. Without the bishop’s order, no one else shall lay hands on a possessed person.

VIII. All penitents shall be reconciled on Thursday of Easter.

IX. A presbyter may visit a sick person and anoint him with chrism; but he may not anoint a sick penitent with chrism.

## VI. Innocent to Bishop Aurelius

[Col. 0628C]

Let hands not be imposed hastily; let no one be ordained from the laity.

## Observation of Philippe Labbe, S.J.

The following canons, which had long before been sent by some Roman synod to the bishops of Gaul, were first brought to light from several manuscript codices by the Reverend Father Sirmond in the appendix to volume I of the councils of Gaul. The royal collector placed them out of their proper position at the end of volume XXXVII, after the indices, together with a treatise on the ancient promotions of bishops. We, however, following the conjecture of that most distinguished editor—which is not improbable—have placed them beneath the letters of Innocent I, since neither their form of decrees nor their style of writing is inconsistent with them. The year in which they were issued is entirely uncertain, although, as everyone can see, they plainly display the greatest antiquity [Col. 0628D].

[Col. 0627]

# Letters Attributed to Saint Innocent I

*(D. Constant, Appendix to vol. I.)* (S)*

## Notice Concerning the Four Following Letters

[Col. 0627D]

1. Of those four letters, Nicephorus Callistus transmitted the first to us complete in Greek, book XIII, chapter 34; Glycas, in the fourth part of his *Annals*, transmitted it in a mutilated form, with several passages cut out here and there. Glycas alone preserved the second and fourth letters there likewise in Greek. The third, however, has reached us only in Latin, transcribed by Baronius from a Vatican exemplar. The same Cardinal added a fifth letter to these, under the year 407: the Emperor Honorius’s letter to Arcadius, which he had extracted from an old codex of Cardinal Guglielmo Sirleto [Col. 0628D].

2. All these writings share the same mark of forgery: they place Eudoxia alive after John Chrysostom, although the testimony of Socrates, Sozomen, Marcellinus, Prosper, Zosimus, and the Greek records establishes that she died in childbirth three years before him. Certainly George of Alexandria should not be compared with these authorities. On his authority, the emperor Leo, surnamed the Philosopher, Cedrenus, Nicephorus, and other later Greek writers extended Eudoxia’s life by three years [Col. 0629A].

Moreover, no history reports that this Empress’s great power and influence over Arcadius’s mind and favor were diminished even slightly until her death; yet this is invented in the second and fourth letters. What is read in the first letter departs no less from historical truth than from ecclesiastical practice: there Innocent is said, after Chrysostom’s death, to have excluded Arcadius and Eudoxia from receiving the sacraments; to have removed Arsacius from the episcopal rank even after his death; to have inflicted the same punishment on those who had joined him in his ordination; and to have struck Theophilus not only with excommunication but also with anathema, removing him from all association with Christians.

First, the letters of Liberius to Constantius, of Gelasius, Symmachus, Anastasius II, and Hormisdas to the Emperor Anastasius testify that Roman pontiffs customarily dealt with princes, even heretical ones, in a very different manner [Col. 0629B]. In addition, they do not ordinarily impose so severe a penalty even on a private individual without prior warnings. Where are those warnings here? If Innocent had wished to employ them, he would have learned of the death of Arcadius—who survived Chrysostom by scarcely seven months—before he was able to use that final remedy.

Furthermore, it is certain from Innocent’s own letters that he reserved judgment of the entire Chrysostom case for an ecumenical synod. Accordingly, that pope, having testified that Theophilus was in communion with him just as John had been, repeatedly urged him “to present himself to the synod, if he trusted in his judgment” (Innocent, Letter 5). Likewise, writing to the Constantinopolitans, he says: “We are considering how an ecumenical synod should be convened, so that the turbulent disturbances may at last, by God’s will, subside” (Letter 7, no. 4).

At the request of Innocent, the Emperor Honorius wrote a third time to Arcadius (Letter 9), making no threats against him but merely begging “that he order Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, who is said to be the author of all the evils, whether he wishes it or not, to present himself” at the synod [Col. 0629C]. While Innocent was considering this, the death first of John and shortly afterward of Arcadius delayed the convening of the synod.

Nevertheless, he did not therefore abandon his original plan, nor, while awaiting the desired synod, did he entirely break peace and communion with John’s adversaries; he merely interrupted and suspended them. On this matter Palladius, the author of the *Life of Chrysostom*, speaks as follows near the end of the dialogue, p. 214:

> “The purpose of the Roman Church is this: not to communicate with the Eastern bishops, especially with Theophilus, until the Lord grants an opportunity for a universal synod, which may heal the putrefied limbs of those who perpetrated these acts.”

Here it is not the judgment of the Roman Church that is indicated, but its purpose—or its policy—which it judged should be followed until the synod decided the matter. Indeed, Theophilus never ceased to be counted among the Alexandrian prelates, even by Roman bishops. The same must be said of his other associates, except Arsacius, whom, according to Theodoret (book V, chapter 34), the bishops of the West “did not even deign to greet.”

When Atticus was substituted in his place, however, Innocent himself was content to keep communion suspended, prepared to restore it to him once he had fulfilled the agreed conditions. Accordingly, when Bishop Maximianus amicably asked him to send a letter of peace to Atticus, he replied:

> “Suspended communion is restored to the one who demonstrates that the causes for which it occurred have now been removed and who professes that the conditions of peace have been fulfilled.”

Theodoret relates that Atticus was received by the Westerners after he had restored John’s name to the sacred registers [Col. 0630B].

3. Nevertheless, from what Theodoret writes in the passage cited, the material and occasion for the first letter—and consequently for the others, which agree with the first so closely that I scarcely doubt that they all had one author—seem to have been provided. It is no objection that, although Theodoret says that while Arsacius was alive the Western bishops so abhorred communion with him that they did not even deign to greet him, the first letter nevertheless removes him from office only after his death, not before.

One should not expect complete fidelity from a forger who cannot hold to the truth, even when reproducing what he imitates. Yet from that detail—“even after his death,” which plainly appears to have been deliberately inserted—the time when those letters were composed may be inferred. Certainly, if they had been public when the Emperor Justinian was searching everywhere for examples by which to prove that Theodorus of Mopsuestia could be excommunicated even after death, he would not have overlooked this particularly notable case of Arsacius’s removal after death. Yet nowhere is he said to have brought it forward. This is a substantial indication that those letters did not then exist—that is, in the middle of the sixth century.

That affected expression, “even after death,” also seems to have been inserted for no other reason than to favor those who wanted Theodorus of Mopsuestia to be excommunicated. We may therefore conjecture that the letters were forged in that same sixth century, while the controversy just mentioned had not yet been settled.

# Letter I

A sentence is pronounced against Arcadius, Eudoxia, Arsacius, and Theophilus.

[Note: [Col. 0629] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0629]

## Innocent, Archbishop of Rome, [Note: [Col. 0629D] Nicephorus considered this letter to have been addressed jointly to Arcadius, Atticus, and Theophilus. Before it he states that Innocent, because the legates whom he had sent to Constantinople had been badly and dishonorably treated, became extremely indignant; and that, shortly after John’s death, he sent a letter to Arcadius, Atticus, and Theophilus, subjecting them to excommunication and deposition. He then notes that this letter was composed in the following terms: “The voice of the blood of my brother John,” and so forth. Yet it contains no mention of Atticus. As if wishing to anticipate this observation, after transcribing the whole letter he immediately adds: “Innocent wrote this while fighting for John.” Nor, he says, did he acquit Atticus, who after Arsacius invaded that great man’s—John’s—see (ἔξω αἰτίας ἐποίει, “he held [him] blameless”). The history will explain this matter in its proper place, namely, book XIV, chapter 25, where it is said that peace was restored once Atticus ordered John’s name to be mentioned in the prayers.] To the Emperor Arcadius

[Col. 0629D] 1. The voice of the blood of my brother John cries out to God against you, O emperor, just as once the voice of righteous Abel cried out against Cain, the murderer of his brother; and it will be avenged in every way. Nor did you merely commit this offense: even in a time of peace you stirred up a great persecution against God and his Church. You expelled from his episcopal [Note: [Col. 0630D] In Nicephorus, τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς, “of the episcopate,” is omitted here, although the same word is retained below in section 3.] see, without a judgment having been rendered, the great Teacher of the whole world, and together with him you persecuted Christ.

I do not grieve for him in this way—for he has received his lot and inheritance with the holy Apostles in the kingdom of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ—although that loss is intolerable. Rather, I am distressed because I first consider the salvation of your souls, and then the people who, deprived of his most wise, spiritual, and divine teaching and instruction, are now compelled to suffer hunger.

For not only did the Church of Constantinople suffer the loss of that honey-flowing tongue; the whole earth beneath the sun has also been widowed, having lost such a divine man, through the persuasion of one woman who permitted this outrage to be committed. She, moreover, shall suffer both the punishment present here and the eternal penalty that will shortly overtake her [Col. 0631B].

Although blessed John, after preserving the faith and strengthening those who were wavering, departed this life, he nevertheless obtained for eternal ages the inheritance of everlasting delights and immortal life. But Eudoxia, that new Delilah, who gradually shaved you with the razor of deception, has brought a curse upon herself from many mouths. She has bound upon herself a heavy burden of sins, impossible to carry [Note: [Col. 0631D] In Glycas: “and extremely difficult to carry.” The reading “impossible to carry” is preferable, since it is clear that this passage was modeled on Matthew 23:4: “For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens.”], and has added it to her former sins (Judges 16:19).

2. Therefore I, the least and a sinner, as the one entrusted with the see of the great Apostle Peter, separate you and her from participation in the undefiled mysteries of Christ our God. And any bishop or cleric of the order of the holy Church of God who, from the hour when [Note: [Col. 0631D] Labbe, following the Greek of Glycas: τὸν πεμφθέντα σύνδεσμον, “the bond that has been sent.”] the bond by which I bind you has become known to you, should dare to administer or deliver them to you: I decree that he has fallen from his rank [Col. 0631C].

If, as powerful persons, you compel anyone to do this by force, and transgress the canons delivered to you by the Savior through the holy Apostles, then on the terrifying day of judgment you will discover, first, that this will be no small sin for you; and, second, that no earthly dignity will then be able to help anyone. The hidden things of the souls will burst forth and be displayed before the sight of all.

3. As for Arsacius, whom you thrust into the episcopal see in the place of the great John, we remove him from office even after his death, together with all the bishops who deliberately communicated with him [Note: [Col. 0631D] This is Arsacius who, according to Palladius, p. 94, had promised and sworn to his brother Nectarius, touching the Gospels, that he would never accept ordination to any episcopate. He died after fourteen months had elapsed from his ordination.]. His name shall not be inscribed in the sacred registers, for he is unworthy of this honor, having polluted the episcopate by a kind of adultery.

“For every plant that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matthew 15:13). As for Theophilus, we declare him not only deposed from his see but also punished with excommunication and anathema, entirely alienated from the fellowship of Christians.

## Letter of Innocent, Archbishop of Rome, to the Emperor Arcadius

[Col. 0630C]

[Col. 0630D] 1. The voice of the blood of my brother John cries out to God against you, O emperor, just as once the voice of righteous Abel cried out against Cain, the murderer of his brother, and it will be avenged in every way. You have not only done this, but also, in a time of peace, raised up a great persecution against the Church of God and his priests. You drove the great teacher of the inhabited world from the throne of his episcopate without judgment, expelling Christ along with him.

For I do not mourn for him in this way—for he has received his portion with the holy Apostles in the kingdom of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ—even though the calamity is unbearable. Rather, I am distressed and concerned, first for the salvation of your souls, and for those who have been deprived of and left famished by his all-wise, spiritual, divine teaching and admonition.

For not only has the Church of the Constantinopolitans been deprived of his honey-flowing tongue; the whole world beneath the sun has also been widowed, having lost such a god-inspired man because one woman, persuaded by others, allowed this dramatic outrage to occur. Nevertheless, she will suffer the punishment that comes from this and the future unending penalty that will overtake her not many days afterward [Col. 0632B].

For although blessed John departed this life, preserving the faith and strengthening those who were shaken, he inherited unending ages of imperishable delight and immortal life. But Eudoxia, the new Delilah, who gradually shaved you with the razor of error, brought a curse upon herself from many mouths, binding upon herself a heavy and difficult-to-bear burden of sins and adding it to her former sins.

2. Therefore I, the least and a sinner, as one entrusted with the throne of the great Apostle Peter, separate both you and her from participation in the undefiled mysteries of Christ our God. Moreover, any bishop or cleric belonging to the order of the holy Church of God who dares to undertake to administer them to you, from the hour when you read this bond of mine, is subject to deposition. If, as men in authority, you compel anyone by force and transgress the canons given to you by the Savior through the holy Apostles, you shall know that, first, your sin will be no small one on the fearful day of judgment, and that no earthly dignity will be able to help anyone; rather, their inward things will be poured out for all to see [Col. 0632C].

3. As for Arsacius, whom you introduced into the episcopal throne in place of the great John, we depose him even after death, together with all the bishops who deliberately communicated with him. His name shall not even be written in the sacred diptychs, for he is unworthy, having committed adultery against the episcopate. For every plant that was not planted by our Father in heaven will be uprooted. Moreover, along with the deposition of Theophilus, we add excommunication, anathema, and complete alienation from Christianity [Col. 0632D].

# Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0633] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## The Emperor Arcadius to Pope Innocent

[Col. 0633A]

To free himself and Eudoxia from excommunication.

All men of sound mind know that acts committed through ignorance are punished neither by God nor by the laws, and that no one pays the penalty in another’s name. I have therefore written these things to assure your gentleness—calling the benevolent God as witness to the matter—that I had no knowledge of any of the events that befell our bishops and clerics, and that I am entirely innocent of their condemnation.

For since I had shared their communion [Note: [Col. 0633D] How can Arcadius be said to have shared their communion, when they were not permitted even to greet him, much less to enter the imperial city, as Palladius testifies on p. 32?], there was no reason for me to afflict them. As for your daughter Eudoxia, know that I exacted from her no slight penalties according to her offense, so that, overcome by such grief and anguish, she now lies ill with a very serious disease.

I beg you, therefore, to free us from exclusion and not punish us in many ways. For the Lord himself does not strike twice for the same offense (Nahum 1:9) [Col. 0633B].

## Letter of the Emperor Arcadius to Innocent, Archbishop of Rome

[Col. 0634A]

All men of sound mind know that acts committed through ignorance are punished neither by God nor by the laws, and that no one exacts a penalty on behalf of another. Therefore I have written these things to reassure your gentleness, with the benevolent God bearing witness: I had no knowledge of anything that happened to our bishops and clerics, and I am innocent of their judgment.

For if I had shared their guilt, I would not have had cause to harm them. Concerning your daughter Eudoxia also, know that I repaid her according to her offense, and not moderately, so that, as a result of such grief and distress, she now lies overcome by the gravest illness. I therefore ask that you release us from excommunication and not punish us in many ways. For the Lord will not strike twice for the same offense.

# Letter III

[Note: [Col. 0633D] This letter repeats what had already been written in the preceding one. We therefore suspect that it is the work of an idle man who wished to exercise his style.]

## The Emperor Arcadius to Pope Innocent

He declares himself innocent of the acts committed against Innocent’s legates and against John, says that he has punished their authors, and asks that Innocent relax the sentence by which he and his wife are excluded from the sacred mysteries.

Entirely, O pontiff of God, none of the things that were boldly perpetrated against the legates [Note: [Col. 0633C] Just as Chrysostom, writing to Innocent in Letter 1, no. 5, immediately after he had first been expelled from his church, testified that everything that had then been impiously done had occurred without Arcadius’s judgment, so Nicephorus, book XIII, chapter 33, says that whatever was subsequently done against the legates escaped the idle Arcadius’s notice.] was done with my knowledge. This may be perceived from the fact that I severely punished those from whom these acts originated.

Nor does any guilt in the deposition of that great John attach to me; rather, it attaches to the wretched bishops, who, while professing to uphold the sacred canons, turned the judgment of his deposition back upon their own profane heads. Somehow persuaded by their speech, I too assented to their sentence—would that I had never done so [Col. 0634B]. Thus they themselves are more at fault.

Accordingly, I ordered that those of them who are still here—Acacius and Severianus, and those who followed the criminal Theophilus—be seized with the greatest possible speed [Note: [Col. 0634D] How shamelessly the architect of these letters lies here is proved by Arcadius’s own rescript, which Atticus obtained from this emperor because he was displeased that no Oriental bishops would communicate with him. According to Palladius, p. 95, it decreed: “If any of the bishops does not communicate with Theophilus, Porphyry, and Atticus, he shall be removed from the Church and deprived of his own property.”], and that those who are there be made to pay the penalties due for their deeds.

Let your paternal kindness be satisfied with us, and do not abandon us deprived of the undefiled mysteries. I have also punished your daughter Eudoxia, who sinned; she too, struck by a very serious illness because of these things, lies in bed. Do not, therefore, exact penalties repeatedly, most reverend father; for the Lord does not punish twice for the same offense, as it is written (Nahum 1:9, according to the Septuagint).

But where would the good of repentance be unless forgiveness were granted to those who repent? Therefore, if we were not truly repentant, access to forgiveness would rightly be closed to us. Since we have accused and condemned ourselves for the things we did wrong, let us not be deprived even of the good of repentance, which is forgiveness [Note: [Col. 0634D] The first thing a true penitent ought to have done was to restore to John the honor unjustly taken from him. Yet Innocent obtained this only around the year 415—that is, nine years after John’s death—when the name of this most holy prelate was entered in the sacred registers.]

# LETTER IV

**[Note: [Col. 0635A]** The falsity of this letter, and consequently of the preceding ones, is plainly demonstrated by Innocent’s genuine Letters 19, 21, 22, and 23. In those letters, the pope is shown to have restored peace to those who requested it neither rashly nor except under prescribed conditions, and only after those conditions had been fulfilled. The chief of these conditions was that John’s name **[Col. 0635B]** be restored to the sacred diptychs. But here he shows no concern either for John’s name or for the other bishops attached to him, who were enduring the cruellest exiles as though by Arcadius’s authority. Thus the pontiff, whose wisdom our predecessors praise no less in restoring communion to august persons than in withdrawing it from them, is here rashly represented.**]

**[Note: [Col. 0635]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0635]

## Innocent the Pope to Arcadius the Emperor

[Col. 0635A]

[Col. 0635] He releases Arcadius and permits him to receive the sacred mysteries.

I approved your devotion, which accords with God’s will and which you have displayed on account of his name. Therefore, released from the sacred bonds, approach the Lord’s symbols with steadfast hearts.

## Letter of Innocent, Chief Bishop of Rome, to Arcadius the Emperor

[Col. 0636A]

I accepted your godly devotion, which you have displayed on account of his name. Therefore, released from the sacred bonds, approach the Lord’s symbols in strength.

[Col. 0635]

# Posthumous Notes of Jacques Sirmond

## On Letter II, to Victricius

[Col. 0635B]

### On the letter in general

Paulinus of Nola, who had once seen Victricius at Saint Martin’s in Vienne, briefly and concisely explains the outstanding and admirable virtues and merits of Saint Victricius, bishop of Rouen and confessor of Christ, in two letters addressed to him, especially in Letter 28. Innocent now sends him the form of ecclesiastical discipline observed in the Roman Church, which he wishes both Victricius himself and, through his recommendation, the neighboring bishops also to follow in their own churches, treating it as a kind of teacher and guide. Thus, I think, the reading *didascalum* found in certain copies is more correct than *didascalicum*, as found in others.

### Number 2, “Let us begin, therefore”

The remainder of this preface, together with the conclusion of the entire letter and the first nine chapters except the third, has all been excerpted from Letter 4 of Pope Siricius, which he wrote from the Roman synod to the Africans and which is read inserted in the acts of the Council of Tele. The chapters are expressed more briefly in Siricius, whereas here they are arranged at greater length.

### Chapter 3, no. 6, “as the synod decreed”

He means the Council of Nicaea, whose eighteenth canon, as quoted by Pope Julius in his letter to the Easterners, reads as follows:

> The ancient authority of the apostles, of their successors, and of the canons has reserved to the disposition of the apostolic see all the greater ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops.

### Chapter 8, no. 11, “those coming from the Novatians”

Those who come to the Church from the Novatians and Donatists are not to be baptized, since they have already been duly baptized, but are to be confirmed through the laying on of hands. Concerning the Novatians, or Cathars, this had been decreed by the Council of Nicaea, canon 8, and by the Council of Constantinople, canon 7. Concerning the Donatists, who were called Montenses at Rome, the canon of the African Council of Carthage inserted as chapter 24 indicates the same, to pass over other evidence.

Those who had once been baptized by these groups are therefore to be received without delay when they come. But those who, after passing over from the Catholic Church to them, were baptized again are not to be admitted upon their return except after prolonged penance—a penance which the Council of Valence, canon 3, had ordered to continue until the day of death. Everyone agrees that the Donatists were accustomed to rebaptize. Concerning the Novatians, Ambrose testifies in his books *On Penance*, and Jerome in his *Booklet on Heresies*: “Novatian established the Novatian doctrine at Rome, refusing to receive apostates and baptizing those already baptized.”

### Chapter 11, no. 14, “is prescribed by the emperor”

The law of Honorius enacted five years earlier is relevant here, in the *Theodosian Code*, under the heading “On Decurions,” CLXIII, by which he orders curiales who had devoted themselves to the clergy—according to the distinct grades of their orders—to be restored to the curia, or to provide substitutes in their place, or to surrender their property:

> If any persons, after the second consulship of our father, abandoned the curia and devoted themselves to the company of the clergy, and have already been found worthy to be bishops, priests, or deacons, let them indeed continue in the sacred and more secret mysteries of God; but let them be compelled either to present substitutes for themselves to the curia or, in accordance with the law enacted long ago, to surrender their property to the curia. Let all the rest—readers, subdeacons, or those clerics to whom the privileges of clerics are not due—be immediately assigned to the services owed to their homeland.

### In the same place, “he himself with us”

That Victricius had previously been at Rome is also confirmed by an earlier letter of Paulinus addressed to him. This passage shows, I think, that he came to Rome in the preceding year, when Innocent was pontiff. Paulinus writes:

> For from there we had drawn sorrow and bitterness, because you did not come to us from the City by the short journey we expected, although you had reached the City across such vast stretches of land.

## On Letter VI, to Exuperius

### On the letter in general

He answers the inquiries of Bishop Exuperius, commending his diligence in referring doubtful matters to the apostolic see. Saint Jerome frequently and at length praises Exuperius of Toulouse, as in Letter 4, to Rusticus:

> Saint Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, feeds others while he himself hungers, and has distributed all his substance to the bowels of Christ. No one is richer than he who carries the Lord’s body in a wicker basket and his blood in a glass vessel. Follow his footsteps from nearby.

And in Letter 11, to Ageruchia:

> I cannot mention Toulouse without tears; the merits of Saint Exuperius have ensured that it has not fallen to this day.

Three letters of the same Jerome to Exuperius also survive, prefixed individually to his commentaries on the prophet Zechariah, which he dedicated to Exuperius when Arcadius Augustus was consul for the sixth time and Anicius Probus was consul—that is, in the year immediately following this letter of Innocent, when Exuperius had sent his deacon Sisinnius to Palestine and Egypt to distribute alms to monks.

### Chapter 1, no. 2, “in the words of Bishop Siricius”

In his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 7, Siricius divides his judgment concerning incontinent priests and Levites in the following manner: those who grieved that they had fallen through ignorance and promised continence in the future he permits to remain in their offices, but forbids them to advance to a higher grade; those, however, who attempted to defend themselves by the example of the Old Law he decrees should be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor.

Innocent imposed the former penalty on those who were ignorant of Siricius’s constitution, and the latter on those who, having learned it, did not obey it. That bishops too were included under this law is made clear by Siricius’s words near the end.

### Chapter 2, no. 6, “the severity of the Novatians”

The Novatian heresy held, as Epiphanius explains in Heresy 59, that those who had fallen after baptism could obtain no pardon. Accordingly, they denied penance and expelled every mention of it from their assemblies. Theodoret, book 3 of *The Heretical Fables*, chapter 6, writes:

> καὶ παντελῶς τὸν τῆς μετανοίας τῶν οἰκείων συλλόγων ἐξορίζουσι λόγον.

“And they utterly banish the doctrine of repentance from their own assemblies.”

Yet those who in the Catholic Church were far removed from them did not doubt that everyone could recover through penance the grace they had lost, although some occasionally judged that peace should be denied to certain persons as unworthy, when they requested it only at the end of life. Nevertheless, because this seemed itself to resemble Novatian severity, it was decided that this resemblance should be removed and that the grace of communion should be granted to anyone who requested it at the end of life, in accordance with canon 13 of the Council of Nicaea.

### Chapter 4, no. 10, “they do not have hidden matters”

The reason given here why adulterous men are not excluded from communion in the same way as women is applied generally to all criminals who secretly creep into communion by Augustine in Homily 1:

> Let no one suppose that he ought to despise the counsel of this salutary penance because he happens to observe and know that many approach the sacred altar whose such crimes he does not fail to recognize. For many do not wish to accuse others because they desire to excuse themselves through them. Many good Christians, however, remain silent and tolerate other sins of which they are aware because evidence is often lacking, and they cannot prove before ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know. For although certain things may be true, they are not easily to be believed by a judge unless they are demonstrated by definite proofs. We cannot exclude anyone from communion unless that person has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical court.

### Chapter 7, no. 15, “But the remaining books”

Many pseudepigraphical books once circulated under the names of these authors: the Gospel of Matthias, for example, mentioned by Origen in his commentary on Luke and by Eusebius in book 3 of his *History*, together with his traditions (*παραδόσεις*), which Clement of Alexandria mentions in books 2 and 7 of the *Stromata*; the Gospel of James the Less; and Peter’s *Acts* (*πράξεις*), *Gospel* (*εὐαγγέλιον*), *Preaching* (*κήρυγμα*), *Apocalypse* (*ἀποκάλυψις*), and *Judgment* (*κρίσις*). Jerome mentions all of these in chapter 1 of *Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> The books, however, of which one is entitled his Acts, another his Gospel, a third his Preaching, a fourth his Apocalypse, and a fifth his Judgment, are reckoned among the apocryphal writings.

There were also the Acts of John, the Acts of Andrew and his Gospel, and finally the Gospel, Acts, and Apocalypse of Thomas. Gelasius speaks of these and others of the same kind in the Roman synod.

## On Letter III, to the Synod of Toulouse

### In the title, “to the Council of Toledo”

We have noted that the title of the letter is ambiguous. If it were established that it was written to the Council of Toulouse, there would be nothing absurd in supposing that Spanish affairs were discussed in a synod of Gaul, since we remember that Gallic affairs were treated at Turin. But there seems little doubt that it was written to the bishops of Spain, after the Council of Toledo, though concerning matters dealt with there or occurring afterward.

I am led to this conclusion by no slight argument, which will be set out in chapter 6. I therefore judge that the ancient inscription of the letter should be restored, so that it should read “to the Council of Toledo.”

### Chapter 1, no. 2, “on account of the communion of the Galicians”

At the Council of Toledo, Symphosius and Dictinius, together with other bishops from Gallaecia, had been received into communion after the Priscillianist heresy was condemned, as Hydatius reports in his *Chronicle*, while retaining the honors they had held. The Baetican and Carthaginian bishops, disapproving this, withdrew from the other bishops who had received them. The pontiff therefore wishes efforts to be made to restore those who had withdrawn to common peace.

### In the same place, “that Lucifer”

This was Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia, who became the author of a schism in the Church. He refused to receive the bishops who had fallen at the Council of Rimini, even after they had repented, and separated himself from those who had received them. Sulpicius Severus writes:

> Lucifer condemned those who had been at Rimini so completely that he even separated himself from communion with those who had received them after satisfaction or penance.

### Chapter 2, no. 5, “Rufinus and Minicius”

Canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea orders that a bishop be appointed by the bishops of the province with the authority of the metropolitan. Rufinus and Minicius had acted against this canon: each had ordained bishops without the metropolitan’s knowledge, and one of them had done so even in another province.

The pontiff therefore says that the usurpers must be punished and that those rashly ordained by them should lose the honor they had obtained, in accordance with canon 6 of the same synod, which decrees that anyone made a bishop contrary to the metropolitan’s judgment must not be a bishop.

### Chapter 3, no. 6, “Bishop John”

This John had agreed through representatives to the Council of Toledo’s reception of those returning from heresy. It was later reported that he had withdrawn and acted against his own judgment. The pontiff therefore orders a fuller investigation into him and into the others who appeared to have withdrawn from communion; if they refuse to return to concord, they are to be excommunicated.

### Chapter 4, no. 7, “concerning ordinations”

Because of their great number, he does not grant such indulgence to those who had hitherto been made bishops in Spain through a corrupt custom from various classes of persons whom the canons exclude from the clerical grades that he permits the practice to continue. Instead, he orders that the penalty proposed for those who ordain and those who are ordained unlawfully be applied henceforth.

### Chapter 5, no. 8, “in place of Patruinus”

Writers on Spanish affairs disagree about the episcopal see of Patruinus, who presided over the First Council of Toledo. Some infer that he was bishop of Toledo; others that he was bishop of Braga; still others consider neither opinion sufficiently secure. From this passage it is clear that they had not thought that he was bishop of Mérida; after his death, Gregory had by this time succeeded him.

### Chapter 6, no. 9, “you decree by judgment”

It is evident that this alludes to the decree of the Council of Toledo, which stands first in its acts in these words:

> Bishop Patruinus said: If it pleases you, let us decide by common counsel what all bishops must observe in ordaining clerics. For my part, I think that the regulations first established by the Council of Nicaea must be observed perpetually, and that we must not depart from them. The bishops said: This pleases us all.

Since this is so, it is perfectly clear that Innocent is here addressing the bishops who had attended the Council of Toledo, and consequently that the letter should be entitled “to the Council of Toledo,” as stated above.

# In the Year of Our Lord 417

# Pope Zosimus

[Col. 0637]

## Preliminary Material

## Biographical Notices

### I

*(From the Pontifical Book, in Labbe, volume II of the Councils)*

Zosimus, a Greek by nationality and the son of Abraham, sat for one year, two months, and eleven days. He established many things in the Church. He decreed that deacons should have their left shoulders covered with garments of linen woven from palm fiber [alternate reading: *palleis*]. He granted permission throughout the parishes for the Paschal candle [alternate reading: *candles*] to be blessed. He ordered that no cleric be offered a cup in public, but only in the homes of the faithful, especially of clerics.

He held one ordination in the month of December: ten priests, three deacons, and eight bishops in various places (see Prosper in his *Chronicle*). He was buried on the Tiburtine Way beside the body of blessed Lawrence the martyr, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. The episcopate then remained vacant for eleven days.

[Col. 0639]

## Notes of Severinus Binius

### Zosimus

After Innocent’s death, following an interregnum of twenty-two days, Zosimus became pontiff on August 19 in the year of our Lord 417, the twenty-third year of Honorius and the tenth of Theodosius. Pelagius and Coelestius, condemned by the Africans, appealed to the pontiff. Having presented Zosimus with a completely Catholic statement of faith, they declared that they were ready in all things and held the same opinion concerning the faith as the Roman pontiff might propose should be held.

Persuaded by them, the pontiff, having apparently restored both men to Catholic standing, sent letters to the same African bishops, which we shall append below from a Vatican manuscript together with the statement of faith. The blessing of the baptismal font, as reported by Leo in Letter 65, was confirmed by a miracle. What took place between Zosimus and the fathers of the African council in the case of Pelagius will be explained below.

Meanwhile, at Rome, Coelestius was summoned to judgment and examined concerning his faith and doctrine. He was found to have denied original sin together with Pelagius. For this reason the sacred consensus of the fathers pronounced against both the following sentence of condemnation: unless they corrected themselves and performed penance, they were to be regarded as condemned throughout the whole world.

The Roman presbyter Sixtus, successor of Coelestine in the pontificate—whom they had slanderously accused of being a supporter and patron of the Pelagian heresy—was the first to proclaim an anathema against them and wrote a commentary against them, as Augustine bears witness in Letters 104 and 105. The emperor Honorius proscribed them by an edict.

The supporters of Pelagius from the Roman clergy were excommunicated by Zosimus as rebels and disturbers of everything. When they went to the emperor Honorius to bring a complaint against the pontiff, they were ordered to be avoided under penalty of excommunication, in a letter sent by Zosimus to the presbyters and deacons of Ravenna.

The condemned heresiarchs attacked the pontiff, the Roman clergy, Augustine, and other Catholics with slanders and attempted to make the Roman Church hated by the Easterners, but in vain.

Because a dispute arose between certain African bishops and the Roman pontiff concerning the continuation of appeals made to the apostolic see, he sent Faustine, bishop of Potentia in Picenum, together with Asellus and Philip as legates *a latere*, to Carthage in the year of our Lord 418. Since Zosimus died during these events and the matter passed to his successor Boniface, what was done in this very difficult case, which had been debated for five years, will be explained below. See Baronius under the years mentioned above.

He sat for one year, two months, and eleven days. From the beginning and end of his pontificate it is clear that he held the papal see for one year, four months, and seven days. His letter to the Council of Milevis indicates that Innocent was still alive in the preceding year, 417. The acts of the Sixth Council of Carthage and the letter of his successor Boniface to the bishops of Gaul, written during the consulship of Monaxius, testify that Zosimus did not survive to the end of 418.

Since, therefore, according to the authority of the *Pontifical Book*, Zosimus died on the seventh day before the Kalends of February (January), and since Symmachus’s report to Honorius, dated on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, establishes that Boniface had been substituted for him, it must be said that Zosimus governed the apostolic see not for three years but for only one year, together with the months and days mentioned above. Baronius, under the year 418, no. 75.

### “He granted permission throughout the parishes”

Zosimus decreed only that the same candle, which was accustomed to be lit only in the larger basilicas, should likewise be permitted in each parish. That the blessing of the Paschal candle is more ancient in the Church is taught by Prudentius, who composed a hymn about it. Baronius, under the year 418, no. 26.

### II

*(From the Collection of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, by Constantius, volume I)*

[Col. 0640B]

The pontificate of this pope was brief but sufficiently distinguished by the events that took place in the case of Pelagius and Coelestius. Paschasinus, writing to Pope Leo in Letter 3, states that Easter was celebrated on March 25 in the year 417, while Zosimus was pontiff; Zosimus’s own first letter, dated March 22 of the same year, confirms this.

Accordingly, the ancient martyrologies and other records seemed more worthy of confidence when they assigned Innocent’s death to March 12 than when they assigned it to other days or months. It is therefore not difficult to determine on what day Zosimus was ordained. For his fourth letter, no. 2, leaves no doubt that he was inaugurated on a Sunday, when it lists among the faults of Heros that even the proper day for ordination had not been chosen.

But between the day in March on which Innocent died and the 22nd, on which Zosimus wrote his first letter, there is no Sunday except the eighteenth. It remains, therefore, that Zosimus was ordained on that day.

By the kindness with which he embraced Pelagius and Coelestius, believing them converted, he revealed how inclined he was to mercy. By the zeal with which he later, after their fraud had been exposed, took care that they be condemned throughout the world, he demonstrated to everyone how far he was from approving heresy and how devoted he had always been to Catholic truth. God used him to place the crown upon the condemnation of the Pelagians through a most celebrated decree.

He happily ended his life on December 26, 418, as is established from the report of Symmachus, prefect of the City, published by Baronius under the year 418. According to Prosper, he had spent one year, nine months, and nine days in the pontificate.

# Letters and Decrees

[Col. 0639]

## Letters and Decrees of Pope Zosimus

*(From the edition of P. Constantius, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, volume I)* (S)*

## Notice Concerning the Following Letter

1.
