This letter was first published by Baronius in his *Annals* and afterward by Jacques Sirmond among the councils of Gaul, from an old codex of the Church of Arles now preserved in the Colbert Library. It also survives in another no less ancient manuscript of that library. To distinguish the two, we call the first *Arel.*, the second *Colb.*

A third manuscript was supplied to us by the Royal Library: codex no. 3989, older than the two mentioned above. It begins with the *factum* (or edict) addressed to the illustrious Agricola, prefect of the Gauls under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, which will be published below in its proper place. It is followed by several letters of Zosimus and other Roman pontiffs down to Pelagius, written especially for the benefit of the Church of Arles.

Furthermore, in a manuscript of the monastery of Morbach containing a compilation of canons written about eight hundred years ago, we found the final two chapters of this letter attributed to our Zosimus. In the same manuscript, however, we encountered its first chapter under the name of Pope Sylvester, as though it were a privilege granted to Rheticius, bishop of Autun, throughout Gaul and its seven provinces, and communicated by him to the bishops of that region.

The published manuscript of Fleury likewise presents the same chapter under the name of Pope Sylvester, by whom the same privilege is granted to Paschasius of Vienne. We shall prove in its proper place the falsity of this document, which we have judged should be relegated to the Appendix.

Thus neither this attribution nor the false citation of the Morbach manuscript impairs the authenticity of the following letter. It establishes only that churches which wished to claim some right over others attempted to strengthen that claim by fabricating a privilege in imitation of this letter.

2. The authenticity of the following letter is proved not only by the authority of the ancient manuscripts but also by historical evidence. Certainly, no one can read the petitions of the bishops of the province of Arles to Pope Leo, preserved in Leo’s Letter 40, without immediately recognizing that they plainly refer to this letter and that their petitions are expressed in its words.

Likewise, all the letters of the Roman pontiffs, whether earlier or later, that concern the Church of Arles are so interconnected that anyone who admits one of them will scarcely be able afterward to reject any of the others. Accordingly, Jean Morin rightly mocks Scaliger in *Ecclesiastical Exercises*, 24, because Scaliger judged Letter 348, this letter, and the other letters written for the benefit of the See of Arles unworthy of Zosimus and spurious.

Paschasius Quesnellus answers the objections brought against them in dissertation 5, part 1, chapter 6, at the end of Leo’s works. Finally, the Council of Frankfurt, held in 794 in the presence of Charlemagne, plainly mentions them in canon 8, where it says:

> Concerning the dispute of Ursio, bishop of Vienne, the letters of blessed Gregory, Zosimus, Leo, and Symmachus were read, and these defined, etc.

3. It may rightly be debated whether Zosimus granted the bishop of Arles anything new in this letter. Paschasius Quesnellus, in the place cited, indeed holds that even the provision concerning the *formata* in chapter 1 granted him nothing that he had not possessed since the age of Cyprian.

But we frankly confess that we cannot discover what he says is evident from Letter 1, to Pope Stephen I: that letter contains no discussion of *formatae*. On the contrary, if we consult the canons that Siricius sent to the bishops of Gaul, we cannot doubt that Zosimus derogated from the common law received in Gaul when he decreed that *formatae* were to be given to all clerics by the bishop of Arles.

When Siricius observes that any cleric “cannot minister in another church without letters from his bishop or a *formata*” (Letter 10, no. 17), he clearly indicates that clerics traveling elsewhere were accustomed to receive letters or a *formata* from their own bishop, not from the bishop of Arles.

I would not deny that this belonged to the metropolitan’s right: bishops subject to him, when undertaking a journey far from their churches, were to receive a *formata* from him. Accordingly, the Council of Carthage held in 397 decreed:

> No bishop shall sail without a *formata* from the primate.

There is no need to point out that the primates of each province in Africa served in the place of metropolitans.

That individual bishops gave these *formatae* to their own clerics is clear from the fact that the Second Council of Carthage, held in 407, decreed:

> The *formatae* given by the primates to bishops, or by any bishops to their own clerics, must contain the date of Easter.

The Council of Laodicea likewise decreed in canon 40, according to the interpretation commonly published in Quesnellus’s Code, chapter 58:

> A minister of the altar, or even a layman, ought not to travel anywhere without canonical letters, that is, a *formata*.

Then, in canon 41, it teaches that this *formata* is to be received from one’s own bishop, in these words:

> A minister of the altar, or anyone else, ought not to travel to foreign places without the bishop’s command.

The Council of Antioch, moreover, while directing in canon 7, according to the same interpreter just mentioned, that “no visiting clerics should be received without a *formata*, nor should priests give *formatae*, that is, letters, to distant regions,” nevertheless adds in canon 8:

> Let the bishop’s vicar, whom the Greeks call a chorepiscopus, be permitted to prepare *formatae*.

It is therefore clear that before Zosimus’s time, both in the East and in the West, the established practice was for clerics to request the aforesaid *formatae* from their bishops, and for bishops to request them from metropolitans. Zosimus consequently granted the bishop of Arles something new when he required bishops and all clerics to receive *formatae* from him.

# Letter I, to the Bishops of Gaul

## On the Privileges of the Church of Arles

**I.** That those who come to Rome or elsewhere from Gaul should receive *formatae* from the Metropolitan of Arles.

**II.** That the metropolitan of Arles should ordain bishops throughout the province of Vienne and both Narbonnese provinces.

**III.** That the parishes belonging to the Church of Arles should be restored to it.

Zosimus to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

**[Note: [Col. 0641D]** The seven provinces, whose civil assembly Honorius ordered to be celebrated annually at Arles in a constitution issued in 418, are called in the ancient notices Vienne, First and Second Narbonnese, the province of the Maritime Alps, Novempopulania, and both Aquitanias.]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0642D]

### 1

It has pleased the apostolic see that if anyone from any part of Gaul, of whatever ecclesiastical rank, seeks to come to us at Rome or intends to travel elsewhere in the world, he may not depart unless he has received *formatae* from the metropolitan bishop of Arles, by which he may prove, with the support of his written credentials, his priestly office or the ecclesiastical position that he holds.

**[Note: [Col. 0643D]** *Formatae*, or letters of communion, without which visiting clerics were not admitted to communion, were customarily received when they traveled elsewhere. Presbyters, deacons, and those of the lower grades received them from their own bishop; bishops from the metropolitan; metropolitans from the primate or patriarch. Saint Maximus teaches this near the end of his disputation with Pyrrhus, when he denies that Pyrrhus’s synod was truly a synod, since neither had the bishops brought *systatikai* letters from their metropolitans nor the metropolitans from their patriarchs:

> The assembled men had no *systatikai* letters—neither the bishops from their metropolitans nor the metropolitans from their patriarchs.

But in this passage Zosimus grants a special privilege to Patroclus, bishop of Arles, in Gaul: that all persons of every ecclesiastical rank who depart from Gaul, whether to Rome or elsewhere in the world, should receive *formatae* from him, and that without them they should not be received elsewhere.]

We established this because many persons, pretending to be bishops, presbyters, or clerics, creep into the name of veneration and obtain undeserved respect, since there is no document of *formatae* by which they can be refuted.

Therefore, dearest brothers, whoever comes to us without the *formata* mentioned above—whether he is a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or holds any lower grade—must know that he absolutely cannot be received.

**[Note: [Col. 0643B]** Here the word *auctoritatem* (“authority”), in the manner familiar to the ancient pontiffs of the Roman Church, has the force of a letter.]

It is evident that we have sent this authority everywhere, so that it may become known in all regions that what we have established must in every respect be observed. If anyone attempts to violate these salutary provisions, let him know that by his own act he has separated himself from our communion.

We have granted this privilege of the *formatae* especially to our holy brother and fellow bishop Patroclus, in consideration of his merits.

**[Note: [Col. 0643B]** Thus the Royal manuscript, together with the Arles and Morbach manuscripts. Other copies read “with special consideration.”]

## Chapter II

[Col. 0644A]

### 2

We have also ordered that the metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles retain the special authority that he has always possessed in ordaining priests. Let him bring the provinces of Vienne, First Narbonnese, and Second Narbonnese under his pontifical jurisdiction.

**[Note: [Col. 0643C]** Learned men debate whether Zosimus is here granting Patroclus a new right. The continuator of Peter de Marca, Stephen Baluze, in book 5 of *On Concord*, chapter 30, and Tillemont, volume 10, pages 681 and following, hold that a new right is being granted. Quesnellus, however, in the dissertation cited above, dissertation 5, chapter 6, observes that Zosimus is neither creating a new right nor confirming an institution of very recent origin, but asserting an ancient privilege founded upon the original rights and earliest prerogatives of Arles. Zosimus now favors this privilege when he testifies that he is entrusting to the bishop of Arles what he has always possessed.

The Gallican bishops also support him in their petitions to Pope Leo after the ordination of Ravennius, bishop of Arles, preserved in Leo’s Letter 41. Leo himself, however, contradicts this in Letter 9, chapter 4, where he complains that Hilary, who had ordained bishops outside his own province, had usurped what none of his predecessors before Patroclus had possessed.

It is less ambiguous that Zosimus here calls the bishop of Arles “metropolitan” in the sense in which the Council of Turin understood the term. When the bishops of Arles and Vienne disputed among themselves concerning the honor of primacy in those provinces, that council decreed that whichever of them proved his city to be a *metropolis* should possess the primatial honor of the entire province and, according to the canons, have authority over ordinations. Hence it is clear that the bishop to whom the honor of primacy and the power of ordination belong in the disputed provinces is there called metropolitan.]

But whoever henceforth dares, contrary to the statutes of the apostolic see and the commands of our predecessors, to ordain anyone in the aforesaid provinces while bypassing the metropolitan bishop—or whoever permits himself to be illicitly ordained there—must know that both parties are deprived of the priesthood.

**[Note: [Col. 0644D]** Zosimus confirms to the bishop of the Church of Arles the ancient privilege and authority which, as he says, he possesses: the metropolitan right to ordain bishops throughout three provinces, Vienne and both Narbonnese provinces. Those who ordain bishops in these provinces while bypassing the metropolitan—that is, the bishop of Arles—or those who are ordained in this way are therefore to be deprived of their honor. The matter is treated again and often elsewhere.]

For how can anyone possess the authority of the supreme pontiff who has refused to observe the pontiff’s commands?

## Chapter III
We admonish all, indeed, that each should remain content within his own boundaries and territories [Note: In the Colbertine and Arelatensian manuscripts, as in the printed editions, *contenti sint* (“should be content”) is found. We supply the intervening sentence from the Regius and Morbacensis manuscripts.]: for it is a barbarous and impious confusion to presume upon what belongs to another. We admonish you lest any further complaint on this matter come back to us. For the Church of Arles has set an example: it rightly desires that the parishes of Citharista and Gargarium, situated in its territory, be incorporated into it [Note: Pliny too mentions Citharista on the promontory along the coast of the Massilians, *Natural History* III.4. An ancient inscription on an old tablet preserved at Arles mentions Gargarium: “The pagans of the district of Lucretius who are within the boundaries of the people of Arles, at the place called Gargarium,” and what follows.].

[Note: The printed editions have *Gargariam* (“Gargaria”). The Arelatensian, Regius, and Morbacensis manuscripts more correctly have *Gargarium*, as Sirmondus had noted should be read, on the authority of the old Arelatensian tablet, which bears: “The pagans of the district of Lucretius who are within the boundaries of the people of Arles, at the place called Gargarium.” Sirmondus also observes that the parish of Citharista is mentioned in Book II of the *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles*. In his posthumous notes, published by Labbe at the end of volume II of the *Councils*, p. 1814, it is likewise added that Pliny, Book III, chapter 4, mentions Citharista on the promontory along the coast of the Massilians. Both places are still known.] Thus no priest hereafter should presume upon injury to another priest.

Since the ancient privilege of the metropolitan city of Arles must in no way be diminished [Col. 0645A], to which city Trophimus, the supreme bishop, was first sent from this see, and from whose fountain all Gaul received the streams of the faith, therefore let it possess, with unimpaired authority, whatever parishes it formerly held in any territories, even outside its own provinces [Note: The Regius manuscript has “as it formerly held them.”]. If any matter of business should arise there, we decree that it be referred to its knowledge, unless the importance of the case also requires our examination.

Issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April (22 March, 417) [Note: In the Arelatensian manuscript the letter ends: “In the consulship of the emperor Honorius Augustus and Constantius.” In the Regius manuscript: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth consulship of Honorius and Constantius,” incorrectly. For Honorius held his tenth consulship in 415 with Theodosius, not with Constantius. Baronius gives no chronological note. Garnerius suspects that he deliberately omitted one, because it conflicts with his opinion that Innocent died on 28 July and that Zosimus succeeded him on 19 August. The ancient martyrologies, however—the old Roman, that of Ado, and others—strongly favor the view that Innocent died on 12 March.] in the consulships of Honorius Augustus for the eleventh time and Constantius for the second time.

## Notice concerning the Two Following Letters

1. Baronius was the first to publish both letters, in the year 417, on the authority of an old Vatican codex, together with its blemishes. John Garnerius attempted to purge those blemishes [Col. 0645B], but with a liberty which we do not consider permissible. Nevertheless, his work was sometimes successful, wherever he departed less from the rules of criticism. Capelli’s judgment, by which he considers them spurious, is rightly rejected by the unanimous judgment of scholars.

The first of these letters is plainly indicated by the opening words of the second, just as the second is openly identified by the following words of Marius Mercator in his *Memorandum*:

> “Coelestius hastened with all speed to the city of Rome under Bishop Zosimus, of holy memory. When questioned there concerning the proceedings, copies of which we possess, and when he was to some extent tested by that examiner, he sowed hope through his frequent answers and pleadings, promising that he condemned those articles concerning which he had been accused at Carthage. For this was urged upon him with particular insistence, and he was expected to do it with even greater urgency. For this very reason he was considered worthy of some measure of kindness from that holy priest. And so he obtained a certain letter full of benevolence addressed to the African bishops, which he abused, and still abuses, to deceive many ignorant people.”

Augustine likewise speaks of both letters no less explicitly in his books *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians to Boniface* and *On Original Sin*, as we shall shortly see.

The following words of Facundus, Book VII, chapter 3, p. 277, concerning both letters are also unmistakable:

> “Finally, they will find Blessed Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see, praising, as true and catholic, the faith of Pelagius himself and of his accomplice Coelestius—whom he himself had examined in the proceedings after Coelestius had been convicted in the church of Carthage and had appealed to the apostolic see—against the judgment of Saint Innocent, his predecessor, who first condemned the Pelagian heresy; and, moreover, blaming the African bishops because they believed those men to be heretics, although he still thought the aforementioned Pelagius and Coelestius orthodox, before they themselves had more clearly exposed their tricks to the African bishops.”

For the present, these remarks are sufficient in support of the authenticity of the letters, which will become increasingly clear from what follows. We must now consider whether Zosimus reexamined a case already settled by his predecessor—a case of which Augustine had said in Sermon 131.40: “The case is finished; would that the error too were finished!”—or whether, as Facundus maintains, he acted throughout this affair “against the judgment of Saint Innocent, his predecessor.”

2. As for Augustine, he said that the case was finished insofar as the errors had been openly and authoritatively rejected; but he did not mean that it was finished in the sense of a fixed and definitive condemnation of the persons of Pelagius and Coelestius. For concerning them the Council of Carthage had written to Innocent in Letter 26.6, as though still uncertain:

> “Even if Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or say that they have never held these opinions.”

Nor had the five bishops asserted anything more definite about Pelagius in Letter 28 to the same pope, section 11, since they had sufficient reason to demand it from him:

> “Let Pelagius therefore anathematize his writings . . . Or, if he denies that they are his, or says that writings introduced by his enemies are attributed to him although he denies them to be his, let him anathematize and condemn them.”

Nor had Innocent condemned him and his associate without adding a condition: namely, that if they came to their senses or were able to clear themselves, they would be absolved and received within the Church. “If they do this,” he says in Letter 29.8, “it will lie within the power of the bishops to offer them some assistance and to provide some care for such wounds, which the Church is accustomed not to deny to those who have fallen when they have come to their senses, so that, recalled from their precipices, they may be brought back within the Lord’s fold.”

He confirms the same point still more clearly in Letter 30.6. Specifically concerning Pelagius, he writes in Letter 31.4:

> “Care will not be lacking, if he provides material for a remedy. For he can condemn what he had held and, by a letter, ask pardon for his error, as is fitting for one returning to us.”

Thus invited by these letters, Pelagius and Coelestius acted as follows: the former came to Rome without delay and professed that he would submit to the judgment of the apostolic see; the latter sent a letter together with a statement of his faith, in which he appeared expressly to condemn the errors attributed to him.

Since, therefore, Zosimus did not fail to apply to them an appropriate medicinal care, he did nothing contrary to the judgment of his predecessor. Nor should he be said to have reopened a case which Innocent had finished, so much as to have wished, in accordance with Innocent’s intention, to complete what Innocent had prescribed as the conclusion of the case.

3. Pelagius appeared to have satisfied the wishes of Innocent. For when he noticed, as Augustine observes in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 30, that there were two matters on which he was being discredited—one, that he denied infants the sacrament of baptism; the other, that he excluded God’s help—he cunningly confessed in his statement of faith (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 32) that “infants receive baptism for the remission of sins,” and prefaced this confession in his letter (*ibid.*, chapter 31) with the assertion that free will “is always aided by divine assistance in all good works.”

By this twofold profession—to which, beyond doubt, Coelestius, being present, voluntarily subscribed—he was considered sufficiently cleared, especially with the accompanying letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who intervened as an exceptionally zealous supporter of Pelagius’s case. Zosimus therefore did not delay sending a letter to inform the Africans of Pelagius’s return to the Church and to disclose and express to them his joy on that account (Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 5).

Albina, Pinianus, and Melania were likewise disposed toward Pelagius in the same spirit as Zosimus, when they had heard from the mouth of that crafty heretic, while he was present, what he had professed in writing before Zosimus.

4. It is more difficult to understand how the faith of Coelestius could have been approved. For Augustine testifies (*ibid.*, chapter 33) that “in his statement, which he presented at Rome in the ecclesiastical proceedings, he confessed that infants are baptized for the remission of sins, and denied that anyone has original sin.” The same Doctor reports the actual words of this heretic in *On Original Sin*, chapter 6.

Nevertheless, both Marius Mercator, as we have just seen, and Augustine himself, as must now briefly be explained, offer various defenses of Zosimus.

5. First, although Augustine admits that Zosimus called Coelestius’s statement catholic, he does not therefore teach that it was called catholic because the poisons of his faith contained in it were approved by the apostolic see, but because it had been written with a catholic mind—or under the appearance of a catholic mind.

For in his statement of faith (*Book II to Boniface*, chapters 3–4), Coelestius, before speaking about his particular opinion, had written:

> “If perhaps, as may happen to human beings, some error of ignorance has crept in, let it be corrected by your judgment.”

But Augustine says:

> “This belongs to a catholic mind: if it happens to think otherwise than truth requires, not to lay such views down as certain—which is the mark of heresy—but to reject them once they have been exposed and demonstrated.”

Nor was Zosimus satisfied with this general profession of Coelestius. By repeated questions and answers, he compelled him to reply that he agreed with “the letters of Pope Innocent, of blessed memory, by which all doubt concerning this matter”—that is, concerning the faith regarding original sin—“has been removed.”

When he had made this profession (chapter 4), Augustine says:

> “Who does not see how Coelestius has been bound and fastened with a most salutary bond, so that he would no longer dare to defend the proposition that original sin is not remitted in the baptism of infants?” [Col. 0647B]

For this reason Augustine praises in *On Original Sin*, chapter 7, the pious diligence of Zosimus in treating Coelestius: like a madman or delirious person, Zosimus attempted through his questions and through Coelestius’s own answers to bind him so tightly that he could scarcely escape; and he treated him with such consideration that, “after an interval of two months, until a reply should come from Africa, a place for repentance was granted him.”

Meanwhile, “in order that this too”—namely, that Coelestius did not deny original sin—“might become clearer and more manifest in him, the letters expected from Africa were awaited, since in that province his craft had become somewhat more evident” (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3).

Thus, to use Augustine’s words, “the willingness to amend, not the falsity of the doctrine, was approved.”

Augustine therefore concludes aptly:

> “Certainly, whatever leniency was shown to Coelestius in the meantime, provided only that the firmness of the ancient and most robust faith was preserved, was a most merciful exhortation to correction, not the most disastrous approval of depravity. And the fact that Coelestius and Pelagius were later condemned by the same priest”—Zosimus—“with renewed authority was an exercise of severity that had been briefly suspended but now had necessarily to be brought forth, not a betrayal of what had previously been recognized, nor a new recognition of the truth.”

6. Augustine offers this further reason for the indulgence by which “those two men of considerable ability were treated with somewhat greater leniency than the stricter discipline of the Church required”: namely, that “although perverted by a wicked error, they were nevertheless not contemptible.”

Why they were not contemptible he subsequently explains when he speaks of Coelestius as “a man of exceptionally keen intelligence, who, if he had been corrected, would certainly have benefited many.”

It was also in hope of this benefit that Innocent ordered that a way of pardon remain open to both men, provided that they anathematized the things they had wrongly believed. For he hoped (Innocent, Letter 31.5):

> “that those who had fallen through his [Pelagius’s] words and instructions might finally learn what the true faith contains. For they can more easily be recalled when they perceive that these things have been condemned by their own author.”

Here again Zosimus’s agreement with Innocent is clear. Accordingly, the deacon Paulinus is free from any suspicion of flattery when, below, in Letter 8.2, he affirms that Zosimus followed Innocent’s judgment concerning Pelagius and Coelestius even before Innocent condemned them by a definitive judgment.

The truth of Paulinus’s assertion is also clearly proved by what he brings forward from the proceedings. Nothing therefore prevents us from applying to the praised pope, even before his definitive judgment, Augustine’s words to Julian:

> “What, then, is the meaning of your accusing Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see, of betrayal, so that you may persist in your depravity—Zosimus of blessed memory, who did not depart from his predecessor Innocent, and so forth?” (*Book VI Against Julian*, chapter 12).

7. In this case the same Roman clergy were present with Innocent when Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned on the condition that, if they came to their senses, pardon would not be denied them; with Zosimus, when those same men, who displayed a certain appearance of repentance, were treated with greater leniency; and again with the same pope when, after their mask and fraud had been exposed, those heretics were openly condemned.

For this reason the Pelagians wished to brand those clerics with the mark of betrayal, as though they had approved a doctrine in Zosimus’s earlier judgment which they rejected in his later judgment.

Augustine repels their slander in this way:

> “If—God forbid—it had then been judged in the Roman Church concerning Coelestius or Pelagius that their doctrines, which Pope Innocent had condemned in them and together with them, should be approved and maintained, then it would rather be on this account that the Roman clergy ought to be branded with the mark of betrayal” (*Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3).

It follows that the judgment of the Roman clergy remained constant in those three judgments, and therefore that Zosimus’s agreement with his predecessor was manifest even in the earlier judgment.

8. Augustine also proves this from the fact that, “although so many and such important letters were passing back and forth between the apostolic see and the African bishops, and although ecclesiastical proceedings concerning this case had been conducted before that see in the presence of Coelestius and with his replies, no letter of Zosimus and no statement of his is found in which he either said or wrote anything in support of Coelestius’s perverse doctrine.”

Moreover, even Facundus, although Zosimus himself appears to have approved the faith of Pelagius and Coelestius “against the judgment of Saint Innocent, his predecessor” (*Book VII*, chapter 3, p. 278), nevertheless admits that Zosimus must be judged no differently from Athanasius when he commended Timothy, a disciple of Apollinaris, to Damasus; from Damasus when he received the man commended to him kindly; or from the Palestinian bishops when they judged Pelagius orthodox:

> “For,” he says, “the simple ought not to be charged with a crime because they did not understand the trickery of malicious men.”

That trickery was such that, from Pelagius’s letter then sent to Zosimus, Augustine would have believed this heretic completely corrected, had he not learned elsewhere of his various devices, as Augustine’s own words demonstrate, quoted in the notes to Pelagius’s Letter 42 to Innocent, p. 918, note g.

9. The cause of Coelestius and Pelagius was helped considerably in Zosimus’s eyes by the unfavorable reputation of Heros and Lazarus, who had accused them, although that reputation was undeserved.

For although, even after they had been removed from the episcopate, Marius Mercator calls them “zealous bishops”; the Council of Carthage, in Letter 26 to Innocent, section 1, calls them “holy brothers and fellow priests”; and Augustine, in *The Proceedings Concerning Pelagius*, chapter 1, likewise calls them “holy brothers and our fellow bishops of Gaul,” Zosimus was hearing something quite different about them.

In Pelagius’s letter he read, as Augustine testifies (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 33), Pelagius’s “envious complaints against his enemies,” which fell chiefly upon Heros and Lazarus. Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who intervened as “an exceptionally zealous supporter of Pelagius’s case,” undoubtedly spared them no more in his letter. Nor were the things which his predecessor John had said against them left unmentioned.

Augustine had wisely warned:

> “Whatever Bishop John said about our absent brothers or fellow bishops Heros and Lazarus, or about the presbyter Orosius . . . I believe that [Pelagius] understands that it has no force to their prejudice.”

But Pelagius was not the sort of man to yield to so fair a warning.

Coelestius was also present in the city, omitting nothing that might either create or increase hostility toward them; and Patroclus was present as well. Zosimus listened to him with greater favor and kindness because he was a friend and associate of Constantius, the consul and master of the soldiers, “whose favor,” Prosper says, “was sought through him.”

It was in Patroclus’s interest that Heros, whose position he had seized, should be condemned in reputation. Whatever Zosimus wrote against Heros in his letters, therefore, may reasonably be believed to have been said on Patroclus’s testimony.

But Patroclus, as Prosper teaches in his *Chronicle*, was of such corrupt conscience that he did not hesitate to sell priestly offices through “infamous commerce.”

Because Zosimus did not know this, he thought that he was delivering a fair judgment concerning Lazarus and Heros on the testimony of three witnesses who agreed with one another. He did not notice that, at that very moment, he was condemning absent men on the suspect testimony of their adversaries, whether those adversaries were open or concealed, while he was diligently warning the Africans that absent persons should not be believed against the absent.

So true is it that we perceive more easily what others ought to avoid or do than what we ourselves ought to avoid or do, and that even clear-sighted men sometimes fall into the very fault they censure in others without noticing it.

But how little inclination Zosimus initially had toward error, and how he had been somewhat too credulous toward the deceitful heretics, he later made clear when the truth was exposed. Nor did it happen without divine providence that the man who was destined to proscribe their perverse inventions throughout the world first embraced their authors with exceptional benevolence. For this made it clear to everyone that the poisonous heresy had yielded solely to the force of truth, and not to any private hostility.

## Letter II

[Note: The Vatican exemplar reads: “Here begins a copy of Letter I of Bishop Zosimus in defense of Coelestius against the Pelagian bishops.” This heading has an inexperienced author.]

**Concerning the case of Coelestius. What was done when Coelestius’s trial was resumed at Rome. He will be acquitted unless those who can refute him in person come within two months and prove that he thinks otherwise than he has professed.**

**Zosimus to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, his most beloved brothers in the Lord, greeting.**

1. A grave matter of examination requires a grave [Note: Baronius reads *desiderat* (“requires”); Garnerius more correctly reads *desiderant* (“require”). A similar opening occurs in the constitution of the emperor Honorius, published by Baronius under the year 419, where he addresses Symmachus, prefect of the City: “The judgment of great deliberations should not be hasty, nor should matters which are decreed for perpetual observance be rashly promulgated.” That statement is true when great matters must first be deliberated; but when a great deliberation and prolonged examination have preceded a judgment, matters already judged ought not to be recalled for a new examination. Accordingly, Innocent, in Letter 34, thinks that obstinate and deceitful heretics such as Pelagius and Coelestius should be dealt with by timely correction rather than prolonged discussion. See also his Letter 29.7.] judgment, so that the balance of judgment may not be inferior to the matters themselves which are being handled.

To this is added the authority of the apostolic see, to which the decrees of the fathers have established a particular reverence in honor of the most blessed Peter. We must therefore pray, and pray without ceasing, that by God’s continual grace and perpetual assistance, peace of faith and catholic fellowship may be sent from this source throughout the whole world, clouded by no [Note: The printed editions read *nubibus* (“clouds”); the Vatican manuscript more elegantly has *nebulis* (“mists”).] mist.

For charity, which, as it is written, “is God” (1 John 4:8), rejoices in the abundant fullness of perfection: whenever it has even a suspicion of something, either a vigilant concern for the faith or a controversy prolonged over time [Note: This is how the Vatican archetype reads, except that it has *intentionis* above, where *intentione* appears, and Baronius reads *contentione*. Garnerius altered the entire passage on his own as follows: “if, when there is some suspicion, the vigilant concern of faith or a controversy prolonged over time is corrected by a true amendment.” He appears to have been more concerned to present a grammatical construction than Zosimus’s meaning. The sentence would be smoother as follows: “by vigilant concern regarding the faith—that is, controversy concerning the faith.” One might also accept: “by vigilant concern regarding the faith and by hesitation prolonged over time.”] is corrected by an amendment.

2. The presbyter Coelestius presented himself before our tribunal, requesting that the matters which had been reported about him to the apostolic see otherwise than they ought to have been be cleared up.

Although many occupations, bound by the greater ties of ecclesiastical affairs, were drawing our care and concern in different directions, nevertheless, lest your expectation concerning the arrival and examination of the aforesaid man should remain suspended for too long, we set everything else aside and took our seat on the day of the hearing in the basilica of Saint Clement [Note: Garnerius inserts *quippe* (“indeed”) here and shortly afterward substitutes *magisterio* (“authority”) for *magistro* (“teacher”), without necessity. Later he more successfully restored *tantosque* (“and such great things”), where the editions of Baronius and the councils had *ratosque*, with the support of the Vatican archetype.

Saint Clement is here understood to have corrected ancient errors, not errors of some particular heresy, but rather the old errors of paganism. If, as some conjecture, he had been a Jew, could one appropriately say that, after converting to the faith of Christ, he corrected ancient errors? In support of his martyrdom, which some have called into doubt, this is a notable passage. Rufinus, in his work on Origen, and the First Council of Vaison, held in 442, canon 2, likewise give him the title of martyr.

The Roman clergy also took part in this gathering, at which Coelestius’s case was examined, in addition to the priests who, as is said below, were present from various regions. For this reason the Pelagians, in Augustine, *Book II to Boniface*, chapter 3, with Augustine himself agreeing, attributed to the Roman clergy what was done both at this gathering and at the later one.]—a man instructed in the disciplines of the blessed apostle Peter and who, under such a teacher, had corrected ancient errors and made such progress that he consecrated by martyrdom the faith which he had learned and taught—so that the authority of so great a priest might serve as an example for the present examination and for salutary correction.

3. We therefore examined all that had previously been done, as you will learn from the account of the proceedings attached to this letter. After Coelestius had been admitted, we ordered his statement, which he had submitted, to be read aloud. Nor were we satisfied with this: we repeatedly investigated whether he spoke from his heart what he had written, or merely from his lips; for judgment concerning hidden matters of the soul can belong only to our God, before whom not merely thoughts but even things to be thought are present.

We judged it more concise that you should learn by reading what his words contain [Note: The Vatican manuscript has *teneant* (“may contain”). Shortly afterward Baronius reads “to be read before your holiness.” Garnerius’s correction appears more accurate.].

4. One thing in particular troubles us: although you have Coelestius present there, nothing has been definitively judged.

As for the letters of Heros and Lazarus sent in the earlier report, it is indeed very easy to conclude that they were written in excessive haste because of the fervor of their faith [Baronius: “because of this fervor”]. But when questioned about them, Coelestius asserted that he had never had any conversation with the men named above concerning such controversies; that he had not even known them by sight before they wrote about him; that he had known Lazarus only in passing; and that, after offering satisfaction, he had withdrawn with the goodwill of Heros because of what he had thought differently about an unknown and absent man.

Since the foundation of this unknown accusation was so fleeting and worthless, it was undoubtedly to his advantage that the character of such men should be investigated, if only their position and way of life were consistent, so that absent persons might properly be believed against absent persons [Note: Coelestius and Pelagius are meant. Lazarus and Heros delivered their letter—or, as Augustine calls it in *The Proceedings Concerning Pelagius*, chapter 3.10, their “statement”—to Eulogius, bishop of Caesarea. On the authority of that bishop, the Synod of Diospolis was subsequently convened. As Augustine records in the same work, chapter 1.2, Lazarus and Heros were unable to attend because one of them was seriously ill. The Council of Carthage’s Letter 26 to Innocent, section 1, tells us that the same letter was brought from there to Africa by the presbyter Orosius.] and that such weight in their letters [Note: The verb *esset* (“might be”) has been supplied here by Garnerius, or something similar, such as *videretur* (“might appear”).] might earn them the authority of testimony.

It became clear that these men, despite the regulations governing ordinations and in opposition to the people and clergy, had claimed priestly offices within Gaul though they were unknown foreigners, and had renounced those offices by their own judgment [Note: Concerning Heros, Prosper’s *Chronicle* records: “Heros, a holy man and disciple of Blessed Martin, while presiding as bishop over the town of Arles, was driven out by the people of that city, though innocent and subject to no accusations.” But perhaps his own judgment was added to the violence of the people.

Baronius has *tum eorum* (“then theirs”), and, with the other printed editions, afterward reads *de se poenitudinem secuti* (“having followed their repentance concerning themselves”), omitting *et confessionem* (“and confession”), which is restored from the Vatican manuscript. The same cardinal prefers *nullius* (“of no one”) in place of *illius* (“of that one”). Zosimus means that many are driven by necessity into the error from which they are trying to clear themselves, because they are believed only reluctantly. This seems to be related to what Augustine says of Zosimus in *On Original Sin* 6.7: “The bishop of that see, whose mercy was great, when he saw him [Coelestius] rushing headlong with such presumption, like a madman, preferred to bind him gradually through his questions and the man’s answers, if he could thereby bring him to his senses, rather than drive him by the force of a strict judgment into that abyss toward which he already seemed to be tending.”]. We therefore, although there were other considerations as well, following their repentance and confession concerning themselves, removed them from the priestly office and from all communion.

It is a weighty point that the case proceeded from such men through letters [Note: Garnerius has “through letters and in their absence.” Baronius, as in the manuscript, has “through letters against the absent.” The sense of the speech and the history require either *in absentis* (“against the absent man”) or *in absentia* (“in his absence”). It is clear that the reference is to Coelestius, who was defending himself in Rome alone.] accusing, in his absence, a man who is defending himself in person, who explains his faith, and who challenges his accuser.

5. I have never regretted turning a judgment toward the better. A young man and executor of the Holy Spirit [Note: Supply *fuit* (“was”). Garnerius preferred to suppress the following relative clause beginning *qui* (“who”).] found innocent Susanna, who had been condemned through the false testimony of the elders (Daniel 13:46). The chaste woman is brought back from punishment by a boy, though the aged men had represented her as unchaste.

We must not therefore believe every spirit, as it is written (1 John 4:1), but must examine matters for a long time and with careful weighing, especially where a person’s faith is concerned, since his condition and life are lasting.

Nor did Solomon fail in his investigation of the dispute concerning the truth in the matter of the childbirth (1 Kings 3:23) [Note: Baronius, Labbe, and Garnerius read *rixa mentis* (“a dispute of the mind”); the Vatican manuscript has *rixa veritis*. It became clear to us that this should be restored as *rixa veritatis* (“a dispute concerning the truth”), which Baronius had also noted in the margin. Shortly afterward we supply *statim* (“immediately”) on the authority of the aforesaid manuscript.]. For he did not immediately bring forward the one child when two women were quarreling with one another; rather, cautious as an arbiter in giving credence, he discovered the truth where he understood the affection of genuine maternal love to lie.

It is exceedingly rare for prolonged and disciplined hesitation not to reach the bed of truth [Note: Baronius has *cunctatione* (“by hesitation”); Garnerius’s *cunctatio non* (“hesitation does not”) is preferable.]. It is a sign of an excellent mind to believe wrong things only with difficulty.

For many whose good confession concerning themselves [Note: Baronius has *confessionis pignus* (“the pledge of confession”); Garnerius has successfully restored the passage. Shortly afterward the same cardinal prefers *nullius* (“of no one”) in place of *illius* (“of that one”).] is believed only reluctantly are driven by necessity into the abyss of the very error from which they are trying to clear themselves; and an irreparable wound is made of what is despaired of being healed.

6. Therefore, in the present case, we judged nothing prematurely or before its proper time. Rather, we have made known to your holiness our examination concerning Coelestius’s declared faith. His earlier statement, which he had submitted within Africa [Note: Garnerius supplied the word *datus* (“given”), which had fallen out of Baronius’s archetype, or something similar; he also correctly restored *exinde apud vos* (“from there before you”), where Baronius had *apud nos*, with the support of the Vatican manuscript. That statement had been submitted to the Africans at Carthage.

It can be inferred that it was attached to the later statement which Coelestius gave to Zosimus. Concerning that earlier statement, the Council of Carthage wrote to Innocent in Letter 26.5: “Coelestius has already confessed in his statement, in the Church of Carthage, that even infants are redeemed through the baptism of Christ.”

Augustine often mentions this statement and confession, specifically in the former Letter 89, now Letter 157, section 22, and in *On the Remission of Sins*, chapter 34, where we read: “As regards the baptism of infants, in order that it may be necessary for them, they concede that they too need redemption, as is contained in the statement of one of them; yet he did not wish to express more clearly the remission of any sin.”

Coelestius testified, however, not in that statement but in the proceedings, that he did not wish to do this. When Paulinus pressed him to confess original sin, Augustine reports in *On Original Sin*, section 3, that he replied: “I have always said that infants need baptism and ought to be baptized; what else does he seek?” Augustine comments on this reply in section 4: “You see that Coelestius conceded baptism to infants but refused to confess that the sin of the first man passes into them, the sin washed away by the laver of regeneration.”

Yet, as the same Doctor pointedly says in the former Letter 89, now Letter 157, section 22: “Although he did not wish to say anything more explicit about original sin, nevertheless, by the very term redemption he imposed a considerable obligation upon himself. For from what would they need to be redeemed except from the power of the devil, in which they could not be unless by the bond of original sin?”] as testimony before you, ought also to have been available, so that you might not so readily believe unexamined accusations and reports [Note: It is clear that the word *criminibus* (“accusations”) must be supplied here from the lower Letter 7.1, where Coelestius is said, in the earlier Roman judgment, to have condemned the charges falsely said to have been brought against him through rumor. Hence Garnerius correctly restored *jactatis*, “reported,” in place of *jactantibus*, “those reporting.”

The charges brought against Coelestius, however, had not been brought through uncertain rumor or solely by absent persons, as Zosimus later acknowledged and as Marius Mercator in the *Memorandum*, chapter 1, and Augustine in *Book I on Original Sin*, chapter 3, recorded. They had been brought by the deacon Paulinus, who had been present when Coelestius was judged and condemned.].

Therefore, within two months [Note: This is the passage to which Augustine refers in *On Original Sin*, chapter 7: “Coelestius, like a delirious man, was not believed to have been released from the bonds of excommunication, even though, so that he might rest, he had been treated gently, as though tenderly cared for. But, after an interval of two months, until a reply should come from Africa, a place for repentance was granted him under the appearance of a lenient medicinal judgment.”

This judgment of Zosimus accords with the constitution in the Theodosian Code, Book XI, title 33, single law, which denies the power to defer all hearings beyond two months, even when they are postponed by agreement of the parties. In the same Code, however, Book II, title 7, law 4, nine months are granted when documents or a person from overseas are required.], either let those who can refute him in person come and prove that he thinks otherwise than he has set forth in his statements and profession, or let your holiness recognize that, after the very open and manifest things he has produced, no uncertainty remains.

7. I indeed admonished Coelestius himself, and all the clergy who happened at that time to be present from various regions, that these snares of disputation and foolish controversies—which do not edify but rather destroy—flow from that contagion of curiosity, while each person abuses the foregoing words according to his own ingenuity and undisciplined eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Garnerius reads “or Scripture.” The reading “having despised Scripture” would not be objectionable, and the sequence of the discourse seems to require it.]

For even the writings of great men sometimes become endangered, together with their authors themselves, after a long succession of time, through the interpreter’s discretion [Baronius: “the misery of time”], so that it was divinely foretold that sin is not avoided through much speaking (Prov. 10:19); and the holy David [Note: [Col. 0653D] On the authority of the Vatican manuscript we have rightly restored the word “voice.”] rightly requested a restraint for his lips and a guard for his mouth (Ps. 140:3).

8. I admonish your Charity, both by the authority of the apostolic see and by the mutual affection of love, that your intellectual powers now submit themselves to the precepts and observances of all the holy Scriptures, as they have been received according to the tradition of the Fathers and the ancestors.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] In Baronius, with the preceding *se* omitted, the text here reads *praecepta* (“precepts”), and below *sufficiant* (“may suffice”) instead of *subjiciant* (“let them submit”). Garnerius restored *praescriptae* (“prescribed”) here and *se subjiciant* below. Certainly Zosimus teaches that everyone must obey the Scriptures as understood not according to his own sense, but according to the tradition of the Fathers and the interpretation of the ancestors. Since the Pelagians, however ingenious, do not observe this, but read the Scriptures according to their own sense, Augustine accordingly says in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 42, that “they do not even look upon the things that are plainly stated.”]

What is not abundant there? What is not full of the Spirit of God and of divine utterances—unless each person wishes to believe himself more than he believes God and to use his own judgment concerning himself?

[Note: [Col. 0654B] In the Vatican manuscript this note is corruptly expressed as follows: “Copies of the author having been given to Honorius ...” In the following letter, however, dated 11 Kalends of October, this matter is mentioned. It is therefore clear that this letter was written no later than 21 September. It may also be inferred that the Africans had not received it before October from the fact that Augustine, preaching to the people on 24 September in Sermon 131, no. 10, said: “Two councils have been sent to the apostolic see; replies have also come from there; the case is finished—would that the error might at some time be finished!” By these words he plainly showed that knowledge of the matter had not yet reached him. That it was delivered to the Africans near the end of October is demonstrated by the fact that the subdeacon Basiliscus, who had been sent to Africa to report what had been done before Zosimus in the case of Coelestius and Pelagius and to summon Paulinus, Coelestius’ accuser, to Rome, is recorded as having met this deacon at Carthage on 2 November (Letter 8, no. 4). No one will doubt that Basiliscus, after his arrival and with little delay, hastened to meet Paulinus and make known to him the mandate of the apostolic see. Finally, we do not doubt that this letter was given on some day of the Kalends of October, perhaps on the very day on which the following letter was given, and that *auctoris* (“of the author”) entered the text instead of *Octobris* (“of October”) through the copyist’s ignorance.]

Given ... (in the year of Christ 417), in the consulship of the Emperor Honorius Augustus for the eleventh time and Flavius Constantius.

## LETTER III

Pelagius, having sent letters and a confession of faith, and Coelestius having again cleared himself, it was not easy to believe their accusers, men of such insecure faith; finally, when they condemned what had to be condemned and followed what had to be followed, they had never fallen away either from Catholic truth or from communion with the Church.

ZOSIMUS, bishop, to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, his most beloved brothers in the Lord, greetings.

### 1

After the presbyter Coelestius had been heard by us and had clearly expressed what he thought concerning the faith, and after he had strengthened by repeated professions the same statements that he had presented in his written confession, we shall have written more fully to Your Charity concerning his case.

### 2

Behold, we have received the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who was ordained bishop in the place once held by the holy bishop John. He intervenes as a most energetic supporter of Pelagius’ case.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Pelagius, accused in the Palestinian synod, at first, says Marius Mercator, page 139, by evading the issue and concealing himself under certain ambiguous professions, and by pursuing doubtful arguments or giving doubtful answers, seems at that time to have deceived the hearing of the bishops. Thus he was acquitted. Since John of Jerusalem had presided over that synod, Pelagius easily obtained a letter from his successor Praylius in his own favor, though he carefully avoided revealing his errors to him. How greatly Praylius always detested those errors he later made clear. For when the same heretic was subsequently detected in plain terms, and after the accusers had persisted, he was expelled from the later synod presided over by the bishop Theodotus of Antioch, of holy memory, and was also driven from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem. The writings of that same holy Theodotus, sent to the most reverend bishop of Rome and to Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, of blessed memory, testify to this; we have copies of them in our hands as evidence. Accordingly, in a second letter sent to Rome after Zosimus’ death, Praylius retracted what he had written in Pelagius’ favor while concealing his heretical opinions and pretending to be Catholic.

Concerning that letter and the confession of faith attached to it, Augustine says in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 30: “Pelagius himself recently sent both a letter and a confession of his faith to Rome, writing to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, not knowing that he had died.” We published fragments of this letter, collected from Augustine’s writings, at the end of Innocent’s letters, page 916.]

The same Pelagius also sent very extensive letters containing his defense, in which, without any disguise and so that every opportunity for interpretive deception might cease, he fully set forth the reliability of his profession—what he followed and what he condemned. Their reading was public. Everything was equivalent and expressed in the same sense and with the same propositions as those Coelestius had previously produced.

[Note: [Col. 0655B] What these statements were, and why their reading caused such joy among Catholics, may be learned from Augustine’s *On Original Sin*, chapter 1, where he addresses Albina, Pinianus, and Melania as follows: “You yourselves wrote that you had heard Pelagius, in your presence, reading from his confession—which he also claimed to have sent to Rome—that infants ought to be baptized with the same words of the sacrament as adults.” Those who heard this testified that they had been affected by the same joy with which Zosimus and his assembly were filled.

Hence, Augustine adds in chapter 5, comes what you wrote: that Pelagius answered you that infants are baptized with the same sacramental words as adults, and that you rejoiced to hear what you desired to hear. For, as Augustine reports in the same work, the confession that Coelestius published at Rome and that was cited in the ecclesiastical proceedings contained these words: “We confess that infants are baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the judgment of the Gospel.”

That this form of baptism—its being conferred for the remission of sins—was customary both in Africa and at Rome is established by the canon of the published Second Council of Milevis, by Pope Gelasius’ Letter 5, no. 6, and by other passages. Those who conceded that baptism was to be conferred upon infants for the remission of sins seemed thereby to admit that infants are not born without sin and thus to confess original sin. Accordingly Augustine observes in the same work, chapter 1: “Who, after those words, would have thought that any question on this matter ought to be raised against them? Or, if anyone did raise one, who would not have considered him most calumnious, unless their clear words were read elsewhere?” And in chapter 6 he reveals what those clear words were in the following manner: “Pay attention, therefore, to what Coelestius said most openly. There you will see what Pelagius concealed from you.” Coelestius adds and says: “But when we said that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins, we did not say this in order to appear to affirm sin derived from descent,” and so forth.

Hence, says the published Second Council of Milevis, canon 2, it follows that in them the form of baptism for the remission of sins is understood not truly but falsely.]

Would that someone among you, my most beloved brothers, could have been present at the reading of the letters! What joy there was among the holy men who were present! What astonishment in each person! Some could scarcely restrain themselves from weeping and tears, that men of such complete faith could have been defamed.

Is there any place in which the grace or assistance of God has been left out? Whoever can even conceive in his mind of anything apart from that grace,

[Note: [Col. 0656B] From the Vatican manuscript we have added *ille* (“that man”). Immediately before this, instead of *nec*, we would prefer the reading *exstet*. Here, we understand or suppose that Pelagius’ own words are being noted or repeated—words in which he invoked a curse, saying that if anyone should think that he could conceive anything, even in his mind, apart from that grace, “let that man be subject to the heavenly sentence” pronounced against the blasphemer of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 12:31).

Pelagius’ familiarity with such imprecations is suggested by what Augustine reports in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 2, on the testimony of Albina, Pinianus, and Melania. He addresses them thus: “You wrote to me that you had dealt with Pelagius so that he would condemn in writing whatever was said against him; and that he said in your hearing: ‘Anathema to anyone who either says or thinks that the grace of God, by which Christ came into this world to save sinners, is not necessary not only at every hour or every moment, but also in each of our acts; and may those who attempt to remove it receive eternal punishment.’”

But Garnerius’ reading offers no satisfactory meaning: “Whoever can say or conceive anything besides this and not be subject to that heavenly sentence which was issued by the Holy Spirit.”]

let that man be subject to that heavenly sentence pronounced concerning the Holy Spirit, by which he is granted neither pardon nor remission, either here or in the future.

[Col. 0656A]

### 3

I also see that this Pelagius is being defamed by Heros and Lazarus in their writings. Has no report reached your ears, most beloved brothers, concerning who these storms and tempests of the Church are? Have you truly remained unaware of the life and condemnation of these men?

Although the special authority of the apostolic see has removed them from all communion, learn from this letter as well, though only briefly, the character of these men. It is an old habit of Lazarus to accuse innocence. Through many councils he was found to be a diabolical accuser against Saint Britius, our fellow bishop of the city of Tours.

[Note: [Col. 0656C] Sulpicius Severus does not portray the life of Saint Britius as so free from blame that he excludes every reason for accusing him or intervening against his priesthood. It may nevertheless have happened that, although Lazarus made a true denunciation against Britius, because he did not succeed in having him removed from the episcopate, he seized this as an opportunity from which to say that Britius had received the accuser’s judgment from Proculus, and to persuade Zosimus of this. It certainly does not seem plausible that Proculus, if he had pronounced such a judgment, would later have ordained him bishop of the greatest city. We now read nothing about this matter in the Council of Turin.]

At the Council of Turin, Proculus of Marseilles pronounced upon him the judgment due to an accuser. After many years, by that same Proculus, he was made bishop of the city of Aix, a defender of a tyrannical judgment;

[Col. 0656B]

when the subjugated city resisted [Note: [Col. 0656C] Baronius reads *afflicto* (“afflicted”); Garnerius reads *cumque*, “and when the afflicted city resisted.” What we read below, “the subjection of the whole city,” has persuaded us that here too we should read *addicta*, namely, “the city of Aix, subjected under the yoke of Constantine.” Constantine had been proclaimed emperor in 407 by British soldiers and thereafter possessed Gaul, Britain, and Spain. In 411, at the city of Arles, where he had withdrawn, he was captured and defeated by Honorius’ commanders Constantius and Ulphila, and not long afterward killed.

It is less surprising that Lazarus, having been appointed bishop with Constantine’s support and against the opposition of the people of Aix, was expelled by his own people after that tyrant had been defeated and killed, and that he yielded voluntarily to the man whom he could not resist.]

and broke into the very inner sanctuary and priestly throne, splashed with the blood of an innocent man.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Tillemont, volume 13, page 677, conjectures that this refers to the slaughter of Verenianus and Didymius, relatives of the Emperor Honorius, whom the tyrant Constantine ordered to be killed near the beginning of 409, before sending eunuchs to Honorius to ask pardon for accepting the empire that had been offered to him, as Zosimus relates in book 5, page 818. If this is correct, the text should be restored as “sprinkled almost with the blood of the innocent.” Earlier, Lazarus is called “the defender of a tyrannical judgment” because he was thought to have approved Constantine’s judgment against innocent men.

How much hatred this aroused against Lazarus may be inferred from the fact that Jovius, Constantine’s ambassador, was compelled, in order to clear this deed, to deny that it had been committed by Constantine’s will, as Zosimus again relates at the beginning of book 6. Moreover, from the same conjecture it may be inferred when Lazarus assumed the bishopric of Aix. It follows that he ascended the episcopal throne immediately after the slaughter of Verenianus and Didymius, and therefore around the beginning of 409.]

The shadow of the priesthood remained there as long as the image of imperial power remained in the tyrant Constantine. When that patron was destroyed, Lazarus voluntarily stripped himself of it and condemned himself by his own resignation.

As for Heros, everything was similar: the same tyrant as patron, the same murders, disturbances, chains and imprisonments for the resisting presbyters, and the subjection of the whole city.

[Note: [Col. 0657C] Garnerius reads *afflictio* (“affliction”); Baronius and the Vatican archetype read *renitentibus* (“while they resisted”). Since Prosper states in his *Chronicle* that this Heros, innocent and subject to no accusations, was driven out by his own people, it is easily understood that his only crime was that Constantine had favored him. For this reason he also became suspect to Constantius, who commanded the armies of the Emperor Honorius; and Patroclus, Constantius’ friend, found an opening to invade Heros’ place and, as far as he could, to defame him so that he might not be recalled.]

A similar repentance for resigning the priesthood. It is astonishing if these men did not wish to attack a layman,

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Namely, Pelagius, whom Orosius also calls a layman because he had received no clerical rank. In the proceedings of the Palestinian council, as reported by Augustine in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapters 23 and 24, he is usually called a monk.

Orosius openly removes from Heros and Lazarus the suspicion of falsehood that was unjustly cast upon them by Zosimus in his *Commonitorium*, where he says: “Pelagius was living in Palestine. Some religious bishops—Heros and Lazarus—found books of his in which many and various things appeared to have been written against the Catholic faith. These books, together with letters, were sent to the fathers and bishops in Africa, where they were read at three councils. Those who arranged to send Pelagius’ books are shown to have dealt with him fairly and in good faith, not to have wished to defame him with false letters.”

Therefore, it is clear that those who suggested something else to Zosimus imposed upon him.]

a man striving toward good conduct through long devotion to God, with false letters—men who had contrived so much against brothers and fellow bishops and had brought so many storms upon the Church.

It is not fitting for episcopal authority, and especially not for your prudence, to depend upon the writings of frivolous whisperers.

Behold, Pelagius and Coelestius are present before the apostolic see in their letters and confessions. Where are Heros and Lazarus, whose names are made shameful by their deeds and by so many condemnations?

[Col. 0657B]

Where are those young men, namely Timasius and James, who brought forward certain writings, as was alleged?

[Note: [Col. 0658B] We do not object to the word *protulerunt* (“brought forward”), which Garnerius added on his own; but another word is missing, which may be supplied from the letter of the five bishops preserved by Innocent, Letter 28, no. 6. There we read that, concerning the same young men, “they brought forward the same book, saying that it was Pelagius’.” The passage will therefore be complete if, after *asserebatur* (“as was alleged”), we add “they brought forward Pelagius’ [book].”

From the letter just cited it is clear: first, that the book brought forward was anonymous; second, that it was handed over to Augustine, not to the Palestinian synod; and third, that Pelagius refused to acknowledge it as his own. Hence the five bishops say in the same letter, no. 7: “But if he denies that this is his book...” Since he denied under Innocent that it was his, it is less surprising that he also denied under Zosimus that it was his.]

You must judge whether, if men confessing such things before the apostolic see are present, those matters which were spread about them by wicked and frivolous authors and by uncertain rumor ought to be believed.

[Note: [Col. 0658C] He calls Heros and Lazarus wicked authors, and calls either them or James and Timasius frivolous because of their youth. Their youth, however, possessed nothing of frivolity but much candor and straightforwardness. Nor was anything in this case entrusted to doubtful rumor.

Augustine himself explains how cautiously he dealt with Pelagius in Letter 106, now numbered 186, no. 1. For when rumor had for some time been spreading that Pelagius held opinions hostile and opposed to the grace of God, Augustine says: “It was certainly not to be believed easily, for rumor is accustomed to lie. But we came nearer to believing it when we read that a certain book of his, attempting precisely to persuade people of such things, had been handed to us by servants of Christ who had heard him teaching such things most earnestly and had followed him.”

On the occasion by which he received Pelagius’ book from them, he relates in Letter 252, now numbered 179, to John of Jerusalem, no. 2: “Certain young men, honorably born and educated in liberal studies, abandoned through his exhortation the hope they had placed in the world. Yet when certain things opposed to sound doctrine appeared in them, and they began to be corrected by our admonitions, they gave me a book which they said belonged to that same Pelagius, asking that I reply to him instead.”]

### 4

Love peace, cherish charity, and strive for concord. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:19). Who are more truly neighbors to one another than all of us who ought to be one in Christ?

Not every wind that enters your ears is a messenger of truth. Therefore a presiding and watchful mind is always necessary, lest everything be left to rumor and everything to witnesses.

Review the sacred writings and the divine archives. False witnesses occupy the greatest part wherever we find either accusations or dangers directed against holy men. I say the greatest part—indeed, the whole, since false witnesses rose up against our Lord himself, the Savior of the whole world, both victim and saving high priest, falsely pretending that they had heard him blaspheme [Garnerius: “who claimed that they had heard his blasphemy”].

Consider what deception can now leave untouched, when it has attacked by perjuries the faith directed toward God—indeed, faith itself and truth.

### 5

We have written these things so that henceforth, if some absent and little-known persons should maliciously lie about anyone in this fashion, your feet may stand firm against the battering ram of deceit.

Thus the holy man asks for a lamp for his feet and a light for his paths (Ps. 118:105), so that our footsteps may not be blind and wandering amid deceptive darkness.

And in the Gospel: “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears and knows from him?” (John 7:51).

[Note: [Col. 0658D] The printed editions read *cogitaverit* (“has considered”). We prefer, with the sacred text, *cognoverit* (“has known”), especially since this reading agrees with the confession of faith sent to the apostolic see by those who refused to subscribe to Pelagius’ condemnation.

They first excuse their refusal to subscribe as follows: “We especially admonish Your Holiness not to suppose that it was done as an affront to you that, through fear of God, we do not dare to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons, having been taught through the Scriptures that human will must not be preferred to the commands of God.” They then add all the testimonies of the sacred writings by which Zosimus here demonstrates that one must refrain from judging absent persons, including the passage, “unless it first hears and knows from him.”

This confession is found in the appendix to volume 10 of Augustine, pages 110–113. We suppose that some of its contents, if it is earlier, were transferred by Zosimus into this letter.]

Also in the Old Testament: “You shall not believe a vain report, and you shall not consent with the wicked to become an unjust witness” (Exod. 23, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 0659C] The printed editions read *credas ... consentias* (“you shall believe ... you shall consent”). The Vatican manuscript has *credis ... consenties*. We have thought it should be restored, in agreement with the confession mentioned above, as *credes ... consenties* (“you shall believe ... you shall consent”).]

And lest anyone should perhaps believe the multitude of accusers before judicial examination, he adds: “You shall not follow the multitude into evil, and you shall not accept guilt through them” (ibid.).

And again elsewhere: “Before you interrogate, do not condemn anyone; and when you have interrogated, reprove justly” (Sirach 11:7).

And again: “Speak what your eyes have seen” (Prov. 25:8, according to the Septuagint).

And in the Acts of the Apostles, when the chief priests and elders of the Jews demanded the condemnation of the absent apostle Paul, the Gentile governor Festus delivered a most just sentence, which it is fitting for us also to bring forward in the face of believers as a rebuke. He said: “It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself in order to clear away the charges” (Acts 25:16).

If, then, a man outside the enclosure of our faith maintained this moderation against priestly modesty, belief in absent persons against absent persons is altogether unworthy.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] Garnerius corrected what, in Baronius, had appeared from the archetype as *inclinatio, credulitas de absentibus in absentes* (“inclination, belief concerning absent persons against absent persons”). His correction may be retained until something more certain comes to light.]

For how many people will be found free from injury if, at every blow struck by an attacker, a trusting breast is opened?

### 6

Let earthly moderation teach us. In secular judgments and lawsuits, what care is first taken in selecting and rejecting the judges themselves, and how great is the hesitation; how many delays are inserted; how often an adjournment is ordered (see the Theodosian Code, book 2, titles 6 and 7). Even at the very end of the contest, judgments are prolonged in favor of the innocent accused (ibid., book 9, title 36).

[Note: [Col. 0659D] Garnerius substituted *concessit* (“granted”) for the particle *cum*, against the archetype. The accused is here called *reus*, meaning one summoned as a defendant.]

Appeal is made to the sea and to documents from overseas, so that the truth—which in the present circumstances is generally strangled by narrower constraints—may at least come from a distance.

[Note: [Col. 0659D] The printed editions read *et extramarina* (“and foreign documents”); this has been corrected from the Vatican manuscript. Zosimus seems here to refer to Justinian’s Code, book 3, title 11, law 1: “If a person or documents are requested from the province in which the lawsuit is being conducted, no more than three months shall be granted. But if they are from neighboring provinces, six months shall be observed for the administration of justice; in the case of overseas matters, nine months shall be observed.” This law, issued by Diocletian and Maximian, was later confirmed by Arcadius in the same title, law 7, and in the Theodosian Code, book 2, title 7, law 4.]

I am lying in all these matters unless they have been discovered for the protection and defense of innocence. For it is more tolerable for any innocent person to be found late than to be condemned quickly as guilty.

### 7

It was a serious matter for Lazarus and Heros to be the followers of their own letters. Did they not know that Your Charity would report the matter to the apostolic see? They would certainly have sailed here by the shortest route of calumny.

When episcopal office is being sought,

[Note: [Col. 0660C] The printed editions read *abdicando* (“when resigning”). The Vatican exemplar more correctly has *ambiendo* (“when seeking or canvassing”).]

they scour seas and lands and neglect no support. But when the reputation of innocent men is attacked, they remain idle and delicate—whether as accusers or as witnesses, for in both capacities their name is infamous—in their chambers and little beds, abusing their letters.

[Note: [Col. 0660C] The Theodosian Code, book 16, title 2, law 41, contains a constitution of Honorius dated to the year 412. It first states that clergy must be accused only before bishops; then it adds: “If anyone, whether he is of exalted rank or of any other dignity, should bring an unproved charge against such persons—that is, a bishop, presbyter, or other clergy—let him understand, by the authority of this enactment, that he is subject to the loss of his own reputation.”

Jacobus Gothofredus thinks that this law was issued on account of the disorderly accusation and wrongful deposition of Heros, who, although innocent, was driven from his church by the authority of the eminent Constantius and by popular agitation. But neither this letter nor the preceding one allows room for that learned man’s conjecture. For if the Emperor Honorius had publicly confirmed Heros’ innocence in 412, Zosimus would have spoken differently of him in 417. See the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 39.

Heros and Lazarus are represented by Zosimus as idle and delicate, lying in their chambers and on their beds, because they excused their absence, as Augustine says in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 35, no. 62, on account of the illness of one of them. In the same work, chapter 1, no. 2, Augustine proves that this excuse was true and legitimate in these words: “Because of the serious illness of one of them, as we later learned more credibly, they were quite unable to be present.” Some people, however, had persuaded Zosimus that the same excuse was fabricated.]

And the two plagues cloud all Africa and the entire tranquillity of Catholic serenity in service of their own whims.

Before the tribunal of Christ we shall all stand. No one will be able to be absent there, nor to evade the judgment of the Lord, whose immensity is present in every place and in all things.

### 8
