If it was dear to our God that, for the sake of the lost sheep, the Word should become flesh and, from being Lord, take the form of a servant, in order to restore the freedom that had long been seized, then let it be your joy to recognize that those whom false judges accused had never been torn away from our body or from Catholic truth.

[Note: [Col. 0660D] If Heros and Lazarus are indicated here, the reading should be “not judges but witnesses.”]

Certainly what your expectation desired has now become clear: they condemned what had to be condemned and followed what had to be followed.

[Note: [Col. 0660D] The printed editions read *nostra* (“our”). The manuscript reading *vestra* (“your”) is more harmonious.]

If the master of the household rejoiced at the return of his son who had been dead and came to life, who had been lost and was found (Luke 15:32), and ordered that a clean robe be brought for his use—that is, the emblem of a pure mind—and a fattened calf, how much greater is this richer rejoicing of faith: that those concerning whom false reports have been spread are not dead and have not perished?

We have therefore sent Your Charity copies of the writings that Pelagius sent. We do not doubt that their reading will produce in you, in the Lord, joy over the completeness of his faith.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0661B] The consuls omitted here can easily be supplied from the preceding letter. It is not obscure that this letter was written immediately afterward. Perhaps both letters were also entrusted at the same time to the subdeacon Basiliscus for delivery.] (21 September).

## LETTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0661B] These letters are among those that, as we have noted, are preserved in the Arelate codex, from which they were first brought to light by Baronius, and in another Colbertine manuscript. So that everyone may judge more fairly what is discussed in them, it should be recalled that Prosper, after stating in his *Chronicle* that Heros was driven out by the people of Arles and that Patroclus, the friend and intimate of Constantius, was substituted in his place, adds: “This matter was the cause of great disagreements among the bishops of that region.” This indeed was the cause of the disagreements: on the one side Patroclus, abusing the favor of Constantius and the confidence of Zosimus, defamed Heros in various ways; on the other, the bishops of that region, who knew Heros more intimately, defended him as guilty of no crime.]

Concerning Ursus and Tuentius, bishops illicitly ordained, that they nowhere be received into communion with the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0661C] Proculus, bishop of Marseilles, having taken Lazarus, bishop of Aix, as his associate, ordained Ursus and Tuentius at Citharista, I believe, and Gargarius, which were parishes belonging to the bishop of Arles. In an encyclical letter Zosimus rebukes these ordinations on many grounds.

First, the men ordained had already been condemned, and it was unlawful to ordain them. Next, they had been ordained after the metropolitan bishop of Arles had been disregarded; the bishops of the province had not been summoned; Lazarus had been called in from another province; places belonging to another jurisdiction had been usurped; and finally, the lawful day for ordinations had not been observed.

He therefore indicates that Tuentius and Ursus, as men expelled from the Church, were nowhere to be admitted to communion.]

ZOSIMUS to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces,

[Note: [Col. 0661C] In the Colbertine manuscript the conjunction *et* (“and”) is missing, though it is also found in the heading of the preceding Letter 1.]

to all the bishops established throughout Spain,

[Note: [Col. 0661C] The expression *a pari*, frequent in the later letters of the supreme pontiffs, occurs here for the first time. By this expression are understood several equal and similar copies of the same letter, which were delivered separately to the individuals, provinces, churches, or persons named in the heading.]

with separate copies.

### 1

When the statutes of the Fathers are violated, an injury is inflicted not only upon the prudence and judgment of those who established them to endure forever, but in a certain sense upon faith itself and Catholic discipline.

For what is so holy and venerable as not to depart at all from the path of our ancestors, whose canonical statutes are like foundations laid to bear the weights of the faith?

[Note: [Col. 0662B] The Colbertine manuscript reads *fidei apta ponderibus* (“suited to bear the weights of the faith”). There is nothing surprising in the word *ab*. After *nihil minus*, something such as *praestitum* (“has been done”) or another similar word must be supplied.

It is related below, in section 3, that Tuentius had been contaminated by the stain of Priscillian superstition.]

But nothing could be farther from this in the case of Ursus and Tuentius. One of them, having been healed by the unceasing medicine of this see, could not attain the health of corrected error; the other, having been removed several years ago on account of an accusation brought against him, as the writings or documents of the citizens testify [perhaps: “as the proceedings showed”], received the rank of chief priest from the very man by whom he had previously been condemned.

In both there is blind error:

[Note: [Col. 0662C] Baronius, together with the Arelate manuscript, reads *Et quod* (“and that”); shortly afterward the Colbertine manuscript has *nec vilem* (“nor a worthless”), instead of *nec velit* (“nor should he wish”). One might read: “and that he should neither wish to maintain another’s judgment concerning Tuentius nor his own concerning Ursus.”

The identity of the man who first condemned Ursus and afterward ordained him is clear from what follows: Proculus, bishop of Marseilles, who, as we learn from canon 1 of the Council of Turin, claimed for himself the ordinations of the priests of the second province of Narbonne.

The Ursio whom the same Council of Turin, canon 3, mentions as having been brought into disfavor in a certain usurpation concerning an ordination must not be confused with the Ursus discussed here. Ursio was already a bishop and was not removed from his rank; but here the subject is Ursus, who had been removed by the judgment of Proculus before he attained episcopal dignity.]

so that, although this is the most important matter of all, he neither wishes to uphold the judgment of others concerning Tuentius nor to uphold his own judgment concerning Ursus.

## 2.

But suppose that the men had honorable morals and approved votes: what of the fact that, with our brother Patroclus, metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles, passed over—without whose authority, according to the canons of our predecessors, no ordination could possibly be celebrated—priestly offices are tumultuously and disorderly thrust upon unqualified persons? Nor are even the bishops of the neighboring province summoned, so that the error might be concealed under some semblance of justification; but Lazarus, long ago condemned at the Council of Turin by the judgments of very eminent bishops as a false accuser, after he had attacked the life of the innocent bishop Britius with false allegations, later obtained a priestly office improperly from that same Proculus, who had sat among the others in the synod at his condemnation, and from whom he had voluntarily withdrawn himself, moved by the testimony of his own conscience, by letters of resignation.

It was truly incongruous that a man stripped of the priesthood by his own confession should, after bypassing the metropolitan, ordain another unqualified priest. And, as though nothing were to be done in an untimely manner, not even the proper day for the ordination was observed—so that, since everything was lacking to such men, even the proper time should be lacking. What more can be added to these many and great offenses committed through improper usurpation, except that final matter which surpasses every error: that they were installed in territories not belonging to them, territories that had from ancient times pertained to the city of Arles? If even one fault of this kind had occurred in such cases, the authority of the apostolic see would have destroyed all the rest as well. Here many things converge: the ordination of unworthy and condemned men; the omission of the metropolitan, as well as of the priests of the province; the most shameless usurpation of territories belonging elsewhere; the failure even to observe the solemnity of the proper day; and the admission of Lazarus into the fellowship of an unlawful ordination. All these matters have been examined among us through official records and testimonies.

[Note: Baronius, with the Arles manuscript, reads *synodo*, without the preposition *in*. The compiler of the Fleury library read here: “he had consented to his condemnation.” The reading *assensuerat* would be closer to ours. Yet in the preceding letter, section 3, Proculus is represented not only as consenting to Lazarus’s condemnation but also as the judge from whom Lazarus received the sentence.]

[Note: Baronius here added the word *est*, which is better absent from the other manuscripts. For the passage must be understood as though it read above: “Nor are even the bishops of the neighboring province summoned . . . but Lazarus is summoned,” etc. Two conclusions follow: first, that Ursus’s ordination occurred after Lazarus had been removed from the church of Aix, and therefore after Constantine had been overthrown and killed—that is, after 411; second, that even after this Lazarus was regarded by Proculus as a bishop. Much later Marius Mercator, Augustine, and the fathers of the Council of Carthage, as we have seen, likewise do not cease to call him bishop.]

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads *illicitus*; Baronius, soon afterward, with the Arles manuscript, reads *spoliatum*: erroneously. The text will be clear if constructed thus: “that, stripped of the priesthood by his own confession, he should likewise ordain an unlawful priest.”]

[Note: Zosimus is content to say that the lawful day of ordination was disregarded, without stating which day it was, because he assumes it was known to all through usage. Symmachus, prefect of the City, speaks similarly in his report to Honorius concerning Eulalius, appointed after Zosimus’s death: “When the holy man Eulalius had been brought by the people and clergy to the Lateran church from the funeral rites of the former bishop, he remained there for two days . . . so that the customary day might be awaited, on which he could be solemnly ordained.” Leo, in Letter 5, chapter 6, Letter 9, section 11, and Letter 11, states that one Sunday was consecrated to sacred ordinations by the canons and the tradition of the Fathers. Tillemont shows, however, from the examples of Saints Martin and Chrysostom that this rule was sometimes departed from: the former, he notes, was ordained on Tuesday or Wednesday, the latter on Friday. Cyril too is said to have been made bishop of Alexandria on 18 October 412, a Friday. Nestorius was also consecrated on Tuesday, if Socrates’ account is true that he was inaugurated on 10 April 412; but Liberatus, chapter 4, reports that he was ordained on 1 April, which fell on a Sunday. The learned Renaudot observes, in his *History of the Jacobite Patriarchs of Alexandria*, p. 177, that when at the end of the seventh century they were preparing to bring a certain George into the church for ordination on a day other than Sunday, Mark the archdeacon intervened and denied that it was either customary or ecclesiastical discipline for an episcopal ordination to take place on any day but Sunday. He accordingly charges Elmacinus with error for tracing the Jacobite custom—that a patriarch be ordained only on Sunday—to a decree of Isaac, who was ordained after Mark’s intervention.]

[Note: The same things about Lazarus are read in another letter of Zosimus, which he wrote during these days to the African bishops concerning Pelagius and on behalf of Pelagius; together with another letter likewise written on behalf of Coelestius, Cardinal Baronius first brought it to light and inserted it into his Annals. Although no trace of this particular accusation of Briccius is now found in the acts of the Synod of Turin, I would not therefore say that no such accusation was made there. But because Zosimus attacks Lazarus so bitterly here and, in that other letter, Herotes together with Lazarus—Herotes being bishop of Arles, a man, as Prosper testifies in his Chronicle, holy and innocent—I fear that he was persuaded to do so by the deception and fraud of Coelestius. Since Coelestius was distressed that his own and Pelagius’s heresy had been detected especially by these two Gallic bishops, and had been publicized by their judgment and by the letters that were being circulated everywhere, he thought that every effort should be made to cast suspicion upon their good faith and reputation in the eyes of Zosimus. Nor is it surprising that he was able to deceive others, since he had cunningly imposed upon Zosimus himself so that Zosimus believed him to be a Catholic. For the argument recently proposed by a learned man—that those two letters of Zosimus should be condemned as false in order not to admit that Zosimus had been deceived—certainly cannot be approved by me; nor, if I am not mistaken, would it have been approved by Saint Augustine or Facundus of Hermiane. For what other letter of Zosimus is there in which he called the libellus of Coelestius Catholic, as Augustine relates in Book II, chapter 3, Against the Letters of the Pelagians, if this is not the letter which Baronius published first? Or what other letter is there in which he condemns the Africans concerning the condemned Coelestius, as Facundus writes, if we deny that it is the later letter published by Baronius? But it is better to hear the whole passage of Facundus, in Book VII of On the Three Chapters, addressed to Justinian:

“They will finally find,” he says, “that even the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the apostolic see, contrary to the judgment of his predecessor Saint Innocent, who was the first to condemn the Pelagian heresy, praised the faith of Pelagius himself and of his accomplice Coelestius—whom he himself had examined in the records after Coelestius had been convicted in the Church of Carthage and had appealed to the apostolic see—as true and Catholic; and, moreover, blamed the African bishops because they were believed by them to be heretics, although he still thought the aforementioned Pelagius and Coelestius orthodox, before the Africans themselves had exposed their tricks much more openly. Yet the heretics did not regard Athanasius and Damasus, nor those Palestinian bishops (of all of whom he had already spoken), nor Zosimus favorably; rather, he judges and honors them as Catholics according to the merit of their faith, because the unrecognized cunning of malicious persons ought not to be charged as a crime against the simple.”]

### 3.

And would that only evil morals, and not also Priscillianist superstition, had appeared in Tuentius! The compassion and mercy of this see had long wished to provide for him in this respect, so that thereafter he might remain more reformed. If he had wished to observe more carefully this benefit, granted to him almost without precedent, he ought to have repented of his former error, rather than hurry to the priesthood with such precipitate force that he neither observed the ancient solemnity of the day—which especially ought to have been guarded—nor thought that he should abstain from an unsuitable place.

[Note: Baronius, on the authority of the Arles manuscript, reads “unlawful territories … are assigned.” These foreign and unauthorized territories, in which Zosimus here complains that Ursus and Tuentius were established as bishops by Proculus, some writers, supported by Letter 1, chapter 3, interpret as the parishes of Citharista and Gargarius.]

### 4.

Concerning this matter we have sent letters to your holiness and throughout the whole world, wherever and in whatever part of the earth the sound of the Catholic religion has gone forth, dearest brothers, so that you may not think that Tuentius and Ursus should be received into the communion of the Church, in whatever ecclesiastical rank from which they have been entirely anathematized.

For they are said to be “circulators,” a fact that we have recognized from the judgments pronounced against them by priestly authority, which they encountered in different regions. Rotten flesh must be removed from the holy body, and the sour and accursed leaven must be removed from the mass of sanctification. It was a matter of shame to write more about them, since they have no shame at having done such things.

[Note: It must be that communion together with episcopal dignity was later restored to him, if, as many learned men think, he is the same Tuentius to whose writings Celestine, Letter 20, section 2, recalls having given answers.]

[Note: In the manuscripts, the whole of chapters 2 and 3 of the preceding Letter 1 is appended here, beginning with the words “But we have ordered especially” and continuing through the consular date. We believe that this was added by no one other than Zosimus himself, so that, on the occasion of this encyclical letter, he seized the opportunity to make known to everyone the privilege that he had granted to the bishop of Arles several months earlier.]

### 5.

But we have ordered especially, just as the metropolitan bishop of the Arlesians has always possessed … [and the rest as in Letter 1, chapter 2].

### 6.

We certainly admonish everyone that each person should remain content within his own boundaries; for it is a barbarous and impious confusion to presume upon what belongs to another. Concerning this matter, do not come to us … [and the remainder of chapter 3 of the aforementioned letter].

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [22 September 417], in the consulship of the emperor Honorius for the eleventh time and of Constantius II.

[Note: The manuscripts read “Constantius,” without adding “II,” as consul.]

# LETTER V

[Note: We owe this letter also to the highly regarded Arles and Colbert manuscripts.]

## That the metropolitan bishop of Arles should possess authority over the ordination of bishops in the province of Vienne and in both Narbonnese provinces

**ZOSIMUS to the bishops of the province of Vienne and of Narbonnese II, from the same authority.**

[Note: He rescinds the privilege that Proculus, bishop of Marseille, had improperly extorted from the Council of Turin, namely, that he should ordain bishops in Narbonnese II as its metropolitan. He also censures Simplicius because he sought the ordinations of the province of Vienne, and establishes that the metropolitan of Arles possesses the ancient authority—already existing, as he says, from the time of Saint Trophimus—over the ordination of bishops in both Narbonnese provinces and in Vienne.]

Proculus has been detected as having usurped much against the ancient order in improperly conducting the ordinations of certain men, which we recently examined in a numerous investigation [that is, in a crowded assembly and with numerous examiners], although he, having been long awaited and taking offense at the delay granted him, pretends not to come.

Nevertheless, that presumption moved us greatly: in the Council of Turin, when an entirely different matter was being dealt with, he thought that something should be stealthily introduced to the injury of the apostolic see, so that the surreptitiously obtained concession of that council might provide him, as metropolitan of the second province of Narbonne, with authority over the ordination of priests.

[Note: At the Council of Turin, Proculus indeed vaunted himself as metropolitan of the province of Narbonnese II, and on that account sought two things: namely, that he should enjoy both the honor of primacy and the authority to ordain bishops in that province. He again claimed both for himself under this twofold title: namely, because the churches of that province or parish were his, or because the bishops had been ordained by him. But in canon 1 the holy synod judged, out of regard for peace and concord, that the honor should be accorded not so much to his city, which lies in another province, as especially to him himself, so that, like a father among his sons, he might stand in the honor of primacy. In this passage the fathers of the council openly deny that he is metropolitan of the second province of Narbonne; and, while denying him the authority to ordain bishops, they are content to grant the honor of primacy to him, not to his city, and indeed only in those churches which were shown either to be his parishes or to have had his disciples ordained there.]

And lest he alone, by shamelessly requesting what did not belong to him, should seem to have insulted this see, he associated with himself Simplicius of the city of Vienne, who with no less shamelessness requested that the choice of those to be ordained priests in the province of Vienne also be entrusted to him.

[Note: Paulinus the presbyter, in Gregory of Tours, Book II of the History, chapter 12: “For if you see men worthy of the Lord as priests—Exsuperius of Toulouse, Simplicius of Vienne, Amandus of Bordeaux, Diogenianus of Albi, Dynamianus of Angoulême, the venerable one at Clermont, Alethius at Cahors, or now Pegasius at Périgueux—whatever the evils of the age may be, you will certainly see men most worthy to guard the whole of faith and religion.”]

This unseemly attempt—to extort from bishops holding a council for definite reasons something that should be cut off at the very threshold—was one which neither the statutes of the Fathers nor reverence for Saint Trophimus could permit or alter; for he was the first metropolitan of the city of Arles to be sent from this see. Among us antiquity lives with unshaken roots, and the decrees of the Fathers have established reverence for it.

[Note: The words “dearest brothers,” omitted by Sirmond and Labbe, are restored from Baronius and the manuscripts. Here a certain conflict of opinions is detected between Zosimus and the Council of Turin; nevertheless, they agree in wishing the statutes of the Fathers to remain unharmed and unshaken. For when the bishops of Arles and Vienne were disputing with one another about primacy, the Council of Turin decreed in canon 2 that whichever of them proved that his city was the metropolitan city should have the honor of primacy over the whole province and should, “according to the command of the canons,” possess authority over ordinations. Zosimus likewise professes reverence for the statutes of the ancients. But which of the two—Zosimus or the Council of Turin—was deceived in the judgment they rendered in this case? If Zosimus’s decision was to be canonical, not only the bishop of Marseille but also the bishop of Vienne should have been summoned to the bishop of Arles. Yet only the bishop of Marseille is mentioned here as having been summoned and awaited together with the bishop of Arles. At the Council of Turin, by contrast, the bishops of Marseille, Vienne, and Arles were heard. Nevertheless, in the following letter Zosimus repeatedly affirms that he granted the bishop of Arles nothing new, nothing that he did not already possess by ancient custom.]

And because we command that what has been interrupted be restored to its proper order, dearest brothers, let the bishop of the city of Arles, from the time of Trophimus onward, possess with inviolable authority in both Narbonnese provinces and in Vienne the succession of ordination confirmed through the ages.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of the emperor Honorius for the eleventh time and of Constantius II.

# LETTER VI

[Note: We have this letter from the same copies from which we obtained the preceding one. It is also preserved in a very old Regius manuscript.]

## That Hilary has no right to ordain bishops in Narbonnese I, and that he should not usurp anything there

[Note: To the objection raised by Hilary—that bishops ought not to be made in another province by someone from elsewhere—he opposes the ancient custom of the bishops of Arles, who are accustomed to ordain bishops not only in the province of Vienne but also throughout both Narbonnese provinces. Accordingly, he forbids Hilary to exercise in Narbonnese I the authority that he had deceitfully obtained from the apostolic see. If he acts otherwise, not only will those whom he ordains fail to possess the honor of the episcopate, but he himself will also be deprived of Catholic communion. Against this prohibition of Zosimus stands the second letter of Boniface to the same Hilary.]

**ZOSIMUS to Hilary, bishop of the first province of Narbonne.**

### 1.

We were greatly astonished when, as we were carefully investigating the matter, your report concerning the priests to be ordained in the first province of Narbonne was read to us: while seeking to provide for your assertion and desires, you colored your report under the appearance of propriety, setting aside the truth, and asserting that priests ought not to be made in another province by someone from elsewhere. You ought surely to have suggested not what seemed right to you, but what ancient custom had established.

Therefore, since what you are shown to have obtained deceitfully from the apostolic see has been annulled, it is sufficiently clear that the priest of the Church of Arles was granted by ancient institution the right to make bishops not only in the province of Vienne but also throughout both Narbonnese provinces. For the priest Trophimus, of holy memory, once sent to the city of Arles by the apostolic see, was the first to display to those regions the reverence due to so great a name, and not without reason transferred to other regions the authority that he had received.

[Note: Sirmond and Labbe, together with the Regius manuscript, read “into other [things/men],” whereas Baronius and the Arles manuscript more pleasingly read “into other regions,” which must be supplied. For after Trophimus was sent to Arles, all Gaul received from his source the streams of faith, as Zosimus himself says in Letter 1, chapter 3; and by ordaining bishops he transferred the honor of this name to other regions as well.]

This custom of ordaining, and the primacy of that place, which he had obtained as its first and rightful holder, continued down to recent times and is confirmed by the records kept among us and by the testimony of many fellow priests.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “approved.” If this reading is preferred, the preceding punctuation must be changed, and “into others” retained—namely, successors.]

### 2.

Therefore, although the records kept at the apostolic see alone could have sufficed, we nevertheless bind you also by this authority, so that you may recognize that a limit of just prescription has been imposed upon your presumption, which appeared to have been raised against ancient custom; and you should not think that you may henceforth claim the primacy in the ordination of priests. For you see that this has been conferred upon the bishop of the city of Arles by the apostolic see, by reverence for Saint Trophimus, by ancient custom, and by our recent and most explicit decision.

If you attempt anything contrary to these provisions, dearest brother, which we have established under the judgment of God, not only will those whom you think should be made bishops be unable to obtain the episcopate, but you yourself, separated from Catholic communion, will eventually groan over your unlawful presumption.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads thus; others read, “cannot be.” Canon 6 of the Council of Nicaea decrees: “If anyone has been ordained without the will and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, the great and holy council has judged that he should not be a bishop.”]

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of October [26 September 417], in the consulship of the emperor Honorius for the eleventh time and of Constantius II.

[Note: Sirmond and Labbe read “on the third day”; Baronius’s “on the fifth day” is corrected from the Regius and Arles manuscripts.]

# LETTER VII

[Note: This was copied from the three manuscripts mentioned in the preceding letter.]

## The dignity of metropolitan usurped by Proculus is asserted for Patroclus. It belongs to him to issue formal letters to any member of the Gallic clergy. Hasty ordinations and ordinations “by a leap” are henceforth forbidden.

[Note: This letter testifies that Proculus was condemned and deposed at Rome by Zosimus, and that encyclical letters concerning his condemnation were written. It confirms Patroclus’s privilege of issuing formal letters and his dignity as metropolitan in Narbonnese II, into which Proculus had intruded; and it subsequently decrees that the ordination of bishops must not henceforth take place by a leap.]

**ZOSIMUS to Patroclus, bishop of Arles.**

### 1.

Your conscience knows what I judged concerning the condemnation of Proculus, since you were present at my examination; nor are you unaware of the authority of our proceedings or of the writings that we sent concerning his condemnation throughout the various regions of the world.

[Note: Baronius and Sirmond add “places”; the word is absent from the manuscripts and is sufficiently understood even when omitted. The preceding Letter V here mentions writings sent throughout the various regions. The Regius manuscript has “the authority of the apostolic see.”]

Therefore recognize, by the authority even of the apostolic see, the dignity and office of metropolitan that belong to you, into which Proculus had intruded by stealth through territories not belonging to him, by authority improperly obtained from a synod.

[Note: The printed editions read “by an unlawful synod”; this is corrected with the help of the Colbert manuscripts, in which only “through an unlawful synod” is found. The preposition “from,” because of the preceding word ending in *a*, may easily have fallen out in copying. The meaning is that Proculus usurped the metropolitan position by the authority of a synod, through territories not belonging to him. Earlier, in Letter 4, section 2, we heard Zosimus complaining to Proculus himself that he had installed Tuentius and Ursus in territories not belonging to him—that is, territories not under his jurisdiction. The reading in the Regius manuscript, “through an unlawful synod,” is also acceptable, insofar as Proculus thought that the authority in question could be secretly seized at the Council of Turin, when an entirely different matter was being dealt with, as we read in Letter 5, section 1.]

Let all who come from whatever regions of Gaul, under whatever ecclesiastical title or rank, know that, after being admonished by you, they must send formal letters to us; otherwise they will have only themselves to blame if, setting aside this solemnity, they attempt to come to us ineffectively without consulting you. This rule ought to be observed from bishops down to the lowest ecclesiastical rank, dearest brother.

[Note: The words “to us,” omitted in the common editions, are restored from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The manuscripts read this way, whereas the editions have “ecclesiastical.” See the notes on Letter 2. The Regius manuscript shortly afterward reads “dearest brothers,” which may refer to those into whose knowledge Zosimus wishes this letter to come.]

### 2.

And because some who transfer themselves from any military service to the Church [see Letter 9, section 1] immediately seek the highest place in religion by a kind of leap, although those who come gradually through the ecclesiastical ranks are customarily delayed until they have been examined, therefore, since we cannot invalidate what has been done in certain cases, those who have already been ordained must remain in the rank to which they suddenly attained by a leap.

[Note: In sacred ordinations the Church has always observed two matters, among others. First, that they should proceed gradually through the individual ranks, so that no one should ascend to a higher rank before receiving the lower ones. Anyone who failed to observe this—for example, someone who became a presbyter directly from the subdiaconate, bypassing the diaconate—was said to have been promoted “by a leap.” Second, that each person should complete a proper and lawful period of service in each rank and observe the times prescribed for each. Zosimus writes about these matters in his letter to Hesychius of Salona. If necessity sometimes forced these intervals of time to be shortened, they nevertheless always religiously maintained the first principle: that the orders should be entered in sequence. Thus Paulinus, in the Life of Saint Ambrose, indicates that Ambrose had been admitted to the episcopate as a catechumen: “It is said that after he was baptized he fulfilled all the ecclesiastical offices, and on the eighth day he was ordained bishop, with the greatest favor and joy of all.”]

For if the Apostle commands that a neophyte not immediately be invested with the priesthood [1 Timothy 3:6], and the statutes of the canons have likewise established this [Council of Nicaea, canon 2], we add this by our own decision: whoever henceforth believes that someone should be invested either with the supreme priesthood, or with the rank of presbyter, or with the diaconate, must know that he himself will suffer the loss of his rank, and that what he has conferred will not be valid for that person. At least this fear may deter those whom careful examination ought to have restrained from precipitate ordination.

[Note: Supply “a neophyte,” or “someone transferring himself from any military service to the Church.”]

Our writings must come to the knowledge of everyone, so that you may know that not even this very thing, which is forbidden to all, is permitted to you.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of October [29 September 417], in the consulship of the emperor Honorius for the eleventh time and of Constantius II.

[Note: The Arles manuscript has, incorrectly, “Given on the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Honorius I, etc.” The editions read “Given on the third day before the Kalends”; we follow the Regius manuscript.]

# LETTER VIII, OR THE LIBELLUS OF THE DEACON PAULINUS AGAINST COELESTIUS, GIVEN TO BISHOP ZOSIMUS

Paul­inus congratulates Zosimus because he condemned the heresy of Coelestius, rejected Coelestius’s slander against him, and finally approved his own faith; he also explains why he does not come to Rome.

(This letter may be read among the works of Paulinus, where it is printed below.)

# LETTER IX

[Note: Ancient collections—the collection of Isidore Mercator, the Hispana, that of Hadrian I, that of Dionysius Exiguus, the codex edited by Quesnellus, and others—as well as the copy in the Colbert manuscript written in large Lombard letters, and several Gallic collections preserved in the very old Corbie manuscript, at Fosses, and elsewhere, contain this letter. At its beginning we place the headings composed by Dionysius Exiguus, from whom the author of the Hispana collection and Isidore customarily borrowed them. In their place, the cited Corbie manuscript has the following:

I. That no priest of the Church should be ordained altogether contrary to the commands of the Fathers.

II. That such ordinations must be resisted.

III. Concerning the ordination of clerics: how they ought to reach the honor of the episcopate.

IV. What they ought to observe at each rank.

V. Concerning those married twice and penitents.

The summary of this letter is shorter in the Colbert copy of the codex edited by Quesnellus: in the general index, “Concerning monks and laymen wishing to advance to ecclesiastical ranks”; but at the beginning of the letter itself, “How bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, exorcists, and lectors are ordained, and how many years they should advance through each rank.” The Regius manuscript, otherwise known as the manuscript of Saint Peter of Poitiers, also gives this last summary. Other manuscripts have none.]

### I. That monks or laymen should not reach the supreme priesthood except through the ecclesiastical ranks.

### II. That if anyone disregards the prohibition, he will be subjected to the peril of the higher rank.

### III. What periods are prescribed for each rank of the clergy.

**ZOSIMUS to Hesychius, bishop of Salona.**

[Note: The more reliable manuscripts have this form. After Dionysius, the printed editions read, “Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, greetings”; the Hispana collection and Isidore add the same.]

## CHAPTER I

### 1.

Your affection demands a decree of the apostolic see, in which the decrees of the Fathers concur, and you indicate that certain people from the popular company of monks—whose solitude is greater than any crowd—and also certain laymen are hastening to the priesthood.

This matter is known to have been specifically forbidden both under our predecessors and recently by us, through letters sent to Gaul and Spain.

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript and in two Colbert manuscripts, *transmissis* is missing, with *datis* appearing in another Colbert manuscript. Earlier, the cited Corbie manuscript has *antecessoribus*, while two others have *prodecessoribus* and two others *decessoribus*. We have no letters of Zosimus to the Gauls and Spaniards in which anything specific concerning this matter is decreed, unless perhaps he is referring to Letter 7 above. Although that letter is addressed only to Patroclus, Zosimus nevertheless wished it to come to everyone’s knowledge through Patroclus’s agency. Moreover, in section 2 of this letter he forbids anyone to be promoted by a precipitate leap to any clerical rank, imposing the same penalty here upon both the ordained man and the ordaining man.]

In those regions this presumption is common, although Africa too is not exempt from this admonition of ours: namely, that no one who, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, has not been instructed in ecclesiastical discipline in due order and trained in divine service through the testing of time should dare to aspire to the supreme priesthood of the Church.

[Note: The words “popular company,” absent from Dionysius, Isidore, and the editions of Merlin, Crabbe, and Rome, are restored from four Colbert manuscripts as well as the Regius, Pithoean, and Corbie manuscripts. Its meaning is clear from section 3 below: “The popularity of such people is found even in places where there is solitude.”]

And not only should such ambition be regarded as ineffective, but also its ordainers should be deprived of the rank that they had presumed to confer, contrary to the order and against the commands of the Fathers.

[Note: The Council of Turin, in canon 3, whose heading is “Concerning unlawful ordinations contrary to the statutes of the Fathers,” punished the ordainers with a milder penalty, as we have already observed. Coelestine agrees with Zosimus in Letter 4, section 5. The severity of both toward the same ordainers is somewhat relaxed, and the moderation of the Council of Turin is restored both in the additions to Leo’s Letter 1 and in canon 1 of the Synod of Riez, held in 439. See Hilary’s Letter 10, section 3.]

Therefore we are astonished that the statutes of the apostolic see have not been conveyed to your affection. We praise the steadfastness of your purpose, dearest brother. Nothing else could have been expected from the ancient severity of your episcopal authority than that, standing ready for the defense of the faith, you should confront such ambitions in accordance with the commands of the Fathers.

2. Therefore, if you think that anything is lacking from your authority—which we do not suppose—let us supply it. [Note: [Col. 0670D] The Roman and Council editions read, “Resist . . . resist”; this is corrected from the manuscripts. Immediately afterward, one Colbertine manuscript together with the Regius reads, “With you let the precepts of the Fathers act, with you let it be”; this is less elegant. In fact, the decrees of the Nicene Fathers, canon 2, and of the Sardican Fathers, canon 13, supported by the words of the Apostle who forbids the ordination of a neophyte, are present here. Siricius likewise confirms the same points in Letter 1, no. 13; Letter 6, no. 5; and Letter 10, no. 15, as does Innocent in Letter 37, no. 6.] Resist [Col. 0671A] such ordinations; resist the pride and arrogance that is approaching. With you are the precepts of the Fathers; with you is the authority of the apostolic see. For if secular offices confer the chief position—not upon those who have entered the threshold of public activity, but after many grades and periods of time have been examined [Note: [Col. 0671C] The Regius codex, with one Colbertine manuscript supporting it, reads: “official men [attain] the chief position through secular offices, not having entered through the threshold of public activity”: corruptly. Here “secular offices” means secular officials and judges.]

[Note: The Roman and Council editions, following Isidore, read *examinatis temporibus*, “after the periods have been examined.” Two manuscripts read *examinato tempore*, “after the period has been examined.” The reading we present from the other manuscripts is more polished.]—who is so arrogant, so shameless, as immediately to wish to be a commander in the heavenly army, which [Note: [Col. 0671C] The printed editions, like the Pithoean manuscript and Isidore, read *propensius*, “more eagerly.” With Dionysius and other manuscripts we prefer *pensius*, “more carefully.”] must be weighed more carefully and, like gold, tested by repeated fires, though he has never first been a recruit and wishes to teach before he learns?

Let him become accustomed to the Lord’s camp, beginning in the rank of readers with the rudiments of divine service [Merl. reads *rudimentis*, “with the rudiments”]. Let it not seem beneath him to become, in due order, an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon; and let this not be done by a leap, but at the times established by the ordinance of our predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0671C] The Regius manuscript reads *statis*; Quesnel then has *majorum ordine*. As in Siricius’s Letter 1, nos. 13 and 14, and in Innocent’s Letter 37, no. 6, where various ranks by which one ascends to the summit of the priesthood are listed, so here too no mention is made of the doorkeeper. This order, as can be gathered from Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 15; the Council of Laodicea, canon 22; and the Eighth Synod, session 8, chapter 5, was unknown to the Greeks; among them, however, both deacons and subdeacons performed the function of the doorkeeper. Among the Latins, on the other hand, its acceptance is attested by the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 9, and by Augustine, new edition, Sermon 46, no. 31. A still fuller witness to the same matter is Cornelius, who in Letter 9, no. 3, counts forty-two exorcists and readers, together with doorkeepers, in the Roman clergy. Was he omitted in the places mentioned because this office was not necessarily required of everyone who was to perform it? Siricius, Letter 1, no. 14, with our own Zosimus supporting him below in no. 5, orders that one who is baptized at an advanced age be immediately enrolled among the readers or exorcists, as though receiving either one of those two ranks were sufficient for promotion to a higher one. For this reason Innocent too does not mention the exorcist in Letter 37, no. 6. By the same reasoning, both he and others could pass over the rank of doorkeeper in silence. Indeed, the same Innocent, in the same place, is silent about the subdeacon, and the Council of Sardica, canon 13, about several other ranks. This shows that these passages should not be understood as offering a precise catalogue of all the orders. It is worth noting what is read in the ancient *Constitution* circulated under the name of Pope Sylvester and to be published by us in the Appendix to volume II. Although in chapter 11, no. 16, where the length of time each person must minister in each rank in order to reach the episcopate is prescribed, the rank of doorkeeper is omitted, nevertheless in the same *Constitution*, chapter 3, no. 6, it is said of Sylvester: “Afterward he established ranks within the assembly of the synod, so that neither a presbyter might bring an accusation against a bishop, nor a deacon against a presbyter, nor a subdeacon against a deacon, nor an acolyte against a subdeacon, nor an exorcist against an acolyte, nor a reader against an exorcist, nor a doorkeeper against a reader.”]

Let such a man approach the height of the presbyterate only when his age fulfills the title and his proven merit is attested by the services he has previously rendered. Thereafter he will rightly be entitled to hope for the position of supreme pontiff.

3. This is caused by the excessive laxity of our fellow priests, who seek the pomp of numbers and think that from this crowd some dignity is acquired for themselves. Hence, everywhere, even in places where there is solitude, a numerous populace of such men is found, while they wish to extend the parishes and, to those to whom they can offer nothing else, they lavish the divine orders. This must always be a matter for strict judgment. For everything great is rare. [Note: [Col. 0672C] In Quesnel, as in the Corbie manuscript, *enim* is omitted.]

## CHAPTER II

4. Therefore, so that we might detract nothing from the merits of your affection, we have directed to you especially a letter that will come to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops—not only those who are in that province, but also those who are attached to the provinces neighboring your affection. Whoever, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the apostolic see, neglects this shall know that it must be punished by us with greater severity; and he should by no means doubt that he will have to render an account of his office if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this may be attempted with impunity. [Note: [Col. 0672C] In the Regius codex the particle *post* is added here.]

[Note: Quesnel suppressed the word *impune*, “with impunity,” and consequently, along with the other editions and with Dionysius and Isidore, preferred *posse tentari*, “may be attempted,” although *posse* is absent from the ancient copies of the Codex that he published and from other more authoritative manuscripts.] For whatever is repeatedly done after being forbidden is done in a spirit of insult. (Nicholas I, Letter otherwise numbered 40, no. 4.) [Col. 0672B]

## CHAPTER III

5. [Note: [Col. 0672C] What follows from this point to the end of this letter appears in our Edmund Martène, volume II of *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, on page 350 from the pontifical book of Egbert, archbishop of York, which he thinks was written about nine hundred years ago, and on page 380 from another pontifical of Cahors, with not a few variations, under the title, “Here begins the Sermon of Pope Innocent on Ordaining the Seven Grades of the Church.” But what authority can those two books have to detract from that of the others, which with complete agreement attribute the whole letter to Zosimus?]

The following periods of time are to be observed for each rank. If from infancy he has given his name to ecclesiastical ministries, let him remain among the readers by continuous observance until his twentieth year. [Note: [Col. 0672D] The aforementioned pontificals of York and Cahors read, “if he has learned our examples, and has continued among the readers . . . Thereafter, if he has advanced to a more mature age.” Anyone who compares this passage with the corresponding passage in Siricius’s Letter 1, nos. 13 and 14, will easily detect the corruption. From that letter it is clear that it became customary for infants dedicated to the Church’s ministries to be initiated into the office of reader from infancy.]

If he has come to it already mature and advanced in years, [Note: The aforementioned pontificals of York and Cahors read: *qui tamen post baptismum statim* (Quesnel: *se*) *divinae militiae desiderat*. The other editions read: *ita tamen* (Crabbe: *quod*; the others: *ut*) *post baptismum statim se divinae militiae desideret*. Yet all the manuscripts have *ita tamen ut*, and subsequently *desiderat*. Hence, both from Siricius’s Letter 1, no. 4, and here, with the very ancient Corbie codex and the Lombard Colbertine manuscript, *si militiae* is plainly to be preferred, and *se militiae* is not to be retained. By this arrangement Zosimus, together with Siricius, appears to deny admission to the clergy to those who had not, immediately after baptism, devoted themselves to the service of the Church. They evidently feared that such persons might have committed something contrary to the purity befitting clerics in secular affairs. Accordingly, the modesty of those is to be praised who, conscious that they have at some time committed a serious crime, themselves withdraw from so holy a state and judge themselves unworthy of it.]

then let it be in such a way that, immediately after baptism, if he desires to be enlisted in the divine army, he be kept for five years either among the readers or among the exorcists; thereafter, as an acolyte or subdeacon, for four years; and thus, if he deserves it, let him advance to the blessing of the diaconate. In that order he must remain for five years, if he has conducted himself blamelessly. [Note: [Col. 0673C] The Corbie manuscript reads *ista se gesserit*. Two Colbertine manuscripts have *si inculpate gesserit*, without *se*. The York and Cahors manuscripts read *si inculpabiliter vixerit*, “if he has lived irreproachably.” Quesnel has, as in the manuscripts collated by Hadrien, *adhaerere*, “to adhere,” whereas the other books more correctly read *haerere*, “to remain.”]

After that, with the services rendered in these several ranks supporting him and with demonstrations of his own faith furnished through them, he may earn the priesthood of the presbyterate. From that position, if a more exacting life has led him to good morals, he ought to hope for the supreme pontificate. [Note: [Col. 0673C] In Rabanus the reading is fuller: “and so perhaps it should be read in the York and Cahors manuscripts,” not *acutior*, “sharper,” as it is printed. But it should be retained with the other books as *exactior*, “more exacting.”]

This law must nevertheless be observed: neither a bigamist, [Note: [Col. 0673C] Merl and Quesnel, with Isidore, read: “neither the husband of a widow, nor a penitent.” Other editions after the Roman edition reverse the order: “neither a penitent, nor the husband of a widow.” The words “nor the husband of a widow” are absent from Crabbe and from the collections of Dionysius, Hadrien, the Hispanic collection, and the Lombard collection, as well as from the Regius, Corbie, Fossat, and three Colbertine manuscripts, among others. In the York and Cahors manuscripts, however, what remains of this letter is so interpolated and altered that it reads: “Neither a bigamist, nor one who has returned, nor one penitent after the gravest crimes, can be admitted to these ranks. Otherwise, church defenders who come from the laity and are husbands of one wife, if they observe the aforesaid requirement, and if they have deserved it by their life, conduct, and knowledge of the Scriptures, ought to be admitted to the clerical order.” I have been reluctant to note certain other errors in those codices; but I thought it worthwhile not to pass over this entirely, so that anyone may observe that, when the writings of the saints are corrupted and thus defiled, it can nevertheless happen that they are sometimes read with a degree of authority.] nor a penitent, may be admitted to these ranks. Certainly, church defenders who come from the laity are likewise to be held to the aforesaid observance, if they have deserved to belong to the clerical order.

Issued on the ninth day before the Kalends of March (February 21, in the year 418), in the consulship of our lords Honorius, for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, for the eighth time, Augustuses. [Note: [Col. 0674C] The printed editions, together with the Pithoean manuscript, read “the eighth day before the Kalends of March, Honorius.” From the other manuscripts we restore “the ninth” and reinstate *DD. NN.*, that is, “our lords,” rather than *domino nostro*, “our lord,” as it is written in the Fossat manuscript. Still worse, in the Corbie manuscript those four letters have been replaced by the word *Nonas*. In Baronius, under the year 418, there appears a constitution of the emperor Honorius against the Pelagians marked with the same notation, as follows: “Our lords Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augustuses, being consuls.”]

## LETTER X

[Note: [Col. 0674C] This letter has been reviewed against the Colbertine codex, in which the privileges of the Church of Arles are collected and from which it first appeared in Baronius’s *Annals*, as well as against two other copies, one from the same library and the other from the Royal Library.]

Against the acts of Proculus and unlawful ordinations.

ZOSIMUS TO PATROCLUS, BISHOP OF ARLES.

Since you have learned the matter at hand and have yourself been warned by our frequent letters that, by the authority of the metropolitan—which we confirmed to you by a pronouncement of the apostolic see—you should confront, by suppressing this affair, the acts and efforts of Proculus, by which he still thinks that he can cause some disturbance, resisting him with the severity and censure that you had undertaken for the confirmation of the rules—for you knew that our delegated office had also been entrusted to you, and you knew that he had been condemned—I wonder what Proculus is now permitted or free to do, whether the things he was accustomed to do or worse. [Note: [Col. 0674C] Sirmond reads this way. The Arles and Colbertine manuscripts, together with Baronius, have *oppressus*, “having been suppressed”; the Regius has *oppressos*. Earlier only the Colbertine had *huic rei*, and afterward, together with the Regius, retained *rigorem censuramque*, “severity and censure.”]

Why does he not consider where you obtained this authority of yours, dearest brother, since we have decreed, and continue to decree, that none of those who come from there to our regions is to be received without your *formata*, nor is anyone to be approved whom you yourself, while present in the province, have not approved? After this delegation had been made, a report reached us that Proculus, as though playing his customary games and following his customary practices, had attached to himself certain men fit for disturbances and, after the things we had forbidden him, had performed ordinations. But let those to whose knowledge we wish this letter to come know that none of those who have been ordained either suddenly contrary to the rules or after we had forbidden him can in any way be received. [Note: [Col. 0674D] Baronius, as in the Arles manuscript, reads *quia aut*, “because either.” Immediately afterward, *repente* means “suddenly,” as in the preceding letter, no. 2, *saltu*, and in Letter 7, no. 2, *saltu subito*. Here Zosimus is silent about the penalty that he imposes upon the ordainer no less than upon the ordained in the two preceding letters. Nevertheless, the following letter will make clear that this penalty was by no means remitted to Proculus by him.]

Issued on the third day before the Nones of March (March 5, in the year 418), in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augustuses. [Note: The Regius manuscript reads “the fourth day before the Nones.”]

## LETTER XI

That it was entrusted to Patroclus that they should accept another bishop in place of Proculus. [Note: [Col. 0674D] We received this letter from the very sources from which we received the preceding one.]

ZOSIMUS TO THE CLERGY, ORDER, AND PEOPLE PRESENT AT MASSILIA.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] He attacks Proculus, who, although deposed, nevertheless continued to conduct himself as a bishop as before and, relying on the aid of certain troublesome men, disturbed the Church. He indicates that he had entrusted their care to Patroclus of Arles, so that they might obey his counsel and directions as those of their bishop. Whether Patroclus ultimately prevailed over Proculus is unknown. But one is again led to wonder at Zosimus: how did it happen that he appears more hostile to Proculus, whom Jerome calls a holy bishop in Letter 4, than to Patroclus, whose disgraceful access to the episcopate of Arles and still more disgraceful administration are recorded? For after Herotes had been driven out by the citizens, as Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*—a holy and innocent man—Patroclus was ordained in his place in the year of Christ 312 because he was a friend and associate of Constantius, master of the soldiers, whose favor was sought through him. “And this matter,” he says, “was a cause of great discord among the bishops of that region.” Concerning the priesthoods sold by him, Prosper’s Pithoean *Chronicle* says: “Patroclus, bishop of Arles, dared to sell priesthoods in an infamous traffic.” It is entirely likely that throughout this whole controversy between Patroclus and Proculus of Massilia, Hilary of Narbonne, Simplicius of Vienne, and others, and in the enlargement of the honors of the Church of Arles, the authority and favor of Constantius—master of the soldiers and soon Caesar, who favored Patroclus and the people of Arles—had considerable weight with Zosimus, to say nothing of Patroclus’s methods. Prosper also records the violent death of Patroclus in his ordinary *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 426.]

I am not surprised that Proculus still persists in his customary front and, having completely forgotten modesty, daily commits acts deserving condemnation; nor that, although repeatedly warned and forbidden, he never ceases or desists. [Note: [Col. 0675C] The manuscripts read *oblito penitus pudore*, “having completely forgotten modesty.” How great a reputation for holiness Proculus had acquired, Jerome reveals near the end of Letter 4 to Rusticus in these words: “You have there the holy and most learned bishop Proculus, who by his living and present voice surpasses our little writings, and by his daily discourses directs your journey, nor permits you, by turning aside to another part, to abandon the royal road.” But who can excuse what he did not cease arrogating to himself even when forbidden? Although the Council of Turin, canon 1, as was observed above, granted him permission to assist the bishops whom he claimed to have ordained with the honor of primacy, as a father assists his sons, it nevertheless did not permit him to perform new ordinations. So difficult is it to remain within the fair limits of legitimate power, or to withdraw from what long custom appears to have strengthened once it has been usurped.]

Behold, he confounds the assembly of your affection by the disturbance for which alone he is known; nor does he allow the Church to be harmonious, since he continually acts through his own functions in such a way that, piling the latest offenses upon the earlier ones, he makes some evil that he had previously committed even worse. Although he is no longer a bishop, he makes bishops; and, as a merely human dispenser to others, he claims that he can grant what he was once unable, undeservedly, to retain for himself. [Note: [Col. 0675C] For he had been condemned, as is stated in Letter 7.]

He adds to himself and joins with himself men of restless mind, who alone can favor one who has been condemned, and through whom he may accomplish whatever he, intent upon disturbance, conceives, trusting in this alliance. But I have concern for you, dearest brothers, being troubled that whatever he does by his daily acts of audacity you, the Christian people and those who remain in our charity, can endure, without confronting his deeds or resisting his efforts. Therefore, although in my earlier letters I entrusted your care to our brother and fellow bishop Patroclus, metropolitan of the province, I entrust it again: so that, secure in his counsel and instructed according to discipline, obeying his directions, you may be able to receive a worthy priest. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Those letters are no longer extant; in them the task had been entrusted to Patroclus in the Church of Massilia. Gregory frequently entrusts a similar duty to visitors after a bishop has been removed or has died.]

Issued on the third day before the Nones of March (February 5, in the year 418), in the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augustuses.

## LETTER XII

Zosimus, having more fully explained the authority of his see, informs the Africans that he did not, as they supposed, place complete faith in the words of Coelestius, nor alter the decisions established concerning him by his predecessor. [Note: [Col. 0675D] This letter was recovered by Baronius from a Vatican codex and first published in volume III of his *Annals*, under the year 418; we have collated it with another Vatican manuscript.]

ZOSIMUS TO AURELIUS AND THE OTHER MOST BELOVED BROTHERS IN THE LORD WHO WERE PRESENT AT THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE.

[Col. 0676A]

1. Although the tradition of the Fathers has granted such authority to the apostolic see that no one would dare dispute its judgment, and although it has always preserved this through canons and rules [supplement: “the same see”], and ecclesiastical discipline, still proceeding according to its own laws, continues to pay to the name of Peter, from whom it too descends, the reverence that it owes—for canonical antiquity wished such power to belong to this Apostle, by the unanimous judgment of all, on the basis also of the promise of Christ our God, so that it might loose what was bound and bind what was loosed (Matthew 16:19)—a condition of equal power was given to those who, with his approval, had deserved to inherit the see. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Garner substituted on his own *super sententias*, “over judgments,” and shortly afterward, “and the promise itself of Christ our God.” Here *per sententias omnium*, “by the judgments of all,” is suitably understood as “by the unanimous judgment of all.” This is certainly Zosimus’s purpose: to assert what canonical antiquity granted to his see.]

For he himself has care both of all the Churches and especially of this one where he had sat; nor does he permit any privilege or judgment to be shaken by any breath, whose foundations the very force of his name established firm and unweakened by any disturbances, and which no one rashly attacks without danger to himself. [Note: [Col. 0676C] The same Garner has *cui vi ipsa sui nominis firma et nullis hactenus acta motibus*, “which, by the very force of its name, is firm and has hitherto been moved by no disturbances.” The foundations of the Roman see are marked by Peter’s name, insofar as the apostolic see is named after this Apostle; and the judgment of this see ought therefore to appear all the firmer because it is regarded as Peter’s judgment. Zosimus means this: Peter is that firm rock upon which the Roman see rests as upon a foundation, and which Christ promised would not be overcome even by the dread assaults of hell.]

Since, therefore, Peter is the head of so great an authority, and since the subsequent devotion of all our predecessors has strengthened it, so that the Roman Church is confirmed by all human and divine laws and disciplines—and you are not unaware, dearest brothers, but know, as priests you ought to know, that we govern its place and possess the authority even of his name [Note: [Col. 0676D] The printed editions have *et potestatem*, “and authority.” We restore from the Vatican manuscript the more emphatic reading. Zosimus says that he possesses the authority of Peter’s name because, as we observed above, his see is called the apostolic see, that is, Peter’s see.]—nevertheless, although we possessed such authority that no one could reconsider our judgment, we did nothing that we did not voluntarily report to your knowledge in our letters. We did this for your brotherhood, so that we might deliberate together—not because we did not know what ought to be done, or because we would do anything displeasing as contrary to the welfare of the Church, but because we wished to confer together with you concerning the man who, as you yourselves say in your letter, had been accused among you, and who had come to our see, not refusing judgment, by virtue of his former appeal, asserting that he was innocent; he even demanded that his accusers appear and condemned the crimes that rumor falsely said had been brought against him.

We thought, and know, that all his petition was set out in the earlier letters that we sent you. [Note: This means the preceding Letter 2, to which Zosimus had arranged to have attached the document submitted to him by Coelestius.] [Note: [Col. 0677B] It seems that the reading should be *quae de illo*, “which concerned him.” Here we think reference should be made to what the Africans had written to Innocent in 416 concerning Coelestius. Garner instead substituted *quae ad illas*, “which concerned those.” He assumes that, after the Africans received Zosimus’s preceding Letter 2 and before they began the plenary council in May of that year, they held two councils at Carthage: one from which they sent a protestation with the documents concerning the case of Coelestius, and another whose synodical letter Zosimus is now answering. But since his opinion is very difficult to reconcile with the historical truth—for immediately after Zosimus’s Letters 2 and 3 were delivered to the Africans by the deacon Basiliscus at the end of October 417, they replied to those letters from the Carthaginian synod and entrusted their documents to the subdeacon Marcellinus, who also undertook to carry Paulinus’s libellus, dated November 8, to Rome—it follows that Zosimus is now responding to the synodical documents delivered to him by Marcellinus. There is therefore no reason to invent other letters from the Africans to Zosimus sent before the plenary council of Africa.]

[Col. 0677C] We believed that a sufficient answer had been given to the writings that you had sent concerning him. [Note: [Col. 0677C] The printed editions have *credimus*, “we believe,” where *credidimus*, “we believed,” ought to be restored; we have discovered that the Vatican manuscript actually has *credidimus*. Thus, if we read “the writings that you had sent concerning him” and understand “to Innocent” afterward, Zosimus’s sentence becomes complete and clear. The Africans had written to Innocent in Letter 27 that original sin and the help of grace were denied by Pelagius and Coelestius, and they had added that they preferred that the men be healed within the Church rather than cut off from the Church. Zosimus indicates that he had hitherto believed that their writings, especially insofar as they concerned Coelestius, had received an adequate answer, since he had informed them that Coelestius agreed with Innocent’s letters, in which both the help of grace and original sin were asserted. This is relevant to what Augustine says in Book II of *Against Boniface*, chapter 3. After quoting the Apostle’s words, “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you,” he adds: “This was thought to have been done in him [Coelestius] when he replied that he agreed with the letters of blessed Pope Innocent, in which all doubt concerning this matter [that is, original sin] had been removed.”]

2. But after the letter you sent through your subdeacon Marcellinus, we examined the whole volume. When we had at last read it through, you had so comprehended the entire text of the letter that you seemed to say that we had granted Coelestius complete credence in every respect and, without examining his words, had assented to every syllable, so to speak. Things that require lengthy deliberation are never to be handled rashly; nor should what must be debated with the highest judgment be decided without great deliberation. [Note: [Col. 0678B] Garner here too, instead of *sinuntur*, “are permitted,” inserted on his own *finiuntur*, “are brought to an end,” introducing a meaning foreign both to the truth and to Zosimus’s intention. The passage should be understood as though *tractanda* were repeated in this way: “Things that require lengthy deliberation are never rashly to be handled.” Thus Zosimus demonstrates that he had done nothing rashly when he allowed this matter time and did not hasten to bring it to an end.]

Therefore let your brotherhood know that, after the letters that we previously wrote or after receiving your letters, we changed nothing, but left everything in the same state in which it had long before been, that is, under Innocent. We indicated this to your holiness in our letters, so that the protestation that you had sent to us might remain in force. [Note: [Col. 0678D] The Vatican manuscript reads this way. Other books have *remaneret*, “might remain.” By “protestation” one may understand what they had asked of Innocent. For interpreting *ad nos* as “to our see” presents no difficulty.]

I have appended my signature. Farewell.

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April (March 21, in the year 418), in the consulship of Honorius Augustus XII. Received on the third day before the Kalends of May (April 29).

## LETTER XIII, OR THE CONSTITUTION OF HONORIUS TO AGRICOLA, PREFECT

That a council of the seven provinces be held at Arles each year.

[Col. 0678B] Since this letter concerns Pelagian doctrine, it is better placed among the documents relating to the heresy, which we shall collect in full in one of the following volumes of this century.

## LETTER XIV, OR [Note: [Col. 0678D] In the Roman edition this letter is marked as copied from Cresconius. Yet we have not found it even cited in this writer’s *Canonical Breviary*. Nor does a genuine Regius exemplar of the Dionysian collection mention it either in the general index of titles or present it in the body of the work itself. It does, however, occur in the collection given by Hadrian I to Charlemagne, as well as in ancient exemplars both of the Codex published by Quesnel and of the Hispanic and Isidorian collection, and in certain other manuscripts. In copies of Hadrian’s collection it is incorrectly entitled “Letter to the presbyters of Ravenna,” and in the index of titles “Concerning the presbyters of the Ravennates or Ravennantians.” Nor is it better entitled in the Hispanic and Isidorian collection, and thence in Merl., “To the Ravenna clergy,” or in Crabbe and the subsequent editions of the councils, “To the clergy and presbyters of the Ravennates.” The truer inscription is this: “To his presbyters and deacons stationed at Ravenna,” which the exemplars of the Codex published by Quesnel supply. Quesnel therefore omitted the word *suis* (“his”), by which the ambiguity of the title is resolved. In fact, that memorandum was sent not to the Ravennates but to Roman presbyters and deacons whom Zosimus had dispatched to the imperial court, and it concerned not Ravenna clergy but certain rebellious Roman clergy. At least some of Zosimus’s successors followed his example by arranging to have persons at Ravenna who attended to the Church’s affairs. Thus Gregory, Book III, formerly Letter 54, writes that, concerning a controversy which had arisen, he had investigated and consulted our sons Peter the deacon and Gaudiosus the *primicerius*, as well as Michael the defender of our see, who had been sent to Ravenna by our predecessors for various answers.]

### MEMORANDUM OF POPE ZOSIMUS TO HIS PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS STATIONED AT RAVENNA. [Col. 0679A]

Concerning certain rebellious presbyters and those who had joined their association.

From [Note: [Col. 0679C] In Merlonius, as in the manuscripts collated by the Spanish editors and Isidore, this greeting is prefixed: “Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, [sends] a warning to the presbyters and deacons who are at Ravenna,” except that the word “warning” is absent from the manuscripts mentioned above. The other editions of the councils, and the Roman edition together with the manuscripts collated by Hadrien, have: “Zosimus (in most editions, ‘the bishop’) [sends] a warning to the presbyters,” etc. If a greeting had to be prefixed, we would place first the one preserved by the Regius and Colbertinus manuscripts: “Zosimus [sends] to his fellow presbyters and to the deacons who are at Ravenna.” We follow the copies of Quesnell’s codex, in which there is no greeting. Indeed, such warnings or documents, in which instructions are prescribed for envoys concerning what they must do—as we shall see in the writings of Hormisdas—are ordinarily without such a greeting.] From the report of our brother [Note: [Col. 0679D] Quesnellus has “Archiamus,” as does one Colbertinus manuscript; the other books disagree. This Archidamus seems to be no other than the man whom Innocent commends to Aurelius in Letter 14.] the presbyter Archidamus, we have learned how you were received and what you did, and also how those men were received who, acting with I know not what audacious recklessness, wished to go against the canons and against us to the imperial court. To them we had formerly sent the letter that we now send to you for delivery, replying to the letters they had wrongfully sent (Council of Sardica, chapters 8, 9, and 10). [Note: [Col. 0679D] In the manuscripts collated by Hadrien: “they could not remain with their fellow presbyters”; and in one of them, with the intervening words omitted, “be mentioned.” Baronius thinks that these men are called defendants because they favored Pelagius. But after Honorius’s edict, issued at Ravenna on the last day of April of that same year, by which Celestius and Pelagius were ordered to be expelled from the City and everyone was empowered to report their supporters to a judge, it is not clear how Pelagius’s adherents could have had access to the same emperor in order to accuse Zosimus. The learned man’s conjecture will again be refuted on another ground, which we shall give in the following and subsequent notes.]

But since they could not remain in their own—namely, in our Roman—church with our fellow presbyters, we have sent you these letters to deliver to them, in which by our decree we declared that the aforesaid disturbers had been entirely excluded from communion with our apostolic see, and that they had accepted the sentence pronounced with our subscription.

[Note: [Col. 0680B] Quesnellus alone has “They also,” undoubtedly to bring the sentence into conformity with grammatical rules. He likewise reads “who, by the unbridled deed and council of these men.” In the manuscripts collated by Hadrien, the reading is “who, by the unbridled counsel of this man,” except that in the second corrections of the Coislinian manuscript there appears “by the counsel of whom.” One Colbertinus has “by the unbridled deed and council of this man.” The reading in another Colbertinus, “by the unbridled counsel of this deed,” without the conjunction *-que*, is sufficiently plausible. The Regius retains it, and likewise has “by the unbridled counsel of this deed.” The printed reading, which we have decided to preserve amid this variation, is found in the manuscripts collated by the Spanish editors and Isidore. If the discussion here concerned the supporters of Pelagius, they would have to be accused not of wishing to lend their assent to an unbridled crime, but of wishing to lend it to a perverse belief.] It is for your [Col. 0680A] Charity to judge how those also are to be regarded who wished to lend their assent to this unbridled deed and counsel. You must charge them with this: that, in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons, they have gravely incurred guilt and, in a manner unbefitting presbyters, proved to be rebels.

[Note: [Col. 0680C] In one of the Harlaean manuscripts: “you must charge them next”; above the preposition *juxta* (“according to”) is written *contra* (“against”). Hence Crabbe, opposite the word *juxta*, noted *contra* in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0680C] The printed editions read: “attempted to become.” The words “attempted to become” are absent from the manuscripts collated by Hadrien. Hence it is clear that *exstitere* (“proved to be”) is to be read here, and that *incurrere* above has the same sense as *incurrerunt* (“they incurred”), as it stands in Merlin. The Roman and conciliar editions then read, “Yet we warn you.” Note that here too the charge against the defendants is rebellion, not rash belief.]

But we warn you that you must remain watchful,

[Note: [Col. 0680C] Merlonius has *neque* (“and not”). Other editions of the councils, together with the Roman edition and several manuscripts, have *ne qua* (“lest any”). With one Colbertinus codex we prefer *ne quo*, as though it meant “lest any,” supported by other manuscripts. That same *quo* is retained in the corrupt readings found in another Colbertinus—“concerning whose rash audacity,” etc.—in the Regius—“concerning which their rash audacity”—and in the Pithoean—“lest the rash audacity of those whom the apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized should stir up scandal.” From this last reading Quesnellus constructed the following, which seems alien to Zosimus’s meaning: “lest the rash audacity of certain men, whom it is known to have been anathematized, should stir up scandal in the apostolic Church.” Zosimus’s admonition is not vague, concerning just anyone, but definite and fixed, concerning those whom he had condemned by anathema.] lest the audacity of any of those whom the holy and apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized should break out.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] In two Colbertinus manuscripts and the Regius: “the apostolic Church knows.” In the Pithoean, as noted above: “should stir up the apostolic Church.” It seems that *scitis ab apostolica Ecclesia* (“you know from the apostolic Church”) should be restored.]

As for those who joined themselves to their association, when you have returned we shall consider, with better counsel, what we ought to do. (In another hand:) Given on the fifth day before the Nones of October (October 3, 418), in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time.

## LETTER XV, OR THE WARNING OF POPE ZOSIMUS TO HIS LEGATES

[Note: [Col. 0680D] This Warning, or rather a fragment of a Warning, was copied from the proceedings of the council held at Carthage in 419, toward the end of May; a version of it appears in the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, chapter 1. The Africans briefly summarize its principal points in Letter 1 to Boniface, section 3. That it was written in the preceding year, namely 418, and attached to the proceedings of the African council at which it was read, is shown by those proceedings. Yet they speak of this council in May 419 as though it had just been held. Hence it may be inferred that the Warning read there belongs to the closing part of 418.]

To his own legates.
