Concerning appeals of bishops to the priest of the Roman Church.—II. Concerning the handling of the cases of presbyters and deacons before neighboring bishops, if they have been excommunicated by their own bishops.

To his brother FAUSTINUS [Note: [Col. 0681C] Bishop of the church of Potentia in Picenum, which is now destroyed.] and to his sons, the presbyters PHILIP and ASELLUS, ZOSIMUS the bishop.

[Col. 0681A]

### 1

You are not unaware of the matters entrusted to you. Conduct everything as though you were acting in our presence—or rather, since our presence is in you there, as though we ourselves were acting—especially since you can also possess this mandate of ours, together with the words of the canons that we have inserted into this Warning for its fuller authority. For thus they said, dearly beloved brothers, in the Council

[Note: [Col. 0681C] This was the Council of Sardica, whose canons we still read in the ancient Morbacensis, Fossatensis, and Colbertinus manuscripts, marked with the title of the Council of Nicaea, or placed immediately after the Nicene canons under a continuous series of numbers. This passage of Zosimus proves that the confusion is ancient. Yet Innocent, Zosimus’s predecessor, did not at all regard the acts of Sardica as Nicene, as we observed in the note to his Letter 7. It is nevertheless all the more remarkable that among so many and such eminent prelates flourishing in Africa at that time there was no one who knew the Sardican canons, since Gratus, bishop of Carthage, had attended the Sardican synod and commended its authority at the First Council of Carthage, canon 5. As early as 398 Augustine, in Letter formerly 163, now 44, section 6, had stated that he had heard nothing yet about the Council of Sardica. Nevertheless, it is clear that throughout this entire affair Zosimus acted in good faith no less than the Africans. It was enough for him that the Africans, who in the Second Council of Carthage, canon 10, and again in the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, chapter 13, declare, “The statutes of the ancients must be preserved by us,” should propose the authority of the Sardican synod. Nor did he need to fear that they would reject decrees which they had learned that their own primate had confirmed by his presence. For this reason alone they write in Letter 2 to Celestine, section 4, that they could not concede those decrees which Zosimus had called Nicene: “because,” they say, “we find this written in no synod of the Fathers.” If, then, they had found this established in so solemn a synod, who would doubt that they would immediately have obeyed Zosimus’s will? Learned men observe that, on the occasion of this controversy, they took care to gather into a single codex the canons received in their church—the codex that we still possess—so that nothing might thereafter be demanded of them that was not consistent with the regulations and discipline of their church.]

of Nicaea, when they were decreeing concerning the appeal of bishops:

> “It was also decided that, if a bishop has been accused, and the bishops of that region have assembled, judged him, and deposed him from his rank, and he appears to have appealed and fled for refuge to the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and has wished to be heard, and he has judged that the examination should be renewed, he should write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth of the matter. But if the man who asks that his case be heard again should by his petition move the Roman bishop to send a presbyter from his own side, it shall be in the power of the Roman bishop to decide what he wishes and what he judges. And if he should decide that men ought to be sent who, being present with the bishops, may judge the case, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, it shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges in his most prudent counsel.”

(Council of Sardica, chapter 7.)

[Note: [Col. 0682C] Here, as we learn from Letter 1 to Boniface, section 2, there followed another heading: “That bishops should not sail to the imperial court.” Zosimus could likewise have supported this by canon 8 of the Sardican synod, as well as by Innocent’s letters written on the matter, which the Council of Carthage is said to have confirmed in the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, chapter 94.]

### 2

Concerning the appeals of clergy,

[Note: [Col. 0682C] It is clear that by “clergy of a lesser rank” Zosimus means presbyters and deacons, both from the Sardican canon that follows and from the Africans’ Letter 1 to Boniface, section 3, where they summarize this third heading of the Warning as follows: “Third, concerning the handling of the cases of presbyters and deacons before neighboring bishops, if they have been improperly excommunicated by their own bishops.” Consistent with this is what the Africans decreed in 416 at the Second Council of Milevis, canon 22, which was inserted into the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, chapter 28, in these words: “It was decided that presbyters, deacons, or other inferior clergy, in cases that concern them, if they have complained of the judgments of their own bishops, should be heard by neighboring bishops with the consent of their own bishop, and that the bishops appointed by them should decide between them.” But in the same canon they added: “As for anyone who thinks he should appeal overseas, no one within Africa shall admit him to communion.” The Roman see did not approve this.]

—that is, of clergy of lesser rank—what you are to do is stated by the synod’s definitive answer. We have thought it necessary to insert what you are to do concerning this matter; it was expressed as follows. Bishop Hosius said:

> “I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps being angry—which he ought not to be—should quickly or harshly become enraged against his presbyter or deacon, and should wish to expel him from the church, care must be taken that an innocent man is not condemned or deprived of communion. Let the expelled man have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, for one must not deny a hearing to him who asks for one. Let that bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that either his sentence may be proved or corrected,” etc.

(Council of Sardica, chapter 17.)

### 3

(There had also been added a fourth heading), concerning excommunicating Bishop Urbanus, or even summoning him to Rome, unless he corrected those matters that appeared to require correction (Boniface I, Letter 1, section 2).

## LETTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0682D] Binius extracted this letter from an ancient codex of the monastery of Weingarten. He and, after him, Labbe judged it to differ greatly from the others and therefore to be of suspicious authenticity. I fear, however, that this appearance of difference was introduced not by the author but by the style of an unskilled copyist. Its consular notation agrees with the period of Zosimus. Nor should it be denied that the force with which Zosimus habitually censures what he does not approve appears throughout this letter, from beginning to end.]

Concerning the disregard of the rules of judicial procedure, so that priests are judged in the presence of laymen and the accused is compelled to seek out and bring his adversary to judgment.

ZOSIMUS sends greetings in the Lord to his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Byzacena

[Note: [Col. 0683B] The archetype has “Bysantium,” corruptly. For this does not designate a city but a province; and Byzantium, after its name was changed, was called Constantinople. The province of Byzacena, however, was famous in Africa, and many councils held around this time in that province are cited by Ferrandus the deacon in his *Breviary*: for example, the council of Suffetula, chapter 2; Septimunicum, chapter 11; Marazanum, chapter 44; Themitanum, chapter 61; and Zellense, or Teleptense, held in this very year, 418.]

[Col. 0683A]

### 1

I am astonished that you show no reverence for the dignity of our name, nor offer such honor to the episcopate as ought to be preserved by those whose honor this is. Laymen are to judge bishops,

[Note: [Col. 0683B] At the Council of Aquileia, in Ambrose, section 51, this saying is attributed to Ambrose himself: “Priests ought to judge laymen, not laymen priests”; and likewise, in section 52: “For this too, and on this very account, Palladius must be condemned, because he awaits the judgment of laymen, whereas priests ought rather to judge laymen.” The same prelate, in Letter 21, section 2, praises the elder Valentinian because he established not only by speech but also by his laws that, in a matter of faith or of any ecclesiastical order, the man who judges should be neither unequal in office nor different in legal standing. To this he adds: “Indeed, if a bishop were accused on another matter and his morals had to be examined, he also wished this to belong to episcopal judgment.” Earlier, the emperor Constantius had established in the *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 2, law 12, issued in 355, that no one should accuse bishops before public judges, but that their cases should be decided by the judgment of other bishops. Baronius thinks this constitution was issued at the request of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Certainly that Confessor, in Book 1 of his *To Constantius*, section 1, earnestly begs him to provide and decree that all judges everywhere entrusted with the administration of the provinces, whose sole concern and responsibility is the provinces, should abstain with religious scrupulousness and thereafter neither presume nor usurp the right to investigate the cases of clergy. Later, St. Martin, established at Trier, said to the emperor Maximus, according to Sulpicius, Book II: “It is a new and unheard-of crime that a secular judge should judge the cases of the Church.” One should also read the letter of Leo, bishop of Bourges, and his companions, reported by Sirmond in volume 1 of the *Councils of Gaul* under the year 454; it excludes from the sacred thresholds and keeps from the heavenly altar clerics who proceed to secular examination, as insulting to sacred law and the priestly order. The specific matter noted here is not that bishops are summoned to secular judgment, but that, in an episcopal court, laymen sit among the episcopal judges. The Second Council of Seville also rejects this, chapter 9, where, after asserting that it is unbecoming for secular persons to judge in the Church, it adds: “In one and the same office, different professions are not fitting.” This too is prohibited by divine law, Moses saying: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together”—that is, “You shall not join people of different professions in a single office.”]

and you call this your council, where, by your permission, it is not a priest who judges a layman, but a layman who is present to judge a priest. For a layman, however honored he may be, cannot so flatter himself about any dignity that he might appear to have been rightfully present

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Supply “at the judgment.” Ivo, page 16, chapter 12, cites this decree as though from the Council of Chalon, chapter 6: “When matters that are canonical are being discussed, or when matters governed by a rule are being discussed, no laymen ought to be present except religious men, and only those who are called in their own person.” Here laymen are not prohibited without qualification from attending ecclesiastical judgments.]

at what had been constituted as an ecclesiastical proceeding. Add that the name of tax-collectors, or

[Note: [Col. 0684B] The printed editions have *demonariorum*; anyone familiar with the meaning of the word will not doubt that *temonariorum* should be restored. *Temonarii* are mentioned in the *Theodosian Code*, book 6, title 4, law 21, and book 7, title 18, law 3. Their office was considered degrading, as is clear both from the following constitution of the emperor Arcadius, in the same Code, book 6, title 26, law 14: “Although the glory of the record offices is adorned by innumerable laws, nevertheless we order that their possession first be secure from all degrading duties . . . and that it suffer no abuse from a *temo*”; and from the following constitution of Constantine, in the same work, title 35, law 3: “We exempt all these men from undertaking the administration of collectors or *turmarii*, whom they call *capitulare* officials because they collect the census of persons, or from the service of the *temonarii*.” Most especially this is clear from the words of Arcadius in the same Code, book 11, title 16, law 14: “We order those who there assist our Clemency in carrying out and sealing replies to be exempt from all base offices and from the whole *capitularia*, or, to express what we wish understood by a common declaration, from the office of the *temonaria*.” Accordingly, *temonarii* is a general term for those who conduct and collect taxes. Hence Tillemont considers the bishop of whom Zosimus is speaking to have been, like Paul of Cataquum, whom Augustine mentions in Letter formerly 124, now 96, section 2, a contractor for tax collection, and therefore subject to examination by such men, so that the bishops might pronounce a more equitable judgment concerning him or make clear that the Church did not approve frauds committed against the treasury. Nevertheless, the Third Council of Carthage, canon 15, had already decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or clergy should not be contractors or agents, nor seek their livelihood through any disgraceful or dishonorable business, “because they ought to remember that it is written: No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” Yet there is no contradiction in supposing that the man here designated had exercised such offices before being promoted to the clergy.]

of *temonarii*, is included, and judgment is gathered against the bishop by this assembly.

[Col. 0684A]

Publicans sit, a bishop is heard, and he is heard by men who, while you permit it, do what is unlawful.

[Note: [Col. 0684D] I think one should read “and, while you suffer such things—which is unlawful—he is heard.”]

Who would not laugh at that—or rather, who would not grieve—when he sees ecclesiastical rule wavering in this way,

[Note: [Col. 0684D] The same use of the verb *titubare* (“to waver”) is found in Letter 13 of Zosimus, section 1, where, speaking of his see, he says: “Nor does it permit any privilege or any breeze of judgment to waver.”]

and the force of the canons cast down for this purpose? When and where, it may be asked, is this shown to have happened? What age remembers such an example? What priest has heard of it? Yet there have been countless men who, having renounced the greatest honors, rejected secular power so completely that even clergy of the lowest rank

[Note: [Col. 0684D] This defective or corrupt passage in many copies might be repaired as follows: “so that even clergy of the lowest rank preferred to endure the loss of honor and not be judged by laymen in the ambition of their former dignity. Behold the true and certain rule prescribed for judges. What do you clergy want from the consent of a lay judge, you who blush to hear this name alone without the glory of your former secular status? What do you want? Certainly, allow me to say,” etc.]

preferred to endure the loss of honor rather than be judged amid the ambition of their former dignity. And behold the true and certain rule prescribed for judges. What do you want from the consent of lay judges? Or you clergy, who blush to hear this name alone without the glory of your former secular status,

[Col. 0685A]

listen. What can I say to you—certainly, forgive me—when you sit in judgment together with such men?

### 2

But we must not omit this matter, especially since no severity of judgments and no established procedure has caused it: that the necessity should be imposed on someone of seeking out his adversary and bringing him to judgment, when the accuser himself ought voluntarily to present himself.

[Note: [Col. 0685A] Rather, the accuser himself, if he neglects to appear within the time prescribed by law, is fined, according to the *Theodosian Code*, book 9, title 36; and the Third Council of Carthage, canon 7, removes from communion the bishop’s accuser who is absent on the days prescribed for presenting the case.]

For this reason we have sent this letter in reply to your Charity through our brother and fellow bishop Numunianus. Farewell, brothers; and in the margin: the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December (November 16, 418), in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF ST. ZOSIMUS, POPE

## NOTICE OF WRITINGS NO LONGER EXTANT THAT CONCERN POPE ZOSIMUS

(D. Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, volume I.)

### I

[Col. 0685B]

Here it is enough to recall the letters of Pelagius together with his confession of faith, as well as the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, sent to Innocent but, after Innocent’s death, delivered to his successor Zosimus. There is no need to repeat what we discussed about them at the end of Innocent’s letters.

### II

#### 2

When Innocent was pope, as we have already observed, Celestius was accused at Carthage and deprived there of ecclesiastical communion; he believed that an appeal ought to be made from this sentence. But when his appeal was disregarded (Marius Mercator, *Commonitorium*, chapter 1), he first proceeded to Ephesus, where by stealth he sought a place among the presbyters, and then to Constantinople. Finally, after almost six years, he went to Rome and presented a confession to Zosimus as he was beginning his pontificate, asking to be heard by him.

In this confession, after explaining his faith from the Trinity and the one Godhead to the resurrection of the dead, as it will be, when he came to the matter at issue he prefaced his statement as follows:

> “But if questions have arisen beyond the faith, concerning which there is dispute among many, I have not, as the author of any dogma, established them by a definitive authority; rather, what we have received from the fountain of the Prophets and Apostles we offer for approval to the judgment of your apostolate, so that, if perhaps some error of ignorance has crept in—as may happen to human beings—it may be corrected by your sentence.”

In the same confession, as Augustine testifies in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 33, Celestius confessed that infants are baptized for the remission of sins, but denied that anyone has original sin. The same Doctor reports the words in which he professed this, in *On Original Sin*, chapters 5 and 6, as follows:

> “We confess that infants are baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the teaching of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be bestowed only upon the baptized. Since they do not possess the powers of nature for this, it is necessary that it be bestowed through the freedom of grace. But when we said that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins, we did not say this in order to appear to affirm sin as transmitted by descent; this is far removed from Catholic understanding, because sin is not born with a person, but is subsequently committed by the person, and is shown to belong not to nature but to the will. It is therefore fitting to confess the former, lest we appear to create different kinds of baptism; and it is necessary to guard against the latter, lest, under cover of the mystery, it be said, to the injury of the Creator, that evil is transmitted by nature before it is committed by a human being.”

#### 3

The common opinion of learned men who preceded John Garnerius is that the remaining words of this confession have been lost. Garnerius, however, in Dissertation 5 on Marius Mercator, page 313, thinks that its first and largest part is contained in Augustine’s Sermon formerly numbered 190, but correctly 191, *On Time*, where it has been inserted. Thus, if the words quoted above from Augustine are appended to this portion, he thinks that nothing further is needed for the completeness of the entire confession.

Some indeed believe that the cited portion of the Sermon belongs to Pelagius’s confession. But Garnerius detected between this portion and Pelagius’s confession differences by which he judges them to be neither one work nor the work of one author. To persuade others of this, he presents Pelagius’s confession in one column and the material inserted into Augustine’s Sermon 191 *On Time* in the facing column, distinguishing in italic type the variations found in each. These variations, however, are so slight and rare that anyone may rightly conclude that one specimen presents Pelagius’s confession in its pure form, while the other presents the same confession in a less pure form, interpolated by the person who composed the beginning of the aforementioned Sermon.

### III

#### 4

When Zosimus had received this confession of Celestius and the aforementioned writings of Pelagius, he summoned the clergy, called Celestius before him, and ordered that the case of Celestius and Pelagius be examined and that proceedings concerning it be drawn up. He then entrusted those proceedings to Basiliscus, so that he might take them to Africa; from Letter 8, section 4, it is certain that this subdeacon had arrived there before November 2, 417.

Marius Mercator, who testifies that he had copies of those proceedings in his possession, reports the following about them (*Commonitorium*, chapter 1):

> “When Celestius was questioned, and was somewhat frightened by that examiner, Zosimus, through his frequent replies and statements he began to sow the hope that he would condemn the propositions of which he had been accused by Paulinus at Carthage, promising to do so. For this was being urged upon him more insistently, and expected of him more forcefully.”

Augustine discusses the same matter at greater length in *On Original Sin*, chapter 7. But the actual words of the proceedings to which both writers refer are reported by the deacon Paulinus in the preceding Letter 8, section 2; since anyone can easily consult them, we refrain from repeating them here.

### IV

#### 5

Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, indignant that Zosimus had granted Patroclus, bishop of Arles, the power to ordain bishops not only in the province of Vienne but also in the two provinces of Narbonne, sent him a report (Letter 6, section 1), in which he claimed that it belonged to him to ordain priests in the First Province of Narbonne. Yet he did not claim this right on the basis of ancient custom, as the matter required, but under a certain appearance of dignity and propriety, asserting that priests ought not to be ordained in another province by someone else. Zosimus refutes this report in Letter 6, issued on September 29, 417.

### V

#### 6

Aurelius and the other bishops of Africa, gathered at Carthage around the beginning of November 417, wrote back to Pope Zosimus concerning Celestius, remonstrating with him as though he had placed complete confidence in this heretic and had assented to every syllable of his words without examining them. In this letter they stated that, since Celestius had been accused before them, his methods were known to them. Then, warning that his faith was not sincere, they implored Zosimus not to absolve him hastily, but to leave the matter in the condition in which it had been before the latest examination—that is, to allow Celestius to remain excluded from the communion from which Innocent had deprived him.

Although they explained this at such length that Zosimus did not hesitate to call their letter a volume, they nevertheless did so with such moderation that they drew the mind of this pope, however favorably inclined toward Celestius, away from his preconceived opinion of him, as is clear from Letter 13, in which he replied to them.

#### 7

Some men whose learning we greatly respect think that two letters were sent back by the Africans in response to Zosimus’s second letter: one from the Council of Carthage, which Aurelius hastily convened so that the two-month interval prescribed by Zosimus would not pass without a letter; the other from a second council at which several bishops from different provinces likewise assembled at Carthage at the beginning of November 417.

But if anyone carefully examines the various passages of Augustine and other Fathers by which they think their opinion is supported, he will find none that actually favors it. Of those passages which they apply to a council held in 417, there is not one that cannot more suitably be referred to the council held in the following year, on the Kalends of May (Letter formerly 47, now 215, section 2).

Augustine specifically writes:

> “We have read what was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council, and his reply to all the bishops of the whole world, and what we briefly established against that same error at the later plenary council of all Africa.”

It cannot be denied that Augustine distinguishes two councils here, calling one African and the other plenary. Yet not even one of these, much less both, can be referred to the year 417. As for the council he calls plenary, he clearly shows that it occurred after that celebrated reply of Zosimus to the bishops of the whole world.

Nor is there any ambiguity that, by the name “African council,” this same Doctor means the synod held on the Kalends of May 418, which preceded the aforesaid reply of Zosimus. This can be confirmed both from *On Original Sin*, chapter 7:

> “After replies had been sent from the African council of bishops, read everything that followed, so that you may see how justly a sentence was pronounced against him,”

and from chapter 21 of the same book:

> “After the replies of the African council . . . the faithful learned what Pope Zosimus appended in his letters, which he wrote to be carried throughout the world.”

Prosper agrees with Augustine in *Against the Collator*, chapter 10, or chapter 5, section 15. For what he praises there as having been established in the African council is expressed as follows:

> “The African councils of bishops went astray when by their decrees they established that both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do, and loving in order to do it.”

The same words are found as a defined proposition in the Council of Carthage held on the Kalends of May 418, canon 4, or 5.

No one should be troubled by Prosper’s addition:

> “The 214 priests went astray, who, in the letter that they placed before their decrees, …”

as though he were beginning to mention another council. For by these words he does not mention another council, but another document of the same council—namely, the letter prefixed to the decrees of that council.

[Col. 0688D]

#### 8

Moreover, between the time when Zosimus’s letter concerning Celestius was delivered to the Africans and the time when they wrote the letter to which the same pope replied in Letter 12, an interval of scarcely eight days can be imagined.

Basiliscus the subdeacon received Zosimus’s letter for delivery to Africa, by which Celestius’s accusers were ordered to appear at Rome within two months, so that they might accuse him there in person. There is no doubt that immediately upon his arrival the subdeacon did not delay in meeting Paulinus, the special accuser of Celestius.

Paulinus testified that Basiliscus had summoned him on November 2 and verbally cited him to Rome. Six days later, on November 8, he sent a petition to Zosimus through Marcellinus, a subdeacon of the church of Carthage.

Since Zosimus indicates in Letter 13, section 2, that he was replying to a letter from the Africans delivered to him by this same Marcellinus, it seems to us that the African letter and Paulinus’s confession were both handed over to Marcellinus on that same day, November 8.

Would anyone persuade himself that, during those few days in which Basiliscus arrived in Africa and Marcellinus departed from there for Rome, two celebrated synods were held in the same city, each sending a separate letter to Zosimus?

It is useful to have observed this not only to clarify the historical truth, but especially to prevent anyone from believing that Zosimus replied in a brief and wholly inadequate manner, and not without some mark of negligence—or even arrogance and haughtiness—to matters of the greatest importance, on which two councils had written to him at length.

For that suspicion entirely disappears once only one letter from the Africans is admitted, to which he replied accurately as the circumstances required.

Finally, it could have happened that the Africans, who frequently held councils, had already assembled at Carthage, or were on the point of assembling, when they received Zosimus’s second letter. Hence they wrote back more quickly, as happened in the following year.

### VI
9. It then happened opportunely that Zosimus’s Letter 12 was received by the Africans on 29 April 418. For three days later, that is, on 1 May itself, they held at Carthage, in the basilica of Faustus, a very celebrated council for the same reason. Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, presided, together with Donatianus, primate of the province of Byzacena, and 202 others, assembled from the provinces of Byzacena, Mauretania Sitifensis, Tripolitania, Numidia, Mauretania Caesariensis, and Spain, as we read in the copies of the Code published by Quesnellus, chapter 13. Prosper, *Against the Conference*, book 5, chapter 5, no. 15, and his *Chronicle* likewise report that 214 bishops attended this council, whereas Photius, in codex 53, gives the number as 224. Although Quesnellus’s codex calls it a plenary council, we have already shown that it is no different from the council which Augustine, in *On Original Sin*, chapters 8 and 21, and likewise in book 2 *To Boniface*, chapter 3, calls African.

10. The bishops assembled there enacted eight canons, such as those presented in Quesnellus’s Code, chapter 13, although they have usually and incorrectly been attributed to the Second Council of Milevis; and they sent them to Zosimus with a letter prefixed. Zosimus himself adopted those canons. Certainly, in the *Tractoria*, of which we shall speak shortly, he wished the third, fourth, and fifth to be regarded as decrees proper to the Apostolic See. Prosper preserved and commended a fragment of the letter attached to them in *Against the Conference*, book 5, chapter 5, no. 15, in these words:

> “The 214 bishops erred who, in the letter which they placed before their constitutions, spoke thus to the bishop of the Apostolic See, the blessed Zosimus: ‘We decree that the judgment pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent, from the see of the blessed apostle Peter, shall remain in force until they openly confess that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord we are assisted, not only in knowing but also in doing righteousness, in each of our acts, so that without it we are able neither to possess, think, say, nor do anything belonging to true and holy piety.’”

11. Augustine seems to be speaking of this same letter in book 2 *To Boniface*, chapter 3, where he says:

> “Letters subsequently came from Africa to Rome stating that it was not enough for the more cautious and conscientious people that Coelestius professed his agreement in general with the letters of Bishop Innocent; rather, he had to anathematize openly the errors he had set down in his little book. Otherwise, if he did not do so, many who understood little would believe that those poisons of faith in his little book had been approved by the Apostolic See—because that see had declared the book catholic—more readily than they would believe them corrected because he himself had replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent.”

We believe that the same point is intended by what the same Doctor teaches in the same work, chapter 4, at the end of section 6: namely, that the Africans, writing back to Zosimus, demanded that Coelestius be compelled to repeat and anathematize the very words concerning this question—original sin—which he had set down in his little book and which we cited above in §1, no. 2.

12. Finally, Augustine notes in *On Original Sin*, chapter 8, that these letters, by which the African council replied to the venerable Pope Zosimus, mentioned what the holy Pope Innocent had judged concerning the proceedings of the Palestinian council, by which Pelagius boasted that he had been acquitted. From this it may also be inferred that the fathers of the African council took care to expose the hiding places and deceptions by which that heretic habitually concealed his impieties. Marius Mercator considers it sufficient to indicate only this much concerning those letters: that the bishops writing back from Africa set out the whole case that had been conducted among them concerning Coelestius, sending also the proceedings that had then been drawn up with him or concerning him.

VII.

13. More famous than all Zosimus’s letters is the one which Marius Mercator, published by Baluzius, page 138, observes to have been called the *Tractoria* and sent throughout the entire world. Concerning the same letter Augustine writes to Optatus, Letter 190, no. 22:

> “We have taken care to send you copies of the recent letters, whether those which proceeded specifically to the Africans or those which proceeded universally to all bishops from the aforementioned see, lest they perhaps have not yet reached Your Holiness.”

Augustine’s words may be understood in two ways. The first is that certain special letters to the Africans were attached to letters sent by Zosimus universally to all bishops. The words of this Doctor cited above naturally suggest this, and historical fact confirms it. The second is that the letters addressed specifically to the Africans—because they had provided the occasion for Zosimus to write, by replying from the Carthaginian council held on 1 May—were subsequently sent universally to all bishops.

Marius Mercator, page 134, relates the sequence of events in these words:

> “When the bishops from Africa, where they had assembled on 1 May, wrote back and set out the whole case that had been conducted among them, sending also the proceedings that had then been drawn up with or concerning Coelestius, he was summoned to a fuller hearing, so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised to Zosimus in 417—that is, so that, after the aforementioned articles, which the deacon Paulinus had brought against him, had been condemned, he might be absolved from the sentence of the Africans by which he had been deprived of communion in 412. Yet he not only failed to appear, but also fled from the city mentioned.”

To this we may append the words of Augustine, book 2 *To Boniface*, chapter 3: when his presence was demanded so that, through definite and clear replies, either the man’s deception or his correction might become evident and no ambiguity remain, he withdrew from the examination. “And for this reason,” Marius Mercator continues, “he was most severely condemned by Bishop Zosimus of blessed memory in writings of the greatest length, in which both the articles concerning which he had been accused by the deacon Paulinus are contained and the whole case concerning the aforesaid Coelestius, as well as Pelagius, his still more depraved teacher, appears to be narrated. We also possess copies of these writings here, and we suggest that similar and identical writings—what they call *a pari*—were sent to the bishops of the Eastern churches, to the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem.”

In these letters Pelagius and Coelestius are said by Augustine, Letter 190, no. 22, to have been condemned throughout the Christian world—not yet absolutely and without any hope of pardon, but on the condition that, unless they corrected themselves, they should also do penance. Accordingly, the same Doctor speaks of them in *On Original Sin*, chapter 22, as having first been reduced to a state of penance or, if they refused this, condemned outright.

[Col. 0691C] 14. Zosimus issued that judgment not alone, but together with the Roman clergy, with whom he had also heard Coelestius in the preceding year. Consequently, the Pelagians charged the Roman clergy—as may be seen in Augustine, book 2 *To Boniface*, chapter 3—and at other times Zosimus himself, as the same Augustine relates in book 6 *Against Julian*, with prevarication, as though in this year they had through prevarication delivered a judgment concerning Pelagius and Coelestius different from that which they had delivered the previous year.

15. Of the Roman clergy, Augustine suggests in Letter 194, formerly 105, no. 1, that Xystus, or Sixtus—then a presbyter and later, after Boniface and Celestine, Zosimus’s successor—was the first to subscribe to this judgment. He notes that Sixtus did so when, as Augustine addresses him, rumor was spreading that he favored the enemies of Christian grace:

> “But so that this sorrow might be wiped from our hearts, the same rumor did not fail to report that you first pronounced an anathema against them before a very large gathering. Then, when the letters of the Apostolic See concerning their condemnation had been sent to Africa, your own letter also followed to the venerable old man Aurelius.”

Augustine himself states in Letter 191, formerly 104, no. 1, that these letters of Xystus were transmitted through Leo the acolyte. From this it follows that Zosimus’s letters, if they were sent at the same time, were likewise carried through the agency of that same Leo.

15. There are indications by which the time may be determined when those letters of Zosimus were either sent from Rome or received in Africa. Since they were written in reply to the acts of the Carthaginian council held on 1 May 418, we must first calculate the time in which the acts of that council could have been carried from Carthage to Rome and Zosimus’s letters then brought back from Rome to Carthage.

This can be established with greater certainty because Augustine was then staying at Carthage as a delegate appointed by the mandate of the aforementioned Carthaginian council (Code of the Canons of the African Church, chapter 127), when Zosimus’s letters reached him. After receiving them, he composed the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin* before departing from there for the province of Mauretania Caesariensis. Accordingly, in the *Retractations* he reviews these books immediately before the proceedings which, in his presence, were completed and recorded at Caesarea in Mauretania on 20 September of this year, 418.

If, therefore, we subtract the time sufficient for completing this journey and composing the aforementioned books, we shall readily grant that those letters were received in Africa no later than August and were written during the interval extending from 1 May to the end of August—that is, either toward the end of June or at the beginning of July. The same conclusion will also be confirmed by what we shall say in the following §8 concerning another letter which was sent to the Africans together with this *Tractoria*.

16. That celebrated letter of Zosimus, sent throughout the Christian world, is mentioned not only by Augustine and Marius Mercator, but also by Prosper in *Against the Conference*, book 5, chapter 5, no. 15; in Pope Celestine’s Letter 21, chapters 8 and 9; in Prosper’s *Chronicle* under the year 418; and by Gennadius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Yet when we hear that so authentic and necessary a writing, transmitted throughout the world with such zeal and received everywhere with such joy by all Catholics, has perished through some unknown fate, we are less surprised that so many other ancient monuments have suffered the same fate. But if it is not possible to present the whole work, it will nevertheless be worthwhile at least to read any fragments of it and collect or indicate them here.

17. Marius Mercator, published by Baluzius, page 134, teaches that the six articles on which Coelestius had been accused by Paulinus are contained in Zosimus’s *Tractoria*. Since they are readily accessible in the same Mercator, pages 3 and 133, and in Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 11, no. 23, we pass over them here.

Other material too, according to Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 21, no. 24, was brought forth from Pelagius’s own writings through the efforts of faithful brothers living at Rome, where Pelagius had lived for a very long time; Pope Zosimus appended these passages, as objects of execration, to his letters which he composed to be carried throughout the Catholic world.

Marius Mercator presents more of this material from pages 135 to 138, drawing both from Pelagius’s commentaries on the Apostle Paul and from excerpts from another sermon of his. He reveals on page 138 that these passages were inserted into Zosimus’s *Tractoria* in the following words:

> “All the articles written above, as has already been stated, are contained in that letter of the bishop of blessed memory which is called the *Tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned.”

Among the passages which Mercator transcribes there from Pelagius’s commentaries on Paul is the following argument of that heretic, which Augustine, Letter 190 to Optatus, no. 22, also declares to have been appended, among his other condemnable propositions, to the letters of the Apostolic See:

> “If the soul is not transmitted by descent, but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s stock, should bear an ancient sin belonging to another, since there is no reason to allow that God, who forgives personal sins, should impute another’s.”

18. We report this argument of Pelagius because the chief of the three surviving fragments of Zosimus’s letter bears especially upon it. Augustine, namely, in the same Letter 190, no. 23, first says:

> “For forgiveness of sins is not false even in the baptism of little children; nor is it said merely in words, but it is truly accomplished.”

He then adds:

> “Now, to use the words already found in the letter of the most blessed bishop Zosimus…”

and produces the words in this form.

### Fragment I of Zosimus’s *Tractoria*

> “The Lord is faithful in his words, and his baptism, both in reality and in [Col. 0693D] words—that is, in deed, confession, and true forgiveness of sins—maintains the same fullness among every sex, age, condition, and class of the human race. For no one is made free unless he is a slave of sin, nor can anyone be called redeemed unless he was truly captive through sin beforehand, as it is written: ‘If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free’ (John 8:36). Through him we are spiritually reborn; through him we are crucified to the world. By his death, the document of debt contracted through propagation—the document of the death introduced into us all by Adam and transmitted to every soul—is torn up; and in that document every person born is held liable before being liberated through baptism.”

[Note: From this it may be inferred that at that time this form of baptism was customary both in the Roman and in the African Church, as prescribed in the ancient Gothic-Gallican Missal published by Thomasius in these words: “I baptize you, N., in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, for the remission of sins, so that you may have eternal life.” Hence, as Augustine writes in *On Original Sin*, chapter 5, Coelestius was compelled to confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins according to the rule of the universal Church. Pelagius too was compelled to make the same profession. When Pinianus, Albina, and Melania heard him answer that infants were baptized with the same sacramental words as adults—and therefore for the remission of sins—they wrote that they were not a little pleased, as Augustine testifies in *On Original Sin*, chapter 1. But the same Doctor subsequently observes, in chapter 21, that he had answered deceitfully, as though the remission of sins were spoken of infants merely in the sound of words and were not effected in reality. The Council of Carthage, published under the name of the Second Council of Milevis and whose decrees, as we have already observed, Zosimus approved, counters this deception in Quesnellus’s Code, chapter 13, as follows: ‘It has seemed good that whoever denies that newborn infants should be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but that they derive no original sin from Adam which is cleansed by the laver of regeneration—and consequently that in them the baptismal formula “for the remission of sins” is understood not truly but falsely—be anathema.’ Zosimus now likewise closes every avenue to this deception.]

After quoting these words, Augustine adds the following in praise of this judgment and in commendation of the Apostolic See:

> “In these words of the Apostolic See, the Catholic faith is so ancient, certain, clear, and firmly established that it would be sacrilegious for a Christian to doubt it.”

### Fragment II

19. A second fragment has been preserved in Celestine’s Letter 21, chapter 9. There the same Doctor—Zosimus—is said to have written, when speaking to the bishops of the whole world concerning the assistance of divine grace:

> “What time, then, intervenes in which we do not need his help? In all actions, cases, thoughts, and movements, he must be entreated as helper and protector. For it is arrogant for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places’ (Ephesians 6:12). And as he says again: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?’ (Romans 7:24). ‘The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (1 Corinthians 15:10). And again: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain; rather, I labored more than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God with me.’”

He also embraced as proper to the Apostolic See what had been established among the decrees of the Carthaginian council—namely, what had been defined in its third chapter. To these were added chapters 4 and 5 of the same council, as though they too were proper to that Apostolic See.

[Col. 0694B] 20. Prosper recorded generally that all the decrees of the Carthaginian council held on 1 May 418 were brought to Zosimus and approved by him in the *Tractoria*, in these words:

> “The synodal decrees of the council of 214 bishops held at Carthage were brought to Pope Zosimus. When these had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world.”

Accordingly, Augustine seems not without reason to refer to the same *Tractoria* as approving the Carthaginian decrees in book 2 *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 12, no. 17, where he writes:

> “The authority of the Catholic councils and of the Apostolic See most justly condemned the recent Pelagian heretics, because they dared to assign to unbaptized infants a place of rest and salvation even outside the kingdom of heaven.”

In these words, written by Augustine near the end of 419, we can scarcely doubt that he is referring to the following decree, which Binius published among the other decrees of the Council of Milevis, although it is found in only a few manuscripts:

> “It has seemed good that whoever says that the Lord spoke the words, ‘In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places,’ and so forth, for this reason—that there is to be understood in the kingdom of heaven some intermediate place, or any place anywhere, where infants who have departed this life without baptism may live in blessedness, although without baptism they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which is eternal life—be anathema. For since the Lord says, ‘Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven’ (John 3:5), what Catholic would doubt that the person who has not been deemed worthy to be a fellow-heir of Christ will be a participant of the devil? Whoever lacks the right hand will undoubtedly fall upon the left.”

If this is so, the order must be altered which the same canon occupies among the Carthaginian canons in Quesnellus’s Code, chapter 13. In his arrangement it is third, although it is different from the canon which Zosimus himself calls the third chapter of the Carthaginian council.

### Fragment III

21. Prosper, *Against the Conference*, chapter 10—or chapter 5—no. 15, and Celestine’s Letter 21, chapter 5, supply a third fragment of the same *Tractoria*. Before reporting it, Prosper introduces it as follows:

> “The holy See of blessed Peter erred, which speaks thus to the whole world through the mouth of Pope Zosimus.”

In Celestine’s letter it is preceded by this other introduction:

> “The regular authority of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us toward this judgment, when, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says…”

Zosimus’s words then follow:

> “But we, by God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have referred everything to the consciences of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The same letter testifies how pleasing this judgment was to the Africans.

22. Marius Mercator did not fail to explain how that entire writing of Zosimus was received throughout the universal Church. He writes, in the edition of Baluzius, page 138:

> “The letter of Bishop Zosimus, of blessed memory, which is called the *Tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned, was confirmed by the subscriptions of the holy fathers both at Constantinople and throughout the whole world.”

Prosper expressed this elegantly in *Against the Conference*, no. 57, in these words:

> “Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, added the strength of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils and armed the right hands of all with Peter’s sword for the cutting down of the impious.”

But, to use the words of Marius Mercator as he continues the same account, Julian and his other associates, refusing to subscribe and unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those Fathers, were deposed and deprived of office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly statutes, and were expelled from all Italy.

Although this occurred chiefly under Zosimus’s successor Boniface, as the following passage of Prosper suggests—“Pope Boniface rejoiced in the Catholic faith of the most pious emperors and used against the enemies of God’s grace not only apostolic edicts but also royal decrees”—it nevertheless remains clear that this was done to vindicate the authority of Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, which had been received throughout the entire Church. We shall have occasion to discuss this matter somewhat more fully below, in no. 30.

IX.

23. At the same time as the aforementioned letter of Zosimus, other special letters were sent to the Africans, by which a delegation was assigned to Augustine and others in Mauretania Caesariensis on account of certain other needs of the Church. Concerning this Augustine writes to Optatus in Letter 157, now 190, no. 1:

> “The letters which you sent to Mauretania Caesariensis arrived while I was present at Caesarea, where ecclesiastical necessity, imposed upon us by the venerable Pope Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, had drawn us.”

What that ecclesiastical necessity was, the same Doctor no more explains in Letter 193, where he mentions it again. Possidius too recalls this delegation and the conference held between Augustine and the Donatist Emeritus at Caesarea in Mauretania on 20 September 418 on the occasion of this delegation; but he likewise says nothing about the necessity that had brought Augustine there.

He relates the matter in chapter 14 as follows:

> “The almighty God granted his help, so that afterward, when the venerable Augustine of blessed memory was staying in the city of Caesarea in Mauretania—where letters of the Apostolic See compelled him to go with other fellow bishops, in order to settle certain other needs of the Church—on this occasion he might see Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of that place…”

Yet before these events with Emeritus, Augustine places in the *Retractations*, book 2, chapter 50, the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin* immediately beforehand, and says of them:

> “After the Pelagian heresy and its authors had been convicted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church—first by Innocent and then by Zosimus, with the cooperation of the letters of the African councils—I wrote two books against them, one *On the Grace of Christ* and the other *On Original Sin*.”

It follows that those special letters by which a delegation was assigned to Augustine and his companions in Mauretania cannot have preceded the letters by which Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned by Zosimus. Nor is there any way to regard them as later.

X.

24. The bishops of Africa who, after the Carthaginian council held on 1 May, had remained at Carthage—three from each province, in accordance with the decree of the council—received there the latest letters of Zosimus. They then seem to have summoned to themselves whatever bishops they could call quickly and sent a letter of congratulation to the same pope. One fragment of it survives, quoted with praise in Celestine’s Letter 21:

> “The Africans venerated this speech of his [Zosimus’s in the *Tractoria*], shining with the purest light of truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man as follows:
>
> ‘But what you placed in your letters, which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, “Yet we, by God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have referred everything to the consciences of our brothers and fellow bishops,” we understood to mean that, with the unsparing sword of truth, as though passing swiftly by, you cut off those who exalt the freedom of human choice against God’s assistance.
>
> ‘For what did you do more by free choice than refer everything to the conscience of our humility? Yet you rightly and wisely perceived that this had been done by God’s prompting, and you truthfully and confidently said so. For surely the will is prepared by the Lord (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint), and in order that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children by paternal inspirations. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God (Romans 8:14), so that we may neither feel our own choice to be absent nor doubt that, in each good movement of the human will, his assistance is more powerful.’”

Prosper, *Against the Conference*, no. 15, reports and praises the same fragment in exactly the same words. The letter from which it was excerpted appears to have been written before Augustine and his companions departed for Mauretania and therefore before the end of August.

XI.

25. At about the same time Julian, bishop of Eclanum, wrote two letters to Pope Zosimus. Julian himself mentions them in Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, chapter 18, in these words:

> “I sent two letters to Zosimus, formerly bishop of that city, concerning these questions—but at a time when I had not yet begun to write my books.”

One of them is mentioned more than once by Marius Mercator. In his *Subnotations*, chapter 6, edition of Baluzius, page 15, he addresses Julian as follows:

> “Now hear what you yourself once declared in your letter—the letter, namely, which at that time you dared to send to the Apostolic See, when you refused the assembly at which the whole Church condemned Pelagius and Coelestius.”

From this we are clearly taught that the letter was written when Julian refused to subscribe to the *Tractoria* of Zosimus, sent throughout the world, and thereby to condemn Pelagius and Coelestius. It was therefore not written long after Zosimus issued the *Tractoria* just mentioned; rather, it was delivered to this pope somewhat later.

Before it reached the hands of that holy bishop of the Roman Church, Mercator says in the passage cited, it was carried about through almost all Italy by certain people whom Julian had deceived and was insinuated into the ears of many as though it were something important. Accordingly Augustine also says, book 1 of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 18:

> “This letter is not addressed to Zosimus, but to seduce those who at Rome might be seduced by such persuasion.”

26. In that letter Julian did not yet openly reveal a heretical meaning. Rather, as those who begin to preach or support a perverse doctrine are accustomed to do, he concealed it beneath Catholic words, so that he seemed to reject and condemn the famous six articles brought against Coelestius. For, according to Marius Mercator, among other things he said:

> “Who, then, is an advocate of the proposition that the whole human race does not die through the death of Adam, nor does the whole human race rise again through the resurrection of Christ? He is opposed to the Apostle, who says: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22). Rightly, therefore, is he rejected who contradicts the statement: ‘Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead’ (ibid., 21).
>
> “Likewise, the proposition that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race. This proposition is rightly refuted by us; for it must be believed that it affected not him alone but the human race.
>
> “Likewise, I count among undisciplined questions the proposition that infants are in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression. Those who are born today are not in every respect in the condition in which Adam was before sin, although it cannot be denied that these too, like him, are God’s work.
>
> “Likewise, the proposition that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin is not supported by reason. For he must be believed to have been made immortal, though, if he had not sinned, he could have acquired the power of immortality by tasting the tree of life. It was therefore wrongly said that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.”

27. Repeating and briefly reviewing some of these points, the same Mercator says in the same work, chapter 9, pages 30–31:

> “In your letter, which, as we have mentioned, was sent to Pope Zosimus of holy memory, you take offense at and condemn the person who holds that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin; and you say that this is not supported by reason. ‘For I believe,’ you say, ‘that he was indeed made immortal, but that, if he had not sinned, he could have acquired the power of immortality by tasting the tree of life.’ You also add that the person who contradicts the Apostle when he proclaims, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ is rightly rejected.”

But the same writer immediately indicates in these words how deceptively Julian brought forward these claims:

> “When a simple Christian hears these things, believing that no trick or deception is being offered, he regards you as an excellent and fitting teacher, according to the manner in which the Church is accustomed to be taught by the Apostles, and resolves to listen attentively to the rest of the same Apostle’s teaching which you pursue in this matter.
>
> “For who,” he adds a little farther on, “could suspect from your earlier statement that you thought anything other than all those priests of God who, under Pope Zosimus of holy memory, condemned Pelagius and Coelestius concerning all these articles about Adam which you had previously rejected and condemned?”

But that Julian then held one thing hidden in his heart and had another ready on his tongue, Mercator demonstrates in the same place from another work which Julian composed much later. In it Julian teaches that death extends only to those whom he sees to have imitated Adam’s transgression (Marius Mercator, page 31). Although that transgression was not made natural, it was nevertheless a form of sin; and therefore, although it does not burden those being born, it accuses those who imitate it. Finally, he says (*Subnotations*, chapter 6, page 12) that sin did not pass into all human beings, but death did—death imposed by the severity of judgment as the avenger of transgression.

Mercator does not conceal Julian’s deception: although Julian admitted that infants born today are not in every respect in the condition in which Adam was before sin (ibid., page 17), he proclaimed in a hidden sense that he understood not Adam’s condition before sin, but the smallness and weakness in which infants are born.

28. We know nothing about Julian’s second letter, unless perhaps it is the exposition of faith which James Sirmond extracted from an old Veronese codex and John Garner published in the first part of his edition of Marius Mercator, page 319; it was reprinted in the appendix to volume 10 of Augustine’s new edition, page 110.

Nothing remains of the title in the original manuscript except certain traces of fading letters, which can be explained from the words appended at the end:

> “Here ends the little book of the faith of S. J. C.”

That is, as it is explained in Augustine’s new edition, “of the priests of Jesus Christ.” This interpretation is more convincing than Garner’s, who thought that the word *Siculorum*—“of the Sicilians”—was represented by those three letters, S. J. C.

In place of the obliterated title, the aforementioned Garner substituted the following:

> “A little book of faith sent by Julian of Eclanum to the Apostolic See in the name of eighteen bishops who refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius.”

There is no apparent reason why the learned man asserted that this little book was offered in the name of eighteen bishops, unless he had read Augustine, book 1 *To Boniface*, no. 3, where Augustine says that he was replying to two letters of the Pelagians: one, namely, which Julian is said to have sent to Rome; and another which eighteen men, allegedly bishops and participants in his error, dared to write to Thessalonica—not to just anyone, but to the bishop of that place, Rufus, whom they attempted by their cunning to test and, if possible, draw over to their party.

Yet from the fact that eighteen bishops devoted to Pelagius wrote to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, it does not follow that the little book sent to the Apostolic See was composed by the same number of bishops. Since it is nevertheless clear that it was sent in the name of several persons, it makes little or no difference whether there were eighteen, more, or fewer.

### 29.

The arguments are more certain by which that learned man proves that this document bears the form of a letter. Nor is it obscure that this booklet, or letter, is from bishops writing to the prelate of the Apostolic See, whom they address both as “father,” on account of the dignity of the chief see, and as “brother,” on account of their sharing the episcopate.

If it is also compared with the few fragments of Julian’s letter to Zosimus that we recently transcribed from Marius Mercator, there will appear such agreement of style that one may reasonably judge both writings to have proceeded from the same source. Certainly, just as in those fragments the person who is said to oppose the Apostle is the one who asserts that neither does the entire human race die through Adam’s death nor does the entire human race rise again through his resurrection, so in that booklet anyone is condemned who asserts that neither does the entire human race die through Adam nor does the entire human race rise again through Christ.

Then what is immediately added—“Or if there are any other matters that either conflict with the Catholic faith or belong to UNDISCIPLINED QUESTIONS, we condemn them with a similar execration”—has the same style as the following passage of Julian’s reported above, §26: “That infants are in the state in which Adam was before the transgression, I consider to belong among UNDISCIPLINED QUESTIONS.”

It is no less clear that they wrote this when they were being required to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, and were refusing to do so. Accordingly, in their booklet they deliberately copy out all the scriptural testimonies by which Zosimus, in Letter 3 to the Africans, §5, had proved that judgment should by no means be pronounced against persons absent and unheard. The only surprising thing is that they did not boast that they had learned this from Zosimus himself.

But what they alleged as their reason for refusing to subscribe was a mere evasion. For since Pelagius and Coelestius had often been heard, and since an opportunity to defend and clear themselves had been granted them, whether in person or through written submissions, in Palestine, in Africa, and in Rome itself; and after many evasions—by which they were convicted of having striven for one thing only, namely, to deceive the judges and elude judgment—it finally became clear that they were alien to the Catholic faith and deserving of condemnation.

When Julian and his associates refused to subscribe to so solemn a judgment on the pretext that they themselves were not permitted to pronounce sentence upon absent persons whom they had not heard, who would not judge that they were improperly abusing the fairest rule of equity?

Their ingenuity is also detected in this, that they append to the exposition of their faith in the aforesaid booklet the following words:

“We have written and sent these things to your holiness as they have appeared to us according to the Catholic faith. If you think that they must be held otherwise, write back to us; but if not … let your holiness be certain that we appeal to the hearing of a plenary synod.”

The nature of their speech is apparent there: although they despised both the judgment of the Apostolic See and the subscription of the whole world, shortly afterward they wrote to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica:

“Subscription was extorted from simple bishops, sitting in their own places without a synodal assembly.”

Augustine, refuting them, says among other things (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, chapter 12, §34):

“Their pride, which exalts itself so greatly against God … is understood also to seek this glory, that because of them a synod of East and West should be assembled.”

There is therefore nothing to prevent the aforesaid booklet from being regarded as one of the two letters that Julian mentions as having been sent by him to Zosimus: written, indeed, after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, but before Julian was expelled from his see together with his associates, and thus composed in the year 418.

## XII.

### 30.

The question is whether Julian was condemned by name by Zosimus. Joan Garnerius, explaining why he does not think that Julian was condemned by name by this pope, writes that he is restrained by the booklet of faith, the letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, and almost countless other passages either in Julian’s works or in Augustine’s.

Nevertheless, he cannot deny that Julian, when he refused, together with his associates, to subscribe to Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, was removed from the episcopate, since Marius Mercator’s words on the matter are explicit (*p.* 138 in Baluzius’s edition):

“To this *Tractoria*, Julian and the other accomplices, refusing to subscribe, were not only deposed and deprived of office by imperial laws but also by priestly statutes, and were driven out of all Italy.”

That these “priestly statutes,” by which Julian and his associates were deposed, were enacted in a council presided over by the Roman pontiff is clearly taught by Marius Mercator himself in the preface to his treatise on Nestorius (*Baluzius’s edition*, p. 33), where he recalls that Julian, formerly bishop of Eclanum, was “long ago deprived of office and deposed, together with his associates, BY THE APOSTOLIC JUDGMENT.”

Garnerius there read “by the ecclesiastical judgment” (*p.* 58); but Baluzius restored “by the apostolic judgment” from the authority of the archetype.

Accordingly, when the same writer addresses Julian as follows (*Baluzius’s edition*, p. 119; Garnerius, p. 73):

“For who, in the preceding judgment, could suspect you of thinking anything other than all those who, when Pope Zosimus of holy memory presided, condemned Pelagius, Coelestius, AND YOU, the priests of God?”

he sufficiently indicates that by “the prelate of the Apostolic See, whose judgment declared Julian deposed,” he means no one other than Zosimus.

This, however, was not said in the sense that Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian were condemned by the same synodal statutes; rather, Zosimus, who had condemned Pelagius and Coelestius and had ordered the others to condemn them through the *Tractoria*, subsequently removed Julian from the episcopate because he refused to subscribe to that *Tractoria*.

### 31.

Therefore Augustine also, agreeing with Marius Mercator, calls Zosimus Julian’s condemner (*Against Julian*, book I, chapter 12, §13). To Julian, who accused Zosimus of prevarication, Augustine replies:

“You accuse the successor of Innocent of the crime of prevarication, because he did not wish to oppose the apostolic teaching and the judgment of his predecessor. But I shall say nothing of this for the moment, lest I wound with praise of YOUR CONDEMNer the spirit of one whom I desire rather to heal.”

Certainly that pious concern of Augustine, by which he feared to wound Julian while wishing to soothe and heal his spirit, and therefore wished to refrain from the offensive expression “your condemner,” would have required him to do so unless the truth of some judgment actually pronounced had compelled that expression from him.

Among those who were then condemned together with Julian, Pope Coelestine’s twentieth letter mentions several—namely, Perfidium, Florus, Marcellinus, and Orontius. These men were first removed from the episcopate by synodal statutes in a Roman synod presided over by Zosimus; afterward, under Boniface, Zosimus’s successor, they were driven from all Italy by imperial laws. Marius Mercator does not sufficiently distinguish these two events.

## XIII.

### 32.

On October 3, 418, Zosimus wrote to his legates stationed at Ravenna. He mentions certain insulting letters written against him by some rebellious clerics of his, as well as his own writings with which he had once answered those letters (Zosimus, Letter 14).

But because those men, persisting in their rebellion, had gone to the imperial court contrary to the canons, the same pope, after issuing a decree, removed them from his communion. He sent this sentence, signed by himself, to the aforementioned legates at Ravenna, together with the writings by which he had formerly refuted their insulting letters.

These letters of the rebellious clerics, Zosimus’s apologetic writings, and the sentence pronounced against them have perished.

## XIV.

### 33.

There can be no doubt that Zosimus wrote a letter concerning the case of Maximus, bishop of Valentia. His successor Boniface records that the investigation of this case had been delegated by his successors to a provincial synod (Boniface I, Letter 3, §1).

## XV.

### 34.

As we have seen, the Africans had asked Zosimus to uphold two provisions as though they were Nicene decrees: namely, that bishops should be permitted to appeal to Rome, and that clerical cases should be settled before the bishops of their own provinces.

Although the decrees being produced in the name of the Council of Nicaea seemed new and unheard-of to them (Boniface I, Letter 1, §4), they nevertheless replied in a letter addressed to Zosimus that they would allow those provisions to remain in force for a short time without causing him any injury, until an investigation of the statutes of the Council of Nicaea had been completed—that is, until the truth of the decrees sent to them had been ascertained. Until then, they said, they would comply with them.

We do not know whether that letter was delivered to Zosimus while he was still alive. But this is certain: he did not have enough time to settle the matter.

## XVI.

### 35.

The *Pontifical Book* attributes the following decrees to Zosimus:

“That deacons should have their left shoulders covered with linen cloths; that throughout the parishes there should be permission to bless the paschal candle; and that no cup should be offered publicly to any clerics, except only in the private rooms of the faithful, especially of clerics.”

# Decrees Extracted from the Letters of Saint Zosimus

*(From the collection of councils in Mansi, volume IV.)*

The authority of the Apostolic See cannot grant anything contrary to the statutes of the saints.

*(From Gratian.)*

The authority even of this see cannot grant or alter anything contrary to the statutes of the Fathers. For among us antiquity lives amid shaken foundations, and the decrees of the Fathers have established reverence for it.

## From the Letter to Hesychius, Bishop

*(Mansi, volume IV.)*

### I.

If he is not learned in the Scriptures, he must not become a bishop.

### II.

Whoever ordains an unlearned bishop must be deposed.

### III.

If he has been tonsured from childhood, let him be promoted at the age of twenty.

### IV.

Let a lector and exorcist remain for five years, an acolyte and subdeacon for three years, and a deacon for five years.

### V.

The order of the clergy is: lector, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, presbyter, bishop.

### VI.

A digamist or a penitent must not be admitted into the clergy.

# Letter Attributed to Pope Saint Zosimus

*(D. Coustant, Appendix to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs.)* (C, S)*

## Censure of the Letter

Joannes a Bosco was the first to publish this letter at the end of the Floriacensis Library. Its simplicity is pleasing and seems to breathe antiquity. But its antiquity is first contradicted by the word “archbishop,” used in its very title.

Then the falsity of the claims made in it is demonstrated by Zosimus’s own Letters 5 and 6, “dated on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh consulship of Honorius Augustus and the second of Constantius.” In the first of these letters Zosimus is vehemently indignant with Proculus of Marseille, because at the Council of Turin Proculus himself had thought that this should be surreptitiously arranged: that the council should grant him authority to ordain priests in the second province of Narbonensis; and because he had “taken as his associate Simplicius of the city of Vienne, who with no less impudence demanded that he too be permitted to choose priests.”

Then Zosimus decreed that “the metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles should possess this right by inviolable authority in both Narbonensis and Viennensis.” Letter 6 also confirms this.

Should he be thought to have changed, after only four days, the judgment that he testifies was pronounced after “a lengthy investigation”? The pope’s Letters 10 and 11, dated March 5 of the year 418, absolutely forbid the admission of so improbable a suspicion. From them it is clear that he remained firm in the aforesaid judgment.

The arguments proving this letter false are all the stronger because its fabricator himself acknowledges the authenticity of Zosimus’s letters written in favor of the bishop of Arles and takes it as certain.

## To Simplicius, Bishop of Vienne

*That he should claim the nearer cities within the province for himself until the matter had been more fully examined. That Lazarus had been condemned.*

**Zosimus, bishop, to Simplicius, archbishop of Vienne, greetings.**

It has been revealed to us how you pursued the cases of your diocese at the Council of Turin. Although, before your legate arrived, we had written that the bishop of Arles possessed jurisdiction and pontifical authority over three provinces, out of reverence for Saint Trophimus, nevertheless, if matters are as your letter sent to us reports, we permit your ancient authority to remain for the time being, until the matter has been more clearly examined.

Thus, as was decreed at the council of the most distinguished bishops at Turin, with the counsel of peace, claim for yourself the cities nearer to you within the province, until apostolic charity has investigated the whole order of the matter more fully.

Know that Lazarus, an improperly ordained bishop and accuser of his brother, has been condemned by our judgment.

Given on the day before the Kalends of October—October 1, in the year 417—during the consulship of Honorius for the eleventh time and Constantius.

# In the Year of the Lord 418

## Paulinus of Milan

*(Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum, volume IX.)*

# Prolegomena

### 1.

That Paulinus, who committed to writing the notable deeds of Saint Ambrose, was entirely different from Paulinus, bishop of Nola, was demonstrated most clearly by the great Baronius [Baronius, under the year 397, §46], contrary to the opinion subsequently held by some.

We understand from the author himself that he was a cleric of the Church of Milan, and indeed of a lower order [Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, §42], since he lived under the care of the deacon Castus, just as Majorinus, who had been a lector in the diaconate of Caecilianus, according to Optatus [Optatus, *On the Schism of the Donatists*, book I, chapter 19].

We learn from the same source that Paulinus remained in this office until the death of the blessed bishop, for whom he served as secretary. He says [Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, §42]:

> “A few days before he lay down on his sickbed, while Ambrose was dictating the forty-third psalm, with me both taking it down and looking on, suddenly, in the form of a small shield, fire covered his head and gradually entered through his mouth, as though into a dwelling, like an inhabitant. After this his face became like snow, and afterward his countenance returned to its own appearance. When this happened, struck with astonishment, I became rigid and could not write down what he was saying until the vision itself had passed; for at that time he was bearing witness to the testimony of divine Scripture, which I remembered very well. On that day he ceased writing or dictating. … I immediately reported what I had seen to the honorable man, the deacon Castus, under whose care I lived.”

This is his account.

Afterward Paulinus received the order of the diaconate, as we learn from Augustine [Augustine, *On Original Sin*, §§3, 8, volume X, pp. 254, 256; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book II, §6, ibid., p. 435] and Marius Mercator [Marius Mercator, *Commonitorium on the Name of Coelestius*, §1].
