They show that, in this rank, he vigorously rose up against Coelestius, the associate of the arch-heresiarch Pelagius.

For that reason some have judged incorrectly [Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 4, works, volume I, p. 47; the Benedictines, in their notes to Augustine’s works, volume X, p. 253, note a; Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 963; Ballerini, in his notes to Noris’s works, volume IV, p. 861] that this same Paulinus was the deacon of Ambrose, bishop of Milan. It is clear, however, that when Ambrose died Paulinus was still a cleric of a lower order, as we have just heard the author himself narrate.

The most learned men were misled, no doubt, by the authority of Marius Mercator, who reported the matter rather incautiously [Marius Mercator, cited above]. Augustine, however, was more prudent: he knew Paulinus well at Milan and therefore called him a deacon, but nowhere called him Ambrose’s deacon.

Nor did the father of ecclesiastical annals speak otherwise: he writes that Paulinus was “afterward advanced to the diaconate” [Baronius, under the year 397, §47].

Moreover, Isidore of Seville records that our author was also honored with the dignity of the presbyterate [Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 4]; yet you will find this mentioned nowhere among the earlier authors.

### 2.

Let us now review the literary works of Paulinus. At the urging of Saint Augustine, whom he had known both when Augustine was living at Milan and later in Africa, where Paulinus eventually settled, he wrote the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, as he himself testifies twice [Paulinus, cited above, §§1 and 56].

It is not clear that Paulinus immediately began, or even completed, this work after the death of the most blessed bishop, who departed this life in 397. He was writing after the year 400, when Simplicianus, Ambrose’s successor, had died and Venerius occupied the see of Milan, as we gather from these words of his [Paulinus, cited above, §46]:

> “After his death, no one succeeded him in the priesthood except the man whom he had marked out three times with the word ‘good old man.’ Venerius succeeded that Simplicianus.”

We also know that Paulinus was still engaged in composing the *Life of Ambrose* after Venerius’s death, which occurred in 408 or 409, since he mentions John, prefect of the praetorium, who held that dignity under Honorius in the years 412, 413, and 422, as is evident from the prosopography of the Theodosian Code [Theodosian Code, volume VI, part II, p. 61].

The author’s words are these [Paulinus, cited above, §31]:

> “After John, then tribune and notary, who is now prefect, was sent to protect those who had taken refuge in the church, etc.”

From this it follows that Paulinus did not complete the work continuously but at intervals. In other words, he began committing this little work to writing at Milan at Augustine’s urging; when other concerns intervened, he interrupted it, and later completed it while living in Africa.

He is said to have openly acknowledged this himself. For he writes [Paulinus, cited above, §51]:

> “Nevertheless, while we were staying at Milan, we learned these deeds from Mascezel himself; and since, while staying IN THIS PROVINCE IN WHICH WE ARE NOW WRITING THESE THINGS, he reported the same matter to many priests, we judged that, since they too had reported it, we might more securely include these things IN THIS BOOK.”

And again, more explicitly, near the end [Baronius, under the year 397, §48]:

> “Also in the city of Carthage,” he says, “when I had come TO A BANQUET at the house of Fortunatus, the deacon and brother of the venerable bishop Aurelius, together with Vincentius, bishop of Colossae, Muraneus, bishop of Bulla, and also other bishops and deacons, I reported to Muraneus, who was disparaging the holy man Ambrose, the death of the presbyter mentioned above.”

### 3.

As for the value of this work by Paulinus, we must plainly agree with Baronius [Nourry, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, §1, in the appendix to volume II, p. 31] and other learned men after him that no one may call the author’s reliability into question:

> “For he testifies that he wrote what he either saw himself, or learned from the holy Marcellina about Ambrose, her brother, or gathered from various letters sent after Ambrose’s death by those who reported having seen him in different provinces.”

Nevertheless, one thing is lacking in him, says the learned man [Baronius, cited above]: in narrating events he paid scarcely any attention to chronology. Nor did he take care to append an accurate catalogue of Ambrose’s writings to the deeds of Ambrose that he transmitted to the memory of posterity—something that Possidius did for Augustine [the Benedictines, in the appendix to volume II of Ambrose’s works, pp. I–XIV; beginning of volume XIV of the *Patrologia*].

We have arranged for this *Life of Ambrose*, composed by Paulinus, to be printed from the distinguished Parisian edition of the Benedictines, who published it after collating it with the greatest care against both manuscript and printed codices [in Bollandus, volume I of January, p. 494, §44].

It will not be irrelevant to observe here that Eugippius, presbyter and abbot of Lucullanum, who flourished at the beginning of the sixth century, remembered in the *Life of Saint Severinus*, the apostle of Noricum, the narrative that our Paulinus relates [Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, §43]. We have noted this in order to answer Tillemont, who, reading this *Life of Ambrose* too inattentively, asserted that the narrative reported by Eugippius was absent from Paulinus’s work [Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume X, p. 81].

### 4.

The second work of Paulinus, now a deacon, is entitled *A Booklet against Coelestius Presented to Pope Zosimus*. Tillemont alone thinks that our Paulinus was the author of this booklet [Tillemont, cited above]. Most learned men, however, more correctly affirm this, relying chiefly on the authority of Marius Mercator [Marius Mercator, *Commonitorium on the Name of Coelestius*, §1], as will become clearer from what follows.

The circumstances in which it was written are understood to have been these. We have already established that Paulinus, having left Milan for Africa, settled at Carthage. While living there, he discovered that Coelestius, the companion of Pelagius, was spreading new doctrines throughout the city and filling everything with dissension. He brought the heretic before the African Fathers, who were holding a synod there, by presenting a booklet.

Augustine [Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 11, §23, volume X, p. 204; and *On Original Sin*, chapter 11, §12, ibid., p. 257] and Marius Mercator [Marius Mercator, cited above] recite the wicked doctrines that Paulinus charged against Coelestius.

When Coelestius was ordered by the Fathers of the Council of Carthage to condemn those doctrines, he refused and was struck with anathema by the same council. Fleeing Africa, he went to Asia. Augustine relates how the matter was conducted [Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 3, §3, ibid., p. 254].

The most learned man argues that these events occurred in the spring of 412 [Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 4, works, volume I, p. 47], on the basis of a letter from the Council of Carthage to Innocent, written around the autumn of 416, in which the Fathers state that judgment had been pronounced against Coelestius there almost five years earlier.

Learned men who not long ago jointly published an edition enriched by the works of Noris, however, judged otherwise: they assigned the Council of Carthage in which Coelestius was condemned to the year 411, not 412 [Ballerini, *Works of Noris*, volume IV, p. 577, in *History of the Donatists*, part II, chapter 13, §4].

### 5.

Meanwhile, according to Mercator [Marius Mercator, cited above, §1 ff.], in order to evade the judgment pronounced against him by the African Fathers, that heretic thought he ought to appeal to the Roman See. Soon afterward, disregarding the appeal, he went to Ephesus, where he was also ordained presbyter through clandestine means.

After leaving there several years later, he headed for Constantinople. Expelled by Bishop Atticus, he hastened to Rome, where Zosimus had succeeded Innocent, in order to undergo judgment on the basis of his former appeal.

He therefore approached the pope and, pretending that he wished to submit to his judgment, appealed to the apostolic tribunal against the deacon Paulinus, who had accused him five years earlier. Through this pretense he obtained from Zosimus a letter to the Africans [Zosimus, Letter 2], summoning the accusers of Coelestius to Rome so that they might refute his faith in person.

Zosimus entrusted this letter, together with another dated September 21 of the year 417, to Basiliscus the subdeacon to carry to Africa.

> “When Basiliscus reached Carthage,” says the learned Coustant [Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 963], “he met Paulinus on November 2 [Paulinus, *Booklet*, §4], undoubtedly in that same year 417, to warn him that he should appear before the judgment of the Apostolic See. But Paulinus sent to Zosimus, in place of appearing in person, the booklet of which we are speaking, on November 8—that is, six days after Basiliscus met him—and therefore in the year 417. In that booklet Paulinus thanks Zosimus, not because he had condemned Coelestius, as Baronius thought [Baronius, under the year 418, §11], but because, in the proceedings held at Rome in September 417, he had insisted that Coelestius condemn the articles that Paulinus had charged against him.

> “Moreover, the same booklet was carried to Rome by the subdeacon Marcellinus [Paulinus, *Booklet*, §4]. Zosimus, in Letter 11, delivered on March 22 of the year 417, replies that he had received letters from the Africans through him. It is therefore clear that this booklet of Paulinus, dated November 8, was composed in the preceding year, 417, contrary to the judgment of the father of the *Annals*, who assigns the same booklet to the year 418.”

This is the learned man’s account. Noris [Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 12, pp. 121, 123], Pagius [Pagius, under the year 418, §5], and Tillemont [Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume XIII, p. 1015, note 70, on Saint Augustine] had already reached the same conclusion concerning the date on which Paulinus wrote his booklet.

### 6.

There still remain matters to be answered that Quesnellius and Noris devised in connection with this booklet of Paulinus.

Quesnellius, after quoting Paulinus’s words in which he says that he had been warned by the subdeacon Basiliscus to appear before the Apostolic See and submit himself to Zosimus’s judgment, immediately adds [Quesnellius, notes to the works of Saint Leo, dissertation 13, §10] that Paulinus refused to comply with the summons.

This opinion of Quesnellius certainly seems acceptable to no one:

> “For Paulinus did not refuse to comply, as the learned men rightly argue [Ballerini, *Works of Saint Leo*, volume III, p. 786, note 16]. Rather, after presenting a booklet of excuse, he humbly set out sufficiently effective reasons why he would not come to Rome—reasons that he thought the pope ought to accept.

> “Among these reasons he states that the case was no longer his own but that of the entire Church, and that this had been approved by the African Fathers. There is nowhere any indication that those same African Fathers forbade Paulinus to go to Rome on the appointed day, as Quesnellius thought.

> “One thing alone is easy to conjecture: with their agreement, he did not cross over to Rome, but delivered his booklet of excuse not to Basiliscus, who was just about to depart, but to Marcellinus, who had been designated to carry the acts of the African council to Rome. They thought it expedient that he should present all these things to Zosimus together with the booklet.”

### 7.

As for Noris, he believed [Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 4, p. 49] that as soon as Paulinus learned that Coelestius had been condemned at the Council of Carthage and had appealed to the Apostolic See, he had traveled from Africa to Rome in order to defend before Innocent, the Roman pontiff, the sentence pronounced against that same heretic by the council.

The following words of Paulinus led the eminent cardinal to this opinion [Paulinus, cited above, §4]:

> “There [that is, at Rome] I was then unable to do anything for that reason, because the man who had appealed to the Apostolic See was absent.”

“But,” say the learned men recently cited [Ballerini, book I, chapter 4, observations on the works of Noris, volume IV, p. 862], “Paulinus’s words do not necessarily convey that Norisian meaning. He could truthfully affirm that he could do nothing before the Apostolic See while Coelestius was absent, even if Paulinus himself had always remained in Africa, because he was prepared to go there if Coelestius had not fled to Ephesus while disregarding his appeal.

> “For in both civil and ecclesiastical trials this order is observed: the person who has appealed must appear before the judge, and, at his insistence, the one who prevailed is summoned; the victor is not himself summoned before the judge when the other party has fled.

> “Hence Paulinus says in the booklet mentioned above that he would have appeared immediately if the sentence had been pronounced against him rather than in his favor.

> “Add that, if Paulinus had gone from Africa to Innocent, this appeal of Coelestius would not have been unknown to that pontiff. Consequently, in the three letters that he afterward sent to the African Fathers, he would have made some mention of the appeal.

> “It was for these reasons, apparently, that the writers who later composed the history of Pelagianism with the greatest diligence passed over this journey of Paulinus.”

### 8.

Finally, there exists a third work of Paulinus, the one under discussion, entitled *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. It was long ago published after being transcribed by the care and diligence of the distinguished Joannes Aloysius Mingarelli from a parchment manuscript of the library of Saint Saviour at Bologna [*Veterum Patrum Latinorum*, volume II, part I].

This booklet was not unknown to Saint Isidore of Seville. He speaks of it and its author as follows [Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 4]:

> “The presbyter Paulinus expounded, in the blessings of the patriarchs, a booklet composed with sufficient concision in a threefold mode of understanding.”

The same man, at Augustine’s request, also wrote the *Life of Ambrose*, rich in signs and teachings and not unequal to the Apostles in merits.

Some learned men, including Tillemont [Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, volume XII, p. 310] and Fontaninus [Fontaninus, *Literary History of Aquileia*, book V, chapter 2, §5, pp. 219 ff.], judged that Isidore had carelessly confused this Paulinus of Milan with Paulinus of Nola.

But they were entirely mistaken, because they read the passage of Isidore too inattentively. The holy bishop of Seville correctly and appropriately distinguishes the two Paulinuses, as the diligent Fabricius clearly recognized [Fabricius, scholium on Isidore, in *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 51, at the beginning].

For he states that our Paulinus wrote the *Life of Ambrose*, just as Uranius published the death of PAULINUS [Isidore, cited above].

The same critical scholars also accuse Isidore of having wrongly attributed to Paulinus of Milan the work of Rufinus *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, later dedicated to Paulinus, bishop of Nola—as though one or the other writer were not permitted to discuss the same subject simply because the other had treated it.

In fact, Saint Ambrose was the very first to write about the blessings of the patriarchs [Ambrose, works, volume I, p. 513]; yet his work did not deter Rufinus from undertaking a similar composition. Why, then, should Paulinus not have been permitted, after both Ambrose and Rufinus, to undertake once again an exposition of the blessings of the patriarchs, just as Isidore testifies that he composed such a work, evidently inspired above all by the example of his teacher Ambrose?

Indeed, we understand that Alcuin, without fearing criticism, later devoted himself to examining the same subject [in Baronius, under the year 418, §79].

Nor were the learned men less mistaken who thought that the work attributed by Isidore to Paulinus was identical with the work of Rufinus. They would certainly have abandoned that conjecture, as I believe, if they had been able to compare the two works and examine them carefully.

For the rest, on this same question one may consult the distinguished Mingarelli, who, adducing many arguments, clearly proved that our Paulinus was the author of the booklet.

# Works of Paulinus the Deacon

## I. The Life of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, Written by Paulinus, His Secretary, for the Blessed Augustine

(C)

See this work among the works of Saint Ambrose, volume XIV of our *Patrologia*, at the beginning.

## II. A Booklet against Coelestius, Presented to Pope Zosimus

(C)

### 1.

I beseech the justice of Your Beatitude, venerable Lord Pope Zosimus. True faith is never disturbed, especially in the Apostolic Church, in which teachers of false faith are as readily exposed as they are truly punished: so that false faith may die in them, if they correct what they had wickedly conceived and brought forth still more wickedly; and so that true faith may be in them, the faith that the Apostles taught and that the Roman Church, together with all teachers of the Catholic faith, maintains.

[Baronius, together with the Vatican manuscript, reads: “so that they may die.” The reading in the manuscript of Labbe, “so that he may die,” is preferable. The same Labbe, after Baronius, continues: “among them, unless they correct what they had committed more wickedly, so that true faith may be among them.” We restore the reading of the archetype, which is fuller, supplying before the word “faith” the verb “may be,” which is absent from it.]

But if, like the other authors of heresy who were long ago judged by the Apostolic See or by the Fathers and expelled from the bosom of the Catholic Church, and who have perished by perpetual death, these men too, who have now been detected—or are being detected—persist in their unbelief, let them be handed over to the spiritual sword so that they may be destroyed.

Thus it is with Pelagius and Coelestius, who were condemned by Pope Innocent, the predecessor of Your Beatitude of blessed memory, if they reject the right faith and persist in their perverse doctrine.

[In the printed editions: “they perish.” The Vatican manuscript more harmoniously reads “they have perished,” for this refers to the earlier authors of heresy. On the authority of the same manuscript we shortly afterward restore “are detected,” where the printed text had “will be detected.”]

2. Following this judgment, Your Beatitude, when Coelestius was being heard before the apostolic see, ordered him among other things in these words: “Do you therefore condemn all those matters contained in Paulinus’s memorandum?”—that is, concerning the Questions [Note: Or, “the chapters brought as charges.”]. And elsewhere: “Did you learn what sort of letter the apostolic see gave to the brethren and fellow bishops of the African province?” [Note: The Vatican manuscript lacks “apostolic.” Here the letters of Innocent to the two councils and to the five bishops are being mentioned.] And it was added: “Do you condemn all those things which we have condemned, and hold those which we hold?” And again: “Do you condemn all those things which have been circulated under your name?” And again: “Or those matters which Paulinus set forth in his memorandum?”

And when he said that I could be proved a heretic on the basis of the charges brought against him, filled with the Holy Spirit, you rejected and suppressed [Note: The words “and suppressed” had been omitted in the printed editions.] the words of the madman and slanderer, delivering a judgment of such a kind that I myself was approved as a Catholic, while you would care for him if he wished to be healed. It was as follows: “I do not want you to lead us around in circles. Do you condemn all those things that Paulinus has brought against you, or that have been circulated by report?” Who would not be satisfied with this judgment? Who else would reject one so salutary, so worthy of embrace, so devout, except someone who has strayed from the faith?

And he who had previously professed that he would condemn whatever had been brought against him, if you judged it contrary to the faith [Note: Baronius and Labbe read “if you should vindicate.” The verb “should judge,” correctly restored by us, will not be disputed by anyone who has read these very words of Coelestius to Zosimus in Augustine, *On Original Sin*, book 1, chapter 7: “If perchance, as happens among human beings, an error of ignorance should creep in, let our judgment correct it.” The printed editions have “hear,” and shortly afterward “of so great a see.” But the sequence requires “hears”; and the reading “of so great a see,” with one Vatican manuscript, is supported by what occurs below: “that I may return thanks to SO GREAT a see.” What Paulinus relates here is also confirmed by Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 7. There he expressly teaches that Zosimus dealt with Coelestius so that he would condemn the matters brought against him by Paulinus and assent to the letters of the apostolic see which had proceeded from his predecessor of holy memory. “But he,” Augustine says, “was unwilling to condemn the deacon’s charges; yet he did not dare to oppose the letters of the blessed Pope Innocent, but rather promised that he would condemn everything which that see condemned.” Marius Mercator explains how this promise was extracted from him: “By his repeated replies and pleadings, he had beforehand sown the hope that he would condemn those articles concerning which he had been accused at Carthage; for he was being ordered to do this more insistently, and was more forcefully expected to do it.” Thus he showed reverence for so great a see only insofar as he generally promised to condemn everything it judged condemnable. But when that see pressed him to condemn the matters brought by Paulinus, he argued to the injury of that same see, equivocated, and evaded the promise which he did not wish in his heart to fulfill.], hears, “Condemn them”; yet he not only does not condemn them, but contends to the injury of so great a see. Hence the Roman Church no longer fails to recognize its accused, who with such audacious spirit has dared to contradict and not to condemn what Your Beatitude decreed should be condemned.

3. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God and to Christ the Lord, because he willed the cause of his Church to be conducted in such a way that the apostolic see—from which it was fitting that the heresy be condemned by the voice of two of its pontiffs—ordered those things to be condemned which had been brought by me against Coelestius. I have always desired, and still desire, not his condemnation but his correction. His case now stands not with me alone but with the whole Church of God, as the writings of the African bishops addressed to Your Beatitude testify [Note: In the printed editions the words “of the African bishops” had also been omitted; they are restored from the same manuscript. The writings of the Africans, which had been transmitted through the same Marcellinus through whom Paulinus’s memorandum was also brought, have dropped out; Zosimus mentions them in Letter 11.], since he attempts to oppose the apostolic judgment by denying original sin, which has passed into all human beings and continues to hold Adam’s inheritance until the end of the world—that Adam who first sinned. Unless this sin is forgiven in infants through the sacrament of Baptism, they cannot possess eternal life and the eternal kingdom.

His teacher Pelagius also disputes these matters, although he himself condemned those very doctrines [Note: Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 1, chapter 5, §19, committed this to memory in these words: “For unless, in the sight and hearing of those who sat as judges at Diospolis, he had condemned those who say that Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and not the human race, and that newly born infants are in the condition in which Adam was before sin, and that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life, he could not possibly have departed from there except as one condemned.” The very words by which Pelagius condemned these doctrines are reported by the same teacher in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 11, §24; but in *On Original Sin*, chapter 6, he notes that Pelagius’s profession on this matter was not sincere.] in the eastern tribunal, while this man attempts to assert them in the gathering of the apostolic see.

He also has against him many ancient Catholic teachers of the Churches, eastern and western, from the southern and northern regions, who in their books can instruct him concerning original sin, if he desires to be healed. He has the blessed martyr Cyprian, the blessed confessor Ambrose, Gregory of Nazianzus, and the blessed Pope Innocent. He also has those who may contend with him in the body, if indeed he judges himself fit for so great a struggle; or, at any rate, those whom he ought to follow, if he wishes to learn what is right rather than teach what is wrong [Note: The printed editions read: “if indeed these are fit for so great a struggle”; and shortly afterward, “or certainly those whom you ought to follow.” These have been corrected from the Vatican manuscript.].

Above all, he has Your Beatitude, whose judgment he ought to have obeyed when he heard, “Condemn them.” Finally, he has the infants themselves, whom he ought to pity if he does not wish to pity himself; for to them, to use the words of the Martyr [Note: Cyprian, edition of Pamelius, Letter 59, to Fidus.], sins are forgiven not their own but those of another.

4. Therefore I beg your blessed apostolate to order this memorandum of mine to be received, by which I may return thanks to so great a see for the most just judgments delivered in my favor. I sent it for this reason: although only by word of mouth, the subdeacon Basiliscus met me at Carthage on the fourth day before the Nones of November, with the Acts of the apostolic see sent from Your Beatitude [Note: Read “sent.”], so that I might appear before the apostolic see and submit to the judgment of your holiness. It had been suggested that I had fled from it and would not promise to be present if the judgment had been delivered against me rather than in my favor [Note: More probably, “that Coelestius himself had fled to that see,” should be supplied. Then one should read: “nor would I promise that I would be absent,” although, since I had been summoned and cited only orally and not in writing, no law compelled me to do so. For an understanding of this passage, it will be useful to append some words of Marius Mercator. First, he relates how, in Africa in the year 411, the fathers and bishops of that region, moved by the six chapters brought against Coelestius by Paulinus, resisted Coelestius and ordered him to condemn them because they contained heretical meanings. He then adds: “But Coelestius, in no way yielding, indeed resisting, was deprived of ecclesiastical communion by those very proceedings in which he was frequently heard. He believed that he should appeal from that judgment to the examination of the Roman bishop. Soon afterward, neglecting that appeal, he went to Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there dared by stealth to seek a place among the presbyters, and so forth.” Hence it is clear: first, that the Carthaginian council delivered a judgment against Coelestius in favor of Paulinus; second, that Coelestius did indeed appeal from this judgment to the Roman pontiff, but failed to pursue his appeal within the period prescribed by law. For the Theodosian Code, book 11, title 30, law 45, provides that transmarine appeals must be pursued within one year; Coelestius, however, approached the Roman pontiff only six years later. Finally, Paulinus had good reason for complaint because Coelestius, disregarding the canons, had first sought the rank of presbyter at Ephesus before clearing himself at Rome or being restored to the communion from which he had been excluded.].

Since the man who had appealed to the apostolic see was absent, I could therefore do nothing there [Note: The printed editions read “therefore then.” The Vatican manuscript has the more fitting “for that reason then.” Earlier we would prefer “there” to “then.”]. He ought certainly to have established the merits of his appeal, especially since, when the appellant does nothing, even according to human laws the victor always has the superior position [Note: See Theodosian Code, book 11, title 31, law 1.].

For what would it now have mattered to me to appear, even before your reverence, as a witness to his perverse teaching? I could have rejoiced in him if, after condemning those matters that had been brought against him by me, he had also strengthened the judgment of the apostolic see in such a way that he deserved to be absolved [Note: In the Vatican archetype: “just as the judgment of the apostolic see deserved to be strengthened and I deserved to be absolved.” Baronius, and Labbe following him, present it as: “so that he might have deserved to be absolved once those matters had been strengthened through the judgment of the apostolic see.” We have judged that wording unacceptable. Here *astipulator* means not one who agrees, but a witness.], and if he had not allowed himself to be ordained before being cleared.

5. But he has always been a little fox intent upon deceits; he does not know how to change his character. He did not believe that he could be detected, because he has always placed his confidence in dens, in which he strives to hide the head of his conscience. What could no longer remain concealed, but has been brought into the open more clearly, is cut away by the spiritual sword through Your Beatitude, lest the Lord’s flock—whom you guard with watchful and vigilant care as a good shepherd—should any longer be torn into pieces by bestial teeth.

I sent this memorandum to Your Beatitude through Marcellinus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage. Delivered on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

[Col. 0715]

III. A BOOKLET ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS. (C, G, S)*

PREFACE

[Col. 0715B]

The most sacred and prophetic blessing of the holy Patriarchs, which through the Holy Spirit and through the mouth of the blessed Jacob was distributed to each according to an appropriate quality, cannot be understood entirely in its literal sense—especially since the same blessed Patriarch says: “That I may announce to you what will happen in the last days” (Gen. XLIX, 1). Nor should it be so weakened through allegorical interpretation that the historical sense is altogether emptied, since, as we shall see later, some things were foretold to them in such a way that some came to pass in the near future and others much later; nevertheless, many of them were reserved for fulfillment at the end.

Therefore, whatever we can understand historically in the very words themselves, let us first unfold briefly, laying foundations, with the Lord’s gift [Note: The Martianaeus manuscript had the erroneous reading “I.”]. But those things that in every respect reject the literal sense, let us examine through spiritual understanding, just as they are to be grasped spiritually.

CHAPTER ONE. The Blessing of Reuben

1. “Reuben, my firstborn; you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow; foremost in gifts, greater in authority” (ibid., 3). The literal sense is clear, because the blessed Jacob received his first son Reuben from Leah his wife (Gen. XXXIX, 31–32). If Reuben had conducted himself worthily toward so great a father, the birthright and the kingdom would have belonged to him. Hence Jacob calls him his firstborn, as one to whom the gifts of the firstborn were due. He also calls him his strength, because the power of rule ought to have passed to him.

He did not state these things as indications that they would necessarily come about, whether because he foresaw them or desired them, but in order through these words to urge him to repentance, when he recalled from what great dignity he had fallen through sin.

2. Hence he says: “and the beginning of my sorrow.” For he was the beginning of Jacob’s sorrow when, breaking the reins of chastity, he rushed without restraint to violate his father’s wife (Gen. XXXV, 22). This deed must be believed to have pierced him with no ordinary grief. It is rightly called the beginning of his sorrow, because the other brothers too were accused by the blessed Joseph before their father of a very grave offense (Gen. XXXVII, 2).

3. When he says, “foremost in gifts,” this refers to the privileges of the firstborn, which were owed to Reuben as the firstborn. But when he adds, “greater in authority,” it is openly declared that it belonged to him that kings should be created from his offspring for the rest of his brothers.

4. When he says, “You have poured yourself out like water,” the meaning is this: just as water that is not contained by a vessel flows in every direction, and wherever the place is more inclined downward it lowers itself and falls with its full force, so you restrained your marital lust by no measure. Wherever the impulse of desire drew you, there you poured out the foul reservoir of your lust [Note: Martianaeus read “they drew.”]. But when he adds, “you shall not increase,” he forbids him from proceeding any further in such or similar disgrace. Thus the Lord also said to Cain: “You have sinned; be still.”

5. What these words are directed toward is confirmed by what follows: “Because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (Gen. XLIX, 4). These words plainly magnify the crime of incest that he committed with Balaam [Note: Martian., “Balam.”], his father’s concubine (Gen. XXXV, 22). And lest this perhaps seem forced to anyone, because it was previously said, “I will announce to you what will happen in the last days,” let him hear what the Book of Chronicles says about this matter:

“The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn—for he was indeed his firstborn—but when he violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel, and he was not reckoned as firstborn” (1 Chron. V, 1).

6. Typologically, this firstborn Reuben designates the Jewish people, who were God’s firstborn, in accordance with what the Lord said about them to Moses: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV, 22); and the blessed Jeremiah says: “Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest” (Jer. II, 3). Israel was his strength when, through the Patriarchs and Prophets and through all the other especially strong men, it fought bravely against idolatry and the impure host of every vice [Note: The scribe consistently has this reading instead of “idolatry.” See Trombellius on Hilary’s letter, note 175.].

7. Yet Israel afterward became the beginning of his sorrow, when, at the coming of the Savior, it remained in unbelief and with proud mind refused to receive his teaching [Note: Martianaeus omits the words “afterward became.”] [Note: Martianaeus omits “to receive.”]. Hence the Lord is said to have wept when he saw the city of Jerusalem (Luke XIX, 41), and is reported to have shed tears at the raising of Lazarus because of the blindness of that people (John XI, 38).

8. When it is said, “foremost in gifts,” it is shown that this same people preceded the nations in gifts bestowed by God [Note: Martianaeus omits the preposition “in.”], while the Church of the nations was to follow, destined to be endowed with the same and much greater spiritual gifts. But when it is added, “greater in authority” [Note: Martian., “he adds.”], it is no wonder if that nation is honored which first believed through the prerogative of the fathers, since the blessed Apostle Paul says that the Jew has much advantage in every way (Rom. III, 1–2) [Note: The Martianaeus manuscript erroneously had “surely” instead of “it is no wonder.”].

9. In the meantime he added: “You have poured yourself out like water,” considering in his mind the unrestrained conduct of that people, which was not held in check by the measure of the vessel of the Law and the divine commandments. Rather, casting aside all the bonds of God’s commandments, it poured out the streams of its speech with all its strength toward the killing of the Savior.

That water signifies either good or evil speech is testified by divine Scripture. In a good sense it says: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. XXIII, 4); and in an evil sense: “He who releases water is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. XVII, 14). But when it adds, “you shall not increase,” it shows that this same people, as we also see with our eyes, has been reduced to very small numbers among all the nations.

10. Why it suffered these things is confirmed by the words that follow: “Because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.” By “the bed of the father” we indicate the flesh of the Savior [Note: Martianaeus adds “your.”] [Note: Martianaeus reads “indicating.”]. Nor is this surprising. By his father’s bed he understands the nations and the Lord’s body, because that same people was created by him; for it is written about him: “All things were made through him” (John I, 3).

By “the couch,” the same body is understood. It was as if defiled by the Jews when, at their outcry, the Lord was hung upon the cross, pierced through with a lance, and drenched with his own blood.

CHAPTER TWO. The Blessing of Simeon and Levi

1. “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of iniquity that wage war” (Gen. XLIX, 5). The literal sense is clear: these two brothers, in order to avenge the violation of their sister, deceived Shechem and his father Hamor under the appearance of peaceful friendship and false amity (Gen. XXXIV). He calls them “weapons of iniquity that wage war,” because it was exceedingly unjust to pretend friendship and afterward betray it.

2. “Let my soul not enter their counsel” (Gen. XLIX, 6), that is, he curses every simulated peace. Hence the blessed David also invokes punishment upon such hypocrites: “They speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts. Give them according to their works” (Ps. XXVII, 3–4) [Note: The scribe indeed, but consistently, writes “Davit.”].

When he adds, “and let my glory not be in their assembly,” he certainly did not wish to glory in such a victory, or rather in such slaughter, in which the warrior’s courage could not be praised but the deceiver’s falsehood had instead to be exposed.

3. “For in their anger they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall.” By “the man,” Shechem must be understood, and by him all those who were killed on his account. The destruction of a wall is not in fact said to have been carried out there in the Book of Genesis; rather, this has been drawn from the customary practice of combatants, who from a distance excavate the earth through tunnels, destroy the foundations of walls, and introduce fire, so that the stones, being baked, may cause the strength and stability of the walls to collapse.

4. Let us see with what severity this deed is struck. “Cursed,” he says, “be their anger, because it was stubborn, and their indignation, because it was harsh.” Their anger was stubborn because it could be softened neither by entreaties nor by gifts. Their indignation was proved harsh because it could not be softened even by the killing of those who had committed the outrage, but did not hesitate to rage instead against the whole city [Note: The manuscript reads *crassari* [sic].].

5. When he says, “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel,” this applies specifically to Levi, who was scattered throughout Israel and did not receive a separate inheritance. Rather, by dwelling in the cities and their suburbs, he was, as it is said here, scattered and divided.

It is the custom of sacred Scripture, when it speaks of those associated with one another, to foretell generally what ordinarily happens not to all but to some. Thus the Lord also said to James and John: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” He replied: “You will indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX, 21, 24). Yet John did not drink the cup of passion by shedding his blood.

6. As regards the prophecy of future events, Simeon and Levi designate the scribes and Pharisees; for it is clear that the chief priests came from Levi. They were “weapons of iniquity that wage war,” having a heart, according to the Lord’s reproach, full of iniquity and plunder (Luke XI, 39). They fought against the Lord not with armed combat but with crafty cunning, seeking ways to attack the Lord’s truthful words and deeds with false arguments.

7. The holy man, detesting these things, said: “Let my soul not enter their counsel,” that is, he cursed that counsel in which the Jews gathered and said: “What are we to do, since this man is performing many signs?” (John XI, 47), and so forth. He did not wish his glory to be in their assembly, refusing to glory in the multitude of those who, the more numerous they were, were the worse. Even then he was fulfilling in deed the sense of Scripture, which says: “Do not glory in wicked children, if they become numerous” (Eccles. XVI, 1).

8. He gives the reason why he abominates the counsel and assembly of such men, saying: “For in their anger they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall.” In their anger they killed the Man, namely, the Lord Savior, of whom Zechariah says: “Behold, a man: his name is Rising” (Zech. VI, 12), crying out to Pilate: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John XIX, 15).

And in their self-will they undermined a wall, because, fulfilling their own will, they both crucified the Lord and pierced his side. He is rightly called our wall, because by his protection we are guarded against the assaults of spiritual enemies. Concerning him this promise is made to the holy Church in these words: “Our strong city is Zion, the Savior; a wall and rampart will be placed in it” (Isa. XXVI, 1).

9. The holy man pierces this deed with the strongest spearpoint of his curse, saying: “Cursed be their anger, because it was stubborn, and their indignation, because it was harsh.” They had a stubborn anger and a harsh indignation because they could not be led to believe that he was God even by divine miracles, nor did they spare him—though he was an innocent man who had harmed them in nothing—but pursued him even to death.

10. When he adds, “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel,” this is what we now see. That same people, dispossessed of its ancestral soil and scattered among all the nations, suffers the penalties of its unbelief as a testimony to our faith. The blessed David also prophesied this in a psalm in the person of our Lord, saying: “My God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law; scatter them by your strength” (Ps. LVIII, 12).

They are rightly said to be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel, because the holy Church, which supplants vices, is rightly called Jacob; and because it strives to see God through purity of mind, it is named Israel. Through this Church the Jews wander divided and scattered; spread throughout the four regions of the heavens, it daily bears with their wandering.

CHAPTER THREE. The Blessing of Judah

1. “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies. The sons of your father shall worship you” (Gen. XLIX, 8). These words display both the modesty of this man, according to the literal sense, and his abundance of strength. In dealing civilly with his brothers, he evidently appeared so modest that he was considered worthy of praise by all—a difficult achievement, namely, to reconcile the goodwill of everyone among so many brothers.

He also abounded so greatly in courage that he was able to bend the necks of his enemies. That he possessed great eloquence is testified by the speech in which he pleaded his own need and that of his brothers before Joseph (Gen. XLII–XLIV). Moreover, the historian Josephus relates that he was extraordinarily powerful in speech. That he was regarded as outstanding in strength among his brothers is further attested by the Book of Chronicles, which reports as follows: “Judah, who was the strongest among his brothers, from whose stock princes arose” (1 Chron. V, 2).

When he adds, “The sons of your father shall worship you,” he clearly entrusts to Judah the kingdom that Reuben had lost, saying that he was to be worshiped by the rest of his brothers; this plainly accords with royal dignity.

2. Mystically, Judah already then prefigured the one who was born according to the flesh from his stock, our Lord and Savior, whom all his brothers praise—that is, all who believe in him. Hence, as the first among those who believed in him, he sent a message from the tomb through the women, saying: “Go and tell my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

Nor should we think that this dignity was attributed only to the Apostles, so that they would be called his brothers. He himself testifies that all who believe in him are to be endowed with this dignity, saying: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII, 50).

His brothers therefore praise him: the whole Church, whether still exiled on earth from the heavenly inheritance or already gone before to heaven [Note: Or “advanced.”]. Hence the psalm says: “Let heaven and earth praise him” (Ps. LXVIII, 35). And in the Apocalypse John says: “Give praise to our God, all his servants, and you who fear him, small and great” (Rev. XIX, 5).

His hands [Note: Namely, Christ’s.] are upon the necks of his enemies, because, according to the testimony of the Gospel: “The Father has given all things into his hands” (John XIII, 3). He himself agrees with these words, saying: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII, 18). And the Father speaks to him: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1; Matt. XXII, 44; Luke XX, 43).

The sons of his father worship him—all those, that is, who through him have been adopted into the dignity of sons, according to the Apostle’s words: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.”

3. It follows: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him?” As far as the surface of the literal sense is concerned, these words prefigure the strength of the kings who descended from Judah: such men as we read the blessed David, the blessed Hezekiah, and all the others to have been. Serving the divine will with deepest humility, they subdued the strength of their enemies, by God’s gift, like a lion and a lioness, and inspired such terror in their enemies that no one dared to challenge them to battle while they rested. The Books of Kings bear witness to this.

4. Typologically, however, he calls the Lord Savior a lion’s cub, as one born from a leonine lineage—that is, descended from a royal stock. He is rightly called a lion’s cub, since its nature is said to be that, when born, it sleeps for three days and then rises, awakened by its father’s roar. This image most beautifully corresponds to the Lord’s sleep, during which, sleeping for three days, he cries out to the Father: “But you, O Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up” (Ps. XL, 11) [Note: Or “who,” or “because.”].

But once raised, he went up to the prey, because, stripping the underworld, he triumphantly carried the righteous with him to the heights as splendid spoils. He lay down like a lion and, as it were, like a lioness, because, although he wished to sleep in the flesh in the tomb, he triumphed over his enemies like a victorious lion.

When he adds, “Who will rouse him?” the implied answer is: “Except the Father?” For no one—not merely any mortal human being, but not even any of the Angels [Note: Some verb appears to be missing here.]—could do so, except the one of whom the Apostle Peter said to the Jews: “God raised him from the dead; of this we are witnesses” (Acts III, 15).

5. “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). This statement is understood more clearly by the faithful, because that people continued to be ruled by princes and leaders of its own nation until our Lord and Savior came, the one who was to be sent by the Father.

He is the expectation of the nations, because God the Father waited for the nations to repent until, through the coming of his Son, he should recall them from the worship of idols to knowledge of himself. For whether the Jews were led away to Babylon, they always had rulers from their own people; or, after returning from Babylon, they continued to do so until Herod, a foreigner, was appointed king over them. Their supreme government was also exercised by the high priests until Aristobulus was reached. He was the first after the return from Babylon who, although he was high priest, placed a diadem upon himself and declared himself king.

His successors likewise continued until, when Jewish affairs were falling into decline and Hyrcanus, the last king of the Jews, had been added to their final calamities [Note: Perhaps “had been devoted to” or “had been handed over to.”], Herod, a foreigner, received the Jewish kingdom from Caesar Augustus. In his time, in accordance with this prophecy and the testimony of the Gospel, our Lord and Savior, the one who was to be sent (Matt. II, 1), came.

6. “Binding his colt to the vine, and his ass, my son, to the vine” (Gen. XLIX, 11). The arrangement of these words demonstrates that the blessed Jacob is not speaking to Judah but about the one who was to be sent. For when, speaking to a son, he says, “O my son,” and adds, “your colt” or “your ass,” he most plainly speaks about the one whom he had previously foretold would be sent.

We read that he came into Jerusalem with an ass and a colt (Matt. XXI, 5–7), but that they were not tied to a vineyard or vine. It remains, therefore, that nothing historical should be sought in these words, but that everything should be understood as spoken typologically.

The Lord and Savior bound his colt to the vine when he subjected the untamed people of the nations to the commandments of the Apostles, who were produced from the Jewish vine, concerning which Isaiah says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V, 7).

He also tied his ass to the vine—that is, to the Church—namely, the Synagogue. At the end of the age, recalling it from unbelief, he will subject it, oppressed by the yoke of the Law, to discipleship under the Church; and thus there will be “one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16). According to the testimony of the blessed Zechariah, those two staffs [Note: Or “those,” referring to the two staffs.] will be joined and will become one in the hand of the Lord.

7. “He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX, 11). It is characteristic of the Hebrew language to repeat one and the same thing in different expressions, as here. For what is wine except the blood of the grape?

But although the surface of the literal sense is incoherent—for no one washes either a robe or a garment in wine—the inner meaning is commended by a more pleasing interpretation. The Savior washed his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape because, hanging on the cross, he willed the sacred flesh that was his robe to be drenched with his own blood.

8. It follows: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (ibid., 12). The Savior’s eyes are proclaimed more beautiful than wine because the gifts of the Holy Spirit conferred through Christ are shown to be more splendid than the legal wine.

That the Savior’s eyes signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit is testified by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III, 9). Isaiah enumerates them, saying: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI, 2–3).

These eyes are more beautiful than the legal wine that failed at the wedding (John II, 3), because through the Law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. III, 20), while through the grace of the Holy Spirit its forgiveness is granted to us. And according to the Gospel, “the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I, 17).

9. When it says, “And his teeth are whiter than milk,” the teeth should be understood as the preachers of the New Testament. By breaking up spiritual foods—that is, by explaining them—they transmit many things useful to us into the stomach of memory.

Milk may suitably be understood as the teaching of the Old Testament, prepared for a people still at the beginning, not yet strong enough for solid food. Jesus therefore has teeth whiter than milk because he made the preachers of his Church conspicuous through the purity of holiness.

The difference between the followers of the Gospel and those who observe the Law is testified by the blessed Peter, who says: “You could not be justified by the Law; in him everyone who believes is justified” (Acts XIII, 38–39).

These teeth are therefore white because, washed in the fountain of Baptism, they are rendered utterly pure from the stains of sins. Nothing similar is reported concerning the observers of the Law; it is merely said: “The one who does them shall live by them” (Gal. III, 12). Moreover, all who serve the Law carnally are under a curse, since the same Law declares terribly: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the commandments of this Law, to do the things written in it” (Deut. XXVII, 26).

CHAPTER FOUR. The Blessing of Zebulun
[Col. 0723C] **1.** “Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, and in the roadstead of ships, reaching as far as Sidon” (Gen. 49:13). According to the historical sense, the location of that allotment which he was to receive in the Promised Land by God’s gift is foretold: namely, that the land of his possession would begin on one side at the sea and end on the other at a torrent, as is clearly shown in the Book of Joshua son of Nun (Josh. 19:11), where the boundaries of those possessions are set out. Hence Sidon is also mentioned here, since it lies beside the sea.

**2.** According to the mystical interpretations, however, Zebulun represents the first fruits of the holy Church. Some of the holy Apostles are believed to have belonged to this tribe, because they continually dwelt on the shore of the sea, earning their livelihood from it by hand and skill, until they were called by the Lord to the summit of apostleship, in accordance with the prophecy of blessed David:

“ The princes of Judah are their leaders, the princes of Zebulun, the princes [Note: [Col. 0723D] The codex has *Neptalim*.] of Naphtali” (Ps. 67:28).

They also dwell in a roadstead of ships, because they rest in the Lord Jesus Christ in confident and secure peace. The ships are understood as the Church: they seek, and find, their Lord as the most trustworthy harbor of their salvation. And rightly it is added: “reaching as far as Sidon,” because the same holy Church is not confined to one corner of the world, but, by growing, reaches as far as the peoples of the Gentiles. Sidon is interpreted as “hunting,” signifying, as has been said, the Gentiles, who in beastly manners pursued the worship of idolatry like wild beasts pursuing their lairs in the desert. Later, by the net of the Lord’s preaching and the barking [that is, the preaching] of the holy Apostles, it was deemed worthy to be admitted within the enclosures of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0723D] The codex incorrectly has *amitti*.].

## CHAPTER V. The Blessing of Issachar

**1.** “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he placed his shoulder under the burden, and became subject to tribute” (Gen. 49:14–15). By these words this tribe is signified as devoting itself to the teaching of the Law and applying itself more readily to scrutinizing the commandments of God. For it is said that he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent—that is, that he tasted in his mind how sweet it was to occupy his understanding with the commandments of God. Therefore he is said to have placed his shoulder under the burden: that is, with all his effort he directed his mind toward pursuing the sayings of the divine Word. Consequently, all those beneath him brought him gifts and honor as their teacher and instructor. The Book of Chronicles agrees with this interpretation, saying of this tribe:

“From the sons of Issachar also came men learned in understanding, who knew the individual times, to instruct what the leaders of two hundred should do” [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Vulgate edition has: “what Israel should do; leaders of two hundred”] (1 Chron. 12:32).

**2.** This strong ass, however, bears the type of the Gentile people, who, before they had the Lord as their rider, were brutish and impatient of the bridle, carried along according to their own will. After they were deemed worthy to have the Lord as their rider, they took from him the name of the strong ass. They saw that rest was good when they heard from their rider:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Vulgate edition has: “and I will refresh you”] (Matt. 11:28).

They also perceived that the land was excellent, because, abandoning the empty teachings of the philosophers, they devoted themselves most earnestly to reading Holy Scripture. Thus, since they learned among other things that it is not those who hear the Law who are justified, it is added: “he placed his shoulder under the burden” (Rom. 2:13)—that is, he subjected all his power to the divine commandments, and especially to the love of God and neighbor. For one does not love one’s neighbor unless one bears him. And it is added: “and became subject to tribute”; for he pays a kind of tribute every day, hearing from the Apostle:

“Render to all their dues: fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor, tribute to whom tribute” (Rom. 13:7),

and so forth.

## CHAPTER VI. The Blessing of Dan

**1.** “Dan shall judge his people, as also the other tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Vulgate edition has “in Israel.”]. “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward. I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:16–18).

According to the historical sense, it is foretold [Note: [Col. 0725D] Or: “it is declared.”] not only concerning the other more distinguished tribes but also concerning Dan that he would become a leader of Israel; and, by way of description, what sort of leader he would be is indicated. Samson is prefigured by these words, for he was terrifying like a serpent and a snake; and, to make him appear still more terrifying, he is described as horned, on account of his exceptional power and strength. Thus, during the time of his rule, he blocked the roads and paths of the Israelite kingdom, lest any enemy dare invade the land under his authority by force. But if anyone more monstrous, trusting in his own speed and strength as a horse [Note: [Col. 0725D] The codex is written in such a way that it may also be read: “and trusting in power as a horse”], had wished to attack him, then, with that assailant’s feet gnawed away and his powers exhausted, he would throw his pursuer into confusion and bring him to the ground. And lest anyone deceived by error should regard him as more than a human being, he immediately added who the true leader was to be awaited, saying: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord”—in whose figure, plainly, this man in some measure went before.

**2.** Dan also prefigures the Antichrist, who will be like a serpent in the way and a horned serpent on the path, because, against those who walk in the way and path of God’s commandments, he sets himself as an obstacle, so far as he can, armed with a twofold character against them. In the serpent his cunning is prefigured, because he craftily seeks to deceive those who hold fast to the way of the Lord by the course of their works. In the horns, however, his fury is shown, which he will use against those whom he is unable to deceive by crafty plotting. For *cerasta* in Greek means “horns” in Latin; therefore this serpent is described as horned.

When the Antichrist comes and performs great signs before the eyes of those watching, bringing down fire from heaven, he is the serpent in the way (Rev. 13:13). But when he turns to inflicting punishments and torments upon those who do not believe in him, he becomes the horned serpent on the path, because he seeks to subjugate with the horns of his power those who walk along the narrow path of the Lord. When he exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped (2 Thess. 2:4), he bites the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward: for he takes away worldly glory from those who do not yield to him, so that, enticed by love of present goods, they may fall there where they do not see.

To fall backward means both to collapse here, despairing and shamelessly, where one does not see, and afterward to arrive in the outer darkness. For one who falls forward is ashamed of what lies behind him; but one who falls backward, as we have already said, nourishes anger for himself on the day of wrath with an unrepentant heart (Rom. 2:5). Furthermore, lest anyone, because of the great sublimity of his miracles, should think that the Antichrist ought to be worshiped as God, he added: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord,” as though he were saying: although the Antichrist may shine with many distinguished miracles, I must await your Salvation—which in Hebrew is called *Jesus*—so that, when he comes, he may crush the power of that one with eternal retribution and, finding me among his faithful, grant me a blessed dwelling.

## CHAPTER VII. The Blessing of Gad

[Col. 0726A]

**1.** “Gad, girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded afterward” (Gen. 49:19). The literal sense is clear to readers of the Book of Joshua son of Nun. Gad, who sought and received an inheritance beyond the Jordan from Moses, was deemed worthy to possess it on this condition: that, girded with weapons before Israel, together with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, he should advance fighting against his adversaries (Deut. 3:18), which he later did under Joshua. Yet, after the enemies had been subjugated, when he returned to his own possession, he had to contend with the incursions of neighboring peoples (1 Chron. 5:18). This, therefore, is what he says: first he fought girded before his brothers, and afterward he was girded again for battle.

**2.** Spiritually, however, he signifies the elect among the Jews, who became, as it were, leaders before the new people and brought them into the land once promised. Such were the prophets and holy patriarchs, who pierced idolatry—the mother of all vices—and its innumerable offspring with the darts of their words. Yet they will be girded again, because in the final times, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters, they will be aroused to renewed conflicts, which they will wage against the Antichrist and his satellites.

For now they do not possess an inheritance beyond the streams of the Jordan, since through the grace of Baptism they do not enter the Church, but remain apart, dwelling outside their brothers and continuing in legal ceremonies.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Blessing of Asher

[Col. 0726C]

**1.** “Asher’s bread is rich, and he shall provide delicacies for kings” (Gen. 49:20). According to the literal sense, the abundance of the land seems to be promised to this tribe. For in the allotment of his possession he had Mount Carmel, notable for its fertility; and, since he also bordered on the sea, there is no doubt that he offered even to his kings the delicacies in which he himself abounded, both of the sea and of the land [Note: [Col. 0726D] Perhaps *ipsa* should be read, and shortly afterward *eam*.].

**2.** By these words, however, holy men who were to arise from the Synagogue are foretold. Their bread is rich: namely, prophetic teaching overflowing with the fatness of the Holy Spirit. One of them, inflamed by insatiable eagerness, cried out:

“Let my soul be filled as with fat and abundance” (Ps. 62:6).

They provide their delicacies for kings [Note: [Col. 0726D] The codex incorrectly has: “he provided”], because they display the royal rule to those who desire to maintain the kingdom of righteous moderation over themselves and those subject to them.

## CHAPTER IX. The Blessing of Naphtali

**1.** “Naphtali is a freed stag, giving words of beauty” (Gen. 49:21). Under the teaching of blessed Jerome [Col. 0727A] [Note: [Col. 0727D] In *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, pp. 377–378, vol. IV of Jerome’s works, edited by Vallarsius], we learn that the Hebrew does not have “a freed stag,” but “an irrigated field,” and that by “an irrigated field” is signified the abundance of warm waters, which overflow most plentifully in the suburb of Tiberias. Nevertheless, the tradition of the Hebrews is that this city was especially devoted to the commandments of God. Consequently, they teach that “an irrigated field” signifies the exceedingly rich teaching of learned masters, which used to intoxicate the hearts of the ignorant like a stream, so that they might bring forth the fruits of understanding; and they say that this is explained below, when it says: “giving words of beauty.”

**2.** We, however, understand by Naphtali the holy preachers of the Church, who, sent to the holy Church, know how to make leaps of understanding like stags, fearlessly climb the mountains of contemplation [Note: [Col. 0727D] The codex has, I think incorrectly, “the minds of contemplation”], and thus give words of beauty to the peoples: so that what they have learned, lifted up in the height of contemplation, they diligently provide to those situated below.

## CHAPTER X. The Blessing of Joseph

**1.** “Joseph is a growing son, a growing son, and beautiful in appearance” (Gen. 49:22; 39:6). According to the literal sense, blessed Jacob foresaw that the tribe of Joseph would abound in innumerable offspring; hence he was the father of two tribes, as he had foretold above in blessing them. Therefore, as though blessing two tribes, he repeated: “a growing son.”

**2.** Joseph is clearly understood to have gone before as a type of the Savior, because he feeds Egypt, failing through famine, with the grain of God’s word; and, sold by his brothers, the Jews, he continues to nourish the Church of the Gentiles to this day. To him it is said: “a growing son, and beautiful in appearance.” For he himself, the Son of God and likewise the Son of Man, somehow grew when he took to himself, in the Apostles and the other faithful of that time, the people of Israel who had dishonored God through transgressing the Law. He is likewise a growing son when he spread the knowledge of his name among the Gentiles and continues to grow among them to the end of the world through the illumination of faith and works. Joseph is also beautiful in appearance, because he is “beautiful beyond the sons of men in form” (Ps. 44:3).

**3.** “The daughters ran upon the wall. But they provoked him, and quarreled with him, and envied him, having darts” (Gen. 49:22–23). As far as the event itself is concerned, he calls his brothers “daughters” because of the disgrace of their inhumanity. For it was not the conduct of a manly and steadfast judgment to wish either to destroy an innocent brother or to sell him, but rather that of feminine instability. They ran upon the wall because they thought they had discovered an invincible plan concerning him, so that he would not become their king. They provoked him by stripping off his multicolored tunic (Gen. 37:23) and inflicting unworthy insults upon him. They quarreled with him and envied him, having darts:

“Are you to be our king? Or are we to be subject to your rule?” [Note: [Col. 0727D] The codex incorrectly has “to your speech.”] (Gen. 37:8).

Hence it was said above: “His brothers therefore envied him” (Gen. 37:11). They had darts—that is, hearts prepared to do harm. Thus it is said of the Jews desiring to kill the Lord:

“The arrows of children became their wounds” (Ps. 63:9).

**4.** According to the mystical senses, however, the daughters signify the Jews, who are designated by a feminine appellation because, abandoning [Note: [Col. 0728D] Perhaps “the Lord” should be supplied] the Lord and the solid teaching of our Savior and clinging to Pharisaic superstition, they were troubled in mind. For those who lack solid understanding and whose mind wavers in varied instability are designated by the Apostle with the name of women, when he speaks of evil teachers:

“They enter houses and lead captive little women weighed down with sins” [Note: [Col. 0728D] In the Vulgate edition this is followed by: “who are led by various desires”], “always learning and never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3:6).

They ran upon the wall when they thought they had found a thoroughly fortified plan, as Caiaphas said:

“It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50).

They provoked him when, moved somehow to weariness by their unbelief, he said:

“O faithless generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” (Mark 9:19).

They quarreled with him, saying:

“How long will you take away our soul?” (John 10:24).

They envied him when they said in their council:

“What shall we do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him” (John 11:47–48).

And again:

“Do you see that we accomplish nothing? Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19).

They had darts, concerning which it is written:

“The arrows of children became their wounds” (Ps. 63:9).

**5.** “His bow rested in the strong one, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob; from there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel” (Gen. 49:24). The historical sense, as far as can be understood, is this. By the bow is understood the mind foreknowing future things. An arrow is placed in a bow so that it may strike from a distance; and a mind prescient of future things is accustomed to send the arrows of its judgments farther away. Thus, when it says, “his bow rested in the strong one,” it is as though it said: his mind, afflicted on every side by tribulations, found rest in the strong one—that is, was made firm in God—and, by the arrows of its judgments, with which it foretold what would happen, struck the future ages with barrenness.

[Col. 0728D] **6.** When he says, “and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened,” this refers to the time when, at Pharaoh’s command, he was released from prison and, as is said here, the bonds of his arms and hands, with which he had been ordered [Note: [Col. 0728D] The codex incorrectly has “sent”] to be bound in prison, were loosened by the hands—that is, by the power—of the Mighty One of Jacob, namely, almighty God, by whose help Jacob’s power became glorious.

[Col. 0729A] **7.** Moreover, what follows—“from there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel”—refers to Christ, who went forth from Jacob, deriving his origin from him. He is rightly called the stone of Israel, because he is strength to the one who believes in him.

**8.** This saying also agrees with the Savior in the following way: “His bow rested in the strong one”—that is, the sentence of punishment by which the Jews who refused to receive him and persecuted him even unto death were to be struck. It rested in the strong one—that is, it was fixed in immutable stability with the Father, who said:

“Amen I say to you, not one stone will be left here upon another” (Matt. 24:2).

And:

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate,” and so forth (Matt. 23:38).

**9.** “The bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob” when the bonds of the tomb were undone, and resurrection was not denied him by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob—that is, by the power of the Father.

**10.** “From there the shepherd went forth, and the stone of Israel”—that is, the Lord and Savior went forth from God the Father and presented himself to human sight, as he himself said:

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:26).

**11.** “The God of your father will be your helper, and the Almighty will bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the abyss lying below, with blessings of breasts and womb” (Gen. 49:25). He invokes for his son the help of the God of his father, namely, of the one by whose help he remembered that he had been delivered from such great dangers, and whom he had recognized as almighty through the benefits granted to him.

When he says, “with blessings of heaven above,” this refers to rain and the tempering of the air, by which the earth is made fruitful with crops and the growth of trees is nourished. When he adds, “with blessings of the abyss lying below,” this refers to the fertility of the earth, which is watered by the vapors of the abyss like the hollow of a sponge, so that it may not easily be dried out by the heat of the sun and rendered useless through drought. He blesses him with blessings of breasts and womb, so that he may increase through abundant offspring and not be condemned to barrenness either of men or of women.

**12.** He says: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers” (ibid. 49:26), so that Joseph would not doubt that what the holy Jacob promised him would come not so much from his own, as it were, recent blessing, but because it had long before been promised to his fathers, that is, Abraham and Isaac. For this is what he says: “The blessings of your father have prevailed,” as though he were saying: Do not receive these blessings of your father as his own, or as though they had been given only once; rather, understand that they were first given by God to my fathers, and not once only, but repeatedly. Therefore I pour over your head, by divine authority, the same blessings that were promised to me and to my fathers.

**13.** To the Lord and Savior, almighty God and Father was a helper when he cried out in the psalm:

“Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to your mercy” (Ps. 108:26).

For although, in his indivisible divinity, he gives aid to all who are proclaimed, he, having become human and having been made a little lower than the angels (Heb. 2:7), needed not only paternal aid but also angelic assistance, in order to manifest the twofold substance in himself. Hence he cries:

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34).

And in the Gospel:

“An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43).

The Almighty himself blessed him, saying:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (2 Pet. 1:17).

**14.** He blessed him with the blessings of heaven above and with the blessings of the abyss lying below when, according to the Apostle:

“He gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10).

He exalted him with the blessings of breasts and womb when, through the sons of the Church throughout the world, he grants that he be blessed: some are catechumens, lying as yet within their mother’s breasts [Note: [Col. 0729D] I think *uterum* or *viscera* should be read], while others, like those already born, suck the maternal breasts. For those who have not yet advanced to the strength of faith but are being drawn toward it by teachers hear from the Apostle:

“My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

Those who have already received the beginnings of faith but have not yet become fully established in the firmness of teaching hear from the same Apostle:

“I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. Indeed, even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:2).

[Col. 0730C] **15.** It follows: “Until the desire of the eternal hills should come” (Gen. 49:26). Here nothing historical is intended; everything resounds with the divine. For he foretells that the Israelite people will be sustained by these blessings until the desire of the eternal hills comes. The hills are understood as the saints established in the Church. Although they excel in the merit of their virtues, they remember, in their most devoted humility, that they are hills. Hence the psalm says:

“Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 71:3).

Their desire is known to have always been the coming of the Lord Jesus. Thus Moses first said:

“I beg you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4:13).

And blessed Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord (Luke 2:26). They are called eternal hills because they are understood to have been created by God for eternity. For their intention is not changed into different things, as happens with fools; rather, always tending toward eternity and clinging to the eternal, they themselves also took from it the name of eternity [Note: [Col. 0730D] Read, “borrowed.” Thus above, chapter 5, § 2, we read that the strong ass “borrowed” its name from him]. Of fools it is said:

“A fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27:12);

but of the truly wise:

“The wise man remains like the sun” (ibid.).

**16.** It follows: “Let them be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers” (Gen. 49:26). These blessings were upon the head of Joseph because through Christ every praise and blessing is returned to the Father. Hence he himself says to the Father:

“Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1).

They are rightly said to be upon his head because “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). He himself, the Son, is called a Nazirite [Note: [Col. 0731B] The codex incorrectly has “Nazarene”] among his brothers because he alone is holy with a special dignity, which is what *Nazirite* signifies. Of him Scripture most truthfully says:

“He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22);

and God the Father anointed him with a special anointing above his companions (Heb. 1:9).

## CHAPTER XI. The Blessing of Benjamin
