[Col. 0731B] **1.** “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. 49:27). The tradition of the Hebrews, together with the agreement of blessed Jerome, holds that these words signify the altar of Jerusalem, which is known to have been constructed in the tribe of Benjamin. Like a ravenous wolf, it devoured the morning sacrifice by the cooking of fire; in the evening, after the sacrifices and rites of the victims had been completed, it used to divide among the priests and Levites what remained from the fire and what, by the command of the Law, was owed as food to the priests.

**2.** By this understanding, blessed Paul is signified as destined to arise from the same tribe. Like a ravenous wolf, he ate in the morning—that is, in his youth—because, while consenting to the killing of blessed Stephen and receiving letters from the chief priests and the elders of the Jewish people for Damascus and the other cities, he tore apart as many saints with various forms of slaughter as a ravenous wolf eats prey. Yet in the evening he divided the spoils, when, struck down by the Lord’s voice and vision, he distributed suitable spiritual nourishment of divine teaching to the faithful established within the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0732B] The word *doctrinae* is absent from the codex, but must be added]; giving milk of wisdom to some, as to little ones in Christ, and, still sympathizing with others, grieving with them like a woman in labor; but supplying solid food of teaching to the more perfect.

That the spoils signify the divine commandments is testified by David, who says:

“I shall rejoice over your words, as one who finds great spoils” (Ps. 118:162).

And blessed Isaiah says of the Apostles:

“They will rejoice before you as those who rejoice at the harvest, as those who exult when they divide spoils” (Isa. 9:3).

[Col. 0731]

**In the Year of the Lord 418**

**SEVERUS OF MAJORCA.** I have been unable to find any mention of this Severus in the various libraries of the Fathers, nor has anything else concerning his life been handed down to memory, except what the following letter contains, published by the author of the Annals, volume IV, under the year 418.

**LETTER OF SEVERUS, BISHOP, CONCERNING THE JEWS.** *(C, G, S)*

[Col. 0731C] It was granted to us by the grace of that same Protomartyr that, while writing the antiquities of the Vatican library, we should discover this same letter of Severus complete and suffering no loss. Since we do not know of its having been published by anyone else, we have judged it worthy to transcribe it here in full as an outstanding monument of antiquity. It runs as follows:

“To the most holy and blessed lords, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the entire brotherhood throughout the whole world, Severus, bishop, needy of the mercy of God and the least of all, eternal salvation in Christ our Redeemer.

You understand the customary formula of the Catholics of this period, who, in order to show that they are far removed from the encroaching Pelagian heresy, profess in the very heading that they are in need of the grace and mercy of God.” [Col. 0731D] But let us give the letter itself:

“Since the archangel Raphael admonishes us that it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God (Tob. 12), it is certainly dangerous to be silent about or conceal the works of Christ. Yet, in recounting them, there is greater grace if they are related in common and simple speech. For the most beautiful splendor of virtue is concealed, in a certain sense, if it is surrounded and embellished by overly abundant eloquence. Therefore I too shall undertake to relate the great things Christ has accomplished among us, not in a composed but in a truthful manner.

“The island of Minorca is one of the Balearic Islands, whose name is widely known to all peoples, including through the writings of secular authors. It lies approximately midway across the sea between Caesarean Mauretania and Spain and is enclosed within very narrow boundaries: it is thirty thousand paces long and three thousand paces wide. I have mentioned this so that it may be recognized that the Lord chooses the contemptible things of the world not only among human beings but also among places (1 Cor. 1).

“On this island, therefore, which of all lands is last in smallness, dryness, and roughness, two small towns have been founded opposite one another, bearing names given them by the Punic people: Jammona faces west, and Magona east. In these towns the burden of priestly office was recently placed upon me, the last of all mortals.

“But Jammona still retains the ancient gift from God, that Jews cannot live there at all. Antiquity relates that many who rashly attempted it, whether overtaken by illness, driven back, extinguished by sudden death, or even struck down by lightning, perished. So widely known is this matter that it has instilled fear even in the Jews themselves, lest they dare to attempt it further. Nor do we regard this as unworthy of belief, since we see that wolves, foxes, and every harmful animal are also absent, while there is a great abundance of wild creatures that are good for food.

“What is even more remarkable is that there are very many snakes and scorpions, but they have entirely lost the power to do harm. Thus, since no Jew—who is rightly compared with wolves and foxes in savagery and wickedness—dares even to approach Jammona under the right of hospitality, Magona alone, like a place swarming with snakes and scorpions, was seething with them, so that every day the Church of Christ was bitten by them. But that ancient carnal benefit has recently been renewed for us spiritually: so that that ‘generation of vipers’ (as it is written in Luke 3), which raged with poisonous bites, suddenly compelled by divine power, cast away that deadly venom of unbelief.

“For almost at the very time when I, though unworthy, received the name of so great a priesthood, a presbyter distinguished in holiness came from Jerusalem and remained for some time at Magona. When he was unable to cross over to Spain as he desired, he decided to return again to Africa. For Spain was at that time occupied by the Goths, as has been shown in its proper place; and this presbyter was the Spaniard Orosius.

“He continues: When he had decided to carry to Spain the relics of blessed Stephen, which had recently been revealed, he placed them, undoubtedly inspired by the martyr, in the church of the town mentioned above. Once this had been done, the fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth, and which he greatly desires to burn, was immediately kindled by his love (Luke 12). At once our sluggishness grew warm, and our heart became, as it is written, burning on the way (Luke 24). Then zeal was already burning in faith, and hope for the salvation of the multitude was raising it up.

“Finally, the practices of salvation were immediately interrupted, and not only was the accustomed fellowship broken apart, but even the harmful appearance of long-standing affection was changed into temporary hatred, for the sake of love of eternal salvation. In every street the battles of the Law were fought against the Jews; in every house, battles of faith.

“The Jewish people relied especially upon the authority and power of a certain Theodorus, who was distinguished not only among the Jews but also among the Christians of the same town in both worldly understanding and honor. Among them he was a teacher of the Law and—as I use their own word—the father of fathers; in the city, he had been released from all the offices of the curia, had already served as Defender, and now held the patronage of the municipality.

“The Christians, humble both in heart and in strength but superior in the vigor of truth, appealed for the patronage of Stephen. At last, when both armies had fixed a day for the contest, they withdrew after a truce had been granted. The Jews were eagerly awaiting Theodorus’s return from the island of Majorca, toward which he had gone, perhaps to inspect his property, since the whole synagogue relied upon his strength. As soon as a delegation had been sent to him, he returned and, by his authority, frightened many people; but he did not extinguish the fire of the conflict—he merely lulled it to sleep. For immediately it burst forth with greater violence, and the flame of faith seized even the neighboring town. And so that Solomon’s saying might be fulfilled:

‘A brother helping a brother will exult like a strong and lofty city’ (Prov. 18),

many servants of Christ determined, refusing no labor of travel, to devote all the powers of their minds to this battle.

“While the battle was thus pending, the memorandum appended to this letter demonstrates what weapons we had prepared. We did not wish to publish it as instruction for certain people—for we ourselves are utterly in need of instruction and hope for it more from your blessedness—but so that it might be observed that, according to the measure of our ability, we had undertaken no small concern for the battle we had accepted.

“Christ, however, whose kingdom is not in word but in power, completed everything by his own strength while we uttered not even a word, and, without any sweat of battle, granted his army a victory which no one had either dared to desire or been able to hope for.

“The Jews, therefore, encouraging themselves with examples from the time of the Maccabees, desired even death in defense of their lawful institutions. Accordingly, they began to bring not only books but also stones, stakes, spears, and every kind of weapon to the synagogue, so that, if circumstances demanded it, they might repel by bodily strength the line of Christians fortified by the power of the Holy Spirit.

“Meanwhile, while these preparations were being made and the coming battle was being arranged with great zeal on both sides, both armies were stirred by indescribable and most unmistakable dreams. If I were to make no mention of them at all, I would seem to have concealed no small part of the divine glory. Thus Luke inserted the dream of Saint Paul the Apostle into sacred history (Acts 16), saying that a Macedonian man appeared in a night vision, asking him to come to his aid; and that, warned by this vision, the Apostle diverted the course of his journey, which had been directed elsewhere, toward Macedonia.

“How much greater, then, is the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to reveal to the least and most unworthy of his servants what Scripture did not conceal even when it was shown to the blessed Apostle! Therefore, for the sake of brevity, lest we perhaps cause weariness to your blessedness, I shall insert only two dreams.”

Among us there was a certain devout and most religious woman named Theodora, who, by the virginity of her body, the religious character of her undertaking, and the meaning of her name, deserved to bear the type of the Church. She saw in a nighttime vision a most noble widow send me—who exercise the priesthood not according to my merit but by the abundance of the divine gift—a written message herself [perhaps: “sent beforehand”], in which she humbly offered me all her fields for sowing. By a similar dream He also deigned to gird and admonish me, the last of sinners, for sowing. For another most noble widow, who clearly had the appearance of the synagogue, implored me to take over her uncultivated fields and, when the season of sowing pressed, to cultivate them carefully. Who, then, is this other most noble widow, except she who, impiously killing Christ, widowed herself most cruelly? The dream of both was one and the same. It is clear that nearly thirty days before it was fulfilled we both saw it and, although we did not know its interpretation, reported it to the brethren.

Among the Jews also, by a marvelous ordering of divine providence, so that the association of the name Theodorus and my office might correspond in one man, Theodorus, who was high priest of the faithless people, disclosed the dream he had seen—not only to the Jews but also, well before the appointed time, to a certain close relative, a leading matron of the city itself, and to many other Christians—in these words:

“While I was going to the synagogue,” he said, “twelve men held out their hands before me, saying, ‘Where are you going? A lion is there.’ When, therefore, I began to tremble at hearing the name of the lion, I nevertheless found a place from which I could look in while preparing my flight, and I saw monks there chanting psalms with extraordinary sweetness. My fear immediately increased; and unless I had entered a certain man’s house in the name of Reuben, and from there hurried at a headlong pace to my close female relative, I would by no means have escaped the care of mortal terror. She took me, lifeless with fear, into her embrace and rescued me alike from danger and dread.”

His dream is perfectly clear and requires no interpretation. For who is the lion except he who is “the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David” (Rev. 5)? And who is that close relative except she of whom it is written, “My close relative is one” (Song of Songs 6)? Only this seemed obscure: that, when frightened by the lion, he entered the house of Reuben the Jew. This, however, was afterwards explained to us most clearly by the very lion who had frightened him in order to save him; we shall explain it later in its proper place. For now I shall continue the account of what was begun.

From the city of Jammon there gathered for the departure of the servants of Christ a multitude that had been thought to reside in the town itself. They completed the labor of that most difficult journey with such enthusiasm that they seemed to fly over thirty miles more joyfully than if they had been summoned to some most pleasant suburb for a banquet. Thus we reached Magona. Immediately I sent clerics to announce my arrival to the Jews and asked them to deign to come to the holy Church. They, however, sending back an unexpected message, instructed us that they ought not to enter the church that day—lest, I suppose, they be polluted—for it was the Sabbath, whose observance they said the Christians had corrupted by their actions.

Again I requested that, if they preferred, they await me at the synagogue, since entering the church appeared to be a pollution: certainly we did not wish to compel them on the feast of the Sabbath to perform servile work. There would, moreover, be an honorable contest concerning the Law, and no quarrels or tales should be stirred up. Or, if they were not cleverly avoiding the contest and were offering a straightforward excuse, let them show the commandment that forbade discussion on that day.

When they obstinately contradicted everything, they were finally driven by fear of that lion to gather at the house where I had taken lodging. There I said:

“Brothers, I ask you: why have you gathered piles of stones and every kind of weapon as though against brigands, especially in a city subject to Roman laws? We desire to acquire you; you desire to destroy us. As I understand it, it is not right for us to weary one another with such varied strife. Yet, as I see, you thirst for our blood, while we thirst for your salvation.”

At this they were somewhat frightened and denied that they had done it. Even when our people insisted that this was so, they resisted under oath. Then, to cut through the knot of the dispute that had begun, I said:

“Where the matter can be proved by our eyes, what need is there of an oath? Let us go, then, to the synagogue, and whether your assertion rests on fault or truth will be established with yourselves as witnesses.”

We therefore began to go toward the synagogue, singing a hymn to Christ through the streets in the joy of the multitude. The psalm, which was also sung with wonderful delight by the Jewish crowds, was this: “Their memory has perished with a crash, but the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 9).

Before we reached the synagogue, however, certain Jewish women—by God’s ordinance, I believe—venturing to presume upon their boldness so that the gentleness of our people might be stirred, began to hurl enormous stones at us from above. Astonishingly, although they descended like hail upon the densely packed crowd, they injured none of our people, not even by a blow, indeed not even by a touch.

Then that dreadful lion withdrew a little of his gentleness from his lambs. For everyone, despite our protests, seized stones; and, setting aside the shepherd’s admonition, while zeal for Christ rather than anger suggested one and the same course to all, they judged that the wolves should be attacked with horns. No one can doubt, however, that this was done by the will of him who alone is the good shepherd.

Finally, lest he seem to have granted his flock a bloody victory, none of the Jews even pretended to have been touched— not even out of envy, as is customary. Yet because we must avoid falsehood in every way, one man was found among the entire number of Christians who wished to be like Achan (Josh. 7), who, under Joshua son of Nun, coveted spoils from the devoted things. He was a servant of a certain Christian; alone, while desiring to seize something from the synagogue, he stumbled upon a stone of offense.

One of our people, as though against a Jew, threw a stone at him. It struck his head and reminded him to remember the head of his own body, that is, Christ. Although the wound was not dangerous, it nevertheless compelled him to confess his desire for plunder, and it terrified all the others by this immediate punishment, lest they should fall in the same way.

After the Jews yielded and we took possession of the synagogue, no one took anything from it—not only did no one carry anything away, but no one even considered plundering it. Fire consumed all its ornaments, together with the wall itself, except for the books and the silver. We removed the sacred books so that they would not suffer injury at the hands of the Jews. We returned the silver to them, so that they might not complain either of our plunder or of loss to their own property.

Thus, after the synagogue had been overturned while all the Jews looked on in astonishment, we proceeded to the church with hymns. Giving thanks to the author of our victory, we prayed fervently that the Lord would conquer the true caves of faithlessness and that the unbelief of those darkened hearts would be refuted by the light.

A certain Jew named Reuben was chosen by the Lord to be constituted the firstborn of all. For, bringing joy to many hearts with a most holy cry, he begged to be released from the bonds of Jewish superstition. Immediately made a firstborn Jacob, he received the sign of salvation; and from then on, clinging to our side and our counsels, he rebuked with us the obstinacy of them all.

Nearly three days, if I am not mistaken, had passed, during which our people persisted in prayer and the Jews in faithlessness. Afterwards Theodorus came, surrounded by the column of his multitude, to the place where only the walls of the synagogue seemed to remain; those walls were later overturned when the Jews believed. A multitude of Christians also gathered at the same place.

There Theodorus, speaking boldly about the Law, mocked and perverted everything that was brought against him. Seeing that he could not be overcome by human words, the Christian people implored help from heaven. All of them therefore cried out together, and with the loudest crash of united voices said: “Theodore, believe in Christ!”

The mercy of the most indulgent Lord is marvelous: small things were still being asked, and he had granted greater ones. Indeed, it is not surprising that the Almighty should perform a miracle. For he himself changed the power of this cry in the ears of the Jews—he who once caused the four lepers of the king of Syria, who had besieged Samaria, to take possession of the camp (2 Kings 7), and who, through Gideon, confused the hosts of the Midianites and gave his three hundred men a great victory without labor (Judg. 7), causing the enemy multitude, through terror, to be overthrown by wounds inflicted upon one another.

So now that cry was received by the Jews standing around in a very different way from that in which it was uttered by our people. For they all thought that what had been said was: “Theodorus has believed.” Believing, therefore, that the leader of their faithlessness had been converted to the faith of Christ, they were all terrified together, trembling where there was no fear.

Their women, running up with hair loosened and funerary wailing, accused Theodorus by repeating his name again and again: “O Theodore, what have you done?” Some of the men fled to pathless thickets and clefts in the mountains; others ran through the alleys of the town itself, seeking a place in which they might hide.

Theodorus himself, struck with astonishment, saw the divine judgment being fulfilled among his people. “The impious man flees though no one pursues him” (Prov. 28)—yet not with no one pursuing him. For that dreadful lion pursued them, the lion who, from the place of the synagogue, had sent forth a roar through the monks, as had been revealed to Theodorus, and by that roar had made the resisting enemies tremble.

Theodorus therefore stood in precisely the place where, formerly in his dream, the terror of the lion had been inflicted upon him. As he sought the cause of such great panic and heard only the name of our lion, he saw no ferocity there, as had been reported, but only monks chanting psalms. Abandoned by the whole multitude of his people and preparing to slip away, he too looked for a route by which to escape.

When that most holy Reuben saw him seized by dreadful fear and deprived not only of the color of his face but even of the use of his voice, he quickly approached. Addressing him with gentle speech while he trembled, he exhorted him to the faith of Christ. By presenting him, as a support, with the example of his own belief, and by the figure of the house to which Theodorus had fled in fear of the lion, he seemed in some way to fulfill the interpretation.

But, so that we may recount everything faithfully and so that you, who seek not eloquence but truth, may listen more willingly, I shall introduce the words of Reuben himself and omit nothing from the simplicity of his speech. He said:

“Why are you afraid, Lord Theodore? If you certainly wish to be secure, honored, and rich, believe in Christ, as I too have believed. At present you stand, while I sit with the bishops. If you believe, you too will sit, and I shall stand before you.”

Theodorus received these words deep within his mind and said to us:

“I shall do what you wish. Keep this promise,” he said. “But allow me first to address my people, so that I may receive an even greater reward for my conversion from the rest.”

His promise was received with unimaginable rejoicing by all. Some lovingly rushed upon him and caressed his face and neck; others embraced him with gentle arms; others longed to join right hand to right hand and begin conversation.

Theodorus therefore proceeded to his own courtyard, joyful at every service rendered by our people, yet not entirely free from anxiety. For although, by his promise, he was already entering the house of Reuben, he was still fearful as he went in, because he had not yet come to his close female relative, who after three days received him into her maternal embrace and freed him from all the disturbance of fear.

We meanwhile proceeded to the church with hymns, as was customary. Blessed is the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who gave water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes, so that we might weep over the wounded of our people (Lam. 1).

After the sacred rites had been completed, we left the church and saw that a considerable multitude of Jews had gathered to meet us. With one accord they begged to receive from me, although I was an unworthy shepherd, the mark of Christ. We therefore returned to the church and, giving thanks to the Lord with all our hearts, immediately impressed the sign of salvation upon their foreheads.

But what tongue could adequately tell what was accomplished by the power of Christ among those who had fled to the forests or caves, especially since each of them has his own history of conversion? Just as it is impossible for us to tell everything, so it would be ungrateful to pass over everything. Therefore, aided by your prayers, I shall unfold one miracle of Christ that we learned from men of the highest fidelity and trustworthiness.

Two prominent Jews, Meletius, the brother of Theodorus, and Innocentius, who had recently escaped the devastation of Spain and had come to this island with his servants—as they now themselves confirm even with the dreadful interposition of oaths—came together at a cave, or rather a rocky place, accompanied by two Jews of humble origin. These two had chosen them as leaders of the common flight.

After they had sat there for a short time, terrified and panting, they sent the two younger and bolder men back to the town to investigate and were left there alone. Then Meletius first said:

“Brother, why is it that I cannot tear from my heart a word that, as our religion teaches, is blasphemous? Ever since the Christian people shouted that my brother had been converted, nothing else is suggested to my heart except this word, entirely unknown to me until this day: ‘Christ, in your name.’ The more I strive to drive it from my mind, the more violently and tenaciously it clings to me.”

Innocentius replied:

“This utterance, which your heart, as everyone can attest, neither previously imagined nor ever uttered, has not without reason been inserted so violently into your mind, especially at this time. I think it is from God. Nevertheless, I beg you, exert yourself and, avoiding these fantasies, drive away the intrusion of this troubling thought.”

Then Meletius began to shout and resound with confused cries, so that Innocentius could see that he was wrestling with his own mind, not only from the movements of his face but also from the evidence of his whole body. When he understood that he was making no progress at all, Meletius went further: he spoke certain profane and shameful words, now wrinkling his nostrils and sucking in air while producing indecent noises, now breaking into foul laughter. Yet this madness could not extinguish the name of Christ from his mind, because the fire of healing had already penetrated all his marrow.

“What then,” he said, “brother Innocentius? These words turn against themselves. I cannot force the name of Christ out of me, neither by the scurrility of words nor by blasphemies uttered in obscene sounds. I feel that something else is being given back to me: an incessant cry does not cease to thrust the name of Christ into the ears of my heart, which I strive in vain to block.”

To these words of Meletius, Innocentius replied:

“With these ears, the Christian people testified that your brother Theodorus—your elder in learning, honor, and age—has been converted to the faith of Christ. Could it happen that you too, constrained by the example of your own brother, might abandon the Jewish religion? Why, then, are we wasting more time in this terrible solitude? How long will we be able to endure the hardship of lacking food? Why should we waste away from hunger, dry up with thirst, and stiffen from the cold? And finally—as we are already suffering—why should we be held by the dreadful silence of this solitude?

“Are we fleeing the bonds of brigands or the swords of barbarians? Does that merciful multitude, which we have seen weeping for us, desire our blood? Let us remember, I beg you, whom our people have ever harmed by force or even injured. Let us return to our harmless enemies, whom we have injured in nothing, and let what pleases God be done.”

Meletius replied:

“Brother Innocentius, I know that you are learned not only in Latin but also in Greek letters, and that you meditate continually upon the Law. Yet I think you have forgotten what the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: ‘The soul that sins, it shall die’ (Ezek. 12). If you have read this, why do you think that I can be drawn to the faith of Christ by the example of my brother Theodorus? He has his own soul, and likewise his own sin; that sin will not harm me if I do not abandon the Lord God.

“I call as witness him who led our fathers out of the land of Egypt: if the violence of winter did not prevent me, I would take any ship and migrate alone to any land. Neither love of possessions nor affection for those dear to me would hold me back; I could easily suffer their loss. I ask only not to be compelled to deny the God of my fathers.

“As for your useless plan that we should return to the city, I am astonished that, although you are a very prudent man, you do not foresee in your mind what you think will happen to us if Theodorus—the pillar of our synagogue, in whom we placed all our confidence—has been forced to apostatize.

“It is therefore wiser for us to go to my estate and not expose ourselves any further to the eyes of the Christians. We can hide there for the time being until, at a suitable moment, we emigrate to foreign lands. For hatred of our religion has increased among everyone on this island, so that one who does not leave his homeland cannot retain the faith of his fathers.

“Why, then, should we not accept voluntary exile, to which—as circumstances show—we shall be driven by the hatred of our fellow citizens even against our will?”

With this plan, the judgment of both was confirmed, and they undertook the labor of the journey they had determined upon.

But as they entered a very narrow path, the darkness of their thoughts obscuring the light of their eyes, they lost the very trail they had been following unknowingly and remained in deserted and impassable places. When they were torn by thorns or blocked by rocks [perhaps: “were lacerated by brambles”], after disfiguring their bodies with long wounds, they first reached such anxiety and then such despair and fear that they were compelled to confess that they were suffering these things by God’s just judgment because of their unbelief.

They therefore invoked the name of Christ, which they had previously rejected when it thrust itself forward of its own accord. With their legs now lacerated, they seized the path that led them back to the town against their will and intention. But when they reached the city unwillingly and in terror, making careful inquiries about everything, they heard that Theodorus was still a Jew and had suffered none of the violence from the Christian people that they had imagined.

Astonished and unable to believe what had happened to them, they directed their journey to Theodorus’s house. When he received them there, with the meal almost over, he immediately asked why they had withdrawn from him and from the city. He learned the entire sequence of events, more with laughter than with astonishment.

After three days, when Theodorus was preparing to address his people and summon them to the faith of Christ, he even had to endure a disturbance among the Jews who were offering themselves for confession. For scarcely any one of them failed to testify publicly that he had personally experienced the power of Christ.

At their first council, a certain young man, Theodorus’s cousin, named Galilaeus, began to proclaim with great indignation—so that the mystery appropriate to the names might, as has been said, be brought to its conclusion:

“I call you all to witness that I cannot remain in possession as a Jew. For I have Christians as co-owners with me; if I wish to persist in Judaism, perhaps I shall have to be killed by their hatred. I shall therefore take thought for my life and now go to the church, so that I may escape the death being prepared for me.”

Galilaeus spoke the truth unknowingly. As he prepared for flight for the moment, he seemed to have given the reasons for his conversion, yet at that time he was thinking nothing of the death of the future age.

A respectable man who happened to be passing by, Caecilianus—distinguished not only among the Jews but also throughout the city, so much so that he has now been elected Defender of the City—affirmed that Galilaeus was speaking truly and testified that he had a similar reason and feared similar things. By these words he gave the young man mentioned above such confidence that, in the sight of everyone, he rushed with the greatest speed to seek the help of our Galilaeus in receiving the prize of faith, and asked our humility that he might thereafter be counted by the same name.

Caecilianus was the father of the Jews. After consulting with his brother Florinus, likewise the father and elder of the Jews, he addressed the synagogue in these words, as we learned:

“I, who hold the first place in the honor of the synagogue after Theodorus, do not, like the young Galilaeus, timidly consult and call everyone to witness. Rather, I exhort and admonish you, declaring that, if it is possible, we should all together abandon the error of the crooked path and hasten to the faith of the Church.

“If such power does not draw you to Christ, I certainly cannot impose so great a salvation upon you against your will—nor can my brother Florinus. Yet we, together with our entire household, shall abandon the mockery of this religion, which we cannot uphold, and join the number and faith of the Christians. Otherwise, innumerable testimonies of the Scriptures would surely convict not only you, brother Theodore, who seem more learned than the rest, but all of you, unless they were following the truth, which cannot be overcome.”

We learned that Caecilianus addressed his people in this spirit, and we received many Jews who, together with him, hastened to the faith of Christ that same day, with unspeakable rejoicing.

The prodigies that then occurred from heaven I cannot adequately express [perhaps: “add”], yet I do not dare to remain silent about them. At about the seventh hour we solemnly began to celebrate the Lord’s Mass. For while we were exhorting the Jews who came to the faith of Christ, or recording their names—for we wrote them down—the greater part of the day had passed, while the people, sated with the feasts of so great a joy, had forgotten bodily food.

The whole people was waiting for Mass with us in the church, which stands somewhat apart from the city in an outlying place and where the recently buried relics of the holy martyr Stephen rest. Two monks, whom the Lord had chosen beforehand as witnesses of his miracles, were lying in the grass in the field extending before the church doors.

A man of honor named Julius, coming toward the church with another man from the city, had just begun to pass by them when one of the monks looked back [or: “responded”]. Struck by the marvelous sign, Julius uttered a confused cry, then turned toward himself and, extending his hand, showed what he saw, which he could not explain in words.

There was a globe of exceptionally white light, whose height almost equaled the stature of a man. It resembled the vessels commonly called *orcae*, but it possessed such brilliance and radiance that, as we learned from the report of the brother who first noticed it, the sun seemed to that brother to be falling.

As it appeared to these men, the globe descended in a slow movement as though across the basilica in which the entire people was seated with us. They thought it so near that the same brother, overcome with astonishment, ran forward, supposing that it had fallen behind the basilica. But the other brother pulled him back and halted his step. He too had indeed seen it in this way, but he asserted that it had been farther away, not as one certain but as one making an estimate.

Certain Jewish women who were then looking out from an upper room, among them the wife of that Meletius mentioned above, affirmed that they had seen precisely the same thing, as though it had fallen above the basilica. Yet whether what appeared was an angel or Stephen himself remains uncertain.

At about the fourth hour of that same day—that is, a little before this sign was displayed—very fine hail fell, not everywhere in abundance. The island’s inhabitants call it *Abgistinum* in their pagan language. When a scent of honey began to waft from it, many of those whom it had struck along the road tasted it and found it sweeter than honey.

Many wise men, seeing that on the same day the children of Israel had gone forth from Egypt—from their faithlessness and slavery—compared what had happened with those signs that we read in Exodus (Exod. 16). They believed that manna had been renewed for this people, who, looking upon God with a believing heart, had even earned the name of Israel. They also thought that the column of fire which had preceded the fathers in the wilderness had been displayed, so that it might provide guidance to their children also, who had gone forth from the true Egypt and furnace—as it is written (Exod. 13)—of iron, leading them toward life.

Indeed, as the reading of Exodus bears witness, the likeness of the signs differs in no respect. For what we believed to have been snow matched the small seed of coriander and bore the taste of honey; and it is clear that what appeared had the form of a fiery column.

We also learn that both signs were revealed to the brethren residing at Jammon. Many tasted the rain of honey, and those to whom the ability had been given to seek its meaning and recognize it by taste confirmed it. Likewise, that column of exceptionally white light presented itself to the eyes of many whom the Lord judged worthy.

From this it may be understood that Jews throughout the world are to be visited by the light of faith. For the splendor of heavenly grace shone so brightly upon us, who dwell on this island and in this small world, so to speak, that the sight of the signs reached even to the farthest boundaries of your land.

On the following day, the eager expectation of all reminded Theodorus that he should fulfill his promise. He thought that the wishes of everyone should be postponed on what seemed to be valid grounds, saying that he wished first to bring here his wife, whom he had left on the island of Majorca. Otherwise, if she learned that her husband had been converted without her consent—as often happens—she might persist in unbelief and, especially through the persuasion of her mother, who was still alive and had been made foolish by her counsels, might withdraw from her husband and from religion.

When Theodorus disclosed this to the Christians, who had already assented, the converted Jews resisted with the greatest agitation. The delay was cut short, and Theodorus himself, joyful, hurried to the embrace of his close female relative, just as he had seen in his dream.

After him, the entire synagogue flowed into the Church, as though an obstacle had been removed. Astonishingly, the ancient teachers of that Law believed without any verbal dispute and without any contest over the Scriptures. They merely asked whether they wished to accept the faith of Christ; they declared that they believed in Christ and desired to become Christians.

One man, as they say, was one hundred and two years old, possessing that age as well as the long duration of his unbelief. Without exchanging three words, lively with hope of the future life, the decrepit old man expressed his wish that, at the end of his days, he might return through the faith of Christ to spiritual infancy. He offered us his limbs, already decayed with age, so that he might be regenerated through baptism as quickly as possible.

There were certain Jews who, passing through and arriving there, were watching for an opportunity provided by time and winds. When the opportunity for sailing was granted, they preferred to believe.

Thus Christ allowed only three women, but the most distinguished of the Jews, to remain for a while in the hardness of their unbelief, in order to extend the glory of his power.

Arthemisia, daughter of Lectorius [MS: Lettorius], who recently governed this province and is now said to be a Count, was moved by the conversion of Meletius’s wife. Leaving her husband’s house with one close friend, a nurse, and a few female servants, she overcame her feminine weakness and went to a certain cave. Although it was in a vineyard, it stood in a somewhat more remote place.

In it there was a small and new winepress, and a new vat had been made there. It seemed in some way to represent the people of believers. For we believe and see that the new wine of the New Testament was received not into old wineskins but into new vats.

In that place the matron remained inexorable for two days, offended with her husband. As soon as the third day dawned, she ordered the female servants to draw water. When she sensed that it conveyed the sweetness of honey in both smell and taste, she first began to be angry with the maidservant and indignantly asked why she had put honey into the same jar.

Then, wishing to expose her as though she were denying it, she went to the vat. Drawing a little water with hollowed hands, she discovered that the water she had used for two days had been changed into the sweetness of the sweetest honey.

She called all who were present and asked them to taste it, lest a deceptive flavor be falsely presenting sweetness only in her own mouth. All who tasted it were filled with extraordinary delight. They judged that it was not water tinged with the taste of honey but the purest honey, merely resembling water.

Struck with astonishment, as they prepared to return to the city they made further inquiries and found, when they tasted it, that even the dew lying upon many of the grasses was similar. The matron then went to the city, reported these things to her husband, and through him made them known to everyone. Immediately she consented without resistance to the faith of Christ.

On that same day on which Meletius’s wife was compelled by the honey to cast away the bitterness of unbelief—on that same day, I say, on which the daughter of Israel just mentioned, as though placed in the wilderness, perceived that the ancient pool of Marah (Exod. 15) had been sweetened by the insertion of the wood of the Cross—the whole Church was so filled with a truly wondrous and heavenly fragrance that nearly the entire brotherhood sensed the presence of the Holy Spirit. We had already sensed it on several occasions, but only a very few of us had done so.

It was also a wonder to everyone that during those days, although the weather remained almost continually clear, very frequent rains fell, and rain preceded the Jews who gradually came to the faith of Christ. Observing this, we used to say among ourselves, half jokingly: “Look, it is raining already; know that whichever Jews are going to come to the faith of Christ are approaching.”

Astonishingly, while we were still often saying such things, the door of faith was being knocked upon by certain Jews. And not without reason, as it is written: “The Lord will set apart a rain of free gift for his inheritance” (Ps. 67). There remained women who refused to run after the fragrance of Christ’s ointments.

That venerable widow, as report has it, a female relative of the above-mentioned Innocentius, boarded a ship with her offspring as soon as she saw that the husband of Innocentius’s sister had converted. We not only permitted but even urged this, because neither words nor miracles could bend them to the faith of Christ.

Innocentius’s wife, however, for nearly four days received the word of salvation that we pressed upon her with hardened ears. Rejecting every remedy, she was oppressed by an incurable sickness of unbelief and could be moved by none of the threats, prayers, or tears of her husband Innocentius.

At Innocentius’s request, the entire multitude of the brotherhood gathered at the house where she lived. They were deeply grieved that one woman should oppose the fullness of such great joy, since she was already clearly regarded as their sister.

When we had long poured empty words into deaf ears and accomplished nothing, we hastened to the familiar aid of prayer. We turned to heavenly mercy with the prayers that human impiety had rejected.

Thus, until approximately the third hour, our army sweated in the battles of hymns and prayers against the enemy Amalek (Exod. 17), under the leadership of our commander Jesus. Then, when we were preparing to withdraw, almost despairing—as must be admitted—we gathered our strength again and ordered everyone to pray. We lay prostrate on the ground and wept for a long time.

When, at the completion of the prayer, the people had cried out, “Amen,” she added that she believed and wished to become a Christian. We therefore returned joyfully to our lodgings, since she too had been rescued from the devil’s snares.

On the following day, finally the eighth day after we had come to Jammon, we decided to return, carrying away the best and most splendid joys of victory. But when we had already set out for the journey and were leaving the city, the Lord added to his people, as though for provisions on the way, the one joy that seemed still to be lacking.

That widow, Innocentius’s relative, was brought back from the sea. Suddenly she threw herself at my knees and begged with tears for the help of our faith. I said to her:

“Why, woman, did you wish to abandon your brothers with such fickleness of mind?”

She replied:

“The prophet Jonah also wished to flee from the presence of the Lord, yet he fulfilled the will of God, although unwillingly (Jonah 1). Receive, therefore, not only me but also these orphan girls, and raise them for Christ.”

As she cried this out pitifully, she pressed her two little daughters upon me with tears. Who did not weep for joy? Whom did the greatness of that joy not force to shed tears? I certainly received the sheep whom we had thought to be the only one strayed from the entire flock, and with her twin offspring I brought her back to Christ’s sheepfolds.

Surely during these days in which these events took place, before the beginning of Lent, the feast of Easter was celebrated by us: for it is established that five hundred and forty souls were added to the Church. I do not consider it empty or superfluous, when I have omitted many things because of their infinite number, to mention at the end that no one among so great a multitude of the people of Jammona—who had come from thirty thousand paces away so many days earlier—preferred the care of his household, the provision of their livelihood, or the affection of desire to this work. Still more wonderful, and more worthy of rejoicing, is that we see the very land of the Jewish people, long unproductive but now, after the brambles of unbelief have been cut away and the seed of the word received, producing a manifold harvest of righteousness: so that we rejoice in hope over such new fields, from which we uprooted a notable forest of unbelief, and see the most fertile works of faith sprouting there. For first they overturn the very foundations of the synagogue; then, in building a new basilica, they contribute not only financial resources but also carry stones on their shoulders.

Let your Blessedness know that this was undertaken by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ on the fourth day before the Nones of February, and completed by him eight days later, after the eleventh consulship of our lord Honorius and the second consulship of Constantius the victor. Therefore, if you graciously admit the word of one unworthy and sinful, accept zeal for Christ against the Jews—but for God’s sake and for their perpetual salvation. For perhaps the time foretold by the Apostle has now arrived, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved. And perhaps the Lord wished this spark from the farthest end of the earth to be kindled, so that the whole world might blaze with the fire of charity.

Thus far the letter of Bishop Severus. For, as we have said, this was sent to all the faithful of Christ and, among other places, was also read at Uzalis in Africa, where Bishop Evodius was, as we mentioned earlier.

## In the Year of Our Lord 419

## Saint Boniface I, Pope

*(Coustant, Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, vol. I.)*

[Col. 0745]

[Col. 0745]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0745C] 1. After the funeral rites of Zosimus had been performed, on the following day—that is, December 28 of the year 418—when the presbyters, together with the people, had assembled in the church of Theodora, Boniface, an elderly presbyter, was elected. On the following day, the 29th, which fell on a Sunday, he was unwillingly consecrated bishop of the city of Rome in the church of Saint Marcellus, amid the acclamation of the entire people and with the consent of the city’s leading citizens, approximately seventy presbyters subscribing and nine bishops of different regions standing in attendance.

2. On that same day as Zosimus’s funeral rites, the archdeacon Eulalius, accompanied by other deacons, a very few presbyters, and a multitude of the disturbed populace, went to the Lateran basilica. After remaining there for two days, he was ordained on Sunday by the Bishop of Ostia, whom he had summoned against his will.

3. On that same day, December 29, Symmachus, prefect of the City, informed the emperor Honorius about both ordinations in such a way as openly to favor Eulalius. The emperor replied on January 3 of the year 419 that his vote and support properly favored Eulalius, since the appropriate number of ordaining bishops, the proper liturgical season, and the suitability of the place had rightly conferred upon him the venerable dignity of the name; but since it was clear that Boniface had lacked all these things, his own decision had been awaited needlessly. Boniface, therefore, was immediately to be forbidden the City, or, if he resisted, expelled. Symmachus reported to the emperor on January 8 how this command of Honorius had been received.

4. At the same time, however, the Roman presbyters sent the same emperor a more truthful account of Boniface’s ordination, asking him to order the two elected men, together with those responsible for their elections, to come to his court, so that he might more easily investigate the truth of the matter himself. Their pleas seemed entirely just to him. Accordingly, on January 15 he sent a second rescript to Symmachus, suspending what had previously been decreed. He ordered Boniface and Eulalius, together with their supporters, to hasten to Ravenna by the sixth day before the Ides of February, and indicated that he had summoned in the meantime an appropriate number of bishops from various provinces, so that the case might be examined in a synod.

5. The case was then investigated through a full examination by the bishops. But since it could not be concluded because of the parties’ persistent dispute, and since the bishops who had assembled considered themselves too few to deliver judgment on a matter of such importance, while the days of Easter were also approaching and required the bishops’ presence in their own churches, the pious emperor decided that the entire affair should be postponed until after that solemnity. In the meantime it was decreed that Achilleus should go to Rome to celebrate the Easter solemnities there, and that neither Boniface nor Eulalius should enter the city. In particular, as Honorius puts it, this was determined by “our ordinance and the judgment of the bishops, of whom the greater multitude had assembled in the synod,” and also by the consent and formal declaration of the parties, so that anyone who entered the City to stir up the people might know that he had been specifically condemned.

6. Nevertheless, Eulalius soon forgot his own declaration and entered the City on March 18, where he caused enormous disturbances. Indeed, although ordered to leave the City by Honorius’s letter to Symmachus dated March 25, he did not fear to remain there stubbornly. But by his impatience he condemned himself, and, as Honorius rightly judged, proved by his present conduct what sort of beginning he appeared to have had. For that reason the same emperor sent this rescript to Symmachus on April 3:

“Since, therefore, it is clear that he was rightly expelled from the City after so many offenses, let your Eminence know that we have determined that the venerable bishop Boniface should enter the City, to whose moderation we have rightly judged that our authority ought to be joined.”

He immediately took care that the bishops whom he had summoned from the Gallic and African regions to a council to be held at Spoleto by the twelfth day before the Kalends of June should be informed that the affair had been concluded and settled, and therefore should spare themselves the labor of this journey. That the Africans were informed with exceptional diligence is proved by their letter to Boniface, written on May 31. All the documents from which we have drawn these preliminary remarks may be consulted in full in Baronius, under the years 418 and 419.

7. After the episcopate of the Roman Church had been assigned and confirmed to Boniface, he devoted very considerable effort to claiming for his own church the jurisdiction over the provinces of Illyricum which some were attempting to transfer to the bishop of the city of Constantinople.

8. He died in the year 422—indeed, according to the ancient martyrologies of Jerome, in which none of Boniface’s successors is subsequently recorded—on September 4. Several ancient catalogues of the Roman bishops agree exactly with this date; they define his pontificate as three years, eight months, and six or seven days. For from December 29 of the year 418, on which we said that Boniface was ordained, to September 4 of the year 422, the same number of years, months, and days is counted.

The Latin and Greek writers also agree with the catalogues mentioned above, if one excepts Nicephorus and certain editions of Prosper, in which four years are assigned to Boniface. Yet even this can be reconciled conveniently with the others if “the fourth year” is understood as not completed. Baronius’s opinion therefore cannot stand: he places Boniface’s death not only in the year 423, on the supposed authority of the Chronicles of Marcellinus and Prosper, but also on November 24, in agreement with the pontifical books. For although, in the Chronicles mentioned above, the accession to the pontificate of Celestine, who succeeded Boniface, appears to be assigned to the year 423, it is nevertheless recorded before the death of Honorius, which occurred in August of the year 423.

## Letters and Decrees

[Col. 0749]

## Letters and Decrees of Saint Boniface I, Pope

*(C, S)*

## Notice concerning the Three Following Letters

[Col. 0749A]

Various documents relating to the election and ordination of Boniface, and to the origin of the schism then arising, were first copied by Baronius from a Vatican manuscript and published at the end of the year 418, or at the beginning of 419, in the order in which they were written in the archetype. First comes the report of Symmachus, dated December 29 of the year 418, by which the prefect attempts to persuade Honorius that Eulalius had been duly elected pontiff of the Roman city, while Boniface had been ordained “contrary to the order of sacred law and the rule of custom.”

Then follows the rescript of Honorius to the same Symmachus, dated January 3 of the year 419, in which he declares that he regards Eulalius’s ordination as valid and Boniface’s as void. He therefore forbids Boniface the City, or, if he does not obey voluntarily, orders that “he be expelled against his will while resisting stubbornly.”

This rescript is followed by a second report of Symmachus, dated January 8, in which he informs the emperor that he had received the emperor’s command on that day, “on which the solemnity of the holy day [Epiphany] was to be celebrated,” and that he had immediately taken steps to carry out the orders. But Boniface, although ordered to refrain from the procession that had been announced, had refused to obey.

Symmachus gained nothing by this. The Roman presbyters, unwilling that he should continue deceiving the emperor, thought that his false account had to be countered with a more truthful one. They therefore composed a petition, which Honorius, writing back to Symmachus on January 15, testifies that he had received. It follows that it was sent either on that very day, the day of Symmachus’s second report, or not long afterward.

Among those documents written on this matter, none is more important to reproduce here than the petition just mentioned, since in it Boniface’s ordination and qualifications are explained more clearly and honestly by his own clergy.

## Letter I

[Note: Written in the year 419, before the middle of January.]

## The Roman Presbyters to the Emperor Honorius, or a Copy of the Presbyters’ Petition on Behalf of Boniface

Boniface’s ordination was legitimate, but Eulalius’s was illegitimate.

[Col. 0750A]

1. We ask your Clemency, most pious and most merciful emperors, Honorius and Theodosius, ever august. After the departure of the holy Pope Zosimus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, as custom required and the discipline of religion itself dictated, many of us priests assembled together so that we might deliberate by common judgment concerning the appointment of a successor.

But because the archdeacon Eulalius had occupied the Lateran church, almost all its entrances having been blocked, and had impiously disregarded the funeral rites of the supreme priest,

[Note: Namely, Zosimus. On this point Symmachus’s first report says: “Eulalius was led by the people and clergy from the funeral rites of the preceding bishop to the Lateran church; there he remained for two days with a very large multitude and with several priests, so that the customary day might be awaited on which he could be solemnly ordained.” It follows that Eulalius is reproached here for having spurned Zosimus’s funeral rites either because he departed from them not without disturbance or, rather, because he left them before they had been completed. Thus Eulalius was compelled to wait two days for the lawful day of ordination, whereas Boniface, withdrawing on the day after the funeral rites had been performed to the agreed location, was not compelled to wait for another day.]

surrounding himself with deacons, a very few presbyters, and a multitude of the disturbed populace, we hastened on the following day, December 28, to the same church,

[Note: Namely, the church named after Theodora, as Symmachus’s first report teaches. Yet we may also infer from this that, had it then been permitted, the ordination of the Roman pontiff should have been performed in the Lateran basilica; Honorius confirms this when he approves Eulalius’s ordination also because the suitability of the place commended it.]

where all had previously agreed to assemble, after a general conference had been held there. After taking counsel together with the Christian people, we elected the man whom God commanded us to elect.

For we selected the venerable man Boniface, an elderly presbyter, most learned in the law, approved for his good morals, and—what adorned him still more—unwilling, though consecrated according to the order of divine institution, amid the acclamation of the entire people and the consent of the city’s leading citizens.

[Note: The printed editions read “we asserted”; this is corrected from the Vatican archetype.]

[Note: This is thought to be the presbyter Boniface who, together with other envoys of the emperor Honorius, carried to the emperor Arcadius in the year 406 the letter that is the ninth among Innocent’s letters; and to whom, while he was serving as an embassy in Constantinople, Innocent’s Letter 23 is extant. The earlier report of Symmachus states that Boniface was ordained in the church of Marcellus.]

For approximately seventy presbyters subscribed, and nine bishops of different provinces were present. It is established that the blessing was celebrated at the appropriate time.

[Note: The emperor Honorius first asserted that Eulalius’s ordination, and therefore its legitimacy, rested on the fact that the proper liturgical season had been observed. Earlier Symmachus, as we heard above, had written that the customary day on which he could be ordained had been awaited. Now the Roman presbyters testify that Boniface’s blessing was celebrated at the appropriate time. Boniface’s predecessor Zosimus, in Letter 4, section 2, considers Lazarus’s ordination objectionable on the ground that not even the legitimate day of ordination had been observed. From these testimonies it is evident that, at that time, a specific day had been prescribed for a legitimate ordination. Leo indicates this day at the end of Letter 5: Sunday.]

And previously everything required by the solemnity had been completed.

[Note: Thus the Vatican exemplar. The printed editions read, “the solemnity was celebrated”; the archetype has been restored here.]

[Col. 0751A] 2. But when the aforementioned Eulalius, who had previously been summoned by three of our fellow priests on the authority of many people, so that he would not presumptuously assume anything against the conscience of the greater clergy, had surrounded a very few presbyters, mistreated and consigned to different custody those who had come with letters to prevent this, and had also produced, together with others, the Bishop of Ostia—

[Note: Clearly this was intended to lend authority to his ordination, since, as Augustine observes in the Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists, part 3, chapter 16, section 29, “no metropolitan bishop ordains the bishop of the Roman Church; rather, the Bishop of Ostia does so as the nearest bishop.”]

—who, as is evident, had been summoned when almost at the point of death—for the old man’s illness shows that he was unwilling to be dragged there—he had rushed into a place not assigned to him, disregarding the order of religion and through intrigue. He began indecorously to defend his action through men ignorant of discipline and unacquainted with religion,

[Note: They covertly allude to Symmachus, whose father, alien from the worship of Christ, had fought against Ambrose to restore the altar of Victory and revive pagan superstitions. His son himself reveals that he followed his father’s profane religion when, in his report to Constantius, published by Baronius under the year 419, he states that he did not strive to enter the Lateran basilica in order to expel Eulalius from it because, as he says, “lest someone who was my rival should bring envy upon me for my religion.”]

thinking that he could confuse the divine judgment through human disturbances.

3. Since it is clear that your Clemency was deceived by a false report,

[Col. 0751B] [Note: That is, by the report of Symmachus. Accordingly, in the report given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, the prefect asks the emperor: “It remains for your Clemency that your servants, always approved by their pure service to your Majesty, not be attacked in their absence by the partiality of factions.” Here he indirectly implies that he had been accused of having given a false account in this matter through partisan zeal.]

so that you might enact something injurious to the divine judgment—for whatever the election of so many people confirms is divine—

[Note: The common editions read “of the divine gift,” contrary to the authority of the archetype.]

we ask your Piety to order the previous decisions removed,

[Note: Yielding to this petition, the emperor declared in a memorandum that no prejudice had been established against either party by what had earlier been decreed by us, since the commands already issued had promptly been withdrawn, in accordance with our piety, for the sake of the people’s peace.]

and that Eulalius, who has intruded into another’s place, be brought with his supporters to the court of your Perpetuity.

[Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript. The printed editions read “to the court of your Serenity.” The final words of this petition, in which thanks are given to the Eternal Empire rather than to the Serene Empire, confirm our reading. Honorius, accepting this part of the petition, ordered Boniface and Eulalius, together with all who had supported either ordination, to assemble at Ravenna by the sixth day before the Ides of February. He nevertheless stipulated that an appropriate number of priests from different provinces should be summoned at the same time to judge the two ordinations, and that those who had taken part in either ordination and later subscribed should not sit among the judges, as was established in the memorandum.]

For we declare that the holy Pope Boniface will be present with our priests.

[Note: The printed editions read, “all the presbyters, leaving each one in his title.” We restore the reading of the archetype.]

For, with each presbyter remaining in his own titular church, all will be present to proclaim their will—that is, the judgment of God. Let your Clemency also order all those whom the case concerns to be present; let those who are unwilling to be brought be expelled from the city.

When the inner examination begins, you will find that this not only conflicts with the divine laws but may also displease human ones.

[Note: The common editions read, “which is wholly divine.” The Vatican exemplar has a corrupt reading, apparently beginning with *quod ns divinis*. The sequence of the sentence requires *quod non solum divinis* (“which not only conflicts with divine [laws]”), with only the initial letters represented. The same manuscript later has *horreat*, not *abhorreat*, requiring the preposition *a* before *divinis*.]

For having achieved this, we shall offer your Eternal Empire the greatest and fullest thanks.

## Letter II

[Note: Written in the year 419, May 31. In an old Colbertine exemplar written in Lombard letters, it also occupies a place in the first part of the Dionysian collection. It is inserted in its entirety in chapter 134 of the Code of the African Church. As chapter 133 of that same Code states, the Africans assembled after the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, on the third day before the Kalends of June, with Aurelius presiding, and decided that it should be written for them on the following day. It follows that it was written in the year 419, on the last day of May.]

## From the Entire African Council to Boniface, Bishop of the City of Rome

[Note: In the Colbertine Lombard manuscript the following is added here: “written and with the acts”—read *gestis* for *gesta*—which were prepared there at Carthage by Faustinus. This agrees with what the Africans write in section 3, where they mention the memorandum of Zosimus, attached to the acts that the envoys were carrying with them to Boniface.]

Sent through Faustinus the bishop and Philip and Asellus the presbyters, envoys of the Roman Church.

They declare that they will observe the provisions concerning the cases of clerics and the appeals of bishops contained in the memorandum of Zosimus until they have examined authentic copies of the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

To the most blessed and honorable brother, BONIFACE, Aurelius Valentinus, of the first see of the province of Numidia, and the other 217 members of the entire council of Africa who were present.

1. Since it has pleased the Lord that our Humility should reply concerning what our holy brothers, our fellow bishop Faustinus and our fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, have done with us—not to the bishop Zosimus of blessed memory, from whom they brought us instructions and letters, but to your Veneration, who by divine appointment have been established in his place—we must briefly set forth what was settled by agreement between both parties, not what is contained in the lengthy volumes of the acts. In those matters we remained, while preserving charity, yet not without some labor of dispute, drawing from the acts what now pertains to the case.

[Note: The parties in dispute are meant, namely the presbyter Apiarius and Urbanus, bishop of Sicca, whose names are omitted here because they were already sufficiently known to Boniface and will soon be mentioned.]

Although that man too, if he were still alive, would receive this more gratefully, since he would see the matter settled more peacefully, lord brother.

[Note: The printed editions, except Crabbe and most manuscripts, read “deliberating on these matters from the acts.” The conjectural restoration “drawing from the acts” later received support from one Harlaean and one Coislinian manuscript, in which, as in Crabbe, the reading is *ea gestis delibantes*.]

2. The presbyter Apiarius, whose ordination, excommunication, and appeal had occasioned no small scandal not only in the Church of Sicca but throughout the whole Church of Africa, was restored to communion after asking pardon for all his offenses.

[Note: Crabbe alone has *toti* (“the whole”), which is not unsuitable if, with the printed editions and several manuscripts, it is followed by *Africanae*. But the word *totius* requires *Africae*. The Greek interpreter of the Code of the African Church renders the passage thus: “not only in Sicca, but also in the whole Church of Africa.”]

Our former fellow bishop Urbanus of Sicca, however, corrected without hesitation whatever in his conduct appeared to require correction.

[Note: The phrase “in him” refers not to Apiarius but to Urbanus. The Africans therefore give this testimony concerning that bishop because, as is explained below in section 3, Zosimus had ordered him to be excommunicated unless he corrected whatever appeared to require correction.]

But since provision had to be made for the peace and tranquility of the Church not only for the present but also for the future, since many such things had occurred before and similar or even more serious matters had to be prevented thereafter, it seemed good to us that Apiarius should be removed from the presbyterate of the Church of Sicca, while retaining the honor of his rank,

[Note: Augustine used a similar measure toward Antonius, whom he had appointed bishop of Fussala, and defended this practice by other examples in Letter 261, now 209. Justellus observes that a similar practice was approved both by the Council of Ancyra, canons 1 and 2, and by the Council of Nicaea, canon 8, as well as in the synodal letter preserved in Theodoret, Book I, chapter 9, by which Meletius was allowed to retain merely the title of his former honor.]

and that, after receiving a letter of communion, he should exercise the office of presbyter wherever else he wished and was able.

[Note: The same term, *epistolium*, is used in this sense by the Council of Sardica, above, p. 398, and by Liberius, Letter 10, section 1. In both places, as here, it means a letter of communion.]

We granted this without difficulty when he himself requested it by a personal letter.

3. Before this case was brought to a close in this way, while we were discussing various other matters in lengthy debates,

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads *versabantur*, “were under discussion.”]

since reason itself required us to ask our brothers, our fellow bishop Faustinus and our fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, in the ecclesiastical records, to disclose whatever instructions had been given to them concerning their dealings with us, they did indeed explain certain matters in words without any written document. But when we pressed them especially for what they had brought in writing, they produced a memorandum which, after being read to us, was attached to the acts that they had brought with them to you.

[Note: The Greek interpreter reads “to us.” The reading *est alligatum* (“was attached”) is preferable, with the Regius manuscript and one Harlaean, to *est allegatum* (“was cited”), found in other books; likewise below *alligaverunt* is preferable to *allegaverunt*. They appear to be referring to the acts of the previous year, when the letters of Zosimus were first read.]

In it they were given four instructions to carry out with us: first, concerning appeals by bishops to the priest of the Roman Church; second, that bishops should not sail to the imperial court at an inconvenient time; third, concerning the cases of presbyters and deacons before neighboring bishops

[Note: The word “bishops” is wrongly inserted here in the Colbertine manuscript, and is excluded by what follows: “if by their own”—supply “bishops.”]

if they had been unjustly excommunicated by their own bishops; and fourth, concerning the excommunication of Bishop Urbanus, or even his summons to Rome, unless he corrected whatever appeared to require correction.

[Col. 0754A] [Note: The Vatican exemplar, together with Merlinius and Crabbe, preserves this reading. Other books have “or summoned to Rome.” From this passage a learned man conjectures that Urbanus had committed some offense against the proper judicial procedure in judging Apiarius. Perhaps his entire fault consisted in treating Apiarius’s appeal as null and void, and for this reason dealing somewhat harshly with the presbyter.]

4. Concerning the first and third of these matters—that is, that bishops should be permitted to appeal to Rome, and that the cases of clerics should be concluded before the bishops of their own provinces—we had already taken care, in the previous year, to inform the same bishop Zosimus of venerable memory by letters of our own,

[Note: These letters are not extant.]

so that, without any injury to him, we might for a short time observe these provisions until the statutes of the Council of Nicaea had been investigated.

And now we ask your Holiness to cause us to observe whatever was done or established by the fathers at Nicaea, and to have these matters which they brought in the memorandum applied there among you, namely:

“If a bishop has been accused, and the bishops of that region have assembled, judged him, and deposed him from his rank; and if he appears to have appealed and taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes to be heard, and he judges that the examination ought to be renewed, let him write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth.

“But if the one who asks that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a presbyter from his own side, it shall be within the power of the bishop to decide what he wishes and considers appropriate. And if he decides that men should be sent who will judge in person together with the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, that shall remain at his discretion.

“But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges in his most wise counsel.”

Likewise, concerning presbyters and deacons, from canon 7 of the Council of Sardica:

“If any bishop, being angry—as he ought not to be—and quickly or harshly stirred up against his presbyter or deacon, should wish to expel him from the Church, care must be taken that an innocent man not be condemned or lose communion. Let the expelled man have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and let his case be heard and examined more carefully, since an audience ought not to be denied to one who asks for it.

“And let that bishop who expelled him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be examined, so that either his judgment may be approved or corrected.”

[Note: One or two years after the Sardican council, the Council of Carthage under Gratus, canon 11, decreed that a deacon should be accused by three neighboring bishops and a presbyter heard by six. Augustine, mentioning this decree in Letter 236, now 65, section 2, does not conceal the inconvenience he fears may result from it.]

[Note: The Regius codex reads “it ought to be denied,” and below, together with the Colbertine, “he unjustly rejected,” omitting *eum*. The Greek interpreter likewise did not express it.]

5. These provisions, then, until authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea arrive, have been inserted into the acts from the most truthful copies of the Council of Nicaea. If they were preserved there, exactly as they were established and exactly as they are contained in the memorandum which the brothers sent from the apostolic see cited before us, and if they were preserved in that same order among you in Italy,

[Note: Merlin and Justellus, as well as two Regius manuscripts, one Harlaean, and the Colbertine-Corbey manuscript, read *quae sibi* (“which belong to themselves”). The reading *quae si ibi* (“which, if they are there”), supported by two Coislinian and two Harlaean manuscripts, Crabbe, and Labbe, is preferable and agrees with the Greek, which has: “which, if they are there.” The words “exactly as they were established and” had been omitted in the common editions and most manuscripts; they are restored on the authority of one Harlaean and another Colbertine manuscript.]

we would in no way be forced either to mention or to endure such things as we now prefer not to mention, or to suffer intolerable treatment.

[Note: Merlin, Crabbe, and one Harlaean manuscript read *cogeremur* (“we would be forced”). Other printed editions have *cogemur* (“we shall be forced”); the Regius manuscript has *cogimur* (“we are forced”); many others have *cogeremur*; the Colbertine has *cogemur, vel intolerabilia patiemur* (“we shall be forced, or shall suffer intolerable things”).]

But we trust, with the help of the mercy of our Lord God, that under your Holiness presiding over the Roman Church we shall no longer suffer this arrogance. The provisions that ought to be observed toward us in every respect will be observed with fraternal charity—provisions that, according to the wisdom and justice which the Most High has granted you, you yourself recognize must be observed,

[Note: The manuscripts of Merlin, Crabbe, and Justellus, together with many others and the Greek, read *si forte* (“if perhaps”). This reading was initially attractive in the sense: “But if perhaps the Nicene canons are otherwise in the most truthful copies, we trust, with the help of God’s mercy...” Later, however, together with the Colbertine manuscript and two Harlaean manuscripts, *nisi forte* (“unless perhaps”) was judged preferable. Labbe has *nisi si forte*, adding *si*, which is absent from our manuscripts.]

unless perhaps the canons of the Council of Nicaea are otherwise.

For although we have read very many manuscripts, nowhere in the Latin manuscripts of the Council of Nicaea have we found provisions sent from there in the form in which they appear in the memorandum mentioned above.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscripts read *quae inde* (“which from there”), which is not unreasonable.]

Nevertheless, since we have been unable to find these provisions in any Greek manuscript, we desire all the more that authentic copies be brought from the Eastern Churches, where they are said to be recoverable.
