For this reason we also beg your Veneration to deign to write to the priests of those regions, namely to the bishops of the Church of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople,

[Note: The same manuscript adds: “of Constantinople and Antioch and Alexandria, and others.”]

and to others as well, if it pleases your Holiness, so that from there the same canons established by the fathers at the city of Nicaea may come to us, with you, above all, conferring this benefit upon all the Western Churches with the help of the Lord.

For who would doubt that the most trustworthy copies of the Council of Nicaea, assembled in Greece, are those which, brought from and compared with such diverse and distinguished Greek Churches, agree with one another?

Until this is done, we declare that we shall observe, until their authenticity is established, those provisions brought forward to us in the aforementioned memorandum concerning appeals by bishops to the priest of the Roman Church and concerning the conclusion of clerical cases before the bishops of their own provinces. We trust in God’s will that your Blessedness will assist us in this.

6. As for the remaining matters enacted or confirmed in our synod, since our aforementioned brothers, our fellow bishop Faustinus and our fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, carry them with them, they will make them known to your Holiness, if you deign to receive them.

And in another hand:

May our Lord preserve you for many years for us, most blessed brother.

Alypius, Augustine, Possidius,

[Note: The printed editions read *Marinus*; the Regius exemplar reads *Martinus*, which is supported by the Africans’ letter to Celestine concerning the same matter, where all the manuscripts give the name Martinus. Nevertheless, on the authority of one Harlaean and another Colbertine manuscript, we have preferred to restore *Marianus*. He seems to be the same as Marianus—written *Maurianus* in some manuscripts—bishop of Uzalis, who is named immediately after the envoys at the beginning of the council from which this letter was sent.]

Marianus, and the remaining bishops also subscribed.

## Letter III

[Note: This letter has reached us through the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, Hadrian I, the Hispana, and Isidore.]

## Concerning Maximus, Bishop of the City of Valence, Accused of Various Crimes, So That His Case Might Be Examined in the Synod of His Province

BONIFACE, bishop, to Patroclus, Remigius, Maximus, Hilary, Severus, Valerius, Julianus, Castorius, Leontius,

[Note: The Regius manuscript of the Dionysian collection has *Constantio*, and below *Maurentio*, instead of *Mauricio*.]

Constantine, John, Montanus, Marinus, Mauritius, and the other bishops established throughout the Gauls and the seven provinces.

### 1. From Valentina

[Note: They had accused Maximus, bishop of the city of Valentia, formerly entangled in the sect of the Manichaeans, condemned for homicide in a secular court, and furthermore covered with many disgraceful acts, before Boniface—the clergy of that same Church asserting that, although inquiries had repeatedly been delegated and judicial hearings established in the province, he had utterly refused to appear and had always evaded every trial. Since he had not come to Rome, the pontiff decreed that he should be judged within the province and ordered a synod of bishops to assemble on the appointed day, to examine Maximus’s case there and pronounce sentence whether he were present or absent.]

The clergy of the city (Ivo, pt. 5, ch. 271) approached us, [Col. 0756C] presenting in a written complaint the crimes which, with the whole province as witness, they asserted Maximus had committed. Although inquiry had so often been delegated, they said that he had always evaded the judicial hearings that had been established. [Note: In the same codex: *tota semper* (“always entirely”).] Not trusting his conscience, had not hastened to have everything examined so that, if innocent, he might be cleared. We learned this also from the contents of our documents. [Col. 0757A]

[Note: The printed editions after Crabbe read *vestrarum* (“your documents”); Merlin, with our manuscripts, more correctly reads *nostrarum* (“our documents”). The bishops had not sent documents concerning this matter, of which they knew nothing at the time; rather, documents belonging to their predecessors, who had delegated the inquiry to Boniface, were already available to him. He therefore ordered them to be read aloud and recognized from them that the claims of the clergy of Valentia were true.]

On the contrary, he demonstrated against himself the truth of what had been said: although the charges were innumerable, he is said to have avoided even the hearings summoned by my predecessors under a provincial inquiry, delegated for refuting those charges, and to have been altogether unwilling to appear. (Nicholas I, Letter 39.)

[Note: The Roman edition after Crabbe reads *cui* (“to whom”), though the other books disagree. A fuller reading would perhaps be: “as one who, namely, had avoided the hearings.”]

No one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment in precisely the way in which the innocent person seeks acquittal. But the crafty quibbling of those who think matters must be handled by schemes of cunning will never receive the name of innocence. For whoever thinks that he can evade judgment by delays confesses everything.

[Note: The printed editions read *veniet tamen* (“yet he will come”), and shortly afterward, except for Merlin, *nec proderit* (“nor will it help”); the readings have been corrected from the manuscripts.]

Let him, then, who is said to be such a man come forward at last. It does him no good to have hidden so often or evaded the proceedings so often: wherever he may flee, his acts and offenses—the crimes alleged against him, if they are true—pursue him. I ought indeed even now to have pronounced a sentence worthy of the acts for which he had been accused before our tribunal—acts by which, through repeatedly avoiding the inquiry and the judicial decision, he thought that judgment could be mocked. But lest anyone perhaps judge it premature [Note: Most manuscripts read *praecoquem*; two others, with Crabbe, Sirmond, and Labbe, read *praecoquam*. In Merlin the text is corrupt: *hanc ne aliquis praeco et quem judicaret*.] and say that nothing had been reserved for him who was absent, although we had sought him, we preferred to defer the matter after allowing an interval of time. His accusers also maintained that, secure in his own intentions and character, Maximus would commit acts deserving condemnation all the more the longer he delayed to appear before the established tribunal.

[Note: The printed edition reads *praesentarit*; the manuscripts correct it to *praesentaret*. Moreover, learned scholars rightly judge that “Manichaeans” here designates the Priscillianists.]

[Note: In the Regius manuscript, *nunc umquam* occurs here, perhaps in place of *nunc aequam* (“now a fitting sentence”).]

[Note: The common editions read “a provincial inquiry is delegated.” The verb “is” is absent from the manuscripts. It is therefore preferable, with Sirmond, to read “by an inquiry delegated to the province.” Above we already read “although inquiry had so often been delegated.” Such delegation was consistent with canon 7 of the Council of Sardica.]

They accuse him of having formerly so befouled his mind by the shameful sect, entangled as he was in the darkness of the Manichaeans, that he could not wash himself clean; they produce the synodal records as proof of the deed alleged. And, entangled on every side in disgraceful acts, they say that he had shown no regard for soundness. In his madness and insane recklessness, they assert, he had allowed himself to be subjected to examination before the tribunals of secular judges—something disgraceful even in a person of low rank—and they state, producing the records, that he had been condemned for homicide.

[Note: The Regius manuscripts read *asserent* (“they assert”); the Colbertine reads *assererent* (“they would assert”).]

They bitterly lament that such a man, after committing so many and such grave offenses, still claims for himself the name of bishop in his hiding places, to the disgrace of his own city, and, by claiming the sacred name for himself, wishes to pollute it.

### 2.

Therefore, dearest brothers, because he refused to present himself to be heard—lest, perhaps, after being convicted by the clergy accusing him, he might at last, when brought before episcopal judgment, receive the sentence appropriate to the pronouncement—although, when this sentence has been issued, what loss can there be for one who is said (III, question 9, ch. 10; Ivo, pt. 5, ch. 271, and pt. 6, ch. 338) never to have possessed the shame of the priesthood and not to have guarded his position even for a short time?—we nevertheless granted him a delay. We decreed that the judgment should take place within the province and that a synod should be assembled before the Kalends of November. If he wished to appear, let him answer the charges in person, if he has confidence; but if he neglected to appear, let him not gain a postponement of sentence through his absence.

[Note: Most manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read *edocta fuerint* (“when these things have been taught”); one of the Coislin manuscripts, in its first hand, reads *edocta fuerit*; the Regius reads *edicta fuerint*. From the two latter readings the genuine text seems to be formed: *edicta fuerit*, namely “when the sentence has been issued.”]

For it is evident that the person confesses the crime who does not use the opportunity to clear himself when judgment has been granted and so often delegated. It makes no difference whether everything that has been said is proved in a present examination, since the absence itself, procured so often as an admission, is already established.

[Note: The Regius exemplar reads *posita sunt* (“have been set forth”). *Proposita sunt* (“have been proposed”) would not be objectionable, especially since the beginning of this letter has *proponentes per libellum crimina* (“presenting the crimes in a written complaint”).]

We are sending letters throughout all the provinces, so that he may not plead ignorance as an excuse and may be compelled to come to the province and present himself there before the established tribunal.

[Note: The manuscripts read *dirigimus* (“we are sending”); the printed editions have *dirigemus* (“we shall send”).]

Whatever your Charity decides should be determined concerning this matter, when it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority, as is fitting.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Ides of June (June 13, A.D. 419), in the consulship of the illustrious man Monaxius.

## NOTICE ON THE TWO FOLLOWING LETTERS

[Col. 0758C]

### 1.

Both letters were read in the Roman council under Boniface II and inserted in its acts; afterward they were published by Luca Holstenius in the bipartite Roman collection. Boniface wrote them on the occasion of Perigenes. Perigenes had been born at Corinth, reborn there in baptism, and enrolled in that Church’s clergy. After having passed successfully through all the clerical grades, he had been ordained bishop for the people of Patras by the bishop of Corinth, with the approval of the synod of the whole province. But after being rejected by the people, he was later chosen bishop by the Corinthians themselves.

Some persons opposed their request, because they held it as a matter of religious obligation that the canons prohibiting the translation of bishops might be violated if someone ordained once for a single Church—even though never received by it—were placed over another Church. For this reason the Corinthians approached the Apostolic See with written petitions, asking that through its authority they might obtain what they desired.

Boniface was surprised that no letters from Rufus had been attached to the Corinthians’ petitions, although Achaea, together with the other provinces of Illyricum, had already been entrusted to Rufus’s care. Accordingly, even though he judged their petition equitable, he nevertheless refused to reply to them before receiving Rufus’s letters, “so that both the authority of the Apostolic See and the due honor of its vicar might be preserved” (Letter 2, no. 4), and also “so that nothing premature might seem to be done by this See” (Letter 15, no. 3).

When he had received Rufus’s written response concerning Perigenes, which entirely accorded with the Corinthians’ wishes, he then sent Rufus the letter “the second, which pleased the entire presbyterate,” that is, the whole Roman clergy (ibid., no. 3), and appointed Perigenes bishop of the Corinthian Church.

### 2.

Since this account establishes that Boniface wrote two letters concerning the matter just mentioned—one by which he kept the Corinthians’ expectation in suspense, and another by which he granted Perigenes to their petition—the subsequent letters make it easier to determine which of the two came first.

The letter that was read first in the Roman council was evidently written first also, because Boniface speaks in it as one who had not yet entrusted to Rufus the care of the Churches throughout Achaea and Macedonia, but had learned only from the records of his archives that this care had been entrusted to Rufus by his predecessors. He then adds that this example of his predecessors moved him to make known to Rufus the petition of the Corinthians, who were requesting Perigenes as their bishop. By these words he clearly indicates that he was then writing to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, for the first time concerning Perigenes.

It is equally clear that the other letter was written after Boniface and Rufus had received letters from each other, when Rufus had not only written to Boniface concerning the condition of the Churches entrusted to him, but had also received from Boniface replies “which he had conveyed to the knowledge of each person” (Letter 2, no. 2).

### 3.

Nevertheless, in Tillemont’s judgment (Tillemont, volume XII, p. 667), Boniface appears in the earlier letter to confirm Perigenes’s election, whereas in the latter part of the other letter he gives Rufus its first notice in such a way as to indicate that he had wished to decide nothing concerning it until he had received Rufus’s letters about the matter.

Moved by this consideration, that learned man believes the earlier letter to be suspect of forgery and thinks it cannot be defended by any means unless one says that it was indeed written by Boniface when he had first resolved to approve and confirm the Corinthians’ petition, but was never sent because he later judged that such confirmation should be deferred until Rufus had written to him about the matter.

But this interpretation is prevented both by Boniface’s own Letter 15, where mention is made of two letters sent to Rufus concerning this matter, and by the acts of the Roman council under Boniface II, in which both letters are mentioned—not as produced from the archive of the Roman Church, but as brought to Rome from the archive of the Church of Thessalonica.

Nor can the earlier letter be regarded as suspect without the other letter being exposed to the same suspicion, and indeed all the other documents read in that council likewise being tainted by equal suspicion. For the authority of one or another is not different; the authority of all is equal. Theodosius, bishop of Echinos in Thessaly, produced each of them. When he requested that their authenticity be examined from the archive of the Apostolic See, and Pope Boniface II assented and ordered this, they were read aloud and inserted in the acts.

Yet we have a grave suspicion that the ending of the two following letters has become confused and disordered. Certainly, if the contents assigned to each under number 4 were separated from the two letters, and what has been wrongly attached to one were restored in turn to the other, nothing would remain that did not fit together appropriately. Nor should it seem surprising that in documents sometimes presented in abridged form certain passages have also been moved from their proper place.

## LETTER IV

### That the Corinthians may receive Perigenes, whom they desire, as bishop

**Boniface to his dearest brother Rufus.**

### 1.

The blessed apostle Peter, to whom the citadel of the priesthood was entrusted by the Lord’s voice, is raised to immeasurable rejoicing whenever he perceives that the children of unblemished peace granted to him by the Lord are guardians of the honor bestowed upon him. For what ought he to weigh as a greater joy than the recognition that the inviolable rights of the power he received are being preserved? For consultation, directed by various persons concerning whatever affairs, truly requires an immovable foundation when it seeks the secret counsel of that See, which is known to have been exalted by the gracious favor of the spiritual Rock.

### 2.

Accordingly, as the records of our archive show, letters have frequently flowed from that source to Your Charity. It is certain that the care of the Churches situated in Macedonia and Achaea has been entrusted to your Fraternity, which we know preserves ecclesiastical discipline through knowledge of the canons.

[Note: We still possess Letters 13, 16, and 18 of Innocent, addressed to the same Rufus.]

Nor do we consider this to have happened without reason. For the Apostolic See, in the exercise of its diligence, confers this grace upon Your Dilection. Therefore we make Your Holiness aware of this matter, which is reported to our ears as having been sent from that province whose care was long ago entrusted to your prudence.

[Note: Supply “of that province,” namely Achaea, whose care, together with the other provinces of Illyricum, is clearly shown to have been entrusted to Rufus from the year 412 by Innocent’s Letter 13.]

### 3.

The Corinthians, formerly praised for the preaching of the blessed Paul, whose petition we thought should rather be submitted than narrated, desire to receive—or rather to retain—as priest of their city Perigenes, who, as the document sent long ago by the holy synod concerning him attests, is holy and distinguished by the excellence of his character.

[Note: The bishops of Achaea, who assembled together, had decided that Perigenes should be placed over the people of Patras and ordained, and in the synodal letter then sent to the Apostolic See they praised him as holy and outstanding in the excellence of his character.]

If I should think that the sequence of his ordination must be set forth in full, it will necessarily increase his praise; and it will certainly benefit him if we mention in due order both the one who ordained him and the one who was ordained.

[Note: Perigenes’s own metropolitan, that is, the bishop of Corinth, ordained him bishop for the people of Patras. For this reason he is shortly said to have been substituted afterward in the place of his creator.]

For who would doubt that this was to be counted among his merits? Who would deny that it was the judgment of God that he was not received by the people of Patras at the proper time, and that, after long and careful deliberation, he was kept in suspense over the aforementioned Church, so that he might become pastor of this fold, in whose enclosure he had spent his life from his earliest beginnings?

“Your judgments are a great deep” (Psalm 35:7). We aptly apply this example, and no one would have believed that someone ordained by others could at some time be substituted in the place of the one who ordained him.

[Note: It seems that the text should read: “who had been ordained for another.” Socrates, Book VII, chapter 36, when about to offer several examples proving that bishops may sometimes be transferred, gives this as his first: Perigenes had been ordained bishop of Patras; but because the inhabitants of that city refused to receive him, the bishop of the city of Rome ordered him to be established in the metropolitan see of Corinth after its bishop had died. But he cites no other example from the West. In A.D. 341 the Council of Antioch, canon 16, had forbidden a bishop to rush from a vacant see into another vacant Church without a complete and duly constituted council, and had defined that council as complete when the metropolitan bishop was present. If a metropolitan bishop, with his synod, could lawfully grant a vacant Church to a bishop whose own see was also vacant, then the Roman pontiff could certainly do the same in a province that belonged to his special care. Pope Felix II later exercised the same right when he gave the vacant Church of Nola to John Talaia, expelled from Alexandria by Peter Mongus, as the deacon Liberatus testifies in chapter 18.]

I do not doubt that this was then the sentence of heaven.

### 4.

[Note: The sentence becomes complete if it is read as follows: “Therefore, with the consent of those who there represented—or represent—the authority of the Apostolic See.” We have already indicated that these words, together with what follows, belong at the end of the subsequent letter, and that everything contained under number 4 in that letter should be transferred here.]

Accordingly, with the consent of those who there represented the authority of the Apostolic See, we receive him into our number. And we must exercise the force of censure against those who, contrary to our action, are said afterward to incite the people without the knowledge of our representatives, if they persist.

We also wish Your Dilection, by our command, to act against them, so that we may restrain the license of those to whom we have entrusted no such authority.

## LETTER V

[Note: If the chronological notice of this letter, as is highly probable, belongs with the preceding material, there is nothing by which we can determine with certainty when it was written, except that the discussion from the beginning through the start of section 4 leaves no room for doubt that it follows Letter 4. We also preserve the order in which it was read in the Roman council.]

Rufus’s vigilance in fulfilling the office of vicar of the Apostolic See is praised. The nature of that office is also explained. Boniface mentions that several bishops had confirmed that his own letters had been conveyed to them through Rufus’s agency, and on this occasion digresses into praise of Perigenes.

**Boniface to his dearest brother Rufus.**

### 1.

We believed that, after our letters had been sent for the observance of ecclesiastical discipline, every avenue of presumption would be closed, since we had given Your Dilection the reply required by the assessment of the cases and had established that those things must be observed which ecclesiastical discipline demands.

But, as the report of Your Holiness has now made clear to us, what we wrote prevailed among many, whereas we have learned that among some our admonition was ineffective. We cannot attribute this to Your Fraternity, since we perceive you to be anxious, in both your actions and your letters, because of the care of the Churches and affairs entrusted to you.

We praise the diligence of your vigilance: lest you seem to neglect what has been entrusted to you, you do not fail to indicate by letter whatever the censure of the Apostolic See ought to correct. You have professed that you possess this fear of our God, as befits a most prudent priest. It will be glorious for you if we learn by experience that what has been entrusted to your care has benefited the Churches.

For the blessed apostle Peter looks upon you with his own eyes, as you yourself faithfully stated in your letters, to see how you exercise the office of supreme ruler. Nor can he be far from you who was appointed the perpetual shepherd of the Lord’s sheep; nor can he fail to care for any Church anywhere, in whom we read that the foundation of the universal Church has been laid.

### 2.

Therefore, dearest brother, the whole care of those Churches that you recognize as entrusted to you by us in place of the Apostolic See looks to you: correct what is perverse, restore what has been disrupted, and, if any disputes arise among bishops, distinguish them under fear of divine judgment.

[Note: Labbe preferred *distringas* (“you should restrain”). But a similar passage in Sixtus III, Letter 10, no. 2, prevents us from accepting his conjecture. There that pope says that he granted Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, the power “to distinguish and decide whatever actions arise among the brethren.”]

Use justly and prudently, against all the storms of emerging tempests, the helm entrusted to you by the Apostolic See.

### 3.

You have said that you conveyed our letters to each of those to whom we had previously written concerning the path they ought to follow. Many priests, mindful of the sacred traditions, have professed their agreement with them; we embrace them in fraternal charity. We recognize such men in our co-bishop Adelphius and in our brother Perigenes, to whom the word of the blessed council long ago came as an affirmation.

[Note: The council by which he had first been ordained bishop for the people of Patras, as is explained more explicitly in Letter 4, section 3.]

The judgment of God, I say, was already calling him to the watchtower of the episcopate. We often believe God’s gifts to be contrary to us and turn against ourselves what we later recognize to have benefited us.

The example of the present matter confirms this. Without doubt our co-bishop Perigenes was saddened when no one received him after he had been ordained. Was it not advantageous for him that the people of Patras, with one united voice of opposition, excluded him from their city? But in proportion as he was humbled when no one received him after his ordination, so much higher is he now, when he is sought by his own people, though he had been rejected by outsiders.

[Note: Supply *magis* (“more”). Here *humilis* means humble and abject.]

For this is the evident and manifest judgment of God: he wished Perigenes to wait until the time when he might deserve to preside over this Church, in which he is said to have been born and reborn.

### 4.

[Note: What follows is in no way connected with the preceding material. But if the following passage from section 4 of the preceding letter is substituted for it—“Therefore, with the consent of those who there represent the authority of the Apostolic See, we receive him into our number,” and so forth—everything fits together perfectly.]

Dearest brother, since the burden of the matters entrusted or delegated to you rests upon your prudence, the petition of the suppliants concerns you both because of the special diligence long ago selected for you and because of your proximity.

[Note: The printed editions read “the petition of the suppliants … regards the matter by reason of proximity.” Clearly, *petitio* (“petition”) must be restored in place of *petitionis*. Likewise, *perspectat* (“regards”) appears to have crept in instead of *te respectat* (“concerns you”), from section 2 above: “the whole care of those Churches looks to you.” Boniface teaches that the Corinthians’ petition concerns Rufus for two reasons: first, in a special capacity, since he had long ago been chosen by Innocent to hear such cases; second, in a general capacity, since he was their neighboring metropolitan.]

We have read this petition with no small astonishment, because it was deprived of your letters. After everything has been carried out in the order required by the circumstances, send some written communication to us. We do not wish to send our letter to our co-bishop Perigenes before receiving your letters, since everything appears to have been delegated for his ordination.

You will hasten to do this because of the desire of those who petition. You know better, for you are worthy of understanding, that they are inflamed to this request solely, as I think, by devotion to religion—especially since they assert that he has remained irreproachably in the dignity of the presbyterate for innumerable years and has reached the highest summit by gradual advancement, not by an unwarranted leap.

For the completeness of the confirmation of his episcopate, only this remains: that he has not yet received our greeting in his honor. I do not doubt that Your Charity understands that it is astonishing both that we seem not to have sent our letter to him and that we have perhaps not given a reply to the suppliants.

We have acted so that both the authority of the Apostolic See and the honor of Your Dilection might be preserved.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October (September 19, A.D. 419), in the consulship of the illustrious man Monaxius.

## LETTER VI

[Note: Written in A.D. 420. It is indeed the beginning of the four books that Augustine composed against the two letters of the Pelagians and dedicated to Boniface; but there is no reason why it should not be called a letter, especially since it is composed in epistolary form and such dedications are ordinarily given the name of letters. Augustine decided to dedicate the work in which he refutes the two Pelagian letters to Boniface because he had received those letters from that same pope. Boniface, entrusting them to Alypius as he was returning from Rome to Africa, did not wish them to remain hidden from Augustine, whose name had been inserted in them maliciously, as Augustine recalls in Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 61. From this we can infer the time when this letter, together with the rest of the work, was prepared. Alypius is said to have returned from Rome toward the end of A.D. 419. The place this work occupies in Augustine’s *Retractions* suggests that it belongs to A.D. 420. Julian, in Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, Book I, chapter 85, takes it for certain that it was sent through Alypius to Boniface.]

**Of Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to Pope Boniface**

Augustine, after first praising Boniface, explains the necessity of answering the letters of the heretics. Then he indicates that he has sent this work especially to him—not for him to learn from it, but to examine and perhaps correct it.

### 1.

I knew you, indeed, through the most celebrated reports that praised you, and from very frequent and entirely truthful messengers I had learned how full you were of the grace of God, most blessed and venerable Pope Boniface.

But after my brother Alypius had also seen you in bodily presence, and, received by you with the greatest kindness and sincerity, had mingled mutual conversation with you under the prompting of affection; after he had lived with you and, although for only a short time, had been joined to you by great affection; after he had poured both himself and me into your heart and brought you back to me within his own heart—your Holiness became known to me to a much greater degree, because my knowledge of you was made more certain by friendship.

For you do not disdain—although you preside from a higher place, you do not set your mind on lofty things—to be the friend of the humble and to return the love lavishly bestowed upon you. For what else is friendship, which takes its name from love and is faithful nowhere except in Christ, in whom alone it can also be eternal and blessed?

Therefore, through that brother by whom I came to know you more intimately, I received greater confidence and ventured to write something to Your Beatitude about matters that at this time, through a renewed stimulus, urge episcopal care—if any such care exists in us—to vigilance for the Lord’s flock.

### 2.

For new heretics, enemies of the grace of God—which is given through Jesus Christ our Lord to the small and the great—even though they are now shown more clearly to be avoided through a more open rejection, nevertheless do not cease trying through their writings the hearts of the less cautious or less instructed.

They certainly ought to be answered, lest they establish themselves or their followers in that wicked error, even if we did not fear that they might deceive some Catholics with plausible speech.

But since they do not cease raging against the enclosures of the Lord’s flock and searching everywhere for entrances by which to tear apart the sheep purchased at so great a price, and since the pastoral watchtower is common to all of us who perform the office of bishop—although you yourself preside in a loftier position—I do what I can in my small share of the duty, insofar as the Lord grants me strength through the assistance of your prayers.

I set before their poisonous and treacherous writings writings that may heal and fortify, so that the madness with which they rage may either itself be cured or be prevented from harming others.

### 3.

I have decided to direct chiefly to Your Holiness what I answer in this discussion to their two letters: one, said to have been sent to Rome by Julian, I believe, so that through it he might find or make his own those whom he could; the other, which eighteen men, apparently bishops sharing his error, dared in their cunning to write to Thessalonica—not to just anyone, but to the bishop of that place, whom they were attempting to test and, if possible, convert to their party.

[Note: When Julian denied that the first letter was his, Augustine, *Unfinished Work*, Book I, chapter 18, considered this answer sufficient: “But if you do not acknowledge it, then let it not be yours.”]

I have therefore decided to direct to Your Holiness what I answer, as I have said, to these two letters of theirs—not so much for you to learn as to examine, and, if something should perhaps displease you, to correct.

For my brother informed me that you yourself had graciously given him the letters, which could not have come into your hands without the most vigilant diligence of our brothers, your sons. I give thanks for your most sincere goodwill toward us, because you did not wish the letters of the enemies of God’s grace to remain hidden from me—letters in which you found my name maliciously and plainly inserted.

## LETTER VII

[Note: It is reproduced in full in Gratian’s *Decree*, Distinction 97, chapter 1. It also exists in the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, Adrian, the Hispana, and another collection written in Lombard script. In these collections it is placed before the preceding Letter 3, dated June of A.D. 419. But this does not support Baronius’s opinion, who assigns it to that same year. If it had been written in A.D. 419, since it is clearly dated in July, chronological order would have required it to follow the letter dated in June. If we also consider the occasion on which it was written, it can readily be established that it cannot belong to A.D. 419. Boniface wrote it at the request of all his priests and clergy, who, terrified by his prolonged weakness and illness and fearing for his life, thought provision should be made lest the schism of Eulalius flare up again. Although Boniface soon began to recover, he nevertheless judged that nothing should be deferred that might secure the unity and peace of the Church for the future. But in the preceding Letter 3 there is nothing to indicate that the pontiff was suffering from a prolonged illness. The letter under discussion therefore cannot have been dated earlier than July 1, A.D. 420. It was sent with the solemn delegation of the most distinguished priests.]

Or, a petition that the emperor establish that no pontiff should ever be ordained in the city of Rome through canvassing or factional solicitation.

[Col. 0766A]

**Boniface, bishop, to Honorius Augustus**
My Church [Note: In the Navarre manuscript, “Roman” is added here; it appears to have been transferred from a marginal note into the text. Hence Merlin has “my Roman Church.”], to which our God assigned my priesthood while you govern human affairs, constrains me by its concern, lest, although I am still detained by bodily illness, I fail to appear before the ears of the most Christian emperor on behalf of its cause—a cause for which a gathering, summoned by all the priests and clergy and stirred by disturbances among the Christian people, has been convened. [Note: The printed editions, together with the Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections, read “on account of the assemblies that are being agitated by the priests . . .”; the authority of the best Colbertine and Lombard manuscript corrects this. It would not be easy to explain what those assemblies were, agitated by all the priests and clergy and by disturbances among the Christian people—especially since Symmachus, however hostile to Boniface, after receiving the imperial edicts ordering that this pontiff be recalled to the city, wrote back to Honorius: “What was commanded proved so welcome to everyone that both the most distinguished order and the Roman people approved it . . . So great was the fervor and joy of the whole city that all, as though religion had been restored and security of peace provided, testified to it with fitting thanksgiving . . . No disagreement among the people now remains, and all, by divine judgment, have assented to the will of Your Majesty. The factions having therefore ceased, all began to think what you had established after being admonished by God’s command.” Thus Symmachus wrote in reply to the imperial letter that he had received on 8 April 419. Since, then, the zeal of the parties had ceased, who could understand that those schismatic assemblies had been stirred up? But the whole series of this petition and the emperor’s rescript also make clear that Boniface was concerned to prevent disturbances that might arise in the future, when he had been summoned and petitioned by the clergy.] If anything should happen otherwise than it ought, it will not be you who arrange everything with equitable moderation, but we, through our silent negligence, shall appear to have allowed something that could overturn the tranquillity of the city and the peace of the Church. Since, by God’s favor, you preside over human affairs as a worshiper of the divine religion, it will be our fault if, under Your Glory—which, as is certain, has always been readier in spirit to favor divine matters—what has endured through so long a succession of years, even under those rulers who were bound by no concern for our religion, is not preserved under firm and stable right [Note: In the Dionysian and Hadrianic copies, “that is, lawful,” except that in one Harleian manuscript “or therefore lawful” is written above the line. Isidore, after the Hispanic collection, substitutes “that is, so that he may confidently use what is lawful,” which Merlin also adopted. Other editions introduced on their own “that is, so that I may confidently use what is lawful.” Gratian alone has “that is, so that lawful things may be preserved.” The Colbertine Lombard manuscript has “that is, concerning lawful things.” We therefore judged that “that is, pagan things” should be inferred. Honorius draws the wording of his own statement from this passage of Boniface when he writes in Epistle 10: “Lest under Christian rulers the Roman Church lose what it did not lose under other emperors.”], while under the rule of Your Clemency things that are unlawful are by no means feared.

The Church herself, most Christian Emperor, calls your devotion venerable—indeed in my speech, but with the affection of her own heart [Note: So the genuine Dionysian Regius exemplar reads together with the Colbertine. Other books have “venerable,” while two manuscripts of the Isidorian collection have “calls by address.”]—that Church which Christ our God, the faithful ruler and governor of your empire, has betrothed to himself alone and preserves as an undefiled virgin (II Corinthians 11:2), so that you may not allow any waves of treacherous storms to break upon her, nor her tranquil face to be disturbed by the swelling of an unusual tempest, most glorious and most tranquil Emperor Augustus.

Therefore that Church, betrothed to one alone yet nevertheless your mother, calls upon your piety through this embassy which she has entrusted to her priests, and recalls the past [Note: The past may be understood as the evils the Church suffered under the faction of Ursinus during the time of Damasus, and the present as those suffered in the most recent schism of Eulalius.] and the present. “While you,” she says, “rule religiously, the people who is now yours is safe, as faithful to God as to you, a Christian ruler.” [Note: The printed editions, following Isidore, add: “My people, which is now yours, has increased.” This is a gloss foreign to Boniface’s meaning and is corrected from Dionysius and other better manuscripts. The subject here is the security provided for the people, not the increase of the people itself; this is confirmed by what Symmachus wrote immediately after the schism had been pacified, when he clearly explained that all were giving thanks because religion had been restored and security of peace provided.] [Note: The more reliable manuscripts read this way. One Harleian manuscript has “you who are Christian rulers”; the Navarre manuscript, “you who are the ruler of Christians”; two others, “the ruler of Christ”; Merlin, “you who are the ruler of Christ”; the remaining books, “you who are a Christian ruler.”]

For behold, amid the very mysteries and amid her prayers, which she pours out for the prosperity of your empire, with holy Peter as witness—before whom and concerning whose seat the matter is being treated—she cries out in anxious words for the observance of religion: while prayer is mingled with earnest petition, lest discord, once uprooted and urged on by the tempter, should drag these people away from their accustomed worship into various pursuits. [Note: Later editions of the Councils have “lest it tear us apart,” and below, following Merlin, “disagreements” instead of “disagreement.” Gratian shortened and compressed this passage as follows: “lest discord, once torn away, should divide human affairs while the customary hidden tempter secretly—or, ‘by stealth’—urges them on.” The pronoun “these” may be referred to the people.]

She would press more matters upon you, most Christian prince, unless she were secure with you concerning her own causes and had prevailed, through your faith—while divine worship flourishes together with the empire—in the suppression of idolatry and the correction of heretics. [Note: The editions, except Merlin, read “she would have been increased by more,” but the manuscripts’ authority corrects this.] She has a refuge in your gentle spirit joined with reverence for her religion: whatever advances this cause, you accomplish, and you entrust it to my brothers and fellow priests, men of proven character, whom I and all who constitute the Church send to you in this embassy. [Note: Merlin has “in this pure embassy”; the other editions, “such legates.” The older Colbertine manuscript has “this embassy commands”; the other ancient manuscripts, “this pure embassy.” The reading we restore is closer to that of the manuscripts and is also required by the sequence of the discourse. For, as Boniface declares at the beginning, he himself, having been summoned and petitioned by all the priests and clergy of his Church, sent this embassy to Honorius. Prudently, however, he sends it not only in his own name but also in the name of all who constituted his Church, because, in requesting the free election of his successor, he was asking for something that concerned his entire Church.] We ask that, as they pursue the cause of the sacred religion, you may provide permanently for the established condition of the universal Church in the city of Your Clemency, with the disposition by which you assent to requests.

Given on the Kalends of July (1 July 420).

## EPISTLE VIII

[Note: This epistle is preserved in the same ancient collections as the preceding one and, in addition, in the Vatican copy. From what Honorius wrote back concerning the case of Boniface and Eulalius, whether in petitions, letters, or reports sent to him from Rome, one may infer the time at which this was written. Since the emperor is found to have replied to all those writings within seven days or not much later, we may reasonably judge that he did not allow the month of July of the year 420 to pass without issuing this rescript.]

### OR THE RESCRIPT OF THE EMPEROR AUGUSTUS HONORIUS TO POPE BONIFACE

In it the emperor decrees that if two bishops should again be ordained at Rome, both are to be expelled from the city.

[Col. 0767B]

[Col. 0768A]

Victor Honorius, illustrious victor, forever Augustus, to the holy and venerable Pope Boniface of the Eternal City [Note: Merlin, as in the Isidorian manuscripts, has “of the city of Rome.”].

We have received the writings of Your Beatitude with the congratulation due to reverence [Note: The Vatican manuscript adds: “we have received them, giving the greatest thanks to almighty God because…”], and, after reading them, we gave the greatest thanks to almighty God because we learned that your holiness, restored to the health you desired after a prolonged illness, had recovered. Therefore, as the venerable men return, we mark our joy by the testimony of a sacred letter [Note: The Vatican manuscript omits “and we ask”], and we ask that Your Apostolate deign, in your daily prayers, to offer your zeal and prayer for the welfare and empire of us.

Know, moreover, that it greatly pleased our piety that your holiness is concerned about disturbance among the churches or the people. Our Clemency believed that sufficient provision had been made so that this could not occur by any means. Finally, by the proclamation of Your Beatitude, we wish this to reach the knowledge of all the clergy: if anything should happen by human fortune to your religious office—which we do not desire—let everyone know that all ambition must cease.

And if, perhaps, two men should have been ordained in reckless rivalry contrary to right [Note: So our manuscripts read together with Gratian and Merlin, except that one Colbertine manuscript has “in rivalry.” Other editions have “while contending,” omitting “perhaps”; the authority of the older Colbertine manuscript restores it. As for the law of Honorius, it was indeed suitable for deterring ambitious men, but enemies of peace could abuse it to exclude good men. Certainly, if it had previously been in force, Rome would not count Boniface himself and Damasus among her pontiffs. Yet the iniquity of the times sometimes demands measures that, once the cause has been removed, are prudently abolished.], neither of them shall ever become a priest; only he shall remain in the apostolic see whom divine judgment and the consent of all, from the number of the clergy, shall have chosen by a new ordination.

Therefore this must be observed [Note: The Corbie manuscript, together with the Hadrianic collection, has “Therefore it must be carefully observed.” One Harleian manuscript, in a second correction, has “Therefore I wish this to be observed”; the Navarre manuscript, “Therefore I wish this to be observed.” The common reading is more genuine, and most manuscripts support it.]: all must preserve a tranquil mind and peaceful dispositions in response to the admonition of our Serenity, and they must not attempt anything through seditious conspiracies, since it is certain that no party’s zeal will benefit any of them [Note: The Vatican manuscript omits “its own.”].

## EPISTLE IX

[Note: Since this epistle provided the occasion for the two following ones, it seemed worthwhile to reproduce it here. Baronius thinks it was issued at the persuasion of Atticus, in the year 421. Another law—namely, that no priest should be ordained in the Hellespont or other regions without the judgment of the bishop of Constantinople—which Socrates records in Book VII, chapter 28, was granted only to Atticus; this is evidence that that bishop was not free from ambition. Yet Theodosius admits in Epistle 10 that this constitution was obtained from him not merely through Atticus but also through the petitions of the bishops of Illyricum.]

### By which the rights of the Church of Constantinople are extended into Illyricum

Theodosius Augustus to Philippus, Praetorian Prefect of Illyricum.

With every innovation having ceased, we order that the ancient practice and the former ecclesiastical canons, which have remained in force until now, be observed throughout all the provinces of Illyricum. If any matter of doubt should arise, it must be reserved for the knowledge of the most reverend prelate of the sacred law, the bishop of the city of Constantinople, which enjoys the prerogative of Old Rome [Note: This is the prerogative of Old Rome: that it is an apostolic see. But the city of Constantinople, as Gelasius says in Epistle 9, section 6, received no title among the sees. Indeed, the same pope asserts in Epistle 23, section 10, that no prerogative accrued to churches even from the presence of the emperor. It is nevertheless clear that the privilege which the Council of Nicaea, canon 6, observes the Roman pontiff to possess is here attributed to the bishop of Constantinople. It is all the more remarkable that Theodosius admitted this innovation because, in this very edict, he first declares that he wishes every innovation to cease.], and entrusted to the priestly assembly and sacred judgment.

Given on the day before the Ides of July (14 July 421), in the consulship of Eustathius and Agricola.

## EPISTLE X

[Note: In the Roman council published by Lucas Holstenius, this epistle and the following rescript of Theodosius are recited after the last three epistles of our Boniface. These two documents rightly receive their place here, since they were written at Boniface’s request to vindicate the rights of the apostolic see. Although the time at which they were written is not noted, it may be conjectured from the preceding constitution. When this began to be promulgated, it is highly probable that Boniface did not rest until such an unjust constitution had been rescinded through the help of Honorius. Accordingly, these three writings should not be separated by any great interval. Certainly they do not seem separable, since they are so closely connected in subject and substance.]

### OR THE COPY OF THE LETTER OF THE MOST PIOUS EMPEROR HONORIUS TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS

That he should abolish the preceding constitution.

We cannot refuse intercession before the ears of Your Clemency in any matter in which our assistance is sought. But we necessarily owe greater care and zeal to those matters that contain the desires of the holy apostolic see. Since, by divine favor, our empire is always governed, there is no doubt that the Church of that city is to be revered by us with special devotion, from which we received Roman sovereignty and [that Church] received the beginning of the priesthood. For the embassy sent to our piety requests nothing other than what accords with the discipline and equity of the Catholic faith.

For it asks that these privileges, established long ago by the Fathers [Note: Even under pagan emperors, as the conclusion of this letter suggests. From this it may be argued that the right of the Roman bishop in Illyricum did not begin with Damasus.], and preserved until our own times, should remain undisturbed. In this matter Your Serenity should understand that nothing is to be wholly derogated from ancient decrees, if anything has been written into the rules of the canons [Note: Honorius sets this against Theodosius’s statements, in which he boasted that he was defending antiquity and the ancient canons.], nor should the reverence of so many centuries be wounded by novel prejudices, my lord.

Therefore, after reviewing the expressions of our piety, let Your Majesty, mindful of Christianity—which heavenly mercy has poured into our hearts—order that, with everything removed that is said to have been obtained throughout Illyricum by the deception of various bishops [Note: Namely, the bishops of Thessaly, who either envied the dignity granted to Rufus or secretly favored Atticus.], the ancient order be preserved [Note: Boniface had written to Honorius in Epistle 7: “Let what has prevailed through so long a succession of years, even under those rulers who were bound by no concern for our religion, be preserved by firm and stable right”; and perhaps he had repeated similar words in the petition by which he sought the emperor’s intercession. Certainly Honorius here appears to imitate such wording.], lest under Christian rulers the Roman Church lose what it did not lose under other emperors.

## EPISTLE XI

### OR THE RESCRIPT OF THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS TO THE EMPEROR HONORIUS AUGUSTUS

That he had ordered that, after the things obtained from him by deception had been removed, the privileges of the Roman bishop throughout Illyricum should be preserved unharmed.

Anyone who appears to bring to our Clemency the words of an eternal prince deserves a fitting judgment, holy lord, venerable august father—especially in view of the Christian religion, which has been so infused into the revered thoughts of Your Majesty that, extended more broadly through our hearts, it is preserved there. For God, its author, made the descendants of Christian rulers governors [Note: Vopiscus, in his Life of Probus, quotes these words from Aurelian Augustus writing to Probus, who was not yet emperor, concerning the decemvirs: “For they are the men who, by a certain prerogative of good fortune, know no governors except future princes.” Julius Capitolinus, in his Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher: “In that priesthood he was both governor and prophet.” Lampridius likewise, in his Life of Julian, mentions governors appointed by that emperor to govern the state. Thus Holstenius, who also observes that ecclesiastical writers bestowed the same title of governor upon Christian rulers. In fact, Pope Gelasius, indicating an imperial constitution, speaks of it in Epistle 14 as follows: “The authority of our governors proceeded from it.” These men are not improperly called governors because they preside over the state, just as bishops are called governors because they preside over the Church.], so that, every deception having been frustrated, what was established by our ancestors might be preserved.

And although the words of Your Perpetuity are received by us with swift devotion and every reverence not only in those matters which divine assistance has preserved incorrupt, this matter is especially important, because the name of that illustrious city has until now preserved the welfare of the entire world and of our kingdom. Therefore, with every deception of the petitioning bishops throughout Illyricum removed, we decree that what the ancient apostolic discipline and the old canons proclaim be observed.

Concerning this matter, according to the form of the command of Your Perpetuity, we have sent writings to the illustrious prefects of the praetorium of our Illyricum [Note: Those writings have been lost; only the above-mentioned command remains in the Theodosian and Justinianic Codes, against which they were directed. Their authenticity is especially confirmed by the fact that Boniface’s successors retained the ancient right in the provinces of Illyricum without any dispute.], so that, with the bishops’ deceptions brought to an end, they may take special care that the ancient order be preserved, lest the venerable Church lose the privileges of the Most Holy City established by the ancients—privileges that have consecrated to us the everlasting empire of its name.

## EPISTLE XII

[Note: This epistle is found not only in the Dionysian, Hadrianic, and Hispanic collections of Isidore Mercator, but also in the Collection of Canons published by Paschasius Quesnellus. The Colbertine copy of this collection bears in its general index the false heading: “Pope Boniface to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, concerning Patroclus, bishop of Lodève.” The more accurate heading would be: “Concerning Patroclus of Arles, who ordained the bishop of Lodève contrary to the canons.” We retain the summary prefixed to it by Dionysius Exiguus. In this epistle Boniface rescinds the privileges granted to Patroclus by Zosimus without mentioning either those privileges or his predecessor who granted them. He is praised by Celestine, Epistle 4, section 6, for restoring to the metropolitans the right assigned to them by the canons.]

### BONIFACE I, POPE, TO HILARY, BISHOP OF NARBONNE

That in each province no one is to be ordained bishop while disregarding the metropolitan.

[Col. 0772A]

Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome [Note: Since the clergy of Lodève in the First Province of Narbonensis had complained to Boniface that, after their bishop had died, Patroclus of Arles had ordained another bishop for them, although he was in another province and had bypassed their metropolitan, Hilary of Narbonne, the pontiff writes to Hilary about the matter. He orders him to go to Lodève and exercise the right and authority of a metropolitan; after everything has been completed, he is to report to the apostolic see what he has decided. Thus Boniface rescinds what Zosimus had recently decreed and declares that ordination in First Narbonensis belongs not to the bishop of Arles but to the bishop of Narbonne, as metropolitan.], to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne [Note: The printed editions, following Isidore, add “greetings”; that word is absent from the examples of the older collections.].

1. We are indeed reluctant to place faith in complaints whose insistence strikes the priests of the Lord, especially when they say that those priests have attempted something contrary to the statutes of the Fathers. Yet, as now, a multitude of complainants frequently establishes the truth of such complaints. Behold, as Your Charity recognizes from what follows [Note: Merlin has “of Lucubensis”; Crab has “of Luctenensis.”], the clergy—or the people—of the Church of Lodève have sent their petitions and tears to us, as far as can be understood, with great sorrow. They say that our fellow bishop Patroclus [Celestine quotes this in Epistle 4, section 7], without their petition [Note: The older Colbertine manuscript reads “having annulled their petitions.” The reading of the other books is more correct; from it is confirmed the practice that a bishop should not be ordained for a people “when their petition has ceased,” that is, without their petition, nor should they be compelled against their will to accept one ordained in this way.], in place of their deceased bishop, has ordained some man or other in another province, having bypassed the metropolitan, contrary to the rules of the Fathers [Note: Sirmond and Labbe, together with the older Colbertine manuscript, read “in another.” Another Colbertine manuscript has “from a foreign province,” which is less suitable. Although the canons also prohibit seeking a bishop from another province unless no worthy man is available in one’s own, the present controversy concerns the ordination of priests in a foreign province. Hilary of Narbonne had already complained to Patroclus, because he had ordained priests in another province, as is recorded in Zosimus’s Epistle 6, section 1, asserting that priests should not be made in another province by someone else. When Hilary, one of Patroclus’s successors, subsequently claimed the same privilege for himself, Leo rebuked him in Epistle 11, section 7, with these words: “What does Hilary seek in another province, and why does he usurp what none of his predecessors before Patroclus possessed?” Throughout this affair there was a certain difference in the form or manner of the judgments of the apostolic see. At first the bishop of Narbonne had obtained the power of ordaining bishops in the province of Narbonensis I, as we learn from Zosimus’s Epistle 6, section 1. Then, in the same Epistle 6, that pope removed this right from him and transferred it to the bishop of Arles. Thereafter Boniface, by abolishing Patroclus’s privilege, restored to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, the right that had been taken from him; subsequent pontiffs, especially Leo in Epistle 11, section 7, confirmed it. Yet amid this diversity all are found to have agreed in one judgment: they unanimously proclaimed that steadfast adherence to the observance of the canons was necessary. “Among us,” says Zosimus in Epistle 5, “antiquity lives with unshaken roots, and the decrees of the Fathers have sanctioned reverence for it.” In this, Boniface now and Celestine and Leo later agreed with him, for they too professed with complete agreement that they were defenders of the canons. Indeed, Zosimus did not assign the disputed privilege to Patroclus until Patroclus had proved that his predecessors had always enjoyed it by arguments that Hilary of Narbonne had been unable at that time to refute. But if that same bishop later, having recovered his strength, established that no one before Patroclus had claimed the privilege, it is not at all surprising that he obtained its revocation and abolition once the reason for which it had been granted was removed. Paschasius Quesnellus still defends Zosimus’s judgment on this matter in Dissertation 5 against Leo. On the opposing side stand Baronius, under the years 418 and 422; Peter de Marca, On the Primacy, section 71; his continuator Étienne Baluze, Book V of On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire, chapter 30; and Tillemont, volume X, pages 681 and following.], disregarding the metropolitan. We cannot possibly bear this patiently, because it is fitting that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of the Fathers.

No one, it seems, is unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which commands as follows, so that we may set down its very words [Note: Baronius has “proper,” as does one Harleian manuscript. Quesnellus, Dissertation 12, chapter 7, thinks that “near” should be restored in place of “properly.” Yet he does not find in the Nicene canons either the words quoted by Boniface or words nearly identical with them. Nor is there agreement among scholars about their source. Some think they were taken from canons that have been lost. Others believe that the sixth Nicene canon is being indicated at greater length. Against them the aforementioned eminent scholar says in the same work, chapter 6: “I do not think this canon is being referred to; for it deals more with the chief primates of the greater dioceses than with the provincial bishops of the metropolises. But,” he says, “the passage concerns the ordinary metropolitan bishops of the provinces in canon 4, which deals with the ordination of bishops.” Yet even canon 4, in the collection that he entitled the Code of the Canons of the Roman Church, does not display words nearly identical with those quoted here by Boniface. It reads there as follows: “A bishop ought above all to be ordained by all who are in the province . . . The power, or confirmation, shall belong in each province to the metropolitan.” As for us, although we do not deny that Boniface cited this canon 4, we nevertheless think nothing prevents the same pope from having referred simultaneously to that portion of canon 6 which, in the very ancient Fossatian manuscript, now Colbertine, appears under the heading “On invalidating an ordination performed without the consent of the metropolitan,” and is expressed as follows: “It is entirely clear, moreover, that if someone has been ordained bishop contrary to the will of the metropolitan, this holy synod decrees that he must not be a bishop.” In the Code published by Quesnellus, canon 6 is likewise divided into two parts, and its final part is expressed in the same words. Certainly we would be reluctant to concede to the learned man that this final part prescribes authority for one of the sees that later came to be called patriarchal, rather than for the other metropolitan sees. As for the interpretation of the word “properly,” our conjecture is this: Zosimus did not intend to reproduce here the actual words of the Council of Nicaea, but repeated words that may have been summarized from the Nicene canons in the petition of the people of Lodève, and declared them as though they were his own. In this way Zosimus, as we shall see in Celestine’s Epistle 21, section 11, adopted the decrees of the Council of Carthage in these words: “We also embrace as proper to the apostolic see what has been established within the decrees of the Council of Carthage.”]

“Throughout each province, each metropolitan is to possess jurisdiction, and no one is to have two provinces subject to him.” [Note: The Roman edition and other older editions, as in the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, add “to be able”; that word is more correctly absent from the Dionysian and Hadrianic copies, where “are to be” is understood. At that time, several provinces were subject to the bishops of Alexandria, Antioch, Thessalonica, and some others; and it is clear from the opinion of Innocent—who writes in Epistle 24, section 2, that provinces divided by imperial judgment must by no means be divided in the Church, nor the number of metropolitans increased—that it could happen for two civil provinces to be subject to one ecclesiastical metropolitan. The reading of the old Colbertine manuscript, “that there may be subject sees,” is much less satisfactory. The matter here concerns provinces, not sees.] They judged, since it could not be otherwise, that this must be observed, as the Holy Spirit suggested to them.

2. Therefore, dearest brother, if matters stand thus, and the boundary of your province encloses the aforesaid church [Note: One of the Colbertine manuscripts has “enclosed.” Merlin, as in the Isidorian manuscripts, has “fortify”; other editions, together with the Hadrianic collection, have “fortified” or “more strongly.” We have restored “admonished” with Dionysius and the other better manuscripts.], go to that same place where such an ordination is said to have been celebrated, admonished by our authority—though you ought to do so voluntarily—having been armed with the right of a metropolitan and relying upon our commands, with due regard for the desires and wishes of the petitioners. [Note: One Harleian manuscript, in a second correction, has “you ought to have done,” supported by the Regius manuscript containing the pure Dionysian collection, where “you should have done” appears.]

Understand that, according to the rules of the Fathers, authority to do whatever must be done has been granted to you by us, so that, when everything has been completed, it may become known to the apostolic see through your report what you have decided. For it is clear that the ordination of your entire province has been entrusted to you [Note: Crab adds “of your province,” and this word was thereafter retained, although it is absent from Dionysius, Hadrian, and the other better manuscripts. Certainly “of yours,” not “of his,” should have been added.].

Therefore let no bold transgressor exceed their boundaries, nor let anyone, to their dishonor, defend on his own side things that do not appear to have been granted to him [Note: The Roman edition, as in the Pithou manuscript, adds “by these men”; in its place “according to the rules of the Fathers” must be understood. The same word “Fathers” is likewise understood above, both in “these boundaries of theirs” and here in “to their dishonor.”]. Let the presumption of those who extend the limits of their dignity beyond what is lawful cease, constrained by our authority.

We say this so that Your Charity may understand that we observe the precepts of the canons so carefully [Note: The old Colbertine and Pithou manuscripts have “to observe the precepts of the canons more cautiously.” Some manuscripts, though not the better ones, have “so that this may be.” Pithou has “judgment” instead of “constitution.” Boniface here clearly commends and confirms canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea, which prescribes that confirmation of what is done in each province be carried out by the metropolitan.] that our constitution also determines that each province must always await the decision of its metropolitan in all matters.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of February (9 February 422), in the consulship of our lords Honorius, Augustus for the thirteenth time, and Theodosius, Augustus for the tenth time.

## EPISTLE XIII

[Note: This epistle, which may properly be called an admonitory letter, was recited together with the two following ones in the Roman council brought to light through the work of Lucas Holstenius. The same Severus, notary of the apostolic see, carried those three writings together into Illyricum. Since Nicholas I frequently cites the middle epistle, he thereby lends authority to the other two as well. Moreover, what is said in those letters about Perigenes agrees with the testimony of Socrates concerning that bishop in Book VII, chapter 36.]

Boniface admonishes Rufus concerning the dignity and office of vicar of blessed Peter granted to him, enters into communion with him, and communicates what he wrote to the Thessalians concerning the various matters being disputed in those regions, as well as what remains for Rufus himself to do.

[Col. 0774B]

### BONIFACE TO HIS DEAREST BROTHER RUFUS
1. The injunction laid upon your predecessors concerning the provinces of the apostolic see [Col. 0775A] must diligently be fulfilled by your Charity. For the affairs of the churches situated throughout those provinces must be cared for with ever-watchful attention. Thus blessed Peter entrusted everything to the Thessalonian Church in his place, so that it might understand that the responsibility for many remains with it; and this responsibility must not be diminished by new [Note: [Col. 0775C] By the expression “those new attempts,” Holstenius understands the rescript of Theodosius, extorted in the preceding year in favor of the see of Constantinople against the rights of the Roman see over the churches of Illyricum. The words that follow also seem to support this interpretation: “For one must not yield to the efforts of those whom novelty and the desire for an unmerited dignity inflame.” The phrase “the desire for an unmerited dignity” refers to Atticus alone. By “those whom novelty inflames,” however, one may understand the Thessalonians, who, eager to flatter Atticus, attempted certain innovations, on account of which they deserved letters from Boniface filled with the apostolic see’s displeasure, threats, and correction. Yet if Theodosius’s decree had then remained intact and unrepealed—the decree by which the right of the apostolic see in Illyricum was transferred to the bishop of the imperial city—Boniface would not, in section 2, have spoken so confidently to Rufus: “Exercise over the other contumacious persons also the right of the authority granted to you.”] attempts, which cannot possess any force. For one must not yield to the efforts of those whom novelty and the desire for an unmerited dignity inflame; rather, one must labor and, with the favor of our God assisting, strive so that whoever strives against what is lawful may recognize that resistance confronts him in every respect. Therefore, dearest brother, trusting in the authority already received from you, arm yourself as a capable soldier of our God against the hostile bands. Here you will fear no doubtful matter, dread no uncertain outcome. You have blessed Peter the Apostle, who can fight on your behalf with his own strength. I do not want you to be frightened by the disturbance of a sea stirred up. For it is certain that the faith which you bear hidden in your breast is greater than all things. No tumult, no storm at all, will trouble you. That fisherman does not allow the privilege of his see to perish while you labor. Every swelling of the waves and every storm will cease, with him favoring your efforts to whom alone the sea was passable. He will surely be present, and, with God as author, will restrain the violators of the canons and the enemies of ecclesiastical law—he who always frustrates the wishes of such minds.

2. Exercise over the other contumacious persons also the right of the authority granted to you. For you see that we have left no place unattended. We sent the Thessalonians letters full of threats and correction. To the synod said to be convening unlawfully at Corinth concerning our brother and fellow bishop Perigenes—whose status, as we wrote, cannot be disturbed by any means—we sent such letters that all the brethren might understand, first, that they ought not to have assembled without your knowledge; and, second, that our judgment was not to be reconsidered. For it has never been permitted to reopen a matter once settled by the apostolic see. In that letter of ours we preserved, as was fitting, the honor due to your Holiness, as your Charity will learn from reading it.

3. We wish your Charity carefully to hear the case of our fellow bishop Perrebius, whose petition, sent to us by him, has informed us that his fellow priests are said to be exceedingly troublesome to him, to the point that they believed he should be expelled from his own church. After summoning the fellow bishops mentioned above, whose violence he laments having to endure, your Charity should investigate the matter. Then, so that they may understand that, if anything was done by them contrary to custom, it must first be annulled, your Charity should promptly report everything examined to us, so that our sentence may strengthen the judgment issued by your Fraternity.

[Note: [Col. 0775C] At the Council of Ephesus, at the beginning of act 1, among the other bishops there is noted “Perrebius, bishop of Farmulus,” or “Farmacus”; in one manuscript “Firmacus,” in others “Farmalius,” where “Pharsalius” should be read, for that is a city of Thessaly. In the proceedings of the same act he gives his judgment, in Labbé, volume III, page 489 B, as “Perrebius, bishop of the Thessalian groves,” in Greek τῶν Θεσσαλικῶν σαλῶν [for ἀλσῶν], and in the same work, page 537 A, he subscribes as “Perrebius, bishop of the Thessalonian groves.” This reading is also found in Marius Mercator, Baluz’s edition, page 212, and in the new collection of Councils compiled by the same Baluzius, page 631. On page 610 of that collection, “Parebius,” in Greek τῶν Θεσσαλῶν σαλτῶν, subscribes in Latin as “bishop of the Thessalonian groves.” Finally, in the same collection, page 1148, among the subscriptions to the Council of Chalcedon appears: “Perrebius, bishop of the Thessalonian Sardians.” Rusticus, the deacon of Pope Vigilius, observed that in the Acumetian manuscript “of the Groves” was preferred in place of “of the Sardians.” Amid this variety of readings, which should be preferred is determined from this and the following letter. Since both letters speak of the Thessalians and are addressed to the Thessalians, it follows that this Perrevius or Perrebius was bishop of the Thessalian groves, not of the Thessalonian groves, and that one and the same city of Thessaly was known by two names, namely Pharsalius and “the Thessalian groves.” It is further established from the passages cited that Perrevius was by no means expelled from his church, since he sat as a bishop with the fathers of Ephesus and Chalcedon and subscribed to both councils under that title.]

[Note: [Col. 0776C] Holstenius has “approved.” We have restored the reading “which we have brought forward”; we think that reading must be approved by everyone.]

4. We wish you to recognize that in the letter sent to the Thessalonian brothers we wrote that Pausianus, Cyriacus, and Calliopus [Note: [Col. 0776C] Holstenius understands these three bishops to be the persons referred to in the following letter, section 2: “I hear that certain bishops, disregarding apostolic law,” and he further supposes that Maximus was ordained by these men without the consent of the apostolic vicar. The number three supports this opinion, since three bishops were required for the ordination of a bishop. But if they ordained Maximus, not only he but also they were to be removed from priestly honor. Certainly, concerning such ordinations, we read the following decree of Zosimus, letter 7, section 2: “Let the one who ordained him know that he will also suffer the loss of his rank, and that what he conferred will have no force upon the one whom he ordained.” See note a on that pope’s letter 9, section 1. In the following letter, section 2, Boniface indicates that these men are separated from his communion because they themselves strive to separate from communion with the apostolic see. In Baluzius, New Collection of Councils, pages 699 and 886, Pausianus is read among the subscriptions as “bishop of Hypata in Thessaly,” and as having been attached to the party of Nestorius.] are to be completely removed from our communion, so that they may recognize that they possess no remedy except through the intervention of your grace. As for Maximus, whom your Charity reported as having been wrongly ordained, we judge that he must be entirely deprived of priestly honor.

5. It belongs to your Charity to dismiss Severus, the notary of the apostolic see, exceedingly dear to our hearts, sent from our own side [Note: [Col. 0777C] This means one of those accustomed to cling to our side, and therefore known to us, familiar, approved, and dear to us. We shall say more about the antiquity and use of this expression in the note on Leo’s letter 31.] with all speed once everything has been completed, so that, when he returns more quickly, we may learn the sequence of events.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March (March 3, 422), in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius XIII and Theodosius X.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0777C] As Holstenius observed, Hadrian I transcribed the entire opening of this letter in letter 97, in the Carolingian Codex, Grets’s edition, page 322. Nicholas I quotes its first words in letter 70 and elsewhere. Boniface himself expressed some of its phrases in imitation of the opening of Innocent’s letter 25 to Decentius.]

The authority granted to Rufus, which some were despising, is confirmed, first by asserting the authority of the apostolic see.

To the most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Thessaly, BONIFACE.

1. The institution of the universal Church took the honor of blessed Peter as its beginning, in whom its governance and highest authority consist. From his ecclesiastical discipline, as the cultivation of religion increased, the source flowed throughout all the Churches.
