The decrees of the Council of Nicaea bear witness to nothing else: indeed, it did not dare to establish anything above his merit [Note: [Col. 0777C] Namely, canon 6, where the ancient manuscripts read: “The Roman Church has always held the primacy”—not, as Quesnel preferred, “has the primacy.” Referring to this, Nicholas I says in letter 8: “If the decrees of the Council of Nicaea are carefully examined, it will certainly be found that that council conferred no increase upon the Roman Church; rather, following its model, it took as an example what it assigned particularly to the Church of Alexandria.” To the same point belongs what Gelasius wrote in letter 33, section 1: “The Roman Church was not placed above the other Churches by synodal decrees; rather, it obtained the primacy through the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior.” “These privileges,” Nicholas I says shortly before the words just cited, “were given to this Church of Christ by Christ, not given by synods, but merely celebrated and venerated by them.”], since he saw that nothing could be conferred upon him beyond his merit; finally, he knew that everything had been granted to this man by the Lord’s word. Therefore it is certain that this Church is the head of the Churches spread throughout the whole world, just as they are its members. Whoever cuts himself off from it becomes an outcast from the Christian religion, since he will not have begun to be within the same structure.

2. I hear that certain bishops, disregarding apostolic law, are attempting something new against the actual precepts of Christ [Col. 0777C], while they strive to separate themselves from the communion of the apostolic see and, to speak more truly, from its authority, seeking the assistance of those whom the sanction of ecclesiastical regulations has not allowed to possess greater power.

[Note: [Col. 0777D] These men are now said to be attempting something new against Christ’s precepts; their new attempts were condemned in the preceding letter, section 1. From this it follows that those new attempts belonged not only to Atticus but especially to certain bishops of Thessaly. Their fault lay not only in the illegitimate ordination of Maximus but also in violating the rights of the apostolic see, rights founded upon Christ’s precepts.]

For the precepts of our predecessors are recorded, and we find whom they granted some jurisdiction over the Churches. Whoever intrudes into its laws, when nothing is owed to him, is already a violator of ecclesiastical discipline, claiming for himself what appears to have been denied him by the fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0778C] Namely, Atticus, concerning whose see Pope Gelasius explains the following in letter 18, section 10: “If the dignity of cities is truly at issue, the dignity of the priests of the second and third sees is greater than that of a city which is not merely counted among the sees but, as Leo says in letter 195, section 3, cannot be made an apostolic see by anyone; indeed, as Gelasius continues, it is not even counted among the rights of the metropolitans.” Boniface therefore rightly denies here that Atticus was granted the power to be of greater authority.]

3. Receive, then, our admonition and correction, one of which we offer to the pontiffs and the other to those who dissent. For the Apostle says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. 4:21).

[Note: [Col. 0778D] Perhaps “to those who share with us,” that is, those who remain in our communion; these are contrasted with “those who dissent,” that is, those who strive to separate themselves from Boniface’s communion or authority.]

For you know that both are possible to blessed Peter: to rebuke the gentle with gentleness and the proud with a rod.

4. Therefore preserve the honor due to the head, for we do not wish the members to quarrel among themselves, so that their conflict may extend even to us, while you judge our brother and fellow bishop Rufus worthy of contempt. Our authority grants him nothing new; it follows the favor of our predecessors, by which responsibility for the Churches has often evidently been entrusted to this man.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] At least that of Damasus, Siricius, and Innocent, as Nicholas I also recalls in letter 2 to Michael. It is therefore clear that some people objected that power had been granted to the bishop of Thessalonica as something new; this then gave Theodosius the opportunity to transfer it to the bishop of the imperial city.]

We wish this action to be preserved inviolate for the future, just as the form of this arrangement was preserved by the fathers. It is not fitting for brothers to bite one another because of another’s dignity. Certainly, if correction was seen in someone to have exceeded what was due, since the apostolic see holds the primacy precisely so that it may receive the complaints of all [Note: [Col. 0778D] In place of “licentes,” which Holstenius retained on the authority of the archetype, Labbe substituted “licenter.” “Gliscentes” would not be objectionable. “Licentes” may nevertheless be understood as meaning “things that are permitted,” as though they were things that are lawful. Holstenius observed that Atticus, bishop of Nicopolis, later brought his complaints to Pope Leo when Anastasius of Thessalonica had abused his authority against him, as we shall see in Leo’s letter 14, and that he found Leo to be a fair judge of them.], it was appropriate that, by a legation sent to us, we should be appealed to concerning this matter, since you see that responsibility for all affairs remains with us. Let novel presumption cease. Let no one dare to hope for what is not permitted. Let no one attempt to violate what was done by the fathers and guarded for so many ages. Whoever recognizes himself as a bishop must obey our decision. Let no one presume to ordain bishops throughout Illyricum without the knowledge of our fellow bishop Rufus [Col. 0779A], and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0779C] Here Boniface seems to have passed to condemning and rejecting the ordination of Maximus and to the provisions made in the preceding letter, section 4, or to other matters to be decreed. Hence one may infer that not a little has been omitted here.]

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius XIII and Theodosius X.

## LETTER XV

Boniface declares that it is not lawful for the bishops of Illyricum to investigate and reconsider the case of Perigenes, whom he had given to the Corinthians as bishop after due consultation; and that, if any attempt this, they will not remain in his communion. He explains Rufus’s authority over those same provinces again, and more explicitly at the end.

To the most beloved brothers Rufus and the other bishops established throughout Macedonia, Achaia, Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus, Praevalitana, and Dacia, BONIFACE.

1. Blessed Peter continues, through the Lord’s decree, to bear responsibility for the universal Church, which he knew to be founded upon himself, as the Gospel testifies (Matt. 16:18). His honor can never be free from cares, since it is certain that the highest affairs depend upon his deliberation. This responsibility extends my mind even to the regions of the East [Note: [Col. 0779C] In particular, to the provinces of Illyricum. These had once belonged to the Western Empire, but in 379 were detached by Gratian in favor of Theodosius and joined to the Eastern Empire.], which through that very responsibility we in a certain sense see. For I continually question everyone who comes from there about the peace of the brethren—that is, about the tranquility of the bishops—which is accustomed to be disturbed by someone’s presumption whenever the devil envies it. Since rumor had until now reported to us that everything was being preserved in its proper order, we were utterly astonished, as the nature of the reports required, at the new intention that attempted this injury to the fathers.

2. For we have learned from a reliable informant that a synod is to be convened at Corinth to investigate the status of the man concerning whom we speak with indignation—the man whom the apostolic see, after examining and discussing everything, established as priest for the Corinthians, following the will of God, which, as the passage of time makes clear, wished him to be shepherd of the very fold in which he had grown and for which he had grown.

[Note: [Col. 0779C] Perigenes is meant. But why such obstinacy in rejecting him? Boniface says nothing about what was alleged against him. It is nevertheless not obscure that the bishop of the imperial city and those attached to him had no other reason for rejecting Perigenes than that he had once been named bishop of Patrae. Some Eastern minds held the opinion—which they thought supported by canons 16 and 17 of the Council of Antioch—that a person designated bishop of a church, even if he had never been accepted by it, could not later be placed over another. For this reason Proclus was for some time prevented from being placed over the imperial city, as Socrates testifies, book VII, chapter 35. On the same pretext Bassianus was removed from the episcopate by the Council of Ephesus because he had been designated bishop of Evaza, although he had never assumed the governance of that church; this may be read in the Council of Chalcedon, act 2, especially page 692. Some likewise objected that Gregory, who had been ordained bishop of Sasima by Basil but had been unable to obtain that church, was placed in the see of Constantinople. Nor were there lacking Westerners who complained that he had been elevated to that see contrary to the rules. They held this view not because he had previously been ordained at Sasima, but because they thought he had subsequently truly been appointed bishop of Nazianzus. As for Boniface, he judged that he would do nothing contrary to the rules forbidding the translation of bishops if he granted Perigenes—who had not been accepted by the people of Patrae—to the Corinthians, who were choosing him as their bishop. Approving this judgment of Boniface, Celestine later sent letters to Perigenes as bishop of Corinth. Accordingly, those who were asking that Proclus be made bishop of the imperial city demonstrated, against those who argued that this was contrary to the canons, that Celestine supported their petition, as may be gathered from Socrates, book VII, chapter 40, although he reports the matter in a highly distorted way because of his preconceived view.]

If your Charity were unaware of the history of this ordination, I would gladly unfold from its beginning what had previously been done concerning him [Note: [Col. 0780C] Namely, the synod that had ordained Perigenes bishop of Patrae, in whose letter an outstanding testimony concerning him appeared and has already been quoted again. Shortly afterward: “whose appearance,” that is, “whose minds,” with the plural in the accusative; the text is obscure at this point because of the obscurity of the passage.], so that, through this disclosure, it might become clear to those whose view of his case has been shrouded in obscurity not through ignorance but through partisanship that a special divine judgment had been made concerning him. As we said, heavenly judgment preserved him for the Church of Corinth as her foster child. This action was earnestly requested of us by the consent of all the citizens and clergy.

[Col. 0780B] Yet our command did not establish this abruptly. Rather, as ecclesiastical discipline required, we ordered our brother and fellow bishop Rufus to examine the inner details of the matter more carefully and, with his nearby moderation, weigh the substance of the petition, so that nothing might appear to have been done prematurely by this see, which has often suppressed the presumptions of others. After some time had passed, the letters of our aforesaid bishop reached us concerning this matter, agreeing with the desires set forth above. Following their most evident reasoning, we gave him as pontiff to that Church in which he had passed the earlier part of his life through each successive degree of honor.

3. For carrying this out I immediately sent the aforesaid bishop a second letter of mine, which pleased the entire presbyterate [Col. 0780C], and by its authority I commanded him, following our predecessors, who always judged the Thessalonian Church—faithful to them and serving them in the affection of the college, as the evidence of the archives affirms—worthy of this honor.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] In the common editions, as in the archetype, the reading is “authority”; this is a familiar scribal error, by which scribes double the letter beginning the following word and attach it to the preceding word. The preceding words, “a second letter of mine,” necessarily require “by authority.” Here “authority,” as often in the writings of the Roman pontiffs, means a letter. Thus when Zosimus says below, concerning Perigenes, section 8, “After the bishop had been established by our letters of authority,” the phrase “by our letters of authority” means nothing other than what appears here: “by a second letter of mine.” He first says that this letter pleased the entire presbyterate. This makes it increasingly clear that in those times the Roman pontiffs did nothing in such matters without the knowledge of their clergy. Again, at the beginning of section 9, where we read, “Our authority must not be without its customary admonition,” it is obvious that “authority” means a letter.]

I now grant this same favor to our brother Rufus for the future as well, following the Lord, who exalts the humbled and always humbles the exalted, granting grace to the former and resisting the latter (I Pet. 5:6).

4. How great, then, is the gift of humility, weighed on the scales of divine grace? And how great is the punishment of pride, which the Lord and ruler of the whole world himself opposes? I leave it to your Fraternity to understand who is the teacher of humility and who is the teacher of pride. But far be it from the priests of the Lord that any of them should fall into this guilt, attempting something new and thereby making the decrees of the fathers hostile to himself, recognizing that he has as a particular rival the one in whose hands our Christ has placed the fullness of the priesthood. Whoever rises up in insult against him will not be able to be an inhabitant of the heavenly kingdoms. “To you,” he says, “I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19), into which no one will enter without the grace of the doorkeeper. “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid., 18). Therefore whoever desires to be counted worthy before our God even of priestly dignity—since one reaches God by receiving Peter, in whom, as we mentioned above, the universal Church is certainly founded—must be gentle and humble in heart, lest the rebellious disciple begin to suffer the punishment of the teacher whose pride he imitated.

5. Therefore, to return to the cause of this injury, a synod is being assembled [Note: [Col. 0781C] The corrupt passage might be repaired as follows: “which, always setting the divine counsel above the decision concerning the chosen man, should recognize the secret purpose.” For he complains that the bishops wish to reconsider the judgment of the apostolic see concerning Perigenes, although that see had deliberately followed the secret counsel of heaven in this matter, following the will of God, as stated above in section 2.] whose corrupt wording appears to say that, having always held a consultation concerning its beloved [one], it should recognize the council’s secret purpose; and what the rules absolutely cannot permit will happen: the honor of our brother and fellow bishop Perigenes, whom our judgment placed in the see of the aforesaid Church, will become doubtful and uncertain.

Who, then, has attacked this man? What inexperienced accuser, perhaps only now returning from abroad, has done so? Which bishop certainly ordered a crowd of brothers to assemble, once our letters had been read? Since the place requires it, if you wish to review the sanctions of the canons [Note: [Col. 0781C] Those of Nicaea, namely, whose sixth canon distinguishes the order of the sees, especially according to the reading found in the old Fossatensian manuscript, now Colbertinus, and several others, as follows: “The Roman Church has always held the primacy. Let Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis retain the primacy, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these, since the Roman bishop also has this custom. Likewise, the one established at Antioch. Therefore, in the other provinces also, let the privileges of the Churches remain intact.” Leo refers to this same canon in letter 95, section 3, where he opposes the ambition of Anatolius, who sought the second place in the Church, in these words: “It would be charged to me if, with my connivance, the rule of the paternal decrees—formed at the Council of Nicaea under the instruction of the Spirit of God for the governance of the whole Church—were violated.” That Boniface is referring here to no canons other than those of Nicaea is confirmed again by these words of Leo’s letter 97, section 3, to Anatolius: “I also grieve that your Affection has fallen so far as to attempt to violate the most sacred constitutions of the Nicene canons, as though this time had conveniently presented itself to you in which the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of the second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of the third dignity.” In section 4 Leo approves his legates, who had strongly resisted at the Council of Chalcedon the granting of such a privilege to the see of Constantinople, openly protesting that no presumption of condemned novelty should rise against the decrees of Nicaea.] you will find which is the second see after the Roman Church and which is the third.

For this reason the order of things appears to have been so distinguished that the pontiffs of the other Churches may recognize themselves, under one and the same priesthood, as subject in ecclesiastical discipline to those to whom they ought to be subject while preserving charity.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] The earlier printed editions read “destroyed,” an obvious error that we have judged no longer tolerable. What Boniface teaches here briefly about the unity of the priesthood, Cyprian explains at greater length near the beginning of his book On the Unity of the Church. After observing that the Lord gave all the Apostles equal power, but, in order to manifest unity, established one chair and arranged by his authority that the origin of unity should begin from one, he adds shortly afterward: “The episcopate is one, and each bishop holds one part of it in its entirety.” Augustine addresses Boniface himself in the same spirit above, in letter 6: “The watchtower of pastoral care is common to all of us who perform the office of bishop, although you yourself preside in it from a higher eminence.”]

Indeed, this judgment of the canons has endured from antiquity (Nicholas I, letter 8, to the emperor Michael) and, with the favor of Christ our Lord, remains to this day. No one has ever boldly laid hostile hands upon the apostolic summit, whose judgment may not be reconsidered; no one has rebelled in this matter except one who wished to be judged concerning himself. The great Churches mentioned above—the Alexandrian and Antiochene—preserve their dignities according to the canons, having knowledge of ecclesiastical law. They preserve, I say, the statutes of the fathers, showing deference in everything and receiving in turn the grace which they recognize themselves to owe us in the Lord, who is our peace.

6. But since the matter requires it, the evidence must establish that the greatest Eastern Churches have always consulted the Roman see in important affairs requiring more extensive debate and, whenever need demanded, sought its assistance. Athanasius and Peter, priests of the Church of Alexandria, of holy memory, sought the assistance of this see. When the Church of Antioch was afflicted for a long time, so that delegations repeatedly came from there for this very reason—first under Meletius and afterward under Flavian—it is clear that the apostolic see was consulted. After much had been done by our Church, no one doubts that Flavian received the grace of communion from its authority [Col. 0783A], a grace of which he had been deprived forever unless letters concerning this matter had proceeded from here.

[Note: [Col. 0783C] This occurred shortly after the ordination of John as bishop of Constantinople. At that time Acacius, bishop of Beroea, together with Isidore and several other presbyters and deacons of the Church of Antioch, came to Rome and brought not only the decree of John’s ordination but also the communion of Flavian with Theophilus, as Palladius says in his Dialogue, page 51. On this occasion the Roman pontiff confirmed the peace arranged by Theophilus by letters sent to Flavian. We observed above, page 707, section 14, that these letters should be attributed either to Siricius or to his successor Anastasius. See also what we discussed there, section 13, on this matter. Boniface could have added to Flavian’s example that of Porphyry, who, after taking the place of Flavian when the latter died shortly afterward, wrote to the Roman Church, according to Palladius, Dialogue, page 141, but was not thought worthy of a reply. For, as Palladius relates on page 28, the presbyters of the Church of Antioch had informed the Roman pontiff Innocent that Porphyry’s ordination had been carried out contrary to law and right. It is therefore clear both that Porphyry sought to have Innocent ratify his own ordination and that the Antiochene presbyters took care that the pope would not accept it.]

The most mercifully remembered emperor Theodosius, believing that the ordination of Nectarius could not be considered firm because it had not been within our knowledge, sent courtiers from his own side together with bishops and formally requested that a letter of communion [Note: [Col. 0784C] We find no record of this embassy in ecclesiastical writers. We have only, above, page 567, the letter of the Constantinopolitan synod written in the presence of the emperor Theodosius, by which Damasus and his associates were informed of Nectarius’s ordination and asked to rejoice over it. Perhaps, when Damasus delayed, the emperor judged that the “formata” he desired had to be requested through a solemn embassy. Here “formata” means letters attesting communion, by which the ordination of a newly appointed bishop is approved, although the word is usually understood as letters given to laymen or clergy traveling abroad, as testimony to their faith, order, or rank.] be regularly sent to him from the Roman see to strengthen his priesthood. A short time ago, under my predecessor Innocent, of blessed memory, the pontiffs of the Eastern Churches, grieving that they had been separated from the communion of blessed Peter, sought peace through legates, as your Charity remembers (see Innocent’s letters 19 and following). At that time the apostolic see granted everything without difficulty, obeying the teacher who says (II Cor. 2:10–11): “If anyone has been forgiven anything, I also forgive him; for if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sake in the presence of Christ, lest we be possessed by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices” (Nicholas I quotes this at the end of letter 42)—that is, because he always rejoices in dissension.

7. Since, then, dearest brothers, I believe that the examples I have cited are sufficient to prove what we have said, although your knowledge contains many more, we wish these letters to meet your assembly without injury to your Fraternity. You will see that they have been sent by Severus, the notary of the apostolic see, exceedingly dear to our hearts, dispatched from our side. As is fitting, brothers, let them serve as an admonition, so that no one who wishes to remain in our communion may again bring forward for discussion the name of our brother and fellow bishop Perigenes, whose priesthood the Apostle Peter once already confirmed through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, leaving no question about him for the future. When he was established by us during the period in which the see was vacant, nothing whatsoever is known to have been alleged against him. Let the accusation cease, whose author we recognize by its spite. Let the contrivance of falsehood fabricated against him be dissolved, because by the favor of our God and of all good men he has attained the priesthood.

8. Nevertheless, since room must be left for the accuser, lest we appear entirely to deny him a hearing [Note: [Col. 0784C] Perhaps one should read, “lest we entirely cut off his hearing,” with this expression used in place of “cut off and deny.”], if anything is reported to have been done by him, after he was established as bishop by our letters of authority, against discipline and the purpose of the priesthood, our fellow bishop Rufus, to whom we entrust everything in our place, together with the other brothers whom he himself chooses [Note: [Col. 0784C] Later Leo, in letter 12 to Anastasius, section 14, entrusted this selection of judges not to Anastasius alone but to the metropolitans. Leo issued that decree, however, after Anastasius had abused the authority granted to him.], will undertake to hear the matter [Col. 0784B], and will report everything back to our judgment, whatever the course and order of events reveal to his investigation.

9. Furthermore, since our authority must not be without its customary admonition, we exhort you and repeatedly command you to give this man obedience in every matter by your decisions. As we have often said, let no one presume to celebrate any ordination without the knowledge of him to whom, as stated above, we entrust everything in our place. Those responsible for this presumption will certainly charge it to themselves in the future, when they see that they are outcasts from the communion of the apostolic charity.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March (March 11, 422), in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius XIII and Theodosius X.

[Col. 0783]

## APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF SAINT BONIFACE I, POPE

### INFORMATION CONCERNING WRITINGS NO LONGER EXTANT THAT PERTAIN TO BONIFACE I, POPE

I.

[Col. 0783D]

1. Before June of the year 419, the clergy of the city of Valentina [Col. 0784D] came to Boniface and presented him with a petition against Maximus, their bishop, in which they set out various accusations against him [Col. 0785A]. In particular, they charged that he was enveloped in the darkness of the Manichaeans (Epistle 3), and, as proof of the allegation, produced the acts of a synod. They further asserted, by bringing forward the records, that he had been brought before the tribunals of secular judges because of his own madness and insane recklessness, subjected to examination, and condemned for homicide. They added that, when provincial jurisdiction had been delegated to him by Boniface’s predecessors, he had always avoided the judgment decreed, and nevertheless, to the disgrace of his own city, claimed for himself in his hiding places the title of bishop. To this petition Boniface replied on June 13 of the year 419.

II.

2. Around August of that same year, Boniface received a petition from the Corinthians, in which they signified that they desired not so much to receive Perigenes as to retain him as bishop [Col. 0785B]. Along with this petition they submitted a letter written by the whole synod of Achaea, which had formerly ordained Perigenes bishop for the people of Patras. In that letter the entire course of his ordination was recounted, and he was expressly commended as a holy man, distinguished by the excellence of his character and formation (Epistle 4, no. 3).

III.

3. After receiving the Corinthians’ letter, Boniface sent a copy of it on September 19 of the aforementioned year 419 to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, desiring that the Corinthians should obtain the fulfillment of their wish as soon as possible, but unwilling to accomplish this without Rufus’s letter, which would confirm his previously formed opinion of Perigenes. Yet the man who then wrote to Rufus, “We do not wish” (Epistle 5, no. 4) “to send our letter to our co-bishop Perigenes [Col. 0785C] before we receive yours concerning him,” immediately adds: “Therefore you will hasten to do this for the sake of those who are making the request.”

Rufus, moreover, obeyed Boniface’s wishes all the more quickly and willingly because his opinion of Perigenes was no different from that of the Corinthians. Boniface himself attests this in these words: “After some time had passed” (Epistle 15, no. 2), “the writings of our aforementioned bishop [Rufus], corresponding to the wishes expressed above” (that is, writings testifying that Perigenes was fully worthy of the honor conferred upon him), “came to us.” These writings, however, have not reached us.

IV.

4. As soon as Boniface had also been assured, by Rufus’s testimony, of Perigenes’ worth, he wrote a second letter to that same Rufus [Col. 0785D], entrusting to him his own place and authority for constituting Perigenes bishop of the Corinthians. This letter, which the sequence of events requires us to assign to the end of 419 or the beginning of 420, Boniface did not wish to send until it had been read aloud to the clergy of the City and had received the approval of the entire presbyterate (Epistle 15, no. 3).

V.

5. After receiving the Corinthians’ petition, Boniface considered what he could do by the full force of his authority and what the requirements of discipline demanded. Although he could have replied to the Corinthians and to Perigenes and immediately constituted the latter bishop, he decided to defer the matter. Accordingly, he addressed Rufus as follows:

“I do not doubt that your Charity understands [Col. 0786A] how remarkable it is that we seem neither to have sent our letter to this man [Perigenes] nor to have given a reply to the petitioners [the Corinthians]” (Epistle 5, no. 4).

While this delay continued, Perigenes’ election, or authority, remained suspended. “For him,” Boniface says (ibid.), “the only thing still lacking for the full confirmation of his episcopate is that he has not yet received our address honoring him.”

Since Boniface therefore testifies that the sole reason preventing him from sending his letter to Perigenes was that he had received no letter from Rufus, there can be no doubt that, once Rufus’s letter had been delivered to him, he immediately sent both the deferred letter to Perigenes and his reply to the Corinthians, and also the second letter to Rufus. That both actions were carried out is indicated by these words: “We have given him to be the bishop of that Church in which, through its several grades, he had also passed the preceding part of his life” (Epistle 15, no. 2).

Here the word “we have given” should be noted, since it conveys a particular authority. The action seemed so necessary that, as long as the letter by which Boniface ordered Perigenes to be constituted bishop was lacking, it was judged that something still remained before the full confirmation of his episcopate.

VI.

6. One letter of Boniface, Epistle 5, points to several writings that have not reached us. In it Boniface mentions a letter from Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, in which Rufus consulted him about certain matters relating to the administration of the Churches entrusted to him. Boniface notes that he gave an answer to this consultation of Rufus in proportion to the circumstances of the cases [Col. 0786C] (Epistle 5, no. 1), establishing that those requirements should be observed which ecclesiastical discipline demands—that is, that one must not depart from canonical or apostolic tradition.

At the same time, he says that he added several letters to this reply, to be sent through Rufus’s agency to various bishops of Achaea and Macedonia. In them he prescribed what course they ought to follow (no. 3). Nor does he omit what Rufus replied: namely, that the aforesaid letters had been delivered to each of their recipients, and that Boniface’s admonition had proved effective among most of them, specifically among Adelphius and Perigenes, but had been ineffective among certain others.

In this report Rufus said that he was encouraged to fulfill his assigned duty diligently by consideration of the blessed apostle Peter, whom he regarded as watching with his own eyes to see how Rufus was carrying out his office.

[Col. 0786D] 7. Since those mutual letters of Boniface and Rufus are mentioned in a single letter, Epistle 5, they increasingly demonstrate that the conclusion of that letter has been awkwardly attached to what precedes and properly belongs to an earlier letter. The chronological note with which the same letter concludes must likewise be understood in this way. For since it is clear that the four aforementioned letters were written at different times, if we consult the historical truth, it is not easy to see how all of them could have been written not merely before September 419 but even before the end of that year.

It is quite probable that Rufus, after being anticipated by Boniface’s letter confirming to him the dignity of vicar of the apostolic see, was then first prompted to consult the same pope.

VII.

[Col. 0787A] 8. We saw above, in Epistle 2, that the Africans wrote to the bishops of the Eastern Churches—namely, those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Constantinople—to request authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea. Only the bishops of Alexandria and Constantinople are said to have replied. Dionysius Exiguus inserted these writings into his collection, as did the Africans in the African Code of Ecclesiastical Canons, chapters 135, 136, and 137.

At the head of chapter 133 of that Code this title is prefixed:

“Here begin the replies to the African council of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in which they sent, through the presbyter Innocent, authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea translated from Greek; these letters, together with the same Council of Nicaea, were also sent through the aforementioned presbyter Innocent and Marcellus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, to the holy Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.”

At the head of chapter 137, however, these words are placed:

“Here begin copies of the Council of Nicaea sent on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, after the consulship of the most glorious emperors, Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII Augustuses, to Boniface, bishop of the City of Rome.”

Then follows the creed of the Council of Nicaea, to which this note is appended:

“To this symbol of faith copies of the decrees of that same Council of Nicaea were also attached by the aforementioned bishops, as is contained in full above. We have not thought it necessary to write them out here again.”

Yet those decrees, or canons, on account of which the Africans had thought it necessary to consult the Eastern Churches, are not only omitted here, but have also fallen out of the places cited [Col. 0787C]. Moreover, this heading makes it clear that Cyril and Atticus wrote not to Boniface at all, but only to the Africans, and that the Africans sent to Pope Boniface, on November 26 of the year 419, through the presbyter Innocent and the subdeacon Marcellus, the writings they had received from them.

9. For this reason no credence should be given to the Colbertine manuscript, written in Lombard letters, in which, after the preceding letter of the Africans to Boniface, the following is appended:

“Here begins the letter of Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, to Boniface, bishop of the City of Rome, sent together with copies of the Council of Nicaea translated from Greek into Latin by the most blessed bishops Cyril and Atticus of the Churches of Alexandria and Constantinople, and sent through their presbyter Innocent and Asellus, subdeacon [Col. 0787D] of the Church of Carthage, as was recited above. The faith of the Council of Nicaea with twenty headings.”

The letter itself runs as follows:

“Atticus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, to the holy brother Boniface, bishop of the City of Rome, greetings. I have issued the canons of the holy Fathers in my own hand, and have subscribed them myself. Amen. No one who has even a slight knowledge of the Greek language is unaware that the Greek letters express numbers,” etc.

The remaining words of that document are omitted; it is circulated in several other books under the title *Formata*. Thus some confusion is apparent in that manuscript. The writings of Atticus and Cyril to the Africans, which were transmitted to Boniface, are still preserved in the African Code, chapters 135 and 136.

VIII.

10. Around the end of the year 421, the clergy and people of the Church of Lutubia sent a petition to Pope Boniface. They complained about Patroclus, bishop of Arles, because, without any petition from them—that is, although they were not requesting it—he had appointed someone unknown, in a foreign province, to replace their deceased bishop, having passed over the metropolitan and acted contrary to the regulations of the Fathers. This gave rise to Boniface’s Epistle 12, dated February 9 of the year 422.

IX.

11. Not long afterward, Boniface received a petition from Perrevius, bishop of Pharsalus or of the Thessalian districts, in which he complained about the bishops of his province [Col. 0788B]. They had been so troublesome to him that they had judged he ought to be expelled from his own church (Epistle 13, no. 3).

The pope then entrusted the examination of this case to Rufus and ordered him to summon the aforementioned bishops in such a way that they would understand that, if anything had been done by them contrary to custom, it had first to be annulled. Since the examination of this case was entrusted to him on March 11 of the year 422, we may reasonably conjecture that Perrevius’s petition had been written around the beginning of that same year.

X.

12. Augustine had placed one of his own clergy, named Antony, over the bishopric of Fussala. But when Antony behaved in a thoroughly unworthy manner, Augustine, together with other bishops, was compelled to pronounce a judgment against him [Col. 0788C] (Augustine, Letter 1 to Caelestine, nos. 6, 9). He delivered a judgment full of every moderation.

Nevertheless, once the case had been decided—a decision to which Antony had at first seemed to assent—he did not abide by it. Rather, by crafty persuasion he induced the holy old man, the primate of Numidia, a person of the greatest authority—namely, Valentinus, bishop of Baia, who subscribes the preceding Epistle 2—to commend him to the venerable Pope Boniface as though he were entirely without fault. Having obtained a letter from his primate for this purpose, Antony sent it to Boniface together with a petition in which he narrated, in whatever manner suited him, the proceedings that had been taken against him.

XI.

13. Boniface then replied, at least to the primate, and absolved Antony in such a way that, speaking of him in his letter with pastoral and watchful caution, he added the qualification: “If he has faithfully reported the sequence [Col. 0788D] of events to us” (Augustine, ibid., no. 9).

But the end of his life, intervening soon afterward, prevented Boniface from learning that sequence of events more certainly. Nor should it seem surprising that the most prudent pope attached such weight to the commendatory letter of the primate, since in episcopal judgments (see above, p. 527, C, and p. 533, A) nothing was ordinarily done without the knowledge of the metropolitan, whose place in Africa was held by the primate. In particular, it had been enacted in the year 397, at the Third Council of Carthage, canon 7, with Aurelius presiding:

“Whoever among the bishops is accused shall bring his case before the primate of his own province.”

But, lest anyone blame Augustine for undertaking Antony’s trial without first notifying the primate, let him remember that this too was permitted by the Second Council of Carthage, canon 10 [Col. 0789A]:

“If a bishop should fall into some offense and be under the extreme necessity of being unable to assemble a larger number, so that he might not remain under accusation, he shall be heard by twelve bishops.”

Moreover, Antony was in a certain sense subject to Augustine, since he had most recently been created bishop in Augustine’s territory at Augustine’s own request. Hence the people of Fussala brought his name not to the primate but to Augustine.

[Col. 0789]

DECREES FROM THE LETTERS OF THE HOLY POPE BONIFACE I

These are taken from Gratian’s *Decrees* and from other ancient manuscripts. (S)*

I. A presbyter must not be ordained before the age of thirty.

If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he must on no account be ordained presbyter, even if he is highly worthy. The Lord himself was baptized in his thirtieth year and then began to teach. Therefore, the man who is to be consecrated ought not to be consecrated until he has reached this lawful age.

From canon 2 of the Council of Neocaesarea.

II. Cases that the metropolitan cannot resolve are to be referred to the primate.

If a dispute should arise among bishops of the same council concerning ecclesiastical law or other matters, their metropolitan, first considering the case together with certain others in council, shall decide it. If both parties do not accept the judgment, then the primate of that region shall hear the matter between them and shall determine what accords with the canons and the laws. Neither party shall be able to oppose his decision by vote.

Excerpted from Justinian’s *Novella* 123, chapter 22.

III. Whatever is consecrated to the Lord belongs to the right of the priest.

[Col. 0789C]

No one may be unaware that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether a human being, an animal, a field, or whatever it may be—once consecrated, is holy to the Lord and belongs to the right of the priests (Leviticus 27). Therefore, everyone who takes away, devastates, withholds, or seizes what belongs to the Lord and to the Church must be held without excuse and judged a sacrilegious person until he makes restitution and satisfies the Church. If he refuses to make restitution, let him be excommunicated.

Almost the whole passage is taken from Book 6 of the Capitularies, chapter 405.

IV.

No bishop, whether for a civil or a criminal case, may be brought before or produced for any judge, whether civil or military. For any magistrate who dares to order this shall be punished by condemnation to the loss of his belt of office.

V. Concerning bishops who desire to harm their brethren.

Just as everyone who loves his brother is born of God (1 John 4), so everyone who hates his neighbor is of the devil. For by love alone we distinguish who is shown to have been born of whom, as John says:

“By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed: everyone who does not practice righteousness and does not love his brother is not of God, because this is the message that you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another” [Col. 0790A] (1 John 3).

And shortly afterward:

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.”

And:

“You know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (ibid.).

Behold, a man is reasonably shown to be a murderer when he separates himself from brotherly fellowship. For even if he does [Col. 0790B] not move his hand to kill, nevertheless, because he strives to do harm, he is already regarded by God as a murderer. One man lives, while the other is already convicted as his killer.

Since the blessed apostle Paul agrees with these precepts in harmonious preaching, saying, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger,” and, “Give no place to the devil” (Ephesians 4), reports have reached us that certain priests have allowed themselves to be inflamed by such obstinate discord that not only has the setting of the sun failed to recall them from anger, but not even the passage of many years has inclined them toward the good of charity. For in their hearts that same Sun of righteousness, Christ, has set, so that they can scarcely return to the light of charity.

Accordingly, we decree that the offerings of these and similar quarreling brethren are under no circumstances to be received, in accordance with the determination of the ancient canon [Col. 0790C]. With regard to the persons who are at variance, however, we specially decree that true reconciliation must bind them together before either of them dares to approach the altar of the Lord or receive the grace of holy communion. They shall make satisfaction through penance for twice as long a period as that during which they persisted in discord.

If one of them, while the other refuses, hastens to make satisfaction in charity, he shall from the moment when he is proved to have hastened toward reconciliation be received within the Church as one who is at peace. Nevertheless, the earlier sentence shall remain in force, so that the time spent in anger may be repaid through a doubled period of penitential satisfaction.

VI. If an expelled bishop dares to enter the city.

If an expelled bishop dares to enter the city from which he was expelled [Col. 0790D], or to leave the place in which he was ordered to reside, we command that he be handed over to a monastery situated in another province, so that he who sinned in the priesthood may be corrected by living in a monastery.

VII. To Count Eleutherius.

Your pious purpose has asked how the offerings and tithes of the faithful ought to be distributed. Therefore, following the statutes of our predecessors, we order that four portions be made from the tithes and offerings: the bishop is to retain the first for himself; he is to assign the second to the Church; he is to grant the third to the poor; and he is to understand that the fourth is to be distributed among the clergy. The portions are to be distributed according to the person, place, and merit of the recipients [Col. 0791A], whether they serve in larger churches or minister in cities and villages.

For if they are children of one Church and have one mother Church, why should they not all receive the support of one mother? The one mother Church is like the one Lord, the one faith, and the one baptism. Although she is spread throughout the whole world, and although, because of differences of place [Col. 0792A] and the constitutions of the greater churches, she has acquired different dignities—some being called mother churches, others being subject to the mother churches as daughters to mothers—nevertheless, since this is so, why should not all clergy share in the goods of one mother, when it is clear that they usefully minister to the daughters of one mother?

[Col. 0791]

LETTERS ATTRIBUTED TO THE HOLY BONIFACE I AND NEVER BEFORE PUBLISHED BY MANSI. (C,S)*

LETTER I. TO JUSTUS, BISHOP OF DORCHESTER, TO WHOM HE SENDS THE PALLIUM

To his most beloved brother Justus, Boniface.

[Col. 0791B] We have sent the pallium to your Fraternity by the bearer of this letter, prompted by the endeavors of your kindness. We also grant you permission, when necessity requires and the Lord’s mercy goes before you, to celebrate the ordinations of bishops, so that the Gospel of Christ may be spread among all peoples who have not yet been converted through the preaching of many, etc.

LETTER II. TO THE BISHOP AND PRESBYTER-VICARS SENT BY POPE ZOSIMUS TO THE AFRICAN SYNOD

Boniface, bishop, to Bishop Faustinus and to the presbyters Philip and Asellus.

The letter of your affection bears witness, and the report of the bearers will also make you aware, how greatly the whole choir of the brethren rejoiced and the company of the saints exulted [Col. 0791C] in the Lord after it received through its ears the long-awaited news of your safety. With one harmonious voice, concern for the members shown by their head was also praised and recognized in the letters.

[Col. 0792A] Christ, therefore, has smiled upon you and your desires. He has deigned both to reunite those who were divided and to mend what was torn apart. This must be explained more fully to you by your brothers and fellow presbyters Dulcitius and Felix when they arrive quickly.

[Col. 0792B] Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, under the consulship of Monasius, vir clarissimus.

JOHN DOMINICUS MANSI’S NOTE ON THE FOREGOING LETTER

This letter, which now appears for the first time, is owed to the learning and courtesy of Father Forbenius Forster, who found it in a very ancient Freising manuscript and sent it to us for publication in this collection. I believe scholars will regard it as highly valuable, since it establishes that the dispute which some years earlier had set the Roman and African Churches against one another under Pope Boniface had been brought to an end, and that the two distinguished Churches had finally reached an excellent agreement.

I confess, however, that I do not know by what precise means this came about. I suspect, nevertheless, that the Africans yielded to the Romans in the matter of appeals, rather than that the Romans yielded to the Africans. For the Roman Church insisted so tenaciously upon the right of its primacy that no one can be persuaded that it was willing to surrender any part of it for the sake of the Africans.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 420

SAINT GAUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF BRESCIA

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791]

PROLEGOMENA

(Bibliotheca Schoenemanniana, vol. I)

§ I. The Life of Saint Gaudentius

[Col. 0791D]

Gaudentius’ native place is uncertain. If he was not a native of Brescia, he nevertheless lived for a long time at Brescia, already in the days of Philaster, as his disciple and having been formed by him in ecclesiastical discipline. During this period he won great favor among the people and clergy.

For while he was abroad in the East for religious reasons, Philaster died. At the insistence of the people and through the support [Col. 0792D] of other bishops—support that received considerable weight from the authority of Ambrose of Milan—Gaudentius was elected bishop of Brescia. Upon receiving this news, Gaudentius left nothing unattempted by which he might avoid the burden. But Ambrose and the other bishops, constrained by an oath—by which perhaps the citizens of Brescia had bound themselves to accept no other bishop—sent him letters together with a delegation of citizens [Col. 0793A] that he considered it a religious duty no longer to resist, especially since communion had been denied him by the Eastern bishops themselves unless he promised to return to the people of Brescia.

The beginning of his episcopate, as well as the date of his predecessor’s death, is unknown. No event of his episcopate brought him greater renown than the embassy he undertook on behalf of John Chrysostom to the emperor Arcadius in the year 405, when Aemilius and Cythegius were consuls. Although the embassy failed in its outcome, it made him famous for his constancy and magnanimity; and Chrysostom’s own testimony provides the most eloquent praise of him in this matter.

It is equally uncertain when Gaudentius died. Some assign his death to the year 427; others, among them Tillemont, with greater probability place it in the year 410.

§ II. The Writings of the Holy Doctor

[Col. 0793B]

Among Gaudentius’ genuine writings, besides the ten Paschal sermons with their preface to Benivolus, four sermons on different passages of the Gospel and a fifth on the martyrs of the Maccabees are acknowledged as authentic from Gaudentius’ own words in the same preface to Benivolus.

Four others—namely, the sermon *On His Ordination*, the sermon *On the Dedication of the Basilica*, and those addressed to Serminius and the Deacon Paul—which are rather letters than sermons, are shown by both their subject matter and their similarity of style to belong to Gaudentius. In addition, in Galeardus’s edition one finds two others: one on Peter and Paul, and another on the life and death of Philaster, his predecessor.

That some of Gaudentius’ treatises have perished we learn from the works that survive, as Galeardus noted in his annotation to treatise 14. There he also cites a passage from sermon 8 which, more than almost anything else, serves to reveal the man’s intellectual character and can vindicate Dupin from the charge of rashness:

“As you remember, we discussed the entire text of the reading which describes the Lord dining at Bethany, explaining Lazarus’s reclining place, the circumstances of the location and time, Martha’s service, her sister’s devotion, the power of the ointment, and the significance of the hair with which Mary wiped Christ’s feet after anointing them with precious perfume.”

[Col. 0793C] Nor are spurious works lacking. There is the *Rhythm on Philaster*, and a book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, attributed at various times to Origen, Cyprian, or Augustine, but assigned to Gaudentius by the Oxford editor of Cyprian, although in the notes he refers it to the time of Bede.

[Col. 0793D] Furthermore, Elias Capreolus, in Book I, chapter 3, of his *History of Brescia*, and Ughellus after Capreolus, make Gaudentius the author of a *Commentary on the Creed commonly called that of Athanasius*. Since this attribution clearly arose from an error, and since no such commentary by Gaudentius exists, perhaps—as Galeardus conveniently suggests—the work intended is Rufinus’s *Exposition of the Creed*. This work, rashly attributed by many to Jerome and Cyprian, was at times also attributed to Gaudentius.

§ III. Editions of the Writings of Saint Gaudentius

According to Galeardus’s earlier observation, Capreolus was the first to publish a specimen of Gaudentius’ writings: excerpts from the sermon on Philaster in Book III [Col. 0794A] of his *History of Brescia*, around the year 1500 or somewhat later.

Then, around 1554, Aloysius Lipomanus, bishop of Verona, published a complete sermon on Philaster, a sermon on the dedication of the basilica, and excerpts from the preface to Benivolus, in volume IV of the *Lives of the Saints*, beginning on page 52, fourth edition of Venice. There, on pages 1 and 15, Gaudentius’ works are said not yet to have been printed.

The collected works were first published in the *Orthodoxographi* of Grynaeus in 1569, and were thereafter frequently reprinted, in the same order and number, in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*. They were, however, burdened with very many errors and lacked two sermons, which were finally added in Galeardus’s latest—and the first that could properly be called a separate and accurate—edition of 1720. That edition, later revised by the editor [Col. 0794B], was incorporated into the Quiriniana Collection of the Works of the Bishops of Brescia. We shall discuss the editions individually.

THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY

1569. Basel, printed by Heinrich Petri, in folio. *Treatises of Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, in the Monuments of the Holy Fathers, the Orthodoxographi*, vol. VI, pp. 1793–1860. Seventeen treatises are presented, together with two replies to Serminius and the Deacon Paul, as well as his preface to Benivolus.

1575. Paris, published by Michel Sonnius, in folio. *Sermons and Treatises of Gaudentius of Brescia*, in the Bignean *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VII.

1579. Cologne, in folio. *Sermon of Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, on Philaster, Bishop of Brescia*, in Surius’s *Lives of the Saints*, vol. IV, p. 225 onward.

[Col. 0794C] 1589. Paris, [publisher illegible], in folio. *Sermons, or Various Treatises, of Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, on Various Passages of Scripture*, in the second edition of the Bignean *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. II, col. 209 ff.

THE SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

1610. Paris, in folio. Several treatises and sermons of Gaudentius of Brescia, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. II.

1618. Cologne, in folio. Several treatises of Gaudentius of Brescia, Bishop, on various passages of Scripture, in volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

1624. Paris, in folio. Several treatises and sermons of Gaudentius, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. II, col. 1 ff.

1644 (1654). Paris, published by the Three Booksellers, in folio. *Sermons or Treatises of Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, on Various Passages of Scripture*, etc., in volume II of the fifth edition of the Bignean *Bibliotheca Patrum* [Col. 0794D].

1662. Paris, published by Anthony Bertier, in folio. Several sermons of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, in François Combefis’s *Preaching Library of the Fathers*.

1677. Lyon, published by the Anissons, in folio. Treatises of Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, on various passages of Scripture, in volume V of the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, col. 942 ff.

THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

1720. Padua, printed by Joseph Cominus, in quarto. *The Extant Sermons of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, Now for the First Time Reviewed and Corrected According to Manuscript Codices*. Added are the short works of Rampertus and Adelmannus, venerable bishops of Brescia. Revised and illustrated with notes by Paul Galeardus, canon of Brescia.

[Col. 0795A] Galeardus undertook the publication of Gaudentius at the urging and prompting of Bishop John Francis Barbarigo, recently transferred from the bishopric of Verona to that of Brescia. Barbarigo assisted him with both financial resources and every possible service, and deservedly saw the work inscribed with his name.

Having obtained excellent assistance from Vatican, Florentine, Urbinate, and Brescian manuscripts, the editor devoted constant labor to correcting a very corrupt author, though in such a way that whenever anything had been altered he informed the reader of it. In presenting and reviewing variant readings he was almost excessively conscientious. He says that he preferred his diligence to seem excessive or overly meticulous to refined readers rather than to risk his fidelity in the eyes of learned and scholarly readers.

He added relatively few annotations. These consist chiefly of material useful for clarifying expressions through comparison with similar passages occurring in other writers; some also touch upon ecclesiastical matters. Both kinds display learning, though not extensive scholarship [Col. 0795B].

Much more remarkable are his discussions in the preface of Gaudentius’ life, virtues, and reputation among his contemporaries and later generations; of his genuine and spurious writings; and of their character. On this occasion (§ II) he also attacks Dupin vigorously, since in his view Dupin had judged Gaudentius unfairly. Finally, after briefly reviewing earlier editions, he informs readers of the plan and arrangement of the present edition.

To all this were added testimonies concerning Gaudentius and an index of passages from the holy Scriptures. The index of subjects, however, includes both Rampertus and Adelmannus [Col. 0795C].

1721. Hamburg, in octavo. *The Life of Saint Philaster, Bishop of Brescia, Written by Saint Gaudentius, His Successor*, preserved in an ancient book of the sacristy of the Church of Brescia and being a sermon delivered on the anniversary of Philaster’s feast, together with Philaster. Edited by John Albert Fabricius.

1738. Brescia, from the printing house of John Mary Rizzardi, in folio. *The Extant Sermons of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, Reviewed and Corrected According to Manuscript Codices*, in the Quiriniana Collection of the Ancient Fathers of the Church of Brescia, pp. 185–379. Again revised, with notes enlarged in a second edition, by Paul Galeardus, canon of Brescia.

What Galeardus accomplished on the occasion of this new edition he himself indicates with a modesty rarely found among Italian editors of ecclesiastical writers of later times [Col. 0795D]: [Col. 0796A] he says that new annotations had been inserted here and there into the Gaudentian text and that some of the earlier ones had also been improved. Yet at first glance anyone can easily observe how frequently, and how successfully, this was done.

Above all, he rejoices over a manuscript that was suddenly presented to him—though not very ancient, it had an excellent text and corrections written in the hand of Octavius Pantagathus of Brescia—and he declares that countless readings had been restored to him from it.

1757. Augsburg, at the expense of Ignatius Adam and Francis Anthony Veith, in quarto. *The Sermons of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia*, etc. An exact reproduction of the Paduan edition.

The manuscripts that assisted Galeardus partly contained all the works published up to that time and partly contained one or another of the newly added sermons individually. There were five of the former and four of the latter.

[Col. 0796B] 1. Manuscripts of the Vatican Library, nos. 1243 and 4580, both on paper.

2. Manuscript Urbinate codex, on parchment, no. 75, extremely elegant, with painted and gilded initial letters.

Galeardus writes that these codices, although not outstanding for their antiquity, nevertheless contributed excellent readings in many places toward the correction of Gaudentius. After permission had been granted by Pope Clement XI, the task of extracting readings was undertaken by Francis Blanchinus and Charles Majellus, prefect of the Vatican Library, both holding the rank of Papal Chamberlain.

3. Manuscript codex of the Florentine library of Saint Mark, on paper, mentioned by John Mabillon in his *Itinerary*. Father Albert [Col. 0796C] Salvi, prior of the monastery of Saint Mark at Florence, had arranged the collation and carefully extracted the variant readings and sent them to the editor.

4. Manuscript codex of Octavius Pantagathus of Brescia, a man of great reputation among the learned of his age.

[Note: [Col. 0795] Galeardus did not omit testimonies about him from his contemporaries, namely, those of Gregorius Giraldus, *Dialogue 2, On the Poets of His Age*; Augustine de Thou, *Commentaries on His Life*, Book I; and Onuphrius Panvinius, *On the Book of the Shepherds*, p. 390.]

Although this codex too was not very ancient, it nevertheless—contrary to Galeardus’s opinion—frequently supplied excellent readings differing from those of the earlier witnesses. In addition, corrections in Pantagathus’s own hand had been written here and there in the margin; the editor considered these to be of no small value.

5. Manuscript Urbinate codex no. 150, on parchment.

6. Manuscript Vatican codex no. 1235, likewise on parchment. Both of these two codices, which contain Gaudentius’ sermon on Peter and Paul, also contain sermons of Zeno.

7. Two Brescian manuscript codices on parchment, the older of which bears a note assigning it to the eleventh century. They [Col. 0796D] contain the sermon on the life and death of the blessed Philaster.

[Col. 0795]

PREFACE OF FATHER GALEARDUS TO THE EDITION OF THE WORKS OF SAINT GAUDENTIUS
[Col. 0795D] 1. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, flourished toward the end of the fourth century, at the time when the golden age of the Church produced Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and other outstanding men. While he had gone abroad to the East for religious reasons, after Bishop Philastrius had died, the people of Brescia desired him as his successor, with the support of the bishops and especially of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, whose authority at that time was supreme. Gaudentius, deterred by the burden of the priesthood, began to plead his inexperience and immature age, in order to withdraw himself from the burden of the office imposed upon him. But Ambrose and the other bishops, bound by the oath of the people of Brescia (by which they had perhaps pledged themselves to accept no other bishop besides Gaudentius), sent him letters of such gravity and force, together with a delegation of citizens from Brescia, that the Eastern bishops, moved by their weight and force, would deny Gaudentius communion unless he promised to return and do what was required. Thus Gaudentius, compelled to return, undertook the governance of the Church of Brescia, not without great praise for his virtue and modesty. For not only was episcopal dignity conferred upon him while he was absent and resisting, but—something rare—he allowed himself to be overcome only after being struck by ecclesiastical threats and, as he himself says, subdued by the authority of the holy men who were present.

2. We learn all this from Gaudentius himself in his sermon On His Ordination, delivered before Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Baronius also drew from that sermon the testimony he used in recounting Gaudentius’ election under the year 386, no. 7. Yet he does not seem to have grasped the meaning of Gaudentius’ words, “bound by the oath by which you rashly bound yourselves,” when he attributes the oath to the bishops, although it had been sworn by the citizens. For Gaudentius is addressing the citizens, not the bishops, as is clear from the following passage:

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Gaudentius, treatise On His Ordination.]

“But blessed Father Ambrose and the other venerable bishops, bound by the oath by which you rashly bound yourselves, sent me such letters together with your delegation that I could no longer resist without danger to my soul.”

Therefore, although an oath may have compelled the bishops to recall Gaudentius, Gaudentius’ words, “by the oath by which you rashly bound yourselves,” refer in no way to the bishops, but only to the citizens.

3. While Gaudentius was in the East and was traveling through the cities of Cappadocia toward Jerusalem, in Caesarea itself, the principal city of Cappadocia, he received from certain holy virgins, nieces of Basil, who lived in a monastery, relics of the forty holy martyrs who had suffered in Armenia under Licinius. They declared that these relics had once been handed over to them by their uncle Basil, bishop of that city.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Gaudentius, treatise On the Dedication of the Basilica, calls them “the most worthy mothers of the monastery of the holy virgins.”]

Gaudentius brought these relics, together with other relics of the saints—of John the Baptist, Andrew, Thomas, and Luke—to Brescia, and placed them in a church he had dedicated. He added sacred relics of Gervasius, Protasius, and Nazarius, as well as those of the martyrs of Anaunia: Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander. After praising the martyrs in a public sermon, he decreed that the church itself should be called the “Council of the Saints,” as we learn from the sermon On the Dedication of the Basilica.

This distinguished act of Gaudentius greatly confirms the antiquity of the veneration of relics. Baronius therefore makes fitting use of it under the year 316, no. 44, where, in discussing the forty holy martyrs, he praises Gaudentius’ sermon. He also mentions it under the year 387, no. 7; besides Baronius, Papebrochius does so in the *Acta Sanctorum*, March, vol. II, p. 14, no. 7, and Ruinart in the *Acts of the Martyrs*.

4. In what year Gaudentius assumed the episcopate is not sufficiently clear. It seems to have happened around the year 387, an opinion accepted by nearly all more recent writers. Vossius, Labbeus, Cave, and Natalis Alexander all assign the beginning of Gaudentius’ episcopate to that year. Vossius writes as follows in book III of *On Latin History*:

[Note: [Col. 0798D] p. 744, editions of Leiden, 1651.]

“Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, recorded for posterity the Life of Saint Philastrius, whom he had succeeded in the episcopate. Philastrius died in the year 387, and therefore Gaudentius’ period is sufficiently established.”

Indeed, if the year of Philastrius’ death were certain, there would be no question about the beginning of Gaudentius’ episcopate. What we can at least infer conjecturally is that Philastrius died after the year 384. For Augustine, who came from Rome to Milan in 384 and remained there until 387, writes that he saw Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, at Milan in the company of Ambrose.

[Note: [Col. 0798D] *On Heresies*, beginning.]

Thus it is possible that one, and perhaps the last, of those three years was the year of Philastrius’ death, since Gaudentius certainly became bishop at Brescia before Ambrose’ death, which is assigned to the year 397. It seems, however, that this occurred several years before Ambrose himself died, for Gaudentius often speaks of him and sometimes addresses him as present in the sermon On His Ordination and in the sermons On Peter and Paul, the former delivered by Gaudentius at Brescia, the latter at Milan.

5. How greatly our Gaudentius flourished in the praise of learning and eloquence can be clearly inferred from the fact that his sermons were regularly taken down by shorthand writers while he addressed the people. At that time it was customary that, if one of the ecclesiastical teachers excelled in speaking, his sermons would be rapidly recorded in writing by appointed notaries. We have said more about this in the notes to Gaudentius’ Preface to Benivolus.

Hence the titles prefixed more than once to Gaudentian sermons: “Here begin the recorded treatises on various passages”; “The treatise of the same author recorded on the day of the dedication of the basilica”; and “Here begins the treatise which, on the first day of his ordination, the notaries of certain citizens recorded.”

Gaudentius was so displeased with these transcribers of his sermons that he denied that what had been written down from such work belonged to him. Thus he himself says in the Preface to Benivolus:

“But as for those treatises which, as I have learned, certain idle enthusiasts presumed to collect secretly by placing notaries nearby—without doubt interrupted and incomplete—they have nothing to do with me. What was written down in the precipitous haste of the transcribers is no longer mine.”

Yet at times he revised such treatises at the request of others. He particularly did so, at Benivolus’ request, for the four shorter treatises on various passages of the Gospel and the subsequent treatise on the Maccabean martyrs, as he testifies there. We should therefore have no doubt that these works are genuine and Gaudentian.

To make still clearer how highly people thought of Gaudentius’ eloquence and learning while he was still alive and in good health, and how great the fame of the Gaudentian name already was, it will be worthwhile to set down here the entire passage of Rufinus in the Preface to Bishop Gaudentius, prefixed to the books of Clement’s *Recognitions*, which Rufinus himself translated into Latin. The passage is as follows:

“Indeed, Gaudentius, distinguished glory of our teachers, you possess such vigor of intellect, indeed such grace of spirit, that whatever you say in the ordinary manner of daily speech, whatever you declaim in church, ought to be preserved in books and handed down to posterity for instruction.”

Here, I think, a collection of Gaudentius’ sermons is plainly sketched—one that had already begun to be made by notaries while he was preaching. There can be no doubt that Rufinus is speaking here of our Gaudentius, although he omits the title of his church. The indications proving this are entirely certain and indisputable; we shall produce them below, when we discuss the time of Gaudentius’ death.

6. I have no certain information by which to affirm Gaudentius’ homeland. It is known that he had lived at Brescia before departing for the East, for he says in the sermon On His Ordination:

“Thus I could no longer resist without danger to my soul, since even the Eastern bishops would deny me saving communion unless I promised my return to you.”

His return indicates either his homeland or at least his place of residence. Nor would Gaudentius easily have been so eagerly desired for the episcopate by the citizens of Brescia if his outstanding virtue had not been fully known to them, whether because they shared his homeland or because of his long residence in that city.

In the Preface, too, when addressing Benivolus, he says:

“Just as you are, by the Lord’s favor, the most worthy head of the honored men of our city, so also of the Lord’s people.”

Thus, by calling Brescia “our city” and its honored men—who constituted the principal order of dignity—he seems in some sense to profess it as his homeland.

These indications, however, are altogether slight and uncertain. He could have called the city in which he was bishop “our city,” and could have had his residence there although he had been born in another land. In the sermon On Philastrius, after enumerating Philastrius’ labors by which he had cultivated the Church of Brescia, he says that he too was a part of that work:

“But I am the least part of him.”

Unless Gaudentius was a native of Brescia, we must therefore conclude that he was Philastrius’ pupil, instructed and brought up by him in ecclesiastical disciplines. I see that this last opinion pleased Tillemont.

[Note: [Col. 0799D] *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, p. 581, Paris edition.]

7. There were several other Gaudentiuses not far removed from our Gaudentius in time, equal to him in episcopal office, and therefore not to be rashly confused with him.

There was, under the emperor Constantius, Gaudentius, bishop of Ariminum, who rescinded the acts of the Council of Ariminum after the synod had been dissolved and was therefore stabbed with a sword by the soldiers of the proconsul.

There was also Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Tamugadi in Africa, whose two letters to the tribune Dulcitius, together with the reply he sent to Augustine, Augustine refuted in two brilliant books.

At nearly the same time as our Gaudentius there was Gaudentius, bishop of Novara, born at Eporedia, a disciple of Eusebius of Vercelli and his companion in exile.

Only two Gaudentiuses, namely the bishop of Ariminum and the bishop of Novara, are mentioned by Volaterranus (*Commentaries*, book XVI, p. 476, Gryphius edition), who rather carelessly omits the Brescia Gaudentius, distinguished by his writings and by the fame of his name.

The name Gaudentius also frequently occurs on Brescia inscriptions. For in Octavius Rubeus’ collection of Brescia inscriptions, p. 246, there is Cornelius Gaudentius, Corrector of Venetia and Histria, as follows:

```text
COR GAVDEN
TIVS VP COMET
CORR VEN ET
HIST CVRAVIT
```

[“Cornelius Gaudentius, a man of perfect rank, count, corrector of Venetia and Histria, caused this to be made.”]

And on p. 296, Gaudentius, husband of Nusia:

```text
NVSIAE CONIVGI
SANCTISSIMAE
INCOMPARABILI QVAE
VIXIT ANN. XXIII.
M. VII GAVDENTIVS
MARITVS BENEMERENTI
```

[“To Nusia, his most holy and incomparable wife, who lived twenty-three years and seven months, Gaudentius, her husband, to his well-deserving wife.”]

[Note: [Col. 0799D] After these had been published in the Padua printing, a stone was found at Gayni in the Riviera of Salò, near Tusculanum, bearing the same inscription in a slightly different form, as follows:]

[Col. 0800D]

```text
LORENIAE VENVSTAE CONIVGI SANCTISSIMAE
QVAE VIXIT ANNOS XXIII M VIIII
GAVDENTIVS MARITVS BENEMER
```

[“To Lorenia Venusta, his most holy wife, who lived twenty-three years and nine months, Gaudentius, her husband, to his well-deserving …” The surviving inscription breaks off.]

But let us return to our Gaudentius.

8. The ten paschal sermons take precedence over the rest of Gaudentius’ sermons. Labbeus correctly observed that they were not written before the year 387.

[Note: [Col. 0800D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 338.]

Their Preface mentions the disturbances which the Arians, relying on the authority of the empress Justina, stirred up against Ambrose in the city of Milan in the year 386. I myself think they were written somewhat later, perhaps after the year 390, because in the same Preface, when Gaudentius speaks of that persecution of the Arians against Ambrose, he seems to indicate a somewhat more distant time:

“For the Jezebel of our own age, when she was persecuting the most blessed Ambrose, thought that you too, at that time being Master of the Records—namely, Benivolus—had forgotten the saving faith, and was compelling you to dictate against the Catholic churches.”

Moreover, when he adds to these paschal sermons, which he had recently delivered in church and was sending to Benivolus, four shorter treatises and, in addition, a fifth on the Maccabean martyrs, and states that he had formerly spoken these before the same Benivolus, he makes it sufficiently clear that, before reciting these paschal sermons, he had already spent a long time in the office of bishop and preacher.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] “Which, you have reported, I formerly spoke before you.” Gaudentius, Preface to Benivolus.]

He sent these paschal sermons to Benivolus at his request, indeed almost under compulsion, with a Preface addressed to him. At Benivolus’ request he also revised the five treatises appended to the paschal sermons, which Benivolus had handed over to Gaudentius for correction after they had been recorded by notaries.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] “I shall return them to you corrected, since you compel me.” Gaudentius, [Col. 0802D] Preface to Benivolus.]

Thus we owe Benivolus the greater and more important part of the Gaudentian sermons that have reached us.

9. Gaudentius adorns this Benivolus, who was a citizen of Brescia, with the highest praises. While serving at Milan under Valentinian as Master of the Records, Benivolus was compelled by Justina, Valentinian’s mother, to dictate a law confirming the faith of the Council of Ariminum. He not only steadfastly resisted but also voluntarily renounced his courtly honors, preferring, as our author says,

[Note: [Col. 0802D] In the same place.]

“to live as a private citizen rather than serve as a dead man.”

Sozomenus relates the story in book VII, chapter 13 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, in Valesius’ translation:

“Justina summoned Benivolus, who at that time was in charge of the Records Office, and ordered him immediately to dictate a law confirming the faith once recited at the Council of Ariminum. When he refused to do so—for he belonged to the Catholic communion—the empress, enticing him with the promise of a higher rank, began to urge him. Yet she could not persuade him. For Benivolus took off his belt and threw it at the feet of the empress, declaring that he wished to accept neither his present dignity nor any higher one as a reward for impiety.”

Besides Sozomenus, the ecclesiastical historians Rufinus and Nicephorus praise Benivolus’ exceptional steadfastness and greatness of spirit.

Yet there were people who wrote the law that Benivolus had refused to dictate. It is preserved in the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title “On the Catholic Faith,” in these words:

“We grant permission to assemble to those who hold the views set forth when, during the reign of the deified Constantius, priests had been summoned from the whole Roman world and the faith had been expounded by those very men who are known to dissent at the Council of Ariminum, and which was also confirmed at Constantinople and shall remain forever. Let the freedom to assemble also be open to those whom we have ordered to meet.
