Let those who think that permission to assemble has been granted to them alone know that, if they attempt anything tumultuous against the command of our tranquility, they shall, as authors of sedition and of the disturbance of the peace of the Church,

[Note: [Col. 0802D] Another reading: “and even of its injury.” Valesius.]

pay the penalty with their heads and blood. Nevertheless, the punishment shall remain in force for those who attempt secretly or covertly to petition against this provision of ours. Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, at Milan, in the consulship of the emperor Honorius and Evodius (386).”

Valesius wonders in his notes on Sozomenus how it happened that the aforementioned law entered the Theodosian Code, since it plainly favors the Arians. Gothofredus, however, observes that this law is absent from the Justinian Code, as having been disapproved.

We have shown in the notes to Gaudentius’ Preface that the office of Master of the Records, which Benivolus held, was a distinguished one. There I have also said more about Benivolus. I remember reading in Ambrose’ letter to Marcellina that the Memoriales and the *Agentes in Rebus* were court offices:

“Records and memorial writings are also called the histories of the ancients,” as Arnobius says in *Against the Pagans*, book VI, and Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*.

10. The Gaudentian sermons breathe piety no less than learning; and their usefulness for strengthening and illuminating the Church’s doctrine is readily apparent from their reading.

In sermon 2 the Discipline of the Secret is explicitly indicated. The mystery of the Eucharist is expounded so aptly, fully, and clearly that I can plainly see that few among the ancients treated such a subject more suitably for settling the controversies of our own times.

Testimonies drawn from this sermon were used to assert the truths of the Catholic Church by John Stephen Duranti in his books *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*, printed at Rome in the Vatican Press, 1591; by Louis Bail of Abbeville in the *Library of Preachers*, published at Paris by Jean de La Caille, 1666; by Ferrarius in *On the Rite of the Sacred Sermons of the Church*; by John Cardinal Bona; and by not a few others among our writers who considered it worthwhile to study the Gaudentian writings.

Gaudentius also gives a splendid testimony concerning relics and the invocation of the saints. He asserts these doctrines most clearly in the sermon On the Dedication of the Basilica, in the sermon On Peter and Paul, and in the sermon On the Life and Death of Philastrius, his predecessor.

When Alan the Englishman cites this sermon against the opponents of ecclesiastical history, *Dialogue* 3, chapter 4, p. 319, Plantin edition, 1566, he numbers our Gaudentius among those Fathers whom the Magdeburg Centuriators omitted and who wrote during the first five hundred years after Christ concerning the faith of the early Church in the matter of relics and the invocation of the saints.

In treatise 9 he eloquently and earnestly defends the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God. In treatise 8, although he forbids parents to impose perpetual continence upon their children, he nevertheless teaches that virginity is better than marriage.

Near the end of treatise 5 there is a highly noteworthy passage about the staff, where he indicates that a staff was given to apostolic priests—that is, bishops—for the correction of their subjects. This may provide support for the ancient use of the staff, concerning which Isidore writes in book II, chapter 5 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

Certainly, the ancient monks of Egypt carried a staff, as is clear from Cassian, book I, chapter 9 of *On the Institutions of the Coenobites*:

“Carrying it,” he says, “spiritually admonishes them that, amid so many barking dogs of vice and invisible beasts of spiritual wickedness, they must never walk unarmed.”

But it would take too long to go through each point. It will therefore be enough to have touched upon a summary of the principal matters, from which the reader may readily judge the usefulness and importance of the Gaudentian sermons.

11. In Gaudentius’ time, around the year 405, serious disputes had arisen in the East because John Chrysostom, expelled from the see of Constantinople, had been driven into exile. The bishops of Italy, assembled under Innocent I, obtained from the emperor Honorius a letter to his brother Arcadius requesting that a council be held at Thessalonica, so that the two parties, from East and West, might more easily meet together to restore peace to the Church.

The envoys chosen to travel to Arcadius were, according to Palladius, the holy men Aemilius, Cythegius, and Gaudentius.

[Note: [Col. 0803] Palladius, *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, chapter 4. Nicephorus gives the same account, book XIII, chapter 33.]

Together with the presbyters Valentinian and Boniface, they set out for Constantinople under official commission, carrying letters from the emperor Honorius, Pope Innocent, and the bishops of Italy—Chromatius of Aquileia, Venerius of Milan, and the remaining bishops—as well as the instructions of the entire Western council.

But the embassy undertaken with such concern and labor had a wholly unhappy outcome. When the bishops who had departed from Italy reached the shores of Greece at the beginning of spring in the year 406, they were seized at Athens by a military tribune, placed on ships, and taken to Constantinople.

When they arrived there, they were excluded from the city and thrown into custody at a Thracian town called Athyra. It is incredible how many and how great were the hardships with which they were harassed, and how much they had to endure in order to defend the commission entrusted to them with the constancy it required.

They were accused, among other things, of disturbing another’s territory beyond their own borders and of being present there in contempt of the Eastern Empire. Then each was separately shut up in custody, tortured, and subjected to many sufferings so that they would produce their instructions and letters.

When no force could break their spirit, the letters they had brought from the West were forcibly taken from them. They had declared that they would hand them over to no one except the emperor.

At last they were tempted with promises and gold to enter into communion with Atticus, who had occupied John Chrysostom’s see. But when they accepted neither promise nor condition offered to them, and instead asked insistently to return to Rome, a certain Valerian, zealous for evil, placed them in a filthy and age-worn vessel, plainly plotting their destruction, and ordered them to return to Rome.

Sailing with extreme danger, they reached Lampsacus only with difficulty. After changing ships, they arrived at Rome four months later, where they reported individually to Pope Innocent what had happened to them.

This was the substance of that embassy, and everyone can see how greatly it adds to Gaudentius’ praise.

12. Chrysostom himself adorns these bishops with splendid titles of praise, as is clear from his letters to the bishops who had come from the West, letters 156, 157, 158, and 159 of Fronto Ducaeus’ 1636 edition. In one place he praises their outstanding zeal and their eagerness of spirit in defending the truth; elsewhere, the dedication and readiness they displayed in repairing the damage suffered by the Churches; and elsewhere, their firm and sincere benevolence, courage, steadfastness, and endurance. In yet another place he praises the greatness of their diligence, vigilance, care, and concern.

More distinguished than all these praises, however, is Chrysostom’s testimony concerning our Gaudentius. It perhaps suggests that he was the principal bishop in dignity among those who undertook the embassy, since Chrysostom addresses a separate letter to him alone. This is letter 184, which reads as follows, in the translation of the same Fronto Ducaeus:

**To Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia.**

“We are not ignorant of your affairs; rather, as though present, we know well your zeal, vigilance, cares, and labors undertaken for the sake of truth. We give you immense thanks, and, though living in such great solitude, we draw no slight consolation from the ardor and sincerity of your charity. Having tested it here, we have learned that it remains equally whole there, and that it has in no way been weakened either by the length of time or by the distance of the journey. For this reason we are deeply grateful to you, and we urge you to continue in your undertaking and always to display the same zeal. For you are not unaware how many Churches’ salvation is now at stake, and how outstanding this right action will be. Thinking on these things, therefore, my most reverend and devout lord, deign to persevere in the same zeal. Thus it will come to pass that, after enduring small labors, you will store up in heaven immortal rewards for these noble struggles.”

This letter establishes how much diligence and zeal Gaudentius contributed to alleviating Chrysostom’s sufferings, and how much praise he rightly earned from the labors of this embassy, undertaken courageously for the restoration of peace in the Church.

Although among the ancient writers on ecclesiastical matters, except for Aemilius, whom they call Beneventanus, the title of the see is not added to the other bishops who led this embassy, no one can rightly call it into question that this Gaudentius was from Brescia, when so clear a testimony of Chrysostom exists.

Elsewhere, too, Chrysostom seems to praise Gaudentius’ labors in letter 160, addressed to a bishop who had come from the West. It seems highly probable to me that this letter also belongs to our Gaudentius; in it Chrysostom continues to recall the labors which Gaudentius had endured both at home and on so long a journey for the benefit of the Church.

Perhaps no one more ready than our Gaudentius, or more suitable for undertaking this embassy, could have been appointed. For, having previously lived in the East, he must be thought to have won great renown there for piety and religious devotion among the bishops of that region. They could persuade him to come to the episcopate only by threatening him with excommunication.

Thus nearly all the more recent writers after Baronius, who had a fuller understanding of the entire matter, assign the distinction of this embassy to Gaudentius of Brescia. Among them are Morerius, Cave, Dupin, and, above all, the most diligent Tillemont.

13. When Gaudentius died is uncertain. Some place his death in the year 410; others, among them the learned Labbeus, in the year 427.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 338.]

Tillemont reasonably thinks that Gaudentius lived until 410 because Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, sent him around that time the books of Clement’s *Recognitions*, translated into Latin by Rufinus himself.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, p. 588.]

The following Preface by Rufinus is prefixed to this translation:

**To Gaudentius, bishop.**

“Indeed, Gaudentius, distinguished glory of our teachers, you possess such vigor of intellect, indeed such grace of spirit, that whatever you say in the ordinary manner of daily speech, whatever you declaim in church, ought to be preserved in books and handed down to posterity for instruction.”

And shortly afterward:

“It is fitting, surely, that you, who have also read these works in Greek, should be informed of the purpose of our translation, lest you suppose that in certain passages we have preserved the order of the translation less carefully.”

How well all this fits our Gaudentius is easily understood: his treatises, as those of an outstanding and eloquent man, were regularly collected by transcribers, and he was trained in knowledge of the Greek language, as is clear from his sermons.

The chronology also agrees perfectly. For Rufinus did not flee to Sicily until after Aquileia had been devastated by Alaric, no earlier than the year 410; he seems to have died there in that year or the next.

Therefore, although Rufinus omitted the title of the see, I have no doubt that these words were written about our Gaudentius.

Elsewhere, too, Rufinus mentions this translation of Clement’s *Recognitions* as having been undertaken for Bishop Gaudentius, in the conclusion appended after his translation of Origen’s Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, in these words:

“After this, indeed, a work calls us which was assigned long ago but is now urgently pressed upon us by blessed Bishop Gaudentius: namely, the books of Clement, bishop of Rome and companion of the apostles, which are being translated by us into Latin so that I may give you, as their successor, knowledge of them.”

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Another reading: “of a companion and successor,” and “of the book of the *Recognitions*, so that it may be translated into Latin.” Cotelerius.]

Cotelerius, in his note on Clement’s *Recognitions* in the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 485, Antwerp edition, 1698, had understood this Gaudentius to be Gaudentius of Novara. But he immediately returned to the correct view, or rather restored the reading “of Brescia.”

14. Rufinus also asserts in the same Preface that Gaudentius claimed this translation of Clement’s *Recognitions* from him by hereditary right, since it had long before been commissioned by the virgin Silvia:

“The work which the virgin Silvia, of revered memory, had long ago commissioned, so that we might render Clement into our language, you subsequently claimed by hereditary right.”

Who this virgin Silvia was is a very complicated question. At Brescia, in the Church of Saint John the Evangelist—formerly called outside Brescia—there is the body of blessed Silvia the virgin, whose memory is celebrated on 15 December.

Some Brescia writers, calling her the mother of Gregory the Great, others his sister, have been seriously mistaken. For I do not see how she could belong to the family of Gregory the Great. In truth, from that family I find no distinguished women besides Silvia, his mother, who is known to lie buried at Rome,

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Baronius under the year 604, no. 30.]

and his paternal aunts Tarsilla and Aemiliana, together with Gorgonia, who was greatly degenerate from them.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Baronius under the year 581, no. 4.]

I therefore think that similarity of name caused her, through a common error, to be transferred to Rome and into the family of Gregory the Great, although neither her homeland nor her lineage was sufficiently known.

It seems to indicate that the Silvia buried at Brescia is the same Silvia whom Rufinus mentions in the Preface to Gaudentius that Rufinus says the translation was commissioned from him by Silvia and later claimed from him by Gaudentius by hereditary right, as well as the fact that both Silvia and Gaudentius share a burial place in the same church and at the same altar. Both points show that this Silvia was joined to our Gaudentius by affection and perhaps also by blood.

Cotelerius thinks that the Silvia mentioned by Rufinus is the same as Salvia, whom Palladius discusses in chapter 143 of the *Lausiac History*.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] In the *Apostolic Fathers*, note on Clement’s *Recognitions*, [Col. 0806D] p. 485.]

Tillemont supposes that she might perhaps have been Silvia, sister of Rufinus, prefect of the East, who, after returning from the East to the West, died at Brescia.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, p. 589, and vol. XI, “Saint Olympias,” article 1, p. 418. On Silvia, sister of Rufinus, prefect of the East, Baronius under the year 395, no. 28.]

In such obscurity concerning the facts, I would not dare to affirm anything certain. Rather, if someone should later bring forth better and more reliable evidence from the treasury of ecclesiastical history, I shall offer no resistance; indeed, I shall consider myself greatly indebted to him.

15. From what has been said thus far, it may reasonably be affirmed with Tillemont that Gaudentius remained among the living until the year 410. Whether, however, with Labbeus and Ughellus, we should say that he lived until 427, I do not know.

What is certain is that Gaudentius himself states in the sermon On the Life and Death of Philastrius, his predecessor, that he had already spent fourteen years in the episcopate. It seems possible that he lived on for some time after the year 406, when he served on the Eastern embassy, since he had been advanced to the episcopate while still very young and at an immature age.

Tillemont, however, observes that Optatianus, Gaudentius’ successor, is found subscribed to the synodal letter of the Council of Milan to Pope Leo in the year 451, after four intervening bishops—Paulus, Theophilus, Silvinus, and Gaudiosus.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, p. 591.]

He therefore says that it is not very credible that, within so short a period—namely, the twenty-four years between 427 and 451—four bishops could have occupied the see. For that reason Gaudentius’ death should more properly be placed around 410 than around 427.

Gaudentius’ body lies at Brescia in the Church of Saint John the Evangelist, formerly called outside Brescia, in the same chapel as Theophilus, his successor in the see of Brescia after Paulus, and the virgin Silvia, whom we mentioned shortly before.

Their bodies were transferred and placed there in the year 1595. The *Acta Sanctorum*, under 27 April, p. 494, relates the history of this translation.

Gaudentius’ name has also been entered in the Roman Martyrology under 25 October, with the following eulogy:

“Saint Gaudentius, bishop, distinguished for learning and holiness.”

This certainly suits Gaudentius, as is clearly shown both by his writings, which everywhere reflect Christian piety; by the notable moderation of his spirit, through which he was compelled, unwilling and resisting, to enter the episcopate; and by the courageous deeds he performed for the restoration of peace in the Church.

And this concludes what we have to say about Gaudentius. We must now discuss his writings, both genuine and spurious.

## § I. On the Genuine and Spurious Writings of Gaudentius.

16. In reviewing Gaudentius’s genuine writings, we shall not need to expend much care or labor, since among learned men there is either very little controversy about them [Col. 0807C] or none at all. Thus no one has ever doubted that the ten Paschal Sermons, together with the Preface to Benivolus, are a genuine work of Gaudentius; likewise the four following sermons on various passages of the Gospel, and the fifth on the Maccabean martyrs, concerning which Gaudentius himself bears witness in the same Preface to Benivolus, in these words:

> Moreover, I shall send back to you, once corrected—as you compel me to do—the four shorter treatises which, as you have reported, I once delivered in your presence on various passages of the Gospel, and the fifth on the Maccabean martyrs.

From this passage of Gaudentius it seems possible to infer that the Paschal Sermons were indeed delivered by Gaudentius in church, whereas the following sermons were recited privately before Benivolus; for he says: “which, as you have reported, I once delivered in your presence.” The words of Rufinus in the Preface to Gaudentius, quoted above, seem to indicate the same thing: “if anything is said by you in the manner of daily conversation, if anything is proclaimed in church”; by these words he plainly designates both private discussions and public sermons delivered by Gaudentius.

Perhaps gatherings of Christians used to be held at Benivolus’s house, where they devoted themselves continually not to gambling and drinking-parties, as is customary today, but to questions of divine doctrine and to the pursuit of piety. Gaudentius readily made himself available to teach them, so that he might obtain a richer fruit from his learning and labor.

The remaining sermons of Gaudentius—namely, On His Ordination, On the Dedication of the Basilica, and the two following sermons, of which the first is addressed to Serminius [Col. 0808A] and the second to Paul the Deacon—are readily recognized as Gaudentius’s from both the nature of their subject matter and the character and similarity of their style. They have therefore always been printed as Gaudentian works in the Libraries of the Fathers together with the others.

17. Since two further sermons have been added to this edition of ours, it will be proper to inform the reader of our judgment concerning them and to explain the reasons that moved me to add them to the other Gaudentian works as genuine.

While I was considering this edition of Gaudentius, I happened by chance upon an edition of the sermons of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, published at Verona in 1586 by order of Augustine Valerius, cardinal and bishop of Verona, and printed by Jerome Discipulus. As I examined it more carefully [Col. 0808B], I came across a passage in the Preface in which the editors and revisers of that edition warned the reader that they had omitted a sermon of Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, which had been added to the printed sermons of Saint Zeno in the earlier edition, because it was not found in the old manuscript codex of Saint Zeno.

I eagerly seized the opportunity of obtaining another Gaudentian sermon, if such a thing existed. After diligently seeking it out, I acquired the earlier edition of Zeno’s sermons, which was widely circulated at Venice in 1508. There, in Book Three, I found the desired sermon under this title:

> Sermon 48 of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, on Peter and Paul.

Its style also suited Gaudentius. Thus I was already beginning, without reluctance or hesitation, to claim it for its true author; my only wish was that [Col. 0808C] the authority of some manuscript codex might lend support to our judgment.

My desire was fully satisfied. At our request, conveyed by letter from the most illustrious and distinguished man John Francis Barbadicus, bishop of Brescia, the learned and most courteous Charles Majellus, prefect of the Vatican Library, promptly sent us a copy of the same sermon, transcribed from Urbinate Codex 150, p. 146, and collated with Vatican Codex 1235, p. 197. In both codices it bears the name of Gaudentius.

Accordingly, supported by two codices—which supplied not only authority for the sermon but also variant readings—we gladly admitted it into the family of Gaudentius’s other sermons and assigned it a place after those published in the other editions.

[Col. 0808D] 18. Another sermon of Gaudentius, placed last, had appeared several times in Lipomanus and Surius’s *Lives of the Saints*, under July 18, with Gaudentius’s name prefixed, under this title:

> *The Life of Blessed Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia, written by Saint Gaudentius, his successor.*

I admit that this title did not seem entirely to preserve the simplicity of antiquity. But since Lipomanus and Surius testified that they had received the sermon from an old book of the treasury of the Church of Brescia, I did not doubt that a collation with a manuscript codex could improve not only the title but also the sermon itself, which had been somewhat corrupted.

Both objectives were achieved with the help of two Brescia manuscripts, in which the sermon is found [Col. 0809A] with this heading prefixed:

> Sermon of Blessed Gaudentius, Bishop, on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, Bishop and his predecessor.

There is also an outstanding testimony concerning this sermon from Rampertus, bishop of Brescia in the ninth century, who quotes a passage from it in chapter 5 of his sermon *On the Translation of Blessed Philastrius*, in these words:

> As we read in the published sermon of the bishop Gaudentius, concerning the life of the most blessed bishop Philastrius, he was, with astonishing kindness, accessible to every age, condition, and sex.

I have therefore been completely astonished that Ludovicus Ellies Dupin, the French author of the *Ecclesiastical Library*, could raise a question about Gaudentius’s authorship of this sermon. Rampertus also uses the authority of the same sermon elsewhere, namely in chapter 9; and after Rampertus it is used by Baronius, Alanus the Englishman, Labbeus, [Col. 0809B] Vossius, Cave, and other later writers.

When I noticed that this fact had not been sufficiently observed by the compilers of the *Library of the Fathers*—for they had omitted the sermon—I considered it my duty to number it among the other Gaudentian sermons as a sincere and legitimate work of Gaudentius.

19. These, then, are the genuine works of Gaudentius that survive; for we have also noted that not a few have perished, in Treatise 14. I shall now speak of the spurious works.

First there is a Commentary on the Symbol commonly called the Athanasian Symbol. Although, so far as I know, no such Commentary survives at all, Elias Capreolus, in Book III of his *History of Brescia*, makes Gaudentius its author; Ughellius and others follow Capreolus.

It is plainly evident that they were deceived by a false belief, since that Symbol, which learned men agree was composed near the end of the fifth century by Vigilius of Tapsus, or by some other writer, could not possibly have been known to Gaudentius, who lived in the fourth century or scarcely reached the beginning of the fifth. We removed this error of those writers in the annotations to Ughellius [Note: [Col. 0809D] Vol. IV, Venetian edition, col. 528.]

I do not see how this false report could have gained currency, unless perhaps by “Commentary on the Athanasian Symbol” one should understand Rufinus’s exposition of the Creed, which many rashly attributed to Jerome and Cyprian and which was sometimes also attributed to Gaudentius of Brescia.

Among the spurious works of Gaudentius there is next counted a Rhythm on Philastrius. Rampertus tells us in his sermon *On the Translation of Philastrius* that this work once bore Gaudentius’s name [Col. 0809D]. But its style and the character of its Latin language plainly belong to a later period. Nothing Gaudentian seems to be found in the poem except the thoughts that its author borrowed from Gaudentius’s sermon on Philastrius. Accordingly, with the support also of Rampertus’s judgment, I have gladly rejected the attribution of that poem to Gaudentius. See also what we have discussed more fully concerning the same poem at the end of Gaudentius’s sermons.

[Col. 0810A] The celebrated book *On the Singularity of Clerics* may likewise be counted among the spurious works of Gaudentius. It has at various times been attributed to Origen, Cyprian, or Augustine; and since it has so far acknowledged no certain author, De Herrera should have numbered it among anonymous works.

John Fell, in the Preface to a recent edition of Cyprian, judged that it could be ascribed to Gaudentius of Brescia:

> The little work *On the Singularity of Clerics*, he says, may have some place assigned to it, on the condition that either Origen, or Gaudentius of Brescia, or some other writer living around the year 1000—when this dispute was especially heated in the West—should be willing to claim it as his own.

But who is this writer living around the year 1000? He is entirely unknown. Fell later, in his notes on that treatise, brings its author back to the time of Bede, that is, to the eighth century, in these words:

> It seems that the book was written around the time of our countryman Bede, when the controversy concerning clerical celibacy was especially heated, particularly in the West. The argument, drawn from a revelation, corresponds to that century.

When I encountered these statements, I certainly wished to know the learned man’s judgment. For what indication, I ask, has ever been found that would assign this little work either to the tenth century—this is what he meant by “the millennium”—or to Bede’s time?

Erasmus inferred that it was written by a bishop, although perhaps no one saw the fact, from the words the author adds to his work [Note: [Col. 0809D] Venetian edition of Cyprian with the scholia of Erasmus, 1547, no. 8.]:

> But you, dearest sons, I address not merely by persuasion, but by authority.

[Note: [Col. 0809D] Amsterdam edition of Cyprian, 1700, p. 151, col. 2.]

Yet the discussion of martyrdom contained in this work [Note: [Col. 0810D] Ibid., p. 150, col. 2.] cannot in any way suit the time of Bede, or indeed the age of Gaudentius or Augustine, when, once peace had been granted to the Church, occasions for martyrdom were no longer frequent.

In my judgment, therefore, this little book must be assigned either to the time of Origen or to that of Cyprian.

William Cave clearly noticed Fell’s error. In reviewing Cyprian’s works, he reports Fell’s judgment concerning the author of this little treatise:

> The most learned editors of the Oxford edition, says Cave, believe that it was written around the time of Bede.

Yet, since we are human, he was ashamed to criticize them, although shortly before, in his discussion of Origen, he had declared that the author of this little book, which was of respectable antiquity, was at least not later than Jerome’s time [Note: [Col. 0810D] *Literary History*, section 3, p. 80; [Col. 0810D] ibid., p. 76.]

Moreover, that little book contains absolutely nothing that can be applied to the controversy concerning clerical celibacy, although it does condemn the cohabitation and intimacy of clerics with women. An author appropriate to that subject certainly did not need to be sought in the tenth century. Cyprian himself [Note: [Col. 0810D] Epistle 4, Amsterdam edition, 1700.] and other Fathers of that age frequently treated the same subject, and the councils dealt extensively with it, so that, once this corruption—which disfigured the morals of the Church—had been removed, ecclesiastical discipline might be preserved intact.

21. Such, then, is what may be said concerning Gaudentius’s genuine and spurious writings [Col. 0811A]. We need not be delayed by the doubtful testimony of Barthius, who seems to conjecture, from similarity of subject or style, that Gaudentius, together with Eucherius, Maximus, Caesarius, and other writers of this kind, was one and the same author under different names.

Thus he writes in Book XLII, chapter 18 of the *Adversaria*:

> I cannot refrain from warning about these sorts of writers. The sermons that we possess under the names of Valerian, Eucherius, Maximus, Caesarius, Gaudentius, Eligius, and others of this kind are so often similar to one another that there is considerable suspicion either that later writers imitated the style of their predecessors, or that the works of a few writers were given different titles by the copyists according to the preference of particular places.

I do not understand what Barthius means. Either he wishes to attribute the sermons of others to Gaudentius, or Gaudentian sermons to others. If the former, I do not see how he will easily persuade anyone else; he certainly does not persuade me. For even if a similar passage on the same subject occasionally appears in two writers, it does not immediately follow that one and the same person was the author of both works. Nothing is more common than for one writer to imitate another writer on the same subject and sometimes to reproduce his thoughts in exactly the same words.

But if Barthius meant to suggest that Gaudentius’s sermons belong to another writer, then the learned man must have been entirely out of his mind, since nearly every Gaudentian sermon contains indications clearer than daylight that Gaudentius is their genuine and true author.

I consider it unnecessary to enumerate these indications individually, since an attentive reader can notice them without much difficulty. Nor should anyone be surprised that Barthius seriously went astray when speaking of our Gaudentius, since he was a learned man who was excessively hasty in forming judgments; for this reason Cotelerius calls him a minor critic [Note: [Col. 0811D] In the note to Hermas in *The Apostolic Fathers*, p. 75, Antwerp edition, 1698.]

There is also a certain account by Octavius Rubeus in the *Lives of Saints Faustinus and Jovita*, p. 40. There, citing Gaudentius as witness, he mentions a certain porphyry urn in which, he reports, the bodies of those same holy martyrs had once lain. But, so far as I know, Gaudentius nowhere reported anything of the sort in his writings. These are mere ravings and trifles that Rubeus gathered from popular rubbish and attributed to Gaudentius in order to give them some credibility.

I am therefore reluctant to spend more time either reviewing or refuting them. Dismissing Rubeus, let us proceed to other matters.

§ II. The Judgment of a Recent Writer concerning Gaudentius Examined

22. Among the many writers of this age who have devoted distinguished efforts to the study of ecclesiastical history, Ludovicus Ellies Dupin claims a prominent place. He composed his *Ecclesiastical Library* through continual study and prolonged labor.

When he reviewed the writings of Gaudentius, however, he showed himself so harsh and hostile toward our author [Col. 0812A] that anyone who approached Dupin without having read Gaudentius and accepted his statements would necessarily regard Gaudentius as a writer of no importance. If such a person then wished to undertake the reading of Gaudentius, he would certainly waste his time and labor.

To make it completely clear to the reader how unfair a judgment Dupin formed concerning Gaudentius, allow me to quote here Dupin’s own French words, after which the reader may decide for himself what is just in this matter.

Concerning Gaudentius’s first sermon he writes [Note: [Col. 0811D] Dupin, *Ecclesiastical Library*, fifth century, part I: “Gaudence, Bishop of Bresse”]:

> He begins the first of these sermons with a thought that has more subtlety than solidity, in order to explain why Easter is celebrated in spring, after the bad weather of autumn, the severity of winter, and before the heat of summer. It is, he says, to show that Jesus Christ, who is the Sun of justice, dispels by his light the darkness of the Jews’ error and softens the hardness of the pagans’ hearts, while by his rays anticipating the heat of the fire of the day of judgment. He adds that, since the world was created in spring, it was fitting that it should be restored in the same season.

Whether Gaudentius should be criticized at this point, I do not see clearly enough, nor perhaps has anyone else seen it differently. Not everyone is endowed with Dupin’s lynx-like eyes. But if it seems absurd to anyone to seek suitable explanations of the seasons in which the Lord’s mysteries took place, or to investigate carefully the correspondences between things, that person must set all antiquity behind him and accuse Ambrose, Jerome, [Col. 0812C] and Augustine of frivolity and tastelessness.

Nor, if Gaudentius allowed something to his imagination by calling Christ the Sun of justice and relating the various changes of the seasons to this image, did he therefore speak with insufficient solidity. For, as Dupin himself noted, Gaudentius immediately adds a more suitable explanation a little farther on, where he says [Note: [Col. 0812D] Treatise 1, p. 26]:

> Therefore the Son of God, through whom all things were made, on the same day and at the same time, raises up the fallen world by his own resurrection, at the time when he had created it from nothing, so that all things might be restored in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth.

This opinion of Gaudentius—that the world was created in spring—was common among Greeks and Latins in that period, as we have observed in the notes on this passage of Gaudentius.

[Col. 0812D] 23. Dupin then continues in the following manner concerning Gaudentius’s second sermon:

> After having explained the mystery of the Eucharist very clearly, he speaks of the dispositions with which one must approach it. He finds all of them represented by the ceremonies with which the Jews ate the paschal lamb. But he draws these correspondences from such a distance that one would have difficulty noticing them. For who would believe that the leather belt with which the Israelites girded themselves was a figure of the mortification of vices? Who could guess that when it is forbidden to break the bones of the lamb, this means that one must observe the precepts found in Scripture? Who would imagine that when it is said that the remains of the lamb must be burned, this signifies that one must consume by a living faith the doubts one may have concerning the mystery of the Eucharist? These allegories, and others like them found in this passage, are somewhat forced, and I strongly doubt that many people will find them agreeable.

The substance of Dupin’s criticism is that Gaudentius used allegory immoderately. This mode of interpretation seems to have displeased Dupin greatly; for shortly afterward he says of two other treatises:

> These two instructions—the eighth and ninth—are full of various allegories.

But this matter is one that Gaudentius shares with nearly all the ancient Fathers. In explaining Scripture, they considered it improper to neglect allegory even when the subject itself was clear and evident.

Augustine’s well-known statement is this [Note: [Col. 0813D] Sermon 44, *On the Words of the Lord*, after the beginning]:

> Our Lord Jesus Christ willed that the things he did bodily should also be understood spiritually. For he did not perform miracles merely for the sake of miracles, but so that the things he did would be marvelous to those who saw them and true to those who understood them.

Gregory likewise says in Homily 2 on the Gospels:

> The miracles of our Lord and Savior must be understood in such a way that they are believed to have truly occurred and yet, through their significance, are understood to indicate something to us.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Compare Augustine, *The City of God*, XV, chapter 27.]

Nor would I strongly object if some things said in this genre were occasionally somewhat slight, since figurative speech is of such a nature that it often drives the speaker into difficulties and rough places and compels him to explain the proposed subject through the most unrelated thoughts.

Perhaps, however, this manner of speech pleased the people greatly, since the populace generally seeks not so much a serious and eloquent speaker as an astonishing and clever one. The ancient Fathers therefore knew that, under the law of charity, they were debtors both to the wise and to the foolish, and they used a manner of speaking that they plainly recognized as more suitable and useful for attracting and holding the people.

In any case, Dupin could not have called Gaudentius’s allegories wholly unusual or unheard-of. To pass over other examples, Gaudentius teaches that what remained of the lamb had to be burned so that we might understand [Note: [Col. 0813D] Gaudentius, Treatise 2, p. 40] that, if anything remains of the mysteries that we cannot yet comprehend, it must be burned with fire—that is, entrusted to the divine Spirit—so that what we do not yet understand may be consumed by the spirit of ardent faith.

This same interpretation belonged to Gregory the Great, Homily 22 on the Gospels:

> We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly entrust to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot penetrate concerning its mystery.

The same interpretation is found in Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, in his treatise *On the Last Words of the Lord*:

> We burn the bones of the lamb with fire, because we perceive and receive visibly, according to their appearance, the sacraments—which are, as it were, the flesh of divine power and coverings of truth. But we neither break nor diminish the substance itself; rather, we cast it into the flames, that is, we commend it to spiritual understandings, because the divine mysteries are spirit and life.

Indeed, it is also found in Gozechin the Scholastic, in his letter to Walcher [Note: [Col. 0813D] In Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Analecta*, p. 384]:

> These men—that is, the followers of Berengarius of Tours—eat the same paschal lamb, which, ineffably transforming the same sacraments into himself, established and consecrated them for us, either raw or cooked in water, not roasted with fire. What remains of it—and always will remain, since no mortal, however learned, has ever been or ever will be able in this life to penetrate fully, with complete understanding, the mystery of the incarnate Word—they do not burn with fire.

Thus, what Dupin asserted no one could imagine [Note: [Col. 0813D] “Who would imagine…?”] was said by these three authors, whom Dupin himself, I believe, would not deny to have been learned, serious, and honorable men, and especially men of sound mind.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] The same opinion is found in Eligius of Noyon, Homily 15, although there he does not speak of the remains of the paschal lamb but of Christ’s body itself.]

24. Perhaps we could have forgiven all these things in Dupin, provided that, when he concluded his treatise on Gaudentian writings, he had not displayed far more serious and savage anger against Gaudentius.

Let us hear our critic pronounce judgment on Gaudentius’s entire style of speaking:

> It is not necessary, says Dupin, to portray the character of Saint Gaudence; it is sufficiently known from what we have said about him. His style is simple and careless; it is full of forced allegories, extraordinary thoughts, and remote allusions. [Col. 0814C] His sermons are dry and barren; they instruct very little and do not move one at all. Finally, they possess none of the force, eloquence, beauty, or precision of the sermons of the Greek authors whom we have just discussed.

Thus Dupin speaks of Gaudentius, and, unless I am mistaken, not very generously. To make the reader clearly understand how unjustly and improperly he criticizes him, and how great was Gaudentius’s abundance of learning, doctrine, and force of expression, I have decided to present here several examples from Gaudentius’s sermons. From them anyone can readily understand what sort of discourse Dupin criticized so severely.

Gaudentius, Treatise 1, comparing Christians with Jews and Gentiles, says:

> And now, in comparison with the Jews and Gentiles, who are known to be submerged in the deep night of unbelief, and in comparison with those who dwell in the darkness and night of heresies and luxury, we seem to be—and plainly are—in the light. But our own days are overshadowed by certain clouds and do not possess the joy of serenity, as the Prophet says: “My days have declined like a shadow.”

In Treatise 4, addressing the newly baptized, he says:

> You, therefore, newly baptized, who have been invited to the banquet of this blessed and spiritual Passover, see to it that you preserve your souls from every defilement of foods infected by pagan superstition.

Then, after several intervening remarks:

> Preserve, newly baptized, the ornament of saving grace. Be sober in all things, lest you lose it when intoxicated. Come diligently to the church. Apply yourselves vigilantly with us to prayers, hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs. Let these be the works of your leisure, by which, rendering the service owed to Christ the Lord, you may obtain from him the reward of eternal life. Let your banquets therefore be sober and your beds chaste; let your spirit be modest, your speech gentle, and your walk mild.

Is this the dry and empty style of speech, entirely devoid of doctrine and every kind of ornament [Note: [Col. 0815D] “His style is simple and careless. His sermons are dry and barren; they instruct very little.”]?

In Treatise 7, to excuse the law forbidding the eating of leavened food from the charge of cruelty, since disobedience was threatened with the punishment of death, he says:

> If he had ordered it to become leavened, diligence would have been necessary there, so that it would not be lacking; what he ordered belongs to laziness, not labor. He commands negligence in order to test obedience; and do you not wish him to condemn the soul that has applied diligence in order to despise him?

In Treatise 11, explaining the words of John 7, “Do not judge according to appearance,” he argues as follows:

> This is a universal judgment, a teacher appointed for the preservation of equity, set before all, known to many, loved by few. For we are commanded not to flatter the persons of the rich of this world and, through a most unjust judgment, to favor unbelievers; nor, through timid silence, merely to tolerate the impious, cruel, rapacious, luxurious, and dishonorable, who deserve every condemnation, while proclaiming them with unjust praises. Nor are we to do what is more deformed than every disgrace: in pursuit of shameful profits, conspicuously to serve another’s money, forgetful of Christian liberty.

Does Gaudentius’s speech really lack all ornament and brilliance [Col. 0815C]? Or, on the contrary, does it not overflow with splendor, vigor, and abundance?

All these examples were also available to Dupin. From them he could have perceived both Gaudentius’s doctrine and his eloquence and genius, had he not brought a perverse and hostile disposition to his reading.

Tillemont, who was not afflicted by such a disorder, judged Gaudentius differently. To set one Frenchman against another, I gladly transcribe his words [Note: [Col. 0815D] *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, vol. X, p. 586]:

> Although his style—that of Gaudentius—may seem rather simple, it nevertheless possesses elegance, and one sees in it a very gentle genius, at the same time very agreeable. As for the substance of his works, their doctrine and instruction are excellent.

25. But let us continue for a little while longer listening to Gaudentius. No one defends his cause more vigorously than Gaudentius himself.

At the end of Treatise 5, he speaks as follows concerning the correction of subjects:

> If the wolf ceases to be a wolf and grazes with the lamb, as the Prophet says, and if the lion, ceasing to be a lion, eats straw with the ox, there is no need of a staff. For if the wickedness of savage behavior is transformed into such gentleness that the gentle seek and receive the nourishment of life together with the innocent and pure little sheep, the workers of Christ, Christ says to each of the apostolic priests that they should carry no staffs of correction on the road, when they have already begun to possess the holy land in obedient and modest disciples.

And in Treatise 3, the passage beginning “Nor should you consider this pointless” deserves the greatest attention. There he discusses free will so brilliantly that nothing could be more elegant or learned.

In the Preface, the entire passage [Note: [Col. 0816D] Preface to Benivolus] concerning the reasons why those who practice piety are sometimes afflicted by bodily pains or various tribulations is explained with such eloquence and learning that Gaudentius plainly seems to reign in it and to surpass all praise:

> There are found to be three reasons why those who practice piety are sometimes afflicted by bodily pains or various tribulations: the first is correction, the second purification, and the third testing.

A little farther on he says:

> Therefore, for the sake of testing, he describes the marvelous Job and the history of Job with many ornaments of thought and language.

Thus no one could be so dull-witted or so lacking in understanding—if Dupin is excepted—as not to perceive the eloquence and force of Gaudentius’s speech.

But I would surely labor in vain if I wished to review everything. Gaudentius needs no longer defense, especially among those who have Gaudentius’s sermons in their hands. I therefore refer the reader to them, so that after reading them he may judge Dupin’s criticism as seems fair.

§ III. Concerning the Plan and Arrangement of the 1720 Padua Edition

26. From the invention of printing down to the present day, there have been several editions of Gaudentius, none of which, however, can so far be called accurate or complete.

Elias Capreolus was the first to publish a specimen of the Gaudentian sermons: namely, excerpts from the sermon on Philastrius, in Book III of his *History of Brescia*, around the year 1500 or a little later.

Then, around 1554, Aloysius Lipomanus, bishop of Verona, published a complete sermon on Philastrius, a sermon on the Dedication of the Basilica, and excerpts from the Preface to Benivolus in the *Lives of the Saints*, volume IV of the Venetian edition. There, on pages 1 and 15, Gaudentius’s works are said not yet to have been printed.

Later, in 1555, a work entitled *Orthodoxographa* appeared at Basel, in two volumes, printed by Henry Peter. It contains nothing of Gaudentius. In a second printing of the same work, however, enlarged in the same city in several volumes in 1569, Gaudentian sermons are found in volume VI, folio 1799, in the same order and number in which they were afterward so often repeated in the *Libraries of the Fathers*. I therefore think it sufficiently probable that this was the first edition of the Gaudentian sermons.

27. Various editions of the *Libraries of the Fathers* subsequently appeared, after the first Paris edition prepared by Margarin de la Bigne in 1576. Gaudentius was always printed in all of them. But, as is inevitable with such large collections, they abounded throughout in substantial errors that awaited a correcting hand. Moreover, they lacked two sermons which, having been cast out, wandered far from their parent: [Col. 0817A] namely, the sermon on Peter and Paul and the sermon on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius.

It was therefore entirely worthwhile to undertake a new edition of Gaudentius. Besides, so far as I know, he had never been published separately, and very few people undertook the study of the enormous collections of the *Libraries of the Fathers*, deterred by the great bulk of the work.

While matters stood thus, and our Gaudentius lay almost in darkness, badly treated by the printers, it happened most fortunately—and, so to speak, under good auspices—that in 1714 the outstanding and immortality-worthy prelate John Francis Barbadicus was transferred from the bishopric of Verona to that of Brescia. As soon as he had assumed the administration of the Church of Brescia, he spontaneously formed the plan of publishing Gaudentius.

If I wished to enumerate the benefits that this great man conferred upon this edition, which I willingly undertook at his command, I should never finish speaking. He never ceased to assist us with both his labor and his resources, especially so that variant readings from manuscript codices might be available to us. With the greatest zeal, whenever necessary, he was always prepared to lend us his authority and services generously.

He also more than once courteously encouraged our industry, urging us to press forward with our undertaking, and examined with his own eyes the still rough and unpolished drafts of the work. Finally, he never ceased steadfastly to protect and support the edition until it appeared in print, even contributing money generously toward the expenses of the type.

### 28.

So that the reader may know what resources we used in preparing this edition, we had at our disposal collations from the Vatican Library of three manuscript codices: namely, the two Vatican codices 1243 and 4580, both written on papyrus, and also the very elegant parchment Urbinate codex 75, whose initial letters are adorned with painting and gold. Although these codices are not of great antiquity, they nevertheless supplied us with exceptional assistance in correcting Gaudentius at very many points, as will be evident to anyone reading them throughout.

In order that their variant readings might be excerpted with less difficulty and more promptly, His Holiness Pope Clement XI, Supreme Pontiff—whose permission was also granted for the codices themselves to be transferred from the Vatican Library to the Quirinal Palace—kindly allowed this, in accordance with his overflowing clemency and benevolence toward all. Under his pontificate and while he remains in good health, the humanities will never be without honor.

The task of making the excerpts was graciously undertaken by the distinguished and learned men Francesco Bianchini and Carlo Majello, prefect of the Vatican Library, both of them *ab honore sacri cubiculi* [honorary chamberlains] of His Holiness Pope Clement XI. I therefore gladly declare here that I shall always owe them everlasting thanks for their services.

To these three manuscript codices was added a fourth, the paper Florentine codex of the Library of San Marco, which the eminent Jean Mabillon had mentioned in his *Itinéraire italien*, p. 178. Its variant readings were carefully described and sent to us by the most reverend Father Albert Salvi, prior of that same monastery of San Marco in Florence.

With these four codices we collated Gaudentius’s first nineteen treatises, as well as the Preface to Benivolus. For correcting these treatises we likewise consulted three editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*: the Paris edition of 1589, the Cologne edition of 1618, and the Lyon edition of 1677.

The sermon *On Peter and Paul*, which is not found in the four manuscript codices mentioned above, was collated with another parchment Urbinate codex, no. 150, and likewise with parchment Vatican codex 1235. Both of these two codices also contain sermons of Zeno, bishop of Verona; their age appears to reach approximately five hundred years.

Besides these two codices, for the collation of the sermon *On Peter and Paul* we used the old Venetian edition of the sermons of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, from the year 1508, in which this sermon first appeared, with Gaudentius’s name by no means concealed, as we noted in the annotations to that same sermon.

For the sermon *On the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius*, variant readings were supplied to us by two Brescian parchment codices, the older of which bears a date indicating the eleventh century. We also used two editions, namely the Venetian edition of Lippomano from 1554 and the Cologne edition of Surius from 1579, in which the sermon had been published among the *Lives of the Saints*.

Moreover, since I knew that the Ambrosian Library in Milan possessed the first edition of Gaudentius—or at least the first, as I believe—which appeared in 1569 in the *Orthodoxographi Patrum*, I had its variant readings for the first nineteen Gaudentian treatises printed there together with the Preface to Benivolus transcribed for me by the distinguished Giuseppe Antonio Sassi, prefect of that library, a man of exceptional learning and the greatest courtesy. But since this edition appears to agree almost entirely with the corruptions of the other editions, it was of no use to us.

### 29.

The order of Gaudentius’s sermons, or treatises, has been preserved by us as it also appears in the other editions. The sermon *On His Ordination*, which Gaudentius delivered before all the others, ought therefore also to have stood first in order. But the Preface placed before the Paschal sermons caused these earlier sermons to come first, since it mentions the four that follow and, fifth, the martyrs of the Maccabees. For that reason, in this edition we have retained the order established for us by Gaudentius himself in the Preface and received in the other editions.

The Gaudentian sermons are followed by a rhythmical poem on Philastrius. For this, consult what we said in the notice prefixed to that poem at the end of Gaudentius’s sermons.

### 30.

It then seemed appropriate to join to Gaudentius Rampertus and Adelmannus, bishops of the same Church, conspicuous no less for learning than for piety. I was strongly moved—indeed, I might say filled with hope—to provide the complete letter of Adelmannus; but I eventually realized, and only with difficulty, that this desire, conceived in my mind, had been entirely futile, when I saw all our efforts come to nothing.

Rampertus, however, recovered at more than one point from the great wounds he had received, and was accurately divided into sections with the help of the two Brescian codices praised shortly before. These codices were of the greatest use to us in preparing this edition. For besides Rampertus, whose manuscript exemplar you would seek elsewhere in vain, they contain Gaudentius’s sermon on Philastrius and also a rhythmical composition in honor of Philastrius, assembled from the thoughts expressed in Gaudentius’s sermon.

The Church of Brescia once possessed a flourishing library of manuscript codices, and some remnants of it still survive. Among them is a parchment manuscript of Augustine’s *City of God*, in large folio format, as well as a work of the same size and character, a collection of sermons and sententiae on all the Epistles of Saint Paul drawn from Augustine’s works. This collection was formerly attributed to Bede but is now assigned to Florus of Lyon.

There is moreover a splendid testimony concerning the Brescian Library by Saint Charles Borromeo in the records of the Apostolic Visitation of the city of Brescia, which he himself conducted in 1581 and which survive in manuscript in the episcopal archive of Brescia. He writes:

> The Church of Brescia, enriched by God’s favor with many ornaments, ought also to have this mark of piety: whenever need arises for the most accurate correction of ecclesiastical codices corrupted by the ravages of time or by the corruptions of heretics, it should bring forth from its own bosom the monuments of the ancient Fathers—especially those correctly written—which it once diligently sought out and preserved for a long time.

### 31.

These, then, were the resources available to us for preparing this edition of Gaudentius. If the reader wishes to know what we have accomplished in it, I would prefer that he learn this from the work itself rather than from my words.

Our principal effort was directed toward presenting Gaudentius’s text as accurately corrected as possible, chiefly with the assistance and aid of manuscript codices, while informing the reader at each individual place whenever anything had been altered. We wished not to appear, as very learned men rightly condemn, to take up the censor’s mark and change everything at will.

In supplying and reviewing the variant readings, I have generally shown myself more thorough. Who, however, could review or record everything? Nevertheless, I preferred that our diligence should seem excessive or tiresome to delicate readers rather than that we should risk losing the confidence of serious and learned readers.

Nor am I unaware how difficult a task I have undertaken in attempting to correct and publish an ancient author, especially in a place where, besides other obstacles, we suffer from the greatest scarcity of better books. Yet it was decided that it would be preferable to attempt something—even if rough and imperfect—than to leave our Gaudentius neglected in darkness for a longer time.

Would that some taste for these studies might one day arise in these regions, and that heterodox men might not always, as has happened, seize from us the honor of publishing ancient authors, an honor that for a long time belonged especially to Italian minds. They have done this skillfully enough in the cases of Cyprian, Sulpicius, Einhard, and many others, so that, by twisting their authority toward error, they might more easily weaken our cause, deprived as it is of the stronger fortifications supplied by antiquity.

Indeed, how displeasing it is to them that the study of ecclesiastical history—which rests chiefly upon the writings of the ancients—should flourish among us is revealed by a single statement that we gladly accept, even though it was unwillingly extracted from our enemies:

> The *Annals* of Baronius have done more harm than the *Controversies* of Bellarmine.

[Note: Georgius Hornius, Preface to Sulpicius Severus, Amsterdam edition, 1665.]

Nor should anyone perhaps consider the work devoted to correcting ancient books futile or empty. On this subject we must certainly listen to the eminent Jean Mabillon in his Preface to the edition of Saint Bernard:

> To select from variant readings those that seem more suitable and restore them to the text is a task that requires a nearly constant use of ancient books, a taste acquired through practice, and a more mature judgment than the general body of scholars supposes—those who think that we are catching spiders’ webs while we pursue what they consider trifles.

Let such people think of us whatever they wish, provided that our labor is approved not by human applause but by the public utility of the Church and of scholarship.

### 32.

Before I finish, it is only right that some testimony of grateful feeling toward those whose services and assistance I chiefly used in preparing this edition of Gaudentius should remain.

First, besides those whom I have already mentioned in their proper places, I must here recall the distinguished Alexander Burgos, an outstanding devotee not only of literature but also of genuine piety. He has devoted to public use a very well-stocked library collected from every direction, and while I was staying at Padua he always wished it to be open to my use.

I also acknowledge that I owe much to the nobleman of excellent character Francesco Giuseppe della Corte, canon of the Brescian Church, and to my brother Giulio, my companion in study. They willingly undertook the labor of collating exemplars and variant readings for me.

The Reverend Father Antonio Piccoli, archpriest of the church of Santa Maria di Terentiano in the diocese of Brescia, compiled and arranged the index of the Scriptures.

If the reader encounters anything polished or anything corrected in this edition, let him attribute it all to Giovanni Antonio and Gaetano Vulpio, brothers. Through their diligence and labor we have achieved that, in the future, we should not greatly miss the elegance or accuracy of foreign editions.

## § IV. On the Plan and Additions of This New Edition

### 33.

These, then, are the matters I had prefaced to the edition of Gaudentius published at Padua in 1720. The reader will now learn briefly what we have accomplished on the occasion of this new Brescian edition.

For a long time, as I reread Gaudentius, many matters had occurred to me that seemed to require a second examination. I was ready to apply my hand to them willingly, so that, if an opportunity for a new edition should ever arise, it might appear not merely with the old apparatus but also equipped with more recent additions.

The authority of the most eminent Angelo Maria Quirini, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, librarian and bishop of Brescia, opportunely joined this undertaking. As soon as I realized that he was considering the plan of this new edition, I understood what my duties were and what I had to do in obedience to the will of so great a prelate. I considered it a great honor to obey not only his commands but even his nods.

Thus, while I was engaged in scattering new annotations here and there through Gaudentius’s text, and in improving some of the earlier ones, as it seemed to me, a manuscript codex of Gaudentius’s sermons unexpectedly presented itself to me. It was not of great antiquity, as was shown by its handwriting and the small form of its letters; but its value was increased by the fact that it had once belonged to the library of the learned Octavius Pantagathus, as corrections written in the margins in his own hand, recognizable by the familiar formation of his letters, clearly indicated.

I do not think that Octavius Pantagathus of Brescia, a man of great reputation among the learned of his age, can be unknown to anyone possessing even moderate learning. Although during his lifetime he entirely refused to make any monument of his talent public or to leave the fruits of his labors to posterity, he nevertheless enjoyed an exceptional reputation for learning. He is celebrated for that reason in the writings of nearly all who lived in his age, and abundant testimony to this appears among the authors of that period.

Among many others, Lilius Gregorius Giraldus writes of Pantagathus in dialogue 2 of *On the Poets of Our Time*:

> Brescia has many learned men, but no poets, as Verona, its daughter, does. Among the learned, however, the great Father Octavius is everywhere to be found, except that he abstains from writing and does not sell his wealth in a public shop.

Jacopo Augusto Thuanus gives a similar account in book 1 of his *Commentaries on His Life*:

> Octavianus Pantagathus had already departed to a better life. His name was great in letters, and Onuphrius Panvinius was a disciple worthy of so great a teacher.

No one is more expansive or generous in praising Pantagathus whenever he happens to speak of him than Panvinius himself. I shall cite only one of the many passages in which he testifies that he held him in the highest esteem, namely book 2 of his *Commentary on the Book of the Fasti*, p. 390. Speaking there about the origin of the indictions, he writes:

> In order to demonstrate when, how, and by whom this was done, and from whom I received the information, I am compelled first to say a few words in praise of the man whose diligence above all enabled me to illuminate and bring to light a matter most obscure, buried beneath the darkness of antiquity, and hitherto known to no one. For I consider it the mark of an honorable and grateful spirit to indicate from whom one has received something and through whom one has advanced; to deprive no one of the praise he justly deserves, and especially not that man from whom I drew the beginnings of everything that I have elaborated, accurately and perfectly arranged, throughout this entire work.
>
> This man is Father Octavius Pantagathus. If he did not already bear this name, he would rightly deserve to bear the name *foremost*. Although I consider it wrong to say only a little or merely in passing about his praises—for they could scarcely be explained in entire volumes—nevertheless, because of my singular respect for him, I could not restrain myself here, where I must explain those matters that flowed, as though from a purest fountain, chiefly from the sharpness of his intellect, the keenness of his judgment, and the variety and excellence of his deeper learning. Nor can I refrain from briefly saying what I truly think of so great a man. Thus, those who knew him may regard it as a great part of their good fortune that they knew him; while those who did not know him may receive from me an account of this man, at once the best and the most learned. For this is my judgment: in our age no one is considered superior to him either in talent, diligence, or learning.

So much for Pantagathus.

### 34.

To return to the codex commended by the name of so great an owner: as soon as I began comparing it with the printed editions, I immediately recognized its usefulness and excellence.

At first glance I had wondered whether it might perhaps have been copied from one of the manuscript exemplars I had used in the earlier edition, and therefore whether no benefit could be obtained from it; indeed, I feared that spending hours examining such a manuscript would be nothing other than wasting time and effort.

But the opposite proved true. It became clear with little difficulty that it had not been taken from the Florentine codex, from the Urbinate, or from either of the two Vatican codices. Indeed, it very often differs from them, as I noted in treatise 5 at the words “He will ascend as though in secret,” and in treatise 10 at the end, at the words “both the shepherd and the pastures.”

Rather, I found it better and more accurately corrected than those codices, as is shown by the passages that, with the aid of this same codex, I either restored, confirmed, or improved: in treatise 4, at the end, at the words “they stammer that they thirst for the Spirit”; in treatise 9, around the middle, at the words “Therefore, when we consider”; in the same treatise, at the end, in the final note; and also in treatise 13 at more than one point.

Moreover, quite a few passages that had been despaired of and left in a damaged state through the fault of copyists, and for which the manuscript codices had provided no assistance in the earlier edition, recovered through the aid of this book. A fine example appears in treatise 3, after the middle, concerning the two destructions of Nineveh; and likewise in treatise 6, before the middle, at the words “For the sons of the Egyptians by nature.”

It is also of no small importance that in treatise 4 this codex restores “they will take with them their nearest neighbor” in place of the corrupt reading found in the other books, “he will take with him his nearest neighbor.” In treatise 8, after the middle, it supplies “with the liberality of divine love” where “with the freedom of divine love” had been incorrectly read. I pass over many other examples, which the diligent reader will easily discover for himself through his own care and study.

Accordingly, with the assistance of my brother Giulio, who had discovered and purchased the book at a price beyond gold, I collated this codex from beginning to end with Gaudentius’s sermons, carefully entering its variant readings and corrections in their proper places.

If the prudent reader judges that some brightness and light has thereby been added to Gaudentius, I shall conclude that I have undertaken work truly worthwhile and received no small fruit from my labor. If not, I shall be content with this new testimony of my diligence and respect toward our Gaudentius.

## Testimonies Concerning Gaudentius

**Saint John Chrysostom, Letter 184, edition of Fronton du Duc, Paris, 1636**

### To Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia

Nothing concerning your affairs is hidden from us; rather, as though present, we know well your zeal, vigilance, cares, and labors, which you have undertaken for the sake of truth. We give you immense thanks, and, living in such great solitude, we draw no small consolation from the ardor and sincerity of your charity. When we tested it here, we learned that it also flourished there in its full integrity and had in no way been weakened either by the passage of time or by the length of the journey.

**Palladius, *Dialogue on the Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, chapter 4, edition of Émeric Bigot, Paris, 1680**

When therefore Saint Aemilius, bishop of Beneventum, and Cythegius and Gaudentius, together with the presbyters Valentinianus and Bonifatius, had received the letters of the emperor Honorius, of Innocent, and of the Italian bishops Chromatius of Aquileia and Venerius of Milan, together with those of the others, as well as the memorandum of the Synod of the whole West, they set out for Constantinople by public conveyance.

**Rufinus, Preface to his translation of the books of Clement’s *Recognitions***

For you, Gaudentius, distinguished ornament of our teachers, possess such vigor of intellect—or rather, such grace of spirit—that whatever you say even in the ordinary manner of daily speech, whatever you declaim in church, ought to be preserved in books and handed down to posterity for instruction.

**Roman Martyrology, 25 October**

At Brescia, the birthday of Saint Gaudentius, bishop, distinguished for learning and holiness.

**Rampertus, Sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, chapter 5**

As is read in the celebrated sermon delivered by the bishop Gaudentius, namely the life of the most blessed pontiff Philastrius.

**The same, chapter 9**

His life and holiness were known by the bishop Gaudentius, his successor, who for fourteen years, and perhaps longer, observed the day of his passing as a holiday, speaking to the people about him.

**Nicephorus Callistus, book 13 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 33, Paris edition, 1630, revised by Fronton du Duc**

Moreover, having received into their hands the decree of the synod convened in Italy concerning John, Aemilius, the God-loving bishop of Beneventum, Cathegius [sic], and Gaudentius, together with the presbyters Valentius and Bonifatius, set out from Rome for Byzantium.

**Petrus Crinitus, book 8 of the *Commentaries on Honorable Disciplines*, chapter 1**

Among our own writers are Tertullian, Hilary, Cyprian, Augustine, Jerome, Rufinus, Ambrose, and Gaudentius. Their commentaries seem to me like treasures, containing such varied and manifold knowledge of learning and of all things that they embrace almost the whole of antiquity, all laws, and the principles of philosophy.

**Elias Capreolus, book 2 of the *History of Brescia***

Gaudentius, our bishop immediately after Philastrius, and the learning, counsels, and gravity with which he was endowed, can be understood above all from his oration on Philastrius.

**Aloysius Lippomanus, Preface to volume 4**

If you wish to know who Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, was, and how great his authority and reverence in the Church were, you will readily recognize them from his writings. He flourished in the time of Saint Ambrose and, as Ambrose himself testifies, was the successor of Philastrius, a bishop of great holiness who preceded the time of Saint Augustine and wrote a book on heresies. Gaudentius was also a contemporary of Benivolus, a most holy man, celebrated both in ecclesiastical history and in the *Tripartite History*, to whom he also addressed certain of his writings.

**Possevinus, *Sacred Apparatus***

The works of Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, who succeeded Philastrius through the efforts of Saint Ambrose, in whose time he lived, exist. He undertook a journey to Cappadocia in order to bring back the relics of martyrs from there and to ennoble his own church with those relics [perhaps: *his church*]. He delivered an oration at the dedication of the basilica, in which he says more about those martyrs. There also exist treatises, or sermons, to which he prefixed a useful and worthwhile preface.

**Baronius, under A.D. 386, no. 7**

Gaudentius was appointed in place of Philastrius, who had died not long before and whom we saw present with Ambrose at the Council of Aquileia. Although he was still young, he excelled in learning and virtues. The force and greatness of the effort he applied he himself explains in the opening of the sermon that he delivered at the time of his ordination.

**The same, under A.D. 451, no. 16**

They were indeed bishops of flourishing Churches. Brescia, ennobled by the blood of martyrs and also by holy bishops—Philastrius, Gaudentius, and many others—is distinguished among them.

**Bellarminus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers***

Gaudentius, Philastrius’s successor in the bishopric of Brescia, wrote extremely useful treatises on various subjects, which still exist.

**Labbeus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume 1, p. 337**

Gaudentius succeeded Philastrius in the Brescian episcopate from the year 387 until the beginning of the fifth century—according to some, until 410, or, as can be inferred from the beginning of the episcopate of his successor Paul, until 427. Ferdinand Ughelli, in volume 4 of *Sacred Italy*, teaches that Paul attained episcopal rank in 427. Gaudentius died on 25 October and was buried at Brescia in the Basilica of Saint John the Evangelist.

**Gaspard Barthius, book 18 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 1**

Gaudentius’s treatises on Exodus are plainly good.

**Ferdinand Ughelli, volume 4 of *Sacred Italy*, Venetian edition, column 528**

Thereafter, through the efforts of Ambrose, the most holy bishop of the Milanese, the Brescian people raised Saint Gaudentius to this see—that is, the Brescian see—in the year 385, while he was still in the flower of his age and traveling in the East to visit the holy places. He was a man distinguished for learning and holiness.

**Philippus Ferrarius, *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, 25 October**

Gaudentius, disciple and successor of Saint Philastrius, was taken up to the Brescian episcopate while still a young man and against his will. He was consecrated by Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, with whom he was especially intimate.

Gaudentius made a pilgrimage to Palestine and enriched his Church with many distinguished relics. He received some of them from Palestine, some from Caesarea in Cappadocia, from the nuns who were nieces of Saint Basil, and others from Rome and Milan. He wrote many works, for he excelled in learning. Some of them are read in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, testifying to his distinguished erudition.

**Aubertus Miraeus, *Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers***

Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia in Italy, was appointed to that see in succession to Philastrius through the efforts of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, as Gaudentius himself testifies in the sermon he delivered on his ordination. He also discusses the journey to the East that he undertook in the sermon on the dedication of the church. He wrote various treatises, which Bellarmine lists in his catalogue; they also exist in the *Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*.

**Cardinal Giovanni Bona, Preface to the book *On Divine Psalmody***

Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, distinguished for piety and wisdom.

**Acts of the Saints, 10 March, p. 14, § 1, no. 7**

Among the earlier Latin Fathers flourished Saint Gaudentius, who, through the efforts of Saint Ambrose, was made bishop of Brescia around the year 385. Among his works there is a homily on the Forty Holy Martyrs, delivered on the day of the dedication of the basilica that he had erected in their honor. He reconstructs the story of their martyrdom and indicates the circumstances in which he brought their relics from the East to his own Church, at least part of which we shall presently present. In other respects he followed Saint Basil very closely.

**Gerardus Johannes Vossius, book 3 of *On Latin History*, chapter 2**

Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, committed to memory the life of Saint Philastrius, whom he had succeeded in the episcopate. You have it in Surius, volume 4, under 18 July. Philastrius died in 387; hence Gaudentius’s period is sufficiently clear.

**Natalis Alexander, *Selected Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, chapter 6, article 34**

Gaudentius, Philastrius’s successor in the Brescian episcopate, flourished from 387 until the beginning of the fifth century. He delivered many treatises, or sermons, on various subjects, which exist in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*.

**William Cave, *Ecclesiastical Literary History*, fourth-century writers**

Gaudentius, of whom there is either no memory at all or only a very rare one among the ancients [Note: Whether Cave could rightly have said this may be gathered sufficiently from the ancient testimonies of John Chrysostom, Palladius, Rufinus, and others, which we cited above], was traveling through the Eastern provinces for the sake of religion and was staying at Caesarea in Cappadocia around the year 387. Meanwhile, when Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, had died, Ambrose and the other bishops of Cisalpine Gaul designated him as Philastrius’s successor while he was absent. To prevent the election from being frustrated by anyone’s deceit, it was confirmed by the oath of each individual bishop.
