When Gaudentius learned of this and refused to return to the West, the bishops sent a delegation to him and also to the bishops of the East, asking them to compel the unwilling Gaudentius to return by ecclesiastical censures. This was done. Gaudentius was compelled to return, and he brought with him relics of the Forty Martyrs, which he had received from the sacred virgins, nieces of Saint Basil, who were living at Caesarea. He then assumed the governance of the Brescian Church.

In the year 405 he appears to have undertaken, together with certain other bishops, a delegation in the name of the Roman synod and the emperor Honorius, in order to make the emperor Arcadius, who was somewhat hostile toward Chrysostom, more conciliatory. It is not sufficiently clear in what year he died.

### Note

How highly the testimony of the distinguished Sebastian Tillemont, cited above in Preface § 24, ought to be valued may be shown by the following words:

> Although his style—that of Gaudentius, of course—may seem rather simple, it nevertheless possesses elegance, and one sees in it a very gentle genius, and at the same time a very agreeable one. As for the substance of the matter, his learning and instructions are excellent.

Dupin himself acknowledges this, and his bold judgment concerning Gaudentius’s writings is thereby refuted. In his *Ecclesiastical Library*, Dupin says the following about Tillemont:

> The *Mémoires* display almost infinite research and are composed with every possible accuracy. The notes found at the end of each volume are excellent and marked by very exact criticism.

His Eminence, the patron of this edition, ordered that this notice be added as the conclusion to the testimonies concerning Gaudentius, so that the authority of Gaudentius’s writings might stand increasingly firm—an authority that Dupin rashly attempted to damage.

# Extant Treatises or Sermons of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia

### Preface

**Gaudentius to Benivolus, servant of Christ**

[Note: Galeardus published this title as follows: “Preface of Gaudentius, bishop, to Benivolus, servant of Christ. Gaudentius to Benivolus, servant of Christ,” adding the following notes.]

**To the servant of Christ.** The title was evidently added by a copyist’s ingenuity. These words are entirely foreign to the customary manner of addressing letters. It is also absent from two manuscripts, the Florentine and the Urbinate. Nevertheless, since it is consistently found in the printed exemplars that we were able to see, we judged that it should be retained.

The Florentine codex reads: “Gaudentius to Benivolus, servant of Christ,” and so does the Urbinate. I have no doubt that this inscription is genuine, and for that reason I arranged for it to be placed before this Preface. The same wording appears in the manuscript codex that belonged to the learned Octavius Pantagathus, my fellow countryman: “Gaudentius to Benivolus, servant of Christ.” The Urbinate, however, alters it slightly: “The servant of Christ Gaudentius to Benivolus.”

Although I know that the style of this work is entirely unlike that of a letter, nevertheless Ferrarius has already shown in book 2 of *On the Rites of the Sacred Church’s Sermons*, chapter 3, that the Paschal sermons of Cyril of Alexandria—delivered from the pulpit to the people but afterward shaped in the form of letters—were often composed in this way, as were those of our Gaudentius and of others.

Salvianus inscribes the Preface to his books *On the Government of God* as follows: “Salvianus sends greetings in the Lord to Saint Salonius, bishop.” Gaudentius himself, in treatise 18, addressed to Serminius, *On the Unjust Steward*, writes: “Gaudentius, bishop, to Serminius, servant of Christ.”

**Benivolus.** Both Vatican codices read: “To Benivolus, servant of Christ.” The Florentine reads: “To Benivolus, servant of Christ,” in the dative form. In the Urbinate we find the name Benivolus twice at the very beginning.

Accordingly, we have conformed our edition to the agreement of the manuscript exemplars and the Paris edition. The reading “To Benevolus, servant of Christ” had crept into the other editions. That the form published by us was the ancient manner of writing is proved by an old inscription in Rubeus, p. 263, dedicated to Marcus Aurelius Dubitatus and Gaius Centullus Fortunatus:

> To Industrius and Benivolus,
>
> who discharged many military offices,
>
> in recognition of his filial devotion,
>
> Marcus Aurelius Dubitatus, a man of distinguished rank, their father,
>
> and Gaius Centullus Fortunatus,
>
> a young man of distinguished rank.
>
> [*INDVSTRIO AC BENIVOLO / PLVRIMIS MILITIAE HONORIBVS / FVNCTO / PRO SVAE PIETATIS MERITO / M. AVR. DVBITATO V. I. PATRI / ET C. CENTVLLO FORTVNATO / ADVLESCENTI* (sic)]

See also Valesius’s note on Sozomen, book 7 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13. More will be said below about Benivolus, at Gaudentius’s words: “A teacher of memory.”

**Preface of Gaudentius, bishop.** The Florentine codex gives this title: “Discourses of Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia.” In the Urbinate codex: “The treatises of Gaudentius to Benivolus begin auspiciously.” See annotation 1 to the following sermon.

[Col. 0827] 217 It had been the common desire that you might have been able to hear in person the things which I expounded from the divine utterances during the Paschal days just past. Although your presence is always rightly welcome to us in the assembly of the Church of Brescia, it is especially so on feast days. For, just as you are the most worthy head of the honorati of our city, so also, with the Lord’s consent, you are the most worthy head of the Lord’s people, because you strive to keep God’s commandments with no less diligence than you show in learning them: striving to make your robust profession of the Catholic faith equal to the merits of an excellent life, so that sincere faith may possess works worthy of the radiance of its purity.

[Note: Those who held civil offices, whether in a city or in the provinces, or who had obtained honours in military service or discharged a military dignity, were called honorati, as Valesius explains in his notes on Marcellinus, p. 15. Alciatus, Praetermissa I, also calls honorati those who had held a palatine or curial dignity but abstained from administration. Ambrose perhaps means them in his Oration on the Death of Valentinian: “I had already promised that I would depart, responding either to the honorati who requested it or to the prefect, so that provision might be made for the tranquillity of Italy.” See Petrus Nannius, Scholium on Ambrose V, ep. 33, no. 4, Froben edition. The designation honoratus was quite suitable for Benivolus, who had been Master of Records in Valentinian’s palace; see below, the following page.]

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate codices and two Vatican codices read: “with God granting it.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read thus: contendens, “striving.” They have habeat sincera fides, “let sincere faith possess,” a reading which I nevertheless do not approve.]

In this there is the greatest fruit for the teacher and an immortal benefit for the hearer, as the Apostle says: “Not hearers only, but doers of the law shall be justified before God” (Romans II).

[Note: The eight Paschal days were formerly solemn for the newly baptized; indeed, for all Christians, since during them they continually devoted themselves to praising the Resurrection and to the most holy preaching, as the ancient records of earlier generations show. Among them sermons delivered to the newly baptized throughout that week are frequently found. John Chrysostom, Homily 33 on Genesis XIII, translated by Fronto Ducaeus, says: “When the day of the Resurrection dawned, it was necessary that we should teach your Charity about the Lord’s Resurrection; and on the following days, because of the miracles then performed, the demonstration of the Resurrection had to be brought forward again. During those days we also took the Acts of the Apostles into our hands, preparing continuous banquets from them for you, and exhorting by frequent, daily admonitions those who had recently received the grace of Baptism.” Hence Augustine, in the preface to On Eight Questions to Dulcitius, calls these holy days; and Valentinian lists them among the feast days exempt from the administration of justice, Book II, On Holidays, of the Theodosian Code. Valentinian’s decree is also confirmed in the edict of King Theodoric, chapter 154. The Trullan Synod, canon 66, says: “From the holy day of the Resurrection until the new Sunday, throughout the whole week, the faithful ought continually to devote themselves in the churches to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, rejoicing in Christ and celebrating the feast, applying their minds to the reading of the divine Scriptures, and enjoying the holy mysteries with gladness and abundance.” Gaudentius likewise says below: “What I remembered having expounded to the holy brotherhood on each day of that most sacred holy week.”]

For the Apostle says: “It is not merely hearers of the law, but doers who will be justified before God” (Romans II).

[Note: Thus the Vulgate also reads, as it did among the ancient Fathers. The Florentine codex and two Vatican codices read “before the Lord”; the codex formerly belonging to the distinguished Brescian Octavius Pantagathus reads “before God.” In that codex, a little above, instead of “the greatest fruit of the teacher,” it has “the greatest fruit of the speaker,” which is a better and perhaps truer reading.]

Nor is it surprising that you now conduct yourself in this way in the fear of the Lord, since, before you had yet received the grace of Baptism, you fought so for the truth of the heavenly faith that, being imbued with the admirable teachings of that man apostolic in every respect, our father Philastrius, you gave proof of such great constancy.

[Note: From this passage we learn that Benivolus, when he resisted the commands of the Empress Justina, was still a catechumen; this is not clear from Rufinus, Sozomen, and Nicephorus.]

[Note: He calls Philastrius “father,” whose successor he himself had been in the see of Brescia. So also in the Sermon on the Life of Philastrius: “But I, the least part of him, earnestly desire with all my wishes that I may somehow be able to protect the field well sown by my father and received in succession that was not sufficiently suitable.” More about Philastrius is found there.]

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate codices, as well as the codex of Octavius Pantagathus, read “you approved by testimony”; this seems better, although I did not wish to alter the reading, since the received reading is equally good.]

For the Jezebel-queen of our time, the patroness and accomplice alike of Arian perfidy,

[Note: Justina, wife of the elder Valentinian and mother of Valentinian II, is meant. See the following notes.]

when she was persecuting the most blessed Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan,

[Note: Sulpicius Severus, speaking of Valentinian, says in Dialogue II: “An Arian wife had attached herself to his harsh and proud disposition.” This was Justina. While her husband lived, she did little harm to the Orthodox; after his death, she stirred up the greatest disturbances. Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History II.15, Froben’s 1523 edition, says: “Justina, a foster-mother of the Arian heresy, boldly disclosed to her son, who was easily deceived, the poisons of her impiety, which she had suppressed while her husband lived.” Socrates, Tripartite History IX.20, says: “Justina, the mother of Valentinian, being an Arian, was indeed unable to harm the Orthodox while her husband lived. After his death, and when her son was still very young, she came to Milan and was hostile to Bishop Ambrose.”]

also compelled you at that time—judging you, the Master of Records, to have forgotten the saving faith—to dictate against the Catholic Churches.

[Note: For Justina’s persecution of Ambrose, see Paulinus, Life of Ambrose; indeed Ambrose himself, V.33, to his sister Marcellina, where, like our Gaudentius, he denotes Justina by the name Jezebel: “What shall I say, that bloody Jezebel also persecuted Elijah? That Herodias caused John the Baptist to be killed? Yet each persecuted one individual; but my merits are far smaller, while my trials are more grievous.” Those seeking further information about Justina will find Zosimus, Book IV, and Valesius’s notes on Marcellinus, p. 611, where he also refutes Socrates’ tale about Justina. She died in exile, as may be inferred from Rufinus II.17.]

She

[Note: Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History II.16, calls this Benivolus “presiding over the record offices”; Nicephorus, History XII.19, says that he served in the clerks’ division, in the archive of the sacred constitutions. The imperial record offices are frequently mentioned in the Theodosian Code. Those who presided over them and held the first place were called masters, as Valesius aptly notes in his notes on Marcellinus, page 253. The record offices were chests or shelves in which commentaries and documents—that is, written records—were kept. There were chiefly four: those of petitions, records, dispositions, and letters, as Salmasius relates in his notes on the Life of Alexander Severus in the Augustan History. Hence those appointed over the individual offices were called, from the office to which each belonged, Master of Petitions, Master of Records, and sometimes simply Master of Petitions or Master of Records, as in Lampridius’s Life of Alexander Severus: “After midday he always devoted himself to signing and reading letters, so that the Masters of Letters, Petitions, and Records were always in attendance.” They were sometimes called Master of Petitions or Master of Records, as here by Gaudentius. Marcellinus likewise says, in Book XXIX, that a certain Festus, formerly an advocate and then governor of Syria, later Master of Records, became proconsul of Asia.]

to have forgotten the saving faith, and compelled you to dictate against the Catholic Churches. To prevent you from doing so, you freely despised both the dignity of the promised promotion and worldly ambition and earthly glory for God’s glory, choosing rather to live as a private person than to serve in office as a dead man.

[Note: The splendid deed of Benivolus is recounted by the ecclesiastical writers cited above. Sozomen, Tripartite History IX.20 and Ecclesiastical History VII.13, agrees with Rufinus and Nicephorus that, rather than abandon the cause of the faith, he took off his belt and threw it at the queen’s feet. Casting off the military belt for Christ’s faith, as a demonstration of constancy and contempt for pagan emperors and other governors, was customary among Christian soldiers, as is shown more fully by the acts of the saints published by Gallonius, On the Torments of the Martyrs, ch. 4, p. 191, Antwerp, 1668. Compare the Roman Martyrology on Victricius of Rouen, 7 August; the Armenian soldiers, 5 September; and Menas the Egyptian, 11 November.]

[Note: This passage has been emended on the agreement of the manuscripts. The printed editions have “political,” which is exceedingly inept. Rufinus supports the emendation in the passage cited above, II.16: “Lest Benivolus should seem to frustrate the queen’s undertaking, a higher honor was promised him. He, who wished to be nobler in faith than in honors, said: ‘Why do you promise me a higher rank as a reward for impiety? Take away even the one I have; only let my conscience of faith remain unharmed.’ Saying this, he threw his belt at the feet of those giving the impious command.”]

For truly he dies before God who departs from the truth of the apostolic faith, from whom Christ God, who is life, is cut off, when he denies the homoousion of the eternal Trinity.

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts read coaeternae, “coeternal.” The Paris edition has eo aeternae, incorrectly. The Arians of Gaudentius’s age strongly attacked the term ὁμοούσιον (homoousion), as well as οὐσίας and ὁμοουσίας, “essence” and “consubstantiality.” See Sulpicius Severus, Book II of the Sacred History, and Jerome’s letter to Damasus, Benedictine edition, volume IV, letter 14.]

But, to return to the matter at hand, when your body was still weak from the great illness, it prevented you from attending the aforesaid festival; hence you were exceedingly distressed, counting this as a fraud inflicted upon you, because of pressing sins, against your spiritual benefits.

[Note: Thus in four manuscript codices; the printed editions read nunc, “now.” But the Pantagathus codex has tuum tunc, “your body then,” as also in the following dolebas omnino, “you were altogether distressed”; a little below it has propterea veluti, “therefore, as it were.” This final word, highly suitable to the passage, is absent both from the printed editions and from the manuscripts.]

Accordingly, you urgently demanded a particular remedy for this loss, asking me to write down what I remembered having expounded to the holy brotherhood on each day of that most sacred week.

[Note: The Urbinate codex and two Vatican codices read this way; the agreement of these manuscripts restores the genuine reading. The Florentine codex has pervectos, “advanced”; the printed editions have perfectos, “perfected,” entirely incorrectly. In all three of those codices one also reads unde ipse excidit, “from which he himself fell,” instead of unde ipse cecidit, “from which he himself fell.”]

I would plainly not have dared to entrust this to writing, conscious as I am of my mediocrity, unless your devout persistence had compelled me. It is enough for me if I am at least able to instruct the people entrusted to me by the living voice.

[Note: The manuscripts agree in this reading, which plainly ought to be retained, since it corresponds to what he said above, “you urgently demanded.” Below also: “Moreover, I shall send you four shorter treatises, corrected, since you compel me.” The printed editions have religiosa constantia, “devout steadfastness,” a reading which we thought ought not to be retained, although it is supported by the book of Octavius Pantagathus cited above.]

Knowing, then, that a true lover of divine wisdom does not seek the pomp of empty eloquence in asserting useless matters, but desires the salutary teaching of suitable explanations from the holy Scriptures,

[Note: The manuscripts have virum, “a man.” Barthius observed that the phrase inanis eloquentiae pompam quaerere, “to seek the pomp of empty eloquence,” should be understood in a less favorable sense, like “the pomp of the world” or “the pomp of demons.” See Barthius’s notes there, page 11. Cicero uses pompa similarly in Letters to Friends II.16: “This troublesome pomp of my lictors is added”; and in Tusculan Disputations IV: “Those burnings of the spirit and whetstones of virtue from the rhetorical pomp.” Hence pompatice ingredi, “to proceed pompously,” in Amos VI.]

I shall undertake to write to you in precisely the same thoughts, and perhaps even the same words, in which I remember having spoken in the Church, so that, when you read it, you may easily recognize my speech, whatever it may be.

[Note: The first of these is about the paralytic; it is counted as the eleventh, together with the three that follow. Thus the earlier Paschal sermons number ten.]

Moreover, you have reported that I formerly spoke before you on four shorter treatises from various Gospel passages, and a fifth on the martyrs of the Maccabees. Since you compel me, I shall send them back to you corrected, so that, if you judge them worthy of any useful remembrance, you may have them transcribed together in the latter part of this little booklet.

[Note: The Florentine codex reads schidae; both Vatican codices read schedae. Jerome, Epitaph on Nepotian: “Our Nepotian tramples gold and pursues little sheets.” And in the Preface to Job: “May the poor permit me and mine to have little sheets, and not books so handsome as they are corrected.” Scheda and schedium are discussed by Barthius, Adversaria XII.18, where he also cites this passage of Gaudentius.]

As for those treatises which, as I have learned, certain idle enthusiasts presumed to collect after having been secretly assigned stenographers, interrupting them and leaving them incomplete,

[Note: “With stenographers secretly placed there.” In former times hearers wrote down, secretly and openly, the sermons of speakers. A notable passage occurs in Gregory Nazianzen, Oration to the 150 Bishops, translated by J. Billius: “Farewell, lovers of my sermons, and of the courses and gatherings, and of the pens both conspicuous and hidden.” There, “conspicuous and hidden pens” signifies nothing other than stenographers, who, whether placed secretly or openly, rapidly recorded in writing what Nazianzen said, as Ferrarius rightly judges, Book II, On the Rites of the Sacred Church, Council 28. I should note in passing that Birkeimer badly understood the passage of Nazianzen. Where the Greek has καὶ γραφίδες φανεραὶ, καὶ λανθάνουσαι, “both conspicuous and hidden pens,” he translated “and also manifest and hidden slanderers,” an inept rendering that undermined Gregory’s entire meaning. See what we said above about the exceptors in the Preface to Gaudentius, no. 5. Many treatises of Gaudentius were recorded by stenographers, as their titles below will show. After sermons had been taken down, the preachers themselves usually received them from the stenographers and corrected them with greater care and diligence, as is clear from Gaudentius himself and from Gregory the Great. When sending his homilies on Ezekiel to Bishop Marianus, Gregory writes: “The homilies which, as I spoke before the people, were recorded on the blessed prophet Ezekiel I had left aside, overwhelmed by many cares. But after eight years, at the brothers’ request, I tried to seek out the stenographers’ sheets and, going through them, corrected them, with the Lord’s favor, insofar as the pressure of my tribulations allowed. Gaudentius himself said a little above: ‘Moreover, I shall send you four shorter treatises, which you reported that I formerly spoke before you on various Gospel passages, and a fifth on the martyrs of the Maccabees, corrected, since you compel me.’ The title indicates that the treatises of Gaudentius which follow the Paschal sermons were recorded by stenographers: “Here begin the recorded treatises on various passages.” Yet sermons were not indiscriminately or universally recorded, but only those of speakers who excelled in delivery, as Ferrarius explains. On stenographers and their signs, see Lipsius’s letter to Leonard Lessius, First Century of Letters to the Belgians, letter 27.]

are none of my concern. They are no longer mine, since it is clear that they were written down in the hurried haste of the recorders.

[Note: The Florentine codex has quae constet, “which is established.” The manuscripts have concisa, “cut short.” This corresponds to what he said above, “interrupted and incomplete.” The codex of Octavius Pantagathus likewise reads esse concisa, “to have been cut short,” as it does in the preceding phrase quae constet.]

Nevertheless, I fear that under the title of my sermon errors hostile to the sound faith may be mixed in by others, and that those who were the authors of such reckless presumption may become liable to everlasting condemnation.

[Note: The Florentine codex, two Vatican codices, and the Paris and Cologne editions read this way. The Lyon edition omits mei, “of my.”]

Therefore, since I could not refuse the service you requested, I shall first briefly show you that the wounds of illness are not always inflicted upon our bodies in proportion to the accumulation of our sins.

The nature of the human body, from the time it received the sentence of mortality—“You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis III)—is subject to various infirmities, without distinction of persons. And although we rightly confess that we are sinners, the qualities of our merits are not thereby to be weighed according to the vigor or weakness of the flesh, since idol-worshipers frequently enjoy bodily health and the good things of this age, while, on the contrary, those devoted to divine worship are shaken by the affliction of illnesses and tribulations.

For we read that the Gentile Abimelech reigned (Genesis XX), while holy Abraham endured the hardships of exile (Genesis XII); and that holy Jacob was a hired servant of that idolater Laban the Syrian (Genesis XXIX:30).

[Note: The Florentine manuscript reads ydolatrae, “of an idolater.” Baluzius observed long ago, in his notes on Salvian, page 237, that Latin codices almost always have idolatria and rarely idololatria. The codex of Pantagathus also has idolatrae here, confirming Baluzius’s observation. See below, Sermon 4, on “the paths of idolatry,” and Sermon 9, on “the Jewish people rejected because of the adultery of idolatry.”]

And that righteous Moses, while the impious Pharaoh reigned, hid in fear in the land of Midian (Exodus II, III); and that the extraordinary Elijah fled from the face of the persecuting queen Jezebel into the wilderness (III Kings XVIII, XIX).

But in the New Testament John, the greatest of the prophets, after the long squalor of a deadly imprisonment (Matthew XIV), after the unjust insults of chains (Mark VI), is beheaded in prison.

[Note: Thus read the Urbinate and both Vatican codices. The printed editions have decollatus, “beheaded,” as part of the text.]

And the sacrilegious Herod, who ordered him killed, reclines at table with his nobles, military commanders, and the leading men of Galilee,

[Note: The word primoribus, “leading men,” is absent from the manuscripts. Perhaps the scribes removed it, thinking it superfluous, since principibus, “nobles,” had already been used. Yet the Gospel text, Mark VI:21, mentions both “nobles” and “leading men”: “Herod made a supper on his birthday for his nobles, military commanders, and the leading men of Galilee.” The Greek reads: Ἡρώδης τοῖς γενεσίοις αὐτοῦ δεῖπνον ἐποίει τοῖς μεγιστᾶσιν αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοῖς χιλιάρχοις, καὶ τοῖς πρώτοις τῆς Γαλιλαίας, “Herod made a supper on his birthday for his great men, and the commanders of thousands, and the leading men of Galilee.”]

drunk not only with wine but also with the Baptist’s own blood.

And as it is written in the Apocalypse concerning Babylon—whether the city, the nation, or each individual soul confused by the darkness of errors and the mingling of carnal vices (for Babylon is interpreted as “confusion”)—“I saw a woman drunk with the blood of the saints” (Revelation XVII).

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts read. Babylon is absent from the printed editions. See Jerome, On the Interpretation of Hebrew Names.]

But the Savior himself teaches in the Gospel where this patience of God will lead, saying:

[Note: The words “in the Gospel, saying,” are absent from the Vatican and Florentine codices, which read “the Savior teaches in the Gospel.” The codex of Octavius Pantagathus has “the Savior himself teaches.”]

[Note: There is much debate among commentators whether this narrative is history or a parable. Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Ambrose hold that it is history; John Chrysostom, Cyril, Theophylact, and Bede, that it is a parable. It is not clear from this passage what Gaudentius thought.]

“There was a certain rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. But a certain poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate, full of sores,

[Note: The manuscripts have “desiring to be filled,” a reading also supported by the Vulgate.]

and desired to be filled with what fell from the rich man’s table.

[Note: All the printed editions read this way. The manuscripts add “and no one gave him anything,” which the scribes may have inserted from the Vulgate. The Greek copies read: καὶ ἐπιθυμῶν χορτασθῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων τῶν πιπτόντων ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης τοῦ πλουσίου· ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ κύνες ἐρχόμενοι, “and desiring to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table; but even the dogs, coming…” This reading is supported by the most ancient manuscript Gospel codex of the monastery of Saint Julia in the city of Brescia, written in large gold and silver letters on purple parchment, which is preserved as a precious antiquarian κειμήλιον, “relic,” among the nuns of that convent. Isidore Clarius, Brescian bishop of Foligno, translated it in the same way. Capreolus, Book V of the History of Brescia, page 27, also records that in the monastery of Saint Julia at Brescia there are preserved very ancient codices dyed in pure green and blue colors, written in gold and silver.]

But dogs also came and licked his sores. It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man died and was placed in the punishment of hell.

[Note: This reading is found in the Florentine codex and in the Paris, Cologne, and Lyon editions. The Vatican and Urbinate manuscripts have “in the bosom of hell.” The Greek copies read: ἀπέθανε δὲ καὶ ὁ πλούσιος, καὶ ἐτάφη. Καὶ ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ, “But the rich man also died and was buried. And in hell, lifting up his eyes…” The Brescia Gospel codex of the monastery of Saint Julia, mentioned above, and the translation of Isidore Clarius agree with this. This mode of punctuation, which is present in the Greek text and is more consonant with the apostolic doctrine of Christ’s descent into hell, is observed and defended by the learned author of On the Moderation of Minds against John Phereponus, Book III, chapter 9, page 412, Venetian edition.]

And he begged that the tongue of that poor man, moistened in water,

[Note: The manuscript codices have “in water.” In what follows, Gaudentius did not follow the text κατὰ πόδα, “word for word,” but rather expressed its sense.]

might be cooled by his finger, but, placed amid the torments of an unquenchable flame, he could not obtain this.

[Note: In the manuscripts, the words “for this punishment, and shortly afterward, ‘and on the other hand,’” are absent.]

Prosperity is reserved for the wicked for this punishment; and, conversely, the tribulation of the righteous is led to that blessedness, so that those who have endured the narrownesses of this life with faithful patience and departed from this age may deserve to rest with the holy patriarch Abraham in eternal life.

Therefore the Lord said: “Enter through the narrow gate, because wide and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it” (Matthew VII). “How narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Luke XIII).

For this reason the holy Apostle also declares that he glories in his infirmities: “For when I am weak,” he says, “then I am strong” (II Corinthians XII).

The same most blessed Apostle Paul also testified that holy Timothy suffered from continual illnesses, writing to him: “Do not continue drinking water, but use a little wine, because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (I Timothy V).

[Note: Two Vatican codices and the Urbinate have noli adhuc, “do not continue”; the Vulgate also supports this reading.]

Perhaps some rich person might ask, saying: “Then did God give riches maliciously, if he torments the rich man because of them?”

[Note: This has been restored from four manuscript codices. The printed editions read si propterea, “if therefore.”]

He wishes human error to appear to sin not only with pardon but even with reason.

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate codices have “already with reason.” This elegant saying of Gaudentius is aptly quoted by the celebrated orator of our own time at the beginning of the second of his sermons published at the end of Ludovico Antonio Muratori’s learned Polyhistor, On Christian Charity, Modena, 1723.]

Not maliciously but providentially God made you rich, so that through works of mercy you might find medicine for the wounds of your sins.

“For almsgiving delivers from death, and it cleanses from every sin” (Tobit XII).

He is not tormented because he was rich, but because, while he himself feasted, the poor Lazarus was hungry.

Moreover, holy Abraham himself had been rich, but he was the servant of travelers and of the needy, giving much.

[Note: This passage seems to me suspect. The Florentine codex reads: “And he distributes much property of the needy.” The Urbinate and two Vatican codices have: “And he distributes very much property of the needy.” I do not wish to investigate these readings further, since I see nothing underlying them. In the margin of the Pantagathus codex, in Pantagathus’s own hand, is written: “of the needy with great generosity.”]

Holy Job also held the kingdom of Arabia; but, as it is written, no widow and no poor person left his house with an empty lap.

[Note: Gaudentius’s passage was cited by Pineda in support of those who believe that Job was a king. The Septuagint and nearly all the Greeks are numbered among them, and Gaudentius may perhaps have followed their authority. As for the region, Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel IX.4, cites Aristaeus, who wrote in a Jewish history that Job lived on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia. The most ancient appendix added to the Book of Job at the end of the Septuagint version agrees, saying that he lived in Ausitis, on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia. See Grotius’s notes on Sulpicius Severus, page 65. I was surprised that the distinguished commentator on Job asserted that the land of Uz was situated in Arabia by Pliny and Ptolemy; for Ptolemy indeed mentions the Ausitae as inhabitants of Arabia Deserta, a point long ago noted by the learned Bochart, Phaleg II.8 and IV.9, and by Spanheim, History of Job, chapter 3. They are thought to have descended from Uz, son of Nahor, mentioned in Genesis XXII:21. But Pliny is entirely silent about this region.]

Finally, when he was afflicted by sufferings, the works of mercy that he had exercised to no purpose were reproached to him through the woman: “And behold,” she said, “what you suffer” (Job II).

[Note: These words are absent from the Vulgate and the Septuagint. Perhaps it is a fragment from the ancient Old Latin version, of which only a few shreds now remain to us.]

Oh, the poisonous cunning of the dreadful serpent! Since he could not turn God’s servant away from good works, he endeavored to make him lose the fruit of his piety through regret for having done good.

Let unfruitful rich men therefore beware of the terrible example of that merciless Rich Man, their companion, lest they be led to similar torments. Rather, let them give alms generously, frequently, and gladly. “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Corinthians IX).

Let them distribute their wealth to the needy and acquire treasures for themselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth corrupts and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew VI), so that, when they depart from this age, they may find refreshment in the bosom of that truly rich Abraham.

This brief answer to the question that had arisen should be sufficient. But I mentioned the matters discussed above so that none of us may be scandalized in his thoughts, and none of us dare murmur against God if we see the unjust, idolaters, and blasphemers enjoy continual bodily health, flourish in worldly honors, and overflow with transient riches, while, on the contrary, we are worn down by various tribulations, afflicted by bodily pains, and subjected to the necessities of poverty.

[Note: Four manuscripts supply this phrase unanimously. The printed editions formerly read “none of us murmur”; the rest had fallen out through the carelessness of scribes.]

[Note: The manuscripts also agree in this reading. The printed editions had “with the health of their body.”]

God, the ruler of all, knows by what providence he chastises his own and for what reason he spares the wicked in this world.

Nor are we entirely ignorant, having been instructed by the most blessed Apostle, that God’s long goodness toward the wicked either calls those who perceive it to conversion or reserves the ungrateful for a more just sentence of punishment: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s goodness invites you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will render to each according to his works” (Romans II).

[Note: The Lyon edition and the Vatican codices have “leads you to repentance,” a reading supported by the Vulgate. The Greek copies read εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει, “leads you to repentance,” or “draws and invites you to it.” In the Florentine codex and in the Cologne and Paris editions, “to patience” entered through a scribal error; the same mistake occurs in the Pantagathus manuscripts, but Pantagathus himself wrote poenitentiam, “repentance,” in the margin.]

That universal retribution is reserved for the day of judgment. In this age, however, some blasphemers or apostates are at times consumed by incurable torments, so that others may be frightened by their punishments.

As for worshipers of piety, when they are sometimes afflicted either by bodily pains or by various tribulations, three reasons are found: the first, correction; the second, purification; the third, testing.

[Note: The manuscripts read corporeis, “bodily.”]

[Note: John Cassian, Conference VI.11, carefully discusses these three kinds of temptation in the same sense; he seems to have taken this division from Gaudentius’s passage. The Vatican codices have written in the margin: “Much is missing here.” This is not entirely improbable, although he immediately takes up the several parts of the division. The reader should weigh the matter. Yet, after these words had already been printed, the codex of Octavius Pantagathus removed all doubt from me; in it the passage is written in continuous order so that no suspicion of a lacuna remains.]

If God sees a person adhering to the apostolic faith frequently committing certain sins, he chastises that sinner of his in order to correct him, so that he may bend him toward repentance by a salutary admonition; and he chastises the negligent lest, by delaying a tolerable punishment, he become liable to the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate codices have “if he sees a sinner.”]

He also chastises the person who lives chastely and justly but has nevertheless been sprinkled with certain stains of evil thoughts, now by the scourge of tribulations and illnesses, so that the future fire may find no filth in him, but so that, cleansed of every stain through small wounds of the briefest duration, he may deserve to pass more securely into eternal rest.

This is the loving God’s prudent care and compassionate severity toward his sinners. For it is written: “Whom God loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII).

[Note: The Florentine and two Vatican codices have “whom the Lord loves”; they nearly always read this wherever “God” occurs.]

Hence each of us rightly proclaims God merciful, taught by the Prophet’s eloquence: “The Lord has chastised me severely, but he has not handed me over to death” (Psalm CXVII).

[Note: The reading ductus eloquio, “led by eloquence,” is strongly favored by both Vatican codices and is also found in the Pantagathus codex; Pantagathus himself, however, wrote doctus, “taught,” in the margin.]

But as for the righteous and blameless—such as holy Job, of whom it is written (Job I) that he was a blameless man and a true worshiper of God—Almighty God permits them to be tested for this reason by the loss of possessions, the bereavement of loved ones, the straits of persecution, or the goads of bodily pains.

He tests them not for his own sake, since he knows all things before they happen, but for the sake of angels and human beings, so that they may recognize them as righteous from their deeds, since they cannot look into consciences, which God alone knows, he who searches hearts and reins. For he knows the hidden things of the heart, as the Prophet’s word testifies (Psalm VII).

And therefore perhaps the blessed Apostle, placed amid the snares of many tribulations and persecutions, said: “We have become a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings” (I Corinthians IV).

God wishes his righteous to be tested before the angels so that the blessed angels may recognize the perfected righteousness of the saints with joy. For the blessed angels in heaven rejoice, as the Lord Jesus says, even over one sinner who repents (Luke XV).

But he wishes the perfection of the righteous to be proved before human beings,
so that they may be provoked by their example to persevere in their love of God. God also wishes to thrust the proven righteousness of the saints upon the Devil, so that he may grieve that they have duly advanced, through the merits of good works, into friendship with God and into the kingdom of heaven from which he fell [Note: Thus read the Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts; their reading seemed preferable to that found in the printed editions: “so that, from the merits of good works,” although this reading too is not altogether bad. Moreover, the Pantagathus manuscript reads as here, “so that he may grieve that they have advanced through the merits of good works,” and likewise below, “he may grieve that they have advanced.”] [Note: Thus the Urbinas manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts, from whose agreement we restore this passage to its genuine reading. Florentine manuscript: “have arrived” (*pervectos*). Printed editions: “have been perfected” (*perfectos*), quite wrongly. In those three manuscripts one also reads “from which he himself fell away” (*unde ipse excidit*) for “from which he himself fell” (*unde ipse cecidit*).]—may grieve, be indignant, envy, and groan, yet nevertheless dare not bring any charge against the divine judgment. [Note: In the Urbinas manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts: “for the sake of testing.”]

Therefore, for the sake of testing, the remarkable Job (Job 1) suddenly becomes poor from being wealthy, is found without children from having been the father of ten children, wounded from being vigorous [Note: The words “and healthy” are not found in the manuscripts.] and sound, from being in the height of prosperity [Note: *Exarare* means “to cut up the earth with furrows,” and is sometimes transferred to the human body. Horace, *Epodes* 8:]
. . . . . . . . . . And old age furrows

the forehead with wrinkles.

That passage is paralleled by Virgil, *Aeneid* VII:

. . . And furrows the shameful forehead with wrinkles.

Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 12: “They saw him made poor from rich, deprived of children though the father of a fruitful family, covered with ulcers, furrowed with wounds from head to foot.” Victor of Vita, *The Vandal Persecution*, book I: “They tore apart the forehead on which Christ had fixed the standard of his cross, showing the sinews more wrinkled than furrowed, and bellowing.” The author of the *Life of Blessed Fulgentius*, chapter 11: “Again the mad hand of the torturer grows savage, and blessed Fulgentius is furrowed by countless lashes.”

He is seen furrowed by worms; from the most glorious condition he is found exposed to reproaches—reproaches both from friends who reproached him and, what was more grievous, from his own wife, who is said to have been preserved not to console his sorrows but for his final temptation. For she urged him to speak blasphemous words, repeating to him the works of his righteousness [Note: Four manuscripts read, “reproaching him with”] which he had performed in vain, since he had come to so many kinds of misery. Therefore, she said: “Say some word against the Lord, and die” (Job 2).

The crafty serpent, the devil, again suggested through the woman that the death deserved by the blasphemer should be sought as a remedy for his miseries, so that he might snatch the palm of patience from the strongest warrior and heap destruction upon the defeated; for the fury of blasphemy does not bring healing to sufferings but adds the torment of death—the death that neither grants an end to miseries nor is the beginning of the punishments that the avenging God has prepared for blasphemers.

But that most blessed man, recognizing that the devil, by the crafty argument of his ancient art, was again administering the poison of death through the woman, answered thus: “You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women” (ibid.), striking, evidently, one woman [Note: Namely, the woman, although the ancients also frequently used the plural for a single person. See the eminent Noris, *Dissertation 4 on the Cenotaph of Pisa*, chapter 3, and Étienne Baluze, in his notes on Lupus of Ferrières, letter 1. The manuscripts read, “of whom all.”]. And he added: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

And elsewhere: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, naked I shall return again to the earth. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1) [Note: The Urbinas and two Vatican manuscripts read: “Naked I came forth, he says, from the womb.”].

Amid the loss of all his possessions, amid the funerals of so many children, amid the most atrocious tortures of his own body, and the inward pains of conjugal reproach, the true worshiper of God praises and magnifies the almighty Lord. Therefore, if we too are worshipers of God [Note: Thus the manuscript copies read. The printed editions, less aptly, read: “worshipers of the Lord.”], let us imitate the triumphant patience which, though stripped of all possessions and children [Note: Baluze observed that *pignora* was used by Salvianus for children, although it was also common among the ancients. Quintilian, book VI, chapter 1: “Therefore that appeal to the judges through their dearest pledges, especially if the defendant has children, a wife, and parents, will be useful”; and shortly above: “Age, sex, and pledges also carry weight in these matters”—he is discussing the peroration—“I mean children, parents, and relatives.” Ovid, *Tristia* III.11:

> Because I am deprived of my country and of my pledges;

and likewise Claudian, *Against Eutropius* I.222:

> Why are you piling up these heaps of gold? What pledges  
> Will follow such great riches?

Augustine, Sermon 1 *On the Innocents*: “They are pledges not entrusted but created; not deposited but exposed.” Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book II, to Gratian, chapter 2: “Although exhausted by maternal longings, she endured the absence of her dearest pledges.” Gaudentius himself, *Treatise on the Maccabean Martyrs*: “He endured as many martyrdoms as the pledges he consecrated”; and shortly afterward: “An eighth also was added to the number, to meet with her dear pledges on the eighth day of Christ’s Resurrection.” See also Alberico Gentili, *On Marriage*, book II, chapter 3, and Bernegger’s notes on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 21.]—and even of the flesh of his own body—possesses an unshaken faith. [Note: The manuscripts read: “possesses. For the true worshiper of God.” The rest is lacking also in the book of Pantagathus, as are likewise the words that follow shortly: “in every time of distress.”]

For that man is truly a worshiper of God whose faith does not fail amid adversity, whose tongue does not cease to bless the name of his Lord in every time of distress and in every blow of tribulation, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth” (Psalm 33) [Note: These words too were removed by the scribes from the manuscripts].

If you are a sinner, recognize that what you suffer is for your correction, or at least for your purification, as I explained above. But if you are righteous, you will not dare presume upon the name of “righteous”; nevertheless, you will understand that what you suffer occurs as a test of your glory. For it is written: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 27).

Therefore the holy Apostle also says: “Tribulation produces endurance, endurance character, character hope, and hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5). Since, then, various torments are inflicted in this age either for the testing of the righteous, for the correction of sinners, or for the punishment of sacrilegious persons—and since these blows are deadly for some but beneficial for others—the Book of Psalms accordingly writes with the greatest distinction concerning the obstinately wicked: “The death of sinners is most evil, and those who hate the righteous shall err” (Psalm 33). It plainly testifies to the most evil death of those sinners who, desiring to remain in the crime of their offenses, hate the righteous man who strikes them [Note: The word “sinners” is absent from the Lyon edition].

But concerning those who can be corrected: “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Psalm 31); concerning the saints: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Psalm 33).

It is not at all difficult for anyone spiritual to judge this difference from the fruits of each person [Note: Thus the printed editions and all the manuscripts read, except the Florence manuscript, which has *spiritali* only here; elsewhere it has *spirituali* and *spiritualis*. The Pantagathus manuscript has *spiritati* here and elsewhere, and *spiritalis*], since the Lord says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:20). For some of the wise men of this age, ignorant of heavenly wisdom, judge that everything among us is confused [Note: Christian religion was commonly called by the Gentiles a vain and mad superstition, and Christians were called fools, atheists, and worshipers of no deity; therefore Gaudentius says that the philosophers of the Gentiles judge everything among us confused. The matter is well known and frequently treated by writers who would not allow the Christian name to suffer under the odium of that most foolish calumny. See Tertullian, *Apology*; Minucius, *Octavius*; Justin, both *Apologies*; Lactantius, book V, chapters 14, 15, and 18. Philosophers were especially hostile to Christians in Justin, *Apology* I.], whereas the spiritual person discerns and judges all things, as the Apostle says, while he himself is judged by no one (1 Corinthians 2).

For certain men wise according to the age, ignorant of heavenly wisdom, wishing to assert that everything which God, the creator of all things, providentially governs with just moderation is accidental [Note: This is the true reading, supplied by the Florence manuscript, on whose authority we corrected this passage. The Urbinas and two Vatican manuscripts read *fortuita adstruere*, with a fourth letter added after the first; the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus reads *fortuita astruere*. Thus the agreement of the other manuscripts besides the Florence one establishes the true reading. The printed editions corruptly read *fortunae adstruere universa*.], speak as follows [Note: The Epicurean position is refuted by Seneca throughout *On Providence*. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.23, citing that work, aptly says: “If anyone wishes to know more fully why God allows wicked and unjust people to become powerful, blessed, and rich, while allowing the devout to be humble, miserable, and poor, let him take up Seneca’s book entitled *Why Many Misfortunes Befall Good Men, Though Providence Exists*. In it he expresses many things not with merely worldly incompetence but wisely and almost divinely. See Lipsius, *Physiology*, book I, dissertation 16. Elmenhorst indicates this passage of Gaudentius against atheists in his notes on Minucius Felix, page 42.]:

“If this world were governed by God’s providence, good and bad alike would never be indiscriminately overwhelmed by blows of tribulations, pains, miseries, and illnesses, because it would not accord with divine equity to inflict similar blows upon people of unequal merit.”

But the hostility aroused by this problem [Note: Among philosophers, *problems* properly means investigations and conjectures concerning hidden matters, by which the more remote secrets of nature are explored more by a certain acuteness of mind than by certain inquiry; such examples are found in Aristotle and Plutarch. In Judges 14 the term *problem* is used for the riddle Samson proposed at the feast of the Philistines.] is easily dispelled by the familiar example of truth [Note: Four manuscripts read *facillime evacuatur*; the Florence and Urbinas manuscripts read *visitato*, as does the book of Octavius Pantagathus, but in his own hand *usitato* was written in the page margin].

It is known to everyone that the edge of iron and the burning of fire are inflicted either for destruction, when the nature of the crime being punished demands a penalty, or for healing, when they are medicinally applied for the sake of curing. In the same way, almighty God adjusts the same kinds of blows according to the character of people’s merits: punishing some, correcting others from their vices, cleansing others, or certainly advancing them to greater glory.

So that this may be understood still more clearly, I shall add a few testimonies from the holy Scriptures. We read: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of desolation” (Psalm 120). And elsewhere: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those who have been shaken out” (Psalm 126).

He calls the blessed Apostles the children of those who have been shaken out [Note: We have added these words on the authority of the best Urbinas and Florence manuscripts, where they were lacking in the printed editions, to no small detriment of the passage. The book of Octavius Pantagathus also has them; but in two Vatican manuscripts the order is slightly changed: “He proclaims the blessed Apostles to be the children of those who have been shaken out.” Augustine likewise understands the Apostles as the children of those who have been shaken out in his exposition of Psalm 126.], those whom the hand of the almighty Lord Jesus, chosen for faith after their fathers had been shaken far away from God’s grace on account of their unbelief, directed [Note: Thus the manuscripts agree unanimously. The printed editions read: “directed.”] swiftly through the whole world like flying arrows, so that their preaching, in accordance with the teaching of the most blessed Paul, might become for some “the fragrance of death unto death,” but for others “the fragrance of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2).

For the doctrine of truth gives life to the obedient and kills the rebellious; it overthrows vices and raises up virtues; it casts down unbelievers and exalts the faithful. For Christ Jesus, whom the Apostles preach, as the holy Simeon says in the Gospel, “has been appointed for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke 2) [Note: The Florence and two Vatican manuscripts read: “and for the resurrection.”].

But so that you may know that the Apostles—who, having received their name from their office, are called in Latin *destinati*, “those who have been sent” [Note: That is, “sent”; for *destinare* means to send messengers, as in Suetonius, *Galba*, chapter 16: “Immediately they sent a delegation to the praetorians with instructions.” The Greek word *apostles* derives from ἀποστέλλω, “I send someone with instructions”; hence Gaudentius says that the Apostles received their name from their office. Gaudentius himself, *Treatise on the Dedication of a Basilica*: “An apostle is one who has been sent by God; for one who has been appointed is called an apostle.” Barthius cites both passages of Gaudentius, *Adversaria* XLIII.8. Concerning the name and office of an apostle, see also Casaubon, *Exercitation* 13 on Baronius, §4, where this passage of Gaudentius could also suitably have been mentioned. See also, if desired, Isidore, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 17.]—are the children of the Jews shaken out from God’s grace, listen to what Christ answered those blaspheming Jews:

“If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 11)—that is, the Apostles [Note: These words are not found in the manuscripts, but we judged that they had necessarily to be retained], chosen from your own lineage. And, in order to show more clearly of whom he was speaking, he added: “Therefore they themselves shall be your judges.” For elsewhere he says to the Apostles: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the resurrection, when the Son of Man comes in the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

“Like arrows, therefore,” he says, “in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those who have been shaken out” (Psalm 126). And immediately it is added: “Blessed is the one who shall fulfill his desire from them” [Note: The two printed editions read this way; the Urbinas manuscript reads: “who fulfilled.”] (ibid.) [Note: The Florence manuscript reads: “Immediately it says,” as does the book of Octavius Pantagathus, which shortly afterward reads: “Blessed is the one who shall fulfill.”].

Thus you may clearly understand that God’s arrows sometimes bring death and sometimes bestow blessedness, as they did for the holy and most blessed Job, who says: “For the arrows of the Lord are in my body, and their fury drinks my blood. When I begin to speak, they spur me on” (Job 6).

And shortly afterward: “If only the Lord would grant this, and my request would come, and the Lord would give me what I hope for; may the Lord who began it wound me, but not kill me forever.”

There are also many passages of this kind scattered throughout the whole body of the holy Scriptures, which, for the sake of brevity, I pass over without fear [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “I pass over safely”], since I am speaking to one who knows the Law, and who, instructed by a few testimonies, can easily gather similar examples. From these proofs you will more fully understand and see confirmed the goodness of God, who by provident chastisement either corrects his servants from sin or advances them to glory [Note: The Florence manuscript reads: “from which demonstrations [you may understand] the goodness”].

You will also recognize the true justice of that same Lord when he punishes obstinate sinners with deserved torments [Note: This passage suffered considerable corruption. The printed editions read: “and with the same deserved torments,” from which Gaudentius seemed absurdly to infer that God punishes the impious with torments deserved by the righteous. We therefore followed the testimony of four manuscripts and restored the true reading, which is also supported by the book of Octavius Pantagathus: “and punishing the obstinate impious with the deserved torments of that same Lord.”], as the blessed Apostle also teaches: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” (Romans 3)—namely, upon those who suppress the truth in unrighteousness.

Concerning our own chastisement, by which we are scourged by God, Scripture testifies as follows: “When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11) [Note: The manuscripts read: “so that we may not be condemned with this world,” a reading also found in the Vulgate. We have detected more than once that scribes altered their texts to conform to the Vulgate].

Concerning the righteous he speaks thus: “In everything we suffer tribulation, but we are not distressed; we are perplexed, but not abandoned; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but do not perish; always carrying in our body the death of our Lord Jesus, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be manifested in our body” (2 Corinthians 4).

And elsewhere the same blessed Apostle Paul, after saying that he had been caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, where he had heard unspeakable words [Note: The manuscripts read: “up to the third heaven”], immediately adds: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, so that I might not be exalted. For this I besought the Lord three times, that he might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12) [Note: The manuscripts read: “where he had heard”; the Florence and Urbinas manuscripts read: “where he heard”; the two Vatican manuscripts, “where he heard”].

Another Scripture, agreeing with this meaning, speaks still more clearly [Note: We restored this reading from four manuscripts. The printed editions read *evidentia*, “evidently”]: “As gold is tested in the fire,” it says, “so righteous people are tested in the furnace of humiliation” (Ecclesiasticus 2) [Note: The Florence manuscript seems to preserve the true reading: “For in fire”]. [Note: Relying on the authority of four manuscripts, which read thus with remarkable agreement, we removed the blemish inflicted on this passage by scribal ignorance. The printed editions read *ut utique gustum*, altogether wrongly. The scribes had been deceived by the similarity of letters, taking *ae* for *g* and adding *u* of their own. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXII.15, vainly attempts to defend the corrupt reading *ut utique gustum* by collecting ancient examples. Our conjecture concerning the origin of the scribal error is strikingly confirmed by the old Basel edition of 1569, entitled *Monumenta Patrum Orthodographa*, in which our Gaudentius first appeared; it reads *utique ut gustum*. This was already noted in the Italian *Ephemerides of the Learned*, vol. XXXVI, p. 38. The manuscript once owned by Octavius Pantagathus here reads *actum* for *aestum*, changing *e* into *c* and omitting *s*; this was easy for scribes writing hastily and, in part, from the similarity of the letters. To conceal nothing, the letter *r* is written above the line in that manuscript, so that it reads *utique ut arctum perpessi tentationum*. Although this correction differs greatly from the true reading, it nevertheless commends the writer’s diligence.]

They are to endure the heat of temptations and, bowed down beneath the burden of tribulations, are not to be raised into pride by the merits of their righteousness, murmuring that they suffer something unjust in opposition to the dignity of their deeds. Not long afterward, however, the repayment of an immortal reward will follow them. Rather, remaining in voluntary humility, they will become more approved in Christ, being endowed with holy virtues and humble in heart [Note: We have published the manuscript reading. Other editions have “holy”—that is, “endowed with virtues and humble in heart”—“more approved.”].

So too were the venerable martyrs, who, faithfully trusting with the blessed Apostle that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory that shall be revealed” in the saints (Romans 8), accepted with the greatest equanimity every punishment and all the torments inflicted upon their bodies for the name of the Lord Christ [Note: Four manuscripts read: “for the name of God Christ”; this reading also occurs in the book of Pantagathus]. They were to have as the rewarder of their victorious patience the very Son of God, who will bestow the kingdom of heaven upon his servants faithful to him unto the end.

His eternal power and divinity, with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, remains throughout all ages.

## TRACTATES OR SERMONS BEGIN

## SERMON I. THE FIRST SERMON ON THE READING FROM EXODUS

### On the Night of the Vigil

[Note: On the night of the vigils, the author of the sermon *To Catechumens against the Jews* (among works ascribed to Augustine, Benedictine edition, vol. VIII, appendix) says: “The nature of this great assembly and of the night you have passed requires us to explain it to you, and to demonstrate the true and eternal salvation received in so great a sacrament on this day. For if, beloved, we consider the works of darkness during the night now past and wish, with the Lord’s help, to explain what we have done, we shall find that in the night we performed not works of night but works of day.” It was customary for Christians to keep vigil through the night of Pascha, which Gaudentius calls, by antonomasia, the night of the vigils. Thus Tertullian, *To His Wife* II.4, says: “Who will willingly endure his wife’s being taken from his side for nocturnal assemblies, should occasion require it? Who, finally, will calmly put up with her spending the night at the solemnities of Pascha?” Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew* IV, on chapter 25, Benedictine edition, vol. IV, p. 120, gives the reason for this solemn all-night vigil: “It is a Jewish tradition that Christ will come at midnight, in likeness of the Egyptian time when Pascha was celebrated, the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the dwellings, and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated by the blood of the lamb. Hence, I think, the apostolic tradition has remained that on the vigil-day of Pascha the people may not be dismissed before midnight, while they await Christ’s coming; and after that time has passed, they may confidently celebrate the feast-day.” Likewise Lactantius, book VII, chapter 19: “This is the night which we celebrate by keeping vigil because of the coming of our King and God. There is a twofold reason for this night: on it he both received life when he suffered, and later he will receive the kingdom of the world.” Ado of Vienne likewise calls it the night of the vigils in his *Chronicle*: “Despair having been put away, he returned to the Church and, there, on the vigil-night of holy Pascha, conceived the Rogations in his mind.” Alcimus Avitus, on the first institution of the feast of Rogations: “These things were prolonged amid public fears and private rumors until the approaching night of the solemn vigils, on which annual custom required the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection to be celebrated.” See Lindenbrog, *Observations on Marcellinus*, p. 545.]

[Note: In Galeardus’s edition the title is: “The First Treatise on Exodus Begins, on the Night of the Vigils, Concerning the Observance of Easter”; this note is appended to it. The Florence manuscript bears this title: “The First Treatise on Exodus Begins, on the Night of the Vigils, Concerning the Observance of Pascha,” with which the manuscript book of Octavius Pantagathus agrees, although it has *Paschae* rather than *pascae*. The Urbinas manuscript reads: “The First Treatise on Exodus, on the Night of the Vigils, Concerning the Observance of Pascha, Begins.” Three editions have: “The First Treatise of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, on Exodus, on the Night of the Vigils, Concerning the Observance of Pascha.” It is remarkable how much license scribes took in corrupting and confusing such titles. The ancients regularly used the formal words *Incipit* and *Explicit* to mark the beginning and end of each work, as the very learned Baluze observed, among others, in his note on Salvianus, page 30. He also published Vincent of Lérins’s *Commonitorium*, on the authority of ancient copies, in this form: “The treatise of Peregrinus concerning the antiquity and universality of the catholic faith begins.” Thus, in the manuscripts that follow, our Florence manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts read: “The first ends; the second begins.” Since the same notation is made in the manuscripts for the first seven treatises on Exodus, I wished to mention it once here. But if anyone should prefer that such matters be omitted as trivial, let him know that, in Baluze’s words, we love even “rubbish and half-consumed stones” because of their antiquity; and let him also remember that we undertook to present the variant readings of the manuscript copies in their entirety and with the greatest diligence. The Fathers of old called addresses to the people and sacred sermons *tractatus* and *tractare*. See Ferrarius, *On the Rites of the Sacred Ecclesiastical Assembly*, book I, chapter 2, where he repeatedly cites Gaudentius.]

### On the Observance of Pascha

[Note: The ancients commonly declined the name *Pascha* in this way; examples are readily available to anyone. *Paschatis* is now more common, as Vossius observed, *On Analogy*, book I, chapter 20. It is a third-declension form, like *aenigma*, *dogma*, and other verbal nouns borrowed from Greek, although τὸ πάσχα is derived not from Greek but from Hebrew—unless other evidence should prove otherwise, a notable passage of Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 2, On Holy Pascha*, certainly demonstrates it. In Jacobus Billius’s translation it reads:

> This Pascha—this, I say, the great and venerable *phaska*—is named by the Hebrews according to their language; the word means “passing over,” historically because of the flight and migration of the Israelites from Egypt into the land of Canaan, but spiritually because of our progression and ascent from these lower things to higher things and to the land of promise.

We have also observed that, in many passages of Scripture, certain names have been changed from a more obscure meaning to a clearer one and from a harsher sound to a more elegant and honorable one. The same thing, we notice, happened here. Some thought that this name referred to the saving Passion; then, adapting the word to the Greek language by changing φ into π and κ into χ, they called this day *Pascha*. The word was afterward established by custom and usage, with the multitude approving it by their vote as the more pious term. The Florence manuscript reads: “Concerning the observance of *pasce*.”]

At the proper time the Lord Jesus wished the most blessed festival of Pascha to be celebrated, after the autumn mist, after the harshness of winter, before the heat of summer. For it was fitting that Christ, the Sun of Justice, should dispel both the darkness of the Jews and the severity of the Gentiles, before the heat of the future judgment, by the gentle light of his Resurrection, and restore everything to the condition of its peaceful beginning—everything that had been confused by a gloomy veil under that prince of darkness.

For God created the world in the season of spring [Note: Gaudentius followed the consensus of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, who assign spring to the creation of the world. Ambrose is representative of them all; we may rightly call him Gaudentius’s father and teacher, *καὶ διδάσκαλον*. In *Hexameron* I.4 he says: “At this beginning of the months, therefore, he made heaven and earth, because the beginning of the world ought to have been taken from the place where spring’s temperate weather was suitable for all things.” And in *On the Mystery of Pascha*, chapter 2: “At this time—that is, in spring—the God who created visible and invisible things, suspending the structure of heaven with the earth fixed beneath it, illuminated the day with the sun’s heat, assigned the moon’s brightness as a solace for the night, and adorned the vaulted heaven with the ornament of shining stars.” This same opinion was also pleasing to the pagans, as is shown, among other evidence, by the famous verse published by Pithoeus:

> New spring, now tuneful spring: in spring the world was born;

provided that the correction of the poem presented by Lipsius, *Select Essays* I.5, is genuine. Those who favor autumn seek their reason in the ripening of crops; among them Joseph Scaliger holds a leading place, *On the Correction of the Calendar*, book V, whether from love of antiquity or of novelty, I do not know. Certainly in this matter he departed not only from the opinion of others but also from that of his own father. The Florence, Urbinas, and two Vatican manuscripts read *veris temperie* (“in the temperate season of spring”) instead of *veris tempore* (“in the season of spring”); the Pantagathus manuscript agrees with them and in the following passage also reads *verax utique* (“truly”).].

For in the month of March God said through Moses: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it is the first among the months of the year” (Exodus 12). Truly, God would not call that month the first unless it were first [Note: He is covertly criticizing the opinion of the rabbis, who placed the beginning of the civil year at the new moon of the month of Tishri, near the autumnal equinox, and thus began the year not with the month of Nisan, corresponding to our March, but with the seventh month, after the crops had been gathered. Riccioli refutes them at length, *Reformed Chronology* I.1, arguing that this is a recent rabbinic invention motivated by hatred of the Paschal month in which Christ suffered. I fear, however, that he cannot adequately defend his opinion, since the view that the ancient Hebrews had two years—one natural and one sacred—which began at different times, has long prevailed among almost everyone on solid evidence. See Sigonius, *On the Hebrew Republic* III.1 and 9, and Buxtorf, *Jewish Synagogue*, chapter 17.], just as he would not call the seventh day the sabbath unless it were the first day belonging to the Lord.

Therefore the Son of God, through whom all things were made (John 1), on the same day and at the same time, revives the fallen world by his own Resurrection, at the time when he had first created it from nothing, so that everything in heaven and on earth might be restored in Christ (Ephesians 1:10) [Note: The Florence manuscript reads: “and the things that are on earth.” The two Vatican manuscripts read: “and the things that exist in heaven, and the things that are on earth.” In the Pantagathus manuscript, the earlier phrase *quo eum prius* (“when he had first”) was incorrectly written *quo enim prius*, but it was corrected in Pantagathus’s own hand to *quo etiam prius*.].

For, as the Apostle says, “from him, through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (Romans 11:36).

Nor should any of us be disturbed if the calculation of the moon and the Lord’s day sometimes compels us to celebrate Pascha in the second month, that is, in April. In the divine Scriptures, days are counted according to the course of the moon. But the Gentiles established the Calends, Ides, Nones, and the names of months and days [Note: Macrobius, book I, chapters 12 and 15; Johannes Rosinus, book IV of *Roman Antiquities*, chapter 7; Hadrianus Junius, *On Years and Months*.], as, for example, [incomplete fragment] “whom the antiquity of human memory held to be the first month,” the pagan [Note: The familiar passage is Ovid, *Fasti* III:

> From you we derive the beginning of the Roman year;  
> Let the first month proceed from your ancestral name.].

Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, Book XVIII, chapter 5: “The Gentiles assigned the names of their gods to these days, whose number of seven returns in a cycle, and also to the months; for, out of regard for Romulus, since they believed him to be the son of Mars, they dedicated the first month to Mars and called it March.”

Thus they named this month March after Mars; and the Sabbath-day, which the rational hearts observed as the seventh day, that man decreed should be called Saturn’s day.

[Barthius, *Adversus*, book XVIII, chapter 1, on this passage of Gaudentius: “He calls the Jews rational because the Gentiles wandered about the world like brute animals without the true light.”]

[From this Faustus slanderously alleged that Saturnian chains had been imposed upon Christians. Augustine refutes him thus in Book XVIII *Against Faustus*, chapter 5: “Nor does your insult frighten us, because you call the rest of the Sabbaths Saturnian chains. It is empty and foolish; nor would it have occurred to you to say this, unless because you worship the sun on the day which they call the Sun’s day. But just as we call that same day the Lord’s day because we venerate on it not this sun but the Lord’s Resurrection, so the fathers observed the Sabbath rest without venerating Saturn, when it was right that it should be so observed.”]

The sacred Scriptures, however, whenever they either report or prescribe anything concerning times, speak in this way:

[Two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate read: “On the tenth day of the seventh month, that is, on the tenth day of the lunar month.” The Florentine reads: “On the tenth day of the second month, that is, on the tenth day of the lunar month,” which agrees with the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus. Accordingly, since the conjunction has been removed from the printed text, it seems that the passage should be read throughout as follows: “On the tenth day of the second month, that is, on the tenth day of the lunar month.”]

“On the tenth day of the second month, and on the tenth day of the lunar month; or on the fifth day of the seventh month; or on the twentieth day of the ninth month; or on the fourteenth day of the first month,” as we have likewise just heard in the Book of Exodus (Exod. 12; Lev. 23). There the observance of Passover is described, and it is commanded that unleavened bread be eaten for seven days of that same festival.

[The Urbinate manuscript reads: “They are purified.” It has: “He commanded.”]

God nevertheless also commands this: if anyone in the first month—whether unclean in soul, that is, defiled by contact with a dead person, or situated on a distant journey outside the chosen place of sacrifice at Jerusalem—

[The Florentine manuscript reads: “at the sacrifices in Jerusalem.” The Urbinate: “at the sacrifices of Jerusalem.” The two Vatican manuscripts place “Jerusalem” after “the place.” Many more recent scholars maintain that this place designated for sacrifices at Jerusalem was the Temple, so that Passover could not be celebrated outside it. Gaudentius plainly disagrees with them in the following tractate, where he says of the paschal lamb: “For they were killed individually by households.” See our observations on that passage.]

—could not celebrate Passover, let him celebrate it in the second month.

[In the Jewish calendar, on the fourteenth day of the month Iyar, or April: the second Passover was to be celebrated by those who had not been permitted, or had been unable, to celebrate Passover in the first month. See Num. 9.]

For God foresaw that the peoples of the Gentiles, still unclean through images of dead human beings and situated far away outside the holy place of the Church, were in fact we who had been far away and had been brought near through the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13). He grants permission that, if the Sunday and the appropriate lunar number do not coincide for us in the first month, we should celebrate in the second month.

[We have added the conjunction, which is found in the manuscript copies but absent from the printed editions. This same discipline concerning the time of celebrating Passover is also recognized by Philastrius, chapter 58.
