Rebuking the Quartodecimans, who asserted that Passover must always be celebrated in March, and who, by doing so, failed to observe the Sunday of Passover but celebrated it on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day, he adds: “Because of this error they do not recognize the true and saving day of the Passover of our Lord, the one day appointed and confirmed by the Lord for the whole world, according to the numerical course of the moon, the months, and the intercalations; and because they do not calculate these things, they do not know what they are celebrating.” Consult, if desired, Fabricius’s notes on this passage of Philastrius.]

And therefore we can celebrate neither before the fourteenth lunar day nor beyond the twenty-first, because there are only seven days of the paschal unleavened bread, during which we seek the Lord’s day. For Christ, the promulgator of the Law and of grace, wills us neither to pass over the appointed days reckoned according to the course of the moon nor to pass beyond, through thankless neglect, the day of his Resurrection.

[Feuardentius quotes this passage of Gaudentius in his notes on Irenaeus, Book V *Against Heresies*, chapter 23, at these words: “On that day the Lord endured death, obedient to the Father, on which Adam, disobedient to God, died. On the day on which he died, on that same day he also ate. For God said: ‘On the day on which you eat from it, you shall die.’ Thus, recapitulating this day in himself, the Lord came to his Passion on the day before the Sabbath, which is the sixth day of creation, on which man was formed, granting through his Passion the second formation, the one that comes from death.” From this passage of Irenaeus one may infer that Adam ate and died on Friday, though Gaudentius does not say this; he says only that on the Friday on which God made man, God suffered for man. Eutychius, Patriarch of Alexandria, likewise asserts in volume I of his *Annals*, p. 15, that on Friday—that is, on the day of Venus—at the ninth hour Adam and Eve rebelled and were expelled from paradise.]

For on the Friday on which he had made man, he suffered for man; and on the Sunday, which in the Scriptures is called the first day of the Sabbath-week (Matt. 8; Gen. 1), on which the world had received its beginning, he rose again. Thus, as on the first day he created heaven and earth—and afterward, in making man, fashioned him from them—so on the first day he might also restore the whole human race, for whose sake he had made the world.

This is what I have briefly said about the reckoning of Passover. But now it is time for us to explain the power of the things we heard in the Book of Exodus.

[The Florentine manuscript reads *disseramus*, as does the book of Pantagathus. There is no reason to alter the common reading. *Edisserere* means “to explain” or “to clarify.” Cicero, *On the Orator*: “Who is more subtle in teaching and explaining?” But *dissero* is also used with the same meaning. Jerome, Letter to Asella: “I have often explained the divine books, as I was able.”]

Let us first consider what Exodus is. Exodus is called a departure. The departure was from the captivity of Pharaoh and of the Egyptians, the people who were then Israel, not our people.

[The particle is absent from the manuscripts. Those who hurry frequently pay no attention to such little words, as we have already detected three times on a single page.]

[The two Vatican manuscripts read: “now ours.” This is an error (*σφάλμα*, a slip), as the words immediately added by Gaudentius show. The book of Pantagathus has: “not ours.”]

Why, then, is it read to you if it benefited only others? What is it to you if it was not for you? But now learn from the Apostle that the things written are more universally for you than for them. “The Law,” he says, “was a shadow of the good things to come” (Heb. 10)—of those good things, to be sure, which have been fulfilled in us.

For when Christ, the Truth, came, he granted us in reality the good things that he had previously given to the Jews in shadow, when he said to the disciples: “Amen, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see the things that you see, and did not see them, and to hear the things that you hear, and did not hear them. But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear” (Matt. 13).

Thus Exodus is blessedly and perfectly completed in us when the true Moses, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God by nature, not by appointment,

[So also in the following sermon: “How God is one by nature and many by appointment.” Philastrius likewise, chapter 134: “What the image of God is by the nature of its property, and what it is by the grace of appointment”; and shortly afterwards: “the begotten image of the paternal and everlasting substance, properly so, not a servant created from nothing by appointment.” Gaspar Barthius, Book XVIII of *Adversus*, chapter 1: “To posit is opposed to truth, and denotes an imaginary supposition only. This usage is drawn from calculation, in which an imagined sum, once posited, produces a true one.” Petronius Arbiter: “If you reckon correctly, there is shipwreck everywhere.” Juvenal, *Satires* 9: “Let the calculation be set down; let boys be present with the tablet.” These are from Barthius. Nor is this an unusual Latin idiom: *pone eum esse victum*, “suppose him defeated,” for “imagine him defeated,” as in Terence, *Phormio*, act IV, scene III, 25: “But suppose him defeated: still, after all, it is not his life that is at stake, but his money.”]

is taken from the water of the Jordan,

[Barthius, *Adversus*, book XVIII, chapter 1, on this passage of Gaudentius: “Christ is said to have been taken from the Jordan through Baptism; through this taking is fulfilled what had been prefigured in the type of Moses, whom the king’s daughter drew out of the river as an infant.” I thought this should be added, lest anyone be offended by the unusual expression “taken from the Jordan,” while reading the rest of this author without difficulty.]

and by the rod of his cross leads us through the water of Baptism out of the captivity of Pharaoh, the devil, and snatches us from all his Egypt of darkness. He calls us from darkness into works of light, away from the deeds of the world, where blessed Paul rebukes some who are still placed:

[The manuscript copies read: “he says.”]

“You ought to have gone out from this world; but now I wrote to you not to associate with…” (1 Cor. 5).

[The passage has the sense: “You ought to have gone out from this world; but now I wrote to you not to associate with…”]

Let us now consider what those who are led out of Egypt hear from God: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year,” he says (Exod. 12).

We read in the Book of Numbers (Num. 30) that whoever makes a vow, promising to abstain from the use of marriage or from any pleasures of food or drink until a fixed time, and then violates it through any lapse, must not have the days already passed counted for him, but must return to the beginning.

[This entire phrase is absent from the manuscripts. The passage in the Book of Numbers reads: “If he makes a vow and binds himself by an oath to afflict his soul through fasting or abstinence from other things.” Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, question 59, volume IV, emphatically maintains that this passage can in no way be understood as referring to abstinence from intercourse. Perhaps it should be read: “that he abstain from any pleasures, whether of food or drink.” The manuscript of Pantagathus has: “that he abstain either from pleasures, or from anything whatever, whether food or drink,” but something seems to be missing. See Barthius, *Adversus*, book XVIII, chapter 1, where he examines this passage carefully.]

In this way, the days that the Israelites spent in Egypt were not counted for them; but when they groaned, having turned to the Lord away from their harsh labors, and the Lord struck the firstborn of the Egyptians,

[The four manuscripts unanimously have *primitiva*, “firstborn.” Thus also below: “their firstborn were struck,” and the book of Pantagathus likewise retains this reading in both places.]

who would not allow them to serve the Lord, then they heard: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year” (Exod. 12).

For there are certain days, months, and years of superstition which the Apostle abolishes when he reproves them:

[The Apostle’s passage is: “You observe days and months and seasons and years. I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. 4). Concerning these superstitious days, the author of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, among Ambrose’s works, volume V, Froben edition, writes: “They observe days who say, for example, ‘One must not depart tomorrow; after tomorrow, nothing should be begun,’ and so they are more easily deceived. They observe months who examine the course of the moon, saying, for example, ‘On the seventh moon tools must not be made.’ Again, on the ninth moon it is not appropriate to bring a purchased slave into the house. Through these practices adverse events more readily tend to occur.” The ancients commonly called days *fasti* and *nefasti*—names derived by analogy from the law, since on certain days it was permitted or forbidden to transact public business—as Suetonius relates, *Tiberius*, chapter 53, although Gellius, Book V, chapter 17, disapproves of that manner of speaking. Horace, *Odes* II.13: “He also placed you on an unlucky day”; and Livy, Book I, chapter 20, on Numa: “He established unlucky and lucky days,” because at certain times it would be useful to conduct no business with the people. Gellius in the same place and Virgil, *Georgics* I.276, note which these ominous and black days were:

“Each day the moon itself has assigned, in differing order,  
fortunate times for tasks. Avoid the fifth …”

[The printed text contains a long lacuna here.]

and a little later:

“The seventh after the tenth is favorable for planting the vine,  
for taming captured oxen, and for adding the threads to the loom;  
the ninth is better for flight, hostile to theft.”

Vopiscus, in his *Tacitus*: “He never allowed a night to pass without writing or reading something, except the day before the Kalends.” On this passage Salmasius writes: “The days before the Kalends, Nones, and Ides were regarded by the ancients as unlucky and black.”

[The manuscripts read: “which the Apostle strips away when he reproves them.”]

There are other days, however, which God commanded and counts.

We too were once in Egypt, ignorant of God and unaware of light and truth. Unclean spirits—the true Egyptians—were driving us to make bricks, that is, to serve earthly creations. But when we turned to God, crying out against our harsh labors, the Egyptians were struck with many plagues, and their firstborn were struck down. For our salvation is the punishment of the demons.

We, however, breathed again and were brought to life;

[The manuscripts read: “for we did not see before.”]

for previously we were not alive in those days when, being dead, we worshiped the dead.

Then, accordingly, we heard at the proper time: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year” (Exod. 12).

When that new day dawned for us which the Lord made (Ps. 117), when we came to know the holy month of new crops,

[The Florentine manuscript and the Paris edition read this way, and this seems to me the more correct reading. Exodus 23 says: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread at the time of the month of new things”; and chapter 34: “You shall observe the feast of unleavened bread at the time of the month of new things,” that is, of fruits. Ambrose gives the reason for this designation in Book X, Letter 83, concerning the celebration of Passover, addressed to the bishops established throughout Emilia: “Nor do I think it absurd that we should derive an example for observing the month from the place where Passover was first celebrated. Hence our predecessors, in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, rightly observed the very month of new things, because in Egypt grain is cut in this first month.” Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 18: “It is certain that plowing begins after the seeds of the preceding year have first been cast into the mud of the receding Nile”—he is speaking of the Nile—“that is, at the beginning of November. Later, a few people weed what they call *botanismon*; the remainder visit the fields with the sickle only shortly before the Kalends of April. The harvest, however, is completed in May.” See Sigonius, Book III, *On the Hebrew Republic*, chapter 9, Cologne edition: “The month of new things, that is, of crops,” as in Exodus 13: “You shall go out in the month of new crops,” and Deuteronomy 16: “Observe the month of new crops.” The Lyons edition has, absurdly, “the month of renewed things”; but the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus has “the month of new things.”]

and the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of retribution.

This interpretation more appropriately applies to the faithful. For among catechumens only the firstborn of the demons have been killed; but for those who deserve to approach the grace of heavenly Baptism, the entire army of the devil is drowned and killed, so that they may truly and deservedly hear, as those reborn in Christ: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year” (Exod. 12).

This explanation also suits penitents, whom the darkness of sins and the gloom of this Egypt had again possessed. For if they groan toward the Lord,

[We have preferred this reading, found in the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate, to the common reading, which has “looking back and fleeing.” The book of Pantagathus also has “repenting and fleeing.”]

repenting and fleeing from the most wicked works of darkness, they will obtain the light of heavenly forgiveness, return to eternal light, and attain salvation.

For it is written:

[Gaudentius quotes this passage from the Septuagint version; one will search for it in vain in the Vulgate, which reads: “If you return and be quiet, you shall be saved.” Cyprian uses this testimony of Isaiah in the same way as Gaudentius, in the treatise *On the Lapsed* and in Letter 34, Amsterdam edition of 1700; likewise Jerome, in his letter to the Deacon Sabinianus and in his letter to Rusticus on repentance.]

“When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved, and you shall know where you were” (Isa. 30:15, according to the Septuagint), “when you trusted in them.”

“You shall know,” he says, “where you were.” For a person then understands that he was in the errors of Egypt’s darkness when he returns to the light of truth and righteousness.

This same discourse may also be understood in a pious sense of that perpetual light which will be granted after the completion of the age to the righteous and faithful, when the night of death has been utterly conquered by the Sun of righteousness, so that they may then hear: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year” (Exod. 12).

[The four manuscript copies read: “when it shall have perished.”]

That will indeed be when the entire power of the Egyptians shall perish, and, freed from this Egypt, we shall eat the true manna and drink from the rock, Christ himself,

following the footsteps of the spotless Lamb and saying: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has received me” (Ps. 62).

And therefore every holy person, while still established in this world,

[The manuscript copies read: “without distinction, longs for it,” which seems more Latin, although I did not wish to displace the received reading. Jerome, to Heliodorus: “Behold the gift which you had received when you were about to serve as a soldier; you long for the enemy camp.” The *Passion of Saint Vincent*, in Ruinart’s *Acts of the Martyrs*: “so that in this way you may be able to long for the truth that has been proved.” Ennodius of Ticinum, Book IV, Letter 34: “I long for my downfall with changed judgment.”]

longs for that future light which the world cannot now contain, saying: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. 41).

“For now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” says the holy Apostle,

[The Florentine manuscript reads this way; the printed editions have “but then.”]

“but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

At present, in comparison with the Jews and Gentiles who are known to be submerged in the deep night of unbelief, and in comparison with those who remain in the darkness and night of heresies and luxury, we seem—and plainly are—to be in the light. But even our days are overshadowed by certain clouds,

and they do not possess the joy of clear serenity, as the Prophet says: “My days have declined like a shadow” (Ps. 101).

There, however, the Lord himself will be our eternal light, so that we may no longer merely be saved in his shadow but may always live in the splendor of his glory.

[The Florentine manuscript reads: “all honor.” This is Gaudentius’s customary concluding formula in nearly all his tractates. Ferrarius, Book I, *On the Rite of Sacred Ecclesiastical Assemblies*, chapter 32, shows at length that sermons of the ancient Fathers were commonly concluded with an invocation and glorification of the divine and most holy Trinity.]

To him be all honor, power, and glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, before all things, now, and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon II: The Second Sermon on the Reading from Exodus

[The printed editions had read this entirely incorrectly: “After those who had returned from the font, the newly baptized.” We have therefore faithfully reproduced the reading of the Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts. A poem on the Resurrection, commonly circulated under the name of Lactantius, has:

“The shining army emerges from the gleaming waters.”

The newly baptized were indeed said to emerge from the bath, just as those approaching Baptism were said to enter it. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 1, translated by John Grodecius: “First you entered the portico of the baptistery”; and *Mystagogical Catechesis* 2: “As soon, therefore, as you entered, you removed your garment.” The Urbinate reading is also acceptable: “After the newly baptized had returned from the font.” Gaudentius himself seems to support it toward the end of this tractate, where, speaking of Christ’s Baptism, he says: “He enters the waters of Baptism in order to consecrate them, and from there, filled with the Holy Spirit who had descended upon him in the form of a dove, he returns from the Jordan, as the Evangelist testifies: ‘Jesus, filled with the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.’”]

After the newly baptized had emerged from the font.

[These words are absent from the two Vatican manuscripts. In the Florentine manuscript they are written in the margin of the page. They are found in the three editions—Paris, Cologne, and Lyons. The Urbinate manuscript reads: “After the newly baptized had returned from the font,” which is not appropriate for catechumens to hear, although the same things are openly displayed to everyone in the Gospels. The book of Pantagathus has a passage on the nature of the Sacraments in almost the same form, except that it reads “emerged” instead of “returned,” which is also the reading we have printed.

There were chiefly two Sacraments whose hearing by catechumens and the as-yet-unbaptized was considered religiously forbidden: Baptism and the Eucharist. Concerning Baptism, Cyril of Alexandria, Book VII *Against Julian*, writes: “I would certainly say many other things about these matters—that is, about the mysteries of Baptism—and demonstrate from Moses and the Prophets that this Sacrament was prefigured and is not new or recently originated, except that, as I have already said, I hesitate before the ears of the uninitiated.” Concerning the Eucharist, John Chrysostom, Homily 72 on Matthew, translated by Fronto Ducaeus: “Only the initiated know how full of mercy the mystery of the Eucharist is.” Ambrose, about to speak of both Sacraments in his book *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 1, prefaces it as follows: “Now the time urges us to speak about the mysteries and to disclose the very meaning of the Sacraments; if we had thought it necessary to make this known before Baptism to those not yet initiated, we would be judged to have betrayed rather than disclosed it.” Cyril of Jerusalem, in the Preface to the *Catecheses*: “Present these catecheses for reading to those approaching Baptism and to those who are already faithful and possess this washing. But do not give them to catechumens or to others who are not Christians; otherwise you will have to render an account to the Lord.” This was the discipline of the Secret, by which the Fathers excluded the uninitiated from the sight of the mysteries, so that they might be inflamed with a greater desire for our sacred rites. See Ferrarius, Book II, *On the Rites of the Holy Church*, chapter 18; Bona, Book I, *On Liturgical Matters*, chapter 16. In this tractate Gaudentius secretly treats of the Eucharist, and hence a little farther on he says: “Now only those things from the reading are to be selected which cannot be explained in the presence of catechumens, yet nevertheless must necessarily be opened to the newly baptized.” Bona praises this passage of Gaudentius in the cited Book I, chapter 16.]

Concerning the nature of the Sacraments, which it is not appropriate for catechumens to hear, although the same things may appear openly written in the Gospels to everyone.

When Christ rose from the dead, vengeance was wrought upon the Egyptians through the Sacrament of Baptism; while the underworld trembled, as he returned to raise up his own body, the enemies of God—for they were enemies of his people—were destroyed. For the prophetic Spirit cries out:

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee from his presence. As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God, and may the righteous feast” (Ps. 67 [68]).

The merciful Father sent redemption to his people, mindful of his holy covenant (Ps. 110 [111]), which he established with our fathers, Abraham and his offspring, forever (Luke 1). [Col. 853B]

[Note: Irenaeus, Book IV Against Heresies, chapter 16, in the Paris edition of Feu-Ardent, 1576: “But this Jesus did by drawing us away from the worship of stones, transferring us from our hard and unfruitful thoughts, and establishing in us a faith like Abraham’s.” Feu-Ardent interprets the passage as follows: “Clement of Alexandria interprets this passage in the same sense and almost the same words: God raised up children of Abraham from stones, when, against the truth, he stirred the righteousness and hardness of heart of those who had become harder than stones, he raised up the seed of devotion toward God, perceiving power from those stones—namely, the Gentiles who believed in stones” (*Oration to the Greeks*). Gaudentius of Brescia speaks in the same way in Treatise 2 on the Gospel. He cites the passage incorrectly, however, for it is Treatise 2, *On Easter*, or *On Exodus*.] For God was able to raise up children of Abraham from these once exceedingly hard stones—the Gentiles (Matt. 3; Luke 3).

Now let all those whom the Lord redeems speak, those whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies and gathered from the lands [Note: In two Vatican manuscripts it is read: “He gathered the children of Abraham, whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies, from the regions of the sunrise.” The rest was omitted by the copyist. This defect also occurs in the manuscripts of Octavius Pantagathus, to the considerable detriment of this passage.] from sunrise and sunset, from the north and the sea: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 106 [107]).

For at Israel’s departure from Egypt, at the departure of the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judea alone became his sanctification (Ps. 113 [114]); but now blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways (Ps. 128 [129]). Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered (Ps. 32 [33]). For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek: the same Lord is rich toward all who call upon him [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “who call upon him.”] (Rom. 10), because, as it is written, “Everyone [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *quicumque invocaverit* (“whoever calls upon him”), as does the manuscript of Pantagathus. The Florentine manuscript likewise has *quicumque invocaverit*.] who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (ibid.).

Therefore, since all of us who call upon the Lord receive salvation after the Egyptians have been destroyed, let us learn to eat the Passover—not like the foolish Jews, who even after the coming of the truth still follow the shadow, each one killing and eating a sheep in every household on the fourteenth day of the first month [Note: At this point the manuscripts of the two Vaticans and the Urbinate rescued the text from profound darkness, and we have faithfully presented their reading. The printed editions had the hopelessly corrupt reading *quem quisque* (“whom each person”), while the manuscript of Pantagathus had *ovem quisque* (“a sheep, each person”), as also in the following words, “killing and eating.” The correct reading, so often confirmed, leaves us no reason to doubt the excellence of this manuscript.] [Note: To make the whole passage corrupt, the printed editions had *occidebant et comedebant* (“they were killing and eating”). We restored *occidens et comedens* (“killing and eating”) from the Florentine, Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts. We therefore owe the corrected passage to the Urbinate and Vatican manuscripts.] .

For when the one whose shadow that sheep had been—the true Lamb of God, the Lord Jesus, who takes away the sins of the world—came, and said, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6), the Jews now practice the matter carnally in vain; unless they do it spiritually together with us, they cannot have life within themselves. [Note: The two Vatican manuscripts read *spiritaliter*, as below they read *spiritalis* and *spiritales*; this reading also occurs elsewhere in the manuscript of Pantagathus. See above, the Preface to Benivolus, p. 227, and the end of Sermon 11, at the words “to adhere to spiritual things.”]

For the Law is spiritual (Rom. 7), as the Apostle says, and “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). What spiritual realities were prefigured in the very history of Exodus (Exod. 12), where the celebration of the Passover is narrated—the tenth day, the fourteenth day, the sacrifice of the perfect, male, year-old lamb at evening, the blood to be smeared on the doorposts, the gathering of neighbors, the footwear [Note: Three editions have *calceamenta*; the Florentine has *calciamenta*, which I consider the better reading. It is likewise a Salvianic expression in Book I *On the Government of God*: “unbroken footwear”; and Baluze, in his notes on Salvian, p. 46, replaced *excalceatos* with *excalcios*. Vossius noted *calciari* and *calciare* in Pliny the Younger and Suetonius. Gaudentius likewise has *calciati* and *calciamenta* in more than one place.] , the staffs, the leaven, the unleavened bread [Note: So read the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions and the Urbinate read incorrectly *quae azymae* (“which are unleavened things”). Below, in Treatise 7, it says that the unleavened bread is to be eaten with bitterness. See our notes there.]—we must, with the Lord’s help, begin to explain from tomorrow. [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts read *immolatio paschae* (“the sacrifice of the Passover”).]

For now, however, we must select from the reading only those things that cannot be explained in the presence of catechumens, yet must necessarily be opened to neophytes.

In the shadow of that legal Passover, not one lamb was killed, but several; [Note: Therefore, not in the Temple, as some more recent writers maintain. So too above: “each person killing and eating a sheep in every household.” And below, in Treatise 4: “The whole synagogue did not kill one lamb; rather, a few killed individual lambs in each household.” Philo, Book III *On the Life of Moses*, translated by Gelenius, says: “At that time”—he is speaking of the feast of Passover—“the common people do not, as at other times, bring victims to the altar to be slaughtered by the priests; rather, at the command of the Law, the whole nation sacrifices, each person slaughtering the victim with his own hands.” And in the treatise *On the Decalogue*: “Passover is said to occur when individuals sacrifice as a people, without waiting for the priests, themselves exercising the priesthood each year for one day.” To diminish Philo’s authority, Natalis Alexander, vol. I of *Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, p. 280, says that Philo was speaking in the manner of an orator. Lamy, however, in his treatise on the ancient Jewish Passover, published in French, p. 134, rejects Philo because he favored the schism of the Alexandrians. In fact, the reasoning and arguments of these authors are strongly reinforced by the testimony of Zeno, bishop of Verona, who says in Sermon 7 on Exodus: “I do not see how a Pharisee could celebrate the lawful Passover, since that eminent and famous Temple lies buried in its own dust, leveled to the ground by a pitiable devastation.” And in Sermon 13 on Exodus: “Receive briefly, Christian, that the Jews cannot celebrate the lawful Passover. Since Solomon’s Temple has been overthrown and lies buried in its ruins through hostile devastation, where do they sacrifice?” Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus: “Let us neither sacrifice a lamb nor celebrate the mystical Passover, because the Law forbids these things to be done without the Temple.”] for individual lambs were killed in the households, since one could not suffice for everyone, because it was a figure, not the reality, of the Lord’s Passion.

For a figure is not the truth, but an imitation of the truth. Human beings too were made in the image of God, yet for that reason they are not God. Nevertheless, in the sense in which an image of God is spoken of, let God also be spoken of: in nature there is one God, while in representation there are many. [Note: The printed editions have *dicunt*. Although the error here is self-evident, our duty requires us to note that manuscript codices read *dicitur*.]

Therefore, in the truth in which we exist, one died for all; and he himself, in the mystery of bread and wine, is offered in each individual church, nourishing us as the sacrificed one, giving life as the believed one, and sanctifying those who consecrate as the consecrated one. [Note: The illustrious de Marca produced this entire passage of Gaudentius, in which he so clearly discusses the truth of the Sacrament of the Eucharist, in his *Dissertation on the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, numbering Gaudentius among the ancient Fathers who openly and lucidly professed the truth of this mystery.]

This is the flesh of the Lamb; this is the blood. For the bread that came down from heaven says: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6).

The blood is rightly represented also under the appearance of wine, because when he himself says in the Gospel, “I am the true vine” (John 15), he sufficiently declares that all wine offered in the figure of his Passion is his blood. Hence the blessed patriarch Jacob had prophesied concerning Christ, saying: “He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49).

He was going to wash the robe of our body, its garment, in his own blood. [Note: Here too a considerable corruption was concealed, which we corrected with the support of the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “He was going to wash the robe of our body, its garment, in his own blood,” with an awkward construction. The Florentine has “its garment, he was going to wash it in his own blood”; the two Vatican manuscripts have “its garment, he was going to wash it clean in his own blood”; and the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus agrees with them.]

Therefore the very Creator and Lord of natures, who brings bread forth from the earth, makes it again from bread into his own body—for he both can and promised to do so—and he who made wine from water makes his blood from wine. [Note: The word *facit* (“makes”) had dropped out of the printed editions; we supplied it from the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts. It also appears in the book of Pantagathus.]

How, then, this Lamb ought to be eaten, we must discern from the reading itself: “You shall not eat anything raw from it, nor boiled in water, but roasted over the fire; its head with its feet and entrails” (Exod. 12).

There are two spiritual understandings in these words; if you follow one, you will recognize both. The entire body of divine Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, contains the Son of God: either promising that he will come in the flesh, or declaring that he has already come. [Note: The Florentine, Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts read: “From this point the blessed Andrew said to his brother Simon Peter, ‘Whom…’”; the manuscript of Pantagathus agrees with them. Either reading can be supported by the Gospel text.]

Thus, when Philip was found by Christ, he found Nathanael and said to him: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph from Nazareth, whom Moses wrote about in the Law and the Prophets” (John 1).

And what more need I say, beloved? [Note: One of the two Vatican manuscripts reads “in Christ”; the other, “in Christ himself.” The reading supplied by the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus is altogether more suitable to this passage: “And what more need I say? It is contained most clearly in him.”] Everything is contained in him, both the whole Law and the Old and New Testaments; and, so to speak, he is the soul of the Law.

For he himself spoke through Moses when he said to him: “I will open your mouth and inspire what you ought to say” (Exod. 4). [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read *cum dicit* (“when he says”).]

He also spoke through the Prophets when he says: “I who was speaking in the Prophets—behold, I am here” (Isa. 52). He also spoke through the Apostles, when the Apostle Paul says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13). [Note: The manuscripts read: “of the one who speaks in me, Christ.”]

These flesh-pieces of the spotless Lamb—that is, the inward parts of his teaching—must not be consumed raw, without interpretation, nor boiled in water, that is, dissolved and cooked by the explanations of those who, like water, flow downward and perceive nothing heavenly; rather, they must be roasted, he says, over the fire—that is, solidified and baked by the divine Spirit. For fire tends upward.

Hence the Lord said to the Jews: “You are from below; I am from above” (John 8).

Therefore, since we have said that the members of the Lamb of God are his Scriptures, let us see what is meant by the head with the feet and the entrails: namely, that in the head you should understand the divinity, according to the testimony of the four Evangelists; [Note: The Paris and Cologne editions have *in capita*, incorrectly; the Lyons edition and Florentine manuscript have *in capite*, correctly.] [Note: That is, with reference to the Incarnation, which Hilary also called *corporation* in his prologue on the Psalms. Philaster calls it *incorporation* in chapter 69: “Others are those who go astray concerning the incorporation.” Likewise Cassiodorus, Book II of *Divine Readings*, chapter 32: “who bestowed such great gifts upon the human race that through the benefit of incorporation he broke the bonds of sins.” Gaudentius himself says in Treatise 14: “If all works are in faith, how much more is this work of his most sacred incorporation!” And in Treatise 19: “He represents in another way the humility of his future incorporation.” From Gaudentius’ view seems to have been taken the passage in the book *On the Essence of Divinity*—among the works attributed to Augustine, in the Benedictine edition, vol. VIII, whoever its author may ultimately be—which reads as follows: “In another way, the feet of the Son of God are understood as his incarnation, which is subject to his divinity as feet are to the head,” or because the Incarnation itself took place toward the end of the world. “For just as the divinity is figuratively represented by the head, so his humanity is represented by the feet.” The two Vatican manuscripts, the Urbinate, and the manuscript of Pantagathus read: “Take the feet as referring to the incorporation.”]

and that you take the feet as referring to the incorporation accomplished toward the end of the age. For the feet are the extremities of the body. In the entrails, however, understand the hidden mysteries.

“And you shall leave none of it until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it. Whatever remains of it until morning you shall burn with fire” (Exod. 12): that is, if anything of the mysteries remains over, it is to be revealed in the morning of that future resurrection—things which we cannot now comprehend. “For now I know in part,” says the Apostle, “but then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. 13).

These things must be burned with fire—that is, handed over to the divine Spirit—so that whatever we cannot now comprehend may be consumed by the spirit of ardent faith. [Note: The manuscripts again read *dicit* (“says”) for *dixit* (“said”).]

As for what he said, “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12), this commands that whatever in the Scriptures is stronger and more powerful must not be broken or shattered, but remain solid. Those who do not keep this command rightly receive woe from the one whose bones they break.

“Woe to you,” he says, “scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matt. 23). These are the bones of the lamb. [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts have *cuminum*, with *u* substituted for *y*, as often happened. See Cassiodorus, *Orthography*, chapters 1 and 4. The manuscript of Pantagathus agrees.]

And elsewhere he says to them: “You make void the word of God in order to establish your traditions” (Matt. 15).

God adds the following to the preceding words in Exodus: “Thus you shall eat it”—namely, the lamb: [Note: So read the printed editions and manuscripts; the Lyons edition has “Let your loins be girded.”] “your loins girded, 242 and your footwear on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste.” [Note: So read the printed editions and manuscripts. One of the Vatican manuscripts has “eat him.”] “For it is the Lord’s Passover” (Exod. 12).

Concerning the footwear and the staffs there is a lengthy explanation, which will be discussed at another time. [Note: The printed editions read *longa ratio est* (“there is a lengthy explanation”); the manuscripts instead have *alio tempore* (“at another time”). Below, in Treatise 5, the longer explanation is given.]

Concerning the girding of the loins, since I have often discussed it at greater length, I shall now speak briefly. [Note: The Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts read “has been explained to you more fully.”] It is written in Jeremiah: “And you, gird your loins, and you shall speak to the people” (Jer. 1). And to holy Job: “Gird your loins like a man; I shall question you, and you shall answer me: Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38, 40). [Note: The manuscripts read: “but you shall answer.”]

The Apostles also hear: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). Why this is commanded so insistently is shown in John the Baptist, who was girded around his loins with a leather belt (Matt. 3).

What the significance of the loins is, the Apostle indicates to the Hebrews: “Levi was still in the loins of his father”—that is, the priestly race—“when Melchizedek met him” (Heb. 7). [Note: The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts restored this passage, which was read corruptly not only in the printed editions but also in the manuscripts as “in the priestly order.” The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus has “the priestly race.”]

Whose loins? Clearly those of holy Abraham.

The leather belt around the loins therefore signifies the putting to death of vices. For the hide that is prepared for use belongs only to a dead animal. Therefore, by God’s command, we must first put to death the desires of the flesh, and thus receive the body of Christ, who was sacrificed for us, who serve in the Egypt of this age. [Note: The word *saeculi* (“of this age”) was absent from the printed editions; we added it from the Urbinate and two Vatican manuscripts. It also occurs in the book of Pantagathus, though through a minor scribal error “of the Egypt of this age” is written for “of the age’s Egypt.”]

“For a person should examine himself,” as the Apostle says, “and thus eat of this bread and drink from the cup” (1 Cor. 11).

When it says that it must be eaten in haste, it commands that we should not receive the Sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood with a sluggish heart and languid mouth, but with complete eagerness of spirit, as those who truly hunger and thirst for righteousness. “Blessed,” says the Lord Jesus, “are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5).

Concluding the reading that had been set forth, he brings his splendid teaching to a most fitting close, saying: “For it is the Lord’s Passover” (Exod. 12). [Note: De Marca produced the whole passage up to “Truth does not know falsehood” in his *Dissertation on the Sacrament of the Eucharist*. Since the passage is so illustrious, we rightly indicated in the preface to Gaudentius, no. 10, that this sermon was of the greatest use to our writers in asserting and defending the mystery of the Eucharist.]

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11). [Note: One Vatican manuscript has: “For it is the Passover, the Lord says, that is…” Another: “For it is the Passover, he says, of the Lord.” The Florentine has: “It is the Passover, says the Lord.” The manuscript of Pantagathus, better than the others, has: “It is, he says, the Lord’s Passover.”]

“It is,” he says, “the Lord’s Passover”—that is, the Lord’s passing-over. Do not think that what has been made heavenly through him who passes over into it is earthly; he made it his own body and blood.

For what we explained above in general concerning the eating of the lamb must be observed specifically in tasting these same mysteries of the Lord’s Passion: you must neither think that the flesh and blood are raw, as the Jew does, and reject them, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6). [Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts reads: “How could he give his flesh?” The Lyon edition has “to give his flesh to eat”; the other editions and the manuscript codices have “to give his flesh to eat.”]

Nor should you boil the Sacrament itself in the pot of a fleshly heart, always subject by nature to bodily fluids, imagining it to be something common and earthly. [Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine have “that common eternal thing.” The other Vatican manuscript has “that and earthly thing”; this is certainly the truer reading and agrees with what was said above: “Do not think that what has been made heavenly is earthly.” The Urbinate has “that common earthly thing.” The printed editions have “that common and earthly thing,” while the manuscript of Pantagathus has “that common and earthly thing.”]

Rather, believe that through the fire of the divine Spirit it has been made what was proclaimed, because what you receive is the body of that heavenly bread, and it is the blood of that sacred vine.

For when he gave consecrated bread and wine to his disciples, he said: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26; Luke 22).

Let us believe, I beg you, the one in whom we have believed. Truth does not know falsehood.

Therefore, when he was speaking to the astonished and murmuring crowds about eating his body and drinking his blood, and they said, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John 6:61), in order to wipe away with heavenly fire those thoughts which I said must be avoided, he added: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:64).

And therefore we are commanded to eat together the head of his divinity, the feet of his incorporation, and the inward parts in the mysteries, so that we may believe all things alike, exactly as they were handed down, not breaking his most solid bone: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26; Luke 22).

But if anything even now remains in the understanding of each person which this exposition has not grasped, let it be burned up in the heat of faith, since our God is a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29) [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts, and also the Urbinate, read “a burning fire.”], cleansing, instructing, and illuminating our hearts for the understanding of divine things, so that we may know the cause and meaning of this heavenly sacrifice instituted by Christ, and return unending thanks for his ineffable gift.

For this is truly the hereditary gift of his new covenant, which he left us on that night when he was handed over to be crucified, as a pledge of his presence. This is the provision for our journey, by which we are nourished and fed along this way of life until we go to him when we depart from this age. Hence the same Lord said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you do not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

For he wished his benefits to remain with us; he wished our souls [Note: The Florentine manuscript and the Urbinate add *redemptas* (“redeemed”).] to be sanctified by his precious blood through the image of his own Passion. And therefore he commands his faithful disciples—whom he established as the first priests of his Church [Note: So it is read in the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate. The printed editions incorrectly have “the first and priests of his Church.” The manuscript of Pantagathus has “the first priests of his Church.”]—to perform continually these mysteries of eternal life, which must be celebrated by all priests throughout the individual churches of the entire world, until Christ comes again from heaven.

Then both the priests and all the faithful peoples together, keeping before their eyes daily the pattern of Christ’s Passion, carrying it in their hands, receiving it with their mouths and in their breasts, will preserve the imperishable memorial of our redemption [Note: The Florentine and Urbinate restored this reading. For both the printed editions and the manuscripts had corrupted it to “an indelible memory.” The manuscript of Pantagathus, however, retains “an indelible memory.”] and, against the poisons of the devil, obtain the sweet medicine of everlasting protection, as the Holy Spirit exhorts:

“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33 [34]).

The fact that he established the Sacraments of his body and blood to be offered under the appearance of bread and wine has a twofold rationale.

First, so that the spotless Lamb of God might give a clean sacrifice to a cleansed people to celebrate—without burning, without blood, [Note: This is a new kind of word, which copyists may have inserted because they did not understand it. The Florentine, Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts have *sine bromo* (“without bromo”). The book of Octavius Pantagathus likewise reads *sine bromo* and omits the following gloss, “that is, by the law of flesh.” *Bromos*, Greek βρῶμος, is, in Pliny, Book XXII, chapter 25, the seed of an ear-bearing plant; it grows among grain and is of the oat kind. In Book XVIII, chapter 11, Pliny says: “Bromos, exceptional rye.” Thus “without bromo” means for Gaudentius “without any foreign admixture,” which suits the Eucharistic bread very well. It is therefore not unreasonable to think that *sine bromo* is the true reading, supported by the agreement of the manuscripts. Octavius Ferrarius included the word *brodium*, derived from Gaudentius, among the origins of the Italian language; besides him, Aegidius Menagius also rendered excellent service to the study of Italian among the French. As Lipsius observed in *On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language*, chapter 3, the Italian language arose a thousand years before his own age. I am delighted that the seeds of the Italian language, already beginning to sprout, are found in our Gaudentius, although this does not mean that the Latin language and its use had altogether ceased in Gaudentius’ age. For, as Janus Rutgersius observed in Book I of *Various Readings*, chapter 13: “If some little word, as the purity of Latin speech was declining, adhered to Roman speech from the dregs of another language, it does not immediately follow that the whole language had perished.” Fontaninus, in *Horta Colonensis*, appendix, pp. 332–333, suggests that the vernacular arose from Latin badly pronounced and badly constructed, and that it thereafter divided into various dialects according to the differing character of regions and peoples. Whether rightly or wrongly, let others judge; I do not strongly oppose allowing each person to think freely about the matter as he wishes.] without *brodium*, [Note: This gloss appears to have been added by copyists. It is also absent from the manuscripts.] that is, by the law of flesh, and something that would be ready and easy for all to offer.

Second, just as bread must be made from many grains of wheat ground into flour, formed with water, and necessarily completed by fire, so in it the body of Christ is reasonably represented: we know that he was made one body from the multitude of the whole human race, perfected through the fire of the Holy Spirit. [Note: This passage plainly seemed to require correction, even though the corrected form was not found in the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts. The editions and two Vatican manuscripts have *qui novimus* (“whom we know”).]

For he was born of the Holy Spirit. And since it was fitting for him in this way to fulfill all righteousness, he entered the waters of Baptism in order to consecrate them; thereafter, filled with the Holy Spirit who had descended upon him in the form of a dove, he returned from the Jordan, as the Evangelist testifies: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4).

Likewise, his blood is wine gathered from many grapes— [Note: This gloss is absent from the manuscripts.] that is, from the grapes of the vine planted by him—pressed in the winepress of the cross, and through its own power grows fervent in the capacious vessels of the faithful who receive it. [Note: So read the two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine, and the Urbinate. The printed editions have “the saving Passover of the Savior,” a scribal error absent from the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

Receive this saving sacrifice of the Passover, all of you who come forth from the power of Egypt and Pharaoh the devil, with us in the full eagerness of a devout heart, so that the inner parts of your souls may be sanctified by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, whom we believe to be present in his Sacraments; his immeasurable power remains forever.

## SERMON III. ON THE THIRD READING FROM EXODUS. FIRST SUNDAY OF EASTER
God speaks through the prophet: “Behold, I make a new heaven and a new earth; and the moon shall shine like the sun, and the sun sevenfold” (Isa. LXVI, XXX). Although he foretells the future renewal of the elements after the end of this age, creation itself will certainly be delivered, as the Apostle says, from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII).

[Note: [Col. 0861D] This passage seems somewhat favorable to the chiliasts (χιλιασταῖς); but see Jerome on Jer. XIX and Augustine, *City of God* XX.7, lest you unjustly accuse Irenaeus, Justin, Lactantius, and other men of the highest reputation of error together with Gaudentius. For there were two kinds of chiliasts, one spiritual and the other carnal. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.24, is relevant to this passage of Gaudentius: “Then those darknesses by which heaven was clouded and blinded will be removed from the world; the moon will receive the sun’s brightness and will no longer diminish. But the sun will become seven times brighter than it is now.”]

For, dearest brethren, neither will the elements fail in such a way that they cease to exist, nor shall we die in such a way that we do not rise improved.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Some editions shortly before read *vel elementa sic deficiunt* (“nor do the elements so fail”); here, however, the manuscripts read *sic morimur* (“so do we die”). The manuscript of Pantagathus has *sic deficiunt* in the former passage and likewise *sic morimur* here.]

Yet even today we see the Lord’s promise fulfilled: we behold the souls and bodies of the neophytes renewed in the likeness of heaven and earth.

We also see the moon—that is, the Church—which grows in peace and diminishes in persecution. It diminishes in the mass of its fullness, not in the light of its splendor; and now we see it shining like the sun throughout the whole world. Moreover, because Christ, the Sun of justice, now shines upon the earth seven times more brightly than he shone before, his rays bear witness: they illumine every human being who comes into this world (John I).

For now that fiery sevenfold Spirit flashes forth from him—the Spirit who, like fire, sat upon the Apostles (Acts II)—and today burns in each believer.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] This is how I read it in the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts. The printed editions read *igneus ipse* (“fiery itself”).] Before Christ suffered and rose again, God was known only in Judea (Ps. LXXV); now the splendor of the Lord’s glory passes through all nations. “His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its end; and there is no one who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. XVIII).

Therefore, since the world has been restored today, let us celebrate with rejoicing the birthday of the world’s reformation. “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. CXVII).

When I speak of the birthday of the world, I mean our own, who have been reborn in Christ. Previously we were indeed alive to sin, but dead to righteousness; now, dead to our former transgressions, we have begun to live for God.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] The Florentine manuscript reads *vivere Deo accepimus*; likewise one of the Vatican manuscripts. The other reads *vivere Deo coepimus*. The Urbinate reads *vivere Deo jam accepimus*. The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus reads *vivere Deo accepimus*, but in Pantagathus’s own hand *coepimus* is written in the margin.]

We have been made conformed first to Christ’s death and then to his resurrection. “For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life,” celebrating the festal day and glorying in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Although Gaudentius understands this allegorically below of Christ, we do not think it irrelevant to note here what learned men have rightly observed—Lapide on John XII and Reizius in his notes on Godwin, p. 244, Utrecht edition, 1698—namely, that Christ came to Jerusalem on that very day for the feast and for his own cruciform Passover (*Pascha suum σταυρώσιμον*) on which God had commanded the lamb to be set apart in Egypt, namely, the tenth day of the month Nisan. For he came to Bethany six days before Passover (John XII.1), that is, on the ninth day of Nisan; on the following day he set out for Jerusalem (v. 12), to present himself to God as an offering.

“Eligius, bishop of Noyon, had previously observed both points in his fourteenth homily. Discussing the commandment concerning Passover given to the Jews in the Old Law, he says: ‘All these things, fulfilled in the true Lamb of God, Jesus Christ, must be fitted to his Passover and ours, so that what was then done figuratively may now be done in truth. For that Lamb, as we have said, is Christ, who came to Jerusalem to suffer on the tenth day of the first month of the Hebrews, called Nisan among them and March among us.’”]

He was accepted on the tenth day of the first month and sacrificed by the Jews at evening on the fourteenth day for the sake of the world. But what that tenth day and that fourteenth day signify, I shall explain, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it, in order to fulfill yesterday’s promise.

God said to holy Moses:

“Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, saying: On the tenth day of this month, let each man take a sheep for the households of his families, a sheep for each household. But if there are few in a household, so that they are not sufficient for a sheep, he shall take with him his nearest neighbor, according to the number of persons; each one shall reckon for himself what will be sufficient for the lamb. The lamb shall be perfect, male, and one year old for you. You shall take it from the sheep and the goats, and it shall be kept for you until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole multitude of the assembly of the children of Israel shall kill it at evening. They shall take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they are to eat it” (Exod. XII).

The manifold wisdom of God speaks through the Law in such a way that, in the same words by which it commands what is presently to be done for salvation, it foretells what is to come. At that time the shadow of the truth that would follow saved the Jews in these observances, while at the same time signifying that their descendants, forgetful of divine benefits, would slaughter the very one whose shadow had saved them.

For Christ, coming into this world from them, was led like a sheep to the slaughter (Isa. LIII). We, however, are protected from every assault of the raging plague by bearing the blood of this Lamb—the sign, namely, of his Passion—either on the two doorposts, that is, in faith and works or in heart and mouth, or on the lintels of our foreheads.

[Note: [Col. 0863C] Both Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine, and the Urbinate read *in liminibus* (“on the lintels”). The agreement of these manuscripts should certainly have warned that in the earlier edition *liminaribus*, a barbarous form, ought to be replaced by *liminibus*. Below also, at the beginning of Sermon 6, we find *quod illud limen*, and at the end *in limine frontis*. Therefore we should not depart from the manuscript reading. The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus has *luminibus* through a copyist’s error, but even this reading supports the genuine form.]

That the lamb is taken on the tenth day and sacrificed on the fourteenth,

[Note: [Col. 0863D] The manuscripts read *haec significari* (“these things to be signified”).]

I understand to signify that the Jewish people would accept the Son of God in the Decalogue of the Law and would crucify him at evening, born in the fourteenth generation after the Babylonian deportation, as it is written (Matt. I).

“At evening” means either at the evening of this world, because he suffered in the final times of the age, or at the setting of the sun itself, because when the Lord was crucified, the sun went down. “From the sixth hour there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour” (Matt. XXVII). What could have been more truly evening?

Nor should you regard as pointless the fact that, although above the command was given in the imperative—“Let them take a sheep for each household”—below it is expressed in the indicative: “The whole multitude of the assembly of the children of Israel shall kill him at evening.”

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Both Vatican manuscripts, the Urbinate, and the Lyon edition read *ad vesperum* (“at evening”), just as Gaudentius himself does shortly before, more than once. The Vatican manuscripts above, and the Urbinate as well, read *istius solis* (“of that sun”) instead of *ipsius* (“of the sun itself”). Although these points are minor, we have thought it right not to omit them.]

“He shall kill,” he says—not “let them kill.” What the synagogue of the Jews was cruelly going to do was foretold; it was not commanded that it should happen.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] These words are absent from the manuscripts, certainly through copyists’ error; otherwise the sense is not complete. The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus is likewise affected by this defect.]

Nor did it happen because it had been foretold; rather, it was foretold because it was going to happen, so that God might display his foreknowledge in those events that were going to occur through the freedom of human choice.

We have spoken of freedom of choice because the Jews wanted to do what they did; and certainly, if they had not wanted to do it, they would not have done it.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] So reads the Florentine manuscript. The two Vatican manuscripts and the printed editions have *voluissent* (“if they had wished”). Incorrectly. The manuscript of Pantagathus reads *si noluissent non fecerant* (“if they had not wished, they would not have done it”), but in Pantagathus’s own hand *facerent* is written in the margin.]

Certainly it is a great sacrilege even to think that God, who is not only good and just but goodness and justice themselves, would either command or compel anything

[Note: [Col. 0863D] I do not know how the word *admirabiliter* (“wonderfully”), found in the manuscripts, crept in here. It was perhaps written in the margin by someone to whom this entire passage of Gaudentius greatly pleased; then, through the copyists’ ignorance, it was admitted into the text. The manuscript of Pantagathus suffers from the same defect.]

to be done that he condemns as having been done.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] The two Vatican manuscripts have *et in opere justitia* (“and justice in deed”).]

Or should we perhaps suppose that, if the Israelites had repented, the omnipotent Son of God would have been unable to save the world by any other means?

[Note: [Col. 0864C] Pantagathus had rewritten *quin si* (“indeed, if”) in the margin; and in the same manuscript, where the printed editions below read *usque in hodiernum diem* (“until the present day”), it reads only *usque in hodiernum* (“until the present”).]

“For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. XI.34).

Consider in the Gospel how Christ awaited the repentance of the Jews. He reproaches the cities in which his many mighty works had been performed because they had not repented:

“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, which are exalted to heaven, you shall be brought down to hell; for if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Nevertheless I tell you, it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you” (Matt. XI; Luke X).

[Note: [Col. 0864C] This is the passage indicated by the learned author of *On the Moderation of Minds against John Phereponus*, III.7, p. 385, Venice edition, in which, while discussing God’s foreknowledge, he praises several Fathers, including Gaudentius of Brescia.]

God’s foreknowledge is not deceived; but neither is the freedom of will once granted to human beings taken away, so that nothing may be judged concerning one who has not been free in acting.

[Note: [Col. 0864D] The Florentine manuscript reads *judicari* (“to be judged”), a reading which may be correct and is more pleasing to me, although I have not wished to alter the text. The manuscript once owned by Octavius Pantagathus likewise reads *judicari*.]

God condemns persistence in evil and embraces the conversion of the penitent. But you may say: “Could God have lied, when he foretold that they would do what they did?”

[Note: [Col. 0864D] The reading of both Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate is *poterat Deus, qui facturos eos praedixerat* (“Could God, who had foretold that they would do it, have lied?”); the manuscript of Pantagathus agrees.]

We do not grasp the greatness of the power of his omnipotence, who calls those things that are not as though they were (Rom. IV.17).

[Note: [Col. 0864D] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, incorrectly, *non consequimur* (“we do not attain”).]

We would have thought that he could lie if what he had foretold had not come to pass. Therefore, did he also lie to the Ninevites? For he said: “Three days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III, according to the Septuagint); yet it was not overthrown, because the people repented at Jonah’s preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0864D] The manuscript copies have *subvertetur* (“shall be overthrown”), a reading supported by the Vulgate. But why does Gaudentius say “three days”? The Septuagint certainly reads this, as does Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.44. The Vulgate, however, reads “forty days.” See Melchior Cano, *On Theological Places* XI.5.]

But understand. The word of God is a two-edged sword (Heb. IV).

Nineveh was destined to be overthrown in another way, and it was overthrown in another way.

[Note: [Col. 0865C] This passage had lost all its elegance through faulty punctuation, which we have restored with the aid of one manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus; it alone correctly distinguishes the clauses in this manner. The printed editions had hitherto read awkwardly: *et eversa est. Aliter evertenda fuerat* (“and it was overthrown. It was destined to be overthrown otherwise”). The inserted period transferred *aliter* (“otherwise”) to a foreign position and impaired not only the elegance but also the clarity of the sentence. Restored to its proper place, the word gives the passage its genuine purity and integrity. Although this emendation is so suitable and easy, it escaped our investigation in the earlier edition, while both the printed editions and the manuscripts alike tolerated and preserved the error.]

It was destined to be overthrown by destruction if it had persisted in its wickedness; its iniquity was overthrown because it repented.

[Note: [Col. 0865C] Augustine expresses this meaning admirably in his commentary on Psalm 50: “Nineveh stood—was Nineveh overthrown? It appears one way to human beings and another way to God. I think, however, that what the Prophet foretold was fulfilled. Consider what Nineveh was, and see that it was overthrown: overthrown in evil, built up in good.”]

As God says to human beings: “As heaven is distant from earth, so my thoughts are distant from your thoughts, and my purposes from your purposes” (Isa. LV).

It is written: “Do not seek what is beyond you, and do not investigate what is above you; for many have been ensnared by their suspicion” (Ecclus. III.22).

Therefore, dearest brother, believe the Lord to be just, true, and gracious in all his words and works, so that you may attain perfect wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0865C] The word *crede* (“believe”) was lacking in the printed editions, although it is wholly necessary to support this entire passage. We restored it from the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate; the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus also has it: *Justum crede Deum, charissime* (“Believe God to be just, dearest brother”).]

“For the lamb shall be perfect, male, and one year old for you,” he says (Exod. XII), so that you may understand nothing mediocre concerning the Perfect One, nothing weak concerning the Male, and nothing incomplete concerning the One-Year-Old.

He is perfect because “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. II).

He is male,

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Both Vatican manuscripts, the Urbinate, and the Florentine read as follows: *quippe quia vir nasci dignatus est ex Virgine* (“since he deigned to be born a man from the Virgin”).]

since he deigned to be born a man from the Virgin, so that he might provide for both sexes.

He is one year old because, after that baptism which he received for our sake in the Jordan,

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Vossius, *On the Vices of Speech* III.2, once notes *Baptismum* in the accusative instead of *Baptismus* in the nominative, although he doubts whether this is a copyist’s error. Apart from this passage of Gaudentius, who uses the neuter gender, the form is also found in Pope Anastasius’s Decree, quoted by Agobard, *On the Privileges and Rights of the Priesthood* 17: “Baptism, whether administered by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient undefiled.” It is also found in Peter Damian, in the book called *Gratissimus*, chapter 9: “Three chief sacraments are regularly celebrated in the holy Church: baptism, the saving mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, and the ordination of clerics.”]

the period of one year is completed up to the day of his Passion.

[Note: [Col. 0866C] Several ancient Fathers held this view, especially those who dated Christ’s death to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, under the consulship of the two Gemini. Among them are Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Lactantius, Augustine, and Jerome. I see what others have thought to the contrary. Feuardentius, above all, in his note on Irenaeus I.1, argued rather heatedly that the distinguished Fathers Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, and our Gaudentius—not mentioning the others—had been carried away by the fervor of controversy into failing to notice the passage in Irenaeus in which Valentinus and his followers are criticized for holding nearly the same opinion. With respect for that good man, Feuardentius might have made such an accusation more sparingly against men of this stature. Here we need only note that our Gaudentius seems to have borrowed this from Philastrius, who, in chapter 106, speaks of the years and time of Christ as follows: “The things which the Lord did and taught in one year—these alone he commanded to be written down. For the things done and said by him during the first thirty years were not written, according to blessed John, who says that the world could not contain all the books if everything he had done were written.”]

Only those things were written in the Gospels that he either taught or did during that year—and not even all of those. For the Evangelist John says:

“Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, whom Scripture records him as having chosen after his baptism,

[Note: [Col. 0866D] The manuscript of Pantagathus reads *eorum quippe quos post Baptismum in Scriptura legis*, with *elegisse* (“to have chosen”) or *vocasse* (“to have called”) understood: “namely, those whom you read in Scripture that he chose or called after his baptism.”]

which are not written in this book. But these things are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have eternal life in his name” (John XX).

Of the things he did before that year, the same John bears witness in the concluding words of his book:

“There are also many other things that Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would be written” (John XXI).

Only Luke the Evangelist briefly mentioned that the Lord Jesus, when he was twelve years old,

[Note: [Col. 0866D] The printed copies read entirely incorrectly *duodecim annorum praeditus* (“endowed with twelve years”). We have emended this from the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts, which read *duodecim annorum praedictus* (“said to be twelve years old”); the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus agrees.]

was found by his parents in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and questioning them, and that he said to his parents:

“Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke II).

This is the acceptable year of the Lord, which the Lord Jesus, reading in the synagogue from the book of Isaiah concerning his own person, declared in these words:

“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke IV.21).

[Note: [Col. 0866D] All printed editions and manuscripts read *de Isaiae libro ex persona sua* (“from the book of Isaiah in his own person”). The phrase *ex persona sua* is wholly incompatible with the context; therefore we have restored *ex Isaiae libro de persona sua* (“from the book of Isaiah concerning his own person”). We trust that this emendation will commend itself to every sensible reader.]

This is the year whose crown—the victorious circle, surely, to be blessed by the works of Christ’s goodness—the Prophet joyfully announced in the psalm:

“You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance” (Ps. LXIV);

namely, the hearts of believing peoples, which, having received the seed of the word of life, will overflow also with a hundredfold fruit.

If, when the legs of the thieves hanging on the cross with Christ were broken, the Savior’s legs were not broken, as the holy Evangelist testifies, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says, “You shall not break a bone of him” (John XIX),

[Note: [Col. 0866D] Both Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read *non confringetis* (“you shall not break”), a reading also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus, as is the following phrase, *cujus est omnis honor* (“to whom belongs all honor”).]

then according to the preceding interpretation this Lamb of God, one year old, ought to be sacrificed, so that everything written concerning him might be fulfilled in him:

[Note: [Col. 0867C] The two Vatican manuscripts read *cujus est*. This doxology was very familiar to the Fathers, as we also noted above at the end of Sermon 1, especially to Antiochus the Monk. Tilmannus observes, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, vol. XII, p. 215, that Antiochus concluded all of his 130 homilies with the words εἰς τοῦ Θεοῦ δοξολογίαν (“to the glory of God”). The same can be affirmed of our Gaudentius, Cyril of Jerusalem, and many others.]

“To whom belongs all honor, power, and glory, with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now and always, and throughout all ages. Amen.”

## SERMON IV. ON THE FOURTH READING FROM EXODUS

[Col. 0867A] We have taught in three discourses about the observance of the carnal Jewish Passover, which is filled with spiritual types: once yesterday, and twice when addressing your charity during the vigils.

[Note: [Col. 0867C] So reads the Florentine manuscript and the Lyon edition. Eligius of Noyon likewise says in his fourteenth homily: “He wishes none of us to be considered excluded from this festival of the mystical Passover.” The other editions have *Judaicae paschae* (“of the Jewish Passover”). Vossius, however, *On Analogy* I.20, asserts that πάσχα is masculine in Hebrew and Chaldean, but neuter in Greek and Latin.]

We have clearly proved that the slaughter of flesh and blood, commanded figuratively, rightly ceased when Christ, the Lamb of God, arrived; for, according to the Apostle, he is “the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X).

For even the most blessed Paul, while he was still in Egypt,

[Note: [Col. 0867D] The Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts read *dum esset* (“while he was”), a reading also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

celebrated the Passover with the Jews according to the Jewish rite. “But after it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb,” he says, “and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood” (Gal. I).

[Note: [Col. 0867D] The Urbinate and two editions read *juxta priscam scribendi formam qua ad ante q retinebant* (“according to the ancient spelling in which *ad* was retained before *q*”), as Cellarius notes, *Orthography*, p. 29, Padua edition, 1724. The Lyon edition and three manuscripts read *acquievi* (“I submitted”). Varro, *On the Latin Language* V, has *adquirere*, from *ad* and *quaerere*; Aldus, in *Orthography*, has *adscisco*, not *ascisco*. Although the inscription on the cenotaph of Lucius Caesar reads *aspiciendi*, not *adspiciendi*, which certainly departs from the consensus of grammarians, Dausquius is criticized by Norisius, *Cenotaph of Pisa*, dissertation 4, chapter 6, p. 483, for defending that reading. *Adfligo*, *adgravo*, *adquiesco*, and similar forms are frequent in Salvianus’s books *On the Government of God*—unless this represents the copyists’ hand rather than the author’s authority, as Scaliger says in *On the Causes of the Latin Language* I.19.]

Therefore, since one to whom the Son of God has been revealed ought not to linger over carnal matters, let us seek the remaining parts of the spiritual mysteries set forth in the present reading.

“You shall take it from the sheep and the goats,” he says (Exod. XII).

From this the Jews should have understood that God’s Law must be interpreted spiritually, since they read that the lamb to be sacrificed was to be taken from sheep and goats, although nature makes this impossible: if it is a lamb, how can it be taken equally from sheep and goats?

But the entire meaning lies in the ambiguity of the expression: the immaculate Lamb, the Lord Jesus, deigned to assume from the Virgin the flesh both of the righteous and of sinners. For he assumed a body not only from the patriarchs and prophets but from the whole mass of the human race.

He himself declared in the Gospel that the righteous are compared with sheep and sinners with goats, saying that the sheep are to be called to the right:

[Note: [Col. 0868D] The two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate have *Venite, benedicti* (“Come, blessed ones”); the manuscript of Pantagathus agrees with them. The Florentine has *benedicti* (“blessed ones”), followed by *haedos a sinistris* (“goats on the left”).]

“Come, blessed ones,” he says (Matt. XXV);

while the goats are to be driven away to the left: “Depart, accursed ones.”

Thus, taken from sheep and goats, he was killed by the whole multitude of the assembly of the children of Israel, when they all cried out to Pilate: “Crucify him” (Matt. XXVII; John XIX).

According to the historical account of the legal Passover, however, the whole synagogue did not kill one lamb; rather, a few persons killed individual lambs in each household. But there the chief priests and elders persuaded the people to ask that the robber Barabbas be granted to them and that Jesus be destroyed.
