[Note: [Col. 0868D] So read the manuscripts and printed editions: *concedi latronem* (“that the robber be granted”).]

For they destroyed Christ the Savior, and they were judged out of their own mouth, so that the word of God might die among them—that is, the utterance of the Prophets, through whom he himself spoke.

And, as it is written in the Prophets, their wise men would fail, while that robber Barabbas, the devil, whom they had so insistently demanded, would live among them.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] Four manuscript copies read in this way. The manuscript of Pantagathus, however, has *Quod autem viveret* (“But that he would live”). I have not removed the common reading because of the agreement of the other manuscripts, although the latter form answers better to what he said earlier: *viveret vero in illis* (“while he would live among them”).]

That the seditious murderer lives among them is demonstrated by the uprisings they stirred up against the Apostles and which, whenever they find an opportunity, they do not cease to carry on even now against all the saints.

But Christ lives for us. For he rose for us, because he was no longer seen by the Jews; nor, after his resurrection, did he enter the synagogue of the Jews, but he entered among the assembled disciples (John XX; Luke XXIV).

[Note: [Col. 0868D] Thus read the manuscript copies and the printed editions. The editions have *ingreditur ad nos* (“he enters to us”).]

He also enters among us, who are assembled in the house of the Church, and he shows us the reality of his venerable body—provided, that is, that we have either deserved or are deserving of being his disciples.

For the blessed Apostles, to whom it was truly entrusted to prepare the Lord’s Passover in the upper rooms,

[Note: [Col. 0869B] Three manuscripts read *pascam Domino* (“I shall prepare the Passover for the Lord”), a reading also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus. The Urbinate has *pascha Domino* (“the Passover for the Lord”); a little farther below the two Vatican manuscripts have *pascae sacrificium* (“the sacrifice of the Passover”), while the manuscript of Pantagathus has *paschae sacrificium*.]

when they saw that only a few of the Jews in the house of the Church were insufficient to complete the sacrifice of the Passover, summoned their neighboring Gentiles, according to what had been commanded in the Law:

“But if there are few in the household,” he says, “so that they are not sufficient for a sheep, the neighbor shall take with him his nearest neighbor,” and so forth (Exod. XII);

for they truly were not sufficient for him who endured death for the sins of the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Four manuscripts, as well as the manuscript of Pantagathus, read *pro totius mundi vita* (“for the life of the whole world”), which certainly accords better with Gaudentius’s elegance.]

For only a few of the Jews believed in the Lord Jesus. Hence the Apostle says:

“So also at the present time”—

there is no doubt that, just as in the time of Elijah, when God said to him, “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings XIX)—

“so also at the present time, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI),

namely, from the Jewish people. For out of so great a multitude scarcely a few are found to have been converted to faith in Christ.

Therefore the prophet Isaiah also bears witness concerning these remnants of the Lord and the mercy of God, saying:

“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I).

You, therefore, newly baptized, who have been invited to the banquet of this blessed and spiritual Passover, see to it that you preserve your souls from every pollution of foods infected by pagan superstition.

Nor is it enough for a Christian to guard his life from the deadly food of demons; he must also flee every abomination of the Gentiles and every path of idolatry, as though they were certain poisons of the serpent, the devil.

For parts of idolatry are sorcery,

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Incantations were customarily employed in sorcery. Quintilian, *Declamations* 14: “Poison mixed with dreadful songs and the terror of deadly incantations”; and Solinus, chapter 30, concerning Africa: “An herb consecrated by legitimate incantations.” Hence *praecantatrix* (“female incantress”) in Plautus, *Miles Gloriosus*, Act III, Scene 1, line 98.]

incantations,

[Note: [Col. 0869C] Virgil, *Pharmaceutria*:

“Bind, Amaryllis, three colors with three knots;

Bind them, Amaryllis, now, and say, ‘I bind the bonds of Venus.’”]

The subligatures that Gaudentius here calls *alligatures*. Philastrius says in chapter 21: “They carried and carry on their breast alligatures and protective charms.” Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II.20, calls them *ligaturae*: “To this category also belong all ligatures, and remedies which even the medical profession condemns, whether in incantations or in certain signs which they call characters”; and in *Tractate 7 on John*: “When your head aches, we approve if you place the Gospel on your head, and do not run to an amulet.”

Subligatures, vanities, omens, lots, the observance of all things (*observatio omnium*; presumably “of omens,” *ominum*), funeral rites—I mean those practices from which the evil of idolatry raised the head of its error. For people first began, for the sake of their own appetites, to prepare meals for the dead, which they themselves would eat; then they also dared to celebrate sacrilegious sacrifices for them, although those who observe funeral rites do not themselves offer a sacrificial gift to their dead.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] Florentinus reads *observatio hominum*, where without doubt *ominum* should be read; the aspiration was wrongly added by an unskilled copyist, and the same error also occurs in Octavius Pantagathus’s manuscript. Earlier printed editions had read, rather ineptly, *observatio omnium* (“the observance of all things”), a form of expression wholly unworthy of Gaudentius’s style. This was the received reading that had hitherto been imposed upon us; but likewise *omnibus* is corruptly found for *ominibus* even in the excellent edition of Livy prepared from Daniel Heinsius’s recension and printed at Amsterdam by the Elzevirs in 1634. There, in the preface to Book I, p. 5, we read *cum bonis potius omnibus* (“with all good things”) instead of *cum bonis potius ominibus* (“with rather favorable omens”). Likewise, in the Amsterdam edition of Einhard, edited by Johann Hermann Schminkius in 1711, *superiora omnia* (“all the foregoing things”) is printed by typographical error for *superiora omina* (“the foregoing omens”); Schminkius adds in the errata: “Read *omina*, for these two words are very frequently confused with one another.” Victorius and Lambinus judged that Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IV.4, where we read, “Caesar, having praised your honor and fairness most highly, and your prudence, suddenly said that, when the Senate was pleading concerning Marcellus, he would not refuse even on account of the man,” should instead read, “not refuse even on account of the omen.” But, as Gebhard thought, this was more ingenious than true; therefore the Graevian edition, and likewise Cellarius’s Leipzig edition of 1708, still retain the earlier reading, “not even on account of the man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0870C] The days and festivals of the dead. Jerome, *Commentary on Jeremiah*, Book III, chapter 16: “It is customary for mourners to bring food and prepare a banquet, which the Greeks call *perideipna* (περίδειπνα), and which among us are commonly called *parentalia*, because rites are performed for parents.” They are called *charistia* in Ovid, *Fasti* II, and *parentalia* in Ausonius, in the *Book of Parental Rites*. See Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities* IV.9.]

For the sake of their appetites they first began to prepare meals for the dead, which they themselves would eat; after that they also dared to celebrate sacrilegious sacrifices for them,

[Note: [Col. 0870C] Augustine, *Against Faustus* XXII.17: “The transgressing angels, whose two greatest vices are pride and deceit, demanded from their worshipers what they knew was owed to the one true God; they wanted to be considered gods, with the vanity of the human heart granting them the opportunity—especially when images were made out of longing for the dead, and divine honors were paid with greater flattery to those received, as it were, into heaven, in whose place they offered themselves on earth as demons to be worshiped, and demanded that sacrifices be made to them by the deceived and ruined.” Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “Our ancestors, imprudent, credulous, and marked by an unformed simplicity, while they religiously worshiped their kings, while they desired to see them after death in images, while they delighted to preserve their likenesses in statues, made sacred observances out of what had been adopted as consolations.” Compare Wisdom chapter 14.]

although those who observe funeral rites do not themselves offer a sacrificial gift to their dead,

[Note: [Col. 0870D] This passage was entirely corrupt; the Vatican manuscripts supplied its correction. The printed editions read: “although they themselves sacrifice no less to their dead in the funeral rites,” an enigma that not even an Oedipus could understand. The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts read: “although they themselves offer no less sacrifice, who perform the funeral rites,” as does the manuscript of Pantagathus. This is not entirely correct. We have therefore faithfully reproduced the reading of both Vatican manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0870D] We learn from Augustine, *Sermon 15 on the Saints*, that this pagan custom had become especially prevalent on the feast of the Chair of St. Peter. Speaking of that day, he says: “Although devout observance has rightly introduced this solemnity into the churches, I wonder why so pernicious an error has today increased among some unbelievers that they bring food and wine to the tombs of the dead, as though souls departed from their bodies required bodily food.” These meals of the dead were called *silicernia*; hence Tertullian, *Apology* 13: “How does a *silicernium* differ from Jupiter’s feast?” See also, if you wish, Servius on *Aeneid* V, “*Libavitque dapes*”; Joseph Scaliger’s emendations to Festus; the learned notes on Terence, *Adelphoe* IV, scene II; and what the distinguished Johannes Antonius Vulpius has set forth on Catullus, poem LIX.3.]

while, upon the tables of the tombs, they pour wine with hands trembling from drunkenness,

[Note: [Col. 0871C] This passage was very badly handled not only in the printed editions but also in the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “pouring wine, they stammer the spirit.” Horace appropriately used *balbutire scaurum* (“to stammer the letter s”) in *Satires* I.3; but what it would mean to “stammer the spirit,” I cannot understand. The two Vatican manuscripts read, “they stammer the spirit from thirst.” The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts read, “they stammer the spirit again from thirst,” where it is clear that a copyist made the syllable *re* the end of the preceding word and the beginning of the following one. Accordingly, with the support of the two manuscripts and a modest conjecture, we have restored: “they stammer that their breath thirsts.” The manuscript that once belonged to Octavius Pantagathus agrees with the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts; in this passage the two Vatican manuscripts prove superior.]

they stammer that their breath thirsts.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Gaudentius derived this from the teaching of Ambrose, who had forbidden porridge, bread, and unmixed wine to be brought to the memorials of the saints, as Augustine testifies in *Confessions* VI.2. Hence Gaudentius adds shortly afterward: “Be sober in all things; gather diligently in the church.” Augustine himself, in the same sermon 15: “Someone says that he is preparing for his loved ones what he himself devours; what he gives to his belly he attributes to devotion.” And shortly afterward: “Cease, therefore, brothers, from this pagan error of unbelief”; and again: “The souls of our brothers and parents are not at all delighted by bodily foods.” They can be offended by these rather than delighted.]

Beware, I beg you, of all these things, lest God, angered against those who despise and oppose him, who refused to have him reign over them, hand them over to the torturers of hell. “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII; Luke XIII).

Preserve, neophytes, the adornment of saving grace. Be sober in all things, lest you lose it when drunk. Gather diligently in the church. Apply yourselves with us, watchfully, to prayers, hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs. Let these be the works of your leisure; by rendering through them the service owed to Christ the Lord, may you receive from him the reward of eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] On the moderation and frugality of the banquets of the ancient Christians, see Minucius Felix, *Octavius*: “We cultivate banquets that are not only chaste but also sober; for we do not indulge in feasts, nor do we conduct a banquet with unmixed wine, but we temper cheerfulness with seriousness.” On the public and private banquets of the ancient Christians, see further Elmenhorstius, notes on Minucius Felix, p. 308.]

Let your banquets, therefore, be sober and your beds chaste; let your mind be modest, your speech tranquil, and your gait gentle. Pray that God may preserve in you the benefits of his grace, and that your faith may advance more and more, through the generosity of Christ the Lord and Savior, whose power and divinity are one and the same with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, before all things, now, always, and throughout all ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. THE FIFTH ON THE READING FROM EXODUS

255. We have deliberately postponed the order of the reading from Exodus, in which the law concerning the celebration of Passover is described,

[Note: [Col. 0872B] The Florentine, Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts read “the celebration of Passover,” a reading supported by the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

so that, in opening up the mysteries, we might preserve the proper order of reverence.

[Note: [Col. 0872B] The printed editions ineptly read “so that the mysteries might be reserved.” The two Vatican manuscripts read “so that the mysteries might be revealed.” The preposition *in* is supplied by the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts; it is also supplied by the manuscript of Pantagathus, though shortly afterward it agrees with the printed editions in reading “in the mysteries being reserved.”]

For it was necessary,

[Note: [Col. 0872C] He calls it “most splendid” because the ancient Christians used to celebrate it with torches and fires. Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 2 on Easter*, translated by J. Billius: “Indeed, splendid for us was yesterday’s festival of brightness and lights, which we celebrated both privately and publicly, with nearly every kind of person and all who were distinguished by office and rank, illuminating the night with abundant fire.” On this passage Nicetas comments: “Splendid also was yesterday’s celebration of lights—that is, the gathering held toward evening on the Great Sabbath. For they passed the vigil through the seventh hour, singing, lighting lamps, and awaiting the imminent resurrection of our Savior.” Likewise Zeno of Verona, *Sermon 1 to the Neophytes*: “After the most devout, chaste fasts of sacred purification had been completed, after the sweetest vigils of the brightest night had passed beneath their own sun.” On the night of the vigils, see what we noted above in Tractate 1, p. 231.]

that on that most splendid night of vigils, in the second treatise, not the continuation of what had been said but what was appropriate for neophytes should be explained, so that inexperienced neophytes might learn the discipline of eating the paschal sacrifice, while the instructed faithful might recognize it. Along with these matters I also discussed one aspect of the clothing of those who eat, suited to the occasion, while reserving two aspects both for them and for the catechumens. For he says:

“Thus you shall eat it”—that is, the lamb—

[Note: [Col. 0872D] The Lyon edition adds *erunt* (“shall be”); the manuscript of Pantagathus reads, “Let your loins be girded.”]

“with your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands” (Exod. XII).

Then we spoke about the girding of the loins; now let us explain the sandals and the staffs. These matters are proposed today because on the following and the third day it will be necessary to explain those points from the beginning of the reading that I deliberately passed over earlier. The true Lamb of God, whom John the Baptist points out, is Christ. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). We ought to eat his flesh, both the faithful in the mystery

[Note: [Col. 0872D] That is, in the sacrament. Among the ancient Fathers, *sacramentum* and *mysterium* signify the same thing; many further examples could be given. Zeno of Verona, *Sermon 1 on Abraham*: “Let him hasten at last to complete the sacrifice; let delay not make sin; he is prepared by the necessary sacraments.” What he here calls “sacraments,” shortly afterward he calls “mysteries”; thus he makes the two terms synonymous. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]

and all believers together in faith, and we must entrust him to the innermost parts of our heart,

[Note: [Col. 0872D] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads “to store him in the inner parts”; the manuscript of Pantagathus reads “to commend him to the inner parts.”]

so that we may have not only our loins girded with chastity

[Note: [Col. 0872D] This is how the Paris edition and the manuscript copies read. Two editions read *cinctos* (“girded”) instead.]

but also be shod, as the Apostle says, “in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). For just as earthly sandals are protections for bodily feet, resisting either the harshness of cold, or the bite of serpents,

or the piercing points of thorns, so the precepts of the divine Law, by which we are commanded to fortify the steps of our minds, resist both the serpent the devil, the most bitter North Wind of the Gentiles, and the thorns and thistles of heretics who prick from every side. We who celebrate the Lord’s Passover must therefore use sandals of this kind. Since, as the Apostle says, “the Law is spiritual” (Rom. VII), and “our Passover has been sacrificed, Christ” (I Cor. V), our loins must be girded and our feet shod.

For what benefit is it to a person to possess bodily chastity alone, if, unwary and without the protection of the sandals of the Law, he becomes subject to the evils mentioned above, or, as happens daily, exposes the heel of his heart to be eaten by serpents?

[Note: [Col. 0873C] The Lyon edition reads this incorrectly, without grammatical construction.]

If he thinks evil, if he covets what belongs to others,

[Note: [Col. 0873C] So read the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts. The printed editions omit *si* (“if”), though the particle is also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

if he plots deceit, if he nourishes anger, if he lies in wait for his neighbor, if he devotes himself to lying, if envy consumes him, if he wastes away in jealousy, if with a poisoned mouth he slanders the good; and while he tries to tear the innocent with the dart of a lying tongue,

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Three manuscripts read “with the darts of the tongue”; this reading is also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

may he himself instead be mangled by the bites of demons who speak through him?

What good did it do you to have your loins girded, if, failing to keep the sandals of the divine commandments, you have handed over the steps of your heart—that is, the foundations of your soul—to the most savage cutting apart?

Some may perhaps think it contradictory that, although God here commands us so emphatically to be shod, elsewhere the same Lord God commands holy Moses and

[Note: [Col. 0873C] Three manuscripts read “holy Jesus son of Nave,” and the manuscript of Pantagathus agrees with them. Perhaps Gaudentius wrote it in this form; but the ignorance of the copyists, who did not know that the holy Joshua was also called by this name, preferred the more familiar designation. Ecclesiasticus XLVI: “Jesus son of Nave, strong in war, successor of Moses.” Jerome, on Matthew II: “Read the book of Jesus son of Nave.” Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.11: “Jesus son of Nave succeeded Moses.” Philastrius, chapter 17: “Both Josiah and Jesus son of Nave”; and chapter 27: “After the death of Moses and the succession of Jesus son of Nave.” Gaudentius himself, Tractate 11: “Son of Nave.”]

holy Joshua: “Remove the sandals from your feet” (Exod. III; Josh. V).

There is indeed a profound reason for this, and it must be laid out through the winding paths of many propositions; but because brevity is suitable both to the labor of the preacher and to the memory of the hearer, I do not wish to draw you out at greater length. The question is resolved where the sandals are removed, when the reason is immediately added: “Remove,” he says, “the sandals from your feet; for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III; Josh. V).

It is therefore shown that the land of Egypt, where that earlier command is given, is not holy, and for that reason sandals are commanded to be worn there; but in the holy land they are ordered to be removed. The reasons for this, however, must be explained clearly.

As long as we live in the Egypt of this world, we who celebrate the Lord’s Passover must use the sandals of the Holy Scriptures, because our step cannot be secure unless it is covered by the Lord’s commandments, until we enter that holy land of promise which has been prepared for the righteous. For, says the Lord Jesus, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. V)—not, of course, this land possessed by sinners, but that land in which there are no thorns or thistles, no serpents or scorpions, since the devil and the other unclean spirits do not approach there.

For then he and his followers will be in the eternal fire that God prepared especially for the devil

[Note: [Col. 0873D] The Florentine, Urbinate, and manuscript of Pantagathus read “especially for the devil himself.” The two Vatican manuscripts read “the Lord, especially for the devil himself.”]

and his angels (Matt. XXV).

We also have John the Baptist, who said of the Savior of the human race, the Lord Jesus: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen the strap of his sandals” (John I).

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Three manuscript copies read: “We also have Saint John the Baptist saying.”]

But Christ is different. He was shod not for his own sake but for ours, because the earth could not bear the naked footprints of his majesty. When he speaks of sandals, he indicates the steps of the Holy Scriptures, by which he walks and circulates his knowledge among all who dwell upon the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] This is how three manuscript copies and the Paris edition read. The other two editions do not have *ejus* (“his”), though the word is also retained in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

And therefore John the Baptist denies in the Gospel that he is either capable or worthy to loosen the strap of his sandals—that is, his discourse; whether in order to expound one of his commandments, or to strip bare and clearly display

[Note: [Col. 0874C] This expression is frequent among the Fathers, who called the Word of God, clothed in flesh, “shod.” Ambrose, *Sermon 17 on Psalm 118*, Froben edition, vol. IV, p. 725: “By the thigh we recognize the sign of generation, according to the words, ‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one’; this signifies that the Son of God, when he emptied himself, girded with the divinity of the Word and shod with human generation, came forth from the Virgin to grant salvation to all.” Gregory, *Homily 7 on the Gospels*: “The incarnate Lord appeared as he came, as though shod, because in his divinity he assumed the deadness of our corruption.” And shortly afterward: “The Lord declares that he will extend his sandal into Idumea, because, when he became known to the Gentiles through the flesh, the divinity came to us as though shod.”]

the venerable footprints of the Word of God, which are still shod in this present age. “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” he says, “but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII); where nothing will remain hidden that will not be revealed, nor concealed that will not be known (Matt. X), when the Lord Jesus comes to that future feast (John VII), and “will ascend,” not “as though in secret,” as among unbelievers,

[Note: [Col. 0874D] We have corrected this on the authority of the Urbinate and both Vatican manuscripts. The Florentine reads, “because he will ascend in secret.” The printed editions corruptly read, “because he ascended in secret.” The manuscript of Pantagathus reads, “as though he will ascend in secret.” It therefore differs here from the Florentine, above from the Vatican manuscripts, and elsewhere from the Urbinate; consequently, this reading cannot have been taken from any one of those manuscripts, with which it so often disagrees.]

but as it is written: “God will come openly, and our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. XLIX).

For this reason, in another place the Apostles are forbidden in the Gospels to carry sandals on the road, when the Lord says to them in Matthew’s Gospel: “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts, nor a bag on the road,

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Three manuscripts add, “nor have two tunics,” a phrase also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus; but it is absent from the Vulgate and does not occur in the Greek of Matthew, which has no *ἔχοιτε* (“you may have”).]

nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; for the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Matt. X).

Elsewhere, however, they are commanded to have them, as the evangelist Mark describes: “And Jesus went around the villages teaching. And having summoned the twelve, he sent them two by two, giving them authority to drive out unclean spirits; and he commanded them to take nothing with them on the road except a staff: no bag, no bread, and no coins in their belts, but, he says, to be shod with *caligulae*,

[Note: [Col. 0875C] The two Vatican manuscripts read *calciatos caligulis* (“shod with little boots”), as does the manuscript of Pantagathus. The Florentine reads *galligulas*, where *g* appears to have been placed for *c* at the beginning of the word. Nevertheless, Julius Nigronius clearly demonstrated that *gallica* was a kind of footwear designed to protect the feet, more suitable for travel than for the city, in *On the Caliga of the Ancients*, chapter 2, §17; in §18 he also cites this passage of Gaudentius. In Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*, *gallica* and *gallicula* are found for *caliga* and *caligula*. *Caligula*, a small *caliga*, was an ancient type of sandal said to rise to mid-shin; Gaius Caesar, son of Germanicus, took his name from its use. See Vossius, *On the Vices of Speech* I.29.]

and not to put on two tunics” (Mark VI).

For the sake of unbelievers and people of little faith, the Apostles are commanded to have sandals on the road of preaching, so that they may preach the Word of God shod and covered in mystery, because of the thorns and thistles of blasphemers. But to those who listen with a faithful mind, as though already in the holy land—perfect in heart and faith, where they could safely proclaim bare testimonies about God—they are commanded not to carry sandals, so that there they may set forth the footprints of his divinity openly.

And therefore blessed Peter shod himself in the prison with his sandals

[Note: [Col. 0875C] The Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts read “his sandals.” The Urbinate and the manuscript of Pantagathus do also.]

(Acts XII), and so he went out again against the Jewish enemies and opposing powers, so that, with his feet shod “in the preparation of the Gospel,” he might tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy (Luke X).

And Moses says in the blessings, either to each individual believer or rather to the person of Christ: “Iron and bronze shall be your sandal” (Deut. XXXIII)—certainly so that he may crush

[Note: [Col. 0875C] The two Vatican manuscripts read *utique ut confringat* (“certainly, that he may crush”).]

the heads of dragons over the waters—that is, so that he may crush the dominions of the dragon-demons who are over the waters of the Gentile peoples. That waters are compared with peoples and Gentiles is revealed in the Apocalypse of John:

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The two Vatican manuscripts read “is revealed to John”; the Florentine, “is revealed by John”; the manuscript of Pantagathus, “is revealed by John.” Whether an aspiration should be written before the third letter of this word will be determined by the distinguished Cellarius, *Orthography of Latin*, p. 43, Padua edition, 1724.]

“The waters,” he says, “which you saw, where the prostitute Babylon sits, are peoples and nations” (Rev. XVII).

I also need a staff while I am still celebrating Passover in Egypt,

[Note: [Col. 0875D] In addition to what we said about the staff in the preface to Gaudentius, no. 10, several things should be noted here about its antiquity and use. First, its antiquity is commended not only by this distinguished passage of Gaudentius but also by another passage in the *Life of Caesarius of Arles* in Mabillon, *First Section of the Benedictine Acts*, for August 27, Book II, no. 17: “The cleric whose duty it was to carry his staff”; and in the *Life of Saint Burchard* in Surius, October 14, chapter 1: “It is clear how much more precious before him who regards the lowly and knows the lofty from afar is Pastor Burchard with his pastoral staff than modern shepherds, who, while feeding themselves, scarcely lack some display even in their staffs.” Isidore describes its form, chapter 219; its use as a sign of correction toward subjects is indicated here by Gaudentius: “But if the wolf ceases to be a wolf and feeds with the lamb, and if the lion, ceasing to be a lion, eats straw with the ox, there is no need of a staff.” And shortly afterward: “Christ says to each of the apostolic priests that they should not carry staffs of correction on the road when, in obedient and modest disciples, they have already begun to possess the holy land.” Isidore likewise, *On Ecclesiastical Offices* II.5, on the ordination of a bishop: “When he is consecrated, a staff is given to him, so that by its indication he may rule or correct the people subject to him, or support the weaknesses of the weak.” Thomassin, Part I, Book II, chapter 58, and Macrius, *Hierolexicon*, under *Baculus*, will provide more; yet neither recognized this splendid passage of Gaudentius.]

so that, if I am an imitator of my holy Moses,

[Note: [Col. 0876C] *Moysis* had wrongly entered the earlier edition in place of *Moysi*, which the old copies have and which must certainly be retained according to the ancient practice of using the second-declension form in the genitive—for example, *Ulyssi* and *Achilli* for *Ulyssis* and *Achillis*. On this see Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar* IV.9, and the other authorities cited by the distinguished Fabricius in his notes on Philastrius, p. 19 of the Hamburg edition, and p. 7 of the present work.]

my Hebrew—meaning my Israelite understanding, which was deemed worthy to see God—I may rescue him from destruction by striking down the Egyptian.

Everyone needs this for himself,

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Understand: “needs this work,” as is clear from what follows.]

as long as he serves the Law. But if someone is apostolic, and, after the Egyptian has been overthrown through Jesus, has become great and powerful, he no longer carries a staff for himself,

[Note: [Col. 0876D] The manuscripts read, “he carries a staff if he carries one”; these final words are absent from the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

but for those to whom it is necessary to say: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV).

He carries it also for those who come to us in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matt. VII). But if the wolf ceases to be a wolf and feeds with the lamb, as the Prophet says (Isa. XI), and if the lion, ceasing to be a lion, eats straw with the ox, there is no need of a staff.

For if the wickedness of savage behavior is transformed into such gentleness that, together with the innocent and pure little sheep, the workers of Christ, the gentle seek and receive the nourishment of life, and are such as ought to be instructed to perfection in love and a spirit of gentleness,

[Note: [Col. 0876D] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions incorrectly have “such indeed are.”]

Christ says to each of the apostolic priests (Matt. X) that they should not carry staffs of correction on the road when, in obedient and modest disciples, they have already begun to possess the holy land.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] The Lyon and Cologne editions corruptly read *corruptionum* (“of corruptions”). The Paris edition and the two Vatican manuscripts read *correptionum* (“of corrections”), a reading also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

May the Savior of the human race, God the Lord Jesus, grant this concerning you to my humble self,

[Note: [Col. 0876D] This is how I read it in the Urbinate and the two Vatican manuscripts. Three editions incorrectly read “to my faintheartedness”; the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus also prefers “to my weakness.”] To him belong one divinity and the same omnipotence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, before all things, now, always, and throughout all ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. THE SIXTH ON THE READING FROM EXODUS
By as much as God the Father has deigned to reveal through his power and Spirit, according to the measure of our strength; by as much as the coequal omnipotence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has granted; by as much as the one and same divinity of the everlasting and unoriginated Trinity has inspired, we have opened up for your love, from the first vigils of Easter until this day, [p. 260] what was the significance of the name of the book of Exodus; what was the power of Passover, whose observance is first decreed there; and why this month in which God commands this to be observed is called the first among the months of the year; what Egypt was; what that tenth or fourteenth day signified; what the lamb of sacrifice was, and why it was to be taken from sheep and goats; what the day’s evening was, what that threshold was, who those doorposts were, and who that blood was; and for what reason they were commanded to eat neither raw flesh nor flesh cooked in water, but flesh roasted by fire, and to eat hurriedly the head with the feet and entrails; what bone was not to be broken from it, what burning of the leftovers was required, and what mystery was represented either in the footwear of the feet, or in the staffs of the hands, or in the girding of the loins.

[Note: Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts read: “by as much as the one and same divinity of the everlasting and unoriginated Trinity inspired.” The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus agrees with this reading; and at the beginning of the sermon, in place of “by as much as God the Father,” it has, by Pantagathus’s correction, “by as much as the powerful God.” The printed editions, moreover, read here: “by as much as the everlasting and unoriginated Trinity inspired.”]

[Note: Thus three manuscripts read it. The editions, however, have “and what observance was there”; shortly afterward, in place of “this month,” the manuscript of Pantagathus reads “that very month.”]

[Note: Thus in three manuscripts. The editions incorrectly read “what Egypt was for the Egyptians”; in the book of Pantagathus: “what Egypt was.”]

[Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts reads “the lamb to be sacrificed.” The book of Pantagathus has “the lamb of sacrifice”; shortly afterward, in place of “what were those doorposts,” it reads “who were those doorposts.”]

[Note: Thus three manuscripts read. The editions have “what those doorposts.”]

[Note: The Florentine manuscript reads “or in the staffs.” The Urbinate manuscript and the manuscript of Pantagathus do likewise.]

It remains for us to discuss the striking down of the firstborn of Egypt, the unleavened bread with bitterness, and the seven days of unleavened bread.

“I shall pass through the land of Egypt on this night, and I shall strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man to beast; and against all the gods of the Egyptians I shall execute vengeance: I am the Lord. And the blood shall be for you as a sign in the houses in which you shall be there; and I shall see the blood and protect you; and there shall not be among you a wound of destruction when I strike Egypt. And this day shall be for you as a memorial” (Exod. XII).

[Note: We have added a particle from the manuscripts which the printed editions lack.]

[Note: Three manuscripts and the book of Pantagathus have “every firstborn.”]

At that time, on that night, God did indeed strike all the firstborn of the Egyptians, just as he had threatened Pharaoh through Moses, when Pharaoh refused to release the people of Israel—whom the same Lord graciously deigned to call his firstborn son.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “He did indeed strike, at that time on that night, the firstborn.” The Urbinate manuscript agrees, but instead of *primonatos* has *priminatos*, as does the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus.]

[Note: Three manuscripts read “when he was unwilling.”]

When the Egyptians, stunned by the slaughter of so many sudden deaths, expelled the Israelites in the middle of the night—the Israelites whom they had previously refused to release as captives—then much greater things were accomplished by this same God for our people against the true Egyptians, and what then occurred figuratively has been fulfilled in us. Therefore, mindful of our redemption, we ought not to conceal his gifts of mercy in ungrateful silence.

On the day when the Lamb of God, the Lord Jesus, was sacrificed, toward evening—for darkness was already approaching, and immediately after he had been crucified it covered the whole earth [Matt. XXVII]—on the night of that day he struck the firstborn of the Egyptian demons, that is, the images of dead human beings, which they themselves had first fashioned in this world in order to be worshiped through them.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate read “which covered”; the Florentine, “which had covered.”]

But when the text adds, “Against all the gods of the Egyptians I shall execute vengeance” (Exod. XII), perhaps you will say: Who are these gods of the Egyptians, if the demons whom the pagans consider gods are themselves the Egyptians?

[Note: All of this was lacking in the printed editions. It is nevertheless credible that the words were omitted by a copyist, since they occur in four manuscripts and are also recognized by the book of Octavius Pantagathus. Both the agreement of the manuscripts and the entire context of Gaudentius’s argument therefore advised restoring them to their proper place.]

Listen, then: not only are the demons Egyptians, but also all their worshipers who persist obstinately in unbelief are Egyptians, since they are sons of darkness: by nature they are sons of the Egyptians, and are sons of demons.

[Note: The manuscript of Pantagathus alone commands that this be restored; it alone has the true reading here. The printed editions, with no intelligible sense, read: “because the sons of the Egyptians are sons of demons.” But once the word “by nature” is removed, who could grasp Gaudentius’s meaning? It also seems that shortly before, instead of *quicumque*, one should read *qui cum*, so that the sense is complete. The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts, in place of “by nature sons of the Egyptians,” read “for they are sons of the Egyptians”; but this too confirms the correction by the copyist’s ineptitude.]

Hence it is said to all unbelievers: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII). For just as all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, according to the teaching of the apostle Paul (Rom. VIII), so all who are led astray by the spirit of the devil are sons of demons.

Divine Scripture therefore calls the devil and his army Egyptians, because, by rebelling against their own Creator, they are estranged from God, who is light. For the holy Apostle says: “What wonder, if Satan transforms himself into an angel of light?” (II Cor. XI).

[Note: The manuscripts have “as an angel of light.”]

In this way he proves that Satan is an angel of darkness, though he attempts to display himself as if he were an angel of light, so as to deceive. By a similar reasoning, all unbelievers who oppose God and are deprived of the light of his divinity are called Egyptians. Yet the Lord himself urges them toward salvation, saying: “While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light” (John XII).

[Note: The agreement of the manuscripts shows that this should be read in place of the wording found in the editions, “the faith of the will.” The manuscript of Pantagathus also rejects that reading and prefers “voluntary faith.”]

Therefore, if voluntary faith can make them sons of light, their being sons of darkness is a fault of the will, not of nature.

On the night, then, when the Son of God, leaving his lifeless body upon the cross, passed with his soul into lower Egypt, in order to visit the souls placed in hell, he executed vengeance upon all the unclean spirits, the gods of the Egyptians, destroying in their firstborn the powers of their dominion.

For, near the time of his Passion, the Lord Jesus says: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world is cast out. And I, when I have been lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

[Note: Three manuscripts and the book of Pantagathus have “when I have been lifted up from the earth.”]

The Lord Jesus therefore recalled to himself all his creation, which the most wicked usurpers had subjected to themselves through a rebellious spirit of divinity, so that all things might be subject to the rule of him through whom all things were made.

[Note: Three manuscript copies have “the most wicked usurpers.”]

He protected—and will protect—those who believe in him from the wound of destruction through the sign of his cross, when it is said: “And the blood shall be for you as a sign in the houses: you shall be there; and I shall see the blood and protect you” (Exod. XII).

[Note: Four manuscripts have “he protects,” a reading supported by the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

[Note: The Florentine, Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts read: “in the houses in which you shall be”; the manuscript of Pantagathus has the same reading, which is supported by the Vulgate.]

Before we pass on to the other matters that follow, however, we must ask how he can say, “I shall protect you,” as though from another destroyer, and then Moses says: “The Lord will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and he will see the blood on the threshold and on both doorposts, and he will pass over the door” (Exod. XII).

What, then, is the meaning? Did the Lord pass through to strike the Egyptians by the hand of the destroyer? Far from it. For shortly afterward he says: “He will not permit the destroyer to enter your houses.” If he himself struck them, how can it be said that he will not permit the destroyer to enter?

Therefore, attentive reader, consider carefully in the text of the reading itself that where it says “the Egyptians are struck,” it does not say “by the destroyer”; but where it says that the Hebrews are to be protected, it says not “by the one who struck the Egyptians,” but “from the destroyer.”

[Note: Three manuscripts read “the Egyptians are to be struck.” The book of Pantagathus also has “the Egyptians are to be struck,” rather than the reading of the editions, “I shall strike the Egyptians.”]

[Note: The Urbinate manuscript and the Lyon edition have “by the destroyer,” as does the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

The destroyer, however, does not strike the Egyptians, whose friend and prince he is; for, as the Lord says in the Gospel of the most blessed Mark, if “Satan has risen against himself,” he is divided and cannot stand; he cannot do this, or his end has come (Mark III).

[Note: Thus the printed editions. In four manuscripts and the book of Pantagathus: “He is divided, he says; he cannot stand; his end has come.”]

But, dearly beloved, the destroyer does wish to strike the Hebrews, while God strikes the Egyptians. For he is plotting retaliation against the servants of God, indignant that his own satellites have been struck by God; for the devil is then most inflamed when he is being extinguished.

At that time he rages against God’s servants, when his first power is slain in the firstborn, while God destroys from among us either idolatry, or superstition, or the other chief errors of the demons.

[Note: The manuscripts again have “in the firstborn”; shortly afterward, the Florentine and Urbinate, in place of “either idolatry or superstition,” read “either the superstition of idolatry.” The book of Pantagathus has “the superstition of idolatry.”]

For that most wicked one is imagined as murmuring against God: “You are striking my Egyptians on account of your Hebrews, and I, on account of my Egyptians, will pursue and kill your Hebrews.”

[Note: Thus the manuscript copies read. The editions, however, have “on account of the Egyptians.” This Gaudentian interpretation seems to conflict with Wisdom XVIII.15–16, where the destroyer appears to have been sent by God to strike the Egyptians: “Your all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from the royal throne, a stern warrior, into the midst of the land of destruction.” The one who destroyed those murmuring against the Lord in the wilderness is likewise called the destroyer. Judith VIII.25: “Those who uttered the reproach of their murmuring against the Lord were destroyed by the destroyer.” And I Cor. X: “As some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.”]

For the enemy said: “I shall pursue and seize the spoils; I shall fill my soul; I shall kill with my sword; my hand shall rule” (Exod. XV.9).

[Note: Thus the printed editions. The Florentine, Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts have “I shall divide the spoil,” a reading also found in the book of Pantagathus. Gaudentius likewise has “I shall divide the spoil” in tractate 12. The Vulgate and the Septuagint read “I shall divide the spoils.”]

But his threat is frustrated if we earnestly obey the Lord’s command, by which he warned that we can be kept safe.

[Note: We have corrected this passage on the authority of the Urbinate and Vatican manuscripts. The Paris edition reads incorrectly “I warned you”; the Cologne edition, worse, “I warned you gravely”; the Lyon edition, most badly, “I warned you, that we might perish gravely.” The manuscript copies agree with the book of Octavius Pantagathus.]

For it is added: “And you shall keep this ordinance as a statute for yourself and for your sons forever” (Exod. XII.24)—namely, that we should always be zealous to celebrate the Lord’s Passover according to the ordinance, and vigilantly do the things commanded to us, lest through our contempt or negligence the destroyer find an opportunity to rage, when the protection of God our protector has ceased.

Let each one of us, then, be on the Lord’s side, the Lord who struck the Egyptians; let him be an Israelite, always contemplating God in his mind, so that he may be protected from the destroyer’s wound.

Let him—or rather, let us—have on both doorposts, that is, in the heart and in the mouth, the saving Passion of the Lord. How? As the Apostle teaches: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

Let us also have on the threshold of the forehead the sign of the Lamb’s blood, so that God may not permit the destroyer to enter among us. For this did not happen only then, either in the history of the Law or at the time of the Lord Jesus’ cross; even now, always, God the avenger of his people strikes the Egyptians.

Always the destroyer, the devil, attempts to enter the houses of the Israelites, desiring to kill them; always the Son of God watches over his own and protects them wherever he recognizes the sign of his Passion.

To him be glory with the Father and with the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII: SEVENTH SERMON ON THE READING FROM EXODUS

Yesterday we said that, after the stronger portions of the Passover commandments had been discussed, three further topics remained from the proposed reading of Exodus. We have already interpreted the first of them—the killing of Egypt’s firstborn—as best we could. Now, with the Lord’s grace supplying abundance, we propose to explain the two remaining topics: the prohibition of leaven and the seven days of unleavened bread.

“For seven days,” he says, “you shall eat unleavened bread; but from the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread from the first day to the seventh day, that soul shall perish from Israel” (Exod. XII).

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “the leaven shall be exterminated.” In the Jewish calendar, on the fourteenth day of the month Abib, or Nisan: Passover, the removal of leaven. This removal had four stages: the cleansing of leaven, the search for leaven, the removal of leaven, and the execration of leaven. See Buxtorf, *Synagoga Judaica*, chapter 17.]

[Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts, and likewise the Florentine, read “may he perish”; the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus reads “let that soul perish.” This punishment is the same as that which the Lord threatened against those neglecting circumcision in Gen. XVII, and it is called the cutting off of the soul from Israel. On the various opinions of interpreters concerning it, see Constantin l’Empereur, notes to Bertram, *De Republica Hebraeorum*, book I, chapter 2; and Godovinus, book III, chapter 4, section 19. The former’s words are: “For the most part, our theologians hold that this phrase designates expulsion from the assembly of the Church and the faithful. Fewer refer it to capital punishment. Amid this diversity, I consider the opinion of those by no means absurd who think that a premature death is indicated.”]

Certain ancient heretics—including the mad Marcion and the detestable Manichaeus—because they were led astray by the spirit of error and insisted that all the Scriptures of the Old Testament ought to be rejected, attempt throughout many chapters of Scripture to assert that the God of the ancient Law is evil, as though either the God of the New Testament were someone other than the one who was indeed foretold in the Law and came, or as though anyone could be legitimately good in comparison with the goodness of God.

They hold that angels or human beings are judged to possess some share of goodness if they know, worship, revere, and love the good God; for the Lord Jesus testifies that “the good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. XII).

[Note: We have added *τὸ bonus* (“the good”), on the basis of the manuscripts, which read “the good man brings forth good things from the good treasure.” The manuscript of Pantagathus also has this reading. The editions read “the man brings forth good things from the good treasure.” The reading adopted here is supported by the Vulgate.]

[Note: Thus the Florentine, Urbinate, and Pantagathus manuscript read. The two Vatican manuscripts instead have “But the Lord.” The editions read: “But you may say: the Son of God.”]

But God the Son of God, possessing perfect goodness with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and knowing that the goodness of the Trinity is one, just as its divinity is one, considered it offensive to be called good according to the condition of created goods, and said: “Why do you call me good?” (Matt. XIX).

That is: “Do not call me good when you do not know me; first learn who I am, and when you have recognized the true God, I accept your calling me good, because no one is good except one, God” (Matt. XIX).

[Note: The editions read “who I am.”]

For that Jew had addressed the Son of God—God and man—as though he were merely a man, though certainly a good teacher: “Good Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?” (ibid.). Therefore the Lord said to him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God.”

There is one God, in whom there is no division of deity. Throughout all the books of the holy Scriptures we read of the Father as God, the Son as God, and the Holy Spirit as God—not “gods,” because the Unity of majesty does not permit them to be called gods. In the Trinity there is only a distinction of persons, not a diversity of nature.

If Marcion and Manichaeus had deserved to perceive this, they would certainly never have said that the one God of the New Testament is good, while another God, who spoke through the Old Law, is evil.

[Note: The manuscripts read “For they even dared,” a reading also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus. This entire passage of Gaudentius could have been cited to illuminate Philastrius, where he discusses Marcion and the Manichaeans, chapters 45 and 61; for he explains their errors more fully and distinctly, as we also noted in the *Spicilegium* to Fabricius’s notes, above, p. 175.]

They even dared to attribute cruelty to him in the aforementioned Law of Unleavened Bread, saying that a human soul was destroyed on account of the leaven of bread—something, they claimed, that could not be more cruel.

For in their madness they did not understand either how great the usefulness of the commandment was, or that God has greater reason to punish when he is despised with a stubborn spirit in small matters, where there is no difficulty in observing the commandment. God more readily forgives necessity than presumption.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “the Lord forgives”; the book of Pantagathus, “God forgives.” The editions have “may he forgive”; and a little earlier, where “with a stubborn spirit” occurs, the manuscript of Pantagathus restores “with a stubborn, nevertheless, spirit,” which is undoubtedly better.]

Thus holy David is not charged with sin because, compelled by the necessity of hunger, he ate the holy loaves which no one but the priests was permitted to eat (I Sam. XXI).

Here, however, let us see what necessity could have arisen. God commanded the Israelites that during the seven days of Passover they should not make leavened bread for themselves (Exod. XII). If he had commanded that leavened bread be made, diligence would have been necessary so that it should not be lacking. What he commanded required idleness, not labor. He commands negligence in order to test obedience; and do you not think that he condemns the soul which has applied diligence in order to despise him?

But now let us see what the reason for the usefulness of this very commandment was—historically for the Jews until Christ’s coming, and today for us, what edification it contains according to spiritual understanding.

When the children of Israel were being oppressed in Egypt by the grievous injuries of captivity, they groaned and cried out to the Lord God, asking him to deign to rescue them (Exod. III). God immediately chose Moses and Aaron from among them, through whom they might approach Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and ask him to release them.

[Note: The Florentine has “when he was releasing them”; two Vatican manuscripts have “when he resisted,” as does the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

When he did not release them, after being scourged along with his people by many plagues, he received this final plague of punishment: on that night all the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck by divine action and perished, the very night on which the Jews were required by God’s command to celebrate the sacrifice of Passover.

At midnight, therefore, a cry and wailing arose throughout all Egypt, for there was no house in which there was not a dead person. Then the king of Egypt, fearing that he himself and all his people might likewise perish, compelled Moses and Aaron at that hour of the night to lead the entire populace out of Egypt.

When they were urgently pressed to leave, let us observe what they did. “And the people,” he says, “took their flour mixed before their dough was leavened, and they tied it up in their garments and placed it upon their shoulders. Having departed, when they came to Succoth, they baked the dough which they had brought out of Egypt,” he says, “unleavened cakes baked under ashes” (Exod. XII).

[Note: The Septuagint likewise calls them *ἐγκρυφίαι ἄζυμοι* (*enkryphiai azymoi*), “unleavened cakes baked under ashes,” although the Hebrews insist that the word *ἐγκρυφίαι*, “baked under ashes,” is not found in the Hebrew text, lest they be forced to admit that their present custom of baking unleavened bread in an oven conflicts with the authority of sacred Scripture. My brother Julius, a man joined to me not so much by blood as by similarity of studies, explicitly testifies that this practice was once observed in a certain synagogue in Italy, so that unleavened bread was eaten baked under ashes. Perhaps, however, the more recent Hebrews, as in many other matters, have departed from the ancient custom.

Concerning unleavened bread, see Athenaeus, book III, chapter 25, where he calls *ἄρτον ἄζυμον* (*arton azymon*) “unfermented,” “lacking leaven”; this may be the bread which Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 11, calls *speusticus*, named from haste. From these passages learned men have rightly inferred that not only the Jews but also other peoples used unleavened bread.]

Thus, so that they might remember this necessity and God’s benefits, he commanded them to celebrate Passover for seven days of the first month in such a way that they would not eat leavened bread (Exod. XIII), and always to declare to their children the reason for which they had been commanded to do this—namely, so that the ungrateful people, reminded by an image of the events, might be compelled to give thanks to their liberator.

And therefore the command is given to them so emphatically: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; but from the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread from the first day to the seventh day, that soul shall perish from Israel” (Exod. XII).

God did many other things for them, both at the Red Sea and in the wilderness. But although I say nothing of their other evils, forgetful of God’s mercies, in addition to the fact that they had made a golden calf and, worshiping it, had said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII), they also rejected with sacrilegious minds Jesus, the Son of God, who had been their liberator and was coming to them.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “they also rejected him himself,” and it plainly seems that this is the correct reading, for the Son of God was not yet called Jesus until after he had taken flesh from the Virgin. The book of Pantagathus also has “they also rejected him himself.”]

Hence the holy evangelist John recalls, not without complaint: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I). That is, he came to those whom he had freed from the bondage of Egypt; whom he had led across the Red Sea on dry ground; before whose eyes he had overwhelmed Pharaoh and the Egyptians when the walls of the surrounding waters collapsed; whom he had fed with heavenly manna in the wilderness; for whom he had brought forth springs from a dry rock; to whom he had entrusted the words of the Law; whose prophets had foretold his coming in the flesh; to whom above all he had come, saying: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV).

These people not only refused to receive him, but also slaughtered him by the punishment of the cross. Nevertheless, he endured the death of the body he had assumed for this reason: both to display the omnipotence of his majesty by rising again through his own power, and, death having been removed and conquered, to restore life to believers, while fully condemning the wickedness of those who crucified him.

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate have “in the death that had been removed”; the manuscript of Pantagathus agrees. One Vatican manuscript has “in the death that had been brought forth”; another, “in the death that had been mutilated and conquered.” This is a printers’ or copyists’ play.]

Therefore, rising on the third day, he transferred himself to the Gentiles, as had long before been threatened: “The kingdom shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI.43).

[Note: Three manuscript copies have “it shall be taken away from you,” a reading with which the manuscript of Pantagathus agrees. The Urbinate has “it shall be taken away from you.”]

Therefore, since we who faithfully follow Christ have been granted knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God, let us see what our same Lord and Teacher taught should be understood by this leaven.

“Pay attention to yourselves,” he says, “and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (Matt. XVI; Mark VIII; Luke XII). When he repeated this more clearly, the Apostles understood that they were not to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the wickedness of corrupting doctrine.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “where it appears,” that is, “where the leaven of wickedness has been made.” The Urbinate and the manuscript of Pantagathus agree.]

[Note: Two editions, namely Cologne and Lyon, along with four manuscript copies, read “there death draws near inwardly,” that is, “the devil.” The Paris edition reads “destruction draws near inwardly,” a reading not wholly implausible in view of what follows: “Know that the one who habitually makes the leaven of death has entered there.” But the authority of a single edition did not seem sufficient reason to depart from the agreement of the editors and manuscripts; the manuscript of Pantagathus also has “destruction draws near.”]

Therefore the capable preacher of the Gospel, the apostle Paul, cries out to us: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V).

Let us therefore beware of the leaven of malice. For when the leaven of wickedness, made by the devil from the mixture of sins and iniquities, appears, destruction approaches that soul.

[Note: It is clear that this is the true reading, found in the manuscript copies, for shortly afterward he adds, “know that the one who has entered.” The editions read: “when you see in your soul, within you, evil thoughts.” It also seems that one should read “when you see evil thoughts having entered into your soul,” although the manuscripts have “in your soul.” The book of Octavius Pantagathus reads: “When therefore you see evil thoughts having entered into the soul.”]

When, therefore, you see evil thoughts entering your soul and devising ways to turn you away from the worship of God or to make you commit some sin, know that the one who habitually makes the leaven of death has entered there. Therefore take care lest such leaven be found in you and your soul be destroyed by God.

“Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?” (I Cor. V; Gal. V). See, then, that you do not even in a small matter allow yourselves to yield either to the error of the Gentiles, or to the iniquity of the Jews, or to the wickedness of heretics, who corrupt the whole lump of faith with the rancor of treachery, through the devil’s leaven.

[Note: The word “rancor” is absent from three manuscripts, but an interval remains in this form: “of treachery . . . corrupt.” If only lacunae were always marked in manuscripts! The Urbinate reads “they corrupt the whole lump of faith by their treachery,” but we have preferred the common reading.]

And when he taught that unleavened bread was to be eaten with bitterness, he taught that no one can lead a sincere life without the sorrow of the flesh.

[Note: Four manuscript copies, namely the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts, read “to be eaten in bitterness.” The editions read “unleavened bread with bitterness is to be eaten.” Above also he said “unleavened cakes baked under ashes,” and the Church in an ancient Easter hymn:

> And pure unleavened bread  
> For pure minds, sincerity.

Likewise Lev. II: “Unleavened cakes mixed with oil”; and Lev. VII: “They shall offer unleavened cakes anointed with oil.”

The command that they should be eaten with bitterness was given in Exod. XII.8, so that the unleavened loaves were to be eaten with wild lettuces, or a mixture of bitter herbs. How the Hebrews observed this rite of the Law at the Passover supper is explained at length by Scaliger, *De Emendatione Temporum*, book VI, p. 572. They dipped these bitter herbs into a rather thick sauce resembling mustard, and they say that this sauce was a sign of the clay in which their ancestors labored in Egypt. R. Maimonides, *On Leavened and Unleavened Bread*, chapter 8, section 7: “They used to dip unleavened bread into the sauce called *charoseth* and then eat it; afterward they put bitter herbs into the *charoseth* and ate them.” See Buxtorf, *Synagoga Judaica*, chapter 18; Godovinus, *Moses and Aaron*, book III, chapter 4, sections 6 and 16.

The same is found in an ancient Hebrew ritual book cited by Baronius under A.D. 34, no. 43: at the second Passover table, when a round unleavened cake was distributed, the head of the household said: “This is the bread of affliction which our fathers ate in the land of Egypt. Whoever is hungry, let him come and celebrate the Passover.” Yet Buxtorf himself argues that Baronius reported this neither properly nor accurately, *Dissertation on the Lord’s Supper*, thesis 1, §14, no. 7. In Deut. XVI.3, unleavened bread is called “the bread of affliction”: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, the bread of affliction.”]

Bitterness appears to be fasting and every abstinence from bodily delights. But the Lord’s Passover is celebrated in no other way; the unleavened bread of sincerity is not eaten in any other way.

When, however, you have gone out of the Egypt of this world in conduct or in body, you will eat the nourishment of manna; you will receive the bread of heaven; and, having been brought into that promised land of the saints, you will enjoy at once the pleasantness of paradise and the eternal sweetness of the Lord himself.

It is a sweet bitterness, followed by the recompense of such great sweetness.

Therefore, from the first day either of our regeneration or of our conversion, let us cast out the leaven of wickedness from the proper dwellings of this earthly habitation; and for the seven days of our entire life—for these same days recur throughout the ages—let us eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and purity, so that we may deserve to obtain the gifts of the heavenly promises.

[Note: The editions read awkwardly “or of our way of life”; we have restored “or of our conversion” from two Vatican manuscripts, and the manuscript that belonged to Octavius Pantagathus reads likewise.]

May almighty God the Father deign to grant these gifts to us, through his coeternal Son, who lives and reigns with him and with the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now and always, and throughout all ages.

[Note: The Florentine and Urbinate add: “Here ends the seventh sermon on the reading from Exodus.”]

Amen.

## SERMON VIII: FIRST SERMON ON THE READING FROM THE GOSPEL

[Note: Galeardus’s edition reads: “Here begins the first treatise on the reading from the Gospel,” and adds the following: The two Paris and Cologne editions and the Florentine manuscript: “Here begins the first sermon on the reading from the Gospel, which is eighth in order.” The book of Pantagathus: “The seventh treatise on the reading from Exodus ends. Here begins the first sermon on the reading from the Gospel, which is eighth in order.” Two Vatican manuscripts have only: “The first, which is eighth in order.” The Urbinate: “The first sermon on the reading from the Gospel, which is eighth in order, begins.” The Lyon edition: “The eighth treatise on the reading from the Gospel.”]

After the conclusion of the treatise which we have brought to your affection up to yesterday from the Book of Exodus, where the law concerning the celebration of Passover is described, let us now, with the Lord’s help, discuss something from the Gospel reading that was recited a little earlier [Col. 0886B], so that by the facts themselves we may prove that the same God is the author both of the Old Testament and of the New.

For we heard that Jesus, the Savior of the human race, had been invited to a wedding [Note: The manuscripts read *had gone*; likewise, a little later, *he changed the water into the taste and nature of wine*], and that there he changed water into the taste and nature of wine. The history itself plainly has an order corresponding to the truth. For the same one who had instituted marriage from the beginning also blessed it (Gen. II), and by his power changed the creature he had made into whatever he wished [269].

As for the power of almighty God, no doubt concerning the deed can enter the soul of a believer. Yet someone among us may reasonably wonder that he went [Col. 0887A] to a wedding celebration—that is, into a house of feasting [Note: The word *went* was absent from three editions; we supplied it from the Florentine manuscript and the two Vatican manuscripts. It is also found in the manuscript book of Octavius Pantagathus, but is absent from the Urbinate. Savaro noted that Gaudentius here calls the wedding feast a *festivity* in his commentary on Sidonius, Book I, Letter 5, and cited a similar passage from Optatus and Sidonius. In this sense, he says, the word *festivum* means both “festive” and “pleasant”].

Indeed, dearest ones, almost the whole text of the Gospels indicates that the Lord Christ, while living among human beings, brought help in desperate circumstances and was especially present to those in sorrow: when he rebuked the blaspheming Jews; when he convicted the scribes and Pharisees of deceit, trickery, greed, and vanity (Luke XI); when he reproached and threatened unbelieving cities (Matt. XI); when he tormented unclean spirits (Luke VIII), in order to aid his captive image [Note: Both the printed editions and the manuscripts read this way; but the book of Pantagathus reads, “to aid the captivity of his image.” Perhaps one should read, “to aid the captivity of his image”], and, after driving out the demons, restore the possessed minds to health; when he cleansed the lepers who pleaded with him (Luke XVII); when he restored paralytics who were living only through the use of the tongue with which they could plead, rather than merely curing them [Col. 0887B] (Matt. IX); when, while walking securely upon the waters, he approached as the calmer of those endangered by the storm at sea (Matt. XIV); when he either restored to blinded eyes the gift of their lost light or infused new light into those blind from birth (Luke XVIII; John IX; Matt. IX); when, skilled in healing, he stood among the sorrowful crowds of the sick; when he removed the various griefs of pleading parents, restoring their dear ones who were dying to health, and the dead to life (Luke VII; John XI).

For this purpose the Son of God, God without beginning, at the end of the age took the beginning of flesh from a Virgin and deigned to live among human beings: to come to the aid of this perishing world, since, as he himself says, the healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill (Matt. IX). A physician, indeed, is accustomed to enter the house of sorrow rather than that of joy [Col. 0887C]. For he is needed either by those afflicted with the pain of wounds, or by those suffering from the disease of illness [Note: The two Vatican manuscripts read “of ailments”], or by those weakened by a lingering wasting of the inner organs [Note: So read the two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine and the Urbinate manuscripts, in agreement with the book of Pantagathus. The phrase *lenta viscerum tabe defectis* means “weakened by a lingering wasting of the inner organs,” with *defectis* meaning “those who are failing,” as in Columella, *On Agriculture*, Book V, chapter 6: “to remove a tree weakened by age”; and Quintilian, Book III, chapter 8: “besieged, unequal to the task, and weakened by lack of water and food.” Salvianus likewise writes, *On the Government of God*, Book V: “Whenever the highest authorities have judged that the tax burdens of weakened cities should in some measure be reduced.” The editions read absurdly, “abandoned by a long wasting of the inner organs.”]—because prosperity has no need of a physician’s service.

What, then, does this Gospel reading recited today mean when it declares that the Lord was invited to attend a wedding feast? It means that there the wine—that is, the power of spiritual joy—had failed, and the mouths of the thirsty guests languished from the lack of joy-giving wine, since, as the Prophet says, wine gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII) [270].

But before we reveal the spiritual understanding [Note: So read the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate edition: “the knowledge of spiritual things”], let us explain the event historically [Col. 0888A]. Christ does not reject the celebration of a wedding for this reason: that he may testify that he is the same God who in the beginning formed man and woman from the clay of the earth and granted them conjugal permission, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I).

This institution so greatly displeases the wretched Manichaeans. I think that, because of their impurity, it is not marriage itself that displeases them [Note: The manuscript of Pantagathus reads: “but the law.” The law—“which does not join many women to one man, but one woman”—the scribe accidentally omitted the clause *nor one woman to many men*. We have therefore preferred the other reading, which is fuller and supported by the agreement of the editions and manuscripts], but the law, which joins neither many women to one man nor one woman to many men [Note: We deleted *also*, since it is absent from three manuscripts. The editions ineptly read, “but also one woman.” See St. Augustine, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, chapters 18 and 19, where much is found that illuminates this passage of Gaudentius], but one woman to one man.

For those execrable Manichaeans do not wish to live according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul: that each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband (I Cor. VII). Therefore Christ blessed the lawful marriage which he had established from the beginning, when, invited, he did not refuse to go to the wedding [Col. 0888B]; and yet he taught that virginity is better, since he deigned to be born through it.

God proved that the holy Virgin was his dwelling place [Note: Three editions read “the light of modesty.” The Florentine manuscript reads “the pillar of modesty,” a reading which we have preferred to the common one; we also find “pillar of modesty” in the book of Pantagathus], where, upon entering, he preserved an everlasting pillar of modesty: he was born without injury to his mother’s integrity and conceived without violation.

Therefore the Apostle, the vessel of election, invited others to the good which he had attained, saying to the unmarried: “It is good for them if they remain as I do” (I Cor. VII). He urges them by the example of blessedness, not compels them by the force of a law. Concerning virgins, he says: “I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful; for it is advantageous for a person to be so” (ibid.).

And after a lengthy exhortation in which he preferred the blessedness of chastity [Col. 0888C] to the condition of marriage [Note: In the two Vatican manuscripts: “he finally concluded his statement”; in the manuscript of Pantagathus: “his statement finally concluded”], he concluded with this final judgment: “Therefore, both he who gives his virgin to marriage does well, and he who does not give her does better” (I Cor. VII, 38) [Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts reads “he who gives his own virgin,” which seems to have been supplied by a scribe because of what follows].

I believe that the blessed Apostle did not say this to the parents of virgins, since it is clear that they cannot rule another person’s will by their own judgment, but that the same holy Apostle offered the choice to every human being, both man and woman: that each should either preserve his or her own virginity—that is, his or her own flesh, born virgin—by choosing the better and free course, or, having recognized the condition of things, give it to marriage if unable to remain continent.

Parents, however, and all the relatives [271] whatsoever of virgins, whether boys or girls, should not flatter themselves concerning the freedom mentioned above, since we have explained that they cannot rule over other minds [Col. 0889A].

[Note: Gaudentius plainly censures the practice of his age, by which boys and girls were customarily assigned permanently to the Church and to virginity not only from the cradle, as Salvian says in Book II *Against Avarice*, but even before they emerged from the womb. Hence Jerome, to Laeta: “I had intended to teach you how you ought to bring up our Paula, who was consecrated to Christ before she was born; whom you conceived by vows before conceiving her in the womb.” And shortly afterwards: “Whether or not to offer your daughter was within your power; although your case is different, since you vowed her before you conceived her; but that you do not neglect her once offered concerns your own danger.” The most learned Baluzius made public some notable records of the later age on this matter, in his notes on Salvian, p. 243; these show that this custom remained in force in the Church even in later centuries, until Celestine III abolished this entire right of paternal power over children, whose decree is reported in the chapter *Cum simus*, *De Regularibus*. On this matter there is Canon 48 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, referred to in 20, question 1, chapter *Monachum*, and likewise Canon 5 of the Council of Worms. But see the most eminent Cardinal Bona, distinguished no less by learning than by the purple, Book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 7, no. 6.
