I name him here the more readily as a mark of honor because a certain recent writer, though suppressing his name but later entering it in the index, in the preface to the *Mystagogia*, p. 178, somewhat unfairly called him “a very commonplace man”—whatever dignity that writer afterwards attained, a man of utterly slight repute while he lived and of none after his death. Moreover, Gaudentius’s opinion is today the doctrine of the whole Church. What I said above—that the custom of assigning boys and girls to perpetual virginity prevailed in the Church not only in ancient but also in later centuries—may also be illustrated by the records and forms for the offering of boys in monasteries which Mabillon publishes, vol. III of the *Analecta*, p. 469. See also Mabillon’s observations on the aforesaid forms in the same vol. III, p. 473.]

They certainly cannot impose perpetual continence, because this is known to be a matter of the will; but they can nourish the will toward what is better [Note: We have preferred the reading of the manuscripts. The editions read “the will at that time”]. They are obliged to warn, exhort, and encourage; to desire more eagerly to bind their children as offerings to God than to the world; to present from the offspring of their own stock either ministers worthy of the divine altar in the order of the clergy, or girls dedicated to chastity, nurturing them among the number of holy women; and, adorning the Church of God with such nourishment, to obtain the blessedness that is their due.

“For it is written: ‘Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and members of his household in Jerusalem’” [Col. 0889B] [Note: The illustrious Vossius, in his notes on Ephrem the Syrian, showed me where this testimony occurs; I had not indicated it in the earlier edition. For when he had used this testimony in *Paraenesis* 16, p. 287, Antwerp edition, 1619, with these words—“For it is written: ‘Thus says the Lord: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and members of his household in Jerusalem’”—Vossius added: “This passage is Isaiah XXXI according to the Septuagint, with whom this author’s reading agrees.” In the Vulgate it reads: “Whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem”; Symmachus likewise has: “Who has fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem”; while Aquila and Theodotion have: *φῶς αὐτῷ ἐν Σιὼν*, that is, “light for him in Zion,” and “a furnace in Jerusalem.” St. Jerome discusses this variation in Letter 101, addressed to Pammachius concerning the best manner of translating. These remarks are from Vossius].

This splendid prophetic saying also contains a loftier meaning, which must be unfolded in its proper place through a full discussion. But since we have been profitably drawn into this treatise by our concern for chastity, while explaining the reason why the Savior went to the wedding, let us meanwhile briefly offer salutary advice to our neophytes, intending to show in what follows how the spiritual meaning of this reading is to be explained figuratively.

You can recognize that you have been regenerated and reborn through Baptism by the very name by which you are called infants. Therefore, if any of you who are bound by marriage desire to preserve your virgins rather than give them to marriage, let them have wives as though they did not have them; and great will be their reward [272] before God our Lord, because they will have preserved their flesh in the condition in which it was reborn through the sacrament of Baptism.

I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you (I Cor. VII). For even if you have served a lawful marriage after the washing of Baptism, you have not sinned. Take care only that you do not abandon the faith in any other respect [Note: Three manuscripts read, “so that you do not sin otherwise,” that is, “so that”; the manuscript of Pantagathus has the same reading, which is perhaps truer and better, although I have not wished to displace the common reading], and that, having become faithful, you flee fornication.

But you will be able to keep this only if you avoid drunkenness and dishonorable banquets, where [the …] of shameful women [Note: This is a Plautine expression, *Truculentus*, Act IV, scene III, line 6: “Although you are both of snakelike disposition.” What follows—“where the lyre and flute sound; where, finally, every kind of musical instrument [sounds]”—shows that singers were employed at Christian banquets, as is also clear from Jerome, *On Avoiding Suspicious Companionship*: “Meanwhile some singer will sound at the table, and amid the psalms flowing in sweet melody, since he will not dare [to look at] other men’s wives, he will look more frequently at you, who have no guardian.” Prudentius also strongly condemns this custom in *Hamartigenia*, 316:

“Was it for the empty strains of a girl’s lyre,

and the sounds of strings, and the banquet-song

of heated wickedness, that God bestowed open ears?”]

[The supplied text breaks off here.]

[Col. 0890B] The following words indicate that Gaudentius was also greatly displeased by this same custom: “Let the house of a Christian and baptized man be free from the choir of the devil.”

The writhing movement of the serpent stirs up unlawful desire; where the lyre sounds, and the pipe; where, finally, every kind of musical instrument resounds amid the cymbals of dancers. Unhappy are those houses that differ in nothing from theaters. Away with all such things, I beg you. Let the house of a Christian and baptized man be free from the choir of the devil; let it be wholly humane and hospitable. Let it be sanctified by continual prayers; let it be frequented by psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Let the word of God and the sign of Christ be in the heart, on the lips, and on the forehead; [Col. 0890D] These words, “among drinks, among conversations,” which we have added from the Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts, are absent from the printed editions; they are, however, also supplied by the Pantagathus manuscript. We have likewise removed the particle *and*, which the manuscripts do not have, from the words “on entering and on departing,” although three editions print it. Among food, among drink, among conversations, in baths, in bedrooms, on entering, on departing, in joy, in sorrow; so that, according to the teaching of the most blessed Paul, “whether you eat, or drink, or do anything else, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 0891A] (I Cor. X), who has called you to grace.

For he both grants forgiveness for past sins and promises rewards for a reformed life. But having explained these matters morally for the common edification, I now come to the promised allegories of the Gospel reading itself. And although I do not consider myself adequate for explaining the mysteries of Christ—I who do not yet deserve to presume upon the authority of the most blessed Paul, who says, “For we speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (I Cor. II)—[Col. 0891C] The Vatican manuscripts consistently retain “comparing spiritual things with spiritual,” as also below, “spiritual understanding”; the Pantagathus manuscript agrees with them, as we noted above at Treatise 2, p. 239. I nevertheless desire to reveal to you, from this same reading of the divine Gospel, a heavenly and secret understanding, insofar as the Lord will grant it. The manuscripts read, “from the same [reading].”

A little earlier, while explaining the beginning of the discourse I had undertaken and making clear the reason why the Savior had been invited to the wedding, I passed on to the edifying treatment of the preservation of virginity, and there I seem to have lingered somewhat. But now I shall repeat the evangelist’s narrative itself, so that we may seek the spiritual meaning more suitably in the words.

“And on the third day,” he says, “there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited, together with his disciples, to the wedding. And they had no wine, because the wedding wine had been consumed” (John II).

[Col. 0891C] We have restored here the reading of the Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts. For an interrogative had wrongly crept into the printed copies, which read as follows: “How had the wedding wine been consumed?”—then, “The true history of the event.” Thus the entire order had been disturbed and corrupted, for the text seemed to pass immediately from the proposed question to another matter. That this is the true reading Gaudentius himself also indicates at the end of the treatise, where, explaining the whole passage again, he reads it as we have printed it. Four manuscripts also have “the true history of the event,” but we have preferred the common reading. Moreover, the book of Octavius Pantagathus also has “the true history of the event”; indeed Gaudentius himself says at the beginning of the following sermon, “first according to the history of the event,” and around the middle, “but the servants, not those according to the event itself.”

Having recognized, as was necessary, the true historical account of what happened, let us now explain spiritually what this third day is on which the wedding is said to have taken place. It was a day of light, dearest brothers, and therefore it is most appropriately compared with the commandments of the Lord, who is the true light, as the Prophet testifies: “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII). And again elsewhere: “Like light,” he says, “are your commandments upon the earth” (Prov. VI).

Accordingly, the Lord Savior rightly admonished that one must walk in the light, saying: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world” (John XI). For truly, if anyone walks in the light of God’s commandments, he cannot stumble at all.

The first day, then, was under the commandment, from Adam to Moses; the second day was under the Law of Moses; the third day [Col. 0892A] is under the grace of the Savior.

[Col. 0891D] We have restored this from the Florentine manuscript. The printed editions have *hodie* (“today”).

On this day the heavenly Bridegroom himself, the Lord Jesus, lover of believing souls, joined to himself as bride the Church from the Gentiles, to whom he would give the precious ring of his seal and the earrings of faith—for “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Rom. X), namely, the Son, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I). [Col. 0892C] To this bride the same Son of God, God the Word, would also give golden bracelets, namely, of approved works and righteous deeds, and would bestow, one by one, the remaining precious necklaces that are ornaments of spiritual virtues. [Col. 0892C] We have adopted this reading from three manuscripts. The printed editions corruptly read, “whose bridegroom is the same Son of God, God the Word”; moreover, the transposition of the closing punctuation—or end of the parenthesis—added fault and obscurity. The Pantagathus manuscript reads, without any closing punctuation, “to whose bride the same Son of God, God the Word.”

And so that you might recognize that on this third day these spiritual nuptials are celebrated by Christ among the Gentile peoples, they take place not in Judea but in Cana of Galilee. [Col. 0892B] This will be shown more clearly, besides the testimony of the holy Isaiah (Isa. IX), who mentioned “Galilee of the Gentiles,” through the interpretation of the names themselves.

For Cana is said to mean “possession,” while Galilee, interpreted from the Hebrew language, is called either “rolling” or “wheel.” [Col. 0892D] Consult Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*. This method of interpretation, drawn from etymologies, displeased some greatly; nevertheless, it is defended by the example and authority of great names.

[Col. 0892D] We have reproduced the reading of the Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate manuscript, by whose assistance this whole passage stood greatly in need. It is evident that the people of the Gentiles, who had formerly fallen into the error of idolatry, now hasten with the speed of a swiftly moving wheel toward the worship of Christian truth. [Col. 0892D] The Vatican and Urbinate manuscripts read thus; the printed editions instead read, “prepare themselves with the speed of a certain running wheel.” Incorrectly: for shortly afterward he adds, “hastened swiftly like a running wheel,” from which it is sufficiently clear what the true reading of the present passage is; it is also supported by the excellent book of Octavius Pantagathus. Thus the prophet David also sang figuratively, speaking to God: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI).

For God thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. XVII). The voice of this thunder clings to the hearts of this people, who hastened swiftly from pagan superstition to faith in the Lord Jesus, like a running wheel.

For this reason we rightly believe that the blessed Apostles were also called by Christ “sons of thunder,” namely, *Boanerges* (Mark III). [Col. 0892D] Four manuscripts now have “called,” which is what is said in Hebrew, *Boanerges*, as does the book of Pantagathus.

For we read elsewhere in the Gospel that certain people from among the Gentiles, desiring to draw near to Christ, sought access through the apostle Philip, who was from the city of Bethsaida in Galilee—perhaps trusting in their familiarity with him. “Sir,” they said, “we wish to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told [Col. 0893A] Jesus (John XII).

[Col. 0893D] The Pantagathus manuscript reads, “They tell Jesus,” and the other words that correspond to it; thereafter it proceeds with the material that, as your Charity remembers, I explained in detail in its proper place, just as it is found in the printed editions. Gaudentius’s words make it clear that some of his treatises have been lost; this has also been noted elsewhere, at the beginning of Treatise 14 and in the Preface to Gaudentius, no. 19.

The following words are connected with these: in the place where, as your Charity remembers, I explained everything in detail, the Lord immediately embraced the messengers of the Gentiles with joy and, foreseeing in the few believers the faith of countless peoples, said to the Apostles: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John XII).

And shortly afterward, turning his voice toward the Father, he said: “Father, glorify your name.” Immediately a voice came from heaven and said: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”

When the crowd of Jews standing around heard this voice of God the Father echoing back from the heights of heaven, it thought that it was thunder, because it did not grasp the words. [Col. 0893D] Thus the Florentine manuscript and the Paris edition; the other editions, namely the Cologne and Lyons editions, read “of the surrounding Jews.” For the people, according to the prophecy of the holy Isaiah (Isa. VI), hearing with the ear but not truly hearing, had heard only the sound of the divine voice, [Col. 0893B] without understanding the words.

Therefore the Lord, both in the Gospel addressed to all and in the Apocalypse after the heavenly teaching, cries out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII; Rev. XIII). [Col. 0893D] The conjunction is absent in the printed editions; we have added it from the manuscripts.

For he knew that everyone possessed ears, but that not everyone possessed the ability to hear. Indeed, no one can be counted as having heard if, dulled by the sluggishness of the heart, he does not know what he has heard.

But the Apostles—and through the Apostles those who were hastening to the faith of Christ—having ears capable of hearing, deserved to understand the divine utterances, which, in proportion to their greatness, are compared in the Apocalypse with thunder (Rev. IV, VI, VIII, X). They were deemed worthy to be taught from heaven, by the testimony of the Father, the saving knowledge of the truth.

Cana, however, is a small city in Galilee of the Gentiles. In that region of Galilee lies also the city of Capernaum, where the blessed evangelist Matthew testifies that Christ lived, saying: “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee; and leaving the city of Nazareth” (Matt. IV)—that is, another Galilee—“he came,” he says, “and lived in Capernaum, a maritime town in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. [Col. 0893D; 0894D] The Florentine manuscript reads, “Capernaum, maritime, in the territory of Zebulun”; one Vatican manuscript and the Pantagathus manuscript do likewise. So also the Vulgate: “he lived in maritime Capernaum.” So that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The people sitting in darkness have seen a great light; and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, light has dawned’” (Isa. IX).

The most blessed evangelist John also records that the Lord Jesus left the land of Judea and went again into Galilee. “He had to pass,” he says, “through Samaria” (John IV, 4). There he describes him as delayed for a while on the journey because of the Samaritan woman, and then adds: “After two days he departed from there and went into Galilee.”

“For Jesus himself,” he says, “testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country. When he came into Galilee,” he says, “the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all the signs that he had done in Jerusalem during the feast; for they themselves had also come to the feast. He came, therefore, again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made wine from water. Now there was a certain royal official whose son was ill in Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, who was beginning to die” (ibid., 43).

When he had immediately healed the absent boy by the power of his word, like a heavenly physician, the holy evangelist concluded in this way: “This was again the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea into Galilee” (ibid., 54).

Therefore, to return to the interpretation of the names and to the figurative meaning: in Cana of Galilee—that is, in the possession of the Gentiles—the spiritual wedding is celebrated in the presence of Christ.

[Col. 0894D] Thus one manuscript of the Vatican reads; another has, “The Prophet speaking in his person.” The printed editions corruptly read, “The prophecy and his person.”

The Prophet, speaking in his person to the Church in the *Song of Songs*, says: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon” (Song IV)—that is, from that pagan offering of incense. For we interpret *Lebanon* as “incense,” from the Greek, which those Magi coming from among the Gentiles believed ought rather to be offered to Christ (Matt. II).

Finally, Lebanon is also seen to be a lofty mountain among the Phoenicians, compared with the proud rule of the Gentiles. Hence above all the bride, the Church, is summoned when she hears the voice of Christ saying: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon” (Song IV).

[Col. 0894D] Thus the Florentine manuscript. Two editions have, “This bride is called the Church”; but our reading is much better and more suitable. The Paris edition has, “This bride is summoned as the Church.” The Pantagathus manuscript has, “This bride is summoned as the Church.”

That is, you will come and pass over from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, [Col. 0894C] and from the lions’ lair, from the mountains of leopards. [Col. 0894D] The manuscripts have, “from the lions’ dens.” Aquila’s version has *katoikētēriou*, “from the dwelling-place of lions”; the Septuagint has, “from the hiding places of lions.”

This means that, abandoning the forests of dreadful idolatry and leaving the lairs of monstrous beasts—namely, the dwelling places of demons—she should hasten to the worship of almighty God and embrace the faith of him who deigns, by the grace of divine love, to call her his bride.

But someone may say: If God, according to the Apostle’s teaching, “desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II), why are these saving nuptials celebrated especially among the Gentiles at the consummation of the age, while the peoples of the earlier age were not joined to the divine marriage?

I shall show you, beloved, that the first-formed man, Adam himself, was joined to divine intimacy, having received from the Bridegroom the insignia of the divine image—the ornaments of wisdom, understanding, and eternal life.

But after the faithfulness of the commandment had been adulterated through the pandering of the devil, immortality was taken away together with the freedom of divine love. [Col. 0894D] Up to this point both the printed editions and the manuscripts read this way, certainly incorrectly; but in the book of Pantagathus, *liberalitate* (“generosity”) has been restored by Pantagathus’s own hand in place of *libertate* (“freedom”), which had appeared earlier. The correction is unquestionably right: it was not freedom that was lost to us through the fall of our first parent, but the insignia of divine generosity—the ornaments of wisdom, understanding, and eternal life that Gaudentius had just enumerated—which perished in that lamentable loss.

Nevertheless, until the flood and until the Law itself, there remained the revived love of certain righteous people toward God, and the restored union of God with a few holy persons.

But because, as I said, apart from a very few saints, the whole earth was fornicating against the Lord, and the human race, in its mad lust, had joined itself to countless gods of idols, God immediately chose the stock of the righteous seed of Abraham. [Col. 0895D] One Vatican manuscript has, “the most righteous stock of the seed of Abraham”; another, “the stock of the righteous man, namely Abraham.”

And with the tablets of a legitimate union, written by his own finger, he established a covenant between himself and that people through his servant Moses (Exod. XX).

From then on, that people, conceiving the divine commandments and becoming fruitful with a holy offspring, began to be most dear to God, whose union it had deserved. [Col. 0895D] Here likewise a serious corruption had entered, which we have corrected from the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions have, most badly, “whose cup it had deserved from God.” Let someone now go and say that all this labor of emending from manuscripts is idle.

[Col. 0895D] The Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate read this way, and it must certainly be read so, since the entire passage speaks of the bride, marriage, and wedding. The printed editions absurdly have *secuta prole sanctorum* (“with a succeeding offspring of saints”). The book of Octavius Pantagathus also has both this correction and the following one.

But as time went on, presuming too much upon God’s love, it declined through luxury into lust, and through lust burst into contempt and rebellion. [Col. 0895B] Therefore it was beaten frequently and in various ways because it had succumbed to adulteries with idols. For it was often delivered over to the sword and often to captivity; but, as it is written, it was unwilling to accept discipline.

For this reason God speaks to it through the Prophet: “You shall no longer be called soft and delicate; but sit,” he says, “on the ground, and take a millstone and grind” (Isa. XLVII). And what after all this? “Your disgraces,” he says, “will appear.”

And again the Lord complains about it through the Prophet: “Have you seen,” he says, “what the house of Israel has done to me? It went upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and there it fornicated with idols.” [Col. 0896D] The manuscripts have this, in place of the printed editions’ very faulty reading, “it contrived wood and stone.” The Vulgate reads, “It committed adultery with the stone and with the wood”; the Septuagint, “It committed adultery with wood and stone.”

“And I said, after she had fornicated in all these ways: Return to me. And she did not return. And I dismissed her and gave her a bill of divorce” (Jer. III).

Let us flee from idols, I beg you, lest we likewise deserve to hear that we have been repudiated. [Col. 0896D] Three editions consistently read thus; for that reason we did not wish to alter it. The manuscripts read better, “lest we likewise deserve to be repudiated.” Whom, however—

Let us hear what bill of divorce the Jewish people received: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

After the Lord’s Passion, an even fuller bill of divorce is given by the Apostles to the synagogue of the Jews, when it is said: “It was necessary that the word of God be announced to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles, as has been commanded us” (Acts XIII).

Therefore, once the Jewish people had been left desolate and rejected, our people from the Gentiles is taken in marriage. [Col. 0896D] The passage designated in Hosea reads as follows: “And I will say to the one who was not my people, ‘You are my people’; and he himself will say, ‘You are my God.’” But in the Epistle to the Romans IX, 25, the same testimony is quoted in this form: “As he says in Hosea: ‘I will call the one who was not my people, my people; and the one who was not beloved, beloved.’” Gaudentius appears to have taken the wording from the New Testament.

“For I will call the one who was not my people, my people; and the one who was not beloved, beloved” (Hos. II).

The Lord had indeed foretold through the Prophet that the nuptials I have described had been celebrated first on the day under the commandment and second under the Law. Therefore the holy evangelist does not simply say, “There was a wedding on the third day,” but, placing a conjunction before it, says: “And on the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there” (John II).

Where? Certainly among the Gentiles. For it is established that blessed Mary derived her ancestry through her mother from the people of Moab. For Boaz begot Obed from Ruth, that Moabite woman. Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot King David (Matt. I). From his seed Joseph was born, to whom the virgin Mary was betrothed—of the same tribe, since otherwise it was not permitted—she who bore Jesus, who is called Christ.

There, therefore, was the mother of Jesus. “Jesus also was invited, together with his disciples, to the wedding” (John II).

A great mystery of piety! He who is the Bridegroom is invited. He is invited by the voices of the Prophets praying in this way: “Lord, incline your heavens and descend” (Ps. CXLIII). And again: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Ps. LXXIX). There are many other similar prayers of the Prophets, humbly inviting him.

The saints are also invited together with Christ, like the faithful friends of that same heavenly Bridegroom, when it is said through the Prophet: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard” (Ps. XVIII). For, filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts I), they were to speak in the languages of the various Gentiles.

Therefore the prophetic spirit, declaring things that were unquestionably going to happen as though they had already happened, added: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

And to show more clearly who these people were and whose heralds they were, he added: “He set his tabernacle in the sun; and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.”

Then the evangelist’s narrative follows: “And they had no wine” (John II).

That the wedding wine had been consumed clearly expressed that the Gentiles did not have the wine of the Holy Spirit. But when he says that the wedding wine had been consumed—that is, that it had failed—he did not speak absolutely, so that you might perhaps believe that it had failed for those to whom it had not yet been given.

For he did not say, “The wedding wine had failed for them”; he merely says that the wedding wine had failed, as though he were saying, “the nuptial wine.” Therefore it is understood that the wine had failed, not of these weddings but of the preceding ones. The nuptial wine of the Holy Spirit had failed, since the Prophets who had ministered among the Jewish people had ceased. [Col. 0897C] The Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts have, “with the Prophets having now ceased,” as does the book of Pantagathus.

For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. There was no one who could give the thirsty Gentiles enough of the spiritual wine to drink. But the Lord Jesus was awaited, so that he might fill new wineskins with new wine through Baptism. For he says: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (Matt. IX; II Cor. V).

Yet all things became new in such a way that their origin remained from the old, since the wine was not produced from nothing but from the ancient element of water.

Do not therefore suppose that the Law of the letter is to be despised, from which the Holy Spirit, through the action of Jesus, is drawn by faithful ministers. For this reason human beings perished in the ancient flood and are now reborn in Baptism, because “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III). The letter by itself kills; tempered with the Holy Spirit, it regenerates.

It is established that all the people of that time perished in that flood except those who deserved to be found within the Ark (Gen. VII), which bore the figure of the Church. Similarly, those who are separated from the apostolic faith and from the Catholic Church cannot now be saved at all.

Therefore let each one of you strive with every effort to remain in the house of the Lord, practicing works appropriate to the grace received. [Col. 0897C] The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions, however, have “each one of us,” and shortly afterward the manuscripts have “reborn into new human beings,” which we have nevertheless declined to adopt. The book of Pantagathus correctly has “each one of you” in both places, and “reborn into a new human being.”

For anyone reborn into a new human being must now guard against his former sins. Preserve, I beg you, your new wineskins, neophytes, lest, returning to your former life, you lose the new wine after the wineskins have burst. For new wine will burst old wineskins; the wine will be spilled, and the wineskins will perish (Mark II; Luke V).

[Col. 0897D] We have faithfully reproduced the reading of two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript, through whose help this entire passage has been restored. In the printed editions, the text first had “regenerated human beings”; then, in place of “in your wineskins,” two editions absurdly read “in your vines”; finally, they had “guard and preserve yourselves, you faithful,” whereas the manuscripts read, “may the faith itself, once guarded, preserve you.” The book of Octavius Pantagathus also supports the agreement of the manuscripts.

Therefore preserve the complete newness of the regenerated human being, and preserve the heavenly wine in your wineskins. [Col. 0897D] Gaudentius seems indirectly to criticize the wholly foolish and stupid heresy of the Ascodrogites, concerning whom see Philastrius, ch. 75, and Augustine, *On Heresies*, to Quodvultdeus, ch. 62; Augustine, however, calls them not Ascodrogites but Ascites. The Ascites were so called from the wineskin: for ἄσκος (*askos*) in Greek is called *uter* (“wineskin”) in Latin. They are said to go about in bacchic frenzy with an inflated, covered wineskin, as though they themselves were the Gospel’s new wineskins filled with new wine. Gaudentius is not remote from this point shortly before, where he says: “Preserve, I beg you, your new wineskins, neophytes, lest, returning to your former life, you lose the new wine after the wineskins have burst”; and above, in this same sermon, p. 278: “The Lord Jesus was awaited, so that he might fill new wineskins with new wine through Baptism.” So that the faith itself, once guarded, may preserve you through the Savior of the human race, Christ Jesus, our Lord and God, who reigns with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, before all things, now, and always, and throughout all ages. [Col. 0898C] In two Vatican manuscripts there follows: “Here ends the first sermon on the Gospel reading.”

Amen.

## SERMON IX: SECOND SERMON ON THE GOSPEL READING
We explained yesterday to your Charity, from the Gospel reading that relates how our Savior made wine from water at a wedding, first according to the literal account of what happened and the reason why he deigned to go there; then according to the spiritual understanding of the heavenly mystery, [Note: [Col. 0898C] The words “what the day was” are absent from the printed editions, which have only “what the first day was.” Yet the former reading fits very well, since above, in the preceding treatise, he explained first of all, allegorically (ἀλληγορικῶς), what the day is. Thus read the two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine, and the Urbinate, as we have printed them; and the codex of Octavius Pantagathus also agrees with them.] what the day was, and which was the first day, which the second, which the third; what the nature of the wedding was; who that bridegroom was and who that bride was; the place where [Note: [Col. 0898D] Thus three manuscripts read. The printed editions have “this wedding.”] that wedding took place; that this was not the first wedding celebrated; and why the Mother of the Lord Jesus is said to have been there. Then we explained why the bridegroom himself was invited to the wedding, or by whom; and how the disciples too were invited together with him. Then we explained what that wine was which they lacked, and what the shortage of wedding wine signified; and how, after the Jewish people had been rejected because of the adultery of idolatry, the Church of the Gentiles was joined to divine love. [Note: [Col. 0898D] The Cologne and Lyons editions incorrectly read, “he rejects the Jewish people because of the adultery of idolatry.” The Paris edition has, “he rejects, because of the adultery of idolatry, the Jewish people,” which comes closer to the authentic reading. We followed the authority of the manuscripts, although so manifest an error did not need correction by deletion. Here too the Florentine codex consistently retains *idolatriae*, as does Pantagathus’s book. See what we noted above in Gaudentius’s Preface to Benivolus, p. 221.] [Col. 0898C]

Therefore we must beware, beloved in every respect, [Note: [Col. 0898D] In Pantagathus’s manuscript, in his own hand, *omnigenae* is substituted for *omni genere*, which is utterly unsuitable. It would indeed be pleasing if *omnigena* were Latin, but the word is *omnigenus*, as examples drawn from Lucretius, Gellius, and others cited by lexicographers show; although *indigena* and *alienigena* are also Latin words. Prudentius used *verbigena* (*Cathemerinon*, hymn 3.2) and *Christigena* (*Hamartigenia* 789). *Nubigena* and *Phoebigena* occur in Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.] lest we again be defiled by some contagion of idolatry and deserve not only to be rejected but also to be condemned forever; for if anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. “For God’s temple is holy,” says the Apostle, “and that is what you are.” Take the greatest care lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ Jesus, as the same most blessed Paul warns (1 Cor. 3; 2 Cor. 11); and lest we be driven away from him who loved us and gave us the pledge of the Holy Spirit in our hearts.

Let us therefore hold fast the grace of the Holy Spirit, poured into us by the generous gift of the heavenly Bridegroom, lest we return to our former poverty. Of this poverty the Mother of the Lord then spoke in a mystery to him, saying, “They have no wine” (John 2). But now let us hear, with minds astonished, what the Lord answered her. Jesus said to her: “What have I to do with you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” [Note: [Col. 0899D] In Pantagathus’s manuscript, “with attentive minds” (attentis) is written in the margin by his own hand, which is certainly better; for there, as in the other books, the reading was “with astonished minds” (attonitis).]

According to the plain sense, it will be sufficient to establish that blessed Mary was called “woman” because of her sex, just as Eve is described in Genesis: “And the Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh. And the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and he brought her to Adam.” And certainly he prefigured her as a virgin. “And Adam said: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman” [Note: [Col. 0899D] Four manuscripts read “she shall be called woman,” and the book of Pantagathus agrees with them.] “because she was taken from her man” (Gen. 2).

But perhaps someone of little faith and scant prudence will say that the virgin Mary indeed conceived Christ not from a man but from the Holy Spirit, as the archangel Gabriel says to her in the Gospel (Luke 1); [Note: [Col. 0899D] Thus the manuscript codices read, whose agreement we have followed. The printed editions read: “nevertheless, after Christ’s birth the Virgin could no longer be so called by Christ.”] yet, once Christ had been born, she could no longer be called a virgin beyond the fact that she had given birth. Therefore Christ did not say, “What have I to do with you, virgin?” but, “What have I to do with you, woman?” [Note: [Col. 0899D] We have restored the little word “from” (de) from the manuscripts; it was absent from the printed editions.] Hear, then, the divine reasoning concerning the hope and life common to us all.

Christ is born not for himself but for us. For he is born who always was; he is born who in the beginning was both the Son of God and the Word of God and God. For this reason, near the end of the age, he was born from a Virgin, so that the Word made flesh might dwell among us (John 1), while nevertheless remaining God, as he had always been.

The Son of God is born as man so that the world might at least in this way behold its Creator; [Note: [Col. 0899D] Thus the Paris edition reads. The Cologne and Lyons editions have “might desire”; the Florentine codex has “might comprehend.”] and he is born from the Holy Spirit of a Virgin so that by the Holy Spirit he might reform from the same substance the human being whom he had fashioned from the clay of the earth. If we believe in the Virgin’s conception, we must also believe in the birth. Both seem impossible to man, but to divine omnipotence they are small matters. For what is difficult for God—leaving aside his greater works—who made the earth from nothing, flesh from earth, and woman from man? In such a way that neither the remaining part of the earth was anything other than what it had been, nor did Adam possess less of what God had taken away, nor was the woman merely that which had been taken from the man.

Adam recognizes his bones and flesh intact in the woman, saying, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2); and do you refuse to believe that the Virgin, remaining intact, recognized as her son him [Note: [Col. 0900D] The manuscripts read “him who performed these things, the intact Virgin, as her son.” The printed editions have “the intact Virgin as a son.”] who performs these things? He is believed to have been conceived without violating his mother; why should he not also be presumed to have been born without violating her? The uncorrupted Virgin gave birth to what the untouched Virgin conceived. He could not violate her integrity by being born, since he had come to restore nature.

If anyone, still weighed down by earthly thinking and hindered by carnal understanding, follows this more slowly and hesitates in an unbelieving heart concerning God’s omnipotence, let him learn from the Gospel of John (John 20) that the same God, after his resurrection, entered twice to the Apostles, when they were gathered in a house because of fear of the Jews, with the doors certainly closed—and he entered in bodily form. But lest he be thought to be not in true flesh but in a phantom, he offered his hands and his other limbs to the Apostle Thomas to touch, in his doubt. Likewise, after entering, he testified to all the disciples together in the Gospel of blessed Luke: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24).

O wondrous faith! The doors were not opened, yet he himself entered within with a true body; he was not only seen by apostolic eyes but also handled by their hands! The marvelous truth of this event, whose explanation faith alone grasps, proclaims the omnipotence of its author. Nor is the event denied because the feebleness of the human mind has not comprehended the greatness of the divine work. [Note: [Col. 0900D] The two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read “did not find,” as do the Urbinate and Pantagathus’s codex.]

By that same power of divinity, therefore, he entered the dwelling of this world through an inviolate woman, preserving even by his birth the enclosure of virginal modesty, just as after his resurrection, with the doors barred, he was able to enter the house bodily. [Note: [Col. 0900D] Thus four manuscripts and the book of Pantagathus read. The printed editions have “who after the resurrection.”]

What is especially relevant to resolving this question is that the Apostle recalls that Christ was born of a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. 4). Thus she is called “woman” while being a virgin, on account of the reality of her sex, not through any loss of integrity—just as God the Son of God is proclaimed to have been made under the Law for the dispensation of our salvation, although he himself is the giver of the Law.

I have said all this for the blessedness of Mary, since Christ called her “woman,” although by a divine birth she began to be a mother in such a way that she remained an even more sacred virgin. [Note: [Col. 0900D] Three manuscripts—namely, the two Vatican codices and the Florentine—read “why her.”] But when he says, “What have I to do with you? My hour has not yet come” (John 2), [Note: [Col. 0901C] Thus read the same three manuscripts and the codex. The printed editions, however, have “that response to this.”] this response does not seem to me to correspond literally to Mary’s suggestion, unless the Lord is understood to have spoken spiritually in a mystery. Since the wine of the Holy Spirit could not be given to the Gentiles before Christ’s passion and resurrection—for the Evangelist testifies that “the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39)—he appropriately answered his mother at the beginning of his signs: “What have I to do with you, woman? My hour has not yet come,” as though he were saying:

“Why is your suggestion so premature, woman, when the hour of my passion has not yet arrived, the hour in which, after all the powers of teaching and divine works have been perfected, I have determined to die for the life of believers? After my passion and resurrection, when I have returned to the Father, then the wine of the Holy Spirit will be given to them.”

Therefore that most blessed woman too, recognizing the profound mystery of this response, understood that her suggestion had not been disdainfully rejected in the present, but that, according to the spiritual meaning, it had then been deferred in mystery. Otherwise she would never have commanded the servants, “Whatever he tells you, do it” (John 2), unless, filled with the Holy Spirit after the divine birth, she had recognized not only the power of Christ’s response but also foreseen the entire sequence by which he would then make wine from water.

For what would remain hidden from the Mother of Wisdom, who was capable of God and a temple fully worthy of so great a power? [Note: [Col. 0901C] This passage suffered from an obvious punctuation error, which we have corrected in this way. In the printed editions the question extends through the following words—“historically confirmed by the truth of the event?”—a scribal error in punctuation that made the sentence not merely obscure but nonsensical. The book of Octavius Pantagathus likewise has our punctuation.]

Since the truth of the event has been historically established, let us now pursue the figures proposed spiritually. Just as you understood the bridegroom and bride, the day and days, the wedding and the place, the lack of wine and the kind of wine, so also understand the Lord’s mother figuratively as the people of the holy Patriarchs, Prophets, and all the righteous, from whom the same Lord is said in the Gospel to have derived the origin of his flesh (Matt. 1). For the book of the generation of Jesus Christ is written as the book of the son of Abraham and of the remaining ancestors.

This mother of the Lord—the generation of the Patriarchs and Prophets—interceded for us Gentiles with the eternal Son of God, born from them according to the flesh, so that he might grant us, in our poverty, the joy of heavenly wine. [Note: [Col. 0901D] We have supplied “his” (suum) from the two Vatican manuscripts.] There are also sayings similar to those which the Apostles, making their request on behalf of the Canaanite woman, a Gentile woman, heard: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (Matt. 15)—that is, to the Gentiles, who had previously been placed in superstition and, like dogs, were accustomed to lick the unclean blood of idol-sacrifices, barking with rabid mouths against the Lord God whom they did not acknowledge. [Note: [Col. 0901D] The Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts read “He hears things similar to those,” as does Pantagathus’s codex; this suitably corresponds to the clause that follows, which the Apostles heard when they made their request.] [Note: [Col. 0901D] The Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts read “that is, the Gentiles who previously”; the Florentine, the two Vatican manuscripts, and the Paris edition read *idolothytarum*. The Cologne and Lyons editions absurdly have *idolatrarum*. Likewise, in the sermon on the Maccabean martyrs the manuscripts read, “they rejected meats sacrificed to idols amid their tortures,” where the printed editions have merely *idolothyta*. At that time the Church’s teaching against eating sacrificial offerings, deriving from apostolic instruction, was especially vigorous. Thus Gaudentius himself, above, tractate 4, p. 253: “See how you preserve your souls from every defilement of foods which Gentile superstition has contaminated.” And Augustine, Gaudentius’s contemporary, in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 16: “It is better to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols.” Christians so abhorred food sacrificed to idols that they detested not only eating it, but every representation and image of it. Therefore Tertullian, rebuking a Christian schoolmaster, says in *On Idolatry*, ch. 10: “He consecrates the very first fee of a new pupil to Minerva, to her honour and name, so that, although he has not been profaned to any idol, he may be said, in word alone, to be connected with food sacrificed to idols.” Rigaltius corrected the printed editions’ erroneous understanding of this passage. Hence emperors hostile to the Christian name, in order more easily to detect the faithful, prescribed by edict that sacrificial food be eaten. Lactantius, speaking of Maximinus in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 37, says: “He was the first to devise that every animal which he ate should be sacrificed not by cooks but by priests, and that nothing at all should be placed upon the table unless it had been tasted in offering, sacrificed, or sprinkled with wine, so that whoever was invited to dinner should leave thence defiled and unclean.” See the notes of Baluzius and Cuper on this passage of Lactantius.]

For we Gentiles were once dogs, and the Jews were once sons. Therefore the Lord did not wish to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs. But after the heavenly bread itself came to his own, and his own did not receive him (John 1); after our same Lord was recognized by Gentiles who had once been dogs, while the sons barked against him with blasphemous mouths; after they cried out together against Pilate, who resisted their demand that Christ, whom they believed to be their king, be sentenced to crucifixion, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19)—God again accuses them through the Prophet: “I have begotten and raised sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1).

“But they shall return toward evening,” as the Prophet says, “and shall suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. 58). For the Jews themselves will eventually return, late, at the evening of the world. For it is written: “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. 10; Rom. 9:27; Hos. 1:10); and the Apostle Paul confesses that the Jewish people have been struck with blindness until the fullness of the Gentiles enters (Rom. 11:25).

They will return at the consummation of the age and will suffer hunger for the word of God, like those dogs that desired to be filled with the crumbs falling from their masters’ table (Matt. 15). Thus the Gentiles, previously dogs, are adopted as sons, and the sons are compared to dogs. For all unbelievers are beasts—not by nature but by their behavior—because “man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish animals and became like them” (Ps. 48). [Note: [Col. 0902D] The printed editions read “and man.”]

Although the Jews had committed things similar to those of the formerly sacrilegious Gentiles, with greater crime, Christ nevertheless loved those whom he loved no longer for their own merit but for the merit of their righteous fathers; and although they were already unworthy, he still called them sons in order to convert them (Matt. 15), and in paternal mercy did not wish to abandon them. [Note: [Col. 0903C] The Vulgate copies read “who were already unworthy, namely”; the manuscripts read “whom, although already unworthy.” We have chosen this reading, removing the word that had intruded furtively.]

He did not wish to withdraw from them too soon and give to the Gentiles himself, the heavenly bread and author of life; not until the steadfast faith of the Gentiles had refuted their faithlessness, and not until he himself, coming in the flesh, had taught and instructed them; chastised them with the benefits of healings; because they proved ungrateful, judged them by divine powers; because they neglected to bend toward faith, condemned them. [Note: [Col. 0903C] Three manuscripts agree fully on this reading, in place of “helped” in the printed editions. I think this is the true reading, because judgment is followed by condemnation; hence the text immediately adds that he condemned them because they neglected to bend toward faith. The rest of the passage has likewise been restored according to the manuscripts.]

And thus, when their wickedness had finally been completed in his Passion, after his own resurrection he migrated to the Gentiles, to whom he would give himself as the bread of life and offer, through the water of Baptism, the cup of the Holy Spirit.

Now let us see to which servants this mother of the Lord Jesus says, “Whatever he tells you, do it” (John 2), and what was commanded and what was done. [Note: [Col. 0903C] The printed editions read quite incorrectly “illuminating the eyes of the flesh.” We have therefore followed the reading of the Vatican manuscripts. The Florentine reads “the eyes of your heart”; Pantagathus’s codex reads “the eyes of our heart.”]

With the Lord and Savior himself illuminating the eyes of our heart—he who is the light coeternal with eternal light—we have understood that, apart from blessed Mary, his proper mother, the people of the holy Patriarchs and Prophets are also his mother, as the source of Christ’s origin, having acted as an embassy before him on behalf of our poverty. [Note: [Col. 0903D] Pantagathus’s manuscript adds “the mother of the Lord,” which is certainly better. A little later it has a small but appropriate transposition: “the cause of origin, to be Christ’s mother.”]

Now let us consider to which servants he speaks when he says, “Whatever he tells you, do it.” I do not understand “servants” to mean only those who were serving at that wedding feast according to the literal event; rather, according to the meaning of the spiritual banquet, [Note: [Col. 0903D] Thus the two Vatican manuscripts read. The Florentine has “of the spiritual banquet.” The three editions ineptly read “according to the transformation of the spiritual matter.”] I understand first the Apostles, the ministers of the New Testament, and then the apostolic priests, to whom both the Law and all the teaching of the holy Prophets make known that whatever the Lord Jesus commands them they must perform with ready obedience. What he commands the servants is stated in the sermon that follows.

Meanwhile, listen to what the Evangelist says: “There were six stone water jars standing there, according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures” (John 2). Although this wedding took place in Galilee of the Gentiles and bore the figure we have described, it was nevertheless then being celebrated among Jews; and there really were six stone jars standing there according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. [Note: [Col. 0903D] Shortly before this, Pantagathus’s codex has “by the Jews,” adding the preposition; here the Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts read “six stone jars standing,” and the same codex agrees. Witnesses cited by Dominicus Macer in his *Hierolexicon* report that at Oveti in Spain, Ravenna in Italy, and elsewhere, some of these jars are preserved in the highest veneration as porphyry vessels. For the vessel at Ravenna, see the eyewitness testimony of Bernard de Montfaucon in his *Diarium Italicum*, p. 101. The distinguished Nicolaus Fabricius Peireskius had arranged through Gabriel Naudé to obtain its measurement and capacity, so that he could furnish his learned treatise on weights and measures, then in preparation, with rarer monuments, as Peter Gassendi relates in Peireskius’s *Life*, book 5, under the year 1633.]

For the Jews had this custom: [Note: [Col. 0904C] This is the reading of one Vatican manuscript, the Urbinate, and the Florentine, which we have preferred to the others as more fitting and better; Pantagathus’s codex has it as well. The other Vatican manuscript reads, “before entering the synagogue, or after returning home from public business, they dined.” The printed editions read, “before entering the synagogue, after returning home from public business, before dining.” On this Jewish purification or washing, see Godwin, book III, ch. 2, and Stuckius, *Antiquities of Feasts*.] before entering the synagogue, or after returning home from public business and before dining, they washed the skin of their bodies with water. The quantity of water sufficient to wash the body was two or three measures, according to the size of the bodies. [Note: [Col. 0904D] We have removed from this passage an inept gloss, which none of the manuscripts supports but which the printed editions alone give in this form: “Either two measures or three, that is, two or three amphorae.” A measure, μετρητὴ (*metrētē*), was an Attic measure of ten *congii*, that is, twelve *sextarii* larger than an amphora, as Budaeus states in book 5 of *De Asse*, p. 580, Lyon edition, Gryphius, 1542. He is nevertheless mistaken in saying that Cratinus called the amphora a *metrētē*, as Jungermannus correctly shows in his notes on Julius Pollux, book 10, chapter 20.]

I cannot pass over without comment the Jews’ unclean purification. They wash polluted bodies and immediately pollute the washed bodies; they are always washing and always unclean; and, as the saying goes, they are washing a brick. The brick they had prepared in Egypt for Pharaoh the devil (Exod. 1), presenting themselves as weapons of wickedness for sin, for the construction of hostile cities. For they are earthly and have not been solidified by the fiery heat of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, until they dissolve into death, they do not cease washing their brick, which is destined to be polluted. Indeed, like pigs, they return from water to mud.

These are the pigs whom the angry Lord handed over to the legion of demons (Matt. 8), so that they might be driven headlong into the lake and killed by everlasting death. Flee the example of uncleanness, neophytes, lest you become participants in their punishment.

The Apostles decreed for us one Baptism according to the divine judgment. [Note: [Col. 0904D] Three manuscript codices read “according to the divine sentence,” and the book of Pantagathus also agrees.] For he says: “Whoever drinks from this water will never thirst” (John 4). You have been washed once in saving Baptism; do not return from the font to the mud. Preserve the purity that has been given you.

What has once been lost cannot be repeated. [Note: [Col. 0904D] Pantagathus’s book does not contain the word “lost” (amissum), but its omission causes no harm, since in that form “once” refers to Baptism, of which he had just said: “The Apostles decreed for us one Baptism according to the divine sentence.”]

But now let us see what those six stone water jars signify allegorically among the Gentiles [Col. 0905A], each holding two or three measures [Note: [Col. 0905C] So reads the Florentine manuscript, as does the book of Pantagathus. Two Vatican manuscripts read “two measures each, or three.” The editions read “two measures, and three.”]. Six faculties are reckoned to exist in every human being: sight of the eyes, hearing of the ears, smell of the nostrils, speech of the mouth, touch of the hands, and movement of the feet. When we were Gentiles, all these faculties were stone within us and dead, as the holy prophet David testifies in his denunciation: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. 113). He deliberately kept silent about the other, baser metals, so that he might condemn the base even more strongly in the case of precious materials. Therefore, since the idols of the nations had sufficiently wealthy craftsmen, let us state in what sense they were condemned: “They will be,” he says, “insensible metals, silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see; they have ears, and they will not hear; they have nostrils, and they will not smell; they have hands, and they will not touch; they have feet, and they will not walk” (ibid.). And what follows? [Note: [Col. 0905C] Two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine manuscript, and the Urbinate read: “Let all who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them.” The book of Pantagathus likewise has this reading.] “Those who make them will become like them, and all who trust in them.” [Note: [Col. 0905C] A fine emendation supplied by the Vatican manuscripts, since this passage had been badly corrupted. [Col. 0905D] The printed editions had read: “Therefore let us consider one thing.” The inexperienced copyist was deceived by the similarity of the letters, or because the worn horizontal stroke crossing the middle of *f* appeared to be an *s*. The Florentine and Urbinate read: “Therefore, when we consider”; but the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus correctly reads *confideremus*, “when we place our trust.” Since in this passage it is found superior to the Florentine and Urbinate, it commends the copyist’s diligence.] Therefore, when we placed our trust in idols, these six faculties were, according to the prophet’s judgment, dead and stony within us, “without proper function, without appropriate movement” [Note: [Col. 0905D] Three manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have: “without function, without appropriate movement, without suitable function,” which was a copyist’s or printer’s error. The manuscript of Pantagathus likewise reads: “without suitable function, without appropriate movement.”]. But when we turned from dead idols to faith in the living God, we were given life, hearing from him: “Because I live, you also will live” (John 14:19). And again: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives—that is, whoever now believes—if he believes to the end, will never die” (John 11).

Having therefore turned to the faith and been given life through Baptism [Col. 0905C], we lift our eyes to the Lord; we draw in the fragrance of his knowledge with an insatiable spirit; and in silent affection we testify that “the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” (Song 4). With our ears we receive the divine readings; with our mouths we confess, praise, bless, and beseech the Lord; we stretch our suppliant hands toward heaven; we run on foot to the church; and with knees bent to the ground we adore the one Godhead of the Trinity.

Therefore Jesus called the ministers—namely, the Apostles and their successors, the priests who serve in the various Churches—and said to them: “Fill these jars with water” (John 2); that is: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28). And plainly because these same ministers had heard the venerable Mary say, “Whatever he tells you, do it,” they filled them to the brim—for they were augmenting Baptism by pouring into it the fullness of teaching.

He rightly said, “having called the ministers.” For Paul was “called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God” (Rom. 1); and all the Apostles likewise were called: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4). “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8) [Note: [Col. 0905D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript read, “those whom he justified, he also illumined,” and the book of Pantagathus agrees with them. But the Vulgate retains “glorified,” as does the Greek edition, which has *toutous kai edoxasen* (“these he also glorified”).]. Having called the ministers, therefore, Jesus entrusted them with the task of celebrating Baptism.

Nor do I pass over, in the final part of this discourse, the fact that these jars of ours are said to hold two or three measures each. Concerning this, some of our people have said: “Two or three measures: the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0906C] The book of Pantagathus does not contain the earlier words, but only the latter ones: “two or three measures”; then follows “namely, the Father and the Son,” which I think is a copyist’s error.]. [Note: [Col. 0906C] The Macedonians, or Pneumatomachi, were afflicted by this error. Philastrius, *On the Semiarians*, ch. 67: “There are also Semiarians who think rightly concerning the Father and the Son, believing that there is one substantial quality and one divinity; but they proclaim the Spirit neither to be of the divine substance nor true God, but made and created.” This error had recently been condemned at the Council of Constantinople, A.D. 381, where, in Baronius, no. 30, the impious opinion of the Semiarians, or Pneumatomachi, is condemned with the utmost execration and detestation. John Albert Fabricius, in the testimonies to Philastrius, cites from the author of the *Praedestinatus*, ch. 52: “Philaster writes that Macedonius called the Holy Spirit the Godhead of the Father and the Son; by this statement he seems to deny the Holy Spirit his own proper attribute.” He then adds: “These words are nowhere found in Philastrius, but were taken from Augustine, ch. 52, as Cotelerius, vol. I of the *Monumenta*, p. 773, rightly noted.” See also, if you wish, the same Philastrius, ch. 86, who, speaking of certain other heretics (perhaps the Adelophagi), says almost the same as he had said above concerning the Semiarians, or Pneumatomachi: “They think rightly concerning the Father and the Son, but do not rightly understand the Spirit, believing the Holy Spirit to be created and made.”]

And they have maintained that some of the Gentiles being baptized are able to receive knowledge of the Father and the Son alone, while others, more capable, can receive knowledge also of the Holy Spirit. But I judge that whoever does not receive the Holy Spirit receives neither the Son nor the Father.

For no one can be baptized except into the complete and inseparable Trinity, since no one confesses the Lord Jesus Christ to be Lord by the propriety of his nature [*proprietate naturae*], as he ought, except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). And “no one goes to the Father except through the Son” (John 14), as he himself testifies: “No one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him” (John 6).

Therefore, whoever diminishes one person of the Trinity to be worshiped has denied the whole Trinity [Col. 0907A] [Note: [Col. 0907C] The Vatican reading, which seemed altogether superior to the others, is followed here. The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus, however, reads: “who denied one person of the Trinity to be worshiped, denied the whole Trinity.” The Urbinate and two editions read: “who has rejected one person of the Trinity to be worshiped,” incorrectly. The Lyon edition reads: “who has refused one person of the Trinity to be worshiped.” The Florentine manuscript reads: “Whoever has diminished one person of the Trinity to be worshiped will deny the whole Trinity.” “Will deny” is also found in three editions.].

Since, therefore, there is neither more nor less in the confession of faith delivered through Christ’s ministers in the sacrament of Baptism, let us see whether our jars each hold two measures or three [Note: [Col. 0907C] So read the manuscripts. The editions instead have “either two, or three.” The book of Pantagathus earlier reads “how many measures” in place of “which measures.”].

The holy apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, declares that, among the various kinds of spiritual virtues, which must be abolished as better things advance [Note: [Col. 0907D] The editions read: “which must necessarily be abolished as merits advance.” But what kind of virtue is ever abolished through the advancement of merits? We have therefore restored the reading of the Florentine manuscript, the Urbinate, and two Vatican manuscripts, which have “as better things advance.” This also better agrees with the Apostle’s meaning, since shortly before he had said: “But earnestly desire the better gifts.”], three things will remain forever: hope, faith, and charity. “Hope, faith, and charity remain,” he says, “these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13).

Faith is that by which we confess the Trinity to be of one substance. Hope is that by which we await the future resurrection of the flesh and the rewards that will follow according to our merits. Charity is that by which we love Christ so greatly that we endure being put to death for his name with equanimity.

But although all who have been baptized in the apostolic faith do believe in the Trinity and hope for the future, not all have dared, with the holy Apostle, to say from the heart: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8). For this reason, some of our jars hold two measures, while others hold three.

May the Lord Jesus, rich toward and above all who call upon him, grant that we may receive three measures, perfected in his charity, even without an open battle of persecution; so that, with minds prepared in the love of God to endure every present punishment, we may stand firm and, through the triumph of an unseen contest, earn a radiant crown of a victorious conscience [Note: [Col. 0907D] So the editions read. The manuscripts have “standing firm.”].

Therefore, after the most blessed Apostles, having fulfilled the office of ministers of the faithful (Acts 2, 6), had filled the jars of believing peoples with the water of venerable Baptism, and the Lord Jesus had changed this water into wine by invisible power, so that those baptized by them might immediately testify by the sudden gift of tongues to the taste of the divine Spirit working within them, among whom the first, Stephen the martyr [Note: [Col. 0907D] The Urbinate reads: “full of grace and power,” as does the book of Pantagathus.], “full of grace and truth, was performing great signs and wonders among the people in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”—

then the Lord Jesus himself said to those same ministers: “Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast.” And they took it.

“When the master of the feast had tasted,” he says, “the water that had become wine, and did not know where it came from—but the ministers knew, because they had drawn the water—the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: ‘Everyone first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, the inferior; but you have kept the good wine until now’” (John 2) [Note: [Col. 0907D] So read two editions. The Florentine reads: “But when the master of the feast had tasted, he says, the water that had become wine.” The Lyon edition reads: “The master of the feast, the water that had become wine.” Two Vatican manuscripts read: “the water that had become wine, and he did not know where it was from,” in place of “where it might have been from”; the manuscript of Pantagathus has the same reading.].

Let us first explain the history of the event itself, and then return to the proposed meaning of its spiritual interpretation.

When weddings took place among the Jews, one man—so far as we have learned from tradition—was appointed from the priestly order to govern the legitimate observance of the discipline and to oversee conjugal modesty. At the same time, he would assign the servants and regulate the arrangements for the banquets; and for this office he was called the master of the feast, that is, the supervisor of the dining room [*triclinium*].

The ministers of the banquet were therefore ordered to bring him a taste of the wine made from water. The master of the feast tastes it without knowing where it came from; and, having summoned the bridegroom, praises to him the flavor of the wine reserved until that time.

Through all these events the Savior’s power is shown, in this sign also, to have been not a phantom but reality, since the master of the feast testifies that what the ministers brought him to taste at the Lord’s command was not merely wine but good wine [Col. 0908C] [Note: [Col. 0907D] Casaubon unjustly criticized this passage in *Exercitationes* 13 on Baronius, §19, where he censures Gaudentius for confusing the master of the feast with the supervisor of morals. It is said that there were three offices among those who received guests at banquets: (1) the master of the household; (2) the master of the banquet, who was also called *architriclinus*, or supervisor of the dining room; and (3) the supervisor of morals, called by the Greeks *oinoptēs*, “wine-inspector,” whose duty it was to ensure that the guests did not exceed proper limits in drinking. Athenaeus discusses the *oinoptai* in Book 10, chapter 7; he also assigns them another duty, on the authority of Philinus, reporting that there were three *oinoptai* who supplied lamps and wicks to those dining. Since Petronius, in the *Satyricon*, also assigns this duty to the *tricliniarch*, or master of the dining room—and since the *tricliniarch* had already risen and poured oil into the lamps as they were going out—I do not see why the office of the *oinoptēs* could not sometimes have been one and the same as that of the *architriclinus*. Popma omitted the office of the *tricliniarch* from his little book *On the Duties of Servants*, published by the Plantinian press in 1608, although it had already been noted in the Cinellian shelves, XIX, p. 105. There is also an inscription attached to the commentaries on Petronius: “M. Ulpius, imperial freedman of the deified Trajan Augustus, cupbearer; likewise *a laguna* [uncertain], tricliniarch.” As for Casaubon’s further claim that he did not remember ever reading that it was the custom of the Jews to appoint one and the same man as *oinoptēs* and *architriclinus*, that eminent man was carried away by an excessive desire to refute Baronius, who had relied on Gaudentius’ authority. There is absolutely no reason why we should not prefer Gaudentius affirming this matter to Casaubon denying it.].

Returning now to the spiritual line of interpretation, let us consider who this master of the feast is. I think that the master of the feast is the most blessed Moses, a man of the tribe of Levi, God’s faithful steward in all his house. He was placed in charge not only of those ancient nuptials of the people of Israel, who later deserved to be rejected, but also of those now being celebrated among the Gentiles.

For who among us could have learned, without the master of the feast Moses, that the Lord our God is one God and that there are no other gods? And, lest you think that the statement about one Godhead is complete in itself, there the Trinity is proclaimed by him, since he speaks of the Lord as God and Lord. For he did not simply say, “Hear, Israel: your God is one.” Rather, what does he say? [Note: [Col. 0909D] So read the Paris edition and the manuscripts. In the Cologne and Lyon editions “Lord” is missing; they read: “Hear, Israel: your God, the Lord, is one.” The omission of this single word overturns the whole meaning.] “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deut. 6). This means that God is one in the Trinity; the Godhead and dominion of the Trinity are one, while the true distinction of the subsisting persons remains.

Likewise, the two wings of the Seraphim, bearing the image both of the Law and the Prophets and of the Old and New Testaments [Note: [Col. 0909D] Two Vatican manuscripts read “two wings of seraphim.” The Florentine has “two wings of seraphim”; the manuscript of Pantagathus has “two wings of the Seraphim”; the editions have “two wings of the seraphim.”], proclaim the hymn of the Trinity to be worshiped and continually cry: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” “Lord,” not “Lords” (Isa. 6) [Note: [Col. 0909D] We have followed the Vulgate reading, although four manuscripts read in the same way: “they proclaim the hymn to the Trinity to be worshiped,” as does the book of Pantagathus, which shortly afterward has “and continually cry out together” in place of “and continually cry.”]. For the one and the same Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit does not admit a plural number.

Furthermore, who among us, as I have said, could have known without the master of the feast Moses that in the beginning God made heaven, earth, and the sea, and everything in them? Or from what source man was formed as male, and woman as female; or from whom the whole succession of the human race is known to have multiplied? Furthermore, what the first blessedness of paradise granted was; what was the beginning of humanity’s guilt, by which the offense of man provoked God; what generations belonged to the righteous and which to the wicked; and why, or when, the flood occurred, together with all the other things written in the Law of Moses? And, to put it briefly, whose soul would have deserved to be joined to divine Love and to Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom, without the provisions of this master of the feast? [Note: [Col. 0910D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “Whose soul has deserved to be joined to the divine Lamb and the heavenly Bridegroom.”]

For Moses himself, who had foretold the coming of Christ to the people of Israel, saying: “The Lord our God will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me; you shall listen to him in everything that he will speak to you. But every soul that does not listen to that prophet will perish from among the people” (Deut. 18)—

when he saw them resisting Christ, whom he had proclaimed, turned to the Gentiles and, together with the holy Apostles, reproached the Jewish people: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be announced to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord commanded us” (Acts 13): “I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49) [Note: [Col. 0910D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the book of Pantagathus read: “I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be for salvation.”].

Therefore, after the Lord Jesus had made wine from water in us, to show—as the Apostle says—the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy (Rom. 9), and had seasoned each of the baptized with the flavor of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0910D] So read three manuscripts. The editions have “and had likewise seasoned the baptized.”], converting the water of the legal letter through the hearts of believers into spiritual wisdom [Col. 0910B], then he said to the ministers: “Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast” (John 2).

The Apostles draw from the jars of the baptized Gentiles both the spiritual flavor and the grace of evangelical power [Note: [Col. 0910D] So read the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts, which have shed remarkable light on this passage. The editions had read: “spiritual flavor in faith, grace of warmth in action”; thus the grace, color, beauty, charm, and elegance of the passage had been entirely destroyed through the fault of the copyists. The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus agrees with the Vatican and Florentine manuscripts.]: flavor in faith, grace of color in action. One is perceived; the other is seen. And they carry it to Moses.

For what priest ministering to Christ would not compare the whole wisdom of the New Testament with the Law of Moses, hearing that the Lord himself both commanded this and carried it out? For when he had cleansed a leper by the touch of his power, he immediately sent him to the Law, saying: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them” (Matt. 8).
