The master of the feast tasted the mystery of Christ hidden from the ages [Col. 0910C] [Note: [Col. 0910D] Three manuscripts read “which was not known to the other nations”; but this does not fit the passage at all, since shortly afterward it says, “as it has now been revealed.” The term *generatio* (“generation”) here stands in place of a temporal expression.], which had not been made known to other generations among the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy Apostles and Prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel. “Of this,” Paul says, “I became a minister” (Eph. 3).

The Gentiles therefore became sharers, through each Apostle as an evangelical minister, in God’s promise in Christ—namely, the promise that the Apostles themselves had first received and would afterward minister to others.

For when Christ remained with them after his resurrection for forty days, as Luke the Evangelist testifies at the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles, “he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which,” he said, “you have heard from me; for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1) [Note: [Col. 0911D] So read the manuscripts, correctly; the Vulgate agrees with them. The editions have *baptizamini*, “be baptized,” perhaps through a typographical error.].

At the end of his Gospel he likewise records the same Lord speaking to those Apostles: “Behold,” he says, “I am sending the promise of my Father into you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).

Although, therefore, the master of the feast Moses did not know that such grace had been bestowed through the gift of Baptism—a grace known to the Apostles, who were ministers of the word—nevertheless, astonished that the taste of the Holy Spirit was present in the jars of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0911D] The editions read “but, having marveled”; we have deleted this and restored the reading of four manuscripts, with which the book of Pantagathus also agrees.], he praises the bridegroom’s generosity, since he had kept such wine for the Gentiles.

The Jews possessed this wine at the earlier wedding [Note: [Col. 0911D] We have retained the common reading, since the manuscripts have “the Jews, while drinking”; but in what follows we have adopted the reading of the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts, since the editions read “but they also became drunk with something harmful.”], but they did not drink it for their salvation; rather, they became drunk and were wounded by a destructive heaviness, being weaker in mind and unable to bear the power of the divine Spirit [Note: [Col. 0911D] Two Vatican manuscripts read “weak in mind”; the Florentine reads “weak in mind,” and the manuscript of Pantagathus has the same reading. Shortly afterward, instead of “filled with the Holy Spirit is not drunk,” it substitutes “is filled with the Holy Spirit and is not drunk.”]. But whoever is strong in faith, filled with the Holy Spirit, is not drunk.

For the cup of God is glorious precisely because it makes drunk (Ps. 22): the intoxication produced by the divine drink makes the minds of those who drink it sober. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, but be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Eph. 5). Stephen too, full of the Holy Spirit and not drunk, saw the heavens opened [Note: [Col. 0911D] The manuscripts add “and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.”], and Jesus at the right hand of God (Acts 7).

For this reason the most blessed Peter also condemned drunkenness, saying (Acts 2): “For these men are not drunk, as you suppose,” he says, “since it is only the third hour of the day. Rather, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your young men shall see visions, and your elders shall dream dreams’” (Joel 2).

This was the beginning of signs that Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee, that is, in the possession of the Gentiles. He manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him (John 2).

Nor is it insignificant that he says “disciples,” not “Apostles.” To indicate the multitude of believers, he used the name “disciples,” not “Apostles.” For all who believe are his disciples; but, as blessed Paul says, “Are all Apostles?” (1 Cor. 12).

Let us now strive and pray, beloved, that after this beginning of signs which the Lord Jesus performed by giving the Holy Spirit in our hearts, he may also perfect in us the remaining signs of virtue. “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another healing in one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another discernment of spirits [Note: [Col. 0911D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read: “to another gifts of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits,” a reading also found in the book of Pantagathus.], to another prophecy, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of utterances. But all these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Having therefore these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh, perfecting the sanctification of the spirit in the fear of God (2 Cor. 7) [Note: [Col. 0912D] Two Vatican manuscripts read this way. The Vulgate reading, “in the fear of God according to the spirit,” is extremely corrupt. The Florentine manuscript, exercising its own authority—which is difficult to imagine anything more absurd, since it seems to attribute virtue and power to the Holy Spirit in the Apostle Paul—reads: “in the fear of God. According to the Spirit, therefore, by the exercise of his own authority.” The result is scarcely more satisfactory. The book of Octavius Pantagathus correctly reads: “in the fear of God, but the Holy Spirit.” We have also noted above in this same discourse that this manuscript seems superior to the Florentine. It also has below: “lest anyone, deceived by hostile persuasion, should suspect,” where the editions read “should suspect, deceived by hostile persuasion.”].

But the Apostle proclaimed that the Holy Spirit distributes the gifts of heavenly graces according to the decision of his own authority, saying: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills, and not as he is commanded” (1 Cor. 12). This is so that no one, deceived by hostile persuasion, might dare suspect that within that substance of the Trinity to be worshiped there is anything subordinate, less powerful, or contrary to itself, since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one will equally in all things and one power throughout all the ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. THE EIGHTH ON THE READING FROM EXODUS.

Having finished here what I had proposed to discuss, both concerning the reading from Exodus and concerning the Gospel reading, I reserved for the Lord’s Day something appropriate that is written in the final part of that reading, where God first announces the law of the Passover. For after the warning he had given—“Everyone who eats anything leavened from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall perish from Israel” (Exod. XII, 15)—he added, saying: “And the first day shall be called holy, and the seventh day shall be called holy for you; you shall do no servile work, except what must be done for every person” (ibid., 16).

[Note: Codex Pantagathi has the better reading *after the pronouncement with which he had said*; shortly afterward, having removed the conjunction, it added *from Israel*.]

That the first day of the world is the Lord’s Day is proved by the seventh day, the Sabbath, on which God is said to have rested, as Scripture says: “And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works that God had begun to make” (Gen. II).

Divine Scripture speaks cautiously, not saying absolutely that God rested from his works, but that he rested from the works that God had begun to make, lest you suppose that the almighty One, who makes all things by the command of his word, had grown weary, when you hear that he rested; rather, understand that, after all the things of this world had been completed, from which he is described as having rested—that is, ceased—he did not cease to carry out other things pleasing to his will. Thus the Lord Jesus testifies in the Gospel, saying: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17).

[Note: The words “you hear” and the rest that follows up to “is described as having ceased” had fallen out through the fault of the copyists; we restored them on the authority of the Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions had, rather ineptly: “when he is described as having rested and ceased, although he does not cease to perform other things pleasing to his will.” In the Pantagathi manuscript, after “when he is described as having rested, that is, ceased,” the rest is also missing.]

God’s rest, therefore, is not a remedy for labor, but the completion of works begun; for after he perfected the world, he did not cease to govern his work. At his command, indeed, the nature of all things either carries out its course when ordered, or withdraws when restrained.

For in the days of holy Noah (Gen. VIII and IX), by his providence he either destroyed the world, polluted by various iniquities, through the Flood, or restored it after the Flood. He himself rained sulfur and fire from heaven upon the four cities of Sodom, where males practiced shameful acts with males (Gen. XIX), contrary to the ordinary course of nature, so that the fiery rain might extinguish those whom illicit passion had inflamed to attack the order of nature itself.

[Note: Urbinas and two Vatican manuscripts read: “which he had inflamed to attack the law of nature”; the Pantagathi manuscript agrees.]

He himself chose the patriarchal race from among the nations, namely, the Hebrew people. For the sake of their liberation, he afflicted the kingdom of Egypt with nine plagues and destroyed it with the tenth (Exod. XII, XIII, XIV, XV).

He himself divided the Red Sea. When the wave of the fluid element was stiffened into the strength of walls, the waters froze—for they froze like a wall—and the waves froze in the midst of the sea, as the faith of that triumphant song testifies in Exodus (Exod. XV). He, then, divided the Red Sea, which the Greeks call the Erythraean Sea, in order both to prepare a passage for his people and a pitfall for their pursuers.

For when the Israelites had gone out through the bed of the sea on dry ground, and all the Egyptians had entered hastily after them by the same passage, God immediately restored to the astonished waters their natural fluidity, which he had taken away; and when the waters overwhelmed the armed ranks of the cavalry, Pharaoh himself together with the chariots and the entire army, he slew them all. The walls of water that had protected the believing people cast down the hostile force by their own collapse.

[Note: This is how the printed editions read; but two Vatican manuscripts and the Pantagathi manuscript have: “He himself rained down manna as food.”]

He himself rained down manna as food upon his worshipers in the wilderness (Exod. XVI), he who had rained down fire upon criminals guilty of unspeakable sacrilege: he rained down manna in his gentleness, he who in indignation had rained down flame.

But since the plan of this treatment does not permit me to review individually and in order the matters belonging to the first and seventh days, I shall pass over what is unnecessary and touch briefly upon a few points. He himself split the rock, and waters flowed (Ps. LXXVII) for so many thousands of thirsty people in the desert (Exod. XVII); he struck down countless peoples of the enemy and destroyed very many kingdoms of hostile nations.

He also dried up the Jordan River, so that he might lead the believing people into the promised land. He himself dried up the Jordan River (Josh. III, IV), who had turned the arid rock into a liquid stream:

> For at the presence of the Lord the earth was moved,  
> at the presence of the God of Jacob,  
> who turned the solid rock into a pool of water  
> and the cliff into springs of water (Ps. CXIII).

Then he established in Zion the Law that he had given on Sinai, increased it in Jerusalem, and, after the offense of his beloved people, extended that same Law to the nations.

For after the Son of God came in human form—through whom all these things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John I)—he was rejected, and even crucified, by those who had once been his sons, whom he had protected and exalted. Through the Prophet he cries out:

> I begot sons and exalted them,  
> but they rejected me.  
> The ox knows its owner  
> and the ass its master’s manger,  
> but Israel does not know me,  
> and my people have not understood (Isa. I).

[Note: This agrees with not a few of the ancient Fathers, who used allegory in interpreting this testimony of Isaiah. When the learned Johannes Antonius Vulpius Bergomas, well trained in many branches of both Greek and Latin learning, noticed this passage of Gaudentius while we were conversing amicably at Padua, he appropriately wondered whether the more recent writers who, following Casaubon and Tillemont, had agreed with the ancients in explaining mystically those words of Isaiah—“The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger”—could derive any support from it. They had thought that the Prophet’s words could in no way be understood historically of an ox and an ass standing beside the Lord’s manger, and consequently that the whole story, on whose authority these brute animals are placed near the Lord’s cradle, was a badly assembled fable.

Nevertheless, if all other considerations were equal, he thought that nothing prevented the Prophet’s words from also being understood historically, even though the Fathers had explained them mystically with sufficiently unanimous agreement. For what is more common among the ancients, and especially in our Gaudentius, than to draw the historical deeds of Christ, and the very Gospel narratives, toward an allegorical meaning?

He also added, quite ingeniously, if I am not mistaken, that painters should not on that account be blamed, even if the truth of the event, supported by the credulity of so many centuries, were in no way certain. For such brute animals could have been placed beside the cradle of the newborn Lord as figures and symbols of the Jewish or Gentile people, by unanimous ecclesiastical agreement, in order to show that Isaiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled at Christ’s birth under this sign. I approved the learned man’s opinion and therefore judged it worthy of being appended to this passage.]

As though he were saying: Since in former times the brute animals of the Gentile peoples recognized the ruler of heaven as their owner and Lord, clothed in the rags of human sins and placed in the narrow manger of Judaea (Luke II), whereas the Israelite people were unwilling to recognize their liberator:

> I will take away, as it was foretold, from Judaea and from Jerusalem the strong male and the strong female.

That is, the incarnate Word; the power of bread and the power of water; the power of heavenly food and the power of regenerating water; the prudent man of fifty, namely the jubilee year of remission; and the wise architect (Isa. III), namely the Holy Spirit, through whom I may build for myself a new Church from the Gentiles.

For the Lord took away all the gifts and benefits of salvation from the ungrateful Jews, both those he had granted and those he had promised, and bestowed them upon those from every nation who had been converted to his faith with willing service.

When, then, did the Lord rest, who has always been at work, of whom we are completely certain from the few works I have briefly recalled, and whom we plainly see working every day?

[Note: The manuscripts read: “we always see him at work.”]

For the fact that the elements, both heavenly and earthly, serve the human race is his work. How could they fail to despise the small and earthly human being unless they obeyed the command of their Creator?

We ourselves also—our being born, our knowing in part these very works of the Lord, our seeking life by living, our conducting and speaking ourselves piously while bearing hope of things to come—these, I say, are the works of God, of God.

It is also a great work of his mercy that he patiently tolerates even the wicked and unbelieving, waits for them mercifully, and, if they repent, embraces them like a merciful father.

The Son of God plainly rested then also from all the works that God had begun to make, when, after all the wonders had been completed and the entire work of the Passion of the sixth day had been fulfilled, he rested buried on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “and when the entire work of the Passion of the sixth day had been fulfilled.” The Florentine manuscript has “when the entire work had been fulfilled on the sixth day of the Passion,” as does the Pantagathi manuscript.]

But since God’s rest is an active rest, that rest could not be inactive. For after his body had been placed in the tomb, his divinity descended with the soul of the man into the underworld and called the souls of the saints from their places. Matthew the Evangelist testifies that their bodies had risen, saying:

> And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose;  
> and, he says, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection,  
> they entered the holy city and appeared to many (Matt. XXVII).

That the Savior’s soul descended to visit the underworld is testified not only by the Epistle of blessed Peter (I Pet. III), but also by the prophecy of blessed David, which says:

> For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld,  
> nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption (Ps. XV).

For the Son of God did not descend into the underworld with the soul of the man he had assumed in order to leave it there, but to call back the souls of many whose bodies were to rise.

For this reason, he who had always existed in the form of God, taking the form of a servant, also accepted the cross, so that by rising on the third day he might triumph over the death he had accepted—a death which the Lord of life could not be permitted to suffer permanently.

Therefore, since after his Passion the Lord Jesus was going to rise from the dead at the dawning of the Lord’s Day and was going to confer the first sanctity upon the first day of his resurrection, the ancient Law foretells this, saying: “The first day shall be called holy, and the seventh day shall be called holy for you” (Exod. XII, 16).

It declares that the first day of the resurrection is to be called holy; it says that the seventh day, already called, will be holy. This means the seventh thousandth year, concerning which the Prophet says to the Lord:

> For a thousand years in your sight  
> are like one day (Ps. LXXXIX).

Thus, therefore, all festivity had to be transferred to the first day of Christ’s resurrection, so that we might await both rest and holiness on the seventh day, when it is said: “The first day shall be called holy,” and immediately added: “And the seventh day shall be called holy for you. You shall do no servile work, except what must be done for every person” (Exod. XII).

[Note: We corrected this passage with the help of the Florentine manuscript, since it had been printed corruptly as follows: “the festivity was to be transferred to Christ on the first day of the resurrection.” The Pantagathi manuscript also gives the reading of the Florentine manuscript.]

[Note: The Florentine manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Urbinate read in this way. The printed editions had “because he called the first day the Lord’s Day”; but that gloss—“that is, the Lord’s Day”—may perhaps have been added by a copyist, although it also occurs in the Pantagathi manuscript.]

For all of us who now call the first day—that is, the Lord’s Day—holy, believing that it was sanctified by the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, also await that truly holy day:

[Note: This appears to have been taken from Irenaeus, Book V *Against Heresies*, chapter 28, and Lactantius, Book VII of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 14; but Augustine refutes this opinion in his commentary on Psalm LXXXIX and in Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 53, saying: “Therefore we vainly attempt to calculate and determine the years that remain to this world, since from the mouth of Truth we hear that it is not ours to know.” See also the same Augustine, Letters 78, 79, and 80. At that time a Jewish tradition was also current among Christians that the world would last for six thousand years and, when these were completed, would perish and be destroyed in the seventh millennium. Huet demonstrates this tradition in *Evangelical Demonstration*, part 9, chapter 8; and Johann Albert Fabricius in the *Pseudepigraphal Code of the Old Testament*, published at Hamburg in 1713, p. 1079. Compare Cotelerius’s notes to the Epistle of St. Barnabas, pp. 45–46, in the *Apostolic Fathers*, Antwerp edition of 1698, and Feuardent’s note on Irenaeus, p. 368, where he cites this passage of Gaudentius.]

—the day of the seventh thousand years, which will come after these six days, that is, after the six thousand years of the world. When these have been completed, there will be rest truly for the holy and for those who faithfully believe in Christ’s resurrection.

[Note: The common reading was “there will be rest of true holiness,” which we rejected as manifestly corrupt, restoring the reading of the Florentine manuscript. This correction is strengthened by the authority of two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate, which read: “there will be rest for the holy and for those who faithfully believe.” In the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus, with the word “truly” omitted, the reading is likewise: “there will be rest for the holy and for those who faithfully believe.”]

For there will be no struggle there against the devil, who will then be held bound in punishment; no contest against the vices of the body, which will no longer be subject to desires.

For the spiritual body will rise, as the Apostle says:

> What is sown in corruption will rise in incorruption;  
> what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory;  
> what is sown in weakness will rise in power;  
> what is sown as an animal body will rise as a spiritual body (I Cor. XV).

And again, shortly afterward, the same most blessed Paul says:

> This corruptible body must put on incorruption,  
> and this mortal body must put on immortality.

[Note: These words had fallen out of the printed editions, but we judged that they had necessarily to be restored from the manuscripts. They are also present in the manuscript that formerly belonged to Octavius Pantagathus.]

And when this mortal body has put on immortality, then, he says, the word written will come to pass:

> Death has been swallowed up in victory.  
> Where is your victory, O death?  
> Where is your sting, O death? (ibid., 3)

And what the sting of death is, the connected statement of the blessed Apostle himself makes clear:

> The sting of death is sin,  
> and the power of sin is the Law (I Cor. XV, 56).

Indeed, dear ones, the sting of death is sin, because death comes through sin; but the power of sin is the Law, because without the Law sin is dead. For sin is not counted where there is no Law.

Adam, too, would not have died because he ate from the fruit of that tree, unless he had eaten against the prohibition, despising the law of the commandment. Nor does anyone today incur the guilt of sin if he is not bound by either the natural law, or the law of the commandment, or the Law of the letter.

The natural law is that by which the Gentiles, who do not have the Law of the letter, naturally do the things that belong to the Law (Rom. II). For the nature of the rational human soul understands by a certain natural law that it should recognize its Creator, not harm its neighbor, and not do what it does not want to suffer. Hence every person is without excuse who either denies his Creator or does the evil that, through the law of nature, he knows to be evil.

[Note: Philastrius also calls the commandment the state of human nature before the Mosaic Law, chapter 133, distinguishing these three stages: in the first age one is under the commandment, in the second under the Law, and in the third under the grace of the Savior, p. 111. See also what the most distinguished Fabricius observed there, as well as chapter 109, p. 85. Thus Philastrius likewise says, chapter 150: “The Law of the letter is placed midway between the commandment and grace”; and chapter 146: “In the commandment, the Law, and the grace of Christ are found all the gifts of dignity that were bestowed upon peoples in the first, second, and final ages through their various merits.” Gaudentius agrees with Philastrius not only here, but also above, Sermon 8, p. 273: “The first day was under the commandment, from Adam to Moses; the second day was under the Law of Moses; the third day is under the grace of the Savior.” What Gaudentius adds here—that the written Law was therefore given so that, for a negligent person, a written reminder of either the natural law or the law of the commandment might be supplied, and so that forgetfulness might have a tutor—is the same as what Philastrius says in chapter 133: “The Law is a reminder of the commandment and a confirmation of that first one”; and shortly afterward: “When this had been forgotten among the Jews, the reminder of the letter followed again”; and again, in chapter 150: “The Law is a reminder of the commandment.”]

Again, the law of the commandment is:

> You may eat for food from every tree that is in paradise;  
> but from this one you shall not eat (Gen. II),

together with all the commands that the Lord is known to have given before Moses by word alone.

The Law of the letter is:

> You shall not kill;  
> you shall not commit adultery;  
> you shall not bear false witness (Exod. XX),

and the other commandments which, after half the number of the world’s years had already passed—

[Note: This means three thousand years, according to the opinion concerning the consummation of the world at the end of the sixth millennium, which was discussed above. Gaudentius seems to have followed the calculation of the Greeks, who placed the Flood two thousand two hundred and forty-two years after the creation of the world. I infer from Sulpicius Severus, Book I of the *Sacred History*, chapter 5, that this calculation was also accepted among the Latins in Gaudentius’s time. But since, if this calculation is accepted, considerably more than three thousand years intervene between the creation of the world and the Law, Gaudentius perhaps meant that half the number of the world’s years had already elapsed. Today those who have published investigations into the reckoning of time differ extraordinarily from this calculation.]

—are prohibited by the Law of the letter, so that, for a negligent person, a written reminder of either the natural law or the law of the commandment might be supplied, and so that forgetfulness might have a tutor and concealment a compelling force. The Apostle says:

> For the Law was our tutor in Christ (Gal. III).

Now the Law—whether of nature, of the commandment, or of the letter—rules a person when his age begins to be capable of the Law.

Hence comes the statement of the Apostle Paul, born of Jewish parents, a Hebrew of Hebrews. He says: “I was once living without the Law,” to show that only the age of infancy lives without the Law, since infancy is not yet capable of the Law. “But when the commandment came,” he says, “sin revived, and I died” (Rom. VII).

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine manuscript, and the Pantagathi manuscript read this way. The printed editions have: “the age of the infant alone.”]

This is what he meant: sin, which was dead to one who did not know it, began to live for one who understood it; and I, who had previously lived without the Law, became liable to death unless I turned away from sin, which now, once understood by me, generates death. Thus the commandment that was given to me for life began to become death for me.

That seventh thousandth year, then—to return to the subject—will be the truly blessed day, when the struggle of this contest that we now endure has ended, the victors will receive the desired rest and enjoy happy repose:

[Note: The same manuscripts give this reading, which no one will deny to be more suitable if he considers what follows, since “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.” The printed editions instead have: “no servile work there, and doing no work of sin”; but the entire force of the statement is lost. The Lyons edition has: “doing no servile work”; the rest has fallen out.]

They will do no servile work there—that is, no work of sin—for “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin,” as the Savior says (John VIII). They will do only what must be done for every holy person: joined with the ranks of the angels, they will offer our Lord perpetual hymns and thanksgivings forever.

Certainly, according to the historical sense, the commandment given to the Jews was that on the Sabbath days they should rest from every work of sin and practice only those things that were appropriate to the soul.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript have: “so that even on the Sabbaths they might rest from the work of sin; then, that they might practice only those things appropriate to the soul.” The Urbinate and the Pantagathi manuscript also agree with this reading.]

But because, neglecting this salutary observance, they had turned the entire law of the Sabbath toward idleness and luxury, it is clear why God now declares that he hates not his own Sabbaths but theirs.

[Note: These words are plainly absent from three manuscript copies, but they must be retained so that the sense not be defective and mutilated. They are also missing in the Pantagathi manuscript, but in Pantagathi’s own hand *therefore* has been substituted for *wherefore*, and *they have turned* is read for *they had turned*, and *to hate* for *he hated*. Thus the whole passage reads: “They have turned the entire law of the Sabbath toward idleness and luxury; therefore God hates his Sabbaths.”]

In the Gospel readings I have often explained to your fraternity—

[Note: See the following treatise. It is plainly evident from this passage that the following four treatises, on various Gospel passages, were written before the ten paschal treatises. Gaudentius had hinted at the same thing in the Preface, saying: “Moreover, I shall send you the four shorter treatises that you said I had formerly mentioned to you, on various Gospel passages, and a fifth on the martyrs of the Maccabees, corrected for you because you compel me, so that, if you judge them worthy of any useful remembrance, you may have them transcribed together in the final part of this little booklet.”]

—that when the foolish Jews accuse the Savior of violating the Sabbath, we have shown by clear proof that he rather fulfilled the law of the Sabbath through the works he performed on the Sabbaths. We learned this from no other source than the very Law that we read together with the Jews. For it is written:

> There shall be one Law for the native-born and for the foreigner (Exod. XII, 49).

The native-born were certainly the Jews, citizens of the patriarchs and of the Prophets. The foreigners, whom the Greek language calls *proselytoi* (προσήλυτοι), were we Gentiles, as the Apostle says: strangers and sojourners from the covenants and the promises, having no hope in them and being without God in this world (Eph. II).

But after we believed, the same blessed Paul says to us:

> You are no longer strangers and foreigners,  
> but you are fellow citizens with the saints  
> and members of God’s household (ibid.).

Thus we have one Law with the Jews. But they receive it in a carnal sense, seeking no spiritual understanding in it; we, on the other hand, find Christ in it, in whom all the treasures of heavenly wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. II).

Finally, in this reading from Exodus too, which sets out the order for celebrating the Passover, we find the true Lamb of God together with all the mysteries of our life:

[Note: We corrected this from four manuscript copies, and the Pantagathi manuscript also supports it, since the printed editions had “one Lamb of God.”]

recognizing him as the true God and man, the Lord of the flock and the sheep,

[Note: The manuscripts differ. The two Vatican manuscripts offer nothing sound, reading “the shepherd together and the Passover”; but the Florentine manuscript has, quite correctly, “the shepherd together and the pasture.” *Pascua* in the feminine gender is also found in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 22: “What pasture is more carefully provided for them than one that turns a human being away from contemplation of true divinity through false enchantments?” Likewise Vossius, Book V *On the Vices of Language*, reports that Arnobius the Younger, on Psalm CX, wrote: “Appointing shepherds and pastures for them.” See Meursius’s note on Minucius Felix, p. 336, Leiden edition, with the notes of the Variorum edition of 1672. We have retained the common reading, which is supported by the authority of the Urbinate manuscript; the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus agrees with the reading of the Florentine manuscript, from which we have already found it differing more than once. It is therefore impossible for it to have been copied from the Florentine, Vatican, or Urbinate manuscript, since it differs so frequently, now from one and now from another.]

the shepherd together with the pasture. For the merciful and compassionate Lord gave himself as food to those who fear him (Ps. CX).

For through the grace of the Son of God we have recognized that the entire Law of the ancient observance has been fulfilled in the truth of the New Testament, showing how the law of the Passover had been given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John I). To him be all honor, power, and glory with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages. Amen.

[Note: The two Vatican manuscripts add: “The Tenth on the Paschal Treatises ends.” The Florentine manuscript and the Urbinate instead have: “When the ten paschal treatises are finished, the excerpted treatises begin,” and so forth; this is the heading of the following sermons.]

## Sermon XI

[Note: Galeardus has here the following title: “The excerpted treatises on various passages begin; the first is on the Paralytic, and is eleventh in order.” He adds the following note: There is no doubt that this is the old and genuine reading of the title, and the more carefully corrected editions give it, namely the Paris and Cologne editions, whose exemplar we followed. The two Vatican manuscripts read without distinction: “The excerpted treatises begin, the first on the paralytic”; but the words “and eleventh in order” are absent. Therefore, although I was unwilling to delete them, I suspect that they were added by a copyist, since Gaudentius, plainly having finished the ten paschal treatises, proceeds as though to another work. The Pantagathi manuscript reads: “When the ten paschal treatises are finished, the excerpted treatises on various passages begin, the first of which is on the paralytic”; the same reading is found in the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts. Gaudentius himself testifies in the Preface that these treatises, excerpted by notaries, as the title states, were reviewed and corrected by him, in these words: “Moreover, I shall send you the four shorter treatises that you said I had formerly mentioned to you, on various Gospel passages, and a fifth on the martyrs of the Maccabees, corrected for you because you compel me, so that, if you judge them worthy of any useful remembrance, you may have them transcribed together in the final part of this little booklet.” The Lyon editors were content with this heading alone: “On Various Passages, the First Being on the Paralytic”; they had additional material in the rest of the heading. But in that edition, as we have already observed, you will seek *akribeian* (ἀκρίβειαν), or exactness, in vain.]

### On Various Passages, the First: On the Paralytic
### 301

I remember that in the preceding treatise I promised your holy love that, with the Lord’s help, I would explain more fully for what reason the Lord testified that he had performed one work: whence the utterly sluggish Jewish populace suffered distress (*scrupulum*) [Note: It seemed that *scandalum* (“offense,” “stumbling-block”) ought certainly to be restored here; nevertheless, I do not readily depart from the agreement of the manuscripts and editions. Certainly the Jewish populace suffered not only a *scrupulus*, that is, anxiety and distress, because of Christ’s miracle, but also *scandalum*: they were seeking, namely, to kill him. Yet since Octavius Pantagathus’s manuscript likewise retains *scrupulum*, I have not altered it. The same manuscript in this passage substitutes *ingratissima* (“most ungrateful”) for *plebs ignavissima* (“the utterly sluggish populace”); that reading is certainly better than the Vulgate reading, but no other manuscript supplies it. Since, however, it appears to have been written in the margin of the manuscript in Pantagathus’s own hand, I did not wish to introduce it into the text.] and inflamed with the most unjust fury, assailed the giver of blessing with blasphemous curses, saying, “You have a demon. Who is seeking to kill you?” (John 7), and even contemplated handing over the Lord of life to the punishment of death.

We have indeed proved [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “of the Evangelist himself.”] from the testimony of this Evangelist that Christ performed not one work, but many—indeed innumerable—works. For at the end of the book he writes:

“There are also many other things that Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that not even the world itself could contain the books that would be written” [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript read *quae scriberentur* (“that would be written”). But perhaps the reading should be *dicat* (“he may say”), to which the Pantagathus manuscript also agrees. The printed editions read *fortasse dicit* (“perhaps he says”). The Vulgate reads: “I suppose that not even the world itself could contain the books that ought to be written.” On this hyperbole in the Gospel text, see, if desired, Fabricius’s notes on Philastrius above, p. 79; also Fabricius himself, *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, part I, p. 321, and part III, p. 517; likewise Grotius, in his *Critici* on Pearson, at this passage in John.]

But perhaps an attentive listener may say: [Col. 0921B] “In the earlier parts of the Gospel the Lord says, ‘I have done one work, and you all marvel’ (John 7); in what follows, that whole accumulation of miracles is celebrated, and therefore [Note: This reading was taken from two Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read: “nothing seems to have been left in question concerning this.”] nothing seems to have been left in question concerning this.”

Yet, reviewing the earlier statements of this book from the preceding discourse, I find that, up to this point in the Gospel, Christ our God had performed very many wondrous works. He had already seen Nathanael before Philip called him while he was under the fig tree. He had already changed, by his own power, the utterly simple liquid of transparent water into the color and taste of wine. He had already healed, by a word, the dying son of the royal official, the heavenly Physician doing so before he visited him, while the request was still being made. He had already disclosed the hidden faults of that Samaritan woman and, once she had confessed them, cleansed her with a spiritual fountain (John 1, 2, 4). He had already healed—or rather restored—the limbs of the paralytic that had been dead for thirty-eight years, by the command of a single voice (John 5). He had already satisfied the hunger of five thousand men with five barley loaves and two fish (John 6), distributing the meal with an even greater miracle: after so many hungry companies of people had been satisfied, a larger heap of leftovers was found than the quantity of food that had been set out. He had already walked upon the sea (ibid., 19), so that the swelling water did not touch the soles of the one who walked.

[Col. 0922A] But in this catalogue of miracles he had still performed one work which seemed to offer the ignorant Jewish populace, raging against him, a plausible opportunity for violence: namely, that he had healed the paralytic on the Sabbath (John 5:10), although the Law had commanded Sabbath rest. Thus Christ, who had come not to abolish the ancient Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5), endured the Jews’ persecution as though guilty of violating the Sabbath.

At this point, dearest brothers, I am compelled to set aside the present sequence of the reading and explain the meaning of the Sabbath, lest the persecution of the righteous by the wicked be thought to have been just. For that paralytic who is recorded as having been healed by Christ on the Sabbath suffered slander from the Jews because, on the very day on which he had been healed, he appeared to be carrying his bed.

“It is the Sabbath,” they said, “and it is not lawful for you to carry your pallet” (John 5:15).

The healed man replied: “The one who made me well—that one told me, ‘Take up your pallet and walk.’”

And later: “It is Jesus,” he said, “who made me well.” Still inexperienced because of his Jewish infirmity, but already grateful for the health he had recovered, and unable to give an account of the deed before his slanderers, he pointed out the author of both the command and the work: “The one who made me well—that one told me, ‘Take up your pallet and walk.’” And he added: “It is Jesus,” he said, “who made me well” (ibid.); or, “It is the son of David who made me well”; or, “It is the son of Joseph who made me well.” For these names were then commonly used among the Jewish people 303 of Christ the Lord and Savior. [Note: Three editions read: “For all these names were then commonly used among the people.” We preferred the reading of the manuscripts.]

But what of it? “It is Jesus,” he says, “who made me well.” For, being a Hebrew, he knew that the name *Jesus* derives from the power of healing. Jesus is indeed called “Savior,” as the angel declares when speaking of Christ to Joseph in a dream: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). “Therefore,” he says, “the one whose name itself is salvation made me well.”

And how could salvation be prohibited from saving by the prescribed law, or altered by the condition of the Sabbaths so that it would no longer be salvation? Let us nevertheless see, dearest brothers, whether the Law itself excluded the work of salvation from the Sabbath.

“For six days,” it says, “you shall do your work, but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God” (Exod. 20). [Note: Thus read four manuscripts, agreeing with the Vulgate and with the Pantagathus manuscript. The Septuagint reads, “Sabbaths to the Lord your God.” The printed editions have: “It is the Sabbath of your Lord.”]

“You shall not do any work of yours on it” [Note: The word *tuum* (“your”) had dropped out of the printed editions; we restored it from the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts. It must certainly be read thus, as the following exposition of this passage demonstrates. The Pantagathus manuscript also supplies *tuum*.] “except what is done for every soul.”

The human race, and especially the Jews, is inclined toward bodily works rather than divine ones. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read: “rather than divine ones; and therefore one day of the week was appointed.” The Pantagathus manuscript also has both readings.] Therefore one day in the week—the Sabbath—was established, on which they would be compelled to abstain from bodily works and devote themselves solely to divine things.

For [Note: The reading found in two Vatican manuscripts seems correct: “namely, they were not permitted either to cook food or to travel on the Sabbath, so that no one, under the pretext of human necessity …” The Florentine reads the same. Since the Vulgate reading seems equally correct, however, I have not departed from it. The prohibition against cooking on the Sabbath found in Exodus 16 properly applied to the period of the manna, according to Godwin; yet the Jews extended it to all time. For this nation, inclined toward superstition, added much of its own to the decree of the Law, about which Moses had defined nothing. See Buxtorf, *Synagoga Judaica*, chap. 16; Petrus Cunaeus, *De Republica Hebraeorum*, book II, chap. 24; Godwin, *Moses and Aaron*, book III, chap. 3.] neither cooking food nor traveling on the Sabbath was permitted, lest anyone, under the pretext of human necessity, place earthly things before divine things.

But after the Jews, neglecting the spiritual duties that the Lord had commanded them to perform for the salvation of the soul, had turned all the lawful observances of the Sabbath toward idleness and luxury, the Lord continually cried out to them through the Prophet:

“I cannot endure your new moons, your Sabbaths, and your great day; your fast, your holidays, and your festivals my soul hates” (Isa. 1). [Col. 0923B]

“Your Sabbaths,” he says, “not mine; for what you do is not mine. My fast and my Sabbaths, which I commanded to be observed, command fasting from vices, cessation from evil works, [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, omitting the conjunction, read: “to cling to good deeds.” The Pantagathus manuscript has the same reading, as it does in the following phrase, “and from seductive luxuries.”] and adherence to good actions.”

But, on the contrary, your Sabbaths and your fasts are disturbed by quarrels [Note: Four manuscript copies read: “and seductive luxuries.”] and are full of enticements and luxuries.

Therefore the very giver of the Law, coming in human form, [Note: The reading found in four manuscripts and in the Pantagathus manuscript seems altogether better, as follows: “When he was performing works of salvation for every soul on the Sabbath, he taught by examples what he had commanded with provident reason.” The word *exemplis* (“by examples”), perhaps written in abbreviation, deceived an ignorant scribe. Reading carelessly, he made *de exemplis* into *fecit enim*, and thereby utterly confused the sense of this passage. The same Pantagathus manuscript shortly afterward reads: “He was not destroying the Law, but rather fulfilling it.” This is also found in two Vatican manuscripts.] when he was performing works of salvation for every soul—for on the Sabbath he was teaching by examples what he had commanded with provident reason—was not destroying the Law, but rather fulfilling the Law. For it is written:

“You shall not do any work of yours on the Sabbath” (Exod. 20): “yours,” he says, that is, human work.

And it is added: “except what is done [Note: Thus read two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine manuscript, and the Pantagathus manuscript. We therefore removed an absurd additional gloss that had entered the printed editions: *pro omni anima, sive omni animae, et ad salvandam animam* (“for every soul, or for every soul, and for saving the soul”). This exception in the Sabbath law is commonly called among the rabbis *periculum animae* (“danger to life”), as Casaubon testifies, *Exercitationes* 1 on Baronius, § 9. Hence the familiar Jewish proverb: “Danger to life overrides the Sabbath.”] for every soul,” that is, for saving the soul.

Therefore we read that the earlier righteous men worked on the Sabbaths for the salvation of souls. For seven days Jesus son of Nave, at the Lord’s command, went around the city of Jericho with the Levites and the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant; and [Note: The printed editions read *motu divino* (“by divine impulse”); the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts read *nutu Dei* (“at God’s command”), to which the Octavius Pantagathus manuscript also agrees. We have therefore changed the single word *motu* to *nutu*, leaving the rest untouched. The following words are read in two Vatican manuscripts as: “and the souls of the Jews are delivered from the danger of war.” The Pantagathus manuscript has the same reading, but it does not differ greatly from the Vulgate. Some Jewish teachers report that the city of Jericho was captured on the Sabbath itself; so true is what Gaudentius says here about the exception to the Sabbath law in such a case.] the hostile walls fell at God’s command, so that the souls of the Jews might be delivered from the danger of war (Josh. 6).

You will also discover that the Sabbath is counted among the seven days, beginning the reckoning from any day. Therefore, when it is said, “It is Jesus who made me well” (John 5), the Jews are warned, by the shared meaning of the name, not to condemn works of the same kind.

Therefore [Col. 0924B] the Lord Christ, when he healed on the Sabbaths either a withered hand, or a man with dropsy, or a paralytic, as truly the Lord of the Sabbath, defended his own action by the testimonies of his Law, saying to the Jews:

“Is it lawful to do good on the Sabbaths to an animal; to save a soul, or to destroy it?” (Matt. 12). [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts give the small but highly appropriate alteration: “Is it lawful to do good on the Sabbaths, or not?” The Octavius Pantagathus manuscript, mentioned shortly afterward, also supports it. We nevertheless did not introduce it into the text, since the received reading is defended by three editions and by two manuscripts—the Florentine and Urbinate—in which the text reads: “Is it lawful on the Sabbaths to do good to an animal?” The sense is: If it is lawful on the Sabbaths to do good to an animal, as we learn from the Lord himself in Matthew 12 and Luke 14, why should it not be lawful on the Sabbaths to save a soul?]

He wished to bring them into the meaning of the Law which, as I have explained above, he had expounded, while at the same time reproaching them for not understanding what their work was, and what was meant by “except what is done for every soul” (Exod. 20). [Note: Four manuscripts read: “your work,” as does the Pantagathus manuscript.]

Thus Christ works for the salvation of the soul on the Sabbath; he works on the Sabbath and fulfills the Law, while interpreting the condition of the Law, clarifying the distinctions among works, and doing what [Note: The printed editions read quite incorrectly: “which the Law displays concerning the Sabbath holidays.” The works Christ performed were not displayed in the Sabbath law but excepted from it. We took this correction from both Vatican manuscripts, whose reading is also supported by the Pantagathus manuscript.] the Law excepted from the Sabbath rest, while making the very Sabbath day, sanctified by its blessing, still holier through his benefits.

For, granting divine assistance on it to every believing soul, he rendered to the Sabbath the works that were owed to it. [Note: The Paris edition, more corrected and accurate than the others, reads thus, and the manuscript copies agree with it. Two other editions contain an absurd break: “But in order to show that, with the Father, who was then also working …”]

But to show the Jews that he had always worked together with the Father, who was then also working in the flesh, he said to them:

“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

And for this reason the Jews persecuted him all the more unjustly: not only because he was abolishing the Sabbath, but also because he was calling God his own Father [Note: Here too the printed editions read *Dominum* (“Lord”), but we restored *Deum* (“God”) from the Urbinate and two Vatican manuscripts. The authority of the Gospel text, from which these words are taken, confirms the correction; the Pantagathus manuscript likewise supports it. See what we noted above, pp. 130, 133.], making himself equal to God (ibid., 18).

The blessed Evangelist clearly taught that he who is truly the Son of God the Father is equal to God by the proper identity of nature.

Although, therefore, the testimonies of the ancients had preceded, [Note: Namely, the example of the ancient Fathers mentioned above, in the siege of Jericho. The printed editions read awkwardly: “yet the Lord desired nothing of this kind of affection.” The two Vatican manuscripts, by whose aid we have corrected the passage, read: “yet the Lord desired to offer no such assertion.” This reading was later also found in the Pantagathus manuscript.] the Lord did not wish to set anything of this kind before them, lest, because such examples were rare and ancient, they should be considered uncertain by some or accidental. Rather, he preferred to confront them with daily and customary examples, so that they could not in any way deny that they had been most justly refuted.

“I have done one work,” he says, “and you all marvel” (John 7:21).

What work was that? “Because I healed the paralytic on the Sabbath.”

And he added:

“For this reason Moses gave you circumcision” [Note: The Urbinate and two Vatican manuscripts, as well as the Pantagathus manuscript, read: “not because circumcision is from Moses.”], “not because circumcision is from Moses,” he says, “but from the Fathers”—that is, from Abraham, who was the first to be circumcised (Gen. 17), and from the other Patriarchs.

“And on the Sabbath,” he says, “you circumcise a man. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath,” he says, “so that the Law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I have made a whole man well on the Sabbath? Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7:22).

It is as though he were saying: “The Law commanded only this: that what is for the soul should be done on the Sabbath. And the same Law prescribes concerning circumcision that whoever, on the eighth day after birth, does not circumcise every male, [Note: Both Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read: “every male shall perish; that soul shall be rooted out.” The Pantagathus manuscript likewise has this reading. The Vulgate at Genesis 17 reads: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall be destroyed from his people.” The Septuagint reads: “That soul shall perish from his race.”] that soul shall be rooted out from his people. Therefore it is for the soul that you circumcise a man on the Sabbaths; likewise it is for the soul that I have made the whole man well on the Sabbath. [Note: This conclusion is absent from the Pantagathus manuscript, although it occurs in the same form in the Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts.] Therefore it is lawful to do a good work for the soul on the Sabbath.

“But if you judge that I have violated the Sabbath in this work, you yourselves continually declare yourselves guilty of violating the Sabbath. Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7:24).

With such reasonable patience our Lord Jesus conquers his enemies. He had indeed descended from the Father into this world in order to conquer by suffering.

But let us briefly consider the force of this final saying:

“Do not,” he says, “judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.”

This is, I think, a general principle, a teacher of equity that must be retained, set before all, known to many, loved by few. For we are commanded not to flatter the persons of the rich of this age and, in an utterly unjust judgment, favor unbelievers [Note: Thus read two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine. The printed editions read: “and impious, unbelieving, rapacious people”; the Pantagathus manuscript reads: “let us favor unbelievers and impious, cruel, rapacious people.”], the impious, the cruel, the rapacious, the luxurious, and the shameless—not merely to encourage them by timid silence, but even to proclaim, with unjust praises, those deserving of every rebuke.

Or, what is more deformed than every kind of foulness, while seeking sordid profits, let us become conspicuous servants of another’s money, forgetful of Christian liberty. Nor, enticed by the beauty of anyone’s bodily form, should we be moved by a crooked judgment away from the region of truth and right opinion. For it is written concerning contempt for wealth:

“If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61);

and concerning the neglect of bodily beauty, God speaks to the priest Samuel when he is to choose a king from the sons of Jesse:

“Do not be astonished,” he says, “at the height of their stature or the beauty of their faces, [Note: In the Florentine manuscript: “Man sees in the face, but God in the heart”; the same reading occurs in the two Vatican manuscripts and in the Pantagathus manuscript. In those manuscripts, however, the word is *Dominus* (“the Lord”), whereas here it is *Deus* (“God”).] for man sees in the face, but God sees in the heart” (1 Sam. 16).

[Note: David was anointed three times: first by Samuel, 1 Samuel 17; second at Hebron, after Saul’s death, 2 Samuel 2; and third again at Hebron, after the death of Ish-bosheth, 2 Samuel 5. John Gregory had warned in the preface to his *Sacred Observations*, vol. IX of the *Critici Sacri Anglici*, that one should not expect the particular psalm mentioned here by Gaudentius in recently printed books. Yet it is found in the recent edition of the Psalter carefully prepared by the eminent Thomasio, p. 650. It also appears—making me all the more admire the man’s excessive confidence—in the Roman edition of the Septuagint of 1588, at the end, outside the regular sequence, under the title: “This Psalm is an autograph of David and is outside the number, when he entered single combat with Goliath.” Besides Gaudentius, Athanasius also mentions this psalm in the *Synopsis* (or whoever was the author of that *Synopsis*) and in his *Discourse to Marcellinus on the Interpretation of the Psalms*. Apollinaris of Alexandria, a presbyter of the Church of Laodicea, rendered it in Greek verse around the year 360. Among more recent writers, Olympia Fulvia Morata produced an elegant Greek and Latin metaphrase of it, which Johann Albert Fabricius includes in *Codex Pseudepigraphus Veteris Testamenti*, p. 908. Marcus Antonius Flaminio also seems to have reproduced this psalm in that polished poem which he prefixed to his *Paraphrase of Thirty Psalms*:

“I was a boy, cast aside in my father’s house,

[Col. 0927D]

and smaller than all my brothers;

I pastured a little flock upon the mountain.”]

And therefore blessed David, the least and despised, was raised by sanctified oil to the kingdom; and he boasts in a special poem that from humility he had grown, through God’s grace, to the highest summit of dignity, saying:

“I was little [Note: Gaudentius uses this abbreviated formula in more than one place, as in Sermon 4: “His neighbor will take his neighbor with him, and so forth”; Sermon 14: “If I take up my wings, and so forth”; Sermon 19: “Why do you wish to kill me? A man, and so forth”; and elsewhere. Fabricius also observed that Philastrius used the same formula, chap. 150: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, and so forth”; and chap. 144: “The work of the Law written in their hearts, and so forth.” Ennodius of Ticinum likewise uses it, book IV, letter 4: “I transfer to your jurisdiction, with perpetual generosity, that slave of mine who is subject to my jurisdiction, and so forth”; and Fulgentius of Ruspe, letter 5: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, and so forth.” Cicero too uses it, *De Oratore* 2: “If a son had been born to me, and he died before me, and so forth”; and below in the same book: “Bring Asellus forward, and so forth”; and in the *Topica*: “In a partition there are, as it were, members, such as the head, shoulders, hands, sides, legs, feet, and so forth.” Menagius noted that the Italian expression *e caetera* (“and so forth”) arose from this usage of the Latin language, under the entry *E caetera* in *Origines Linguae Italicae*.] among my brothers, and so forth.”

Therefore Christ rightly says in every respect:

“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7:24).

And which one of us, dearest brothers, is found capable of observing each of the things I have mentioned?

“Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times” (Ps. 105:3).

Since, then, as I said above [Note: “As I said above.” The Florentine, the two Vatican manuscripts, and the Pantagathus manuscript read: “as I stated previously.” A scribal play.] this is a general principle, it is nevertheless directed specifically against the Jews, who judged Christ, though he performed wondrous works, merely as a man according to his outward appearance, while failing to see God in his mighty deeds.

This saying also strikes heretics who blaspheme the Son of God with no little force, because, observing the humility of the flesh he assumed, they attempt to measure the substance of his boundless divinity.

But we, brothers, saved by his grace through faith (Eph. 2:8), should judge with righteous judgment, maintaining equity [Note: “In every action of our way of life.” Four manuscript copies and the Pantagathus manuscript read: “in every act.”] in every action of our way of life.

For it is the rational judgment of the soul to choose to serve God rather than the world; to determine to obey Christ’s commandments rather than be corrupted by the devil’s counsels; to resolve to cling to spiritual pursuits [Note: “To cling to spiritual pursuits.” The Urbinate and two Vatican manuscripts read *spiritalibus* (“spiritual,” with the alternative spelling), which the Pantagathus manuscript also retains. See above, Sermon 2, p. 239; Sermon 8, p. 272; Sermon 9, p. 289.] rather than become entangled in bodily vices; and to judge eternal blessedness in the world to come preferable to the world’s brief pleasures.

Let us therefore walk with the impartial judgment of an upright heart in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, so that we may merit from the eternal Son of God a share in eternal life, whose omnipotence with the Father and the Holy Spirit remains throughout all ages.

[Note: “Amen.” The Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts add: “The discourse on the paralytic ends”; in the Pantagathus manuscript: “Here ends the discourse on the paralytic.”]

Amen.

## Sermon XII: The Second on Various Chapters

### Concerning what the Lord Jesus said: “Now is the judgment of this world”

[Col. 0928A]

### 308

After that voice of God the Father by which he had said that the Son, already glorified, would again be glorified, and after the Savior had spoken to the crowds standing around him—as we recently discussed, explaining that the testimony of this voice had been given not for his own honor but for the instruction of our faith—the Gospel reading now under consideration indicates what the same Lord immediately added:

“Now is the judgment of this world” (John 12:31).

I think, dearest brothers, that we must consider what sort of judgment he then said was imminent. If he had wished us to understand the future judgment by which this world will be judged through fire, he would not have said, “Now it is,” but would have said, “Then it will be.” But because he was speaking of a present judgment, it is fitting to examine what that present judgment of the world was.

Will it be thought that Christ judged the world at his first coming, when he is known rather to have saved it, as he himself testified, saying:

“For God did not send his Son to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17)? [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Pantagathus manuscript read *ut salvetur* (“so that it may be saved”), whereas the printed editions read *ut salvaretur* (“so that it might be saved”). The Vulgate agrees with our reading.]

And in the Gospel of blessed Luke we read that, when a Samaritan village refused to receive the Savior, the Apostles James and John, indignant, said to him:

“Lord, do you wish us to command fire to descend from heaven upon them and consume them, just as Elijah did?” [Note: The Urbinate manuscript reads *prohibuit eos* (“he forbade them”). The Vulgate, both in Greek and Latin, reads differently: *στραφεὶς δὲ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς*, “but turning, he rebuked them.”]

But he, angered, forbade them (Luke 9:54).

O merciful anger!

What, then, is the meaning of his saying, “Now is the judgment of this world” (John 12:31)?

“Judgment,” brothers, can be understood in two ways. The sentence of one who decides is called judgment, and the punishment suffered by one who undergoes it is also called judgment: one judgment belongs to the agent, the other to the sufferer. [Note: The reading of the Florentine manuscript is: “The judge performs judgment; the defendant suffers judgment; and it is the judgment of both.” We have added the words “and it is the judgment of both” to the text as genuine, removing an absurd gloss that had entered the printed editions in this form: “The judge performs judgment; the defendant undergoes—that is, suffers—judgment.” The two Vatican manuscripts read: “The defendant suffers judgment, and it is the judgment of one,” which, although somewhat corrupt, confirms the Florentine reading. The Octavius Pantagathus manuscript likewise has the same reading. It is therefore scarcely doubtful that this should be restored to Gaudentius’s genuine text, which should read: “The judge performs judgment; the defendant suffers judgment; and it is the judgment of both,” agreeing with the Florentine manuscript.]

When Scripture says that the world either performs or suffers judgment, it does not refer to the natures of irrational elements, but signifies the inhabitants of the world. Thus, when the house of Israel is mentioned, it does not mean walls or roofs, but the Israelite people.

Therefore Christ, ruler of all, after the unusual birth of the holy Virgin, after the manger had been worshiped with the lavish homage of the Magi, after the manifold teaching of heavenly speech, after the cures of various illnesses accomplished by the command of his powerful word, and after this present testimony of the Father, [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads: “when he was already very near”; the Pantagathus manuscript retains the Vulgate reading.] when he was already close to his Passion, says:

“Now is the judgment of this world” (John 12).

It is as though he were saying: “Now—now—is the judgment of this world: whether, after the voluntary Passion, it will choose to believe in him rising by his own power, so that it may be saved through faith, or whether, with the Jews, it will judge that it must deny the Judge who will deny those who deny him, saying to them: ‘I do not know you. Depart from me into the eternal fire, workers of iniquity’” (Luke 13).

Or rather—and this interpretation is more usefully approved by the authority of the surrounding discourse—“Now is the judgment of this world” (John 12:31); that is, the hour has drawn near when the world will judge the Creator and Judge of the world, itself destined to be judged.

In the same way he speaks in the Gospel of Luke to the chief priests and elders, [Note: The word *magistratus* (“magistrates”) is absent from the Urbinate manuscript, as it is also from the Pantagathus manuscript. I therefore suspect that both this word and the following word *templi* (“of the temple”) are additions by scribes who admitted into the text an inept marginal gloss. As far as I know, strategoi had no connection with the temple but were concerned with military affairs, as is sufficiently clear from Julius Pollux, book I, chap. 10. Hence *strategia* means a prefecture or military command in Pliny: in book IV, chap. 11, he says of Thrace, “It is divided among fifty *strategiai*”; and in book VI, chap. 9, concerning Armenia: “It is divided into prefectures, which they call *strategiai*.” Plautus likewise, *Curculio*, act II, scene III, line 6, counts the *strategus* not among sacred but among secular magistrates:

“Neither strategist, nor tyrant, nor market-superintendent,

nor town-governor, nor village-governor …”]

Therefore, although I think the reading should be “to the chief priests and elders, and the temple commanders who had come to arrest him,” I nevertheless did not wish to alter the text; I leave my conjecture to the judgment of the reader. After I had published this at Padua in 1720, the *Acta Lipsiensia* for October 1722, p. 488, informed me—although not without some bitterness—that *strategos of the temple*, στρατηγοὺς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, occurs in Acts 4:1 and 5:24. Luke 22:4 could also have been added, passages which perhaps escaped the diligence of one occupied with another task at the time. Nevertheless, the learned Lightfoot doubts, in *Horae Hebraicae* on Luke 22, whether the tribune or centurion of that garrison ought rather to be called στρατηγὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, “commander of the temple,” or στρατηγὸς τῆς Ἀντωνίας, “commander of the Antonia”; consult him if you wish, as well as Grotius on Matthew 26:45, to whom it is clear that this garrison was not ordinarily stationed in the Temple, but was transferred there from the Antonia on feast days. Yet those learned men were greatly displeased that I had ventured, albeit modestly and lightly, to pluck a few hairs from Barthius—whose claim to the highest scholarly distinction I do not thereby wish to diminish. But, with their permission, concerning Barthius and his errors—for he was a human being, as are we and all the others—Reinesius, in his letters to Christian Daumius, must certainly be consulted, besides others and indeed Fabricius also, p. 17 of this edition. Thus the editors of the *Acta Lipsiensia* ought not, on account of a single word of Cotelerius, which I merely restored, to have brought so great a quarrel against me.]

and the temple commanders who had come to arrest him:

> “As though against a robber you have come out with swords and clubs; when I was daily with you in the Temple, you did not stretch out your hands against me. But this is your hour,” he said, “and the power of darkness” [Col. 0929C] (Luke 22).

The power of darkness is, in fact, the power of this world, or of worldly people who, established in the darkness of faithlessness, refuse to look upon the light [Col. 0930A] of truth. And because God has permitted human beings the free choice to do whatever they wish, [Note: [Col. 0930D] The two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine read, “exercise [power] against the Christ of God.”] they exercise a sacrilegious power against Christ. Hence, when Pilate said, “I have authority to crucify you, and I have authority to release you,” the Lord answered him: “You would have no authority unless it had been given you from above” (John 19).

Finally, to show that the judgment of the world of which he had spoken meant his Passion, the Lord joined the statements together, saying: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast down, or will be driven out” (John 12), [Note: [Col. 0930D] From this it is clear how great at that time was the authority of the Greek exemplars, even where they departed from the Vulgate. The Greek edition reads ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω, “he will be cast out,” or “he will be driven out,” just as Gaudentius translates it a little below.] as we read in the Greek exemplars.

For the Passion of Christ was destined to be the overthrow of the devil. Hence the holy prophet David speaks concerning him: “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 50). Although this verse can also be understood in another sense, it nevertheless fits the present one well. For the Lord Jesus is judged and conquers in his Passion; he dies and triumphs.

But why is the devil called the prince of this world? Pay attention. The devil is called the prince of this world by usurpation, not by nature. For, having led the human race astray so that, after abandoning God, it might worship Satan himself through images fashioned by human hands, he seized the principate by force and exercised tyranny, to such an extent that the world did not recognize its true Prince when he came, being blinded by the devil’s own deceptions. For Christ was in this world, as the Evangelist testifies, “and the world was made through him, and the world did not recognize him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1).

Therefore the Lord allowed himself to be judged by the judgment of this world [Col. 0930C], in order to cast down or drive out this enemy of the human race, since the two are understood to be one and the same; [Note: [Col. 0930D] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads, “understand that one in an equal sense”; another, “understand that both are in an equal sense.” Neither reading has anything reasonable about it; moreover, the book of Pantagathus also had “one in an equal sense,” but in the space above the preceding line it was corrected by Pantagathus’s own hand to “and in what sense one.”] and understand in what sense they are one. [Col. 0931A]

The devil did not dwell in level and lowly places, [Note: [Col. 0931C] The printed editions absurdly read, “where he was driven”; and indeed the correction was evident even without the support of either Vatican manuscript, in which “whence he was driven” is read. This reading is also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus.] whence, after being driven out, he could be thought to have passed to another place without falling from his own position. Rather, when he is expelled from the height of heaven, he is necessarily hurled downward.

Clearly, the Greek has significantly placed ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω, that is, “he will be cast out,” or “he will be driven out,” so that it might be understood that he must also be driven from the souls of believers who are already heavenly, as from the heavens themselves; so that, once he has been expelled, Christ the Lord might reign in us.

Therefore he added: “And I, if I have been lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12). That he unambiguously indicated that he would be lifted up from the earth on the gallows of the cross is made clear by the Evangelist’s explanatory statement:

> “Now he said this to signify by what death he was going to die.”

[Note: [Col. 0931C] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “Therefore, when I have been lifted up, I will draw all things.” The Florentine manuscript, however, reads, “Therefore, when I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things”; and the book of Pantagathus certainly has the same reading, although here too *ego* (“I”) was restored by his hand.]

“I, when I have been lifted up from the earth,” he said, “will draw all things [Col. 0931B] to myself” (John 12:33)—namely, that, when lifted up on the cross, he would call the whole world to his faith.

But when he says, “I will draw all things to myself,” and not “all people,” I think he signifies that all the classes of creatures which were either sacrificed to idols [Note: [Col. 0931C] We discussed sacrificial offerings above, in the notes to treatise 9, p. 283. Concerning dedication, see Brissonius, *Formulae*, book 1, p. 125, Paris edition, 1583, and Laurentius Pignorius, *Symbolica*, letter 32. There is also a notable passage on the dedication of idols in Arnobius, book 6, where he speaks in the voice of the Gentiles: “For we do not determine that bronze, or materials of gold and silver, or other substances from which statues are made, are gods or divine powers in themselves; but we worship and venerate in them those whom sacred dedication introduces and causes to dwell in images fashioned by artisans.” Shortly afterward he adds: “This is the first thing we desire and ask you to hear: whether they do this unwillingly”—that is, “drawn by the right of dedication.” Minucius, in the *Octavius*, says: “When, then, does this thing come into being? Look: it is cast, fashioned, carved. It is not yet a god. Look: it is soldered, constructed, erected. It is still not a god. Look: it is adorned, consecrated, prayed to. Only then is it a god, when that human being has wished it and dedicated it.” Hence among us we have the dedication of a church, the dedication of an altar, and similar practices, which the Christian religion transferred from the profane rite of the Gentiles into the sphere of sanctity. Consult Baronius, note on the Martyrology, 9 November.] or dedicated, Christ promised to recall to his blessing and consecrate to his name.

For, in accordance with the judgment of the apostle Paul, it is necessary that every tongue confess him and that the whole world become subject to God (Philippians 2). To this God, namely, who ascended above the heaven of heavens toward the east, as the Psalmist says (Psalm 67); [Note: [Col. 0932C] The Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts read: “To this God who, ascending on high,” a reading supported by the book of Pantagathus. The Septuagint likewise has “ascending on high,” but the Vulgate has “you ascended on high.” Justin, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, cites the passage as follows: “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive.” Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 67, quoting the Apostle’s passage in Ephesians 4, likewise has: “He ascended on high, he took captivity captive.”] to this God who, when he ascended on high, led captivity captive (Psalm 67).

We must take the greatest care, dearly beloved brothers, [Col. 0932A] lest we render Christ’s victory void through our own fault—the victory by which he triumphed over the devil, redeeming us from his captivity by his precious blood and taking from him his dominion over the human race—by subjecting ourselves again to that tyrant’s rule through the enticements of the flesh, submitting to his cruel kingdom in insult to the Redeemer. Thus he may rightly complain while rebuking and reproaching us: “What profit is there in my blood?” (Psalm 29.) [Note: [Col. 0932C] The Florentine manuscript and one of the Vatican manuscripts read, “his blood poured out for you without cause,” where *ergo* (“therefore”) seems to be required instead of *eos* (“them”). But the Urbinas and the other Vatican manuscript more correctly read, and I would prefer their reading even to that of the printed editions: “poured out for you without cause.” These readings had already been published when the manuscript book of Octavius Pantagathus supplied a better reading than the others: “for my blood was poured out for you without cause.”]

“My blood was poured out for you without cause,” [Note: [Col. 0932D] This is how it is read in four manuscript codices, through whose help we corrected a passage somewhat corrupted in the printed editions.
