For they had punctuated it: “if you conduct yourselves in this way. Therefore, turn back, author”—although that reading too may be defended. In the book of Pantagathus it reads: “if you conduct yourselves in this way, therefore live accordingly.”] “if you conduct yourselves in this way. Therefore conduct yourselves so that the devil, the author of evil desires, may again rule over you, [Note: [Col. 0932D] The Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts read, “that he has stripped the spoils from so great a victor.” The book of Pantagathus has: “that he has stripped the spoils from so great a victor, mocking the robbers”; but by his hand “the robber to us” has been restored in the margin.] while the proud robber mocks, claiming that he has stripped the spoils from so great a victor.”

[Note: [Col. 0932D] In the two Vatican manuscripts: “for the enemy said,” as also in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

For he said:

> “Pursuing, I shall overtake; I shall divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled. I shall slay with my sword; my hand shall rule” (Exodus 15).

For this reason the most blessed apostle Paul exhorts us, saying:

> “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires; nor present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but present yourselves to God as those living from the dead” (Romans 6).

And again elsewhere:

> “For this reason Christ both lived and died and rose again, so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (Romans 14),

namely, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them [Note: [Col. 0932D] The word “but” appears superfluous. It is also absent from the Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts. The Vulgate reads: “but for him who died for them and rose again.” The manuscript book of Octavius Pantagathus has: “but for him who died for them and rose again.”] and rose again (2 Corinthians 5).

Therefore, instructed by such instruments, brothers, let us dedicate our entire life to the service of Christ, whose kingdom with the Father and with the Holy Spirit endures throughout all ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. THIRD SERMON ON VARIOUS PASSAGES. [Note: [Col. 0933C] This is how the Florentine and Urbinas manuscripts read. The printed editions, together with the Vatican manuscripts, instead have “On the Nativity of the Lord.” I nevertheless think the former reading is correct, since the sermon touches only briefly on the Nativity of the Lord and the whole treatise is directed against Jewish greed and in favor of the poor. The manuscript of Pantagathus has “Likewise, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord”; and indeed the word “likewise,” although omitted by us, is also found in four other manuscripts. Dupin, a critic of Gaudentius, approves this sermon altogether; he prefers it to the others and judges it better and more useful.]

On the birthday of the Lord. Against Judas’s avarice and on behalf of the poor.

[Col. 0933A]

Throughout all the books of divine Scripture, the Son of God is proclaimed not only as God, but also as man and as the son of man. [Note: [Col. 0933C] The conjunction is absent in four manuscripts and in Pantagathus’s book.] In the Old Testament he is foretold and promised, whereas in the New he is manifested and believed; for the old Law, as the Apostle says (Heb. 10), [Note: [Col. 0933C] The manuscripts read: “was a shadow of the good things to come, which were to be fulfilled.”] was a shadow of the good things to come—namely, of those good things known to be fulfilled in Christ—through which the man born today of the human race, through the most blessed Virgin, restored the image [Col. 0933B] corrupted by the poisonous bite of the serpent. [Note: [Col. 0933D] Thus the printed editions; the manuscripts, however, read “cut apart by the serpent’s bite.” We encountered a similar reading above, in the Preface to Benivolus, where the manuscripts have “to have been cut apart by the headlong haste of those receiving it,” while the printed editions have “to have been written down.” In both places we have retained the common reading, and shall continue to do so, although Octavius Pantagathus’s codex also has here “cut apart by the serpent’s bite.”]

so that he whose maker he had been from the beginning of the world might be its restorer at the completion of the age. [Note: [Col. 0933D] We printed the reading of the Florentine manuscript, which seemed altogether superior to the others. The Vatican manuscripts agree, but contain a slight fault in their reading, having “at the consummation” instead of “in the consummation.” The Urbinate has: “so that he who had been the world’s craftsman from the beginning might be its restorer at the completion of the age.” The Urbinate, Pantagathus’s, and Vatican codices more correctly read: “so that he who had been the maker from the beginning of the world might be its restorer at the completion of the age”; in this they agree with the Florentine. The printed editions have it incorrectly: “so that just as he had been the maker of the world from the beginning, so he might be its restorer up to the completion of the age.” For Gaudentius is not speaking of the making of the world, but of the restoration, through Christ’s birth, of the image of the human race.]

Who would be sufficient to admire this mercy worthily? Who could be an adequate proclaimer of such great goodness? 313 [Note: [Col. 0934C] These words are absent from four manuscripts, where the text reads: “Who could prove an adequate preacher of such great goodness, the immeasurable and incomprehensible God?” This reading is also found in Pantagathus’s codex.] Who would be sufficient to proclaim that, for the sake of our life, the immeasurable and incomprehensible God willed to become what man is, and that the creator of all the heavenly virtues descended to the lowliness of this earthly flesh?

Nevertheless, he became man for us in such a way that he did not cease to be what God is. For although the Word became flesh, as the Evangelist testifies (John 1), nevertheless, because he remains what he had been before becoming man, it is immediately added: “and dwelt among us.” By these words both the inhabitant is revealed [Note: [Col. 0934C] I do not know by what misfortune the manuscripts have been badly mutilated at this point, for approximately thirty-eight lines are missing from the words “and a dwelling place” up to “may preserve that.” Octavius Pantagathus’s book is likewise not free of this defect. The discerning reader will judge how great a loss to the sermon this causes; but hurried workmen often produce such monstrosities.] and a dwelling place is likewise shown. [Col. 0934A]

Thus he began to be what he previously was not, without ceasing to be what he was. The Virgin Mother herself also bears witness to this omnipotence of the Son of God and of man. Conceiving by the Holy Spirit, she brought forth the God-man whom she had carried in her chaste womb in such a way that, in the undefiled mother of so great a name, her integrity remained even more glorious after the divine birth.

We rightly called it a divine birth, because he who was born in the flesh through the Virgin is God; for the archangel Gabriel said to her: “The holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). From the moment he assumed the flesh of our weakness, the same Son is both of man and of God, because the one born from Mary is none other than he who, entering through his mother’s ears, filled the Virgin’s womb. [Note: [Col. 0934C] A rather harsh reading, but one suited to Gaudentius’s style; unless the sentence is punctuated in this way, it is difficult to understand. The printed editions suffer here from faulty punctuation.]

That is to say, he himself, by the Holy Spirit, formed his man [Col. 0934B], since Wisdom built herself a house (Prov. 9): he was already making the dwelling place of our body his own, and, clothed in that dwelling, he came forth without any injury to his mother’s integrity. For the most blessed Mary, giving birth to the incorruptible one, is both mother and virgin.

I have said these things briefly to demonstrate the mystery of the Son of God’s incarnation. Now I come to explain that part of the Gospel reading which had previously been passed over while others occupied themselves with other matters. For, as you remember, we discussed the whole passage that describes the Lord dining at Bethany, explaining Lazarus’s place at table, the circumstances of place and time, Martha’s service, her sister’s devotion, the efficacy of the ointment, and the reason for the hair with which Mary wiped Christ’s feet after anointing them with precious myrrh. [Note: [Col. 0934D] The printed editions corruptly read *myrrho*, which we corrected by restoring *myro*, although, because of the lacuna indicated above, there were no manuscript aids available. The Benedictine editors of Jerome likewise restored *myro* in the Preface to the Books of the Old Testament, vol. 1, col. 321, when they found *myrrho* in the manuscripts, reading: “But I also ask you, handmaids of Christ, who anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious myrrh.” The Greek word is μύρον (*myron*), in Latin *unguentum*, “ointment”; besides Jerome and Gaudentius, Hilary also uses this word in his commentary on Psalm 132. Thus this *myron* extinguishes all foul odors wherever it is poured. Cassian likewise writes (Conference 14, chapter 14): “For a pot once contaminated by terrible substances more easily spoils the most fragrant myrrh.” The word also occurs in the Vulgate, Judith 10: “She washed her body and anointed herself with the finest myrrh.” Hence *myrothecium*, a repository for ointment, occurs in Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* 2.1: “I used up the whole myrothecium of Isocrates.” It is therefore futile—as is clear from these examples—for the author of the Hieronymian Questions, out of an excessive eagerness to oppose, to dissent from the certain correction of the Benedictines.]

We explained how Judas, while wishing to appear the patron of the poor, was convicted as a thief, an adversary of pious and appropriate devotion. But we omitted—or rather reserved—what the Lord Jesus said in response. “Let her alone,” he said, or “Allow her”: [Note: [Col. 0935C] From this one may infer that our Gaudentius was not unskilled in textual criticism, since he was so diligent in comparing copies of the Bible. He says: “Let her alone,” or “Allow her”; for both readings are found in Greek and Latin copies. But *Allow her* seems more suitable to the sense, because of what follows in the plural: “For you always have the poor with you.” He also notes variant readings elsewhere, Sermon 12, p. 310: “Now the prince of this world will be sent downward,” or “will be driven out,” as we read in the Greek copies.] both readings are found in Greek and Latin copies; but the sense seems better suited when one reads *Allow her*, and so forth, because of what follows in the plural: “For you always have the poor with you.”

Let us therefore ask, beloved, why the Lord responded in the plural to the words of Judas alone: “Allow her, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial: for you always have the poor with you, but me you do not always have” (John 12; Matt. 26; Mark 14).

Truly admirable, and exceedingly provident, is Christ’s patience! [Col. 0935B] He speaks to all the disciples together [Note: [Col. 0935D] We restored the reading with the assistance of the Urbinate codex, which is also supported by Pantagathus’s book. Both Vatican manuscripts have: “so that the insult of the hostile Judas may be restrained.” Although this reading is not free from corruption, it nevertheless somewhat confirms our emendation. The common reading in the printed editions is worse: “so that he might restrain the insult of the hostile Judas.”] so as to restrain the insult of the hostile Judas. He does not attack him harshly as a fraudster; rather, concealing his crime—although the Evangelist knew him to be a thief—he gently instructs everyone alike, teaching meanwhile that what Mary had done had necessarily been performed toward him as a mystery of burial.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Thus one of the Vatican manuscripts; the other has “if there were any who wished,” with which the Urbinate and Pantagathus’s codex agree. The printed editions read “if they wished anything.”]

As for the poor, there would always be an opportunity to give to them, to those who wished to do so, because they would always be with us. [Note: [Col. 0935D] The word *now* is absent from the printed editions; we supplied it from four manuscripts, with which Pantagathus’s book also agrees.] But no one would have long to minister to him in the flesh, because, after the imminent Passion, he would rise and immediately carry the body he had assumed into heaven.

Therefore Christ dispels Judas’s words by the gentleness and generality of his admonition, lest he either give Judas himself an opportunity to excuse his madness, or cause any of the Apostles to be troubled by someone who might perhaps suspect that Judas’s suggestion was pious; or certainly lest he leave some stumbling-block for anyone who would read the passage later.

For Judas, although acting out of a desire to defraud and hatred of the Savior, had nevertheless uttered those very words of deceit under the pretext of piety: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii,” he said, “and given to the poor?” (John 12).

Exceedingly irreligious and wholly importunate, he revealed the disposition of a greedy fraudster [Col. 0936A] while attempting to conceal his own crime under the appearance of religion. [Note: [Col. 0936C] The reading of both Vatican codices seemed preferable; we substituted it for the common reading, which had “with the feeling of a greedy fraudster.” The phrase that immediately follows—“namely, his own crime”—connects better with it. Pantagathus’s codex likewise has “the feeling of a greedy fraudster”; and shortly afterward, where the common copies read “he was burning to turn the price of Christ’s burial to his own profit,” the same book has “he was dragging it to his own profit.” This was written in the margin by Pantagathus’s own hand, while the text itself, omitting what follows, contained only: “the price of Christ’s burial he was burning…”]

He was plainly irreligious and importunate, because he not only regarded as superfluous what had been done for Christ’s honor, but also censured it in utterly wicked language. He was also a fraudster, because, carrying the money box, he carried away what was put into it for the needs of the poor, as the Evangelist complains (John 12:6). He was greedy as well, because he was not satisfied with daily stealing the poor’s allowances [Col. 0936B], but was also burning to turn the price of Christ’s burial to his own profit. Yet he turned it not into the momentary gains of his greed, but into the perpetual losses of salvation.

For not long afterward he lost his life along with all that either the impious thief had gathered through the frauds he had committed or the sacrilegious betrayer of Christ had received as the reward of his wickedness. Strangled by consciousness of the crimes mentioned above, he inflicted upon himself the death he deserved with a noose he had prepared, and was immediately [Note: [Col. 0936D] The printers read “he must be snatched away”; but two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate have “he must be snatched away to the punishments of hell,” while Pantagathus’s book has “he must be snatched away to the punishments below.” Concerning what Gaudentius says here about Judas—namely, that he inflicted upon himself the death he deserved with a noose prepared by himself—see the learned dissertation of Jacob Perizonius, *On the Death of Judas*, published at Leiden in 1702.] snatched away to the punishments of hell.

That the ointment had served the ministry of the Lord’s burial, the same Savior more clearly declared in Matthew’s Gospel: “By pouring this ointment upon my body,” he said, “she has done it for my burial” (Matt. 26). [Note: [Col. 0936D] We strongly infer, from the agreement of the manuscripts, that Gaudentius wrote *myron*, or *myron* in this passage, rather than *unguentum*. For the Florentine and Urbinate read “but that *myron*”; the Vatican manuscripts likewise read “but that *myron*”; and Pantagathus’s codex has *mirum*, which Pantagathus himself corrected in the margin of the book as follows: μύρον, “ointment.” Thus, as I suspect, *unguentum* is a gloss inserted into the text by ignorant copyists after the true reading had been displaced. From Gaudentius’s repeated use of this word we eagerly took a clue for emending another passage in the sermon on Peter and Paul.]

Although the Lord Jesus was the judge of consciences, he nevertheless did not wish to rebuke Judas too sharply for his hidden motives, lest, since he seemed to have spoken with plausible reason, he should perhaps be thought to have been corrected unjustly [Note: [Col. 0936D]. Thus four manuscripts, whose reading we followed [Col. 0937B], for it corresponds perfectly to what precedes: “he should perhaps be thought to have been corrected unjustly.” The printed editions have, incorrectly: “and from this to have conceived such a reason for his anger that he handed him over to be killed by his enemies, whom he had kept hostile without any sin.” Perhaps the copyists found, where the line ended, “and from this, the justice of anger,” from which they made “his anger”; then, repeating *such*, which stood at the beginning of the following section [Col. 0937C], they produced “to have conceived such a reason.” Pantagathus’s codex reads: “and from this to have conceived a just cause for anger.”] and thereby to have conceived a just cause for anger, so that he might hand over to his enemies for killing one against whom he had been hostile without any fault.

Christ therefore wished to say nothing harsh in proportion to the merit of that criminal mind, lest Judas appear to betray him in anger. For the Lord, the truly just judge, wills that each person be the cause of his own deserts; he wills that the just suffer for justice alone; and he wills that the wicked, if he persists in wickedness, be judged guilty of death by his own choice.

For God formed man, as Scripture testifies (Gen. 1:26), and made him according to the image of his likeness, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He placed before him fire and water, saying: “Stretch out your hand toward whichever you choose” (Ecclus. 15). God, he says, placed before man water and fire—that is, refreshment and punishment, remission and retribution, life and death. 316

Who, I ask, would not flee punishment, suffering, and death, and choose refreshment, remission, and life? But the one who avoids death is he who walks along the paths of the life-giving commandments; the one who receives the gift of life is he who avoids mortal acts through the labor of spiritual disciplines. [Note: [Col. 0937C] Thus the Florentine, Urbinate, and Pantagathus’s book. The Vatican manuscripts have “he who, for the sake of labor,” while the printed editions read “he who, through the labor of mortal studies.”]

Therefore it is said: “Behold water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you choose” (Ecclus. 15)—that is, the work is yours. Works are shown by the hand, because we can neither be subjected to torments without guilt nor earn a reward without struggle. The Apostle says: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” (Rom. 3); and again: “No one is crowned who competes in the contest unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2).

Our contest is against the vices of the flesh, against the desire for money, against anger of spirit. These are the weapons of the devil. We must resist them with the helmet of faith, the breastplate of self-control, and the shield of mercy, in which, as the Apostle says, we can extinguish all the burning arrows of the wicked one (Eph. 6).

[Note: [Col. 0937C] Dupin did not understand this passage quite correctly, translating it into French: “He exhorts to almsgiving, which he does not scruple to compare with Baptism, saying that just as the water of Baptism extinguishes the fire of hell, so the abundance of alms extinguishes the fire of covetousness which remains after Baptism, or at least prevents it from being kindled.” This is entirely wrong. Gaudentius says: “the fire of sins is extinguished, provided that after conversion it does not blaze up again through renewed crimes”; but Dupin did not grasp this.]

For just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving resists sin (Ecclus. 3:33)—that is, just as the water of saving baptism extinguishes the flame of Gehenna through grace, so by the flood of almsgiving that whole fire of sins, accumulated after faith has been received, is extinguished, provided that after conversion it does not blaze up again through renewed crimes. [Col. 0938B]

The person who, in penitence, seeks a remedy for sins through almsgiving must now cease committing what requires penitence, lest what is extinguished on one side be kindled on the other. [Note: [Col. 0937C] The Lyon edition was terribly corrupt here, reading “he must now cease doing penance”; but Pantagathus’s codex, together with other manuscripts and editions, has “he must now cease doing what requires penance.”]

We called it a flood of almsgiving so that you might perceive the abundance of giving. [Note: [Col. 0937D] Thus two Vatican manuscripts, whose reading seemed more correct than the others here. Pantagathus’s codex read “but each one is of the flesh,” quite wrongly; in the margin, however, *quotus* had been restored in place of *carnis*, giving “but how few there are,” with a question mark at the end of the clause. This reading suits the entire passage extremely well. The Cologne and Lyon editions have “but how rare you are”; the Paris edition, “but how rare is anyone.” Three editions agree in another error, reading “for the refreshment that benefits him,” which we corrected on the basis of the two Vatican manuscripts.] Yet how few there are who scatter even a drop of almsgiving that will benefit their own refreshment.

A Christian leaves the church and passes by the poor man praying with deaf ears. [Note: [Col. 0938C] Four manuscripts read: “A Christian leaves the church, if indeed he is a Christian.” This may perhaps be the genuine reading, and Pantagathus’s book also indicates it. Cyprian has something similar in the same context, *On Works and Almsgiving*: “What is a treacherous heart doing in the house of God? What? The man who does not believe Christ at all is called and named a Christian? The name Pharisee suits you better.” From this one may confirm the ancient custom of the Church, when the poor stood at the doors of temples to receive alms. John Chrysostom, *Homily 28 to the People of Antioch*, translated by Bernard of Brescia, writes: “Therefore the poor sit before churches and the monuments of the martyrs, at the doors, so that from such a spectacle we may derive great benefit”; and in *Homily 30 on 1 Corinthians 12*, translated by Germanus of Brescia: “For what is baser and more contemptible than beggars? Yet they too perform a very important service in churches, fixed at the temple doors.” The familiar passage is Acts 3:2 concerning the lame man, whom they placed daily “πρὸς τὴν θύραν τοῦ ἱεροῦ,” that is, “at the door of the temple,” to ask alms from those entering. This custom was preserved even in later centuries, as the Council of Bourges of 1585 states, title 9: “The church custodians shall take care that beggars do not wander through the church or enter the choir under pretext of asking alms during divine worship or the sermon; rather, they shall await alms at the doors of the churches.” There is also the constitution of Pope Pius V, *Cum primum*, constitution 5, issued in 1566, by which beggars asking for alms were excluded from church enclosures.]

These were times full of the calamities of war, by which the Roman world was oppressed. Jerome, *Epitaph on Nepotianus*, writes: “My spirit shudders to trace the ruins of our times. For twenty years and more Roman blood has been shed daily between Constantinople and the Julian Alps. The Goth, the Sarmatian, the Quadi, the Alan, the Huns, the Vandals, and the Marcomanni devastate, drag away, and plunder Scythia, Thrace, Macedonia, Dardania, Dacia, Thessalonica, Achaea, Epirus, Dalmatia, and all the Pannonias.” Compare Zosimus, book 4 of the *New History*. Gaudentius Merula, book 2 of *The Antiquities of Cisalpine Gaul*, chapter 14, after quoting the passage from Jerome just given, adds: “I am surprised that he did not add Cisalpine Gaul, which, as Flavius Vopiscus reports, was devastated by the Marcomanni—especially the territory of the Insubres around Milan—who later, under the emperor Aurelian, inflicted such a defeat on the Romans at Piacenza that the Roman empire was almost dissolved.” Vopiscus’s passage is in *Aurelian*, chapter 18. [Col. 0939C] Merula, however, makes a shameful mistake when he wants the disaster inflicted on the Roman empire by the Marcomanni under Aurelian, in the third century after Christ, to be the event mentioned by Jerome, who recounts only events of twenty years or somewhat more. Which barbarian invasion Gaudentius chiefly has in mind, whether that of Eugenius and Arbogastes, when, after Valentinian was killed, they invaded Italy around the year 392, or another invasion by Radagaisus and Alaric after the year 400, I cannot determine.]

Thus God will hear us when we plead; thus, amid the dangers of the barbarians threatening us, we shall deserve to be protected by divine aid. For it is written (Tob. 12) that fasting with almsgiving is good. Both ought to be practiced in order to mitigate the Lord’s anger.

But perhaps you cannot fast—and you cannot because you do not wish to—or at least give food to the hungry. You cannot remain fasting for three hours longer than usual. [Note: [Col. 0939C] Three manuscripts have: “You will not be able to remain fasting; you surely understand what he suffers.” The Florentine and Pantagathus’s codex have the somewhat better reading: “You will not think yourself able to remain fasting; you surely understand what he suffers.”] You can surely understand what he suffers who fasts unwillingly through want, whom your cruelty makes fast, while you, stuffed with abundant dishes, do not even consider relieving the hunger of the needy with a small amount of food.

You plead scarcity; you bring forward necessities; you complain of difficult times. You beg more shamefully than the needy person. Indeed, you are ungrateful to God while making false complaints.

But let us suppose that there has been scarcity: do you alone feel it, I ask? Does that poor man not feel it? [Note: [Col. 0939C] In Pantagathus’s manuscript the word *lucrari* is absent, so that the reading is: “What, then? What new silver you daily contrive…” One other manuscript also agrees with this reading, so that the inept word *lucrari* seems to belong only to the editions. It also corresponds very well with what follows: “you build houses of marble.”]

What of the fact that you daily contrive to acquire new silver? You build houses of marble; you purchase silk garments; you buy necklaces precious with gold and gems. [Note: [Col. 0939D] An outstanding passage of Gaudentius, which, so far as I know, has hitherto been noticed by no one. It makes sufficiently clear that in that age the Church had a particular concern for the poor and needy. On this subject there is a dissertation by Jean de Launoy, *On the Church’s Care for the Wretched and the Poor*, although it considers chiefly the arrangements of later periods rather than the discipline of that age. Cyprian, Letter 7 in the latest edition, formerly book 2, letter 24, writes: “I ask that you diligently care for the sick and all the poor; and if there are any needy travelers, supply their expenses from my own funds, which I left with our fellow presbyter Rogatianus. Since those funds may perhaps already have been entirely distributed, I have sent him another portion through Naricus the acolyte, so that the work of assisting those in distress may be carried out more generously and promptly.” What the Church’s discipline was in the administration of ecclesiastical property, from its beginning up to the reign of Constantine the Great, is outlined by Thomassin, part 3, book 2, chapter 12. There, in section 10, on the basis of Justin Martyr’s *Apology* 2, he indicates that the head of the Church was appointed guardian of all the needy.]

I am ashamed to say, and regret to recall, how many peasants living on their estates in the pomp described above have either died of hunger or been supported by the Church’s alms. 318 What a dreadful crime! People have died in whom lay the whole wealth of the owner. Thus, blinded by excessive greed, they provide neither for the needs of the present time.

Let us therefore begin with our own people, beloved, and do good to the needy and miserable. Let us supply food, drink, and clothing to those in want, because the Lord is the just rewarder of such works. When he comes in his majesty (Matt. 25), he will grant the kingdom of heaven to those placed on his right hand in proportion to the merit of their having nourished the poor. [Col. 0939C] [Note: [Col. 0940C] The editions read “on the right-hand side”; the manuscripts read “on the right hand.” The difference would perhaps not deserve mention, except that our diligence might be approved by readers.] But, on the contrary, he will decree that the inhuman and impious be burned in eternal fire, saying that in the poor he himself was either nourished by their piety or neglected through their cruelty.

So great is the love of our Savior for his poor. Let us therefore strive to love Christ also in the poor, who loved us in every way and who, like a good shepherd, laid down his life for his sheep (John 10).

But if I begin to explain by what duties you must prove your love toward the Lord, I do not know whether you will love me while I am speaking; I do not know whether you will listen to me willingly—unless perhaps you are so religious that, just as a little earlier you rejoiced in divine benefits, so you also desire to obey his commandments and eagerly learn what duties of love toward God must be practiced. [Note: [Col. 0940C] Thus two Vatican manuscripts, the Urbinate, and two editions. The Paris edition has “and likewise in the commandments,” which is not sufficiently correct; Pantagathus’s book has “and likewise the commandments.” The whole of Gaudentius’s anticipation here should be observed, by which he renders his hearer remarkably receptive and attentive.]

The Lord himself [Col. 0940B] says what kind of love each believer ought to have toward him: “He who has my commandments and keeps them,” he says, “is the one who loves me” (John 14).

For that person loves God perfectly [Note: [Col. 0940C] We followed the reading of the Florentine codex, since the other copies, both manuscripts and printed editions, offered nothing sound and read as follows: “who either has his commandments in his mouth or keeps them in his works.” What follows shortly afterward—“For those who merely report the divine commandments with their mouth in a superficial confession”—plainly demonstrates the truth of our reading. It is also supported by Octavius Pantagathus’s codex, which here is superior to the Urbinate and Vatican manuscripts; indeed, shortly before it reads *certainly* rather than *perfectly*.] who either holds his commandments in his heart or keeps them in his works.

For he who merely repeats the divine commandments with his mouth in a superficial confession, and neither retains them in his mind nor observes them in his deeds, cannot at all say: “I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the upright and in the congregation” (Ps. 110). Rather, he must hear God rebuking him through the prophet together with the synagogue of the contemptuous people: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29; Matt. 15).

“Do not be deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal. 6). Do you suppose that the lukewarm and careless Christian loves God, who permits idols to be worshiped on his estates; [Note: [Col. 0940D] Thus the remnants of paganism and the shrines of idols had not yet been entirely removed in Gaudentius’s age, around A.D. 400, as may likewise be inferred from other passages of Gaudentius: tract 8, p. 277, “Let us flee, I beg, from idols, lest, likewise rejected, we deserve to hear …”; and tract 4, p. 253, “You therefore, neophytes, see how you preserve your souls from every pollution of foods which pagan superstition has defiled.” The celebrated debates of Ambrose and Symmachus concerning the Altar of Victory clearly show the same thing. Hence the writers of Brescia make themselves wholly ridiculous when they maintain that, from the second century after Christ onward, the entire city of Brescia, under Bishop Apollonius, as Ughellus reports, had been converted to the Christian faith. Gaudentius certainly says, not obscurely, in his sermon on his own ordination, that the Church of Brescia was founded in the faith by his predecessor Philastrius: “After that most learned voice of my father Philastrius of venerable memory, which, flowing abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit, founded this Church in the faith of the Trinity to be adored.” Philastrius was bishop of Brescia around A.D. 380.] who allows the shrine of a demon and the altar of the devil to stand as an insult to God [Col. 0941A]; who does not cease committing adulteries and debaucheries; who daily steals what belongs to others and daily covets it; who eagerly seeks to kill his neighbor by whatever means, so that he may more freely satisfy either his pleasure or his greed, even if he cannot fulfill it?

[Note: [Col. 0941C] The printed editions have “by the constant practice of sexual immorality”; but the Florentine manuscript and the two Vatican manuscripts have “the constant practice of sexual immorality,” as does Octavius Pantagathus’s book.]

For the constant practice of sexual immorality does not restrain the lust of the flesh but inflames it. The Prophet says: “All of them are adulterers; their hearts are like a burning oven” (Hos. 7). Nor does the rapacity of the predator suppress greed; it provokes it. For it is written: “He who loves money will not be satisfied with money” (Eccl. 5).

Nor does he love God who does not have mercy on the poor, in whom Christ himself testifies that he is either cherished or neglected. “What you did not do,” he says, “for one of the least of these, you did not do for me” (Matt. 25). The Apostle John likewise says in his epistle: “Whoever sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, the love of God is not in him” (1 John 3).

He therefore lies when he claims to love Christ who does not love him in the needy person, who denies by his deeds the love he promises in words. Let each person therefore strive to prove by works of mercy that he loves God, so that the love of God may cleanse him from every sin.

But do you wish to know how greatly almsgiving lightens the burdens of sins? Hear the counsel that the prophet Daniel gives to the sinful rich man: “Now, O king, let my counsel please you; redeem your iniquities with almsgiving, and your sins with compassion toward the poor” (Dan. 4).

But perhaps you think that what you deny to the poor has been preserved for you or your children. [Note: [Col. 0941D] The Florentine, two Vatican manuscripts, and Pantagathus’s codex have the same reading: “you think that you will preserve for them what you deny to the poor.”] I do not want you to be so dangerously anxious. [Col. 0941C] For you do not know what the following day will bring forth. [Note: [Col. 0941D] The printed editions consistently cite Ecclesiasticus, chapter 8, at this point. We discovered that the citation is erroneous, for that chapter contains only: “Do not give counsel before a stranger, for you do not know what he may bring forth.” Proverbs 27, however, reads in the Vulgate: “Do not boast about tomorrow, since you do not know what the coming day may bring forth.” The Septuagint has: “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the day that comes may bring forth.” John Chrysostom, *Homily 22 on 2 Corinthians 10*, translated by Erasmus of Rotterdam, reads: “For you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.”]

Our God is powerful enough to give to them as well as to you. Indeed, whatever you give to the poor, you have bestowed both upon yourself and upon your children. Nothing can be lacking to those with whom you have made Christ a fellow-participant. [Note: [Col. 0941D] The Florentine and Urbinate have “to those with whom you have made Christ a fellow-participant.” The two Vatican manuscripts have “to those with whom he made Christ a fellow-participant.” Neither reading is important enough to make us depart from the printed editions. Pantagathus’s codex agrees with the Florentine and Urbinate.]

He knows how to repay who testifies that he receives in the poor. Give confidently; for there is a suitable recompense-giver who promises the kingdoms of heaven.

Divine Scripture says: “Store up almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you before God” (Ecclus. 29). This is what it means to say: “Sell your estate and purchase protection”—by whose intervention, assured of having obtained pardon, you may deserve to behold the coming Judge as a free man.

In the Gospel, however, he says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19).

[Col. 0942B] If we are commanded to distribute everything, let us consider what guilt awaits those men and women who habitually wear silk, purple, and gold garments, if they do not clothe the naked with some kind of covering. Some women load their own limbs or those of their daughters with gold and pearls, and pass by with dry hands the crowds of needy people begging. [Note: [Col. 0941D] This was the custom of noblewomen, as is made clear by Claudian’s well-known poems concerning the belt and the trappings of the royal horse, sent by Serena to the Augusti Honorius and Arcadius. The dress of the women of Brescia seems also to have been especially notable, since in luxury and wealth it rivaled that of queens. What Gaudentius said shortly before—“Some women load their own limbs or those of their daughters with gold and pearls”—is not unlike the following passage of Claudian:

“Diligently she loaded with gems sought from the sea  
the reins that would suit the swift Xanthus and Balius.”

Similarly, Publius Syrus in Petronius:

“What is the use of the precious pearl to you, Indian gem?  
Is it so that, laden with sea-born ornaments, a matron may walk about…?”

And Horace, *Epode* 8:

“Nor let there be a married woman who walks about  
laden with rounded pearls.”]

[Col. 0942D] Zeno of Verona, Sermon 2, On Avarice: “You reject a false idol, O handmaid of Christ; believe me, you worship it in yourself, whose adornment, whose image, you do not lay aside. You proceed to the Church of God with your whole body gilded by varied workmanship, burdened with accursed metal.”  

They also fashion for brute animals—horses and mules—delicate ornaments of silver and gold [Note: [Col. 0942D] A small alteration, but very appropriate here, was suggested by the Pantagathus manuscript, which reads inutilia ornamenta, “useless ornaments,” instead of subtilia ornamenta, “delicate ornaments.” Since, however, subtilia occurs in the other manuscripts and editions, I have been unwilling to change it.] ; yet they do not give a human being, made in the image of God, even the vilest clothing or food. And do they suppose that they will find some respite on the day of judgment unless, at least from now on [Note: [Col. 0942D] The Florentine manuscript also assisted at this point, since the editions and manuscripts alike had absurdly read opera pietatis accipiant, “receive works of piety.” Jerome, To Eustochium, On the Preservation of Virginity: “Take up the shield of faith, by which the fiery arrows of the devil are extinguished.” Augustine, Confessions, book IX, chapter 12: “Evodius took up the psalter”; and book VII, chapter 21: “I eagerly took up the venerable writing of your Spirit.” The Pantagathus manuscript also reads opera pietatis arripiant, “take up works of piety,” quite correctly.] they take up works of piety? I beseech you, let us be merciful to the poor, so that we too, in accordance with the Lord’s saying (Matthew 5), may obtain mercy.

Both the rich and those of moderate means [Col. 0942C] ought eagerly to give alms, each according to [Col. 0943A] his ability: “For we brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away” (1 Timothy 6). “Naked I came forth,” says holy Job, “from my mother’s womb; naked I shall return again to the earth” (Job 1). Each person carries away with him from the resources he has received whatever he has spent for the work of religion, whatever he has done out of love for God, obeying his commandments. For on the day of judgment it will be said:

[Note: [Col. 0943B] The passage in Ignatius’s Letter to the Smyrnaeans is altogether similar: “It is fitting for those who have turned to God to repent; for in hell there is no one who confesses. For, behold, the man and his works are before his face.” Perhaps at that time the opinion prevailed that these words had been spoken by Christ the Lord, as Nierembergius maintains in On the Origin of Sacred Scripture, book XII, chapter 15. The same statement, “Behold the man and his works,” is found in the Meditations circulated under both Augustine’s and Bernard’s names—under Augustine’s in chapter 39, and under Bernard’s in chapter 2. Nierembergius is mistaken, however, in thinking that these were the words of Christ the Lord; they are undoubtedly taken from Isaiah 62:11, and were rendered by the Septuagint as follows: Ἰδοὺ ὁ Σωτήρ σοι παραγέγονεν, ἔχων τὸν ἑαυτοῦ μισθὸν, καὶ τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ πρὸ προσώπου αὐτοῦ — “Behold, your Savior has come, having his reward with him, and your work before his face.” On this, see Usserius, Prolegomena to the Letters of Ignatius, chapter 11, at the end. The letter of Ignatius cited by Nierembergius is one of the interpolated letters in Cotelerius, p. 91; for the prophetic testimony is absent from the genuine Letter to the Smyrnaeans, although it also occurs in precisely the same words in Clement, Potter, p. 642.]

“Behold the man, and his works”; it will not be said: “Behold the man, [Note: [Col. 0943C] We have faithfully reproduced the complete reading of three manuscript codices, namely, two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinas. The editions read et potentia ejus, et haeredes ejus, “and his power, and his heirs.” The sentence opera requirit qui praecepta commisit, “He requires the works of the one who entrusted the commandments,” plainly contains a gap introduced through the fault of the copyists. The Florentine manuscript reads: “and his power, and his heirs. He requires the works of the one who entrusted the commandments.” The Pantagathus book has: “and his riches, and his heirs. He requires the works of the one who entrusted the commandments.” From a comparison of both manuscripts, the complete reading can be recovered.] and his power, and his riches, and his heirs.” He requires the works of the one who entrusted the commandments; he is the rewarder of mercy who taught piety, who established that love for himself should be demonstrated by observance of the commandments. For he regards as done for himself [Note: [Col. 0943D] This is the reading of one of the Vatican manuscripts. The other manuscripts read quidquid egeno praestiterit, “whatever he has done for the needy.” The copyist’s error was easy: while carelessly reading what may have been written in abbreviation as praestit. erit, he fused two words into one. Two editions read quidquid egeno praestiteris, “whatever you have done for the needy,” a reading supported by the Octavian Pantagathus book. The Cologne edition, incorrectly, has quidquid egeno praesteris.] whatever has been done for the needy. Hence elsewhere we read: [Note: [Col. 0943D] Thus the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinas, as well as the Pantagathus manuscript. The Florentine manuscript also has it, but changes pauperis, “the poor person,” to pauperibus, “the poor.” The editions read: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to God; for he will receive.” Eligius of Noyon likewise has this in Homily 11: “For through almsgiving to the poor he lends to God.” Cyprian, however, in the treatise On Works and Almsgiving and in the treatise On the Lord’s Prayer, reads this testimony as follows: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to God.” Similarly, in the treatise On the Dress of Virgins: “Lend God your patrimony.” On these passages, see Gronovius, Observations on Ecclesiastical Scripture, chapter 1, p. 10.] “He who has mercy on the poor lends to God” (Proverbs 19). And indeed he lends; for from the Son of God himself he will receive great things in return for small, and heavenly things in return for earthly things—he whose kingdom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, endures forever and ever.

## SERMON XIV. ON VARIOUS CHAPTERS, FOURTH

[Note: [Col. 0944C] This title is read in this form in two Vatican manuscripts and in the Pantagathus book. The Florentine manuscript instead has: “Here begins On the Promise of the Coming of the Paraclete.” The Urbinas has: “On the Promise of the Coming of the Paraclete.” The editions have: “On the Promise of the Paraclete.”]

### On the Promise of the Coming of the Paraclete

322 The ineffable providence of the only-begotten Son of God graciously discloses little by little to his disciples the truth of saving faith, which human hearts cannot receive all at once. [Col. 0944A] He had already taught at length in the preceding discussions about the unity of his divinity with the Father, [Note: [Col. 0944C] That some of Gaudentius’s treatises have been lost is clear not only from this passage, but also from the beginnings of Treatises 11 and 12. For the things he indicates there that he had promised to explain, or had discussed immediately beforehand, are no longer extant. The same is true of what he says in Sermon 2, p. 242: that he had frequently discussed at greater length the girding of the loins; this is found nowhere. Likewise, in Sermon 13 he recalls the following: “We discussed, as you remember, the whole sequence of the reading that describes the Lord dining in Bethany, explaining Lazarus’s reclining, the circumstances of the place and time, Martha’s service, her sister’s attentiveness, the power of the ointment, and the reason for the hair with which Mary wiped Christ’s feet after anointing them with precious perfume.” All these things are likewise missing from the present collection. So too is the material he indicates that he explained in Treatise 8, p. 274, in these words: “These matters are connected with what I discussed in detail in its proper place, as your affection remembers, when the Lord, graciously embracing the envoys of the Gentiles and foreseeing the faith of innumerable peoples in the faith of a few believers, said to the Apostles: ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.’” See the notes attached to that passage.]

as I explained in the preceding Treatise: showing that there is so little division between the Father and the Son that he even said that the speech he uttered was not his own unless it belonged to the Father. For he had said: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me” (John 14:24). By this statement it became sufficiently clear that all who despise the teaching of the only-begotten Son are despisers of the Father, since the Son says that the word he calls his own is not his unless it is the Father’s. The Son’s word is therefore his if it is the Father’s, because, he says, “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine” [Col. 0944B] (John 16:15). And elsewhere he says to the Father: “All things that are yours are mine, and mine are yours” (John 17:10), namely, through the unity of the divine substance, which does not permit anything to be called its own that does not belong to its nature.

Now he immediately adds that the same unity of the Holy Spirit must also be believed, foretelling that the fullness of his teaching is to be brought to completion through the Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0944D] This is the reading of the editions; the manuscripts instead read: “he foretells that it is to be brought to completion through the Paraclete himself.” The Urbinas has Paraclitum, and elsewhere also reads Paraclitus for Paracletus; but scholars have not sufficiently agreed whether Paracletus or Paraclitus should be read. The following passage from Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, On the Sunday Gospels, deserves to be copied here in full: “When a Greek came to the royal palace while that Gospel was being read and Paraclitus was said, he declared that Paracletus ought to be said. Yet we do not dare to change it, because of custom.” Scaliger, On the Causes of the Latin Language, book I, chapter 26, wishes Paraclitus to be called barbarous, though Jean-Baptiste Thiers defends the word in his Dissertation on Retaining the Word Paraclitus. Quintianus Stoa, our fellow citizen, Epography 4, chapter 4, p. 276, Venice edition of 1568, printed by Hieronymus Scotus, maintains that Paracletum must unquestionably be pronounced with a long penultimate syllable. The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus consistently has Paracletus, Paracletum, Paracleto.] saying: “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you. But that Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and remind you of everything that I have said to you” (John 14:25). [Col. 0945A] 323

By these words he deigned to announce beforehand to the blessed Apostles both his own return to heaven after the impending Passion and the coming of the Holy Spirit upon them from heaven, when he says: “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you. But that Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send.” Yet the Holy Spirit was not only in heaven and absent from earth; nor was the Son going to ascend to heaven in such a way as to abandon the earth; nor does the Father possess only the heavenly throne, where the Son was to return and from which the Holy Spirit is said to come. [Note: [Col. 0945C] Thus the Paris edition and the Pantagathus book. The Vatican manuscripts instead have: “whence the Holy Spirit is said to come.” Two other editions, incorrectly: “whence the holy Spirit is forbidden to come.”]

For the most blessed prophet refers such a confession to the Father: “Where shall I go,” he says, “from your Spirit? And from your face where shall I go? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present; if I take up my wings straight ahead and dwell at the farthest end of the sea” (Psalm 138). [Note: [Col. 0945D] The Florentine manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Pantagathus book have: “from your face, where shall I flee?” From this passage, and from many others, it is evident that Gaudentius used some distinctive version, unless perhaps it was the ancient Italic version, since what he cites often leaves either no trace or only a very slight one in the Vulgate or in the Septuagint.]

“If I take up,” he says, “my wings,” and so forth. It is good that he has his own wings, by which, once he takes them up, he penetrates wherever he wishes. But how could the prophet, remaining in the body, ascend into heaven, descend into hell, or travel beyond the furthest seas? What wings, then, does he have? The mind of the believer takes up the wings of faith, [Note: [Col. 0945D] The editions most corruptly read: “so that, as things higher than earthly things, wholly in the spirit...” We have corrected the error from the two Vatican manuscripts, supported also by the manuscript text of the Octavian Pantagathus book.] so that, elevated above earthly things and wholly established in the spirit, it may be able to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the length, breadth, height, and depth of the knowledge of God (Ephesians 3).

Heretics, lacking these wings of faith, discuss God while rolling about among earthly things; weighed down by the burden of earthly thoughts, they are dragged from the sublimity of divine understanding to things perishable and carnal. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Thus the Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts. The editions have: “weighed down by the burden.”] Nor can they approach knowledge of that immense divinity, [Col. 0946A] to which only the faithful mind has access—the mind that perceives, believes, confesses, and proclaims the unity of the Trinity worthy of adoration; and because it cannot express this adequately, it glories in that very fact above all.

“Where shall I go,” he says, “from your Spirit? And from your face where shall I go? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present; if I take up my wings straight ahead [Note: [Col. 0946C] Both Vatican manuscripts have: “and dwell at the extremity of the sea”; the Florentine: “and I shall dwell at the farthest end of the sea”; the Pantagathus book: “and I shall dwell at the farthest end of the sea.”] and dwell at the farthest end of the sea; for even there your hand will hold me, and your right hand will guide me” (Psalm 138). [Note: [Col. 0946C] The manuscripts offered virtually no assistance in restoring the reading, although an obvious error was present in the editions, which had indivulsam instead of indivisam. We have therefore safely removed the word. The Urbinas reads invulsam Trinitatis naturam, “the unplucked nature of the Trinity,” which has no meaning. The Pantagathus manuscript, the only sound one at this point, has indivisam Trinitatis naturam, “the undivided nature of the Trinity.” Thus it both remedies the error of the other books and admirably confirms our conjecture published in the earlier edition of Gaudentius. Although I knew that indivulsus occurs in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book I, chapter 11, in the phrase indivulsus comes, “an inseparable companion,” I had not therefore supposed that Gaudentius wished to use this unusual word when speaking of the Trinity. Our emendation was made still more certain by what follows shortly afterward: “Lest anyone suppose that the Holy Spirit was divided from the Father, or that the Son was believed to be separated from him.” Vigilius of Thapsus, On the Trinity, book V: “The ineffable fullness of the undivided substance of the Trinity.” Tertullian likewise, Against Praxeas, chapter 8: “Root and shoot are two things, but joined together. Fountain and river are two forms, but undivided.” And shortly afterward: “For behold, I say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Spirit another—not, however, another Son from the Father by diversity, but by distribution; nor by division another, but by distinction.”]

This confession marks the undivided nature of the Trinity.

“Where shall I go,” he says, “from your Spirit?”—that is, from the Paraclete himself, whose fullness the Apostles received, confessing God’s promise to have been fulfilled through Peter’s mouth, when he testified: “This is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘In the last days, says the Lord, I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh’” (Acts 2; Joel 2).

“And from your face where shall I go?” (Psalm 138)—from the Son, namely, who is the face of the Father, because the Father is seen in the Son, according to the declaration of the Lord and Savior himself. When Philip pleaded, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” he answered: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has also seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14).

Lest anyone suppose that the Holy Spirit was divided from the Father, whose Spirit he is, or that the Son was believed to be separated from him, whose face, right hand, wisdom, and power he is, he does not say: “If I ascend into heaven, your Spirit is there,” or “your face and your Spirit are there.” Rather, he says, “You are there”—with the Son, certainly, and with the Holy Spirit—because the one and identical divinity of the Trinity worthy of adoration is always everywhere.

But so that one faith and a distinct confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit might be handed down to believers, Scripture therefore says that the Father sends both the Son and the Holy Spirit—[Col. 0947A] although neither the one who sends nor the one who is sent can be believed to be God if he is in one place [Note: [Col. 0947D] The editions read entirely incorrectly: “and is not in one place,” that is, “let us believe the Son himself;” therefore we have preferred the reading of four manuscript codices, which is also supported by the Octavian Pantagathus book.] and not in another.

Let us believe the Son himself when he speaks, for he is the truth: “I am not alone,” he says, “because the Father is with me” (John 8). And again concerning the Holy Spirit: “If I,” he says, “cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). And the evangelist Luke: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4).

Since, then, the divinity of the Trinity is nowhere absent, it is a dispensation of our salvation that one is proclaimed as sending and another as sent. For the human mind could not otherwise grasp that the Father is Father, the Son Son, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit, unless it learned the distinction from the naming of the sender and the one sent. And again, it would not recognize the one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit unless it read that the one sent is in no way separated from the sender.

For neither did the Father, as has been said, abandon the Son who was sent; nor is the Holy Spirit, who was to be directed to the Apostles, ever shown to have been absent from the Father and the Son. Nevertheless, only the Son of God was incarnate. For, as we read, “the Word became flesh” (John 1), not the Father and not the Spirit.

How the Son of God fulfilled this mystery of the Incarnation while preserving the unity of the Trinity is demonstrated by that omnipotence by which the same Son of God ascended into heaven with the body of the man he had assumed, yet remained with his disciples until the end of the age. “Behold,” he says, “I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.” “Until the consummation of the age,” he says, “I am with you” (Matthew 28): not only with the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0947D] Thus the Florentine manuscript and the Pantagathus book. The editions have: “but with the disciples.”], but certainly also with all believing disciples.

We must therefore believe that God is not otherwise than he himself revealed in his own speech that he is. We must not examine his works with a rebellious spirit, but admire them with faithful devotion, because “the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith” (Psalm 32). If all his works are in faith, how much more is this work of his most sacred incorporation!

Let us therefore cease, neglecting faith, to assault the divine mystery with insulting questions. The scrupulosity of one who hesitates does not discover an understanding of God’s works through excessive curiosity; rather, it loses the faith which is known to be the guide of salvation and life.

That excessive scrupulosity destroys faith can easily be understood from one example of divine operation: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1). Since I cannot grasp how its Creator made it from nothing, if nevertheless I do not believe and confess that it was made, I declare God a liar through sacrilegious hesitation.

All his works, [Note: [Col. 0947D] Thus the two Vatican manuscripts, the Urbinas, and the Pantagathus book. The editions have: “and the chief divine work.”] and especially the divine work of the Incarnation of the Son of God—as the holy Scriptures proclaim—must therefore be received by the faithful devotion of every believer’s mind; and what the heart has believed with steadfastness must be confessed with the faithful service of the mouth. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

In promising that the fullness of his teaching would be repaid through the Holy Spirit, he wished him to be believed [Note: [Col. 0948D] The reading of the two Vatican manuscripts. The editions have, less correctly: “equal in his omnipotence,” which cannot fit the passage in any way. The Pantagathus book has: “to be believed equal to his omnipotence”; and for retribuendam, “to be repaid,” which precedes, it has the somewhat better tribuendam, “to be bestowed.”] equal to his omnipotence. For in the Trinity there is not Lord and servant, God and angel, Creator and creature; rather, there is otherness and identity—other in person, the same in nature [Note: [Col. 0948D] This passage was afflicted by no small corruption in the editions, which we have cleansed with the aid of four manuscript codices. In all of them we find, without distinction: aliud persona, idem natura, “another in person, the same in nature.” The editions incorrectly read: “another in person. That is, nature.” The Pantagathus manuscript gives the entire passage as follows: “but another, and the same. Another in person, the same in nature.” In the margin, however, Pantagathus’s own hand has written: “another and the same; another in person, the same in nature,” which I would also prefer to the other readings.] —another in person, the same in nature—and therefore not gods, but God, because the unity of the Godhead does not admit division.

Finally, Christ says there concerning the Holy Spirit: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14)—that is, in the name of God, so that he is to be confessed as God, just as the Son is. And therefore the Son of God says of himself: “I have come in my Father’s name” (John 5:43), which the prophet had also foretold concerning him, and which the children in the Gospel confirmed in their praise when they cried: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21).

Rightly, “in the name of the Lord”: not in the name of a servant, because he is God; not in his own name, because he is the Son. For the Father’s name is in the Son. Thus, I repeat, the Son says of himself: “I have come in the name of the Father” (John 5). But concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “Whom my Father will send in my name” (John 14).

And when he ordained that the work of Baptism should be celebrated in the Trinity, he did not say “in names,” but “in the name” (Matthew 28). For the Father is God, and the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, as I have repeatedly demonstrated to your affection by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. Therefore the name of the Trinity is one, and its power and divinity are one, enduring forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON VARIOUS CHAPTERS, FIFTH

### On the Birthday of the Maccabees

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The title of this same treatise, On the Maccabean Martyrs and Their Birthday, appears in this form in Galeardus’s edition, [Col. 0949C] which appends the following note. We have established this title on the authority of the Florentine, Urbinas, and two Vatican manuscript codices, to which the Pantagathus book also agrees. The Cologne and Paris editions instead have: “A Treatise of the Same Author on the Maccabean Martyrs and Their Birthday.” The Lyons edition has only: “On the Maccabean Martyrs and Their Birthday.”]

### On These Blessed Martyrs
If any of you, dearly beloved brothers, perhaps wonders that Jewish men who suffered punishments for the sake of the precept of the Law are now honored as holy Martyrs by the Christian people, he will certainly understand, if he has come to know the whole purpose and rationale of the holy religion, that this was established by our forefathers with sound and supreme judgment.

These men were Jews before the coming of the Lord and Savior, living under the Old Law alone; and they bore the surname Machabees [Note: [Col. 0949C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions incorrectly read *trahant ex genere* (“they derive from the race”).] by descent, just as today [Note: [Col. 0949C] *Aniciorum* must certainly be written, although the manuscripts read *Anitiorum*. You will find many monuments of the Anicii in Gruter’s Inscriptions, pp. CCCLII, CCCLIII, and elsewhere, in which *Anicius* and *Anicia* are invariably and consistently read. The printed editions mistakenly have “the offspring of the Aricii”; had some foolish person among us read this in an earlier age, he would doubtless have entered this family into the Roman census as well. Aldus, *On Orthography*, p. 34: *Anicius*, not *Anitius*. So too the Capitoline inscriptions and others that Jerome repeatedly cites. Jerome, *To Demetrias*, Ep. 98, Benedictine edition: “The illustrious stock of the Anician blood, among which there is scarcely anyone—or no one—who has not deserved the consulship.” The two Benedictine and Erasmian editions of Jerome read “the blood of the Anitii”; but this was a typographical error.] the offspring of the Anicii [p. 327], or whatever such names may now be called, which claim a noble stock descending from an accumulation of earthly riches—although true nobility does not arise from riches but is recognized in character.

How much nobler were these seven boys than King Antiochus! Indeed, [Col. 0949B] [Note: [Col. 0949D] This is the reading of the Florentine manuscript, which seemed sounder and more accurate. I have never been able to bring myself to approve the reading of the Urbinate and both Vatican manuscripts, where we find: “how manifest in these is the nobility of God,” although three editions retain it. The book of Octavius Pantagathus likewise prefers the Florentine reading: “how manifest in these is the nobility of faith.”] how manifest in these is the nobility of faith, and how ignoble and marked by the punishment of treachery is he! These men worship God the Father; he, the devil. These venerate the law of their fathers; he, rebelling against God, acknowledges himself to be the devil’s son.

For he compelled them, contrary to the precept of the divine Law, to eat swine’s flesh (II Macc. VII)—without doubt flesh polluted by profane sacrifice, for to the defiled and faithless nothing is clean (Tit. I). But even if, as some maintain, that flesh had not been sacrificed to the devil, [Note: [Col. 0949D] Thus the two Vatican manuscripts, the Urbinate, and Pantagathus’s manuscript. The Paris and Lyons editions read *quia hoc ipsa scribentis historia* (“because this is what the history itself of the writer [says]”); the Cologne edition reads, less correctly, the same. Gaudentius means the history of the Maccabees as it is read in the Bible. Josephus, however, in his treatise *On the Maccabees*, ch. 5, asserts that the swine’s flesh had been sacrificed to idols: καὶ κρέων ὑείων, καὶ εἰδωλοθύτων, “both swine’s flesh and flesh sacrificed to idols.”] since the history itself does not state this more explicitly, nevertheless it was a very grave and extreme offense to violate the divine precept, whether by rewards that sought to entice them or by punishments that tortured them.

God had commanded the Jews (Lev. XI; Deut. XIV) [Note: [Col. 0949D] The printed editions have “not to eat the pig and other things like it”; but *illi* (“to it”) is absent from the manuscripts. The prohibition of the Law concerned not only pigs and animals like pigs, but also many other animals that had nothing in common with pigs. See Leviticus XI and Deuteronomy XIV. Gaudentius likewise says below that the Jewish people had been commanded to abstain from pork, from similar four-footed animals, and also from certain birds and fish.] not to eat pork or anything similar. [Note: [Col. 0950C] The manuscripts read this differently. The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts have: “and this was of twofold purpose, brothers”; the two Vatican manuscripts and Pantagathus’s book: “and here there was the fruit of a twofold purpose.” I would not prefer either reading to the vulgate text.] And this was for a twofold reason, dearly beloved brothers: either so that a luxurious people would not nourish the flame of fleshly vices with hot meats—for such foods are said to produce excessive heat in bodies—or so that they would not live in the manner of swine.

For swine are always unclean. After coming out of a spring or river, they roll themselves again in the mud; they never look toward heaven, but with their heads always bent toward the earth they serve their bellies. And therefore the Lord (Matt. VIII) permitted a legion of demons to enter a herd of swine—that is, the herd of those who are nothing but animals of the belly, who never look upon heavenly things but, always devoted to uncleanness, are [Col. 0950B] smeared with the mud of vices. [Note: [Col. 0950C] Thus Philastrius, ch. 73, speaking of the Borborians: “These men, going into the mud and then forgetting themselves there, distort their faces and limbs with mud.” Claudianus Mamertus, *On the Status of the Soul*, II.10: “Why do you stain Christ’s bride with the mud of falsehood?” Cicero likewise, *Against Verres*, III: “Everything was stained with the utmost disgrace and shame, as well as with extraordinary folly and inhumanity.” And *Against Verres*, V: “I do not want them, judges, to be so marked in this city that they seem to have been smeared not with wax but with mud.”]

God therefore wisely commanded either abstinence from gluttony or restraint from unclean actions; for “the Law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. VII). [Note: [Col. 0950D] The printed editions incorrectly read: “the divine commands seem salutary”; but the manuscripts agree on: “for the divine commands are salutary.”] The divine commands are indeed salutary, for “the human being who does them will live by them” (Deut. IV, 1).

But suppose that there is no harmfulness in swine’s flesh, and that it supplies no fuel for bodily temptations; [Note: [Col. 0950D] Thus the printed editions. The two Vatican manuscripts have “since all things are clean today”; the Florentine, “although all things are clean today”; Pantagathus’s book, “because all things are clean today.”] indeed, that today “all things are clean to the clean,” sanctified through the word of God and prayer (Tit. I, 15; I Tim. IV, 5). Nevertheless, the power and authority of God who gave that command must be considered: [Note: [Col. 0950D] Gaudentius also uses *tunc temporis* (“at that time”) above, Treatise 11, p. 303: “These names were customary among the Jewish people at that time concerning Christ”; and Treatise 6, p. 260: “In us were fulfilled the things that at that time were occurring figuratively”; perhaps elsewhere as well. Philastrius frequently uses the same expression: p. 117, “when necessity pressed at that time”; p. 121, “in the city of Salem, so called at that time”; p. 77, “the Apostles and believing Gentiles who at that time believed in Christ the Lord and Savior.” Although this manner of speaking may have seemed barbarous to someone, it is nevertheless also found in Justin, Book I, ch. 4: “From the obscure nation of the Persians at that time.”] he had ordered this to be observed at that time.

No one can examine the commanding Lord without penalty for his sacrilege, or despise him with impunity. For there could have been no evil in that tree which the good Creator had planted among the other trees of Paradise; its fruit was so beautiful and sweet that it aroused desire in the eyes and offered an enticement to the palate. For it is written: “And the woman saw that the fruit of the tree was pleasing to look upon and sweet to eat; and she took it, ate it, and gave it to her husband” (Gen. III).

But if you perhaps say that not everything pleasing in appearance and sweet is also good, because there are some evil things that seem pleasing and sweet, I yield, I agree, I consent. For, as Scripture says, honey drips from the lips of the adulterous woman, who for a time [Note: [Col. 0951C] Thus the printed editions. The manuscripts instead read: “she fattens your throat, but at the end…”] fattens her throat; but at the end you will find her more bitter than gall and sharper than a two-edged sword [Col. 0951B] (Prov. V).

Certainly there is nothing evil either in the appearance or in the sex of a woman; but evil is indeed found in the will of the sinner, who through the intemperance of desire transgresses the lawful right of marriage. Likewise, although the nature of wine is good, drunkenness is rightly condemned.

Hear now the divine Scripture’s general judgment concerning all created things: “And God saw everything that he had made, [Note: [Col. 0951C] The Lyons edition reads: “and they were very good.”] and behold, it was very good” (Gen. I). Yet because the reason of truth required it, [Note: [Col. 0951D] We thought this passage should be emended in this way. Two editions read: “and human servile condition had received the law of the ruling God.” Lyons has: “the law of the condemning God”; the Florentine: “that human servile condition might receive the law of the condemning God.” Three other manuscripts have: “and human servile condition might receive the law of the ruling God,” followed incorrectly by “with freedom of its own will granted.” We read instead, “with freedom of its own will granted,” a reading willingly retained from the editions. Pantagathus’s book has: “so that human servile condition might receive the law of the ruling God, with freedom of its own will granted.” The scribal error of writing *libertate* for *libertati* is easy to explain.] so that human servile condition might receive the law of the ruling God, while freedom of its own will was granted, God chose one tree from all the trees of Paradise—not an evil one, certainly, but one in which the knowledge of good and evil might appear; [Note: [Col. 0951D] The two Vatican manuscripts read: “but one in which there would be the knowledge of good and evil, namely, in which”; the same reading appears in Pantagathus’s book. The Urbinate has: “but one in which there would be knowledge of good and evil, namely, in which.” We have retained the reading of the editions.] in it he would test the obedience of his servants, so that the obedient might possess the reward of immortality, or the one who despised him might receive the sentence of unending death. [Note: [Col. 0951D] Reading of the Urbinate. All the other manuscripts and the printed editions have: “or the reward of immortal life”; Pantagathus’s manuscript: “or the reward of immortality.”]

The man ate because he wished to; he did not keep the command because he did not wish to; he is punished with death [Note: [Col. 0952C] Four manuscripts and Pantagathus’s book have: “because he was able to keep the command but did not strive to do so”; and shortly afterward: “and its fruit was good,” where the printed editions read: “and the fruit was indeed good.”] because he was able to keep the command but did not wish to. The tree was good, and its fruit was good; but the transgression of the command was evil, and contempt of God was evil. Thus evil is not in the fruit of the tree, [Note: [Col. 0952C] The Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts and Pantagathus’s book have: “but in the human being’s will”; and shortly afterward the same book reads “to bring about destruction,” where the printed editions and the two Vatican manuscripts have “to prepare destruction.”] but in the will of the transgressing human being.

Therefore, if the fruit of a single little tree, rashly tasted by our first parents contrary to God’s command, acquired death for the human race, the transgression of the divine command could also have brought destruction upon the Maccabees, who were then under the Law. Their observance of that command has now won them honor and glory, because they preserved the faith of God courageously and steadfastly in that very matter.

For the one who does not violate the laws of God’s command preserves faith in God. They did not refuse to eat what was forbidden because they were horrified by its appearance; rather, they most justly feared insulting God who had forbidden it. “The one who is faithful in a very little,” says the Lord, “is faithful also in much” (Luke XVI).

These men were faithful in much [Note: [Col. 0952D] Four manuscripts read in the same way: “if they rejected sacrificial meats amid tortures.” This seems the more suitable reading, corresponding to what follows: “forbidden meats.” He compares what was forbidden with sacrificial meat and infers that eating sacrificial meat was the more serious matter. See above in the notes on Treatise 9, p. 283. Pantagathus’s manuscript has: “if they rejected sacrificial meats”; then: “and they were faithful in little if they merely refused to eat meats that were forbidden,” a reading also found in the other four manuscripts.] when they rejected meat sacrificed to idols amid their tortures; they were faithful in little when, merely in order not to eat forbidden meat, they handed over their own bodies to be devoured by punishments. The more remarkable faith is that which is not violated even in small matters.

These most blessed brothers provided a model of endurance for future martyrs after Christ’s Passion, so that they might understand [Note: [Col. 0952D] Four manuscripts have “with what effort” instead of “for the Redeemer,” as does Pantagathus’s book.] with what greatness of spirit and steadfastness they ought to fight for the name of the Redeemer, for whose command they themselves had contended so stubbornly. [Note: [Col. 0952D] Thus four manuscripts and Pantagathus’s book. The printed editions instead have: “had contended so stubbornly.”]

Let no one think it absurd that shortly before I compared them with the Anicii. [Note: [Col. 0952D] In Greek, *Ἀνίκητος* means “unconquered,” from *α-* and *νικάω*, “I conquer, I overcome.” Hesiod, *Theogony* 489: *ἀνίκητος καὶ ἀκηδής*, “unconquered and carefree.” An ancient inscription in Reinesius, class I, no. 49: *ΗΛΙΩ ΑΝΙΚΗΤΩ ΕΥΧΗΝ*, “A vow to the Unconquered Sun.”] For in Greek speech we call the Anicii “the unconquered.”

The cruelty of the most savage tyrants inflicted various kinds of punishment upon their bodies. When the crafty persecutor had been unable to overcome the steadfastness of their faith in six brothers [Note: [Col. 0952D] The two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine have “by the cruelty of the tortures”; Pantagathus’s manuscript has the same. A little above, that book reads “the tyrant’s savagery” instead of “the ferocity of the tyrant.” We have not thought it necessary to alter the text in either place, although “the tyrant’s savagery” also occurs in the Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts.] by the cruelty of punishment, he turned, in the case of the seventh, because he was younger, from torments to enticements [Col. 0953A]. He tortured the boy with promises of riches and offers of honors, yet he could not turn him aside.
