For he was the brother of his brothers and the son of that mother who, while gladly seeing and urging each of her sons to be punished for God’s name, endured as many martyrdoms as she consecrated children: [Note: [Col. 0953C] The well-known saying of Gregory the Great concerning blessed Felicity is relevant: “She came first to the punishment, but arrived eighth.” The Lyons and Cologne editions incorrectly read “having suffered seven times in her own womb”; but Paris and the manuscripts read “having suffered.”] having suffered seven times in her own womb, she herself approached the number as the eighth, so that on the eighth day of Christ’s resurrection she might meet her beloved children.

Hence it is not without reason inferred that this most blessed mother foreshadowed the image of the holy Church, [Note: [Col. 0953C] Thus the Paris edition and four manuscript codices. Two other editions have “demonstrated”; Pantagathus’s book likewise prefers “foreshadowed.”] which is accustomed to bear spiritual children for God, thinking nothing of flesh and blood.

But if anyone now demands from me the remnants of my earlier discussion, asking why those foods which had been forbidden in the Law for the sake of continence are not also now prohibited for the same reason, I shall answer briefly, as I understand it. I believe that the many observances of the legal precepts were removed from the midst in such a way that the general precepts would remain in their former condition.

We said that, for the sake of preserving chastity, the Jewish people had been commanded to abstain from pork, from similar four-footed animals, and also from certain birds and fish [Note: [Col. 0953C] Three editions read incorrectly “forbidden.” The two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate have “commanded,” which is also the word found in Pantagathus’s book.], while the types of rational figures remained attached—figures which the spiritual teacher ought to explain individually in their respective places.

But since earthly minds seemed to be burdened rather than instructed by the complexity of many commands, divine providence, tireless also in this respect toward the human race, promises through the prophet Isaiah: [Col. 0953C] “For the Lord,” he says, “will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Isa. X, 23).

And therefore blessed James, together with the other Apostles, established this decree to be observed in the Churches: “That you abstain,” he says, [Col. 0954A] “from things sacrificed,” [Note: [Col. 0953D] We supply the words “and from fornication” from four manuscripts, in which they had previously been absent from the printed editions. Their necessity is clearly demonstrated both by the agreement of the Vulgate and by the following context of Gaudentius’s sermon. Pantagathus’s book also supplies them.] “and from fornication, and from blood” (Acts XV), [Note: [Col. 0953D] Gaudentius’s reading, in which he interprets “from blood” as equivalent to “from things strangled,” is strongly illuminated by a passage of Ambrose, *Epistle to the Galatians*, ch. II: “The Greek sophists, who did not understand these three commands, although they knew that one must abstain from blood, adulterated Scripture by adding a fourth command, ‘and from what is strangled.’ I think they will now understand by God’s will, because what they added had already been stated above.” Compare Irenaeus, Book III, *Against Heresies*, ch. 12, Feuardent’s edition, p. 188.] that is, from things strangled.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] The old reading, badly corrupted, has: “except miserable homicide”; but the error is self-evident, and we have deleted it, relying also on the manuscripts. Gaudentius, however, openly disagrees with those who maintained, as Augustine testifies (*Against Faustus*, Book XXXII, ch. 13), that the apostolic decree to abstain from blood should be understood as referring to homicide and killing; for he says that the Apostles omitted homicide. What he understood by the words “from blood, that is, from things strangled,” he immediately makes clear by adding: “lest we be polluted by the blood that has died within the entrails of strangled animals.” This makes me wonder how Macrius, in the *Hierolexicon*, could assert that here Gaudentius takes *suffocato* (“what is strangled”) to mean the shedding of blood.] They omitted homicide, [p. 331] adultery, and magic, because it would not be appropriate for things punished even by the laws of the Gentiles to be named in the Churches. They also omitted all those minute details of legal observances and sanctioned only the matters mentioned above, which were to be kept: lest we be polluted either by foods sacrificed to the devil and thus made profane, or by the blood of dead animals remaining in the entrails of strangled creatures, or lest we violate through the impurities of fornication our bodies, which are temples of God.

Thus they permitted everything to be eaten while commanding that fornication be avoided. It must now be a matter of our restraint [Note: [Col. 0954D] The two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine have “to loosen the reins of license only to this extent”; shortly afterward, where the editions have “but so that chastity,” they read “but insofar as chastity.” Pantagathus’s manuscript gives the whole passage as follows: “It must now be ours to loosen the reins of license with greater moderation only to the extent that we are not carried headlong into luxury, but insofar as chastity can remain safe.” The Urbinate agrees.] to loosen the reins of license only so far that we are not carried headlong into luxury, but [Col. 0954B] so that chastity may remain safe. Blessed Paul, knowing that it could not be preserved without restraint upon the appetite, says: “All things indeed are clean, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; but it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense” (Rom. XIV, 20); [Note: [Col. 0954D] These words are absent from four manuscripts; I therefore readily suspect that they were a gloss added by scribes. They are also absent from Pantagathus’s book.] that is, who suffers offense when he eats.

He immediately added this salutary counsel: “It is good,” he says, “not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended, or scandalized, or weakened” (Rom. XIV, 21). Who is a closer brother than our outward human being? So that our license may cause him neither offense, weakness, nor scandal, we must use the license of foods, not abuse it, so that we may know [Note: [Col. 0954D] The Florentine manuscript reads: “that we were not born for the sake of eating, but for the sake of living”; Pantagathus’s book also favors this reading. The editions have: “that we were not born for the sake of eating, but for living.” One of the Vatican manuscripts, which we have preferred here to the others, reads: “that we were not born for the sake of eating, but for living well.” The word *bene* (“well”) was carelessly omitted by scribes, nearly making Gaudentius agree with the school of Epicurus; it therefore had to be restored to the text.] that we were not born for the sake of eating, but for living well.

Therefore, the condition of the flesh must obey the command of the soul, lest unrestrained license, as Solomon says (Prov. XXX), cause the servant to rule, the fool to be filled, and the maidservant to drive out her mistress, when the Law commands: “Cast out the maidservant and her son, for the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI).

Let us therefore cast out the maidservant, desire, and her son, sin, so that we may become heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. He, carrying the wood of his cross upon his own shoulders (John XIX, 17), thereby fulfilling in the reality of the assumed human being the image of the Passion that he had foreshadowed under the shadow of the Law in holy Isaac (Gen. XXII, 6), redeemed our life with his precious blood from the destruction of eternal death. For he himself is our redemption. To him be all honor, power, and glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0955B] This sermon was delivered by Gaudentius before Ambrose, bishop of Milan, as is evident below.]

## SERMON XVI. THE SIXTH SERMON ON VARIOUS TOPICS

[Note: [Col. 0955B] Ferrarius correctly observed, *On the Rites of the Holy Church*, Book III, concerning Councils, ch. 12, that sermons were sometimes delivered by the ancient Fathers not only on the very first anniversary of a bishop’s ordination, but also when that anniversary recurred. He proves this clearly with examples drawn from Augustine and Leo the Great.]

On the occasion when, on the first day of his ordination, certain citizens’ notaries recorded the holy Bishop. [Note: [Col. 0955C] Concerning the *exceptores* (“recording clerks”), see what we stated above in the Preface at the words “with notaries secretly appointed,” p. 220.]

[Col. 0955B]

Conscious of my ignorance, and deterred by the shame of my own immature age from undertaking the dignity of the priesthood, I was rightly asking the highest priests for permission to remain silent. [Note: [Col. 0955C] The discipline of those times generally required that bishops be appointed only when they had already reached mature and advanced age; Siricius, in his Decretal Letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 9, set that age at forty-five years. Nevertheless, there are many examples of eminent men who, having received dispensation from the age requirement, were promoted to the episcopate while still young; this was granted to their virtue, so that they might be exempted from the laws. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book VI, chapter 30, speaking of Gregory Thaumaturgus and Athenodorus, translated by Henri Valois, says: “Accordingly, they made such great progress in divine utterances that, while both were still very young, they were appointed bishops of the churches in Pontus.” I pass over John Chrysostom, Epiphanius of Ticinum, and Remigius. [Col. 0955D] The present treatise offers us a striking example of Gaudentius’ modesty.]

For I fear, first, that the power of heavenly words may be weakened by the speech of my smallness. [Note: [Col. 0955D] Inferior editions read incorrectly, “lest the way of heavenly words”; but four manuscripts read, “lest the power of heavenly words,” a reading that also appears in the codex of Octavius Pantagathus.] Then I am ashamed that I cannot provide the desired fruit of instruction to so great an expectation. Therefore, since I feel myself altogether unequal to your desire, [Col. 0956A] I have tried with all my strength to avoid this burden. But blessed Father Ambrose and the other [333] venerable bishops, bound by the oath with which you rashly pledged yourselves, sent me such letters together with your embassy that I could no longer resist without injury to my soul; and saving communion, too, would have been denied me by the Eastern bishops unless I promised to return to you.

Thus, constrained by such a predicament and subjected to the authority of the holy men present, I undertook this office of the high priesthood, though not worthy of it by merit, [Note: [Col. 0956C] In a similar way, when Remigius was elected to the church of Rheims at no more than twenty-two years of age, he pleaded his age as an objection, as Flodoard relates, History of Rheims, book I, chapter 11: “Accordingly, when the most holy young man was oppressed by these difficulties, since no avenue of escape was open to him anywhere and he could in no way satisfy the people by persuading them to abandon the course they had begun, he began to complain publicly about the weakness of his age, proclaiming that ecclesiastical regulation did not admit that age to so great a dignity.” And Ennodius, in his Life of Epiphanius, says that Epiphanius, ordained bishop in his twenty-eighth year, addressed the priests and ministers as follows: “Although, dearest brothers, at the beginning, when I was stumbling in immaturity, the burden of your judgment and of the dignity I had undertaken weighed me down.” But the people passed over such complaints with deaf ears. Hence, a little earlier, the same Ennodius reports the opinion of Rusticus, a most distinguished man, concerning Epiphanius’ age, in these words: “We know, and have perceived through profound reflection, that this young man ought not to be judged immature because of his age; nor should tender years be presented as some obstacle to men of weighty counsel.” In four manuscripts the reading is, “nor suited by age,” as also in the book of Pantagathus.]

nor suited by age, nor mature in learning. Consider, then, what I suffer: although I do not know how to speak, I cannot remain silent. For I am compelled to obey the command of my elders beyond my powers, having neither the freedom to keep silent [Note: [Col. 0956D] We have judged that this should be restored from four manuscripts, since it accords better with “although I do not know how to speak.” The printed editions had “nor confidence to speak forth”; the codex of Pantagathus, “nor eloquence to speak forth.”] nor [Col. 0956B] the eloquence to speak forth.

But perceiving, by the authority of divine Law, that the commands of spiritual fathers are salutary, I dare to break into speech and bring a slight discourse to your ears. Perhaps you receive it patiently for this reason: because it may seem useful to the people of Christ to learn, from the example of the preacher, obedience, which is preferred even to sacrifice and placed before all the commandments of God (1 Samuel XV).

For when the Hebrew people, after those wonders in Egypt, were being called to the knowledge of the one God, they first learned obedience, [Col. 0957A] as the guide to keeping the heavenly commandments. Thus Scripture testifies: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy VI). And again: “Hear, O Israel, the commandments of life” (Deuteronomy IV).

The word “Hear,” as I think, does not signify merely the act of hearing, but proclaims obedience for the observance of the Law, as the Lord again bears witness when he says: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah I). But if, according to the judgment of the blessed apostle Paul, “not the hearers but the doers of the Law will be justified before God” (Romans II), then this hearing will no longer appear superficial, since it is honored with the rewards of the good things of the land—not of just any land, but of that once promised, that land flowing with milk and honey.

For the land of the promise is the flesh of Christ, taken from the mass of the human race formed from the earth and overflowing with the sweet juices of divine grace. We are nourished and fed by the purest milk of his teaching; by [334] the sweetness of his heavenly gifts we are refreshed; by his abundance the hearts of believers grow rich; and by his good things the minds of the obedient and the souls of the faithful are fattened, both in this age and in the age to come. [Note: [Col. 0957C] So the editions. Two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine manuscript, and the codex of Pantagathus read, “by the heavenly sweetness of gifts.”] [Note: [Col. 0957C] Two editions, namely Cologne and Lyons, incorrectly read *signantur* (“are marked”); but the Florentine manuscript, together with the book of Pantagathus and other manuscripts, reads *saginantur* (“are fattened”).]

To what, then, does this discourse relate? Surely to this: that your affection may clearly understand how great a force compelled my littleness to obey difficult commands and to open my mouth in the presence of so many priests—and especially after that most learned voice of my venerable father Philastrius, [Note: [Col. 0957C] Philastrius, the glory of the church of Brescia and Gaudentius’ predecessor, concerning whom we said above in the Preface to Benivolus: “You were imbued with the admirable teachings of our father Philastrius, in every respect an apostolic man.” More about him below, in the sermon on the Life of Philastrius.] which, pouring forth abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit, founded this church in faith in the Trinity to be worshiped, established it in true hope and perfect charity, raised it to the virtues, and left it in peace. [Note: [Col. 0957C] So read the two Vatican manuscripts and the book of Pantagathus. The Paris edition reads, “which flowed abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit”; the Cologne and Lyons editions, “because it flowed abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit.”]

Let this brief statement suffice as an excuse for the boldness that might have been censured in me. [Note: [Col. 0957C] The manuscripts read: “Now, since the well of the sacred readings is deep”; then, “I shall beseech our common father Ambrose.” This reading also occurs in the codex of Octavius Pantagathus.] But now the well of sacred readings is deep (John IV, 11), and since I have no vessel for drawing up the word, I cannot meanwhile supply living water to you who thirst. I beseech our common father Ambrose, after the slight drizzle of my discourse, to water your hearts himself with the mysteries of the divine Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0957D] It may perhaps seem strange that Ambrose, being present at the sermon, should be praised by Gaudentius. It is therefore worthwhile to hear a passage from Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 28, “On His Father’s Funeral,” in which he addresses Basil, who was present, in these words, translated by Jacques de Billy: “Man of God, faithful servant, and steward of the mysteries of God, and man of spiritual desires—for Scripture calls by this name men who are sublime and exalted, placed above the things visible to the eyes.” And in Oration 16, “On the Election of Eulalius as Bishop of Doara,” turning to him, he says: “But now, best and most perfect of shepherds, be present and receive your people with us and before us: the people whom the Holy Spirit has entrusted to you, whom the angels offer, and whom your life and conduct have committed to you.” [Col. 0958D] The first discourse of Ennodius, delivered on the anniversary of the episcopal see of Laurentius, bishop of Milan, is also excellent; in it he heaps the highest praises upon him while he is present. Ferrarius collects similar examples in book II, chapter 6, of *On the Rites of the Sacred Church Councils*.]

For he will speak by the Holy Spirit, with whom he is filled, and rivers of living water will flow from his belly; and, as the successor of the apostle Peter, he himself will be the mouth of all the priests standing around.

For when the Lord Jesus asked the apostles, “But whom do you [335] say that I am?” (Matthew XVI), Peter alone answered on behalf of all believers: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” What gift did this confession immediately receive? Clearly, blessedness and the most glorious authority of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, when Peter alone speaks, the faith of the other believers is by no means excluded. Rather, the proper order is maintained, since the first place in speaking is rightly granted to the chief of the Apostles; [Note: [Col. 0958D] So read the editions; but in three manuscripts—the Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts—the reading is, “lest it seem more like some disorder.”] otherwise it would have seemed more like a tumult than an answer if all had answered then together and competitively.

Someone might say that, just as those three faithful young men in the furnace (Daniel III), so all the Apostles ought in this examination to have professed the same thing with one harmonious voice. But it must be considered that Judas Iscariot, because he had not believed in his heart, could not confess with his mouth; and, being unbelieving, he neither deserved blessedness nor, before the perpetration of his dreadful crime, could he be condemned by the sentence of the just Judge. [Col. 0958C] [Note: [Col. 0958D] So read the same three manuscripts. The editions read, “to be condemned beforehand by sentences”; but in the three manuscripts mentioned above, the book of Octavius Pantagathus agrees with them both here and in the preceding reading.]

After Judas had already been condemned for his crime, all the Apostles, with Christ risen, receive the keys in Peter; indeed, together with Peter they receive from the Lord himself the keys of the heavenly kingdom, when he says to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John XX, 22). And again he says: “Go, teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII).

For the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened only by this key of the spiritual sacraments. Let all these apostolic priests now pray for the mercy of God the Father, who raised the needy from the earth and lifted the poor from the dung heap, to make him sit with the princes of his people (Psalm CXII); and may he deign to grant me, the least of all, the power of the Holy Spirit for holding the helm of his Church, [Note: [Col. 0959C] Four manuscripts read, “with the princes, that is, with these princes of his people”; Gaudentius may have said this to indicate the bishops standing around him.] [Note: [Col. 0959C] The two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbinate read, “to hold the helm.” The Florentine manuscript reads, “to hold,” as do three editions.] through his only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, with whom God always lives and reigns, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, before all ages, and now, and forever, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. THE SEVENTH ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

[Note: [Col. 0959C] This is not entitled in the codex of Galeardus as the other titles are. It instead reads: “Here begins his treatise delivered on the day of the dedication of the Basilica of the Council of the Saints,” and adds the following note. The most distinguished man Charles Majellus, prefect of the Vatican Library, to whose assistance this edition of ours owes very much, courteously pointed out that this is the genuine reading of the title, found in the Vatican and Urbinate manuscripts; it should therefore be preferred to the printed reading, which has “On the day of the dedication of the Basilica of the Forty Holy Martyrs.” [Col. 0959D] I willingly and readily followed the judgment of that most learned man, all the more willingly because I found the same reading, “Basilica of the Council of the Saints,” confirmed by the Florentine manuscript; and that this is altogether the true and legitimate title of the sermon is shown by Gaudentius himself in this treatise, near the end: “We decree that this very basilica, dedicated to their merits, ought to be called the Council of the Saints.”]

On the day of the dedication of the Basilica of the Council of the Saints.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] “Councils of the Saints,” or “Councils of the Martyrs,” were the names given to places where the bodies of many martyrs rested, as Baronius reports from Molanus in his note on the Martyrology for June 23, where he cites this treatise of Gaudentius. But our fellow citizen Octavius Rubeus made a disgraceful error in his Life of Saints Faustinus and Jovita, p. 65, when he thought that the Church of the Council of the Saints was so called because assemblies of the faithful were held there. If he had read this treatise of Gaudentius, he could by no means have been ignorant of the origin of the name. [Col. 0960B] This Basilica of the Council of the Saints, about which Gaudentius speaks in the present treatise, no longer exists in Brescia; or, if some other church has arisen in its place, it does not retain the name. In a manuscript catalogue of the bishops of Brescia, though it is not particularly ancient, I read the following: “Gaudentius, who lies in the church of St. John outside Brescia.” This church appears to be the same one that was also called the Basilica, or Church, of the Council of the Saints, founded and built by Gaudentius, as the treatise delivered by him on the day of its dedication testifies. A little later, under Theophilus, it says: “Theophilus, who lies at the Council of the Saints, that is, in the church of St. John outside Brescia, in the chapel of the Capreoli.” But Florentinius, in his *Chronological Catalogue of the Bishops of Brescia*, printed at Brescia in 1614, says under Theophilus: “The most ancient lists of the holy pontiffs record that his bones, now preserved in St. John the Evangelist, lay in the church called the Council of the Saints, whose memory we lament has been extinguished.” I develop these matters more fully in my annotations to the Brescia Martyrology, which, God willing, will one day be published.]

336 Our weakness, dearest brothers, is wholly unable to render thanks worthy of the divine gifts and heavenly benefits [Col. 0960A]. For God granted that we should possess the venerable relics of the saints; then he himself bestowed the ability to found this basilica in their honor; and today he has permitted us, having obtained the presence of the chief priests, to be worthy to celebrate its dedication. For holy bishops and apostolic men have assembled to pay the blessed fathers and their teachers the homage of devotion that is their due, so that we might be enriched by the fullest abundance of spiritual blessings; although the troublesome presence of the barbarians has taken away the greater part of the solemnity of this day, [Note: [Col. 0960C] Gaudentius perhaps indicates an incursion of the barbarians, either still impending or already carried out, concerning which see above, Tractate 13, p. 317: “Thus God will hear us when we entreat him; thus, amid the dangers of the barbarians that threaten, we shall deserve to be protected by divine aid.” See what we noted there.] preventing the other holy bishops whom we believed would attend from arriving. Now I shall begin to enumerate these men whose blessed relics make us illustrious.

First is John the Baptist [Col. 0960B], indeed the last but the greatest of the prophets: last in time, because “all the Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. 11:13); [Note: [Col. 0960D] Three manuscripts read “but deservedly first, but superior in dignity”; and shortly afterward, “you went out into the desert.” The manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus also supports both readings.] but deservedly first and preeminent in dignity, because Christ speaks of him thus to the Jews: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way’” [Note: [Col. 0960D] We supplied the words “before your face” from the manuscripts, since they were lacking in the printed editions; they are also found in the book of Pantagathus.] [Col. 0961A] (ibid., 8). By a single testimony of the Savior, the most blessed John the Baptist is declared to be both an angel, an apostle, and an outstanding prophet. Truly he is God’s angel, for he is Christ’s forerunner and messenger; truly he is an apostle, for he was sent by God and is called one who was commissioned as an apostle. “There was,” it says, “a man sent by God, whose name was John” (John 1:6). He is therefore called a holy prophet, and more than a prophet, because he deserved to point out with his finger the Christ foretold by his own voice and by that of all the prophets, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid., 29).

After him we have the most blessed Andrew, first a disciple of John himself and then of the Savior; Christ is recorded to have chosen him as his first apostle. “Andrew,” it says, “the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard John say, ‘Behold the Lamb of God,’ and had followed him. He first found his brother Simon and said to him: ‘We have found the Messiah’ (which is translated Christ). And he brought him to Jesus” (ibid., 40).

Third is the blessed Thomas, who after Christ’s resurrection alone desired, and alone obtained, the opportunity to touch Christ’s limbs with hands that were indeed inquisitive, but certainly worthy. That was the expression of ardent desire, not unbelief, when he said to his fellow disciples, who had seen the Lord while he was absent: “Unless I see and touch him, I will not believe” (John 20:25). He was deeply anxious lest he should not enjoy with his eyes what he believed in his heart, lest he be deprived of the sight of that light in which the other apostles gloried in having been illuminated. [Note: [Col. 0961C] The reading of the Florentine manuscript and both Vatican manuscripts, which the following words show to be better and more suitable, is: “The Lord therefore satisfied the hungry man.” Three editions have “the Lord therefore satisfied him,” in corrupt form. The manuscript of Pantagathus has “the Lord satisfied the hungry man.”]

The Lord satisfied the hungry man, whose promise remains: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). He appeared to the apostles a second time (John 20:26) to fulfill Thomas’s desire. His longing benefited the others as well; nor does he himself have anything less than the others because he saw Christ later. For he compensates for the disadvantage of having seen him later by sight as well as by touch. If he had been faithless, as some suppose, Christ would not have deigned to appear to him after his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0961C] Barthius, Adversaria XXII, chapter 6, lists this passage of Gaudentius among expressions that are neither grammatically nor correctly spoken in Latin, adding that it ought to have said “had not been.” He then gives a similar passage from Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne: “It could have ended sooner, if the treachery of the Saxons had allowed,” where it should be “if it had allowed”; and from Fulgentius, Letter 1, chapter 1: “The excessive violence of fever would take away my means of living, unless the true physician of souls and body deigned to grant a remedy,” where it should be “unless he had deigned.” This is Barthius’s argument. I certainly praise the learning of so great a man; but since the three editions available to me clearly read “had not been,” Barthius must have used some other, more ancient edition. In the manuscripts one finds “had not been,” for so one of the Vatican manuscripts reads; another has “would not have been.” The Florentine and Urbino manuscripts likewise have “had not been,” as does the book of Octavius Pantagathus. We have therefore preferred to retain the genuine simplicity of the manuscripts rather than the inept corrections of the printers, especially since, apart from the passages cited by Barthius, this sort of expression is not uncommon among ecclesiastical writers. Thus Augustine, Confessions X.10, at the end, has “unless, when someone reminded me, they were dug out, I could not think of them,” for “unless they had been dug out, I could not have thought of them”; for he had said above, “I had learned, I recognized, I said,” as is clear to anyone reading the text. Likewise in Confessions X.18: “Unless I remembered it, I would not find it, because I would not recognize it,” for “unless I had remembered it, I would not have found it, and I would not have recognized it”; for he had earlier said, “I remember that I had sought and found it.” Similarly in Confessions II.2: “Or certainly I would have attended more carefully to the sound of your clouds while awake,” for “I would have attended”; and shortly afterward: “Then I would have listened more carefully to these voices,” for “I would have listened”; for he immediately adds: “But I, wretched man, grew inflamed and went astray.” By contrast, Fulgentius uses “would have deserved” for “might deserve” in his Sermon on Saint Stephen: “Stephen was able to overcome the savagery of the Jews, so that he might thus have deserved to triumph happily”; and shortly afterward: “so that he might have deserved to receive the crown,” while he held charity in place of weapons.] not having been willing to do so. For it is written: “He is found by those who do not tempt him, and he appears to those who have faith in him” (Wis. 1:2).

When the Savior said to him, “Do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John 20:27), [Note: [Col. 0962D] Four manuscripts read: “Do not be unbelieving, but faithful.”] and, “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (ibid., 29), he wished to instruct in him all who would believe afterward, so that our people—like Thomas, who was absent when Christ appeared to the apostles—might lend unquestioning faith to their report [Note: [Col. 0962D] The Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts have “unwavering faith.”] and not demand to see in the flesh the one whom they had learned from the apostles’ testimony to have risen after the suffering of the cross and to have been seen. For after he returned to heaven, being present in this world only through his powers, he ought not to appear bodily every day to each and all believers according to anyone’s wish.

Let it be enough for us that Saint Thomas’s curiosity satisfied the scruple of future doubt. His absence, and his more eager search to see and touch the Lord, were entirely arranged for our salvation, so that we might know more clearly the truth of the Lord’s resurrection. Blessed Thomas, although rightly reproved for his necessary curiosity, affirmed it when he said to him: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). [Note: [Col. 0962D] The four manuscripts read this way; the printed editions instead have: “The curiosity and doubt of Saint Thomas brought an end to future scrupulosity.” This is wrong, since Gaudentius acknowledges no doubt or unbelief in Thomas above; it would therefore be foolish to admit here what he rejected earlier.]

Fourth is Luke the evangelist, who, following the blessed apostles with equal merit, wrote both the book of the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles with remarkable discernment [Col. 0962A]. [Note: [Col. 0962D] We restored this passage, which was corrupt in the printed editions, with the help of four manuscripts; the book of Pantagathus agrees with them here and in the preceding reading. Three editions have “with imitative examination”; but no sane person would presume to imitate Luke writing the Acts of the Apostles, as I think, and the book of the Gospel. The Greek word is πράξεις (*praxeis*, “Acts”).]

At present we possess the blessed relics of these four men. They preached the kingdom of God and righteousness, and, killed by unbelievers and the wicked, are shown always to live in God through the power of their works [Col. 0962C–0963A].

John was killed in the city of Sebaste in the province of Palestine, Thomas among the Indians, [Note: [Col. 0963A] What is said here—that John was killed in the city of Sebaste—does not sufficiently agree with Josephus, who in Book XVIII, chapter 7, reports that he was taken to prison at Machaerus and killed there. Cellarius defends Josephus’s view in his dissertation on John the Baptist and in his dissertation on John the Baptist’s imprisonment and execution, against the distinguished Lightfoot on Matthew 14:10. He was indeed buried at Sebaste, or Samaria, a city of Judea, as Jerome suggests in his letter to Marcella; but that city and province obeyed Archelaus, not Herod. See Baronius, for A.D. 33, nos. 4 and 5. The Urbino manuscript reads “in the city of Sebastena.” For the place of John’s burial, see also Cellarius’s dissertation on John the Baptist’s imprisonment and execution, no. 15.]

and Andrew and Luke at Patras, a city of Achaea. [Note: [Col. 0963B] For material illustrating this passage of Gaudentius, here is what you will find in Mabillon’s Notes on the Calendar of the Church of Carthage, volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 415. Since the following occurs in that calendar—“The 13th day before the Ides of October: Saint Luke the Evangelist and martyr”—Mabillon adds this observation: “Two things here do not agree with the others, namely the day and the title ‘martyr’: for Luke is usually recorded on the 15th day before the Kalends of November, and the title ‘martyr’ is not generally attached to him. Nevertheless, this is suggested by Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 1 against Julian, and Paulinus and Gaudentius state it openly.” Nicephorus describes the manner of his martyrdom in Book II, chapter 43, where he says that Luke was hanged from an olive tree because there was no supply of dry wood from which a cross could be made. Gaudentius identifies the place as Patras, a city of Achaea, in Sermon 17, or the Tractate on the Dedication of the Basilica of the Forty Holy Martyrs. This is Mabillon’s account.] They are reported as having completed their course.

After these we have Gervasius, Protasius, and Nazarius, most blessed martyrs, who a few years ago deigned to reveal themselves to the holy priest Ambrose near the city of Milan. [Note: [Col. 0963C] I have sometimes wondered whether, from this passage of Gaudentius, in which he makes so distinguished a mention of the blood of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, anything might be added to the account of the miracle that Gregory of Tours relates in *The Glory of the Martyrs* I.47. During their translation, when a panel accidentally fell from the roof of the church and struck their heads after being exposed for the veneration of the faithful, a great quantity of blood flowed from them. “From this,” says Turonensis, “the blessed blood was collected, staining the linens, coverings, and ecclesiastical veils; it is said to have flowed in such abundance that linens capable of receiving it had to be found.” Their relics, collected in abundance from this, were carried throughout Italy and Gaul. Gaudentius’s passage might seem to refer to this blood, recently poured from the saints’ heads. Since their translation, under Ambrose’s direction, took place in 386, while Gaudentius’s sermon on the dedication of the basilica was delivered shortly after 397, as we shall say below, some of this blood could certainly have been conveyed to Gaudentius, having flowed from the saints’ heads in so remarkable a miracle. This conjecture was strengthened by the printed editions’ reading: “whose blood we possess, collected in gypsum,” followed shortly afterward by: “we also possess the blood that is a witness to their passion.” It consequently appeared that Gaudentius was speaking, in a sense, of two kinds of blood: first, blood collected in gypsum at the time of their martyrdom; and then again blood miraculously sprinkled during the translation upon linens and coverings. But after collating the manuscripts, we found that instead of “we also possess the blood,” the reading must absolutely be “for we possess the blood.” Thus it appears in all three manuscripts—the Florentine and the two Vatican manuscripts—and the book of Pantagathus also agrees. It is therefore clear that Gaudentius speaks of only one blood: that shed at the time of the saints’ passion and collected by the faithful in gypsum according to ancient custom. Nothing, then, is added by Gaudentius’s authority to Turonensis’s account. On the glass and earthen vessels in which the faithful used to collect the martyrs’ blood, see Aringhius, *Subterranean Rome* III.22.]

We possess their blood, collected in gypsum, and require nothing further; for we possess the blood that is a witness to their passion.

We have also received the holy ashes of Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander [Col. 0964A], [Note: [Col. 0964B] This is the reading of the two Vatican manuscripts. Three editions corruptly have “of the martyr Sisinnius and Alexander”; but the error was obvious even without the manuscripts. See what we said about these martyrs in the notes to Ughellus, volume IV, column 523 of the Venetian edition. They are mentioned in the Roman Martyrology and also in Usuardus on May 29.] whom, shortly before, a sacrilegious people in Anaunia, devoted with particular zeal to the worship of their venerable religion, killed and burned with flames, so that they might become a holocaust to God himself, who in the most righteous rebuke had forbidden them to offer his Christians as sacrifices to demons. [Note: [Col. 0964B] The printed editions read “whom recently at the altar of Agatinus,” by which expression ignorant copyists had thoroughly tormented Gaudentius’s readers; for who could ever guess what that altar was or where on earth it existed? We have therefore restored “in Anaunia,” since the Florentine, Urbino, and two Vatican manuscripts unanimously read “in Anaunia, devoted to the venerable one,” making the correction easy. These martyrs suffered in the valley of Anaunia, commonly called Val d’Anagna or Val di Non, in the diocese of Trent; hence some call them the Anaunian martyrs, and Augustine likewise calls them so in Letter 158 to Marcellinus the Count. The reading of the other manuscripts is also supported by the book of Pantagathus, which reads “in Anania,” omitting the fifth vowel, which conjecture easily supplied. It is clear from this passage that Gaudentius composed this Tractate shortly after the year 397, which was the year of these martyrs’ passion, as Rumartus confirms from the calculations of learned scholars in the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 683 of the Paris edition. For Gaudentius says, “whom recently in Anaunia”; it is therefore easy to infer a date from these words.]

Now what worthy account shall I give, after these ten, of the Forty Martyrs, who deigned to accompany me on my journey when I was traveling through the cities of Cappadocia toward Jerusalem? [Note: [Col. 0964C] On the pilgrimage to the East, which was once a major expression of piety and religion, you will find a notable passage of Jerome in his letter to Marcella, written in the name of Paula and Eustochium. It corrects Hornius, who in his Notes on Sulpicius Severus, p. 371 of the Amsterdam edition of 1665, says that before Constantine it was considered unusual for Alexander—as recorded in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.11, Valesius’s edition—to have gone to Jerusalem to worship and see the holy places. Jerome, on the contrary, expressly says: “It would take too long now to pass through every generation from the Lord’s Ascension to the present day, naming which bishops, which martyrs, and which men eloquent in ecclesiastical doctrine have come to Jerusalem.” Origen too, who flourished for nearly a whole century before Constantine, testifies in Book I against Celsus that in his own time the cave at Bethlehem was still famous among unbelievers because Jesus, who is worshiped by Christians, had been born there. Especially in the age of Gaudentius and Jerome, pilgrimage to Jerusalem had become widespread; hence Jerome says in his letter to Desiderius: “It is part of faith to worship where the Lord’s feet stood.” Consult Baronius’s note on the Martyrology for May 4, letter e, so that you may see more clearly how Hornius is blind in broad daylight. Bochartus records many more of Hornius’s errors in his observations on Sulpicius Severus, in his dissertation addressed to Isaac Vossius, found in volume I of his works, p. 1058.]

For in the very greatest city of Cappadocia, which is called Caesarea, where those most blessed men have a distinguished shrine [Note: [Col. 0965A] That is, a church, which in Greek fashion was called a *Martyrion* (μαρτύριον, “martyr-shrine”). Consult Baronius, Note on the Martyrology for July 6. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 8: “Clergy established in poorhouses, monasteries, or martyr-shrines shall be subject to the bishop of the city in which they are located.” Cyril likewise calls the church of the Resurrection at Jerusalem a *martyrion* in Catechetical Lecture 14. Compare Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* IV.46–47, and there the notes of Henry Valesius, as well as his letter on Anastasis and the Jerusalem Martyrion.] we found certain women devoted to God, most worthy mothers of a monastery of holy virgins, altogether like Mary and Martha, whom Jesus rightly loves—sisters in nature, faith, zeal, and integrity of chastity.

To these women the venerable relics of these martyrs had once been entrusted by their maternal uncle, the supreme priest and blessed confessor Basil [Col. 0965A]. [Note: [Col. 0965C] The Florentine and two Vatican manuscripts supplied this passage, which in the editions reads: “from their uncle, the priest and confessor Basil.” But Gaudentius also calls bishops “supreme priests” above. In the manuscript of Pantagathus, as in the others, the reading is: “from their uncle, the supreme priest and blessed confessor Basil.” On Basil’s nieces, see the distinguished Muratorius in his *Greek Anecdotes* on poem 130 of Gregory of Nazianzus, where he quotes this passage of Gaudentius.] They granted these relics to our desire readily and faithfully, proving that they considered us worthy custodians of so great a gift, while also confessing under the testimony of the Lord that they had always prayed to our God that so precious a possession might be transferred to heirs who would cultivate it with equal faith and diligence [Note: [Col. 0965D] Four manuscripts agree on this reading without variation, and the book of Pantagathus agrees with them. Three editions incorrectly have “who would imitate them with similar faith and diligence”; likewise, shortly below, we propose “to cultivate” for the manuscript reading “to examine carefully.” We have therefore corrected both passages.] and who would be both successors to and enlargers of their zeal and veneration [Col. 0965B], [Note: [Col. 0965D] This entire passage was missing, greatly damaging the sense of the place; we restored it from the Florentine, Urbino, and two Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and would daily await their migration from this world.” Incorrectly; the defect in the common reading is also supplied by the book of Pantagathus. This error of the copyists led the exceptionally learned Tillemont astray. Since he entirely failed to grasp the sense of this passage of Gaudentius, he interpreted it as though Basil’s nieces were seeking heirs of these relics who would become successors to and enlargers of the women’s zeal and veneration and would then learn—from these dead ashes of the martyrs—to await their own migration from this world every day. Thus, in volume X, p. 581 of the Paris edition: “Who would imitate, and even increase, the respect and veneration that they had for these martyrs, AND WHO WOULD LEARN FROM THESE DEAD AND LIVING ASHES to live each day in expectation of death.” This is entirely wrong, though the carelessness of the copyists cannot be attributed to the learned man.] since they themselves were advanced in years and daily awaited their own departure from this world.

Behold, their faithful prayer has been heard. Today we present the venerable relics of the Forty Martyrs to believing peoples, to be cultivated [Note: [Col. 0966C] The printed editions incorrectly have “to be examined carefully,” as indicated above; likewise, shortly afterward, where the editions read “for the purpose of establishing your love,” the manuscript of Pantagathus and the two Vatican manuscripts give “for the purpose of instructing you.”] although it is recognized that, from that earlier time onward, they have never lacked the solemnity properly due to them through our ministry, which has been devoted to their splendid benefits for our salvation.

But I shall now briefly recount in what order these most blessed men attained the glory of martyrdom, although I confess myself unequal to celebrating their praises. [Note: [Col. 0966C] There is an excellent homily of Basil the Great on the Forty Holy Martyrs, whose authority the Fathers of the Seventh General Council repeatedly used to refute the opponents of the holy images. Ruinartus rightly observed in the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 581, that the holy Fathers Gregory of Nyssa, Ephrem the Syrian, and our Gaudentius borrowed much from it.]

They plainly possess a herald worthy of their merits and most deserving of honor: Basil, a man of blessed memory, a confessor and bishop of the Church of Caesarea, whose extraordinary eloquence and discourse seasoned with apostolic salt blunt the poverty of my talent [Col. 0966A]. For what new thing can I contribute that he did not pour forth abundantly in praise of them, richly adorn, and expressly set forth through the wealth of his eloquence? It is indeed exceedingly difficult to praise the same virtues in different speeches.

Nevertheless, for the purpose of instructing your devotion, I shall attempt at least to repeat the history of their deeds. These men were soldiers stationed in the regions of Lesser Armenia, flourishing in age, tall and distinguished in body, commendable in their experience of warfare, and honored with military pay in proportion to the merit of their virtues; [Note: [Col. 0966D] Gregory of Tours likewise has this expression in *History of the Franks* II.2: “A certain girl, very wealthy in possessions and flourishing in senatorial nobility according to the dignity of the world—and, nobler than all these things, distinguished by the Catholic faith.” Salvianus too has in Letter 1: “Among the other virtues of chastity and wisdom, there is also nobility of faith, which is always an ornament to every adornment.” See Joannes Savaro’s Note on Sidonius Apollinaris, Book III, Letter 12, where he praises this passage of our Gaudentius.] and, surpassing all these qualities, they were Christians [Col. 0966B]; adorned with every moral excellence by the goodness of their venerable religion and equipped with the spiritual weapons of heavenly doctrine.

As soon as the trumpet of persecution sounded, love of faith girded Christ’s bravest soldiers for battle. For when the savage edicts of the sacrilegious king began to be proclaimed by the judge, commanding that no one, whether civilian or soldier, dare declare the Christian name, but that the whole people be compelled to sacrifice to demons [Note: [Col. 0966D] The three editions absurdly have “through other edicts,” but the two Vatican manuscripts have “when the savage edicts”; shortly afterward, one of them corruptly has “they began to propose and adjudicate,” while the manuscript of Pantagathus reads “when the savage edicts of the sacrilegious king began to be proclaimed by the judge.” The same manuscript also correctly has “to display” where the editions read “to utter the Christian name,” or, as the margin supplies, “to display before themselves.”], they voluntarily came forward, loudly declared that they were Christians, and stated that no terrors could separate them from this saving worship.

The terrifying persecutor, observing the young men’s steadfastness, laid aside his authority and addressed them with flattering words, urging them not to persist in this obstinacy, not to become insulting toward their emperor, not to despise his commands, and not, though otherwise most devoted, to provoke the king’s greatest displeasure by this action. For this particular obedience they ought rather to hope for benefits and honors from him. It was surely disgraceful for warrior men to perish by a most shameful death among the cowardly and guilty. They ought to consider the flower of their youth and the pleasantness of this light and life, which [Note: [Col. 0967C] Here too the two Vatican manuscripts provided assistance, since the printed editions incorrectly read “without regard for that reasoning.”] they were being foolishly persuaded to cast away without regard for any consideration.

When the Christian men—deservedly admirable—heard such words, they not only rejected the poisonous flatteries of the pernicious tempter with steadfast hearts, but also refuted them with an exceedingly forceful reply.

“What are you trying to do, you utterly wicked man?” they said. “Daring to rebel against God, do you attempt to trip up his servants with deceitful words? Why do you strive to bend us away from the worship of the true and living God toward the dead images of demons? Why do you attempt, through the perishable promises of earthly honors and the illusions of empty things, to corrupt our minds and draw them away from the strength of heavenly faith? We curse gifts that bring the loss of salvation; we reject honors that take away that everlasting glory; we repudiate the friendship of the king, which desires to separate us from the love of God; and we reject this temporal life of our bodies, which, if preserved at the cost of our faith, brings destruction upon the soul. Finally, we are not frightened even by present punishments.

“We surrender our flesh to whatever torments you wish to inflict, lest, by denying Christ God, we should be cast into the everlasting tortures prepared from the beginning for the devil and for you, his servants.”

Then that judge of iniquity, inflamed by such words, doubled the fury that shortly before he had wished to satisfy more subtly by devising a novel form of punishment [Col. 0967C]. [Note: [Col. 0967C] The four manuscripts read this way; the editions repeated the word. The book of Pantagathus also prefers “he intensified.” What follows, drawn from Basil, clearly shows that these holy martyrs were not submerged in water, as most have thought, but were exposed above the frozen ice of the pool itself in the severe winter, so that they might be killed by the cold. See Baronius’s Note on the Martyrology for March 9, and Ruinartus, *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 586. The extremity of the cold and the severity of those regions can be sufficiently gathered from what the Roman soldiers suffered while stationed in Armenia under Corbulo. Tacitus reports in Book XIII, chapter 35: “Many limbs were burned by the violence of the cold, and some died while on watch; a soldier who was carrying a bundle of wood was recorded to have frozen so severely that his hands, clinging to the load, dropped away with the truncated arms.” John Chrysostom likewise complains of the bitter cold of Armenia in Letters 4 and 6 to Olympias.]

For he observed that the nature of the region was stiffened by excessive cold [Col. 0968A] and that the season was one in which the harshest violence of winter pressed down with greatest force as the north wind blew. [Note: [Col. 0967D] Fronto Ducaeus used this passage of Gaudentius to defend the true reading of Basil’s Sermon on the Forty Martyrs, where, for τὴν φύσιν τῆς χώρας ὅτι κρυμώδης—“the nature of the region, because it was cold”—Volaterranus had translated “the nature of the region, rugged and steep with hills,” evidently having read κρημνώδης in some manuscript instead of κρυμώδης.] Mountains were covered with snow and fields with frost; liquids were forced by the sun’s fires to acknowledge their own nature; the courses of rushing rivers were numbed by immense ice. [Note: [Col. 0967D] Raphael Volaterranus, translator of Basil’s sermons, placed this pool outside the city. In his translation of the sermon on the Forty Martyrs he rendered its location as follows: “The holy men of God were therefore ordered to spend the night in the open air at a certain pool which was beside the walls of the city.” He made a slight but significant error in translating περὶ ἣν ἡ πόλις κατάκειται, “around which the city lies,” as “which was beside the walls of the city,” as Baronius long ago noted in his entry for March 9 in the Martyrology. Gaudentius more correctly said that the pool lay below the city, although he too does not fully convey Basil’s meaning, since Basil explicitly writes that the martyrs were tormented in the middle of the city and in the pool around which the city was settled: ἐν μέσῃ τῇ πόλει, “in the middle of the city.” Moreover, the passage cited by Baronius reads κατῴκισται in the better editions of Basil instead of κατάκειται, as follows: λίμνη μὲν περὶ ἣν ἣ πόλις κατῴκισται, “a pool around which the city had been founded.”]

The pool also, lying beneath the city in which these events took place, spread widely in every direction; while the strongest ice remained, it provided a solid road for groaning wagons.

Having considered the savagery of the place and season [Col. 0968D], the Gentile enforcer of sacrilege ordered this punishment to be imposed on the saints: their bodies were to be stripped and bound, and they were to spend the night in the frosty severity of the open air, while baths steamed at a distance within their sight. There the cunning persecutor promised a swift remedy to those who were overcome, eager thereby to destroy their souls even more. [Note: [Col. 0968D] The book of Pantagathus has the better reading: “Having therefore perceived either the violence of the place or of the season”; it likewise has “before their sight” shortly afterward, where the editions read “in their sight.”]

But the most blessed martyrs, burning with the Holy Spirit, cast their clothing far away and hastened eagerly to the arena, looking heavenward toward the crown prepared for so great a contest. Then, by mutual exhortations to endurance, they kindled their strength, placed the glory of the heavenly kingdom above their present sufferings, and repeated among other things:

“If, for the safety of an earthly king, we have scorned to fear hostile swords, why should we not, for the faith of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal King, endure with even temper every torment inflicted upon our bodies, so that we may pass more swiftly into the blessedness of eternal light and everlasting life through the short path of a glorious death?”

Amid the frosts, Faith burned, and their heavenly souls glowed with desire for Christ. The sharpness of excessive cold scorched the shining skin of their frozen bodies; but their devout minds, possessed by love of God, contemplated the delights of paradise. The cold pierced the innermost parts of their organs, so that an internal icy torturer pressed upon the marrow of their bones with the most grievous torments. [Note: [Col. 0968D] So reads one Vatican manuscript; the other has “icy terror,” a reading supported by the book of Pantagathus.] Yet the strength of their souls remained unmoved. Looking toward the goal of their course, it rejoiced in the approaching completion, awaiting with faithful endurance the promised gift of God [Col. 0969A].

But one of their number, unable to endure even the very brief remaining period of pain, which was already his final suffering, began miserably to ask that he be taken to the baths. [Note: [Col. 0969C] The three editions have “to the bath,” which we have corrected on the authority of both Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript, which read “to the baths”; the book of Pantagathus has the same reading. Varro denied that *balnea*, “baths,” was used in the plural; his words in Book VII of *On the Latin Language* are: “Custom does not form a plural from what they call *balneum*.” So also below, where the editions read “the unhappy man is led to the bath,” we have restored “to the baths,” following the same manuscripts; for a private bath was called *balneum*, while public baths were *balneae*, as Varro likewise testifies in Book VIII of *On the Latin Language*: “They are called by the plural name *publicae balineae*, not *balinea*, contrary to the way private people say one *balneum*, while they call several *balneas*.”]

Meanwhile, the soldier who had been charged with opening that bath of death to any who were overcome was watching from an elevated place with keen eyes, waiting to see how the contest of those remarkable men would end. He saw the commander of the heavenly army descending with a multitude of angels and distributing bright garments and rich rewards, one by one, to the bravest warriors. Only that wretched man, whose faith the devil had broken, did not receive them.

The unhappy man was led to the baths, where, as soon as the warmth he had believed would restore him breathed upon him, he was deprived of life and lost both life and crown.

A sorrowful deed was immediately followed by an unexpected cause for rejoicing. Suddenly the observer of the vision described above took his place; he stripped his limbs for the desired punishment and loudly and repeatedly declared himself to be a Christian. The power of that marvelous spectacle had suddenly made a true Christian out of one who had been a pagan. He was immediately seized as guilty of his profession; willingly he was bound and cruelly fastened with cutting bonds. He remained bound, gloried in his punishment, and was exalted by the hope of divine recompense. Amid the sufferings Christ’s faith grew; amid the torments love increased. For with apostolic conviction he declared: “No force of punishments, no enormity
...will be able to separate from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom. 8:9). In the midst of tortures the new martyr, instructed by the Holy Spirit, is taught and makes progress; he dies and triumphs. The adorable Trinity, with greater glory, both washes and purifies its witness, who faithfully perseveres amid the torments, through martyrdom itself in place of baptism, and brings him to the kingdoms of heaven.

Finally, this fortieth saint dies together with the saints, so that the sacred number might be completed—the number which the Savior had honored by fasting—as the blessed martyrs themselves are remembered to have prayed. After this, he ordered the executioners to burn the bodies of the dead, which had been carried some distance away, in the fire. They left one behind, who was thought still to be alive, in case the very isolation might somehow turn his will for the worse. Thereupon his venerable mother, who had nourished such a son on the good milk of heavenly wisdom, ran to the corpse of her breathing son and with her own hands placed him on the cart by which the bodies of the others were being dragged to the pyre.

“Go,” she said, “my son; go along this good road, safe with your companions of the same age, and glorious to the Lord.”

O admirable and truly worthy mother of a martyr! Indeed, she herself was already a martyr, for she did not spare her own entrails, while she rejoiced that her own limbs were being punished in her son for the name of Christ.

Nor will we be silent about what happened afterward: when the ashes of the burned bodies were being thrown into the river at the persecutor’s command, there were devout hands that either secretly stole away a portion of the ash [345] or purchased it at a price. Hence the Church of Caesarea rejoices, and our brotherhood rightly glories, recognizing that a saving gift has been reserved for it by God’s providence.

We have received a portion of the relics, and we are confident that we possess no less, while we embrace all forty, honoring them in their own ashes. Thus the faithful woman in the Gospel (Matt. 9; Luke 8), who was saved through Christ’s fringe, grasped the hem of his garment and drew forth the power of the Godhead: by the touch of the fringe, faith drew healing for the believer, and she obtained the salvation she had confidently sought.

Therefore the very portion that we have been privileged to receive is the fullness. For these forty martyrs cannot in any way be divided from one another, since their relics are inseparable and indivisible. Just as that fiery Spirit of God joined their souls together in the unity of saving faith—for “the whole company of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32)—so the fire that consumed their members reduced them to one body of ash.

Thus we possess both these forty and the ten saints mentioned earlier, gathered from different regions of the earth. Accordingly, we decree that this very basilica, dedicated through their merits, ought to be called the COUNCIL OF THE SAINTS. For it is fitting that, as we are about to approach the venerable relics of so many Martyrs, we should acknowledge that we are proceeding to the COUNCIL OF THE SAINTS.

Therefore, helped by the patronage of so many righteous persons, let us run as suppliants in their footsteps with complete faith and every desire, so that through their intercession we may deserve to obtain everything we ask, magnifying Christ the Lord, the giver of so great a gift; to him belong all honor, power, and glory, with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, before all things, now, and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Thus the two Vatican manuscripts and the Pantagathus manuscript, which also reads in the following sentence “this fortieth saint”; but the printed editions corruptly read “and washes, and corrects.”]

[Note: The Florence manuscript and the two Vatican manuscripts add the word “this,” which is absent from the printed editions; they read, “finally this fortieth saint dies together with the saints.”]

[Note: Who gave the order? Clearly, the unjust judge, by whose command Gaudentius also recalls that the other events he related above took place. Perhaps the text originally read *jussi carnifices* (“I ordered the executioners”), but the copyists’ negligence altered it; this appears in the Pantagathus manuscript, where the same hand has written *jussi* in the margin instead of *nisi*, which appears in the text.]

[Note: The printed editions do not have the Greek article *τὸ* (“the”); but it is found in three manuscripts and in the book of Octavius Pantagathus.]

[Note: Gaudentius says this in anticipation of the objection that could be raised concerning the holy relics being thrown away, as Baron rightly observed in his entry for March 9. But Baronius errs when he adds that Gaudentius asserts that the martyrs suffered this at Sebaste, a metropolitan city of Lesser Armenia. Although everyone agrees that the place of their martyrdom was that city, Gaudentius does not say so here.]

[Note: The Florence, Urbino, and two Vatican manuscripts read “a portion of the relics,” as also below, “a portion of the relics”; this reading is likewise supported by the Pantagathus manuscript. This passage of Gaudentius greatly illuminates the ancient custom among Christians of redeeming the bodies of holy martyrs at a price, a practice frequently mentioned in the Acts of the Martyrs.]

[Note: This distinguished passage of Gaudentius is cited by John Ferrandus, *Inquiry into Relics*, book I, chapter 4, article 2. On the basis of it and of testimonies from Gaudentius himself and other Fathers, he argues that this is how certain churches came to claim possession of an entire martyr’s body, when they in fact had only a very small portion of it deposited on altars, in memorials, or in reliquaries.]

[Note: Jerome, Letter to Marcellus: “Everywhere we venerate the tombs of the martyrs, and, placing the holy ash before our eyes, we touch it even with our mouths, if permitted.” Pliny, book XIX, chapter 1, speaks of asbestos linen: “From it the funeral tunics of kings separate the ash of the body from the remaining ash.” The Florence and two Vatican manuscripts read “venerating them in the holy ashes.” The Pantagathus manuscript reads “venerating them in their own ashes.”]

[Note: The printed editions are correct, although four manuscripts read “let us hasten to their footprints”; we judged that reading entirely unacceptable, even though it also appears in the book of Octavius Pantagathus.]

# SERMON XVIII. EIGHTH ON VARIOUS CHAPTERS

Or, the response of the holy Bishop to Serminius concerning the dishonest steward.

[Note: Since nearly all the titles of these treatises have been corrupted in the printed editions, in expressing this one also we preferred to follow the agreement of the manuscripts, in which the reading is *ad Serminium*, rather than retain the common reading *ad Germinium*. The Pantagathus manuscript reads *ad Herminium*, which is not displeasing and may perhaps be the true reading, although I have preferred the agreement of the other manuscripts. The Lyon edition, worse than the others, has the following disordered arrangement: “On the dishonest steward. Treatise XVIII. Response to Germinius.” Who this Serminius—or Herminius—was, whom Gaudentius calls learned in sacred and secular literature, I am entirely unable to say.]

To the servant of Christ, Serminius, Gaudentius, bishop.

[Note: On this parable of the steward, see Jerome in his letter to Algasius, Question 0; and, drawing on Jerome, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, Book III *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 108. Valla observes that in this passage of Luke 16 the word *dispensator*—“administrator”—is more appropriate than *villicus*—“steward.” For, according to Varro, a *villicus* is appointed for the purpose of cultivating the fields and takes his name from *villa*. From this Valla concludes that Jerome was certainly not the author of the New Testament Vulgate, since in his letter to Algasius he translates this passage differently, saying: “Give an account of your administration, for you will no longer be able to administer mine.” But the Vulgate has: “Give an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to act as steward.” On this matter see Martianay’s annotations on Jerome’s book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, volume II of the Benedictine edition, p. 529, as well as his fuller notes on the same book, p. 519.]

346 It is always fitting for a wise man to reflect on words of wisdom and to apply to their understanding every acuity of intellect and every vigor of mind. Therefore you, who are learned both in the writings of worldly wisdom and in the true wisdom of God, which you have learned through the sacred Scriptures, do not cease applying yourself to investigating the inward meanings of the words of Christ, whom, as the Apostle teaches, you know to be the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions corruptly read *quorum dispersionem*—“whose dispersion.”]

Among the other sayings of the divine Law, whose exposition you frequently demand, you specifically requested this as well: that I should explain in writing the very difficult parable of the dishonest steward, for which none of us seemed to you a sufficiently capable interpreter.

[Note: Thus the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbino manuscript. The printed editions instead have: “of which no one of you seems capable to you.” The Florentine manuscript likewise has “of which no one of us,” namely, among ecclesiastical interpreters. Tillemont, following the common reading “of which no one of you,” inferred that this Serminius had not been from the territory of Brescia and had found no sufficiently capable interpreter of the proposed question where he lived. This may also have been approved by Pantagathus, who wrote *vestrum*—“of you”—in the margin of his book, although *nostrum*—“of us”—occurred in the text.]

You perhaps wish the explanation itself to be committed to writing so that you may possess a written record of my response concerning the passage which, as you yourself admit, is most obscure.

[Note: In the Pantagathus manuscript, his own hand has written in the margin: “I would explain it in my own words; and I would commit the explanation itself to writing.” This perhaps agrees altogether better with the sense, if for *id eo* one reads *idque*, or even *idque ideo*; for what follows—“I will not fear either to speak when questioned or to write”—answers it very well.]

But I shall not fear either to say, when questioned, or even to write, according to the limited capacity of my understanding, what I think, provided that the integrity of the faith is preserved.

[Note: The manuscript and the editions alike read thus; but the Lyon edition has it incorrectly, although the faithful meaning is preserved.]

First, dearest brother, the words of the passage itself must be set forth, and only then should the meaning of the statements be opened.

The blessed Luke reports in his Gospel:

“The Lord Jesus was saying to his disciples a parable: ‘There was a certain rich man who had a steward; and he was reported to him as though he were wasting his possessions. And having summoned him, he said to him: “What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you will no longer be able to act as steward.”’

“‘But the steward said within himself: “What shall I do, because my lord is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”

“‘And calling each one of his lord’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my lord?” He replied:

[Note: The Florentine manuscript reads: “And he too was reported to him”; but the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbino manuscript read: “And he too was reported as though wasting his possessions.” The Pantagathus manuscript has: “And he too was reported to him as though wasting his possessions.”]

“‘“A hundred measures of oil.”

[Note: Thus the Paris and Cologne edition; but the Lyon edition and four manuscripts read “a hundred casks,” with which the Pantagathus manuscript agrees. A *bath* (Greek βάτος) is a kind of liquid measure among the Hebrews, containing a tenth part of a *cor*. Ezekiel 45: “A bath of oil is a tenth part of a cor; ten baths make a cor.” Latin translators generally render it *cadus*—“cask”; hence it was easy for copyists to substitute the common word for the more unusual and learned term. Perhaps it was a gloss placed in the margin which later crept into the text.]

And he said to him: “Take your written account and sit down quickly and write fifty.”

“‘Then he said to another: “And you, how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred kors of wheat.” And he said to him: “Take your written account and write eighty.”

“‘And the lord praised the dishonest steward because he had acted prudently; for the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light. And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

“‘He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much; and he who is unjust in what is least is unjust also in much. Therefore, if you have not been faithful in dishonest mammon, who will entrust to you what is true?

[Note: Three editions incorrectly read “what is yours”; but both Vatican manuscripts have “what is true,” and the Pantagathus manuscript likewise. The sentence cannot properly be read otherwise, even though the Florentine and Urbino manuscripts agree with the printed editions. Isidore Clarius of Brescia, bishop of Foligno, writes in his scholia on this passage: “From lesser deeds an inference is drawn concerning greater ones. Therefore, if you have not been faithful in administering riches, which are a kind of false thing, who will believe you concerning those things which are true—namely, the administration of the gifts of the Spirit? And if in these riches, which are a kind of property belonging to another, you are found unfaithful, how will you be fit to have entrusted to you the administration of those things which are properly yours—the gifts of the Spirit?”]

“‘And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?’

“‘No servant can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other; or he will endure the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon’” (Luke 16).

[Note: Thus the two Vatican manuscripts, the Florentine manuscript, and the Urbino manuscript; but instead of *oderit*—“will hate”—they read *odiet*, as does the Pantagathus manuscript. The Lyon edition has: “For either he will hate the one and love the other; or he will cling to the one”; and the Vulgate has the same form. The Paris and Cologne editions read: “For either he will hate the one and tolerate the other, or he will despise the other.” Three words, “and love the one,” have dropped out.]

It is the mark of a perfect teacher, for the instruction of disciples, to set before them likenesses drawn from things commonly encountered in human life, so that the hearer, made fit for the zeal of action, may be formed by the instruction of comparison and may not hesitate to undertake a work whose possibility and necessity the image of the parable has shown.

Therefore the Lord Jesus, the true teacher of saving commandments, wishing to urge his disciples—whether they were then apostles or are now all believers—

[Note: The printed editions read *invitare*—“invite”; but three manuscripts more aptly read *incitare*—“urge,” which is also found in the Pantagathus manuscript.]

to practice almsgiving faithfully, set forth the likeness of the steward, so that the example of this person might signify that nothing in this present age is ours, but that the administration of our Lord’s possessions has been entrusted to us, either for using enough of them with thanksgiving or for distributing them to our fellow servants according to each one’s need. Nor is it lawful for us to misuse at will the possessions entrusted to us or to appropriate them for extravagant expenses, since an account of the distribution must be rendered to the Lord when he comes.

Finally, after the end of the parable he added:

“‘And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings’” (Luke 16:9).

That is: make the poor your friends from the earthly possessions which human iniquity claims for itself, refusing to share anything from God’s property with God’s people. For *mammon* in the Syriac language means money or riches.

“Make for yourselves,” he says, “poor friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings,” when that same substance has been distributed and consumed for the needs of the poor.

[Note: Four manuscripts unanimously read: “so that when the same substance has failed”; the same reading occurs above: “so that when it has failed, they may receive you.” This seems quite correctly expressed and is also found in the Pantagathus manuscript. Nevertheless, I did not wish to alter the received reading, which is supported by the Vulgate.]

The poor themselves, that is, are friends who obtain salvation for us; and in them Christ, the eternal rewarder, will acknowledge that he has received the services of our humanity. Therefore they will not receive us by themselves and in their own right, but through him who is refreshed in them by the fruit of our obedience and faith, and who will receive the ministers of this piety into the eternal dwellings of the heavenly kingdom.

For he says:

“‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you gathered me in; naked, and you covered me; ill, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me’” (Matt. 25:34).

When they modestly and reverently excuse themselves, saying:

“‘Lord, when did we see you in these needs and minister to you?’” (ibid., 37),

he will answer them:

“‘Amen I say to you, when you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me’” (ibid., 40).

Let no one, therefore, think it absurd that those for whose sake we are received are said to receive us, since our very receiver, the Lord Jesus, who is not subject to human needs, declares that in them he was hungry and thirsty, a stranger and naked, ill,
