[Note: The editions read “imprisoned,” but four manuscripts more correctly have *carceratum*—“imprisoned”—and the Pantagathus manuscript has the same. Salvianus, Book II *On the Government of God*, speaking of David in repentance, writes: “He is changed in appearance and heart; he casts off the entire king with his ornaments; he is driven by fasting, dried up by wasting, poured out in weeping, imprisoned by solitude.”]

and imprisoned.

“Make for yourselves,” he says, “friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.”

[Note: Here too three manuscripts—the two Vatican manuscripts and the Urbino manuscript—have “so that when you fail.”]

And shortly afterward:

“If you have not been faithful in dishonest mammon, who will entrust to you what is true?”

[Note: Again the printed editions incorrectly read “what is yours,” but four manuscripts and the Pantagathus manuscript have “what is true.” Nevertheless, the same manuscripts shortly afterward have, not quite correctly, “if you have not been faithful in what is another’s, what is true”; whereas our edition reads “what is yours.” That this passage should be read in the present form is shown by what immediately follows: “Certainly, whatever is in this age is another’s to us.” See what we noted above, p. 347.]

Indeed, dearest brother, who would think it proper to entrust the true riches of heavenly things—which a faithful and just distributor enjoys rightly and deservedly—to one who does not know how to administer earthly possessions faithfully, although they usually provide material for iniquity?

“For glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:3).

Immediately, then, that saying of the Lord is joined to this:

“And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:11).

Certainly, whatever exists in this age is another’s to us. For while hoping for a future reward, we are commanded to live in this world as guests and strangers, so that each of us may confidently dare to confess to the Lord:

“I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13).

But for believers the proper and eternal possession is that heavenly one, where we know that our heart and our treasure are to be (Matt. 6), where we presume by faith that we already dwell with the whole affection of our mind, since, according to the teaching of the blessed Paul, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

The kingdom of heaven is therefore ours, if we serve the Lord who promises it in humility of heart and gentleness of spirit.

“For blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

That kingdom, however, cannot be attained by anyone who has not proved himself a capable and faithful steward of the alien inheritance of this age, temporarily entrusted to him. Therefore the Lord said elsewhere:

“How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God!” (Matt. 19:23).

And at the end of this reading he said:

“You cannot serve God and mammon” (Luke 16:13).

For the servants and disciples of Christ ought to command money, not serve it, lest, while we obey its greed, money ruling us separate us from the love of Christ’s service.

[Note: The Lyon edition most ineptly reads *donante*—“while giving.” Gaudentius seems to have had in mind Horace, *Epistles* 1.10:

“Money amassed either commands or serves each person.”

Thus also Seneca, *On the Happy Life*: “For the wise man, riches are in service; for the fool, they are in command.”]

Money must therefore be scattered among the needy, according to the command of God, the Creator of all things, since it is neither ours, nor can any miser retain it without iniquity and his own destruction.

For, according to the Savior’s saying, riches block the entrance to the kingdom of heaven for those who retain them, and it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God (Matt. 19:24)—namely, that rich man who, because of the horror of shameful greed, is weaker than a camel.

[Note: From the words that follow, “The burden of money is heavy,” Gaudentius seems to have understood the Gospel saying “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle” as referring to a living camel. Jerome in Matthew 19 also favors this interpretation. The Pantagathus manuscript has *camelo informior*—“more misshapen than a camel”—instead of *camelo infirmior*; the two Vatican manuscripts agree, so that it corresponds to the preceding phrase, “because of the horror of shameful greed,” which can appropriately be said only of a living camel. Others, however, take the word to mean a sailor’s rope to which an anchor was attached, in which sense it occurs in Suidas. Perhaps Gaudentius, wishing also to accommodate himself to this interpretation, says shortly afterward that the way leading to life seeks those who are unencumbered and slight, like a slender thread. This was a Hebrew proverb, concerning which Samuel Bochart writes at length in *Hierozoicon*, part I, book II, chapter 5, where he adduces several Hebrew passages that are highly relevant to illuminating the proverb.]

The burden of money is heavy. It presses the minds of those who cling to it down to the earth under the weight of greed and does not permit them to rise to higher things or to look toward heaven, where our life is, although the blessed Apostle teaches:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:1ff.).

Since the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted (Matt. 7:14), it does not admit those burdened with bundles of earthly riches. It seeks people who are unencumbered and slight, disciplined by complete self-restraint and—as I might put it—like a slender thread, who may easily pass through the opening of that mystical needle once they have become spiritual.

This is the meaning and usefulness of this parable. First, one must obey it according to what is commanded; then its more hidden meaning, if it can be found, must be sought, because the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power (1 Cor. 4:20).

And not merely hearers but doers of the Law will be justified before God (Rom. 2:13). Nor can anyone clearly comprehend the inner knowledge of divine speech, since the Apostle declares:

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and untraceable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34).

And elsewhere, when he perceived the mystery of the divine word concerning Adam and Eve to be exceedingly great and was unable to speak of it worthily, he said:

“This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

Do you wish to know that eternal life is attained not through knowledge of secrets but through the accomplishment of good works? When a certain rich man questioned him, the Lord answered in the Gospel:

“If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17).

Although that man boasted that he had kept them all, one commandment could not be extracted from him at that moment: that he should be merciful to the poor and transfer his treasure to heaven. For immediately after hearing this saying he went away sorrowful.

[Note: Thus the printed editions; but the Florentine manuscript and the two Vatican manuscripts have “one present commandment could not be extracted from him,” and the Pantagathus manuscript reads the same.]

And not without reason was he sorrowful, because, possessed by the evil of greed, he could not possess the joy of the heavenly treasure.

Certainly, the love of money is the root of all evils, as the Apostle laments:

“Some, desiring it, have gone astray from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:10).

For he suffers a destructive error of faith and pierces himself with many sorrows who, through love of earthly things, departs from Christ like this young man—while he evades Christ’s commandment, while he is led away from the Lord’s presence, sorrowful and mourning, by voluntary blindness toward the punishments prepared for the greedy and contemptuous.

For to those placed on the left because of their lack of fruitfulness it will be said:

“Depart from me into the eternal fire, which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels; for when you did not show mercy to those in need, you did not show mercy to me” (Matt. 25:41).

I now come to the point you have pressed upon me so earnestly, and I shall state as briefly as I can what I think about it, prejudging no one who wishes to interpret it in his own way, provided that his explanation does not violate the tradition of the apostolic faith.

I think that the dishonest steward is the devil, who for this reason was sent into this age for the correction of the human race,

[Note: The two Vatican manuscripts have *ad correptionem*—“for correction.” I suspect that the original wording was “for the correction of the human race he was sent into this age”; but the Pantagathus manuscript offers the better reading: “for the correction of the human race he was released into this age.”]

so that, fleeing from the savagery of this most cruel steward, we may run humbly to the mercy of God, through whose mercy and power we may be defended against all his assaults. For this steward himself has been placed under the authority of the Lord God—the true rich man who, as the Apostle teaches, is rich toward all and above all who call upon him.

“For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. 10:12–13).

The devil dissipates his lord’s possessions when he rages toward the destruction of the human race—that is, toward our death, since we are God’s possession—as the Son of God himself testifies by repeating what his Father said through the Prophet:

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

And again:

“For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession” (Ps. 134:4).

When God therefore saw that the demon’s audacity had advanced so far that he had usurped and killed those whom he had been permitted only to test for the sake of correction, he threatens him with expulsion,

[Note: The two Vatican manuscripts, the Urbino manuscript, and the printed editions have *comminatus*—“having threatened”; shortly afterward they have *interminata*, whereas from the Vatican manuscripts we have restored *interminatae*. The Pantagathus manuscript also supports both corrections.]

so that his savagery might be broken by fear of unending punishment.

But that most wicked being, counting the death of human beings as his profit, burns anxiously because the Lord was going to take away from him the power of ruling.

[Note: The printed editions add a conjunction, but it seemed superfluous. They read: “because the Lord would take away from him the power.” The two Vatican manuscripts have: “because God would take away from him the power.” The Pantagathus book reads: “because the Lord would take away from him the power.”]

And because he neither wishes to do good nor is ashamed to ask mercy in repentance, he reasons how he might prevail over the Lord’s debtors—that is, those entangled in the debts of sins—not only by openly attacking them but also by deceiving them through a flattering fraud under the pretext of false goodwill, so that, seduced by false kindness, they may receive him into their houses and be judged with him forever.

The devil considers this a great remedy for his own punishments: to acquire many companions in punishment.

For the crafty enemy, disturbed when Christ came and threatened him, devised a poisonous plan by which even those who were fleeing from him as he pursued them might follow him as he withdrew.

He hastens, by new devices and various kinds of temptation, to trip up human beings, knowing that at the end of the age he is to be completely removed from their domination.

For after Christ’s coming he is inflamed with doubled fury against the human race, knowing that he has only a short time, as it is written concerning him (Rev. 12).

He falsely promises to release the debts of his fellow servants, which are in the Lord’s power, when he offers indulgence to sinners in either faith or conduct—when he persuades them that those crimes are not counted as sins which even the people who commit them know to be serious offenses.

They acknowledge the amount of their debt when they cannot deny that they are wholly liable to God, both for despised faith and for neglected conduct. But those who render what belongs to God are no longer debtors to God.

Do not be surprised if he thus lies to people about the remission of debts, whom by this art he tries more subtly to kill. He dared to promise the kingdoms of the world to Christ, the creator of all things, shamelessly asserting that they were his own:

“All these things are mine,” he says, “and I give them to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you fall down and worship me, all will be yours” (Matt. 4).

O the ineffable patience of Christ, who permits the tempter to speak for this reason: that, having assumed humanity, he might demonstrate in himself the art of fighting and conquering!

O the unbridled audacity of the lying devil! He senses God, yet he tempts him. He knows the Lord of all creation, to whom he falsely claims that the kingdoms of the world belong, and he promises to give him possession of creatable things,

[Note: The Pantagathus book has *crealium*, which approaches the reading of the printed editions, and the two Vatican manuscripts likewise have it. But in the margin of the Pantagathus manuscript *creaturarum*—“of creatures”—has been supplied; this is less displeasing, since what the devil promised Christ were certainly not things capable of being created but things already created.]

through whom he knows that all things were created.

For from the beginning, as it is written, the devil was a murderer, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him (John 8:44).

But let us now come to the particular figures about which the question is asked.

As we touched on above, wheat is the faith of Christ, the beginning of human life. For he is the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to this world (John 6:33).

And again he himself says:

“He who believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John 11:25).

Oil, however, is good works. The foolish virgins who did not have these works (Matt. 25), when the lamps of their souls had gone out, remained in darkness, excluded from the bridal chamber of the heavenly kingdom.

Our souls must not merely be virgins in faith and remain undefiled; they must also always carry with them the oil of every good work in their vessels, lest the lamps of faith within us be extinguished through lack of works.

For just as the flesh is dead without the soul, so faith without works is dead, according to the saying of the holy James (James 2:26).

The light of faith will indeed be constant and everlasting if it is abundantly enlivened by the richness of good works.

[Note: The printed editions read “is illuminated by richness”; but the reading of three manuscripts—the two Vatican manuscripts and the Florentine manuscript—seemed more suitable: “is enlivened by richness.” The Pantagathus book also has this reading. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* 2, line 405:

“And the whole being will be enlivened by warm marrow.”

Hence *animator*—“the enlivening one”—in the same author, *Hymn on the Martyr Romanus*, line 788:

“The sole enlivening one and maker of you knows…”]
ψυχοδότης (*psychodotēr*), that is, “one who gives the soul and the life-giving spirit,” as Georgius Fabricius notes in his commentary on Prudentius, Weitzius, p. 401.] may be enlivened by abundance. The devil therefore surrounds the human race with false promises, so that they may not recognize the debt owed in faith and works; until, by the sentence of the Lord and Judge, they are thrust back into the prison of hell, to be made to pay the last farthing through punishments (Luke 12:59).

But when he persuades that one hundred measures [Col. 0979B] of oil—that is, of works—should be rewritten as fifty, and forces one hundred cors of wheat—that is, of faith—to be reduced to eighty, this is a more hidden fraud and a very subtle ambush of the enemy: for, when he has withdrawn people from idolatry, he entangles them in various errors of pernicious doctrines, diminishing the sum of saving faith; and those who have been removed from wicked deeds and desire to persist in good works, he overthrows through a pestilential love of boasting.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] The whole of this is absent from the Lyon edition, where it reads: “But what concerns one hundred cors of wheat.”]

For he strives to distort our faith and our works from the number one hundred—the perfect number, and the one placed on the right—toward the deceitful shortcuts of the left; perverting the apostolic faith through the left-handed sense of heretical persuasion, and often leading the merits of good works and deeds performed on the right toward left-handed conduct.

For how many has the devil released from the strength of the right-hand side into the vices of carnal pleasures through left-handed counsels! How many, eagerly desiring to pay their spiritual debts through acts of religion, he has deprived of the heavenly reward by injecting a desire for human glory, so that they do not obtain the promised rewards of the [354] right-hand side, while in those very good works they hasten to please not God but human beings!

[Note: [Col. 0979D] The printed editions read incorrectly, “for he deprived those enticed by the heavenly reward of the glory of human ambition,” as though *illectos* were intended. We have removed this manifestly corrupt reading. The word *illectos* improperly intruded in place of *injecta*, through an easy scribal transposition caused by carelessness; for in four manuscripts and in the book of Pantagathus there is unanimous agreement on: “by injecting a desire for human glory.” Even in these witnesses there is a slight defect, namely the preposition improperly inserted; once it is removed, the passage is restored to its integrity.]

Therefore Christ the Son of God and Lord, warning his disciples [Col. 0980A] not to make a practice of performing their righteousness, almsgiving, fasting, and prayers before human beings, lest through the vice of boasting, which is assigned to the left-hand side, they lose the reward of the right-hand side, says: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6).

It is therefore plainly evident with what poisonous cunning that unjust steward changes the duties owed to religion from the right-hand side to the left. Nor is this without significance: a greater number is lost to the Lord, to whom we are debtors, from the works represented by the oil than from the wheat compared with the example of life-giving faith.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] The printed editions have this most shamefully: “for he is less shameful who is removed from right faith than he who is removed from works,” as though unbelief were a lesser fault than the others. But four manuscripts, whose reading we have printed, came to the aid of this badly damaged passage, restoring: “for the crowd that is withdrawn from the faith is smaller”; the same reading is also found in the manuscript of Pantagathus.]

For the crowd that is withdrawn from right faith is smaller than that which is withdrawn from suitable works, as the Savior testifies: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

But the Lord praises not the goodness, piety, or justice of the unjust steward, but his cleverness and shrewd prudence, because he had arranged his deceit with subtle wickedness. He praises him at once threateningly and prudently.

[Note: [Col. 0980C] Here and shortly afterward, the book of Pantagathus reads *providenter* (“providently”), so that providence is attributed to the teacher and prudence to the disciples.]

Threateningly, indeed, in that by the very designation “unjust” he condemns the devil’s wickedest prudence; but prudently, in that he instructs the disciples who hear him to oppose with every precaution and with all prudence such a cunning and wickedly prudent enemy, in accordance with his schemes and arguments.

For that serpent was in paradise more prudent than all the beasts (Genesis 3), and with the poisonous bite of seduction he killed the first-formed human beings. The blessed Apostle, detecting the twisting designs of this serpent, says: “For we are not ignorant of his schemes” (2 Corinthians 2:11).

Hence also the Savior says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10), which the Apostle Paul explains in other words when he says: “Be children in malice, so that you may be mature in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14:20).

Christ commanded us to be prudent, not poisonous; wise, not harmful; but, like the snake, laying aside the old garment of sin, we should be remade into the new human being, preserving with every care our head, which is Christ, and handing over all our limbs to persecutors [355] to be torn apart for his sake, so that the faith of God, which is the head of our salvation and life, may remain whole and unwounded.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] The *Physiologus*, first published under the name of Bishop Epiphanius at Antwerp, from the Plantin press, in 1588, with Gonzalo Ponce de León as editor and translator, has the following in chapter 15: “Therefore we too, in a time of danger, ought to surrender the whole body to death and guard only the head; that is, not to abandon Christ, just as the holy martyrs did.” The same statement occurs in Epiphanius, book 1, volume 3, *Against the Ophites*. Isidore of Pelusium, letter 126, to Count Herminus, translated by J. Billius, says: “The Lord commands us, most ingenious man, to be prudent as serpents; namely, that in every temptation we preserve our head, that is, our faith in Christ. For however many adversities and blows may press upon a serpent, it keeps its head safe and unharmed.” The aforementioned Ponce de León cites these and similar passages in his notes on the *Physiologus*, where he also cites this passage of our Gaudentius.]

[Note: [Col. 0981C] Thus Flor. and Urb., to which is joined the manuscript of Pantagathus. Cusi reads: “Therefore, most beloved”; but Gaudentius addresses Serminius, or Herminius, to whom this treatise or letter was written; hence shortly afterward he also concludes: “Farewell, dearest son in Christ.”]

[Col. 0981A] Therefore, dearest one, let us imitate the prudence of this steward, not his faithlessness; let us emulate his cleverness, not follow his wickedness. As skilled as he was in doing harm through his work of iniquity, so well instructed in salutary pursuits, and equipped and armed with every prudence, ought we to be: “putting on the breastplate of faith and the helmet of salvation” (1 Thessalonians 5), “and the sword of the spirit” (Wisdom 5), and the unconquerable shield of righteousness, with which, as the Apostle exhorts, we can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one (Ephesians 6); lest he strike us unawares everywhere with the arrows of his suggestions, lest he overwhelm us when unarmed, lest he kill us while asleep; and lest, even if we are awake and armed, he destroy us because we do not know how to wage war.

[Note: [Col. 0981C] The Paris and Cologne editions read *prudentes enim* (“for prudent”), as does the Lyon edition; but shortly afterward they have “whom the Lord calls more sons of the age.” Perhaps the text originally read *prudentes enim magis* (“for they are more prudent”). We have preferred the reading of the Florentine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts, which we later also found in the book of Pantagathus.]

For unclean spirits are sometimes found to be more prudent than the sons of the age—that is, the sons of darkness—whom the Lord so calls, than the sons of light, whom God, who is light, deigns to call to the adoption of sons

[Note: [Col. 0981D] This is a hexameter verse, as is also the following from treatise 1:

“He could not celebrate; in the second month let him celebrate.”

Thus it appears in Eucherius, in the *Paraeneticus to Valerian*:

“And when circumstances prosper, you confess that you did not deserve it.”

Barthius mentions these among the little verses that escaped their authors unintentionally, book 4 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 13.]

reborn through the sacraments of the heavenly washing.

[Note: [Col. 0981D] This conclusion is absent from the Florentine manuscript and is likewise missing from the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus.]

Farewell, dearest son in Christ.

## SERMON XIX. NINTH SERMON ON VARIOUS PASSAGES

Or, the response of the same holy Bishop to the deacon Paul, concerning what the Lord Jesus said to the Apostles: “For the Father is greater than I.”

[Col. 0981C] 356 Before this passage of the holy Gospel, whose meaning you earnestly demand from me in a letter, Paul, my brother, most dear to me by kinship of flesh and spirit, Christ, the Son of the living God, is known to have spoken many things about the one and perfect substance of his divinity with the Father, when he said to the Jews: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); when he answered the holy Philip: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9); and when he spoke collectively to the blessed Apostles: “Believe me, that I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:11).

After these statements, and many others of the same kind, by which he proved himself to be *homoousios*—consubstantial—with the Father, and of the same essence, he was now about to introduce something that would increase the fullness of knowledge in minds strong in faith, but offer a stumbling-block to the doubtful and nourishment for blasphemy to the faithless—for the word of God (Luke 11:34) is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many. He therefore warned the eleven blessed Apostles, and likewise those who would follow in the footsteps of their faith, lest at the hearing of the words he was about to speak

[Note: [Col. 0982C] Florence, Urbino, and two Vatican manuscripts judged that *turbellam* should be restored here, which fits much better with what follows: “lest your heart be troubled.” *Turbella* means a small crowd or a slight disturbance, as in Plautus, *Pseudolus*, act 1, scene 1:

“You know very well, by Hercules …  
how many little disturbances I am accustomed to cause.”

And in *Bacchides*, act 4, scene 9: “I cause such great disturbances.” For this passage Meursius thought *turbellas* should be written, like *suada* from *suadela*, and *fuga* from *fugela*. Indeed, in this passage of Gaudentius the manuscript of Octavius Pantagathus reads *turbelam*, not *turbellam*, which especially confirms Meursius’s conjecture. When scribes encountered an unfamiliar word, they foolishly erased it and substituted *scandalum*; hence the printed editions read: “the mind of someone might suffer scandal.” Zeno of Verona used *turbulentare* in his sermon on patience.]

might suffer disturbance. “Let not your heart be troubled,” he says, “nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: I am going away, and I am coming to you. If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:27–28).

The Arian heretics have this as their most notorious question [357] by which they contend with sacrilegious speech that the Son of God is less than his Father, producing his own testimony because he says: “For the Father is greater than I.”

[Note: [Col. 0982D] Because the controversy was then especially active. The printed editions corruptly read *formosissimam* (“most beautiful”), but Florence, one of the Vatican manuscripts, and the manuscript of Pantagathus all have *famosissimam* (“most notorious”).]

The wickedness of their hearts blinded them (Wisdom 2:21), so that they did not recognize the reason for this statement from the words that preceded it—or rather, so that they would not follow the truth once they had recognized it.

There are two substances in Christ: one proper to him, the other now his as ours; that is, one is divine and the other human.

[Note: [Col. 0982D] In the manuscripts of Pantagathus, when the reading was *alia nostra jam sua* (“the other ours, now his”), Pantagathus himself revised the passage as follows: “one proper, the other ours. One is his, that is, one is divine,” which no one will doubt is much more correct. Perhaps, however, the addition *jam sua* (“now his”), which is introduced without purpose, should simply be deleted, and the text should read: “one proper, the other ours”—that is, one divine and the other human.]

For the Son of God, from the time when the undefiled Virgin bore him, conceived by the Holy Spirit, and through this manner of birth the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1), began also to be the Son of Man—the one who in the beginning was with the Father as the Son of God, namely God the Word.

From then on, through the stages of life, the Creator of time advances into a perfect man, as the Evangelist testifies: “But the child grew and became strong, and was filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was in him” (Luke 2:40).

Understanding that this growth advanced for the sake of our growth, the Apostle Paul said: “Until we all arrive,” he says, “at a perfect man, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13); although the perfect divinity, which always will be what it was, and will be without end, required no increase.

Everything, therefore, that Christ, established in this twofold substance, either said, did, or endured manifested at one time the omnipotent nature of God, and at another the weakness of the humanity he had assumed.

His birth in the flesh shows a human being; the extraordinary birth from a Virgin proves God. The narrow cradle of the manger and the customary wrapping in cloths signify human infancy; but the voices of angels announce to the shepherds that the one who was born is God.

For when the angel said: “Do not be afraid; for behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger,” suddenly there appeared with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:10ff.).

Then Herod persecutes the little child; but the radiance of the obedient star declares him to be a great God

[Note: [Col. 0983D] Barthius, book 22 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 20: “A noteworthy account concerning the Magi, who came to Jerusalem from distant Bactria to worship Christ, as Prudentius writes. But it is not commonly known that the ancients judged that they undertook this journey not in their own name, but as envoys chosen from the entire chorus of Eastern sages. Hence Juvencus writes, book 1:

‘They bore the name of Magi.  
Then, joyful, the noblemen came to Jerusalem  
by the long roads, and approached the king …’

Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, to his brother Paul: ‘Then Herod persecutes the little child; but the radiance of the obedient star declares him to be a great God, whom the Magi, envoys of all the nations, devoutly worshiped, presenting to the heavenly King the honor due to him through the offering of mystical gifts.’ Gaudentius is also speaking mystically here. This is Barthius’s note.]

whom the Magi, envoys of all the nations, devoutly worshiped (Matthew 2), presenting to the heavenly King [358] the honor due to him through the offering of mystical gifts.

Jesus, a boy of twelve years, is found in the temple by his anxious parents (Luke 2); but in his words the crowd of teachers seated around him marvels at him as the Wisdom of God.

And he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Isaiah 53), approaches the baptism of John like a sinful human being, intending to wash away our crimes in his own body; but there too the voice of his Father immediately thunders from heaven, revealing the distinctive character of the divine nature: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him” (Matthew 3:17).

[Note: [Col. 0984D] A most elegant synopsis of the Gospel history, similar to those he composed above in treatises 8 and 11. These repeated examples show how fortunate Gaudentius was in natural talent and how distinguished in verbal abundance.]

The devil approaches him as a human being, the tempter (Matthew 4); but after the devil has been defeated, the ministries of angels who serve Christ as God immediately attend him.

He often avoids the uprisings of the raging Jews as a human being (John 8); but as God he drives out legions of demons, as though they were servants, by the command of his word (Luke 8).

He sits beside the well, wearied from his journey, as a human being (John 4); but as God, the searcher of human minds, he reveals the hidden things of the Samaritan woman. He not only reveals them, but also cleanses her through the washing of water that springs up into eternal life.

He faithfully cleanses the one who prays: “Cleanse me from my secret faults” (Psalm 18). For the woman says to him: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst again” (John 4)—that is, with the burning of sins extinguished.

To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep belongs to a human being; but to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves belongs to God (John 6). To give living water (John 4), one draught of which grants the drinker that he will no longer thirst, but that it will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life, belongs to God alone.

And he who is exhausted by the labor of an earthly journey like a human being again walks upon the waters like God.

For when the Lord (Matthew 14) had ordered his disciples to sail across the strait until he dismissed the crowds, after the crowds had departed he went up [Col. 0984B] and prayed on the mountain. But in the evening, when the little boat was already being tossed in the middle of the sea by waves stirred up by a contrary wind (Mark 6; John 6), he, borne along by the power of his majesty, walked upon the surface of the sea; the swelling water did not touch the soles of him who walked.

The Apostles, in danger during the fourth watch of the night, see Christ approaching from a distance. Peter asks: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matthew 14:28). But he, unwilling to deny anything to faithful desire, says: “Come.” And Peter, he says, descending from the boat, walked upon the waters to reach Jesus. But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid; and when he began to sink, [359] he cried out, saying: “Lord, save me.” Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and seized him, saying to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:29–30).

While he walks upon the earth and feels weariness, he is human; but when he walks securely by his power across the waves and lifts up Peter as he sinks, he is God.

At the same time, let the Arians consider in this passage that a certain deadly drowning is prepared for those who are doubtful in the faith of Christ, unless by a true confession they turn as suppliants to his omnipotence.

Elsewhere also the holy Evangelist describes the Lord Christ as sleeping while sailing (Matthew 8:24), when the disciples, placed in the utmost peril of the storm, awakened him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (ibid. 25). Then, rising, he commanded the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm.

He sleeps as a human being, and rising he commands the elements as God. For he restrained the swelling waves by his word, and immediately the rebuked storm fell silent; and at the voice of their Creator,

[Note: [Col. 0984D] The correction was obvious, but it was nevertheless drawn from the three manuscripts, Florence and the two Vatican witnesses. The printed editions read incorrectly *plena confestim* (“full immediately”); but in the manuscript of Pantagathus the immense mass of the gulf lay immediately flat, where *infinita* (“boundless”) appears in place of *inflati* (“swollen”).]

the immense mass of the swollen abyss immediately lay flat.

But lest, by reviewing such individual examples, I seem to wander too far from the purpose of my discourse, I shall add a few more words of our Lord Jesus Christ, from which you may perceive in him both the condition of human nature and divine power.

[Note: [Col. 0985C] From this verse to the end of this treatise, everything is extraordinarily disordered and confused in the four manuscripts: nearly one hundred lines are missing here and there, while what remains is continually displaced and can scarcely be brought into proper order except by an Ariadnean thread. The manuscript of Pantagathus suffers from exactly the same defect. A learned man rightly observed in his notes on Longinus, Salmurian edition, p. 385, that at the end of almost all manuscript codices the text usually bristles with more errors, when weariness, negligence, or excessive haste corrupts what remains.]

He says to the Jews: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man, and so forth” (John 8:40). And elsewhere, when Peter confesses, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), he declares him blessed, because he was found worthy to have this faith infused into him by God the Father; thereby confirming through this utterance that he himself truly is the Son of God.

And he who had said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18), says again: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26).

And the same one who said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), says again: “Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me” (Luke 22).

For this reason, the one who, speaking in the person of God, had said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10), speaking in the person of the humanity he had assumed, says: “For the Father is greater than I” (John 14).

Now, for one who understands what has been said, the following explanation will make more clearly evident [360] for what reason that which is written is said, and what exactly is meant by the words, “For the Father is greater than I.” Yet it is already plainly clear from the testimonies cited above that the Son of God, begotten by the Father without any beginning, after he deigned to be born from blessed Mary, is both God and human being; and that at one time, according to the flesh, he either did, spoke, or suffered humble things

[Note: [Col. 0985D] Thus read four manuscripts; three editions, however, have the inept reading *delegisse*. The manuscript of Pantagathus has *vel egisse* (“or done”).]

while at another he taught in words and demonstrated through miraculous deeds the immeasurable sublimity of God’s nature.

[Col. 0985C] Nevertheless, the most wicked Arians do not follow this rule of distinction; rather, with the deceit of Jewish innkeepers,

[Note: [Col. 0985D] The agreement of the manuscripts persuades us that this is the reading. It also agrees with what follows, namely, “human things with divine things.” The editions, however, read less correctly, “they mix water with wine.” Later in this same treatise humanity is also compared with water and divinity with wine: “so that the water of the Incarnation might become the wine of the Godhead,” which heretics, adulterating the word of God, still mix with wine as though it were water.]

they mix water with wine—that is, human things with divine things—and thus confuse that pure and apostolic faith by an adulterating mixture, attributing to God ignorance, weakness, fear, inability, doubt, pain, hunger, thirst, weariness, and the other sufferings of a human being.

The Son of God assumed and bore these together with humanity without detriment to his divinity, in such a way that he counted as his own the insults he suffered in the flesh, while nevertheless his divinity, retaining the power of its nature, remained impassible.

Hence the holy Apostle, while preserving the condition of divine incorruptibility, speaks of the Lord of majesty as crucified (2 Corinthians 13).

Indeed, his Passion, accomplished not in the divinity, which is impassible, but in the humanity he assumed, brought aid to the world destined to perish; for by the wound of this humanity we have been saved.

Not that his divinity could have been wounded, but because he himself assumed our weaknesses, bore our sins, and suffered pain on our behalf, according to the teaching of the Prophet (Isaiah 53). For he himself was neither weakened,

[Note: [Col. 0985D] Four manuscripts read either “or he himself bore” or “or he himself [bore] the pains of the wounds of crucifixion,” that is, of the wounds Christ endured when placed upon the cross; the manuscript of Pantagathus has the same reading. Perhaps Gaudentius wrote *crucialium*, a corrupt Latin word, just as Commodianus used *cruciarium Domini* in instruction 32:

“If you have not worshiped the crucifixion of the Lord, you have perished.”

In that passage Rigaltius interprets the word as referring to Christ’s cross or suffering.]

nor did he sin, nor did he himself feel the pains of cruel wounds.

For how could it have happened that he who by the power of his command had cured the manifold diseases of sickness and by his authority had restored repeated life to the dead should himself

[Note: [Col. 0986D] We have restored this passage according to the manuscripts, since the editions contained a defect. They read: “according to the divine nature, he was subject to sufferings in the flesh.” But in that form Gaudentius would seem to support not his own case but that of the Arians, declaring in some fashion that Christ, according to his divine nature, had been subject to Passion in the flesh. The error arose because the words *in carne* (“in the flesh”), which we have restored to their proper place below, had been transferred here through the carelessness of scribes.]

have been subject to Passion according to the divine nature?

He therefore endured, as a human being, the insults of the Passion in the flesh, and as God he performed miracles by his own authority. Hence the Apostle says: “He was crucified through weakness, but he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13).

Thus, [361] when he is led to the Passion, by the touch of his right hand he creates a new ear for Malchus (Luke 22:51), which had been cut off by Peter’s sword in opposition to the purpose of his patience; and while hanging upon the cross he grants paradise to the confessing thief (Luke 23); and while placed in the tomb he raises the bodies of the saints (Matthew 27).

[Note: [Col. 0986D] An anachronism? For the bodies of the saints did not rise immediately after Christ’s death, but after his resurrection, as appendages of the Lord’s resurrection, in the words of Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 33. Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Nepotianus*, says: “At his resurrection, many bodies of those who slept arose and were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem.” On this passage, see the notes of Martianaeus, Benedictine edition, volume 4, p. 267.]

And when he rises, he is seen with the same arrangement of limbs in which he had suffered (Luke 24), and he enters, with the doors closed, to the Apostles gathered within one house (John 20); and when he ascends into heaven, he does not abandon his faithful disciples, promising that he will remain with them until the consummation of the age (Matthew 28).

If the Arian heretics followed this distinction, they would never turn the mystery of our life into an insult against the Son of God by asserting, in blasphemous words, that he is lesser than God the Father—he whom the chosen vessel testifies to be equal to the Father—thereby explaining the whole reason for which the Son of God, who is also man, said: “For the Father is greater than I.” He says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, existing in the form of God, did not consider it robbery that he was equal to God” (Philippians II).

The Apostle testifies that he is equal; Arius attempts to assert that he is lesser. The judgment is left to the hearers: whom they think should be believed—whether the Apostle Paul, who was chosen by Christ as teacher of the nations and, like a wise architect, laid the foundation of faith (I Corinthians III), and who, caught up to the third heaven, heard heavenly secrets (II Corinthians XII); or the accursed Arius, who, in the time of Emperor Constantine, pretended with his poisoned heart to confess the Catholic faith; who sought admission to the king’s friendship and to the rank of the presbyterate, from which he had deservedly been expelled and to which he tried to be restored; who, like Judas the betrayer, burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out (Acts I), lest a wolf should enter under a sheep’s clothing to devour the Lord’s flock.

[Note: These events occurred after the Council of Nicaea, when Arius, having been received by the synod of Jerusalem, pretended repentance before Constantine. Compare Socrates, book I, chapter 26, Valesius’s edition; Sozomen, book II, chapter 27; Athanasius, *Apology II*; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69. This passage of Gaudentius considerably illuminates the history of the Arian heresy, and is therefore also cited by Baronius under A.D. 336, no. 56, among the testimonies of the Fathers with which he mocks Arius’s shameful death. Gaudentius seems to have imitated Ambrose, who says in book I of *On the Faith to Gratian*, chapter 9: “Whom, then, shall we believe? John, reclining upon Christ’s breast, or Arius, rolling about amid his own spilled entrails?”—so that we might recognize that Arius’s treachery was like that of the betrayer Judas, whom a similar punishment condemned. For Arius’s entrails too were spilled—shame forbids saying where—and thus he burst open in the middle.]

Arians who follow the assertion of this wicked man will likewise follow the example of his death. But we, who follow the apostolic faith and teaching, should lend the ears of our minds with faithful devotion to the explanation of the blessed Paul given above.

[Note: The reading of the Urbinate manuscript, which seemed better than the others. The Florentine manuscript has: “we who follow apostolic teaching”; the two Vatican manuscripts: “we who follow apostolic faith.” Both of these readings agree with the Urbinate. The printed editions instead have: “we who pursue apostolic discipline.” The Pantagathus manuscript reads: “But we, following apostolic teaching.” Perhaps *qui* is superfluous.]

For he continues: “But he emptied himself”—namely, by voluntarily humbling himself in goodness. And he adds: “Taking the form of a servant,” certainly not becoming a servant; “he was made,” he says, “in the likeness of man” (Philippians II). “Whatever was made, in him is life” (John I): namely, what was made in him according to the flesh is our life, as he himself testifies: “I came that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (John X).

Then he adds: “And being found in appearance as a man” (Philippians II); for no one has ever seen the appearance of God, that is, God himself properly speaking (I John IV). Then he humbled himself, “becoming,” he says, “obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians II). For in voluntary humility, in accordance with the Father’s will, he willingly endured the cross so that his death might become the life of believers.

Therefore, he says, “God exalted him.” Whom did he exalt? Clearly, the one who underwent the punishment of the cross and death—not God in isolation, who is always exalted by nature. “And he gave him the name which is above every name” (Philippians II).

The name above every name is God; and it is certainly not given to God that he might be God.

[Note: Thus the Florentine and Urbinate manuscripts agree, as does the Pantagathus book. The two Vatican manuscripts read less correctly: “It is certainly not given to God that he should be Lord.” The printed editions have: “It is certainly not given to him that he should be God.”]

For in the beginning, with the Father, the Son was God the Word. But the man assumed by the Son is raised into God, so that the Son of God, who had always been, might likewise be God together with the substance he assumed from the Virgin—wholly God again.

[Note: Thus the Paris edition and four manuscripts, together with the Pantagathus book. Two editions have: “and the Son of God who had always been,” as above. The Son of God was the Word; but our reading is “the Son was God the Word,” based on the Paris edition, four manuscripts, and the Pantagathus manuscript.]

Thus, in the name of Jesus—who is God and man—every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians II). That is, after the mystery of the Passion and the triumph of the Ascension, the whole Son of God, together with that which he deigned to assume for our sake, should be worshiped in the glory of God the Father—remaining, of course, in the divinity of his own nature—by all the powers of heaven, earth, and the underworld.

Before, therefore, he suffered; before, having triumphed over death, he ascended victoriously into heaven; before he returned to the bosom of the Father’s divinity with the whole substance with which he had been born from the Virgin; before the Lord Jesus was recognized and worshiped by every rational creature of heaven, earth, and the underworld in the glory of God the Father, he rightly said to his disciples: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

He was still lesser, the Son of God born in the flesh, until he placed the nature of the man he had assumed in his ancient glory.

[Note: The editions read: “until he assumed the nature of man into his ancient glory.” We have therefore restored here the reading of mutually agreeing manuscripts, except that the Urbinate has “the material of the assumed man,” as does the Pantagathus manuscript.]

And therefore elsewhere he says to the Father in his own person: “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII). This means that he should possess, together with the whole substance of his bodily birth, the glory of divinity which the Son, as God with God the Father, had always possessed before the foundation of the world.

[Note: The Pantagathus book reads somewhat better: “with the substance of bodily birth.”]

For this reason he also speaks in this way after his resurrection to certain people who were hesitating about this dispensation: “O foolish men,” he says, “and slow of heart to believe in all that the Prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke XXIV).

He did not without reason testify that he was lesser, but in that passage where he was conveying to his own Apostles, in explicit terms, the reason for his Passion, resurrection, and ascension.

[Note: Thus four manuscripts; the printed editions instead have: “then, Arius.” The Pantagathus manuscript reads: “Not you, Arius.” It seems, however, that it should be written: “to the Apostles: Not you, Arius,” and that the punctuation mark indicating the end of the sentence should therefore be removed, so that “not you, Arius” refers to what he had said: “but in that passage.”]

Do not, Arius, suppose that his statements concerning the perfect substance of divinity, which he made before the Passion, can be nullified by the native argument of your unbelief, with which you wickedly destroy the salvation of your soul through cunning. The speech of Christ is entirely distinct in its clarity, whether he teaches about his divinity or speaks about his incarnation.

For through the Prophets he announces the sublimity of his deity in one way when he says: “Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against you: I am the Lord your God” (Psalm XLIX). In another way he indicates the humility of his future incorporation when he says: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm XXI).

And after many other words, so that you may not doubt that the entire fabric of the prophecy belongs to him: “They divided my garments among themselves,” he says, “and upon my clothing they cast lots” (ibid.). The Evangelists testify that this was done by those who crucified Christ with regard to his garments (Matthew XXVII; John XIX).

Therefore no believer should be troubled that the Son, placed in this world according to the flesh, said that he was lesser than his Father. He even deigned at that time, through the Prophet, to compare himself to a worm. This was not without the profoundest reason for the mystery.

It is established that the larva of the future bee, which generates without intercourse, is born, and that its labors bring health to kings and commoners, as it is written.

[Note: Where is this written? This is one of those passages not found in the Hebrew text or the Vulgate edition, though it occurs in the Septuagint and in many Fathers. As Samuel Bochart observed in the preface to his *Hierozoicon*, after the passage about the ant at Proverbs VI, 8, the Greek text adds certain words about the bee, cited by many Fathers; the Arabic translator rendered them, and Castalio also rendered them thus: “Or go to the bee and learn how industrious she is, and what august work she performs, whose labors kings and private persons beneficially enjoy.” The Septuagint reads: “Or go to the bee and learn how industrious she is, and what venerable work she performs, whose labors kings and ordinary people offer for health.” The four manuscripts and the Pantagathus codex have “offer for health”; and a little below, instead of “we offer for the health of the common life,” they have “we offer.” But we did not think the received reading should be changed in either place; for the Law forbade Jews to offer honey—the product of the bee’s labor. Leviticus II: “Every offering offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven; neither anything leavened nor honey shall you burn in sacrifice to the Lord.” See Saubert, *On the Sacrifices of the Ancients*, chapter 25.]

[Note: Gaudentius is speaking in accordance with Pliny’s account, whose words in book XI, chapter 16, are as follows: “The mating of bees has never been observed. Many have thought that they must be produced from flowers composed and arranged suitably and usefully. Some have thought that they arise from the mating of one individual, called the king in each swarm. Having rejected this opinion, he adds: ‘What is certain is that they brood after the manner of hens. What has been hatched first appears to be a little worm, white, lying crosswise and clinging in such a way that it seems to feed.’ Aristotle, however, attributes mating to bees in book III of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 10, in the translation of Theodore Gaza: ‘If offspring appeared to be generated without kings, bees would necessarily also be generated from themselves without mating; but since those who care for these animals deny this, it follows that kings both generate themselves and generate bees.’ Virgil’s account of the shepherd Aristaeus in *Georgics* IV is well known; there he seems to have followed poetic imagination, for Bochart easily taught in the Preface to his *Hierozicon*, page 48, that bees could arise not only from an ox but also from a lion, as is related in Judges XIV—namely, that bees were found there, not born. Consult Augustine, *On the City of God* XV, chapter 27, and there the notes of Ludovicus Vives on the words: “But there are other creatures in which there is nothing male and female, such as bees.” Cardan, in book IX of *On Subtlety*, asserts that bees are generated from honey; but Scaliger mocks Cardan in *Exercitation* 191, which is certainly worth consulting. Today the mating of bees is so well established that it can no longer be called into question.]

The labors of Christ’s Passion, whom the Virgin Mother brought forth as a bee destined to remain virgin,

[Note: Thus four manuscripts and the Pantagathus book; the editions read: “the Virgin Mother gave birth.”]

we offer, in the figure of his body and blood, for the health of the common life, both to kings—that is, high priests, from *ruling*—and to all the lesser members who follow, whether of the Levitical order or of the faithful people. With conscious mouth we bear witness to the recognized sweetness of the mysteries: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm XXXIII).

[Note: There is a large lacuna here in the manuscripts: sixty-five complete verses are missing, from these words to “For the one whom he announces as bent down.”]

But woe to the heretics who attempt to assert that what is sweet is bitter, wishing to remove equality from the Son precisely where he is known to remain wholly in the glory of God the Father, after the mystery of the Passion has been completed.

For thus he says to the blessed Apostles, who were listening with the desire of their minds for the majesty of his Ascension: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I” (John XIV).

He was declaring that for this reason he would ascend into heaven after his Passion and resurrection in both substances, divine and human: so that he who, because of the humility of the incarnation, appeared on earth to be lesser than himself and therefore lesser than his Father, might, having trampled down the sting of death and ascending victoriously into heaven, remain equal to the Father, as he had always been; and so that the same one who had always been God, now also man, established as God in the eternal glory of the Father, might reign without end.

For the one who earlier made wine from water in a figure, when he said to the most blessed Mary: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John II), himself, after the hour of his Passion, completed the truth of the preceding riddle to this extent: the water of the incarnation truly became the wine of the divinity. By adulterating the word of God, the heretics still mix water, as it were, with wine, although the whole Lord Jesus—both what is from God the Father and what is from the Virgin Mother—is the only-begotten God in the glory of God the Father.

God was not diminished in man; rather, man advanced into God. Thus, just as the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I), so flesh would become God and dwell in heaven.

Accordingly he added: “And now,” he says, “I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened, you may believe” (John XIV, 29). That is: For this reason I said that if you loved me, you ought to rejoice that I was going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I, so that when it has happened, you may believe me equal.

“When it has happened”—what? Clearly, this: when, after my Passion, I have ascended into heaven, remaining in that glory which I have always possessed with the Father and in the presence of the Father.

Therefore, after he rose from the dead, certain people who doubted were rebuked by him, and they heard that it was necessary for Christ to suffer all these things and so enter into his glory, which he testified that he had always possessed before the foundation of the world.

For this reason the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (II Corinthians V, 16). He is God and man, and both are now God, established at the right hand of God the Father, because “the cup in the hand of the Lord is full of unmixed wine mixed. And he has poured from this into that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied” (Psalm LXXIV).

And although I know, dearest one, that the text of this psalm was previously explained by earlier writers in another, and indeed reasonable, sense, I nevertheless, in the freedom of faith, following the suitability of the words, have applied it to the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: The rule which Augustine gives for interpreting Scripture is well known, in book I of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 36: “Whoever thinks that he has understood the divine Scriptures, or any part of them, in such a way that by that understanding he does not build the twofold love of God and neighbor, has not yet understood them. But whoever derives from them a meaning useful for building this love, even if he does not say what the person he is reading is demonstrably shown to have understood in that passage, is not dangerously deceived and is not lying altogether.” Gaudentius speaks somewhat differently above, in the treatise *On the Steward*, page 351: “I now come to what you have so earnestly demanded of me, and I shall explain as briefly as I can what I think about it, prejudging no one’s preferred interpretation, provided that his explanation does not violate the tradition of the apostolic faith.”]

For God was thus either bent down or humbled in man, that, while remaining God, he might be what he had been, and might exalt the man for whose sake he had humbled himself. For the Word became flesh so that he might dwell among us (John I); and so man was again transformed into God that, although raised into God, he might retain the substance of his own nature.

Therefore the Prophet says: “For the cup in the hand of the Lord is full of unmixed wine mixed; and he has poured from this into that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied.”

“It is full,” he says, “of unmixed wine mixed” (Psalm LXXIV). He calls the wine mixed, yet testifies that it is itself unmixed, so that we may believe him to be the same God whom, for our sake, we confess also to be man.

For the one whom he announces as bent down he likewise says is full, so that he who emptied himself by taking the form of a servant does not cease to be fully God. “For in Christ all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Colossians II), and “from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John I, 16).

“This cup,” he says, “the sinners of the earth will drink” (Psalm LXXIV). Properly, according to this interpretation, he says: “The sinners of the earth will drink,” because the sinners of heaven—angels who became demons—are not worthy to drink the cup of salvation. But the sinners of earth will receive the cup of salvation against the poisons of demons and the diseases of vices, and they will invoke the name of the Lord (Psalm CXV). For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans X).

This cup is assigned to sinners to drink because the healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill. “I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew IX). For wisdom of God invites such people to this cup of saving mixture when, with a sublime voice, it exhorts and says: “Whoever is foolish, let him turn in to me.” And to those lacking sense it says: “Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs IX).

The fool is invited by the wisdom of God for this reason: that he may become wise; and the sinner, that he may be converted and live.

All of us are summoned generally to this cup of divine mercy. “For all have sinned,” as the Apostle says, “and lack the glory of God” (Romans III, 23)—that is, the healing of his majesty.

[Note: On this apostolic passage, à Lapide rightly observes that, when Paul says “all lack the glory of God,” Cyril in *On the Right Faith to the Queens* understands “glory” to mean Christ, who is the glory of the Father precisely insofar as he is our Redeemer and Justifier—as though Paul were saying: all need Christ the Redeemer. Others, more genuinely in accordance with the Apostle’s meaning, understand “glory” here as the grace by which God is glorified. Hence Jerome, book VI on Isaiah, chapter XVI, and Augustine, book I of *On the Merit of Sins*, chapter 27, citing not so much the Apostle’s words as his sense, read: “All lack the grace of God.” Although all these senses tend almost to the same point. The Lyons edition reads “and lack the grace of God,” and again shortly afterward “and lack the grace of God”; for the healing of his majesty. But the Florentine codex and the Pantagathus book have “glory of God” in both places.] If all have sinned and lack the glory of God, whom shall we finally call healthy, for whom the physician’s office is not necessary, except perhaps those who have already been healed by him and no longer require medicine?

Moreover, no saint has failed to need the medicine of Christ, since faith in him alone has made them saints, as Scripture testifies in the letter of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Hebrews (Hebrews XI). For this reason the same Apostle, giving thanks, proclaimed: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (I Timothy I).

Nor should anyone flatter himself concerning his own salvation without the gift of God in Christ, when the chosen vessel confesses himself to be the first of all sinners.

[Note: This means “worse” or “more evil,” not “more worthy,” as Barthius thought in his *Annotations* on book I of Paulinus of Petricordia’s *Life of Saint Martin*. Gaudentius’s use of this passage helps to illustrate Paulinus’s words:

“True love had subjected those very people who were previously more worthy.”

He says “more worthy” through an abuse of the age. He then cites a passage from Alcimus Avitus and Gaudentius. Barthius could have used another passage of Gaudentius, where in treatise 17 he calls the person “more worthy” the prior one. But “prior” is rightly used, and superior in dignity.]

Therefore, since we have been gathered from among sinners and have deserved to drink the faith of Christ, having become participants in the altar and having received the gift of charism, let us proclaim God’s gifts with a voice of exultation and confession, saying:

“You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me. You have anointed my head with oil; and how excellent is your intoxicating cup!” (Psalm XXII).

Thus, with the mercy of the Lord following, may we merit from the eternal Son of God the everlasting dwelling of his house, whose kingdom will have no end, because he conquered death and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Three editions read quite nonsensically, “with the matter of the Lord following”; but the four manuscripts have “with the mercy of the Lord following.” The Pantagathus codex has, instead of “may we merit,” “may we possess”: “with the mercy of the Lord following, the dwelling of his house”; this seems more congruent with the sense, but the syntax of the following words opposes it.]

[Note: The remainder is missing in the four manuscripts and in the Pantagathus codex, which immediately adds: “The sermons of Lord Gaudentius to Benivolus end.” But that conclusion is more properly suited to the end of the sermon on the Maccabean martyrs; for there end the sermons sent by Gaudentius to Benivolus, according to what Gaudentius himself wrote to him in the preface, p. 220.]

## SERMON XX. THE TENTH SERMON ON VARIOUS PASSAGES. On Peter and Paul.

[Note: Galeardus has: “The Sermon of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia on Peter and Paul,” with the following note. This title is borne by the old Venetian edition of the sermons of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, in which this sermon first appeared in 1508; it is found there in book III, sermon 48. It also exists in the Urbinate manuscript 150 and the Vatican manuscript 1235, with which it was collated, and is entitled: “Of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, on Peter and Paul.” There can therefore be no doubt that it is genuinely the work of Gaudentius. The revisers and editors of the sermons of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, which were reprinted at Verona by Hieronymus Discipulus in 1586 at the command of Augustine Valerius, cardinal and bishop of Verona, also bear witness to this same sermon. Their words are these: “We warn that the sermon of Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, has been omitted. It had been added to the printed sermons of Saint Zeno, but is not found in an old manuscript codex.” It is also found among the papers of Octavius Pantagathus under this title: “Of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, on Peter and Paul.”]

[Note: He seems to be designating Ambrose; for in his sermon *On Ordination* he says: “The blessed father Ambrose and the other venerable bishops.” And below, in the same sermon: “I beseech our common father Ambrose.”]

The venerable bishop of Christ, and our common father, through the affection with which he detained me when I was departing, has now compelled me, even while I was making excuses, to address your affection once again with a discourse of mine.

[Note: These words sufficiently indicate that this sermon was delivered at Milan; it is clear from what follows that Gaudentius preached in that city more than once. In ancient times, visiting bishops were accustomed to be invited to preach by the bishop of the city to which they had come, as Ferrarius has observed at length in book II of *On the Rites of the Holy Church*, part V, chapter 5. When Saint Cardinal Charles Borromeo saw this praiseworthy and pious custom of the ancient religion being neglected and discontinued, he restored it to the Church of Milan both by action and by decree, as is recorded in his acts.]

And therefore, according to the smallness of my understanding, I shall touch upon something concerning the praises of the most blessed Apostles, encouraged nevertheless by the protection of those whose natal feast it is.

[Note: The Urbinate and Vatican manuscripts agree. The printed editions erroneously read “by their prayers.”]

We understand that three births have been granted to the human race by the eternal Trinity.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript also has this reading; the Urbinate has “human conditions,” which is plainly a copyist’s error.]

One is carnal and belongs to everyone; two are spiritual, according to the merit of each person’s faith. The first is that by which we are created from nothing into the substance of worldly life. The second is that by which, in Baptism, we are regenerated from iniquity and error into the truth of righteousness. The third is that by which the most blessed martyrs, for confessing the name of Christ, are born through torments into the kingdom.

Such a pattern came first in Christ, who, born from the Virgin,

[Note: Thus the printed editions. The Urbinate manuscript has: “born from the Virgin as man.” The Vatican manuscript likewise.]

is reborn in the Jordan,

[Note: We have corrected this from the Urbinate and Vatican manuscripts; the earlier printed text read: “is born in the Jordan.”]

and on the gibbet of the cross, of precious …

[Note: Blood is sometimes used for juice or liquid; hence Manilius, book V:

“And the blood of the green grove withdraws from the woodland, and from the herbs.”]

Similarly, Genesis 49:11: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his mantle in the blood of the grape.” And Deuteronomy 32:14: “And he shall drink the purest blood of the grape.” In the same way as Gaudentius, Cyprian too speaks, in his Letter 10 to the Martyrs and Confessors, Amsterdam edition, 1700: “Blood flowed that would extinguish the fire of persecution, that would lull the flames and fires of Gehenna with glorious gore.” He is baptized in the blood of his own gore. For after that baptism which he had received for our sake in the Jordan, [Note: [Col. 0994C] This is the reading of the Urbinas and Vatican manuscripts; the old edition has “through his Passion.”] he says to the Apostles concerning his Passion: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized” (Luke 12:50). [Note: [Col. 0994C] The Urbinas and Vatican manuscript codices read “from this.”] For he rose from that baptism of Passion to a life already closed by no limit; he returned to the kingdom “whose kingdom shall have no end” (Luke 1:33).

Following the footsteps of this master, the faithful disciples Peter and Paul proceed; today all the Churches throughout the world celebrate with due honor the anniversary of their martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 0994C] Both codices agree; this is plainly the reading required, referring to “throughout the world” and “all the Churches.” The printed editions read “celebrate.”] [Note: [Col. 0994C–D] Thus the manuscripts. The old edition, and Pantagathus’s book, lack “on this day.” Here Gaudentius supplies material for those who maintain that the Apostles suffered on one day and in the same year; see Baronius, under A.D. 69, no. 4. Valesius held otherwise in his notes on Eusebius, book II, chapter 25.]

For on this day, at the city of Rome, Nero’s cruelty killed both of them for Christ’s name, but the Lord’s justice crowned them. [Note: [Col. 0995B–C] A certain learned man thought this had been taken from the apocryphal Acts circulated under Linus’s name; but the matter is confirmed by the frequent testimonies of the Fathers—Origen, Augustine, Prudentius, Chrysostom, and others—whom Baronius lists under A.D. 69, no. 49. Lest anyone object to the unusual character of the matter, Lipsius, *On the Cross*, book III, chapter 8, should be consulted. This makes me all the more wonder that such an opinion could have taken root in a learned man’s mind, especially since those spurious Acts appear to be considerably later than Gaudentius’s age. See Vossius, *On Greek History*, book II, chapter 9. Moreover, Gaudentius’s words are exactly Jerome’s in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he says of Peter: “Fastened to the cross, he was crowned with martyrdom, with his head turned toward the ground and his feet raised on high, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified as his Lord was.”] [Note: [Col. 0994D] That is, while Nero was in Rome—or while he had departed for Greece? If the latter, Gaudentius’s statement that Nero’s cruelty killed the Apostles must be understood only in the sense that, after issuing a capital edict, he ordered them killed through his agents. Yet the former opinion has far more supporters. Baronius reports that the Apostles suffered when Lucius Fonteius Capito and Gaius Julius Rufus were consuls, A.D. 69 (but more correctly 67), after Nero had returned to Rome from Achaia; Pagius contends that they were killed while Nero was in Rome, before he departed for Greece, when Nerva and Vestinus were consuls, namely A.D. 65. Compare Tillemont, notes on the life of St. Peter, note 40.]

Peter was crucified with his head turned toward the ground and his feet raised upward, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord. Paul was beheaded by the sword. Both were noble, both illustrious: two lights of the world, pillars of the faith, founders of the Church, teachers of innocence, authors of all holiness and truth.

We can praise them worthily only if we proclaim them by divine testimonies, by which Truth itself praised them. [Note: [Col. 0995C] This is the reading in the editions and the Vatican manuscript; in the Urbinas manuscript *tibi* (“to you”) is absent. The former reading is supported by the Gospel text.] To Peter, confessing the faith, the Lord says: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16). “And I say to you, Peter: you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth.

What shall I say of Paul? [Note: [Col. 0995C] The manuscripts have *quid dicit?*—“what does he say?”—which seems more fitting, since he is speaking in the person of Christ.] “He is,” he says, “a vessel of election for me, to carry my name throughout the whole world” (Acts 9).

The Church is founded upon one; the other, having himself become a vessel of election, carries among the people the precious myrrh of faith through his teaching. [Note: [Col. 0995C–D] The old edition read: “The other carries among the people, by his teaching, the precious wall of faith, himself having become a vessel of election.” But this reading was altogether harsh and unworthy of Gaudentius’s style. For how can a vessel carry a wall? Further, even if it were not a vessel, how could it appropriately be said that someone carries a wall? Jerome, in his Letter to Heliodorus, writes: “That ram of piety, against which faith is shaken, must be blunted by the wall of the Gospel.” But this has no bearing at all upon our reading: a ram is indeed blunted against a wall, but that a vessel should carry a wall has never been heard by anyone. The manuscripts offered no help here, until a most learned man perceived that an error had arisen from the interchange of letters—specifically, *y* for *u*—and that instead of *fidei murum* one ought to read *fidei myrum*, “the myrrh of faith.” There are frequent ancient examples of this phenomenon: they wrote *Aegyptum* for *Aegyptum*, *Suriam* and *Suracusam* for *Syriam* and *Syracusam*, *Sullam* for *Syllam*, and similar forms, as we also noted above, in treatise 2, from Cassiodorus, *On Orthography*, chapters 1 and 4. Nothing is more certain than this emendation; I therefore adopted it all the more eagerly because Gaudentius is found using the word *myrum* elsewhere as well; see above, treatise 13, pages 313 and 315. I wished to record this more fully here both so that the reader may know to whom he owes the restoration of this splendid Gaudentian passage, and so that the learned man may retain undiminished praise for himself.]

Peter shines through signs and miracles; Paul glories in teaching and persecutions. Peter had previously been a fisherman; Paul, a persecutor; but afterward both became fishers of men. For throughout the whole sea of this world they cast the nets of saving doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0996C] This is how the manuscripts read; the editions previously had “the nets of the Savior’s doctrine,” which in no way seemed worth retaining.]

Peter is commanded to walk upon the waves (Matthew 14:29); Paul, upon the clouds, while he is carried up to the third heaven. [Note: [Col. 0996C–D] Emended from both the Urbinas and Vatican manuscripts. The editions have *divinisque* up to the third heaven. This passage bears upon the well-known question whether Paul was carried up to the third heaven only in spirit, or also bodily, as 2 Corinthians 12 relates.
