Since Gaudentius says that Paul was commanded to walk upon the clouds, he seems to have understood that Paul was truly and literally carried into heaven together with his body: he implies that Paul walked upon the clouds in the same way that Peter had walked upon the waves. He then concludes: “Both walk in the element of an impassable journey, raised on high by the power of faith.” If you wish, consult Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, book II, chapters 13–14.]

Both walk in the element of an impassable journey, raised on high by the power of faith. Whom I should dare to place before the other, I do not know, since the Lord showed them equal in suffering under one confession, joined them in true brotherhood, and bound them together by the bond of unanimity; so that we may rightly understand the prophetic spirit to have proclaimed concerning them: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132). [Note: [Col. 0996D] This is the reading of the printed editions and the Vatican manuscript; these words are absent from the Urbinas manuscript.]

There are indeed Moses and Aaron, of whom it is said that they are brothers. There are the Prophets and the Apostles, brothers in one doctrine and one spirit. [Note: [Col. 0996D] Likewise above, in the treatise on the Maccabean martyr: “What brother is more closely joined than our outward man?” John Cassian, *Conferences*, XII, chapter 11: “This will happen when the flesh, finally ceasing to lust against the spirit, agrees with its desires of chastity and virtue, and they begin to be bound to one another by the firmest peace; then, according to the Psalmist’s saying, they will dwell together as brothers.”]

There are within us an inner and an outer man: if they share one mind, they are brothers. Peter and Paul too are truly blood brothers, whom one and the same faith, through the communion of their own blood, made genuine brothers. I shall even dare to call them twin brothers, whom one mother, through one fortunate confession, brought forth together from her fruitful womb into the kingdom. For blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5).

Let us therefore, brothers, share in the memories of the holy Apostles; let us share in the memories of the saints through faith, conduct, way of life, and speech, so that we may deserve to be aided by their prayers in everything that we ask, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0997B] We have retained the reading found in the editions, although these words are absent from the manuscripts. Perhaps “in the memories of the saints” is superfluous.] [Note: [Col. 0997B] Both the Urbinas and Vatican manuscripts have “of our Lord Jesus Christ.”]

To him be all honor forever and ever. [Note: [Col. 0997B] The manuscripts add “Amen,” a word absent from the editions.]

## SERMON XXI. ELEVENTH ON VARIOUS PASSAGES

Or, an Oration of Blessed Gaudentius, Bishop, on the Life and Death of Blessed Philastrius, Bishop, his predecessor.

[Note: [Col. 0997B–C] This sermon had wandered outside its proper order, as we also noted in our Preface; it therefore rightly occupies this place, since the collectors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* had unjustly omitted it elsewhere. Baronius, Labbe, Cave, and others frequently drew testimonies from it. We have compared it with two manuscript codices of the Archive of the Church of Brescia; the earlier and older of these bears an eleventh-century designation. We also compared it with the Venetian edition of Lipomani, 1554, and the Cologne edition of Surius, 1579, who published it in the *Lives of the Saints* and testify that they received it from an old book of the Sacristy of the Church of Brescia. We have taken the title from both Brescia manuscripts, since it seems more consistent with ancient simplicity than the title published by Lipomani and Surius in this form: “The Life of Blessed Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia, written by Saint Gaudentius, his successor.” The book of Pantagathus gives this title: “The Sermon of Blessed Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, on the Life of Blessed Philastrius, his predecessor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0997C–D] Philastrius’s eulogy found in the Appendix to Ado is for the most part drawn from this sermon of Gaudentius. The very same sermon, as presented by the Paduan edition of Gaudentius, p. 239, carefully corrected and annotated, was republished by the distinguished William Cuper in the *Acta Sanctorum*, July, vol. IV, p. 387; it is worth consulting.]

[Note: [Col. 0997D] In both Brescia manuscripts the word is written *Karissimi*—“most dear ones”—according to the ancient practice by which *k* was used for *c*. I shall not dwell on a familiar matter for which coins and inscriptions provide abundant examples. An old inscription in Rubeus, page 268, reads: “To Monima Crescentia, most dear, Marcus Aelius, her son”; and on page 252: “To Aurelius Vibius, who lived forty-five years, his fellow member and dearest friend.” See Lipsius, *On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language*, chapter 13. Above also, in the sermon on his ordination, Gaudentius calls him “father”: “After that most learned utterance of my father Philastrius, worthy of venerable memory”; and in the Preface to Benivolus: “You, imbued with the marvelous teachings in every respect of that apostolic man, our father Philastrius.” In the manuscripts: “to our blessed father Philastrius”; and everywhere *Filastrius* is written instead of *Philastrius*.]

Most dear brothers, today, mindful of Christ’s promises, we render due honor to our blessed father Philastrius, as to one truly living. For he is a son of the Patriarchs, a companion in faith, and an imitator of their way of life; he was most like them in sincerity, and like the one whom Christ declares to live to God, [Note: [Col. 0998B–C] Supply “he was.” The following words in the printed copies were astonishingly corrupted: “he declares Christ equal to God as living”; but what place here is there for Christ’s equality with God? The discussion concerns not the Arian but the Sadducean heresy, which denied the resurrection. Moreover, Gaudentius appeared to attribute the whole passage to Philastrius, as though he were refuting the Sadducees’ unbelief by cogent arguments, whereas all this was said by Christ, as the Gospel text shows. Thus everything at the beginning of this sermon was full of ambiguity and obscurity, until the earlier and older Brescia manuscript supplied the reading: “and such a one as Christ declares to live to God.” On adopting it, we restored the genuine sense of the passage.] refuting the unbelief of the Sadducees by a powerful authoritative argument, when he says that the one who is called “the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob” is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matthew 22; Luke 20). “For all live to him,” he says (Luke 20:38).

And certainly divine Scripture had foretold that they were dead according to the condition of the flesh, although in a good old age, and buried, as the tombs that remain demonstrate. [Note: [Col. 0998C] The editions again suffered from a serious corruption, reading: “he declares them to have been dead in Christ according to the condition of the flesh”; and afterward: “although he had foretold that they were buried in a good old age.” The words “in Christ” had been added very absurdly; moreover, “declares” and “to be” were superfluous. Both Brescia manuscripts give our reading; the book of Pantagathus has this form: “He had foretold that they were dead according to the condition of the flesh, although in a good old age, and that they were buried.”] [Note: [Col. 0998C–D] Concerning the burial of the Patriarchs: Genesis 25, where Abraham is concerned; 35, where Isaac is concerned; and 50, where Jacob is concerned. The mausoleum in which their remains had been buried still existed in the time of Josephus and Jerome in the city of Hebron, built of the finest marble. See Josephus, *Jewish War*, V, 7; Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*, under “Arboc.” Perhaps during his journey in the East Gaudentius examined these monuments with his own eyes.]

Therefore, what blessed Peter was permitted to say boldly about the patriarch David—that he was dead and buried (Acts 2:29)—although he knew that through prophetic faith David had anticipated life after death, since he had said, “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you” (Psalm 118), and other things of this kind: let us also be permitted to say boldly to you concerning the legitimate son of the Patriarch and High Priest, Philastrius, that he indeed died and was buried, and his tomb is among us, but his life is in Christ with God. Therefore, when Christ, our life, appears, then he too will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3).

That he was truly a legitimate son of blessed Abraham is testified by examples of faith and works (Genesis 12). [Note: [Col. 0998D] The Pantagathus manuscript has: “Faith and works.”]

[Note: [Col. 0998D–0999C] Philastrius’s origin is wholly unknown to us; the ancients too were ignorant of it, as the rhythm on Philastrius, which we recently published in the additions to Ughellus, shows. There one reads:

> From what towers this man was born,  
> None of us remembers or knows;  
> But this we know: that he followed  
> Blessed Abraham.

Since this Rhythm on Philastrius contains much that is excellent, and was at times circulated under Gaudentius’s name, we have appended it to this sermon as a splendid supplement. Ughellus calls Philastrius a Spaniard; Cave conjectures that he was Italian by race, but neither relies on any plausible evidence. See our notes on Ughellus, in the bishops of Brescia, vol. IV, col. 525 of the Venetian edition, and what we added in the Preface to Philastrius, no. 3, of this edition.]

For, believing God with the fullest faith, he too went out from his land, from his kindred, and from his father’s house; and he followed the word of God, stripped of all the impediments of the world. Therefore he quickly deserved to attain what he had striven to follow, unencumbered. Practicing extraordinary self-restraint, ever watchful in the Holy Scriptures, he desired the wisdom of God, regarding Christ the Lord as his portion, in whom all the treasures of heavenly wisdom are hidden (Colossians 2). When he had filled his desire with these things, he became a man of heavenly desires; and, having been chosen through the laying on of the hand of the presbytery as a steward of the divine word, he did not permit the grace of God to be neglected. [Note: [Col. 0999C] Gaudentius seems to have had 1 Timothy 4:14 in mind: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.” By this manner of speaking he may have indicated that Philastrius was then ordained bishop, *μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου*—“with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery”—just as the Apostle there indicates that Timothy was ordained. For it was customary for the presbyters who were present, together with the head of their assembly, to lay on hands, as Grotius notes on this Pauline passage. But perhaps Gaudentius more likely intended to signify that Philastrius had been appointed to the ministry of preaching, in accordance with Acts 13:3: “Fasting and praying, and laying their hands upon them, they sent them away.” This is better supported by Gaudentius’s words: “when, through the laying on of the hand of the presbytery, he had been chosen as the steward of the divine word.”]

But, traveling through nearly the whole circuit of the Roman world, he preached the word of the Lord, proving himself a worthy imitator of the Apostle Paul. For, filled with the Holy Spirit, he fought not only against Gentiles and Jews, but also against all heresies, and especially against the raging Arian impiety of that time, with such strength of faith that he was even subjected to scourging and bore in his body the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0999C–1000B] Philastrius’s book *On Heresies* exists; it was composed with both zeal and devotion. Some nevertheless mark it as lacking in accurate judgment, because Philastrius included in its catalogue of heresies many things that ought not properly to have been classified under that name. He establishes three classes, or orders, of heresies: the first those that existed before Christ’s coming; the second those that arose after Christ’s Passion; and the third those that arose under the Apostles. John Albert Fabricius was preparing a new edition of this little work, as he himself states in his *Latin Library*, page 732, but perhaps he has so far refrained because of the scarcity of manuscript copies. These matters had already been published in the Padua edition of 1720. Soon afterward, when Fabricius’s Philastrius was issued publicly by the Hamburg press in 1721, and when our desire to obtain some manuscript copy of Philastrius had grown ever stronger, through the distinguished generosity of the most eminent Cardinal Quirini, Bishop of Brescia, we happened to discover a manuscript of Philastrius belonging to the monastery of Corbie. We have said more about it in the Preface to Philastrius in this Brescia edition. It proved a notable aid in emending and restoring Philastrius’s book, as will be plainly evident to anyone reading our *Spicilegium*.]

For once he had been a suitable guardian of the Lord’s flock in the city of Milan, opposing the Arian Auxentius, before blessed Ambrose was chosen. [Note: [Col. 1000B–C] Baronius cites this passage of Gaudentius on Philastrius under A.D. 369, no. 27; Rampertus, in his sermon on the Translation of Philastrius, and Ferrarius, in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, 18 July, also used it. Baronius thinks Gaudentius means that Philastrius remained at Milan after Hilary’s departure, in order, insofar as he could, to keep the Catholic people steadfast; for this reason, he thinks, Philastrius endured beatings. See what we said in the Preface to Philastrius, no. 3.] He also stayed in Rome for a considerable time and won many people to the faith through both public and private disputation. [Note: [Col. 1000C] This passage of Gaudentius may have given certain people an opportunity to count Augustine among those whom Philastrius won to the faith. But such claims are more the prophecies of idle minds than conjectures; certainly we do not think them important enough to devote much care or time to refuting them. See our notes on Ughellus and the Preface to Philastrius, no. 7.]

Nor did the faithful disciple of Christ ever cease preaching the word of God as he passed through the villages and hamlets of different regions. After those salutary journeys through many souls, Brescia—once uncultivated but eager for instruction—won him for itself: ignorant indeed of spiritual knowledge, but praiseworthy in its desire to learn.

The good farmer immediately uprooted from the deepest roots the forest bristling with diverse error and, bending eagerly over the plow of instruction, turned the raw earth with all his strength; by constant furrows he transformed the neglected soil into fertile fields, freely planting within its breast the seeds of life-giving commandments. [Note: [Col. 1000C] We have restored this reading from the earlier and older Brescia manuscript. The other manuscript, as well as the editions, has “a forest bristling with diverse error,” a reading that can also be defended and that is likewise found in the book of Pantagathus.]

He also planted a vineyard whose fruit would bring joy, because “wine gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 103). He grafted olives of peace onto wild olive trees, and upon the harshness of wild fruits he grafted shoots of richness and sweetness, so that this apostolic man might have some fruit among you as among the other nations. [Note: [Col. 1000C–D] Above, in the Preface to Benivolus: “Through the marvelous teachings in every respect of that apostolic man, our father Philastrius.” This was a common designation for bishops, as Baluzius notes on Salvian, page 322. Thus Gaudentius also says, in treatise 5: “If anyone is apostolic, and through Jesus has become great and powerful by overthrowing the Egyptian,” and in the treatise on his ordination: “Let all these apostolic priests now pray.” Likewise in the treatise on the dedication of the basilica: “The holy bishops and apostolic men assembled.”]

And he now rejoices with God in the fruits of his completed work, for “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10), and “the laboring farmer ought first to partake of the fruits” (2 Timothy 2). But I, the least part of him, earnestly desire with all my prayers that I may in some way be able to care for the field well planted by the father and received through a succession that was not sufficiently suitable. [Note: [Col. 1000D] Both Brescia manuscripts read this way, and correctly; the editions corruptly read: “the field well assessed by the father, but still planted.” The book of Pantagathus retains the latter reading. What Gaudentius adds—“and received through a succession that was not sufficiently suitable”—elegantly expresses how much he regretted, even after fourteen full years, when this sermon was delivered, that he had been compelled, unwilling and reluctant, to undertake the burden of the episcopate. See what we noted on Sermon 16, pages 332–333, and in the Preface to Gaudentius, nos. 1–2.]

We have just touched briefly upon his zeal for the faith and the greatness of his labors. Now let us recall, most dear brothers, how much gentleness in holy conduct that vehement ardor of spirit possessed; how lofty in humility was that height of knowledge; how ignorant of earthly things was that expertise in heavenly matters. [Note: [Col. 1001B] Both Brescia manuscripts again have *Karissimi*. From this point to the words “I have recalled these few things about the virtues of the man of God,” Capreolus reported the passage quite accurately from a manuscript of Gaudentius in book III of his *History of Brescia*, where he speaks about Philastrius; thus he seems to have been the first to publish a specimen of Gaudentius’s sermons.]

For he was ignorant of human glory and a fierce exactor of divine honor, “not seeking his own things, but those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2). Despising the friendships of the world and worldly duties, and adhering continually to the service of God, he was continually occupied amid human conversations: surely, “there was his heart where his treasure was” (Matthew 6). [Note: [Col. 1001C] The first Brescia manuscript has: “adhering continually to the service of God”; the other, “continually adhering himself to the service of God.” Capreolus reads: “he continually adhered to the service of God.”]

What of this as well: although he despised all the laborious and costly things of this world, he increased the poorest sellers of cheap goods by becoming, with merciful generosity, an extravagant buyer? He considered it a small matter what he gave to the professedly needy. [Note: [Col. 1001C] This is the reading of both Brescia manuscripts, supported by Capreolus. The editions have “what he professed.”]

The same holy man was quick to anger but ready to forgive, surpassing in patience and conquering by kindness; strict in correcting, unrestrained in easing; free in action; with astonishing benevolence common to every age, condition, and sex, and especially joined to all the humble. [Note: [Col. 1001C] Both Brescia manuscripts read “and especially joined to all the humble.” Capreolus has “and likewise joined to the very humblest of all”; perhaps the true reading is found in the Pantagathus manuscript: “and yet more closely joined to all the humble.”]

Even in that style of dress, he was altogether spotless in his poverty: gracious without affectation, contemptible without pretense; plainly one who, though he himself cared nothing for it, revealed the purity of his mind. [Note: [Col. 1001C] Capreolus has this form: “Seeking contempt without deceit, so that he might reveal the purity of his mind”; this reading seems better and more suitable. The rest is absent from Capreolus.]

I have recalled these few things about the virtues of this man of God in a very brief speech— [Note: [Col. 1001C] The earlier and older Brescia manuscript has: “of this man of God, namely the most blessed Philastrius, our outstanding patron, whose feast is celebrated today, in a very brief speech.”] lest this day, on which blessed Philastrius, our patron, departed to the heavenly realms, whose feast we celebrate today, should pass ingloriously in mournful silence. [Note: [Col. 1001C–1002C] Although the common reading is found in one of the Brescia manuscripts—a fact I had failed to mention in the first edition—it is not free from suspicion that the designation “patron,” which is attributed to Philastrius here by the more recent manuscript and above by the earlier and older one, did not come from Gaudentius, but in both manuscripts is an interpolation from later times, when Apollonius and Philastrius were called patrons of the city of Brescia. This title of honor has since long ceased to be applied to them. With God’s help, we shall say more about this in the notes on the Brescia Martyrology.]

For after renewing the observance of this solemnity for fourteen years already and bringing many praises of his merits to your hearing, I see that many more things that can still be proclaimed remain untouched. [Note: [Col. 1002C] This makes it readily clear that the sermon was delivered by Gaudentius shortly after the year 400, since he seems to have received the episcopate around 387, according to what we said in the Preface.] On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, he laid aside the human condition and departed to him whom he loved. Let us therefore venerate the memory of so worthy a priest with due affection, so that through his intercession as well we may more easily obtain the good things we ask for, through the gift of the eternal Son of God, to whom belong all honor, power, and glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen. [Note: [Col. 1002C–D] This is the day on which the Roman Martyrology, as well as Maurolycus, Galesinius, and other more recent Martyrologists, commemorate Philastrius, relying on Gaudentius’s testimony. In both Brescia manuscript codices the following is found concerning Philastrius before Rampertus’s sermon on the Translation of Philastrius; we reproduce it below in the note on Rampertus’s sermon: “In the Martyrology of our Church of Brescia we find written: On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, the Assumption of our most blessed Father Philastrius at Brescia. He lies at Saint Andrew, where the title of the ancient cathedral once stood. In the manuscript Martyrology of the Saibanti Library at Verona, a codex apparently from the thirteenth century and numbered 244, I read: ‘On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August … in the city of Brescia, the burial of Philastrius, bishop of that city.’”]

## Poem in Praise of Blessed Philastrius

### Notice concerning the Following Rhythm

Since this rhythm contains, for the most part, the same material in verse that Gaudentius expressed in the preceding sermon in prose in praise of Philastrius, and since it once also presented Gaudentius as its author, we have placed it here so that the reader devoted to Gaudentius might not feel that anything was missing. Who its author was is unknown. It is nevertheless certain that it is older than the ninth century, for Rampertus mentions this rhythm in his sermon on Philastrius, which you will find below; relying on Rampertus’s authority, we have willingly denied its authorship to Gaudentius.

Certainly neither its style nor its “saliva”—to use Jerome’s expression—suggests Gaudentius as the author. Rampertus’s testimony concerning this rhythm is as follows:

“But he also used regularly to sing a rhythmic hymn about him, which, they say, the bishop Gaudentius had composed with such authority.”

I deny that Gaudentius himself composed it, since the sense of the first line is quite different; moreover, if one pays attention, the rhythm itself contains the letters of its composer’s name, as it were, at the beginnings of the verses.

There seemed certainly to be some basis for conjecture about the author’s name in this testimony of Rampertus, when he says that “the rhythm itself contains the elements of the name of its composer at the heads, so to speak, of the verses, if one pays attention.” Yet from the initial letters of each group of four verses nothing other than “Philastrius, Bishop of Brescia” is produced. Therefore, if anyone can untie this knot, he will be my great Apollo. For I would not believe that Philastrius himself could have composed this rhythm in his own praise.

Perhaps Rampertus understood the author’s name to be contained in another poem that was added by the author himself at the end of that rhythm and is found in the earlier and older of the two manuscript codices of the Church of Brescia mentioned above in the notes at the beginning of the preceding sermon, as follows:

> Once you were perfect, nourishing father Philastrius,  
> In talent, life, understanding, and faith.  
>   
> I, your devoted, humble, little servant,  
> Have striven to set down for you a song of perfect cords.  
>   
> Intercede for your servants by praying on my behalf,  
> Always perfectly, and through the Lord God.

If someone could perhaps prove that the author of that rhythm was a person named, or known by the designation, *Perfectus*, and that for this reason the word was repeated at alternate verse-heads in this poem, I would not strongly resist. But I openly confess that everything here is obscure and uncertain to me; nothing else seems readily apparent except that some pious man younger than Gaudentius pieced together this rhythm in praise of Philastrius from the themes of Gaudentius’s sermon.

Those who first published Rampertus’s sermon acted in bad faith: wishing to make Gaudentius the author of the rhythm, they cut out the words by which Rampertus called this into question. We, however, have restored Rampertus’s testimony in full, as we explain more fully below in its proper place in the notes on Rampertus.

This rhythm is found in the same two manuscript codices of the Church of Brescia in which Gaudentius’s preceding sermon on Philastrius is also preserved. We formerly drew it from those codices, or from one of them, when we published it in the additions to Ughellus. [Note: [Col. 1003] Volume IV, column 526, Venetian edition.]

Since, however, some alteration crept into that edition because of haste, we now present the rhythm again, carefully collated with and corrected from the manuscript copies.

Moreover, so that nothing may remain hidden from the candid reader and lover of truth, we point out that one of these Brescia codices—the later and more recent one—has been corrupted where this rhythm reads that Philastrius was the **seventh** bishop of Brescia. For the following:

> **SEVENTH**, he sat upon the throne of the episcopal seat,

was substituted:

> **TENTH**, he sat upon the throne of the episcopal seat.

But the note itself openly betrays its falsity. For in the earlier and superior codex it is written faithfully:

> **SEVENTH**, he sat upon the throne of the episcopal seat;

Then the law of the poem is opposed to it, and the name FILASTRIUS, which is expressed by the initial letters of each quatrain—if, indeed, this conjecture of ours has any weight—would no longer be present. Finally, in Rampert’s sermon, which precedes the poem in that same later manuscript in which the corruption was introduced, it is explicitly written that Philastrius was the seventh bishop of Brescia, in these words:

> “For this man, the SEVENTH BISHOP, gathering the Church of Brescia to Christ by his preaching at that time, preserved the holy doctrine.”

But I shall briefly explain the purpose and direction of this fraud. A more recent opinion had already begun at that time to gain currency among certain of our own ill-occupied men: namely, that Philastrius had been the tenth bishop of the city of Brescia, whereas previously he had been regarded as the seventh. When some half-learned person noticed that the mark supplied by this poem was highly inconvenient to his opinion, he erased it and covered it with newer ink and red pigment, while leaving untouched both Rampert’s sermon and the older manuscript, which had escaped the violating hand. But let us now turn to the poem itself.

[Col. 1003]

## A Sapphic Pentameter Poem in Praise of Blessed Philastrius, Bishop

(C, G, S)*

**377**

Let every inhabitant sing with me

A fruitful song, where Cleosa flows  
[Note: Perhaps “Clysis” or “Clesis,” as in the manuscripts.]  
—and the Mella flows as well;

Let the curving Ollius, running around,

Sing with me.

**[5.]** May the composer of this song be present,

Our fellow inhabitant of the Benacus shore  
[Note: Alternatively, “our own.”]:

Free man and slave alike, let them resound

The hymns with every voice.

[Col. 1005A] Let the whole joyful populace of the people echo;

Everyone born at Brescia, and the visitor,

Clergy and ranks of the lay people,

Every sex and every age,

Let us be roused to the melody of so great a father,

Whose bones we enjoy forever;

And every bishop who was in this city

In ancient time.

The **SEVENTH** sat upon the seat of the episcopate,

This good and blessed bishop of Brescia,

Noble and wise, who was called

By the name **PHILASTRIUS**.

**[20.]**

No one among us remembers, nor does anyone know,

From whose towers he was born  
[Note: Alternatively, “nor does anyone understand.”];

But this we know: he followed

Blessed Abraham.

**[25.]** Having abandoned his possessions and the things known in his homeland,

And always accompanied by faith,

He continually sought the heavenly doctrine

With the deepest faculties of his mind.

Vigilantly rereading the sacred books,

Abstinent, as though he had been alone,

He wisely instructed himself in a love

Most intensely directed toward heaven.

**378**

A good and simple man, filled with goodness,

Who believed that the Lord and God

Was his own proper portion,

By an everlasting lot.

By divine lot the holy priest

Was consecrated; thereafter he devoted himself

To teaching peoples throughout the world

With holy doctrine.

[Col. 1005C] He himself, by heavenly admonitions, resisted

Barbarian peoples bowed down to idols,

Wicked Jewish men, and the faithless.

**[45.]** A beloved minister of the eternal King;

But he declared that the teachings

Of the faithless Arian sect were false,

Always and everywhere,

Opposing them as though in the deepest sense.

His limbs, struck by continual lashes,

Often poured forth streaming blood

Of rosy hue.

While he continually gave zealous admonition,

The impious were allowed such power against him

That upon his own limbs he bore

The marks of Christ.

**[55.]** But against you, wretched and ignorant Auxentius,

He stood firm in the strength of faith,

Ever refuting the people despite

Your bloody bites.

[Col. 1006A] By faith he himself established many companies

Of people throughout the circuit of the world,

Until he reached Brescia, with the will of the

King of the heavens  
[Note: Alternatively, “king of the peoples.”];

And he found it uncultivated, yet then eager to be instructed,

Although ignorant, nevertheless firmly ready

To receive teaching, with zealous study

And intelligence.

For he stripped the uncultivated people,

Who bore many stains, of their old ones,

Clothing them with new ones, and renewing them

For Christ through wholesome conduct.

**379**

This holy prophet was a man of his age,

Unacquainted with pomp, an ardent

Worshiper of the Lord’s honor,

Seeking nothing for himself;

Well done, faithful one!

He considered the empty honors

Of this age to be of little worth;

He who meditated day and night

Upon the law of Christ.

He despised as small and counted as nothing

All that was great and precious in the world;

But he increased the number of those who sold

At a lower price, as a buyer.

Patient in the affection of a father,

Slow to anger and also quick to forgive;

Sweet, humane, temperate, benevolent,

He was all things to all.

Upright as judge, and a prudent physician,

Who understood spiritual healing:

He mixed liquids of olive oil with Bacchus,

Healing wounds.

And although, as a father, he was always more closely bound

To the lowliest, he himself was bound

To every sex, age, servitude, and

Nobility.

Well done—worthy of wonder and imitation!

He was humble and also gracious in bearing;

Humility was free from filthy behavior,

And grace from arrogance.

The eighteenth day of the month of July carried him away  
[Note: Literally “three times six days.”],

While the clergy wept;

But the crowd of the people mourned greatly

With loud voices.

Therefore we always believe that through his blessed merits

We may be relieved of the burden

Of our sin and may obtain a place

Of forgiveness,

May the everlasting grace of the Father of light,

And of the Son,

And of the Holy Spirit, compassionately be upon us,

With continual remedies

In every year. Amen.

[Col. 1007]

## In the Year of Our Lord 420

## Saint Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage

[Col. 1007]

## Prolegomena

*(Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum of Galland, vol. VIII.)*

[Col. 1007A]

**1.** Aurelius, primate of all Africa, is listed by Saint Fulgentius among the illustrious Fathers and Doctors of the Church in these words  
[Note: Fulgentius, *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, book II, no. 42.]:

> “Who would deny that the blessed bishops Innocent of Rome, Athanasius of Alexandria, Eustathius of Antioch, Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil of Caesarea, Ambrose of Milan, Hilary of Poitiers, John of Constantinople, **Aurelius of Carthage**, Augustine of Hippo, and the other pontiffs, who governed the Churches of God with the greatest vigilance, resisted heretics—whether newly arising or already established—because the Holy Spirit dwelt in them; who neither allowed the ancient wolves to creep into the ecclesiastical flock, nor the new ones to lie hidden disastrously within the Lord’s fold—who, I say, would deny that these men are vessels of mercy, which God prepared for glory?”

So speaks that holy bishop of Ruspe. And Aurelius of Carthage is rightly honored with such praise. “For he was the first of all,” says the very learned man  
[Note: Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 8, near the end.],  
“while Augustine was still silent, to condemn Caelestius for refusing to admit original sin; and thereafter, having convened several synods, he struck his followers with sacred anathema. Hence Saint Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, sang of the Pelagians condemned by him in synod  
[Note: Prosper, *Poem Against the Ungrateful*, verse 90.]:

> “To what other end could the holy  
> Council proceed, whose leader and guiding mind  
> Were Aurelius and Augustine?”

Moreover, he excluded the Donatists from almost the whole of Africa; he converted even the temples of the pagans to the use of the Christian religion; and in seventeen plenary councils held throughout Africa he confirmed orthodox doctrine and discipline with excellent laws.”

**2.** Concerning the period during which Aurelius held office, it is first established that in the year 390 he had not yet been elevated to the episcopal chair. For in that year, at the Second Council of Carthage, convened on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, his predecessor Genethlius presided; yet Genethlius is subsequently known to have ended his life. Aurelius therefore must have obtained the episcopate in the following year, 391, or at the latest in 392. This is Tillemont’s opinion  
[Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. VI, p. 159, and vol. XII, p. 555.].

In what year Aurelius finally died, however, is not so well established that anything certain can be determined. He was still alive in 427, when Saint Augustine committed to writing Book XXII of *The City of God*. There, speaking of the deacons of the Church of Carthage  
[Note: Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8, no. 3.],  
he says:

> “Among whom was Aurelius, and of whom he alone is now in the world of human affairs, already a bishop, to be named with the honor due from us.”

The same is proved by Book II of Augustine’s *Retractions*, written in that same year, where he says  
[Note: The same, *Retractions*, book II, chapter 16.]:

> “For these reasons the venerable old man Aurelius, bishop of that city’s Church, ordered me to write something on the subject, and I did so.”

Moreover, he was still alive in 429, when Augustine’s Letter 231 is said to have been written. In it, while advising Darius about books that Darius had not requested  
[Note: The same, Letter 231, no. 7.],  
Augustine says:

> “If, while you are in Africa, you read all these books, send us your judgment concerning them, or leave them to be sent to us through our lord brother Aurelius.”

Furthermore, as Noris observes  
[Note: Noris, cited above.]—and after him Pagius  
[Note: Pagi, on the year 430, § 26.]  
and Tillemont  
[Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XII, p. 559.]—we learn from the *Commonitorium* of Marius Mercator, presented to Theodosius in 429, that Aurelius was still alive in that very year. For when this writer mentions Ambrose, Innocent, Zosimus, Theodore, and Praylius, he calls them “of blessed memory”; but when he names Aurelius, he does not do so. Thus, concerning Caelestius, accused at Carthage, he says:

> “Regarding the chapters written below, he was accused before Aurelius, bishop of that renowned city, by means of a written complaint from a certain Paulinus, deacon of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, of holy memory.”

Aurelius was therefore still alive in that year, though he died shortly afterward, apparently in the following year, 430. For before Easter in 431, Capreolus was sitting at Carthage, as we gather from his letters read at the Council of Ephesus  
[Note: Council of Ephesus, part II, act 1, p. 1074, vol. III of the edition of Labbe and Cossart.].

When these chronological considerations have been calculated, it follows that the venerable old man, after holding the primacy of Africa for nearly forty years, died in 430  
[Col. 1009A]—the same year in which Saint Augustine gave back his spirit to God—though somewhat earlier, namely on July 20, the day on which his memory is commemorated in the most ancient Calendar of the Church of Carthage, published by Mabillon, where it is recorded in these words  
[Note: Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 164, new edition.]:

> “The thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [so written]: the deposition of Saint Aurilius, bishop.”

**3.** In addition to the addresses to the African Fathers recorded in the Code of the African Church, our Carthaginian bishop wrote various letters, which Tillemont carefully lists  
[Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XII, p. 556 ff.]. One of these is an encyclical letter to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, concerning the condemnation of the heretics Pelagius and Caelestius. The great Baronius inserted it into his ecclesiastical annals from the Cresconian collection  
[Note: Baronius, on the year 419, § 58.].

We, however, followed the copy transcribed by the most learned John Garner, furnished with variant readings and notes, from his third Dissertation addressed to Marius Mercator on the imperial constitutions published in the case of the Pelagians. The subscription of the letter is as follows: “Given on the Kalends of August at Carthage, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta,” that is, in the year 419. Therefore, in our edition, the letter to which it is attached must be withdrawn from that year and placed later, especially if one considers what we have just explained concerning Aurelius’s episcopal tenure.

Moreover, much enhances the importance of this letter what the aforementioned Garner observes  
[Note: Garner, in the note below, p. 130, near the end.]:

> “This was evidently written to the bishops by one who was most learned in the canons, eminent in holiness, extremely jealous of episcopal dignity, most closely associated with Augustine in practical affairs, and almost alone in that respect. Thus knowledge, holiness, concern for dignity, and association with Augustine give Aurelius such authority in this matter as could hardly be greater, even as an example to bishops.”

Thus far the learned man.

**4.** Nor should it be omitted that several men distinguished for holiness and learning wrote letters to this same Aurelius: Innocent I and his successor Zosimus, Paulinus of Nola, Augustine, Alypius, John Chrysostom, and others  
[Note: Tillemont, cited above.]. Saint Augustine also dedicated to our Aurelius, as a mark of honor, that great work *On the Trinity*, as well as his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* and another *On the Work of Monks*. What more need be said? To conclude this account at last in the words of the eminent writer  
[Note: Noris, cited above.]:

> “So much was attributed to Aurelius alone by all the bishops of those provinces that, at the Council of Carthage held under Honorius VII and Theodosius II, the Fathers said to him: ‘It has also pleased all, by common request, that in all letters issued by the council **YOUR HOLINESS ALONE SHOULD SUBSCRIBE**.’”

[Col. 1009]

## Letter of Saint Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, to All the Bishops Established throughout the Provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana

*(From the same source, p. 129.)* (C)

### On the Condemnation of the Heretics Pelagius and Caelestius

To our most beloved and most dearly desired brothers and fellow priests,

[Note: Donatianus presided over the Church of Telepte and the whole province of Byzacena. In that year he appears to have held two synods there: one before Easter, the other around autumn. At the former he received the delegation of the proconsular province, carried out by Vincentius of Culcita and Fortunatianus of Neapolis; at the latter he received Aurelius’s letter together with the imperial constitution. The acts of the former are found in the second volume of the great Collection of Councils; nothing remains of the latter. In recording the former, however, I think an error has crept in: it could not have taken place on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, for that would have fallen on the ninth day of Lent, with Easter falling on March 30. Thus, contrary to the practice of those times, half the Fathers would have been absent from their Churches for a large part of Lent. Nor can the error be adequately corrected by restoring, as seems easy, the numeral X and saying that the synod was held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. That day, too, would have been the first day of Lent, when it would have been unlawful for bishops to be absent from their Churches. But if, retaining the numeral VI, “the Kalends of February” is substituted for “the Kalends of March,” and the synod is therefore said to have been held on January 27, everything fits perfectly: the Nicene canon concerning the holding by primates of a synod of their province before the Lent of Easter would have been observed; the synod would have begun on a Monday, as was customary; and the Fathers would have been present in their Churches at the beginning of Lent. Donatianus, moreover, held a distinguished place in the African Church: he took part in the Council of Carthage before the Conference of 411; he presided with Aurelius over the African Council of 418; he convened the Council of Telepte in 419; in the same year he presided with Aurelius over the African Council and reviewed the canons of the preceding synods, signing second after Aurelius. On the occasion of Donatianus of Telepte, a statement that slipped into the editions of Binius and Christophorus Justellus should be corrected, as though Donatianus had obtained the primacy of his province not by right of age but by right of city. This is wholly contrary to the truth, since in the synodal letter of the Council of Byzacena, Muzonius is called primate and is described merely as an old man, as were the others who presided over the remaining provinces, apart from the proconsular province, by virtue of the privilege of age.]

To Donatianus, of the first see,

[Note: Of the nine bishops whose names are inscribed on the letter, five are named at the Council of Telepte: Donatianus, Januarianus, Felix, Januarius, and Victor. No mention is made of the other four—Palatinus, Primianus, and the two Cajani. I believe that both Cajani, and also Primianus, belonged to the province of Arzugitana, or Tripolitana. Palatinus was a Byzacene. Januarianus was bishop of Tubulbacum; Felix, of Segermes; Januarius, of Cenculiana; Palatinus, of Boseta; and Victor, bishop of Culcita or of the Church of Baha.]

to Januarianus, Felix, Palatinus,

[Note: The manuscripts of Magdeburg, Primino, Gajano, and so forth; Ursinus, Gatano; Baluzius, Galano, and so forth.]

Primianus, Caianus, and the other Caianus, Januarius, Victorinus, and all the others established throughout the territory of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, Aurelius, bishop.

[Note: Two matters deserve notice here. First, Caelestius is named before Pelagius, although Caelestius was the disciple and Pelagius the teacher. Was this because Caelestius was a priest, whereas Pelagius was only a monk? Or because, while Pelagius was concealed at Jerusalem, the whole weight of the affair had long since fallen upon Caelestius, after he had become the leader of the entire movement from being its disciple, as Jerome says in his letter to Ctesiphon? Or because the Africans had no dealings with Pelagius himself, but much with Caelestius? Or because the question of grace was then less heated than that of original sin, the latter portion of the error having fallen to Caelestius to defend, as though by lot? Second, throughout Aurelius’s entire letter there is no mention of the eight canons established against the heresy at the later plenary council. The reason certainly is that subscription was not to be made to those canons themselves, but to the papal *tractoria* of Zosimus, which contained the entire case against both heretics and, at the same time, the judgment of the Catholic Church condemning both together with their doctrines.]

Your holy charity has remembered that you participated in the plenary council concerning the condemnation of Caelestius and Pelagius and their doctrine  
[Note: The reading of Magdeburg, Baluzius, and Ursinus, “their doctrines,” is less suitable to the historical context.]  
most beloved and most dearly desired brothers.

But since, for the honor of God, in whose hand the king’s heart is established (Proverbs 21:4), the authority of the most glorious Christian rulers, who preserve the true and catholic faith,

[Note: The reading of Magdeburg is “who establish.” The heterodox perhaps deliberately erred in flattering the rulers.]

has been added,

[Note: The term “authority” is used to signify a constitution, as is frequently done in the Theodosian Code. The same term is used to signify a law in the single law *On Centurions*, and a rescript in law 31, *On Petitions*, chapter 5. Hence, in the collector’s appendix added to Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, a decretal judgment is called “regular authority.”]

and they wished it to be made known through my humility to all my fellow bishops  
[Note: All printed editions read “he wished it to be made known,” but the rules of Latin required the plural to be restored in place of the singular.],  
I hastened to instruct your honorable fraternity by sending copies, lest some evil, in any part of the province, through the serpentine persuasion of the aforementioned men,

[Note: He calls the heresy excluded from the universal Church because he knew it had been condemned by the Apostolic See. He did not doubt that the letters sent to all the bishops of the world would have to be subscribed by all the bishops of the Catholic party. In the same sense, which was common to all writers of that age, Possidius wrote that the Emperor Honorius followed the judgment of the Catholic Church when he followed the sentence issued by the two highest pontiffs—as though, in that age, the judgment of the Catholic Church and that of the Apostolic See were one and the same in matters of faith.]

which has been excluded from the universal Church of the whole world, might perhaps creep in.

For this reason, therefore,

[Note: We explained at length, in a separate dissertation on this matter (chapter 2), the necessity of requiring a subscription in the Pelagian controversy, which is the subject of the entire constitution; and we traced all the causes of that necessity chiefly to the obstinacy of the Pelagians. Indeed, just as no heresy was more crafty or equipped with more malicious arts than the Pelagian, so none was more obstinate against all the forces of the Church and the age.]

this constitution of the Christian rulers is so necessary that your charity must not remain ignorant of it; and letters from them addressed to me,

[Note: It is not sufficiently clear which letters are meant. Were they some letters distinct from the constitution? The sequence of the discourse favors this. Or were they identical with the constitution itself? The form of the letters suggests this. Or was it the first constitution, which the persistence of the evil compelled them to repeat, and which was sent to Aurelius together with the letter—that is, with the second constitution? This is highly probable. Or, finally, did an imperial mandate or an edict of the praetorian prefect come to Aurelius together with the letter, copies of both of which were sent to the fellow bishops? That is the more likely interpretation.]

having been read together with their copies, your charity will learn how each of you ought to subscribe—whether you are those whose subscription is already recorded in the acts of the synod, or those who were unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa;

for, in the condemnation of the aforementioned heretics, the subscription of all of you was

[Note: Baluzius reads “restored,” which is less suitable to the history and to the writer’s meaning. See the notes.]

complete,

[Note: In the appendix of Salvianus published by Baluzius, the reading is “restored”; in the other editors, “complete.” Both make acceptable sense, though the second is better, since Aurelius is addressing everyone and could require either a complete subscription from all or a restored subscription from a few. What subscription should be considered complete is defined by Leo the Great, in Letter 86, where he writes to Nicetas of Aquileia about the Pelagians.]

so that there is absolutely nothing

[Col. 1013A]

from which any suspicion could reasonably remain regarding anyone’s dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps hidden depravity.

[Note: The Magdeburg manuscript reads “weaker,” whether through dissimulation; this is wholly corrupt.]

[Col. 1014A]

*(In another hand):* I wish you, brothers, to live well and remember me. Given on the Kalends of August, at Carthage, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta.

[Col. 1013]

## Synodal Letter of Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage

From the synodal booklet, in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. II, col. 1184. (S)

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following document are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1013B]

After Theodosius and Nectarius had passed to the heavenly realms, Arcadius, the son of the former, succeeded to the empire, and Honorius, Arcadius’ brother, succeeded Gratian. At that time a local and holy synod assembled at Carthage, comprising one hundred and twenty-seven Fathers; it conducted proceedings against the Donatists—described in the Greek as κατὰ εἰδώλων Δονατιστῶν, a corrupt or elliptical reading—and against every other heresy and the aberrant errors in those regions. Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, presided over it. Having promulgated sacred and divine canons, it endured until the time of the younger Theodosius.  
[Editorial note: The translator appears to have read εἰδωλολατρῶν, “idolaters.”]

[Note: Many statements of the holy bishop made at the Conference of Carthage against the Donatists have also come down to us. Consult the monuments concerning the history of these heretics in *Patrologia*, vol. XI, cols. 1223 ff.]

## Appendix

[Col. 1013]

## Notice Concerning the Following Letter

Baronius explains by what evident signs this letter is shown to be spurious. Writing under the year 374, no. 40, he says:

> “Letters are preserved as having been given in the consulship of that same year, in the name of Damasus, to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, placed by Isidore Mercator at the beginning of his collection. They are preceded by a letter written in the name of Aurelius to Damasus, in which he had requested that decrees of the Roman pontiffs be sent to him from the Apostolic See. But—if I may say so with due respect—what need was there to adorn the vestibule of a great house with falsehoods, thereby casting serious suspicion upon the rest of its contents? How, I ask, could Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, have written to Damasus, the Roman pontiff, and Damasus have returned a letter to him in that very year, especially under those consuls, if, after Saint Augustine had become a Christian, returned to Africa, he found the aforesaid Aurelius serving as a deacon of the Church of Carthage and, after some time, made bishop of that same city?

> “Augustine himself attests this, and in perfectly explicit words, when in his commentary on *The City of God* he mentions his return to Carthage from overseas regions, recounts the miracle of Innocentius’s recovery from an incurable illness, and finally says:

> “‘Holy men visited him every day: Saturninus, then bishop of Uzalum, of blessed memory; the presbyter Gelosus; and the deacons of the Church of Carthage, among whom was Aurelius, and of whom he alone is now in the world of human affairs, already a bishop, to be named with the honor due from us. We often spoke with him about this matter while recalling God’s wondrous works, and we found that he remembered very well what we have related.’

> “So Augustine himself writes. You therefore see how much later the episcopate of Aurelius of Carthage must be placed, and how far it is from the truth that he, already a bishop, wrote to Damasus in this year or received a letter from Damasus. For it is certain that Augustine’s return to Africa, after he had become a Christian, had departed from Milan, and had sailed from the Roman port, took place in the year of Our Lord 389. Thus it is clear that Aurelius was not made bishop of Carthage even fifteen years later, but continued as a deacon.

> “You therefore see how the correct order of chronology disproves the twisted fabrications of others. You will not be surprised, then, if we apply ourselves frequently and diligently to determining the true chronology.”

[Col. 1015A]

## Letter of Aurelius to Pope Damasus (S)*

To the most blessed Pope Damasus, Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

May our humility entreat the glory of the Apostolic See and the grace of your eminence that you deign to send us in writing the decrees that you may be able to find, from the death of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter up to the beginning of your holiness, in accordance with the authority of the Apostolic See, which we have learned is governed through the holiness of your wisdom,

so that through the nobility and prudence of your holiness we may know what was decreed in that holy see during the aforementioned times, and that those who acted against the institutions of the apostolic canons may be identified.

Fare well, most holy pope and most loving father, and pray for us.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. The same, having been read at Rome, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

[Note: The supposed response of Damasus to Aurelius may be read in volume XIII among the apocryphal writings of the holy pope.]

## In the Year of Our Lord 420

## Bachiarius the Monk

*(Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum of Galland, vol. IX.)*

[Col. 1015]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 1015B]

**1.** Bachiarius, a man of Christian philosophy, intending, stripped and unencumbered, to devote himself to God, also chose pilgrimage in order to preserve the integrity of his life. Thus Gennadius  
[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 24.]  
writes; he also adds that Bachiarius wrote a little book on the faith against complainers and slanderers.

No ancient records disclose, however, what country he came from. But from the words of Gennadius just cited, and especially from Bachiarius’s own testimony, I would judge that he went abroad chiefly for the same reason as Paul Orosius; and therefore that our author, like Orosius, was a Spaniard. We understand that Florus, a man of consular rank, also adopted this view, although by a different route  
[Note: Florus, Dissertation 1 addressed to Bachiarius, § 1.].

Bachiarius flourished at nearly the same time as Orosius, that is, at the beginning of the fifth century. Orosius, observing that Spain was infected with the errors of the Priscillianists and Origenists, prepared to leave it and proceeded to Africa. Bachiarius, moved by the same cause, likewise abandoned his homeland and his kindred  
[Note: Bachiarius, *On the Faith*, § 1.],  
saying:

> “Because the stain of a certain heresy had touched our native soil.”

Yet the two men did not have the same purpose. Orosius migrated elsewhere and arrived on the African shores so that, since his fellow countrymen were suffering from the disease of heresy, he might obtain for them the medicine of saving doctrine from Augustine, the bishop of Hippo  
[Note: Orosius, *Commonitorium*, § 4.].

Bachiarius, however, having been brought under suspicion of error, decided to undertake a pilgrimage and at the same time wrote a little book on the faith against complainers and slanderers—not, as Gennadius thought, against the opponents of his pilgrimage, but rather against those who accused him of the error of his homeland  
[Note: Bachiarius, § 2, in the same work.]. He says:

> “As far as I see, it is not speech but region that makes us suspect; and although we are not ashamed of the faith, we are ashamed of the province.”

He appears to confirm this opinion still more clearly when he says  
[Note: The same, *On the Faith*, § 1.]:

> “We are judged by the opinion of certain presiding men, as though we could not be free from the deception of error.”

By these words the author seems clearly to indicate certain bishops who complained that his own faith was suspect or even accused him of heresy. In my judgment, these presiding men were the bishops Eutropius and Paulus, mentioned by Orosius  
[Note: Orosius, *Commonitorium*, § 1.]. Moved by the same concern for the salvation of all, they had undertaken the journey from Spain to Africa and had already delivered a *Commonitorium* to the great teacher Augustine concerning certain heresies.

We leave these conjectures, whatever their worth, to the judgment of learned readers.

[Col. 1017A] **2.** Now, whatever may be established concerning Bachiarius’s nation or homeland, the things we have just reported from Gennadius sufficiently show that he lived as a monk. Clearly, this man, “a practitioner of Christian philosophy,” intending, naked and unencumbered, to devote himself to God for the preservation of the integrity of his life (or “profession,” as the Corbie manuscript reads), undertook a journey … so that, leaving his own land, he might become a fellow-heir of the patriarch Abraham.

This is what the presbyter of Marseilles committed to writing, having learned it from Bachiarius himself, who says [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Bach. *Fid.* § 1)]: “We know our homeland according to the flesh, although now we know it no longer (II Cor. V, 16), and, desiring to become sons of Abraham, we have left our land and our kindred.” Nor does the most learned Florius prove less decisively, by arguments rigorously established, that our author was never elevated to episcopal honor, as many have thought [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Flor. *Dissert.* 1, on Bachiarius, § 7, pp. LIII ff.)]: this certainly cannot be gathered from either of his two treatises anywhere. Rather, the journeys undertaken by a man devoted to Christian philosophy strongly suggest that he persisted in his monastic vocation, since such journeys are scarcely compatible with pastoral responsibility.

Finally, the fictitious claim that Bachiarius was a bishop would be shown beyond all possibility of doubt if these words of his were brought forward [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Bachiar. *loc. cit.* § 7)]: “He is the shepherd,” he says; “where he calls, I shall follow; what he says, I shall ruminate, because he knows that he must render an account to himself for my protection.” Here you have the shepherd assigned to the number of the sheep. Indeed, he was so far from undertaking the governance of others that he was accustomed to bow his head before priests or teachers for sanctification and to humble his heart [Col. 1017C] [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Id. *ibid.*)].

**3.** That Bachiarius devoted himself above all to the cultivation of the sacred writings is plainly evident from the two short works which the changing fortunes of time have not begrudged us. Of these, the first, entitled *Faith*, was brought forth from darkness at the end of the previous century by Ludovico Antonio Muratori, a man outstanding in learning and scholarship [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Murat. *Anecdot.* vol. II, pp. 9 ff. Milan, 1698)]; the second, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, had long since been published for general use, both among the *Orthodoxographi* and in various libraries of the Fathers.

Gennadius mentions the former, as we said above, and testifies that he himself had read it; but he did so with excessive carelessness. For he says that this work had been composed by the author and presented to the bishop of Rome to refute the slanders of his rivals, and at the same time to show that he had undertaken his journey not through fear of men, [Col. 1017D] but through fear of God. The authority of the presbyter of Marseilles misled learned men, among them Tillemont himself [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Tillem. *Mém. eccl.* vol. XVI, p. 473, note 9)]: [Col. 1018A] but that exceedingly perceptive critic would certainly have guarded himself against this had he had the opportunity to read the little work through.

Whatever the truth of the matter may be, the very learned scholar repeatedly praised above was the first accurately to expose and reject Gennadius’s error [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Flor. on Bachiarius, *Dissert.* 1, § 6, pp. XLVII ff.)]; readers are therefore referred to him. The later short work is mentioned by the anonymous writer of Melk, who calls Bachiarius a man of very good judgment [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Anon. Mellic. *de Scriptor. eccl.* chap. 53)]. Not long ago, moreover, the distinguished scholar whom we have just mentioned undertook to prepare an edition of both little books [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Flor. *Bachiar. opusc. edit.* Rome, 1748)]. He based it on the manuscript codices of the Ambrosian Library as well as on previously published copies, and enlarged it with two learned dissertations and clarified it with notes. We have therefore judged this excellent *edition* (ἔκδοσις) preferable to the others; in addition, we have appended Muratori’s observations on Bachiarius’s *Faith*.

[Col. 1018B] **4.** Before bringing the matter to the table, however, it may perhaps not be idle to add one or two observations which Petrus Wesseling inserted concerning our author’s first little work in a letter to H. Venema about fragments of Aquila in the writings of Philo the Jew, published at Utrecht in the year 1748 itself, in which Florius’s edition of Bachiarius appeared at Rome.

First, the learned man examines a passage [Note: [Col. 1017D] (Wessel. cited letter, § 7, p. 29)] which Bachiarius quotes from II Thessalonians II, 3 in these words [Note: [Col. 1018D] (Bachiar. *Fid.*)]: “Unless the *refuga* and the *discessio* should come.” After quoting it, he says: “Bachiarius, as the sequence of the discourse and his very age plainly show, rested in *refuga*; *discessio* is owed to the diligence of another, and an excessively officious one.” So far he.

I would not wish simply to reject this criticism of the distinguished Wesseling as unfair; nevertheless, it may be permissible to make a few observations about it. The Pauline text reads: ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ ἀποστασία—“unless the *discessio* [departure, apostasy] should come.” Thus the Vulgate, and Jerome once and again [Note: [Col. 1018D] (Jerome, *Bibliotheca divina*, works vol. I, p. 1647, Paris edition of the Benedictines; the same, Letter 121 to Algasi[a], question 11, works vol. I, p. 879, Vallarsius’s Verona edition)], Rufinus [Note: [Col. 1018D] (Rufinus, *Commentary on the Creed*, no. 34, p. 97, new Verona edition)], and others.

But Bachiarius must have used an older translation, in which he found *refuga*, just as Augustine certainly read it [Note: [Col. 1018D] (Augustine, *City of God* XX, 19, works vol. VII, p. 596, Paris edition of the Benedictines)]. This word, as Mill observes [Note: [Col. 1018D] (Mill, *Novum Testamentum Graecum*, on II Thess. II, 3, and in the *Prolegomena*, no. 846)], seems to have arisen from an interpretation of the word ἀποστασία, understood as referring to Antichrist himself, as the Greeks explain it. In that sense, “refugee” or “deserter” (ἀποστάτης, *apostates*) would be used.

With this interpretation Sedulius Scotus says [Note: [Col. 1018D] (Sedulius, *Collection on II Thess. II, 3*, in the Paris Library, 1644, vol. I, p. 1011)]: “What he here calls *discessio*, elsewhere he called *refuga* in the Latin copies. Both expressions, however, are to be understood in this way: ‘unless the refugee from the truth should come,’ whether this means the deserter from his own principality, or the departure of the Gentiles, and so forth.”

Sedulius copied this word for word from Pelagius (αὐτολεξεὶ). Yet the passage appears less accurately and with faulty punctuation in the Hieronymian editions, both that of Martianaeus [Col. 1019A] [Note: [Col. 1019B] (Martianaeus, Jerome’s works, vol. V, p. 1083, near the middle)] and that of Vallarsius [Note: [Col. 1019B] (Vallarsius, Jerome’s works, vol. XI, p. 1040)], as well as in Clericus, who republished Pelagius’s commentaries from the Frobenian editions of Erasmus in his *Augustinian Appendix* [Note: [Col. 1020B] (Clericus, *Appendix Augustiniana*, p. 440)].

From what has been said, Bachiarius must have come upon an old Latin codex in which both readings, *refuga* and *discessio*, were found together, and therefore he himself touched upon both at once.

**5.** Wesseling also briefly discussed another passage in our author and said [Note: [Col. 1020B] (Wessel. *loc. cit.*)] that he did not know where Bachiarius had obtained these words [Note: [Col. 1020B] (Bachiar. *Fid.* § 5)]: “Through the good, he worked every desire for me.” “Those words,” he adds, “do indeed give off a Pauline scent, something from the Epistle to the Romans VII, 8, but they are less than genuine. The Greek, as it now stands in the Epistle, offers little assistance, and it is not our inclination to resort to suspicions and conjectures.” [Col. 1019B]

So the distinguished scholar. Yet there is no reason to doubt that Bachiarius had Romans VII, 8 in mind. The Greek reads: Ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, κατειργάσατο ἐν ἐμοὶ πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν—“But sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every desire.”

The standard translator renders it as follows: “But sin, taking occasion, worked through the commandment in me every desire.” Yet there is no need to labor excessively in order to remove Bachiarius from the mark of criticism. He knew that a little later, in verse 12, the Apostle had said: ἡ ἐντολὴ … ἀγαθὴ—“the commandment … is good.” Thus our author directed his eyes to this clause in verse 12 when, in the earlier clause of verse 8, he rendered διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, “through the commandment,” as “through the good,” supplying “commandment” mentally; that is, he followed the Apostle’s meaning rather than the letter.

These, then, are the considerations we have at hand by which Bachiarius’s text, as it stands, may in some fashion be supported. Learned men of sharper judgment may provide better explanations; to their consideration we submit conjectures of this kind [Col. 1020B].

[Col. 1019]

[Note: [Col. 1019D] The Ambrosian Codex is entitled as follows: “Here begins Bachiarius’s *Faith*.” Gennadius, however, seems to have read the same little work under the title: “Book on the Faith.”]

## BACHIARIUS’S *FAITH* (C, S)

[Col. 1019]

[Col. 1019C] **1.** “Everything that was is itself what will be, and there is nothing new under the sun” (Ecclesiastes I, 9, according to the Septuagint). And again the Apostle says: “All these things happened as a figure for us” (I Corinthians X, 6). This is proved by the outcome of the present matter, since the deeds once performed as the sacraments of the evangelical mystery are again renewed in the events of our own age [Note: [Col. 1019D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads this way. Muratori’s edition, however, has “are celebrated”].

Behold now, as far as we understand: Christ asks water from the Samaritan woman, while your Blessedness requires faith from us. As far as I can see, what makes us suspect is not our speech but our region; and those of us who are not ashamed of the faith are made ashamed of our province.

But far be it from us, most blessed one, that among holy men the stain of earthly birth should infect us. “Although we know our homeland according to the flesh, now we know it no longer” (II Corinthians V, 16), and, [Note: [Col. 1019D] These numerals indicate the notes of the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori appended at the end.] [Note: [Col. 1019D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, reports this about Bachiarius’s *Apology*: “He satisfies the bishop of Rome against those who complained and slandered his journey, declaring that he undertook the journey not out of fear of men but for the sake of God, so that, leaving his land and his kindred, he might become a fellow-heir of the patriarch Abraham.” In these final words Gennadius was referring to this passage. Nevertheless, I admit that it is difficult to establish from this alone that Bachiarius undertook any journey.] desiring to become sons of Abraham, we have left our land and our kindred (Genesis XII, 1).

We say this because, just as the Jews do not believe the Samaritans, so they do not believe us, since the soil of our origin has supposedly been touched by the stain of a certain heresy. Thus we are judged by the opinion of certain bishops, as though we could not be free from the deception of error.

The unbelievers once said in a similar way: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (John I, 46). Yet Christ came from there. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Saint Cyprian writes aptly on this subject in his book *On the Unity of the Church*: “The Lord chose Judas among the Apostles, and yet Judas afterward betrayed the Lord. Nevertheless, the faith and firmness of the Apostles did not fall on that account, because the traitor Judas defected from their fellowship.” Saint Jerome likewise writes in Letter 22 to Eustochium: “Nor does he say that the eleven Apostles were broken by Judas’s betrayal.” And against Vigilantius: “The succession of the Apostles was not destroyed by Judas’s betrayal.”]

I ask: did the merits of the Apostles change because of the perfidy and greed of one man, who came forth not merely from the same region but from their very midst? Did the life of the patriarchs become disgraceful because of the fault of their brothers? [Note: [Col. 1020D] The Ambrosian Codex and the Milan edition have, incorrectly in my judgment, “disturbed.”] Did the oracles of the prophets become false because of the inventions of false prophets? When that Levite, Korah, turned aside into heresy, did the rest of his kindred, descended from that stock, contract a stain through their relationship? When the sons of the priest offered alien fire, their brothers continued to carry out the priestly office and, by the honor of their ministry, testified that they were innocent of their brothers’ crime.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] This is the Nicolas who, enrolled among the deacons in the time of the Apostles, gave origin to the heresy of the Nicolaitans; he is mentioned in Acts of the Apostles VI, 5. Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* I, 27, says of him: “The Nicolaitans have as their teacher Nicolas, one of the seven who were first ordained by the Apostles for the diaconate; they live without restraint.” Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* III; Eusebius of Caesarea; Augustine; and others also mention him.]

When the deacon Nicolas turned aside into heresy, the glorious works of God shone forth in the virtues of the assembled brethren. We are charged with the crime of our region. Whoever says this should read about Christ the Samaritan (John VIII, 48): in that province, not only [Note: [Col. 1021B] Bachiarius may be understood here in two ways. Either he calls Christ a Samaritan because Christ often lived in the towns of Samaria, or because the Jews called him a Samaritan as an insult. Saint John VIII, 48, says: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” Augustine observes, both in his *Exposition on Psalm XXX* and in *Exposition on the Gospel of John*, tractate 43, that Christ did not deny being a Samaritan. His words are: “Of the two accusations brought against him, he denied one and did not deny the other; for he answered and said, ‘I do not have a demon.’ He did not say, ‘I am not a Samaritan,’” and so forth. He then derives the reason for Christ’s silence from the term “Samaritan.”] heresy but also the crimes of idolatry have flourished.

In the house of the profane and most wicked Ahab, Obadiah, a servant of the Lord, was found and was worthy to be joined to the bodies of the prophets. In [Note: [Col. 1021D] The passage should be corrected: instead of *Ferepta*, *Sarepta* should be written. This city was formerly situated in Phoenicia near Sidon and still exists in our own time, if recent geographers do not mislead us. Pliny, *Natural History* V, 19: “From there come Euhydra, Sarepta, and Ornithon, towns, and Sidon,” and so forth. The story of the widow mentioned here is taken from Luke IV, where we read: “There were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when heaven was shut up for three years and six months, when there was a great famine throughout the whole land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Sarepta of Sidon, to a widow woman.” The matter is described more fully in III Kings XVII. In Jerome’s time both this town and Elijah’s dwelling still existed; the holy Doctor writes in Letter 27 to Eustochium, in the *Epitaph of Paula*: “Having left Berytus, a Roman colony, and the ancient city of Sidon, she entered Elijah’s little tower on the shore of Sarepta.”] Sarepta of Sidon, among [Note: [Col. 1022C] Sarepta, as stated above, was counted among the cities of Phoenicia. The Phoenicians were also indiscriminately called Canaanites. Thus Saul’s mother is called in the sacred Scriptures at one time τῆς Φοινίσσης, “the Phoenician woman,” and at another τῆς Χαναναίτιδος, “the Canaanite woman.” Likewise, the Canaanite woman mentioned by Saint Matthew XV, 22, is called by Saint Mark VII, 26, a Syrophoenician. The learned Bochart clarified this matter in *Sacred Geography* V, 34, no. 2.] the most wicked race of the Canaanites, a faithful widow is found and chosen as the prophet’s hostess.

Balaam, the teacher of idolatry and head of heresy, was admitted so that he might proclaim Christ. Job descended from the profane and unbelieving stock of Esau. [Note: [Col. 1021D] Consult the addition found at the end of the Book of Job according to the version of the Septuagint and the commentators. Saint Jerome says in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: “Some wrongly think that Job was of the race of Esau. For what is found at the end of his book—because it was translated from the Syriac language, and because he is fourth from Esau, together with the other things contained there—is not found in the Hebrew volumes.”]

Ruth, a relative of Christ’s lineage, is described as a Moabite, whose origin [Note: [Col. 1022D] “Forever” is absent from the Milan edition.] is rejected forever from the doors of the Church. Abraham, the father of faith, descended from the stock of the Chaldeans, for whom the impiety of magic is native and natural. When the Magi worshiped Christ, the ancient reproaches of their errors were not charged against them. Moses, educated in the arts of the Egyptians, was granted the grace of the prophetic spirit. Is error from an earthly province now to be attributed to those reborn in Christ?

**2.** If we acknowledge our homeland, let us also be ashamed of our guilt; for the city into which I have been renewed has become my region, indeed my homeland. Let nothing be attributed to me from earthly relationships, which I remember having renounced. Whoever judges me faithless because of my provincial kinship should know that he himself is faithless, because he has either forgotten or considers uncertain what he knows was confessed in baptism. For undoubtedly the one who accuses me of ancestral error does not abandon earthly kinship.

Certainly, according to the structure of human affairs, a father makes a homeland. How, then, can I be said to have a homeland on earth, when by heavenly command I am not permitted to call or have a father on earth (Matthew XXIII, 9)? [Note: [Col. 1022D] The Ambrosian Codex reads “homeland.” I did not hesitate to correct so obvious an error.]

Do you want me to prove this to you by examples plainly evident in my case, since you attribute the faults of a homeland to me? Did not [Note: [Col. 1022C] These heretics derived their origin chiefly from Novatian, whom Novatus the African assisted in publishing his error. Their perverse doctrine was that no one who had fallen into the crime of idolatry could be admitted into the Church, even if penitent. Saint Cyprian, in whose time this plague broke out and who fought against it more than anyone else, is regarded as a witness to this matter in Letter 52 to Antonianus. Saint Epiphanius, in Heresy 59, no. 1, which concerns the Cathari, says that the Novatians had utterly weakened the virtue of repentance, since they said: μετὰ τὸ λουτρὸν μηκέτι δύνασθαι ἐλεεῖσθαι παραπεπτωκότα—“after the washing, the one who has fallen can no longer receive mercy”; that is, no mercy can be shown to one who sins after baptism. Philastrius, chapter 34 *On Heresies*, and many others report the same. I believe Bachiarius was referring to this in the words that follow, although I readily suspect that some scribal error lies hidden in them.] the Novatians, [Note: [Col. 1022D] Could it be the Donatists?
