The ancient writers often call the African schismatics by this name, especially Saint Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 69, where he says: “The Donatists turned schism into heresy, as though the Church had perished because of the crimes of Caecilianus, whether true or false.” [Col. 1023D] It was therefore characteristic of these people to attribute to descendants the faults committed by their ancestors. The mention of the common people, a term frequently used in the Donatist controversy, also adds considerable weight to this suspicion. In any case, a serious error lies in these words: “they hated heresy no less than the common people”; instead of *odere*, “they hated,” one should write *dilexere*, “they loved,” or something similar.] who dissented from Catholics in this manner, acquire by perverse judgment the leprosy of a shameful heresy because they believed that the succession of past faults ought also to be attributed to their descendants, and did not so much hate heresy as the people?”

If, because of the fault of one person, an entire provincial [Note: [Col. 1023C] This means “to strike with excommunication.” It is so written in our codex. The word is unknown to better authors, but it was used in Bachiarius’s time. Salmasius observed in his notes on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium* that in the manuscript of Augustine’s *Commonitorium to Faustus*, *anathemare* is found twice. Earlier printers substituted *anathematizare* for it, but the distinguished Benedictine Fathers, in their latest edition of Augustine, write *anathemare*. Faustus of Riez also used this word on pages 18 and 19 of the 1586 edition, as did the First Council of Toledo against the Priscillianists. See the distinguished Du Cange, *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*.] generation must be anathematized, then let that most blessed disciple [Note: [Col. 1024D] Something is missing. Saint Leo the Great calls the city of Rome a “disciple of truth.” Perhaps Bachiarius wrote “disciple of Peter.”], namely Rome, also be condemned, since from it not one but two or three, or even more, heresies have now sprung. Yet none of them has been able either to possess or to move the chair of Peter, that is, [Note: [Col. 1023D] It is pleasing to note in passing this proclamation concerning the Roman See. The chair of Peter is called the seat of faith, the inviolate tribunal and sanctuary of religion. Heresies have indeed burst forth even from the city itself, but none has been able to attack the head and bulwark of the Catholic Church; for Christ clearly promised this to Peter. I would add several, indeed the similar words of all the ancients on this subject, were I not restrained by the labor involved in citing so many writers, and were it not preferable to seek rivers rather than streams. The eminent Bellarmine, Baronius, and Sfondratus should chiefly be consulted here.] the seat of faith, or to hold or dislodge it.

Finally, let all the provinces from which streams of differing error have flowed be condemned. That chosen vessel and teacher of the nations (Acts XX, 9), when Eutychus fell from the third story, I suppose, because he was erring somewhat concerning the Trinity, restored the warmth of faith to him and gave him back his life—that is, he granted him pardon. [Note: [Col. 1024C] Saint Luke relates the story in Acts of the Apostles XX, 9: “A certain young man named Eutychus, sitting on the window, while Paul was speaking at length, being overcome by deep sleep, fell from the third story and was taken up dead.” He then adds that Saint Paul restored him to life.]

Perhaps we, still sitting in the window—that is, on the path of light and in the splendor of faith—are condemned too severely, not after examination but on suspicion. They do not know that “with what judgment they have judged, they shall be judged” (Matthew VII, 2), and that “whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be guilty of the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew V, 22). *Raca* means “empty.” And who is empty except one whose inner parts lack the truth of faith and who is like “a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal” (I Corinthians XIII, 1)?

The man who had seen Christ only for one night said to his fellow citizens: “Does our law judge a man unless it first hears what he does?” (John VII, 51). And are these men, who have been followers of the Lord for so many years, judging before they hear and know the matter on which they judge?

[Col. 1024A] If a sentence must be pronounced before investigation, why did the Lawgiver command (Leviticus XIV, 36 ff.) that, before the priest enters and sees the house, it should not be declared unclean lest the house be torn apart by the leprosy of decay or of a ringing sound—that is, of heresy?

Do not, I beg you, most blessed brother, think badly of the province. For your discernment is not unaware that, when the ark of the Lord arrived, Dagon’s head was shattered into a hundred pieces together with both his feet, while his spine is described as having remained intact (I Kings V, 4, according to the Septuagint). We understand Dagon’s head or feet to be the members of the world, that is, the East and the West; [Note: [Col. 1024C] Here all the councils should be understood which had been held against heretics both in the East and in the West. I would nevertheless judge that the First Council of Constantinople and the Council of Aquileia are chiefly indicated by these words. Both were held in the year of Christ 381, that is, only a few years before Bachiarius wrote: the former in the East, the latter in the West; the former ecumenical, the latter convened from nearly all the provinces of the West.] in those regions, under the presence of the Law, the perversity of all errors has been crushed.

It is for you to judge what the middle portion of the spine may be, in which the joints of the knots still remain loosened. Why, I ask, is my province being sought? “I am a stranger, as all my fathers were” (Psalm XXXVIII, 17).

Nevertheless, if it is earnestly asked where I was born, let my confession be accepted, which I answered at the birth of baptism. [Note: [Col. 1024C] From the very beginnings of the Church, it was customary among all Christians—and the custom still persists—for a profession of faith to be made solemnly before baptism. On this subject see Tertullian, *On Modesty* chapter 9 and *On Baptism* chapter 6; Cyprian, Letters 70 to Januarius and 76 to Magnus; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 40, *On Holy Baptism*; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catecheses* 1 and 2; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*; and the other Fathers. Joseph Vicecomes, a doctor of the Ambrosian College, treated the subject most fully in his learned volume *On the Ancient Rites of Baptism* II, 23 ff.] For it was not my homeland that gave me my confession, but my confession that gave me my homeland, because I believed and received (Matthew XXI, 22).

Nor should my Samaritan condition obscure me, because, questioned about Christ at the well, I believed, and, cleansed from the leprosy of unbelief, I recognized him.

Nevertheless, [Note: [Col. 1024D] “Because” is missing in the codex and in Muratori’s edition.] because the principles of apostolic instruction move us—or admonish us [An. “admonish us”] (I Peter III, 15) to present to everyone who asks a reason for the faith and hope that are in us, [Col. 1025A] let us not delay setting forth the rule of our faith to your Blessedness, [Note: [Col. 1025B] This illustrious testimony of Bachiarius would call for me to establish from the treasury of the ancients the authority of the Roman pontiff in determining matters of faith; for, according to Christ’s own testimony, the successor of Peter can neither be deceived nor deceive. But I judge it more prudent to leave this to the fuller treatises of others, lest I burden this little work incongruously with digressions. Let Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*; Bzovius, the same treatise, chapter 17; Cardinal Sfondratus, *Gaul Vindicated*; and innumerable others be consulted.] since you are the architect of that very [Note: [Col. 1025D] The Milan edition reads “of that craft.”] building.

Restoration notes: The three saved textual corrections were applied, and all useful canonical column boundaries from 1025D through 1034C were restored at their associated translated passages. The supplied source contains no 1034A or 1034B boundary.

### 3.

But lest this very thing perhaps arouse suspicion of unbelief—that I answer what is asked only slowly—we believe that God exists; what was, was; what was, will be, never anything else, always the same: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit: one God, and one Son from the Father, the Holy Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

The substance of this one Trinity is one, and these three have one will. Neither is the one who communicates greater, nor the one who receives lesser; neither is the second from the first, nor the third from the second; for thus the prophetic teachings instructed us, saying:

> You shall not go up by steps to my altar (Exod. 20:26).

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1026D] We correct the punctuation of the previous edition. The author refutes certain ancient writers, especially the Arians, who imagined degrees within the Trinity—as though the Holy Spirit were inferior to the Son, and the Son to the Father, whom for that reason alone they called *τὸν ὑπὲρ πάντα Θεόν* (“the God above all”).

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1025D] I could scarcely restrain myself from writing, “What was, is; what is, will be.” My most learned friend changes nothing, but punctuates the passage thus: “We believe that God exists; what was: it was; what was: it will never be anything else, always the same.”

**Editorial note:** I suspect that we should read, “one God the Father,” or “one Father, and one Son from the Father.”

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1025B] From this we may also learn that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. For if the Spirit belongs to the Father and therefore proceeds from the Father because he is the Father’s Spirit, then, since he is also the Son’s Spirit, he must likewise be said to proceed from the Son. This reasoning has such force that St. Augustine, *Tractate* 99 on John, spoke thus: “Why should we not believe that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, since he is himself also the Spirit of the Son?” He repeats the same point in Book XV, chapter 17, of *On the Trinity*. [Col. 1025C] Cyril of Alexandria likewise taught that the Spirit is the Son’s Spirit in his *Letter to Reginus*, cited in volume I, chapter 6, of the Council of Ephesus; add to this Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, and what I noted on St. Paulinus’s *Natales* XI, volume I of the *Anecdota*.

[Col. 1026A] I understand the altar as a kind of foundation of the Faith, from which the nourishment of living food is received; because, by the proper meaning of its name, “altar” signifies nothing other than a high understanding of lofty things. When the name *altare* is divided into syllables and begun from the end, it signifies and expresses a lofty reality.

**Editorial note:** I do not think I am being fanciful if I declare that Bachiarius’s words here refer to the celebrated *discipline of the secret*. For here, in accordance with the practice of the ancients, the wondrous sacrament of the Eucharist is presented under a covering and cloud of words. What indeed is the altar, from which the nourishment of living food is received, if not the most holy sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood? The ancients were accustomed to conceal certain doctrines and ecclesiastical rites, lest sacred things be exposed to the mockery of unbelievers, following Christ’s command that what is holy should not be given to dogs and pearls should not be thrown before swine.

Indeed, certain ecclesiastical mysteries were concealed even from catechumens. St. Augustine bears witness to this in *Tractate* 96 on John: “The sacraments of the faithful,” he says, “are not disclosed to catechumens.” Among the matters chiefly concealed was the unbloody sacrifice of the altar, [Col. 1026B] since it surpasses the understanding of uneducated pagans and of those inexperienced in the faith. I could prove this with six hundred examples, if the learned did not already have at hand the volumes published on this subject by Emmanuel Schelstrate, formerly prefect of the Vatican Library, in which the discipline of the secret is admirably presented and more strongly confirmed. The learned Wilhelm Tentzelius attempted to disparage Schelstrate’s work in published books, but the success of that attempt has already been judged by the learned.

It was therefore enough for Bachiarius merely to indicate so great a sacrament and to call it a profound knowledge of lofty realities, lest a public little book, perhaps falling into pagan hands, expose the venerable mystery to danger. For this reason, later, when speaking about the origin of the soul and introducing the altar, he says: “The foundation of the altar is, as it were, a certain root of depth; in its secrecy let us also join the account of the soul.” You see that, according to our author, both the origin of the soul and the institution of the venerable sacrament belong to the discipline of the secret. [Col. 1026C] But this is more than enough, and rests on mere conjecture.

We must not ascend to this Faith by steps, lest, by thinking unequally, we make a passage from lower to higher; rather, we should enter with the equal step of our heart, so that we understand the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one substance, one power, and one virtue.

For “Father” is the primary name of divinity in itself, which is believed and which is called “God the Father”; the Son is God from the Father, not from himself, but from the Father.

**Editorial note:** The words “but of the Father” are superfluous.

The Father is God, and the Son is God; but the Father is not the same as the Son, although the Father is believed to be what the Son is.

**Editorial note:** In the Gothic-Hispanic book of prayers published by the distinguished Joseph Blanchinus, the ancient Unitarians of those regions are tacitly indicated in these words: “The Son is believed to be not the very one who is Father, provided nevertheless that he is confessed to be what the Father is,” p. 18.

And the Holy Spirit is not the unbegotten Father, but the Spirit of the unbegotten Father. The Son is begotten, not the Spirit’s Son, but the Son himself, upon whom the Spirit was sent by the Father.

**Editorial note:** I have scarcely any doubt that Bachiarius wrote, “but the Spirit of the Son.”

Therefore, since the unbegotten Father is the one whose Spirit he is, the Holy Spirit is incautiously called unbegotten, lest unbelievers suppose there to be two unbegotten beings or two Fathers.

**Editorial note:** Bachiarius asserts that it is careless to call the third person of the Trinity unbegotten, and his reasoning seems entirely sound to me. In the Creed attributed to St. Athanasius and adopted by the Catholic Church, however, we read: “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.” If the Spirit is not begotten, then he is unbegotten, and thus the Church stands against Bachiarius. Indeed, we are taught that the one Word may be called begotten both by John in the Gospel, where he calls him “Only-begotten” twice, and by the Apostles’ Creed and many of the Fathers. Therefore the Spirit cannot be called begotten, and consequently may be called unbegotten.

Yet I shall clearly demonstrate, if I am not mistaken, that Bachiarius thought correctly. First, we must observe that the word *unbegotten* belonged to the Father in such a way that ancient writers regarded it as his personal property. Eusebius of Caesarea, in chapter 19 of Book II of the acts of the Council of Nicaea collected by Gelasius of Cyzicus, says:

> Εἷς ἀγέννητος ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατήρ. Εἷς καὶ ὁ γεγενημένος ἐξ αὐτοῦ μονογενὴς υἱὸς Θεὸς λόγος.

> [Col. 1027B] One is the unbegotten God and Father. One also is the Only-begotten Son, God the Word, begotten from him.

He adds:

> ὥσπερ οὖν οὐκ ἔστι συναγέννητος τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ Θεὸς ἕτερος, οὕτως οὐδὲ συγγεγενημένος.

> Therefore, just as there is no other God unbegotten together with God the Father, so neither is there another begotten together with him.

St. Thomas likewise notes this in *Against the Errors of the Greeks*, *Opusculum* I, chapter 8. Accordingly, the ancient author of the *Questions Attributed to St. Athanasius*, question 5, calls “unbegotten” the proper surname of the one Father:

> Ἰδίον τοῦ μὲν Πατρὸς τὸ ἀγέννητον, τοῦ δὲ υἱοῦ τὸ γέννητον, τοῦ δὲ ἁγίου πνεύματος τὸ ἐκπορευτόν.

> It is proper to the Father to be unbegotten, to the Son to be begotten, and to the Holy Spirit to proceed.

[Col. 1027C] Nor do St. Athanasius in his *Letter to Serapion*, Gregory Nazianzen in Oration 23, *In Praise of Jerome*, near the end, Isidore in Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, section 1, Anselm in the middle of the *Monologion*, chapter 54, and other Fathers speak differently. Among them Augustine, in Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 26, says: “The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten,” a statement he repeats elsewhere.

[Col. 1027A] Bachiarius therefore rightly observed that the Holy Spirit is carelessly called unbegotten, for otherwise that word would no longer be proper to the Father. But it is one thing to say that the Spirit is not begotten, and another to call him unbegotten. The Church itself uses the first expression, but scarcely tolerates the second, lest two unbegotten beings—and therefore two Fathers—appear to exist. This is Bachiarius’s reasoning, and it is also the reasoning followed by St. Augustine in Sermon 58, *On the Season*, the third sermon after the Epiphany octave. He says:

> The Holy Spirit is said nowhere to be either unbegotten or begotten, lest, if he were called unbegotten like the Father, two Fathers should be understood in the holy Trinity; or, if he were called begotten like the Son, two Sons should likewise be thought to exist in that same holy Trinity.

The anonymous author of the book *On the Trinity and the Unity of God*, chapter 1, in volume IV of St. Augustine’s works, likewise says:

> [Col. 1027D] Right faith declares that the Holy Spirit is neither unbegotten nor begotten; for if we call him unbegotten, we will seem to affirm two gods, and so forth.

St. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 50, *On the Nicene Faith*, says:

> We venerate the Holy Spirit as God, neither unbegotten nor begotten.

And in Oration 26, section 3, he acknowledges:

> Πνεῦμα ἓν ἐκ Θεοῦ τὴν ὕπαρξιν ἔχον, παραχωροῦν Πατρὶ μὲν ἀγεννησίας.

> The Spirit has his existence from God, yielding to the Father in this one respect: that the Father is unbegotten.

[Col. 1028B] The same distinguished Doctor repeats this in other places. After all these writers, the eleventh Council of Toledo, in its profession of faith, likewise confesses the Father to be unbegotten while saying: “The Holy Spirit is believed to be neither unbegotten nor begotten, lest, if we call him unbegotten, we should speak of two Fathers,” and so forth.

Hence the learned Ruiz, of the Society of Jesus, in his commentary on St. Thomas *On the Trinity*, disputation 52, sections 3 and 8, holds that, strictly speaking, the Holy Spirit is not unbegotten. Consult him there, and also Vasquez, volume II, on the first part of St. Thomas, disputation 140; it will be evident how prudently Bachiarius adopted this position.

The Son, begotten by the Father before the ages, cannot have another begotten companion, so that he may be believed to be the Only-begotten and so that two begotten beings may not be named. The Father is one and unbegotten, the Son is one and begotten, and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, is coeternal with the Father and the Son, because there is one work and one operation of will in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

**Editorial note:** Thus Ambrose. The earlier edition less correctly has “among unbelievers.”

The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and coeternal with the Father and the Son; but the one is born, while the other proceeds, as it is written in the Gospel of blessed John:

> The Spirit who proceeds from the Father—he will announce all things to you (John 15:26; 16:13).

Therefore, the Holy Spirit is to be regarded neither as the unbegotten Father nor as the begotten Son, but as the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father. [Col. 1028A] Yet what proceeds is not something other than that from which it proceeds. If the person is asked about, he is God.

[Col. 1028D] This threefold conjunction and conjoined division both excludes union among the persons and maintains unity in the distinction of the persons.

Thus we believe in the most blessed Trinity: that it is of one nature, one divinity, one and the same virtue and substance; and that there is no difference between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, except that the one is Father, the other Son, and the other Holy Spirit—Trinity in the subsistent persons, Unity in nature and substance.

We also believe that the Son was born in the latter days from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, and assumed flesh and a soul of human nature. In that flesh we believe and confess that he both suffered and was buried and rose from the dead; and in that same flesh in which he lay in the tomb, after the resurrection he ascended into heaven, from where we await him coming for the judgment of the living and the dead.

**Editorial note:** Who does not know Helvidius’s heresy and its impious doctrines against the virginity of Mary? This notorious scoundrel lived near the end of the fourth century, at precisely the time when I have reasonably maintained in the *Prolegomena* that our Bachiarius wrote. This may also provide some confirmation: our author mentions no heretic except him. I suspect the reason is that he judged nearer and more immediate heresies to require a more explicit refutation than those condemned long before. Jerome answered Helvidius’s blasphemies in a most distinguished book, [Col. 1029B] defending the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary by notable arguments. Epiphanius likewise entered the contest when recounting the heresy of the Antidicomarianites; indeed, he wrote a lengthy letter against the same heretics, which may be read there.

[Col. 1029A] We also confess the Virgin from whom we know that he was born to have been a virgin before giving birth and a virgin after giving birth, lest we be considered participants in the error of Helvidius.

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1029C] These words seem to have been directed against Origen, who in several places—especially Book IV *On the Resurrection*, the exposition of the first Psalm, and the *Stromata*—maintained that at the final day of judgment the very flesh which human beings used in life would not rise again. Yet I think that times nearer to Bachiarius are meant here. Near the end of the fourth century John, bishop of Jerusalem, reheated the same errors of Origen and gave Saints Epiphanius and Jerome occasion to write for Catholic truth. Jerome’s excellent Letter 61 to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem should be consulted. I think that Bachiarius later indicates this bishop without naming him when he says: “Nor, as some most absurdly do, do we say that another flesh will rise instead of this one.”

We confess also the resurrection of our flesh, entire and perfect—the flesh in which we now live in this present age, whether governed by good practices or subjected to evil deeds—so that in that same flesh we may either endure the torments of punishment for evil deeds or obtain the rewards of good things for good deeds. We do not say, as some most absurdly do, that another flesh will rise in place of this one, but this very flesh, with absolutely no member cut off from it and no part of the body severed.

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1029D] Rufinus has “the resurrection of our flesh”; I think the reading of the Ambrosian manuscript followed by Muratori should be corrected accordingly.

This is the treasure of our Faith, which we preserve, sealed with the ecclesiastical Creed that we received at baptism. Thus we believe with the heart before God; thus we confess with the lips before human beings, so that their knowledge may produce faith among human beings, and his image may render testimony to God.

This is the staff of our defense, with which we strike the mouths of those who murmur against us—those who bark at us as we pass along the road of this age, driven by the yoke of custom rather than by the pursuit of reason.

**Editorial note:** The presbyter of Aquileia, section 1, likewise calls the profession of faith that he sent to Anastasius a staff: “So that, if enemies should perhaps bark against me, I might offer you a certain staff of my confession with which they could be driven away.” See St. Jerome, Book XI against Rufinus, section 2.

This is the shield of our faith, by which we repel and avoid the darts of slanderous words and poisoned suspicions, lest the enemy’s word, which is aimed at striking, find in us some exposed limb, stripped of the protection of faith. But let us be silent about these matters, since our concern now is not to strike back at the enemy but only to avoid him.

**Editorial note:** Bachiarius says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and says nothing of the Son. At that time, evidently, the heresies had not yet arisen that compelled the Church to define this question, as happened in subsequent centuries. [Col. 1028C] The first Council of Constantinople, the second ecumenical council, called the Spirit proceeding from the Father in the received Creed, but made no statement about the Son. For a long time the whole Church preserved the Creed as received from the council; Catholic writers therefore omitted the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son without censure, but did not deny it. Later the Western Church most prudently judged that the clause *Filioque* should be added to the Creed. I shall return to this subject below, when discussing the *Quicumque* Creed. See also my notes on line 139 of St. Paulinus’s *Natales* XI, vol. I of the *Anecdota*.

**Editorial note:** Several words are missing. Bachiarius perhaps wrote: “If the person is asked about, [it is] the Spirit; if the nature is asked about, he is God.” Jerome, the foremost critic among the ancients, long ago observed that the repeated occurrence of the same word within a few lines often causes copyists to omit intervening material; see his Book XI, *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapters 40 and 42, Book VI on Jeremiah, chapter 30, and elsewhere.

**Editorial note:** These words, and much that follows, have been taken almost verbatim from Rufinus’s *Apology to Anastasius*. See Dissertation I, chapter 11. This dissertation of the most learned editor is to be presented elsewhere.

**Editorial note:** Rufinus has *sit*. Shortly afterward, on the authority of both Rufinian and Ambrosian manuscripts, we did not hesitate to write *nec inter*; Muratori’s distinguished edition has *ne*.

### 4.

[Col. 1030A] Now, if we are also asked what we think about the soul, we believe that it was made, just as we read in the prophet Jeremiah, where King Zedekiah says:

> The Lord lives, who made this soul for us (Jer. 38:16).

**Editorial note:** The most eminent and distinguished Cardinal Norisius has dealt with this question in *Vindiciae Augustinianae*, chapter 4, section 3, so thoroughly that nothing can really be added. I shall draw a few points from him. It is certain that for many centuries even the most eminent Fathers remained hesitant in assigning the origin of the soul. [Col. 1030B] Indeed, Augustine and Jerome, although they debated this question in various letters, were unable to establish anything certain. Consult Augustine’s letter to Marcellinus and Jerome’s *Apology against Rufinus*, as well as Augustine’s letters to Jerome and to Optatus and his four books *On the Origin of Souls*; nevertheless, both acknowledge that the matter is doubtful.

[Col. 1030C] St. Eucherius, in his commentary on Genesis 3; Pomerius, in his book *On the Soul*; the African Fathers of the sixth century, in the synodal letter sent from Sardinia to Byzantium; and St. Fulgentius, in Book III of *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, all remained hesitant before the same obstacle. The last of these, in chapter 18, praises Augustine most highly for having doubted concerning this matter, and concludes chapter 20 with these words: “How much better, then, that we refrain from contending over this question, in which we recognize that we labor in vain! Especially since we see that what was by no means defined by the holy men who preceded us must be sought by us with all the greater caution and restraint, since we see that those distinguished men did not reach its conclusion.”

Cassiodorus, in his book *On the Soul*, chapter 14, and Gregory the Great, Book VII, letter 53, were likewise uncertain. St. Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 23, included among the doctrines he proposes as matters to be held by faith this statement: “That the origin of the soul is uncertain.” The eminent Cardinal Norisius gathers other authorities from later periods in the distinguished work mentioned above. No one, therefore, will wonder that Bachiarius remained so uncertain in this opinion.

[Col. 1030D] But if we are asked from what it was made, I confess that I do not know, since I do not recall having read anywhere. Therefore, I am not ashamed of ignorance, because I am not taught by reading; nor am I afraid of danger, because I do not presume to assert what I have not read—lest I be found to transgress the prophetic commandments, which order that blood not be eaten, adding (Lev. 18:14):

> For the blood of every flesh is its soul.

**Editorial note:** St. Augustine, in *Against Adimantus*, chapter 12, warns that it was never written that the human soul is blood. He repeats the same point in Book XI of *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, chapter 6. Basil the Great should also be read, *Homily* 8 on the *Hexaemeron*, section 2.

For what is it to eat blood, if not to dispute about the soul? Therefore, we may say that the flesh founded for us in Adam was compacted from the qualities of the world and substance, with God as maker and author; but let us consign the blood to the foundation of the altar—that is, let us leave it to the one who created it to know from what he created it.

**Editorial note:** My learned friend has restored the passage very well as follows: “and substance, with God as maker,” etc.

**Editorial note:** I can readily believe that *fundamus* should be restored. Rufinus, in section 6 of the *Apology*, says: “Up to the present I do not hold anything certain and definite concerning this question; but I leave it to God to know what is true . . . apart from what the Church plainly teaches, namely, that God is the Creator of souls and bodies.”

For the foundation of the altar is, as it were, a certain root of depth; in its secrecy let us also join the account of the soul, about which we cannot dispute.

Therefore, we do not say that the soul is a part of God, as some assert, because God is indivisible, undivided, and impassible, whereas the soul is subject to various passions, as the daily course of events proves. [Col. 1031A] Nor do we say that it was made from some creature, lest we make it inferior to the other creatures over which it has been appointed mistress, if it acts rightly. Rather, we say that it is formed solely by the will of God. His power does not require matter from which to make what he wills; his will itself is the matter of those things whose coming-to-be or existence he commands.

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1031B] The ancient Fathers held that souls are created by God at the conception of each individual human being. As the most eminent Cardinal Norisius teaches in *Vindiciae Augustinianae*, chapter 4, section 3, this view held the stronger authority until the Pelagian heresy. [Col. 1031C] When the heretics then pressed the argument that souls, if created by God, could not be produced with sin, St. Augustine and the most eminent Fathers preferred the other opinion: that souls are transmitted and propagated from the soul of a parent. Augustine’s words acquired such force that for many centuries after him very holy writers doubted the soul’s origin, until the view of the Scholastics prevailed, the transmission of souls became obsolete, and their creation became common teaching in the Church. This is evident from many passages in Augustine, especially Book X on Genesis, chapter 23; Letter 28 to Jerome; and Letter 147. Thus we may also infer something about the date at which Bachiarius wrote: if Pelagius’s ravings had occupied the Christian commonwealth when he composed this *Apology*, he would certainly not have said that the opinion according to which souls come to us by transmission—a view which learned men, following Augustine, judged more congenial to Catholic doctrine—met with less approval from him.

[Col. 1031D] But we do not yield to that assertion in which some take needless delight, believing that souls are generated by transmission, because blessed David contradicts this suspicion when he says:

> Know that the Lord himself is God: he made us, and not we ourselves (Ps. 99:3).

And elsewhere:

> He fashioned their hearts one by one (Ps. 32:15).

Where can transmission find a place when hearts are fashioned one by one, or when it is said, “He made us, and not we ourselves”? Those who say that souls are generated by transmission are thereby said to assert that we make ourselves.

But this **[editorial note: The Milan edition has *scientia*, contrary to the autograph; its reading has therefore been introduced into the text, though perhaps it should read: “But prophetic knowledge rebukes these persons [namely, the supporters of transmission].”]** prophetic knowledge rebukes when it says:

> He made us, and not we ourselves.

Apart from the Trinity alone, we believe and confess that everything which in heaven, on earth, or in the sea has power, is acted upon, or is moved, is a creature.

### 5.

**Editorial notes:** I prefer the reading *esset* (“was”) here. Muratori reads *facit* (“makes”) in the clause “because God does not make evil.” At the description of the angel’s lofty rank, perhaps read *descripta* (“described”), or *quae scripta est* (“which is written”). The Milan edition has *nunc* (“now”), apparently through a printer’s error. Read, if you please—and at my own risk—*qua* (“by which”) in the following construction. At the statement on created food, it seems one should write: “as was said: ‘And it was so. And God saw that they were very good.’”

We understand the devil not to have been made as he is the devil, nor to have possessed a distinct kind of nature by which he was born a devil; rather, we believe that he earned this name, not that God gave it to him. [Col. 1032A] Nor was he unbegotten, because he is not God; nor was he made a devil, because God did not make evil, but he was made a good angel, as Scripture demonstrates:

> Through the good, every desire was brought about for me (Rom. 7:8).

For I believe that he was an evil angel, as the Apostle says:

> A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows (2 Cor. 12:7).

And elsewhere:

> Unless the deserter and the apostasy should come (2 Thess. 2:3).

Therefore, the one who is now a deserter was once, in the sight of the Creator, upon that lofty rank which is written by the prophets, when it is said:

> And you were the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty (Ezek. 28:12),

and elsewhere:

> How did Lucifer, he who rose in the morning, fall from heaven? (Isa. 14:12).

We say that he received from his Maker a nature capable of good and evil, surrounded with the glory and honor of immortality; he also received the dignity of knowledge. But, lifted up in pride, he believed that what was not his belonged to him, because he did not see the Lord who had made him. “I am,” he says, “and there is no other besides me” (Isa. 47:12).

Hence he was assigned to earth and ashes, as it is written:

> Why are you proud? Earth and ashes (Eccli. 10:9),

and:

> The beginning of sin is pride (ibid., 15).

Assigned to Tartarus and everlasting fire, he is destined for perpetual punishment, not immortal life.

[Col. 1033A] We believe that every creature of God which the Creator granted for the use of food is good, as it was done: “And God saw that they were very good” (Gen. 1:30–31).

**Editorial note:** It seems that the text should read: “as was said: ‘And it was so. And God saw that they were very good.’”

**Editorial note:** The Manichaean doctrine is plainly refuted here. Among their other ravings, by which they introduced their most pernicious heresy into the East, they also asserted that the devil had not originally been evil. [Col. 1032B] Let St. Epiphanius be heard, *Against Heresies* 66, which concerns the Manichaeans, section 16. Refuting their opinion, he says:

> Ἅμα δὲ καὶ περὶ διαβόλου οὕτως διαληπτέον, οὐκ ἀπὸ κτίσεως φυσικῶς κακοῦ κεκτισμένου, ἀλλὰ ἑαυτῷ μετὰ χρόνον τὸ ποιεῖν κακὸν ἐφευραμένου.

> [Col. 1032C] We must also understand the matter of the devil in this way: he was not created evil by nature from the beginning of his creation, but later devised for himself the practice of doing evil.

He proves the same point at greater length below, in section 62. Nor was this insane opinion held only by the Manichaeans; it was also held by the Priscillianists, who gathered together the contagion of every heresy. Leo the Great, in Letter 93 to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, chapter 6, describes their error in this way:

> The sixth statement indicates that they say that the devil was never good, that his nature is not the work of God, but that he emerged from Chaos and darkness; that he has no author of his own being, but is himself the origin and substance of all evil. Yet the true faith, which is Catholic, confesses the substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, to be good, and declares that evil has no nature, since God, who is the creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good, and so forth.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 2, and Coccius, Book IV, article 5, volume II, should also be consulted on this matter. [Col. 1032D] This error was condemned in antiquity in the ancient *Chapters against the Manichaeans*, which I appended after Bachiarius’s works. There we read:

> If anyone asserts that the prince of this world, that is, the devil, and the mass of darkness were created, and that he was not made a good angel by God and afterward changed by his own perversity, let him be anathema.

But we consider it useful to abstain from these things for a time, not out of religious superstition or abhorrence of God’s creation, but for the sake of bodily continence, according to the Apostle’s counsel, who says:

> It is good not to eat meat or drink wine (Rom. 14:21).

To use them when one wishes, and to abstain when one chooses, lies within human power.

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1033C] The holy use of fasting was attacked by Jovinianus, whom I believe lived during Bachiarius’s time, and the Catholic Church immediately opposed him. St. Jerome, a most holy man and the first to cut down this heresy, set out the heretic’s errors in two books. In one of them he discusses the usefulness of fasting at length and also learnedly proves that every creature of God which the Creator granted for the use of food is good, as Bachiarius says—although Jovinianus foolishly denied it. St. Augustine, speaking of Jovinianus in his book *On Heresies* addressed to Quodvultdeus, section 82, says: “Like the Stoic philosophers, he said that all sins were equal; that a person could not sin after receiving the washing of regeneration; and that fasting or abstinence from certain foods was of no benefit.” See also St. Ambrose, Letter 82 to Vercellae, and Gennadius, *Profession of Faith*, and so forth.

We approve marriages, which were granted with God as their author; within them we praise continence. We exalt and admire virginity, as an outstanding shoot emerging from a withered trunk’s root.

**Editorial note:** [Col. 1033D] Jovinianus’s other heresy was to place marriage on an equal footing with the sacred vow of virginity. St. Augustine, in the passage cited above, adds: “He made the virginity of consecrated women and the continence of men who choose a celibate life equal in merit to chaste and faithful marriages, so that certain consecrated virgins of advanced age in the city of Rome, where he taught these things, are said to have married after hearing him.” [Col. 1034C] St. Jerome likewise presents this as another of his heresies in Book I against Jovinianus: “He says that virgins, widows, and married women who have once been washed in Christ, if they do not differ from the others in their works, possess the same merit.” Gennadius of Massilia, in the *Profession of Faith* published in the appendix to volume III of St. Augustine’s works, section 68, says similarly: “To equate marriages with virginity consecrated to God, or to believe that those who abstain from wine or meat for the sake of disciplining the body gain no additional merit—this is not Christian, but Jovinian.”

We believe that the distinction between the righteous and sinners arises not from the condition of the Creator but from the choice of the will. With fullest faith we accept repentance for sins and regard it as a kind of second grace, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> [Col. 1033B] I wished to come through you, so that you might have a second grace (2 Cor. 1:15).

### 6

We receive the Old and New Testaments with an equal balance of faith; and, as with the scale of a moving balance running through its marked divisions, so we weigh the events attested by the testimonies with active meditation. Without emptying history of its credibility, we believe that everything we read actually happened; rather, in accordance with apostolic teaching, we search out in these events a spiritual meaning, insofar as the Lord grants it—provided that this meaning concerns the type of Christ and the Church, or contributes to the amendment and correction of morals. This too accords with what the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them as a figure for us” (1 Cor. 10:6).

[Note: Origen’s error on this matter is very well known; the Greatest Doctor often censures it, especially in the book against John of Jerusalem, no. 7. See, if you wish, Dissertation 2, chapter 4. This too is to be presented elsewhere in the Dissertation.]

Elsewhere blessed Peter says: “Every utterance requires interpretation” (2 Pet. 1:20). Every Scripture that does not accord and agree with the ecclesiastical canon we not only do not accept, but condemn as foreign to the truth of the Faith. We do not readily assent to strange and unknown stories concerning the contents of Scripture; nor does a new doctrine quickly enter the recesses of our ears, because we read of a Virgin, new and hidden, whom we suspect to signify a raw or secret doctrine.

[Note: This passage is, if any passage ever was, extremely corrupt. I would gladly restore it as follows: “Because we read that the Virgin is called Alma, that is, hidden or concealed.” Saint Jerome should be consulted on Isaiah 7:14, where, among other things, he says: “Therefore ALMA signifies not only a girl or VIRGIN, but, with emphasis, a virgin HIDDEN or SECRET, one who has never been exposed to the eyes of men.” Bachiarius often plays upon Hebrew names, as we observed in Dissertation 2; anyone may observe the same in the other little book On the Restoration of the Lapsed.]

This doctrine is forbidden to be examined lest it deceive human hearts, under the appearance of truth, through the beauty and sweetness of its words and inventions. It is a virgin doctrine, unknown to any ecclesiastical or Catholic man, but always nurtured among women—that is, among souls that are always learning and, credulous toward every spirit of deception, readily mingle themselves with it, without caring from what source they conceive. Yet the Lord commanded in the Law that marriage should take place only with someone from one’s own tribe—that is, with that understanding of the faith which comes from the seed of the fathers, in other words, from doctrine, and which is ennobled by the lineage and ancestry of Abraham, who first believed while still uncircumcised.

[Note: Read “understanding.” Philo Judaeus and Origen, Philo’s follower, call it νοῦς (*nous*, “understanding”); both explain allegorically in innumerable passages those marriages. Translators, however, often fail to preserve the propriety of the expression and render νοῦς as *mens* (“mind”), a feminine word.]

It is a virgin doctrine that pleases itself only in secret and is ashamed to come out in public.

[Note: The Medicean edition corruptly reads “tanto,” though the autograph supports it.]

Such a doctrine we not only flee, but also condemn with a public voice, declaring it foolish to believe what either we ourselves cannot defend or ought not to reach the ears of the public.

[Note: I would prefer “considering.”]

### 7

[Note: See the excellent Inquiry concerning the Fasts of the Ancient Christians in Cabassutius, chapter 5, in *Notitia saeculi II*. The true purpose of fasting did not consist solely in the Christian people abstaining from food and feasting, but also in withdrawing from other pleasures. This devout practice is frequently described among the ancient Fathers, especially Saint Maximus, Saint Leo, and other early Fathers. The most distinguished P. Thomassinus published a very elegant treatise on fasts. See also my Inquiry concerning the Fasts of the Four Ember Seasons, which you will find in this book, where it is intended to illuminate this passage.]

We observe more carefully the fasts prescribed according to ecclesiastical rule and discipline, so that at the three seasons of the year our “masculine” quality (Exod. 34:23)—that is, the work of virtue which surpasses every other work—may appear. And whenever fasts are proclaimed by the Church, we wish to fast not only from customary usage but also from social intercourse, conversations, and greetings that introduce conversations.

[Note: This is how Muratorius published the passage. But the Ambrosian manuscript reads: “And because, with God as witness, we also write these things.” I consider the learned man’s conjectural correction entirely sound: “And although, with God as witness, we also feel these things as we write them.”]

Although, with God as witness, we feel these things as we write them, nevertheless we do not flatter ourselves about the truth in such a way that, if priests or teachers—who are the heads of the people and the pillars of the churches—should, by disapproving any of the things we have professed, say something more correctly, we would be slow to adopt their judgment.

[Note: Read “disapproving”; *aliquid* (“something”) is a variant reading noted by a copyist in the margin of an earlier exemplar in place of *quodlibet* (“any”). The copyist, inserting both readings, disturbed the sense. A nearly similar error remains in the very ancient book of the Shepherd, book 1, vision 4, no. 2: “Your solitude and your anxiety.” The former word should boldly be deleted. Hermas immediately repeats without the gloss: “Cast your anxieties upon the Lord.” And in vision 3, no. 11: “You have not cast your anxieties upon the Lord.”]

We remember the command that is written: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7).

For we are not so foolish as to refuse to humble our hearts before those to whom we bow our heads for the sake of sanctification. He is a shepherd: wherever he calls, I shall follow; whatever he says, I shall ruminate upon, because he knows that he must render an account to God for my protection (Heb. 13:17).

[Note: Ambrosius has this reading. The earlier edition reads: “These are the things which …”]

These are the matters that, for the present, I have been able to bring before you. If anything seems to have been omitted intentionally or still troubles you, deign to ask without embarrassment, so that I may answer without hesitation and either correct my error or be confirmed in the Faith.

I call every reader of these words of confession to witness that, if anyone takes anything away from them, God will take away his part from the book of life (Rev. 22:19).

[Note: The printed editions wrongly read “from the same things” and “and God.” See Dissertation 2, chapter 1.]

For if anyone believes that we speak one thing with our lips and hold another in our hearts, God can inspect our heart, as I said above. We have offered our lips for confession; concerning them, by which men can judge, we have made satisfaction. Thus, by two witnesses, every word of ours shall stand (Deut. 17:6): by God, whose judgment against us we invoke if we deceive, and by men, whose suspicions we correct through our confession, lest they sin further against us by continuing to think evil of us.

[Note: He imitates the frequently cited apology of Rufinus, who says in no. 8: “Those who, solely out of envy and jealousy, generate offenses, dissensions, and scandals for their brothers will give an account on the day of judgment.”]

If anyone, after hearing these things, persists in disbelief and does not grant us the assent of faith, I do not doubt that on the day of judgment he will have his place either among the unbelieving people or among false witnesses, and that, according to the judgment of Moses’ law, he will receive the iniquity he contemplated against his brother (Deut. 19:19).

### 8

For although we are sinners, nevertheless, because of those three hundred golden shields that Solomon made (3 Kings 14:27), we ought not to make bronze ones.

[Note: Read “therefore.”]

For, according to the Apostle, the shield is a figure of faith: “And taking the shield of faith” (Eph. 6:16). He makes bronze in place of gold who, having removed the truth of faith, produces only a base metallic clang in his confession; and although he appears devout in his profession, he is found guilty because of his vow, confessing what he does not believe.

[Note: The editions read “substance.” We have corrected the text in accordance with the manuscript. Origen’s Homily 11 on Numbers presents a nearly similar allegory: “Where true faith and the complete preaching of the word are found, things are called either silver or gold: the brilliance of gold indicates the purity of faith, while silver tested by fire signifies words that have been examined. Those things called bronze consist only in the sound of the voice, not in the power of the Spirit; and they are, as the Apostle says, ‘sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.’”]

Of such people blessed Paul may be suspected to have said: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). Does it not seem to you that power can be perceived in gold and appearance in bronze?

But we desire to preserve the prophetic assertion, so that before the feet of the king’s horses—who are bishops or teachers, whose feet are swift upon the mountains (Isa. 52:7), proclaiming peace—we may place the shields of our faith.

For the three hundred golden shields signify either the faith of the blessed Trinity or the fullness of all creatures—heaven, earth, and sea. Those runners who place them before the feet of the horses are to be believed when they were able to say: “I have finished the race” (2 Tim. 4:7).

[Note: Perhaps “whether.”]

For, instructed by the law, we are able to preserve this all the way to the end,

[Note: It should read: “this, up to the end.”]

so that Suracim, king of Egypt (3 Kings 14:25)—that is, the devil—may not carry them away from the temple of our heart.

[Note: The Medicean edition reads “Juracium.” In the version of the Seventy it is Σουσακίμ (*Sousakim*). In the Vulgate, at 3 Kings 11 and 14, as well as 2 Chronicles 12, this Egyptian king is called Sesac. Saint Jerome observed that, before his version of Chronicles, names in Greek and Latin manuscripts had been so corrupted that they seemed to be not so much Hebrew names as a collection of barbarous and Sarmatian ones. Saint Jerome says nearly this much to Domnio and Rogatianus in the Prologue to volume 10, p. 431.]

May the assistance of your prayers keep watch over this matter before Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript concludes: “Finished. Amen.”]

---

## BACHIARIUS TO JANUARIUS: BOOK ON THE RESTORATION OF THE LAPSED (C)

[Note: In the printed editions the title is *On Receiving the Lapsed*. See Dissertation 2, chapter 1.]

To Januarius, my brother blessed in Christ, venerable to me in every faith and affection, Bachiarius, a sinner, sends greetings.

### 1

If I had not feared that I might be assigned a place among Job’s feigned friends—who, when they saw his wound, remained in perpetual silence, as though he had no consolation—I almost would have closed the doors of my lips in silence, placing my hand over my mouth and stopping the pipe of my tongue.

[Note: With the help of the Ambrosian manuscript, whose accurately transcribed copy the distinguished Saxius sent, we have restored the genuine reading. Erasmus reads *haberent* (“they had”). Other editions read *haberet* (“he had consolation”).]

[Note: This is the reading of Ambrosius and Erasmus; Grynæus and Magaronius read “with the hissing of the tongue stopped.”]

But far be this from my faith: that I should say there is any wound without consolation, when the Prophet proclaims to me: “Is there no physician in Gilead, or is there no balm there?” (Jer. 8:22).

For Gilead is interpreted as “heap of witness.” And we understand this heap of witness to be the entire canon of the divine books, where there is a mass of indissoluble testimonies, like a heap gathered from stones. In this heap, if he is sought, the true physician, our Lord Jesus Christ, is found.

[Note: Erasmus reads: “the true physician, my God Jesus Christ.”]

And what is balm except the virtue of continence, which joins what has been loosened and glues together what has been torn apart?

Knowing this, we do not hesitate to mingle the laments of our mouth with the consolation of the wound itself that has occurred. For we have heard of the ruin of a terrible calamity; we have heard Satan rejoicing over the downfall of Christ’s soldier.

[Note: This is how Ambrosius, Grynæus, and Bignæus read it. In the editions of the Pseudo-Hieronymian *Rebuke* one finds: “the soldiers of Satan rejoicing over the ruin of Christ.” That is a harsher statement, if not an impious one. The genuine reading is confirmed by Bachiarius in no. 10, where he says that worldly people rejoice when they hear of the ruin of Christ’s soldier.]

And the shout of the voice that the devil’s army raised in its triumph has reached our ears. I call God as witness over my soul (2 Cor. 1:23), because my inward parts were shaken, and my bones were so agitated that I felt every part of my body tormented by the same wound.

[Note: Erasmus reads: “Thus my inward parts were shaken and my bones trembled.”]

For I could not say that this evil occurred without loss to me, since a member of my body was struck by the devil’s arrow, while the Apostle says: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26).

### 2

Yet my spirit is not wholly permitted to give itself over to lamentation or weeping, because I have grounds for anger against you. Behold, our brother went forth with us into battle against our common enemies, and suddenly was struck down by a fall. You judged him not even worthy of the honor of burial, but left him to be devoured by beasts and birds.

[Note: Ambrosius has this in the printed editions: “For behold, against …”]

Where is the mercy of the Christian religion, which our Teacher taught to be better than sacrifice (Matt. 9:13)? Behold, our brother lies struck down by the enemy; perhaps he is still breathing. Yet because you return unwounded, you have not even attempted to bring consolation to his wound.

[Note: The best reading, supplied by Erasmus. “To return” means, evidently, to return from the battle into which they had gone together with the fallen man. Ambrosius reads: “You return without a wound.” Bignæus reads: “You are without a wound; return.”]

Do not be without fear, most blessed brothers: the enemy struck down a stronger man, so that afterward he might gain easier access to the others.

[Note: Ambrosius reads “fathers.” Shortly afterward, in place of *clarior* (“clearer”), which appears in Bignæus’s edition, we have introduced *celerior* (“quicker”) from Grynæus and Ambrosius.]

Why, I ask, do you despise the wounded man, or why do you suppose him to be dead?

[Note: I prefer this reading, although Erasmus’s edition is mutilated: “or, as you think, dead.”]

Saul’s concubine, daughter Respha, was better than you (2 Sam. 21:10). She guarded the bodies of the dead whom David had struck down in vengeance for the Gibeonites, clothed in sackcloth, until water rained upon them from heaven—that is, until a drop of heavenly mercy descended for their forgiveness.

[Note: Erasmus reads “that Respha, Saul’s concubine.” We retain the common reading, which the Ambrosian manuscript does not remedy. I would judge that “daughter of Aiah” should be read, with the name Respha deleted; it may have entered the text from the margin.]

Better was Judas Maccabaeus (2 Macc. 21:40), who believed that prayer should be made even for his dead brothers, who had been laid low by offerings of idols stolen from the city of Jamnia.

[Note: Ambrosius has the corrupt reading *Trimnia*; Grynæus has *Lamyria*; Bignæus has *Lamyrni*.]

### 3

Why, I ask, did our Physician place so many kinds of remedies among the compartments of his books, if none of all his plasters can heal the wound inflicted by the enemy? Was there some wound hidden from the Chief Physician, for which the skill of his art provided no remedy?

[Note: The printed editions read most corruptly, “the Architect.” The Ambrosian manuscript corrects the passage. Erasmus expands it: “Could any wound arise that was hidden from our Chief Physician’s knowledge?”]

[Note: I think “or” should be read.]

If you please, let us open the school of our Physician and, at the beginning of the canon, investigate the kinds of wounds and medicines. Behold, at the very entrance of the school there meet us those two authors of carnal seed,

[Note: Grynæus and Bignæus add “Adam and Eve,” but the gloss is absent from Ambrosius and Erasmus’s edition.]

who, struck by the poisonous tooth of the serpent, were not immediately consigned to perpetual punishment and death,

[Note: The word *perpetuae* (“perpetual”), which Grynæus and Bignæus do not acknowledge, is present in the Ambrosian manuscript and the Hieronymian editions.]

but, cast out from the delights of paradise—that is, from the freedom of the Church and communion in the sacred mystery—were condemned for a time under the figure of grief and affliction, so that they might be healed by the balm of repentance. They were exiled from the tree of life—that is, from participation in Christ—until they might return to him either through the flaming sword (Gen. 3:24), that is, through the fiery suffering of martyrdom, or through the Cherubim of the Lord, whose name is interpreted as “multitude of knowledge.” It is not now the time to speak of these matters individually.

But what of that fratricide, upon whom the Lord commands a sign to be placed for this reason (Gen. 4:15), so that no one might kill him? For he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18:32).

Nor is that patriarch, the first of the fathers, far removed from these examples. He was the first to believe, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:6). When his brother’s son had been captured by an enemy force, he rescued him by taking with him a band of his servants. Afterwards, through a conversation with the divine Majesty—that is, through the merits of his prayer—he delivered him from the affliction of Sodom, that is, from the judgment of Gehenna.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript wrongly has “from the region.”]

And you, therefore, take a band of servants,

[Note: Ambrosius adds “your own.” The printed editions wrongly read “for this,” that is, “for your work.” Erasmus is better: “take a band—that is, by your own work.”]

that is, by your own work, not another’s, and give aid to your captive brother. Speak with the Lord—that is, pray to Christ—lest the fire of the future judgment consume him.

### 4

Imitate the work of the patriarchs (Gen. 34:25ff.), who not only shuddered at the violation of their sister after she had fallen into the hands of foreigners, but also avenged it.

[Note: Ambrosius reads “they rescued.”]

Yet ask who those avengers of the sin were. Were they not Simeon and Levi? And you belong to the tribe of Levi, since you serve in an ecclesiastical office. Simeon is interpreted as “obedience.” Since you, therefore, were obedient to God, why do you delay rescuing or avenging the disobedient soul?

The soul of your brother is your sister. If you allow her to serve among foreigners, you will sin. But perhaps you say: “This man who has fallen is a Levite; no medicine of healing can be given to him.” You are mistaken, brother. Return to the school of the Physician.

Behold, in the second place—that is, in the book of Exodus, where the wound and affliction of the whole people are described—we also find that the Levites sinned. They are said to have been the first to be corrected at the legislator’s rebuke; and in them the crime of sin is not so much condemned as their swift conversion is praised in the speed of their repentance (Exod. 32:1ff.).

Our Lord also recalls this matter in Ezekiel, when he says concerning the Levites: “Those who first departed from me, when Israel went astray” (Ezek. 44:10).

The high priest himself also made an idol at the people’s urging; for him Moses prayed, and by fraternal assistance he was delivered.

But perhaps you say, most blessed one: “At that time neither the Levites had been sanctified nor the high priest consecrated, when this crime was committed.” I do not contradict your discernment, which you have acquired from the volumes of Scripture. Nevertheless, I could answer you according to the apostolic judgment with which he speaks to the Hebrews (Heb. 7:9–10): Levi, hidden in Abraham’s loins, gave and received tithes from Melchizedek.

[Note: Ambrosius reads this. The editions instead read: “He received tithes from Melchizedek and gave them.” From Genesis 14:20 it is not sufficiently clear who received the tithes—whether Abraham from Melchizedek or the reverse. But the Apostle’s authority compels us to understand that Abraham gave them: “Through Abraham even Levi, who received tithes, paid tithes.” For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him. I would therefore restore Bachiarius’s passage as follows: “Levi, hidden in Abraham’s loins, gave and received the tithes of Melchizedek.”]

Or what do you think Aaron himself lacked in pontifical honor or rank, when he struck Egypt with dreadful signs and, going out by night with the people, celebrated the holy Passover?

[Note: Bignæus reads “holy.” The distinguished Benedictine Antonius Augustinus Touttée cites this passage of Bachiarius in his notes on Saint Cyril of Jerusalem’s *Catechesis* 2, no. 10, where Aaron is anticipated and honored with the name “priest.” Cyril says: “Moses, supplicating God for the sinning high priest, persuaded God.” In this sense one can also readily explain Ambrose, Letter 66, no. 3, and *Apology of David*, chapter 4, no. 17. Bachiarius, however, can scarcely be excused.]

Yet we know that the Passover could not be celebrated without a priest.

### 5

But leaving these matters aside, I wish to ask you: What was Aaron when, struck by jealous envy against Moses, he murmured together with Miriam (Num. 12:1–2)?

But perhaps you say: “Envy is less serious than fornication.” Read, then, blessed Paul, who says: “Neither fornicators, nor the envious, nor the revilers, nor the greedy, nor the slanderers shall inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9).

Do you see how those who will not enter the kingdom of heaven are joined together as equal and alike? Observe what punishment envy deserves, by which the prophetess Miriam is struck with leprosy (Num. 12:10), and also what punishment greed deserves, for which Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, is condemned by a similar sentence (2 Kings 5:27).

But you, who do not detest the greedy, who do not shun the envious, who do not avoid the slanderer and robber, condemn the fornicator, your brother returning for a time, to the punishment of eternal death?

[Note: Bignæus’s reading is very poor: “Why, being greedy …” Grynæus, Erasmus, and Ambrosius have “who.” Among the ancients, as Petavius, Morinus, and others note, sins were divided into three classes. The first consisted of idolatry, adultery, murder, and their manifest forms; stricter penance was imposed for expiating these. Those whom Bachiarius refutes here abused this distinction—of which Pacianus’s treatise *On Penance and Confession* shows that the Spanish churches were aware—to deny the remedy of repentance to a fallen brother. But despair of forgiveness is something quite different from the rigor of discipline. Our author believes that the fallen man, even though guilty of a very serious crime, should indeed be admitted to repentance; yet he does not think that he can share in communion before completing its arduous and prolonged course. This follows from the entire little book, and especially from what is read in nos. 4 and 15.]

We do not say this in order to loosen the reins of sinning. Let anyone who reads this understand that we are not speaking to the living but consoling the dead.

Finally, let him rise again; and you will see that we shall immediately give him the verse of the Psalmist: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4). He will receive the rod of correction and the staff that can support the weak.

[Note: Erasmus and Ambrosius have this reading. The printed editions less correctly read: “You will see … we hand over.”]

Let us therefore understand the Apostle’s saying—that neither the envious, nor fornicators, nor those who desire what belongs to others will possess the kingdom of God—in this sense: if the time of his summons finds someone in such a vice.

[Note: Grynæus reads *arcessionis*; Erasmus, *recessionis*. The Ambrosian manuscript supports Bignæus’s edition, which I rightly judged preferable.]

For elsewhere the Lord says: “I will judge each one according to his ways” (Ezek. 33:20). And the Apostle himself says: “What they once were makes no difference to me” (Gal. 2:6).

In his Epistle blessed John commands us to pray for a brother who does not have a sin leading to death (1 John 5:16)—that is, who has not followed the evils of his sins all the way to the end of his life.

[Note: Ambrosius reads “to exhort.”]

As for what you said above concerning the Levites—that they had not been sanctified when they were polluted by sins—what do you make of what is written in the books of blessed Ezra (1 Esdr. 10:18), where, after returning from the Babylonian captivity and having recently rebuilt the foundations of the Lord’s temple, not only the common people but also the priestly family and the family of the great Jesus are found to have been mixed with foreign women, that is, with Syrians, Idumaeans, Moabites, and Ammonites?

[Note: With the glosses removed, the Ambrosian manuscript restores the passage to a sound form. This history is found both in the canonical book of Ezra and in chapter 9 of the Third Book, which the Church has placed among the apocrypha. Bignæus and Tillemont believe that Bachiarius cites the latter; this would not surprise us, since it was customary for Greek and Latin Fathers to quote testimonies from the same book, as Calmet demonstrated in a special Dissertation on this book, volume 3 of the Venetian edition, p. 162.]

Yet all of them, after receiving Ezra’s counsel and withdrawing from the company of foreign women, were freed from the same sin. Hence you see that just as we are stained by the contagion of sin, so we are cleansed by expelling it.

[Note: Up to this point the Pseudo-Hieronymian *Rebuke against Evagrius* extends; see further Dissertation 2, chapter 3.]

### 6

Do not, I beg you, most blessed one, bury our brother, sunk in the depth of a well under the power of an unjust ruler, and overwhelm him with the stones of despair.

Let us imitate that Ethiopian (Jer. 38:7, 11) who, when the holy Jeremiah had been cast into a pit by an unjust king, rescued him by taking the assistance of thirty men and lowering rags and ropes to him.

[Note: Bignæus adds “old.” I would prefer to read “old rags and old ropes.” The Septuagint has Παλαιὰ ῥάκη, καὶ παλαιὰ σχοινία (*palaia rhakē kai palaia schoinia*, “old rags and old ropes”).]

Behold, our brother is in the pit. Let us take thirty men—that is, either the assistance of the blessed Trinity, or, through the toil of soul, flesh, and spirit, let us rescue him who has been sunk in the depth of the well.

[Note: The ancients often distinguish soul from spirit. Saint Pacianus, the light of Spain, says that the Corinthian man was handed over by the Apostle Paul to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, but not of the soul or spirit—only for the destruction of the flesh. *Letter* 3 to Sympronianus, p. 207 of the Roman edition of 1564.]

Let us send him old rags; let us bring to his memory examples of the ancients who, having fallen through sin, were afterward brought from the depths of evils to the heights through repentance. When these examples have been set before his eyes, he will not be able to despair.

A soldier who has been struck in the first battle often fights more bravely in the second and rises up more angrily against the one who struck him.

[Note: Ambrosius reads “persecutor.”]

Behold, we stand at the end of the age. Battles of suffering for Christ’s name are pressing upon us. What is surprising if the man whom the spear of fornication struck down should prevail in the contest of suffering? What if the man whom incontinence and lust had conquered should be victorious in martyrdom?

Was this not what happened to that Nazarite, born by promise (Judg. 16)? When the blandishments of a woman had conquered him to his own destruction, he was later found, at the end of his death, under the suffering of martyrdom, to have struck down a greater army of enemies than before, when he had been a Nazarite—that is, undefiled.

[Note: The opinion of Saint Augustine and others is that Samson did this not because he was deceived humanly, but because he was divinely commanded. Bachiarius attributes to him the praise of martyrdom, perhaps relying on Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews, where he is praised among those approved by the testimony of faith (11:32, 39).]

For just as that priestly family descended from the kinship of Eli (1 Sam. 3:14), concerning which the Lord had sworn that none of them would stand before him because they had provoked the Lord by grave sins—was not that entire kinship reported to have been killed for David by Saul (1 Sam. 23:18)?

And what is this except a figure of martyrdom, so that those whom the grave crime of sin had enveloped might be freed by death inflicted for Christ?

These are the sacred mysteries of the blessed books. Thus the potter does not allow his vessels to perish (Jer. 18:6); he even says that, when they have been broken and dashed upon stones, he can restore them.

[Note: From Ambrosius we add “his own.”]

### 7

Do not despise, I beg you, your dead brother. He is the son of the barren Shunammite (4 Kings 4:20), that is, of the Church. He who has died was born by promise.

For once the Lord promised and pledged his birth to Abraham a second time, in the seed of Isaac (Gen. 22:15; Heb. 11:18), and his head was struck by the heat of the harvest—that is, the chief part of his mind grew hot amid the flame of lust.

[Note: I think there is an error in the word *spei* (“hope”). Perhaps “shameful” should be read. Below, in no. 18, we find “through the flame of shameful desire.”]

Let his mother run to Elisha—that is, let the Church lament anxiously—for he will rise again if we faithfully hope for this from Christ.

And you, most blessed one, imitate Elisha’s work in the dead brother. Place hands upon hands, feet upon feet, and mouth upon mouth.

First, do this so that you may sympathize with him who lies dead; do not, raised up by the triumph of your integrity, tower above him or stretch yourself over him whom sudden death has carried away. Rather imitate the Apostle, who says: “I fear that when I come, my God may humble me before you and I may mourn over many who sinned previously” (2 Cor. 12:21).

Place your eyes also upon his eyes, lest they wander any further toward his destruction; his mouth upon your mouth, lest it speak wicked things; his hands upon your hands, lest they do harmful things; his feet upon your feet, lest they wander into shameful places.

[Note: That is, “your mouth upon his mouth,” and so forth.]

And thus, when your members have been joined to his members for his protection, he will not only have no further opportunity to sin, but will also gain hope of rising again, so that he who died from the cold of sin may be recalled to life by the warmth of consolation.

Remember also to drive everyone from his presence. Let no one see him; let no one be in the midst; let no one presume to claim the right to see him because of kinship.

What do I mean by a relative? Even if that natural mother should be present, let her not be given access to enter.

[Note: The Vulgate edition reads: “Even if that natural mother should be present, let her not …” The following words, recently published by the most holy pontiff Benedict XIV in book 7 of *On the Diocesan Synod*, chapter 57, ought to be inscribed in golden letters. We reluctantly omit much, but it would be wrong to pass over the excellent rule he there prescribes to bishops. He says rightly and wisely in section 4: “Therefore, even if a shameful crime of incest should occur in a diocese once or twice, perpetrated by one or another of the clergy, it will not for that reason be lawful for the bishop to depart from the common rule and, to the people’s astonishment and scandal, immediately decree that henceforth no cleric may live with a niece, aunt, sister, or mother, as though all were considered guilty or suspected of the same enormous crime. Rather, if he finds someone of doubtful reputation whose cohabitation with a relative smells bad even among upright and prudent men, he should impose separation upon the person to whom the limitation of the rule certainly applies, using, however, the circumspection and caution demanded by the circumstances, lest a hidden offense be exposed. Chromatius, a presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, and Eusebius, his brother, distinguished by the office of deacon, lived together at home with their widowed mother and sisters who had professed virginity. Both, devoted to the books of Jerome and Rufinus and distinguished for piety and learning, attained episcopal dignity: the former succeeded our Valerian; the latter most holily governed a church of uncertain name, unless it was Bologna. But what the canons, composed under the Spirit of God, granted to the innocent could not be claimed by the lapsed or penitents whose crimes had been public. Moreover, the Spanish ascetic had filled not merely the city in which he lived but nearly the whole world with the reputation of his sacrilege, as our author says in no. 10.”]

Thus you recognize that Elisha acted in this way with the son of the Shunammite (4 Kings 4:31), our Lord with the ruler’s daughter (Matt. 9:25), and blessed Peter with the widow Dorcas (Acts 9:40).

For a man dead in sins, a very private and solitary place ought to be prepared, where nothing more is taken in than the physician and the corpse.

[Col. 1044A] **8.** Do not, I beg you, most blessed brother, let us abandon one who has been struck and was once pleasing to us, unarmed, whom the enemy found.

[Note: [Col. 1044D] Gryn. reads *impercussum*, with the same meaning. This edition retains certain marks of antiquity; for example, it has *laqueas* and *stimulas*, not *laqueos* and *stimulos*, as the Margarin and Ambrosian editions do.]

The breastplate of righteousness was lacking to him (Eph. VI, 14; II Thess. V, 8), as were the helmet of hope and salvation and the sword of the Spirit, with which Christ’s soldiers are armed. Let him be healed, I beg you, for he is still breathing; and let him return to the battle. Was not that outstanding and courageous David, who in his youth overcame a giant of extraordinary size, later overcome by the foolish nakedness of a woman? (I Sam. VII).

[Note: [Col. 1044D] The editions of Ambrose and Gryn. add this.]

As soon as he acknowledged through the prophet’s words (II Sam. XII) that he had sinned, he immediately fled to the poultice of repentance and healed the scars of his crimes by the satisfaction of confession. Yet even then the enemy did not cease attacking him. For afterward he persuaded him to sin by numbering the people (II Sam. XXIV, 1); and he nearly killed him with the giant’s weapon (II Sam. XXI, 16–17), had not Abishai, the brother of Joab, commander of the army, saved him by interposing the protection of his aid.

[Note: [Col. 1044D] The printed editions read incorrectly, *nisi eum Joab in princeps*. Ambrose preserves traces of the true reading: “by Abishai, the brother of Joab, the commander,” etc.]

Hence also, I believe, he himself says in Psalm LXX: “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. LXXXII, 2). And elsewhere: “Often have they fought against me from my youth” (Ps. CXXVIII, 1).

But you say, “Let there be no memory of him, because he slaughtered himself by a shameful sin.” First inquire, brother, whether this man who fell was found in battle or was wounded at home; for greater mercy is deserved by the man whom the enemy struck in combat than by the man whom a robber stabbed while he slept.

I certainly saw him stationed in battle. He was fighting with the shield of fasting against the allurements of the appetite; he was fighting with the breastplate of silence against the darts of detraction and the other weapons of malediction. But he was struck in the place where he considered himself safer.

For just as Asahel, that brother of Joab, commander of David’s army, who is said by Scripture to have been swift like a deer (II Sam. II, 18, 23),

[Note: [Col. 1044D] In our Vulgate it says, “like one of the roes” (*quasi unus de capreis*) “that dwell in the forests” ([Col. 1045D]). In the Septuagint likewise: ὡς ἡ μία δορκὰς ἐν ἀγρῷ, “like one doe in the field.”]

because, I believe, the purity of an undefiled body had granted him the gift of swiftness

[Col. 1045A]—“For the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15)—

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Gryn. reads, “Abner pursues him.” Ambrose reads, “This man, while pursuing Abner.”]
