is reported to have been struck in the kidneys by the point of the spear of Abner, whom he was pursuing. I think no one can doubt that the fault of fornication is signified by that bodily region. Likewise Abner himself is afterward said to have been struck in the groin by Joab, Asahel’s brother (II Sam. III, 27), because the emblem of fornication deserved to be slain nowhere but in the groin.

But did Asahel fail to receive the consolation of his brothers, when the whole army of David mourned him so? Or was he erased from the book of life—that is, from the memory of the Lord’s teaching? Scripture does not forget him; indeed, it even mentions the swiftness that he possessed before his death,

[Note: [Col. 1045D] We delete the negative particle inserted by Bignaeus, following the manuscript and the first edition.]

when it says, “He was swift like a deer”—that is, he not only avoided the enemy’s snares by the alertness of his mind,

[Col. 1045B] but also became the slayer of serpents, that is, of hostile powers.

**9.** Remember, brother, that we are flesh. That sea—which is the figure of baptism—which blessed John says he saw in the Apocalypse, he describes as being of glass (Rev. IV, 6; XV, 2); and for that reason it is soon endangered or broken in us. Slippery is the path of this world, bound fast by icy iniquity. When the heat of desire has moderately melted it,

[Note: [Col. 1045D] These same manuscripts correct the editions of Margarin, which read *immodicae*.]

it becomes easy for wretched people to slip and fall.

“Stretch out your hand to your fallen brother” (Eccl. XV, 18), who, confounded by the shame of sin, dares neither to raise himself nor to lift his eyes. Fulfill the law of Moses: “If your brother’s donkey falls under its burden” (Exod. XXIII, 5)—that is, the flesh overcome by sin—

[Note: [Col. 1045D] The Septuagint has Τοῦ ἐχθροῦ σου, “of your enemy”; the Vulgate, “of him who hates you.”]

bend toward him, humble yourself, and lift him from his fall.

Why are you ashamed to be joined to a sinful man? Look to him who says, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. VII, 17). Our Teacher, finding a man wounded by robbers (Luke X, 30), judges him not only worthy of care but also restores him to his inn and flock. Having given the innkeeper two denarii—that is, the two Testaments of the divine canon—he promises him a greater reward if, through his diligence, he restores the wounded man to his former condition.

So you too gather up the brother whom the robber devil struck with his band of attendants; entrust him to the innkeeper—that is,

[Note: [Col. 1045D] The Ambrosian manuscript does not recognize this initial letter. [Col. 1046D] Again, at no. 17 he praises the most blessed bishop. We have discussed this title of honor in Dissertation 1, chapter 6.]

to the blessed bishop, who, if he spends anything on him, will receive more from the Lord.

But perhaps you say, “He was wounded; this man is dead.” If you call him dead, then place him, at least beside the bones of Elisha (II Kings XIII, 21). I do not want you to separate him far from Christ’s members, because he will be ashamed of association with the better and will rise to life.

Do not consider it a small torment of correction

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Ambrose has the correct reading, though the sense requires us to read *momentum* instead of *tormentum*.]

if a sinner is admitted into the company of the blessed, because he feels their rewards to be his torments. If someone is praised, he is ashamed; if someone is reproached, he recognizes himself. Placed amid these scourges of words, he continually approaches satisfaction and amendment.

**10.** But what shall we say of the statement that we have heard from certain people: that a woman and a man who are partners in crime and sin should be joined together as though in marriage and wedlock? Let this be far from Christian speech.

[Note: [Col. 1046D] The edition reads *Christi*. Ambrose, whom we follow, is better.]

It is the serpent’s suggestion, that he should take even the corpse of the one he killed. Is it not similar if someone has been gravely struck and is gasping at the point of death, and an earthly physician, having perhaps visited him and suspecting that he cannot live, urges him to be killed? Without doubt the same is being said here: “A brother or sister has been found gravely wounded by the weapon of desire. When marriage to the person involved in the crime is urged upon this one, what else is being said except, ‘Let him or her be killed,’ since he or she cannot live or escape from this wound?”

Do you perhaps not know what punishment awaits one who despairs? That messenger of Saul’s death (II Sam. I, 2 ff.), when he came to David and reported that his enemy had been struck down, was questioned by David about the cause of his death. He answered that he himself had killed him with his sword, adding: “For I saw that he would not live after the stroke of the wound inflicted upon him” (ibid., 10). David immediately condemned him to death, since he had despaired that the man struck by his enemies could live and had slaughtered him after removing all hope.

Indeed, in Davidic fashion, let the garments of heart and breast be torn; let a mournful voice be raised in lamentation; let the Israelite people—that is, the ecclesiastical people—be taught a dirge and say:

[Col. 1046C]

[Note: [Col. 1046D] The Septuagint has στήλωσον, meaning “inscribe a title” or “erect a monument.”]

“Lift your stones upon your heights, and consider your slain: how the mighty have fallen in battle. Let this not be announced in Gath, nor proclaimed in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the foreigners rejoice and the sons of the uncircumcised exult” (ibid., 19–20);

and the rest that is contained in the proclamation of that lament,

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Ambrose’s edition reads, “contained in the lament itself.”]

and let it say or speak: “See, it is forbidden that the fall or ruin of the brother be sown in the territories of Gath or the borders of Ashkelon”—that is, made known to secular people or worldly men. And have we not suffered this, that not only the city in which he lives, but even the whole world, should be filled with the fame of his despair?

Does not that evangelical saying also correspond to this command: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him privately; and if he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others as witnesses” (Matt. XVIII, 15–16), and the rest contained in the discourse of the commandment?

You see, then, what he says: “Lest the sons of the uncircumcised rejoice.” Woe is me, who know these things. For who are the sons of the uncircumcised except the people of this world,

[Col. 1047A] living in the error of their sin

[Note: [Col. 1047C] Ambrose has *et in* instead of *et*. The author of the synchronistic Epistle to a Fallen Monk, among the Basilian writings, no. 21, similarly says: “We have become the tragedy of captives; by Jews and Gentiles our affairs are brought upon the stage.”]

and in paganism? These people rejoice when they hear of the fall of Christ’s soldier, or take consolation from his deed, saying: “Look at the one who was reproached to us by others, whose example we were compelled to follow. Although he had emerged from our body, his life was said to be unlike ours, to our shame.”

Was it not better never to begin what is good than to fall so shamefully, or to be unable to complete what one had begun? They do not know that, in God’s judgment, the soul that is known to have desired good and to have been overthrown by a plotter may perhaps have the greater excuse, than the soul that, rebellious against God and out of the servile terror of despair, has chosen to be handed over to the yoke of captivity rather than experience the danger of combat.

Is not a soldier excused before his king by his own wounds? Often the wound of his scars commends the valiant warrior.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Gryn. and Ambrose agree. In Bignaeus’s edition it is less correctly printed: “his own wounds excuse the soldier,” etc.]

**11.** But setting these matters aside, let the dead man be mourned and the corpse buried; that is, let his sin be concealed and removed from our midst, partly through our labor and partly through the shame of his own confusion. Let us provide the linens of consolation and the spices of heavenly hope. But let him, enclosed within the grave of his secrecy, contain himself, confounded by the shame of sin. Let him be torn by the worm of his conscience, which consumes all the corruptions of sins within him,

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The edition reads *totus*, “wholly.”]

until he emits from himself no stench of an evil reputation.

Did not blessed Tobias earn the pardon of heavenly mercy in this way, by giving burial to his brothers who had died in captivity? I believe this signifies and recommends repentance to those who have fallen under the dominion of the ruler of the world (Tob. I, 18; II, 9).

So let us cover his body as it deserves.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Bignaeus reads *contigamus*. We restore the elegant and correct reading from the older edition of Gryn., based on the Ambrosian manuscript.]

Behold, a prophet went out from Jerusalem (I Kings XIII, 1 ff.)—that is, from the house of the Lord—against Bethel, which was committing fornication against the Lord, that is, against the city of this world. The Lord had commanded him not to taste its food or drink. But because he was deceived by a false prophet—that is, by the spirit of fornication—by the wicked man, he fell into the power and portion of the lion,

[Note: [Col. 1047D] What if Bachiarius wrote *fortem*, “strong,” by which name the lion is suggested in Samson’s riddle (Judg. XIV, 14)? The Vulgate reading, however, can stand, and the Ambrosian manuscript supports it.]

who “prowls around roaring, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V, 8).

Yet the lion remains beside his corpse, so that, unless it is carried to the bosom and grave of the Church, it would become food and nourishment for him. Therefore let us imitate the service of the false prophet and bury with every due honor the man whom the devil struck.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Ambrose reads, “let us bury him with every due honor.”]

Christ is accustomed to raise the dead from such a grave. Only let us not leave his corpse to be devoured by wild beasts or birds—that is, by vices or worldly people.

How, I ask, can we despair of the Lord’s mercy, when he even reproved Pharaoh for having in no way deigned to repent, saying in the prophecy concerning Pharaoh: “I have broken the arms of the king of Egypt; and he did not entreat that healing be given to him and strength restored to him to grasp the sword” (Ezek. XXX, 25)?

[Col. 1048B] **12.** Solomon

[Note: [Col. 1047D] In the margin of Ambrose’s book the name Solomon is written in red letters, perhaps to alert readers that a distinguished and noteworthy sentence occurs here. Fulbert extracted it; we praised him in Dissertation 2, chapter 3. There it is incorrectly read, “to be joined to God, to be united to wisdom.” Bachiarius clearly alludes to that prayer in Wisdom IX, 4: “Give me the wisdom that sits beside your thrones.” From this we learn that Bachiarius attributes this book to Solomon, whose name it bears. This also pleased our Rufinus, who, acting as translator in homily 12 on the Proverbs of Saint Basil, no. 1, renders these words—τρεῖς τὰς πάσας ἔγνωμεν πραγματείας τοῦ σοφωτάτου Σολομῶντος, “We know these three books to be principally those of the most wise Solomon”—as follows: “We know these three books principally to be those of the most wise Solomon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and what is called the Song of Songs,” vol. II, p. 730.]

—that extraordinary man who deserved to be joined to God’s attendant

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Fulbert appears to have the better reading, “through prophecy.”]

—that is, to be united with Wisdom (Wis. IX, 4)—fell into the embraces of foreign women. Ensnared by the bond of lust, he also polluted himself by the error of sacrilege when he fashioned an image of Chemosh, the Moabite idol (I Kings XI, 17).

But since through the prophet he acknowledged the guilt of his error, is he therefore excluded from heavenly mercy?

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Ambrose reads, “of heavenly healing.”]

Perhaps you say: “Nowhere in the canonical books do we read that he repented or obtained mercy.”

Listen, then, brother. Some may perhaps call his repentance acceptable precisely because it is not written in public laws: he repented not before the face of the people but in the secret of his conscience, with God as witness. We know that he obtained pardon from this, because, when he had been released from the body, Scripture records that he was buried among the bodies of the kings of Israel. Yet we know that this was denied elsewhere to sinful kings who remained to the end of their lives in the perversity of their purpose. Therefore, because he deserved to be buried among righteous kings, he was not alien from pardon; but he could not merit that pardon without repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Fulbert cites the passage in this form: “Do not doubt, brother, his repentance, which is not recorded in public laws. And perhaps for that reason it is judged more acceptable, since it was not before the face…” It seems strange that Bachiarius should willingly concede to his opponents that Solomon’s repentance is not recorded in the canonical books, since the ancients who favor Solomon’s salvation rely especially on those words of Proverbs XXIV, 21, where, according to the Septuagint version, the Wise Man testifies concerning himself: “At last I repented.” In any case, Solomon ought to have undergone public repentance in order to remedy the people’s offense.]

That congregation of Korah, when it had been swallowed alive by the opening of the earth for the audacity of its attempt, nevertheless had the little altars in which they had kindled the profane fire ordered by the Lord to be surrounded by the altar (Num. XVI, 37),

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Ambrose reads *areolae*, “little altars.” The Vulgate translator of Scripture has *thuribula*, “censers”; Rufinus, *bacilli*, “little rods,” vol. II of Origen’s works, Benedictine edition.]

[Col. 1049A] because they are said to have been sanctified. We understand these to be their souls, in which they had received the heat of adulterous flames through presumptuous freedom. Therefore they are swallowed alive, but their little altars are forbidden to perish, just as the Apostle also says: “I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved

[Note: [Col. 1049C] Ambrose has the same reading; Bignaeus has “may be saved for the day.”]

on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. V, 5).

Consider, then, brother, to how few it is granted to free their limbs unblemished from the bite of sin in the amphitheater of this world, where one fights with wild beasts—that is, with vices. That man who experienced this said: “Do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. LXXIII, 19).

But since it has been a long time that they have been speaking with you, we must take care lest our loquacity offend you. Therefore, to you, for whose sake we have said these things,

[Col. 1049B] we turn our pen.

**13.** Why do you avoid me, brother? Why do you entrust yourself more to the company of worldly people? Perhaps they

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Gryn. reads *videant*, “let them see”; Bignaeus, *vident*, “they see.” He relegated *rident*, “they laugh,” to the margin of the book.]

laugh at your fault; I mourn it, and, if it must be so, I shall desire to die with you. Why are you ashamed of our presence? Our situation is alike, because I too am confounded by shame over your affair.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] We should read *Annon*. Saint Eucherius uses the same allegory in his commentary on the Books of Kings, book II, p. 197: “Just as Hannon, king of the Ammonites, disfigured David’s servants sent to him and sent them back to David in a shameful and derisive state, so also the devil, the prince of this world, habitually disfigures many religious people through insinuated vices. When he exposes their hidden evils as open and shameful acts of lust, he leaves them naked of the dignity of chastity, as though their garments had been cut away up to their buttocks; and when he strips them of their former strength, he shaves them as though of their beard. Yet the true David, namely our Lord and Savior, does not exclude them from the indulgence of repentance in his merciful regard. He commands them to remain in Jericho—that is, under the ban of repentance—until, by making satisfaction, they recover the spiritual sacraments and strength of mind that they lost by sinning, and can finally stand in his presence.” It seems that both authors drew from the same source.]

As I see it, King Annon of the Ammonites (II Sam. X, 4 ff.) shaved half the beards of David’s soldiers—that is, of Christ’s ministers—and cut their garments up to the groin. This signifies that he removed from them, by shaving half their beard, the masculine appearance and showed that he had made them effeminate by the pleasurable razor of vices.

Half your beard has been shaved, because by one vice you have lost whatever good you had accomplished in God’s virtues. Half your beard has been shaved because, if you wish to labor during the remaining time of your life, what remains will grow again. He cut the garments up to the groin when he revealed before people’s eyes the shameful acts that he himself had persuaded you to commit.

Yet even after this there is hope. Let us sit in Jericho until our beards grow: that is, let us be a reproach and disgrace to the better, and become an anathema to everyone, as Israel was in Jericho, until a bearded appearance—that is, an increase of virtues—grows for us.

Believe me: our king will grieve over the injury. He will avenge us, his soldiers, against the enemy who did these things to us in his dishonor. Our King David was absent from our sight for a little while; and therefore, defeated by our enemies,

[Note: [Col. 1050C] II Sam. XXIII, 11: Μερὶς τοῦ ἀγροῦ πλήρης φακοῦ, “a portion of the field full of lentils.” But who says that the portion of the field was broken? Or does he understand by this name a vessel or earthen flask?]

we broke a part of the field full of reddish lentils, which represent the figure of our modesty and delicate chastity.

But now that our king has opened the remembrance of sin to the eyes of our heart, let us stand, so that at least what remains—that is, the rest of our life—may be defended and kept safe.

Do not, I beg you, let anyone persuade you to turn this crime into marriage and call a matrimonial union what is a crime.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] This entire passage is absent from Ambrose through a copyist’s error.]

I do not want you to provoke and multiply God’s offense. For if what the enemy secretly and fearfully persuaded you to do is rightly called guilt, how will you deserve pardon for what, as though insulting God and his judgment, you publicly begin to claim as your own?

Imitate Amnon, son of David (II Sam. XIII, 15 ff.). When he had burned with illicit passion for the violation of his sister, afterward he hated her more than he had previously loved her; and for this deed he was killed by his brother, because,

[Note: [Col. 1050D] These are mere subtleties, refuted by the sacred text. Just as it is uncertain whether Amnon repented of his most shameful crime, so no one can doubt that David’s paternal affection moved him to spare him, while Absalom’s uncontrolled anger and desire urged him to rage against his brother. Such arguments must be forgiven to allegorists; we are not offended by a few blemishes.]

having recognized the guilt of his error, he did not remain in the crime but vehemently hated the substance of the sin itself.

Hence we also suspect that David was not angry with him, because he soon saw that he had accepted repentance; and that he immediately and impatiently hated what had deceived him for the space of one hour, and by the power of repentance broke its snares.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] The Ambrosian manuscript is extremely corrupt here: “and that, on behalf of the one who was deceived for a single hour by the snare and immediately broke it through patience—that is, through the virtue of repentance—and of the one who was captured,” etc. Gryn.’s edition is mutilated at this point and offers no assistance.]

But the man who has been caught in the net of vices and patiently submits to his enemies—that is, to the hunters—until he is even shut up in a cage and there fattened for a long period for display, will then be pleasing above all to the world’s principalities

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Perhaps *principatibus*, “principalities.”]

when he has been killed.

Until you have escaped the trap of fornication, do not entrust yourself to the snares of drunkenness, through which

[Note: [Col. 1050D] I suspect that *in manus*, “into the hands,” should be restored; but against both the editions and our manuscript, I make no change.]

you may fall into the fury of Absalom (ibid., 28); for luxury and drunkenness possess a kind of kinship in the birth of vices.

**14.** Therefore lift up your spirits, brother; raise the eyes that the shame of conscience has lowered; and do not let hostile despair break you. Behold, Absalom, who had killed his brother, obtained the king’s pardon through the intercession of friends (II Sam. XIV, 23), so that he did not despair of asking even for the kiss of peace and the presence of Christ’s face.

So you too, before those whom you know to be David’s friends—David who was once your father when you had not sinned—be humble and bow low, so that what you cannot obtain by yourself you may deserve through their intercession.

And if they should perhaps be hard of hearing, do not cease begging opportunely and importunately; for Absalom obtained through injury what he could not obtain through friendship, and what he did not deserve according to his merits, he obtained through injury.

[Note: [Col. 1051D] Gryn. and Ambrose have this reading. In Bignaeus, the article τὸ is missing before *pro meritis*.]

Do you wish to know that the saints often pray for sinners through an occasion of injury? That blessed man, one of the four,

[Note: [Col. 1051D] So the editions read; the Ambrosian manuscript has “one of the seven.” We discuss this more fully in Dissertation 2, chapter 1.]

head of confessors and martyrs, when he was being pelted with stones by a mad crowd, at the very departure of Israel from Egypt (Ps. CVI, 1)—that is, of the soul from the body—knelt and prayed to the Father for sinners (Acts VII, 59), following the example of our Teacher, who asked forgiveness for the people persecuting him (Luke XXIII, 34).

Behold, you see where the occasion of prayers arises from the injury and punishment of the saints. We do not say this so that you may obtain the intercession of the blessed by insulting them; rather, we advise you that, if they have not dared to pray on account of the magnitude of your crimes, they may more readily be heard on behalf of the one by whom they have been injured when they endure the injury of your importunity.

[Note: [Col. 1051D] Bignaeus has the very poor reading, “in your opportunity.”]

“Set fire to the barley nearest you in the field” (II Sam. XIV, 30), because “the tongue is a fire”

[Note: [Col. 1051D] Ambrose adds: “And the hand of iniquity often presses upon the members through the tongue.” Gryn. has it somewhat differently: “And the world of iniquity is established through the tongue in the members.”]

(Jas. III, 6), while the field is this world.

Thus, whenever you begin to disparage the fruits of a good life and say, “See what the saints are like, since they do not dare to pray for sinners; where is the daily reward of their work?” then, when it has been set alight by your tongue, the hope of the saints will be stirred toward confidence in prayer. For they will recognize that you have been driven to this necessity for the sake of your own benefit, not through the fault of detraction.

Absalom likewise did not set fire to Joab’s field because he wanted to harm him as an enemy, but so that Joab might at least look toward the man who had ignored him when he flattered him; thus Absalom might deserve the presence of one who was close or friendly to Christ.

For the fruit of the saints, insofar as it is understood according to human beings, is not improperly represented by barley; but insofar as it is according to God, it can be understood as wheat. There is no doubt that, according to the Apostle, the saints sow both, “providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. XII, 17).

Therefore Absalom set fire to the barley nearest him—that is, to the conduct enacted among human beings. But he could not reach what is before God, because the Father alone recognized it.

**15.** But perhaps you say: “Your persuasion requires a man who is quiet or secure; whereas I must fear every day the persecutor of this world, who desires to avenge upon me the disgrace of his nearest kinswoman.”

[Note: [Col. 1051D] Bignaeus has *proxime suum*. The Ambrosian reading, which we follow, seems to confirm Tillemont’s conjecture: namely, that there were people urging the monk to marry the violated virgin in order to soften the parent’s anger.]

If you fear something of this kind, behold the six cities of refuge (Josh. XX, 2 ff.); enter them, if you please.

And if, on account of the consciousness of your sins, you do not dare to enter those that are in the promised land—that is, in the Church—there is Bosor beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, which is interpreted as “narrowness”; that is, a small or modest monastic cell.

[Note: [Col. 1052D] Bignaeus has *citra*, “on this side”; Ambrose, *contra*, “beyond.” We have explained in Dissertation 1, chapter 7, p. LIX, why we follow neither.]

It will suit you very well, because it belongs to the tribe of Reuben, and he unlawfully stained his father’s bed (Gen. XLIX, 4).

There is also Ramoth, from the tribe of Gad, which is interpreted as “exalted death” or “vision of death.” Truly, repentance should be called an exalted death, when, with the members mortified, a man is led to the heights of heaven from which he had previously fallen away.

[Col. 1052B]

Or, in relation to that humble death which generally threatens all flesh, it is reasonably called exalted by comparison with it, because it is far nobler to die through repentance than to be dissolved by this common death.

But if we wish to understand “vision of death,” it can be interpreted in this way: when we are established in repentance and place before our eyes the torments of Gehenna and the underworld, we see the very appearance of death from which we are freed by the benefit of repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1052D] Bignaeus has “until you remember.” The reading of our manuscript seemed better.]

Only remember that you are doing penance in the city of the slave woman’s son, because “everyone who sins is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34);

[Col. 1052C]

[Note: [Col. 1052D] I would gladly delete these words, which are absent from Ambrose.]

and, “taking the form of a servant,” you must humble yourself even unto death (Phil. II, 7–8).

There is Gaulon in the territory of Manasseh, which is interpreted as “rolling about,” so that you may remember that you must roll about in sackcloth and ashes; and this in the territory of Manasseh, which is interpreted as “oblivion,” so that, forgetting the things you did before, you may stretch forward to what lies ahead (Phil. III, 17).

Dwell here, then, so that through narrowness, death, and rolling about you may escape the persecutor’s wrath and find the hope of salvation.

Then, if you accomplish anything beneficial in these places, you will also be able to reach Cades in the promised land, which is in Galilee. It is interpreted as “holy,” so that, when in tribulation you have cast away the work of corruption, access to the holy Church may also be granted to you; and to the inheritance of Naphtali, which is called “the released vine” (Gen. XLIX, 21), so that you may deserve to share in the mystery of the Lord’s blood.

But let the entrance to Hebron not be closed to you either,

[Col. 1053A] which is interpreted as “union” or “marriage.” For let your soul return to its husband—that is, to the Spirit of God—from whom, because of its sins, it had for a time been widowed.

[Note: [Col. 1053C] We restore the true reading with the aid of the Ambrosian manuscript. Philo Judaeus uses a similar allegory in *Quod deterius potiori insidiari soleat*, p. 141. The older editions have *judicata*, “judged.” I note in passing that the word *peccaminum* is favored by Spanish writers: Prudentius uses it frequently, and our author repeats it below at no. 21. In the Gothic-Hispanic Book of Prayers, p. 24, prayers are offered to the Virgin Mary to obtain for us from God the remission of *peccamina*, sins.]

And so you will also be able to enter the sixth city, Shechem, which our Joseph received as an inheritance, and for that reason was buried there.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] Gryn. incorrectly has “the father who,” etc. In the same place Saint Jerome says in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: “Joseph was buried there, and his mausoleum is still visible there today.”]

Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder” or “labor,” so that you may show that through the labor of repentance you have been carried back from your error upon Christ’s shoulders (Luke XV, 4), joined to the ninety-nine sheep, and made the hundredth, since Shechem is recorded as having been purchased from foreigners for one hundred lambs (Gen. XXXIII, 19).

### 16

But why, brother, does sluggishness still delight you as you lie there? Rise, for the physician has come, who says that the putrefactions of sins must be cut away and afterward the wound of the scar itself treated.[^c0110-1] Why are you afraid? Why do you avoid treatment? You did not fear the Zabulitic spear,[^c0110-2] which is weighed down by a mass of six hundred shekels (1 Kings 22:7); why do you evade the knives of the evangelical instrument? You endured the fire and flames of the enemy; why do you fear the Lord’s fire, the fire which he came to cast upon the earth (Luke 12:49), which will consume hay, straw, and wood (1 Corinthians 3:12)? Cut away from yourself the will of your rotten habit.[^c0110-3] Burn your kidneys and your heart; condemn the hostile appearance of your body, through which you have either been deceived yourself or deceived others.

Let your limbs, emaciated by fasting, become horrifying, and accustom yourself to have as your covering the hair-shirt which you had polluted by your filthy conduct; so that, when you are pierced by its touch and roughness, you may always remember the goads of your sins.[^c0110-4] May Moses file down your calf within you, through which you indulged yourself in the wilderness (Exodus 32:20); that is, let the discipline of law and fasting wear down your flesh, so that, reduced to nothing, it may be kept thin.[^c0110-5] You have read, I believe: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). So be angry with your sins, that you may sin no more.

Anticipate the savage torments of avenging Gehenna, and become your own torturer; so that, when the enemy comes, he may find nothing in you that he can punish.[^c0110-6] If the occasion for suffering comes, remember how you must fight in the presence of your King, so that you may be able to amend the fault of one who deserted and fled. But if perhaps the occasion for this blessedness is lacking, you yourself can become your own persecutor; so that, as the Apostle said (Romans 12:1), you may present yourself to God through every kind of death.[^c0110-7]

Enter the prison of your monastery, and seek the darkness of solitude by which you may be recalled to the light you have lost. Let hunger be your substitute for gluttony, and thirst for flame. [Editorial note: This defect is easily remedied if, in place of *gula* (“gluttony”), we read *gladio* (“the sword”): let repentance take the place of martyrdom.] so that, by the hand of the executioner that is your will, through the punishment of abstinence the framework of your ribs may be stripped of its entrails, and, in place of the punishment of fire, the burning of harsh thirst may consume the innermost marrow of your bones. Let wakefulness be for you like a guard over public duties; and, bound by a harsher custom and rule as by a chain of rigid iron, await the forgiveness of heavenly mercy under the image of martyrdom.

Come, come—why do you hesitate? That ladder of Jacob (Genesis 28:12), from which you fell while you were trying to climb, still stands there and has not yet been taken away. Although you have bruised all your limbs in your fall, nevertheless try again to climb. Until you reach the step from which you fell, preserve and guard yourself bravely; for although every ascent is slippery, that one quickly inclines and casts the climber into the depths.

[^c0110-1]: We follow the best reading of Grynaeus. Ambrosianus has, not improperly, *putridae* (“rotten things”).  
[^c0110-2]: The Ambrosian manuscript reads *zabulicam*; the printed books have *zaboliticam*. See note 2 of Rosweidus on Saint Paulinus’s letter to Severus, and elsewhere.  
[^c0110-3]: We follow Grynaeus’s excellent reading. Ambrosianus has, not badly, *putridae*.  
[^c0110-4]: Saint Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, chapter 9, no. 40: “Ask willingly for prison; bind your entrails with chains; crucify your soul with groans and fasts; seek the help of the saints; lie beneath the feet of the elect.” Bachiarius explains the duties of the penitent more fully.  
[^c0110-5]: The corrupt reading of Bignonius is retained. Ambrosius has *liniet* (“will smear”). Read *comminuat, tenuat* (“may crush, may make thin”), and so forth. In Vatican manuscript 3834 it is plainly written *limet*, that is, “may wear down, crush,” as I had conjectured it should be read.  
[^c0110-6]: Ambrosianus: “what the enemy could anticipate in you and punish.”  
[^c0110-7]: I have not found this sentence expressed in these words in the Apostle. But in 2 Corinthians 6:4 one reads: “Let us present ourselves as ministers of God, in great patience, in tribulations, necessities, distresses, blows, imprisonments, seditions, labors, watchings, fastings,” and so forth. Here is every kind of death—namely, laborious repentance, by which he was to wash away the stains of his fallen crime.

### 17

But perhaps you will say that, like the Pharisees, I place heavy burdens on people’s shoulders while I myself do not wish to touch them with my finger (Matthew 23:4). Behold, brother: since the permission to swear is forbidden to us (Matthew 5:37), if you believe anything of my unhappy condition, I promise, by the mercy of the Lord, that I wish to share in this labor which I urge upon you.[^c0110-8] [Editorial note: Ambrosianus reads, “according to the name of the Lord.”] In my desire for your salvation, I not only impose your fellowship upon myself but also offer myself to you. And if perhaps you are ashamed to come to us, send word; I shall hasten without delay to lead you here.

Let your fellowship be dreaded, like Ruth from the Moabite field—that is, the soul coming from drunkenness and fornication—by the man who seeks only his own interests, knows nothing of mercy, and boasts only of being descended from Israel.[^c0110-9] Although I am not like Boaz (Ruth 4:1ff.), I nevertheless desire your soul to be joined to me. Let no one accuse me of presumption, because I am permitted to raise up offspring from the widow of a dead brother (Deuteronomy 20:7, 9), lest I lose the Paschal sandals and become disinherited from Christ’s Passion; and, becoming blind as though at the bridegroom’s word, lest I accept the saliva of a fasting mouth, which is spat upon the ground and trampled.[^c0110-10] Rather, after seed has been poured out, let me enter the widow-soul of my dead brother—that is, one dead through despair. Then, having sought a multitude of seed and gathered an abundance of words from the Scriptures, let me be joined and draw near to this widow, so that, having heard these things, she may conceive without difficulty and give birth to the spirit of salvation.[^c0110-11]

For I remember the words of the apostolic command, where he says: “Save some by snatching them from the fire; console the doubtful” (1 Thessalonians 5:14); and elsewhere: “He who turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death” (James 5:20). It is no small thing if we snatch the tip—or uppermost part—of the ear from the lion’s jaws (Amos 3:12).[^c0110-12] Yet I think that the most blessed pontiff, who in these same places stands with his priests at the divine altar, is imitating no work other than David’s: when a lion or bear has carried off a sheep from the flock, he rises against it, strangles its throat, and snatches the prey from its gullet; or, like the good shepherd, he recalls the wandering sheep, binds the bruised one, and turns back the stray.

[^c0110-8]: Several ancient writers speak in this way. Saint Chromatius, *On the Eight Beatitudes*: “Therefore it is wholly unfitting for us to swear. For what need has any one of us to swear, when we are not permitted to lie at all?” See what follows, volume 11, page 168, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris 1624.  
[^c0110-9]: Compare this with the published texts; we have removed the errors with the aid of our manuscript.  
[^c0110-10]: The words of the Law to which Bachiarius alludes will clarify this obscure and, moreover, corrupt passage: “But if he does not wish to take his brother’s wife, who is owed to him by law, the woman shall approach him before the elders, remove his sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and say: ‘Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother’s house’” (Deuteronomy 25:9).  
[^c0110-11]: The printed editions have *salivam*. The Ambrosian manuscript, however, reads *salivam junioris* (“the saliva of a younger person”). It seems preferable to read simply “the saliva of the mouth.”  
[^c0110-12]: Is it “the tip” or “the uppermost part of the ear”? The Septuagint has *λοβὸν ὠτίου* (“the earlobe”); the Vulgate agrees.

### 18

You, however, brother, by no means consent to a criminal and shameful union. Do not insult him whose anger you will be unable to endure.[^c0110-13] Rather, let that woman whom the guilt of crime made your companion return to her husband. Is the sister of the patriarchs (Genesis 34), after she sinned, said to have married?[^c0110-14] The Lawgiver commanded (Leviticus 20:10) that whoever defiled another man’s wife should be stoned together with her; and therefore he does not permit marriage, but under the name of stones he corrects and reforms the sin by a harsh sentence.

Look at the prophet, who says: “And I said: After you have played the prostitute, return to me” (Jeremiah 3:1). Although the Assyrian king carried away the vessels of the Lord’s temple (Jeremiah 27:16), nevertheless let them return to the temple (Ezra 1:7–11), lest Babylon possess them forever in impurity.

Although the prince of cooks—he who prepares food for his lord, that is, for the worldly prince, from our sins—may have set fire to the Lord’s temple through the flame of shameful desire, nevertheless let Zerubbabel come, that is, the spirit of wisdom, which has already understood the power of women to rule wicked men; and which trusts wholly in truth. Let Ezra come, the library of the Law and the memory of reading. Let Nehemiah come.[^c0110-15] Let Naaman the Syrian come, the strength of confidence and despiser of fear, who does not fear the power of the prince when rebuilding his homeland. and, having stationed the angelic and patriarchal powers at the individual places of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 4:16–17)—that is, at the members of the body—so that what has collapsed may be rebuilt and what has been rebuilt guarded, let him serve the construction with one hand and the guard with the other. [Editorial note: Ambrosianus reads, “that what has collapsed may be rebuilt.”] for Adam was placed in paradise to work and to guard it (Genesis 2:15).

Let the barriers of the gates therefore be rebuilt through the tropological meanings of their names. At the beginning let the Sheep Gate be rebuilt (Nehemiah 3:1, according to the Septuagint), which we suspect to be hearing, through which we test whether the things entering us from outside are good or evil, because “faith comes from hearing” (Romans 10:17). Let us do what the Apostle says: “If you are in the faith, test yourselves” (2 Corinthians 13:5).

Let the Fish Gate be rebuilt (Nehemiah 3:3), that is, the ever-wandering nature of our sight, and the swift, fleeting gaze of the eyes through the paths of the sea—that is, the ways of this world. Sight itself may be regarded as a dragnet: whatever it looks upon, it immediately catches, and what it has caught it sends into the inner storerooms of the heart.

Let the gate at Anathoth be rebuilt (Nehemiah 3:6), whose name is interpreted as “responding sign.” [Editorial note: The Vulgate translator of Scripture has “they built the Old Gate”; the Septuagint has *Τὴν πύλην ἰασαναῖ*, alternatively *τοῦ ἀσανά*. I find no mention of a gate in Anathoth. Thus a corrupted text of the Old Latin version misled Bachiarius.] We suspect this to be the crossbeam of the forehead, where we have received the sign of our salvation and of the Lord’s holiness.[^c0110-16] [Editorial note: Ambrosianus reads, “we receive.”] This is the golden plate on which the high priest is commanded to receive the name of the Lord written as the Tetragrammaton.

Would you like to know why it is not inappropriate for us to understand the gate at Anathoth, “responding sign,” as the crossbeam of the forehead? The prophet joins to this gate the places of the perfumers (Nehemiah 3:8), which, through the tropological meanings of their names, are said to have been rebuilt by other virtues.[^c0110-17] And what are the places of the perfumers except those touched by the sanctification of chrism?

After this comes the Valley Gate (Nehemiah 3:13), which we suspect to be the function of the mouth and taste, through which the fruit of all seeds—that is, the words of God—emerges.[^c0110-18] Let the Dung Gate also be rebuilt (Nehemiah 3:14), which we suspect to be the entrance of the nostrils, or of smell, through which that shameful allure deceived us, and we considered as profits what were dung (Philippians 3:8).

Let the Strong Gate also be rebuilt (Nehemiah 3:15), [Editorial note: Bachiarius used a corrupt text of Scripture here. The Septuagint calls it *Τὴν πύλην τῆς πηγῆς*, “the Fountain Gate”; accordingly our Vulgate reads “the Fountain Gate.”] which I believe to be the function of our hands, or of touch, because we did not hold firmly what we were holding, and another took our crown (Revelation 3:11). Let the walls of the Pool also be rebuilt (Nehemiah 3:15), that is, the form of our baptism and the broken defenses of the mystical font, which are the marks of chastity. For when the wall of continence had been loosened through lust, and the barriers of the sacred waters had been broken, we poured out and lost the water of the font.

The wall is therefore said to be rebuilt so that we may recognize that the Lord’s mercy is so great that even periods of interrupted chastity can be rebuilt and recalled to the former likeness of continence through the power of self-restraint. Thus you too, through the vocabulary of the names and the tropological meanings of the places, should understand that these things said to be rebuilt are functions of the members.

[^c0110-13]: The Ambrosian manuscript correctly reads this. Grynaeus has *insulte*; Bignonius, *conjugio, cujus iram* (“marriage, whose anger…”).  
[^c0110-14]: Ambrosianus has “to have married.”  
[^c0110-15]: I am surprised that this word displeased Jean Launoy so greatly in *Epistolae*, part 4, letter 1, that he accused Cardinal Cajetan of using barbarous and uncouth language. Excessive eagerness to condemn led this otherwise learned man astray in ecclesiastical writings. The ancient translator of Scripture quoted by Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV.13; the author of the Vulgate at Mark 10:42; Saint Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* I.9.10; Saint Jerome in Homilies 4 and 8 on Jeremiah, in addition to Bachiarius—all these, whom no one would call barbarous or uncouth speakers, and many others, use the same word.  
[^c0110-16]: The older edition’s ugly error is not corrected by the Ambrosian manuscript. Bignonius’s editions do not contain this passage: “Ven. Na. Sy. vir. conf. cont. for.” Everyone can see that it ought to read “Nehemias.”  
[^c0110-17]: A certain Ananias, “son of the perfumers” (*υἱὸς τοῦ ῥωκεΐμ*, or *ῥοκεῖμ*), is said to have built a house not far from the Old Gate. In the Vulgate he is called “the son of the perfumer.”  
[^c0110-18]: *Τὴν πύλην τῆς φάραγγος* (“the gate of the valley”). The older interpreters call it the Valley Gate. The name “Frugis” may perhaps have been formed from the Greek word, or Bachiarius may have found it in the Italian version or in some commentary.

### 19

Finally, do not imitate the work of the king of Babylon (Daniel 5:2ff.), so that you believe you ought to drink the wine of perdition from the vessels of the Lord’s temple, and this before your gods—Venus, Mars, and Mercury—that is, fornication, avarice, and rage.[^c0110-19] For it is written: “The fury of a man is unrestrained” (Job 31:11, according to the Septuagint); and elsewhere: “Avarice, which is idolatry” (Ephesians 5:5). You cannot reckon avarice as applying only to money, since avarice is felt especially in lust, for which no limit is ever established.

The Prophet teaches us that virgins are called vessels in the Lord’s temple when he says: “Wheat for the young men, and sweet-smelling wine for virgins” (Zechariah 11:17, according to the Septuagint); and if the liquid of wine is poured into something, what else should it be called but a vessel?

I would gladly be instructed by those more learned than I: on what authority of Scripture is a corrupted woman encouraged to marry, when blessed David did not permit even his concubines, whom his son had defiled through shameful intercourse, afterward to marry or have husbands (2 Samuel 20:3)? Did he not preserve them as widows, providing them with sustenance, until the end? David—that is, the Lord Christ—does not wish his wife to be possessed by another man in his sight.

Finally, the daughter of Saul whom he had lost for a time during the persecution (2 Samuel 3:13ff.), he afterward demanded should be returned and restored to him. Although she had also been joined to another, she was nevertheless taken away from him and assigned to the one whose she had formerly been. You have polluted David’s wife: do not presume to do this any longer. Rather, as the man who had taken her did, return and restore her, weeping and mourning.

[^c0110-19]: This passage from Job is reported mutilated and insufficiently corrected. The Greek version of the Elders reads: “For the fury of anger is uncontrollable, to defile a man’s wife.”

### 20

Perhaps that ancient counselor, wiser than all the beasts (Genesis 3:1), suggested to you that you could perform the repentance we urge upon you in your old age, and that for now you might satisfy the desire of your longing under the name of marriage.

But do not extinguish with the moisture of vices the evangelical spark that proceeds from the fire of the entire book, where it says: “Fool, this night your soul will be demanded of you” (Luke 12:20). If even among those whose marriages are honorable such unions cannot last forever, how will they endure among you, where they are joined to crime?

Let the one who says that this crime ought to be corrected by marriage come forward, and let him say that a union arising from so great a crime should be called marriage.[^c0110-20] For marriage is a word belonging to a religious designation (Hebrews 13:4), since it was granted by God’s authority.

Behold, the Apostle cries out concerning honorable marriages: “Those who have wives as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:29). And who says: “Let an adulterer have her, use her, and enjoy her”?[^c0110-21] But I see toward what defense he turns. For, he says, it is written: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9). This was said concerning a virgin or a widow. This woman is no longer a virgin. At that time she was burning, and she married; now let her be refreshed and live. She is not a virgin, because she has been corrupted; she is not a widow, because her husband lives forever.

Why, then, do you urge her to marry? Do you wish to know the apostolic judgment concerning this error? He says in his Letter: “Fornication is certainly heard of among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife” (1 Corinthians 5:1). Here something similar has happened. This young woman who sinned was the wife of that Father who begot us through the word of truth (James 1:18). I believe she was joined to him in marriage when, following the example of Rebecca coming from Mesopotamia to Isaac, she received the veil with which her head was covered (Genesis 24:65).

Concerning this deed the Apostle says: “I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Corinthians 5:3). Did he say, “I commanded him to marry the woman he had corrupted”? No. Rather: “I handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.” For Satan means “adversary”; by this, I believe, he indicates that everything contrary to pleasures and everything contrary to the will should be felt by the flesh that sinned, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[^c0110-20]: The Lyon edition has “to be called a marriage because of so great a crime.” In the same words, in *On the Faith*, no. 5, it professes that marriage was granted by God’s authority.  
[^c0110-21]: Ambrosius has “Let an adulteress have her.” Saint Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*, chapter 5, no. 21: “Someone will say: ‘It is better to marry than to burn.’ This saying concerns one who has not made a vow, one who has not yet been veiled. But she who has pledged herself to Christ and received the holy veil has already married; she has already been joined to an immortal husband. And if she wishes to marry according to the common law of marriage, she commits adultery and becomes a servant of death.” See Dissertation 2, chapter 5, and the author of the book *On Virginity*, formerly attributed to Basil the Great, no. 39, at the end of volume 2 of the Benedictine edition.

### 21

And you also, brother, whoever has persuaded you to this, curse him. For observe that animals worn out by age are never slaughtered in sacrifices; everywhere either a lamb, a calf, a goat, or a kid is offered (Exodus 29 and elsewhere)—that is, sins which are still tender, small, or moderate.[^c0110-22] In one place, however, we read that Elijah offered a bull (1 Kings 18:33), but this happened only once. This was permitted to the one Savior, who slaughtered the sins of the entire people, grown old through long persistence.[^c0110-23]

But do not think that your sin is still a tender kid. Believe me: it is a goat. Behold through how many regions of the earth the stench of your conduct—that is, the evil reputation of your disgrace—has traveled. How, then, can what smells so strongly not be called a goat?

The Prophet calls blessed the one who seizes Babylon’s little ones and dashes them against the rock (Psalm 136:9). And you are waiting until your enemy becomes a giant? But if you wish to know, he is already a giant. For as soon as the sons of God desired the daughters of men, giants were born from them (Genesis 6:4). This is the form of a giant: enormously excessive and beyond the stature of the remaining sins.[^c0110-24]

And if someone perhaps says that David also received into his marriage the woman whom he had adulterated (2 Samuel 11:27), the cases are not comparable. She was the king’s wife, whereas the other was a soldier’s wife. As an earthly man, he could be killed by the treacherous plotting of an artful scheme; but this King is heavenly, and his wife has been corrupted and violated. No mortal passion approaches him who is not temporal but eternal.

And yet David, while Uriah the Hittite—although his own soldier and an earthly man—was absent, presumed to have intercourse with Bathsheba. Did he not try not merely to urge Uriah, but even to compel him (2 Samuel 11:13), after he had craftily ordered abundant food and drink to be served, to lie at home in his own bed?

How will you claim intercourse with an adulteress while her husband is alive and present—and, what is more, while the King, immortal and everlasting, is also present?

But perhaps you will say: “When he learned the cause of the adultery, her husband cast her out and rejected her.” You deceive yourself, brother, because through the Prophet he himself cries out: “Where is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her?” (Isaiah 50:1). And elsewhere: “Does the one who falls not rise again? Or does the one who turns away not turn back? Why has my people not repented of their evils, and, held fast in their evil intention, refused to return to me?” (Jeremiah 8:4–5).

Behold, at the Lord’s command the prophet took a prostitute as his wife (Hosea 1:2ff.); and you say that a soul has been cast away by God into destruction?

Nor do I oppose this marriage, if you can produce from it such fruit as came forth from Bathsheba and David: the one whom the Lord, through the prophet, called Jedidiah—that is, “beloved of the Lord”—“in the word of the Lord” (2 Samuel 12:25). Among men he was called Solomon, that is, “Peaceful,” and he held authority over the whole world—that is, over the whole human being.

Such a son is born from repentance. Such a child is brought forth by the groans and laments of mourners. Finally, blessed David himself, after he had been discovered with an adulteress in his youth, is found in his old age with a virgin (1 Kings 1:1ff.), so that we may understand that after sin a long chastity imitates virginity.

You too, then, imitate David. Let the woman whom you had as your companion in the fault of corruption become your companion in the labor of repentance—not so that you may repent while joined together, but so that, separated from one another, you may be joined by carrying out one work between you; for a still-smoking brand from a fire is quickly seized by a devouring flame.

[^c0110-22]: Against Bachiarius, I suspect that “or a goat” has slipped in here. The words that immediately follow also have the flavor of a gloss: “In one place, however, we read that Elijah offered a bull. This was permitted only once, to the Savior.” If these are removed, I would read: “…sins.” But this was permitted only once, to the one Savior.  
[^c0110-23]: Bignonius has “there were born among the giants and the rock.” These words, unless I am mistaken, preserve traces of the true text: “Giants were born on the earth, and Rephaim.”  
[^c0110-24]: The printed edition has *Dirigiam*. In the Ambrosian manuscript it is *Dirigam*. Eucherius and others, less corruptly, have *Ididam*. But this name does not mean “in the word of the Lord”; it means “beloved of the Lord.” Bachiarius follows the version of Theodotion, which reads: “His name was Jedidiah, in the word of the Lord” (*τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἰεδιδία ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου*), and: “He called his name Jedidiah”—“beloved of the Lord”—“in the word of the Lord.” See Origen’s *Hexapla*, collected by Montfaucon, volume 1, page 333.

### 22

Above all, therefore, brother, do not let hostile despair grow within you, asserting—as that unbeliever does—that the fallen cannot be restored, when the Lord says: “All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven human beings; but whoever has sinned against the Spirit will not be forgiven” (Matthew 12:31).

I say that this very despair concerning the Lord is sinning against the Spirit, because “the Lord is Spirit” (John 4:24). It is therefore not forgiven him because he has not believed that the Lord can return to him what he has lost.

What, then, can stand in the way of our forgiveness? Our Lord is almighty. Is it impossible for the Almighty to erase sin? Our Lord is good, “for no one is good except one, God” (Luke 18:19). Can this fault occur in that supreme and perfect goodness, that he should not hear the one who pleads?[^c0110-25]

Come, then, my friend, rise up. Having lost your profit and substance amid the waves of the world, hold fast like a shipwrecked man to the one plank (Luke 15:13)—that is, to knowledge of the divine canon—which will bring you to the shore where it says:

“If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows. But I will not scatter my mercy from them, nor will I harm them in my truth” (Psalm 88:31–34).

Of whose sons is this said? Are they not the sons of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the womb of the ecclesiastical font and the hidden, intricate vulva of the mystery brought forth; whom, once born, the cradle of the Cross received, and the breast of the Gospel nursed?

Would you like to know that the baptized, not the catechumens, are called sons? Observe what he himself said to his Apostles: “I shall no longer call you servants, but sons” [Greek: *φίλους*, “friends”] (John 15:15). You too, therefore, if you know that you were a son—that is, if you possessed something apostolic within you—you are not permitted to despair even in this condition.

But if you have always performed the service of a servant—that is, of a sinner—greater courage must be given you to rise again. For the fall of one who falls from a low place is lighter; and the man burdened by less weight of anger is the one who, having always remained in error, turns himself at last toward a right life,[^c0110-26] rather than those who, after holy deeds, have lived shamefully and have sewn an old garment onto new clothing (Mark 2:21).

And what of what he says to his churches in the Apocalypse, which are compared, among the number of the faithful, to seven-branched lampstands under angelic protection? “Remember from where you have fallen, repent, and perform your former works; otherwise I am coming to you quickly, and I will remove your lampstand” (Revelation 2:5).

And in the earlier part of the book he says that he saw an innumerable multitude (Revelation 7:15), who washed their robes in tribulation and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; and he says that the Lamb of God will lead them to the springs of life (Revelation 7:17). We understand this number, nevertheless, to be the number of penitents, because they were saved only through tribulation and mourning.

[^c0110-25]: Read without hesitation: “into that supreme and perfect goodness.” If I am not mistaken, this appears in Lactantius, or in another author older than Bachiarius.  
[^c0110-26]: “Or: path.”

### 23

You too, then, wash your robe in the fountain of tears.[^c0110-27] Perhaps you will be able to imitate the fine linen of chastity. What if he gives you purple, and you pour out the juice of your blood for his name? Scarlet can abound for you if you blush at the things you previously did. Nor will hyacinth be lacking to you if you grow hot with bruising your body and bring it into servitude (1 Corinthians 9:27).[^c0110-28] Thus, perhaps, with these colors you may at some time be mingled into the Lord’s tabernacle.

This, dearest brother, compelled by love and grief for you, I have attempted even beyond my strength and ability. You will have a double punishment on the day of judgment if, like deaf serpents, you reject the words of our incantation (Psalm 57:5), or if you believe that the word of one who begs, the counsel of one who warns, or the affection of one who grieves should be despised.[^c0110-29]

May Jesus Christ, the Son of God, restore to you twofold the goods taken from you through the envy of the devil; and may you be reconciled to the Lord in such a way that you may also deserve to intercede with the Lord on behalf of us, who are your friends, in our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

[^c0110-27]: We restore this corrupted and dislocated passage of the older editions to soundness on the authority of the Ambrosian manuscript. As for the mystical explanation of the colors, our author departs little from Origen, who says in *Homily 11 on Exodus*, no. 3: “With fine linen one may compare virginity; with scarlet, the glory of confession; with purple, the splendor of charity; with hyacinth, the hope of the kingdom of heaven.”  
[^c0110-28]: Ambrosianus has “you will be clothed in it.”  
[^c0110-29]: Read “and.”  

**In the year of our Lord 420**

**Zacchaeus the Christian and Evagrius the Monk**

(*Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Galland, volume 9)

[Column 1061]

[Column 1061C]

## Prolegomena

[^c0110-30]

### 1

That the books of the *Dialogues* which bear the name of Zacchaeus are extremely ancient is clear from the antiquity of the manuscript codices, indeed from the very reading of the books themselves. To establish the author’s date with certainty, however, seemed to us so laborious and difficult that, after a careful and diligent examination and after consulting highly learned men, nothing has so far emerged as certain.

Indeed, this author seems to have concealed his name so deliberately and almost by design that he attached only the fictitious names of Zacchaeus and Apollonius to his *Dialogues*. Although he declares that he drew his teaching from the monuments of earlier Fathers, he gives the name of not one of them, nor does he identify the kind of writing from which he drew it. Accordingly, learned reader, we are compelled to offer you here only a few conjectures.

### 2

The profession of our Zacchaeus is not nearly as obscure as his date. For since, according to Cassian,[^c0110-31] monastic observance can be taught only by those who have experienced it, it may be gathered from what he writes throughout almost the whole of Book 3 that he earned his standing in the monastic life; and he himself indicated this somewhere.

From this, perhaps, his date can be determined. Since around the sixth century nearly all the monks in the West embraced the rule of the holy father Benedict, if our Zacchaeus had survived until that time, he would have taken his monastic instruction from the rule of Saint Benedict, just as he took the dogmas of the faith from the holy Fathers. But comparison makes it clear that he did not do this.

Nor do the arguments that follow obscurely suggest that he undertook this work before the beginning of the fifth century. Before that period, in the part of Europe where he was then living, there were not available the numerous illustrious volumes of the Fathers to which he could send his Apollonius as to fountains from which he had drawn this entire catechesis. Nor, before that time, had the matters he discusses in Book 2 against the Arians, Photinians, and other such obscurantists been explained so explicitly by the Latin Fathers that they could not be reviewed without tedium; he himself says as much.[^c0110-32]

These considerations lead us to assign the origin of the *Dialogues* to the fifth century.

[^c0110-30]: The author of this investigation is Acherius, from volume 1 of the *Spicilegium*, at page 1.  
[^c0110-31]: Cassian, preface to the *Institutes*.  
[^c0110-32]: Zacchaeus, *Consultation*, Book 2, chapter 1.

### 3.

This is also suggested by the fact that Zacchaeus himself attacks only those heretics who in his own time were making the greater tumult and enjoying the greater influence: the Manichaeans, Marcionites, Photinians, Sabellians, Patripassians, Arians, and Novatians. But concerning the heresy of Pelagius and his followers, which in the course of the fifth century infected the greater part of the world, he says not a word—not even though the opportunity presented itself in several places, especially in Book II, chapter 11.

Meanwhile, it should be observed that our author was mistaken, or that the passage was corrupted through the ignorance of copyists, in his description of the Sabellian heresy, since he attributes to Sabellius what belongs to Macedonius. Furthermore, all the signs by which he foretells that the coming of Antichrist is imminent [Note: [Col. 1063D] The same author, ibid., Book VIII, chapter 8.] correspond exactly with our conjectures [Col. 1063D]. For this is precisely the period when enormous hordes of barbarians poured into Africa and Europe and devastated Gaul, Spain, Italy, and Rome itself, the very citadel of the empire; while in the East royal Constantinople and most of the cities of Palestine were being shaken by a dreadful earthquake, and finally men were afflicted by famine and pestilence. Consult Orosius [Note: [Col. 1063D] Orosius, Book VII, chapter 40, near the end, and chapter 42.], Zosimus [Note: [Col. 1063D] Zosimus, Book VI.], Sozomen [Note: [Col. 1063D] Sozomen, Book IX, chapter 8.], [Col. 1064A] Saint Jerome [Note: [Col. 1064D] Jerome, Letter 16.], Lucas of Tuy in his *Chronicle*, and Marcellinus Comes [Note: [Col. 1064D] Marcellinus, *Chronicle*, p. 27.].

What he relates at length concerning the institutions of cenobites living in cities, and concerning sacred hymnody, also supports this conclusion [Note: [Col. 1064D] Zacchaeus, *loc. cit.*, Book III, chapter 6.]. For before the year 400 very few, indeed perhaps no, monasteries were seen in the cities of Europe. As for singing, Augustine expressly writes that it was introduced into the Church by blessed Ambrose as the fifth century was approaching [Note: [Col. 1064D] Augustine, *Confessions*, Book IX, chapter 7.].

Finally, his style, generally swollen and muscular; his repeated use of expressions familiar to writers of this period; his clear refutation of the astrologers and of the heresies against which the Fathers of that time directed their pens; his noteworthy mention of supplications by which rain was kept away; and many other details of this kind appear more than sufficiently to confirm our conjectures [Col. 1064B]. Thus far, then, we have indicated conjectures—not only our own, but also those of eminent men: Sebastian Le Nain de Tillemont, Charles du Fresne, Seigneur du Cange, Jean-Baptiste le Cottelier, the Reverend Fathers Jean Garnier, S.J., and Pasquier Quesnel, priests of the Congregation of the Oratory of the Lord Jesus, and, above all, our own Francis Delfau.

### 4.

There may perhaps be a critic of more discerning judgment who will think that some weight is added to these arguments by what the author writes [Note: [Col. 1064D] Zacchaeus, *loc. cit.*, Book I, chapter 21]—namely, that in his own time the signs of the Lord’s death contained the relics of the blessed tomb. By these relics he may be understood to mean the shroud in which Christ’s sacred body was wrapped: Eudocia is said to have carried it to Constantinople at the beginning of the fifth century, and, according to Walter—whose authority for this matter may be judged for oneself—Theodosius II sent it with great ceremony to Besançon in the year 439.

There may also be someone who will derive a conjecture concerning the period in which our author lived from the fact that in one place [Note: [Col. 1064D] The same author, *loc. cit.*, Book I, chapter 28.] he criticizes—not all worship, but, as he says, the incautious homage offered by the people to the images of the emperors. For toward the end of the fourth century that custom was in force: painted or sculpted images of the emperors were carried about in solemn procession and received with the public acclamations of the crowd. Yet that worship often degenerated into superstition because of the weakness of the multitude, which cannot restrain its emotions whenever flattery or the display of public joy excites them. Circumstances also sometimes contributed to this. Those images were displayed not only in profane places but also in sacred ones, as were the statues of Eudocia erected at Constantinople near the basilica—statues which became for John Chrysostom an occasion both of righteous zeal and of envy.

Zacchaeus seems to have had this in mind when he says that priests forbade such a custom of incautious homage. For just as the Fathers judged that the images of emperors ought to be honored, so they always disapproved of immoderate worship that seemed to approach religion, or even superstition. Indeed, emperors who were devoted to piety did not tolerate excessive eagerness in venerating their own images. A remarkable law of the emperor Theodosius bears on this matter, and I shall quote it here to clarify the point [Note: [Col. 1065D] Theodosius, *Code*, single law concerning imperial images.]:

> Whenever statues or images of us are erected, whether on customary feast days or on ordinary days, let a judge be present without the ostentatious pomp of adoration, so that he may show that his presence has been added as an adornment to the day or place and as a reminder of us. Even at public games, when likenesses are displayed, let them show only that our divine power and praises flourish in the minds and secret thoughts of those assembled; worship exceeding human dignity must be reserved for the heavenly Deity.

Animated by the same spirit, Honorius, an imitator of his father’s piety, rebuked his brother Arcadius because not only was a statue of the empress Eudocia displayed at Constantinople for the people to worship, but it was also carried through the provinces like the image of fabulous Cybele.

In any case, it would be futile to twist this passage of Zacchaeus into support for the veneration of sacred images, since the Church—which proclaims their pious worship—rejects immoderate and superstitious worship, just as Zacchaeus does in the case of imperial images.

### 5.

“But indeed,” someone may object, “our conjectures seem to be contradicted by the fact that Zacchaeus says nothing about the Apollinarists, Donatists, Priscillianists, or Pelagians.” But he himself forestalls this objection by expressly stating that he had not undertaken to list every such plague. It might nevertheless be said that at the beginning of the fifth century the doctrines of Pelagius and Nestorius had not yet been condemned so explicitly that there already existed distinguished works from which, in his customary manner, he could extract Catholic doctrine. This again demonstrates the man’s exceptional modesty and confirms the conjectures advanced concerning his date.

In any case, that mighty champion of religion suppressed not only the heretics of earlier periods but also those of his own age, and he seems to have portrayed them from life in their true colors [Note: [Col. 1065D] Zacchaeus, Book II, chapter 11.]. “For those very men,” he says, “who, abandoning the apostolic tradition, followed teachers of perfidy, changed the name of religion together with its meaning.”

The same author says that Peter is not only the foundation of the Church [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, ibid., chapter 18], but also affirms that the authority of all priests is gathered into Peter’s person—contrary to the view of the innovators. Again, against the Novatians, he elegantly and forcefully defends the authority to absolve from sins as having been granted by Christ to priests [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, ibid.].

Apollonius, now enrolled in the Christian army, confesses the Church’s sacrifice and the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, preface to Book II.]. In place of the obsolete sacrifices of cattle and birds, he records that the heavenly offering of the faithful is celebrated through a pure oblation [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, Book II, chapter 7.]. He repeatedly champions free will, sound and unimpaired. He gives illustrious testimony to the power of sacred relics [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, Book I, chapter 21], affirming as an eyewitness that things we read of the saints having done while alive are also performed before the ashes of the dead.

He commends monasticism—which Luther attacks as an invention of the devil—as a singular work of Almighty God [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, Book III, chapters 3, 4, and 6.]. Finally, he teaches that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, Book II, chapters 2 and 3.], which, in my judgment, is the same as saying that he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

### 6.

“Although, since nothing is blessed in every respect, this author is not without certain blemishes, an educated reader who wishes to excuse him will apply benevolent interpretations to them, as is proper, so that his authority may remain sound in every respect. Meanwhile, we offer several cautions, lest simpler readers be rashly offended in certain places.

First of all, he seems to have contracted something of the soot of Pelagianism—the stain of that age—which perhaps caused him to refrain from attacking the Pelagians and the Nestorians who arose from them. ‘The reason for the Incarnation,’ he says [Note: [Col. 1065D] The same author, Book I, chapters 8, 15, 17, and 21], ‘is either the preservation or the restoration of the human race.’ He immediately seems to establish this restoration in law and example.

He attributes the premature deaths of infants to the inequality of the elements or to the crimes of their parents, not to original guilt [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book I, chapter 36], in order to demonstrate that God is not unjust. He adds that they are treated more mercifully lest, being born of wicked parents, they should at some point become like their authors; and here he seems largely to locate original sin in the evil example of parents [Col. 1066C].

Nowhere, however, does he mention the grace of the Savior, whom he regards merely as the arbiter of merits [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book I, chapter 33.]. Finally, he thinks that the whole necessity of the law lies in our will [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book I, chapter 36.].

A Catholic reader will wipe away this stain with the same sponge by which Saint Augustine removed it from the Greek Fathers: namely, that doctrines of this kind had not yet been explicitly explained by the Church. Yet this excuse is unnecessary, since he himself intimated both original sin and the necessity of Christ’s grace to the extent sufficient before a fuller definition.

‘This,’ he says [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book I, chapter 14], ‘was the chief reason, or will, for assuming humanity: that the sin contracted by man might be removed through man.’ And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book II, chapter 8]: ‘No one can be saved without the washing of spiritual water’ [Col. 1066D]. Again [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book II, chapter 16]: ‘Freed from the universal ruin, you are restored to the hope you had lost.’

He also elegantly supports the grace of the Redeemer [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, ibid., chapters 5 and 8]. Then [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book III, chapter 10]: ‘Let him alone provide the means for accomplishing it, who by his gift has permitted one to desire great things.’ Finally [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same author, Book II, chapter 20]: ‘Let him not refuse to contribute what he has enabled one to will’ [Col. 1067A].

Moreover, he says [Note: [Col. 1067D] Zacchaeus, chapters 8 and 18] that we are justified by faith—in precisely the sense in which blessed Paul wrote of faith that works through love; otherwise, ‘even if I have all faith, it profits me nothing.’ Furthermore, when he teaches [Note: [Col. 1067D] The same author, ibid., chapter 19] that it is sufficient to adhere to the canonical Scriptures, he does not abolish the traditions which he there asserts, and whose neglect by the heterodox he laments.

Elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1067D] The same author, Book I, chapter 33] he thinks that a period for repentance was granted to the angels, perhaps not in the sense of the School; unless by that period is understood the interval that intervened between sin and punishment.

### 7.

“Perhaps you ask, reader, whose countryman Zacchaeus was. Frankly, I cannot think of anything to assert. Some curious investigators of antiquity declare him to have been either a Gaul or an Italian [Col. 1067B]. If, however, I may indulge in conjecture, I would call Zacchaeus an African, on account of the affinity of his style with the African writers who were composing works in that age or shortly before it.

“It remains for you now to learn from me, reader, from which library the manuscript codices were supplied from which we undertook to transcribe Zacchaeus’ work.

When the distinguished men Charles du Fresne, Seigneur du Cange, and Jean-Baptiste le Cottelier—both of them most learned—were examining and inspecting the manuscript codices of the celebrated Thuane Library, they came upon two manuscript copies of the three books of the *Dialogues* of Zacchaeus the Christian and Apollonius the philosopher. They turned them over and over, and finally, after examining them as best they could, judged them worthy of the light of publication. Without my knowledge, they requested the two manuscripts from the learned librarian Joseph Quesnel [Col. 1067C], who, being closely bound to me in friendship and known for his kindness toward everyone, generously lent both of them to me.

My very dear friends immediately brought them to me and presented me with a treasure that had until then been hidden and unseen. I received it with the greatest delight and promised to bring it into the light.

### 8.

“But indeed, when I began to read and examine those codices, I came to a halt at the very beginning. The latter manuscript lacked a title, although it plainly bore the marks of eight hundred years; its first page was almost effaced; the words throughout the entire work were repeatedly transposed, and syllables had been awkwardly divided and joined.

In the other codex, written in a somewhat older hand, a title was indeed present, but the characters repeatedly escaped the eye, as they did throughout the volume, since it had been weakened and rotted by rain and decay. Moreover, this codex was not merely damaged: it had been written so carelessly and incompetently by some ignorant person that the order of the text was frequently inverted—for example, in Book I. Just as he indiscriminately inserted much material from Book II into a single chapter, so in Books II and III alike he disturbed the sequence of the text and altered its meaning.

While I remained anxiously perplexed, and no path presented itself through which I could escape from so great a labyrinth, the Reverend Monsieur Faure, a doctor of the Sorbonne [Col. 1068A] and a most skilled investigator of antiquity, informed me that he had discovered the *Dialogues* of Zacchaeus in the library of the fathers’ congregation of Saints Vitonus and Hidulphus at Saint-Arnulf of Metz.
