I immediately wrote about this matter to the Reverend Father Dom Pierre Descrochets, a highly learned priest of the same congregation and subprior of Saint-Arnulf. He, being endowed with singular courtesy, promptly and graciously sent me a codex elegantly written around the year 600.

But, astonishingly, that codex contained the same transpositions and repetitions as the older Thuane manuscript. Nevertheless, I confess that it was of the greatest assistance to me, for from it I resolved in many places the knots that remained and wiped away blemishes. And, to say what I think, it is reasonable to believe that the Arnulfian codex was copied from the aforementioned older manuscript of the Thuane Library and once belonged by right to the Abbey of Saint-Arnulf of Metz.

Some of our own men, I do not deny, gave assistance in collating with immense labor the apograph that we used for this edition against the manuscript codices, and in elucidating the darkness that very often enveloped the mind. Among our own associates, Monsieur Gabriel Gerberon and Monsieur Jean Mabillon were also at hand.”

### 9.

[Note: [Col. 1068D] The following was added to Acherius’ *Disquisition* by the distinguished Louis-François-Joseph de la Barre, who prepared a new edition of the *Spicilegium*.]

“Thus far Acherius. His labor would have been diminished to no small degree if he could have seen the *Altercation of Theophilus the Christian and Simon the Jew*, which the Reverend Father Dom Edmond Martène published in the fifth volume of the *Anecdota*. Since the author of that *Altercation* is Evagrius, who was writing around the year 420, as we learn from Gennadius [Note: [Col. 1067D] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 50] and from Marcellinus Comes under the year 423, the learned man whom I named above rightly judged that it can scarcely be doubted that the same man wrote these *Consultations*.

“There are other matters about which we think it worthwhile to warn the reader. For what Acherius says—that the relics of the blessed tomb may perhaps be understood as the shroud in which Christ’s sacred body was wrapped—is, in my judgment, altogether improbable. It is sufficiently established that this shroud was not carried to Constantinople by Eudocia, the wife of Arcadius, at the beginning of the fifth century, but by Aelia Eudoxia, the wife of Theodosius the Younger, and not before the year 440. Everyone knows that the latter woman visited the city of Jerusalem; but I know no one who has written that she traveled throughout Palestine. Moreover [Col. 1068D], these *Consultations* had already been written before Theodosius the Younger had married Eudoxia.

“What the same author added concerning the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son is even less accurate. For in the passages he indicates—namely, chapters 2 and 3 of Book II—not a single word can in any way be referred to that question. If he was thinking of chapter 19, where the text formerly read, ‘The Holy Spirit is also from the Father and the Son,’ we wish first to inform the reader that we have removed the word *simul* (‘together’) and restored in its place, on the authority of the best codex, the word *similiter* (‘similarly’), which entirely changes the meaning, as may be seen in the notes.

“Then, even if the word *simul* is retained, it is not clear that Zacchaeus or Evagrius held the same view concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit as all Latins do today. For it is evident from the second book, chapter 17, of Anselm of Havelberg’s *Dialogues* that there were formerly men who confessed that the Holy Spirit is both the Father’s and the Son’s, indeed that he is from both the Father and the Son, but who nevertheless did not wish it to be written that he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

“It remains to inform Acherius that, when he published these *Consultations*, the manuscript codex of Saint Martial of Limoges had not yet been made available to him. This codex was written before the year 1010 at the command of Ademar of Chabannes, from which various readings were later excerpted and published at the end of volume XIII of the *Spicilegium* [Col. 1069B]. We gladly acknowledge that these readings were of considerable assistance to us in correcting the text, but in such a way that many more readings were excerpted from the codex of the monastery of Vendôme by Dom Martène, who arranged for them to be published at the end of the fifth volume of the *Anecdota*.”

Thus far Monsieur de la Barre.

### 10.

Now, lest we appear to have come here wholly empty-handed, we would like to contribute a few observations. First, with regard to the author’s date, we must examine the opinion of Fabricius [Note: [Col. 1069D] Fabricius, *Select Arguments*, etc., chapter 5, p. 255.], who thought that a different view should be taken from that of the others.

When the following words of Zacchaeus were brought forward [Note: [Col. 1069D] Zacchaeus, *Consultations*, Book III, chapter 8], “Kingdoms clash with kingdoms, and they drive from the thrones of rightful seats emperors unsuspected of such acts,” he thought that the author, in writing this, was clearly referring to what was done by Odoacer, king of the Heruli, in the year 470 after Christ [Col. 1069C]. He repeats the same view elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1069D] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina medii aevi*, vol. II, p. 350, Hamburg edition.].

At the very least, he should have assigned the passage to the year 476. But leaving this aside, there is no need to resort to the period of that barbarian leader in order to make the author’s words fit the truth. Why should the disguised Zacchaeus not have been referring to the frequent invasions of Italy by Radagaisus and, above all, Alaric, which occurred at the beginning of the fifth century? For we know that at that time the Western Empire was miserably harassed and that Rome itself was captured and plundered. These matters were sufficiently known to the public and require no documentary records for their confirmation.

### 11.

We would further point out that we have added another short work to the three books of Zacchaeus’ *Consultations*, a work which Wolf [Note: [Col. 1069D] Wolf, *Bibliotheca Hebraea*, vol. III, p. 1141, no. [Col. 1070D] 2273.] and Fabricius [Note: [Col. 1070D] Fabricius, in the work cited above.] rightly acknowledge as belonging to the same author along with the other works mentioned earlier.

Its title is *Altercation between Theophilus the Christian and Simon the Jew*. The distinguished Martène and Durand published it [Note: [Col. 1070D] Martène, *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, pp. 3–18.], and they discussed it learnedly as follows:

> “This work, venerable on account of its antiquity, was supplied to us by an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Vendôme, in which it is immediately appended to the three books of the *Altercations* or *Consultations* of Zacchaeus the Christian and Apollonius the philosopher, as though it were the fourth book of the *Altercations*. Thus it appears to be the offspring of the same author: after refuting philosophers under the name of Zacchaeus the Christian in three books, he attacked the Jews in a separate work under the name of Theophilus.
>
> “Three conjectures in particular may persuade us of this. First, the title is the same in both works. The three books of the *Consultations of Zacchaeus the Christian and Apollonius the philosopher* are given the title of an *Altercation* in the Limoges codex of Saint Martial and in the Vendôme codex. In the Limoges codex it reads: *Altercation of Apollonius the philosopher with Zacchaeus the Christian*. In the Vendôme codex, however, it reads: *Here begin the chapters of the first book of the Altercations*.
>
> “Indeed, the same is found in other codices used by our Acherius when he published them in volume X of the *Spicilegium*. At the end of the first book one reads: *The book of the Altercation of Zacchaeus the Christian and Apollonius the philosopher is finished.* At the end of the third book: *The Altercation of Zacchaeus and Apollonius is completed.*
>
> “Second, the manner of writing is also the same in both works: namely, the form of a dialogue or disputation in which a gentile or a Jew proposes his objections and difficulties, and the Christian explains and resolves them in such a way that in the end he persuades and prevails.
>
> “Third, the style is likewise identical everywhere—swollen and muscular—as will be clear to anyone who compares the two *Altercations*. Since Acherius proves very convincingly in his preface to volume X of the *Spicilegium* that the books of the *Consultations of Zacchaeus the Christian* were written at least at the beginning of the fifth century, learned readers will easily perceive what judgment should be formed concerning the date of the *Altercation of Theophilus the Christian and Simon the Jew*. Its great antiquity is certainly demonstrated by the very version of Scripture used by the author, a version familiar to the earliest ecclesiastical writers. From this you may infer how highly it ought to be valued by everyone.
>
> “After I had written these things, I discovered in Gennadius that the author of this *Altercation* was Evagrius, who flourished around the year 400. For he writes as follows [Note: [Col. 1070D] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 50]: ‘Another Evagrius wrote the *Altercation of Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian*, which is known to everyone.’
>
> “Marcellinus Comes agrees with him in these words [Note: [Col. 1070D] Marcellinus Comes, *Chronicle*, under the year 423]: ‘Evagrius wrote the *Altercation of Simon the Jew and Theophilus the Christian*, which is known to almost everyone.’
>
> “The distinguished Sebastian de Tillemont had likewise conjectured with me that this Evagrius was the author of both *Altercations*. Moreover, the *Altercation* that we are presenting here was formerly kept in the monastery of Centula, as is shown by the catalogue of the books of that monastery made in the time of Louis the Pious, which Hariulfus cites in his *Chronicle of Centula*, volume IV of the *Spicilegium*.”

Thus far the learned author.

### 12.

Before leaving this subject, we would also like to call attention to something which occurred to us when we observed it in Zacagnius’ notes on the disputation of Archelaus with Manes.

Explaining a passage in which that bishop of Carrhae states [Note: [Col. 1071B] Archelaus, *Disputation*, chapter 31, in our *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III, p. 588] that Moses handed down an imaginary law, Zacagnius writes, among other things [Note: [Col. 1071B] Zacagnius, ibid., note 4]:

> “The ancient translator of the monk Evagrius also uses this word in the disputation of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, with Simon the Jew, chapter 13, where he calls the Sabbaths an imaginary rest of that seventh day on which sacred Scripture testifies that God rested after completing the creation of the world.”

The passage of Evagrius to which Zacagnius refers, as it appears in our printed edition, reads as follows [Note: [Col. 1072B] Evagrius, *Altercation*, below]:

> “Having been taught evil Sabbaths,” he says, “that is, the *imaginary rest* of the seventh day was handed down,” and so forth.

In writing what we have just quoted from him, the learned man was doing something quite different from what he intended. For he is found to have made many mistakes in that annotation.

First, he confuses our Evagrius with that very famous Evagrius of Pontus, whose surviving works we have published elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1072B] *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VII, pp. 533 ff.]. He could easily have avoided this error if he had consulted Gennadius, who carefully distinguishes the two men [Note: [Col. 1072B] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapters 11 and 50.].

Next, he invents an ancient translator of our writer, as though the latter had written in Greek, even though he is acknowledged to have been a Latin author. Finally—and this is the chief point—he identifies the author of the disputation with Simon the Jew as Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Thus he seems to have thought that this bishop disputed with the Jew and that Evagrius later committed his disputation to Greek writing, whereas our Evagrius fabricated that *Altercation* as having taken place between **Theophilus the Christian** and Simon the Jew. But enough on this subject.

[Col. 1071B]

[Note: [Col. 1071D] In the manuscript codex of Saint Martial of Limoges it reads: *Altercation of Apollonius the philosopher with Zacchaeus the Christian*. But that the title we have published is the correct one is clear from the fact that the author himself uses the word *consultationes* in the preface: *to conduct consultations concerning objections* (*paulatim consultationes de contradictionibus facere*).]

## THE THREE BOOKS OF THE CONSULTATIONS OF ZACCHAEUS THE CHRISTIAN AND APOLLONIUS THE PHILOSOPHER. (C, G, S)*

[Col. 1071]

## BOOK ONE

### PREFACE

[Col. 1071C]

Among certain people, the contradiction of the gentiles, because it is excluded from all true wisdom and is exiled and empty, seems rather to be despised than refuted. For in contempt of it there is a useless weariness, whereas in instruction there is a double benefit: our religion, which is both holy and simple, is made known to everyone, and those who have been instructed usually believe what they had despised in ignorance.

It therefore seemed worthwhile to set down a great matter, though in a humble style, and to disclose in a single body of belief what many have indeed said more clearly but scattered in different places; then, by introducing the characters of an inquirer and a respondent, gradually to conduct consultations concerning objections.

And so, lest the gentiles complain that judgment had been passed against them as though they were absent, and—as he says—lest “I say” and “he says” be inserted too frequently, it seemed appropriate to introduce a Philosopher representing the gentiles. In the preface to his proposition, while arguing arrogantly about our belief, he briefly explains what we ought to believe. Afterwards, examining everything piece by piece, he will recognize, as the causes of his questions increase, that human beings have no fate; and, after recoiling for a while especially because of astrology, he will finally surrender to faith, as he does in the case of the other matters.

Our own speaker, gradually and gently descending to an exposition of the revered religion, will touch briefly upon a few of its principal points out of the many things that cannot be expressed. He will demonstrate that the reason which alone is sought by disputants of this sort has been entrusted spiritually to faith whenever it is lacking to earthly understanding, and he will dwell not on the solidity but on the indications of things; for when light is brought near to blind eyes, if it is not seen because of its brightness, it is felt by its warmth.

## CHAPTER I. Whether Christ can be God and man

### APOLLONIUS

The occasion, Zacchaeus, has brought you and those present here before me, so that what we once used to say abusively in our opening remarks may now be freely brought forward and tested. For if you inquire carefully, you will easily understand that all sects of religion and all the rites of worship have proceeded from rational beginnings. But your sect of belief is so superfluous and irrational that it seems to me capable of being accepted only through folly.

For what is so absurd, and so contrary to human reason, as that Christ—whom you call the Son of God—should be believed to be both God and man, one and the same? That a virgin should give birth after conceiving without seed? That God should be born from a woman; that afterward, through the successive stages of life, he should learn, feel, suffer, and endure the lowliness of earthly acts? Then, fixed to a cross, that he should undergo death, and finally, after dying, raise himself from the dead?

Nor is it enough for the authors of this persuasion to add their assent to so foolish a tradition [Note: [Col. 1073D] So in the codex of Saint-Arnulf, and considerably better than the reading in the text, *rationi* (“to reason”). Below, on the authority of the Vendôme codex, we have written *vigentem* (“flourishing”), where the printed editions have *Vincentem*. In the Limoges codex, somewhat earlier, the reading *nisi et ut mortales* (“unless also as mortals”) is, in my judgment, incorrect.], unless they also condemn the immortal gods of the gentiles with tiresome harassment.

Moreover, they despise the world, which flourishes through its eternity, as though it were temporary and brief; and, while they themselves live without any decree of Fate [Note: [Col. 1073D] So in the Vendôme codex; in the printed editions, *de gentilibus* (“concerning the gentiles”), through an ugly scribal error.], they promise themselves the blessedness of immortality after the resurrection of dead bodies.

Can you or do you dare to give an account of this practice—if it is to be called an account at all, rather than the foolish persuasion of men—by demonstrating it through an examination of present realities, so that either, once defeated, you may withdraw from your error, or, overcome on the same terms, you may join me to your tradition with the testimony of this council?

### ZACCHAEUS

[Note: [Col. 1073D] We restored this from the Limoges codex, in which the reading is *audere*, and from the Vendôme codex, in which the remaining words follow as in the printed text. In the printed editions: *audire quidem quivis facile potest, et de Deo verum* (“anyone can easily hear, and the truth concerning God”).]

Anyone can easily dare to speak what is true, even about God, provided that something compatible with your wisdom and not contrary to such justice can be expressed from divine matters [Note: [Col. 1074D] In the Vendôme and Limoges codices, *talique*. Not much later, where the text reads *sed per se omnia scire*, the word *sed* is absent in the Vendôme codex.].

For it is the position of your school that the wise person forms no opinion, believes nothing, is not deceived, knows everything by himself, does not tolerate hidden or unknown things, grants no greater possibility to the Creator than to the creature, and judges the meaning of God in the same way as that of man. Above all, you maintain this purpose in disputing against Christians. Hence your argument also began from this point: that you first condemned what you later wished to investigate.

## CHAPTER II. How Christ is the Son of God

[Col. 1074A]

### APOLLONIUS

The ease with which you have embraced your belief, and the confession undertaken against the reason and law of the whole world, compelled me to speak more vehemently and argue more strictly. Nevertheless, if you have confidence in answering, first disclose this faith to me: how do you wish Christ to be regarded as God or the Son of God, when you do not afterward deny that he is also man? Surely he must be proclaimed either God or man, because it is clear to everyone’s understanding that one may become the other, but that both cannot exist simultaneously.

### ZACCHAEUS

That subtlety belongs to your sophistries: you refuse to believe what you first destroy after accepting one part, and you extend your hands toward small matters in order to overthrow the whole. Therefore silence is especially appropriate toward you, since it is a lighter fault not to honor than to injure; yet you do not wish to believe in God [Note: [Col. 1074D] In another codex: “you do not wish to believe in God,” which is why we restored the preposition *in*, absent from the text. Above, I read *non deferre honorem* (“not to show honor”).], and you cannot speak without offending him.

## CHAPTER III. That this struggle should not be without purpose

### APOLLONIUS

I, for my part, believe that the exchange of these discussions is always useful to those who doubt, and I affirm from experience that by certain streams of inquiry one reaches the fountain of truth [Note: [Col. 1074D] This is certainly how it must be read, for the reading in the printed editions, *venire*, cannot stand. A little farther on, the Vendôme codex correctly has *propterea* (“for this reason”); the first edition incorrectly reads *praeterea* (“besides”).].

For this reason, the doctrines of all sects exist so that, by listening, you may understand what you previously did not know. What is heard can more easily be believed when reason supplies support than what has not been heard can be recognized. Therefore, if it is appropriate, set forth the propositions one by one, lest, while we contend in vain, those who are present become filled not with the unexpected understanding but with weariness.

### ZACCHAEUS

It is wholly fitting that the mysteries of heavenly counsels be known. The truth concerning Christ’s divinity is so simple and self-evident that, although no one can express it worthily, anyone can easily understand it if he offers the will to believe.

Even I, who am the least of Christians, would not remain silent on this matter, were I not commanded by the rule governing such altercations to avoid occasions for them. For where there is no progress, conflict is restrained. Therefore, if you strive merely to dispute and to be defeated with impunity while refusing to believe, seek out the Epicureans, Platonists, and the displays of the other similar sects. We do not have such a custom (1 Corinthians 11:16).

## CHAPTER IV. Whether the poets say anything about Christ

[Col. 1074D]

### APOLLONIUS

Set these matters aside and do not depart from the condition proposed: namely, that one side should follow the person who, before these same listeners, has prevailed at the end. And since, as you rightly say [Note: [Col. 1075D] So in the Limoges codex, which then adds *ac pene*, perhaps better read *ac bene*. The printed editions have: “And since, as you yourself say.”], no one can justly regard speaking on behalf of religion as a burden, I shall discuss everything concerning Christ point by point.

First, disclose an evident argument, so that if you can prove him to be God or the Son of God, I may more readily assent to the other things you report as having been done or as still to be done by him. Nor will I be ashamed freely to believe what the gods could not prevent.

ZACCH. And I too believe through him, [Note: In the Vindobonensis manuscript: “who can raise up,” perhaps a better reading.] because he can raise up inhabitants for himself even from stones (Matt. 3:9), that you can easily be led away from the error of paganism, if, laying aside the arrogance of false wisdom, you do not immediately reject in your heart the one whose majesty you either knowingly neglect or ignorantly seek, once you have recognized him in reality. [Col. 1075B] For behold, your gods will hear him speaking, fortified by faith in Christ, and they will not prevent him. But I am astonished that you, who prefer the appearance of complete learning, should inquire doubtfully whether Christ is God or the Son of God, when you cannot be unaware that the books of your own authorities also bear witness to his divinity and bring forward the cross that you mock. [Note: In the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul, “to prefer.”] From these I shall meanwhile produce two examples. [Note: When we sought this passage in Plato, we found the following written in Book X of the *Laws*: that circular or spherical motion is most like the Mind by which all things were created and are governed. Everyone understands that this is absurd; but I do not know whether what some ancient Christians inferred from that passage—that Plato mentioned the Lord’s cross—is not even more absurd.]

For Plato, whom you proclaim to be the most learned and wisest of men, when he was speaking of the revelation of Christ’s majesty, also indicated his sign in these words, asserting that a God would come whose sign is circular and crossed. The Sibyls, likewise divinely prophetic, as you claim, uttered the distinctiveness of the holy name together with the dignity of its nature. [Note: This is the true reading of the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts; for the reading preferred by the printed editions—“as you agree”—does not seem free from error, since it could be concluded from it that Zacchaeus himself regarded the Sibyl’s verses as divine.] The same Sibyl later signified God and the cross in a single verse, [Col. 1075C] which you refute in many arguments, setting out the poem as follows:

> Blessed is that God who hangs upon the lofty tree.

Observe: although expressed in words that are far apart, the confession of both is nevertheless made explicit. He indicates that it will happen, because he understood that Christ would be manifested in human form; she calls him blessed, because she foresees divine power in human frailty and victory in the death of that same human being. Yet it is not appropriate to conclude from this that they attained true wisdom merely because they were sometimes permitted, as if in a dream, to speak it; nor was it so that paganism might seem to have earned foreknowledge from God. Rather, it was so that even your own authorities might speak of Christ as God and the Son of God—authorities who, although they are almost universally mistaken, [Col. 1075D] [Note: In the Vindobonensis: “even in this.” I do not know whether the author here implicates Plato or the Sibyl in this error; nor do I much doubt that the mistake is verbal and belongs to the copyist.] were plausibly correct in this instance.

## CHAPTER V. Not only about poetic statements, but also about present-day miracles

[Col. 1076A]

APOLL. You recall appropriately, for the moment, what each of them said; but since there is freedom to test the matter, allow your preceding conclusion to be restrained by an argument of equal force: those whose authority ought not to be accepted in everything [Note: We have restored the negative particle, absent from all the manuscripts, so that the sense would be coherent.] may perhaps have made a human error in this matter. Therefore, if Christ is truly God or the Son of God, this must be taught not only by the writings of the ancients but also by examples present before our eyes.

ZACCH. How unjust is the purpose of pagan conviction! When it argues on its own behalf, it uses its own authorities; when it is refuted, it does not believe them. Our faith is not so impoverished, nor our defense so needy, that in proving itself it should rely only upon external testimonies and seek outside itself what it possesses within. Hear the unclean spirits of demons—your gods—terrified at the invocation of this name, not denying that Christ is God and the Son of God. When torments are raging and questions are being put to them, they do not say what pleases them, but confess what is forced from them. And if you disparage our belief and faith, at least believe your own gods; or, if shame does not restrain the one party, let human beings deny what even demons confess.

## CHAPTER VI. What may be said in answer concerning demons

APOLL. Why do you persist in throwing at me, as your whole argument, various inventions about demons and the shifting opinion of uncertain spirits? [Note: I would prefer “on your behalf,” if the manuscripts supported it.] If this is your only proof, you should return more honorably to the authority of those previously mentioned.

ZACCH. It would be fair for you first to believe the testimonies of your own authorities, and then to weigh, with no light regard, the unwilling confession of demons. For unless they were driven by invisible torments, they would certainly speak freely on their own behalf more readily than they would always lie against themselves. But since the riches of God are immeasurable in every matter, and especially since his majesty is displayed in honoring his name and summoning human beings to faith, true majesty is spread abroad. [Note: The printed editions read “of majesty,” incorrectly; the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts read “majesty,” correctly.]

Therefore, if these things are insignificant, unheard-of remedies of healing follow, as do God’s unspeakable benefits extended even to the dead. At Christ’s command, then, the blind are given sight, hearing is restored to the deaf, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the dead are raised (Matt. 11:5). If you do not believe that these things were performed by him, recognize that they have been performed by human beings in his name. For if he were not God or the Son of God, or were falsely believed to have assumed human form, he would neither assist when invoked nor provide signs beneficial to those in need. It can plainly be understood that God does not assent to falsehood, nor can human beings obtain signs through falsehood.

## CHAPTER VII. What necessity God had for descending to earth

APOLL. What you say might seem not to be foreign to faith, if what follows belief deserved to be believed. For, to pass over other matters for the moment, what reason or necessity did God have for coming to earth?

[Col. 1077B]

ZACCH. No necessity encompasses God, since he is always free and subject to no suffering. Everything is subject to him by itself, and he himself is subject to no one. Nevertheless, his judgment is absolute and certain: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). Therefore, if you raise a mind wandering in darkness toward the light of heavenly understanding, so that you believe that God can do whatever he wills, you will not indeed discover any necessity, so far as he himself is concerned, for his coming to earth—or rather, since he is always everywhere, for appearing visibly in human form—but you will understand that his will was rational.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why God assumed an incorruptible human being

[Col. 1077C]

APOLL. Just as it cannot be doubted that God can do whatever he wishes, so it is clear that he does not wish what is contrary to or unworthy of himself. Therefore, if there was no necessity, explain rationally his will.

ZACCH. First impress this upon your mind: whatever that same God displayed, assumed, and endured among human beings was done either to preserve or to restore the human race. In this matter he so loved the benefits he had always bestowed from the beginning that he granted more forgiveness to those pardoned [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis manuscript; the printed editions have “than he weighed out punishments,” which is less correct.] than he balanced evil by punishments. For humanity’s sake, the books of Scripture are filled with examples of the past, exhortations concerning the present, and the hope and fear of things to come, so that, if faithful promises did not allure people to recognition and worship of the Creator—which is the sum of righteousness [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has the excellent reading “which is the sum”; the Lemovicensis has “righteousness,” followed by the rest as in the Vindobonensis. The printed editions read “which is the sum of righteousness,” yielding a different and less suitable sense.]—the dread of the announced judgment might restrain them. Since these arrangements accomplished little through the prophets, the Savior granted his presence, so that the work of our salvation might be completed by the power of his preaching, and correction might not always be thought to come from a human being alone. For in Christ divinity shone forth in teaching, deeds, and signs; and he invited us to imitate righteousness and holiness, not by force, but through miracles. Therefore, when he was about to undertake so great an act of condescension, how ought he to have descended to earthly things except by bearing him in the material of frail human beings—a corrupt reading found in all the manuscripts? [Note: I would gladly read: “in his own fragile human nature.”] This was the one who was to see him present, hear him teaching, and imitate him at work.

## CHAPTER IX. Why God was born from a woman

APOLL. Let it be granted that a plausible rational purpose for coming to earth appears, since God is said to have come out of compassion for humanity. Was it impossible for him to form an incorruptible body from some more exalted substance, and, having assumed it, to bring help to humanity without burdening himself with corruptible human matter?

ZACCH. Since God does everything by his own will, he assumes nothing as though compelled by something burdensome to himself. [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis; the printed editions read “he assumed.” Not long afterward the Lemovicensis has “but so that he might wish it to appear what it was”; I do not know whether that is better.] But just as he cannot be deceived, so he himself does not deceive. What was real, therefore, ought to have been made by him; it was not fitting that, in the manner of magical illusions, an apparition should be displayed in place of a human being, but that he should be what he wished to appear to be. Therefore, since he was coming in a true human being for the salvation of all, he had to be born and, through the stages of life, undergo the development of age, so that he might both teach what a human being can do and not command anything to be done that he himself had not first done through the human form he had assumed.

## CHAPTER X. How, born from a Virgin, he escaped human frailty

APOLL. Let there be, if you wish, a brief conclusion to the dispute on this point as well. Was it not at least unworthy for him to take shape within a woman’s womb? Or is it believable that he was conceived without seed?

ZACCH. I said earlier that understanding follows faith, and that the human mind grasps what is higher and closer to God only through faith. For if God, whenever he wished, could create a human being from non-existent matter, or from any other material, as you said shortly before, then surely he could do so more easily from existing matter—his own matter—so that everything would be true, it would be more wondrous, and it would not involve the mingling of seed. Or what animal or element is dearer to God than a human being? What material could be more suitable for so great a formation than the holy Virgin, within whom the Spirit of God formed a body from the flower of the purest womb, in which the Son of God lived and dwelt among human beings?

And lest it seem incredible that this could have been done through the Spirit of God, consider what the spirit of the world can do. It is certainly not God, but one of God’s works: how easily it binds naturally loosened earth through cold, turns waters into ice, and produces snow from the same waters, changing weight into lightness and color into whiteness; how it hardens crystals by its blasts, so that they do not recover the softness of their own nature. After all this, believe that something was impossible for God which you understand to be possible for a creature.

## CHAPTER XI. How God grew through the various stages of life

APOLL. Do you also testify that a Virgin gave birth? Since the creation, as you assert, [Note: We have added the negative particle, which was entirely necessary, from the Lemovicensis manuscript.] was effected not from incorruptible God but from corruptible matter, how did it exceed the limits of its own frailty?

ZACCH. O wisdom of the world, which perceives nothing divine in your persuasion! You hear that the salvation of all was effected within a human being by the work of God; and when you understand that he was conceived without disturbance of the body, you do not believe that he emerged without its dissolution! Where, then, would God’s benefit or power be, if the sacred union merely shared its name with human frailty but not its honor?

[Col. 1079B] You especially refuse to believe that Christ is God because he is proclaimed to have been born from a Virgin contrary to the custom of human birth. But I believe that he thereby passed more fully into the glory of God: although, even as a human being, he was in some respect unlike our condition, he properly completed the order of birth and did not violate the integrity of his mother’s body through the necessity of his birth. [An alternative reading: “of being born.”] It is therefore beyond doubt that, since the creation was from the Spirit of incorruptible God, the birth too was incorruptible; and that what was fragile in humanity was preserved by the power of divinity, rather than what belonged to God being diminished by human frailty.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Christ’s virtues

APOLL. Grant that Christ’s divinity and birth were as you say, since, on account of the God whom you continually introduce into your reasoning, it must also be judged possible for a Virgin to give birth. What purpose was served by his crying as an infant in a cradle, then remaining in childish ignorance, or not passing beyond the unstable period of adolescence into more mature years, in which, by divine power, he might immediately have begun with the strength of manhood to perform the deeds he was to perform? [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis; the earlier edition has “as possibility,” which gives a less suitable sense.]

ZACCH. The course of his life, joined to the will of his divinity, answers you on this point: he who had endured the delays of a developing womb also observed the proper time of life, and did not disdain to live as a human being after he had deigned to be born in this way. For when would he have been believed to have truly assumed a human being, [Note: Here too we follow the Vindobonensis; previously the text read “unless these,” an ugly error that arose because the copyist had not grasped the meaning of the word “to pass through.”] if he had hastened past these stages of life? But perhaps he ought to have despised something belonging to humanity, since he came to teach humility and patience. How much more modestly did he prove himself both God and human being, display miracles, [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis and Saint-Arnoul manuscripts; the text has “endured,” incorrectly. “Produced” would be somewhat better in both places.] and refuse to reject weakness!

For this reason he is recorded as having grieved in sorrow, slept in weariness, desired food in hunger, wept in mourning, and groaned in death, so that while the sublime works described above demonstrated the true God, the things that provoke lament spoke of a true human being. He both endured by assuming what belongs to us and, when he wished, accomplished by a word what is possible only for God.

## CHAPTER XIII. If Christ raised others, how did he not escape death?

APOLL. I remember that various healings and the raising of the dead were brought forward earlier; yet I do not see in them any special reason for admiring Christ. For more skilled magicians also raise the dead, and physicians provide remedies for every weakness.

ZACCH. I am not unaware that magical incantations call forth not the spirits of the dead but those of demons, and that by means of an apparition they briefly pretend to be what they are not. They also add a condition to their falsehood, so that either they answer without being seen or, if they are seen, they remain silent. Thus the image of shadows mocks the feeble wishes of the foolish.

But the souls of the dead, once their bodies have been released, are led to their appointed dwelling places; according to their merits they remain either among the blessed until the day of future judgment, and are not subject to the invocations of magicians, or are confined in certain prisons and prevented from coming to the upper regions. Thus demons fabricate their likeness, either because the dead disdain to come or because they are detained, so that the demons may always be involved in the deception they love and frustrate those who believe such things by imitating the truth.

The remedies of physicians, on the other hand, through many mixtures of herbs, benefit neither immediately nor everyone; and whenever a more serious disease has taken root in the sick, either the entrails are scorched and tormented by fire, or the hidden destructive growth is cut away by iron. Nothing is accomplished as a remedy by command, and nothing is perfected by speech alone.

Certainly we can all admit that medicine can diminish what exists in a human being, but cannot add what does not exist. The works of Christ must be judged the opposite. A blind man who had no material basis for sight from the beginning, and who possessed empty places where his eyes should have been, received sight when he was smeared with clay, just as the first human being had originally been formed. A man who did not know how to walk was ordered to walk. Blood that had flowed away from a woman’s veins was stopped by a word. A severed ear was restored by a command. Leprosy did not flee because of medicine, but because of a word.

Moreover, a corpse wasted away in the tomb was ordered both to come forth and to live; and he did not merely appear suddenly to those who saw him, but participated in all human activities and rejoiced that he would live for years. Who besides God could feed so many thousands of people with only five loaves [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis, more correctly than the earlier edition, which has “very many more.”] that they were satisfied?

Who walked upon the sea with his feet and freely trod that immense element as he walked, fixing firm footprints while the waves served as a path? Who could command the winds and restrain with a word the storms raging in the tempest? Who could turn water into wine and, from the same substance into the same substance, produce an advance into a better kind without the nature understanding the transformation?

Christ did these things while living as a human being, in order to prove himself both human and God, and he did them before many witnesses. Therefore, if an echo is to be equated with the one speaking, or foam with springs, or a shadow with the true light, then human works may be joined to the powers of God without an unworthy comparison: in the one case, the only delay in these remedies is that they are commanded to be beneficial; in the other, what is accomplished through labor disappears almost before it is perceived.

## CHAPTER XIV. Who the devil is, and what the sin of humanity was

APOLL. If God, as you strive to make us believe, performed the preceding miracles while remaining in a human being, did he also wish to receive and endure the cross? Or for what reason did he, who rescued others from death, not escape death himself? Or how could he benefit others who could not benefit himself? In this matter he ought especially to have strengthened the faith of those who doubted him by showing that he would liberate others, since he had first demonstrated this in his own liberation. On this point either the reason must be revealed, or it is entirely just not to demand belief.

ZACCH. Here too your judgment is mistaken: you think that divinity suffered injury in being fastened to the cross. But divinity is incomprehensible and free; it could neither suffer nor be held. Rather, through the human being he had assumed, Christ celebrated a certain triumph over the devil. When he set the victory of the flesh upon the wood, he overcame the devil through a human being, without injury to himself—the devil who had led humanity into sin, to the injury of God.

Thus it was a human being, not divinity, who was given to the cross; and he who had sinned through the wood was fastened to the wood. The chief reason or will for God’s assuming a human being was this: that the sin contracted by humanity might be removed through a human being, and that faith in the resurrection might begin from the one who plainly ought to rise first. For, pure and free from every sin, he wished to suffer for all, so that he might be preferred to all not merely by power but by merit.

You see, therefore, what the splendid manifestation of divine power and the victory of life consist in: he did not deserve death, but took it away from those who did deserve it; and he fastened the guilt of matter to the standard of spiritual triumph, not his own guilt. [Note: The Lemovicensis has “his particular guilt.” Below, we have restored “he had given” from the Vindobonensis, whereas the printed editions read “to give.”] Since no other human being is free from sins, anyone else who gave his life would have given it only for himself. He had to die for all who owed nothing to sin on his own behalf; and since he could not be condemned, he nevertheless consented to be killed, lest perpetual death hold us captive.

## CHAPTER XV. If God is impassible, why does he become angry and punish?

[Col. 1081D]

APOLL. Set aside for the moment the question of who this devil is, or where he comes from, whom you affirm to have been the instigator of some sin. If it does not weary you, explain the human sin itself, whose enormity, as you assert, was so great that it could not be expiated except through Christ’s cross alone. For once the character of the crime has been examined, it will become clearer what this proclamation of the cross, so greatly exalted, accomplished.

ZACCH. It is certainly no burden to explain the beginnings of the ancient offense and to relate in a straightforward account what degree of evil the transgression of the first human being produced, so that you who desire to hear only the causes of sin may also come to know more closely the Creator of the human race.

When God had made all things from nothing, he fashioned the human being, the inhabitant of the world, from clay. To the still crude and lifeless body he gave spirit and sensation: spirit, by which we draw in the common air and move our limbs; sensation, by which we differ from the other animals. Then he added the distinctive freedom to live, granting unrestricted authority over all things. Immortality was then permitted [Alternative reading: “promised”] on a condition, and a law was placed within the will—not a law whose difficult observance would bring danger upon one who did not know it, but one which, once revealed, would guard the great grace of the Creator, together with the benefit of immortality, so that it would not be seized.

Thus, when the human being had been placed amid the delights of paradise—a most pleasant place, unspoiled by any harshness or variation of the winds—ample permission was given to eat from the fruit of every precious tree. Yet the use of one particular tree alone was forbidden among the many, so that, by always looking upon that forbidden tree, the human being might remember the one who had forbidden it and might not forget that the author who was set above all things was above him. He would thereby recognize that everything had been subjected to him in such a way that he himself was subject to the one who had subjected everything to him. At the same time, this was so that the rational human being, unlike brute animals, would not grow sluggish without observance, but that, through the special sense he alone had received, he might understand both to take care and to earn reward between commandment and benefit.

[Col. 1082C] The devil, jealous of this blessedness, used the serpent, which was more prudent than the other animals, and first enticed the woman—that is, the human being of the inferior sex, more easily disposed to believe—to violate the prohibition by tasting the tree. Through her he afterward deceived the man by a similar falsehood, asserting that they would become like God if they did not abstain from the fruit of that tree, which God had supposedly set apart for that very reason: so as not to share heavenly knowledge with human beings.

Deceived by these tricks, they were driven into the most depraved sin, daring, though unable, to wish to become like their Creator through transgressing his commandment. By this fraud they were deprived of the benefit of immortality and expelled from paradise. Removed from that inviolate temperate climate and destined to live beneath this corruptible air, they were immediately clothed in skins, and harsh labor was assigned to them in the search for food, so that they might till soil that would provide nothing willingly; and, sweating among thorns and thistles, even if they gathered much, they would nevertheless remain subject to the sentence of death.

This was the first transgression of the prohibition, the cause of all evils and the beginning of death. Yet God’s patience did not immediately carry the sentence into effect as punishment; rather, it softened the force of the harsher decree by interposing time, so that forgiveness might be merited through the labor of repentance, and so that those who had fallen might teach the observance of righteousness even to their descendants, for whose sake those who had grievously fallen through their own fault might be restored to the life they had lost. [Note: The Saint-Arnoul manuscript has the best reading; I do not see why Acherius relegated it to the margin and replaced it with “whose.” In what follows there are almost as many variant readings as words, but they are of no importance.]

These intervals of mercy and the course of the saving path were not maintained by satisfaction through conversion; instead, the growth of vices increased, and the abuse of succeeding generations consumed them. Thus, when the sentence of death later gathered strength, only the outpouring of the flood could extinguish the stain of burning crimes.

## CHAPTER XVI. How human beings were created after the flood

APOLL. It is dangerous to pass over matters that provoke reflection. For if God is both impassible and good, how is he now angry or punishing? Anger indicates one who is subject to suffering, and vengeance is evil.

[Col. 1083B]

ZACCH. God is the impartial judge of human actions: he gives rewards to the good and punishment to the wicked. He is good when he gives recompense, and just when he punishes. Therefore anger does not indicate one who is subject to suffering, but one who disapproves; and vengeance is not evil, but just.

## CHAPTER XVII. The origin of the Jews

APOLL. Reverence must be yielded to divinity, especially since one must always believe of God what is worthy of his honor. Therefore, returning the narrative to the point at which it was suspended, explain carefully, if it is worth hearing, how human beings were either made or born after the flood.

ZACCH. It is entirely worthy to reveal God’s healing action toward us from the beginning, and to set forth the seed of the human race preserved in Noah, showing that its descendants came from him, rather than inventing Deucalion and Pyrrha in childish fashion by throwing stones behind one’s back.

Thus, after the earth had been cleansed by the flood, Noah alone—because he alone was found righteous—was preserved with his descendants for the propagation of the human race. Yet the sentence of death still remained, as it does now, so that immortality might be restored together with resurrection according to the merit of one’s way of life. For some time the pattern of righteousness endured among human beings; the discipline of example remained vigorous, and reverence was preserved through fear.

But just as prolonged prosperity always produces security from abundance, abolition of restraint from security, and abuse from abolition, so they forgot fear and forgot the author of their being, and from vices they burst into sacrileges. No longer content to dwell upon the earth, they built a tower as though they intended to ascend to heaven, and human hands dared to assault the heights of the clouds.

O unfathomable goodness of God, and compassion worthy of being expressed by no one! Disobedience to God deserved death, yet desiring God’s dwelling was met with impunity.

Consider the gentleness of divine clemency: the reckless are not punished in their crime, but are led away from crime; and where heavenly judgment ought to have raged, signs of power are displayed. Moreover, a path of repentance and understanding is opened. For since at that time there was still one language for all, their language was divided into the numerous nations now scattered throughout the world, and in the midst of their most fervent work each person spoke only what he alone understood.

While their boldness persisted in the construction of their crime, suddenly those who were asking did not know how to ask, those who were serving did not know how to obey, and what was brought to the builders as though necessary became an obstacle. Thus the undertaking was abandoned not through punishment but through weariness, so that afterward fear of the miracle might reach everyone with astonishment, without an example of punishment, as each person explained to his own people why he had lost the knowledge of the former language and passed into the new language of his nation.

But what does it profit to have covered crimes with the flood? What does it profit that indulgence, not punishment, destroyed this engine of madness? Behold again, O human being, you confuse the elements in insult to God, transferring the honor and worship of invisible majesty to visible creatures. If you look to height, God is above; if to greatness, he is more immense and is everywhere; if to splendor (Wis. 13:3–5), the Creator is brighter, and the one who made beauty must necessarily surpass in this virtue what he made. Finally, let this be the distinction between Creator and creature: let the things we see possess such power to inspire admiration that they do not cause us, with reverence, to lose sight of those things which we cannot see because of their majesty.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why they were led into the wilderness after leaving Egypt, and why the Law was given

APOLL. If the things you recall are true, God’s care for humanity and his patience are immeasurable and without end. But since you have mentioned that, after the work on the tower was abandoned, nations were formed throughout the earth through the diversity of languages, explain carefully, following the order of events, how the sect of the Jews arose with Moses, or for what reason, after so many centuries had passed, the broad extension of the Law emerged, when the law is naturally implanted in human understanding, if the capacity for knowledge exists. [Note: Here too we follow the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts; the earlier edition read “were made.”]

ZACCH. From the first human being up to the time I mentioned, knowledge of God was maintained through successive generations. Although the law was not written in letters, as you yourself have acknowledged, it was naturally implanted in human understanding. But after both had been abolished, Abraham, a man of singular faith, was chosen. God appointed him the father of all belief on account of this merit: at God’s call he first left, without hesitation, his home, country, and relatives, intending to go into unknown and foreign lands, lest he should remain among his kinsmen in the servitude of idols and lose the grace of faith that he had already earned and was going to increase, or at least retain it with less fervor.

Again, in the extreme old age of himself and his wife, when their limbs were already growing cold with age, he did not despair of a son who, God had promised, would be born to him, believing that the difficulty of nature would be overcome by the possibility of the divine promise. Later, when this son was his only one, he brought him without hesitation to the altar to be killed at God’s command, striving to give the Creator precedence over affection, and at the same time trusting that the one whom fire had consumed for God’s sake could be restored to him whole even from burned ashes. [Note: Thus in the Lemovicensis manuscript; from it we have also restored the difficult reading below. The printed editions had “had burned,” followed by “then clear divinity,” which makes no sense. We omit the other minor matters.]

Yet the Godhead, never harsh toward believers, did not allow this excellent man to be deprived of his son, but only to be tested. At the moment when the sword was already about to strike, he placed a ram beneath the raised weapon as a gentler sacrificial victim, so that his devotion might be completed without loss of piety, and so that he might nevertheless receive the grace of faith because he had placed God before affection.

By such faith, therefore, he earned for his descendants the promise of a land flowing with abundance, and, as the forefather of the Jewish people, he was the first to receive circumcision. Not because the foreskin prejudiced righteousness or faith, or because God had created anything superfluous in a human being that he later commanded to be cut away, but so that the offspring of the chosen man might be recognized among other nations by a bodily sign.

Accordingly, this same people, because of the scarcity of the regions in which they lived, migrated into Egypt—not because God was unable to provide abundance for them in any place whatsoever, but so that, when he later led them out of Egypt, he might teach how great he was through miracles.

A great nation arose from this offspring, and a small number grew into a multitude that provoked envy, so that when the Egyptians feared that the Jews would become stronger than themselves, they tried to burden them, as though they were subjects bound to deserved slavery, with degrading labor. Moreover, through the savage force of an edict, they put the male sex to death from the womb, so that exposure would eliminate those born and labor would take up those who were strong. [Col. 1085C]

Under these afflictions, the foreign people approached the God whom their ancestors had handed down to them, and, for their liberation, asked for the divinity worshiped by their fathers. As a result, against the force of the cruel edict, Moses was first secretly raised by his parents. Then, after being exposed because of fear of the command, he was found by Pharaoh’s daughter and instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; afterward he received commands for liberating God’s people. Otherwise, if he had not been trained in all their wisdom, he might have seemed either to have accepted and carried out what he had received by accident as an uneducated man or to have done so with only mediocre understanding. [Note: Thus it is read in the Vindobonensis manuscript, though incorrectly; the earlier edition has “instructed,” which is preferable.]

God spoke to him through the fire from the bush and displayed signs that would prevail against the Egyptians. Through these signs, both those whose slavery was being ended might believe and those who were going to resist might be terrified, so that both peoples might be preserved amid the display of miracles. When God’s hand was clearly perceived, the obstinate were warned to turn from their impiety, and the afflicted were liberated.

Then, when Moses, at the command of God, was demanding the release of the aforesaid people, the Egyptian magicians joined Pharaoh, their king, in resistance, striving to deceive him by imitating the miraculous signs Moses had performed. [Note: This too is the reading of the Vindobonensis manuscript, which we have preferred to the reading of the printed edition, *quae fecissent* (“which they had done”).] For a while, likeness does not yield to truth, and illusion to signs; yet resistance is permitted to a certain extent—not so that the falsehood of the profane might prevail, but so that the power of God might shine forth more broadly. For when they appeared to produce the various kinds of plagues in the matter of the signs, just as Moses did, they could not undo what they themselves had done. And, as this monstrous science is accustomed to do, they knew how to inflict harm but did not know how to bring aid, praying for the cessation of the evils they themselves had brought upon others from the one whom they were attempting to imitate. Thus at last they were compelled to release the people by the force of signs beyond imitation and by their confession of their own inability. [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts; in the printed editions: “the people, untouched by the unimitable signs,” a very bad reading.]

By God’s judgment they were instructed, as they were about to depart, to feign a celebration of joy in the guise of a brief departure, and to obtain from their hosts the possessions needed to adorn the absent festivities, retaining them as the due reward for their long labor—not with the intention of fraud, but as the honor of payment. The Egyptians, deceived—for they still knew nothing of the retention of their wealth—pursued those whom they had compelled by entreaty to undertake the journey, when their malice revived with anger after the people had been released. As the Egyptian army approached, those who feared for their escape were left without hope: enemies pressed upon them from behind, while the sea barred their way in front.

God came to the terrified, and, at the height of their despair, heavenly aid fought on their behalf. First, darkness interposed during the day, defending those who went before as though by an impenetrable barrier; then, by a reversal of the elements, the onset of night, brought to their aid, protected the trembling people from the attack of their pursuers. Next Moses was commanded to strike the immense sea with his staff and, by that command, to remove the waters of the deep so as to provide a path for those crossing. On either side a lofty battle-line of waves was raised, and one might have said that the billows stood arranged like troops prepared for battle at a signal, while the sea, solidified in the likeness of a wall, was divided by intelligent obedience. Dry ground was opened for those who walked across, and the depths of the sea were emptied between towering masses on either side. When the people had reached the opposite shore and the pursuers were closing in upon those who were departing, the sea, struck again by Moses in the same manner, came together upon itself. It was as though the vastness of the avenging element, in defense of God’s injury, were gathering in a more violent returning surge: an innumerable multitude of chariots and horses, with their chosen riders, was submerged, and the company of warriors, mingled with the sand, was covered over as though it had never existed.

From these beginnings, under Moses as leader, the people of the Jews—whose origins went back to Abraham—were brought forth; and after crossing the sea they were led as far as the wilderness in which they remained for forty years. [Note: We have restored this entire passage with the help of the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts; in the earlier edition it was badly printed: “through this night … a guide went before them.”] By night a pillar of light went before them as a guide for their journey. By day the same pillar, advancing in a cloud lest weariness should overcome the exhausted, protected them from the violence of the heat. Thus they made use of God’s aid while the elements themselves served them, so that in his benefits they enjoyed not only the favor of heavenly power but also the indulgence of paternal care; and while they stood amazed between wonder and necessity, they feared neither the signs nor the dangers.

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether the Law brought more to human beings than nature did

**APOLLONIUS.**—Knowledge of the foregoing is indeed welcome; but unless it is fortified by the fullness of reason, it is weak. What, then, was the reason that, after crossing the sea and being freed by such great miracles, they were led into the wilderness? Or why, afterward, were they afflicted in the deserts by so long an exile? Since, moreover, the dreadful barrenness of those regions supplied them with neither food nor the other necessities of life, how were such multitudes fed? Or for what reason was this punishment imposed so severely upon those who had been freed? Or how was the Law afterward given? Explain it.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—That removal was not a punishment, nor were the necessities of life lacking in the deserted and desolate places. Their sustenance was more precious than ordinary human provision, and the circuit through the wilderness itself was appropriate. The principal reason for the delays was that the preceding examples of miracles might there be increased; and because we always cherish what we are accustomed to, provision had to be made lest those who, as was soon proved, might at some point begin to desire a return to Egypt should reach the promised land immediately by a short and direct route. Even amid the greatest abundance, the accustomed desires of those familiar with a known region [Note: There is no doubt that this passage has been corrupted by the copyists. I think it may be emended to *cognitae regionis*, that is, “of the known region,” namely Egypt, “the accustomed desires.” What follows, *post eremi injuriam* (“after the hardship of the wilderness”), cannot stand; I therefore read *post eremi moram* (“after the delay in the wilderness”).] and the profane rites of their religious practices, from which they were especially restrained, might arise. Furthermore, they had to be prevented from being immediately terrified by the wars required to expel the nations from those same regions, although, with divine providence preceding them, those wars would not bring them harm.

It was also so that, after the hardship of the wilderness, the promised dwelling-place might please them more; although its incomparable beauty in itself commended it, remembrance of what had gone before would make it more welcome. And observe the divinity’s clemency in his patience. When they did not await food with humble prayer but noisily complained of its absence, he provided them with a kind of cloud of food, and human bodies fed upon the food of angels. The outpouring of the nightly provision not only left no room for complaint but remained in excess for their use.

Throughout all the time I have described, in a marvelous manner neither footwear nor clothing wore out; likewise, no growth of hair or nails prevailed, but, as though immortality had already been restored, simple wholeness preserved the human form unchanged.

There Moses was summoned up the mountain to receive the Law; and, held in God’s address for forty days and nights, he brought back the commandments written on stone tablets. Alas for the crime! He found those whom he had left corrupted by sacrilege, while they were still refreshed by manna and heavenly delight. [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis manuscript; the printed editions have *referti* (“filled”), whereas below, following the same manuscript, we have restored *Deum* (“God”).]

For when that same people accused Moses of delaying as though he would not return, they quickly forgot the God who had led them out of Egypt, satiated by the abundance already mentioned. In their luxury they began to demand gods whom they might worship, and, casting the jewelry of the women into the fire, they declared that it was to be devoted to that religion which reproduced the form of the idol worshiped in Egypt. Moses returned and faithfully raged against the crime. He reduced to powder the head of the bull that had been fashioned in the likeness of the Egyptian abomination, and in indignation shattered the tablets brought down with the Law, judging those unworthy of God’s writings whom the execration of such an undertaking had polluted.

He did not cease from the force of his anger until what had been committed was expiated by the slaughter of many, when executioners had been sent throughout the camp, and the offense against God had been appeased; then the commandments, restored on the tablets, were brought back. Their restoration demonstrated that God does not hate those whom he permits to be corrected, but does not wish to destroy those whom he chooses to chastise in this way.

Thus the circuit of the wilderness lasted forty years, and so did these benefits of God toward the people he had once received. Then the Law was divinely given, which, in its promulgation, brought not a novelty of precepts but a restoration of natural justice. [Note: Thus in the Vindobonensis manuscript; in the earlier edition, *sui edictione* (“by the promulgation of itself”).] What previously only a very few wise people knew, all might now observe and read through; and ignorance could no longer provide an excuse, since a person would not seek by the senses alone what he did not perceive to be innate in himself, but would recognize it by sight as well.

## CHAPTER XX. Why human salvation came so late

**APOLLONIUS.**—It is clear knowledge that the Law clings naturally to human faculties and that everyone possesses an understanding of what is harmful and beneficial, what is fair and unjust. We know that we love what is our own and hate what is opposed to it; likewise, goodness consists in granting another what pleases him, while wickedness inflicts upon another what displeases him. [Note: The Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts read this way, and considerably better than the earlier edition, which had *prospera* (“prosperous”).] Therefore, unless the nature of the ordinances is explained, I cannot understand what more the Law given through Moses contributed than nature had handed down.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—Recognition of God, together with love and fear of him, is the first law. For what does it profit us to know God if we do not have it at heart to love and fear him? Then follows the complete order of justice: to devote oneself to piety and, with purity of mind, to advance into the observance of good works. Moreover, a present punishment is attached to offenses, and expiations are joined to transgressions. Finally, at the conclusion of the ordinances it is commanded that you do not do to another what you would not want done to yourself, and, conversely, that you do to another what you would want done to yourself.

The creation of this world is likewise included; and the same Maker who fashioned it from nothing set forth the harmony of the elements, indicating that they are his work, though human error has represented them as coeternal with him.

After Moses, as the intervals of time passed and the worship of idols increased through the abuse of salutary commandments, the frequent rebuke of the prophets was added. They announced and preceded the coming of Christ, whom we have already experienced and now await, with many kinds of healing. For God threatens more often than he punishes, desiring the severity of heavenly anger to be feared rather than exercised. [Note: This too is the reading of both manuscripts, and it pleased us more than the reading formerly printed, *exerceri* (“to be exercised”). Not much later, the printed text had *trucidantes* (“slaughtering”); from the same manuscripts we restored *cruci dantes* (“handing over to the cross”). At the beginning of the following chapter, following these manuscripts, we printed the text differently from Acherius; but the changes are not such that it is necessary to inform the reader of each one.]

But the obstinate nation of the Jews not only refused correction but scorned even to be reproved. They punished the prophets sent at God’s command with various penalties, so that the tradition of human superstitions might not lose the honors it had presumed to claim. By their deliberate perversity they showed that they perhaps expected to be corrected by God’s presence; yet afterward, after the signs and wonders, they refused to believe in him, though they knew that he would come and recognized that he had come.

## CHAPTER XXI. Whether the consummation was predetermined, or whether the order of events brings about the end

**APOLLONIUS.**—If, then, his coming was so necessary that he would not refuse to suffer for all, himself providing the pattern of righteousness and displaying the hope of a new resurrection in his own death, why were both God’s benefit and human salvation delayed for so many ages?

**ZACCHAEUS.**—As you have been able to observe, the human race has always been protected and preserved from the beginning by God’s great dispensation. If you briefly survey the whole matter, you will see that the order of divine providence converged toward this end: that the human race would not have to be destroyed by God’s just judgment.

The sentence of death could have been fulfilled immediately at the first transgression, so that the violators of the command might be punished; yet time for living was granted in accordance with the measure of repentance. Later, as crimes increased, the earth was corrupted; but the pollution of the element was washed away in such a way that, through Noah, the remnant of the human race was preserved.

After the Flood, a strong and numerous multitude rose up to build a tower. They were not extinguished for the enormity of their undertaking; rather, they were scattered with a sign of wonder so that they might be corrected. Later, when faithlessness did not cease, Abraham was set apart amid a kind of flood of vices, just as Noah had been set apart in the Flood for the preservation of the race, so that faith might be propagated. Through his descendants the people multiplied, became polluted by the contagion of Egypt, and were recalled to the worship of God not by the severity of judgment but by benefits and signs. Again, in the wilderness they departed from the true Creator by making carved gods. As though human beings had then first been made, or as though they had no law in their understanding, the Law of God was transmitted in written words through Moses.

Yet when impiety continued to spread, the preaching of the prophets was added. At intervals, divine vigilance always stands watch either to prevent the living from straying or, by punishing them moderately, to correct those who remain in error. [Note: Thus the often-praised manuscripts read; the printed editions have *divina providentia* (“divine providence”).]

Finally, the very Creator of heaven, earth, and humanity, like the master of a great household who has sent his faithful servants ahead, bestowed the coming of his power, not rejecting the assumption of an earthly body for the salvation of human beings. Turning the passion and death of the cross toward the very body he had assumed, he displayed both the fullness of the Law and salvation.

You ask why he did not come earlier. Is it not obvious that the final events had to be delayed and the end postponed, so that the fullness of the times might preserve the fullness of justice, and so that, through the length of the interval between tradition and judgment, oblivion might not take away what God’s great favor had provided? If Christ had come either in the middle period or at any earlier time, then not only abuse but also forgetfulness would have carried away faith along with abuse, and no concern for righteousness would have troubled human hearts, since it is harder to believe in ancient examples when faith is scarcely granted to recent ones.

Look: even now the relics of the blessed tomb contain the marks of the Lord’s cross and death, and the place, marked out by the present multitude, bears heavenly witness to his ascent after the sight of the resurrection. Almost still, the footprints impressed upon the ground remain, and the regions traversed by his works display examples of his virtues. Yet many do not judge Christ to be God either because he died, or because, if he was God, they do not believe that he could have died and risen again after death—although, among other things, death proves him human and resurrection proves him God.

Moreover, the deeds of the apostles’ way of life remain, and we are almost taught by those living among us to follow the pattern of righteousness, since we often see happening even before the ashes of the dead what we read that the living accomplished. [Note: The reading of these same manuscripts is excellent; the earlier edition had *sequi prout*, very badly. What follows, *vix propinquitate*, is corrupt but can readily be emended if one reads *sic propinquitate* (“thus by proximity”).]

It is scarcely through the nearness of the end and the terror of the approaching judgment that we are compelled to abandon idols and worship the true divinity. Between the first coming of Christ, which we know, and the second coming, which we await, we are constrained by the saving brevity and the very narrowness of the times, so that we neither admit forgetfulness of the commandments nor despair of the fulfillment of the promised blessedness.

You therefore see that it was necessary for the intervening ages to prevent the nearness of the second coming from putting the end at risk, while the impending terror of judgment would compel the preservation of righteousness—especially since that coming would bring the greatest and perfect things, and what is perfect cannot be anything but final. Consider how many the earlier coming would have saved, certainly more than the later one will, had the later one found them alienated from faith; for those whom remedies of such healings have not cured will be condemned by the order of the announced judgment. The expectation of perpetuity can equally become a cause of despair: one may know God through the Law yet refuse righteousness, doing what appears righteous while refusing to know God through the Law.

## CHAPTER XXII. Whether bodies are restored for the resurrection

**APOLLONIUS.**—We do not deny that souls, once they have laid aside their bodies, return to God—that is, to their proper author. But we suppose that the stain previously contracted through human actions is purged by ethereal fire, so that the souls, pure and simple, may again be mingled with God, from whom they are in any case derived. Therefore, if you wish this to be regarded as the judgment, it is not a predetermined consummation of all things that brings about the end, but the sequence of those who die.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—Your definition is wholly mistaken. For how would human souls undergo judgment if they were from God? The simple substance of divinity cannot be purified, since it cannot be polluted. Purification must involve suffering, and, as we know, the divine substance does not undergo it. Human souls, therefore, are not from God but made by God; they are the work of the Creator, not participants in divinity.

When the time of the judgment mentioned above arrives, the souls of all who have died will one day receive back their bodies, so that with those same bodies they may either receive the reward of their just deeds or suffer for their unjust acts. Christ, however, will visibly come again from the heavens. We shall stand before his tribunal, and by his judgment the merits of all will be weighed. He who suffered under judgment will judge, leaving no trace of injustice: he will restore immortality to the faithful in the kingdom, and everlasting torment in suffering to the unbelieving.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On those who have been neglected and devoured by beasts

**APOLLONIUS.**—Can this also be asserted by wise people: that the ancient ashes of the dead, and the faint residue of bones remaining in tombs consumed by the passage of ages, can again be assembled into bodies, and that the former vigor of their limbs can be solidified by gathering uncertain dust? I would more readily agree that souls can be subjected to any judgment than that the bodies of the dead can be recalled to the order of life.
