**ZACCHAEUS.**—You have forgotten both my admonition and your own pledge, if you contend that anything is impossible for God. If he made what did not exist so that it came to be, can he not make what once existed exist again? Or is it not more difficult for us to make what has never existed than to restore what has existed?

But human judgment cannot grasp this power of God if present creatures do not teach it, if the seasons do not mark it by the variety of their forms. Different trees are stripped bare by the harshness of winter, and, when their leaves have fallen, you might believe that they have perished, along with the hope of their shoots. But when the season of spring breathes more gently, the moisture held in their roots ascends to their heights in a marvelous way, creating in the flowers a whiteness and a form that the wood had not possessed. Fruits are added to the apples, and a kind of covering appears in the leaves; what was not in the tree is seen in its season.

And what of seeds cast into the fields? Do they not display complete evidence of the resurrection? The inner parts of the earth are opened so that bare grains may be entrusted to the furrows; what the soil has not covered has no power to be born again. Consider the Creator’s power even in small things: unless seeds decay, they do not rise again, and unless they first die, they do not come to life again. Were the green shoots submerged in the furrows, or did they lie hidden beneath their stalks? From where, then, does a single seed become many? From where, with their ears, does a new whiteness of straw emerge? How does the force of the shoot climb from the root into the ears, or how afterward is white softness changed from green grasses into grain? Certainly you would not believe that such things could happen in the same way unless you always saw them.

What, then, God established from the beginning—that the earth should return in this manner what pertains to human nourishment—will he not do in the restoration of the human being himself? One who has become a witness of God’s wonders must necessarily marvel most greatly in himself after the resurrection at what he previously praised in subordinate things. Once you have considered the reason behind all these matters, you will know that the ashes and remains of the dead are seeds of bodies, from which Christ, at the coming of his majesty, will raise up forms according to their merits. For it is not enough for divine clemency merely to restore what has existed, unless the splendor of the good also adorns their bodies and the shame of the wicked obscures them with deformity.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the mass of heaven was made, or will pass away at its end

**APOLLONIUS.**—Let us assume for the moment that the ashes of the dead are restored to bodies from tombs as though from familiar repositories; and, since souls know the bodies in which they were contained, [Note: This latter word has been added from the Vindobonensis manuscript.] that they confidently reclaim them from those same places. But what of those who have been submerged in the waves, struck down in wars, or, after being killed by robbers, have lacked burial rites, leaving their limbs as food rather than in tombs? Is it credible that they can be restored in the same bodies they possessed, when even the remains of their ashes cannot be found?

**ZACCHAEUS.**—If you believed that God can do all things, you would finally judge this easy to accomplish, and you would not decide through human argument whether what he had said must be done could be done. Faith therefore has the highest merit above all virtues, because it does not doubt that what God has said will be fulfilled.

The explanation of this matter is as follows. All the elements and every creature respond to us with no discernible sense or understanding; they appear to exist as mindless servants solely for the performance of their proper ministry, either because we are unworthy to command them or because we do not know the secrets of the world. But they both understand and fear God, and obey his commands so completely that they promptly fulfill his orders at his nod.

Thus whatever digestion of bodies takes place through fish, beasts, or birds is mingled either with the waters or with the earth. Yet it cannot in any way happen that nothing remains of what has existed in whatever form. The more precious material, wherever it has fallen, these two elements preserve; they keep it within themselves, distinguished as though by a special color, to return it at the resurrection. Nor can what must be sought out by divine power and will emerge of its own accord ever remain as though lost. Thus, while all things serve, the remains of scattered limbs will return to their proper form and body, so that in the miracle of the resurrection the merit of faith will be increased in believers precisely where an increase of unbelief arises in others.

## CHAPTER XXV. Whether the world will be restored to something better

**APOLLONIUS.**—Your whole argument has for some time been directed toward this: since you recall that the individual elements were made from nothing, you also reduce to an origin and enclose within an end the world which we believe to be from itself and destined to remain through its own eternity. Although I follow the order of your argument, in which you previously said that it was made by God, nevertheless confirm by reason how you wish us to believe either that the immeasurable mass of the heavens was made or that it will not always exist as it now does.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—All the elements, therefore, which you count as coeternal with God were, as I have already said, made by him from nothing and joined together in this form of the world by a marvelous harmony. Just as they received their beginning from God’s creation, so they will receive their permanence from his beneficence. They are therefore not coeternal with the one by whom they were made, since no one doubts that anything whatsoever is not only unequal to its author but subject to him.

This is most clearly evident to the understanding: the world was composed of many things. From this it can easily be perceived that divinity is not within it but above it, since divinity does not need the assistance of another; it is one, simple, and perfect in itself, because incorporeal. Therefore God is invisible and incorruptible. The things involved in and contemplated through this world are not so; even those generated from the world itself show that they are corporeal.

Moreover, whatever we see being done or created by the same power under divine ordering belongs not to its own will but to its assigned function. Observe the passages of the sun and the courses of the moon, and how each day, through the alternation of the seasons, each must repeat either its rising or its setting. With the arrival of night the sun loses the day, which nevertheless it illuminates when it is not, as though shut out, excluded by the obstruction of clouds. The moon suffers diminution and, under the ordinance of its ruler, either loses or receives the fullness of its light.

There is also the varying course of the stars; the signs serving reason; the sea swelling in accordance with marked months; and, observing the measure of its increase and decrease under the established ordering of the hours, either resting in calm weather or being disturbed by a storm. The earth, soaked by rains, becomes soft, and again is either tightened by frost or dried by heat. Indeed, trembling in fear at the sight of God, it confesses by its movement that it is subject to his command. The air itself is often corrupted by a more destructive breath and, once burdened, becomes pestilential. Rains are overcome by pious prayers to the Lord, and prolonged fair weather is again changed by supplication. Everything either serves the order imposed upon it or, under religious prayer, is turned toward the necessary use of humanity.

You worship all these things, individually and collectively, assigning them names in place of God. If this is so, they are falsely judged to be gods, and the error is obvious. But if there are beings who rule these things at God’s discretion, it is manifestly foolish to make those who are subject equal to the one to whom they are subject. There are not many gods, but one Maker of things born and living, who made all things, rules them, and by equal authority decrees either that they will remain or that they will fall.

You see, therefore, that no beginning should be attributed to God alone, from whom the origin of all things proceeded. Nor should those things be judged coeternal with his majesty which he himself will make eternal, just as he will make the human being eternal. When he comes, those things will be destroyed and changed for the better, so that what is now polluted by our crimes, though unwillingly and groaning, either through suffering or through sight, may endure immortal together with humanity. For those things immune from suffering are nevertheless contaminated by sight. *(Romans 8:20, 22.)*

Thus, when the elements too are renewed for the better together with humanity, the memory and authors of vices will perish; even those elements will be purified which lost their innate purity not through deeds but through knowledge of deeds.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Why idols are worshiped in vain if they give answers in temples

**APOLLONIUS.**—It is indeed difficult to believe that a world standing firm amid such an astonishing display of powers could ever be destroyed or restored. But since you affirm that it will be changed by God’s power, what will exist without it? Or what kind of restoration could make it more glorious, when its magnitude and beauty are so great that neither its magnitude can be grasped by reason or knowledge nor its splendor increased? What definition or judgment, then, should be followed on this subject? It is consistent with the instruction you promised that you should not remain silent.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—You are right that, for our understanding, the reason lying wholly within God’s providence is incomprehensible. Yet a manifold splendor will increase the form of the present beauty, since a far greater light will come to it from the Creator than the light he has implanted in creatures. [Note: We have added the word *est* (“is”) from the Vindobonensis manuscript. Below, the same manuscript and the Lemovicensis have *omnium specierum nulla* (“none of all species”).]

We must therefore measure invisible things by visible ones and estimate incorruptible things from the wonder of corruptible things. When the righteous rise into eternal joys, a new heaven and an unformed earth will be revealed. A light multiplied beyond the sun will pour forth from the sight of God, because the sun is much farther from God than we are from that same sun.

Those whom the merits of different degrees of righteousness have raised to this life will instead possess the splendor of the sun. Each will enjoy the honors of the happiness he has attained in such a way that neither will the higher be exalted nor the lower despised; rather, each will love his own joys so that the difference of brightness will be balanced by equal immortality.

Then no interruption of night will violate the continuity of day and light. God, present to the eyes of those who see him, and the divinity ever accompanying the joy of the blessed, will drive away darkness and join day to them. No envy will afflict the wretched, no suspicion torment the unwary, no pain of mind or inward anguish will trouble anyone. No necessity, opportunity, or will to sin will make death either deserved or feared.

Everything will bloom with fruits; the appearance of all things will not be altered by any change of seasons. Fragrance will rival beauty. There will be no troublesome rains with their darkness, nor will cold or heat corrupt the freedom of perpetual breezes. A gentle temperateness will remain forever, and no remembrance of the past will disturb the immeasurable joys of that blessedness. Thus, even if the future destruction of the present world did not remove its use, the righteous would nevertheless rejoice that it had passed away rather than grieve.

## CHAPTER XXVII. If God alone is to be honored, why are human beings also honored, and why are images sculpted in the vessels of God?

**APOLLONIUS.**—The exhortation concerning the future is great, as you say, but it has not yet been demonstrated that the empty divinities of the pagans are called by a vain religion, or that their gods are devoid of honor, since reliable answers are given from the inner sanctuaries and future events are learned in temples. If these answers are both true and beneficial to those who inquire, you Christians try in vain to destroy what you cannot take away. [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has the excellent reading: in the earlier edition, corruptly, *nondum gentilium potuit vana religione* (“the vanity of the pagans could not yet”). Other matters were later corrected with the help of the same manuscript, but they are too minor to require individual notice.]

**ZACCHAEUS.**—Those things which the inspection of entrails customarily displays in temples, and which the inner sanctuaries seem to foretell as future, are not always true and, in my opinion, have never benefited anyone. If they are adverse and come from God for the purpose of correction, they cannot be changed except by him. What benefit is there in knowing what has been announced if the foretold events cannot be avoided? But if they are not from God, they can be neither good nor true; and just as they do no harm, so they provide no benefit.

Whether they are false or certainly possess some truth through the outcome, they are all fabrications of demons. These wish people to hope in them and are accustomed to deceive those who hope, so that when they have drawn human beings away from the worship of God, they may also strip them of his benefits and separate them from his goodness.

These beings haunt the temples of the pagans; under the names of dead human beings they have established their dwelling in your inner sanctuaries. Since they have no other place on earth in which to remain, they rush headlong through the air beneath the clouds, examining everything in their winged movements. They either announce what they have already seen or foretell as things to be avoided the adversities they wickedly intend to bring about themselves.

Although they are wicked and unreliable spirits, polluted by every crime and guilt, they nevertheless do not lack the benefit and vigor of an incorporeal nature, of that substance whose dignity they lost along with heaven. They must know more than human beings, whose creation is higher and whose senses are not enclosed within an earthly body.

And what, I ask, is their divination? Are they not likewise terrified, together with the human beings whom they have captured through vices, by the invocation of Christ? They voluntarily wish to foretell certain things and announce matters concerning the absent or the future as though they were manifest, whether they hope for relief from torments or imitate those who will foretell such things in order to deceive.

Yet all their pretense of divination concerns earthly matters and actions. They foresee nothing, before it happens, that belongs to God; they know nothing heavenly before they see it; and, what is even more astonishing, they do not even discern the thoughts in human hearts. [Note: We have restored to the text the entire passage concerning knowledge of heavenly things from the margin. The phrase *quod sit Dei* (“which belongs to God”) is scarcely tolerable; I would gladly read *quod solius est Dei* (“which belongs to God alone”).]

You are not ashamed, then, to attribute the worship of true divinity to such beings, and to entrust human life and hope to those whose constant practice is deception and whose ingenuity in misleading passes for divination? You also either fashion images of them, baked by fire, or offer them for worship in wood and carved objects. Among these, the god is more venerable to you who has been more finely polished by the craftsman’s hand; divinity is considered more illustrious if the painting is more beautiful. Yet no effort is made to seek the Creator, nor is understanding applied to recognize the true God.

Is it not manifest madness to subject a human being to these as though they were God, when by believing in God you could subject them to yourself, and to seek the supports of life from those whose guilt is beyond doubt? If you think they will be useful and therefore trust that they ought to be appeased, believe them helpful to anyone when they are favorable—if, when scorned by the faithful, they do harm; if they injure those by whom they are despised for God’s sake. Since they fear us, they rule over you. [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts correctly read; the earlier edition corruptly had *vobis prosunt* (“they benefit you”).] And consider how they ought to be regarded—beings who can never do good, nor always do harm, although doing harm is easier for them and they never cease to desire it.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Why Christians do not believe in fate
APOLL. — Your rebuke does indeed have the appearance of truth, but it can be refuted by examining the matter further. For we worship the images or likenesses of those whom we either believe to be gods according to true religion, or, instructed by the traditions of the ancients, do not know that they are not gods. [Note: Both manuscripts have *ducti*, perhaps better. Not much later, where the text reads “you accuse us of sacrilege,” the same manuscripts have only “you accuse us.”] But you, to whom this is an abomination, why do you venerate images of human beings—whether painted in wax or cast in metal—with reverence for kings, even through public worship? And why do you give human beings the honor that, as you yourselves proclaim, is due to God alone? But if this is both unlawful [Col. 1096D] and contrary to the law, why do you Christians do it, or why do your priests fail to forbid it, so that knowingly, under cover of official duty, you do what you accuse us, in our ignorance, of committing as sacrilege?

**ZACH.** — I neither ought nor can approve this, because the manifest declarations of God do not permit us to worship the elements, angels, or any powers of heaven, earth, or air. For this is a special designation of divine office, and its reverence is higher than every earthly veneration. But just as flattery first drove human beings into this kind of evil, so now custom scarcely recalls them from their error. Yet in this you detect only heedless service, not any divine worship. [Note: We have restored this from conjecture. In the printed editions and manuscripts the reading is *cultum, sed*, but it is corrupt.]

Certainly, because of the likeness of beloved faces, people’s eager enthusiasm does more than those to whom the honor is offered may require, or than those who offer it ought to perform. And although more vigilant Christians abhor this custom of careless homage, and the priests do not cease to forbid it, the person whose image is greeted is nevertheless not called a god; incense is not burned to the images, nor do they stand upon altars to be worshiped. Rather, they are displayed in memory of their merits, so that they may provide posterity with an example of commendable deeds [Col. 1097B], or rebuke those who are present for their abuse.

You see, therefore, that there is nothing in this resembling your errors, which you criticize; nor are more careless services justly attributed to profane acts. For even those to whom this matter may be referred would either refuse to have it done if consulted, or would not reject any customary practice of empty glory. Assuming nothing divine rashly, they acknowledge that they are mortal and unworthy of God’s honor; to him they owe both what they are and, perhaps, by faith, the merit of having become what they are.

**CHAPTER XXIX. Why Christians do not believe in fate.**

**APOLL.** — At the beginning of this proposition you could have noticed that I touched upon the objection only lightly, because the complete observance of your profession, as you claim it to be, ought to admit absolutely nothing by which God could be provoked. But now, setting these matters aside, if you think it appropriate, state clearly why you do not want fate to exist for human beings, or for what reason you hold that there is no necessity imposed by decree; since these things are found and established through the course of the stars and the reckoning of the moon in such a way that no one can easily avoid what the configurations fixed by his own birth have destined for him. [Note: We have added the final word from the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts.]

**ZACCH.** — I believe you understand that the word *fate* (*fatum*) is taken from the interpretation of the term, and that what is thought to be called by this name is not the form of some thing but of a word. But if there is any necessity imposed by decree—which it is impious to believe—then God is either ignorant of human life or unjust: unjust, if he himself assigns good and evil to those who have not yet experienced them; ignorant, if he allows them to be decreed by another while he remains inactive. [Col. 1097D]

For if it is necessary that people be good, why are merits attributed to the will? If they are evil, why is punishment attributed to their deeds? Therefore the law too is superfluous, and I do not know why the laws of the world are established, if whatever a person does rightly is to be attributed to outcomes, and whatever he does wrongly to necessity. Moreover, why does God, the same creator of good things, either threaten judgment or promise blessedness in so many volumes of Scripture? [Col. 1098A] What do the devout prayers of human beings accomplish, or what does earnest supplication achieve, if some power of decree fixes upon people, inexperienced and emerging into the light at birth, something that cannot be avoided and that appears to be imposed upon them?

On the contrary, God is just and never unequal in judgment. Just as he himself formed all things, so he governs all things, establishing a law from the beginning that we should be good alone—or rather, since we are created and born in this way, that we should not change. And not merely that we should not be evil, but that we should not even wish to be evil, so that we may always do good, rather than, as those who deserve evil, eventually suffer it.

But this supposed foreknowledge of all human wickedness was invented by the devil, its author, so that those who do not recognize this deception of his may be more secretly misled under the harmless appearance of mathematical science. [Col. 1098B] Among all the arts of his crimes, none does he pursue more perniciously against the uncertain, and by none does he more subtly draw people away from the worship of God, than by persuading us that, although we know that we owe to God the fact that we are formed and born, we owe to fate the fact that we live.

We are deceived unless, for some people, the chief concern of their entire religion is not to be ignorant of the future. Whether they wish it or not, they become subject to the one through whom they believe these things are made known; and while they pursue such matters, they depart from faith and religion. Worse still, evil is not avoided under the appearance of innocence, because people do not believe it can be avoided; nor is what is expected necessarily to occur requested from God if it is thought certain to happen.

Consider, moreover, the very theater of these magical practices: the quality of the signs, the position of the moon, the day, the hour, and the name of the person consulting are investigated. Behold, divination is already uncertain, since the questioner or the respondent may be mistaken. Then every possible degree of favorable outcome is produced, and adverse events are foretold together with the possibility of escape. Here too the fraud of the aforementioned craftsman is plainly visible: he admits that events are uncertain when he declares that they can be escaped.

For God does not assign adversity to the innocent, nor does he impose evils upon those who have not experienced them. [Note: We preferred to publish this reading, although no manuscript supports it, rather than the previous reading, *inexpertis magna*. At the end of the chapter we likewise restored *posse*, where the printed edition had *posset*.]

You see, therefore, that the fraud of the devil’s art mocks both divine patience and human curiosity, and that, as though in the reckoning of the moon and the course of the stars, a hidden wound and poison of treachery lies concealed. Thus, amid the knowledge and foreknowledge of future events, reverence for God and love of justice are diminished among human beings, since God must either be believed to have appointed evils for those being born, or to be unable to remove what another has appointed. [Col. 1098D]

**CHAPTER XXX. If the devil causes harm in hidden ways, how can he cause harm in the courses of the moon or stars, since they are present?**

**APOLL.** — As I understand it, the power of this devil is great, since, contrary to God’s will, as it appears, he has inserted into the course of the moon and stars those things by which he might harm human beings. Yet how are we to believe that things observed there come from elsewhere? I think that the devil can deceive people through hidden falsehoods, but that mathematical science itself agrees simply with the signs and stars. It should not therefore be judged harmful merely because it removes nothing from the events of life; rather, it should be considered useful, since it either announces prosperity or declares what must be avoided.

**ZACCH.** — I said earlier that mathematical astrology is the more grievous evil because it is considered innocent. But although it is concealed and enclosed by an investigatory subtlety, its activity is nevertheless revealed, as I explained, by its substance and its end. It is not from God, and therefore it must not be believed to be connected with the stars. It is first uncertain and untrustworthy, then empty in its operation, and therefore it is pointless to observe it, since it will be of no benefit.

It is great folly to fear what it predicts, since such things can be escaped even according to the confession of the predictor, and especially can be overcome by prayers directed to God. But it is utter madness to hope for something favorable from it, since it can so easily either be deceived or deceive. Yet suppose it sometimes announces the truth: what sense is there, while bearing manifest guilt, in awaiting doubtful outcomes from such omens rather than, secure in faith, hoping for healing from God or for merit?

Know this above all: the devil has a certain principate among crimes, and various ministries of unclean spirits serve him. Under his wicked division, some carry the torches of lust and kindle the fuel of sexual excess; through others desire is driven headlong, and avarice employs its own officials. [Note: The reader should be warned that the word *officium* is understood here, as in the manuscript and in the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the empire, to mean the ministers or officials of a governor. The words enclosed in parentheses survive from the clause in which Zacchaeus wrote that demons presided over immoderate joy, having received this office from the chief demon.]

Others persuade people to bloody love of possession, and to the frauds that are sisters of theft. *(They rejoice at what they recognize.)* These preside over sorrows, and certain ones are appointed to inflict terrors upon those who fear. The multitude of others is exercised in tortures, so that the bodies of unhappy human beings may be shaken more cruelly by torment. By some, madness is increased as the moon waxes, as though a stain from the fullness of its pure light came upon those who are seized; under a certain measure or intensification of evil it is either increased or begins.

Some await the practice of magic and devote themselves to imagining and fabricating the figures of the dead. Those more skilled in these divinations run ahead of them, and mathematical astrology, as though simple, embraces the most subtle forms of deception. Others foretell omens by birds and indicate the flights of birds by definite quarters of the sky. [Col. 1099D] Thus, with that instigator or governor of all falsehoods presiding, demons serve under various wages of crime, setting before the human race snares that cannot be avoided or endured—if, indeed, everything were believed or done just as they always want it to be believed or done.

**CHAPTER XXXI. Who the demons are, and who the devil is.**

**APOLL.** — The question set aside earlier has appropriately returned to the answer: who, then, are these demons whom you previously stated more explicitly to have dwelt in the temples of the Gentiles and now to preside over or participate in all crimes? Who is their prince in the same way—the one whom you call the devil? And how were they cast down to these activities, if they once possessed some dignity of a higher nature? For the things you mentioned above can be accomplished by them only through their kind and quality.

**ZACCH.** — Their nature is even now what it was at the beginning, because whatever God has once created he either changes for the better or does not himself abolish. But they lost their heavenly dignity not through their Creator, but through their own will. Since you ask the causes of their offense, learn both from the account given in Scripture. When God created all things, he made two kinds of creatures especially important, granting each intelligence according to its function: angels in heaven and human beings on earth. The angels are incorporeal and truly spirits; we, however, carry heavenly intelligence within earthly bodies.

And although, by the Creator’s gift, the will of both is free, human beings nevertheless have greater opportunity to sin, since they must be on guard both in mind and in body. For the soul sins through its desires, and the body through its actions.

These, then, are closer to God who are freer; and because they are always ministers and intermediaries of his commands, they therefore know more. [Col. 1100B] Thus whatever you see being done on earth through ranks of powers and dignities is a shadow of heavenly things. So there too, according to what God has granted, the order and discipline of the one who presides serve God’s commands; and at the will of the ineffable Majesty, the obedience of archangels governs the innumerable multitude of angels. [Note: We have added the small word *ut*, absent from the printed editions and manuscripts, because it seems necessary. Below, we printed *et disciplinae* from the Vindobonensis, whereas previously the corrupt reading was *est disciplinae*.]

The one who is now the devil and prince of demons was originally the first of all the angels. Though he surpassed the others in creation and rank, when he was lifted up by pride he was made lower than all. For he wanted to appear to be God, which he was not; and because he had been made first among all, he assumed the honor of the Creator by comparing himself with the Divinity. Because of this presumptuous attempt, he was cast out of heaven together with some of the lower angels who had given him their assent. After he had dragged them with him to earth, as though restoring the principate he had lost, he made his attendants out of angels; and, as I mentioned shortly before, he consoles himself for his exclusion from heaven through the offices of crimes and the evils of those who have fallen. [Col. 1100D]

He first incited and persuaded the human being, through the serpent, to violate the law of the commandment; and thereafter he has continually turned the goodness of our creation into crimes through the allurements of life. And although this was accomplished through human hands, Christ was nevertheless crucified while he—the devil—pressed it forward.

Envy, arrogance, cruelty, and a lust mingled with excess are always his delight and joy in filthy hearts. And lest he should expose his subtle wickedness by pursuing only impious or polluted things, he mixed what was honorable into the shaping and effects of crimes. He strove to appear to approve virginity and to claim that chastity ought to be dedicated to idols, so that what he destroys in reality he might pursue in name. Even when people have been purified, he offers them something more of his deceit, and willingly allows any sect to be followed, provided that no one can know God in ignorance or worship him, once known, according to his will and law. [Col. 1101A]

These, then, are the demons, and this is their prince, the devil. Christ’s name terrifies and torments them, hidden within the innermost parts of human beings. They construct all the snares mentioned above against everyone; and those whom they cannot capture through enticements, they try to draw away from the hope of immortality by making them displeasing to God in whatever way they can—through the enjoyment of present things and disbelief in what is to come. [Col. 1101B]

**CHAPTER XXXII. Why God, who foreknows the future, created the devil, who would become the enemy of human beings.**

**APOLL.** — If the devil is as evil as you say, and so persistent in crime, then God, who foreknew the future, ought neither to have created evil nor raised it to so great a height of dignity, lest he create an adversary for himself or an enemy for human beings. If knowledge is available, let an account of the reason for this act follow.

**ZACCH.** — God made nothing wholly evil in his work, nor is anything harmful implanted in these creatures; rather, it was desired by them, because everything was made to be pleasing, not to cause harm. But first God granted free will to the angels, just as he later did to human beings. Otherwise they would have differed in no respect from speechless animals except in nature: as I have already said of human beings, arranged in a certain torpor of ignorance, either everything would be permitted to them or nothing would be permitted.

Would God, then, the source of all reason, have created irrational ministers for himself? Or what reason would there be in their understanding if no power existed in their will? Finally, what obedience or worship of God could there be except the likeness of servants following the commands of one who orders them? But if the Creator is to be accused because of the voluntary evil of each individual—which it is impious to say—then all things can be accused in the same way, because everything was made for good use, yet has evil outcomes if you wish to use it otherwise.

Is fire evil? And yet whatever you bring near it improperly is burned. The earth buries, but only when it collapses. The seas were not gathered together for shipwrecks, and yet, when approached by ships at the wrong time, they submerge them. Were high places constructed for falling? Yet unless we stand most cautiously at the summit, we fall. Iron was given to human beings for turning the earth into furrows and cutting wood, and from it wars took up swords. Is death placed in a rope? Yet many end their lives by a noose. Who assigned stones to stoning, or wood to crosses? Were the highest dignities given to kings for the purpose of making tyrannies easier to assume? How good is the creation of wine! Yet when taken too freely it produces madness. The very juices of plants that are mixed into beneficial medicines either harm more violently when poisonous or, taken in excessive quantities, kill. Marriage was permitted for the purpose of producing children, and from lawful intercourse illicit adulteries are admitted.

What, I ask, could God have done more justly than create a rational race of angels and human beings, depriving it neither of freedom nor of the knowledge needed for caution? But if God, who foreknew the future, ought not to have created such a being or preferred it to the others, then he ought not to have made human beings or preferred them to all other creatures, since he knew that they would sin. And, as you say, even the elements ought not to have been made, if they were not going to be useful to anyone, or because all of them can cause harm if you do not use them in the way for which they were made.

How much more persuasive is this order of divine providence: to entrust the highest place first to one who was going to attempt unlawful things, so that the more attentive concern of justice might teach those who came afterward to love and fear the Creator, and at the same time might show that he could be tested with impunity neither by angels nor by anyone else, since he had cast down even an archangel for presumption. You see, therefore, that by God’s creation he was made good, and by God’s gift established in a high place; but by his own will, which he had received as free, he changed goodness into evil and lost dignity through arrogance.

**CHAPTER XXXIII. If the devil sinned with his companions, why was he not immediately killed?**

[Col. 1102C]

**APOLL.** — What you have said about the creation and fall of the devil also appears to accord with reason. But explain clearly why, after an act of such great audacity, he and his attendants were not immediately destroyed, as I have already asked.

**ZACCH.** — God’s judgment proceeds not only from power but also from reason. In condemnation he does not want the sentence to consist solely in the judgment of the judge, unless the conscience of the offender also turns back to him through a certain postponement of punishment, since he always grants mercy to those who desire to return to him. [Note: We restored this from the Vindobonensis; previously the reading was *qui condemnationem*.]

Although he is just in all his equity, he is nevertheless more inclined toward mercy, and he does not hurry to vengeance in swift indignation, since no one succeeds to his judgment. He therefore strives to save, not destroy, what he has created; hence he is characterized by indescribable patience and not by precipitous vengeance. If that same devil and the other companions of his destruction, before the growth of their subsequent crimes and the betrayal of the heavenly secrets that they knew in part, had offered hands subject to repentance, cleansing the crime of pride through an appeal grounded in humility, angelic honor would surely have returned to them. They would not now be wallowing in the filth with which they oppress those whom they have captured in the snares of wickedness and recruit, in the unhappy condition of their vices, as a consolation for their own destruction.

Consider further the contest between human beings and demons, between wrongdoing and justice: from the forces of luxury and virtue contending with one another arises the reward of immortality. God, the judge of merit, watches us fighting every day and calmly observes spiritual snares being overcome by fragile bodies. The sin of so exalted a creature surely had to be punished in this way, and the angel’s pride, raised against God, had to be subjected to human beings, so that the one who did not want his own creator to rule over him might first suffer the authority of those subject to him. And although he drags human beings, masters of their own will, toward the worse side, nevertheless many attain the seat of God through the testing of virtues and faith. [Col. 1103B]

You see, therefore, that through God’s providence the devil and his accomplices are preserved until the future judgment, even for the sake of a certain benefit to humanity. The Creator’s patience thereby gives the fallen a place for repentance; and if the periods of indulgence have accomplished nothing, they are condemned by their own rather than by God’s sentence. Their guilt increases daily from outside, because, although we are exercised toward justice by their attacks, human frailty nevertheless prevails all the more for this reason: these beings lost what they possessed in the angelic nature without anyone opposing them. [Note: Here too we follow the Vindobonensis. The earlier edition had *prae se*, which made no sense. At the end, the reading *quod hi nullo*, found by Acherius in one manuscript, was also found by us in the Vindobonensis; it is considerably better than the printed *quam nullo*.]

**CHAPTER XXXIV. Why God did not send an angel who would either restore humanity or destroy the devil.**

[Col. 1103C]

**APOLL.** — I understand the substance of your assertion to amount to this: that Christ, the Son of God, came already to earth, or will come again, not only to restore humanity but also to condemn the devil and his companions. If this is so, an angel too could have been sent who, without injury to God, would destroy the wicked after separating them from the good, and punish the prince of the wicked himself together with his companions by divine authority.

**ZACCH.** — The first reason Christ, the Son of God, had for wishing to come to earth was either that he should not allow humanity, which was going to perish, to perish, or that he should restore what had been lost. But this too is joined to his providence: just as in the first coming he overcame the devil and his companions in the human being, so in the second he will judge him in the human being. It would not have been difficult for God, through any power of the heavenly host, to bring the present age to an end and punish those already mentioned. But because the aforementioned author of wickedness had wanted to appear to be God, as I have already explained, it was necessary for the Son of God to be made visibly manifest, so that it might be known before angels and human beings who each one was, and so that the pretender might be refuted face to face. Thus no doubt about the understanding of the one Majesty would thereafter remain in either creature.

To these reasons is added the fact that the same one who had originally formed human beings, made immortal under a condition, ought to restore them to something better. For it would have been unfitting if a corruptible human being, made by God, were made incorruptible by an angel after having earned this through the testing of faith. What, moreover, is more worthy of God’s generosity than that he should grant his presence as the consummation of blessedness, and bestow upon the restored what he had denied to the untested? Thus, at last, freed from all these things, we may see reigning in his own majesty the one whom we follow through such sufferings of evil, whom amid the world’s hostility and dangers we confess and believe, as we desire. [Note: The Lemovicensis manuscript has this reading; the printed editions incorrectly have *prima et quidem*. In the same place Acherius notes that one manuscript reads: “God the Son came to earth in order that …”]

**CHAPTER XXXV. Why the wicked prosper and the righteous are oppressed.**

**APOLL.** — Faith in what you have explained has been established in my mind. But so that no hesitation may remain, now reveal to one who believes, I ask, what power causes the wicked to prosper or oppresses the righteous; and, since, as you have shown, God has such great concern for humanity, why such a perverse difference nevertheless governs both groups, so that, although in the wicked there are both the will and the action of evil, an abundance of good things nevertheless falls to them contrary to justice, while prosperity is denied to those who more justly ought to be wealthy.

**ZACCH.** — The understanding of this matter is easy, and the entire explanation need not be sought in spiritual experiences, since ordinary life plainly teaches how everything either flows abundantly to the wicked or is lacking to the good.

The wicked, reversing the order of their actions, not only complete what they stubbornly seek but also plunder what belongs to others. They devote the whole span of life to every kind of profit and place their hope in money. The good, however, avoid even honorable efforts at gain because of the opportunity for wrongdoing; they do not stubbornly guard what they have acquired well, prefer peace to quarrels, and hope for the author of justice as their avenger.

Moreover, pity never moves the wicked, nor do they even scarcely extend themselves to small gifts. But for the good, the expense of the poor is an occupation, and expenditure in good works is always ready. Since the overturning of morals arises above all from abundance, the instigator of crimes, nourishing his own followers, supplies lavish wealth to those who rejoice, so that luxury may creep in through the success of their pleasures. Then abundance turns toward banquets, and captive drunkenness is irrigated by vices.

From this comes the lesser concern of the wealthy for God, and confidence in present things does not allow them to hope for the riches of the future. But God, whose patience is long, allows the swollen to be thrown into dissipation and strengthens those who are constricted by suffering. He will render the promised judgment to all, so that each person may receive there what he has done here and suffer forever what he has inflicted here by despising and tormenting those beneath him and subject to him for a time.

**CHAPTER XXXVI. If God is just, why are infants, who know nothing of evil, afflicted with various evils?**

**APOLL.** — The parts of this question have also been plainly laid open. And unless I feared that it would be burdensome to add something as though to heap upon what has already been explained, I would not ask in vain what this means: that infants, wholly unaware of vices and sins, are afflicted with various evils; that sometimes, as they emerge from the womb, weakness seizes them, or premature force snatches them away to death; that savage madness torments the innocent; and that the piety and justice of the Majesty, unquestionably ready for all, does not come to their aid. Therefore, if, as I said, it is not tedious, speak briefly and show everything.

**ZACCH.** — You ask more than may be sufficient for one who believes, and in your inquiry you go beyond the boundaries of necessary knowledge. [Note: Acherius himself noted in the margin that this ought to be read, although all the manuscripts had *progrederis*. Below, we restored *ut in nullo* from the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis; previously it read *ut nullum*. The words subsequently enclosed in parentheses are absent from all manuscripts except one of Saint Arnulf. That same manuscript, where you read *quid sentiri debeat*, has the fuller reading *quid usus attentioris vitae docuerit*.]

But so that you may not waver or hesitate in faith at any point, and so that the argument of unbelievers may have no place at all against God’s justice, consider what ought to be understood.

(God made human beings from four elements: dry, moist, hot, and cold. The cold elements are placed in the spleen, the hot in the gall, the moist in the blood, and the dry are reckoned in the bones. As you understand, this remarkable harmony of opposites, joined together, preserves the Creator’s work in the human being and, by the ingenuity of divine art, displays a more excellent form than the individual elements had previously retained in themselves. Thus it appears that whatever is renewed by the Creator always advances toward something better.

These elements therefore flow together in equal proportions at conception, and they meet from every region of the internal organs in such a way that the offspring do not exceed the Creator’s balance in any respect. But this integrity of birth is moderated either by the sparingness or by the excess of one or the other parent; and whatever has prevailed improperly in the developing child within the womb, or shortly after it emerges from the womb, produces either illnesses or death.

For there are two veins in the human being that hold the chief authority among all channels of breath and blood. From their own seat among the vital organs, they are dispersed through narrow passages and illuminate the whole body, preserving by their known courses the explored and accessible path of life. If some force closes either of those veins, it produces the ruin of unmistakable weakness and death. Hence infants very often either become deprived of all light or are immediately snatched away by premature death.) [Col. 1105C]

Sometimes too the swift end of infants occurs because of the sins or merits of their parents: the good are tested by the removal of those they love, while the unjust are punished; and those who do not perceive themselves to be rebuked by other pains and losses are afflicted even by bereavements. But the righteous are tested by a greater fire of faith, when, having remained steadfast in lesser matters, they are also tested through the loss of those they love. [Note: The Vindobonensis has the correct reading; the earlier edition had the corrupt *probantur affectum*. Shortly afterward, where we have written *arguuntur exitiis* from the same manuscript, the reading was previously *arguuntur exitu*, less correctly.]

But when an unspeakable demonic madness torments those who are not yet conscious of good or evil, the cause lies with their parents, though in different ways. If the parents are unjust and are not corrected by the punishments mentioned above or by similar ones, they are also rebuked through the deaths of their innocent children.

Those, however, whose conduct is upright and who overcome demonic wickedness on their own are nevertheless wearied by such attacks. Nor are they free from the exercise of troubles, since the deceitful power cannot otherwise prevail to harm them. It always wraps the cunning of evil in this, so that, whether these things occur because of vices or because of faith, it may persuade anyone it can that God is either unjust or negligent. [Note: Here too, following the authority of the Vindobonensis, we have corrected what previously read *si quis forte*. Below, from the same manuscript and the Lemovicensis, we printed *malis vitae*, whereas Acherius had written *ex malis vitae*.]

But however the devil may torment either the little ones or their parents, God’s justice is absent from neither. For the transfer of infants from the evils of this life to something better is itself a benefit, lest, born from wicked parents, they should eventually become like their authors. And for those who gave them birth it must be counted a benefit that, through the temporary pain of their affliction, they are either rescued from sins and become good, or are increased in merit and grow in faith. [Col. 1106B]

You now have the reasons for your questions and a clear understanding of all your uncertainties. Therefore, now submit yourself to God and render the faith promised in your agreement; reject this wisdom of the world and believe the utterances of true wisdom. Cease seeking higher things from yourself, and entrust the explanation of the heavenly secrets to the knowledge and counsel of their Author.

For although you have now learned many things, and some matters concerning the inner aspects of faith remain, do not think that a human being can know everything that belongs to God—except what God himself has thoroughly taught a human being to know, or has permitted him to understand through divine inspiration. Therefore, go forward and testify to the faith received in the simplicity of your heart by the confession of a devoted mouth. Do not be terrified by the heavy burden of the commandments: the service of God is light, and the whole necessity of the law lies within the human will. Once you have discovered it to be fully revealed, you will rejoice in its recognition; and although repentance over past error may goad you, a greater joy will nevertheless come from confession. [Col. 1106C]

**CHAPTER XXXVII. What the fullness of the law is: confession of belief in God.**

**APOLL.** — The will you have sought has long been ready. But just as places intended for foundations must first be cleared of rubble, so the mind had to be cleansed of doubts [Col. 1106D] and filled with knowledge, so that the firm purification of ancient matters might provide an open approach to faith. Since the complete revelation of the law could not previously remain in a mind too occupied, now repeat it after arranging it briefly, so that what I had almost refused to accept when I heard it may, after being examined in many ways, be received with reverence.

**ZACCH.** — I shall certainly repeat it, and I shall express in briefer words what must be impressed upon the innermost parts of the soul. For Christians, integrity of faith is the fullness of righteousness: namely, to know, worship, fear, and love God; neither to adore nor worship things made by human hands; and not to eat profane food sacrificed to idols.

Behold, no longer is the blood of abundant victims or the odor of polluted fire demanded. You will have worshiped God earnestly if you give yourself wholly to God, observing two chief commandments above all: that you love God more than yourself, and that you love a human being as yourself. For no one can benefit himself by himself as much as that one can benefit either everyone collectively or individuals. And what is fairer than that, just as you love a human being, you should wish to be loved by him, if you desire to be comforted?

So act as you desire good things to be granted. Certainly, do not exclude the hope of the most blessed eternity for the passing pleasure of a very brief time; do not preserve the vanity of present things while destroying faith in the future. Since it is clearly more advantageous to choose one of two alternatives, I will not say according to God’s judgment but according to that of any honorable person: to place one’s hope in what is to come and despise present things, rather than, for the sake of the passing use of present things, let lasting things pass away.

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.**
APOLLONIUS.—Everyone both perceives and can understand that God’s majesty is one and simple, and that all visible and invisible things were created by him; that whoever does not believe in the full faithfulness of his law and promises, and in the fullness of justice and merit, is deprived forever of the effect of the divine possibility of resurrection; and that whoever denies that you, Christ, are the Son of God and remain God in man, and neither confesses nor proclaims you as the Redeemer of the human race, having carried the triumph of the cross up into heaven; whoever does not expect you to be the future requiter of holy labor or avenger of crimes—let such a one, groaning in fellowship with the devil, go forever as an exile into darkness and, plunged into the terrors of deep night, be rolled amid the fires of blazing mire.

[Note: [Col. 1107C] Thus both the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts, and correctly. In the earlier edition: “but they cannot understand either.” Below, where it reads *when carried up into the heavens*, Lemovicensis has *your*, Vindobonensis *when lifted up*.]

But let it be far from me now to know more than I ought about God and his works, or to wish or seek to know anything except what I have been taught by him—lest punishment accompany the fault of ignorance or delayed belief. Let the defiled seats of idols collapse, and let the temples of accursed abomination be emptied; and let divination itself—which, as I see, is either deceitful or false because of the manifold frauds of demons—perish beneath the reverence due to holy religion.

[Note: [Col. 1107C] The manuscript of Saint-Arnould and the Vindobonensis read *of the defiled one*. Not much later, where the text has *they flooded with joys*, we preferred the reading of the Saint-Arnould manuscript to the reading placed in the text by Acherius, *they filled with joys*. At the end, the Lemovicensis and Vindobonensis manuscripts read *recognized too late*; the earlier edition has *recognized too late* in the feminine.]

I will follow God Christ and the way of salvation, loving him before my soul and all my inward being, and loving in myself only what he has loved. But you, who were the minister of the divine gift in me, and who will receive grace from its author, hand on to me, I beg you, the fullness of faith; hand on the sacraments of the inner mystery, and suffuse perishable matter with the renewal of a higher hope. For if you believe anything, you who have attended our discussions, the joys of the true light have so flooded the soul that, although I regret having remained ignorant of God Christ and his loving-kindness for so long, I nevertheless hope that it is blessedness eternal to have recognized and believed him, even so late.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1107]

## PREFACE

Since the best and most desirable path toward the practice of justice is to live piously and to guard the ordering of life itself through observance of one’s deeds and understanding; and since among all good pursuits the foremost is either always to speak to God or faithfully to speak about God, assigning what is greatest in a human being—the service of tongue and mind—to the praises of its Author; yet without being so exalted by the fervor of pious devotion that vows supported by faith overstep the proper measure of thought and confession, or that a bolder advance should trample the sacred boundaries of divine proclamation beyond what is permitted—

[Note: [Col. 1107D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts, correctly. The earlier edition has *observance*, incorrectly. Not long afterward, following the manuscript Vindobonensis, we wrote *the authority of its author*; in that manuscript the intermediate words *of affairs* do not appear.]

—we therefore approach first, ready not through confidence but through faith, an explanation of the holy Trinity; then we shall proceed in a straightforward exposition against the Jews and afterward against the heretics, and shall also expose the schismatic error of the Novatians.

[Note: [Col. 1108D] The excellent reading of the same Vindobonensis manuscript; in the printed editions: *let him tread with a bolder step*, less well, as I judge.]

Thus an instruction gathered from many volumes will serve in place of a compendium, without laboring through everything in each individual case. Since we have found that a matter is better handled through persons, we shall lead our Zacchaeus and our Apollonius through the aforesaid stages of the case with more robust knowledge, so that, as in the earlier little work, the rivals of our religion may be condemned; and so that the one whose zeal for learning is kindled may desire to live for God and die to vices.

Now, therefore, in a gentle exchange between the persons mentioned, everything will both be brought forward and tested, so that with suitable brevity it may be shown what ought to be accepted and what avoided; while the belief of the faithful is strengthened by heavenly examples, and the unbelief of the profane is destroyed, above all, by arguments drawn from their own understanding.

## APOLLONIUS

If anyone is capable either of expressing in words or of grasping in mind, as is fitting, his gratitude to God for the benefits bestowed upon him through God’s mercy, I above all ought to discharge this duty of confession and thought. By his inspiration or your teaching I have escaped from so many snares of error, laid down the bonds of death, and, stripping off the earthly human being, passed by God’s adoption into the hope of heavenly joys. Having moreover become a participant in the eternal sacrifice—indeed, by receiving God, a part of God himself—

[Note: [Col. 1109D] Scarcely anything in the whole work is more remarkable than this testimony of Apollonius, now a Christian, to Christ’s real presence when he is received.]

—I ought with all the strength of my soul both to seek what brings salvation and to destroy what is crooked. But since, in returning gratitude, we are not even adequate to what we perceive through understanding, this alone is the path of repayment available to those unequal to the task: if God, the giver of all forgiveness, should, in the condescension by which he attends to our thoughts, look upon the vow owed to him and accept the will in place of the deed.

Therefore, however much I may have attained, being possessed of indescribable joy, my fear of ignorance is nevertheless greater now that something like knowledge has begun in me. A great anxiety troubles my soul: if I am conscious of spiritual secrets, may I be found either ignorant or hesitant concerning as much of the fullness of the sacred mystery as it is lawful to hear and speak.

For when you first laid down the principles of faith in me, you asked for a simple belief in the Father, from whom all things are, and in the Son, through whom all things were made. Later, as the tradition of the unfolding mystery began, you also required from me a confession of the Holy Spirit, and my whole belief was directed toward the Trinity.

## CHAPTER I  
### Whether there is a third Person in the honor of religion

APOLLONIUS.—Remembering your promise, reveal whether there is a third Person in the honor of religion, or whether the name is assumed from customary multifold reverence rather than from a distinctive designation. If you disclose these hidden things of heavenly wisdom, whatever has been successfully completed in my reception of the arriving faith will be strengthened by more perfect knowledge. It will then follow that you should also explain the teachings of the heretics and all the perversities of schisms, so that they may be avoided more quickly, provided that you first show how what has already been granted ought to be believed.

[Col. 1109D]

ZACCHAEUS.—Those who are always girded for the service of spiritual warfare ought indeed to be trained by continual instruction, as though awaiting imminent battles, and ought to detest idleness. Yet many reject as though it were a work of novel learning what you seek, although it has been set forth both at length and sublimely; and everything concerning all former ambiguity has been so fully discussed that now not only untrained interpretations of the meaning but even words themselves are unavailable unless they have been repeatedly impressed upon the mind.

Moreover, in any edition, it is a well-known annoyance either to rub up what is already familiar or to produce, with the author suppressed, what has been included in more distinguished monuments. Hence it may perhaps suit both of us better to consult the examples of the ancients and draw this kind of doctrine from the works of illustrious writers: for it is undoubtedly more profitable for you to learn what has been perfected by more learned men, and safer for me to remain silent about matters of the greatest importance.

## CHAPTER II  
### Whether the Holy Spirit is God

APOLLONIUS.—I too believe that some have discussed these matters more broadly as our faith grew, and that across so many courses of years and ages the talents of spiritual men have not been possessed in silence but through their merits. Nevertheless, what is spread before untrained minds becomes known only slowly, and lengthy exposition burdens the mind before it teaches.

And so, once the excuse has been removed, let the fervor of what is useful exclude the fear of envy, and let the love of unconquerable faith overcome the grace of the undisturbed leisure you embrace; while the meaning of an old proverb eases our modesty. For what can anyone say that has not been said before? Or what knowledge concerning our affairs is so obscure that the practice of those who preceded us has not illuminated it?

[Note: [Col. 1109D] We have printed this from the Lemovicensis manuscript; the printed editions read *so that the fervor of that man*, incorrectly. A little above, where it reads *not possessed in silence but through their merits*, no one will doubt that some fault is present, but we found nothing in the manuscripts by which the error could be repaired.]

Therefore, first reveal this to me with certainty concerning the Holy Spirit: is he God, or is he some thing belonging to God? Is he to be believed a gift of divinity, or its fullness? Whatever you teach the one who is simply going to believe the sacraments of faith must be proved by testimonies.

[Note: [Col. 1110D] A fine emendation supplied by the Vindobonensis manuscript: the earlier edition had corruptly printed *they dictated*. Not long afterward, from the same manuscript, we have printed *the opportunity for recitation* in place of Acherius’s *the opportunity for silence*.]

ZACCHAEUS.—Although your demand may be burdensome and the force of so great a question may create a certain difficulty, since what must be said is arduous and must be contemplated more through faith than through words, nevertheless, because you do not cease to demand great things from the humble, and the fervor of the Lord arouses an opportunity for explanation, we are commanded not to keep the substance of faith pressed into the ground—that is, locked away in the secrets of the heart—but to lend it freely to those desiring knowledge and multiply it as though at interest.

Let us therefore, trembling before the exposition of ineffable majesty but confident in confession, open our lips to their Author. There is one God; and although the Trinity is distinguished by persons and names, it does not differ from itself or from its own eternity. Rather, the divinity that existed before the ages, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is truly and properly one and the same. It can neither be divided by our interpretations nor, when the Trinity is turned back into one Person, confused.

Thus the Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is God. In the Trinity there is not one God, but the Trinity is one. This is the complete faith; this is our belief. Therefore we neither permit Gods to be supposed nor allow them to be called Gods, but confess one God in the persons and names mentioned above.

For ineffable divinity did not manifest itself so that it could be enclosed, grasped, or contained by words within names and persons; rather, it manifested itself so that what it was might be and be known, giving believers an understanding of itself to the extent that the narrow limits of human speech could bear.

But do not think that these things were previously withheld from you; rather, they were previously not believed by you. For, coming from the multitude of idols, you would have thought that gods were being proclaimed here also, unless the beginnings of tradition contained in the fullness of faith had remained silent.

## CHAPTER III  
### Whether this expression can be confirmed by the Holy Scriptures

APOLLONIUS.—So far as can be understood, the faith hoped for is present in the interpretations, and the reasoning of the exposition accords with the truth. Nevertheless, the stability of pure belief requires that the same statements be confirmed by sacred exchanges, and that some summit of truth be established by reading once argument has ceased. For it may seem incongruous to speak about God without bringing forward especially those things by which he himself wished to make himself known.

Accordingly, from the many matters that I do not think can be enumerated at present—and I do not demand that they now be enumerated, since for the moment I seek the order of doctrine, not the body of history—give authority to what has been stated by saying what is clear and little in extent. For, as I said, these things, cast down as though on a slender foundation, will totter unless, supported by human speech, they are also strengthened by divine examples.

ZACCHAEUS.—You rightly demand that greater faith be given to those things that Divinity itself has uttered openly in testimony to itself, and rightly ask that a few be brought forth from innumerable examples. For proof of true majesty, although it possesses plurality, does not require plurality; and a few things suffice for one who believes, while unbelievers remain ignorant even if they investigate many.

Therefore, first from the books of the Old Testament, and afterward from the New, recognize the Holy Spirit as sharing the substance of the one divinity. The Book of Genesis begins thus:

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. 1:1, according to the Septuagint).

He is the Beginning who, when the Jews asked who he was, said: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). Hence elsewhere it was said by him: “In the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. 39:8; Heb. 10:7).

[Note: [Col. 1111D] In the Vindobonensis the whole clause is written thus: “He is designated by the name of the Beginning, who said of himself: ‘I am the Beginning,’” and so forth. Below, where the text reads *the rudiments of its own fire*, the Lemovicensis manuscript supplies the reading; the printed editions corruptly had *its own signs*.]

The Spirit of God moved over the waters so that, being about to produce all living things from them, he himself might provide the unformed beginnings of his own fire [reading uncertain], which now pours the gifts of sanctification into the purified.

David likewise testifies under God’s inspiration:

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

See how full this brevity is, and how clearly it returns to the mystery of unity. By placing the Father in “the Lord,” and the Son in the significance of “the Word,” he named the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the mouth of the Most High. And lest the utterance be reckoned merely a sound in the Word, he teaches that the heavens were made through him; and lest the Spirit be understood as merely breath, he demonstrated in him the fullness of power.

For where there is power, there must necessarily also be a subsisting Person; and where there is “all,” it is signified not as something taken away from the two but as something completed in the third—not so that the third alone possesses what is in the whole, but so that the one who appears last in name should not possess less.

Again the same prophet explains the Trinity as he prays:

“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a principal Spirit” (Ps. 50:12–14).

The principal Spirit belongs to the Father; the right Spirit belongs to the Son; the Holy Spirit is distinguished by the addition of his proper epithet. Do not be troubled by the addition of these names, that the principal and right Spirit has been designated by prophetic language as holy.

Although there is one property in each, because the Spirit is God, a diversity of names has been added so that the confusion of persons might not arise in our understanding. For what is holy is necessarily right; nor can it again be right unless it is holy. The Spirit is principal because the only-begotten Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him.

Of this Isaiah, speaking in the person of God concerning Christ, wrote:

“I have spoken; and I called him and brought him, and made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things. I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; when they came to be, I was there. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:15–16).

Likewise, when the angel announced to Mary the mysteries of the sacred birth, he brought forth concerning the same reality statements of equal force:

“The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Later, when the Lord spoke about the calling of the nations, proclaiming the Holy Spirit within the one name of divinity, he said:

“Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

The apostle Paul likewise wrote:

“He who confirms us with you in Christ the Lord, and he who anointed us is God, and he who sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. 1:21–22).

And again, while praying for heavenly blessings upon the Corinthians, he added:

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Cor. 13:13).

Therefore, remembering the truth proposed, do not ask for the multitude of statements that is abundantly available. For, as I said, it is the practice of believers to believe God on the basis of a few things; to remember many is rather the task of diligence advancing by itself than of one who teaches.

## CHAPTER IV  
### What should be answered to the Jews

APOLLONIUS.—A simple assertion had already established belief that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly God. But since it is easier to give assent to words than to derive understanding from the senses, it was necessary to examine firmly what had been accepted and to confirm voluntary confession with heavenly teachings.

Now, as you uncover the perverse doctrines of the sects opposed to us, begin, if you think fit, with the Jews: why does this stubborn people deny God and Christ the Son of God, and refuse to acknowledge the Lord of all creation in either birth—although, before all the nations that are now being saved or have been saved, they knew the knowledge of future things through the Law and the Prophets, and could in no way have been ignorant of what had to be done for the salvation of the world, since they both knew God and were not deprived of God’s utterances?

ZACCHAEUS.—Your judgment is not mistaken: the birth of our Redeemer, both according to God and according to humanity, which now remains in one and the same person, is contained throughout the entire body of the Scriptures. The mysteries of the sacred Advent were openly revealed to the Jews; and I would not be reluctant to summarize them from memory if the order of my discourse followed attentive understanding throughout.

But since our intention is directed toward simple understanding, not toward controversy, let it suffice for your hearing to behold the whole light in a portion of its radiance, and to pass briefly through both matters. Thus, in the Book of Genesis, when the destruction of Sodom is recounted, an act of one will, as always, but not of one Person, is shown, since Scripture says:

“And the Lord rained from the Lord out of heaven” (Gen. 19:24).

Again, when Moses, at God’s command, was stationed on the rock and saw what was behind him, he indicated the distinction of the Trinity in number, saying:

“Lord, Lord, Lord, merciful and compassionate” (Exod. 34:6).

Through David, these are the words of the Father speaking to the Son of God:

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

Through Solomon, the Son himself bears witness concerning himself:

“When the Lord prepared heaven, I was there with him. When he set apart his throne and made the clouds upon the mighty winds; when he established the springs beneath heaven; when he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him arranging all things; I was the one in whom he rejoiced. Daily I delighted before his face, when he rejoiced over the completed world” (Prov. 8:27–31, according to the Septuagint).

Again, when he raises the question of his own name and that of the Father, he sets forth the reality of his true birth, saying:

“What is his name, or what is the name of his son?” (Prov. 30:4).

Let these statements concerning Christ according to his divinity suffice for the present.

As for the faith in his assumption of a body, Moses, first commanded to proclaim this to the people, speaks thus:

“The Lord your God will raise up for you from among your brothers a Prophet like me; you shall hear him” (Deut. 18:15).

“And whoever does not hear that Prophet, I will avenge it, says the Lord” (ibid., 18:19).

The Savior confirmed this testimony when, rebuking the same Jews in the Gospel, he said:

“If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

Again, when God commended Jesus son of Nun to the fierce people under the very name of Moses, he admonished them to recognize, in the name of the earthly leader, the title of the future heavenly one. For God said to Moses:

“Behold, this is Jesus who stands before you. Take care not to despise him, for he too will obey you; and my name is in him” (Exod. 23:20–21).

Finally, through the patriarch Jacob the truth of the prophetic blessing was most clearly fulfilled, when it was announced in these words that a leader and prince—that is, a king and priest—would belong to the Jews until his time:

“A leader shall not fail from the thighs of Judah, nor a prince from Israel, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he is the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10).

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The Vindobonensis manuscript reads *who is to be sent*; not long afterward it likewise reads *the cornerstone in Zion*.]

Balaam likewise announces the same thing in Numbers, saying:

“A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. 24:17).

The Magi, always retaining this in the eastern regions, were the first to announce the Savior’s birth after observing the star; and what had once been prophesied by the author of their art was fulfilled through them when they recognized it by their contemplation of the eternal light.

Finally, through Isaiah God speaks:

“Behold, I send into Zion a chosen cornerstone, precious; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 28:16).

The same prophet likewise recalls that he would be born from a Virgin:

“Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23).

Again, under the words of those same Jews groaning at the future judgment, when they will see Christ in the majesty of the Father, he brought forth these words:

“There is no God besides you; for you are God, and we did not know” (Isa. 45:14).

Jeremiah explains this through the words of the faithful people:

“This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found every way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).

Micah also disclosed the place in which he was to be born:

“And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha, are you truly too small to be counted among the thousands of Judah? For from you one shall go forth for me who will be ruler in Israel, and his origins are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5:2).

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The manuscript of Saint-Arnould reads *he will go forth, so that he may be*; the same manuscript shortly afterward has *his processions are from the beginning, from the days of eternity*.]

Many other passages are read and available that teach with the greatest clarity the mystery of both births in Christ God.
