But the proper method is to refute the impious and rebellious by the authorities of their own writings; and, as I have already indicated, my purpose is to answer your question rather than the intention of those who resist. Reason may require length when there is a contest; it is just that the concerns of those seeking counsel should be satisfied with brevity.

## CHAPTER V  
### Whether the Jews are deceived in other matters besides their refusal to believe that he is the Son of God

APOLLONIUS.—There is no doubt that faith cannot be withheld from these testimonies, and that even the Jews themselves could not fairly reject such proofs unless they prefer to go mad—especially since, drawn from their own books, they shine with such clear integrity that, even if one examines them without an advocate, they prove themselves.

Nevertheless, I would like to become more certain through what examples these same Jews are driven in another direction, and to be instructed not only by correct examples but also by contrary ones. For that truth of doctrine can finally be called complete which shows those who are in error not only what may correct them but also the ways in which they corrupt themselves.

ZACCHAEUS.—You retain what has often been impressed upon you: there is one God—that is, one divinity of the Trinity—and in the designation of this name the meaning is of one substance, not of one Person. But the occasion of their error and unbelief is that, on Mount Horeb, these words are spoken to them in the voice of God:

“Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4).

And again:

“I am God, and there is no God besides me” (ibid., 32:39).

And a third time:

“I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6); “I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 42:8).

Not “to no one,” but “to another”—that is, I will give it only to the one through whom I have determined in predestination that the immortality lost by you from the beginning should be restored for the better. He truly cannot change who admits neither loss nor increase.

Since there is truly no other Divinity, it is necessary that another God not be named. Yet this was said to the Jews concerning the unity of Divinity not as to people who did not know it, but as a warning to those about to transgress toward idols, so that they would neither interpret nor worship as gods those whom they recognized as one in substance and majesty.

It is also clear that, when God was arranging the creation of the world and of humanity, the mystery of the Trinity was displayed, as Scripture says:

“And God said, ‘Let us make humanity in our image and likeness’” (Gen. 1:26).

When he says “our,” he plainly reveals that the speaker is not one alone; and when he says “in our image and likeness,” he indicates an equality within distinction, so that in the same work the knowledge of the Trinity may be made clear: in it there is neither empty plurality nor a likeness that disagrees, since the subsequent words are transmitted in this way:

“And God said, ‘Let it come to be’; and God made; and God blessed.”

God the Father therefore announces what is to be made; the Son accomplishes what was said; the Holy Spirit confirms it through blessing. It is necessary, then, that the author of the whole creation be one God, even though the word of the one declaring it is “Let us make.”

Finally, the ancient blessing through Moses unfolds and confirms this rule of faith, in which he is commanded to bless the people through the mystery of a threefold invocation. For God said to Moses:

“Thus shall you bless my people, and I will bless them: ‘May the Lord bless you and guard you; may the Lord illuminate his face over you and have mercy on you; may the Lord lift up his face over you and give you peace’” (Num. 6:23–26).

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Thus the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts; the earlier edition has *in the majesty of substance*, less correctly. Below, from the Vindobonensis manuscript, we supplied the little word *thus*, which was absent, where it reads *thus shall you bless the people*. The same manuscript supplies the reading we printed at the end, *to be performed and effected*, where the printed editions were mutilated.]

From this you understand that it makes no difference to the indivisible and unchangeable God if words expressing human activity do not correspond to every precise feature of the sentences, since it has been left to the evident understanding of believers that whatever is said to be created or effected by God is always believed to be performed and effected by the Trinity.

## CHAPTER VI  
### Whether the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion were foretold in the oracles of the prophets

APOLLONIUS.—Christ’s birth as God and man has been demonstrated by specific documents, and it has appeared beyond doubt that the Holy Spirit, remaining in the same substance, fulfills the mystery of the perfect Trinity. Now confirm the same matter, if possible, by an exposition of the Scriptures: whether the Passion of the Lord’s cross was also foretold, or whether indications of that venerable death were marked out in any part of the body of the old Law. Thus, with our concern somewhat relieved, let the order of the instruction begun illuminate this part of the sacred work, which the exposition of the simple tradition revealed earlier.

ZACCHAEUS.—There is plainly an open proclamation throughout all the Scriptures not only of the Passion but also of the resurrection and ascent into heaven; and the prophetic voices sang in advance that the kingdom of God among us would begin with Christ’s Passion. David speaks above all in this way:

“Say among the nations, ‘God has reigned from the wood’” (Ps. 95:10).

This does not mean that we have not always been under God’s rule from the time of our creation; but as long as we disagreed with his worship and will, we were considered strangers. Hence Moses prophetically rebukes the aforesaid people, saying:

“Your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear day and night, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deut. 28:66).

Concerning this it is likewise written in Numbers:

“God is not suspended as a human being is, nor does he suffer threats as a son of man does” (Num. 23:19).

For truly, in that reproach, he endured everything because he said that he was the Son of God, and he was handed over to death not as a human being, since the cross received one accused of no crime.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Acherius appended this to the passage: “That is, he was not handed over to death because he said that he was a human being; but, to tell the truth, this interpretation does not please me, for Zacchaeus seems to be saying that Christ was handed over to death by the Jews because he said that he was the Son of God, and that he was not condemned like other human beings, since the cross received him although he was charged with no sinful offense. Thus the words he transcribed above from the Book of Numbers apply to this. The reading *suffers threats* is not supported by the Lemovicensis manuscript, in which the word *threats* is omitted.”]

Through the prophet Amos the Spirit speaks of midday, as happened in his Passion, and of the coming night:

“And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that the sun shall go down at midday, and the day of light shall be darkened over the earth” (Amos 8:9).

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Another manuscript has *and on that day the light*.]

And Jeremiah says:

“She who gives birth was terrified, and her soul was afraid. The sun went down while it was still midday, and she was confounded” (Jer. 15:9).

Under the words of the Lord himself, Isaiah also most openly declared the torments and the insults of mockery, saying:

“I gave my back to whippings, and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spittle” (Isa. 50:6).

For this reason David had foretold:

“They pierced my hands and my feet, and they counted all my bones. They themselves looked upon me and saw me. They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:17).

It is known to all that his garment was divided by the soldiers who handed him over to the cross, and that one of all his garments was transferred by lot before the judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] The Lemovicensis manuscript supplied this excellent reading, since the earlier edition had *with judgment ceasing*, which could scarcely be tolerated. Below, we preferred *piercing* to the printed reading *piercing through*; the Vindobonensis manuscript supports this. From the same manuscript we also printed *for his suspension*, whereas the earlier edition preferred *for the suspension of him*. The same manuscript gives the passage from Exodus cited by Zacchaeus somewhat differently: it reads, “Take the lamb, and they shall eat it at night”; the Lemovicensis also has “Take it.”]

Likewise, the admixture of vinegar and gall that those same Jews gave the Lord hanging on the cross was foretold long beforehand by David, who says:

“They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22).

Thus also, through Zechariah, he lamented the severity of the wounds, saying:

“They shall look upon me whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10).

For when they pierced his side with a lance, since in their fury they were not permitted to break the bone of one already dead, they fulfilled what had long before been said to Moses. For the Lord said to Moses:

“They shall take a mature year-old lamb from the sheep and goats, and the whole multitude of the assembly shall kill it toward evening, and they shall eat it that night; and you shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12:3 and following).

Finally, the Spirit prophesied that thieves would be joined to his suspension, saying:

“And he shall be reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12).

The Scripture also did not remain silent about the bargain concerning the wretched Judas, who was one of the apostles and betrayed the Savior after receiving thirty pieces of silver. It even designated the amount of money, saying:

“And they set as his price the value of thirty pieces of silver” (Zech. 11:13).

These testimonies suffice to prove the Passion.

Now recognize the resurrection in the very words of the Savior speaking to the Father, David giving the fullest testimony:

“You will not abandon my soul in Hades, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10).

The prophet who foretold this could not have spoken of himself, since he will remain in the corruption into which he was joined to his fathers until the day of the universal resurrection. Likewise through Isaiah:

“Now I shall rise; now I shall be glorified; now I shall be exalted; now you shall see; now you shall be put to shame” (Isa. XXXIII, 10).

That this was truly foretold concerning the Savior is demonstrated by the two-day interval granted to the underworld and by the ascension that followed: he willingly laid down his body and, willingly taking it up again as his own, raised it aloft. The prophet Hosea indicated this number of days after his resurrection more clearly, saying:

“God has revived us on the third day; after two days we shall rise” (Hos. VI, 3).

Isaiah, indicating the whole truth of his passion and ascension, placed these words in his prophecy:

“He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. And who will declare his generation? For his life will be taken from the earth” (Isa. LIII, 7–8).

David, likewise, under the words of God the Father speaking to the Son, proclaimed not only the ascension but also the judgment, saying:

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1).

Since, then, the prophet testifies that the Lord spoke to the Lord, who could doubt that the Father is indicating to the Son—passing from humanity into the glory of divinity—the power of heavenly judgment and the force of the majesty he is to exercise? The Son himself says in the Gospel that this was never said to any of the angels or human beings: that, seated at the right hand of God the Father, he would trample subject enemies beneath the feet of his name.

Zachariah also asserts that this one was shown to him, speaking as follows:

“And the Lord showed me Jesus the great priest standing before the face of the angel of the Lord; and the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, devil; may the Lord rebuke you, who has chosen Jerusalem. Is this not a brand snatched from the fire?’” (Zech. III, 1–2).

That is: Has not the passion already been completed, and, with human frailty laid aside, has not everlasting power succeeded to Christ?

Daniel likewise gives a similar prophecy concerning the same one:

“I saw: behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days. Those who were standing by presented him, and royal power was given to him; and every land, race, and every glory shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be corrupted” (Dan. VII, 13–14).

The Jews hear and recite these things; they know them, yet they do not believe in Christ, whom they know was abjured by their fathers. They pretend not to know, although they have always lived even under the same law they display in such a way that what they confessed with their lips they denied simultaneously in heart and deed.

## CHAPTER VII. Why a portion of the ancient law was cut away, and which books transmitted the observance of righteousness

[Col. 1118D]

[Note: In the Vindobonensis manuscript, *intulerunt* is read. Below, in the heading of chapter 12, from the same manuscript and from the Lemovicensis, we have restored *qui duos dicunt* (“who say that there are two”), where *qui nos dicunt* (“who say us”) was incorrectly printed; and in the following chapter we have supplied the word *credit* (“believes”).]

**APOLLONIUS.**—It has been shown sufficiently and abundantly that the Lord’s resurrection and heavenly ascension shine forth through divine testimonies, and that all these things are radiant with spiritual proofs. Thus, even if some part of the crime committed could be defended by an excuse of ignorance, the truth, spread abroad more widely, would compel the unbelief of those now present to be condemned, since the deed of the humility proclaimed beforehand fulfilled the authority of the heavenly decrees, and the faith of the growing peoples teaches this.

Now explain why a portion of the ancient law was cut away, or what reason for antiquating the earlier books introduced a form of more righteous observance, since the same author is the creator of both, and, possessing the substance of the same divine majesty, neither does his will disagree with reason nor does eternity accord with foreknowledge.

**ZACHARIAS.**—It is a faithful and true confession to hold that the commands of both belong to one God, and to acknowledge that the law handed down through Moses was not abolished by Christ but fulfilled, as he himself solemnly declares in the Gospels:

“I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17).

For the law had long been a promise of evangelical preaching, God speaking thus through Isaiah:

“The law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3).

That is, the doctrine of righteousness and faith, brought to completion through Christ, will be recognized in the Church.

And again Micah says:

“The law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge among many peoples, and he will rebuke and expose powerful nations” (Mic. IV, 2–3).

Otherwise, once the old law had already been given, what other thing could be announced as needing to be added except the Gospels? Concerning this Jeremiah likewise spoke:

“Behold, days are coming, and I will complete over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant—not according to the covenant which I established with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. XXXI, 32).

That is, I will establish a gentler covenant in the Gospels. Those things will cease concerning which it is written:

“I gave them commands that were not good, in which they would not be justified” (Ezek. XX, 25);

but:

“The one who does them will live by them” (Gal. III, 12).

Some things, therefore, were established more severely in the law for this reason: that they might humble a rebellious people, made wanton by long habit of paganism, rather than allow them to be lifted up into justification; and that, as though by a certain disciplinary guard, they might restrain through fear of present punishment those whom the threat of a delayed judgment could not yet preserve, since they were still living far from the end of the age.

[Note: Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript and another seen by Acherius; nevertheless, *justificaturi* (“of those who would justify”) was printed. Above, after “That is, I will establish a gentler [covenant] in,” something is missing which we cannot restore without the aid of manuscripts.]

Hence the command:

“An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Lev. XXIV, 20);

and:

“Do not eat; do not touch” (Lev. XI, 8).

Hence the prescribed observance of months and the festival of new moons; hence the regulated course of the Sabbath, and freedom almost shut out from the whole range of human actions by enforced leisure.

The consecration of sacrifices of cattle and birds was demanded at first by the reason of their accustomed abomination: since they could not suddenly be prevented from these practices, it was more prudent gradually to abolish what had to be rejected than immediately to punish what had to be prohibited.

Another clear reason is this: although they sacrificed victims according to pagan ritual, they were nevertheless taught to offer to God what they had previously been accustomed to present to idols. Since they were occupied with the actions of many sacrifices, neither time nor opportunity was given them even to think about transgression; and what they might desire was not taken away from them, while there always remained something that the intention of their devotion could not fulfill.

[Note: This is how we found it in the Vindobonensis manuscript, from which we also printed below *intentio non valeret* (“the intention could not fulfill”). The printed editions have *praebeatur . . . intentionem valeret*, incorrectly.]

Finally, they soon hear the prophet:

“What are your many sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full. I do not want the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, or the blood of goats and bulls; nor should you come thus before my presence. For who required these things from your hands? You shall not continue to tread my court. If you bring fine flour, it is vain; incense is an abomination to me. I cannot endure your new moons, Sabbaths, and great day. My soul hates fasting and festival days. You have become a burden to me. I will not forgive your sins” (Isa. I, 11, 15).

That is, your crimes are not to be cleansed by these expiatory offerings. Rather, he prophetically demonstrated what the purification of our baptism would be, saying:

“Wash yourselves; be clean” (ibid., 16).

That is, when the time of that visitation arrives, pursue the mysteries of spiritual washing:

“And if your sins are like crimson, I will make them white as snow; but if they are like scarlet, I will make them white like wool” (ibid., 18).

In the *phoenicium*—the crimson dye—the darkness of sins is signified; in the scarlet, a bloodstained mind is represented.

Thus the change announced through Christ was turned toward better things. In place of the obsolete sacrifices of cattle and birds, the heavenly offering of the faithful is celebrated in purity, and we are fortified against every ambush of the hostile enemy by the addition of a spiritual sacrifice. In the assumed human being the decree of God the Father is fulfilled:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

When, therefore, the time of the Gospels dawned, grace immediately released those whom the bondage of the law held captive, and the Lord’s sacred mouth proclaimed:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 28–30).

So that the severity of the punishments mentioned beforehand might not remain, and so that a fatal outcome might not snatch away the remedy of saving repentance available to the guilty, the Lord decreed that punishments should be reserved for judgment, preaching in the Gospel:

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. XII, 19);

for unless just correction follows, no one exacts vengeance more rightly than the one who is not deceived in establishing the guilt of the deed committed.

Thus the lethargy of the Sabbath has also been abolished, and no time has been excluded from good work for the faithful, he himself speaking in the Gospels:

“It is lawful to do good on the Sabbaths” (Matt. XII, 12);

and:

“The Son of man is Lord of the Sabbath” (ibid., 8).

Moreover, the freedom to eat what is suitable has been granted, since, as he himself testified:

“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth” (ibid., 15, 11).

Thus all those things which were a torment to the rebellious are dissolved through the liberty granted by Christ. With only a few things ceasing because of superstition, those which truly deserve righteousness have been added.

[Note: I can scarcely persuade myself that Zacchaeus wrote it this way. Since he wished to say that certain things had been abolished, in which there was some superstition, I think the sentence would not be badly expressed if one wrote *ob superstitionem* (“because of superstition”); but whether anyone can recognize that same meaning in the common reading, I do not know with sufficient certainty. In the Lemovicensis, what follows reads *quae veram justitiam* (“which [things] true righteousness”), perhaps better.]

For this reason the law slipped in between the beginnings and the fullness of faith: it would break the savage minds of the Jews by the difficulty of such sanctions and persuade them more readily to receive the grace of the indulgence that was to come. The forgiveness of a long bondage and the liberty once desired would otherwise have made that grace still more attractive even to unbelievers.

## CHAPTER VIII. What righteousness the Jews have in circumcision

[Col. 1121A]

**APOLLONIUS.**—Not without reason, when considering this matter, I had anticipated that there was some plan of divine providence: that, at the beginnings of this uncultivated people, things should be commanded as though useful and pleasing, although it would later be fitting for them to be abolished.

What sanctification or merit, I ask, is there in circumcision for these same Jews, who even now flatter themselves that it takes the place of baptism, although you established in the preceding book that it was constituted only as a sign of the chosen offspring? Without doubt it is clear that they will be deprived of the rewards of righteousness if, trusting only in this mutilation of the body, they place in it the evidence of their entire hope—when, having rejected injury to the flesh, they ought rather to rejoice in the bloodless gifts of the Holy Spirit.

**ZACHARIAS.**—You correctly recall that the exposition in the preceding book was of this kind: that carnal circumcision was a sign of faith, not the condition of righteousness, as Scripture records:

“And God said to Abraham: ‘You shall keep this covenant of mine between me and you, and your offspring after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you’” (Gen. XVII, 10–11).

[Note: The Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts read *rationabiliter custoditam* (“observed reasonably”). Not much later, the Vindobonensis and another manuscript seen by Acherius read: “For that Jesus was ours in word and deed.”]

That this was observed bodily until Christ is proved by the subsequent deed of Jesus son of Nun. After the departure from the wilderness in which those same Jews had lived for forty years, and in which no one had been subjected to this injury because there was no mingling with foreign peoples in the wilderness, he was commanded to mark the people and, according to the custom handed down by the fathers, to impose upon those about to cross the Jordan the recognition of their ancestral faith. Scripture says:

“And the Lord said to Jesus son of Nun: ‘Make for yourself stone knives, and sit down and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time’” (Josh. V, 2).

This indeed also happened according to the letter, but it was extended more especially to us through prophetic interpretation. For that Jesus was Jesus in name only; our Jesus is so both in name and in deed, as the angel announces to the shepherds in the Gospels:

“Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke II, 11),

whom you will call Jesus, “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21).

In the second sons, the peoples of the nations are understood; and in the stone cuttings, the discipline of the Gospel corresponds. Hence Moses first prophesied such things, saying:

“In the last days God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your people [the reading is uncertain; another manuscript has ‘the seed of your people’], to love the Lord your God” (Deut. XXX, 6).

Jeremiah likewise announces that it is not flesh but hearts that must be circumcised, saying:

“Circumcise yourselves for your God; but also circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Jer. IV, 4).

[Col. 1122A]

The Lord, moreover, very clearly declares in the Gospel to a ruler of the Jews that no one at all can be saved without the washing of spiritual water or attain possession of his kingdom. For he says:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not see the kingdom of God” (John III, 5).

Concerning this he had previously foretold through Isaiah:

“Do not remember the former things, and do not recall the ancient things. Behold, I am making new things, which will now arise, and you will know them; and I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the waterless place, to water my chosen race and my people whom I acquired, so that they might declare my virtues” (Isa. XLIII, 18–21).

And again:

“If they thirst in the wilderness, he will bring them water from the rock; the rock will be split and water will flow, and my people will drink” (Num. XX, 8).

And a third time:

“From his belly will flow rivers of living water” (John VII, 38).

Thus, according to the Apostle:

“Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the observance of God’s commandments” (1 Cor. VII, 19).

This has been fulfilled in faith in evangelical belief and through the grace of baptism. It no longer marks either a people or a sex as circumcision once did; rather, turning injury to the flesh into a spiritual sign, it excludes neither sex nor separates one nation from another. Saving all equally in itself, it counts uncircumcision among vices and hands down circumcision in conduct, because what belongs to true sanctification is discerned in faith; what belongs to genuine faith is attributed to works of righteousness, not to injury of the body.

[Note: So the Vindobonensis reads; but the word *circumcisio* (“circumcision”) must then be added, so that the text reads: “not now also, as before, circumcision.” The printed editions have *nonnumquam* (“sometimes”), incorrectly. Acherius conjectured *non umquam* (“never”). At the end, *quod manifestae fidei* (“what belongs to genuine faith”) is the excellent reading of the Vindobonensis; by contrast, the earlier edition’s *quia manifestae fidei* (“because of genuine faith”) is very poor.]

## CHAPTER IX. Why the patriarchs were permitted to have several wives in marriage

[Col. 1122C]

**APOLLONIUS.**—There is also a certain proof of this dispensation, as I had understood it, and a vain presumption of the Jews, who believe that they ought to regard as a gift in place of baptism what, prescribed according to the circumstances of the time, preserved not the condition of faith but the knowledge of their lineage.

What reason was there, when the patriarchs retained the merits of righteousness, that they were permitted to have several wives in marriage and union? It was not counted as a sin—God certainly knew of it—which is now so prohibited and punished that it is judged not only an offense worthy of God’s displeasure but also entirely deserving of human vengeance.

[Note: Here the verb *sciendi* (“of knowing”) is understood differently from its common usage, namely as *scitum* in the expression *plebiscitum* (“popular decree”). Below, *ultione hominum aequissimum* (“entirely deserving of human vengeance”) is the final wording supplied from the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis.]

**ZACHARIAS.**—There are several reasons given by different people for this permission, but this should be considered the principal one: that, with the order of perfection set aside, belief in God might first be established; and that the law, being introduced in order to strengthen faith, would not remove what it found to be apparently harmless, but would mark as unlawful only those things that were truly believed to be deadly.

Hence Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness, and devotion passed into merit, Scripture saying:

“Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV, 3).

Furthermore, the Divinity, nurturing a small people, wished it to rejoice in numerous descendants, so that it might be increased above the others as the people he loved above the rest, and so that the curse of the law might be avoided by the one whose seed had continued in offspring.

[Note: These four words were added from the Vindobonensis. In the Lemovicensis the rest agrees with the Vindobonensis, but it reads *quae prae caeteris diligebatur* (“which was loved above the others”).]

But this excuse is common to all and belongs not to a few but to the people. In the case of the patriarchs, however, the reason is judged to be external: since each believed that Christ, promised from his own seed, would eventually come from him, and since they had not yet read that he would be born without human seed, they burned with love for such a great offspring and entered into marriages with many women, judging it exceedingly weak to assign hope of the most exalted offspring to one marriage alone.

For the first promise was made to Abraham in these words of God:

“In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18).

The patriarch Jacob is honored in nearly the same way by this utterance, the Lord speaking to him:

“I am your God. Increase and fill the nations, and from you will come the Church of the nations; kings will arise from your loins. The land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you and to your seed after you” (Gen. XXXV, 11–12).

David, in the Spirit, recalls these promises more plainly for himself, saying:

“The Lord swore to David, and he will not repent: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne’” (Ps. CXXXI, 11).

A similar order of this promise is maintained through Isaiah, who says:

“A shoot will go out from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1);

“in him the nations will hope” (ibid., 10).

In the shoot, the venerable integrity of Mary is shown; in the fragrance and grace of the flower, Christ is signified, as he himself teaches in the Song of Songs:

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II, 1).

Therefore these simple desires of those eager for offspring were softened by the Lord speaking through Isaiah, when, by means of the sign of the virgin birth, salvation for the human race was revealed. The prophet thus speaks to Ahaz of the promise of this gift:

“Behold, the Lord will give a sign: a virgin will conceive” [and bear a son] (Isa. VII, 14).

[Note: We added the final phrase, following the authority of the Vindobonensis. Below, the same manuscript has *pariet filium et caetera* (“will bear a son, and so forth”); but the Lemovicensis is much better: *Ecce* (“Behold”).]

Here is the third reason.

The first reason, therefore, is that they did not simply misuse what had not been prohibited, and that the Divinity wished the foolish people to be increased through their efforts toward a numerous offspring.

[Note: I scarcely believe that this passage is free from error. Below, the manuscripts Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis have *accessione multiplicis* (“by the addition of multiple [marriages]”), whereas the earlier edition has *accersione* (“by incitement”), which is corrupt.]

Added to this was the following: because they thought that Christ, promised from their own race, would come to them after a long time through the addition of multiple marriages, the careless desires of the holy men continued until the preaching of continence, already near at hand, revealed that he would be born from a virgin. Then the restorer and founder of our salvation, gradually fulfilling it as righteousness increased, would bring about what he had once postponed through the dispensation appropriate to an immature age.

## CHAPTER X. What offense the nations committed; and why God, having rejected the Jews to whom the Law was first given, daily embraces and teaches the nations

[Col. 1124A]

**APOLLONIUS.**—As I think, and as I believe is evident to the understanding of all, the simplicity of the holy patriarchs has been absolved from every suspicion of more savage desire, especially since God, the examiner of minds, would not have granted such people the prerogative of righteousness if he had shown that they had presumed upon what was forbidden and not permitted by the dispensation.

But now that the reasons seem to have been fully examined, an unexpected question intrudes: what special offense did the nations commit, by which for so many ages and generations they were excluded and kept away from God’s instruction, while now, summoned by hope of eternal gifts, he embraces and teaches them—after the Jews have been completely expelled from God’s grace, although they had both prior use in receiving the law and the first lot in the election?

**ZACHARIAS.**—From the beginning God rejected none of those who believed, nor were the nations displeasing to their Creator before they, forgetful of his benefits and of their own creation, senselessly worshiped creatures in place of his reverence and honor, and, venerating images of human beings and cattle, made themselves deservedly like those things which they had preferred to themselves, although they had been made superior by God. Scripture records:

“The images of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (Ps. CXIII, 4).

“Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (ibid., 8).

Solomon likewise says:

“Human beings made them, and one who had received a spirit fashioned them. No human being can fashion a god like himself; since he is mortal, with wicked hands he fashions a dead thing. He himself is better than those he worships, since he has lived, whereas they never have” (Wis. XV, 16–17).

And again:

“Attending to the works, they did not recognize who the craftsman was, but either fire, or spirit, or air, or the circuit of the stars, or excessive water, or the sun, or the moon they considered to be the rulers of the world and gods” (Wis. XIII, 1–2).

Since, therefore, they had placed the confidence of all their hope in such things, neglecting the Creator, they received the reward of their own work: they rushed of their own accord into every kind of impurity and became estranged from God’s instruction, serving only vices. Plunged into crimes, they did not recognize the way to attain immortality until they believed in the mediator between God and human beings.

Hence it is written in Deuteronomy that the Church from the nations is to be preferred to the synagogue:

“You will be the head among the nations,” it says, “but the unbelieving people will be the tail” (Deut. XXVIII, 44).

As long as faith and righteousness flourished among the Jews, God’s love for them also did not depart. He himself protests through Isaiah in the Canticle:

“Now I will sing to my beloved a song concerning my beloved vineyard” (Isa. V, 2).

In the Canticle, the one who complains is the beloved in Christ, and the vineyard is the synagogue. For he also says in what follows:

“And now, man of Judah and you who dwell in Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard. What more should I do for my vineyard that I have not already done for it?” (ibid., 3–4).

“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (ibid., 7).

The man of Judah is the Savior, as above; those who dwell in Jerusalem are those whose feet run in the faith of the Church.

[Note: Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript reads, correctly; the earlier edition has *quorum spes* (“whose hope”), corruptly. The same manuscript and the Lemovicensis read below *quod ante non* (“which had not previously”), whereas the earlier text had *quod certe non* (“which certainly had not”).]

Thus the Lord urges them to recognize a condition as though equal between himself and the Jewish people: what more wonders and benefits could he provide for it that he had not already done? To it belonged the exceedingly grievous liberation from slavery in Egypt and hands freed from the basket; countless signs against Pharaoh and all the Egyptians; visible assistance of the preceding divinity in the pillar of cloud and light by day and night; and an impenetrable separation from the darkness of the persecutors.

There was also the unheard-of flight through the sea and the defense provided by the warring element against the violence of those pressing upon them; manna in the wilderness; and the enjoyment of a long life without deterioration of beauty or clothing. Likewise, the expulsion of nations unequal in force and number, and the establishment of an inheritance in possession of a land flowing with abundance.

[Note: The printed text has *in patribus*, very incorrectly; the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts have *in paribus*, also incorrectly. There is no doubt that we have supplied the true reading here, as likewise below where the printed text read *ac pene in abusionem*.]

What of the frequent bloodless rebukes given to sinners, the transgression erased by the punishment of only a few, the deaths of sinners remitted, and the persistence of leniency reduced almost to the point of abusing the giver’s generosity?

[Note: So the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis read; the earlier edition has *pretiosius potuit* (“could have been more precious”), which is inferior.]

In the face of such evils of raging unbelief, what could have been added as a remedy except that, by the will of both the Father and the Holy Spirit, the Son of God should be sent as a remedy for those perishing? He deigned to assume the material of our frailty and to receive the whole human being in God, so that he might save the whole person, if that person believed, through his adoption.

But it remained for the unbelievers that the sentence should be fulfilled against them and their descendants now living:

“With their eyes they will see and not see; with their heart they will understand and not understand; with their ears they will hear and not hear, lest at some time they should turn and I heal them,” says the Lord (Isa. VI, 10).

And again:

“Woe to the sinful nation, the people full of sins, wicked children” (Isa. I, 4).

And a third time:

“The daughter of Zion will be abandoned like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a watchman’s hut in a cucumber field, and like a city that is under siege” (ibid., 8).

Confirming what he had once spoken through the prophet, the Lord approved it in the Gospel, saying:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you: how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 37–38).

That is: what formerly was God’s dwelling is now the dwelling of demons, because whatever true religion abandons, profane superstition claims for itself.

When, therefore, the destruction of the Jews was completed in the killing of Christ, faith in the promises was opened to the belief of the nations. And just as from the beginning great salvation was promised not to the dignity of lineage but to the merits of faith, the Lord taught this when the same Jews, as though to prove their faith, boasted that they were children of Abraham:

“You are born from the devil as father,” he says, “and you do the works of your father” (John VIII, 44).

“If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (ibid., 39);

that is, faith would appear similar in you. Just as he believed in me amid every difficulty of human hesitation, so you too should believe with equal gentleness.

Nevertheless, the Divinity does not wish their hardness of heart to remain, out of compassion for them; but he permitted it to exist because of their unbelief. According to the Apostle:

“Blindness has happened in part to Israel, so that the faith of the nations might enter” (Rom. XI, 25).

Therefore, to obtain the goods of eternity, the Jews’ privilege of lineage is not sufficient unless faith also supports their origin. Nor are we saved merely by their offense, unless we likewise fear the example of those who were exalted and then humbled. Believing that one single and undoubted way is open in Christ to both peoples, let us hold fast the undefiled gifts of faith, as he himself taught us in the Gospel, saying:

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one goes to the Father except through me” (John XVI, 6).

And:

“The one who believes in me will be saved” (John VI, 47).

That is: just as there is one God, so one people of believers should serve the Creator’s will forever. He does not reject worship, while, without depressing either side by God’s justice, he rejoices that those whom unbelief condemned in their ancestors are absolved through confession.

## CHAPTER XI. The kinds and errors of heretics

[Col. 1126C]

**APOLLONIUS.**—Great is the foolishness of the Jews if they do not know such evident things; more condemnable is their obstinacy if they understand them and despise them. But whether they are ignorant or understand and refuse, they cannot be free from guilt: either the prejudice of negligence in their misuse or the guilt of unbelief must be borne by them.

Leaving them, then, to their own destruction, if that is what they choose, explain to me the kinds and characteristics of the heretics, so that, standing firm in the faith as on an immovable rock, I may not be shaken when the waves of unbelief begin to attack me, since I know them in advance. For although I believe it is characteristic of a simple mind not to know their corruptions and errors, it is nevertheless a stronger faith, as a precaution, to know them.

[Note: So the Vindobonensis reads; the printed editions have *genera erroresque* (“kinds and errors”). A little farther on, where the text reads *ut etiam haeretici* (“so that even heretics”), the same manuscript has *ut jam nec haberi haereticos se credant* (“so that they no longer even believe themselves to be considered heretics”), which is less correct. See the beginning of the following chapter.]

**ZACHARIAS.**—The plagues of the heretics are so great and so innumerable that it is difficult not only to count them but even shameful to name them. The detestable tradition of evident corruptions has so blinded wretched people by turning them away from the faith; the subtlety of diabolical fraud has so immersed itself in the minds of the perishing that even heretics believe they have heretics of their own.

Leaving apostolic tradition behind, they followed teachers of unbelief and changed the name of religion along with its meaning. According as each person found it pleasing to deceive and seduce the ignorant people and to acquire honor from crime, one taught that God should be believed only in part, another that he should be wholly denied.

Moreover, although they retained the name of Christ, they gave their groups their own names, so that they might not be entirely removed from sacrilege, having abandoned the name of Christ and taken the name of their religion from a human being. For what difference is there whether someone receives his name from an idol or from a human being, if he ceases to be called Christian?

Thus each heresy is now named from the author by whom it transgressed, and they take such delight in the particularity of their crime that they do not even then understand that they have been cut off from the unity of religion, since they have lost the faith even in their name.

Thus the Manichaeans are named from Manes; likewise a derivative group takes its name from Marcion. Photinus divides his followers even by his name. Sabellius similarly demands that a part of his assembly be called after him. Error imposed the name on the Patripassians; and Arius, holding the citadel in the devil’s inheritance, names his flock of the lost after himself.

Moreover, innumerable portents of such prodigies are reported, whose despicable stupidity makes them unworthy even of refutation. Yet, joined as an appendage to the impiety of those already mentioned, they do not cease to attack the Church and Christ.

But because nothing is ever stronger than truth, when the waves have been shattered on every side, the great mass remains immovable. They are broken by their own blows, while the purpose of the unbelievers rises only to this end: since they disagree among themselves, each wishing to destroy our faith, all of them together establish it.

For the Manichaean asserts that there are two gods and two principles, wishing one to be believed good and the other evil: the good one, namely, who softened the truth of the ancient commandments by the publication of the Gospel; the evil one, who made this world and spoke through Moses and the other prophets. Moreover, they assert that the Redeemer of the human race did not truly possess flesh but only its appearance.

Marcion, however, confesses the Son of God according to divinity but denies him according to humanity.

Photinus, for his part, says that the son of Mary, the human being assumed in time, is the Son of God, but he insists that he did not exist before the ages.

Sabellius, with the unbelief by which he blasphemes against the Son of God like the others, also denies the Holy Spirit and assumes the whole truth of divinity in the Father alone.

[Note: So the Vindobonensis reads, and considerably better than the earlier edition, which has *tantum ac Filio sacramentum verae Trinitatis* (“only the mystery of the true Trinity with the Son”). Sabellius could not have acknowledged the Trinity there, since he maintained that there were only two persons.]

The Patripassian indeed asserts that the Father exists, but immediately says that the Father himself is the Son, and that the same one descends from innate substance into birth and passion; likewise, he says that the Holy Spirit is also the same in person, not a third.

[Note: So the Vindobonensis reads correctly: *ab innata substantia* (“from innate substance”). The printed editions have *ab inita*, which is corrupt; nor is the Lemovicensis reading *ab unita* (“from united substance”) any better. Acherius wrote *ab ingenita* (“from unbegotten substance”) in the margin, from a certain manuscript—or did he conjecture that this was the reading? He also notes that the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul has *subsistentia* (“subsistence”), which is not satisfactory.]

Arius climbs to lofty heights only to fall to the depths. He confesses the Trinity in persons and names but excludes the unity of divinity, declaring the Son of God, through whom all things were created, to be a creature rather than the Creator. Moreover, he adds degrees of dignity to the names, making lower in honor the one whom he subsequently speaks of in name.

[Note: This is how it is written in both the Lemovicensis and Vindobonensis manuscripts, but incorrectly. The printed editions add *gradus* (“degrees”): “he adds degrees of dignity.”]

These are the principal sects of the heretics, and such disastrous persuasions of men are swept into diverse doctrines that they either divide the simple substance of the inseparable God and the ineffable majesty of divinity by their interpretations, or dishonor them by degrees of rank. They invent things unworthy of God and deny what is eternal or proper to him.

## CHAPTER XII. Against the Manichaeans, who say that there are two Sons of God

[Col. 1128B]

**APOLLONIUS.**—It can undoubtedly be judged from these people what sort of heretical sects those are which you say are ranked in the first place, since they can be condemned even by such men. But since our stated purpose is to establish everything by examples, explain by the character of their interpretations by what Scriptures they have constructed these divisions and gradations of perfidy, and by what understanding they have been brought to such precipices. For although I have not yet heard what arguments they put forward, I nevertheless immediately perceive that the wretched are in error, and that only the integrity of the Catholic faith remains: for it neither rejects the fullness of the Trinity and its spiritual ordinances, once established and approved, nor fails to preserve what it has accepted.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—If better things can properly be said concerning bad things, it would certainly seem more pardonable not to know God than to confess him impiously. But since those also are condemned by the decrees of heavenly statutes who have neglected to know God through the Law, the same condition will embrace those who perversely refuse to believe, with everlasting punishments, as Scripture testifies: “The one who is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). “Those who have sinned without the Law shall also perish without the Law” (Rom. 2:12).

Rightly calling these men Antichrists [Note: [Col. 1128D] Perhaps one should read *calls them*, with reference, of course, to Scripture: for example, 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7], since by hidden treachery they destroy true religion and pretend that they believe in and proclaim God in order more easily to attack the faith.

The first Manichaeus, entering upon the impiety of his own tradition, in order to assert two gods and two principles, made the authoritative statements of the faithful Scriptures unfaithful, especially adopting that saying of David in which he says: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power” (Ps. 109:3) [Col. 1128D]. He did not understand that the beginning which is truly proclaimed as abiding in Christ is in the Word; that it concerns the day of the Passion and of the judgment soon to come; and that the whole of divinity is fulfilled not in two but in the Trinity.

They further say that the one who made this world is evil, because it is written: “The world is placed in evil” (1 John 5:19) [Col. 1129A]. But the elements that we see are not harmful, nor should they be believed either to generate or to possess anything evil. Having been arranged by God’s work, they were “very good” when they were made, as Scripture says: “Behold, all things were very good” (Gen. 1:31; Sir. 39:21). Rather, “in evil” signifies our iniquity, and “in the world” the human race, as John teaches when he proclaims the Savior’s coming. For he says: “He came into this world, and the world did not recognize him” (John 1:10).

If they assert that the author of the Gospels and of the Law is different because in the Law present vengeance is prescribed, while in the Gospels a place is granted to forgiveness, the Law indeed demands repayment for injury and establishes an equivalent condition for what has been lost; yet “God does not avenge twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1:9). The penalties paid in the body, according to the character of the punishment for the offense, are, as we believe, to be weighed by the outcome of a milder judgment [Col. 1129B].

Here, moreover, a time for making satisfaction is admitted; but unless a worthy fruit of repentance and corresponding deeds follow, there is eternal fire and the everlasting worm, the Lord himself declaring in the Gospels: “Their worm shall not die, and the fire shall not be extinguished” (Mark 9:43, 45, 47; Isa. 66:24). “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12).

Therefore there is not one God in Christ and another principle, but the same author of the Law once promulgated and now fulfilled. Nor is anyone in the Trinity evil, because one is called good. Rather, since the unity of divinity is expressed in the one God, the equality of goodness and unity must likewise be indicated. In the Law, the severity that guards justice must not be considered evil; and in the Gospels goodness must not be believed to exist without justice [Col. 1129C].

They further add that Christ did not possess true flesh, but that an insubstantial appearance, arising from some unknown substance or fluid, was displayed in place of a human being [Note: [Col. 1129D] This is how both the Lemovician and Vindobonensian manuscripts read; the earlier edition has “from I know not what material,” from an unknown source [Col. 1130D]].

What, then, did the whole preaching of the prophets foretell concerning his bodily birth? What did the angels say on different occasions? Was John perhaps not sent, or is that declaration of God the Father concerning him false: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way” (Mal. 3:1)?

Finally, what did the infusion of the Holy Spirit within the most blessed Virgin accomplish? Why was the period of the swelling womb not set aside, according to their account, for its abolition? Where are the complete signs of a blessed childbirth, and a birth superior to the condition of all other mothers? An infant crying in the manger [Col. 1129D], growing in age and wisdom as a child, and disputing divine understandings among the chosen assembly of elders?

What, I ask, would that criminal impiety not have said if the founder of the salvation of all had not done these things—if the unbelieving crowd of Jews, despising the preacher and understanding only an opinion about his origin, not the mystery of his true birth, had remained silent instead of saying: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter? And are not his mother and brothers with us?” (Matt. 13:55)?

These, then, are the stages of a true human being, and a definite progress through the common years, as the Gospels testify: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace with God and men” (Luke 2:52) [Col. 1130A]. He therefore fears to be what he was born as, he who pleased God by his justice and purity of life, and his companions by gentleness and humility.

Add to this the use of a manifest body. Although his life was of inimitable holiness [Note: [Col. 1130D] In the Vindobonensian manuscript it reads here, “of immeasurable holiness.” Below, where he hears “God,” the earlier reading was “he would hear”], the nature of human weakness nevertheless requires the protection of clothing. He hungers, thirsts, mourns, rests, suffers, and is likewise moved to tears; he neither rejects nor omits any further human action. Indeed, he is tempted by spiritual deceits and conquers, and at the confession of his enemy it is investigated whether he is the same Son of God.

Angels ministered to him for the encouragement of victorious steadfastness. He was handed over with a kiss, arrested, and subjected to suffering. And if wretched perfidy wishes to have the true man proved, let it hear him crying from the cross before he died: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:1). Where there is humility and injury, understand a human being; where there is power and divinity, believe God, as the Apostle teaches: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19).

For behold, weak and subject, rising on the third day, as he had foretold, he returns to the place appointed for the Apostles, scarcely believed by those who were astonished; and, having broken the jaws of the underworld, he appeared in order to establish his seat in heaven.

Thanks be to you, Thomas, who alone among all believed more slowly; who, touching the places of the nails and demanding the signs of the whole Passion, openly insisted that what was one day to be denied by the perfidious should be proved to you.

They would certainly more readily claim that one whom they invent to have lived without a body returned incorporeal [Col. 1130C], gathering from this the supports of their earlier deception: that he crossed the sea on foot; that he entered, without forethought, through closed barriers that remained standing; and that, received by a shining cloud, he ascended to his Father’s throne, whence he will come again.

Yet they should not be unaware that Peter, at the same Lord’s command, walked upon the waves; nor should they fail to know that an angel released him from prison when his chains fell away of their own accord. They should acknowledge that Paul, in order to escape the reproach of boasting, went—whether in the body or outside the body, yet known to God—as far as the third heaven. Finally, let them recall that Elijah was taken up in a fiery chariot and, while those looking on watched him leave, undertook a journey unknown to human beings.

Those who now refuse to believe such powers in the Son of God, while denying the mystery of the true Incarnation and concealing what he did, refuse to grant that the human being possessed what he merited and do not believe that God could have done what he did.

## CHAPTER XIII. Against the Marcionites and Photinians, one of whom denies that the Son of God was bodily, while the other believes that he was corporeal for a time but cannot be eternal

**APOLLONIUS.**—The impiety of this sect has been exposed, and its plainly execrable doctrine has been shown worthy of condemnation, although it was already discerned at the beginning of the account. Nevertheless, it has been made more conspicuous by its own particulars. It now follows that you should explain, while preserving the proper order of each matter, what perversity the others have in their own tradition and what defense each offers; for an arrangement made by specific distinctions will remove confusion from our understanding, since the light of exposition makes clearer what, wrapped in the darkness of error, always flees the light of truth [Col. 1131A].

**ZACCHAEUS.**—It was stated above that the Marcionites believe the Son of God according to divinity but reject him according to humanity; while the Photinians, conversely, say that the Son of God came into being from the time of his earthly birth and deny him before the ages.

Observe the truth amid contending perfidies in a single comparison: neither confesses it in its entirety, and neither rejects it in its entirety. For the Son of God, born from the Father in the Word before the creation of all the ages, eternal from the eternal, true from the true, cannot be anything other than what has always been in the Father, as he himself teaches in the Gospels: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16:15).

Yet these things are not claimed from him as though they belonged to him alone, but are common in such a way that they are complete in each. Again: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:16). And: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

Likewise it is said to the patriarch Jacob: “Build an altar to that God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of your brother Esau” (Gen. 35:1). Again, in the Gospel he spoke thus to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world was made” (John 17:5).

He is the one who went before the people coming out of Egypt in the cloud. Isaiah plainly testifies that he was seen by him. Finally, when Jesus son of Nun asked him in battle, he declared that he would be the commander of the heavenly army [Note: [Col. 1131D] This is how it reads in the Vindobonensian manuscript; in the printed editions, “finally he said himself to be the commander …” A little later, because the Vindobonensian manuscript has “heavenly,” we have written “heavenly,” where the printed edition had “who is heavenly”].

“For no one,” he says, “has ever known the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). He always presented himself to human sight because, being about to make the heavenly fellowship a wonder to our frailty (sic), he was already preparing to be understood in the human being whom he was to become. Let these statements concerning divinity suffice for the Marcionites.

Let the Photinian heresy in turn acknowledge his bodily birth. The Lord says to the prophet Nathan: “Go, say to my servant David: You shall not build me a temple” (2 Sam. 7:5), “but I shall raise up your offspring after you, and I shall prepare his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish his throne forever; and I shall be his father, and he shall be my son” (ibid., 12–13).

Likewise the patriarch Jacob had prophesied earlier concerning the same person in Genesis: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; your father’s sons shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the shoot you have risen for me as a son; lying down, you have slept like a lion and like a lion’s whelp. Who shall raise him up?” (Gen. 49:8–9).

Perhaps it is not unknown that this is the nature of the noblest wild beast: a lion is born without breath, with only the complete form of its body, and, lying thus for two days, receives the use of common life from the breath of its parent. Hence this raising up is compared with regard to the Savior, and it rightly adds: “Who shall raise him up?” No one, certainly, except the Father [Note: [Col. 1131D] The Vindobonensian manuscript reads, “these things to the Savior.” Below, the Lemovician manuscript has “the tongue shall be full” [Col. 1132D]].

But Judah was not worshiped by his brothers. Rather, because he assumed a body from the same tribe, the Savior is signified in Judah by the words of the prophetic blessing, while believers are counted among his brothers, as he himself testifies in the Gospels: “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 12:50).

Isaiah likewise says: “Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees. Our Lord renders judgment; he himself shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear” (Isa. 35:4–6).

[Col. 1132B]

We already know that this was accomplished in the Gospel, but we trust that it will be accomplished more fully in the resurrection, when limbs joined to dry bones are renewed and, after the dust of the bodies we have assumed, we are clothed with the gifts of spiritual form. The Apostle teaches: “This mortal must put on immortality, and this corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53).

Thus we are to be conformed to the bodily form of Christ, whom Jeremiah, proclaiming that he would come in the flesh, says: “And he is a man, and who shall know him?” (Jer. 17:9, according to the Septuagint). For it would not have been necessary to speak of God with the addition “man,” unless it were to show that in God there was also a human being.

David, moreover, says in the words of the Lord himself: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). This testimony was confirmed in the Gospel by the Father’s twofold voice: first, when he sent him into the Jordan to be baptized by John [Note: [Col. 1132D] Earlier it read, “when he sent himself into the Jordan,” an ugly scribal error. Below, where it says “who now [bears] the form,” I suspect there is some corruption]; and second, when, suffused with the splendor of future glory, he sat upon the mountain between Moses and Elijah.

Thus these words of God the Father thundered concerning the same person at both times: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). That is: hear no longer Moses, who then displayed the figure of the Law, nor Elijah, who introduced the figure of the Prophets, but hear this one, who possesses speech with authority and, in the power of the law of grace.

For Scripture had foretold concerning him: “The sun of righteousness shall rise for you, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. 4:2). Paul likewise says in his preaching: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4), “who was made for him according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). John similarly says: “Every spirit that confesses Christ to have come in the flesh is from God; but whoever denies this is not from God, but is Antichrist” (1 John 4:2).

You see, therefore, that the doctrines of the Photinians and Marcionites can be refuted very easily. Yet the ancient serpent has bound minds steeped in deadly deceits with terrible chains, so that they defend the stain of an irreconcilable sect by a certain presumption of steadfastness. Nevertheless, through the confession of both, the truth of manifest divinity shines forth: the discordant and dull malice of those who dispute confirms the part denied by one, while denying the part confessed by the other.

## CHAPTER XIV. Against the Sabellians, who deny that the Holy Spirit is God and think that he should be believed to be a gift rather than the giver

**APOLLONIUS.**—The examination of the exposition we desired is also clear in these matters, and the undisputed perversity of both sects has stripped bare the inventions of their wretched distortions. Let the order of the discussion now proceed to the remaining heresies, and let the sequence already begun pass through the disclosure of them all, so that the light of faith, brought into the volumes of hearts as though into the hidden recesses of venomous serpents [Note: [Col. 1133D] This is how the Vindobonensian manuscript reads, as does another manuscript seen by Acherius; he nevertheless preferred to print “the volumes of sins”], may uncover what has been concealed within them—not because such people deserve recognition, but lest, while unknown, they more easily creep into minds made vulnerable by doubt and harm them.

[Col. 1133B]

**ZACCHAEUS.**—I believe you remember that it was noted in the preceding heading that the Sabellians especially deny the Holy Spirit and, in the impious traditions, call him a gift rather than the giver. They claim the authority for this evil principally from sacred testimonies, because he is read both to be given and to be received, as the Savior says to the Apostles: “And breathing upon them, he said: Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

Certain disciples, when questioned by Paul, likewise said that they had neither received the Holy Spirit nor even known whether he existed: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 19:2).

The reasoning behind these statements is as follows. He is indeed given, not because he does not give himself, but so that it may be shown that he is present in the one who bestows him. For just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Holy Spirit is in both, and again both are conspicuous in him [Note: [Col. 1133D] Here we have repaired a lacuna in the earlier edition from the Vindobonensian and Lemovician manuscripts. The earlier edition contained only: “so the Holy Spirit is seen in both,” with “and conspicuous” written in the margin].

For this reason he is said to come after the Savior’s ascension, although he is first given by the same Savior; and the one whom he promises to send later from himself he shows already to be in himself. Likewise, promising that after his coming and his own ascent he would remain with us until the consummation of the world, the same Lord says: “And behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world” (Matt. 28:20). And again: “Unless I go, that Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7).

So closely connected and inseparable is the giving in the outpouring that it proves beyond doubt that another divine person is active in what is awaited, while the one who ascends to the Father is nevertheless with us, and the one who is promised as destined to be present is rightly believed to have been given by the one who is about to ascend.

Although the Apostles had received the gift of the Holy Spirit before the Savior’s ascension, they afterward received its fullness in him, as the book of Acts teaches: “And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty wind approaching, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues appeared to them, and fire sat upon each of them” (Acts 2:2–3) [Note: [Col. 1133D] In the Vindobonensian manuscript, “divided”; “and fire sat.” Acherius had also read “divided” in one of his manuscripts and “separated” in another. We have immediately added the word “Spirit” from the Vindobonensian manuscript].

The Spirit is also made manifest through speech, as the same Scripture records: “And the Spirit said to Philip: Approach the eunuch’s chariot” (Acts 8:2). And again: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

The Lord, moreover, commends reverence for the Holy Spirit with a threat, saying: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32).

He sanctifies the hearts of the faithful and forms and directs them toward every perfection of heavenly grace, as the Lord proclaims: “When that Paraclete whom I shall send to you from my Father comes” (John 15:26), “he himself shall direct you, and he himself shall convict the world concerning their sins” (John 16:8, 13).

He is therefore not a gift but the giver; not some gift but the bestower of gifts. He is not sanctified, but sanctifies; he never appears among creatures, but always in the substance of the Trinity, as the Apostle teaches: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; divisions of operations, but the same God. Yet one and the same Spirit works all these things” (1 Cor. 12:4–6, 11) [Col. 1134B].

It is utterly foolish to suppose that he is the same as an angel or as one of the heavenly powers, since an angel cannot be poured into many persons, whereas this is possible for him by virtue of his own divinity [Note: [Col. 1134D] This is how the Vindobonensian manuscript reads; the printed editions have “to consider.” Below, from the same manuscript, we have written “a person in the divinity,” where the reading was “a person into the divinity”].

Angels merely occupy the place to which they are sent by God or to which they return. He, however, is present in one place in such a way that he is always everywhere, as the Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Ps. 138:7), and so forth.

The same prophet indicates that angels were made as follows: “You make your angels spirits,” he says, “and your ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). But Scripture clearly shows that the Holy Spirit is God, saying: “For God is Spirit” (John 4:24).

He is free in his generosity, simple in majesty, and consenting to the will of the Father and the Son, not subject to them, as the Apostle testifies: “The Spirit distributes to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). He fills all things and is not diminished; he is received by all and receives nothing himself. He governs pious minds with holy moderation and is found to need nothing. In judgment he is just, and ready in his bestowal.

The end of Ananias also showed this to be just; and Cornelius proved that God is not believed in vain before Peter’s teaching. Yet these things alone do not testify or prove that his person subsists in the divinity [Col. 1134D].

The living image of the living God came in the form of a dove from the heavenly seats above; and by him the Redeemer of the world, who was to be worshiped by the angels, was anointed and made Christ, as Isaiah himself recounts in the Gospels: “The Spirit of God is upon me; therefore he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18; Isa. 61:1), and so forth.

Thus, by these testimonies and countless others besides, the ruined error of the Sabellians is exposed. They specifically reject the Holy Spirit and pollute the fullness of solid majesty by their sacrilegious tradition. They do not observe that he is shown, as the usefulness of our case has required, either in the Father or in the Son, or again in the same two while they remain in him.

For although the complete salvation of our faith is to believe and confess that God is one in every respect, as he is, faith cannot lack the confession that the Trinity is not without a third.

## CHAPTER XV. Against the Patripassians, who suppose that the Father suffered

**APOLLONIUS.**—The error and cause of the Patripassians are indeed different from those of the Sabellians just mentioned; but, as I believe, the outcome and recompense of their perfidy should be compared with that of their predecessors. They exclude the Holy Spirit, who remains in the power and substance of God, from the unity of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 1135D] Both the Lemovician and Vindobonensian manuscripts read this, except that the latter incorrectly has “those repenting.” The earlier edition reads, “they exclude him from the unity of their own divinity,” and, while reviewing all the Scriptures, “the Trinity”], and, resisting all the Scriptures, attack the faith of the Trinity.

But after leaving these also among the profane, let the perversity of the rest be refuted, lest they think that what has not been uncovered in the exposition was suppressed rather than omitted; and lest, when mention of what the authority of Scripture perhaps does not conceal is passed over for those who inquire, a dying ember grow into some kind of fire.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—I had warned at the beginning of the first inquiry that the fullness of the ineffable majesty can be understood to some extent by faith, but cannot suitably be expressed in words. For since it is the efficacy of truth, not the condition of a differing substance, that produces the distinction of names and persons, and since even the mind is unequal to contemplating divinity, no one doubts that the substance of speech is much weaker than that of the mind.

The authors of all errors therefore seize upon this difficulty of human weakness. Among them, the Patripassian chose this aspect of impiety: since the Son, the firstborn, is from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, the Father and the Word are the same; the flesh assumed and the Passion are likewise seen to be from him; and the Holy Spirit too is the same.

Nor is he proclaimed as an origin within the Trinity; rather, he alone is proclaimed, to the detriment of the distinction of divinity, unless the Trinity is believed to have been reduced into a communion [Note: [Col. 1135D] The Vindobonensian and Lemovician manuscripts read “of the one proclaiming”; immediately afterward the manuscript of St. Arnulf reads “into union.” Below we have written “is recognized,” as Acherius advised should be read, although the text has “to be recognized”]. Of this, as I have very frequently recalled, what cannot be grasped by the senses is to be considered ineffable rather than nonexistent [Col. 1135D].

Not only is injury from the Passion absent from the Father; it is recognized in many ways to be absent also from the Word. For it was not the incorporeal divinity that was fastened to the cross, but the body; and whatever the Son of God endured beneath the honor of heavenly power is attributed not to the Word but to the assumed human being.

Since sin was in the first human being, how would the redemption announced to the human race through so many ages have come about unless the blood of a true human being had expiated it anew? Although many testimonies have already taught his death, lest this heresy build an argument against itself by claiming that nothing has been brought forward, we shall take a few examples from the abundance of them.

David, therefore, says in the words of the Lord himself: “I became obedient unto death” (Ps. 21:—; Phil. 2:8) [Note: [Col. 1136D] Acherius noted at this place that the author either quoted from memory or alluded to Psalm 21, in which, however, nothing of this kind is found].

And again: “They placed me in the tombs like the dead of the age” (Ps. 140:3). And a third time: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87:5).

O immeasurable power of God and inscrutable wisdom of God! Why is he a little earlier “like the dead of the age,” but now “without help, free among the dead”? It is because, as he himself had foretold: “The Son of Man had to suffer and be crucified by the scribes and chief priests, and, having conquered death, return from the underworld on the third day” (Matt. 16:21), so that, for the accomplishment of our salvation, he might receive dominion over the living and the dead alike; and so that this example of the highest love might be established, namely, that we should drink the cup of suffering for him which he had not refused for all.

The Trinity is therefore manifest in persons and names, but its divinity is one. We do not accept the union of the Patripassians, but embrace the Catholic unity in God.

The groups mentioned above therefore dissent from this interpretation and attempt to impose falsehoods through hidden means, affirming that what is from the Father exists only in him, while attributing to the divinity the injuries that belong specifically to the human being.

## CHAPTER XVI. Against the Arians, who say that the Son and the Holy Spirit are inferior to the Father

[Col. 1136C]

**APOLLONIUS.**—I feared that some evil more powerful or more deeply hidden might reside within the concealed entrails of this perfidy. For at the first appearance of your account I did not see the members of our faith so clearly revealed, and I attributed the darkness wrapped in harmful deceits to ignorance rather than to malice.

Thus the plausible order of your doctrine mingled the author’s torn frenzy with destruction and with its adherents. Now explain in like manner what the Arians claim against the truth of our belief, so that, if they are shown to possess wickedness either of the same kind or more concealed [Note: [Col. 1136D] In the manuscript of St. Arnulf, “or more dreadful”; immediately afterward the Vindobonensian manuscript has “let them cling”; the earlier edition has “let them adhere”], they may cling to the groups mentioned above, rightly judged execrable if by their deceitful traditions they diminish what they do not refuse under the title of their profession [Col. 1136D].
