**ZACCHAEUS.**—I said earlier that the Arians occupy the citadel of perfidy and should be considered all the more responsible for ruin because, while professing loftier things, they display an apparently complete faith, although they reject the integrity of faith.

For they say that the Son of God is not the Creator but a creature, and that he is superior to the rest only in this respect: that, having been made first from God the Father, he was not begotten; and that he is likewise subject to time because he was born.

They confirm this impiety by the cunning of such a statement: “There was a time,” they say, “when he was not.”

O savage malice of the impious! Could God at any time not exist? Or how could he be begotten if they also assert that he was made according to divinity? Since it belongs uniquely to God always to have been, what else can one born from him and within him be except what the Father is?

Or how is he the Father if in the Word there is some kind of assumption rather than a true birth? If he is a true Father, then there is a true Son; and if he is unlike the Father in nothing, then at last there is a true image of the one who begot him.

There is also the concordant saying in the prophet: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44:1). And again: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

But immediately they substitute for these the statements spoken, under the words of the Lord himself, in the person of the assumed human being: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). And: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38).

Finally, they seize upon writings of a more elevated meaning from the words of Solomon: “Wisdom was created before all things” (Sir. 1:4). And: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22).

If they do not consider these to have been foretold, as I said, in prescience concerning the author of our redemption, and if they think that Solomon, in the same Spirit, understood something different from the others, let them hear the equality of substance and the one divinity. Let them recognize that the Father and the Son, although not the same in persons and names, are nevertheless one in majesty:

“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

And again: “Philip, have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

And a third time: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16:15). What the Son wills, the Father wills also; and: “As the Father works, so the Son also works” (John 5:19).

Likewise he asks to be glorified by the Father, yet in turn declares before human beings that the Father has been glorified by him.

How, then, can he be enclosed within any extension of time, when time was created by him? Or what beginning can be attributed to him through whom the beginnings of all things came forth?

Consider the blind persuasion of the Arians, and its sense, which exceeds the limits of every impiety. Suppose that by their opinion they could pass beyond the beginnings of things and bring prejudice against solid majesty. Is it not manifest madness to attribute the name of an inferior substance to God, to whom you owe everything, and to define the immense as though you could reduce it to something small?

What, O wicked human being, did he deserve from you—indeed, what did he not deserve above all others—when, after forming you last of all, he granted you such gifts, that you return evil for good and prefer to be weeds rather than wheat?

Although you were made later than all creatures, you were made superior through him whom you profanely strive to mix among the things he himself made.

You are, from the trampled clay—as you yourself do not deny—an image and likeness of God in understanding, appearance, and power. You rule over the earth from which you were taken. You, the weaker, rule over stronger things. Carried across the deep on modest beams, you travel; the elements serve you when subjected, rather than ruling over you.

For you, the yearly seasons change, whether pleasant or useful, and the variety of things brings forth the fruits arranged for all seeds. For you, the birds of the air descend, and what is born in the waters is nourished and lives.

I pass over the fact that, freed from the general ruin, you are restored to the hope you had lost; that, stripped of immortality through yourself, you are clothed with it through him as though worthy from the beginning; and that, as if this generosity were small, you will moreover ascend to heaven if you prove worthy.

No longer burdened by the location of your material nature, you will be joined to the choirs of angels and, as the possessor of everlasting joy, will behold the invisible God throughout the ages.

What more is there? If you preserve the faith of Catholic adoption, you will remain forever an heir of God and co-heir of Christ.

Yet, driven back by these and similar arguments, they nevertheless strive to cling to their wicked interpretations, taking from the Gospels the statement that he did not know the hour and day of his coming.

Let it be granted to them that the assumed human being did not know this before he received, in God’s glory, authority over earthly and heavenly things. But did the divinity of the Word also not know? Or, since the Son is always in the Father and the Father in the Son, can one know something while the other does not?

And will he be completely ignorant of something to be done by him according to the Father’s will, when within the very principle of the Father’s will there is not subjection but agreement? David, speaking in the Spirit under his words, teaches: “I desired to do your will, my God” (Ps. 39:9).

He does not therefore obey as a subordinate, but does the Father’s will in his own will. He is said to be sent, but so that he may be understood to be another.

Even according to his humanity he knows all things, and he foretells future events in such a way that it is clear that not knowing the day of the consummation was more fitting for us than that he should have been entirely ignorant of it.

Finally, for this reason we are also kept ignorant of the end of our own life, so that the anxiety of an uncertain end may make us more attentive to justice, and so that we may more easily avoid death if we fear its coming every day.

For Scripture, providing this general warning, foretold it by saying: “Fool, this night your soul shall be demanded of you; whose shall those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12:10).

Likewise the Apostles are warned, the Savior saying: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17), “because you do not know when the Son of Man will come” (Matt. 24:42).

That is: Fear and uncertain expectation are more useful for you, lest confidence destroy those who are secure and knowledge of the future deceive those who fear nothing. When hope of a long life has been cast aside, you should profitably fear to dare what you do not believe can be corrected within the available time.

Nevertheless, all the perfidy of the heretics concerning Christ’s two births is overthrown especially by two testimonies, as the Gospel of John thunders forth:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God; and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3).

And again:

> And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (ibid., 14).

You see, therefore, that no ground is left to the Arians on which they may rightly dissent from the integrity of our faith: since the same Son of God is proclaimed both as the only-begotten before the ages and now as the firstborn; possessing the reality of an earthly body while not abandoning heavenly power [perhaps: “losing”], he embraced in his two births what he had previously possessed through divinity alone.

## CHAPTER XVII. Against the Novatians, who dissent from unity and do not believe that one who has once fallen can be restored

[Col. 1139B]

**APOLLONIUS.**—The error and perversity of all the sects had already become clear in the first exposition; but, so that it might appear more readily, the firmness of the teaching that followed necessarily contributed, and the method running through each point suitably exposed whatever the tradition of wicked interpretation had concealed. Therefore, so that no instruction may now be lacking to the mind, disclose, I ask, what cause separates the Novatians from us, so that, having departed from catholic belief, they not only form assemblies outside the Church but, as I believe, also attack the faith of the one from whose peace they withdrew out of hatred for unity.

**ZACCHEUS.**—You rightly understand that the unity of faith cannot belong to those by whom the unity of the Church has been abandoned; for it makes no difference in what manner someone departs, if he voluntarily separates himself from its body, since the Lord says this in the Gospels:

> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters (Luke 11:23).

These people were once with us, but they were torn away by a certain Novatus as their leader. Yet they are not to be equated with heretics, because they dissent not from catholic confession but from charity; and, rebellious only against mercy, they withdraw from God those whom they do not permit to be restored once they have been entangled in the enemy’s snares.

They call themselves “pure”—to use their own word, *Cathari*—ever forgetful of the divine admonition by which the Spirit first says in Job:

> For who is pure from defilement? No one, even if his life on earth is only one day long (Job 14:4–5, according to the Septuagint).

Hence the Psalmist, expressing the same thought, says:

> In sins my mother conceived me (Psalm 50:7).

And John says in his Epistle:

> If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8).

Thus they do not believe that those things should be punished by more severe judgments which, because they have never been brought to confession, are most cunningly suppressed, as though they could remain hidden forever. But that those who confess, together with the correction of their present conduct, are not only not denied pardon for the past but are even granted the privilege of righteousness, God himself speaks as follows, declaring these things through Isaiah to those who have turned:

> Tell your injustices first, so that you may be justified (Isaiah 43:26).

Observe the reward together with pardon, and the recompense of a certain honor in simple confession: God promises the fruit of righteousness to the one against whom the Novatian pronounces harshly; and he promises that the one whom the Novatian expels lest he be saved can be absolved with grace.

Yet they did not possess the legitimate primacy of the priesthood or the highest seat in the episcopate. Rather, as discord grew through intrigue, as though in a kind of tyranny, they follow the aforesaid author of the schism and, excluded from participation in devout communion, prefer to hand people over perpetually to Satan rather than recall them to God through the exhortation of spiritual grace.

[Note: I have preferred to print this as it appears in the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts, since previously *exclusos* (“excluded”) had been read. Following the same manuscripts below, we have written *intellexit* (“understood”) rather than the erroneous reading *posuisse intellexit* (“he understood that he had placed”). I hesitate to record the other, less significant matters.]

They refuse to accept the innumerable examples of Scripture by which it is known, beyond any doubtful interpretation, that the fallen ought both to be summoned back and the returning received. The Book of Psalms begins in this way:

> Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked and has not stood in the way of sinners (Psalm 1:1).

Blessed, therefore, is the one who did not go away in such a manner as to disdain returning, but who, accepting the progress offered by better counsel, ceased to mingle with the wicked after understanding that he ought rather to be corrected.

Likewise blessed is the one who did not stand in the way of sinners—that is, the one who, having entered into vices, did not remain in them. The Psalmist teaches this in what follows, prefacing an excuse for sins that creep upon us and, conscious of our weakness, saying:

> Who understands his offenses? (Psalm 18:13)

That is, offenses can be committed more easily than they can be recognized.

In his prayers he adds that he may be cleansed both from the sins of others and from his own hidden sins, confidently affirming that he will be blameless if those things in which he previously sinned do not rule over him. Behold, even one who condemns in himself crimes that will not return is made pure from the greatest offense; and one who has chosen to become what he did not wish to be, while refusing to enjoy what he loved, glories in the honor of the blameless.

God expresses a similar judgment through Ezekiel, saying:

> Why will you die, children of men? Turn to me, and I will turn to you (Ezekiel 33:11).

That is: This path along which you proceed is the way of hell, and true death lies in despair of pardon. I am not sparing in abolishing crimes, since I so gently warn people not to commit them again; and I disclose the inviolable rule of my judgment in these words:

> I do not desire the death of the one who dies; only let him turn back and live (ibid.).

And:

> If the wicked person turns away from his wickednesses that he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and does justice and judgment, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of all his offenses that he has committed shall be remembered (ibid., 14).

Yet Novatian prevents God’s gift and the most worthy decree of devout remission from being restored not only in the abolition of sin [Note: The Lemovicensis manuscript reads “to be reduced into abolition …”; the final word is recognized by both Vindobonensis manuscripts, which then omit *excretae indulgentiae* (“of indulgence poured out”).], but also obstinately refuses to allow it to extend to pardon. Lest he depart entirely from these people and their like, he rejects the force of indulgence displayed in every correction, dismissing even the lightest and fewest matters, although the Savior states in the Gospels that everything is cleansed through almsgiving and that, just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Sirach 3:33).

Finally, leaving the entire flock, the shepherd of faith searches for one sheep; and when he has found it, placing it upon his shoulders, he assigns greater joy to the recovery of what was lost than he had in what was safe.

The Apostle says that the Galatians are formed again within him like a birth, although he had previously brought them forth in the regeneration of the mind, in vain, because their vices were growing strong again. Hence Peter and James, the brother of the Lord, affirm that a multitude of sins is restrained through an act of charity, declaring in similar words:

> Charity, he says, covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8; James 5:20).

Having clearly considered these things, you understand that the Novatians, blinded by atrocious obstinacy, desire to satisfy their own wickedness rather than God’s will: for toward their neighbors—even those who, after remorse for their past deeds, are perhaps better than the judges themselves—they condemn confessed sins and do not release those that have been expiated, although these sins can be forgiven and ought not to be concealed.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What should be answered to the Novatians

**APOLLONIUS.**—The reasoning is plain and evident: not merely by God’s judgment, with whom the fullness of mercy resides, but even by the judgment of righteous human beings, those who, having trampled down the perversity of their vices, turn toward better things are not to be regarded as irremediable [the negative is supplied editorially]. Those who were previously negligent either through the ignorance of youth or because they were overtaken by the errors of various circumstances resume the path of faith; and, casting aside the allurements of the flesh that they had previously preferred, they wash away through acts of heavenly conduct whatever they had previously polluted through love of earthly things.

But perhaps these things were permitted before the infusion of baptism, and perhaps the Novatians possess some authority by which they maintain that those polluted after spiritual washing cannot be cleansed; and perhaps they assert that the inviolable gift of the Holy Spirit can be conferred once through human beings but, once lost, cannot be restored. Their assertion may perhaps be supported externally by the claim that they do not deny a place for repentance in themselves, but that pardon must be hoped for from God, and that satisfaction must be completed for deeds, not reckoned as merit.

What, then, should be said or demonstrated to those who persist in such an intention? Explain it in the customary manner of exposition, so that through the occasion of our discourse correction may be urged upon the perverse and pardon upon the afflicted; while the obstinacy of the irreligious is exposed, and whatever hope is approved for those who despair is made clear.

**ZACCHEUS.**—It is indeed more blessed to preserve the gifts of spiritual grace undefiled and to reserve the incorruptible gift of heavenly indulgence for the future judgment [Note: Thus the manuscript of St. Arnulf, which, though Acherius had seen it, he nevertheless preferred to print as *puro deferre judicio* (“to reserve for pure judgment”). Below, we preferred the Vindobonensis reading *gesta dimitti* (“that deeds be forgiven”) to the earlier edition’s *gesta committi* (“that deeds be committed”).], as David teaches in full:

> Blessed are the undefiled in the way (Psalm 118:1).

The Apostle likewise says:

> May we be able, brothers, to preserve whole soul and body and spirit for the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

But the unwary ignorance of youth leads some, and the heat of earthly allurements leads others, onto the inclined path of sins. David speaks of this under the words of his own excuse, with the Spirit saying:

> Do not remember, Lord, the sins of my youth and my ignorances (Psalm 24:7).

For it is a just plea to ask that the pattern of remission be applied to deeds committed in weaker years and that wrongs committed under the privilege of age be dismissed; for in this same testimony the prophet does not relate an idle story, but points out how the weakness of age is more heedlessly liable to fall.

At whatever stage of life they may be, let them not occupy the Novatian position as though it were a special one [Note: Thus the Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts; the printed editions read “lest they hold even a special [position].” The same manuscripts correctly read “silent falsehood,” where the earlier edition incorrectly had “such great falsehood,” and, finally, the Lemovicensis has “since he is polluted in his own conscience,” where previously “since he alone is polluted” was read.]; let them hear Solomon proclaiming similar things without exception of age:

> Who can boast that he has a pure heart, and that he is clean from sin? (Proverbs 20:9)

The silent falsehood is therefore excluded: however pure someone may appear to human eyes, he is not for that reason innocent, since he is polluted in his own conscience and before God.

Divine mercy has therefore permitted this weakness of our frailty to be cleansed through a threefold degree of indulgence. In the beginning, it grants everything through baptism; afterward it covers sins that have crept in through repentance; and it decrees that none be reckoned at all if the fervor of martyrdom absolves someone from every stain of the body. The Psalmist says:

> Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin (Psalm 31:1).

Thus all things are forgiven in baptism, since only those things contracted afterward are charged against a person. In repentance, sins are covered—but if they are repeated, they revive. In martyrdom, however, none can be imputed, because they are first erased by the precious shedding of blood and do not return to condemn a body that has been blessedly extinguished.

Yet they will deny that grave sins can be forgiven with the support of repentance, although they know that it belongs equally to their office and profession either to bind what is severe or to release what has been cleansed. The Savior’s sentence makes this fully clear with reference to Peter, in whose person the power of all priests is gathered:

> Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven (Matthew 16:19).

Therefore, sins are permitted to be forgiven without exception, provided only that, once sent into abolition, they do not return; and provided that, as it is written, the dog does not return to its own vomit (2 Peter 2:22), nor the washed sow desire to wallow again in the mire [Note: This entire passage is badly corrupt. I would read it thus, if the matter were left to my judgment: “desiring to plunge herself … destined to suffer … having fallen …”]. Such a person would suffer greater danger after remedies than he had endured when he was falling into the evils at their beginning. The Lord gives this warning in the Gospels:

> Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you (John 5:14).

Do not doubt it: God always judges the present, not the past. For he says:

> In whatever path I find you, in that I shall judge you, says the Lord (Ezekiel 33:20).

But if, after baptism—that is, after receiving the Holy Spirit—there is no place for grace to be restored to us, how did Aaron, already a priest, recover the rank of high priest after being delivered from a grave offense? And how did Miriam, after the infliction of leprosy, deserve to be cleansed from heaven, when she had been separated so that she might not pollute anyone? For the camp signifies the spiritual assembly of the Church, while leprosy represents the image of mortal sin.

Why did the patriarch David, requiring expiation for two blood-guilts, ask that the former Spirit of grace be renewed in him, clearly and confidently promising God that the conversion of the wicked might be summoned by the example of his pardon? Moreover, after praying that he be granted the opportunity to speak in God’s praises, he obtained authority to preach, saying:

> You will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise (Psalm 50:17).

But God said to the sinner:

> Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant upon your lips? (Psalm 49:16)

Unless, perhaps, they contend that the prophets had a different Spirit from the one we now receive—or that they had no Spirit at all—and thus make God under the grace of the Gospels harsher than he was under the Law. They will have to admit that Peter, that is, the very foundation of the Church, although he did not remain in his offense, nevertheless had been in an offense; and they should understand that, remembering the Lord’s warning, he washed away through the bitterness of his tears the guilt not of treachery but of weakness.

Likewise, the return of that profligate man in the Gospel, who had exhausted the wealth of his spiritual substance and confessed that he had sinned against heaven, is not rejected as polluted or refused as wasteful. Rather, he is received by the kisses of the father as he bends over his neck—that is, by catholic peace. Certainly he could not have been a son except through the prior adoption of baptism.

He also rejoiced in the preparations for the great banquet—that is, he was honored with divine communion. Receiving faith in the ring and the garment of grace in the robe, he is moreover fed with the flesh of the calf—that is, he is made a participant in eternal inheritance through the reception of the sacred body—and receives the full adornments of apostolic dignity.

Finally, the Savior indicates that even blasphemy, which surpasses all sins, can be forgiven, and does not refuse to abolish what has been committed against him, if through the labor of true conversion we merit that, under his command, heaven should agree with the judgment of priests. With this confidence, the Teacher of the Gentiles invites those who are cleansed from vices through faith not only to pardon but also to honor, saying:

> Whoever cleanses himself from these things will be a sanctified vessel, honored and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work (2 Timothy 2:21).

Thus, just as the Trinity exists in the unity of divinity, so there is a threefold cleansing in the one name of baptism. The Lord says to the Apostles:

> I still have a baptism with which I must be baptized, of which you know nothing (Luke 12:50).

He himself underwent these stages in the body, leaving an example of them for all. He was baptized in the Jordan; he endured the likeness of repentance in the desert; and what was the highest purification, he completed in his passion.

Hence you perceive that the Novatians, living amid every occasion of sin, most foolishly reject against themselves what they understand God to have provided for their sake. The Church alone, being close to God both in faith and in mercy, is rightly called queen above the vile crowd of concubines. Holding the place at the right hand, she condemns the children of the left on high; she offers complete faith to those who come to her and does not bar the way to those who desire to return to her. While she proclaims manifest divinity to the faithful, she prefers to recall the perishing through the readier hope of pardon rather than, perhaps, to drive those needing correction into despair.

## CHAPTER XIX. What constitutes the complete fullness of the divine mysteries

**APOLLONIUS.**—It is clear that the Novatians foolishly refuse to forgive sins and, forgetful of their own frailty, rejoice more in the condemnation of the fallen than in the correction of the converted. But unless repeated questioning produces weariness, add this one final firmness to the completion of the work: embracing the whole body of belief, enumerate the heights of the divine sacraments, and establish for memory what you have handed down to minds possessing eternal hope, so that frequent confession may be able to recall, in a few words, what faithful instruction has fitted into the form of catholic brevity.

[Col. 1144C]

**ZACCHEUS.**—The reasoning already traversed in each matter, and the text of all the interpretations made clear, might indeed have been sufficient. But lest some scruple arise from the variety of meanings, or some ambiguity from the plurality of answers, hold fast to the sacred order of the whole faith and always recall these things.

There is one God, the Father, who has always possessed this particular characteristic: that he is Father. He receives nothing from another but brings forth everything from himself; he is unchangeable, invisible, incomprehensible, and eternal.

There is therefore also the Son, distinct from the Father in name and person, not in substance, of full majesty like the Begetter, likewise perfect and everlasting. He is not, according to the opinions of the faithless, to be believed to have begun in time because he was born; rather, remaining with the Father before time, he was manifested to us in time in the assumed Savior. He is and must be believed and confessed as one and the same, now and forever, because the manifestation of his divinity does not permit that he ever was not; nor does the assumption of true flesh allow us to deny that he was born from a Virgin through the creative action of the Holy Spirit.

There is also the Holy Spirit, to be regarded as other than the Father and the Son only in person and name, not in majesty or substance [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript has a considerably better reading than the earlier edition, *a Patre simul ac* (“from the Father simultaneously with …”). In the common reading, the words *a Patre ac Filio* (“from the Father and the Son”) must necessarily be referred to the verb; in the Vindobonensis they refer to the following word *alius* (“other”).]. He was not begotten as the Son was, but proceeds from the Father. He is equal in power, divinity, honor, and will; he always does and accomplishes the same things as the Father and the Son. He forms wisdom, gives faith, bestows gifts, grants sanctification, remits sins, distributes graces, and is always joined with the Father and the Son in every goodness of their works. He was never created, but is always creating.

It is fitting that he be perpetually believed in and confessed, adored, worshiped, and feared; and that he be loved with the utmost purity of heart, so that, just as he is always the same in the Father and the Son, so the fullness of the Father and the Son may be believed to be in him.

You have the true and simple account of the matters you asked to understand, and the disposition of a brief answer suited to knowledge. It remains, as you remembered was said at the beginning, that as an energetic reader you diligently attend to the fuller volumes of our predecessors; and, content even with this brevity, glory in the knowledge of higher teaching, believing that we have answered your private wish rather than produced a public edition.

Indeed, the immensity of heavenly secrets prevents us from proceeding farther, and the greatness of ineffable majesty restrains senses blunted by their own weakness. Already, as the hours incline toward sunset, a shadow near to darkness spreads abroad; and minds attentive through frequent interpretation ought both to be refreshed and to relax.

But guarding these things with the full labor of mind and body, never abandon faith, never abandon confession [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript reads: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not [seek] what is lower than you,” etc. Above, from the same manuscript, we printed “faith … confession,” whereas previously “with faith … with confession” was read.]. Do not exceed what is permitted while pursuing what is forbidden; and, desiring impossible things, strip yourself of salutary things. God gives this warning:

> Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not investigate what is stronger than you (Sirach 3:22).

That is: What has not been disclosed to you concerning heavenly or infernal matters by the law itself, do not listen to or believe at all. For those whom the devil cannot deceive through the vices of the flesh, he overthrows through such zeal and vanity; appointing judges of hidden knowledge, he compels them to search beneath stone after stone, so that they may find a serpent.

Therefore, let it be enough to cling to canonical teachings. When seeking knowledge of the divine histories, take care only not to be ignorant of what has been written; and with the greatest diligence continually remember Christ the Lord crucified, who will come in judgment upon the bodies that rise again and will reign forever with the elect.

You will believe these things with confidence; you will proclaim these future events, so that, joined to the assemblies of the saints, you may both be granted and enjoy the most delightful honor of eternal life. [Note: We preferred to print this rather than the earlier edition’s reading, “if among the intervening …”.] Thus, preserving the rule of righteousness amid the storms of sins and the surges of the collapsing age, you may merit, especially through the integrity of your faith, the things that will remain forever after this age.

## CHAPTER XX. Confession to God

**APOLLONIUS.**—The publication of the earlier little book was indeed substantial, and its clear understandings taught knowledge of the matters and faith [Note: Thus both the Lemovicensis and Vindobonensis manuscripts; the printed editions read “clear to understandings.” Near the end, where the text reads “through the effect of a cherished prayer,” it read “effect.”]; but the present work must be credited no less to usefulness than to the grace of what preceded it. For although, as you yourself professed, you had surveyed what many had traversed, brevity nevertheless brought an advantage that the words of lengthy works rarely attain; and the fruit is considerable.

First, you learned through a clear exposition the divinity of the threefold unity; then the fall of the Jews in their faithlessness and the ruin of every kind of impiety among the heretics; and finally, convicted in your own folly, Novatian, you learned through evident testimonies of Scripture how much you deprive yourself of God’s indulgence.

A brief conclusion of the faith has moreover been added, and everything has settled so deeply in the heart that it is desirable to live amid these matters, and to complete one’s desire in them—provided only that the unbegotten Creator of all things, through the God whom he begot from himself and within himself, and whom he now embraces as dwelling in the flower of an assumed body and remaining in both births, may hear us and fulfill us through the Holy Spirit; and may not refuse, through the effect of the fostered prayer, to grant the will that he himself has produced.

May he kindly protect and guide his servant, who creeps with little steps among his commandments, confessing the Trinity in persons and names and God in majesty and substance; and by the benefits of his mercy may he reward both confessions, if by living I fulfill his will and, preserving the faith handed down by the fathers, may be present at the joys of the future resurrection.

# BOOK THREE

## PREFACE

As we now prepare this third little book, we shall describe the form of catholic conduct—not the form by which we wish to exalt ourselves, but by which others may be instructed. By arranging the stages of observance, it will demonstrate through divine judgments what can or ordinarily does come about in a human being. It will so temper the highest matters with what is small and moderate that it will in no way detract from the humbler by what it contributes to the greater; rather, the Apostle’s saying will be carefully observed:

> Let each person hold the faith he has within himself and, without judging anyone, glory in the Lord (Romans 14:22).

In this way he will guard more cautiously in his own affairs what he has judged more severely in those of others. [Note: The Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts read *aestimaret* (“would judge”). Below, from the same manuscripts, we printed “divine promise” where “divine provision” had stood; and near the end, “what it is fitting to dare,” where previously “what it is fitting to hear” was read.]

Applying ourselves for a little while to this work, we shall exercise our customary characters in a suitable discussion; and we shall invite a disciple, initiated by a learned teacher, to undertake the demanding honor of this profession and to approach the discipline of strictness. By presenting the actions of exemplary monks, we shall introduce the prospect of final perfection. For the reader who briefly examines these matters, the obscurity concerning the Antichrist will be resolved; and, when these points have been considered individually, the final faith in the resurrection will be disclosed. Although it was long ago rightly believed and accepted, it will nevertheless be confirmed in simple words by divine promise.

First, therefore, Apollonius, as in the other books, returning to the intervals of the postponed conference, will take up again, as though after a two-day delay, the teaching supported by authority and friendliness. As he surveys the members of the order mentioned above, he will desire more earnestly to serve righteousness and, assigning the remainder of his life to God, will not refuse even to die for his name, once he has recognized, with the proper measure in each matter, what it is fitting for a human being to desire and what it is fitting to dare. For to believe everything through confidence alone is insufficiently secure, while to submit to weakness in everything deserves no merit.

## CHAPTER I. What is the suitable form of life

**APOLLONIUS.**—If it were fitting, O Zaccheus, that what we often observe in mute animals could also be discerned in the minds of certain human beings, then this saying of an old maxim would certainly have been especially confirmed in me. For just as other animals always return to those places where they were once well fed, and cannot be enticed by richer fodder to forget what they received when hungry, so we, after the hunger and thirst for the word—as I now understand it—seek your conversations eagerly and cling confidently to the discussions we have experienced, from which we have received food of heavenly knowledge and draughts of divine understanding.

For behold, scarcely yet freed from the vast errors of paganism, breathing the novelty of the regeneration recently poured into us, we already know the integrity of the faith through your instruction [Note: Both the Lemovicensis and Vindobonensis manuscripts read “the integrity of faith”; the earlier edition incorrectly had “the integrity of the faith.”], and, attacking all the members of the heretics, we embrace the gift of catholic confession. Trusting, with God as our author, we possess the coverings of a house built upon the rock; if the giver of all good things grants it, we shall see from the watchtower of the Gospel the conduct of earthly life and the blind vanities of the age.

But although knowing our own Creator as he is is the first good, and although the foundations of true salvation are secure in the acceptance of faith, the ordering of belief is one thing and the ordering of life another. Although the solid mass of the spiritual building is not overthrown when the floodwaters of wickedness strike it, the metals of righteousness do not shine if no works of virtue come to its aid.

Therefore, since we ceased some time ago from such pursuits in time but not in mind, return to us, as you remember, with the discussions postponed during our rest; and, consulted by us, state what form of life it is most fitting for us to undertake. Thus, while you salutarily urge spiritual indulgence, establish from Scripture those commands which, while preserving faith, do not omit the grace of works of virtue [Note: The Lemovicensis and Vindobonensis manuscripts read “works of virtue”; the earlier edition had “virtues of works.” Below, where the text has “to fortify the undertaking with safe beginnings,” the printed edition has a corrupt reading; the manuscripts do not provide a better one, except that the Vindobonensis has *proposita* (“proposed”).].

**ZACCHEUS.**—I remember that our conversation was interrupted by the close of day, and that, as the questions multiplied, time rather than eagerness was lacking. For this reason we now yield to you on the condition that, while asking us for a form of life, you accept a degree of knowledge suitable not to our boasting in ourselves but to our desire to benefit others through God.

Yet the warning is not inappropriate: to fortify what is proposed with safe beginnings and, while desires remain fixed upon observance, always to strive for an ascent toward higher things. For the Lord says in the Gospel:

> Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down with himself and calculate the expense? (Luke 14:28)

Otherwise, if the work is interrupted, what was begun may be ridiculed through carelessness, and what was previously a matter of desire may become an object of hatred.

Similarly, when undertaking war against enemies, the reason for foreknowledge teaches those who are about to fight to assess their own strength and, after weighing the force of the opposing army, either to make a treaty or to engage in battle. Otherwise, a late complaint of weakness may compel them to turn their backs on the pursuer, and, after repentance for a rash deed, they may suffer either a mournful or a shameful outcome in the place from which they have been displaced [Note: The Vindobonensis and Lemovicensis manuscripts correctly have the present reading; the earlier edition had a corrupt text.]

Therefore, the first path, without exception, is firmly to believe in God and, once you have believed well, to fear him more; and, as we have often already said, to love with your entire heart the one whom you fear. This is not because he is equally capable of doing good and evil, but because he prefers to bestow good things, and never punishes us for wrongdoing as we deserve.

The next good is the purity of a simple life and a devotion to charity toward one’s neighbors, with wicked deeds hated. For it is written:

> You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your innermost being (Matthew 22:37);

and:

> Your neighbor as yourself (ibid., 39).

In this passage, the reference is not only to kinship; rather, one is rightly called a neighbor who, overwhelmed by misfortunes, is helped by one who prospers, and who, warmed by adopted mercy, returns to God in grateful affection what he does not possess through kinship of blood.

Hence Solomon’s saying:

> Store almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will itself plead for you against every evil (Sirach 29:15).

And again:

> Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God (Proverbs 19:17).

David likewise says:

> I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken (Psalm 36:25–26), nor his seed seeking bread. All day long he has mercy and lends, and his seed shall be in blessing.

Job likewise says:

> I rescued the poor from the hand of the powerful; I assisted the orphan who had no helper. The mouth of the widow always blessed me, when I was the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame, and the father of the weak (Job 29:12, according to the Septuagint).

And the Lord taught in the Gospel that he is lifted up in the persons of the humble, saying:

> Truly I tell you, what you did for one of the least, you did for me (Matthew 25:40).

The Apostle also says:

> Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessing will also reap in blessing. Let each one give according to what he has resolved in his heart, not with sadness or from compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:6–7).

Through Isaiah, the Spirit discloses the whole work of mercy, saying:

> Loosen every bond of injustice; release the suffocations of powerless transactions; send the crushed away into rest; and destroy every unjust contract. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy without shelter into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise the members of your own seed. Then your timely light will break forth, your garments will quickly arise, your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will call, and I will hear you; while you are still speaking, I will say, “Behold, I am here” (Isaiah 58:6, 9).

Therefore, property acquired without fraud is acceptable if it is possessed in this way. Sin lies not in moderate means but in the desire for riches, as the Lord declares:

> Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation (Luke 6:24).

And again:

> It is difficult for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven (Luke 18:24).

Honorable marriages do not displease God, and the chaste affection of the marriage bed, solemnized for the procreation of children, is approved, as Scripture says: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). And again [Col. 1149C]: “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. XIX, 6).

[Note: [Col. 1149D] The Codex Vindobonensis reads, “let him not separate.” The words enclosed in parentheses survive from the passage in which Zacchaeus was discussing the lawful use of clothing and food.]

[From this follows clothing not devoted to luxury, but to cleanliness.]

And according to the Apostle: “Everything sold in the market is food without guilt” (I Cor. X, 25), because, as the same Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV, 17). Yet excessive use of either is harmful, as the Lord warns: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down by wine and drunkenness” (Luke XXI, 34). He had already foretold this through Solomon: “For whom is woe? For whom are bloodshot eyes? Is it not for those who linger over wine and pursue the places where banquets are held?” (Prov. XXIII, 29, according to the Septuagint). Hence the Apostle gives Timothy instructions to take wine because of his weakness (I Tim. V, 3), but in moderation. He says this also elsewhere: “Let no one deceive you” (Col. II, 18); “drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

In this form of life, therefore, and in the discipline of sober conduct, let the mind be ready for God [Col. 1150A]; and let other fasts and persistent prayers in supplication either win or produce righteousness, so that the saying taken from the Gospels may accompany and protect one who lives in this manner: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

These words will be sufficient for ordinary people, if the fervor of higher attainments is absent. That the promises of eternal life are granted to such people is made clear by the authority of all the Scriptures: so that, if among the brightest stars of the future kingdom [Note: [Col. 1149D] This passage is written as follows in the Codex Lemovicensis: “if exceptional splendor does not raise up the lesser ones, sins, etc.” Below, the same codex reads, “let no power subtract.” What follows is difficult or impossible; Acherius disliked it and conjectured that it ought to be read as “or as impossible.” But this word is better omitted, for the discussion here is not of commandments, nor even of counsels in general, but only of particular counsels that one might reasonably say are impossible for most people, since they do not appear to have been called to follow them. — [Col. 1150D] Acherius’s reading nevertheless seems preferable; it is also confirmed below, where we read “which, as you yourself said, are proclaimed as virtually impossible.”] exceptional splendor does not raise up the lesser ones, and sins do not overwhelm them, the diversity of dwellings in the Father’s house, as he himself recalled, may console them; and, in sum, the Lord’s exhorting decree comes to mind: “All who have believed in me shall not be put to shame” (Rom. IX, 33).

That is, no power may separate from Christ those whom pure faith has once bound to him, and they may be saved by the integrity of the saving sign—those who reject what is difficult or impossible because of the labor involved, or who have feared to undertake it because it is arduous and great.

## CHAPTER II. What rule of the higher life must be maintained

**APOLLONIUS.**—The truth of this teaching and the soundness of the counsel are clear: we are to love God above every affection, and, even if we do not attain the highest things, not to fall short even of the ordinary ones; and, if the honor and splendor of higher attainments do not come, the judgment should not condemn the wretched eternally.

[Note: [Col. 1150D] Acherius rightly observed that the reading should be *excidamus* (“fall short”). Below, “for labor does not so, etc.” is plainly corrupt; but the manuscripts offer nothing by which the error can be corrected. Perhaps it should read, “the harshness discourages the weak, so that, etc.”; but I would prefer, “the harsh man discourages the weak, so that, etc.”]

But truly, this is characteristic either of a sluggish or distrustful spirit, one that expects nothing exceptional from God’s generosity: for a person to grow numb over small things when the highest things have been set before him, and to value the convenience of this life so highly [Col. 1150C] that he disregards the kingdoms of immeasurable ages; or, despised in some common condition of the crowd, to mourn too late that he did not seek what, once the course of this age has been completed, he can no longer deserve.

Let us therefore not hesitate to explain from sacred utterances what form of life and what higher manner of conduct belong to a loftier purpose; for labor does not so reject the weak that no confidence in divine calling should encourage them, even though the things that, as you yourself said, are proclaimed as virtually impossible, and whose merit is not secured by the circumstances of the times, may perhaps be lighter in practice than they are believed to be.

[Note: [Col. 1150D] Here too one sees an example of the copyists’ negligence; no suitable meaning can be extracted from these words. “Is not worn down,” that is, “is not diminished,” would not be objectionable; but what follows would then have to be read differently. Perhaps the text should be “and it is lighter in practice”; nevertheless, I would prefer “the harsh man discourages the weak,” and so forth.]

**ZACCHAEUS.**—The way that leads to life is indeed narrow and difficult (Matt. VII, 14); but since all things are possible to those who believe, insofar as the measure of our frailty permits, the heights of divine gifts must always be sought under the invocation of God. This is especially so because the Lord, acting in our body and doing nothing at all that a human being cannot accomplish, gave this command to the Apostles [Col. 1150D]: “Behold, I have left you an example to follow” (John XIII, 15).

That is: Let the excuse of impossibility disappear. I teach you to be able to do what I myself did not refuse to do. Therefore, “If you wish to be perfect,” as the same Lord said to the young man who consulted him, “go, sell all your possessions, and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

That is: Forget and reject earthly things; desire heavenly things; and, as he adds, “you will abound in the riches of spiritual treasure” (ibid.). Such, then, is the reason for voluntary poverty before God: having become poor for a time, you remain rich forever; and, despising the fleeting dignity or pleasure of the world for love of that treasure, you will obtain possession of heavenly delights.

The indissoluble bonds of this world must therefore be broken, and certain burdens of possessions and estates must be cast aside, so that, desiring to reach our Redeemer, we may not be oppressed by any necessities of sin. Although, when the will to sin itself is absent, the necessity is likewise absent, the occasion must nevertheless always be feared; and sometimes guilt creeps in beneath honorable actions. [Note: [Col. 1151D] Thus the Codex Vindobonensis and the first edition read: “with him himself thus bearing witness in the Gospels.” Not much later, from the same codex, we wrote “I shall no longer say,” where the text had “I no longer say”; and below the Codex Lemovicensis reads “under the dominion of the spirit,” where the reading had been “in the dominion of the spirit.”]

The Gospel itself bears witness to the truth in this way: “Whoever does not sell all that he possesses” (Luke XIV, 33), “and take up his cross and follow me, cannot be my disciple” (ibid., 27).

Therefore we must strive first to be his disciples and afterward his friends. For the condition of slavery comes to an end when spiritual merit takes its place, as he himself says: “If you do what I command you, behold, I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XV, 14).

This labor is welcome to those who live in this manner, and for the hope of such things every hardship is preferable to all pleasures: gracious humility, patient contempt, meager food, and poor clothing; and, with the flesh subdued under the dominion of the spirit, one must learn to turn one’s efforts away from vices—to conquer anger, owe nothing to envy, cultivate gentleness, detest arrogance, reject the vanity of human glory, and restrain the tongue, that most savage evil, from slander.

Thus, when the garments of the old person have been worn away, the Apostle’s saying may not be repeated in vain: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 30); and let us be his imitators (I Cor. IV, 16), as he is Christ’s, confidently making our own the words: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philipp. III, 20). And: “The Lord is our portion” (Lam. III, 24).

When we are always intent upon these things, we neither admit through sight or hearing anything by which sin is admitted or imagined as something to be admitted.

## CHAPTER III. What the institutions of monks are, and why they are hated by many

[Col. 1151D]

**APOLLONIUS.**—The requests of this inquiry have been sufficiently fulfilled, and the merits of true perfection have been made so clear that a certain fervor of the soul for testing them has arisen, separating the practice of the present life from every occasion of sin.

Explain now what the congregation or sect of monks is, and for what reason they are considered worthy of hatred even by our own people. If they pursue honorable things and do not dissent from the unity of the faith, they ought rather to be imitated than avoided. For, as I think, it is the same crime and sin to hate the good as it is not to avoid the wicked; since it is impossible in any way that one who loves the wicked should prefer to be good, or, conversely, that one who displays any appearance of goodness should not be driven by the goads of wickedness and should not truly be what he unjustly condemns in others.

[Note: [Col. 1152D] Thus the Codex Lemovicensis reads; the printed editions have “thus, in truth, that.” Below, where we printed “you know that it will be,” I would prefer “you almost know that it will be.”]

**ZACCHAEUS.**—You rightly assess such a purpose and judge that those who pursue this life ought not to be hated by the faithful, lest, under the uncertain judgment of the mind, offense against the good be incurred in place of offense against the wicked; for it is written: “Those who hate the righteous will offend” (Ps. XXXIII, 22). “Woe to those who call evil good” (Isa. V, 20).

There are many forms of this observance, and under the one name of the purpose there are different kinds of monks. Yet the cause of all is such as you know it to be among every order: because of the variety of conduct there is also a diversity of wills. Hence the profession itself is irreproachable and holy; but some, under the cover of this way of life, commit deeds worthy of hatred, and, although they are charged with different guilt, they nevertheless depart generally from the profession.

Among these, those whose spirit is most corrupt are they who pretend for a time to abstinence and continence. They first insinuate themselves through the pursuits of slippery intimacy; then, deceiving women whom they have ensnared with vain opinions, they entice them into the use of miserable desire—either by coveting gifts and seeking the foul profits of avarice, or by overcoming their subordinates through deceit and drawing them away from their purpose of devoted chastity.

Others begin faithfully and strive to serve righteousness with an ardent purpose; then, having undertaken what they did not consider carefully enough, they cannot endure it and abandon what they began. Or they are softened by the persuasion of the envious or of those who shrink from undertaking such a life, and they depart from the rigor of their institution. Once accustomed to more relaxed practices, they return to every bodily enticement; and, making their first commitment void, they praise the order of common life so as to condemn the practice of the more rigorous purpose.

You therefore understand that the integrity of enduring discipline must not be condemned in advance because of these people and their like, nor the glory and honor of those who complete it sublimely in the most holy labor be diminished; for, as has been said, it is the person rather than the order that displeases, and what many preserve with courage cannot rightly be despised because of a few.

Those truly carry out the measure of this profession who, as has already been said, have entirely cut off the bonds of the world, devote themselves to the practice of the law, and, awaiting the promises in full, strive to fulfill the commandments in full. Yet even among them there is considerable difference in observance. Although it is dear to all to deserve the glory of future things, some strive for the highest, while others strive for what is ordinary.

Some, as though at the lowest grade of this sect, content with a small degree of observance, live only as celibates—either rejecting marriage because they have never experienced it, or, warned by the memory of what they have lost, avoiding a second marriage if they had a first. In the latter case, what commonly happens is that they either do not find in a second marriage what they lost in the first, or else suffer later what they lacked in the deceased.

These people participate in the affairs of ordinary communal life and do not seek seclusion, retaining the customs of this life. Thus, even if they can remain free from sins, they nevertheless become subject to occasions of sin; for, while the law of the body pulls in another direction, those who can see evil yet refuse to look at it accomplish great things with greater difficulty.

Their clothing is neither dishonorable nor contemptible; their food and drink are the same as those common to everyone, or they abstain rarely and restrict themselves in only a few things. They do not burn with zeal in the discipline of psalmody, nor do they break the night’s rest with vigils. They supply the poverty of those who ask with a moderate, manageable income, not with lavish wealth. Their faith is warm, though not burning; their mind is religious, though not wholly devoted to religion.

This way of life belongs to those of the better sort. They first live in more remote places, even if they reside in cities, and although they do not ostentatiously display the order of their way of life, they consider it a sin to suppress their willingness to receive the exhortations of others.

There is one place for all to meet, but their places of residence differ. Their clothing is humble and their food unappealing. It makes no difference what sort of drink you have, or by what cheap liquid you are satisfied, provided that it restrains the pleasure of drinking and removes the force of bodily necessity.

They devote themselves frequently to psalmody, and their devotion to praising God is distributed at fixed hours. They labor in continual fasting until evening, and perform the work of the day according to their knowledge. [Note: [Col. 1153D] We preferred to publish this reading rather than the first edition’s “by each person.” Below, where we printed “always singing psalms,” the Codex Vindobonensis formerly read “always deceiving.”]

Nothing that anyone possesses is private; whatever anyone lacks is held in common. Therefore sluggishness is hateful to all, and food is considered unsuitable unless it comes from labor.

They spread rushes over their beds, and cover their bodies for sleep with small coverings. They also have appointed times for prayer during the night and established vigils. Moreover, they are never deceived about the coming of day: dawn always rouses them while they are diligently singing psalms, and morning devotion compels them to offer praises to God.

Those whose observance is of the first rank inhabit only the wilderness and the desolate places of the desert. Properly called by their name, they lead a solitary life, either tempering the sun and rain by living in rocks hollowed out as dwellings or in underground caves. They eat old bread without additions of other foods and drink pure water from springs.

Their clothing is either made of skins or of haircloth, and the whole practice of their life is a contest of mind and body. Their prayers to God are unceasing, and supplication takes the place of sacrifice. If they ever cease from prayer, divine praise is sung through psalmody, and the mind’s cheerfulness is kindled by the exercise of religious joy.

Moreover, they often engage in conflict with a manifold host of demons, and their victorious constancy frequently confronts the deceits of unclean spirits. They persist continually in fasting and keep nights of vigil. They either lay their small bodies on the ground without supports, or endure for a short while upon a rock [Note: [Col. 1154D] Thus it is read in the Codex Vindobonensis; the first edition has “slightly thrown down.”], so that sleep seems not to be practiced through an injurious brevity but driven away.

Such is the diversity of monks, and such is the heavenly discipline of those who live spiritually upon earth. For the name of God, a vowed death is appointed to all, and the solemnity of a holy departure is desirable, since no injury suffered in the world is compensated; this also is to be rewarded with sublime honor and will remain without any change of time.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether faithful monks undertake these things by God’s command

**APOLLONIUS.**—Great indeed is the proclamation of such virtues, and glorious is the service of those who minister to God’s will [Note: [Col. 1154D] We supplied this missing word from the Codex Vindobonensis.] and praises [Col. 1154B], since by such pursuits the destructive allurements of this life are avoided and the rewards of eternal blessedness are sought.

Nevertheless, show in orderly explanation, beginning from the instruction already given, that each of the practices you have mentioned above as being carried out by faithful monks proceeds from the command of God who gives the warning. For it is undoubtedly clear that they would possess uncertain authority if they had not been undertaken on the authority of the one by whom they are believed to be rewarded.

**ZACCHAEUS.**—The first and particular reason why monks seek seclusion is that they may avoid even the occasion of sin, as has already been said; and that those whose will is upright in their purpose may be unable to undertake any other kind of action. Finally, they seek it so that, when they undertake war against the world, no allurements of the world may break them.

For faith fervent in the spirit is hostile to the things of the world, as John proclaims in his Epistle, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; for everything that is in the world—the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age—is” (I John II, 15–16).

James likewise says: “Do you not know, brothers, that friendship with this world is hostility toward God? Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age will be constituted an enemy of God” (James IV, 4).

David specifically indicates that humble clothing and the continual labor of fasts are acceptable to God, saying: “When they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth, and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. XXXIV, 13). And again: “I made my clothing sackcloth” (Ps. LXVIII, 12). And: “I mingled my bread with ashes and tempered my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI, 10).

The Lord, praising John’s clothing, says: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. XI, 8; Luke VII, 25). There he indicates that luxurious dress belongs where the use of pleasures is abundant. For his clothing was made of camel’s hair, that is, it lacked even the softness of wool. He was also girded with a belt of skin, and, drinking neither wine nor strong drink, he ate locusts and wild honey. He did not seek the abundance of an elegant and elaborate banquet, but used only what, in an excellent way of life, would bring neither luxury nor expense.

Hence, when Elijah was about to undertake his great journey at God’s command, the angel provided him only water and cheap bread. Daniel, in order to obtain the fulfillment of his desires, did not partake of drink or food.

Finally, the Lord himself conquers the devil through fasting and humility, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7), so that through his poverty we might become rich and be saved from injury (II Cor. VIII, 9).

Yet when he wished to govern the Church received from the Gentiles in the same way, he also commended abstinence in these words: “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Rom. XIV, 21), “in which there is indulgence” (Eph. V, 18).

That is, so that the humbled mind might think more deeply about God, and the subjected flesh might be removed equally from luxury and expense—things with which we are occupied both in seeking them and in spending them. But if we are rather intent upon the kingdom of God, the saying will not be absent concerning the provision of necessities: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear” (Luke XII, 22), “for the Gentiles seek all these things” (ibid., 30)—those, namely, whose belly is their god and whose entire hope is in their throats (Phil. III, 19).

For such people, eating and drinking, after the manner of animals, are their sole and chief concern. The Lord immediately confirmed the confidence he had proclaimed concerning these matters by this example: “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither plow nor sow nor gather into barns, and your Father feeds them” (Matt. VI, 26). And again: “You of little faith” (ibid., 30): “Your Father knows that you need all these things. Therefore seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be given to you” (ibid., 32–33)—that is, they will be provided when they are not expected.

Hence the Apostle declares that, in order that everything may be possessed, nothing should be possessed with anxious concern: “As having nothing and possessing everything” (II Cor. VI, 10).

You therefore understand that those who despise everything subject everything to their own possession; and that, in the judgment of the foolish, those who are rich in God’s promise are considered poor. They despise small things for a time in order to deserve great and everlasting things; and they are content to lack in this world the things that others produce, at the cost of their integrity and life, accumulating them throughout the whole age—only for them either to perish shortly while those same people are still alive in the world, or to be left behind, destined to perish with the world, when those people eventually depart from it.

## CHAPTER V. From which Scriptures continence or virginity is proclaimed, and whether it is commanded that marriages be separated for the love of God

**APOLLONIUS.**—It has clearly been shown that contempt of the world, together with humble clothing and the purpose of continence, shines forth in the oracles of sacred instruction; and that those merit more in heavenly things who have presumed little upon earthly things. Monks are trained through harsh observances for this purpose: not merely to cut away vices, but also the material that gives rise to vices.

Now therefore disclose, from the same authorities of Scripture, the evident command concerning continence and virginity. Why, in the end, do those who are celibate not merely because circumstances have made them so, but because they abstain from lawful unions, rightly condemn what is unlawful, yet nevertheless reject or spurn what is lawful? [Note: [Col. 1155D] Thus the Codex Vindobonensis reads; the first edition has “if therefore.”] If these practices have indeed come, as was said above, from a divine command, they are salutarily required. But if they are separated from heavenly instruction, why are things commanded as though they ought to be done when they are difficult to observe and fruitless in labor?

**ZACCHAEUS.**—To Adam it was said at the beginning: “It is not good for man to be alone” (Gen. II, 18). Soon afterward the command concerning procreation followed: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 28; IX, 1).

But the woman, made for him and from him, was first a comfort to him rather than a marriage partner, until disobedience made them exiles from paradise—those whom obedience would have kept within paradise. After being expelled from that blessed dwelling, the man recognized his wife, as the Book of Genesis teaches: “And Adam knew his wife, and she conceived and bore a son” (Gen. IV, 1).

Thus marriage preceded the labor to which humanity was subjected, and unions were established beforehand for those who were to endure thorns and thistles. The hardships of procreation followed, and another decree preceded the woman’s giving birth: “In pain and sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. III, 16).

Those born in this way are, as we see, taken away by various misfortunes and sorrows. Hence the Apostle says in preaching: “Such people will have tribulation in the flesh” (I Cor. VII, 28).

Nevertheless, the beds of marriage are not dishonorable (Heb. XIII, 4), nor is an undefiled marriage bed without fruit. From it comes, of course, the offspring of saints; and what is praised in virginity belongs also to marriage, though the reward of continence is higher.

Virginity is the loftier state. It need not fear being the lesser, nor should it insult the lesser because it is greater. [Note: [Col. 1156D] We preferred to publish this reading, whereas the earlier edition had “but according to a Catholic interpretation.” Below, where the text reads “Israel was diminished,” the Codex Lemovicensis has “Israel was devoured.”]

Let the Catholic interpretation therefore assign distinct praises of chastity to honorable marriages; let it reckon the merit of continence to those who abstain, and attribute the reward of virginity to those who remain undefiled. This is not to condemn what is good, but to commend what is better.

Hence there is this evident testimony to continence in Scripture: “The Lord knew that Israel had been diminished, and no one had been left except those who practiced continence.” Foreseeing this in the Spirit, Solomon said: “A time for embracing, and a time for keeping far from embracing” (Eccl. III, 5).

The old command is that the earth be filled through procreation; the new, that heaven be filled through continence and virginity. Hence the Lord says through Zechariah: “Holy stones are rolled upon the earth; wheat among the young men, sweet-smelling wine among virgins” (Zech. IX, 16).

Finally, the Gospel mentions different kinds of eunuchs. But a special possession of the kingdom is assigned to those who have made themselves eunuchs for its sake and out of love for it—that is, not those whom the necessity of inability compels, but those whom the will makes continent.

For thus it is written, as the Lord explains: “There are eunuchs who were made so by men; there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 12). Of them it is said through Isaiah: “I will give them a better place than sons and daughters” (Isa. LVI, 5).

Yet he declared that this reward is so arduous and exalted that when the Apostles said in one place, “If such is the situation of a man with a woman, then it is not expedient to marry,” he replied: “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX, 10).

Therefore there is no command concerning those who practice continence, but a recommendation; nor is virginity imposed as a necessity, but it is praised so that it may be a matter of will, as the Apostle bears witness: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who himself has knowledge of God. I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, for it is good for a person to be thus” (I Cor. VII, 25–26).

John, however, declares in the Apocalypse that only those who have not been defiled by unions with women cling to the footsteps of the Lamb, saying: “These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes; these are the ones who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins” (Apoc. XIV, 4).

Better things are therefore reasonably preferred, but what is lower is not thereby evil. No sin is signified in marriage; rather, as you learned shortly before, continence is commended because of the necessity of the impending end, lest the Gospel’s “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” apply (Luke XXI, 23). At the same time, those who have been occupied with marriage may at some time devote themselves to strict satisfaction; remembering the burdens of their sins, they strive more earnestly to restore themselves to God, since those who have committed unlawful acts rightly abstain even from what is lawful.

## CHAPTER VI. What the practice of psalmody and prayer is, and from where these commands came to monks

**APOLLONIUS.**—I also knew that the purpose of virginity and continence possesses lofty merit, especially when those devoted to reverence for God consecrate their human will; for they undertake things worthy of common veneration and imitate a life or conduct of angelic dignity.

But because I believed that this was a command, not merely advice, authority from the Scriptures ought to be supplied. Now briefly explain how frequent the practice of prayer and psalmody should be, and from where such devotion to these teachings came to the monks. For although there is great value in constant supplication, the practice of singing seems idle, since prayer itself, being less frequent, is more attentive, and the divine majesty ought to be honored with serious rather than playful praises.

[Note: [Col. 1157D] Thus reads one codex seen by Acherius; nevertheless, he preferred to publish the reading found in another codex, “from the monks.” Below, where we printed “the prosperity of actions,” the Codex Lemovicensis reads “the prosperous and living action.”]

**ZACCHAEUS.**—It is right that we present ourselves before God’s sight intent upon prayer and serious in all things, asking with submissive minds for a prosperous ordering of our deeds. But it is necessary that the one who asks more frequently obtain his request more quickly, since the Lord declares in the Gospels: “Amen I say to you, even if he will not give it because of friendship, he will give it because of persistence” (Luke XI, 8). That is, if he can obtain little through merit, persistence in asking will prevail.

Hence again: “Pray without ceasing, so that you may be considered worthy to escape the evils that are to come upon you” (Luke XXI, 36). Through Solomon the Spirit says: “Do not hinder yourself from praying always” (Ecclus. XVIII, 22). The Apostle likewise says: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks to God, for this is his will” (I Thess. V, 28).

In the text of the sacred song, however, everything is serious and everything venerable, and it is so worthy of holy worship that through it divinity is always either praised or entreated. Divine mercy provided for this when it took account of our weakness and misuse, mingling gentle things with sad ones and pleasant things with severe ones, so that it would not allow us to depart in any way from remembrance of itself, since it made us delight not only in speaking of its benefits but also in singing them.

Moses first taught this after the crossing of the Red Sea: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exod. XV, 1). David likewise, when choosing what he should offer God above all things in return for blessings, settled upon the delight of singing and psalmody. For he says: “I will sing to the Lord, who has granted me good things” (Ps. XII, 6). And: “I will sing psalms to your name, O Most High” (Ps. IX, 3). And again: “Exalt yourself, O Lord, in your strength; we shall sing and chant your mighty deeds” (Ps. XX, 10).

Through Jeremiah, God says that those devoted to such practices will be multiplied in glory: “There will be among them the voice of those who sing praises; and I will multiply them, and they shall not be diminished” (Baruch II, 32, 34).

The three youths, untouched in the furnace of fire, repay their deliverance with a song of praise. After singing a hymn with the Apostles, the Lord proceeds to the mountain, so that the freedom of the holy festival might have an example of completed authority in him who had instructed us in all things. [Note: [Col. 1158D] Zacchaeus certainly wrote this; there is no doubt that the reading in the first edition, “freedom for those things,” is corrupt.]

That this should be celebrated at fixed hours of day and night David established by reporting his own practice, saying: “I will cry out in the evening, in the morning, and at noon” (Ps. LIV, 18). And again: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII, 164). And a third time: “By day I will cry out, and you will not hear; and by night, and it will not be reckoned foolishness to me” (Ps. XXI, 3).

Therefore neither king nor prophet was ashamed to rejoice in the praises of God; indeed, he taught us so thoroughly that by these things we please God that, when he showed that he would keep night watches of spiritual songs, he also declared the time of the office: “At midnight I rose to confess your name, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 62).

[Note: [Col. 1158D] Perhaps the word “God” or “Lord” should be added.]

In the Gospel the Savior perhaps also affirmed that he would come at these same hours, when the firstborn of Egypt were struck down as the angel inflicted the blow; and what Christ will do at the end against the powers of this world was marked beforehand by the figure of that plague.

Finally, Paul and Silas, having engaged in such meditation, were heard by the other prisoners in the jail, and no punishment restrained them from this solemnity.

You therefore perceive that the frequency of psalmody and prayer is celebrated in the offices of righteous saints, who await their common end—or, if it should come, their individual end—in security under such a practice. Through this delight of the mind, the honor of faith and the cheerfulness of souls increase; and amid the cares of the world and of their professed restlessness, joyful grace obtains what more sorrowful discipline cannot prevail to obtain.

## CHAPTER VII. Whether the Antichrist will come, and how the world will end

[Col. 1159B]

**APOLLONIUS.**—The knowledge brought forward in the narration of the saints’ deeds has rightly been used to explain the consummation [Note: [Col. 1159D] There can be no doubt that this should be read in this way; previously it read, “in the narrative of the consummation.”], and the world’s apparently unending end has been offered so that we might inquire more freely.

With what kind of conclusion, then, will present events end, or in what manner will the periods mentioned in the preceding books be brought to a close? From where, moreover, do such confident threats of the nations and such arrogant quarrels of the profane arise?
