If the spirit of acedia rises against you, do not leave your house, and do not turn aside in the time of sadness. For just as one rubs silver, so your heart will become bright if you persevere. The spirit of weariness drives away tears; the spirit of sadness, however, afflicts prayer.

If you desire riches, you will be very anxious, and if you embrace them, you will mourn most bitterly. Let no scorpion remain in your bosom; so too, no evil thought in your heart. Do not spare the killing of the serpent’s offspring, and you will not give birth to their thoughts. For just as fire tests gold and silver, so temptation tests the monk’s heart.

[Col. 1183C] Remove pride from yourself, and put vainglory and boasting far from you. Whoever is deprived of the glory he sought will be saddened; but whoever has obtained it will become proud. Do not give pride to your heart, and do not say in the presence of the Lord, “I am powerful,” lest the Lord abandon your soul and wicked demons humble it. Then your enemies will trouble you from the air, and terrible nights will receive you.

Knowledge guards the monk’s manner of life; but whoever departs from it falls among robbers. From the spiritual rock a river flows; the soul that does good drinks from it. A clean soul is a chosen vessel; an unclean one will be filled with bitterness. Without milk an infant will not be nourished; and without freedom from passions the heart will not be exalted.

[Col. 1183D] Freedom from passions precedes charity; love, however, precedes knowledge. Wisdom will be added to knowledge; prudence, however, produces freedom from passions. The fear of the Lord produces wisdom; faith in Christ grants the fear of God. A glowing arrow sets the soul on fire; but the man who does good extinguishes it. Knowledge rejects shouting and blasphemy; wisdom, however, flees deceitful words.

Honey is sweet, and the honeycomb is pleasant; but the knowledge of God is sweeter than both. Hear, monk, the sayings of your father, and do not make his instruction fruitless. When he sends you, obey him, and in thought act together with him; for in this way you will escape evil thoughts, and wicked demons will not prevail against you.

If he entrusts money to you, do not squander it; but if you have earned a surplus, do not keep it for yourself. A bad steward will afflict the souls of the brothers; and one who remembers evil will not have mercy on them. Whoever squanders the monastery’s property defrauds God; and whoever neglects it will not go unpunished.

[Col. 1184A] An unjust steward distributes badly; but the just steward will distribute as is fitting. Whoever speaks evil of his brother will be destroyed; but whoever neglects the needy will not see the light. A layman serving his brother in sickness is better than an anchorite who does not have mercy on his neighbor. The foolish monk neglects the tools of his craft; the wise, however, will take care of them.

Do not say, “Today I will stay, and tomorrow I will leave,” because you have not considered this matter wisely. The wandering monk will meditate on false sayings; but he will mock his own father. Whoever adorns his clothing and fills his belly feeds shameful thoughts, and will have no fellowship with the saints.

[Col. 1184B] If you enter a village, do not approach women, and do not linger to converse with them; for just as someone who swallows a hook is pulled away, so your soul will be dragged away. The long-suffering monk will rejoice in freedom from passions; but whoever provokes his brothers will be hateful. The Lord loves the gentle monk; but he drives away the turbulent one.

The lazy monk will murmur; and the sleepy one pretends to have a headache. If your brother is saddened, console him; and if he is suffering, suffer with him. By doing this, you will gladden his heart and heap up a great treasure for yourself in heaven.

The monk who pretends to guard his father’s sayings will curse his father’s dog and disparage the lives of his sons; but the Lord will destroy him. Whoever seeks an occasion will separate himself from the brothers; but he will accuse his father. Do not lend your ear to sayings directed against your father, and do not stir up the soul of one who dishonors him, lest the Lord become angry at your works and erase your name from the book of the living.

[Col. 1184C] Whoever obeys the father of the monastery loves himself; but whoever contradicts him will fall into evils. Blessed is the monk who keeps the Lord’s commandments; and holy is the one who observes the sayings of his fathers. The lazy monk will suffer many losses; and if he persists in boldness, he will also proceed to lose his habit.

Whoever guards his tongue directs his ways; and whoever guards his heart will be filled with knowledge. The double-tongued monk troubles the brothers; but the faithful acts quietly. Whoever trusts in his own self-restraint will fall; but whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

[Col. 1184D] Do not give yourself over to the satiety of your belly, and you will not be filled with nighttime sleep; for in this way you will become pure, and the spirit of the Lord will come upon you. The anger of the psalm-singing man will subside; and whoever is long-suffering will be fearless. From gentleness knowledge is generated; from fierceness, however, ignorance.

As water gives growth to a plantation, so humiliation of anger exalts the heart. Whoever pursues banquets will have his light extinguished; but his soul will see darkness. Weigh your bread on a balance, and drink your water by measure; and the spirit of fornication will flee from you.

[Col. 1185A] Give wine to the old, and offer food to the sick, because they have worn out the flesh of their youth. Do not undermine your brother, and do not rejoice at his downfall; for the Lord knows your heart, and will hand you over on the day of death.

The prudent monk will be free from passions; the imprudent, however, will drain evils dry. The Lord will blind the evil eye; but he will rescue the simple from darkness. As the morning star in heaven, as the palm tree in paradise, so is pure understanding in a gentle soul.

The wise man will examine the sayings of God; the foolish, however, will mock them. Whoever hates the knowledge of God and rejects consideration is like one who pierces his own heart with a spear. The knowledge of the Trinity is better than knowledge of incorporeal beings, and contemplation of it is better than the explanations of all the ages.

[Col. 1185B] Gentleness is the gray hair of the old; their life, however, is true knowledge. A gentle young man endures much; but who will bear with a fainthearted old man? I saw an angry old man, exalted beyond his proper time; yet the younger man had no more hope than he did.

Whoever scandalizes laypeople will not go unpunished; and whoever provokes them will dishonor his name. Fire will destroy the one who disturbs the Lord’s Church; the earth, however, will swallow the one who resists the priest.

Whoever loves peace will eat its honeycomb; and whoever gathers it will be filled with honey. Honor the Lord, and you will know incorporeal beings; serve him, and he will show you the explanations of the ages. Without knowledge the heart will not be exalted, and a tree will not blossom without moisture.

[Col. 1185C] The flesh of Christ is the virtues of deeds; whoever eats it becomes free from passions. The blood of Christ is the contemplation of deeds; whoever drinks it will be enlightened by it. The breast of the Lord is the knowledge of God; whoever reclines upon it will be a preacher of divine things.

The one full of knowledge and the doer of good met each other; the Lord stood between the two. Whoever acquired love acquired a treasure; and he received great grace from the Lord. Wisdom knows the counsels of demons; prudence, however, has investigated their cunning.

Do not despise the holy decrees that your fathers established. Do not abandon the faith of your baptism, and do not reject the spiritual seal, so that the Lord may be present with your soul and protect you on the evil day. The sayings of heretics are messengers of death; whoever receives them will destroy his soul.

[Col. 1186A] Now therefore, my son, hear me, and do not approach the doors of unrighteous men, nor walk upon their snares, lest you be caught. Separate your soul from false knowledge; for I have often spoken to them, and I investigated their dark sayings and found the poison of asps in them. There is neither prudence nor wisdom in their ways. All who receive them will perish, and those who love them will be filled with evils.

I saw the fathers of their doctrines, and in the deserts I engaged with them. For the enemies of the Lord confronted me, and demons contended against me in words, and I did not see the true light in their sayings. The lying man will fall away from God; but whoever deceives his neighbor will fall into evils.

[Col. 1186B] God’s paradise is better than a garden of vegetables, and the Lord’s river than a great river that darkens the earth. Heavenly water is more trustworthy than the water of the Egyptian sages who draw from the earth. For just as those who climb wheels descend downward, so those who exalt their words will be humbled.

The wisdom of the Lord exalts the heart; his understanding purifies it. The explanations of providence are obscure, and the contemplations of judgment are scarcely intelligible; but the man who does good recognizes them. Whoever purifies himself will behold intelligible natures; the monk who is gentle, however, will know the explanations of incorporeal beings.

Whoever calls the Trinity a creature blasphemes God; and whoever despises his Christ does not know him. Contemplations of creatures enlarge the heart; but words of prudence and judgment exalt it. Knowledge of incorporeal beings raises the understanding and brings it near to the holy Trinity.

[Col. 1186C] Remember, you all, him who gave you brilliant proverbs in the Lord, and do not forget his humble soul at the time of prayer.

## II. TO VIRGINS

[Col. 1185]

[Col. 1185D] Love the Lord, and he will love you; serve him, and he will enlighten your heart. Honor your mother as the mother of Christ, and do not provoke the gray hairs of her who bore you. Love your sisters as the daughters of your mother, and do not abandon the way of peace.

Let the rising sun see a book in your hands, and your work after the second hour. Pray without ceasing, and remember Christ who begot you. Avoid gatherings of men, lest an idol come to be in your soul and become a stumbling block for you at the time of prayer.

You have Christ as your beloved: cast all men away from you, and you will not live a reproachable life. Put anger and hostility far from you, and let the memory of evil not remain with you.

[Col. 1186D] Do not say, “Today I eat, and tomorrow I will not eat,” for you do not do this wisely. It will be harmful to your body and painful for your stomach. Eating meat is not good, and drinking wine is not best; but you ought to offer these things to those who are weak.

A turbulent virgin will not be saved; and she who lives in luxury will not see her bridegroom. Do not say, “The servant-girl has saddened me; I will repay her,” because there is no servitude among the daughters of God. Do not lend your ear to empty words, and flee the stories of wandering old women.

Do not watch the festivals of drunken women, and do not go to another’s wedding; for every virgin who does these things is unclean before the Lord. Open your mouth to the word of God, and restrain your tongue from much speaking.

[Col. 1187A] Humble yourself before God, and his right hand will exalt you. Do not turn away from the poor in a time of tribulation, and the oil of your lamp will not fail. Do everything for the Lord, and do not seek glory from human beings, for human glory is like the flower of hay, but the glory of the Lord remains forever.

The Lord loves a gentle virgin; an angry virgin, however, is hateful. An obedient virgin will follow mercy; one who contradicts, however, is very foolish. The Lord destroys a murmuring virgin; but he delivers the grateful one from death.

Ugly laughter and shameful immodesty: every foolish person will become entangled in such things. She who adorns her clothing will also fall away from chastity. Do not linger with worldly people, lest they turn your heart aside and make your righteous purposes fruitless.

[Col. 1187B] Pray to the Lord with tears at night, and let no one perceive you praying, and you will find grace. Desire for walks and longing for other people’s houses turns the soul from its proper state and corrupts its ready will.

A faithful virgin will not be afraid; but the unfaithful one will flee even from her own shadow. Envy consumes the soul, and jealousy devours it. She who despises a weak sister will also be far from Christ. Do not say, “This is mine, and that is yours,” for in Christ Jesus all things are held in common.

Do not investigate another’s life, and do not rejoice at your sister’s ruin. Rather, assist virgins in need, and do not exalt yourself in your nobility. Do not utter a word from your mouth in the church of the Lord, and do not lift your eyes, for the Lord knows your heart and observes all your thoughts.

[Col. 1187C] Repel every evil desire from you, and your enemies will not grieve you. Sing psalms from your heart, and do not merely move your tongue. The foolish virgin will love silver; the prudent, however, will add her bread.

Just as the force of fire is difficult to restrain, so a virgin’s wounded soul is scarcely curable. Do not give your soul to evil thoughts, lest they defile your heart and drive pure prayer far from you. Heavy is sadness, and intolerable is acedia; tears to the Lord are stronger than both.

Hunger and thirst make evil desires wither; good wakefulness, however, purifies the understanding. Love drives away anger and hostility; gifts, however, confuse the memory of evil. She who secretly slanders her sister will stand outside the bridegroom’s chamber, cry out at his doors, and have no one to hear her.

[Col. 1187D] The lamp of the merciless virgin will be extinguished, and she will not see [Col. 1188A] her bridegroom coming. Glass falling from a rock will be shattered; and a virgin joined to a man will not be innocent. A gentle woman is better than a spirited and angry virgin.

She who draws a man’s words out through laughter is like one who casts a snare around her own neck. As a pearl in a golden sling, so is virginity practiced with reverence. The songs of demons and flutes loosen the soul and destroy its strength; guard that strength in every way, lest you become reproachable.

Do not take pleasure in laughter, and do not rejoice with those who revile, for the Lord will abandon them. Do not reproach your sister who is eating, and do not exalt yourself in your abstinence, for you do not know what the Lord has thought, or who will stand in his presence.

[Col. 1188B] She who pities her own bloodshot eyes and wasting flesh will not rejoice over the freedom from passions of her soul. Severe is abstinence, and chastity is scarcely kept straight; but nothing is sweeter than the heavenly bridegroom.

The souls of virgins will be enlightened; the souls of the unclean, however, will see darkness. I saw men corrupting virgins through their teachings and making their virginity vain. But you, daughter, hear the teachings of the Church of God, and let no outsider persuade you.

God founded heaven and earth, and provided for all things, and rejoices in them. There is no angel incapable of wickedness, and no demon evil by nature; for God made both with free will.

[Col. 1188C] Just as a human being consists of a corruptible body and a rational soul, so also our Lord was born without sin: eating, he ate, and crucified, he was crucified; his appearance before human eyes was not fictitious.

There will be a resurrection of the dead, and this world will pass away; and we will receive spiritual bodies. The righteous will inherit light; the impious, however, will inhabit darkness.

The eyes of the virgin will see God, and the ears of the virgin will hear his words. The mouth of the virgin will kiss her bridegroom; the virgins’ sense of smell, however, will run in the fragrance of his ointments. The hands of the virgin will touch the Lord, and the chastity of her flesh will be acceptable to him.

[Col. 1188D] The virgin’s soul will be crowned, and she will live forever with her bridegroom. A spiritual garment will be given to her, and she will keep festival with the angels in heaven. She lights an unquenchable lamp, and the oil will not fail in her vessels. She will receive eternal riches and inherit the kingdom of God.

My sayings, daughter, have been spoken to you; let your heart keep these words. Remember Christ who guards you, and do not forget the adorable Trinity, of one substance.

## Volume back matter

[Col. 1187D]

## INDEX OF THE SUBJECTS CONTAINED IN THE WORKS OF SAINT CHROMATIUS, TOGETHER WITH THE PROLEGOMENA AND COMMENTARIES PERTAINING TO THESE WORKS, FROM COL. 247 TO 436 OF THIS VOLUME

[Note: [Col. 1187] In this index, Arabic numerals refer to the column numbers printed in bold type in the text.]

(In this index, Roman numerals represent the prolegomena, while Arabic numerals represent the text columns according to the order of the Utmensis edition.)

### A
Abbot Alcuin. See Alcuin.

Adultery. What did Saint Chromatius write about dismissing adulterous wives? [Col. 1188] XLII, 59. What did Dupin, Tillemont, and Sixtus of Siena think about this passage of Chromatius? 126, 130. Who is to be understood as “our adversary,” with whom, according to the Gospel, we must be reconciled while we are still on the way? 50. Various opinions are reported by Saint Chromatius, ibid. and 51. He himself, however, understands this adversary together with others as the Holy Spirit, 52.

Aglietti, Francesco, commended, LIII and LVII.

Alaric, Duke of the Goths, invaded Italy in the year 400 and again in 407 or 408, and threw the region of Aquileia into turmoil, L and LII. On Alaric’s first invasion, see also Fontanini, 116, and De Rubeis, 144. On the second, see the same De Rubeis, 164.

Alcuin, abbot, or Flaccus Albinus. He transmits Saint Chromatius’s text on the mystery of the Trinity and offered us helping hands for correcting that text, which is read in a badly corrupted form both in the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum* and in the latest edition of Gallandius, X, LXXIX, 17, 18, 125. He was the first to call Chromatius’s writings a booklet on the eight Beatitudes, perhaps on the basis of the manuscript he used, XXIII. We likewise know that he was the very first to call Chromatius a Roman bishop, indeed the bishop of the Roman Church, 124 and following, and 144. Yet not in such a way that he himself believed Chromatius actually to have been bishop of the city of Rome and supreme pontiff, 126. Indeed, he was not even the originator of this title, 165.

Ambrose, Saint, Bishop of Milan. Regarding human laws and conjugal chastity, he taught the same things that Saint Chromatius later taught at Aquileia, XLIV. The testimony of this holy teacher concerning Saint Chromatius, LXXV. See also 113. His outstanding teaching on oaths is cited, 130. Was Saint Chromatius ordained bishop by Saint Ambrose? 112 and following, 140, 161 and following.

Anastasius, Saint, Pope. In his letter to John of Jerusalem he says absolutely nothing about Origen’s condemnation having been sent to Chromatius of Aquileia, 115. Saint Anastasius distinguished Origen’s case from that of Rufinus of Aquileia, 146 and following.

What is the *angariatio* (compulsory service) of a thousand paces in the Gospel, and what is the spiritual meaning of this passage? 65, 66.

The human soul. The various opinions of the holy Fathers concerning the origin of the human soul, 151.

The third anonymous brother of Saint Chromatius, invented by Fontanini, was rejected by De Rubeis, XIV, 109, 110.

An ancient anonymous author writes that Saint Chromatius also rendered valuable service concerning ecclesiastical liturgy, XLVII, LXXX.

The years of Christ were marked neither in the fourth nor in the fifth century; rather, the practice began much later, LIII, LIV.

The apostles as the salt of the earth, 31 and following.

The apostles as the light of the world, 36.

Aquileian Church. In the fourth century this Church possessed commentaries on the Gospels, the work of Fortunatianus, Bishop of Aquileia, whom Saint Jerome mentions, XXV. In this Church also, during Saint Chromatius’s lifetime, the practice of daily—or at least very frequent—Communion of the faithful flourished, XXXVII. The Aquileian Church was sometimes called the Church of Forum Iulii, and the bishops of Aquileia were called bishops of Forum Iulii, because they had a permanent seat in the city of Forum Iulii, especially during the eighth and ninth centuries, LI. Saint Chromatius is said to have rendered valuable service to the sacred liturgy in the Aquileian Church, XLVII. With what eulogy did Saint Jerome honor the clergy of the Aquileian Church? See the dedication of this work, 110. The Aquileian and Milanese Churches had this distinctive custom: the bishops of each ordained one another in the church of the bishop who was to be ordained, 140. The city and territory of Aquileia were repeatedly tested by military forces, both Roman and barbarian, from the year 388 through 408, L, LI, LII.

Arcadius Augustus. His brother, Augustus Honorius, sent him a letter concerning Saint John Chrysostom, and also sent Saint Chromatius of Aquileia’s letter, written to him on the same matter, LXXVIII. Fontanini conjectures that, on this same occasion, Chromatius sent Arcadius a special letter on Chrysostom’s behalf, 117.

Saint Chromatius attacked the Arian heretics and the Arian heresy, both as a presbyter and as a bishop, LXXI, 17, 95, 127.

Asquini, Basilius, published the inscription of the Aquileian Via Gemina after Bertoli, with a lacuna of three lines, LXI. He maintains that the name of the emperor Hadrian, not Diocletian, stood in this lacuna, LXIII. Cortinovius and Filiasius adopted Asquini’s opinion, ibid.

Augustine of Aquileia, successor of Saint Chromatius, 120, 159.

Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo. He taught that human life, however greatly it may excel in the fruitfulness of justice, is not lived without the remission of sins, XXXV and following. He admirably settled the controversy that had arisen in his own time concerning daily or, rather, intermittent Communion of the faithful, XXXVIII and following. He deeply lamented that the friendship between Jerome and Rufinus had been broken, 152.

Bachiarius, monk. His opinion concerning oaths, 130.

The baptism of Christ and of John, and the difference between the two, 13. Why did Christ wish to be baptized by John? 14. John needed baptism because he could not be without sin, 15. The grace of baptism mystically foreshadowed when the people of Israel were led through the Jordan into the Promised Land, 16. What is signified by the heavens being opened when the Lord was baptized? 19.

Baronius, cardinal. His judgment concerning the letter attributed to Saint Chromatius and Heliodorus and addressed to Saint Jerome, *On the Birthdays of the Saints*, etc.; and concerning another letter attributed to Saint Jerome and addressed to the same men, 102 and following. Fontanini attempts to weaken Baronius’s conjecture that Saint Chromatius was ordained at Aquileia by Saint Ambrose, 112 and following. De Rubeis considers this conjecture not groundless, 139 and following. Indeed, he asserts it to be highly probable, 161 and following.

Barthius, Caspar. How highly did he esteem Saint Chromatius’s writings? 129. He writes that no one explained the word *Mammon* in the Gospel better than Chromatius, ibid.

Barre, René Laurent (De la Barre). He published an edition of Rufinus’s works in which Chromatius appears to be called *Pontifex Maximus* by Rufinus, XLVIII, XLIX. What does Vallarsius think of this title attached to Chromatius? ibid.

The Basel edition of 1528, the first edition of Saint Chromatius’s writings, was of very great importance for correcting the editions of the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum* and the latest edition of Andrew Gallandius, X. The title of this first edition, together with John Sichard’s dedicatory letter, LXXXIII.

Basil the Great, Saint, was called “Beselehel” by Saint Gregory Nazianzen; in what sense? XLV.

The evangelical Beatitudes are certain very firm steps by which holy souls can ascend to the kingdom of heaven, 4. What is the highest step of the evangelical Beatitudes? 9. They are Jacob’s ladder, whose summit reached from earth to heaven, 10. The Magdeburg Centuriators noted this comparison, but Fontanini rightly rebuked them, 131.

Bertoli, Giovanni Domenico, was the first to publish the Aquileian inscription of the Via Gemina, including the three-line lacuna that had long been absent from Gruter and others, LXI. He thought that Diocletian’s name had been carved in this lacuna and wrote against Asquini, who had instead assigned the place to Hadrian, LXIII. Nevertheless, Bertoli’s opinion was abandoned by Cortinovius and Filiasius, who, together with Asquini, support Hadrian, ibid.

Who Beselehel was, and in what sense Rufinus of Aquileia called Saint Chromatius the Beselehel of his own time, XLV and following and LXXVI.

Blondellus, David, is refuted by Fontanini for having written that Chrysostom, concerning his unjust condemnation, appealed equally to the Roman Pontiff, to Venerius of Milan, and to Chromatius of Aquileia, 118 and following.

Boni, Mauro, possesses a very rare first edition of Gennadius’s *On Illustrious Men*, in which Nicetas is called bishop of the city of Rome, XLIX. At Venice he recently discovered a leaden coin or seal bearing the name of Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, together with the numeral CCCCXX; its figure is presented here and it is discussed, LIII and following. In the same place he also discovered a large number of inscribed leaden pages or plates containing ancient records, from an old Corrarian literary society about which no writer, until now, had said anything, LVI.

C. The letter of the Latin language, formed as two right angles placed back-to-back, does not demonstrate fifth-century antiquity but reveals a later age, LV.

This edition of the writings or booklets of Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, is dedicated to the Metropolitan Chapter of Udine; and why?

Cassiodorus. His testimony concerning Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, LXXVIII. This testimony perhaps gave some fabricator the opportunity to pass off letters of his own composition as the letters of Jerome mentioned there and subsequently lost, ibid., 134, 135.

Ceillier, Rémy. He admits that the writings attributed to Saint Chromatius are worthy of that name, but would like stronger proof that they are genuinely his, XX. We, on the contrary, assert that nothing is lacking for a complete proof, XXI. Ceillier is defended against the false and foolish assertion of the French journal entitled *Journal des Savants*, XXII. Ceillier observed that Chromatius cites the history of Judith without any doubt concerning the book’s divine authority; from this the discipline then in force of daily, or at least very frequent, Communion is inferred, XXXVI. Another text concerning marriage mentions the human laws then in force on this matter in the Roman Empire, contrary to evangelical teaching, XLI and following.

The name Chromatius occurs several times among both Latins and Greeks, as Fontanini observed; he himself mentions three Chromatii besides our Aquileian, 110, 111.

CHROMATIUS, SAINT, Bishop of Aquileia. Why are his surviving writings or booklets being published in this new edition? V and following. How highly was Saint Chromatius esteemed by the earliest lights of the Church of his age? VI and following. Among our own writers, Fontanini above all, and De Rubeis, wrote learnedly about him, VII. Their complete works are presented in this volume, 109, 139, 161.

The arrangement of Saint Chromatius’s writings according to the new order of this edition, 1.

The statements made by Saint Chromatius at the Council of Aquileia in 381, while he was still a presbyter under Bishop Valerian, XII, 95, 100.

Lost writings of Saint Chromatius and their list, XII, 97.

Writings falsely attributed to Saint Chromatius, XII, 99 and following, 133 and following, 158.

Fontanini lists the various editions of Saint Chromatius’s writings after the first Basel edition and before the latest edition of Gallandius, 121 and following.

Fontanini also supplied a list of Chromatius’s surviving, lost, and spurious writings, though not a sufficiently accurate one, 137.

Saint Chromatius had a brother named Eusebius, but not a third brother whom Fontanini called Anonymous, XIV, 109, 110.

Chromatius was of Aquileian origin, XVIII. Fontanini proves this, 109. Nor does De Rubeis wholly oppose it, although he suspects that Chromatius’s homeland was rather Romatium or Romatinum, from the Port of Pliny called Romatinum, 140.

He could readily have belonged to the Aquileian family of the Eusebii, as Angelo Maria Cortinovius conjectured, XIX.

In what year did he enter the episcopate, and by whom was Saint Chromatius ordained? 111 and following, 139 and following, 161 and following.

With how many and how great friendships did he flourish? 113 and following. Although Rufinus and Jerome disagreed with one another, he always honored them and even attempted to reconcile them, 115.

Chromatius never received the title *Pontifex Maximus* from Rufinus, ibid., XLVIII, XLIX.

Saint Chromatius undertook the defense of Saint John Chrysostom’s cause, 117 and following, 156 and following.

Saint Chromatius took the greatest pleasure in the study of Sacred Scripture, 141 and following.

The surviving writings of Saint Chromatius are genuinely his, despite the cautious statements of Tillemont and Ceillier, XIX and following. Fontanini had previously proved this, 126 and following. We likewise confirm it from John Clericus, XXI.

How highly the older editions of these writings regarded them, 128.

What is the style of these writings? 133.

What does De Rubeis write about these writings and the spurious ones? 157 and following.

What Saint Chromatius’s writings actually are, why and in what order they were composed, and on what occasion, XXII and following.

Apart from the first treatise or sermon, which properly concerns the Eight Beatitudes, all the rest are two significant fragments of his Commentary on Matthew, composed for the use of pious reading, XXV.

On what occasion Saint Chromatius probably wrote his Commentary, from the beginning of the Gospel of Saint Matthew to its end, XXVI and following.

What are the doxologies frequently used by Saint Chromatius? XXVII and following.

Their variety, and the probable reason for it, XXIX.

The use of doxologies in the letters of the apostle Paul and also of Peter, XXVII. Likewise in the First Letter of Pope Clement to the Corinthians, ibid.

The observation of the distinguished Morcelli concerning the varied use of doxologies among the ancient Fathers, XXIX and following.

Saint Chromatius mentions the histories of Judith and Esther—or true histories—and has no doubt about the divinity of these books, XXX and following.

He also regards the books of Wisdom and Sirach as divine, XXXII.

Saint Chromatius’s text concerning Saint John the Baptist is examined, XXXIII and following.

Likewise, another text concerning the daily Communion of the faithful, XXXVI and following.

Also the text concerning marriage and the human laws then in force, contrary to the teaching of the Gospel, XLI and following.

Rufinus calls Saint Chromatius the Beselehel of his time, XLV, LXXVI. In what sense did he call him by this name? XLV and following.

According to an ancient anonymous author, Saint Chromatius deserves recognition in the Aquileian Church also for ecclesiastical liturgy, XLVII.

Why was Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, called a Roman bishop and even bishop of the holy Roman Church? XLVII and following.

The opinions of Fontanini, De Rubeis, and Abbot Frobenius on this matter are reported, XLVII, XLVIII, LXXIX, LXXX.

Our own opinion is asserted and supported, XLIX and following.

Although Fontanini and De Rubeis do not give the same year for Saint Chromatius’s death, it nevertheless cannot be extended beyond the year of Christ 408, LII.

On the occasion of this year, a lengthy discussion is offered of a recently discovered leaden seal or coin bearing the name of Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, and the numeral CCCCXX, together with a bishop’s crozier, LIII and following.

It is concluded that this seal or coin is a thousand years later in date and does nothing against what Fontanini and De Rubeis wrote concerning the year of Saint Chromatius’s death, LVII.

See Fontanini and De Rubeis.

How probably did Saint Chromatius take the route by which he could turn from Aquileia toward the Port of Romatium or Romatinum? LIX and following.

See Rufinus, Chrysostom, Baronius, Tillemont, Ceillier, etc.

Chrysostom, John, Saint. Testimonies concerning Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, LXXVII. Chrysostom informs Chromatius of his sufferings, and Chromatius undertakes the defense of his cause, 117 and following, 156 and following. Chrysostom thanks Chromatius for undertaking the advocacy of his cause, LXXVII, 118, 157.

The city set upon a mountain: which city is it? 37.

Clericus, John. He does not always value the ancient catalogues of authors and writings so highly that all writings not listed in them must be regarded as spurious or doubtful, XXI.

The Rufinian codex of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, preserved in the Collegiate Chapter of Cividale, ought to be considered highly authoritative, although it may not be older than the twelfth century, 115.

Daily Communion of the faithful. See Daily.

The Bishop of Concordia, who for a long time has not had his seat at Concordia but in the city of Portogruaro, is, in ordinary speech and writing, called not the Bishop of Concordia but the Bishop of Portogruaro, LI, LII.

Concupiscence too—not adultery alone—is held liable to the crime, 54 and following.

Sacramental confession, in the early centuries of the Church, did not precede the daily Communion of the faithful then in practice, except among those who felt themselves bound by some serious sin, XXXIX and following.

Cortinovius, Angelo Maria. He illustrated several recently discovered Aquileian monuments concerning the family of the Eusebii; according to him, the holy men Chromatius and Eusebius, brothers, perhaps belonged to this family, XIX. He supplied a more accurate form of the inscription of the Aquileian Via Gemina in the three-line lacuna, LXII. He ingeniously filled the gap by inserting the name of the emperor Hadrian, LXIII. See Filiasius.

The Corrarian literary society, formerly existing at Venice, was only recently discovered; until now no writer, Venetian or foreign, had mentioned it, LVI, LVII.

The sign of the cross on the seals of ancient bishops, LVIII.

Cyprian, Saint. He mentions the confession of conscience among the priests of God, even for improper thoughts, XL.

De Rubeis, Bernardus Maria. In his *Monuments of the Aquileian Church*, etc., he discussed many matters concerning Saint Chromatius with great learning; his complete work is also presented here, XIV, 139. In his *Dissertations* he likewise touched on various learned matters concerning Saint Chromatius against Fontanini; these too are given at the end, XIV, 161. The coins of the patriarchs of Aquileia are cited; De Rubeis made them known to scholars through engraved plates and illustrated them, LV. Nevertheless, this distinguished man is mistaken when he asserts that Palladius of Helenopolis testified that John Chrysostom had written to Chromatius of Aquileia about his sufferings: Chrysostom himself testified to this at the end of the letter, 156 and LXXVII. He might perhaps write differently today about Fortunatianus, Bishop of Aquileia, before Saint Valerian, 161. See Fontanini.

God, although Lord of all, of whom in particular is he graciously Lord? 92.

The devil: whose lord is he understood to be? 92.

The French journal. See *Journal des Savants*.

Statements made by Saint Chromatius, while he was a presbyter of the Aquileian Church, at the Council of Aquileia in 381, 95.

How highly does the Lord esteem fraternal love? 48, 49, 50.

Diocletian Augustus. Bertoli thought that this emperor’s name had once stood in the three-line lacuna of the Aquileian inscription of the Via Gemina, LXIII.

The dangers of the rich and the deceitfulness of treasures, 87, 88. How can the rich also obtain the heavenly treasure? 89.

What a remarkable beginning for heavenly teaching! It does not begin with terror but with blessedness, 4.

Doxologies used by Saint Chromatius, and for what reason, XXVII and following. Their diversity, and the probable reason for it, XXIX. The use of doxologies in the letters of the apostle Paul and also of Peter, XXVII. Likewise in the First Letter of Pope Clement to the Corinthians, ibid. The observation of the distinguished Morcelli concerning the varied use of doxologies among the ancient Fathers, XXIX and following.

The Church is a city set upon a mountain, 37, 38.

Those who give alms ought not to sound a trumpet; and why? 70, 71.

According to the Gospel, the bishop is the eye of the Church; and, according to the Lord’s teaching, Chromatius says that he is to be cast away from the body of the Church if, through perverse faith and shameful conduct, he has become a scandal to the Church, 57. Again, the bishop is the eye of the body of the Church if he proves to be a Catholic and faithful teacher; otherwise, if blinded by heresy, etc., 91.

Estius asserts that Saint John the Baptist was not without venial sins and therefore said to Christ: “I ought to be baptized by you,” XXXVI.

[Col. 1193] In the older manuscripts of Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Chronicle*, the little compartments are absent in which the years of the Lord, dated from his Nativity, now appear in the printed editions, LIV.

Rufinus translated Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin at Chromatius’s command and dedicated it to him, LXXV, 115 and following, 143.

Eusebius, Saint Chromatius’s brother, was first a deacon of Aquileia and later was elevated to episcopal dignity, XV. He may easily have been bishop of the see of Bologna and consequently the same man who attended the Council of Aquileia in 381 and is numbered among the holy bishops of the Church of Bologna, XV, XVI. The difficulty arising from the dates assigned to Saint Eusebius of Bologna by the distinguished Lambertini is explained, XVII, XVIII. Several outstanding monuments excavated from the ruins of Aquileia have made known to us, within comparatively recent years, a certain Aquileian family of the Eusebii, XVIII. The distinguished Angelo Maria Cortinovius illustrated these monuments in published booklets and not implausibly conjectured that both brothers, Eusebius and Chromatius, belonged to this family, XIX.

Saint Cyprian mentions the confession of conscience made by the faithful before the priests of God, even for improper thoughts, XL.

Filiasius, Jacobus, follows Cortinovius in inserting the name of the emperor Hadrian into the inscription of the Via Gemina; yet he apparently did not know of Cortinovius’s correction in the three-line lacuna, LXIII.

Flaccus Albinus. See Alcuin.

Florius, Count Francesco, provost of the Metropolitan Church of Udine. He composed proper lessons for the Office of Saint Chromatius, VIII. See them at LXXXI. He showed a certain inclination, in his Roman edition of Bachiarius, to identify Saint Eusebius of Bologna with Eusebius, the brother of Chromatius of Aquileia; subsequently he extended this inclination so that he had at hand what could be presented as proof of the matter, though only under the name of conjecture, XVI.

Florius, Count Filippo, praised by the preceding Francesco Florius, XVI.

Fontanini, Justus, Archbishop of Ancyra. In his *Literary History of Aquileia* he wrote outstandingly about Saint Chromatius; his complete work is also presented here, XIII, 109. Gallandius too highly commends this work, LXXXVIII. Nevertheless, he gratuitously asserted the existence of a third brother of Chromatius, whom he calls Anonymous, XIV, 109, 110. Fontanini is also mistaken when he asserts that Eusebius, Chromatius’s brother, was still alive as a bishop in the year 400, 110. Likewise when he says that in 371 Chromatius was still a deacon, ibid. He is similarly mistaken in asserting that Saint Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem mentions the transmission of Origen’s condemnation to Chromatius, 115. He gratuitously asserts that Saint Chromatius was called *Pontifex Maximus* by Rufinus of Aquileia, and that this was an honorific title, 115 and following. The cause of this error, however, was that he could not have seen Vallarsius’s edition of Rufinus, which appeared long after Fontanini’s death and in which Barre’s earlier error was corrected, 116. See Barre.

In 1713 Fontanini was writing his work on Chromatius; he died in 1736. Consequently, many things later clarified by scholars were unknown to him, ibid. Fontanini discusses the year of Chromatius’s death, his successor, and the cult he received in the Church, 119 and following. He also discusses the title of Roman bishop attributed to Saint Chromatius, 122 and following. This learned man is mistaken when he asserts that Chromatius’s text on the mystery of the Trinity, which he reports from an Alcuinian manuscript, is read in exactly the same words in the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 125. He refutes Blondellus, 118 and following, and likewise the Magdeburg Centuriators, 110. Chromatius is also vindicated from their calumnies, 130 and following. See Chromatius and De Rubeis.

Fortunatianus, Bishop of Aquileia, wrote a Commentary on the Gospels, concerning whom Saint Jerome speaks, XXV. Although he has a bad reputation because of Arian doctrine, he has nevertheless most recently had defenders who contended for his orthodoxy, XXVI. For that reason De Rubeis might perhaps write differently about him today as well, 161.

Frobenius, abbot, the latest editor of Alcuin’s works, gives his opinion concerning why Saint Chromatius was called a Roman bishop, XLVIII, LXXIX, LXXX.

Galen, the physician, asserts that the emperor Trajan restored nearly all the roads of Italy, LXIV. What if, by writing “Trajan,” he intended Trajan-Hadrian? LXV.

Gallandius, Andrew. Concerning Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia: from his prolegomena to volume VIII of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, etc., LXXXV. He praises Fontanini as the man who adorned the Chromatian field better than anyone else, LXXXVII.

Garnerius, John. He interpolated Saint Pope Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem, although he did so as a supplement and without any intention of deceiving, 115, 146, 148.

Saint Chromatius speaks of the Gentiles as still existing in his own time and ready to undertake persecution if it were provoked, 51. Fontanini makes the same observation, 127.

Gregory, Saint Nazianzen. He called Saint Basil the Great “Beselehel,” XLV.

The edition of Saint Chromatius’s writings by John Grynaeus, among the *Orthodoxographia* of the *Monuments of the Holy Fathers*, Basel, 1569, was of very great importance for correcting the editions of the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum* and the latest edition of Andrew Gallandius, X. Grynaeus has an excellent opinion of Saint Chromatius’s writings, 128.

Hadrian Augustus. Against Bertoli, Asquini, Cortinovius, and Filiasius rightly think that this emperor’s name, rather than Diocletian’s, once stood in the Aquileian inscription of the Via Gemina, LXIII and following. We also conjecture that the name of the same emperor appeared in another recently discovered Aquileian inscription of the Via Annia, LXII. The epithet “Invincible,” appearing in both inscriptions, first began to be given to Hadrian on stones, as Bertoli observed, LXV. This emperor founded the Hadrianum at Aquileia; after the peace of the Church, it was eventually dedicated to Christian worship, LXIV. Why was Hadrian’s name erased from both these inscriptions? LXV and following.

Henry IV, emperor. Coins of this emperor, recently found at Venice in the Ark of Saint Mark the Evangelist, display the letter C formed by two right angles placed back-to-back, LV.

Heroldus, John, has an excellent opinion of Saint Chromatius’s writings in his *Orthodoxographi*, etc., 128.

Jerome, Saint. Several testimonies of this holy teacher concerning Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, have been collected together, LXXI and following. Three letters attributed to Saint Jerome and addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus, 100, 101, 106. At Chromatius’s request, Jerome translated various books of the Bible into Latin, 113 and following, 141 and following. Jerome’s silence concerning Chromatius’s writings in his *On Illustrious Men* does nothing to support depriving Chromatius of those writings, 128. The dispute between Jerome and Rufinus concerning Origen’s doctrines, 142 and following. Jerome’s words about Rufinus’s condemnation should be interpreted in a milder sense, 149. See Chromatius and Rufinus.

Today, what does the word in “our daily bread,” which we request, signify? 79.

Honorius Augustus. Testimony concerning Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, LXXVIII, 117, 156 and following. See Arcadius.

Hypocrisy and hypocrites, especially in the offering of prayers, are condemned in the Gospel, 72.

Love of enemies is urged in the Gospel, 68, 69.

Two Aquileian inscriptions concerning the roads belonging to Aquileia: the Annia and the Gemina, LX and LXII. They appear to have been erected for one and the same emperor because both roads were restored by the same person, LXII. This person is said to have been Hadrian, LXIII.

Envy is always the companion of a good deed, 8.

The iota and the apex of the Law: what might they also signify mystically? 44.

Fasting, not for human glory—as with hypocrites—but for future hope, 83. We should conceal the work of fasting beneath a cheerful face, 85. Examples of this fasting are given, ibid.

John the Baptist, Saint. According to Chromatius, he was baptized by Christ and needed baptism because he could not be without sin, XXXIII. This matter is treated more fully, ibid. and following.

Job showed himself in all things to be an evangelical man and fulfilled the Lord’s command before he heard it, 55.

The *Journal des Savants*, March 1745. The journal’s carelessness in reviewing Rémy Ceillier’s opinion concerning Saint Chromatius’s writings is noted, XXI and following. See the Trevoltian writers.

An oath. “It is altogether unfitting for us to swear,” Saint Chromatius said; and for what reason? 60. Why did our God often swear? 61. The Lord forbids us to swear by the elements; and why? ibid. and 62. Sixtus of Siena examines Chromatius’s opinion concerning oaths, 130. Saint Ambrose’s outstanding teaching concerning oaths, ibid.

Justice: how should we seek it so that we may truly be blessed? 25, 26. We must thirst for justice to such an extent that for its sake we must despise both bodily punishments and death itself, 30. What was the justice of the scribes and Pharisees? 45. What does it mean not to perform our justice before human beings? 69, 70.

Labus, John, first made public an Aquileian inscription recently discovered at Aquileia, which now gives us our first notice of a certain Aquileian road called the Annia, LIX.

Lambertini, Prospero, later Pope Benedict XIV. He mentions Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Bologna, without mentioning this holy man’s Aquileian origin, XVII. He assigns the dates of Eusebius’s Bolognese episcopate; the difficulty arising from these dates against identifying him with Eusebius, Chromatius’s brother, is either greatly reduced or removed, XVII, XVIII.

Washing the face: what does it mean according to the Gospel? 86.

Proper lessons for the Second Nocturn, for the Office of Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, LXXXI. See Francesco Florius.

The Lord did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them; and how? 43, 46.

To prefer human laws to divine laws is to commit an offense, XLII.

Let no one flatter himself concerning human laws that are contrary to God’s law, XLIV.

Lipsius, Martinus. How excellently does he write about Chromatius’s writings in his *Micropresbyticon*? 128.

Lirutus, John Joseph, published copperplate engravings of, and illustrated, coins that circulated in the province of Forum Iulii, LV. Among others, he presents a Venetian coin bearing the letter C formed by two right angles placed back-to-back, ibid.

The forms of the letters appearing on Chromatius’s seal or coin indicate that it was made after the year 1000 of Christ, LIV.

The lamp: for what purpose is it lit, and whom do they signify by the name “lamp” in the Gospel? 38, 39. Who are those who obscure the lamp with the veil of a blind mind? 39, 40. The ancient types of this evangelical lamp are explained, 40. What does it mean to carry a lamp in one’s hands? 41. By the name “lamp” we may also understand the Lord, who first appeared in humility like a lamp and later shone like the sun upon the very candlestick of the Cross, 41, 42.

What is the lamp of our body? 89, 90.

Salutary mourning: what is to be understood by it? 6.

Who are those who mourn and are blessed? 23.

The Lord calls his disciples the light of the world; and for what reason? 37.

Lupius, Antonius Maria, presents a fragment of a Latin stone on which the letter C appears, consisting of two right angles placed back-to-back, LV.

Mabillon, John, is cited concerning the ancient seals of bishops and concerning the sign of the cross that they placed before their own names when they subscribed acts or documents, LVIII.

The Magdeburg Centuriators are refuted by Fontanini for what they write concerning Chromatius’s age, 110. Chromatius is also vindicated from their calumnies, 130 and following.

The Evil One from whom we ask to be delivered at the end of the Lord’s Prayer: who is he? 81, 82.

What is Mammon, which sometimes also captivates religious minds? 92, 93. See Barthius.

The commandments of God, which in the judgment of worldly people are considered insignificant and small, are not small before God but necessary, 44.

Count Leonardo Manin, Venetian patrician, commended, LVI.

According to Chromatius, by “hand” in the Gospel a presbyter is signified; the Lord commands that he be cut off from the body of the Church if he holds perverse faith or does not live rightly, 57.

What are the right and left hands in Scripture? 71.

Marchinius, John Francis. What does he assert concerning the Book of Esther and the Book of Sirach? XXXI and XXXII.

Marriage. Saint Chromatius’s teaching on the bond of marriage from evangelical law, contrary to what the human laws established by pagans then permitted, XLI and following and 59. The testimony of the first teachers of the Church on this matter, for the instruction of the faithful, XLIII. What Saint Chromatius taught the people of Aquileia concerning the human laws of the Gentiles regarding marriage had shortly before been preached to the Milanese by Saint Ambrose, XLIV.

A lie. It is not lawful to lie, even without an oath, 60. Every lie is traced back to the devil as its author, 62.

The frequenting of the marketplace gives Saint Chromatius the occasion to deliver a sermon to the people, 3. Under the image of the marketplace, spiritual goods are offered, ibid. and 10. What does Fontanini infer from this marketplace mentioned by Chromatius? 127. The same Fontanini defends the word *mercatus* as Latin against Florentinius, 134.

The mercy of God is not obtained except by the merciful, 27.

The merciful person, even toward enemies themselves, will prepare for himself a greater accumulation of mercy at the Lord’s coming, 7.

A person cannot be meek unless he has first become poor in spirit, 5.

Who are truly to be called meek and therefore blessed? 24.

The Lord ascended the mountain to give the Beatitudes to his disciples; and why? 19 and 20.

Morcellus, Stephanus Antonius. An observation concerning the varied use of doxologies among the ancient Fathers, XXIX and XXX.

Purity of heart and cleanness of conscience will allow no cloud to obstruct the vision of the Lord, 7.

Who are truly to be considered pure in heart, whom the Lord calls blessed? 27. They shall see God; and when and how? ibid. and 28.

Neumanus, Franciscus, concerning the Greek letters omicron and omega formed in a square shape on ancient coins, LVI.

Nicetas, Saint, Bishop of Aquileia, was called bishop of the city of Rome in a manuscript of Gennadius and likewise in the very rare first edition of Gennadius’s work, XLIX. On this difficulty Fontanini does not at all support Baronius; prevented by death, he was unable to clarify the matter, 122.

The Chromatian leaden coin or seal, recently discovered. See Seal.

O. The Latin letter, displayed in a square form, appears on the Chromatian leaden seal or coin, LIII. This form—
The square shape excludes antiquity from this letter in the age of Chromatius and instead reveals an age a thousand years later, LVI and following. What does plucking out the eyes and cutting off the hands mean in the Gospel? 56. Sons and neighbors are designated by the name “eyes”; if they cause scandal, they are to be cast away from us, 56. By the name “eyes,” a bishop too is understood to be signified by Chromatius; and he teaches that such a bishop is to be cast away from the body of the Church if, through corrupt faith and disgraceful conduct, he has become a scandal to the Church, 57. Again, the bishop is the eye of the body of the Church if he proves to be a catholic and faithful teacher; otherwise, if blinded by heresy, etc., 91. How should prayer be made by us? 72, 73. In prayer there is no need for a cry of the voice, but for a cry of faith and the devotion of a religious mind, 73. Various examples of devout prayer, ibid. There is no need for an abundance of words in prayer, 74. Chromatius explains the Lord’s Prayer section by section, 74 and following. In this brief prayer are contained all the things necessary for our faith and salvation, 82. This Lord’s Prayer seems to be that “word cut short” which Isaiah had foretold, ibid. Origen. The errors of this otherwise most learned man were denounced by Saint Chromatius to his congregations, 115, 145. Fontaninus is mistaken when he asserts that mention is made of the condemnation of Origen transmitted to Chromatius in a letter of Pope Saint Anastasius to John of Jerusalem, ibid. Nevertheless, the errors of Origen were condemned by Pope Anastasius, and Origen’s books were forbidden to the faithful, 146 and following. Origen himself was denounced to the people as a heretic, ibid. Pope Saint Anastasius distinguished Origen’s case from that of Rufinus of Aquileia, ibid. and following. See Rufinus, Jerome.

Paciaudi, Paolo Maria. He lists writers, both Catholic and non-Catholic, who have dealt with Saint John the Baptist and matters relating to him, XXXVI. Who are the peacemakers, and what is the more important and sublime peace-making? 8. The peacemakers are those who preserve the peace of the Church under the unity of the Catholic faith, 28. We ought to preserve the peace of the Church with every effort, 29. Palladius of Helenopolis. His testimony concerning Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, LXXVIII. It is not Palladius but Chrysostom himself who says that he wrote letters also to Chromatius of Aquileia concerning his exile and sufferings, 156. What is “our daily bread,” which we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer? 78. The title “Pope” attributed to Saint Chromatius by Saint Jerome, LXXI, LXXII, LXXIII. This form of address as a title of honor was then commonly used for bishops, XLVIII. This perhaps was the reason why Saint Chromatius could more easily be written by unlearned scribes of a later age as a Roman bishop and even as the supreme pontiff, ibid. and LXXX, 165.

What a gift of grace it is that we have God as Father and may freely call him Father, our God and Lord! 75. Saint Paulinus of Nola thinks that the adversary with whom, according to the Gospel, we must be reconciled while we are still on the way is to be understood as the Holy Spirit, 132. Who are the poor in spirit? 5. The poor in spirit are already beginning to be meek, 6. Not all the poor are blessed, 21. The Apostles themselves first set before us an example of blessed poverty, ibid. Fontaninus excellently defended the doctrine of poverty taught by Chromatius against the calumnies of the Magdeburg Centuriators, 130 and following. The peace of the Church. See Peacemakers.

Forgiveness of sins is not obtained from God unless we ourselves forgive those who sin against us, 79, 80, 82. The bishop’s staff visible on the reverse side of the seal, or Chromatian lead medallion, indicates that this object is later than Chromatius; above all, this is shown by the form of the staff, LIX. During a persecution on account of the name of Christ, we ought to accept and endure everything with joy, 30. Chromatius prepares the minds of Christians for times of persecution, 64, 65. Rufinus did not at all call Chromatius “supreme pontiff” as a title of honor, as Fontaninus believes, 115, 116. He is seen so called in the edition of Rufinus’s works prepared by René Laurent de La Barre, which Fontaninus perhaps used; but this was an error of the antiquarians, as Vallarsius writes, XLVIII, XLIX. Chromatius is not so called in the notable Rufinian manuscript of the Collegiate Church of Cividale, which ought to be regarded as highly authoritative, 115. In the year of Christ 400, or thereabouts, when Rufinus dedicated his translation of Eusebius’s History to Chromatius, the title “supreme pontiff” had not yet been transferred into Christian usage, nor did it serve to designate the supreme hierarch of the Church, the Roman pontiff, 115, 116. The single passage from Tertullian that the most distinguished scholars cite in support of this title, already attributed to the Roman bishop, has no bearing on the matter, 116.

“Hand” signifies a presbyter in the Gospel. See Hand. The daily communion of the faithful in the early centuries of the Church. On this subject, XXXVII. It was also practiced in the Church of Aquileia in the time of Saint Chromatius, ibid. and 79. A question that arose at approximately that time, perhaps among the Africans, concerning the daily or rather intermittent communion of the faithful was beautifully resolved by Saint Augustine, XXXVIII. Sacramental confession did not precede daily communion except in the case of those who felt themselves bound by some grave sin, XXXIX and following. What is Raca in the Gospel, and why does the Lord forbid calling one’s brother Raca? 47. Radagaisus, leader of the Goths, entered Italy in the year 404 or 405 and attacked the territory of Aquileia, L. How should the coming of the kingdom of God, which we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer, be understood? 77. Why was a bill of divorce permitted among the Jews, and why was that permission taken away by our Lord and Savior? 58. The places of episcopal residence, as they are called, were not yet so fixed and established in the time of Saint Chromatius as they became in later centuries, L. Saint Chromatius was called a Roman bishop; and for what reason, according to the opinions of Fontaninus, De Rubeis, and Abbot Frobenius? XLVII, XLVIII. Our opinion on this matter is set forth and supported, XLIX and following. Romatius, or Romatinus Portus, mentioned by Pliny, where we suppose that Saint Chromatius once stayed, XLIX, L and 140, 163. Saint Chromatius perhaps ended his life at this Romatius, or Romatinus Portus, LII. Rubeis. See De Rubeis.

Two Rufinuses, distinct from the Aquileian, occur in the letters of Saint Jerome, 150. Did either of these write the little work of recantation that was attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia? 150. Rufinus, the presbyter of Aquileia, called Chromatius, his contemporary, the “Bethaleel” of his time; in what sense? XLV and following, and LXXVI. Testimonies of the same Rufinus concerning Saint Chromatius are cited, LXXV and following. Saint Chromatius baptized Rufinus at Aquileia while he was still a presbyter, in the year 371 or 372, 110. Chromatius always held Rufinus in high esteem; indeed, after disputes had arisen between Rufinus and Jerome, he tried to reconcile him with Jerome, 115, 153. Chromatius enrolled Rufinus, who had already become a presbyter from a monk, among the clergy of Aquileia, 153. With what praise did Palladius of Helenopolis write about Rufinus of Aquileia? Ibid. Besides Chromatius, other exceptionally holy men also maintained friendships with Rufinus of Aquileia, 154 and following. A parchment codex, approximately from the twelfth century, containing the Latin version of Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History made by Rufinus, exists in the archives of the distinguished Collegiate Church of Cividale; a conjecture concerning this codex, 115. Rufinus certainly did not call Chromatius “supreme pontiff,” ibid. and XLVIII, XLIX. Rufinus’s Prologue to Chromatius on the History of Eusebius, which he translated into Latin, LXXV, 115 and following, 143. The dispute between Rufinus and Saint Jerome over the doctrines of Origen, 142 and following. Pope Saint Anastasius distinguished Rufinus’s case from Origen’s in his letter to John of Jerusalem on this matter, and he did not absolutely condemn Rufinus himself, 146 and following. Whether the little work of recantation published by Norisius, etc., belongs to Rufinus of Aquileia, 149 and following. Rufinus grieved excessively at the death of Chromatius and did not wish to remain any longer at Aquileia; yet he was uncertain where he should go, 159 and following. See Jerome. See Chromatius.

The Lord impresses upon us in the Gospel contempt for worldly affairs, 65. What is “the salt of the earth,” and in what way were the Apostles called the salt of the earth? 31, 32. The virtue of salt is explained; and what does heavenly grace, represented by salt, accomplish in us? 32. The ancient figures of this salt are explained, 33, 34. What does it mean for salt to become foolish? 35. The example of Judas Iscariot is proposed: although he too had been salt, after becoming foolish he changed from a member of the household of faith into an enemy of the truth, ibid. What does it mean for foolish salt to be trampled underfoot by people? 36. What is the sanctification of God’s name, which we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer? 76. Lost writings of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, 97. [Col. 1198] Writings falsely attributed to Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, 99.

Serry, Jacobus Hyacinthus. He discusses learnedly many matters concerning the sanctification of Saint John the Baptist in his mother’s womb, XXXV. Sichard, Johannes. Dedicatory letter of the writings of Saint Chromatius to Sigismund Ilsung, LXXXIII. How splendidly does he speak in it about the writings of Saint Chromatius? LXXXIV and 128. The seal, or recently discovered Chromatian lead medallion, whose image is also reproduced, has no connection whatsoever with the age of Saint Chromatius of Aquileia, LIII and following. Indeed, it was made after the year 1000, LIV and following. For what probable reason do we think that it was then made? LVIII. On the seals of ancient bishops, see Mabillon.

Sixtus of Siena. A warning concerning forged letters addressed to Jerome under the names of Chromatius and Heliodorus, and to Chromatius and Heliodorus under Jerome’s name, 99. Here too, by comparing several passages of Chromatius with statements of the ancient Fathers, he explains them lucidly, 129 and following. Mention of the Holy Spirit: when and why was it introduced by the Fathers into the doxologies? XXX. Chromatius thinks that the Holy Spirit is to be understood as the adversary with whom, according to the Gospel, we must be reconciled while we are still on the way, 52. The Magdeburg Centuriators criticize this opinion of Chromatius, but with utter malice, as Fontaninus demonstrates, adding also the example of Saint Paulinus of Nola, 132.

Stua, Johannes Petrus a. After Fontaninus, he freed Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, from the stain of Arianism in a special dissertation, XXVI. What is the temptation into which we ask not to be led in the Lord’s Prayer? 80. Examples of useful temptations, 81. The possession of the earth promised to the meek will take place not in the present life but in the future; and in what way? 25. The Magdeburg Centuriators slander this doctrine of Chromatius, but quite ineptly, as Fontaninus observes, 132. Selected testimonies of the ancients concerning Saint Chromatius of Aquileia, LXXI and following. Theodosius the Great Augustus besieged the tyrant Maximus at Aquileia, captured him, and put him to death in 388. He also defeated the tyrant Eugenius in battle in the territory of Aquileia in 394 and condemned him to death, L. Theodosius, staying at Aquileia for some time, annulled the acts of the tyrant Maximus, 112. The Lord wishes us to store up our treasures in heaven; and how is this to be done? 88. A person who preferred to store up treasure for himself on earth cannot have his heart in heaven, 89. Tillemont would have liked stronger monuments to exist asserting that writings were published under the name of Saint Chromatius of Aquileia, XX. Fontaninus satisfied him on this point, 126 and following. We too add something concerning this matter, XXI.

Tiraboschi, Girolamo. On the time when, at least among Italians, the practice of dating documents by the years of Christ began, LIV. Title of the first edition of the writings of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, together with the dedicatory letter of Johannes Sichard, LXXXIII. We too retained the title “Treatises” that Gallandius gave to the writings of Saint Chromatius, although we departed from his arrangement, IX. Trajan Augustus. He restored almost all the roads of Italy, according to the testimony of Galen the physician, whose words are cited, LXIV. Nevertheless, two Aquileian inscriptions bearing erased names and indicating the Via Annia and the Via Gemina were not set up, because the Best Prince did not deserve this injury, ibid. The editors of the *Journal of Trévoux*, in November 1744, faithfully reproduced Ceillier’s article on Chromatius of Aquileia, unlike the authors of another journal called *des Savants* in the following year, XXII.

We ought to regard the tribulation of our brothers as our own and therefore share with those who ask, or request something mutually, 66, 67. The mystery of the Trinity. Saint Chromatius’s celebrated text on this mystery, which appears in a most corrupt form both in the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum* and in Gallandius’s latest edition, is presented restored to its integrity, X, XI and 17, 18. Turre, Michael, Count of, is praised, 115. What does “anoint the head” mean according to the Gospel? 85. Vainesius, of the Maurist Congregation, observes that the letter C formed with two right angles at the back came into use in eleventh-century inscriptions, LV. He also says that the Latin letter O, used in inscriptions in a square form, belongs to the Middle Ages, LVII. Saint Valerian, bishop of Aquileia. Saint Chromatius succeeded him in the episcopate; and in what year? 111 and following, 139 and following, 161 and following.

Vallarsius, Dominicus, editor and commentator on the works of Saint Jerome, observes that the Anno Domini dates cited in the *Chronicle of Eusebius* translated into Latin by Saint Jerome are a much later addition, LIV. He also explains the origin of the title “supreme pontiff” given to Chromatius in Rufinus’s Preface to him, etc., from the Rufinian edition of René Laurent de La Barre, XLVIII and 115 and following. It is necessary to work not only with words but also with deeds, 44, 45. Why are useless and idle words forbidden? 47, 48. The Aquileian Via Annia. A recently discovered inscription at Aquileia is presented, revealing an Aquileian Via Annia previously unknown to all writers on Aquileian antiquities, LIX, LX. This inscription is genuine, and nothing corrupt has entered it, LX. A site near Aquileia is investigated where this Aquileian Via Annia probably ran, LXVIII. Saint Chromatius perhaps used this road, situated near the waters, to travel from Aquileia to Romatinus Portus and to return from Romatinus Portus to Aquileia, ibid. The Roman Via Annia. There is nothing about it in the ancient writers and very little in inscriptions, LXVI and following. Nevertheless, it was among the roads that extended through the regions of Italy lying between Rome and the Eridanus, LXVII. The Via Appia. Bertolus mentions a certain Aquileian Via Appia recorded in old documents; but this is more probably the Via Annia, of which the inscription on the recently discovered stone speaks, LXVII. [Col. 1200] The Aquileian Via Gemina. Bertolus, Asquinius, and Filiasius reproduce the inscription of this road with a lacuna of three lines, indicated by a continuous series of dots. But Cortinovius, after carefully inspecting the stone, corrected the lacuna itself by inserting blank spaces and ingeniously supplied the name of the emperor Hadrian, LXI, LXIII.

Retribution of vengeance is forbidden by the Lord, and why? 63, 64. What is the will of God whose fulfillment we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer? 77, 78. Zaccaria, Francesco Antonio. After Fontaninus, he cleared and defended Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, from the stain of Arian doctrine and from the charge that Pope Liberius had lacked steadfastness, XXVI. The brothers Leopoldus and Sanctes Zucculi are praised and cited as witnesses for the recently discovered Aquileian stone indicating the Aquileian Via Annia, LX. Zurla, Placidus. His letter concerning the recent discovery by Mauro Boni of inscribed lead sheets, from the old Corrarian literary society of Venice, previously unknown to all writers, LVI and following. [Col. 1199]

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND WORDS CONTAINED IN THE WORKS OF ST. GAUDENTIUS

From column 791 to column 1006 of this volume.

Where the valley of Anaunia is situated, ibid.

Ansoaldus, bishop of Brescia, 400.  
Whether bees are born without sexual union, 363 and n. ibid.

The Apostles received the name from their office, 228. From where they are so called, n. ibid. Sons of those cast out, 228 and n. ibid.  
Whether the Apostles Peter and Paul suffered at Rome while Nero was ruling, 368 n.

To seize upon works of piety, 320 and n. ibid.

The author of the work On the Moderation of Intellects, praised, 222 n., 248 n.  
The author of the Mystagogical Foreknowings, 271 n.  
The author of the Hieronymian Questions, corrected, 314 n.  
The authors of the Acts of Leipzig, corrected, 309 n.  
Unleavened bread is to be eaten with bitterness, 277 and n.  
Unleavened cakes baked under ashes, 265 and n. ibid.  
Babylon, the same as confusion, 221.  
Bacchinius (Benedict, abbot), praised, 332 n.  
The rods of correction, 259.  
The rod, 258 and n. ibid.  
“Stammering the spirit” was wrongly read in printed editions, 254 n.  
*Balneae*, not *balnea*, 343 n.  
Baluzius (Stephanus), 221 n., 226 n., 239 n., 283 n. Praised, 231 n., 253 n., 271 n.  
The work of Baptism is celebrated not in names but in the name, [Col. 1200] 326.  
*Baptismum* for *baptismus*, 249 and n. ibid.  
Baptism by immersion was still retained in the age of Adelmannus, 309 n.  
The barbarians threatened Italy in Gaudentius’ time, 317 and n. ibid.  
The importunity of the barbarians, 336.  
Barthius (Gaspar), 220 n., 355 n., 357 n. Corrected, 230 n., 366 n. Praised, 338 n.  
The Basilica of the Council of the Saints, formerly at Brescia, 336 n.  
The nieces of Basil living in a monastery at Caesarea, 340. They attribute to Gaudentius the relics of the Forty Martyrs received from their uncle, ibid.  
Basil, praiser of the Holy Forty Martyrs, 341.  
The *batus*, a measure of liquids, 347 n.  
The Benedictine editors of Jerome, praised and defended, 314 n.  
Benivolus, 217. Head of the honored men, ibid. His piety and religion, ibid. Instructed in the teachings of Philastrius, 218. Master of memory, ibid. Justina vainly attempts to induce him to write against the Catholic Churches, 219. He chooses to live as a private citizen rather than serve as a dead man, ibid. He seriously falls ill, ibid. He demands that Gaudentius write the Paschal Sermons, ibid. He compels him to correct other Sermons, 220.  
Bertramus (Bonaventure), 264 n.  
Birkeimer’s error, 220 n.  
Blanchinus (Francis), 336 n.  
Bochartus (Samuel), 350 n., 364 n.  
Bona (John, Cardinal), 238 n. Praised, 271 n.  
Borromaeus (Charles), praised, 367 n.  
Brissonius (Barnabas, Cardinal), 311 n.  
The luxury of the women of Brescia is censured, 320 and n. ibid.  
Brodium, 244 and n. ibid.  
Budaeus corrected by Jungermannus, 285 n.  
Buxtorfius (John), 232 n., 263 n., 267 n., 303 n.  
Caesarea, the greatest city of Cappadocia, 340.  
The Caesarean Church, 345.  
What is meant by reeds both clear and obscure, 220 n.  
Footwear, 239 and n. ibid.  
The Kalends, Ides, and Nones, so called by the pagans, 232.  
*Caliga* and *caligula*, 258 n.  
The camel through the eye of a needle, a Hebrew proverb, 350 n.  
What Cana signifies, 274. Where it is situated, 275.  
Canus (Melchior), 248 n.  
Singers employed at Christian banquets, 272 n. They are censured, 272 and n. ibid.  
Imprisoned, 348 n.  
Casaubonus, 295 n., 304 n. Corrected, 289 n.  
Cellarius (Christopher), 251 n., 258 n.  
Our contest is against the vices of the flesh, 316.  
The Chiliasts are of two kinds, 245 n.  
The Christian religion commonly traduced by pagans, 227 n.  
To be a Christian surpasses everything, 341 and n. ibid.  
Christ rises on the same day on which he had created the world from nothing, 232. On Friday, on which he had made man, he suffered for the same man, 233. Received on the tenth day of the first month, he is sacrificed on the fourteenth, [Col. 1201] 246 and n. ibid. His preaching was completed within the period of one year, 249 and n. ibid. After he rose again, he did not enter the synagogue of the Jews, 252. He was called by various names by the Jewish people, 302. Raised upon the cross, how he drew all things to himself, 315. Christ, God, is foretold in the Old Testament but demonstrated in the New, 312. Why he treated Judas gently, 314, 315. Compared with a worm, 363.  
Chrysopolitanus (Zacharias), 346 n.  
Food is to be used permissibly, not abused, 331.  
The Cinellian bookcases, praised, 289 n.  
Clarius (Isidore), of Brescia, 222 n., 349 n., 365 n.  
A manuscript Gospel codex of the monastery of St. Julia at Brescia, 222 n.  
Having forgotten the mire of vices, 327 and n. ibid.  
The stains of evil thoughts, 224.  
Serpentine gestures, 272 and n. ibid.  
The Council of the Saints, 336 and n. ibid.  
The Council of the Saints, formerly a basilica at Brescia, 345.  
The inward pains of conjugal disgrace, 225.  
What Christian banquets ought to be, 254 and n. ibid.  
Cotelerius (John Baptist), 297 n.  
Cruciform wounds, 360 n.  
The Lord’s crosses, 360 n.  
Cuneus (Peter), 303 n.  
Cuperus (Gisbert), 283 n.  
David anointed three times, 306 n. His autograph psalm outside the order, 306 n.  
Dausquius (Claudius), 251 n.  
Dedication or sacrifice to idols, 311 and n. ibid.  
*Defecti* for *deficientes*, 269 and n. ibid.  
God’s deeds are not to be investigated with a rebellious spirit, 325.  
He keeps faith who does not violate the rights of God’s commandment, 329.  
Foreknowledge does not err, 218.  
The world is governed by providence, 227 and n. ibid.  
Rest is active, 296.  
How rest is to be understood, 294.  
The arrows sometimes bring death, sometimes bestow blessedness, 229.  
How the Son of God is less than the Father, 363.  
No one investigates or despises the commanding God without punishment for sacrilege, 328.  
God makes the rich not maliciously but providentially, 222.  
Why he chastises the just, 226.  
In nature he is one; in position, many, 239.  
He forgives necessity more readily than presumption, 265.  
The word “God,” often removed in manuscripts and “Lord” substituted in its place, 300 n.  
The works of the right hand, 353.  
How the Devil is called the prince of the world, 310.  
After Christ’s coming he is inflamed with doubled fury against human beings, 352.  
The days in Scripture are counted according to the course of the moon, 232.  
Which are the days of superstition, 235 and n. ibid.  
The Discipline of the Secret, 238 n.  
Divinity compared with wine, humanity with water, 360 and n. ibid.  
What good things the doctrine of truth confers, 228.  
Sunday, the first day, 232. In the Scriptures it is called the first day of the Sabbath, 233.  
The Lord, creator of natures, makes his own body from bread and his blood from wine, 240.  
What a Christian’s house ought to be, 272.  
Unhappy are houses that differ in nothing from theaters, 272.  
The houses near the Flaminian Way, 396 and n. ibid.  
Doxology customary among the Fathers, 250 n.  
Dupinius, critic of Gaudentius, 312 n. He praises Gaudentius, ibid. and n. He does not grasp Gaudentius’ meaning, 316 n.  
The two substances in Christ, 357.  
The winter church at Brescia, 389.  
The Church compared with the moon, 245. It grows and wanes, ibid.  
The Church of St. John outside Brescia, 336 n. Whether it is the same as the Basilica of the Council of the Saints, ibid.  
What the ancient discipline of the Church was in the administration of ecclesiastical property, 318 n.  
*Edissero* and *dissero*, 234 n.  
Almsgiving is to be practiced generously, frequently, and gladly, 223.  
Almsgiving extinguishes the fire of sins, 316.  
Those who give alms rarely are censured, 319.  
Elmenhorstius (Geverhart), 228 n., 254 n.  
The elements, both heavenly and earthly, serve the human race, 296.  
The renewal of the elements after the end of this age, 245.  
Bishops called high priests, 332 and n. ibid. Apostolic men, 373 n. Accustomed to preach on the day of their ordination, 332 n. Formerly invited to preach in foreign cities, 367 n.  
The Eastern bishops deny communion to Gaudentius unless he promises to return to Brescia, 333.  
The bishops present at the sermon are praised, 336 and n. ibid. [Col. 1202]  
Formerly, after the sermon of a preaching bishop or presbyter, the sermon of another bishop standing by would sometimes follow, 336 and n. ibid.  
Examples of bishops who opposed their age in order to withdraw from the episcopate, 334 n.  
The error of certain Christians concerning the Holy Spirit, 288.  
“And so forth,” 307 and n. ibid.  
The hyperbole of the Gospel text, 302 n.  
Gnawed away by worms, 225 and n. ibid.  
Exodus, the same as departure, 234.  
The removal of leaven, 263 n.  
It was not the Destroyer but God who struck the Egyptians, 262. He was their friend and prince, ibid. He wishes to strike the Hebrews while God is striking the Egyptians, 262 and n. ibid.  
*f* changed into *s*, 286 n.

**Fragment excerpted from Bernard de Rubeis’ Monuments of the Church of Aquileia.** 407  
**Chapter X.** Valerian dies, and Chromatius is elected: was he ordained by St. Ambrose? His homeland is investigated. He obtains from Ambrose an interpretation of Balaam’s prophecy; and Jerome dedicates to him and to Heliodorus of Altinum a Latin translation and commentaries on several books of Sacred Scripture. Rufinus returns to Rome from his pilgrimage in the East, where he translates Origen’s books *On First Principles* into Latin. A disagreement begins with Jerome; Rufinus seeks Aquileia. Chromatius himself induces him to undertake a Latin translation of Eusebius’ *History*. Alaric, king of the Goths, makes his first invasion of Italy. 407  
**Chapter XI.** On the condemnation of Origen; Rufinus himself is charged, and writes an apology. Theophilus of Alexandria, Anastasius of Rome, Venerius of Milan, and Chromatius of Aquileia condemn Origen’s doctrines. The pontiff distinguishes Rufinus’ case from Origen’s and reserves Rufinus to divine judgment. Jerome’s statements are explained. The pamphlet of recantation published under Rufinus’ name is disowned by the same Rufinus. 413  
**Chapter XII.** Augustine grieves over the broken peace between Rufinus and Jerome and urges Jerome to silence. [Col. 1208] Chromatius supports him after Rufinus has been entered on the register of the Aquileian presbyters. Paulinus of Nola maintains friendship with the same Rufinus. Rufinus dedicates his works to Chromatius, Gaudentius of Brescia, and others. He vigorously defends in the West the cause of John Chrysostom, driven from the see of Constantinople.  
**Chapter XIII.** Chromatius dies, and his works are reviewed. Augustine ascends to the see of Aquileia. Rufinus leaves Aquileia. 426  
**Excerpt from Bernard de Rubeis’ Dissertations of Various Learning.** 429  
Chapter XVIII, numbers 5 and 6. Ibid.

# ST. INNOCENT I, POPE
## Prolegomena

Same place. **LETTERS AND DECREES.** 463

**LETTER ONE.**—Innocent confirms to Anysius the authority over the churches of Illyricum that Anastasius and his successors had granted to him. 463

**LETTER II.**—Various regulations concerning discipline. 468

**LETTER III.**—On the disagreement and corrupt discipline of the churches of Spain. 485

**LETTER IV.**—Concerning John, bishop of Constantinople: how unjustly he was driven from his city and his church by Theophilus’s faction, and how many evils were perpetrated both then and afterward. 494

**LETTER V.**—Innocent I, pope, to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria: that he cannot withdraw from communion with John unless John is condemned by a lawful judgment. Theophilus is summoned to a canonical synod. Same place.
